# Section on the Treatise
## Signature a 2

<image-desc>A page from a 15th or 16th-century printed edition of Avicenna's Canon of Medicine. The text is printed in a Gothic (blackletter) typeface in two columns. A large, ornamental red drop-cap "F" opens the page on the left. In the right column, a decorative blue drop-cap "F" on a gold and patterned ground begins the first chapter. There is a lush floral border ornament at the bottom right corner consisting of blue, red, and green acanthus leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

Fever is an extraneous heat. We are excused from those things which are customarily said at the beginnings of books, because they were discussed at the beginning of the first *Canon*. We do not intend to focus on childish matters, but on necessary things according to the members of the fourth book. After Avicenna determined in the third book the illnesses appropriate to specific organic members, he saw fit in this fourth book to determine particular illnesses that are not appropriated to a single member.

<insert>
**The fourth book of the Canon begins, concerning particular illnesses which, when they happen, are not appropriated to one member; it contains seven Sections (Fens). The first Section is on fevers and contains four treatises. The first treatise is on ephemeral fever.**
</insert>

I also speak of "decoration" <note>cosmetics or physical appearance</note> just as he himself said in the preface of the *Canon*, because this pleased him. He was also able to place the knowledge of fevers and abscesses before the knowledge of diseases of specific members, just as Rhazes <note>original: "Rhaly"</note> did in the eighth and ninth of the *Theory* and in the third and fifth of the *Practice*. First, therefore, it pleased him to determine the illnesses not appropriated to one member; second, concerning decoration, at the beginning of the seventh Section. The first part is in four, just as there are four such illnesses or particular dispositions not appropriated to one member: namely, fever, abscesses, the loss of continuity <note>wounds or fractures</note>, and poisonous dispositions. First, he determines fevers; second, abscesses; third, the loss of continuity; fourth, poisonous dispositions.

The first part is in two: first, he determines fevers regarding their essence, causes, signs, and cure; second, regarding their termination (the crisis). The first is in two: first, he determines fevers in a general sense; second, in a specific discourse. The general things we consider about fever are its essence, its distinction into types, and its existence in a subject according to the aptitude of the subjects. First, he provides the definition and division of fever; second, he shows the bodies susceptible to it; third, he determines the periods of fevers.

Regarding the definition of fever, it should first be considered that many definitions are given by authors: by Galen in *On the Differences of Fevers*, in the commentary on the *Aphorisms*, and in the *Book of Diet*; also by Johannitius, Averroes in the *Colliget* and the *Canticles*, by Rhazes in the *Signs of the Heart* and the *Theory*, and by Isaac in his discourse on fever. All are good definitions, but this one by Avicenna is more complete. Let us explain it: "Fever" is named from "fervor" <note>boiling heat</note>; in Greek it is called *pyretos* from *pyr*, which is fire. Thus, fever is called a heat of the nature of fire.

<margin>b</margin> **It is heat.** The "Conciliator" <note>Peter of Abano</note> doubts whether fever is heat, since there are "cold fevers," as Avicenna says later. He brings up many childish arguments. We say with Galen that fever is essentially in the genus of "heat contrary to nature," which shows injury to function. If you wish to investigate this, see our question on the subject of fevers, where we deduced that in the heart and the whole body there is a "hot disease" that injures all operations; this disease must be called fever, as there is no more fitting name. Fever is a heat which is a quality, not a body. When it is said some fevers are cold, it is understood either because the matter is cold (like phlegm or melancholy) or because a cold accident follows it, such as shivering.

<margin>c</margin> **Extraneous.** All agree that the "extraneousness" of heat is twofold: one is totally opposed to life, like the heat of the dead; fever is not this, because the works of life continue. The other is an extraneousness opposed to health, which removes the perfection of functions and brings impediment; such is the heat of a feverish person. Therefore, it appears that in a feverish person, the heat is composed of the natural and the contrary-to-nature.

---

### On the definition and types of fever. Chapter 1.

Fever is an extraneous heat kindled in the heart and proceeding from it by means of the spirit and the blood through the arteries and veins into the whole body: and

A. in such measure it necessarily deprives life. But not every amount of "napellus" <note>monkshood/aconite</note> kills; rather, the works of life stand with it. If it is the nature of heat contrary to nature that it is "febrile heat," it formally impedes the operations of the heart.

B. **Kindled in the heart.** We have already declared that in the whole body there is one natural heat, which is the principle of all operations. This is the health of the complexion. Disordered heat and added extraneous heat is fever. It follows that fever is the primary suffering of the heart, then of the rest of the body. Averroes said well that fever injures all operations. Albert of Bologna says that in every putrid fever, the humors of the heart are in a state of heating. If the heat is in the members, it is "hectic"; if in the spirits, it is "ephemeral."

C. **And proceeding from it into the whole body.** This is common. But it does not seem to proceed to the whole, because sometimes the extremities are found cold. Furthermore, do the blood, veins, and arteries go to all parts of the body? They say that from the inflamed heart, the fever is carried to the whole by means of the blood and spirits in the vessels. Because the heart sends proportionate heat through these, it also sends disproportionate heat through them. A solemn doubt: when a man is near death from a killing fever and the extremities are cold, is he said to have a fever? We say he can be said to have a fever in every part, yet also have a "cold disease" due to the loss of natural heat. A second doubt: can the fever be carried by the spirit alone or the blood alone? Avicenna says "spirit and blood." An external cause can transform the spirit alone (as in ephemeral fever) or the humors alone (as in pestilential fever).

<summary>This page introduces Book IV of Avicenna's Canon, defining fever as an "extraneous heat" originating in the heart and spreading via the blood and spirits. It includes scholastic commentary on the nature of this heat and how it differs from natural body warmth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the definition of fever, specifically addressing whether fever is a primary disease or a secondary symptom (accident) of another condition like an abscess or blockage.</meta>

# Book

<margin>a</margin> Suppose that an external heat occurs from the outside, gradually occupying the whole, or finally the whole heart. Take the final state: now the heart is inflamed. Before the heat carries the members away, I ask whether the person has a fever. It is certain that they do, because there is external heat in the whole heart, but the distribution <note>original: "delatio"</note> has not yet occurred. Therefore, those arguments are apparent and resolved by me in our question; for they conclude the opposite of what I believe to be true.

<margin>b</margin> **And it is inflamed.** He declares here that fever is an external heat, and this is what harms natural operations—that is, those which are in us by nature as living beings: natural, and vital. As Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli the Elder, a 10th-century physician</note> says in the declaration of this definition. And Dionysius says it regarding "natural" things, taking "natural" as distinguished against "animal" and "vital" functions. For although all are harmed, the natural ones seem to be harmed more, because the heart is more their principle. Consider this, because it has an opposition depending on the principles of medicine to which we wish to return. And Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the primary authority for this text</note> suggests that not just any inflammation is a fever, but inflammation that harms operations. Therefore he adds that it is not the inflammation of febrile heat like the inflammation of a man working or being angry; for the flame in those is not "finalized" <note>reached a pathological extreme</note>, rather they grow warm and thus remain healthy.

### It is inflamed in it with an inflammation that harms natural operations, not like the heat of anger or labor, since it is not finalized and does not impede operation so that it is restrained. And there are some of the greats who divide fevers into two primary divisions: namely, into fever as a disease and fever as an accident <note>a secondary symptom</note>; and they place fevers from abscesses in the category of accidental fever. And the intention of their discourse is that a disease-fever is that between which and its cause (which is not a disease) there is no medium, such as the fever of putrefaction. For putrefaction is its cause without a medium, and putrefaction is not a disease in itself, but rather the cause of a disease. But the fever of an abscess is an accident existing in the affected part, while the abscess follows it; and the abscess is a disease in itself. And to the one contradicting, it is as if he says: if because the fever of an affected part follows its heat and follows from its pain, it is similar to being an accidental fever, then it must be that many ephemeral fevers are accidents; and if it follows the putrefaction which is in...

<margin>c</margin> **And there are some.** He begins to determine the divisions of fevers: first according to the opinion of others, second according to his own and the customary one. The first part has three sections: first he posits their opinion, second he exemplifies it, third he insists against it. He says first that there are "some of the greats," namely Rhazes <note>Al-Razi, 9th-century Persian physician</note> in the 16th book of the *Continens*, second chapter, and the 17th book, fifth chapter.

<margin>d</margin> **And the intention.** He declares what they understand by this: namely, he wants that fever to be a disease whose immediate cause is not a disease. For example: a fever following putrefaction has that putrefaction as its joined cause, and yet putrefaction of a humor is not a disease in itself. But that fever is called an "accident" whose immediate cause is a sickness. For example, a fever whose cause is an abscess; for the fever following an abscess follows something that is a sickness, namely the abscess. For an abscess is a sickness, and this is what he said at the end: the fever of an abscess is an accident of the affected part while it is an abscess.

<margin>e</margin> **And to the one contradicting.** Here he gives an objection against the division—specifically against the claim that the fever of abscesses is an accident. First this, second he shows what should be held in this contradiction. In the first part, he says that he who would wish to contradict would argue thus: if the fever of abscesses is an accident, this is in one of three ways. One is that it follows the heat of the abscess or the pain, and from this it is called an accident. But this is inconvenient, because then many things would be accidents, namely those which arise from pain and heat. For example: from anger, drinking something hot, labor, and similar heating causes, which is nevertheless false. The second way is that the fever of an abscess is called an accident because it follows the putrefaction of the abscess. But for this reason it ought not be called an accident of the abscess, because the abscess as an abscess (which is a composite term) causes that fever accidentally, because it causes it through the putrefaction which is a part of that abscess-forming sickness. But what causes through a part, causes accidentally; or it happens to the abscess that it causes fever because it causes it through putrefaction, which is something external to the abscess insofar as the abscess is a sickness. And thus the abscess causes it mediately, not immediately. The third way is that the fever of an abscess is not called an accident by any of the said ways, but in another way: that the fever of an abscess is called an accident because through the fever itself one comes into the knowledge of the abscess, and we investigate its knowledge through the fever. Just as accidents lead to the knowledge of diseases. And this third way is not valid, because through the fever of putrefaction we investigate the putrefaction itself...

<margin>column 2 upper margin</margin> ...and we arrive at the knowledge of it. And this is understood when he says "but not significantly," meaning it was not understood as an accidental fever through this, but rather through one of those two ways. They did not understand it as an accidental fever except that it follows an abscess—that is, unless it is an accident of the abscess through this. Or because they find the discovery of the abscess through that fever. Therefore the disposition is similar, etc. But it is doubted whether this objection seems to be valid. For if I find an abscess through a fever, then through it I find a disease, and from this it can be called an accident. But if through the fever I find putrefaction, I do not find a disease but a cause, because putrefaction is a cause. And thus such a fever following putrefaction without an abscess is a disease. It must be said that Avicenna leaves the solution of this noted through what he had said: noting that through frequent fever we do not properly find the abscess except the mode of putrefaction of the abscess, not the abscess in itself. For example, a choleric abscess of the liver is not properly found through fever; but when there is fever and other signs, judgment is given that there is an abscess in the liver, then you judge that the matter is choleric, that which putrefies; because that fever is a continuous tertian. You find therefore the putrefaction of the abscess through the fever, then the disposition of putrid fevers without an abscess is similar.

### ...from the abscess: then the abscess is not its primary cause insofar as it is an abscess; rather it extends to the putrefaction which is in it. Therefore its cause, which is essential, is putrefaction; and the abscess is not its cause except by accident. And we say that if they did not mean an accidental fever by this, rather they only understood it because it follows an abscess, they find it through the discovery of the affected part. Similarly, therefore, is the disposition of putrid fevers in comparison to putrefaction. Truly, occupation in such contradictions is that which contributes nothing to the science of medicine, and makes physicians proceed from their art to inquiries which perhaps for a long time divert them from their art. And let us proceed, therefore, according to what is customary. Let us say, therefore, because the fevers of abscesses and obstructions are accidental fevers, and other fevers are diseases, then it is fitting that we say: since all things that are in the human body are of three kinds, namely the containing members, that which is in them of humors...

<margin>f</margin> **Truly, occupation.** He wants that one should not be occupied in this contradiction, because it contributes nothing to medicine alone. For the question is only whether a fever following an abscess can be called an accident; but you know the nature of that fever.

<margin>g</margin> **And the abscessing:** and know the causes and cure, whether it be an accident or a substance, or a disease. It contributes or harms you nothing in medicine. We ought not to dispute about names, as above in the first book.

<margin>h</margin> **And makes them proceed, etc.** Because he will strive to want to interject whether the same thing can be both a disease and an accident; whether an abscess by reason of its totality can cause fever; whether the putrefaction in the abscess which causes the fever is a disease in itself; and many other things to which, when he proceeds, he spends much time, and thus is hindered.

<margin>i</margin> **Perhaps.** Let there not be a man who, by the goodness of intellect and exercise, quickly dispatches himself from these questions; and perhaps it will behoove him to overstep medicine. It is doubted whether the division of fevers into accidental fever and disease-fever is good. It is said that it is, because they find it in the seventh part of the *Aphorisms* <note>of Hippocrates</note>. Also Rhazes in the 16th book of the *Continens*, where he says "I say that this is true and visible, that as often as we divide fever, they are bipartite: whence we say that all fevers will be either from disease or from accident." Avenzoar <note>Ibn Zuhr, 12th-century Andalusian physician</note> posits the same. Dionysius responds: fever is considered in two ways, either in its essence, and thus it is not divided into disease-fever and accidental fever (for what is essentially a disease cannot essentially be an accident, since these are distinct reasons). Or fever is considered in comparison to the physician's knowledge and operation. And thus he can divide the fever. For he will call that fever an accident which follows another disease. For he will cure that fever with the cure of an accident, namely by intending toward the disease which the fever follows. Another view is that which others gave: that this division is good because it is useful to the physician. For in it he varies the cure; and therefore Avicenna immediately concedes this division as customary.

<margin>k</margin> **Let us proceed.** Here he posits the division according to his own opinion: and first he posits the division into primary and principal genera. Second he posits the non-principal divisions. And the first is divided into two. First, by affirming the aforesaid division, he premises the foundation by which he divides fever into primary genera. Second, he makes the division. By "fever of obstructions" he understands when it is immediate, not when it is by means of putrefaction. By "fever of abscesses and obstructions" he understands those following other diseases like a lung ulcer. And what he says, "let us proceed according to what is customary," refers to the said division and to what is to be said. To the said one indeed, because it is customary and useful to the physician. Namely, notwithstanding the contradiction made, we affirm it saying that fevers following diseases are accidents, and others are diseases. But Avicenna does not solve the reason of the contradictor, since he concludes the truth from the nature of the thing; to the physician, however, it is conceded that he may call a disease an accident. And this being affirmed, then let us posit the more principal division. And it appears that it refers to what is to be said, which is customary: namely, that fever is divided into the first three genera.

<margin>l</margin> **Since the cause:** And as if arguing. Just as Galen <note>the Greek physician</note> in the first book *On the Differences of Fevers*, expressing the body in names, and the first natural subjects of heat are three: namely members, humors, and spirits. Therefore there are three genera of fevers according to the different kindling in one of the three subjects. First, therefore, positing the antecedent, he declares it by a simile in the parts of a bath. Second, he posits the general consequence. But it is doubted: since many other things seem to be in us, like hair, superfluities, elements, and others. It must be said that there are only three things in us which are the immediate foundations of natural heat: namely humors, spirits, and members; and therefore according to these three, heat beyond nature is distinguished.

<summary>This page discusses the classification of fevers, debating whether they should be categorized as primary diseases or secondary "accidents" resulting from other conditions like abscesses or obstructions. It concludes that while philosophically complex, the distinction is practically useful for physicians in determining treatment.</summary>
<keywords>fever, inflammation, abscess, putrefaction, Avicenna, Isaac Israeli, Galen, Rhazes, disease vs accident, medical classification, humors, spirits</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory analysis of fevers, specifically focusing on the classification of fevers (hectic, humoral, and ephemeral) and the physical temperaments most susceptible to them.</meta>

# Treatise I

<margin>a. Humidity. Note: He does not say "earth," so that he might include humors and humidities, and perhaps chyle <note>chyle: a milky fluid containing fat droplets, drained from the small intestine during digestion</note>.</margin>
<margin>b. Diffused vapors. By "diverse vapors" he means those which are not yet spirits—as at the end of the second stage of putrefaction—or those which are corrupt spirits, or not true spirits.</margin>
The subject of the present [discussion] is either extrinsic and not properly [the subject]; properly speaking, surfaces are also not the proper subject of natural heat, nor are parts properly so, except through a certain reduction. From which it can be inferred that a fever ignited in the blood more truly has the essence of a fever than one ignited in yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>, and properly in yellow bile it exists on the surface or similar.

<margin>c. And air. Through this, Avicenna wishes to show that just as one part of a bath—which perhaps seems less significant—can heat the others (as hot air can inflame the walls and the nearby bathwater, even if they themselves were cold, namely the wall and the water), so in the same way one of these parts of ours—for example, the spirits—can inflame the other parts, and thus also the members and the humors. And this is what he adds: "similarly the genus of bodies," because an incorporeal genus is indeed found, such as temperament <note>original: "complexio"</note> and virtue.</margin>
and spirits, the comparison of which is to the walls of a bath. And the hidden humidity, its comparison is to the water of the bath. And the other spirit, vital and natural, and the diffused vapors, their comparison is to the air of the bath. And when the air of the bath is cooled, it is not necessary that it extinguish that which is near it; rather, it is possible for it to remain and return and heat that which is near it. Similarly, there is one of these three genera outside of which no corporeal genus is found in man. ¶ For if a fever is ignited in the radical members by a primary ignition, just as a burning is ignited—for example, as in the walls of a bath, or by a blacksmith's bellows, or by a cook's pot—then that genus of fevers is called **hectic fever** <note>original: "febris ethica"; a fever associated with wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note>. ¶ And if a fever is ignited by a primary ignition in the humors, and then ignites the members from them as it happens—as when hot water is heated in a bath and the bricks are fired because of it, or hot broth in a pot and the pot is heated because of it—then that genus of fevers is called **humoral fever**. ¶ And if a fever is ignited by its primary ignition in the spirits and vapors, and then ignites the members and humors from them—just as it happens when the air of a fire reaches a bath and is ignited in it, heating its air and reaching the water and walls—then that genus of fever is called **ephemeral fever**, since it is ignited in a subtle substance which is resolved with speed. And it rarely passes a day and its night unless it is converted into another genus of fevers. Therefore, the division of fevers is not by a method close to the division occurring through differences. ¶ And fevers are divided in another way. ¶ For it is said that among fevers there are acute fevers, and there are those that are not acute. ¶ And among them are chronic, and those not chronic; and among them are nocturnal, and those are diurnal. And among them are healthy and "right" <note>regular/predictable</note>, and those having horrible accidents <note>symptoms</note>. And among them are remitting, and those that are inseparable. ¶ And among those inseparable ones, there are some which have remissions, and some which have intensifications. And there are those which have exacerbations, and those which are uniform. And there are those which are cold, having rigor or shivering. And there are those which are simple, and those which are composite.

<margin>d. Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; 9th-century Persian physician</note>. He declares the conclusion or consequence that gives the mode of each genus of fevers. First, of the hectic, he says: "if it is ignited by a primary ignition," meaning first in the members. He said this to give an example of this fever alone, not complicated by another genus of fevers. He said the same of every other genus, always repeating "by a primary ignition." Hectic (ethica), i.e., habitual, because it is habitually present, or because it possesses the "habit" of the body and its parts. Then he gave an example of humoral fever... He called them "fevers of the humor" to include both putrid and non-putrid ones, although Galen... places *sinochas* <note>continuous non-putrid fevers</note> without putrefaction as intermediates between putrid and ephemeral fever. Then he gave the example of the ephemeral, and gave the reason for its name: because it lasts one day and rarely passes it. It is called ephemeral from the *ephemeron*, a fish that lives for one day, as Isaac says... It is of short duration because the heat is ignited in a subtle thing, i.e., spirits or vapors, which are of a nature for fast resolution. Experience finds that this resolution is completed in one day. Air and water are quickly ignited. One must consider Avicenna's various ways of speaking... for a hectic fever, it suffices for the heat to be ignited in the members; it does not require heat in the humors or spirits... Hectic is when heat is ignited in the radical members, which are properly members as distinct from fat and tallow, and perhaps flesh... But you will ask how hectic is transmitted? It must be said that it requires the spirits and humors to be heated, not for the *existence* of the fever, but for its *transmission*. Transmission is not of the essence of fever, just as being "down" is not the essence of a heavy object, but the potential to be so. In putrid and ephemeral fevers, it is not enough for heat to be ignited in humors or spirits; it must pass to the members, otherwise it would not be a fever since the members are what live. Therefore he said "if it is ignited in the spirits, then ignited in the members," adding "and humors," which was not necessary for the existence of ephemeral fever, though it follows necessarily. He then concluded these things, which will be declared in the question.</margin>

### On the predispositions to fevers. Chapter II.

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap 'Q' in red ink with swirling flourishes.</image-desc>

**Q**uestion: Some ask whether the bodies most strongly predisposed to fevers are hot and moist bodies, especially when the moisture is stronger than the heat; and these indeed have foul-smelling sweat, urine, and excrement. ¶ And hot and dry bodies are likewise predisposed to hot fevers; they begin first as ephemeral, then hasten toward putrefaction.

<margin>f. And among them. He presents the seventh division, and it is clear. From the things said above, I want the solution to the question to be noted: whether fever is heat, and whether it is heat beyond nature, and whether it is added, and whether it is a passion of the heart. ¶ It is doubted here whether fever is a single disease. It seems not, because it is a bad temperament, hot and dry... in many places in medicine the subject is multiple and not one, i.e., the body. ¶ To the contrary: because Avicenna says it is heat. Antonius responds that fever, by the mode of its composition, is one disease like an abscess, and therefore dryness stands as the "material" heat... but from its components, it is a composite disease, i.e., hot and dry. Accept this solution if it pleases you. ¶ There is another response by Dy. [Dionysius?] which those of Bologna follow: that fever is one disease because it is either "becoming" or "made." If "becoming," it is one disease because there is one thing moved (the heart) and one thing moving (the body's heating). If "becoming" is one disease, then so is the "made" fever. ¶ Also, when things follow each other in some effect—one by itself, the other by accident—one is not of the essence of the other. Since heating follows fever by itself, but dryness follows the heat, therefore dryness is not of its essence. Against the first: the thing moved is twofold, i.e., the heart as heatable and as dryable. The mover is twofold, i.e., the agent heating and drying (for example, yellow bile). Against the second: the drying of yellow bile does not necessarily follow the heating.</margin>

<margin>e. And they are divided. He presents various other divisions... not in the first or proper way. He presents seven primary divisions: some are acute (absolutely), others not acute (i.e., becoming acute). Others are chronic... This division is not primary because sharpness can exist from accidental diversities like subtlety, heat, the quantity of matter, and location. Second division: some nocturnal, some diurnal. This is also accidental, based on the hour of movement... Third division: some are healthy and "right" (i.e., *synochas*), others are those in which there is doubt due to wicked accidents. This is from symptoms... Fourth division: by continuous and interpolated (intermittent), which is neither primary nor essential. Fifth division: a sub-division in which he hints at three species of *synochas* (continuous fevers): always decreasing (called *paraugmastic*), always increasing (called *augmastic*)... and those standing equally (called *homotenous*)... Sixth division: those that are similar (not having a "type" or pattern) and those having rigor, etc.</margin>

Although heat happens, it does not happen to it (i.e., to the dryness) by itself but from the operation. ¶ Let us therefore state three things. First, that fever is essentially one disease. The reason: fever is a distemper in the natural heat. But for a distemper to exist, the hot quality alone suffices, with every other quality (moisture or dryness) set aside. ¶ Second, that in reality, fever is for the most part found only as a composite disease. It is not "one" in the way whiteness is one quality, for it is not found alone in reality but always joined to another (e.g., hot or cold). The reason: exceeding heat immediately dries, and the drying that is immediately joined to fever is through the resolution of spirits which it immediately causes. One must imagine that in all members there is a mode of natural or healing humidity through the presence of the substance of the spirits, which are moist bodies of the nature of air. Therefore, fever is rarely seen to be free from this drying. This happens not only from a dry cause, but from heat drying the other humidities of the members... Third, we say that if it is possible to imagine a fever being only a distemper in heat without a distemper in dryness, then not every dryness is a disease. If there is a man having many and thick spirits, when a fever arrives, the distemper in heat will stand for some time without the drying of the resolution of spirits. And if someone is of superfluous humidity, the fever will not immediately make him fall into a "dry" disease. Thus, authors who wanted the essence of fever said it is a hot disease; those who saw what happens for the most part in fact said it is a hot and dry disease. Regarding the reason, it must be said that the question does not ask about unity or multiplicity on the part of the subject... but asks about the unity in the essence of fever: whether it is one quality or two.

<image-desc>Blue decorative initial 'I' with red penwork.</image-desc>

**I**n the next part: Since he has placed the definition and division of fevers, he shows which bodies are more prepared for fever; and this first. Second, which are not prepared... ¶ He therefore first places four orders. In the first are hot and moist bodies, specifically when the moisture is more abundant than the heat. They said (i.e., Galen in *On the Differences of Fevers* and Rhazes in the *Continens*) the cause is because they have the matter and the efficient cause of putrefaction, which are heat and moisture... They doubt this because he says "if the moisture is stronger." For a multitude of moisture preserves from putrefaction (as said in the *Meteorology*)... a multitude of moisture in which the ruling heat is suffocated is the cause of putrefaction, as appears in our humors. And therefore a hot and moist man with much moisture is apt for putrefaction; hence his excretions would stink, as Avicenna and Galen say. ¶ In the second order are hot and dry bodies which, by the sharpness of their humors, are apt to incur bilious fevers; because they are easily inflammable bodies having fiery spirits, therefore...

# BOOK III

...first they encounter an **ephemeral** <note>original: "ephimeram"; a one-day fever</note> fever: because they are dissolvable and drying: these are also prone to **hectic** <note>original: "ethicas"; a wasting fever associated with consumption</note> fevers. And consider that **Avicenna** does not place an order in his way of speaking among these bodies: because he did not say "these bodies are hot and dry" after those: because perhaps it is difficult to judge which of them are more disposed. For hot and moist bodies are more disposed to putrefaction: but hot and dry to burning. In the third order are bodies hot and temperate in moisture and dryness: the reason is because they have spirits apt for burning and melancholic ones on account of having much heat with a temperament of moisture: which is conforming to the multiplication of spirits which are properly spirits of the heart, more hot than they are moist. In the fourth order are bodies exceeding in moisture and temperate in heat and cold. But it is doubted because hot and moist bodies with much moisture were the most prepared among all: because they are placed as the first of the prepared bodies; but excessively moist bodies temperate in heat approach those more closely. Therefore it should be said that bodies hot and temperate in passive qualities are more prepared for ephemeral fevers: from which, beginning there, they are changed to putrid ones: because an excess of heat also causes putrefaction when it has sufficient blood in the body, and other humors with it. But excessively moist bodies temperate in active qualities are more prepared for putrid fevers: and therefore he says that such bodies, hot and temperate in moisture, are not prepared for a putrid fever at the start: because they begin more with ephemerals, but moist bodies in active qualities begin with putrid ones. This is the way **Avicenna** suggests. However, ill-disposed bodies are cold and moist, and cold and dry. But you will ask which of these bodies are more ill-disposed. It should be said that for ephemeral fevers, cold and moist bodies are inherently more ill-disposed: because they are more remote from simple burning: but for putrid fevers, cold and dry bodies are more ill-disposed. But you will ask about the temperate complexion: and about the cold complexion and the dry one as well. It should be said that he gave it to be understood that a temperate complexion resists the fall into sickness more. But he understands "cold" to be ordered through cold and dry in the end, just as in resistance, or perhaps the opposite. And so on. And he ordered this in the eighth term. And when it is asked which bodies are more prepared for fevers: **Avicenna** saying here that they are hot and moist: but below in the chapter on ephemerals that they are hot and dry. And **B.** <note>likely a reference to a commentator or specific text</note> affirmed this in the eighth term. It is answered with one voice by the predecessors that in a fever we consider the "fall" and the "cause of the fall." We consider the fall in general: every fever is an extraneous heat with dryness: and as such, hot and dry bodies are more prepared. Then hot and moist. And you order them subsequently: and the reason is: because such bodies have a complexion more conforming to fever, as fever. We also consider the fall specifically as to all types: and then into putrid fevers fall more the hot and moist: but into hectic and ephemeral, the hot and dry. We consider the fall even more specifically: and then into a sanguine fever the hot and moist are more prepared to fall; into a choleric, the hot and dry; into a melancholic, the cold and dry; into a phlegmatic, the cold and moist. If however we consider the cause of the fall since it is, as is frequent, twofold: namely extrinsic: which for the most part is heat and heating things, and as such hot and dry bodies are more prepared. But the intrinsic cause is putrefaction; for this, hot and moist bodies are more prepared. This discussion however would have many objections which I omit to be brief. And perhaps because here the question is about fever as fever: and then the answer is not about fever as fever: but about this type or that: because to see fever as fever puts nothing in reality. And by responding concerning each type and whatever species, it does not have a single answer. And therefore **Avicenna** said "they said": and you consider it.

---

<margin>a</margin>
**The hours of fevers.** Since he has determined those prepared for fevers, he determines their hours and times. And first he notifies them. Second, he places the signs. There: "second: knowledge." The first in three parts. First he places the division. Second he declares it. Third he adds the completing causes. There: "and the principle." There: "third: and the status indeed is verified." The declaration is there at the beginning: first because the determination of the times of a disease belongs to the treatise on humoral fevers because to those the times are properly owed since they are fevers properly speaking: however, because they can also apply improperly to ephemerals: therefore he placed the discourse on the hours of fevers here in the general discourses. It should also be considered that one might dispute whether every disease has times and whether every fever does. We however are excused from this through the science of the principles of medicine; for we disputed in the second book of the first part where we showed how time applies to successive things and how to permanent things. It should also be considered that a certain decline is true: and in this, one does not die, as **Galen** proves in the third [book] on crises in the previous chapter. And this is because it is impossible for the sick person to die at the hour when the virtue <note>term: "virtue" (virtus) refers to the body's natural healing power or vital force</note> perfectly overcomes: but it overcomes in the true decline. Furthermore, in the stronger hour it does not suffice. But in the "status" <note>term: "status" refers to the peak or plateau of the illness</note>. Therefore it cannot fail in the weaker. If however the decline is false, it happens that one dies in it: and this is because the subtle part of the matter is resolved and the gross part remains worse, as often happens in **hemitrite** <note>original: "hemitriteis"; a semi-tertian fever</note> fevers: as below in the second section, the chapter on the signs of various types. Or it is on account of the proximity of the virtue near death as happens to him who raises his head and dies. Third section, chapter on **syncope** <note>fainting or sudden loss of strength</note> or on account of the permutation of matter, for when it is in the process of changing, an alleviation is seen: just as happens when a person with **quinsy** <note>original: "squinanticus"; peritonsillar abscess</note> becomes **peripneumonic** <note>original: "periplemonicus"; lung inflammation</note>: or it is phlegm because the natural heat is resolved: and the fever seems to cease when rather the natural heat has ceased: or because although the virtue has evacuated much matter, and a little of the disease remains. Equivalently however the virtue is consumed: and the resolution is made in the fight so that together with that little disease that remained, the heat fails: it was therefore a victory of the virtue, a **Cadmean victory** <note>original: "uictoria katimica"; a victory that ruins the victor</note> as the *Conciliator* <note>Peter of Abano</note> says in difference 107, of which mention is made in the first [book] on critical days, eighth chapter, and is explained in the sixth book, second section, 12th comment. For **Cadmus** of the thing had two sons who, fighting between themselves, both died. And according to this mode **Averroes** conceded in the third [book] of the *Colliget* that in the universal decline the infirm person can die. However, that the onset of a new disease could be the cause of death is not to be doubted: and this **Avicenna** understood when he said "on account of that which we shall say." Namely, in the second section of this chapter on the hours of death: concerning the cause commonly. That is, concerning the cause of death commonly happening in the decline which can also happen in other times.

<margin>b</margin>
**And the principle.** And this part has four just as there are four times. And it should be considered that this notification of the principle <note>term: "principle" (principium) refers to the onset or beginning stage of the fever</note> can be common to the universal and particular principle: for in both the heat is suffocated by the matter: just as the fire of a small flame is suppressed by moist wood: as **Galen** in the second [book] on the differences of fevers: speaking of the beginning of a **paroxysm** <note>a sudden attack or increase of symptoms</note> says. But against this, because a paroxysm can arrive in the "status" in which the matter is digested: and he himself says that in the beginning no trace of maturation appears.

### On the hours of fevers. <sig>aa.iij.</sig>

<margin><gloss>Heat is suffocated by the matter. That is, the harm to operations appears: because the sickness is in act: as **Averroes** says in the third [book] of the *Colliget*. For this notification of the general principle is known from the first book, second section. But here it was necessary to notify the principle of material fevers: and it is notified from the relation of the heat to the matter, as he did here. Secondly it should be said that although the matter in the universal status is digested, nevertheless its motion in the beginning of a paroxysm is suffocating of the heat and conclusive: such that even in the pulse a deepening appears, and in the urine a thinness.</gloss></margin>

**The hours of fevers** are like those of other sicknesses: the **principle** [onset]; and the **increase**; and the **status** [peak] at the end; and the **decline**. And there are sometimes particular causes of each paroxysm: and the fear is from the principle up to the status; but at the decline the sick person does not die from the fever itself, except through that which we shall say concerning the cause commonly. And the principle indeed is the hour in which the natural heat is suffocated by the submerged matter...

...it pleases me more: that the matter making the paroxysm in the universal status is not that which is digested: but new matter which is moved: and you consider these things. It is doubted whether in the principle of the whole fever a sign contrary to digestion can appear. It seems so: because black or green urine can appear. Furthermore, a man can die in the principle: but this is entirely from the malice of the matter. To the contrary however it is said that a sign contrary to digestion—which is a certain sign of crudity—and that is contrary in act, not in aptitude: like crude urine. Another is a sign truly contrary to digestion, depriving it in act and potential, like bad black or green urine, indicating the matter to be such by the action of putrid heat contrary to natural action. We shall say therefore that in the principle of putrid material fevers, a sign entirely contrary to digestion does not appear, nor of digestion: but a sign of crudity appears. And the reason is: because since it is in the principle, the bad heat could not yet make a manifest impression in the matter, nor yet the natural heat. For these fevers either from the beginning have indeterminate signs of health or death: and then not yet does the good or bad imperfection appear in the matter: or they have signs more determined toward health. And then also not yet does a manifest sign appear of the impression of heat in the matter on account of the brevity of time. And when it appears, the principle is separated from the increase and the increase begins. Or they have signs toward death: and then also not yet does the manifest impression of putrid heat in the matter appear, on account of there having been little time in action. And when it appears, the increase of the mortal disease begins. Against the first statement: in the increase of the disease there are indeterminate signs of health: and with this a sign of appearing digestion can appear. Against the second: if the fever in the principle has a sign toward health, this seems to be from the signs of digestion. For these are what give confidence of health: as **Galen** often writes in the first [book] on crises and in the commentary on the Aphorisms regarding paroxysms. Against the third: if from the principle the fever is determined toward death: therefore signs contrary to digestion appear: because the matter is ultimately malignant. To the first it can be said that in the increase in which signs of digestion appear, manifest signs of health are determined: and because in that increase a man cannot die; and the cause of the disease; nor yet from such a disease will a man die if the matter be uniformly conquerable just as it begins: but this is rarely found. To the second it should be said: that when from the principle of the fever we judge it healthy, it is an estimative judgment not collected from any sign of digestion: but from many other signs collected into one. To the third it should be said: that signs of death are not taken from signs contrary to digestion, but also from others. For the matter can kill from the principle by quantity alone, even if the power is not malignant. To the contraries: first to the first: it should be said that black urine appearing in the principle of the fever—at that instant in which the blackness or greenness begins, the increase begins: and thus the principle was manifestly hidden by brevity. To the contrary: some fever can begin from black matter like black bile or **leek-green bile** <note>original: "choleraprassina"</note> as **Isaac** [Israeli] felt in the fifth book of *On Fevers*, chapter on the tertian. But then for whatever instant the fever begins, for the same the such tinting of the urine could appear. It should be said: that such a sign of digestion—namely, such black or green urine—does not appear from malice induced in the matter by the action of putrid heat: but from the malice which it had before it caused the fever: and therefore this ought not to be proportioned to the fever any more than the contrary. For example: let some fever begin from some digested, sanious matter. Given that some sign of digestion appeared in the principle, it would not be from the action of natural heat convening with the fevers: but from the disposition before the fever. To the second it should be said: that if a man dies in the principle of the fever, he does not die from the manifest addition of malice made in the febrile heat: because that would already be the death of the increase and not of the principle: but he can die from many other causes known from the matter and the virtue. It can be said also otherwise as suggested in the text: that in the principle of the fever a sign of digestion or its contrary cannot appear from the nature of the fever which then begins, or of the virtue fighting against the fever: but from the nature of the matter which it has before the fever. And it follows from this that in the principle of the fever the matter can be undigested, receiving no potential for digestion: and this will not be from the nature of the fever: because it does not yet corrupt the matter: but from the nature of the matter before the fever: and therefore if the fever begins from **eruginous bile** <note>original: "cholera eruginosa"; verdigris-colored bile</note>. And it is asked whether in the principle of this fever the matter is digested or crude. It should be said that it is crude as to this, that it is able to be digested: and able to receive the contrary of digestion: because it is impossible for it to be digested by the power of any virtue of any man: but it is called crude and not digested while it manifests the effect of febrile heat which now is neither any action of the virtue resisting that fever: but let there be a manifest action of another bad disposition from which that eruginous bile was generated. The action of the heat of the fever however will manifest then that matter will be transmuted for the worse: and then the increase of the mortal disease will begin: but the action of nature cannot be manifested since it is impossible for this matter to be rectified: but we say that if escape from this fever of eruginous bile were possible at the time it begins...

# Treatise I

...increase through the addition of corruption in the matter in one who is destined to die: at that time digestion begins in one who ought to be liberated; yet it may be impossible to be liberated. And then suppose that someone begins to suffer a fever from matter of such malice that no further malice can be added to it: when will the increase of this mortal disease begin? It must be said that he will die at the beginning of the fever without an increase. Otherwise it can be said—and you should consider this.

<margin>a</margin>
**And the beginning.** He says afterwards that a "beginning" is found in every sickness—speaking materially of the beginning defined here. Consider this: that the beginning is hidden for three reasons (the first and second causes may be considered as one type). The first cause is the shortness of the time of the beginning; hence the sickness immediately appears to be in its final stage, as seen in the paroxysm of acute <term>ephemera</term> <note>a fever lasting only one day</note> and <term>synoche</term> <note>a continuous non-intermittent fever</note>, which immediately passes into the peak, decline, or increase according to the three species of synoche. The second cause is the weakness of the symptoms at the beginning; hence they do not deprive a man of his accustomed acts, which is a strong point as noted in the first book on crises, the seventh case. The third cause is the quick appearance of a sign that excludes the beginning, namely digestion or true indigestion. When the matter is subtle and scarce and the [body's] power is strong, a "cloud" <note>original: "mubes", referring to sediment in urine</note> will immediately appear, a sign of maturation or "feigned" digestion. For it sometimes happens that certain phlegmatic matters, on the same day the fever begins, are broken down and expelled with the urine in the bodies of those living idly; hence they produce in the urine a certain feigned <term>hypostasis</term> <note>sediment</note> which looks laudable but is not, and an unskilled physician judges the disease healthy when, as malice proceeds, death soon occurs. Regarding this feigned hypostasis and the way to avoid error concerning it, he speaks in the first book, second <term>fen</term> <note>a division of Avicenna's Canon</note>, the chapter on hypostasis.

...in the limb for so long until no trace of maturation, or its contrary diversity, appears. **And the beginning** is indeed found in every sickness. Yet sometimes it is hidden, as is its hiding in synoche, epilepsy, and apoplexy. And sometimes the beginning is hidden by the fewness of symptoms, and it is thought there is no beginning in it. And similarly, sometimes on the first day of acute fevers, clouds and signs of maturity are seen, and it is thought there is no beginning, but it is not so. **And the increase** is indeed the hour in which the innate heat is moved to resist the matter by a manifest motion, and signs of digestion or signs contrary to digestion appear. **And the peak** <note>original: "status"</note> is the hour in which the battle between nature and the matter is vehement, and the victory of one of the two over the other appears; it is the hour of the struggle. Its duration in those having acute paroxysms is one paroxysm, and it is not recognized except by the one that follows it, or two paroxysms, and it is recognized in the third; therefore it does not exceed those two except in <term>macronoric</term> <note>long-term or chronic</note> diseases; for perhaps many paroxysms are similar in all their judgments, and there at the peak...

<margin>b</margin>
**And the increase.** He indicates the confirmation of the "increase" from the symptoms and by another reasoning of the matter. From the symptoms indeed when he says: "it is the hour in which the innate heat is moved to resist." By this he wants us to understand that the heat which was previously submerged in the limb (that is, in the place of the matter) is now expanded. It appears like a fire which was previously suffocated under green wood but now conquers and its flame rises high. Therefore, to the touch, the heat is greater and more apparent, the pulse more manifest and consistent, and symptoms appear. Secondly, he identifies the increase from the alteration of the matter when he says "signs of digestion appear," meaning manifest or clear signs of digestion, because such signs are in the time before the increase from the beginning. For signs of hidden digestion can be found in the beginning, as Galen says in the first book on crises, chapter seven. Therefore he says "by a manifest motion," meaning by this not only the manifest appearance of signs of digestion or its contrary, but also the manifest appearance of the aforementioned symptoms. It is doubted: if innate heat moves to resist the matter by a manifest motion, how then will a sign contrary to digestion appear? It must be said that in the motion to resist, it does not always resist successfully; rather, it is resisted by the addition of a degree of corruption in the matter. Or it must be said that "innate heat" here is taken for the innate quality of the feverish person, which is not single but double: namely, natural and contrary to nature. Both rise from the suffocation of the beginning. When therefore it has awakened and now conquers this whole heated aggregate: if the naturalness of the natural heat conquers, then it penetrates the matter and inflames it with a perfect flame (that is, digestive as far as possible), and from this a sign of digestion appears (for example, a white cloud begins to appear). But if the malice and the unnatural flame of heat conquer, then malice proceeds in the matter and malignant corruption is added to it by a manifest motion, so that signs contrary to digestion appear (for example, the urine begins to turn black).

<margin>c</margin>
**And the peak.** He indicates the definition of the "peak" <note>original: "status"</note>. First from the symptoms that follow the vehemence of the struggle; and therefore he says "it is the hour of the struggle." These symptoms are pains, restlessness, alienation <note>delirium</note>, and others frequently numbered by authors. Secondly, from the alteration of the matter when he says "victory appears." For if in this struggle the natural heat completes the induction of the form of perfect digestion, perfect signs of digestion appear. But if the foreign heat prevails, contrary signs will appear in the ultimate malice of the urine. But someone will object: first, because in the beginning or increase such a state can be said to exist in which such a vehement struggle occurs with the victory of the disease over nature, as when it kills then. It must be said that just as a true crisis toward health occurs at the peak with preceding signs of digestion, so the crisis opposite to it (toward death), which can be called a true crisis, occurs at the peak with preceding signs contrary to digestion. Second, someone will say the symptoms Avicenna intended should have been placed second, since they follow after the "digestion" made while nature is already attempting expulsion. It must be said that one should not worry about the posterior or anterior positioning of the speech. Or it must be said that the finality and vehemence of symptoms occurs not only from the struggle of dividing and expelling the matter, which occurs after digestion (as Galen indicates in the commentary on the fourth section: "in whatever diseases beginning"), but it is also the struggle of the completion of digestion. Properly, putrefaction is added to the matter just as digestion is, as we have discussed elsewhere. It is therefore a vehement struggle because whether the disease becomes healthy or mortal, it is in its greatest being; and regarding this he said "let the struggle be vehement." Third, he identifies the peak by the time of duration: in acute diseases the peak does not last long, usually one or three paroxysms; but in "macronoric" (chronic) ones it can last for many paroxysms, which perhaps are similar in their dispositions because they are all paroxysms of the peak. He said "perhaps" because of the contingent variations in these. A novice first doubted how he says that in the peak the victory of one over the other appears, since this happens in the decline. It must be said that in the decline (in a healthy disease) the victory of the [body's] power appears in the act of evacuating the matter; but in the peak it appears to the prognostic judgment through confirmed signs of digestion, and thus judgment appears regarding health, or through contrary signs it appears regarding death. A second doubt: how is the peak the end in one paroxysm when a paroxysm has a decline, and in the decline the disease is weaker, whereas in the peak it ought to be stronger? Furthermore, they say in the following paroxysm there will be a decline, but in the decline the disease ought to be weaker; but this will not be so—rather it will be stronger at least in the peak of the paroxysm that occurs in the decline of the preceding paroxysm which was at the peak. Therefore, in the decline, the disease will be stronger in some part than in the peak. A third doubt: how does he say it is known in the paroxysm that follows, when Galen in the first book on crises teaches how to know the peak when it is present and when it is future? To the first it must be said: since the peak is the most troublesome hour, in acute cases it cannot last long, but in chronic cases it can. And then we say that if the fever is continuous, in the hour of the decline of the paroxysm of the peak, the disease is stronger than in the peak of the paroxysm of the decline. If the fever is intermittent, we can perhaps understand the same; yet it is safer to say that the peak in that case is discerned more from the alteration of the matter. To the last it must be said: although the peak is known in the present when it is, yet the knowledge is confirmed when it has passed and the decline appears.

...a trace of digestion or its contrary is [not] seen. **And the decline** is indeed the hour in which the innate heat now dominates the matter and conquers it, and it exists in the separation of its gathering (that is, thing after thing); and then the heat of the hidden warmth is alleviated and expelled to the extremities until it is resolved, and many times it is thickened.

**And the peak** indeed varies in sicknesses. For the peak of very acute sicknesses lasts up to four days, and ephemera fevers are of this sum; however, they themselves are not numbered as "acute" because it is not enough for the sharpness of a sickness that its peak be near; rather, it must be among sicknesses involving fear <note>danger of death</note>. And acute fevers (not "very" acute) follow these, and they are those whose peak reaches up to 13 days and beyond. And the knowledge of acute sicknesses in their orders and of chronic ones is helpful in the regimen of the patient's food, according to what we shall say in the following.

**And most** fevers indeed complete the beginning, increase, and peak in one paroxysm, and make another paroxysm in declining. And fevers indeed vary in these times; of them indeed there are:

<margin>d</margin>
**And there.** This he adds to declare what he said: "the victory of one of the two appears," etc.

<margin>e</margin>
**And the decline.** It should be considered that he maintains a high method in defining the decline, which does not involve the part of the alteration of the matter since it was already perfectly altered in the peak. Therefore, it shares with the peak the fact that the matter is digested; decline is in a healthy disease, and therefore there cannot be a disposition contrary to digestion in it. He defines it therefore by its cause: the victory of heat over the matter. This victory is in the act of suitable expulsion. For expulsion is suitably done when the harmful is separated from the helpful, with the helpful retained and the harmful expelled; and therefore he says "it exists in the separation of its gathering" (that is, in expulsions). For in symptomatic <note>unhealthy/irregular</note> expulsions, natural heat does not stand in the separation of the gathering; rather, the whole aggregate of good and bad is precipitated and expelled. In this [natural] separation, however, a graded expulsion occurs (part after part), just as it was separated part after part. In a suitable critical expulsion, therefore, we consider three things. First, the proper form of expulsion, which is a regulated, graded separation of good from bad (which does not happen in a symptomatic one); and this he says: "it exists in the separation of the gathering... thing after thing" (that is, matter after matter), so that it is called expulsion and not precipitation. We consider second the effect that follows from this: that the heat of the viscera where the matter was held is alleviated; and therefore he says "the heat of the hidden [warmth]." Third, we consider the place to which it is expelled: because it is to the extremities (that is, outside the body). And this is what he says: "until it is resolved" (that is, it entirely recedes, or the matter is finished in this evacuation). For we have shown elsewhere that this word "resolved" is used by Avicenna in many various meanings. Hence in the second book, chapter 4, when he speaks of stupefying medicine, he says the complexion of the limb is "resolved" (meaning the complexion of the limb is destroyed). And because sometimes it is not expelled to the extremities so that it is resolved (entirely finished), but is retained in some limb and a crisis occurs by "mutation" (that is, an abscess), therefore he adds "and many times it is thickened" (that is, some part becomes an abscess in the expulsion of the matter). This is Avicenna's usual way of speaking elsewhere. Others, however, explain "thickened" as the matter becoming thick through the expulsion of the subtle parts and the remaining of the gross. But if it is asked whether the aforementioned definitions of increase, peak, and decline apply to these times of the paroxysm (for it has already appeared that they apply to the beginning): it must be said that all these definitions entirely suit the three universal [stages] and can suit the times of the paroxysm. For in the increase of a paroxysm, the heat is moved over the matter under which it lay suffocated in the beginning; in the peak of the paroxysm there is a struggle and final inflammation in the matter; and in the decline the heat now dominates the matter. But these ways of speaking are not as proper in particular times as in universal ones. Avicenna in the following chapter will set down the way of having heat in the times of the paroxysm.

<margin>f</margin>
**And the peak.** Here, to complete the science, he sets down four chapters. In the first he wants to indicate...
