<meta>This page continues the discussion of the duration and stages of diseases, specifically focusing on how to recognize the "status" (peak) and the "acuteness" of a condition based on clinical signs.</meta>

# Book III

...division of diseases which he sets forth. Galen <note>G. refers to Galen, the 2nd-century Greek physician</note> in the third book on critical days, and in the commentary on the third book of the *Prognostics*, comment 11, and in many places, says that some diseases are very acute and terminate in the first four days. And this "ephemeral" fever <note>A one-day fever</note> sometimes terminates on the fourth day, such as that which arises from an obstruction or similar cause; yet it is not considered "acute" for the reason he states. And Galen’s discourse in the commentary on the *Aphorisms* regarding acute diseases says some are "absolutely acute," of which Hippocrates <note>Hyp. refers to Hippocrates</note> says they terminate in 14 days. Beyond that law, taking "acute" broadly, they can extend to 20 days; and if they are taken improperly as "tropic" acute diseases, they terminate in 40 days, as Galen said in the first book of the *Prognostics*, comment 27. He also notes that there are other chronic diseases which extend to months and years. Secondly, the cause is known to him who acts from a regimen universally ordered toward the "status" <note>The peak or plateau of a disease</note>, as Hippocrates understands in the first book of the *Aphorisms* when he said: "to those, therefore, whose status is continuous." He speaks in "orders" because acute diseases are of diverse orders: some terminate on the 1st day, some on the 7th, some on the 14th; and similarly, chronic ones vary. Each requires its own feeding, as will appear in the chapter on the feeding of feverish patients. The third cause is the discourse of Galen in the first book on crises, already mentioned above, that several [diseases] complete themselves in one paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or increase in symptoms</note>, i.e., they have their beginning, increase, and peak in one paroxysm, and in the second they decline. Or many complete the peak in one paroxysm, but the other stages occur in several paroxysms before that peak paroxysm. The fourth cause is that certain fevers have a long increase and a long decline, as appears in *augmastic* and *peraugmastic* fevers <note>Technical terms for fevers with specific patterns of increasing intensity</note>; and thus it is understood that some have a long beginning and some a long peak. This cause awaits declaration in the chapter below regarding the fever which is due to putrefaction, etc.

<margin>a **And ephemeral.** Against this: Rhazes <note>9th-century Persian physician</note> in the 15th book of the *Continens*, chapter 7, classifies ephemeral as a long disease. It must be said that here the discourse is about the ephemeral of a single paroxysm, not the whole ephemeral. But against the fact that three universals are taught to be recognized here: it must be said he uses this discourse as a starting point.</margin>

When you see paroxysms prolonged due to thick matter, then the disease will not be acute. All this was said to let you know that the certainty of this sign depends on the verified nature of the matter. And the discourse can be the other member of the division, so that we say material illnesses either have paroxysms—like interpolated and proportional continuous fevers, where paroxysms are long or short—or they do not have paroxysms, like *sinocha* <note>A continuous inflammatory fever</note> and dropsy. And then they either have signs of acute (i.e., hot) matter, and the disease will be acute and short, or signs of cold, thick matter like dropsy, and then the disease is not acute. **And if it remained.** This text can first be explained thus: if the paroxysms invade at the same hour, as in the discourse of that aphorism in the fourth part: "to whom exacerbations or paroxysms..." but this exposition does not seem to be admitted by Avicenna, since this does not speak of anticipation or postponement, nor consequently of equal invasion. Secondly, it is explained to mean that if the illness in its own genus does not have any critical change or any trace of a crisis, it will not be acute but long, as in that aphorism of the fourth part: "in fevers, an abscess not resolved at the first crises," etc. And these expositions are difficult. Thirdly, it can be explained thus: if the paroxysm remains with its disposition, i.e., midway between long and short, then the disease will be of a medium disposition, like a *prolatic* fever <note>A fever that is extended or delayed</note> compared to choleric and melancholic ones. Fourthly, it remains in part, i.e., the sign signifying its disposition, i.e., midway between signs of thick matter and subtle matter, which signifies a matter that is as if medium; the illness will not be of that [high] acuity. And these two expositions are our own.

<margin>b **Apoplexy.** Against this: it is from cold, thick matter. It must be said that some apoplexy arises from hot matter; or it must be said the disease is acute on account of the matter being hot (and such is not apoplexy for the most part), or on account of the accidents or the nobility of the location [the brain]. And such is apoplexy and also quinsy <note>Severe throat inflammation</note>; for they kill quickly by the severity of the accidents, or recovery happens quickly.</margin>
<margin>d **Tertian.** Properly continuous or interpolated.</margin>
<margin>e **And sometimes.** Increases in the circuit: whether the conditions of the periods or paroxysms are four: length and shortness. He teaches to recognize the times of the disease through this. The second is their safety or lack thereof; he teaches to recognize through this in the section "and sometimes from strength." The third is anticipation and postponement; he teaches to recognize through those in the section "and they are recognized." The fourth is the multitude or paucity of accidents; he teaches to recognize from this in the fourth section. It should be considered that Avicenna takes "time" broadly here, i.e., for a great span of time to which a tertian fever can extend; and therefore he said from 3 hours to 14. Yet authors usually take the time that commonly occurs for the most part, as Galen in the second book on crises, when he says 12 hours. Avicenna below: It is doubted whether from the shortness of paroxysms we argue the peak is near, and from length that the peak is remote. It seems not, for Galen in the third book on crises, chapter 3, argues from the length of the parts of a paroxysm that a fever is continuing, or is continuous; but he appropriates shortness to interpolated fever. A continuous fever is shorter and more acute than an interpolated one. In the 18th book of the *Continens*, chapter 6: Furthermore, when paroxysms are long, then it is the peak, because in the peak, labors and accidents reach their limit. To the contrary, for Avicenna, it must be said that in the same illness we do not signify this mode; but when paroxysms are long, then it is the peak as Galen argues. In different ones compared to each other, length and shortness can happen either from the nature of the matter—and then we signify as Avicenna says, that this judgment is for phlegmatic or quartan fevers, or impure tertians signifying a distant peak, while short ones signify a near peak—or it can happen from the mode of motion or location of the matter, whence it is continuous or interpolated. And then we do not judge as Avicenna says; and this judgment given from the length and shortness of the paroxysm is confused, and is not verified unless the nature of the matter is first inspected. Therefore Avicenna said: "they signify that the matter is thick." The first thing that falls under judgment from the length of a paroxysm is that the disease is long; and then this judgment, which was confused, is certified when you see that the matter is thick, from which the contrary signs cease.</margin>
<margin>f **And if it were not.** This discourse can be a discourse in itself, as if to say: if you see signs of thick matter and subtle matter which signifies a matter as if medium, the illness will not be of that acuity. And these two expositions are ours.</margin>

---

### Knowledge of the hours of universal illnesses and specifically the peak. Chapter 54.

**K**nowledge of the hours of universal illnesses is sometimes from the species of the illness: for spasm, *ficus* <note>A growth or tumor</note>, epilepsy, apoplexy, and quinsy are among the very acute. And pure tertian and *causon* <note>A burning fever</note> are among the not very acute. And quartan and paralysis are among the long-lasting. And sometimes from the motion of the illness: for if the paroxysms are short, they signify that the peak is near, like pure tertian, for the time of its paroxysms is from 3 hours up to 14 hours; and if they are prolonged, it signifies that the matter is thick and the peak is distant, as in impure tertian. And if there were no paroxysms there, but rather its matter was acute like *sinochi*, then the illness will be acute. And if its signs were signs of cold, thick matter or leaning toward thickness, then the illness will not be acute; and if it remained with its disposition, then the illness will not be of that acuity. And sometimes it is from strength: if weakness arrives quickly, the illness is acute; or if that does not appear, the illness is not acute. And sometimes from age and season: for in hot weather and a hot age [of life], the peak of the illness hastens; and in cold times and cold ages, the peak of the illness is delayed; and the disposition of regions is similar. And from the pulse: for if it is fast, frequent, and large, then the illness is declining toward acuity, and if not, then it is not acute. And from the rigor <note>Shivering or chills</note>: for if it is of a long duration, then the illness is declining toward length; and if it is of a short duration, then the illness tends toward acuity. And sometimes there is no rigor at all, then its extension is shortened. **And the hours of the illness are sometimes known from the part of the hours of the paroxysms.** For if they were...

---

**K**nowledge. He determined this in the hours of fevers by showing what they are; here he teaches how to recognize them. And because the "status" (peak) is the time of which every physician especially has knowledge, as in the book on crises and the first part of the *Aphorisms*, he speaks specifically of the peak. First he teaches how to recognize universal times, second particular ones. There: "knowledge however." The times of a disease are known either by signs which Galen calls "pre-appearing" (following Hippocrates) or by signs "post-appearing." And first he teaches to recognize it by the first signs, i.e., pre-appearing; second by the post-appearing. There: "sometimes they are known from the part of digestion," or there: "and sometimes they are known from the disposition of evacuations." It should be considered that the signs called pre-appearing are three: the species of illnesses, the circuit, and the incitements of the times of the year with their likes, as appears from the *Aphorisms*, comment 7 on paroxysms. First, therefore, he teaches to recognize universal times by the species of illnesses. Second by the circuit of increases, i.e., they are incited by the seasons of the year. There: "and sometimes from motion." It should be considered that the knowledge had from this is only very useful. For I only know that the peak is near or far from the beginning. For if I know the disease is acute, I know the peak is near the beginning, and the times are short, just as a spasm is acute because it kills quickly, i.e., a universal spasm. But Thaddeus <note>Thaddeus of Florence, a 13th-century medical professor</note> asks what should be said of a "humid" spasm. He answers: that it is more acute because it arrives more suddenly. We do not intend to dwell on this, because considering the being of these spasms when they are already in action, one will see that the discourse of Thaddeus is not entirely true.

<margin>g **And sometimes from strength.** Here he teaches to recognize the times of the disease from strength, because with strength appearing strong, the paroxysm is called "safe"; but with the same falling, it is called "bad." And therefore he says he teaches to recognize the times of the disease from safety and lack of safety. Secondly from certain others. There: "and sometimes from age." It is doubted whether from weakness of strength we argue a short or long disease, since according to the last chapter of *On the Differences of Fevers* and to the contrary here in Avicenna. If you wish for a confused and plural solution to this doubt, see Thaddeus on the aphorism of the fourth part: "that disturbed urines like those of cattle..." The clear solution is that the disease is either mortal—and then the weaker the strength, the shorter the disease, as is known, and thus Avicenna speaks here where he says "sometimes," because in a mortal disease—or it is healthy, and then the weaker it is, the longer it is; and thus Galen speaks.</margin>
<margin>h **And sometimes.** Here he poses other signs that appear, so as not to change the terms of Hippocrates and Galen which they use in the *Aphorisms* regarding paroxysms and consistencies. In the first book on crises, he will divide these parts otherwise and more clearly: so that it may be said that from the causes we recognize the universal times of the disease. First, the species of the illness. Second, the quantity of paroxysms. Third, strong or weak strength. Fourth, age. Fifth, times of the year. Sixth, regions. Seventh, pulse. Eighth, rigor, etc. And I say this way is clearer, because it is difficult to preserve the significance of the terms of Hippocrates and Galen by which they say: that some signs are pre-appearing and some are post-appearing. For those are poorly distinguished, as we have said elsewhere. However, it is to be believed that among the Greeks these terms signify properly, and among us; and what he says is evident.</margin>
<margin>i **And from the pulse.** The cause is because a fast, frequent, large pulse signifies an internal burning, and therefore the crisis will be soon. He said however that "if it is not acute," he did not say it is "long," because it could be short and safe.</margin>
<margin>k **And from the rigor.** The reason is that a longer rigor signifies thick matter that is slow to inflame; and conversely a short rigor. He says afterward that when there is no rigor in any way, its extension is shortened, i.e., the retention or remaining of the fever. But to the contrary: because an untrue tertian is longer than a true one, and yet sometimes it does not begin with rigor, as Avicenna poses below. It must be said that "rigor" here is taken broadly, i.e., for the "typus" <note>The periodic pattern of a fever</note>, whether it be rigor, or shivering, or horror, or coldness around the limbs, or a chill. It happens that a fever has a "typus" because it is continuous, and then it is short; or because the matter is benign as in sweet phlegm, and then it is also short. To what Avicenna says below: it must be said that although there is no rigor, there is nevertheless some "typus" there; or it can be said that if there is no rigor or "typus," it could be extinguished from the thicker part of such matter which is moved slowly, so that as it is moved, it is heated and does not produce a "typus"; then such a fever will be longer, and this is not Avicenna's discourse here.</margin>
<margin>l **And they are recognized.** It should be considered according to Galen in the first book on crises and Rhazes in the 18th book of the *Continens*, chapter 7, that some anticipation of paroxysms is "absolute," such as when the second precedes the first by one hour, and the second the third by one hour, and so on. And such anticipation signifies neither increase nor postponement of decline. And the reason is: because this can be from the nature of the illness. For some fever is found which always anticipates from the beginning to the end; some which always declines; and this is what Avicenna says: "since from illnesses there are..." etc. Another is anticipation that is not absolute, but "superfluous." For example: the second paroxysm precedes the first by one hour, and the third the second by two or three, and the fourth the third by three or four. And such anticipation signifies an increase, and the opposite postponement signifies decline. And this is what Avicenna says: for if they were preceding according to a superfluous anticipation, i.e., exceeding much, so that one precedes the predecessor in its anticipation and <margin>m</margin> adds to it; and this is what he says "tending toward addition," then it is in the increase; and that such...</margin>

# Treatise on the Fen
<note>The "Fen" refers to a specific division or "book" within Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine.</note>

<margin>a</margin>
**Anticipation** <note>original: *antecessio*; the fever fit arriving earlier than expected</note> signifies **increase**, and not just any symptoms that appear: for there are some illnesses that run their course until the end, etc. Secondly, it must be considered that the text which says: *if it has so remained*, can be explained in two ways. First, if the anticipation is not only absolute, but an anticipation of that which is superfluous: and this is what it means by *the superfluities have remained*. Then the illness will be in its **peak** <note>original: *statu*; the "status" or height of the disease</note>. In another way, according to Avicenna: one should not be certain in giving a judgment of increase through anticipation, however much it may be superfluous, unless there are also added accidents <note>symptoms</note> and the rest. Similarly, a judgment of the peak is not given by the paroxysms remaining at an equal onset unless there are no extreme symptoms. For an equal onset can absolutely signify the beginning of a disease, or a long disease, as appears from the *Aphorisms*, fourth part: *To whom the exacerbations...* Therefore he said: if the anticipation and the superfluities have remained (that is, the symptoms in their extremity), and this speech refers to what he says: *as one precedes the superfluity of the other*. That is, one precedes that which it adds over the other, tending toward an addition, namely of symptoms. But he spoke distinctly about this knowledge of the times of the disease from the perspective of symptoms immediately after; however, he said this about it so that he might certify the knowledge from the perspective of anticipation and postponement.

### ...proceeding according to anticipation superfluously: so that one precedes the superfluity of the other, tending toward an addition: then the illness will be in its **increase**. For among illnesses there are those that run until the end of their hours according to increase: and these are sometimes of the tertian type <note>fever recurring every third day</note> and of the continuous type. But if the anticipation has stayed, and the superfluities have stayed: then without doubt the illness will be in its **peak**. ¶ And that which keeps to one hour is of a long duration: and if they are postponed, then the illness is in its **decline**. Similarly, the disposition of the hours is known from the increase of the symptoms of the fever, and their staying, and their decline, and from the addition of its paroxysms in their length and shortness. And perhaps they vary and do not resemble one another. ¶ And sometimes they are known from their disposition. For when in some paroxysm there occurs sweat or a flux of the belly, and the second paroxysm which follows it is similar in intensity to the first and in its strength or above it: then its evacuation is because of the quantity [of matter] and not because of strength: and the illness is judged to be long. And sometimes they are known from the side of **digestion** and the contrary of digestion according to what we have said; for example: when sputum appears with some digestion, or urine in which there is some cloudiness, then it is the beginning of the increase.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ *And keeping to one hour.* This is that aphorism: *To whom the exacerbations or paroxysms...* And it requires a great deal of discussion. For it is commonly said that the equal onset of paroxysms is a sign of rawness <note>original: *cruditatis*; undigested humors</note>: and with the symptoms remitted, it signifies a long illness, because it exists in the beginning with thick or raw matter. But in his commentary on that aphorism, he wants the fixedness and stability of the onset to signify matter needing a long time for digestion, as if he wants there to be an equal battle between nature and the matter: and the speech is similar to the third [book] of the *Prognostics* and the commentary. This is an equal battle: because nature holds it in the same way in its dispositions with respect to its power. Therefore it is neither defeated so that health occurs, nor winning so that death occurs: therefore the disease is long. But with this, irregularity also signifies, or can signify, a longer disease. And it is a doubt whether an equal onset signifies a longer disease than irregularity: and perhaps it ought to be said that irregularity which happens by a fall of power signifies a shorter end toward death. But irregularity from a diversity of matter can signify a longer disease insofar as it signifies diverse matters: and you should consider this. It is doubted first why anticipation and superfluity signify increase, postponement signifies decline, and equal staying signifies the beginning or the peak. And he says that if the matter were uniform of itself, it would always invade at an equal time. Therefore, when nature manifestly moves against the matter, as it does in the increase, then the paroxysms are accelerated. When nature fails it, then the paroxysms are postponed: and this is in the decline. This speech is much diminished, as it appears: because it is given that it can be reduced to two causes. The first is the equality and inequality of the battle: for in the beginning and the peak the battle seems equal enough; in the beginning indeed equal because not increased, but the matter stays raw; in the peak indeed equal because not able to be increased. And therefore the paroxysms, which are paroxysms of battle, are equal in the hours of onset. In the increase and decline, however, there seems to be a certain inequality of battle: in the increase indeed through the agitation which nature makes in the matter, and therefore the matter moves quickly. Whether it be a good agitation which nature makes in the matter, or a bad one which the matter makes in nature, or a bad putrid heat in the matter. In the decline, however, it is because of victory. The second cause is the quantity and motion of the matter with a similar disposition of qualities which is in the beginning and the peak. For that which is moved first and second in the beginning and peak is equal in quantity and quality: but in the increase and decline it is unequal and dissimilar, as is known: because these are possible to have otherwise; therefore it happens in the beginning that anticipation occurs, and also postponement. And in the increase postponement, and in the decline anticipation. And you should consider this. It is doubted secondly why some fevers proceed always by adding, like certain tertians and quotidians <note>daily fevers</note>: and some always by postponing: as are certain tertians and quotidians. These men say, namely **Thaddeus** <note>Thaddeus of Florence, a famous 13th-century physician</note> and all who follow him: that the cause is the deformity of the matter in thickness and thinness. For if the thinner matter begins to putrefy first, and successively the thicker, in that case the paroxysms will always go by postponing, because the thicker matter will be moved more slowly. But if the thicker matter begins and proceeds to the thinner, they will always go by anticipating. But then Thaddeus insists: how can thick matter be moved before thin? It must be said it is because of some proper disposition, just as in someone **phlegm** putrefies and not **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>. But if you consider the speeches of these men, they cannot give this cause except in fevers that pass from thick matters to thin, or vice versa. ¶ But now sense shows certain tertians quite pure, and from matter quite uniform in substance, to have proceeded always by anticipating: and in some always by postponing: and the intake of the most prepared things is quite similar. But we will say here that there can be many causes, of which we will say some are on the part of the body, and some on the part of the matter: on the part of the body indeed it happens that a man is quite sensitive in his members, but close to bloodiness and moist in them: and in the beginning the choleric matter meets them covered: but as the paroxysms proceed it is always more uncovered, and they are bitten more and more quickly by the new matter: wherefore the paroxysms hasten. In some other body, however, the matter which is moved paroxysmally could gradually add an obstruction to the sense, wherefore the paroxysms will postpone. On the part of the matter: for because of many contingent causes the fever can begin in the first paroxysm with some quantity of matter, and it is possible for all the second matter to be more ample or more biting than the first, even if it is digested or is in decline, and thus the paroxysms will always anticipate. But it is said: according to this, in the decline a paroxysm could be made from more ample matter than in the peak. It must be answered in two ways: first, that that last paroxysm was the peak and the decline. Or it must be said: that it is not inconvenient, but although the matter be more ample, it will be more obedient to the power [of nature]. And you should consider that many causes can accelerate the paroxysmal motion, even if the fever is in decline.

### ...then when that is multiplied and appears, or its contrary, then it is the **peak**. And again when digestion appears or its contrary quickly from the sputum or a cloud [in the urine]: then know that the peak is near: if it is delayed, then know that the peak is far off. The knowledge of the particular hours is taken thus: for the hour of the beginning of the paroxysm is the hour in which the **pulse** is constricted: and you already knew his intention: and the color of the extremities becomes leaden: and the extremes are chilled: and specifically the tip of the ear and the nose, until the hour in which the spreading of heat is felt.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ *And similarly.* It should be considered that the symptoms here are understood as pains, heats, thirst, wakefulness, etc. And what he says is clear.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ *And perhaps.* As if he says: in fevers of heterogeneous members there is no order of onset: and therefore from these signs of anticipation and postponement and length and shortness we cannot know the times of the disease. And perhaps he wants that diversification, insofar as it signifies diverse matters, to signify a long disease.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ *And sometimes.* He teaches to know from another sign, that is, **evacuation**: and consider that such an illness is long if it is to be healthy: because there can be a short mortal fever. And in this is included that aphorism of the fourth part: *In fevers a great sweat coming on, the fever not failing...* etc.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ *And sometimes.* Here, as they say, he teaches to know the times of the disease from signs appearing afterward: although it could begin there: and sometimes it is known from the disposition of the evacuation. Note that the signs appearing afterward are signs of the **crisis** <note>the turning point of a disease</note> of which evacuation is one: and he has already spoken of this and the signs of digestion and its contrary. And he says these signs are of health and death, although they are appearing afterward; they cannot [be used] to know the times of the disease, because signs of death, since they are common to the three times, are understood from what was said before. And consider that he took the signs of digestion in the sputum and urine, meaning others as well: and he taught to know the times of the disease, when they are and when they will be, as appears in the text. And the knowledge from these signs is certain: but from the signs said above it is not so certain, as first concerning the crisis.

### ¶ And sometimes there are associated with the beginning an alteration of color and sluggishness and distress: and slowness of movements: and depth of sleep: and softening of the eyelids and heaviness of speech: and a shivering between the shoulder blades and in the back, and perhaps a strong rigor happens in it: and sometimes there happens a flow of saliva and a leaping of the temples and a ringing of the ears: and sneezing and a commotion of the members of the body.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ *Knowledge of the hours.* Here he teaches to know the particular times. And first he does this according to the given common [rule] of the lengthening and shortening of the paroxysms. There: *and know*. The first part in two: first he does this. Second he puts an example. There: *and if it seems to you*. The first in four according to which he notifies the four times. It must be considered that the symptoms of the beginning of a paroxysm all follow the motion of the suffocations of natural heat under the matter: and therefore the pulse is constricted. And you knew this in the first book, second [part], fourth [chapter] below, in the chapter on the signs of putrid fevers. And from this, because the heat flees, the color becomes leaden: and the extremes are chilled. These symptoms are then diversified according to the diversity of matters: and according to the diversity of bodies: and the parts in which the impression appears: whence the extremes are chilled specifically, etc., because they are cold with little flesh, *Prognostics* I. And therefore sometimes the color is much altered. ¶ He said this: *alteration of color*, as in a fainting fit. *Sluggishness* in a phlegmatic one: *distress* when the matter moves around the part of the stomach and the respiratory organs. *Slowness* in a phlegmatic one and also *depth of sleep*, etc. Whence certain phlegmatic ones begin paroxysms with a stupor. *Shivering* when the matter is somewhat choleric. *Flow of saliva*: the matter being moved in the stomach or head. *Commotion of the members*, that is, a shaking: as in the tremor of a type and of other symptoms. The cause is clear.

### And the power [of the body] is indeed more vehemently weakened because of the weakness: which is in the beginning or the peak.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ *And more vehemently.* It must be considered that weakness happens by way of suffocation: and this happens more in the beginning of a paroxysm. And by way of strong inflammation: and this happens more in the peak of a paroxysm: and therefore death happens more in the beginning than the peak of a paroxysm: but in the increase or decline: as below in the second section, the chapter on the hours of death. And thirdly concerning the crisis, fourth chapter. In the decline indeed death and weakness happen by way of resolution <note>the "dissolving" or wasting away of the body's strength</note>. And this is rarer, as Saliceto says there. ¶ This is what Avicenna wanted here when he says *and more vehemently*, etc. That is, it happens more that the power weakens in the beginning and peak than in the decline of a paroxysm: in the increase, if the power fails, it is because of the addition of heat, just as in the peak: and this happens more in the peak. In the decline indeed it happens more frequently that with the febrile heat thinned out, a man is more relieved than his natural heat is simultaneously resolved by accident.

### ¶ And the first half of the hour of increase is the hour in which the pulse begins to appear and to become large and to become fast. And the heat is spread in the whole body according to equality.

<margin>h</margin> ¶ *And the hour of increase.* It must be considered that there is an hour of symptoms having an affinity to the beginning in which there is suffocation, and an affinity to the peak in which there is now an eruption made and a venting of heat: therefore he divided the increase into two parts: and he did not do this because it is longer in proportion, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus</note> says, because it is common for the increase to be short and the beginning and peak to be long, as will appear later. But he said this because of its deformity <note>variation</note>.

### ¶ And its other half is the hour: in which this spread heat does not cease to be increased with equality.

<margin>i</margin> ¶ *According to equality.* That is, proportionally.

# Book IV

<margin>a</margin> **And the time of the peak.** This is called the "status" <note>Latin: *status*, meaning the peak or plateau of a disease</note> because the accidents <note>symptoms or secondary conditions</note> remain in their ultimate state; therefore, with heat added to its limit, the pulse becomes faster and more frequent. But you might say: it does not seem to be larger, because the strength <note>vital faculty</note> is more weakened in the peak than in the growth stage. It must be said that the added necessity forces the strength to enlarge the pulse more than at other times; and elsewhere we have touched upon it being stronger. Nevertheless, natural strengths, assuming some necessity, work vehemently, as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the influential Greek physician</note> says in his commentary on the pulse, treatise 4, first commentary.

<margin>b</margin> **And the time of decline.** He doubts because he says that sweat occurs. Then, indeed, the decline happens as they sweat. It must be said first that the word "then" does not denote a strict sequence, but indicates two modes of decline: one without manifest evacuation, and another with manifest evacuation. Secondly, when the matter begins to be propelled toward the skin, even if sweat does not yet appear, the hidden heat can begin to be alleviated.

<margin>c</margin> **And many times.** This is the discourse of the third book on the crisis, chapter four. Therefore, return to the pulse to distinguish a true decline from the peak; for in a true one it proceeds toward improvement, but in a false one <unclear>it fluctuates</unclear>.

<margin>d</margin> **And if you wish.** He doubts how he attributes "shuddering" <note>Latin: *horripilatio*, goosebumps or shivering</note> to tertian fever <note>a fever that recurs every third day, typically malaria</note> when everyone says it happens with "rigor" <note>intense cold/shaking</note>, as Galen says in the second book on crises. It must be said that by "shuddering," he understands a gradual process from a small chill to a great rigor. For first, in a tertian fever, a certain shuddering of the skin begins, and some cold follows, because the heat begins to intensify; but when the bile is carried strongly over the sensitive members, then there will be manifest rigor. These terms—shuddering, cold, and rigor—are used with much variety among authors, as will be said below in its own chapter.

<margin>e</margin> **In many dispositions.** Because a non-true tertian is governed in which rigor does not occur, as the author will set down below.

<margin>f</margin> **And know that the sickness is sometimes prolonged.** Namely, a tertian or a paroxysm <note>a sudden attack or increase in symptoms</note> or whatever material disease it may be. He doubts because there are other causes of prolongation besides those he sets down below in the first chapter on putrefaction: namely, the rest of the matter and the weakness of sensation; and errors in the regimen <note>lifestyle/dietary rules</note>; and in the second chapter on the signs of prolongation, he places the cause as "thickness in the viscera." It must be said that he summarized it, and you should complete this knowledge from what is to be said. For not everything can be written in one place; and if you consider the rest of the matter and the thickness in the interior parts, it is reduced to the thickness and coldness of the matter. Malice of the regimen is reduced to extrinsic causes, which he puts here as an example, such as cold weather; weakness of sensation is reduced to weakness of the strength. But you might ask: why does he say the weakness of strength or innate heat "helps" that, when it is actually the principal cause? It must be said that every cause which is outside the nature of the disease and the nature of its cause can be called "extrinsic" in prolongation and shortening. However, causes taken from the disease itself or its cause are more proper and intrinsic; and these can be called "co-helpers," while those are "principals." He doubts whether the method of distinguishing particular times (namely of paroxysms) and universal times of the whole disease is the same. It seems so, because just as universal times are distinguished and identified by the fact that the pulse is submerged, oppressed by heat, or expanded (as appeared above), so too are the particular times of paroxysms. Here the Author <note>Avicenna</note> follows Hippocrates, who teaches that the same signs used to know universal times also teach one to know paroxysms, as appears in the aphorism on paroxysms and consistencies. On the contrary, Avicenna speaks distinctly about the distinction between particular and universal times and brings forward distinct signs. It must be said that by a certain general and proportional distinction, these times are distinguished in a similar way. For just as in the universal beginning of a disease the heat is suffocated because the matter is raw, then it is manifested more fully in the matter, then it reaches its peak, then it declines; so it happens in the beginning, growth, peak, and decline of a paroxysm. However, by a special and appropriated distinction, they are distinguished in a different way, as everyone commonly says. For the universal times of a disease are distinguished either by the alteration of the matter or by the accidents, as appears in the first book on crises. But the particular times of paroxysms are distinguished neither by the alteration of the matter nor by the accidents, but by the way the heat behaves in expansion or enclosure. That the times of paroxysms are not distinguished by the alteration of the matter and the action of nature is apparent because there can be a time in which the action of nature on the matter has not yet occurred, and yet the paroxysm will have all its stages, just like a paroxysm at the beginning. And it is possible that a paroxysm has its decline, and yet there will be no decline of the disease; indeed, a person could die in the decline of a paroxysm. This does not happen in the decline of the whole disease once the action of nature on the matter has been completed. For when the strength overcomes and expels it, the sick person cannot die, as proven in the third book on crises, chapter five. But in the decline of a paroxysm, it can happen that the natural heat is resolved <note>dissipated</note> along with the matter, and the sick person dies. Nor are the times of a paroxysm distinguished by accidents like the universal times of a disease. And this is proven by Dionysius: first, that the times of a disease are distinguished by the accidents of "foreign heat" <note>feverish heat</note> insofar as it is foreign and against nature, and thus the distinction is by the accidents of the disease. But the distinction of paroxysm times is by the movement of the heat as heat—I mean movement inward and outward—and by its addition or resolution. Second, because the peak of a paroxysm is not a peak regarding the accidents such that the accidents are most intense in it; for it could be that the growth and peak of a paroxysm are mild, and the beginning of the paroxysm will have more difficult accidents, so that in such a beginning the sick person will die if it is a mortal illness, as taken from Galen. And because of this, Dionysius infers that the distinction of paroxysm times by accidents is accidental to them, but by the movement of heat it is essential. For the beginning of a paroxysm is when the heat is constricted and the extremities are cold; the growth is when it expands; the peak is when it is fully expanded; the decline is when it is resolved. It is not so with universal times regarding accidents, because then it will be the peak when the accidents of the disease are intense, and the decline when they are remitted. And therefore, the peak of the disease regarding accidents can coincide with the beginning and growth of a paroxysm, and the decline of the whole disease regarding accidents can coincide with the peak of a paroxysm. Dionysius adds, however, that it must be understood that there is some agreement between the times of a paroxysm and the times of a disease distinguished by accidents: because both in the decline of the disease regarding accidents and in the decline of a paroxysm, a person can die. For it is possible that the accidents of the disease appear to be remitted because the natural strength is overcome and conquered, not resisting or fighting the disease; and because of this, the accidents of the disease appear remitted, and yet the sick person tends toward death. Although this is a decline of the disease regarding accidents, it is not a decline regarding the essence of the disease. And as it is something outside of nature compared to the strength and its action. And therefore Galen’s reasons, by which he proves in the third book on crises that in the decline a person does not die, prove it regarding the decline in terms of the operation of nature, but not regarding the decline in terms of accidents. And this is also what Avicenna meant when he said: "and many times indeed." Although Avicenna’s discourse refers to the decline of a paroxysm, it can nevertheless refer to the decline of the disease regarding accidents, because the decline

### And the time of the peak is the time in which the heat remains spread with equality: and the accidents with their disposition: and the pulse is larger than ever: and it is more vehemently fast and frequent. And the time of decline is the time in which the diminution begins, and the pulse begins to be tempered and equalized. Then that in which the body begins to sweat and leads to the eradication [of the disease]. And many times indeed a disposition occurs near death which is like a decline: and it is as if the sick person has escaped: and it is not necessary that you be occupied with this: rather, you should know the disposition of the pulse when it is enlarged and becomes strong. And if it seems right to you, I will give you an example of tertian fever. Note, therefore, that since in most dispositions tertian fever begins with shuddering: then cold and rigor; afterward the rigor is calmed and the cold is lessened and the heating begins; afterward the heating is equalized: then it is increased; afterward it reaches a peak: then it begins to be diminished until it is eradicated.

### And know that the sickness is sometimes prolonged: either because of the multitude of the matter: or because of the thickness of the matter: or because of the thickness

of the disease regarding accidents can coincide with the decline of a paroxysm. ## For the clarification of this question, many premises are first sent forth. First, that every disease having four universal times (if healthy) or three (if mortal) depends on some matter through whose varying disposition its times are distinguished. This proposition is apparent because one distinction of the universal times of a disease is on the part of the matter. The second proposition is that any paroxysm has its own matter on which it depends, and this is a known proposition. The third is that the matter through whose disposition the universal times of the disease vary is one from the beginning of the disease until the end of the decline in a simple disease; but in a composite one, there are two from the beginning to the end. The reason: because authors distinguish universal times by this: that which in the beginning is raw now begins to be digested (i.e., in the growth stage); but in the peak it is digested or turns toward digestion; in the decline, this is called the time when the raw matter is expelled. So says Galen in his booklet on the universal times of disease, and in the first and second books on crises, and Avicenna. But this would not be the case if the matter were different and changing. On the contrary, in an intermittent tertian fever, there cannot be one single matter, because on the day of rest it is not there. Furthermore, how could there be one single matter from beginning to end in a quartan fever <note>a fever recurring every fourth day</note> that lasts four years? It must be said that in intermittent fevers, the times of the disease are not properly distinguished by the alteration of the matter in the same way as in continuous fevers; for continuous ones are one continuity in their parts. And if the times are distinguished by the alteration of the matter, it will be by the alteration of the antecedent matter standing in the veins. Therefore, the sign of digestion that you consider on the day of rest is not compared to the continuous cause, since there is none, but to the antecedent cause; not that it must be one and the same from the beginning of the whole fever until the end. Since therefore the antecedent cause moves toward a paroxysm while it is raw, then those paroxysms are the "beginning" paroxysms; when it is softer, they are the "growth" paroxysms. And from this you may infer corollaries. First, that the universal times of a disease are properly distinguished in continuous diseases, in which one matter runs from the beginning until the peak, reserved for the crisis. And therefore, in continuous fevers, prolongation—in which many crises occur—greatly confuses the times of the disease; so that after signs of digestion and the mode of crisis have already appeared regarding that matter, the signs of digestion are lost again, and reappear again, and crises happen again. And all this is because of the precipitation of many new matters to the site of putrefaction, so that it is not called one matter, but can be called many having a beginning, growth, and peak. And this led Galen to posit these acute "convertible" diseases after he saw that an acute fever absolutely lasts 14 days; that one which lasts 14 days will be fairly uniform in its exacerbations if it is of the exacerbating type, or entirely uniform if it is a *synochus* <note>a continuous non-intermittent fever</note>; and that which terminates before this time (namely on the 11th, 6th, 7th, or 5th day) is a true continuous fever having one manifest distinction of the times of the disease. Or they are prolonged further, properly to the 40th day, by "conversion" or a kind of relapse, as Galen indicates in his commentary on acute illnesses. The second corollary is that in modern times, because of the [dietary] habits of men and the multiplication of matters that are frequently precipitated toward putrefaction besides the primary matter that starts the fever, the times of the disease are greatly confused regarding the alteration of the matter; and now digestion will appear in the urine for some days, and afterward rawness will return again, as if another disease were starting over. And according to this, we have seen a continuous fever lasting 30 days, even though it was enough for our ancestors when they said it lasted 40. The fourth proposition is that any matter that causes a paroxysm or exacerbation is distinct in number from another that causes another paroxysm. The reason is that whatever matter causes a paroxysm causes the patient to be ill and is afterward resolved and finished, so that it can no longer carry the foreign heat. Therefore, if the paroxysm returns again, it must be that the matter is different; and so it is understood by Galen in the second book on the differences of fevers and by Avicenna below. The fifth proposition is that the matter which is disposed through distinct universal times from the beginning of the disease until the end is not that which causes the paroxysm on the day of the paroxysm or the fourth day; but that which paroxysms is accumulated with it. The reason is that one remains (namely the matter by which the times are distinguished) and the other is expelled, either every day or every third or fourth day. The sixth proposition is that if there is a continuous fever from one matter from the universal beginning until the end, to the decline, and this fever has exacerbations, the matter that causes the exacerbation is not the same in number as that which runs through all the times of the disease; but it is another, and there are as many in number as there are exacerbations. And although many of these propositions can be reduced to one, we have divided them into many so that we may speak more clearly. From these propositions, I first infer that continuous fever is of three modes: one in which from its beginning a single matter is moved to putrefaction, or is entirely occupied by unnatural heat, and that whole matter remains from the beginning until the end of the fever (namely to the beginning of the decline) with no addition of other matter made to it; and such is a true putrid or non-putrid *synochus*. On the contrary: in a putrid *synochus*, for example, there would be no succession in heat if some part of the blood were not continually added to the prior part which was previously putrefied. Furthermore, Galen in the third book, chapter one, distinguishes the species of *synochus* by the fact that what evaporates from the blood is equal to what is ignited, or more or less. Therefore, a new accession occurs in the blood, namely of newly ignited blood, which was not ignited at the beginning of the fever; otherwise, that variety would not occur. Furthermore, a continuous resolution occurs from the blood in a fever; therefore, if new blood does not approach the fever, all the blood would always be declining. Furthermore, suppose a blood-fever in which there is evaporation only in a measure that would not cause a fever; if therefore in the first evaporation of blood there were no accession of other blood succeeding in that evaporation, the fever would cease in the first evaporation; and thus some blood-fever would cease in less than a sixth part of an hour. Furthermore: every day blood is generated from the food that is eaten, and that is mixed with the heated blood; therefore it will be heated. Let us say that we can imagine a quantity of putrid blood with which the fever begins, and with no extrinsic quantity added to it, it will be one continuous fever from the beginning until the end; for example: the fever begins with one pound of blood...

I say that with that blood, with nothing added from the outside, the succession of this fever will persist in its heat and evaporation: for all that blood is heated even in all its formal parts <note>In medieval science, "formal parts" refer to the essential qualities or "form" of the substance, whereas "material parts" refer to the physical substance itself.</note>, but not yet in its material parts. Therefore, as the heat occupies all the material parts in the beginning, it will cause continuous evaporation. Then, if the amount of vapors being released is greater than the material parts being added, it will be a "declining" sanguine fever; if they are equal, it will be "equal-toned" <note>original: *homotonea*; a fever that remains at a constant intensity</note>; if less, it will be an "increasing" fever. And just as we imagine this in one pound of blood, so we can imagine it in the blood of the whole body, or in the blood which is in the large veins attached to the back. ### General Discourse on Ephemeral Fevers. Chapter V.
</insert>

Many difficulties could be raised here, which I will omit. Following this path, the objections cease: for it is conceded that a new part of blood is added during the "accession" <note>the start of a fever spike</note> which is a material part of the whole inflamed blood, or it is a part according to its matter or form moved to the victory of the degree of external heat. To the last argument, it must be said: although that actually happens, it is not necessary to be inherent in this fever. Or it must be said that it is not necessary for blood generated from new food to receive that external color by which it could cause fever, although it sometimes does; for instance, someone who eats meat during a *sinocha* <note>a continuous, non-putrid fever</note>. And we shall say this secondly: we can imagine at the beginning of a sanguine fever a certain quantity of putrid blood, and that a continuous addition is made to it, not indeed at a determined time (as on the third or fourth day, for then it would be a continuous exacerbating fever), and the blood has this by its nature. Therefore, that first quantity which first putrefied on the first day in a *sinocha* runs from the beginning to the end, if it happens to be a pure continuous fever; and that other blood which is continuously added to it is consumed with the first. This mode is explained when we speak of the manner of continuity in fevers.

The second mode of continuous fevers is those which start from the beginning with a certain quantity of matter, and this matter proceeds from the beginning to the end, as we say in the case of sanguine fever. With this, every day (if it is phlegm), or on the third day (if it is bile/cholera), or on the fourth day (if it is melancholy/black bile), some part of the matter is moved, causing an "exacerbation" <note>a temporary increase in the severity of symptoms</note>. But it is doubted whether this fever is seen as one, or as a double fever—one continuous and another intermittent. Secondly, it is doubted whether such a mode of continuous fever is caused by blood or by another humor. It must be said: if we imagine a quantity of putrid bile <note>original: *cholera*</note> in the veins capable of maintaining the fever until the day of the crisis <note>the turning point of a disease</note>—for example, according to Galen, until the seventh day—then we would have imagined a truly continuous bilious fever having only one paroxysm <note>a single continuous attack</note> in which the universal stages of that fever are distinguished. This was the view of Galen and Avicenna in the second chapter on the differences of fevers, for they categorized certain fevers of red bile as true *sinochas* (continuous fevers), divided into increasing, beyond-increasing, and equal-toned. However, certain commentators corrupt that text. And if we imagine along with this that every third day, or on the third and fifth days, some part of the bile within the veins is moved, then we would have imagined an exacerbation. Because this part of the bile which causes the exacerbation is moved in the same place and added to the matter that causes the continuous fever, they are not called "two fevers." But if that bilious matter which is moved in the third-day exacerbation were outside the veins, then the patient would have two fevers: one continuous and the other intermittent. And one might subtly say: if the bile causing the exacerbation in that continuous fever is so great that it could spark a fever on its own—even if it were not that specific bile—then the fever would be truly continuous until the day it ends; one being truly continuous, the other not truly continuous but composed of those several exacerbations, which is the "third mode" of continuity we shall discuss. But if that bile is so small that it only makes the continuous fever stronger when it is moved, but cannot cause a fever by itself, then it is one truly continuous fever. It does not seem far-fetched that some matter can increase a fever yet not be able to cause the whole fever itself. Thus, a small amount of putrid bile could increase that fever which it could not cause alone. The Commentator <note>likely Averroes</note> intends this possibility in the third treatise on the regimen. To the second, it must be said: we can imagine a true continuous fever from every humor, namely phlegm and melancholy, just as we say of bile and blood. But there is a difference: the matter of exacerbation in other humors does not have a determined day like bile (every third day) or phlegm (every day). The reason for this difference is elsewhere in our writings. But if blood is added to it continuously, it does not have a movement on a determined day, but is continuous, because such is its nature. But it is doubted whether that true continuous fever can be free from the fortification on the third day; and thus, could a continuous fever of phlegm or melancholy be free from their spikes? We say that "possibility" is a broad thing; therefore, I do not see it as impossible. Indeed, just as a quantity of bile moved within the veins causes one paroxysm—during and after which it is possible for no other bile to be moved—and it will last seven, ten, or more or fewer hours, so a quantity of bile can putrefy within the veins and maintain a fever throughout, even if no other bile is moved to putrefaction in this whole time. But just as the former is rare, so this is rarer. It must be imagined, therefore, that with some quantity of bile moved to putrefaction within the veins, a particular disposition is created by which some bile will be moved in parts, causing an exacerbation. And since it is conceded that a true continuous *sinocha* fever can be made from a humor other than blood, look for the full explanation below in the chapter on putrefaction and the chapter on *sinocha*.

The third mode of continuous fevers is through the conjunction of several paroxysms or exacerbations: where, before the first matter is resolved, the second is ignited. Hence, such a continuation occurs more in putrefaction inside the veins, as is stated below in the chapter on putrefaction, in fevers other than sanguine ones. For such continuation is more appropriately assigned to fevers other than sanguine ones, as would appear to one understanding the book *On the Differences of Fevers*. And it is doubted whether any of the fever matter from the first day remains until the crisis. It must be said that it is possible for the crisis to be so near that on the seventh day some part of the bile, for example, or phlegm remains, which by itself could not cause the fever, but causes it together with another or other matters subsequently moved. And if the authors have left these two things undetermined, it is because these truths are certainly indeterminable. One thing is: how long can one fever from a humor other than blood last when moved within the veins to putrefaction in such a way that no new matter is joined to it? For concerning bile outside the veins, they said it lasts from four to twelve or thirteen hours; concerning phlegm, eighteen hours; concerning melancholy, twenty-four hours. But concerning those putrefying inside the veins, they did not say; this was because they saw that a second

<column-break/>

exacerbation arrives before the first is finished. Therefore, you cannot know for certain whether the first would have lasted; but if we suppose a great quantity of bile and that it putrefies near the heart and no other bile can be moved, we will have imagined a true continuous bilious fever, just like a single paroxysm of a single fever from matter outside the veins, having no other paroxysm before, after, or with it. They did not set a certain duration for this continuous fever, unless we call it a "burning fever" <note>original: *causon*; a high, burning fever often associated with bile</note>, even though we know that burning fevers are found for the most part to exacerbate, albeit secretly. Another thing they left undetermined is how long the matter that remains from the first exacerbation of a fever lasts in the body, which matter is joined to another matter that causes the second exacerbation. Know that those remains of matter and other matters that are corrupted in feverish people are what cause the many varieties of "creunts" <note>possibly a term for clinical signs or discharges</note>, even though they are not the primary cause of the fever.

There is a doubt concerning the aforementioned: whether, while one matter causes a true continuous bilious fever without anything added from the outside, such 

<margin>
The causes of all species of ephemeral fever are primitive causes: essentially heating, and heating by accident from the sum of occurrences and things taken in: namely, in food and drink, and in bodily and mental passions.
</margin>

matter could exacerbate every third day; and this through its agitation or a new mode of putrefaction. For the opinion of Galen and Avicenna was that a new paroxysm or exacerbation is caused by new matter newly aggregated and moved. We shall speak of this below, and we have said something in the question on the prolongation of fever.

There is a second difference between the two solutions of the question in three conclusions. First: if the fever has only one paroxysm, like a *sinocha* or a tertian of one paroxysm, the distinction of the whole disease and the times of the paroxysm are the same; it is more convenient to say these are the times of the whole fever and the times of the paroxysm. Second conclusion: if the fever is continuous through one matter running from the beginning to the end, and besides this, it has paroxysms or exacerbations from other matter supervening upon it, although it is the same in species, the distinction of the times of the whole continuous fever and the distinction of the times of a single paroxysm is not the same, just as a paroxysm or exacerbation is not the whole disease. It is, however, similar: because just as the whole matter is disposed differently from the beginning to the end—in the beginning, increase, peak (*status*), and decline—so is the matter of a single paroxysm. And just as the matter of the whole fever in the beginning is raw and suffocating, in the increase it begins to be possessed by heat (either digestive or putrid), in the peak it is fully possessed, and in the decline it is evacuated; so in a similar way, the matter which suppresses the heat at the beginning of an exacerbation is occupied by heat in the increase, occupied fully in the peak, and this either by natural heat (if it is a paroxysm from which one should be cured or feel better after) or by heat beyond nature (if it is a paroxysm in which the symptoms lead to death or a worse disposition). There is a similar distinction regarding the accidents <note>symptoms</note>: because just as at the beginning of the whole disease the symptoms are mild, and in the increase they are added to, etc., so at the beginning of a paroxysm the symptoms are mild or small, and in the increase they are added to, etc. And I mean the symptoms which belong to the paroxysm, such as the febrile disease; for its symptoms as a "prince" <note>primary symptom</note> alone—for example, coldness of the extremities and sunken eyes—are relieved in the increase, but the symptoms that follow the degree of heat or malice proceed by increasing from the beginning to the peak, just as in the whole of a fatal or healthy disease. 

The third conclusion is that if the fever is continuous and exacerbating because of the prolongation of the paroxysms, the judgment is almost the same as for intermittent fevers, and this question seems to ask about that. Thus, consider an intermittent fever that has its beginning in three paroxysms, its increase in three, its peak in three, and its decline also in three paroxysms. For example, if one of these paroxysms is taken, I say that the distinction of the times of the whole fever and the distinction of the times of a single paroxysm is not the same, but I say it is similar in all respects. For we call the first three paroxysms the "beginning," because in all of them the symptoms are mild and the matter is raw compared to the other three which are the paroxysms of the "increase." Also, three paroxysms will be called the "peak," because the matter then being moved is digested and the symptoms are at their limit. In the same way, in any one paroxysm taken from these: at its beginning, the matter is a suffocator of heat; in the increase, the heat occupies the matter; in the peak, the heat has occupied the whole matter; in the decline, it evaporates. Also, in the beginning, the symptoms are mild, in the increase they grow, and they are at their peak in the status; in the decline, they truly decline, and the patient could die in a false decline. Now it appears that the distinction of the universal and particular times of the disease is similar, and thus the same. The arguments of Dionysius <note>likely a reference to a specific medical authority or commentator</note> against this are solved when it is said that the times of paroxysms are not distinguished by the alteration of matter; I deny this when it is proven, because although the matter is raw in the beginning of the whole, the paroxysm will still have all the stages. It must be said that the matter of the paroxysm at the beginning is raw compared to the matter of the paroxysm of the increase and peak; yet that raw matter which makes the paroxysm of the beginning behaves one way at the start of the paroxysm, another in the increase, and another in the peak, in which dispositions it resembles the matter of the whole fever, although this disposition is not that one, as he says. To the second argument, when it is said a paroxysm can have its decline while the disease does not decline: the reasoning is faulty because it argues that this decline is not that one, but it does not prove that it does not happen in a similar way—namely, through a similar disposition in the matter. I say similar and not identical, because as we said above, the universal decline is principally from the vital power, but a particular decline can occur by putrid heat evaporating. Both are therefore similar because they involve the evacuation of matter. To the reasons by which it is proven that the distinction of these times does not occur regarding symptoms: it must be said to the first that just as symptoms in universal times follow the action of heat acting upon the matter in the limbs, so they do in the times of a paroxysm. To the other, when it is argued that symptoms are not more intense in the peak of a paroxysm: I say on the contrary, the symptoms of the disease of one fever increase throughout the whole paroxysm. And when it is argued that one can die in the beginning: it must be said that a person can also die in the universal beginning. Let us say, therefore, that just as someone who dies in the universal beginning would have had more difficult symptoms in the peak if they had lived until then, so someone who dies in the beginning of a paroxysm would have had more difficult symptoms in the peak of that paroxysm if they had lived. The symptoms of the beginning of the paroxysm were sufficient for their death, whereas someone stronger would not have died in the beginning. These are the matters in this inquiry, which should be completed by our other questions.

Before all things. Now he has determined certain common things about fevers, distinguishing them into three primary genera. Here he follows up on each of them: first on ephemeral fevers; second on putrid fevers; third on hectic fevers; fourth he completes the discourse on putrid fevers and certain related matters in one treatise. The second part is on putrefaction; the third is at the beginning of the third treatise; the fourth at the beginning of the fourth treatise. First, he sets down certain general things about ephemeral fevers or gives general knowledge; second, special knowledge. First, he sets down certain more common things to be known beforehand; second, things less common; third, he sets down the general cure. This is what the rubric says: "General Discourse." These general things to be known beforehand can be said of ephemeral fever: first, what it is (which already appeared in the first chapter); second, what its general causes are (useful for cure and knowledge); third, the time of its duration and...

It concludes that the stages of a single fever spike mirror the stages of the entire disease, moving from a raw "beginning" to a "peak" and eventual "decline."</summary>

Transition. ¶ It contributes to the cure and understanding. Fourth, how they stand in the ease and difficulty of cure and understanding, and it is useful for both. Four points are made: first, here. <note>original: "sa. r̄"</note> These fevers are mostly according to the majority. Second, there. Third, <margin>a</margin> This indeed is a fever. Fourth, <margin>b</margin> Men indeed more quickly. The first is divided into three. First, he sets forth the modes of those causes. Second, he declares certain things. Third, he posits the errors of some. Second: <margin>c</margin> Not. Third: <margin>d</margin> They are. It is first doubted: because it does not seem that **ephemeral fever** <note>A fever lasting only one day, from the Greek *ephemeros*.</note> has a cause, because ephemeral fever is a "completed disease" <note>original: *morbus factus*; a disease that has already reached its full state.</note> as they say in the first book on fevers: 7. 8. <note>original: "ter."</note> but a completed thing does not depend on a cause.

A certain person responds: that ephemeral fever has a cause in its "becoming" <note>original: *in fieri*; in the process of being created</note>, which is an effect newly produced; but it does not have a cause in its "secondary state of being." For in its completed state, it is simply the state of being heated in the **vital spirits**; this however does not depend on a cause except in its becoming. We, however, say otherwise: that ephemeral fever is a true "becoming" fever, namely in the members, and its bodily cause is an inflamed **spirit**. <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" were subtle substances that carried heat and life throughout the body.</note> It is doubted secondly because he says that the causes of ephemeral fever are **primitive** <note>External or immediate causes like anger, sun exposure, or fatigue.</note>: to the contrary: because if an ephemeral fever comes from an obstruction <margin>a</margin> or a **bubo** <note>A swelling of the lymph nodes.</note> and similar things: they say that true ephemeral fevers are made by primitive causes. The reason is that in such cases there is a simple inflammation in the spirits lasting one day: such pure inflammation is made by inflammatory causes like anger and the like. <margin>e</margin> ¶ Not a true one, however, can be made by bodily causes. They also say that bodily causes like buboes produce ephemeral fever as if they were primitive causes: and this because nothing bodily reaches the heart from the bubo, but only a simple quality. <margin>f</margin> ¶ Let us see to the contrary of the first: that if ephemeral fever is an inflammation in the spirit apt to last one day, <margin>g</margin> let this be the true definition of an ephemeral fever. It is clear that it can be produced by bodily causes: such as from a bubo and **putrid fever**. Whence Averroes in the third *Colliget* <margin>r</margin> if it lasts longer <margin>h</margin> this is by accident, just as because of its own cause, an ephemeral fever made by anger or the heat of the sun could last for many days as long as the heat of the sun or the anger persists.
