---

True ephemeral fever is made by primitive causes: rarely however by bodily ones, because those more frequently produce putrid fevers. Against the second point, however, it appears that this man does not understand what a "bodily cause" is: for there is a "complexional cause" and a "compositional cause": whether they share a bodily thing or an incorporeal thing: for a bad heat of the liver is the cause of a bad **complexion** <note>The balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> of the stomach: and it is a bodily cause even though it does not share matter. We shall say therefore that for a physician, a true ephemeral fever is not so much that which comes from a bubo or obstruction as that which comes from anger: and this is because another intention of cure comes to it, and because it lasts longer in fact. It must be considered that some heating things are *per se* (through themselves), whether they are so formally or virtually: some are *per accidens* (by accident) and mediated, such as an obstruction.

<margin>a</margin> **From appearing swellings.** We shall say that he placed the primitive causes from which ephemeral fever mostly arises here; he also places bodily causes: and he says "appearing" because internal swellings produce a putrid fever. <margin>b</margin> It is doubted why he spoke distinctly of pains: it must be said that it is doubtful whether it is a primitive or bodily cause.

<margin>b</margin> **Obstructions.** i.e., certain obstructions making ephemeral fever are primitive causes: such as those made by a bath or the coldness of the air: certain ones however are bodily: such as humoral obstructions: and from both, ephemeral fever is made.

<margin>c</margin> **And they do not arrive.** Because someone might ask whether the aforementioned causes can produce other fevers besides ephemeral; he says yes, if the vigor of the heating of those causes passes through: and heats the members or humors in their completed state. For if they do not pass through with the intensity of their heating, but only place the spirit in a heated state, it is an ephemeral fever. But Thaddeus asks whether a heating cause here can produce a **hectic fever** <note>original: *ethicam*; a fever involving the drying and wasting of the solid parts of the body.</note> before a putrid or ephemeral one. He responds that it can, due to disposition and aptitude. But that question falls in the chapter on hectic fever.

<margin>d</margin> **And there are.** Perhaps they said this because such movements and labors more frequently induce pure inflammations. But it is an error: because wine, hot medicine, and the sun can induce pure inflammation.

<margin>e</margin> **And these.** To the contrary, because Isaac says in the second book that ephemeral fever can last four days, and Galen in the 8th *Therapeutics*. It must be said that true ephemeral fever does not last beyond a day: because its heat is retained in the spirit from which it is quickly resolved and evaporated: indeed the spirit itself is quickly renewed: almost in any taking of food: as in the second book of *Therapeutics*, first chapter. But a non-true one can last for many days according to the durability of the cause.

<margin>f</margin> **It is thought.** That is, it is estimable but not certain.

<margin>g</margin> **Retention.** That is, the heat in such a completed state, namely that it is retained in the humors or members to which it passed: and therefore he notably says "retention."

<margin>h</margin> **Although.** They want to say that it is not always true that if they pass the third day a transformation has been made: because some have said that ephemeral fever lasts six days and is consumed with the total consumption that pertains to ephemeral fever: but if it had transformed into another genus, it would not have been so consumed.

<margin>i</margin> **To which.** Namely, to the fever terminated on the sixth day.

<margin>k</margin> **It would not be similar etc.** Because it would last longer. But to the contrary, it could have been transformed into a **tertian fever** <note>A fever that peaks every third day (every 48 hours).</note>, which could also be finished in one paroxysm. Further, it can be transformed into a continuous fever terminable on the fifth day: but it was occupied by the ephemeral: therefore one recedes on the sixth day from the beginning of the ephemeral. It must be said that Avicenna speaks of what happens for the most part: and he speaks by the authority of those men. It happens for the most part that hectic or putrid fevers into which ephemeral is transformed are not finished on the sixth day from the beginning: concerning hectic fevers it is certain. But concerning putrid ones it also appears that they are more frequently longer than five days; even those that happen from ephemeral fever happen to bodies that are somewhat indisposed: because if those bodies had been prepared, then the primitive cause would not have first made an ephemeral fever.

<column-break/>

It could be said that by what he says "with total consumption," he understands a uniform termination without critical accidents <note>Sudden, drastic changes in the patient's condition that signal a "crisis" or turning point.</note> and diversities of accidents that would not happen if it were putrid.

<margin>l</margin> **And this.** It is doubted whether ephemeral fever is difficult to recognize. It seems not, according to Galen in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*: where he intends that their recognition is easy: which he confirms by experience, instructing in the first exacerbation that the person return to their usual habits, as one who ought not to fever further. Namely, because it had been an ephemeral fever.

<margin>f In this there is a manifold way of speaking. Some have said that ephemeral fever alone is easy to recognize: but when complicated with others it is difficult. Others say that recognition with respect to the cure is difficult: for the cure is so easy that to recognize it is difficult in respect to the ease of the cure. Another way of speaking is that of Dionysius and mine: that ephemeral fever is difficult to recognize because its accidents are not very manifest: and especially in the beginning. And this appears because neither the urine nor the pulse is changed much from that which is according to nature, nor even the quality of the body: for in ephemeral fever there is no sharp heat. And perhaps sometimes it does not hinder human activities. To the contrary it must be said in two ways. First, that Avicenna speaks here of the beginning, Galen of the process of the paroxysm; and this is the solution of Thaddeus. Alternatively, that recognition of ephemeral fever in the beginning is not easy, but while it exists and is finished it can easily be understood that it was an ephemeral paroxysm and that the man ought not to fever further.</margin>

transformed into another. ¶ And this fever indeed is easy to cure and difficult to recognize, and similarly the beginning of **hectic fever**. <margin>m</margin> And men indeed who more quickly fall into ephemeral fevers: and who are more vehemently harmed by them if an error is made in them, are those in whom heat and dryness are more dominant, since they arrive quickly at hectic and tertian fever. Next, those in whom heat and moisture dominate, since they arrive quickly at putrid fever. Next, those in whom there is more heat. ¶ Next, those in whom there is more dryness. ¶ And when those who have a dry and hot complexion experience hunger: and with it come wakefulness and labor of the soul and labor of the body, ephemeral fever hastens to them with a certain shivering. Which if it is not succored, and he is not fed immediately, putrid fever will hasten to him.

Concerning their properties, it is that they are not made from **antecedent causes** <note>Internal factors like an accumulation of bad humors.</note>; nor do they begin with

hectic fever is easy to cure: and if it seems that it is not difficult to recognize: because it is a fixed disposition: like a habit and a great transformation. It must be said that the beginning of hectic fever is difficult to recognize: because its accidents are not vehement in its beginning: and specifically the drying of the body. Others said that hectic is easy to recognize with respect to other species of hectic. ¶ Thaddeus says that it is easy to cure because in the beginning the consumption of moisture has not been made. But it is like a certain boiling in the humors: as appears in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*. Indeed Galen posits that it is of easier cure than putrid. Certain **moderns** however, poor in experience in science, wonder greatly at this: because they say that hectic is fixed in the hard members, and therefore is of more difficult cure than putrid. But this discourse is crude. For in hectic fever there is a simple intention: and in the first species, since consumption has not yet been made in the humors, a small labor in cooling leads to the removal of heat and a perfect cure: nor is this difficult although the radical members are heated: for to be heated does not mean great danger. But it means heat at the limit which, as we have shown elsewhere, can be less than a certain heat in motion: in putrid fever, however, since the intention is composite, alteration does not suffice: but it is necessary to evacuate: which is not easily done.

<margin>m</margin> **And men.** These are the discourses of Galen in the 8th of the *Therapeutics*, penultimate chapter. And consider that here the order of bodies is not only of those prepared for ephemeral fever, but of those who are not called so and are feared for transformation into another fever. First therefore in this order is a hot and dry body. Second is a hot and moist body. Third is a hot body only. Fourth is a dry body only. There is another order of these bodies as they are harmed by fasting. And the first is hot and dry. Second dry. Third hot. Fourth hot and moist: as some have said. And you consider.

<margin>n</margin> **And when those.** It is doubted how ephemeral fever arrives with shivering since it does not begin with a **periodicity** <note>original: *typo*; the recurring pattern/chill of a malaria-like fever.</note>, as in the following chapter. It must be said that ephemeral fever by its own nature does not have shivering, because it is a fever not depending on humors, but accidentally from the nature of the bodies in which there are sharp humors: as in choleric people who have labored and fasted, certain sharp vapors rise which cause shivering. Whence, at its onset, Galen fed the man in the 10th of the *Therapeutics*, third chapter.

<margin>o</margin> **From the properties.** Now he has given more general knowledge; here he gives less general knowledge with respect to that. And first, the signs by which we distinguish ephemeral fever from others. Second, he determines its transformation. Third, he places the signs of transformation. Second, there: "when it is expedient." Third, there: "the signification." The first is divided into as many as the orders of signs he posits: and they seem ten in total: although they can be reduced to a larger number by taking any sign. Second: "neither do they begin." Third: "it is an inflammation." And the rest will be clear. It must be considered that an antecedent cause is taken here for a bodily cause: even if it is conjoined. For ephemeral fevers are not properly made from bodily causes, namely true ephemeral ones, as was said. But you say: Averroes in the fourth *Colliget* posits that every ephemeral fever is made by a primitive cause, but it is not converted. It must be said that he speaks of true ephemeral fever.

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Avicenna’s medical theories, specifically focusing on the diagnostic signs (the "collection of signs") of ephemeral fevers—those short-lived fevers lasting only a day—and how they are distinguished from more dangerous "putrid" or material fevers through the examination of heat, pulse, and urine.</meta>

# Sina, Treatise I

<margin>a
He discusses the likeness of cold and the lack of heat, such as is found in a tertian fever <note>A fever that returns every third day, like certain forms of malaria.</note> with respect to a phlegmatic state. Perhaps a strong cold does not result from the heat being driven inward. For such a state occurs because of a "stinging" sensation from which the heat flees. But though a stinging sensation occurring in the spirit is real, it is not long-lasting as it is in a tertian fever or in the shivering of burning fevers; therefore, it does not become a truly strong cold. It is therefore a *likeness* of cold, although there may be a true stinging. And for this reason, the author did not say "a likeness of stinging," but "a true stinging" caused by a hot, sharp vapor; however, it does not last.</margin>
<margin>a</margin> **A**lthough. This is the second collection of signs taken from the movement or the onset of the disease. He means that while putrid fevers <note>Fevers caused by the "rotting" or corruption of the bodily humors.</note> begin with a constriction of heat (whereby shivering, cold, a submerged pulse, etc., occur), this does not happen in an ephemeral fever, since it does not depend on matter <note>i.e., it is caused by the spirits/vapors, not a physical buildup of humors.</note>.

<margin>b</margin> **W**hence perhaps. He declares that what he said is true for the most part, because sometimes a likeness of cold happens because of a malignant vapor. It is doubted why he said "a likeness of cold." Indeed, it seems like true cold caused by the lack of heat in the extremities due to its retraction inward, as in a tertian fever. It should be said that perhaps he calls it a "constriction" [of heat]; although they do not mostly begin with shivering and coldness of the extremities, or a deep-seated heat, or a decline toward sluggishness, sleep, a submerged pulse, or its thinness, diversity, or smallness. Rather, perhaps there occurs in their beginning a likeness of cold, a shivering, and a stinging. The cause of this is the vapor of a bad chyme <note>term: chyme <gloss>the partially digested mass of food and juices in the stomach</gloss></note>, and it is removed quickly. Rarely, a shivering happens because of a multitude of vapors hurting the muscles because of their excessive stinging. <margin>c</margin> **A**nd its inflammation is not a "biting" <note>original: *mordicativa*; a sharp, stinging, or caustic sensation of heat</note> or harsh one; rather, it is good, like the heat of a body that has been exercising or of a drunk person. <margin>i</margin> And when the urine is digested on the first day and the pulse is good, then judge that it is an ephemeral fever. This is because the urine is not altered in it insofar as it is ephemeral, and its sediment is digested and does not decline toward the color of a humor. Sometimes its "cloud" <note>term: nubes <gloss>floating particles or cloudiness in a urine sample</gloss></note> is hanging, and sometimes it is floating with a good color. And sometimes it happens that its color is not balanced; nevertheless, its substance is balanced, and its color is not altered except because of what is associated with it as a cause of urine alteration—

---

<margin>f</margin> **A**nd its inflammation. This is the third collection of signs from the touch of the heat. He says first that the heat is not biting or harsh, contrary to the idea that its heat is rooted in a subtle substance. It should be said that it does not bite like a putrid fever; but the substance becomes subtle, and because of this, it makes an impression quickly, though not a deep one.
<margin>g</margin> "Other." That is, not harsh because it is not dry.
<margin>h</margin> "Good." That is, mild to the touch.
<margin>i</margin> **A**nd of a drunk person. Not "good" compared to a healthy person, but compared to other fevers. This appears because he said "of a drunk person." For the heat of drunkards is bad and sometimes fatal, as appears in the commentary on the Aphorisms: "if anyone who is drunk dies." Nevertheless, it is a heat that is mild to the touch, namely a vaporous heat from wine-like vapors.
<margin>k</margin> "Of one laboring." That is, one who has exercised.
<margin>l</margin> **A**nd when there is urine. This is the fourth collection of signs. It should be considered that by this sign, it is best distinguished from a putrid fever, as appears from the same opinion of Galen in the first book *On the Differences of Fevers*. He was extensive in the beginning on this point, that digestion appears in the urine. And perhaps he added "a good pulse" to distinguish it from an incipient "efficacious" <note>possibly meaning a more serious hectic or inflammatory fever</note> fever, in which the pulse is not so good. <margin>p</margin> It is doubted whether we signify an ephemeral fever by "digested urine" since there is no material fever, and digestion belongs to matter. <margin>q</margin> It must be said that we do not signify it directly by the sign of digestion, but as if indirectly. For we signify that a bad alteration is not in the matter, nor is the body transmuted in its humors toward any corruption that we could signify through its sediment <note>term: hypostasis <gloss>the solid sediment at the bottom of a urine vial</gloss></note>. Avicenna hints at these two reasons: first, that alteration or corruption only happens in the humors when he says "it is not altered except insofar as it is ephemeral," meaning the alteration is in the spirit, not in the humors. The second is that the humors do not infect the urine, which he notes when he says "it does not decline to the color of a humor," meaning the humors are not corrupted or putrid. Whence a sediment similar to them might arise, just as in a choleric fever a yellow sediment can occur, and in a phlegmatic fever a white, viscous one. Therefore, whatever the sediment was before it was an ephemeral fever, it remains almost the same now. <margin>r</margin> From which it appears that if in health one does not have crude urine without sediment, one should expect such a thing at the beginning of an ephemeral fever. Understanding this, Avicenna says "sometimes it is according to [this]," meaning not always, but if the man has it in health. And it appears that a change in the color of the urine from ephemeral fever toward a bad tint is more likely than a change in its substance; for a mere "flame" <note>metaphor for acute heat</note> can be the cause of the tint, even if it is not the cause of a bad sediment. And so he adds: "and sometimes it happens that the color is not balanced." Such a color alteration is not specific to ephemeral fever; rather, it could happen from colors associated with other fevers, like tertians and the like. And perhaps he understands the alteration in color from the flames of the internal organs—for example, from the heating of the liver. For it happens in an ephemeral fever that the urine appears fiery, not because of a cause from the ephemeral fever itself, but because of the "flames" of the liver, which could exist even if there were no ephemeral fever, and could exist in tertians and the like. Or sometimes there is a heat that is not "good," which is apt to be inflamed in the liver more than it is in a frenzy <note>phrenitis</note>. It is doubted whether we distinguish it from a putrid fever by the sign of digestion appearing on the first day. It seems not, because on the first day in some putrid fevers, a sign of digestion can appear, as Galen says in the third chapter. Furthermore—

<column-break/>

<margin>l
It does not seem that the sign of digestion appears on the first day in an ephemeral fever, because it can happen from a nauseating fullness, and then the urine will be crude. <margin>l</margin> Furthermore, digestion is mostly done by the spirit, but that spirit has become "foreign" <note>alienated or dysfunctional due to the fever</note>; therefore, its digestion fails. For the feverish person is sick, and the sick person's digestion is slowed, as Avicenna says below.
<margin>d</margin> It should be said that in ephemeral fevers, insofar as they are ephemeral, digestion immediately appears in the urine—that is, good urine—not only on the first day, but at the beginning of the day, namely when they invade. The reason is that a true ephemeral fever does not include the corruption of humors, as a putrid fever does; and in an ephemeral fever, there is a heated spirit, not one made very malignant by the heating, but rather its own [heat] and mild. <margin>m</margin> Avicenna puts these reasons in the text. However, insofar as it is ephemeral—and so it may appear in true ephemeral fevers—the urine may be "biting" by accident. Nevertheless, because of causes that do this, even if it were not an ephemeral fever, the urine can appear crude, undigested, or bad in color and substance—for instance, if the ephemeral fever is joined with a defect of the liver or stomach, or some bad humors moving from the liver toward the veins. These causes are not from the ephemeral fever *as* ephemeral; for if it were not ephemeral but a tertian or another disposition, it would make that bad urine. And in this way, what he says can be explained: "and its color is not altered," meaning the urine and its sediment, and thus the substance is not altered except by that. <margin>n</margin> From the things said above, collect that there can be many causes by which it happens that at the beginning of an ephemeral fever, digestion does not appear in the urine, whether it be a true ephemeral fever or not. <margin>o</margin> To the contrary, it should be said that on the first day in a putrid fever, a sign of digestion can indeed appear, but not usually at the very beginning of the day, as in the beginning of an ephemeral one.
<margin>p</margin> To the second point, the solution is apparent, because that which is due to nauseating satiety would happen even if there were no ephemeral fever.
<margin>q</margin> To the third, it should be said that although the spirit is distempered, it does not follow from this that the humors have corruption and putrefaction, which would cause the sediment not to appear or to appear bad, as in putrid fevers. But you might say: one having an ephemeral fever will not well digest food in his stomach nor chyle in his liver. It should be said that because of this, "civility" <note>likely meaning "normalcy" or "clarity"</note> does not appear in the urine because that defect is small, as Isaac says in the second book on fevers; or because of this, there will not be corruption in the humors of the liver, as there is in a putrid fever.</margin>
—as we shall say regarding the tertian fever and those similar to it. <margin>d</margin> **A**nd the pulse is inclined toward thickness, strength, and magnitude, unless it is from debilitating passions, or unless there was a biting or cold humor in the stomach, or some other cause among those that change the pulse besides the fever. And indeed, it is rarely diversified; but if it is diversified, it will have an order. <margin>e</margin> **F**or if it is diversified, that will be because of another cause preceding the fever or neighboring it, such as vehement labor, or vehement stinging in the viscera, and similar <margin>f</margin> things. And sometimes it happens that the pulse is hardened because of vehement cold, which thickens and chills; or because of the vehement heat of the sun, which dries; or because of vehement labor, which dries; or hunger, or distress, or wakefulness, or evacuations. And sometimes the expansion is hurried, and the constriction is delayed, and it does not hurry more than the natural rate except rarely and with little velocity, because the necessity of ventilation in it is more vehement than the necessity of leading out the corrupted vapor. For the vapor in it is not corrupted in comparison to its normal state. Rather—

---

<margin>m</margin> **A**nd the pulse. This is the fifth collection of signs. From the pulse, he provides the sign according to the types. First, it is the spirit because of an added necessity, and it follows from this that it is fast, as appears from Avicenna's *Canon*, Book I, Section 2, Chapter on the pulse of different ages. Third, it is strong. Against this: because the virtue <note>term: virtue <gloss>the body's vital strength or power to function</gloss></note> is weak since the person is sick. It should be said that it appears strong because a fast and large pulse *seems* strong, even if it is not, as in the *Introduction to Pulses*. Or it should be said that it is strong in comparison to the pulses of other fevers in which the virtue fails more. For this pulse fails little compared to the pulse of a healthy person; whence Isaac in his second book on fevers, the chapter on the signs of ephemeral fever, says the pulse of those suffering from ephemeral fever does not differ from the pulse of the healthy except in the velocity of the diastole <note>The expansion of the heart/arteries.</note> and the slowness of the constriction—namely, with respect to the velocity of the systole <note>The contraction of the heart/arteries.</note>. Then Avicenna posits cases in which, in an ephemeral fever but not *because* of the fever, the pulse can become small, weak, and rare; such as a debilitating passion like restriction or evacuation, etc. Therefore, the pulse is equal and not diverse; that is, if it is diverse, it is ordered because there is no heavy matter there, but it is vaporous.
<margin>n</margin> "For." Used here for "but."
<margin>o</margin> **I**f it be diversified. Namely, from equality and from order. Because if it becomes diverse and unordered, it will be because of a cause that happened before the fever, like one who suffered from labor, or one that happens with the fever; and this is what he means by "neighboring," such as stinging, etc. Or even mental labor can happen with the fever, though not bodily labor in the same way, since those with fever should rest in bed, as in the commentary on the Aphorisms: "for those with fever, [labor] is not entirely on the surface." How labor and stinging diversify and disorder the pulse may be known from the science of the causes of the pulse.
<margin>p</margin> And similar things. Such as excessive evacuation or the intake of bad foods, and in short, every cause by which the pulse can become unequal or unordered. It is doubted that he says "because of a preceding cause," since he had said that ephemeral fevers do not arise from preceding causes. It should be said that "preceding cause" is taken in two ways. Sometimes for a bodily cause distinct from a "primitive" <note>An external, immediate cause.</note> cause; and it was taken this way above when he said ephemeral fevers do not arise from preceding causes. Sometimes it is taken for a cause coming before the fever or another disposition; and it is distinguished from a "neighboring" cause which comes at the same time as the fever. And in this way it is taken here; for bodily or mental labor is a primitive cause and not a preceding one in the first sense. And whether it is neighboring or preceding in the second sense (i.e., coming before the fever), it can change the pulse. In the fifth way, the pulse is of due softness, not hard; it happens, however, that it is hardened because of the causes he posits.
<margin>q</margin> **A**nd sometimes it hurries. Here he posits a sign by comparing the systole to the diastole, and he means that the diastole hurries—that is, it is fast. And it is weary [or delayed] with respect to the diastole; rather, the systole does not hurry—that is, it is not faster than the natural systole—except rarely and by a little. And that is when there are many vapors; and then he assigns a common known cause, as noted by Haly [Abbas] in the second treatise of the *Techni*, 68th commentary, and by many others. It is doubted that he says "sometimes it hurries," when indeed this is always the case, as Galen hints in the first book *On the Differences of Fevers* and Isaac in the second book on fevers. It should be said first that it is an improper way of speaking; second, that this applies to true ephemeral fevers insofar as they are ephemeral. But true ones are rarely found; rather, for the most part, other causes are joined with them which change the systole by many changes. <margin>r</margin> Third, it can be answered, as we have said elsewhere, that the diastole is greater than the systole, and this is always the case; but the velocity in both of them above the natural rate, or the thickness, is not always manifest, because the added necessity must be fulfilled with magnitude since it is not—

<sig>b</sig>

It emphasizes that because ephemeral fevers affect the spirits rather than the physical humors, signs like digestion and pulse regularity often remain closer to a healthy state.</summary>

# Book

...of great necessity: for its heat is like that of one suffering from a fever. If, however, much heat is added to what is always present, then a clear distinction appears in the speed of the expansion <note>original: "diastole"</note> to the contraction <note>original: "systole"</note>. Although three solutions were our first, the two are more suitable, and the third can be defended, even if it is not in harmony with the words of Galen in the second book *On Crises*, where he says that in an ephemeral fever the pulse increases in speed and often in magnitude.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ **And when it is ambiguous.** This is the sixth collection of signs from the pulse and breathing. Since the pulse can be ambiguous in its contraction <note>original: "systole"</note>, which is not fully understood according to Rhazes <note>An influential Persian physician (865–925 AD), also known as Al-Razi.</note> in the 16th book of the *Continens* at the end of the 11th chapter, and in the first chapter and tenth book of the *Almansor*. We agree with him on this and against Galen, as we proved above in the first book. Therefore, consider the breathing, the contraction of which will be apparent to your sight.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ **The pulse returns.** Because that heat causes a light resolution. And in this sign, for distinguishing an ephemeral fever from a putrid one, Galen speaks very certainly in the third chapter of *To Glaucon*: he says no other fever returns to its natural state in this way, not even if a long time passes between the end of the first and the beginning of the second paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or peak intensity of a disease.</note>, as in tertian and quartan fevers. In those, a sign of the fever always remains, whereas in an ephemeral fever, everything is erased once the paroxysm ceases: and this is what Avicenna understands.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ **It is a good sign.** Specifically, in signifying that it is an ephemeral fever, although it may also be good for other reasons.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ **And you should know.** This is the seventh collection of signs from the good pulse and urine, which change more in those [putrid] fevers than in ephemeral ones. Therefore, a good pulse and good urine signify an ephemeral fever. However, a bad pulse and bad urine do not necessarily mean it is *not* an ephemeral fever, because a bad pulse and urine could exist through the effect of the ephemeral fever, where the badness would not be because of the fever itself but because of another cause, as appeared above. And this is what he says: "When the pulse and urine are not good, it does not mean it cannot be an ephemeral fever." He then proves that a good pulse and urine signify an ephemeral fever, because in ephemeral fevers good urine is often found; therefore, the sign of an ephemeral fever will be good pulse and urine. By this, he hints at the proof of his other statement: namely, that "it is bad urine, therefore not ephemeral" does not follow, because it can be an ephemeral fever with bad urine, even if it is often not bad. Thus he saves the text which says "for it often happens," meaning it happens sometimes that it is this fever. Here our objection ends; a sign is for its existence, and the contrary sign is for its non-existence, as Boethius says in the second chapter of *The Consolation of Philosophy*. If, therefore, good urine signifies an ephemeral fever, then when it is not good, it signifies it is not an ephemeral fever. It must be said that this opposition holds true in balanced causes and effects.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ **And of those.** This is the eighth collection of signs.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ **An easy beginning.** Through the absence of the symptoms mentioned at the start of the paroxysm of putrid fevers.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ **Light.** In heat, or easily bearable by the sick person. Against Galen in the 17th book of the *Continens*, first chapter: an ephemeral fever at the beginning is not slow. It must be said he means "not light," i.e., it should not overwhelm with heat through the form of cold or shivering.

<margin>h</margin> ¶ **An increase not exceeding two hours.** This is found through experience and cannot be proven except that it quickly comes to its peak state in a short time. Whether by "increase" we mean the final heat impressed upon the spirit by an external cause—and I do not believe Avicenna meant this—or we mean the peak of heat when the heated spirits are sent into the limbs—and I believe this is what is meant. For inflamed spirits move quickly through the limbs and inflame them, reaching the peak of heat they can, though not reaching the state of a "hectic" fever <note>A chronic, wasting fever associated with internal organs, much more serious than an ephemeral one.</note>.

---

### ...is good in comparison of itself to it.
### And when it is ambiguous <gloss>a</gloss> to you, the pulse and its constriction: then know it from the breathing: and because the pulse indeed returns <gloss>b</gloss> after its eradication to its natural habit in that body: and this is a good sign. <gloss>c</gloss> And know <gloss>d</gloss> thoroughly that as often as the urine and pulse are good, they signify that the fever is ephemeral: and when they are not good, it does not necessarily mean it is not ephemeral.
### ¶ For many times in it the urine is tinted, the pulse is diverse, weak, and small. ¶ And of those <gloss>e</gloss> things which signify that it is an ephemeral fever: let its beginning be easy <gloss>f</gloss> and light <gloss>g</gloss> and let its increase <gloss>h</gloss> not exceed two hours: and let vehement symptoms <gloss>i</gloss> not accompany its peak: and let no wicked symptoms happen in it: <gloss>k</gloss> and let there be no vehement boiling of heat in it: and let the pains be lessened with it: for if there was a headache or other pain with it, let it not be fixed and inseparable...

---

<margin>i</margin> ¶ **Vehement symptoms.** That is, in intensity or number.

<margin>k</margin> ¶ **Wicked.** In their malice.

<margin>l</margin> ¶ **Pain should not be fixed after its eradication.** Because whether the pain is from a bad temperament <note>original: "complexione"</note> or from vapors, it recedes immediately and perfectly, which does not happen in the eradication of a paroxysm of putrid fevers. It is doubted whether an ephemeral fever has "four times" <note>The standard medical stages of a disease: onset, increase, peak, and decline.</note>. It seems not, because it is a "made disease" <note>original: "morbus factus"</note>. On the contrary, here is Avicenna, who assigns it a light beginning, this increase, a peak that is not "wicked," and a perfect decline. 

It must be said, first, that this discussion concerns true ephemeral fevers, about which there is more doubt. From this, it will appear what should be said about non-true ones, such as those caused by a bubo <note>A swollen lymph node, often associated with plague.</note> and similar things. Second, this fever does not have "times" depending on matter which is altered and expelled during the whole duration of the disease, as in putrid fevers, because an ephemeral fever does not depend on a humor. Third, a true ephemeral fever does not strictly have periodic paroxysms. The reason is that periodization or paroxysm comes from the movement of matter, as it gathers and is expelled from part to part; but a true ephemeral fever has only one paroxysm (or whatever you wish to call it) in which we assign its stages. 

An ephemeral fever having one paroxysm differs from a tertian fever having one; a tertian fever by its nature can have many periodic paroxysms, but happens to have one. An ephemeral fever by its nature has one paroxysm and not many periodic ones, but happens to have several. The reason for the first is that choleric matter, once moved, can by its nature dispose the limbs to gather new matter. The reason for the second is that an ephemeral fever has its product from an external cause, for example, the heat of the sun; it happens by chance that a man returns to the sun, and another ephemeral fever occurs. Fourth, in this one paroxysm of ephemeral fever, we can imagine "time" and succession in two ways: one way regarding the disposition, namely the heat proceeding in the spirit from an external heating cause; and regarding this, it has no "times," because such heat is made in the spirit and then retained. 

But you say: just as when a fluid is heated it is said that rotting and corruption are "in the making" in the humors, so when the spirit is only heated, could there be a "making" of corruption of the spirit? Furthermore, before being heated and while being heated... It must be said that although these things are part of the nature of the thing, they are not well-distinguished by the physician...

<column-break/>

...nor manifest to him. ¶ In another way, we can imagine time and "becoming" in the paroxysm of an ephemeral fever regarding that heat which depends on the limbs from the heated spirit. Thus we can place "times" in ephemeral fever, for while the spirit is in a heated state, the limbs are disposed in various ways. At that moment when the spirits are now in a heated state, the limbs begin to be heated, and this is the **beginning** of the ephemeral fever. Because this is not from matter, these are not the symptoms of the beginning of the paroxysms of putrid fevers, except in an accidental way. In the second part of time, the heat in the limbs increases, and this is the **time of increase**, which ends quickly. In the third part, the final stage lasts—the peak of the degree of heat reached in the limbs—and this is reached not through being heated but by the process of heating no longer intensifying. This is the **state** <note>The peak or "acme".</note>. In the fourth part, the heat recedes from the cooled limbs, and the spirits and vapors evaporate. Because they are subtle bodies, no trace of them remains after the paroxysm, unlike putrid humors. Thus Avicenna distinguishes the times. 

¶ To the argument that "ephemeral fever is a made disease," this is true regarding the spirit, and regarding that, it has no measuring times; but regarding the "becoming" that depends on the limbs from the state of the spirits, it does. 

It is doubted, second, whether an ephemeral fever can have a malice by which it kills. The answer is no, because it is only a disease of which there is doubt; otherwise, it would be an "acute" fever, as Avicenna said above. ¶ Furthermore, it is commonly believed that intermittent fevers are not fatal. Therefore, much less so is an ephemeral fever. On the contrary, an ephemeral fever is a suffering in the spirit, which is the noble part of the body. Therefore, it does not seem impossible that it could kill. 

The common response is that an ephemeral fever cannot be fatal because a fever is not fatal except by great malice of quality or a great quantity of matter, which are not in an ephemeral fever. Note, however, that putrid fevers seem most likely to bring death for three reasons, and this is in their nature: one is excellent hot quality; second is poisonousness in the putrid matter, as in a pestilential fever or an eruginous choleric fever <note>A fever caused by "verdigris-like" bile, considered highly toxic.</note>; third is the resistance of the matter to evacuation. Finally, this cause is reduced to the quality or malice of the retained matter. I say, therefore, that an ephemeral fever of itself for the most part does not kill by either of these causes. For the spirit does not pass to such acute heat, nor is it transformed into a poisonous disposition through repeated transformations and combustions, as happens with eruginous cholera or malignant black bile, nor does it resist expulsion. Nevertheless, very frequently it will occur: it is not incredible that a certain distant possibility exists, namely that an ephemeral fever might sometimes be fatal. For sometimes a disease is fatal not in itself, but compared to the individual, as Galen feels in the book *On the Four Times of Disease*. An excess of quality in a certain ephemeral fever could be sufficient to be fatal to a man. For just as there are different individual healths, so there are different individual proportions of life. Furthermore, if a person is at the peak of heat, if an addition is made that breaks the ultimate proportion of balance, death will follow. It was declared in one of our questions that every degree of heat beyond nature, from the beginning where a man is feverish until the end where death immediately follows, can be placed in reality. ¶ Furthermore, it is not incredible that a heated spirit could be joined by a poisonous property by which it kills. But you say: this is outside the nature of an ephemeral fever. It must be said that this is true for a *true* ephemeral fever, or logically it is true for an absolute ephemeral fever, but not for one of this specific kind. ¶ Just as it is outside the nature of a putrid fever, as putrid, to be made from a poisonous humor, but not outside the nature of *this* specific case, although a poisonous disposition is closer to the disposition of putrefaction than to the heat of an ephemeral fever.

---

### ...after its eradication <gloss>l</gloss> and this indeed signifies that it is an ephemeral fever. ¶ And the most part <gloss>m</gloss> of its eradication happens through sweat: and a moisture similar to natural sweat, not "humoral" <note>meaning sweat caused by an excess of heavy, bad humors.</note>: and if there is a vehement superfluity, it is again in its quantity. Rather, it approaches natural sweat in its quantity, just as it is close to it in its quality. For if you see a very great amount of sweat, then the fever will not be ephemeral.
### And of those <gloss>n</gloss> things by which an ephemeral fever is tested: let the person having it enter a bath. And when they have stayed long enough to experience a kind of unusual shivering <note>original: "horripilationem"</note>, it is known that the fever is a putrid fever; and let the person leave the bath immediately. And if nothing is altered from their disposition, then the fever is ephemeral.
### ->Permutation of Ephemeral Fever. Chapter 7.<-
### ¶ When it is appropriate <gloss>o</gloss> for a patient with ephemeral fever to be fed, and the physician errs regarding it, and not...

---

<margin>m</margin> ¶ **And the most part.** This is the ninth collection of signs. It is doubted that an ephemeral fever ends through sweat since the spirit is not "sweat-producing" matter. Isaac answers in the second book on fevers that this is because of the humidities in the limbs which the heat of the ephemeral fever melts, just as a bath does, which sometimes removes thirst by melting humidities. ¶ Alternatively, it can be said: that vapors spread through the limbs, being heated and pushed to the skin, are thickened there, and sweat occurs; therefore it is not "humoral" nor excessive as in humoral diseases, but small, gentle, similar to humoral sweat but not humoral, and similar to natural sweat. But on the contrary, all sweat is "beyond nature," as in the third book of *Accidents*. It must be said it is called "natural" for this healthy man in this state—for example, from suitable exercise—even though it is not simply natural compared to a perfectly healthy person who ought to expel their superfluities imperceptibly.

<margin>n</margin> ¶ **And of those.** This is the tenth sign. It is doubted because in the last chapter of the 11th book, he teaches to bathe in a putrid fever, and wants it so that if there is no shivering, nor the limb is weak, nor a multitude of raw humors, he will be helped by the bath. ¶ It must be said that in a putrid fever, a bath is not allowed at the beginning; but here, at the beginning of a fever where there is a suspicion whether it is putrid or ephemeral, it is allowed as a test. ¶ For if it is putrid, with many raw humors evaporating and melting, shivering or a "type" <note>A periodic recurrence or pattern of shivering.</note> will occur, but not in an ephemeral fever. ¶ And it appears that this sign does not distinguish it from a "hectic" fever. But he says "unusual": for some, it is a habit immediately when they enter the bath—that is, the tub or vat—that they shiver, either because of the sudden change with much skin sensitivity, or because it immediately moves some sharp superfluities.

<margin>o</margin> ¶ **When it is appropriate.** Here he places the causes of the transition of ephemeral fever into others; first one, and second another where he says "and similarly." It is doubted whether in hot and dry people it changes into a putrid fever. It seems so according to Galen in the 10th book of the *Therapeutics*, third chapter. It must be said that from incongruous abstinence, an ephemeral fever can not only...

# Part 1 Treatise 1

...becoming a hectic fever <note>original: "ethica"; a wasting fever often associated with consumption or tuberculosis</note>: but a putrid one: yet hot and thus they are more prone to a hectic fever: where there is hot moisture. They also abstain from food. Therefore, speaking in comparison of these, he said here that the hot or the inflamed moistness through abstinence or hunger readily incurs a continuous fever <note>original: "synocha"; a fever caused by an overabundance of blood</note>: and therefore the discourse that follows when it says: "or perhaps first to that," namely a fever with putrefaction, can refer to both bodies: but the hot and dry to that which comes from the putrefaction of yellow bile <note>original: "cholere"</note>: and the hot and moist to that from the putrefaction of blood. Some, however, interpret the text as referring to a hectic and intense fever, that is, a bilious <note>original: "cholericam"</note> one.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ **And similarly.** It must be considered that when the pores are not open, ventilation is prohibited, and this is the cause of putrefaction as stated in the previous treatise. Therefore, when ventilation is prohibited, first an absolute heating inflammation occurs; then, as the external heat is fortified, putrefaction happens: and this is what he means by "inflaming with inflammation," for it heats. That is, it inflames first: as if only heating. And it is inflamed afterward with the strength of that which putrefies. That is, it putrefies by inflammation: and therefore it can be explained as "inflaming with the strength of the heat" because of which it putrefies: and he hints that first a continuous fever could occur without putrefaction, then with putrefaction, and he explains two contagious types, namely other fevers which arise from error; for although there are others, these happen more frequently.

<margin>b</margin> **Signification.** He places the signs here, first in general, and second in special. There is a doubt how a decline without sweating signifies a transition, since this truly belongs to an ephemeral fever, because by its nature it does not have sweating at its end, except by accident as stated above regarding prepared matter. It must be said that these signs should be gathered together: for whether it is without sweat or with copious sweat but without a cleansing <note>original: "mundificatione"</note>, and the decline is long, it signifies non-genuine ephemeral fevers, and that type is prone to change into other fevers. Or it should be said that some of these signs signify that it is changing, just as those already changed recede without sweat and without any moisture—that is, now with a roughness of the skin—signifying it is passing or has passed into a hectic fever. But you may ask: by what shall we judge the departure of the prior fever? It must be said: by another quality of the heat: and it could recede without sweat through a hidden onset of its own putrid nature with a pattern <note>original: "typo"</note> that prevents sweating. But if sweat arrives and the fever is not dismissed, or if the decline is long and the symptoms <note>original: "accidentia"</note> do not recede, all of this can indicate a transition into another fever—either a humoral hectic or a putrid one—which you will distinguish by the signs to be discussed. And therefore he adds:

### Signs of the change of an ephemeral fever to other fevers. Lesson 8.

The significance of this is that the fever itself declines without sweat or moisture, or with sweat but without a cleansing through that sweat: and it is a long, difficult decline without a cleansing of the pulse. Rather, something remains in the pulse and a headache remains if there was one: and all of this signifies a change to a fever of putrefied humors or a hectic fever.

¶ For if the causes were vehement or of long duration, it will change into a hectic fever. If it changes to a hectic fever, you will see the touch of the arteries to be very hot: and you will see a fever similar or even in all members, where heat is added upon the fullness: and at the time of taking food: or you will see the pulse keep its equality along with hardness and smallness. And you will see the remaining signs I spoke of regarding the signs of a hectic fever. And when it changes to the genus of fevers called continuous <note>original: "synocha"</note> without putrefaction, you will see an increase and fullness of heat, and an inflammation of the face. And when it changes to putrid fevers, shivering <note>original: "horripilatio"</note> and diversity of pulse and smallness and constriction appear: and there is a stinging, dry heat and a vehemence of symptoms. In the urine, however, perhaps a "digestion" <note>term: digestion (digestio). In medieval medicine, this refers to signs in the urine (like sediment) showing the body is successfully processing the disease.</note> remains from the substance, and in many others no digestion appears in it.

### Treatments of ephemeral fever according to the universal method. Chapter 9.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ **For.** First he places the signs of when it changes to a hectic fever; second, when to a humoral one. It is doubted whether strong and long-lasting causes can also cause a putrid fever. It must be said that it is true, for primary causes can move antecedent ones as said above. He adds that "if to a hectic," etc., as if to say it is possible that from those causes it does not change to a hectic. Or it should be said that these causes are primitive: which for the most part cause ephemeral or hectic fevers, which are simpler flames: then he places the signs of hectic fever which should be declared in the chapter on hectic fever.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ **And when.** Here he places in a brief summary the signs of continuous fever and putrid fever; therefore, look for their own chapters on these. But it is doubted regarding his statement that "in the urine perhaps digestion remains." To the contrary, because this is the beginning of a putrid fever, but in the beginning of a putrid fever the urine is not "digested." It must be said first that "it remains," that is, it is not digested: and "in many," etc. If you ask why he said "in many," since digestion always ceases when putrefaction arrives? It must be said that sometimes the beginning of that putrid fever is so brief that it is hidden: and this is rare: in many, therefore, it is not hidden. Or it should be said that some putrid fever to which they come from an ephemeral one is not very malignant—for example, a certain continuous fever—and then the urine does not appear bad in substance, but good and as if digested: but in color and sediment <note>original: "hypostasi"</note> it is not good, nor digested. And therefore he said "in many others," that is, apart from the substance, such as in color and sediment, it does not appear digested. That is, it does not appear good in that way; rather, in the sediment it will not be digested: because either there will be no sediment, or it will not be digested, or in many putrid fevers in which a change occurs from an ephemeral one. And this is because the humors were previously prepared for putrefaction. And therefore when an ephemeral fever passes into a putrid one, they putrefy vehemently for the most part. And so the urine is not digested; but if the humors were not so disposed, some digestion will remain in the urine.

<column-break/>

<margin>e</margin> ¶ **In all.** Here he places the general rules of cure: first by things consumed, second by external applications, third by evacuation. Take therefore for the first statement: to whom it is granted to delight in food, and to whom not; and to whom at the beginning a "pore-opening" <note>original: "porisimi"</note> is given; and for whom the diet is thinned, and for whom not; and to whom some cold water is granted, and for whom not. ¶ It is doubted whether those having an ephemeral fever—since their strength is strong and the disease brief—should have food prohibited entirely. Furthermore, in an ephemeral fever, there is no intent toward "virtue" <note>The body's vital power</note>. Furthermore, from what Avicenna says, in every fever food would be appropriate because everyone is weakened. It must be said that brief diseases with difficult symptoms, in which we intend to address the "matter" <note>the diseased humors</note>, prohibit food, as in the first aphorism. But a brief, easy disease, in which we do not intend to address the matter, does not prohibit food, but not at just any time, but in the decline, unless it lasts too long or unless for certain causes which Avicenna posits: and the food must be of easy digestion because the sick person is weakened: and for this intent Avicenna brings in that discourse: and he does not want you to feed them just because they are weakened. ¶ It is doubted why we give food to those having much yellow bile <note>original: "choleram"</note> since they are not "pure bodies." ¶ It should be said that to some having an ephemeral fever we immediately grant food for fear of a hectic fever or fainting <note>original: "sincopis"</note> from weakness, such as those consumed by labor and hunger, etc. To some for fear of fainting and falling into putrid fevers, such as bilious people. For when the cause of an ephemeral fever arrives, the yellow bile is moved: causing shivering, and if it flows to the stomach, they faint from the "gnawing" <note>original: "mordicatione"</note> which food removes: but if it is inflamed it will putrefy and become a putrid fever: therefore, with food quieting the sharpness of the bile, there is safety for the bilious from these things. Not only to "pure bodies" do we give food by compulsion, but properly we feed them as a medical treatment.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ **And these.** Namely, with water: and in some it is prohibited because the intent is toward restoration <note>original: "repletionem"</note>.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ **And cold water.** It is doubted why it is prohibited when the fever is vehement, since then it could more safely be granted. It must be said: according to some, "vehement" means a heat that is weakening, or vehement in its symptoms: because from this it is not a true ephemeral fever, but there is a suspicion of a putrid one, or of a transition into it.

<margin>h</margin> ¶ **And it is granted to them.** He places the cure through external applications, namely baths, embrocations <note>term: embrocation (embroca). The act of pouring a liquid medicine or oil over a part of the body, or the liquid itself.</note>, and frictions. He grants the bath of sweet water because of the "accidents" <note>symptoms</note>. That is, because of those things that happen from a bath, which are four: moistening, sweating, rarefying <note>opening the pores</note>, and cooling.

<margin>i</margin> ¶ **Unquiet disposition.** Some have said: that is, it should be done with lukewarm or temperately hot water: or that a bath should be made when the disposition is quiet: these are not contrary indications prohibiting the bath. Otherwise, we say according to the mind of Avicenna that the cooling which happens from a bath does not

In all species of ephemeral fever, it is necessary that those things be brought to the bodies of the patients which nourish them with good nourishment and with speed of digestion: because the one with fever is sick, and the sick person is weakened. But to some of them, it is granted to indulge in food, such as those suffering from labor, anguish, and hunger. And to those in whose bodies there is much yellow bile. Also, because if he were to suffer shivering in the beginning, he should swallow food soaked in water or wine so that it may be more penetrating. And these indeed are fed even at the beginning of the fever, and for some, it is prohibited to indulge in it, and it is hinted to them that it should be made subtle, as in a patient suffering from a blockage <note>original: "opilationem"</note>. ¶ And it is better that the feeding be postponed until the decline, except in those whom we have excepted. And cold water is such that it should not be prohibited at the beginning of the matter, since the strength is strong, so its weakness is not feared, and it is the best cure for cooling. ¶ But if there should be weakness in the viscera and the fever is already extended or has become vehement: then it is better that all those things be taken together, and a bath is granted to them when their "pore-opening" <note>original: "porismus"</note> is consumed in ephemeral fevers through the symptoms, among which is moistening, and among which is sweating and the rarefying of the pores: and among them is cooling in an unquiet disposition: because it is prohibited where a fall into putrefaction is feared. ¶ And one ought not to avoid the bath except for those with a blockage, because a bath generates a putrid sickness: and similarly a patient with a nauseating surfeit, except at the end of the matter and when the pores are dilated and the nauseating fullness descends. There indeed one ought to bathe. ¶ And those with catarrh <note>original: "catarrum"</note> should not bathe unless it is "sun-burnt" <note>original: "adbustium"; possibly meaning a dry or hot type of catarrh</note>.

<margin>l</margin> ¶ **And all** those having ephemeral fevers should not prolong their stay in the air of the bath, but rather in its water when they wish, except those having it from solidity and thickness of the skin: for it is suitable for them to prolong their stay in the air of the bath until they sweat. Embrocation...

happen immediately, but when the disposition is quiet: then the water returns to its own coldness which cools the heat in the body as in the first treatise, second fen, first chapter. Some of the ornate speakers, etc., or "in an unquiet disposition." That is, when the disposition is quiet: because it is a true ephemeral fever, not having signs of a putrid one. He said later that one having catarrh should not bathe. To the contrary, because a bath ripens <note>original: "maturat"</note> cold, raw matter as in the previously cited chapter; some say that a bath that resolves and heats is not suitable for cold matter, but a bath that only heats is. But this is against Avicenna; for he says there: "and it is when the bath heats by resolution," etc.

<margin>l</margin> ¶ It must be said, therefore, that if the matter of the catarrh is cold, raw, and plentiful, a bath of sweet water is not suitable because it acts on the heat. But if it were little, it could ripen it: however, it is safer after ripening, as in the eighth treatise. But in acute catarrh: because it mitigates its sharpness, it is suitable. Read for these the third treatise, fifth fen.

<margin>k</margin> ¶ **And all.** Why? Because cooling and moistening are sought: which is done more by water than by air: but those having solidity and thickness of the skin made by cold things or astringency <note>original: "stipticie"</note> need much opening of the pores, which hot air does more.

<margin>l</margin> ¶ **Embrocation.** To the contrary, because an embrocation is a medicine suitable for that which needs to be dissolved as in the first treatise, fourth fen. The unlearned have said that he speaks of an embrocation made from an actual liquid or for cold. Dino <note>Dino del Garbo (d. 1327), a famous physician and commentator on Avicenna.</note> tries to save the text in two ways. First, that those having solidity of the skin should stay in the air, and not be bathed in waters, nor embrocated with water, because it adds blockage to them. Otherwise, he says that in this he wants to hint that friction should be done first: so that it opens the pores for the washing of the embrocation: because embrocation does not dilate the pores in that way, nor does it impress itself unless friction precedes it in them: therefore it is a continuous discourse for those who have fever from a blockage of the pores or density. And although the ways stated by Dino are good.

<margin>m</margin> ¶ We shall say otherwise with him, that in an ephemeral fever in which a bath of hot sweet water is suitable to resolve by opening the pores, it is better to bathe the whole than to do an embrocation.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of fevers within a commentary on Avicenna’s "Canon of Medicine." The previous page concluded a discussion on how the lack of ventilation in the body's pores can lead to the putrefaction of humors. This page shifts focus to "ephemeral fevers"—brief, one-day fevers—and their various causes, ranging from emotional states like grief to physical factors like labor or external heat.</meta>

# Book III

The reason is that an embrocation <note>original: "embroca"; a liquid medicinal application or lotion</note> made without pouring or with only a little is quickly cooled over the whole body: and it quickly blocks the pores. It does not open the pores through its heat as much as when a man lies under a large quantity of water. Sometimes, however, we prefer embrocation, such as when there is a scorching heat in the head, as understood in the seventh part of the Aphorisms <note>Refers to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note>. If the fever is not caused by yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>: as stated in the seventeenth [book] of the *Continens* <note>The "Kitab al-Hawi" by Al-Razi</note>, first chapter. Thaddeus <note>Thaddeus of Florence, a 13th-century physician</note> then said that an embrocation moves the matter toward the skin and thus blocks it.

<margin>a And in sharper [fevers]. Sharper: that is, from an obstruction, whether it is a stronger obstruction or an external obstruction of the pores.</margin>
<margin>b Resolves. Dionysius explains: that is, it gradually finishes and consumes that matter.</margin>
<margin>c Dries out. That is, quickly and perhaps. Avicenna means that when much matter is present, although friction opens the pores, it does not finish the matter: though it dilates it, which is permitted for its evacuation: but if it is little, it can finish it: and this is what he says: if it meets with very much moisture, it resolves, that is, dissolves and dilates it, therefore it needs evacuation: and if a little stays around the parts of the skin, it dries it out, that is, resolves and evaporates it, so that there is no need for evacuation. Because of these things, he adds: "Of evacuation etc." But Thaddeus says: when I need evacuation, I can rub the body before I evacuate. It should be said that although it is safer to evacuate first, if the pores are blocked, some friction that is not very strong is useful in opening them, whereby the matter is better evacuated.</margin>
<margin>d On fevers. Although here he determines specifically about ephemeral fevers, first he sets forth their species and causes. Second, he treats each one. It should be considered that we accept that ephemeral fever has species according to its causes: yet it should be known that these are not strictly species but are certain differences and variations in the physician's cure. Some are manifest: and from this diversity of causes, the physician can understand the various and proper species of ephemeral fever. We say that proper species are given to ephemeral fevers just as they are to putrid fevers, because of the diversity of the spirits ignited in different ephemeral fevers. For there is a certain ephemeral fever whose heating is first and foremost in the "animal spirit" in the brain; another in the "vital spirit" [in the heart], and another in the "natural spirit" [in the liver], as will appear later in the proper chapter. Avicenna understood this when he numbered three species, and below in the chapter on ephemeral fever from hot foods. It is doubted why every true ephemeral fever is caused by a primitive cause comparable to things coming from outside. It should be said that a cause can be called "from outside," meaning primitive and distinct, preceding and conjoined: and thus it is not taken here. In another way, "from outside" can be explained as from the surrounding air or its mediation, and food and drink, which are called "from outside" with respect to those things that are in us, such as the disposition of the soul or bodies. And in this way it is taken here. Thus, the accidents of the soul are not called "from outside" but "from within" according to this.</margin>
<margin>e And of compared [dispositions]. This has three parts. It should be considered that these dispositions are called "animal": because they are instilled through the soul, though there are degrees in this, for some are more dispositions of bodies (though only insofar as they are ensouled) such as health, sleep, and wakefulness: and therefore they are only present through the soul. Others tend more toward the disposition of the soul, such as the "accidents of the soul" <note>Emotions or psychological states</note>, as understood in the sixth [book] of *On Natural Things* <note>By Avicenna</note>.</margin>
<margin>f And of proportioned. Here he first puts a certain subdivision, second he declares it. It should be considered that by "movement" he means primarily local motion. By "action" he means movement even if it is not local. It pleased Avicenna to call these movements and actions "corporeal dispositions": because they dispose the body more materially and with less subtlety than the degrees of immaterial dispositions. Although some of these are only in the body insofar as it is ensouled—such as pain, labor, syncope <note>fainting</note>, hunger, and thirst—these are nonetheless operations or dispositions of more material powers than sadness, anger, sleep, wakefulness, and the others mentioned above. It is doubted why he puts "tranquility" here when he previously placed it among the animal dispositions. Furthermore, tranquility is not movement, and yet he says "compared to things that are movements." It should be said that one kind of tranquility belongs to the soul, and he spoke of this above; another belongs to the body, and of this he speaks here. To the second doubt, one should supply the text: "and compared to things which are movements" and "the contrary to movement," for Avicenna notably said "not actions" and "contraries" above because something might be a "non-action" and yet not be the contrary of movement.</margin>
<margin>g But you. You ask how syncope <note>fainting</note> is a movement: it should be said that it is the movement of the spirits toward the heart. Or it should be said that it is reduced to the contrary of movement. It is doubted how an obstruction <note>original: "oppitatio," likely *oppilatio*</note> is an action, since it can be in the process of becoming and movement. It should be said that it is not an action, but it is induced by action; or it is not an operation of a [bodily] power, nor reducible to a power's action, just as a defect like syncope is not.</margin>

But if it was through pouring or just by smearing, it only blocks the pores. **And in a sharper [fever]** <gloss>a</gloss> every ephemeral fever that is from an external or internal obstruction, rubbing opens the pores of the one who has it; then if it meets with very much moisture, it resolves <gloss>b</gloss> it, and if it meets with a little moisture, it dries <gloss>c</gloss> it. **None of them, however, requires evacuation unless they have an obstruction from repletion <note>an overabundance of humors</note>, or have a nauseating fullness: and those who have an ephemeral fever from a hardening of the body which is full.**

### Species of ephemeral fever. Chapter 10.

**Of ephemeral fevers** <margin>d</margin> there are those which are entirely compared to the animal dispositions. <margin>e</margin> **And among them are those compared to corporeal dispositions.** <margin>f</margin> **And among them are those proportioned to things that happen from the outside.** <margin>g</margin> **And of those compared to animal dispositions, there is that which comes from anguish, and that from sadness, and that from estimation and thought, anger, wakefulness, sleep, tranquility, fear, and joy.** <margin>f</margin> **And of those proportioned to corporeal dispositions are those compared to things that are actions and movements; and among them are those compared to non-actions and movements, and to their contraries.** <margin>g</margin> **And compared to things which are movements is that which comes from labor, and that from tranquility, and that which comes from evacuation; and among them is ephemeral fever from pain, and among them is ephemeral fever with syncope <note>fainting</note>; and among them is that which comes from hunger, and that which comes from thirst.** <margin>e</margin> **And of those compared to things that are not actions is that which comes from obstruction; and among them is that from nauseating fullness; and among them is that from an abscess; and among them is that from a hardening of the skin.** <margin>f</margin> **Those compared to things that happen from the outside are like those that come from scorching <note>original: "adustione"; usually from the sun or fire</note>, whatever scorching it may be, and like that from cold, and hardening, and from washing. I will therefore speak of each of them along with their cure.**

<column-break/>

"Sometimes it happens." He follows up on each species of ephemeral fever: first those compared to animal dispositions; second to corporeal ones; third to things coming from outside. The first part has eight sections, as there are eight animal causes. First, he determines the ephemeral fever from anguish. However, one must first know how anguish, sadness, and thought differ. Know that these words are used very loosely and it seems they vary according to different languages, and this is already [discussed].

<margin>a is great and... Some masters say that anguish is the soul's pain over a past evil, while sadness is the soul's pain over a future evil. Others say that anguish is the pain or passion of the soul from thinking about some past loss, like the death of a friend or son or lost money; but sadness is the pain of the soul from the fact that a person cannot obtain some good they seek—therefore Avicenna said "because of a sought-after thing." Others say that anguish is like a sudden sadness, whereby the heat is suddenly recalled [inward]; but sadness happens gradually and recalls the heat gradually.</margin>
<margin>b Reason. In the seventeenth [book] of the *Continens*, first chapter, it says that sadness is when one thinks with pain about a loss; and according to this, it seems he includes sadness and anguish together. But Isaac in the second [book] on Fevers and Gilbert in this chapter say that anguish pertains to the spiritual power of the heart, but sadness to the rational power in the brain. Azaravius <note>likely Albucasis</note>, however, says the opposite in this chapter. He says that anxiety, that is, anguish, pertains to the thinking power of the brain, but sadness to the vital power of the heart. These ways are all different, and this is because of the various ways of understanding the words. And we will say what seems more familiar to our language: that these three passions—anguish, sadness, and thought—consist in the fact that the heat is moved inward because of a passion in the soul. But anguish seems to be the pain or passion of the soul due to the loss of a thing for which recovery is not hoped; such as the pain for the death of a son or friend, and because it coincides with a thought of despair, the person is anguished: and their spirits are inflamed and afflicted in the internal parts, and sometimes "corporeal anguish" follows from this, which is being unable to remain still in any position. Sadness, however, is the passion from the loss of a thing where despair has not set in, as when one is sad over lost money, the recovery of which one is busy seeking, and there is not yet despair. It seems, therefore, that anguish is a strong sadness: and therefore it ignites more in anguish than in sadness, though the reverse could be understood. "Thought" seems to be a deep meditation on something, not that anguish or sadness falls there, but simply thought with a certain abstraction, such as the thought of God in which the faithful immerse themselves. From this, it appears these are quite close: and therefore sometimes they are put in one chapter, as by Haly <note>Haly Abbas</note> in the third [book] of the Practice. And from these things, the text also becomes clear.</margin>

### On ephemeral fever from anguish and its signs. Chapter 11.

**Sometimes it happens** <gloss>a</gloss> **from the movement of the spirit to the interior and its hiding in them because of an excess of anguish: a spiritual fever.** <gloss>i</gloss> **Its signs are a fieriness** <gloss>k</gloss> **of the urine and its sharpness** <gloss>l</gloss> **so that the one having it feels its sharpness because of the dominance of dryness in it; and there is a movement of the eye** <gloss>m</gloss> **inclined toward closing; and the eye is sunken because of resolution <note>the 'wasting away' of the eye's humors</note> with quiet and under closure; and the face tends toward a citrine color** <gloss>n</gloss> **because of the depth of the clarity; and the pulse is toward weakness and thinness** <gloss>o</gloss>, **inclined and strongly declining toward hardness** <gloss>p</gloss>.

### On the cure. Chapter 12.

**It is necessary** <gloss>q</gloss> **that the one having it should increase the entry into the tub <note>original: "tine"; likely a bathing tub</note> and place most of their intention on bathing with the water of the bath without its [hot] air; and increase that joining with rubbing** <gloss>p</gloss> **that** <gloss>r</gloss>. **For some oil** <gloss>s</gloss> **is more helpful to them, and the bath** <gloss>t</gloss> **is managed with soothing and cold-scented things; and let them place cooling compresses <note>original: "epithemata"</note> upon the chest, with mucilages and juices and good waters; and let them use many mixtures in their drink, for this is a good medicine for them.**

<margin>b Sometimes. That is, in prepared bodies.</margin>
<margin>i Spiritual fever. That is, an ephemeral fever in the vital spirit, to which anguish is more appropriated according to Isaac.</margin>
<margin>k Fieriness etc. Because of the dominance of dryness, namely from the drying heat. For the heat is enclosed in the heart, and there it agitates, and the anguish inflames the liver and sharpens the urine.</margin>
<margin>l Its sharpness. Namely of the urine, or of the heat itself to the touch when he is feverish.</margin>
<margin>m Movement of the eye etc. Because here there is a deepening of the heat inside without being pushed back out, since the person is in despair.</margin>
<margin>n Toward citrine. That is, darkish or greenish. For thus the Arabs sometimes speak of citrine: and it is understood as quasi-green, as we discussed at length in the third chapter... [reference to previous treatise].</margin>
<margin>o Pulse toward smallness. With the heat having moved deep inside.</margin>
<margin>p Strongly toward hardness. It is doubted why "strongly." It should be said that it is a manner of speaking, or he speaks of a very notable hardness which appears when there is much drying.</margin>
<margin>q It is necessary. Here he sets the cure: now with things that regard the [patient's state], such as things that bring joy; now with things that regard the fever, namely the inflammation, using cooling things; now with things that regard the accidents <note>symptoms</note>, namely the drying, using moistening things.</margin>
<margin>r With rubbing. To cause penetration [of the medicine].</margin>
<margin>s Some oil. Namely sweet oil, or oil of violets, or chamomile, as your judgment determines.</margin>
<margin>t And that the bath. Because at first contact the bath heats; the rest is known.</margin>
