<sig>b 3</sig>

<margin>Sometimes it happens. Here it appears that sadness and pain of the soul arise from the fact that someone is unable to attain some sought-after good; hence it says.</margin>
<margin>When a sought-after thing, namely, cannot be attained.</margin>
<margin>a Laborious motion. Because sadness moves the heat inward, and insofar as it is a worry about possessing something, it moves outward in a certain way.</margin>
<margin>d Except that the movement of the eye is toward the external part with its depth, that is, although it is deep.</margin>
<margin>f Because of the resolution <note>original: "resolutionem"; the dispersal or breaking down of the body's vital spirits</note>. Another [source] has it differently, namely: Because of the resolution which is toward the external parts. Add "it is." And it means that although the eye is sunken and deep because of the resolution and drying out in the movement of the heat, and from inflammation and wakefulness—all of which occur in sadness—nevertheless, because in these things there is a worry about something, the heat moves outward, and thus the eye appears [sunken].</margin>
<margin>p The pulse is not lowered, etc., namely, as in distress.</margin>
<margin>b Rather with weakness, that is, with a release of the depression within it.</margin>
<margin>i But it is false, that is, a certain throbbing from the sudden movement of heat to the outside at times; or a "leap" <note>original: "saltus"; a sudden irregularity in the pulse</note> (which is a change from depth to appearance when suddenly a way appears to him by which he can pursue this thing); the care is evident.</margin>
<margin>k Sometimes similar. Because in a similar way, from the inflammation of the spirit, the urine is perhaps tinted; much thought, however, in things where speculation occurs—and despair does not properly happen, as in distress, nor does hope stand, as in sadness—arranges the eyes uniformly. And although these maintain one form of gaze, in the depth of the eye they decline more inward because heat is drawn inward; but because there is no distress or sadness there, the motion is not toward closing, but toward appearing in the greatest things. For in the highest speculations we are not properly saddened or joyful as in other things which we pursue by reason of good or evil, as understood in the third [book] of the *Problems*, the sixth problem <note>Refers to Aristotle's *Problems*</note>.</margin>
<margin>Diverse pulse. You might ask how it is diverse and yet mostly equal. It should be said: that it is diverse by comparing the expansion <note>original: "diastolem"</note> to the contraction <note>original: "sistoli"</note>, or it is diverse because of some diversity in the movement of the heat which happens because at one moment the object of thought or speculation appears to him as if grasped and understood, and at another moment not so. However, this diversity is small compared to that which is in sadness and distress, and therefore compared to that, it can be called equal.</margin>
<margin>m Toward yellowness. Because of wakefulness and the other things said above; and consider also that by "thought" we can understand the thought alone of pursuing something, besides that there would be sadness there, not only the thought of the spirit.</margin>
<margin>Sometimes it happens. Because anger is a fervor due to the appetite for vengeance. Reason inflames and reddens the face unless fear is present with it, as when an injury is inflicted by a superior. Therefore, the heat is not so abundantly moved outward, and thus a deep redness does not occur, but a bright one, which he calls "citrine" <note>original: "citrinum"; a yellowish-orange color</note>.</margin>
<margin>Fear. That is, fear of another fever, namely, a humoral one; the text here has "tremor," which commonly appears in those who are very angry, in the hands and feet; indeed in the lips, because the moving power of the limbs is weakened due to an evil motion in the spirit, which flees to the outside; and this is what it says because of weakness, or because some sharp humor moves, biting the stomach or limbs, and this is what it means when it mentions the movement of the humor.</margin>
<margin>p Swelling. Because of many vapors moved to the face.</margin>
<margin>q Urine sharp to the touch. Against Isaac [Judaeus], who in this chapter posits that urine...</margin>

### Concerning ephemeral fever from sadness. Chapter XIIII.

Sometimes it happens from an excess of sadness due to sought-after things that a laborious motion occurs, heating the spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; the vital force carrying heat through the body</note> and causing one to fall into a fever. Its signs are these same signs as those from distress, except that the movement of the eye is with its depth because of the resolution which is toward the external part; and the pulse is not lowered or depressed; rather, there is a weakness in it, but there is also a "leap" with it. And its cure is just like the cure for that which is from distress.

### Concerning ephemeral fever from thought. Chapter XIII.

Sometimes it happens from a multitude of thought regarding things, a fever similar to that which is from sadness, except that the motion of the eye is equal, not declining toward closure nor toward protruding, yet declining toward depth; and the pulse is diverse in expansion and contraction, and for the most part is equal; and the face is inclined toward yellowness. And its cure is the cure for that which is from sadness.

### Concerning ephemeral fever from anger. Chapter XV.

Sometimes it happens because of the excessive movement of the spirit toward the exterior in a disposition of anger, an overflowing heat burning the spirit into a fever. Its signs are redness of the face, unless fear is mixed with it, in which case it becomes yellow, and a swelling of the face similar to one who is swollen in sleep; and the eyes are red, tending outward because of the vehement motion of the spirit to the exterior. And sometimes a tremor happens to some of them because of the movement of the humor, or because of a natural weakness; and the urine is red and sharp to the touch because of its sharpness. And sometimes there is a certain clarity with it, and the pulse is thick, full, thumping, and frequent.

### Concerning the cure. Chapter XVI.

Make them rest and see that they are occupied with soothing narratives, good voices, and wonderful games; and have them enter a bath of tepid water, not of excessive heat; and let them be anointed liberally with some oil. For that is more suitable for them than hot water. And let them be fed...

<column-break/>

<margin>...has sharpness. And it is proven because the heat is quickly moved inside and out. It should be said that he understands this in respect to fever from distress.</margin>
<margin>q Sometimes there is a certain clarity. Because it is an inflammation not causing a strong boiling, since much heat is drawn into it; and the opposite can appear as turbid.</margin>
<margin>Make them rest. This cure addresses the causes with rest and things that bring joy. It also addresses the disposition, namely the heat, by transpiring and releasing the sharpness with a bath, namely of little heat; for if it were of manifest heat, it would be harmful. Thus the contradiction with Serapion is removed. And it is more convenient with some oil, such as violet oil, which is better. And therefore he gives cold and moist things; he forbids wine lest it inflame, and because it increases anger, as Serapion says; you should consider the patient's habit.</margin>
<margin>u Sometimes it happens. He signifies the way an ephemeral fever arises from wakefulness; since heat moves much, as was sufficiently said in the first book, second and third sections.</margin>
<margin>t Swelling of the eyelids. Against this, because this seems to happen in much sleep, as above. Furthermore, how do the eyes become deep in these cases? It should be said that from much sleep the face and eyelids swell because of the retention of vapors and the prohibition of resolution; but in much wakefulness, it is because of the corruption of digestion, whence many evil vapors rise to the eyes; and because the eyes and eyelids themselves are fatigued and weakened more, the vapors tend there; and with this, the whole eye can be deep because of the drying out of the good moisture.</margin>
<margin>u Disturbance of the urine. Against this: because wakefulness makes the urine raw, and thus it becomes thin and clear. It should be said that by "disturbance" he means the loss of brightness which happens from a defect in digestion; I do not say it is a total lack of digestion, as Avicenna hints in the first book, second section, in the chapter on the signs of urine colors. Or it should be said that from wakefulness the urine becomes turbid if matters are moved, and if not, it tends toward clarity. Or it should be said that wakefulness tints the urine because of the motion of heat, and discolors it because of its loss from much resolution, and this discoloration he calls "disturbance."</margin>
<margin>r Yellowness. Because of the malice [of the condition], as if the blood were burnt or sharpened. And therefore the faces of those unable to sleep become yellow, as Averroes [says] in the second [book of the] *Colliget*.</margin>
<margin>y Its swelling, namely of the face.</margin>
<margin>3 Because of "excitation." Excitation is an Arabic word and signifies two things: waking up, unless there are fumes; here it means a phlegmatic repletion similar to cachexia <note>original: "cacexie"; a state of ill health and malnutrition</note> as in the *Continens*, the chapter on swollen abscesses. Thus it is understood: the face swells because they become cachectic from bad digestion.</margin>
<margin>a The cure, however. He turns the intention toward the cause, the fever, and the excitations.</margin>
<margin>a Let them take wine in drink. Namely, to moisten and induce sleep; therefore it should be diluted, and it ought to be a mediocre wine, not old or pure, and not taken copiously, because it would induce death by multiplying wakefulness, as happened to the servant of the notary in the third [book] of *Internal Organs*, fifth chapter.</margin>
<margin>Spirit. It should be considered that although he spoke above of bodily and animal tranquility, he nevertheless comprehends both here along with sleep, because sleep is very similar to rest.</margin>
<margin>c Sometimes there would be a flow. You might say "rather, always." It should be said that he says this because of those from whom many vapors are resolved which, being retained, cause fever. But this is not in everyone, but in some, and he signifies this when he says "sometimes."</margin>
<margin>d Vaporous resolution of the pulse. That is, appearing in the pulse because vapors seem to exit from there; or the pulse, that is, the throbbings.</margin>
<margin>e Its cure, etc.</margin>
<margin>g Cools and moistens. Against this, because these things induce sleep.</margin>
<margin>f Temperate exercise. Against this, because what is accustomed to heat does not cool. It should be said that cooling and moistening things are given because of the fever—not just any things, but those that also keep him awake, like a bath or exercise. To the second point, they say "temperate" refers to weak exercise because this person cannot exercise much. Since he has a fever, good exercise, by excluding inflamed vapors, cools and moistens.</margin>

### Concerning ephemeral fever from wakefulness. Chap. XVII.

Sometimes ephemeral fever also happens from wakefulness. Its signs are a preceding period of wakefulness and heaviness of the eyelids, since perhaps he cannot open them, and a deepening of the eye because of resolution; and swelling of the eyelids because of the corruption of food and a multitude of vapors; and disturbance of the urine because of the lack of digestion, and weakness of the pulse and yellowness of the face because of poor digestion; and a swelling of the face because of "excitation" from the bad digestion, but it is not with redness as in the fever from anger.

### Concerning the cure. Chap. XVIII.

The cure for it is to be at leisure and to rest and sleep; and to embrocate the head with those things that cool and moisten; and a moist bath and meals of good foods; and moistening ointments. And wine is among the things most beneficial to them; and they may take it in drink without fear, unless there is a headache.

### Concerning ephemeral fever from sleep and rest. Chapter XIX.

Regarding the spirit, sometimes hot vapors are resolved because of wakefulness and movement. Therefore, when sleep and tranquility are prolonged and they are not resolved, a heating of the spirit and its fever happens from them. Its signs are these: for a preceding period of sleep and great tranquility signify it, especially if it is contrary to one's habit; and a vaporous resolution and the pulse also signify it.

### Concerning its cure. Chap. XX.

Its cure is a sweat-cloth in the air of the bath; and an equal washing with hot water; and a small amount of food, and an inclination toward that which cools and moistens him; and temperate exercise; and things that cool and moisten are necessary, and they should be prohibited from wine entirely; there is no way for them to have it.

Book III

<margin>a And there is no need for him to drink wine. Wine is feared either lest it move vapors to the head, or lest it agitate the humors toward putrefaction, or lest it cause sleep; however, for certain other reasons, it might be granted to some.</margin>
¶ a And there is no need for him to drink wine. "to drink wine."

<margin>b Sometimes it happens. This comparison is general because in both cases there is inflammation from movement toward the outside, although in joy it happens more gradually. In anger, a great sudden joy might occur.</margin>
¶ b Sometimes it happens.

### On the ephemeral fever from joy. Chapter xxi.

<margin>c lesser frequency. Because the heat is not so greatly ignited.</margin>
¶ c

<margin>d The cure is the first. Not entirely similar, for in anger there are things that bring joy, but in joy, there are things that bring sadness <note>original: "tristantia"; here the commentator suggests countering the emotion with its opposite</note>.</margin>
¶ d

<margin>e Sometimes. First, you have the difference between distress and fear, and also the proportion that exists between joy and anger: for in fear, the heat suddenly moves inward; and therefore sometimes they experience a churning of the belly and thirst greatly, as Aristotle says in the *Problems*, book 22, problems one and two; and because it happens suddenly then, it affects the pulse more diversely. You, however, should note that in the general principles of the science of medicine—as we said in the first book of the *Canon*—accidents of the soul are rarely found pure, but are instead vehemently mixed.</margin>
**S**ometimes it happens from joy, with the signs of that which comes from anger, except that the form of the eye is the form of a joyful person, not the form of an angry one. ¶ And the frequency in the pulse is lesser. ¶ And its cure is very close to the cure of that which comes from anger.

### On the ephemeral fever from fear. Chapter xxii.

**S**ometimes an ephemeral fever happens from fear according to the same path as that which happens from distress. ¶ For the proportion of fear to distress is the same as the proportion of anger to joy, because the movement of fear is toward the interior and anger is toward the exterior; and it happens suddenly, whereas the other movements happen gradually. Its signs are the same as the signs of that which comes from distress, except that the diversity in the pulse is more vehement, and the form of the eye is the form of one who is terrified. ¶ Its cure is very close to the cure of that which comes from distress; and it is necessary that he be secured from fear, and that he be approached with news that causes joy, for things that bring gladness are helpful to him.

### On the ephemeral fever from labor. Chapter xxiii.

<margin>f Labor. He determines ephemeral fevers compared to bodily dispositions: first to those which are movements and actions and their contraries; second to those which are not, such as blockages. Although there were seven causes, tranquility has already been addressed in the chapter on ephemeral fever from sleep; therefore, he first determines the fever from labor <note>Labor here refers to heavy physical exertion or exercise</note>.</margin>
**L**abor sometimes reaches the point of creating vapor by heating the body and the spirit, so that it becomes a fever harmful to the body's operations; it is of the greatest harm and weighs heavily upon the vital and animal spirits. The signs are a preceding period of labor, an increase of heat in the joints above other parts, the touch of weariness, and dryness of the body. ¶ And sometimes at the end of it, a moistening occurs if the labor was temperate—that is, when there is no parching or cold in it that prevents sweating. ¶ But if the labor was excessive, the moisture and sweat are diminished; and sometimes a dry cough follows it, because of the involvement of the lungs; and sometimes there is a decline in the constitution, and its pulse is small and weak, and sometimes it declines toward hardness <note>original: "duritiem"; a hard pulse suggests dehydration or "dryness" in medieval theory</note>; and the urine is yellow and hot because of the subtle movement and because of the resolution <note>original: "resolutionem"; the breaking down and dispersal of bodily substances through heat</note>.

<margin>g They doubt why he said "harmful to operations." It should be said that this way of speaking pleased him; or he said it because the operation of human social interaction and immoderate exercise is singularly seen to be hindered. Perhaps he wants to continue the sense thus: "harmful to operations and is etc.," that is, the hindrance in operations is the harm he does to the vital and animal spirits, because these two spirits are especially the principle of movement according to impulse or will.</margin>
¶ g

<margin>h Signs of touch, that is, the perception of weariness, whether it be ulcerous, wasting, or abscess-like <note>original: "apostemosa"; referring to internal swellings</note>, according to the diversity of the body.</margin>
¶ h

<margin>i Temperate. On the contrary, that would not cause a fever. It should be said that it is "spaced out," that is, not excessively flowing. Therefore, when such labor occurs, there is no "communication" there—that is, there is no parching around the matter, like fire or sand, and cold does not prevent the sweat; thus some sweat happens at the end of such an ephemeral fever.</margin>
¶ i

<margin>j If, however, sweat—namely in labor, or the labor was etc.</margin>
¶ j

<margin>k Cough. The lung being harmed by inflammation.</margin>
¶ k

<margin>l Toward hardness. Because of the drying out.</margin>
¶ l

<margin>m Yellow and hot urine because of the subtle movement and because of the resolution. Some say that this refers both to the urine and the pulse: so that the sense is that it is tinted because of the movement of bile <note>original: "chole"</note>, and the pulse is weak because of the resolution. Alternatively: the urine is tinted and appears hot because of the movement of subtle hot humors and because of the resolution—that is, because of the heat that resolves, or because of the dissolution of hot humors which can be associated with the urine. Another text has: yellow, that is, tinted because of the movement of bile, and clear because of the resolution—that is, subtle and clear because a drying out has occurred in these cases.</margin>
¶ m

### On the cure. Chapter xxiv.

<margin>n Treatment. First he sets down the cure. Second, he interposes the opinion of others. Third, he completes the cure. There, "some say"; there, the third part: "and it is necessary." This intention looks toward three things: the cause, which is labor; the weariness induced, by properly moistening; and the rectification of the diet.</margin>
**T**heir treatment is tranquility and bathing in a tub, and of the joints; and the taking of good, moistening food according to the quantity

<margin>o Some say. But Haly Abbas <note>A famous Persian physician</note> says in the third part concerning the regimen of health that in abscess-like weariness the food should be greatly reduced; but such weariness can arise from labor. It should be said that most weariness joined to this fever is of the "drying" kind. Therefore Haly, in the third part of his practice, turns his intention to it, as does Avicenna here. Those who say the regimen should be made lighter either mean the regimen for others—namely those suffering from acute fevers (and this is a false statement, as it seems)—or others suffering from different ephemeral fevers. This is also false because here there can be a strong urge to urinate and a necessity for food because of dryness. Therefore Haly says in the same place: let the dishes be frequently multiplied. We shall also use a lighter regimen in ephemeral fever from blockages; but if the weariness is ulcerous or abscess-like...</margin>
¶ o

Galen <note>The foundational Greek physician</note> intends this, but Avicenna intends that which is more joined to excessive labor, namely the drying kind. Or it should be said that he primarily understands the drying kind, whether it is more joined to it or not.</margin>

And it is necessary that their anointing be more frequent than the anointing of others with some oil, so that their limbs and joints may be moistened from the dryness, and again so that the tension that has happened to them may be softened. ¶ And violet oil is among the best oils for them.

### On the ephemeral fever from evacuation. Chapter xxv.

<margin>Sometimes it happens. He sets down four causes why evacuation causes an ephemeral fever. The first is excessive movement in the spirit; for in the movements of the humors, there is a movement of the spirits. Strong agitation is a common cause of vomiting and loosening of the belly, and perhaps the flow of blood. The second cause is weariness which can follow because of rising many times to the stool, or because the humors move around the muscles. These modes of weariness are modes of pain that cause inflammation. Perhaps the author understood these two causes as one. Also, excessive evacuation—namely a flux—moves and inflames the spirit because of the weariness of rising to the stool. ¶ The second or third cause is that the medicine is hot and dry. The third or fourth cause is the fury of bile <note>original: "cholere"</note> because of bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note>, which can become putrid as it appears; but if it is assigned more to the ephemeral, he says the moisture of the vapors—that is, some moisture apt to evaporate—makes the fury of the bile return, i.e., to fire and inflammation; and this happens in those with abundant bile and bilious blood.</margin>
**S**ometimes it happens from a commotion of the humors after a loosening of the belly, an excessive movement of the spirits that inflames a fever within them because of the great weariness that follows them. ¶ And sometimes purgative medicines cause it, because they heat the body. ¶ And sometimes it follows bloodletting, because it causes the moisture of the vapors and their bloodiness to return to a bilious fury.

### Treatment. Chapter xxv.

**I**t is necessary that the management of the urine be refined through those things which are ordained in their own chapters; and that the sick person be fed with that which comforts him most, and according to the quantity that may be digested of those things which cool and moisten, and which have in them pungent and astringent <note>original: "pontica stiptica"</note> qualities; and let these be placed over the stomach.

<margin>¶ It is necessary. The signs are known, namely the evacuation itself. It should be considered that the intention in this fever is three-fold: first, toward the cause itself, which is the excessive flux—and for this, go back to the third book and consider if it is necessary to restrain it or not. The second intention is toward the cause of the strength <note>the patient's vitality</note>, so that it may be with comforting things; and since with this it is necessary to attend to the flux and the febrile distemper, these comforting things ought to be cold and moist because of the fever, and he puts in them some astringents because of the flux. This food will be, for example, the juice of chicken or partridge meat with a little pomegranate and quince wine. The third intention is toward the fever, as is clear.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the classification of "ephemeral fevers"—brief fevers typically lasting one day—within Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*. Having previously discussed emotional causes, the text here addresses fevers resulting from physical distress (pain, fainting), nutritional deprivation (hunger, thirst), and physiological blockages.</meta>

# Section 1, Treatise I

<margin>a</margin> And concerning this summary: specifically regarding strengthening astringents <term>astringent: substances that contract tissues and reduce secretions</term>.
<margin>b</margin> "Cooler": that is, less warm, as mastic oil is less warm <note>original: "masticino"</note>.
<margin>h</margin> nard-based <note>original: "ardinū" for "nardinum"</note>, as Galen says in the penultimate chapter of the seventh book of *The Regimen of Health*.
<margin>c</margin> "Aromatized": that is, aromatic with a good scent, or he says this because of other things added there. You, however, should consider the compositions of these oils because they vary greatly according to different cities.
<margin>d</margin> "And let it be squeezed": certain unrefined practitioners assign a reason, saying that if it were not squeezed, it would become cold and cause blockages <term>oppilation: a medical term for the blockage or obstruction of pores or vessels</term>; these people are ignorant of the nature of oil, for it strongly resists cooling; indeed, since it absorbs heat, it retains it well. The reason, therefore, is that Avicenna fears the actual levity of oils, and thus he desires their virtue <note>medicinal power</note> but not their actual liquid density. It is doubted whether lukewarmness <note>original: "tepidum"</note> is softening and dispersive by its nature. One might say not, as its heat is close to natural heat and conforms to it. See Galen’s third book on *Therapeutics* and Avicenna here. Some say "lukewarm" is one thing and "temperate" is another, as can be gathered from the chapter on the cure of pure tertian fever, where after he teaches bathing with temperate water, he later teaches splashing with lukewarm water. They say, therefore, that what is temperate and warm comforts, but what is lukewarm weakens. This argument cannot be tolerated because "lukewarm," being below "temperate," diminishes heat and, as it were, weakly binds the pores; but this does not weaken the body. It must be said, therefore, that lukewarmness is deceptively warm, and what is temperate weakens by accident but comforts by nature—specifically by inducing a conforming heat. But because it opens the pores and keeps the sick person exposed, it moves the heat outward; therefore, it weakens, and because it moves and melts the moisture. However, a stronger heat encountered might seem to weaken more by itself, yet by accident it comforts relative to lukewarmness because, with a certain biting quality, it closes the pores. Avicenna observes this particularly regarding the belly—that is, the stomach and intestines—because they are cold, nervous members. Thus they are comforted more by heat and not by lukewarmness, and therefore Galen says in the same place: "all lukewarm things resolve the strength of the belly."

<margin>e</margin> Pain. Why pain causes heat is discussed more elsewhere.
<margin>f</margin> "Let it be managed": he intends that in the cure of pain, one should use those things known in their own chapters, and for the fever, cooling and moistening baths and ointments, just as he says in the chapter on fevers from labor; this happens because weariness is a mode of pain.
<margin>g</margin> "Adopted pain": for example, in the head or joints, but if the whole body is in pain, it is possible for it to be cured by this.

plasters and infusions: strengthening things, warmed but not reheated. <margin>i</margin> For everything lukewarm is softening and dissolves the strength. And regarding this summary: <margin>k</margin> it is wool soaked in nard oil, or a cooler oil, <margin>l</margin> aromatized, <margin>m</margin> and let it be squeezed <margin>n</margin> until the parts of the oil are separated from it; <margin>o</margin> let them be placed over the heart and those parts that need cooling.

### On ephemeral fever from pain. Chapter xxvij.

<margin>p</margin> Pain sometimes heats the spirit so much that a fever is ignited. Signs: pain in the head, eye, ear, tooth, joints, or extremities, or colic, or hemorrhoids, or other pains from boils.

### On the cure of that which comes from pain. Chapter xxviij.

Let the pain be managed with that which is given in its own chapter, then let it be cured with the treatment for that which comes from labor. <margin>q</margin> But if an onset of pain is feared from the drinking of wine, it should not be given to drink.

### On ephemeral fever from syncope <note>fainting or sudden loss of consciousness</note>. Chapter xxix.

Sometimes it happens to one who undergoes syncope, due to the diverse heating from the commotion of the spirit, that it turns into a fever; and sometimes the remnants of the fever remain after the removal of the fear in syncope. Signs: the proximity of syncope and a fall in strength without signs of other fevers (those which are not ephemeral), and the pulse in this condition is of diverse dispositions. <margin>r</margin> For sometimes it falls and is destroyed when cold overcomes it. <margin>s</margin> And sometimes it becomes a drying attenuation in hardness with a crawling sensation <term>vermination: a sensation like worms crawling under the skin</term>.

### Treatment. Chapter xxx.

Its cure is the cure of syncope: you give foods of fast digestion and good chyme <note>original: "boni chimi"; healthy digestive juices</note> among those you have known; and if you need to give wine to drink, do so, and do not worry about the fever. <margin>t</margin> When, therefore, he is freed from syncope and a fever remains similar to that which comes with wasting, let it be cured with that which is in the *Canon* concerning cooling and moistening.

<margin>b</margin> "Sometimes it happens": It is doubted how syncope can be a cause of fever since it leads to coldness and a fall in the pulse. It must be said that because of the confinement of the spirit in the heart and the prohibition of breathing, inflammation happens. Therefore, first the fever happens internally from the syncope; then, when he rises from the syncope, it appears more externally. And so he said "diverse heating happens," and we understand that there can be fever while the syncope persists and also as it recedes—hence he said "remnants." But you might say he should not have said "fever," because according to time, he should have called it the fever itself with its greater duration, since syncope does not last a whole natural day, but perhaps less than an hour. It must be said that this fever happens when syncope occurs frequently, according to Avicenna, "after the removal of fear"; where they occupy a large space of the day or of two days or more, as when they are caused by the stomach, they were frequent according to Avicenna. And therefore Avicenna says "after the removal of fear" and not "after the removal of syncope," because several syncopes preceded, and one should no longer doubt its outcome; for once the fear of syncope is removed, none is expected to come. But once one syncope is removed, another might be expected to occur.
<margin>i</margin> "Signs, etc."
<margin>k</margin> "When cold overcomes": namely, externally.
<margin>l</margin> "In hardness": namely, when cold overcomes or when there is wasting because of the syncopes.

<margin>m</margin> "With termination": that is, with "little worms" <note>vermiculis</note> during the act of syncope sometimes.
<margin>n</margin> Sometimes the intention turns to the syncope with food and drink: namely wine, not fearing the fever, as also in the seventh book of *Therapeutics*.
<margin>o</margin> "In the Canon": namely, on the cure of those who are wasted, book VII, and on hectic fever.
<margin>p</margin> "Sometimes they are sharpened": By lights he may have a way to temper the heat; it is necessary that an ignition be made from hunger.
<margin>q</margin> "When they do not find": namely, the bodies or vapors.

### On ephemeral fever from hunger. Chapter xxxi.

Sometimes vapors in the body are sharpened when they do not find nourishment, and they generate a fever. Its pulse is weak and small, and sometimes it inclines toward hardness. Treatment: Feeding during the fever is like porridges made from barley meal <note>original: "kist ordei"</note> with vegetables; and after those, with good, strengthening foods. Let him be bathed, and let much lukewarm water be poured over his head. Let him sit in it, and let his body be moistened with things like oils of violet, rose, and gourd.

### On ephemeral fever from thirst. Chapter xxxij.

This is very close to that which comes from hunger, and it is more worthy to happen because of the lack of that which settles the strong heat in the vapors with water. Treatment: you give cold water to drink, and juices of cold fruits, especially pomegranates. Moisten the body in a tub, and if possible, let a bath with cold water be taken.

### On ephemeral fever from blockage <note>original: "oppilatione"</note>. Chapter xxxiij.

Blockages occur in the pores of the skin because of its thickness and lack of "bubbling" <note>evaporation/transpiration</note>, and a multitude of foods, and because of cold. And because of washing with cold, astringent waters. And because of the scorching of the sun. And sometimes it happens in the pathways of the veins and their channels, and their orifices, and their courses and ways.

And when he speaks of ephemeral fever from blockage, he refers only to this species. <margin>r</margin> For it often happens that dispersal <note>of heat/vapors</note> is lessened, and repulsion and constriction are multiplied, and breathing is deprived. A great deal of vapor is gathered and not dispersed, and then superfluous heat occurs; and while its inflammation persists in the weakest of the parts of the body, which is the spirit.

<margin>r</margin> ¶ "Nourishment": that is, that from which it is generated.
<margin>s</margin> "Toward hardness": because of the drying, he said "sometimes," because it appears that the fever is a drying and hardening from the deprivation of food.
<margin>t</margin> "Feeding": It should be considered that he places foods that are given while the fever persists, which are cooling like barley ptisan; and those given after the fever, like meat. Therefore the text says "after that," namely the fever. But if the text says "after those," namely the porridges, then the text means that while the fever persists, you should first give cold, non-corruptible foods like barley meal, lest the other foods be corrupted by an ignited and greedy stomach; and subsequently, if they need it, more strengthening foods like meat can be given. Let this rule be gathered here from the general principle given in the first book, and in the third section, the third chapter on the regimen of food.
<margin>u</margin> "Lukewarm water": that is, duly warmed; Avicenna intends to moisten the whole body.

<margin>x</margin> "This is very close": Avicenna wants to imply that because of hunger, inflammation happens in the vapors and spirits, and because of thirst likewise. In thirst, the cooling of heat—which is done by watery moisture—is lacking; and he says: it is more "worthy" that a stronger heat occurs in the vapors (spirits and vapors) because of the lack of that which is settled by water. It should be considered that in thirst the body inflames more than in hunger, as we have shown elsewhere. This is apparent because in thirst one craves coldness or something extinguishing; and therefore it is more difficult and tedious to tolerate thirst than hunger, as Aristotle says in the *Problems*, book 28, problem 27, and book 7. Although he gives another reason, Avicenna implies this: where there is a need for a greater extinguishing agent, there is a greater inflammation. Note that here, by "fruit water," he does not mean a decoction of cassia and tamarind—as doctors commonly understand by "fruit water"—but he means the juice of cold and moist fruits like apples, sweet pomegranates, and oranges, but specifically "water," that is, the juice of pomegranates, to avoid corruption.
<margin>y</margin> "If possible": provided he is not already wasted.

<margin>z</margin> ¶ "Blockages": There were four types of ephemeral fevers made from things that are corporeal and are neither actions nor movements: namely, from blockage <note>oppilation</note>, nauseating satiety, abscesses <note>aposteme</note>, and solidity <note>density of the flesh</note>. Therefore he determines these four, and first the fever from blockage. First the causes, second the signs, third the cure. He gives five causes for the blockage of pores: one is the deprivation of washing, whereby filth is retained (this is what he means by "thickness").
<margin>p</margin> "And for...": The second cause is a multitude of foods, whence many blocking superfluities are made; another cause is the coldness of the air, etc. Another cause is blockage in the veins; this happens in the ways and channels regarding the cavity, and in the orifices regarding the extremity that terminates at the members, and in the "courses" regarding the pores with which they communicate—or he said "ways" regarding small things and "courses" regarding major branches.
<margin>q</margin> "And when he speaks": here, applying the cause to the ephemeral fever, he first chooses which kind he means.
<margin>r</margin> "To this species": Namely, that which comes from the blockage of the orifices or courses or pathways of the veins, because this is properly called "from blockage." For that which comes from the blockage of the pores of the skin is discussed later and previously under "density" or "solidity."
<margin>a</margin> ¶ "For it often happens": Here a general cause of these blockages is taken, because repletion <note>over-fullness</note> adds to the lack of evacuation, manifest or hidden. Secondly, the common cause of the fever's arrival is taken, because superfluous heat occurs according to the mode which...

# Book IV

He says: thirdly, how it becomes effective <note>original: "effi." for "efficiens"</note> and how it is humoral—whether putrid or not putrid. An effective fever occurs when heat remains in the spirit <term>spiritus: in medieval medicine, a subtle substance that circulates through the body to carry life-force and heat</term>, which is a weaker body, namely in the manner of a substance because it is subtle and thin.

<margin>a</margin>
**And of this kind.** He assigns the causes of this blockage of the paths of the veins and their flow, and touches on three modes of blockages according to three types of causes. Namely, a blockage which physicians call "attenuating" <note>original: "attenuatoria"</note> due to the matter in the passage, which may be faulty due to its volume, thickness, or stickiness. A "constricting" <note>original: "coartatoria"</note> blockage arises from the narrowing of the walls due to cold or an abscess <term>apostema: a swelling or internal gathering of pus/fluid</term>. Finally, he mentions blockages from a growth within the vein, for example, a wart. This must be remembered from the second part of the first book, and the fourteenth part of the third book. But you might ask in which vein such a thing could grow. It should be said: in some large internal branch, or over a large portion of the orifices, or as mentioned previously, over a large part of the skin due to ulcers or burns. However, it is rare that this happens, and if it does, what would be the specific essential cause? Since that cause would be inseparable, the effective fever would also be inseparable. Nevertheless, other causes like anger, when joined to this fleshy blockage, excite the fever more than if that blockage did not exist. Secondly, you might say these causes are extrinsic, such as a tightening cold. It must be said that I am speaking of a fact arising from an intrinsic cause, or it must be said that the blockage of the paths is among the intrinsic causes termed "corporeal," even though their causes can be extrinsic. This is similar to what can be said of "solidity," which is called an extrinsic cause and was discussed above. It should be said that this discourse extends to all causes of blockages which he wishes to recall from the first book—not that all those blockages are the cause of an effective fever, and specifically the fever discussed in this chapter, but rather blockages from matter, which is apparent from what he adds: "because the body in this state consists of a great deal of matter."

<margin>b</margin>
**And these.** He posits seven canons <note>rules or principles</note>. The first is known since he posits the cause "because the body consists of a great deal of matter," and because of this, it is more prone to becoming putrid. Also, it is not prepared to be ignited in the same way as the limbs. In the second canon, he posits certain accidents <note>symptoms or secondary occurrences</note>.

<margin>c</margin>
**Adherence.** That is, continuity, just as the inflammation is continuous while the blockage remains.

<margin>d</margin>
**Middle** between igneous. You may ask where the other extreme is. Some say he means between igneous and red, or between citrine <note>yellow</note> and red. Alternatively, "between igneous" means between degrees of "fire-like" heat that is not a weak heat (as in mild ephemeral fevers) nor a strong heat (as in putrid choleric fevers). The third canon is known. Regarding the fourth canon, he says that if the primary blockages are strong, then such an ephemeral fever passes into a putrid fever, as Galen says in the eighth book of *Therapeutics* <note>original: "Sal. viii. tera."</note>. It should be said that if they are extremely strong, such that both the paths of the veins and the pores in the skin are blocked, then it passes into a putrid state. Avicenna does not mean this [specifically here], for he says "they are not thickening" <note>original: "inspissantes"</note>; he means therefore that they are not extremely strong, but only strong enough. Some, however, say "they are not thickening" means they are not from an extrinsic cause, for example, from the coldness of the air, because such an ephemeral fever is not long-lasting; rather, it is easily removed. Regarding the fifth canon:

**It is doubted** how an ephemeral fever can have paroxysms <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or intensification of symptoms, like a "fit" of fever</term> since it is an established fever. Furthermore, because of the "fixity" of the blockage, he says it is fixed—not that it happens and returns in paroxysms. It must be said that true ephemeral fevers, which arise from pure primitive causes (for example, the heat of the sun), do not have paroxysms; that is, they do not depend on movable matter. But you might say: just as one putrid humor predisposes another so that the paroxysm returns, so too a spirit currently inflamed predisposes another. It should be said that putrefaction is a final disposition in the humor resulting from a prior disposition of the humor; therefore, a putrid humor is not generated immediately, but becomes putrid after its generation by the trace of "evil heat." The spirit, however, does not predispose the heart in such a way that when the spirit that first caused the fever recedes, evaporates, or is tempered, another inflamed spirit is generated just like the first. Nor do spirits impress an evil disposition in the way humors do, because humors are thick. Those ephemeral fevers called "true" do not paroxysm, but those that arise from blockages can; this is because the entire blockage might persist or recede, or because while one blockage remains fixed, the vapors multiplied in a certain space evaporate and then accumulate again, or because the blockage, though standing, varies by increasing or decreasing. This is just as if the blocking humor were regenerated and then resolved. This is what he means when he says "it happens and returns because of the fixity of the blockage." That is, although the blockage remains fixed, it can be explained that the fever happens, stays, and subsequently recedes due to its withdrawal. The sixth canon is known. The seventh canon can be understood in two ways because of the first point. It should be known that the phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy: the practice of opening a vein to draw blood for therapeutic purposes</term> which we would perform in this ephemeral fever would be from the left basilic vein <note>original: "basilica sinistra"</note> because through it, vaporous repletion is removed, as stated in the third canon, Fen 11, in the chapter on general canons for curing evil complexions of the heart. And by this phlebotomy, it happens that the fever is cured once the vapors are removed. But it sometimes happens that a commotion occurs in the blood of the left or right side, and from this, pain can follow. Then there is no excuse for phlebotomy; nor does an abscess follow from it, especially since it is a sign that the repletion is of blood; thus phlebotomy was beneficial. However, it remains for your consideration whether it should be from the same side or the opposite. For the text is explained thus: "it causes pain to happen," namely in some part after phlebotomy is performed on the left side (from the left basilic vein). The second explanation is that phlebotomy, from whichever side it is performed, sometimes causes pain to occur on the left side because that melancholic blood is agitated by the phlebotomy and is not drawn out in the first bleeding. Then it is not necessary to repeat it according to the method that seems right to you. Perhaps he means in the left side of the chest when phlebotomy of the right side preceded it, causing a commotion of the blood without its removal. In the repetition of phlebotomy, you must attend to the time: whether on the same day or the following, whether from the same side or another, and whether something else allows for thinning or adapting the blood or not. All of this you must learn from other sources.

<column-break/>

**it will be** an ephemeral fever. When, therefore, it inflames within the blood, it is the famous species called *synocha* <term>synocha: a type of non-putrid, continuous inflammatory fever caused by an excess of blood</term>, which we shall discuss; it is among the highest of the humoral fevers, and it is not due to putrefaction but rather due to inflammation and boiling. But if that passes into putridity, which the blockage and the deprivation of respiration cause, it changes into "putrid fevers" and the like. Indeed, the blockage occurs either from a multitude of humors and blood, or from their thickness, or from their stickiness, or because of some incident among the causes of blockage in the "instrument" <note>the body's vessels</note> rather than in the flow—such as constricting cold, or a narrowing abscess, or the growth of something, or other things you must remember. And this specific fever among ephemeral fevers changes slightly into "hectic" fever <term>ethica: a slow, consuming fever often associated with wasting diseases like tuberculosis</term>, because the body in this state has a great deal of matter. In this fever, there is again thirst, inflammation, an adherence of heat, and urine that is intermediate between igneous and normal. This fever is difficult to recognize, as its appearance is very close to that of the humoral fevers. This fever sometimes remains until the third day, and in the period following that, there are many strong blockages. These are "thickening" <note>making the humors more dense</note> but not "condensing" from the outside. If they are small, the fever's eradication is quick, provided there is no error in treatment. This fever among ephemeral fevers sometimes happens and returns because of the fixity of the blockage, which is the reason why paroxysms occur. This fever often changes into coldness and shivering <note>original: "horripilationem"</note>, which signifies that it has become putrid. And when the fever from blockage causes pain after phlebotomy in the left side, there is no excuse for repeating the phlebotomy, especially when the fever subsides but the pain persists. **Signs:** Sometimes ephemeral fever occurs not from a

<margin>e</margin>
**Signs.** First, he provides the preliminary identifying signs. Second, the true ones (where it says "verifying"). He posits three signs: first, that it does not arise from a "primitive" (external) cause. For example, the heat of the sun. This leads to a "remote estimation" <note>diagnosis by exclusion</note> because other fevers besides the ephemeral and those from blockages can arise without a primitive cause. The second sign is a "long decline," though this is not exclusive to this fever alone. The third is declining without evacuation—namely, the sweat characteristic of a true ephemeral fever, which is similar to natural sweat. This too could apply to other fevers, although it applies very much to that which arises from blockage. Therefore he adds: "Estimation," and then what follows.

<margin>f</margin>
**And verifying.** He posits signs of "repletion" <note>over-fullness</note> from raw, thick, and sticky humors, and signs of blood repletion when he says: "And in those where the cause is repletion," namely of blood. These are things intended to be known from the first canon, second Fen, in the chapter on signs of the dominance of humors.

<margin>g</margin>
**Pulse** is small. Some say this occurs when it passes into a putrid state. But if you consider the excessive blockage and the multitude of matter, these can make the pulse small even before it turns putrid.

<margin>h</margin>
**Cure.** First, he posits the cure more at the beginning; second, in the progress after evacuation (where it says "then it is necessary"). The first part is in three sections: first, he posits the cure for that which arises from blockage caused by repletion and multitude; second, for that which arises from thick, sticky humors.

<margin>i</margin>
**Then.** The last canon. A general rule on this from Galen, book 8 of *Therapeutics*, which suggests two

<margin>a</margin>
**cause** that is primitive <term>primitive cause: an external triggering factor, like heat, cold, or exhaustion</term>, and it has a long decline; then consider that it is a blockage, specifically when it declines without evacuation but with moisture. And to verify your estimation: look for signs of repletion in bodies with a lot of blood and those who generate it, or those with thick and sticky humors. The difference between the two is that if the blockages in them are due to the thickness and stickiness of the humors, the known signs signify them: there is no inflammation of the body, no redness, no distension—at most, just signs of volume. But in those where the cause is repletion [of blood], there are signs of repletion: redness of the face, swelling of the veins, puffiness, tension, and other visible signs. If the blockages are excessive, the pulse is small; if they are not excessive, the pulse need not be diminished. **Cure:** When the cause is a multitude of humors and repletion, you must hurry in the beginning to phlebotomy and evacuation. If you perform phlebotomy while he is not currently feverish, that is better. Sometimes he is feverish; if it is not an emergency, then waiting is more suitable, for phlebotomy makes the humors flow and mixes them together. If, however, there is no excuse [for delay], then phlebotomy and evacuation should not be postponed or slowed. Afterward, apply yourself to things that open the blockages and cleanse the passages. Do not rush to cleanse the passages and open them at the same time as the evacuation. For that might perhaps become a cause for drawing the humors suddenly toward certain passages and making them stick there. This is a matter in which there are many errors; perhaps it increases the blockages if the humors are thick, especially if the passages are naturally narrow. **When** phlebotomy and evacuation sometimes draw out sticky, smoky superfluities that cause constriction by their...

points. Third, he posits the regimen of food (where it says "And food"). The first part is in two: first, he posits the cure through evacuation; second, through agents (where it says "then let it be"). He therefore commands evacuation and gives a suitable hour. But why did he say "multitude," "repletion," and "evacuation"? It should be said that he said "multitude and repletion" meaning a filling multitude in which phlebotomy is directly suitable. But "evacuation" will be with clysters <note>enemas</note> or other things that cleanse the blood, among which is cassia pulp. He said "multitude" regarding the fault of blood alone, insofar as it happens in *synocha* without putrefaction, and in this, phlebotomy is suitable. "Repletion" refers to the fault of other humors in the blood; in such a case, phlebotomy is first suitable to evacuate that humor. Avicenna wants you to know all this; it would be from the first book... and universal pharmacy is useful in the beginning, and particular pharmacy in the hour of rest. Let the evacuation happen in the beginning for fear of falling into putrefaction, for once it is invigorated, it is not easily endured. As in the commentary: "We do not stand thus at the beginning of diseases to loosen them." He says the same regarding phlebotomy. This is presumed to be sufficiently known from the first book on phlebotomy, and the third canon, Fen 11, the canon on quinsy <term>squinantia: an old term for tonsillitis or a peritonsillar abscess that restricts breathing</term>. However, in the hour of rest, because then some humor is at fault along with the blood, or it ought to be at fault less; it is separated from the blood and more easily drawn out by phlebotomy. Because after a paroxysm has occurred, some humor is more fit to be eliminated by phlebotomy; but then the blood is corrupted and mixed with an evil, corruptive mixture. If, however, there were a great necessity—for example, fear of suffocation or fear of a stomach seizure—one chooses the lesser evil during the paroxysm. Regarding the pharmacy that is most suitable then, it is well known.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of ephemeral fevers (febris epimera) caused by blockages. It transitions into the specific treatment protocols involving bloodletting, baths, and dietary management, before moving to Chapter 24, which addresses fevers caused by "nauseating satiety"—what we would today call severe indigestion or overeating.</meta>

<margin>a</margin> He gives reasons why he wants opening and cleansing medicines from the outside not to be given before phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, a standard medieval treatment for balancing humors</term>, or while a great multitude of humors remains. The first reason is that before the evacuation, the matter is stirred up by these opening and cleansing agents (for example, syrup of roots), and this adds to the blockage <note>original: "oppilatio"</note>; a sudden, thin flow blocks the passages no less than thick, sticky matter. The second reason is that it is possible that phlebotomy alone might cure such a fever so that it does not fall into a putrid state. Therefore, it is not helpful to start with diuretics <note>original: "diureticis"</note>; he says this properly because such a phlebotomy in this fever acts against the blockage of the veins caused by an excess of blood, which is nothing other than a true "synocha" <term>synocha: a continuous fever caused by an excess of blood (the sanguine humor)</term>. But since this can be cured by phlebotomy alone, no other remedy is needed, and in this state, we can evacuate blood even until the patient feels faint.

<margin>c</margin> **And if not.** It is doubted whether phlebotomy should be performed here; this seems inconvenient if there are thick and sticky humors, as noted in the fourth book of *On Regulating Health* <note>original: "de re. fa." for "De regimine sanitatis"</note> and the first book of the *Canon* <note>original: "cañ." for "Canon" of Avicenna</note>. Furthermore, it suggests that sometimes excessive phlebotomy might be performed, which seems wrong. It must be said that if sticky and thick humors are in the blood separately, you do not need phlebotomy, but you might need a pharmaceutical <note>original: "farmatia"</note> to reduce them, since it is not entirely "rawness" <note>original: "cruditas," meaning undigested matter</note>. If, however, they are mixed with the blood, a "diminishing" phlebotomy is appropriate, and perhaps even a strong one when you need a powerful evacuation, specifically once the matter has been "digested" <term>digestion: in medieval medicine, the process where humors are thinned or cooked by the body's heat so they can be expelled</term>. In this fever, you primarily need to open the passages and evacuate as much as possible without harm. You must modify the opening and cleansing agents; though they should be strong because of the thickness of the humors, the presence of the fever requires you to move from weak to strong doses carefully.

<margin>b</margin> These treatments should prevent the fever from turning into a putrid state. You should continue even until the patient is close to fainting, provided you do not sense a great multitude of humors but rather sense blockages <note>original: "oppilations"</note> caused by their thickness and stickiness. In that case, you might not need excessive phlebotomy, but rather "opening" treatments. This opening is done with cleansing medicines and foods. Because the illness is a fever, you cannot use hot cleansing agents; rather, use those ranging from pure vinegar syrup <note>original: "syrupu3 acetosuz"</note> to that made with seeds, or from endive water to fennel water. The food should be that which washes away matter and lacks stickiness, such as barley water <note>original: "kist ordei," likely referring to ptisana</note>. Since this food is opening and cleansing, it is not bad to mix it with barley water. Finally, you must observe: after you have evacuated (if evacuation was necessary), see if the fever lessens and if the fever-fit <note>original: "porismos"</note> is weaker than the first one. Consider the urine; if you find it is not lacking in "digestion," and if the pulse does not signify putrefaction, proceed with this regimen. Put the patient in a bath on the third day after the fever-fit during the time the pores are softening, waiting until five hours have passed if the fever lasts that long. Anoint and rub him with cleansing things like bean flour, vetch flour, lily root, or birthwort <note>original: "aristologie"</note>, softened with a little honey and water. If you dare to use something stronger, use the foam of saltpeter <note>original: "spuma barauc," likely baurac/borax or saltpeter</note>. If the bath alters his nature or causes shivering, do not stay in it, as these blockages are not the kind a bath opens. When he leaves the bath, he should not eat or drink wine until the danger of the fever-fit has passed.

<margin>d</margin> **Next.** Care must be placed especially on the process after the bath and friction. First, he shows what to consider before approaching the bath; second, what should be done upon exiting. Regarding the first part, he mentions seven conditions for using the bath. First, that evacuation has already been performed. Second, that the fever is declining overall, or at least the fit <note>original: "paroxismus"</note> is decreasing. If it were not in decline, the bath might agitate the matter. Third, that the urine shows signs of "digestion." Different texts say different things here, but Galen <note>original: "Gal."</note> says there should be no sign of indigestion in the urine. The fourth condition is the pulse. Fifth, it should be the third day. It should be done five hours before a future fit. Finally, he mentions anointing and rubbing. The seventh condition is that if bad accidents occur that suggest putrefaction, do not stay in the bath, because these blockages are prone to turning into a putrid fever and are not easily removed by a bath.

<margin>e</margin> **From where therefore.** He wants to delay food until the suspect hour of the fever-fit has passed, but it is useful to feed the patient if he cannot tolerate the lack of food. If you have treated him well, continue with the bath and food. But if the urine is "raw," it is turning into a putrid fever.

<column-break/>

**Sometimes it happens.** Here he determines the nature of ephemeral fever from indigestion or from "nauseating satiety." First, he gives the manner of its arrival and its rules; second, the signs; third, the cure. Indigestion can be the corruption of food in the stomach or diminished digestion. This refers to food turning sour or smoky <note>original: "fumosuz"</note>. But it is doubted why this fever is not said to come from the corruption of the liver. It should be said that such a fever would be a "putrid humoral" fever. Because "chyle" <term>chyle: the milky fluid produced from food in the stomach before it becomes blood</term> is more distant from us than the humors, it can be reduced to primary causes. This is specifically when only the vapor is inflamed and not putrid. This is a point of speculation mentioned above regarding Galen and the first chapter on causes.

<margin>f</margin> **And properly.** First, he shows the bodies that are disposed to this; second, the disposition itself. A "choleric" <term>choleric: a person with a temperament dominated by yellow bile, usually hot and dry</term> person might have a cold stomach, meaning their pores are not wide; because of the corruption of stomach digestion, they will breathe out smoky vapors rather than sour ones, and the narrowness of the pores prevents these from being drawn out.

If his nature allows him to eat a little and he can tolerate it, give him a drink that opens the passages, such as thin barley water cooked with parsley. If the fever-fit does not repeat, then use baths and feed him. If the fit is diminished and the urine is good, trust in the cure. But if the fit returns as strong or stronger and the urine is bad, the sickness is tending toward putrefaction, and its treatment is the treatment for putrid fever.

### On ephemeral fever from nauseating
### satiety and repletion. Lesson 24.

**Sometimes** it happens that from a nauseating satiety, bad vapors arise, from which heat occurs; the spirits are inflamed, and thus a fever happens. This occurs especially in choleric bodies and in those who do not have wide pores. For the majority of their superfluities <note>original: "superfluitatum," waste products of digestion</note> evaporate as smoky vapors, and sour belching is diminished in them. Those most strongly disposed to this are people who start exercising, moving, or going under the sun or bathing immediately after a nauseating meal. In these people, smoky vapors multiply, especially when they have pain in their bodies, specifically in their viscera.

<margin>g</margin> **And of those.** The cause is that these actions immediately cause the corruption of food in the stomach, move the matter, and prevent evacuation through the bowels or vomiting. They also increase heat.

<margin>h</margin> **Regarding matter.** We must consider the food matter itself and the sour vapor. Therefore, he says two things about the matter.

Regarding the matter of sour belching, it rarely happens that it generates a fever. If it does, it will be weak; indeed, usually, it is not generated at all.

**And we believe** that what is generated from sour belching is nothing but nauseating satiety. These people are greatly helped when their bowels are loosened, and their fever is removed because the excess smoky superfluity is expelled. The treatment differs between those whose bowels are naturally retained and those whose bowels are loose.

<margin>i</margin> **And in those having.** It is doubted because if a fever is generated, it seems it should be a strong one because it would be putrid. It is said that the corruption of food into something sour usually happens from cold; therefore, neither the matter nor the vapor causes a fever, but rather they dull the heat. However, sometimes such corruption happens from a weak, "boiling" heat, and then an ephemeral fever can occur, which will be sharper. Avicenna <note>original: "Auic."</note> says such a fever could be called putrid, so he says it is "not generated"—meaning not as a pure ephemeral fever.

<margin>k</margin> **And we believe.** It is doubted here whether the effect is the cause. Some say the text is corrupt. Others say that if an ephemeral fever comes from sour matter, it is because of some accidental cause, like new heat added to that matter. Alternatively, the sour vapor might add to the nauseating satiety by cooling the stomach.

<margin>l</margin> **And these.** Here he sets out the rules. These are the ones having ephemeral fever from nauseating satiety.

<margin>m</margin> **And if nature.** Some say phlebotomy weakens the power of the liver to hold humors. But consider that a person with this fever might have much inflamed blood in the liver. Once they have evacuated the corrupted food, we perform phlebotomy, and nature—being relieved—expels the bad matter. Another disposition would be much corruption in the stomach and intestines and "sharp bile" <note>original: "cholera acuta"</note> near the liver, where the color of the urine might deceive you.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ephemeral fevers—brief fevers lasting only a day or so—specifically those caused by "nauseating satiety" (severe indigestion or overeating). It moves from describing the physiological symptoms, such as the effect on the liver and heart, to the practical treatment protocols in Chapter 35, involving evacuations, digestive aids, and specific dietary recovery.</meta>

...and corrupts the materials in the liver <note>original: "epate"</note>, and bad vapors ascend to the heart, from which those accidents <term>accidents: in medieval medicine, "accidents" refer to symptoms or secondary occurrences of a disease</term> occur which he writes about. Then the corrupted materials return from the liver to the intestines with manifest sharp acidity; and then there is a flow of the liver—I do not mean a hepatic flux caused by washing, but from the corruption of the materials around the liver. This entire discourse could also refer to a phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy: the practice of opening a vein to draw blood to balance the body's humors</term> performed recently when a person has evacuated three times and it is believed the corruption of food is finished; if phlebotomy is performed then, a strong flux and a hepatic flow follow.

<margin>a</margin> And they resemble the discourse insofar as this shows that a person is deceived by these symptoms, believing there is a fullness indicating a need for phlebotomy, when in fact these symptoms do not arise from fullness—namely, of a nauseating satiety—but rather the whole thing occurs from those hot fumes.

<margin>b</margin> Three days. Within which time it is believed that digestion has been rectified and those bad materials in the stomach have been evacuated.

<margin>c</margin> And know. I believe these periods <note>original: "piodos," likely referring to paroxysms or cycles</note> arise from the repeated corruptions of food as often as a man takes food, namely dinner or lunch. And it hints that perhaps up to seven corruptions of food could remain, which the healthy pulse shows—that is, not indicating putrefaction. Yet eventually, it would pass into a putrid corruption communicated to the humors; it is difficult, though possible, to imagine periods arising from the corruption of food in a single instance.

<margin>d</margin> Signs also. Against what was said above: that it is not generated by acidic belching. It should be said that he was implying it is rarely generated that way.

<margin>e</margin> Urine deprived of digestion and watery. Against what he said above, that the urine is red. It should be said that these signs belong to the one who has acidic belching; for above he already laid out the signs of an ephemeral fever for one who has smoky belches, to which he said the symptoms are similar, etc. Or it is understood to be watery, meaning thin in substance, even if it is tinted in color.

...be eased by two or three evacuations; then let him be bled, and a strong flux of the belly may follow upon it, and perhaps a hepatic flux will occur, which we shall signify by the pulse of the heart and the blackness of the tongue. <margin>c</margin> And the symptoms of an ephemeral fever from fullness are similar to the symptoms of a fever from anger: for the eyes and face grow very red, and there is a powerful inflammation, and the pulse becomes large and fast, and the urine is red. <margin>i</margin> Furthermore, when it lasts longer, it does not exceed three days <margin>b</margin>. <margin>h</margin> And know that an ephemeral fever from nauseating satiety sometimes comes with four or seven paroxysms, and with this, it is an ephemeral fever, yet its pulse is healthy. Signs: <margin>d</margin> Its signs are a change in belching toward acidity or smokiness. Therefore, when the belching changes back to health, it indicates recovery. And indeed, the urine of these patients is deprived of digestion and is watery <margin>e</margin>. And when the cause of the nauseating satiety is wakefulness, there is a swelling in the face and throat, and a heaviness in their eyelids.

->### Of the Cure. Chapter 35.<-

<margin>f</margin> **A patient** with this nauseating satiety is not evacuated unless his nature is either loose or not loose. <margin>g</margin> If his nature is not loose, then it is necessary to loosen it; and if there is any food, or waste, or heaviness remaining in the stomach, then it will be necessary to make him vomit, and afterward you shall loosen him. Consider <margin>h</margin> where he finds the heaviness. <margin>i</margin> And consider then whether it is better to evacuate that with clysters <term>clysters: enemas used to clear the bowels</term> and suppositories, or with something he drinks from above so that it may loosen, or settle, or digest. The nature of the belching signifies which is better; for perhaps it will be necessary, if the food is stuck firmly and vomiting is difficult, not to look toward the fever but to administer *diapiperon* <term>diapiperon: a digestive medicine made primarily of pepper</term> so that it may precipitate and descend with digestion; or let something weaker than it be administered, and let an embrocation <note>a liquid medicine rubbed on the body</note> and digestive plasters, known from the chapter on digestion, and laxatives, known from the chapter on loosening, be applied. <margin>l</margin> Therefore, when it has descended, then it will either exit by itself or be assisted with a suppository, and hunger should be endured by him, just...

<column-break/>

...when the corruption is toward the acidic. Although it rarely happens, or otherwise in corruption toward the smoky, he intends to alter the bad complexion <term>complexion: the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in the body</term> toward another quality; then it is not appropriate, and we do not make such an alteration in the beginning while the food remains, but once it has been evacuated, as appears at the end of the chapter. Or he intends to address the corrupted food, and this is done in two ways: either to settle it—and simple *diapiperon* can do this by the power of the chyme <note>the pulpy acidic fluid that passes from the stomach to the small intestine</note>—or to rectify it, and then it is possible to imagine some parts of the corrupted food which are more coarse and diminished in strength. And although the thin parts were corrupted into smoke, those coarse parts could return to a diminished digestion, which was helped so that digestion might be completed by simple *diapiperon*; and perhaps we need something weaker than that. <margin>q</margin> Alexander, however, rebukes Galen <term>Galen: a famous Greek physician whose work formed the basis of medieval medicine</term> regarding this precept, as appears in the chapter on the corruption of food; however, Galen can be defended in the manner aforesaid.

...as long as no hesitation remains in the destruction of the nauseating satiety; then let him take light food of quick digestion and good chyme, and let the intention be toward hunger and sleep, which alone relieves the anxiety of alleviating the fullness. <margin>m</margin> But if his nature is loose, consider whether the thing being evacuated is that which is corrupted. And if it does so, it should not be restrained until the whole is evacuated, even to its very last part; and wait for the decline of the paroxysm <note>original: "porismi," likely a typo or variant for paroxysm</note>, and then have him enter a bath and feed him, unless there was an excessive flow destroying his strength. In that case, do not have him enter a bath; rather, feed him and comfort <margin>m</margin> his stomach with things you know, some of which are written in the chapters on the loosening of the belly, and among those is wool soaked in oil in which there is an astringent power, or even in oil of nard after it has been pressed and the greatest part of the oil separated from it. <margin>n</margin> And if the loosening persists <margin>r</margin> and you find that what is exiting is not of the kind that was corrupted, mix in warm, fresh oil of quinces <note>original: "cydonys"</note> according to this method, and oil of mastic; and oil of nard is not contrary to them. <margin>o</margin> And perhaps we have administered wax-salves <margin>s</margin> specifically when the condition does not tolerate the tightness of wool over their bellies. And sometimes we need stronger plasters, as with the plasters mentioned for the choleric passion; and give them fruit waters to drink if they can tolerate them, and give him to eat that which has light nourishment and is easy to digest, such as cock's testicles and "stony" fish <note>original: "pisces aradrach," likely referring to rock-dwelling fish considered healthy</note>, and precede that with some fruits and juices and astringent syrups <note>original: "robub stipticis"</note>.

<margin>p</margin> And if his appetite is cut off, remind <margin>r</margin> him with those things you have known, and specifically with those made of quinces. And when the evacuation is finished, it is not bad to administer a strong electuary <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made of herbs and honey</term> of those that digest and comfort the stomach and open blockages; and this should be after the removal of the fever and the symptoms. <margin>q</margin> And the path indeed to phlebotomy is that it should not be done until the fever declines; for then it may be done. And that which is first given in drink is barley water. <margin>k</margin> And let the food be like that...

<margin>i</margin> And hunger should be endured, along with sleep, so that the matter may be consumed and rectified if any of it can be rectified; and consider the amount of sleep and the hour.

<margin>k</margin> And that these [sleep and abstinence] excuse you from the anxiety that must be applied to alleviating fullness with clysters and other evacuations; for sleep during abstinence consumes those materials greatly.

<margin>l</margin> But if his nature is not excessive—namely, that which is of the flux, from which a man becomes debilitated—and this is what he calls the "destruction of strength."

<margin>m</margin> And comfort. This can be continued with the preceding discourse so that he prescribes three things: namely, the bath, food, and anointing. The order shall be: first the bath, second the anointing, third the food. And it can be continued to what he just said: namely, that if you do not use the bath because of weakness and excessive flux, you must nevertheless comfort the stomach, among which remedies is the soaked wool, etc. This precept was above in the chapter on ephemeral fever from evacuation.

<margin>n</margin> And if it persists. Here he places the final points of the cure and intends to address two symptoms: namely, the excessive flux and the loss of appetite. It has as many parts as he sets out. The first point is to constrict the excessive flux when they evacuate what is not corrupted, etc. "Warm," meaning hot, or if there is inflammation, let it be lukewarm in this manner—namely, by soaking the wool and wringing it out.

<margin>o</margin> Wax-salves <note>original: "cerota"</note>. See Galen, book 8 of the *Therapeutics* in this chapter, because these are his words there. For sometimes the sick person cannot bear the weight of wool soaked in oil, and therefore we make a wax-salve which can be applied by itself.

<margin>p</margin> Stronger. Namely, for binding the bowels in a "choleric" state. Third point: and give them fruit water to temper the heat, such as pomegranate and quince wine if the flux is excessive; and give stony fish, namely those cooked in broth; both according to Galen in the same place.

<margin>q</margin> And if it is cut off, etc.

<margin>r</margin> Apply. Namely, that which is cut off. You have known this in the third point. And "with the evacuation," meaning when the evacuation is finished. "Strong electuary," meaning while the evacuation is occurring, one powerful enough to act as *calamentum* <note>a mint-like herb</note>. Or "with evacuation," a remedy you wish to make penetrate the members; and because *diacalamentum* is hot, Avicenna <term>Avicenna: a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university text</term> fears for the fever and symptoms—namely, of inflammations, even if there were no fever.

<margin>s</margin> And the path, etc., "declines." Namely, the paroxysm, and once the evacuation of corrupted foods from the stomach and intestine is done; and that which is done before phlebotomy or before the fever declines, for he needs some drink because of strong thirst. Food, namely while the fever stands in the beginning or during the increase or the general state...
