<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of ephemeral fevers—brief, one-day fevers—transitioning from dietary causes to fevers caused by internal and external abscesses, as well as environmental factors like heat and suppressed habits. The text relies heavily on Avicenna's "Canon of Medicine," examining how localized inflammation affects the heart and overall body temperature.</meta>

...be given, etc., in which rhubarb <note>original: "reubarbarum"</note> is not included: because they are colder: and consider that Avicenna <note>original: "Auic."</note> already intended for some evacuation of the corrupted material to have been performed when you are below, if it is possible.

<margin>a Fevers. Here he determines the nature of fevers from internal abscesses and swellings: and first he gives the method of occurrence; second, the signs; third, the cure—the parts are evident. However, there are diverse ephemeral fevers according to the diversity of the abscesses; moreover, the abscess is diversified by location and cause. First, therefore, he determines the ephemeral fevers according to the diversity of the locations of the abscesses, in which discourse he speaks of other fevers. Second, according to the diversity of the causes, there where he says, "And for the most part." The first part is in two: first he posits which fevers follow internal abscesses; second, which follow external ones, there where he says, "But visible abscesses." One might doubt here: it does not seem that fevers following internal abscesses are putrid, because they are either continuous, and this is not the case because the matter of continuous fever is inside the veins, as stated in the second book on crises and the second on the differences of fevers; and first: they do not cease: as Galen <note>original: "Gal."</note> says in the commentary on the aphorism "whosoever fevers." It must be said that fevers of internal abscesses are for the most part continuous because the material continuously fumes toward the heart due to three causes: namely, because of the multitude of the material; and because of proximity; and because of the width of the veins; and they can sometimes be intermittent, even disordered, as will appear in the fourth treatise; nor is it inconvenient that the material of a continuous fever be outside the veins, namely in abscesses. It is doubted here if they are hectic fevers <term>hectic: "ethica," a wasting fever affecting the solid parts of the body</term> since they do not have a bodily cause. It must be said that internal abscesses, because of a strong putrid fever and the resolution of the nourishing members, can produce a hectic fever, and the cause of that will be bodily in its becoming, not in its completed state. Whether it be possible for these obscure internal abscesses to follow an ephemeral fever: we believe indeed it is not impossible.</margin>

**F**evers following internal abscesses <note>original: "apata," abbreviation for apostemata</note> are putrid. And sometimes a hectic fever is associated with them, and they are not numbered among the ephemeral <term>ephemeral: "ephimerarum," fevers lasting only a day</term> fevers. But visible abscesses, such as boils and eruptions or buboes <term>buboes: "bubones," inflammatory swelling of a lymph gland</term> that happen in them: and specifically large abscesses which occur in the glandular members and in the flesh called soft: such as those that occur in the groin from the superfluities of the liver: and in the armpits from the superfluities of the heart: and under the ear from the superfluities of the brain: sometimes fevers follow them. And they are not cleared away without that which comes from them reaching the heart: until either heat alone ignites it: or heat with putrefaction <note>original: "putredine"</note>: for if it were heat alone, then it will be of the genus of fevers of internal abscesses. And for the most part, what happens regarding these fevers following abscesses that follow primitive causes—both from ulcers and scabies and pains and blows and falls to which materials are expelled and retained in the passages, near the soft flesh—is of the genus of ephemeral fever. And for the most part, what happens regarding these fevers following abscesses whose causes are antecedent <note>meaning pre-existing conditions</note>, such as past fullnesses and blockages, are putrid; and in this way, the fevers are the roots and the abscesses follow, although sometimes it happens the other way around. **H**ippocrates named these fevers "malignant," both those which are ephemeral and those which are not ephemeral. **A**nd indeed, the fevers following them are for the most part ephemeral: and if they are not ephemeral, they are bad. And for the most part, these follow blood-related abscesses: and sometimes they occur following erysipelas <term>erysipelas: "herisipilam," a bacterial skin infection known as St. Anthony's Fire</term> and things similar to it.

<margin>b But abscesses etc. That is, small hot abscesses. Eruptions are hot abscesses tending toward the surface. Or buboes are properly hot abscesses in the cleansing places <note>the lymph nodes</note>: but broadly for any external eruption and so it ends, i.e., and therefore he says "or which," namely, that which first comes into them. Eruption: because then inflation occurs. Let the text be continued thus: "Visible abscesses sometimes follow fevers." And consider that he did not say "they follow ephemeral fevers," because putrid ones can follow: and therefore he distinguished "It will be of the genus of fevers of abscesses," i.e., of the ephemeral ones which follow abscesses. And thus one Jewish translation has it. And this therefore appears: that if a fever follows putrefaction, as toward an abscess, it is not then putrid unless the putrefaction reaches the heart: as in the first book on the differences of fevers, chapter five.</margin>

**F**igure. Their signs are: those things which we said regarding the preceding of the abscesses before them: and the face is inflamed and red, and there is an addition in it beyond the disposition of health: and it is not a fiercely stinging heat. What is the multitude of it in them: since these abscesses are blood-related: unless they are fevers following erysipelas: and then a moistening follows these fevers, and the pulse in them is rapid, which is treated with wild chicory <note>original: "agresta"</note> with gourd and a few almonds. And let its location be cooled, and its fragrance, and troches <term>troches: medicinal lozenges</term> of camphor in which rhubarb is not put.

### On ephemeral fever and abscesses. Chapter 36.

<margin>c And for the most part. He posits the diversity of fevers according to the diversity of the abscesses, which are diversified by the manner of their causes: and first from the manner of the causes diversified by genus; second, by species, there: "the second." And for the most part, the first of these is in three parts. First, he shows which fevers follow abscesses following primitive causes. Second, those following bodily causes, there: "the second," and "for the most part." There: "the third," and "fevers." It is doubted how ulcers and scabies are primitive causes, since they are bodily causes. It must be said that he intends by ulcers "primitive causes making ulceration," such as a cut with a sword. By scabies, they also understand excoriation <term>excoriation: the peeling or rubbing away of skin</term>. Pain, however, in one part: as in the foot, it sometimes draws an "ignis" <note>likely an inflammatory abscess</note> to which a primitive cause is compared. Or it must be said that the said causes are not properly called primitive except in respect to blockages or fullnesses: which although they are mediated, they more directly cause the abscess. Since, therefore, these abscesses are made from the said primitive causes, it signifies a good disposition in the humors. Wherefore they are not prepared for putrefaction: wherefore more pure inflammation and ephemeral fever will occur. But when they occur from antecedent causes: then they are prepared for putrefaction, wherefore more putrid fevers are made from them.</margin>

<column-break/>

Great and frequent pain because of fullness and heat: and the urine is watery and white because of the course of the materials to the abscesses and ulcers.

**C**ure. **I**t is necessary that a precursor be made in it with phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy: bloodletting</term> and a flux of the belly <term>flux: here, a bowel movement or laxative effect</term>. **A**nd let the abscess be treated with that which is necessary in its own chapter: and let the regimen be subtle: and let him not drink wine at all: and let him not be fed except after the complete decline <note>of the fever paroxysm</note>, and necessary for him are extinguishing, cooling, and moistening things: and plasters cooled with snow upon the sick, abscessed member: so that they do not harm the abscess nor make it raw; rather, let the path between it and the heart be cooled with a cooling that penetrates into the depth.

### On ephemeral fever from "earthiness," i.e., from which it becomes hard like a shell. Chapter 37.

**T**his fever again follows the cessation of resolution <term>resolution: the body's natural process of dispersing inflammation or perspiration</term> because of blockages that are not deep-seated. **A**nd indeed many men, when they abandon their customs of bathing, fall into fevers. **A**nd many of them are those in whose bodies choleric vapor <term>choleric vapor: fumes from yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness</term> is generated because of the complexion of their bodies and their food and their bad water: and because of their preceding dispositions from wakefulness. **I**ts cure is extinction and the administration of a bath: and to sweat in it after the decline. And to be rubbed with those things which are like bran and bean-meal, and bitter almonds, and melon seed, and something of "alufen" <note>likely wood-ash or alkali</note> and borax <note>original: "baurac"</note>. **A**nd let his food be extinguishing and moistening, and let his wine be of a very great mixture <note>diluted with much water</note>, and let the bath be repeated many times.

### Ephemeral fever from heat. Chapter 38.

**S**ometimes it happens from the heat of the air and the heat of a bath and similar things to ephemeral fevers. **A**nd for the most part, that does not happen except from the intensity of the heat of the sun, which is its own suspension with the animal spirit <term>animal spirit: "spiritu animali," the subtle substance believed to carry sensation through the nerves</term>; since the first thing to be harmed by it is the head. For its air heats up and reaches the heart, and a fever occurs; then it is spread into the whole body. And sometimes its suspension occurs with the heart because of the heat of the breath: and sometimes the head is guarded from the heat. But that which is from the sun happens for the most part beginning in the brain and head, and because of that, for one who is not "clean" <note>meaning one with excess humors</note>, his head is filled:

<margin>d And fevers. This is the fourth part. In buboes, etc. One might doubt: there seems to be a contradiction: because he says that fevers which follow external abscesses with preceding blockages and fullnesses are putrid, but here he says absolutely that those following external abscesses are for the most part ephemeral. It must be said in two ways: first, that perhaps the three preceding points wish to be explained differently. Namely, most external abscesses in respect to internal ones are made from primitive causes, therefore most external abscesses follow from ephemeral fever; but most internal abscesses in respect to external ones are made from bodily causes, therefore most of those are putrid fevers. Second, it must be said that by considering external abscesses absolutely, more ephemeral fevers follow them than putrid ones: and if they are putrid, they are bad: as Hippocrates said, then comparing certain external abscesses to other external ones which he said above.
e And for the most part. Because they are hot humors.
f Signs. Moistening follows. I.e., sweat with many vapors: or with some subtle dissolved humidities at the skin: let "watery white" <note>urine</note> not be understood as glass-like, but not much colored, as much as the heat of the body shows.
g Cure. He fears the drinking of wine. Let him not be fed except after the decline, i.e., the particular one. "Above," i.e., above the used part that looks toward the heart. And it is not understood that it should not be placed over particular abscesses: because this is contrary to what was said above in the first book, fourth section: and below in the third section of this one: and it is especially done when the material has already flowed to the part: as Thaddeus <note>original: "Thadeus," likely Thaddeus of Florence</note> rightly glossed here and assigns the cause to Avicenna.
h This fever. The chapter is well enough known: "and many of them," i.e., those who fall into fever having abandoned the custom of breathing <note>or perspiring</note>. "They are those" etc. because of a choleric complexion etc. because of their dispositions in wakefulness, because of heating causes from exercises in the arts: or in other "alufen," i.e., ash, alkali, or wax, or water with which the Saracens wash clothes.
i Sometimes it happens. He determines the nature of ephemeral fevers compared to causes or things that come from without. And they are five. First, he determines that which is made from heat: and first, in positing the causes, he enumerates them; second, he shows the diversity in the pores of those, there where he says "and first," he speaks of the heat of fire for those practicing arts around it: "and for the most part" etc. which more commonly occurs to us.
k And it is. First he shows which cause from the aforesaid more greatly alters the brain; second, which alters the heart, there where he says "and that which."
l And first, etc. I.e., ephemeral fever from the heat of the sun first begins, etc.
m Its air. I.e., the spirit which is of the nature of air: by which afterward the vital spirit is heated: since the animal spirit is continuous with the vital spirit: as in the third book of the Canon, first section, chapter on melancholy. Or "air," namely, that which goes to the brain to temper its heat as in the third book of the Canon, fifth section, first chapter; and such air can be communicated to the heart. Or "air," namely, surrounding the head; and lest you believe that a fever from the heat of the sun always starts with the head, he says: "and sometimes," etc., because of the heat of the breath, i.e., of the air which goes with the breath. And because of that, i.e., signs of fullness and heaviness of the head appear: if it is not "clean": and frequently it is not clean: for those humidities of the head are moved and dilated by the heat: as is used in this chapter. And consider that...</margin>

The text contrasts how different spirits (animal, vital, and natural) are affected based on the source of the heat.</meta>

Now Avicenna <note>original: "Auic."</note> says that first it is a fever which, if compared, is also a suffering, so that the expansion [of heat] is not of the essence of the fever.

It is doubted why it is only: canine [heat] <note>original: "canicularis," referring to the Dog Days of summer</note> is from the sun: he replies therefore that it impresses more on the head. Furthermore, in the sixth treatise in this chapter, he intends the same. It should be said that canine heat is partly from the sun and partly from the stars actively radiating, and this impresses more on the head; and concerning this, the word of the wise man <note>likely referring to Galen</note> is understood. Another type arises from malicious burnt vapors of the air, which he calls "poisonous" in the third [book] of the Canon, section three, chapter on the preservation of eye health: and such heat reaches the heart more. And it also reaches people standing in the shade. And otherwise, the contradiction could be removed if you consider this.

**Signs.** In the solar part, that is, in the part alone—meaning in the head alone—or in the solar part—meaning in the part that had contact with the solar rays. In the cordial [heart] part—meaning the chest moves a lot: and specifically perhaps one feels heat in the inner part of the heart: and because the heat of the heart is greater, Bartholomew said that externally it is greater, and the sign is what Avicenna introduces: and he says that properly the fever is of greater heat in the heart, but accidentally not. Otherwise, this speech is verified with respect to other fevers, not simply, and this is declared by the smallness of the panting <note>original: "fistio," referring to rapid, shallow breathing</note> in considering the heat outside. For a fever that has heat similar to the heat in this fever and proportionately corresponded inside, the heat would induce great panting; and yet in this one it does not happen: because they do not thirst much: and in this it is the opposite of that which occurs from the density of the skin from cold, which is less hot outside than inside and causes more thirst than the external heat appears.

</margin>
**Cure.** Let him not touch, etc. He fears heating. The necessity for bathing, which does two things: it excludes vapors and cools; but oil does not exclude them, as is evident.

**Sometimes it happens.** This is an ephemeral fever from the condensation of the pores caused by cold: or etc., it does not lead to that, namely the putrid fever or that one which is neither putrid nor ephemeral, because a mild vapor does not inflame; but rather, being retained, it is a cause of plethoric heat; and if it multiplies greatly, it will cause the manner of a *synochus* <note>original: "sinocho," a type of continuous fever</note>, although it could also cause an ephemeral one.

</margin>
**Signs.** Because of the closing of the pores, the vapor does not immediately appear when the hand is placed [on the skin]. The reason is that if it multiplied much, it would cause the motions of a *synochus* fever, although it can also cause an ephemeral one. The matter is in its smallness, i.e., how this fever is small. Although it is small, as Isaac said. The matter is there in resolution, i.e., the weakening of the power <note>original: "virtutis"</note> as in those. The urine is sometimes tinted: because the heat that was resolved, i.e., previously: is now not resolved: it expels, etc. Mostly therefore it is white: because the heat is obstructed by external cold: and thus let Isaac be understood in this chapter. But you say: the suffocation or muffling of the heat, how can it stand with this being a fever, etc., with those vapors? It should be said that it is muffled in degree and multiplied in quantity so that it makes a fever. Or it should be said that there is muffling in the nutrients, not in the heart, and here is a place for speculation.

And that which is not a [putrid] fever, but occurs from canine [summer] days and from bathing and from other impressions made on the heart.
### Signs.
The signs are when it occurs from the intensity of the inflammation of the head in the solar part of the brain: and perhaps it is with heaviness and fullness if the body has not been cleansed, and a greatness of breath in the cordial <note>heart</note> part. And that which appears from the body of intense heating is hotter in its interior. And concerning those, let this be known: that its thirst is less than that of one whose heat is that [kind of] heat, and in this habit it is contrary or diverse to that which is from density.
### Cure.
It is necessary to begin in its cure with that which cools and with poultices <note>original: "embrocuis"</note> over the head and chest: from cold oils: and specifically rose oil cooled over snow: which should be poured over the head and chest from a distance <note>original: "loco longinquo"</note>: and let cold water be given in drink which follows its course: and without cessation let it be done until the fever declines. Sometimes they are taken and enter a tub, and let the tub not touch him if the fever is with him: and bathe him with lukewarm water and do not permit its air to heat him. And you do not fear the pouring of hot water over his head because it moistens and resolves the fever: and the necessity for bathing is greater than the necessity for anointing. Therefore, when he comes out, then rub his head with cold oils such as rose oil and oil of water-lily <note>original: "nenufare"</note>.

#### On the ephemeral fever that occurs from cold and bathing. Ch. 39.
Sometimes it happens from cold and bathing with cold waters, and the visible pores are condensed and the smoky vapors are narrowed according to what was said of that which occurs from heat: whereby a fever occurs and many times leads to a putrid one. And it does not lead to that fever unless the suffocated vapor is sharp/acute, not mild. For mild vapor does not generate it.
### Signs
And the causes are that the body in it at first when touched is not of intense heat. When the heat is manifest and elevated, and the pulse is not in the smallness that is in that which occurs from anguish, sadness, and hunger, because there is no resolution there. But it is swift because of the necessity—that is, of drawing in air—unless there is intense cold, and perhaps the eye declines toward hardness and is not deep; indeed, sometimes it is swollen because of the narrowed vapors. And the urine is sometimes white because the heat is suffocated, and sometimes it is tinted because the heat which is resolved from the pores is expelled to the path of the urine.
### Curatio
Let them be covered in the fever until they sweat; when therefore it declines, let them enter the bath. And let them be bathed with water inclining toward heat: and with warm air: and let waters be applied to them as poultices in which have been decocted things like marjoram, dill, and water-mint <note>original: "sisfumbrium"</note>; and let them be rubbed with those things we mentioned, because they wipe the pores and soften them; and let the anointing in them be postponed until they sweat and are rubbed and bathed with very hot water. And it is necessary that the bathing with water precede the bathing with air: then let him be anointed with one of the oils that dilate the pores: and let it be poured over their heads, such as oil of dill, wallflower <note>original: "keiri"</note>, and chamomile: and let them be fed light and aromatized foods. And let them take in drink a thin white wine mixed [with water]: and it is better for them than water because of what is in it regarding sweating and provocation. And anointing with some oil for those suffering from labor is more helpful than for those suffering from solidity.

#### On the ephemeral fever from solidity from styptic waters. Ch. 40.
Sometimes it happens to those who bathe in waters causing stypticity <note>original: "stipticitatem," i.e., astringency</note> such as those over which the power of alum or tragacanth <note>original: "draganti"</note> prevails, so that a vehement thickness of the visible pores occurs. Wherefore their vapors are compressed and what we said happens to them sometimes, and indeed many times it leads to putrefaction.
### On the signs. Ch. 41.
The significance of the cause: and that which is signified by the blackness of the skin: as if the extension itself were prepared by the preparation with which hides are prepared <note>referring to the tanning process</note>: and as if the skin were touched when infused in tragacanth water; and it is a disposition in the addition of heat after time: that is, not immediately from the touch of the skin as in others of those which occur from the obstruction of the pores; and the pulse is weaker and smaller and of more vehement speed. And the urine is vehemently white and thin like the urine of a woman: and there is no diminution in their bodies nor deepness in their eyes.
### Cure.
It is necessary that it be cured with a proximity to the cure of those who were before them. Nevertheless, wine is not given to them in drink except after confidence in the vehement amplitude of the pores, unless the condensation is small: for perhaps then the wine opens it. And it is necessary that the refinement of their regimen be greater: and their stay in the air of the bath and their bathing with hot water be greater, and it is necessary that their anointing be delayed more.

#### On the ephemeral fever from wine. Ch. 42.
Sometimes ephemeral fever happens from wine and their cure is the cure for drunkenness. And perhaps they need a solution with fruit water and similar things, and bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note> and vomiting, and especially when their headache persists. And it is necessary that he enters the bath after the decline [of the fever].

#### On the ephemeral fever from hot foods. Ch. 43.
Where hot things cause ephemeral fever: and just as that which is from the sun is for the most part cerebral and in the animal spirit; and that which occurs from the bath is cordial and in the vital spirit: similarly, that which occurs from food is hepatic <note>related to the liver</note> and in the natural spirit.

The text follows the structure of Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine, moving from the immediate causes of fever to the underlying biological decay (putrefaction) of the bodily humors (blood, bile, phlegm, and black bile). It connects these medical theories to daily life, including diet, environmental air quality, and physical habits like bathing or sun exposure.</meta>

<margin>
a According to Thaddeus <note>original: "Atredo," likely referring to Thaddeus Alderotti, a famous 13th-century physician</note>. After the discourse on ephemeral fevers, he discusses putrid ones: and in this, the discourse on blood-based and choleric <note>yellow bile</note> fevers will be completed. Since the previous discourse on ephemeral fevers was somewhat incomplete regarding fevers arising from retained choleric and sanguine vapors, this will be the completion; and the rubric <note>heading</note> says as much. First, he discusses putrid fevers in general, then specifically. There, he covers choleric fevers. The first section has three parts: for the immediate cause of a putrid fever is putrefaction <note>the "rotting" or breakdown of humors</note>. Therefore, he first provides a discourse on putrefaction. Second, he provides the signs of putrid fevers. Third, the cure. There, the second part indicates the signs; the third part, "you should know," covers the cure. First, he provides the cause of putrefaction; second, the different types of putrefaction; third, how the diversity of putrid fevers arises from the diversity of putrefactions. There, the second part states: "putrefaction is indeed fivefold." The third: "the putrefaction of choler..." There are four modes of the causes of putrefaction: some on the part of food, some on the part of disposition (which is blockage), some on the part of the air, and some on the part of the humors which become putrid. There, the second: "either blockage." There, the third: "either through external dispositions." There, the fourth: "and the majority of causes." In the first part, he lists seven causes why food is prepared to putrefy, which is why it is called "bad food": first is the badness of the substance (for example, truffles); second is the tendency toward corruption (like milk); third is wateriness (like peaches, cherries, and the like); fourth is coldness, from which bad blood is produced (like cucumbers); fifth is bad cooking and preparation; sixth is the bad hour in which it is consumed; seventh is bad order (when what should be eaten last is eaten first, or vice versa). All of this is known from the third book, Part II, Treatise 13, in the chapter on the corruption of digestion. Also from the first book, Part III. Because he spoke in those places about the quantity of food as a cause of corruption, he wants you to understand that here as well.
</margin>

Since the previous discourse on ephemeral fevers was somewhat incomplete regarding fevers arising from retained choleric and sanguine vapors, this will be the completion, as the rubric says. ### On the Cure. Chapter 43.

**H**is treatment involves the provocation [of cooling] with known cooling agents. Natural treatment is best with *siracost* <note>a medicinal sugar or manna</note> and tamarinds, and rectifying the liver with things like endive water and oil; and vinegar syrup, cooling plasters made with sandalwood, camphor, rose water, its oil and juice, and cooling oil juices. And quenching the heat with cold and moistening foods. This is the beginning of the discourse on putrid fevers and the completion of the discourse on sanguine and choleric fevers.

### Second Treatise: A Universal Discourse on Putrid Fevers. Chapter 1.

<margin>
b Slow and moist things. This is explained in two ways: first, as things that are slow in their outcome, such as cucumbers, melons, and generally "borarti" fruits <note>perhaps referring to borage or specific gourds</note>; or slow in digestion because of excessive moisture. It appears how this second cause differs from the fourth: it must be said that although they are close in subject matter, the third cause refers to the slowness or badness of digestion due to high moisture, while the fourth cause is due to coldness. If you wish to combine them into one cause, you can. Bad craftsmanship: Thaddeus says this is like if milk or honey is prepared with mustard; but in truth, by "bad craftsmanship" he understands every mode of bad preparation by art, order, or scent. The text can be interpreted this way. It should be considered, however, that Avicenna did not provide a definition of putrefaction because he wants you to understand it from the first book, second section, the chapter on the causes of heating. Some dispute here quite childishly whether putrefaction can occur in us, since it was said in the first book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s De Anima</note> that the soul defends us from putrefaction; but we do not care for such arguments.
</margin>

**P**utrefaction happens either because of bad food when it is prepared, such that what is generated from it is prone to putrefy because of the badness of its substance; or because it quickly undergoes corruption even if it is of good substance, such as milk. Or because it is watery, providing bad nourishment, the wateriness of which the blood absorbs, such as that generated from very slow and moist fruits. Or because it is from those things that do not convert into good blood; rather, a bad, cold humor remains, which the innate heat <note>the body's natural life-force</note> shrinks from, and external heat replaces it; such as that generated from cucumber, melon, pears, and the like. And there are also virtues <note>natural bodily powers</note> among those that do nothing to the food or humor because of the deprivation of respiration of the humors, because it leaves it raw. And such a complexion either generates a bad humor or corrupts that which is generated because of shortcomings in digestion, and because it moves it with a sluggish motion. These causes are helpful in the generation of the blockage that produces putrefaction. Or because of extrinsic dispositions and bad air, such as pestilential air,

<margin>
c Or because of blockage. This is the second branch of the main division, stating putrefaction happens either because of food or because of blockage. It should be considered that by "blockage," he understands all blockages: whether of the veins or the pores of the skin. This is clear from what follows: that blockage prevents respiration (the entry and exit of air) and "evacuation" (the leading out of bad materials and excessive vapors). Alternatively, "respiration" can be said regarding the pulse, and "evacuation" regarding the breath, or vice versa. "And because of the complexion": Some, like Dionysius, say this implies the blockage happens through a bad bodily complexion. Leaving aside the two explanations we made elsewhere, we will give one here: which is that Avicenna wants to clarify two things. First is the cause why the prohibition of respiration and evacuation due to blockage causes putrefaction, finding that blockage preventing ventilation is a cause of putrefaction because of the bad complexion that follows such blockage, whereby it does not perform a good action. Then he resumes the mode in which the bad complexion following prohibited evacuation is a cause of putrefaction, saying it does this either by generating a bad humor or by corrupting what is generated... or because it moves the limbs with a sluggish motion toward their end, so that the delayed humor is seized by external heat and putrefies since the power <note>virtus</note> does not distribute it. These two seem to differ: for it is one thing for the complexion to generate a bad humor, and another for it to dispose what is generated toward corruption... It is secondarily doubted what kind of bad complexion follows prohibited respiration and evacuation. It must be said it can be hot or cold depending on the diversity of seasons—indeed, according to one time in different parts, as we have declared elsewhere in the science of principles.

The causes of the multitude and viscosity and thickness of humors are well-known, and the beginning of a blockage is known.

# Book IV

...it happens incongruously: because the drawn-in air does not temper it as it ought, since it is imbalanced in its heat. The air itself, beginning to turn harmful, improperly grips the parts it touches, and thus it can be said to cause a blockage.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ **Putrefaction.** This refers to the diversity of putrefaction <note>The biological process of decay or "rotting" within the body's fluids</note> based on its location. Consider that it is not called "common" putrefaction because it occupies the whole body and every part; rather, it is called common because it occurs in the common veins. It is said to be "in a member" when it is in one particular place, such as, for example, the matter of an **aposteme** <term>aposteme: a swelling or internal abscess filled with corrupt matter</term>. It happens that matter gathers in one specific part because of the weakness of that part (namely, in its ability to expel waste), or because of an "attractive heat" (whether that heat be excessive or sharp), or because of pain. How pain "attracts" matter is a matter of debate, and we have discussed this in the second book on the differences of fevers. Alternatively, it can be explained by the intensity of the sensitivity of that part, which makes it suffer quickly from any cause. It should be considered that this suffering location can be not just a single simple member, but many parts together in one place. It can also be an organic part with a clear cavity; for example, matter can putrefy in the cavity of the stomach or in a vein. It may be that only one part receives these matters, and if they are not correctly managed by nature, they will undergo putrefaction. From there, the **fumes** <note>In medieval medicine, "vapors" or "fumes" from corrupt fluids were thought to travel to the heart to cause fever</note> are communicated to the heart, and a putrid fever is created, which will be either continuous or intermittent according to the nature of that material. This will vary according to the locations and the substances involved.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ **And humor.** This is another variation of putrefaction based on the substances. It is debated why he did not speak of "humidities," since fevers arise from their putrefaction, as **Averroes** <note>A famous 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> notes in the third book of his *Colliget*. Some believe that a fever of the humidities becomes "ethical" <note>Also known as "hectic" fever, a wasting fever linked to the consumption of the body's moisture</note>; however, although different modes of ethical fever are distinguished by the consumption of heat in the members, they can still putrefy and evaporate toward the heart to cause putrid fevers. **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century author of the *Canon of Medicine*, the primary source for this text</note> understands all of these to be included in the total sum of the humors, whether they are inside or outside the veins.

¶ There is a doubt whether the **spirit** <term>spirit: the vital, subtle substance—distinct from flesh—that carries life and movement through the body</term> can putrefy and cause a putrid fever. It seems so, because air can putrefy (as stated in the first book of the *Canon*), and therefore so can the spirit. Furthermore, putrefaction is the corruption of a mixture, and the spirit is a mixture. Some say that the spirit can putrefy since it is a kind of mixture, but not with the kind of putrefaction that causes a fever. The reason is that the spirit is in constant motion, and thus it is preserved from rotting.

<column-break/>

...are not eradicated without leaving behind hidden remnants. And when they putrefy inside the veins, they cause the fever to "cling," and they are not easily eradicated; nor is it close to one that is easily cured, but rather it is a constant and inseparable presence. ¶ However, it possesses an intensity through which the **paroxysm** <note>A sudden attack or increase in the symptoms of a fever</note> belonging to it is recognized. And when the putrefaction is internal and dominates all the veins or most of what follows from them, there are perhaps no apparent increases or decreases in the fever. ¶ But when it is the opposite, manifest alterations are seen. ¶ And a fever from external putrefaction is not eradicated and then returns, except because the matter that is rotting undergoes a peak of putrefaction at the time of the paroxysm. Its moisture, upon which the heat depends, is resolved and exits the body, since it is not held in the veins in a way that would prevent total resolution. What remains is its "ashy" or "earthy" quality, which cannot carry the fever or the heat—much like what is seen in a manure pile, which stays hot until it all turns to ash, after which no heat remains. And when no heat remains in the humor that was scorched by putrefaction, the fever is destroyed, until matter gathers once more at the site of putrefaction. ¶ And yet, remnants of the heat remain in it.

¶ This should be referred to as yellow bile. Or it might be because of a fever occurring every seven days, or every week, which runs the course of quartan fevers in the nature of their matter. Thus there are certain fevers that run the course of phlegmatic ones, such as the diurnal, nocturnal, and **syncopal** <note>A fever accompanied by fainting</note> humors. ¶ And because quartan and quotidian fevers have many other fevers that run their course, while choleric ones <note>yellow bile</note> do not have them, or have few, he did not say: "yellow bile causes a tertian fever and those that run its course." However, if he had wanted to, he could have said it. 

¶ It is doubted why continuous fever is attributed to blood, when other humors can also cause a continuous fever. It must be said that fever from blood is the "truer" and more uniform continuous fever, not having distinct cycles. But continuous fevers from other humors do have cycles and periods of worsening. ¶ Therefore, when Avicenna said that yellow bile causes a tertian fever, he meant both the intermittent and the continuous tertian; and so on for the other humors, black bile and phlegm. Commonly, however, it is said that blood causes continuous fever because it is plentiful, hot, and moist. ¶ It follows putrefaction consecutively because it is near the heart and contained in the veins. ¶ It is also doubted why yellow bile acts every third day, black bile every fourth, and phlegm daily. Some attribute the cause to the movement of the humors based on their qualities and quantities. Others look to elemental natures: yellow bile is like fire, blood like air, phlegm like water, and black bile like earth. Others refer to the celestial bodies, assigning blood to Jupiter, phlegm to the Moon, yellow bile to Mars, and black bile to Saturn. But if you consider it well, these are all widely remote theories, nothing more than rhetoric. The truth is that black bile is slow-moving, while phlegm is fast-moving. ¶ We, according to our own theories on the prolongation of fevers, say that these cycles are a property of the matter in relation to natural heat, which follows the nature of these humors according to their quantity and location.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ **And the location of blood.** Here he presents the diversity of putrid fevers based on the location of the putrefaction. ¶ This diversity exists because some are continuous and some are intermittent.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ **Truly.** First, he states the mode of fever from putrefaction outside the veins. Second, the mode from putrefaction inside the veins. It should be noted that Avicenna implies two things. ¶ First, that fevers occur because matters putrefy outside the veins (specifically phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile), and he wants these to be intermittent fevers. Second, he adds two conditions...

# Fen I Tractatus II
### Page 11
**C 2**

<margin>1</margin> Regarding matter that occurs outside the veins and is "uprooted" <note>original: "eradicatur"; refers to the fever being completely cleared from the body</note>: the author shows that being uprooted happens differently for different humors. Melancholic matter <note>black bile</note> and choleric matter <note>yellow bile</note> are perfectly uprooted. However, phlegmatic matter, because of the "viscosity" or stickiness of the substance, is not cleared with a complete uprooting before the next fever attack <term>paroxysm: the period of a disease when symptoms are most severe</term> arrives. Instead, it leaves behind hidden remnants of heat. These remnants might not actually be a fever at the moment, but rather a "neutral" state or a non-febrile disposition. Whatever the case, the body is not cleansed from it during the quiet period <note>the interval between fever attacks</note> as thoroughly as it is with other humors. 

But you might ask: since it is granted that blood can putrefy outside the veins, what cycle <term>period: the predictable schedule or interval of a fever's return</term> does it keep? It must be said that when blood begins to change into the nature of another humor, it will follow the movement according to that humor's nature. For example, in the case of yellow bile, this happens to patients with pleurisy when they spit up red phlegm; see Galen’s second book *On the Differences of Fevers*. Perhaps the attack will depend on the nature, quantity, and quality of the humor, and the condition of the body part sending or receiving it. Consider this well.

And when they putrefy, we must consider that we find two modes of putrefaction for the humors—namely blood or the other two <note>phlegm and biles</note>—within the veins. One is "absolutely" within the veins, meaning common to the whole body. From this arises a **continuous fever** that is not uprooted in the way a true intermittent tertian fever <term>tertian fever: a fever that peaks every third day, associated with yellow bile</term> is. Nor is it like a daily intermittent fever, which has distinct "fortifications" or peaks by which its cycle is recognized. A continuous tertian fever afflicts the patient more on the third day; because these modes of putrefaction within the veins belong to yellow bile, phlegm, and black bile, these fevers create "inseparable" continuous states with periodic intensities. 

If we refer to blood, it is said that it possesses a uniform, continuous intensity. Its cycle or movement is recognized in a broad sense. As will be stated below, every humor has a cycle that is natural to it. There is another mode of putrefaction within specific veins—the "common" or major ones, such as those from the collarbone to the groin, or in the veins closest to the heart, or the one ascending from the liver to the heart, or from the heart to the lungs. In these cases, the fever is **uniform and continuous**, having no increases or decreases. The author says "perhaps" because although such matter is most frequently blood (which has no distinct attacks), it can also be yellow bile, which would cause a **causon** <term>causon: a highly inflammatory, burning fever</term>. This might have some small increase or decrease every third day. Conversely, when putrefaction occurs in veins that are not so common or not so close to the heart, the fever would be continuous but have manifest changes in its rising and falling.

¶ A doubt arises: can a "contained" continuous fever <note>one that stays at a constant level</note> be formed from any humor without increases or decreases? It seems so, because any humor can putrefy in the parts closest to the heart. We find not only yellow bile there, but also phlegm and black bile. On the contrary, usually only **causon** and **synocha** <term>synocha: a continuous fever caused by over-abundance or putrefaction of blood</term> are called "contained." **Thaddeus** <note>Thaddeus Alderotti, a famous 13th-century physician</note> said that the specific nature of the humor does nothing to make a fever "contained" or periodic. Humors of different species, like yellow bile and blood, can both cause a contained fever. Rather, he says four things cause this: substance, quantity, quality, and location. When these are combined—the humor is of a substance prone to rot, the quantity is sufficient, and it is near the heart—then a "contained" continuous fever occurs. These conditions are most often found in blood. In phlegm, three of these causes are found: quantity (there is more of it than anything but blood), quality (moisture), and location (it can be near the heart). In yellow bile, there are two: substance and location. Therefore, phlegm moves from day to day, while yellow bile moves more slowly. Black bile, however, has opposite causes: it is scarce, cold, dry, and thick, and its location is further from the heart. Therefore, it moves slowly and cannot form a contained fever. 

Or we might say that a specific effect that happens always or mostly must be reduced to a specific essential cause. Since it appears to us that yellow bile moves every third day, black bile every fourth, phlegm daily, and blood uniformly, it seems some cause per se creates this effect. No cause seems likely except the nature of the humor itself; other causes vary infinitely. Hence, <unclear>every humor</unclear> has the cycle that suits it. These cycles can vary due to accidental causes of location, quantity, or substance. We say, therefore, that a contained fever is naturally made of blood, because it is the nature of the sanguine humor to rot uniformly, without intensifying on the third, fourth, or daily mark. However, quantity, substance, quality, and location assist in this and sometimes change its movement. 

While true periodic fevers (measured by days) are made by other humors, it happens that from these other humors—for example, yellow bile—a contained continuous fever can be made that is not periodic in act, but periodic in potential or "hiddenly" periodic. For instance, choleric matter rotting near the heart's veins naturally wants to increase every third day and decrease on the alternate third. But because of the location and quantity, the first batch of matter is not quickly resolved, and the second batch rots quickly; thus the second matter attacks while the first is still present. This creates a **contained continuous fever**, even though its nature is to rise and fall.

¶ In this way, we can imagine a contained continuous fever in matter outside the veins. For example, if we assume it possible for someone to have several intermittent tertian fevers overlapping in their attacks—though this is very unlikely. What can reasonably happen is a contained fever of yellow bile, which will *appear* contained, but by the nature of the matter will actually have subtle increases and decreases. This is why **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> said "perhaps they are not." It is clear that after blood, the humor most likely to cause this is yellow bile, because a lot of it is found without blood around the heart—specifically in the vein that nourishes the lungs. After yellow bile, we can imagine it of phlegm, which is found in abundance near the lungs, though not as close to the heart by natural position. We have seen a continuous fever where the matter was predominantly phlegmatic, and it had no manifest increase or decrease. From this, we judged the matter was located near the heart. This occurred in the case of **Lord Andreas of Trent**. 

Therefore, it is unlikely for black bile to cause a contained fever, though it cannot be strictly proven impossible. If physicians define a "contained continuous fever" as a uniform fever with great heat, it is clear such a fever will be from blood or yellow bile (though "false" phlegm can mimic a causon with its sharpness). But if they mean a continuous fever without manifest decline or return, then phlegm is very well-suited for it, even if it does not multiply near the heart as easily as yellow bile. 

The preceding argument is supported by two propositions. First: external putrefaction causes intermittent fever. Second: internal putrefaction causes continuous fever. First, he proves that when putrefaction is external, the fever "recedes" (it is not continuous). Second, he gives the reasons why it returns. He usually gives one cause for why the attacks recede and return, and then a second cause. 

<column-break/>

Secondly, he explains why it stays, why it is uprooted, and why it returns. Any mode of dividing this can be valid. In the first part, he proves that when putrefaction is external, the fever is uprooted, arguing thus: when the rotting matter is finished, it reaches a point where it can no longer induce a fever, and so the fever stops or is "uprooted." When the rot is outside the veins, it finishes because the matter is not held in a "contained" place that prevents it from evaporating. It remains as an "ashy, earthy" residue that cannot sustain heat or fever. 

Consider that from this, we solve the common question: does the matter of an intermittent fever start rotting in the veins or outside them? It must be said: outside the veins. The putrefaction comes upon it during the time of the paroxysm <note>the fever attack</note>. This is verified when an intermittent fever is not just "born" but happens as a "crisis" of a continuous fever. In that case, the rot was previously inside the veins—as happens when a patient with a burning causon fever suddenly experiences shivering and sweating. Sometimes matter moves outside the veins and does not immediately rot; sometimes it does not rot at all, as seen in the "cold" of one who does not become warm (see the second book of *Differences of Fevers*, chapter 8). 

Secondly, "ash" and "earthiness" should not be understood literally, but as matter entirely stripped of its evaporating moisture. It can no longer induce febrile heat, much like a pile of manure that slowly stops smoking as it finishes decaying. This is an example from **Galen**. 

The author then assigns the cause of the "return" of the fever, even though the matter was finished: the cause is the **remnant of heat** left over from the first putrefaction. We can say that Avicenna provided a general cause for the return of an attack: the time it takes for matter to re-aggregate at the site of putrefaction. He then explains the causes of this re-aggregation.

It is doubted how new matter is gathered by that "quality" (the leftover heat). We say that since the place where the rotting matter caused the attack is outside the veins, we imagine this heat remains outside the veins. It gathers matter by corrupting the nourishment of the veins; the heat "attracts" the matter so that it does not follow a natural change but is hurried into corruption.

A second doubt: can this "bad quality" be inside the veins where humors are generated? We can easily see that the heat following the rot—which has now receded—could be in internal places like the liver and veins. Through a bad "complexion" <term>complexion: the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an organ</term>, it might gather yellow bile, which is immediately expelled outside the veins once gathered, only to gather again after an interval. But it is harder to imagine heat from putrefaction doing this; we would have to say that even if the rotting humor is outside the veins during the attack, it could infect the veins and liver, leaving behind a "bad heat" that causes new matter to gather.

A third doubt: can a "quality" (heat) alone remaining outside the veins cause the humor to gather? It seems not, because there is no reason why it would gather the *same* kind of humor as before. Some say a bit of the first humor always remains, acting like a "leaven" or ferment to pull in more. This view contradicts Avicenna and Galen. They seem to want the return to be possible through "quality" alone. Furthermore, if a remnant remains, the new matter that arrives is much more than what was left; and what remains is more "earthy" or melancholic, while the new is choleric or phlegmatic. Therefore, we say the remaining quality is not just heat, but heat with a specific "property" matching the previous humor. Thus, it corrupts new matter into that same nature.

¶ I do not wish to be troubled by the question of where the humor is generated. The disposition in the veins corresponds to this, specifically multiplying that humor. When that humor actually exists in the blood, it appears certain that the second attack is of the same species as the first. Since these dispositions can vary, the forms of the attacks also vary.

¶ It is doubted how heat can cause the re-gathering of phlegm or black bile, since these are "cold" humors. We say that perhaps this only happens if there is a disposition of the blood in the veins corresponding to the quality of the liver. We say that this kind of heat causes the blood going outside the veins to turn into *rotting* black bile, not natural black bile or phlegm. It is "actuated" and intensified so that the portion of blood that is phlegm or black bile is corrupted by the remnant heat.

A fourth doubt: if nothing remains between attacks except a "quality," how does the whole fever have unity? Some believe an "ashy" residue must remain to give the fever unity, but it seems this is not necessary. Others say the "antecedent cause" <note>the underlying bodily condition</note> preserves the unity. But this is insufficient, because the attack might not come even if the antecedent cause remains. Furthermore, the fever can return even if no matter exists, because the remnant heat will generate it anew.

We say, therefore, that between attacks nothing remains but the "quality," which is the total cause for gathering new matter. There is nothing else in which the fever can be united except that **bad complexion**. We say a man has "one tertian fever" for the whole time because it is more "one" thing than two different attacks would be. This is like how two tertian fevers—one in winter and one in summer—are distinct.

¶ I want the whole fever to be measured as one continuous febrile event, even if it is intermittent. The matter will be gathered by the power of that heat—first a little, then more, then more again. Then there will be less: this is the **beginning, increase, peak, and decline** of the whole illness. But you might ask: why is there no distinction of "times" of the disease during the quiet hour based on the change in matter?

We say the distinction is perhaps only in the symptoms of one attack compared to another, or in the change of matter. Since the aggregation of matter (from little to much and back to little) can vary, you will see some intermittent fevers vary in their attacks. Attacks that seem to be declining might suddenly surge again, indicating an "increase." If we want to use signs of **digestion** <note>in medieval medicine, "digestion" refers to the body "cooking" or preparing humors for expulsion</note> during the quiet time to determine the stages of an intermittent fever, we look at the disposition of the members. This explains many observations: sometimes you see signs of digestion in the quiet periods after the first attacks, but "crudity" <term>crudity: undigested or unprocessed humors</term> in the later ones, or vice versa, depending on how much power the bad quality has to harm the digestion of the liver and veins. Thus, you cannot always neatly distinguish the stages of the fever. Consider this.

It is doubted whether a man can return to his healthy state between the attacks of an intermittent fever. We say that for the most part, he does not. The rotting matters infect the limbs even if the bulk of the matter has receded. Frequently, some "dregs" of the matter remain, or a new gathering of matter begins due to the body's disposition (repletion of quantity or quality). Thus, Galen denied that an intermittent fever is cleansed as thoroughly as a one-day fever <note>ephemera</note>. However, to the theoretical mind, it does not seem impossible for a man to have febrile attacks and be healthy between them. The reason is: in a choleric man, some yellow bile can multiply within his range of health...

It also discusses how the location of putrefaction—near or far from the heart—determines whether a fever appears continuous or intermittent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how humors—specifically yellow bile (cholera) and phlegm—interact with the veins and internal organs to produce recurring fever cycles. It builds on the previous page's focus on how these substances "putrefy" or rot to generate heat.</meta>

# Book III

...it can be pushed outside the veins, which creates a <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase in symptoms</term>. And when the person returns to health, the fever can return again. This is evident if we remember the man who, because of the width of the bile duct leading to the stomach, vomited <term>cholera: yellow bile, one of the four humors</term> every single day; this is discussed in the second book of *On Complexions*, in the *Tegni* <note>The "Tegni" is the "Ars Medica" by Galen, a fundamental medical textbook</note>, in the commentary on the second book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, and in the ancient commentary. 

If you ask, then, whether someone could have a fever their entire life: it must be said that if such movement of yellow bile is due to a "mobile disposition" <note>a temporary or shifting state</note> existing at the furthest edge of their health—for example, a certain degree or measure of heat—then whenever they are in that state, they will fall from their health into themselves. This is because their health is said to be the cause of it, or because of a cause happening by chance, they fall into fever. 

However, if that disposition is "immobile" <note>permanent or structural</note>—for example, the width of the bile duct or some natural blockage—then that person could always have a fever; that is, for as long as their life lasts, they could suffer paroxysms, especially those of a choleric nature. To use an example: no one should wonder at this, for if the yellow bile that is vomited every day were pushed every day into another part of the body's constitution, they would have a fever every day for their whole life. What we have said is very helpful to those who claim that a person cannot be sick from birth until now, which we have nonetheless denied in our general discussion on this.

<margin>a</margin>
It is certainly doubted whether the quality left behind by putrid humor inside the veins can be the cause of a paroxysm returning within the veins. It must be said that just as putrid humor outside the veins sometimes leaves behind a bad quality alone without matter—from which new matter is gathered again—so we can imagine that when some humor inside the veins is moved toward putrefaction (for example, an ounce of yellow bile, or some part of that ounce, such as three drachms, is dissolved), the remaining quality disposes the body so that new matter is aggregated. We will speak more of this shortly.

<margin>b</margin>
**Or because.** Here the author gives another reason why the fever returns even though the first paroxysm has receded. He does this in two parts: first, he explains the cause; second, he concludes the whole discourse at the point beginning: "The matter, therefore." First, he says that the predicted cause of the return was a remnant of the "quality," just as the primary cause of its return is due to the discovery of the first cause of putrefaction <note>original: "putredo"; the "rotting" process believed to cause the heat of a fever</note>—that is, the principal cause of rotting in the primary matter. 

Therefore, two causes differ: the first is the cause of the "complexion" <note>the specific balance of hot/cold/wet/dry</note> remaining in the limbs from which new matter is re-gathered. But the second cause is the heat of the matter actually rotting, by which other matter is actually and critically disposed toward rotting. And here the example of pigeon dung fits perfectly, which <note>Galen</note> provides: there was a heap of that dung in which one part first rotted and smoked; and while it was smoking, the second part of the same heap was prepared to rot. 

It is first doubted when he admits the cause of the second paroxysm's return, which comes from the "ash" or the residue of the preceding matter. It should be said that perhaps he intends this to be understood in the first cause, which is the "remaining quality." For that quality—whether it be pure or with some residual ash—can attract new matter to the site of the rotting. This second cause, however, stands on the fact that the first putrid matter prepares the second for rotting. And therefore he moves to the second cause that could be brought back. 

It is doubted that if this second cause differs from the first, one must imagine that if a fever has a hundred paroxysms, all the matter was previously accumulated in the form of an "antecedent cause" and bit by bit, part after part, is moved toward rotting according to its cycle, with the first part preparing the second. For this is the example of the pigeon dung in the field that <note>Galen</note> describes. And if the first matter generated the second, then this cause would be the same as the first. 

It must be said that it sometimes happens that the matter for all the paroxysms that are to occur persists under the form of an antecedent cause; such paroxysms are believed to be few, though it is not impossible for it to be so. For example, if there is an excess of a pound of yellow bile in the blood, it is expelled outside the veins bit by bit, and each ounce causes a paroxysm, and the first always prepares the second. But you might ask: why is one ounce of yellow bile moved before another? It must be said it is because one is more "actualized" <note>further along the process of change</note> and more distant from the nature of blood. And what has been said perhaps does not happen frequently. 

However, it happens more frequently that a preceding paroxysm, by its putrid heat, prepares the body for the generation of a second mass of matter—I say "corruptive generation"—and then the first cause differs from the second. The first cause involves the action of the quality remaining after the first matter is dissolved. This second cause involves the action of the putrid heat of the matter while it is actually rotting, from which the second matter is prepared, whether that matter existed before or is newly generated. 

It is doubted how these matters will maintain the periodic movements of <term>tertian: a fever recurring every third day</term> or <term>quartan: recurring every fourth day</term> or daily fevers, since their "movers" are either bad complexions left behind that act during the quiet hour, or the malice of the putrid qualities that act during the time of the paroxysm. It must be said that although these causes are formally different, they frequently run together. That is, the two matters that are moved are of the same kind: for example, if yellow bile precedes, yellow bile follows; therefore, they maintain the cycles. However, they can vary: for a bad quality left behind by rotting yellow bile, or its actual putrid quality, can move not only yellow bile but also phlegm. This explains the variation in cycles. When many "incinerations" <note>breakdowns of matter</note> have occurred, quartan fevers may occur in a man with a hot liver, or a phlegmatic stomach might attract a tertian fever toward a phlegmatic one, and vice versa. Consider this. 

It is further doubted why he says "according to the path of putrefaction." It must be said that the quality acquired in the second matter from the first matter (as the second cause says), or even from the quality left behind by the matter (as the first says), is not yet "actual" rotting, but is a certain disposition toward rotting, as we explained at length in our inquiry on the prolongation of fevers. Let us say, therefore, that if the first matter, while actually rotting, actually makes the second rot, then the fever continues itself through this; it does not have a periodic return of a second paroxysm. But if it at some time prepares the matter for rotting by giving it a quality—by which, on such a day, it will be moved by a movement in which rotting will happen to it, or its rotting will be completed—then there will be a periodic return of the second paroxysm. And this is why Avicenna said, "according to the path of putrefaction." 

Beyond this, it must be considered that the disposition induced in the second matter by the first matter, or by the remaining quality, can be imagined as a disposition so close to rotting that as soon as that matter is moved to the site of rotting, it is seized by it. Or we can imagine a degree of rotting that does not yet appear, either because the degree is too faint or because there is very little matter receiving that degree. But both a weak degree and a small amount of matter can be called a "path" in respect to the subsequent rotting that is capable of actually causing a fever. It should also be considered that the text says:

<insert>
**From the first putrefaction: although the matter does not remain; or because of the discovery of the first cause of putrefaction in the first matter, and it is inflamed in the second matter according to the path of putrefaction. The matter, therefore, of the rotting...**
</insert>

<insert>
**...of the first putrefaction. This can be explained in two ways: one way is that he calls the "first putrefaction" the prior cause in respect to what follows; and then the discovery of the cause of the first putrefaction is the discovery of the putrid heat which is in the first matter. In this way, "first" is linked with the word "putrefaction." In the other way, by "first cause of putrefaction," he understands the immediate and essential cause of the rotting; and then it is said the paroxysm returns either because of the discovery of the first cause—that is, the essential and immediate cause of the rotting—which is first found in the prior matter, then accidentally in the second, etc. And thus the word "first" is linked with the word "cause." But it is doubted what moves the second matter to actual rotting, since the first matter has already receded and the second matter is only on the "path." It must be said that the heat proceeds by disposing it bit by bit. Either, therefore, the heat intensifies itself (as we have held elsewhere, that the same thing can act upon itself) or, from a more ample disposition, once the matter is consumed, the rotting is completed by the heat of the surrounding environment. It is doubted because he seems deficient in stating the causes of the return of paroxysms, because besides these...**
</insert>

<column-break/>

**...there is the disposition of the specific parts that generate the matters and send them to the place of the rotting, as <note>Galen</note> said. It must be said that a paroxysm that has receded returns again: either through a bad complexion left behind by the matter of the prior rotting (whether there is ash with it or not), or because of the alteration made by the first putrid matter in the second matter. And these are the two causes of return which are the causes taken from this: that a person is feverish or was feverish, so they are taken from the perspective of the putrid humor. Avicenna placed these alone because his discourse was continuously about the recession and return of extrinsic putrid fever, and about the continuity of intrinsic fever. But besides the stated causes, there is a cause of return: a new generation of humor made by the organs that send it out. And this cause does not necessarily depend on rotting; indeed, it can happen even if all rotting is excluded. For example: the liver and the veins of...**
</insert>

...this man, in such a time, have multiplied such and such an amount of yellow bile, which in such a time is pushed outside the veins and will cause one paroxysm of a tertian fever; and finally, again, this liver and these veins, after a determined space of time, will produce the same quantity of yellow bile (or close to it) and the fever will return. It is manifest that even if nothing of the putrid quality of the first yellow bile remained, and even if the putrid heat did nothing to the neighboring matters, the fever would still return as long as the same disposition of the liver and veins and the same manner of nutrition remained. For this reason, Avicenna did not include this cause, because this is not a cause of "return" <note>in the sense of a remnant</note> that can be traced back to the rotting of the fever. But you might say: could not that bad quality exist in the liver and veins or another part because of the action performed by the putrid humor? It is manifest that it could. It must be said that then this cause is no different from the first cause that Avicenna provides. 

It is doubted why this is reversed when it is a paroxysm of phlegm. For if the putrid heat of the first matter prepares the second matter for rotting, then the matter that is more quickly prepared by the first matter will be moved sooner. But yellow bile, compared to preceding yellow bile, is fit to be prepared more quickly than phlegm compared to preceding phlegm. And this is proven: because as rotting is compared to rotting, so is the preparation compared to the preparation. For it seems that those preparations are similar to the rotting itself. But the rotting of yellow bile proceeds most quickly—choleric matter is like fire in dry wood—whereas the rotting of phlegm is slow, like fire in green wood. This is so much the case that Rhazes, in the 18th book of the *Continens*, in the chapter on quartan fever, believes the increase of a phlegmatic paroxysm is longer than a melancholic <note>black bile</note> one. 

By the author's logic, the disposition for rotting will happen sooner in yellow bile than in phlegm. In this difficulty, we said much in our inquiry on the prolongation of fevers. But let us say here again that the first and second matter are either in one heap, or the second matter is like a heap from which (because of the aforementioned smoke) one part is first separated while the second remains. I say that as far as substance and quality are concerned—since it is supposed to have the same requirement to cause a fever—yellow bile is more prepared for rotting than phlegm. And I do not see why, if in Peter's body (for example) there are two ounces of phlegm of which one ounce is moved today, and in Martin's body there are two ounces of yellow bile of which one ounce is moved today, the paroxysm of yellow bile would not return sooner than the phlegm. For yellow bile is far more prone to being inflamed. 

Nor is it valid what some say, that the heat of a phlegmatic fever lasts longer than a choleric one; for it lasts only about 3 hours more. But the intensity of the heat of yellow bile seems to do more for the action than the duration of the small heat of phlegm—or at least not less. I say, however, regarding substance and quality: that if the movement of that yellow bile is delayed until the third day, it will only be because of a property following the nature of such a humor. 

Furthermore, one paroxysm of a tertian fever is found to last 18 hours. But if the second matter is to be generated or actualized, then the paroxysm of yellow bile is later than that of phlegm. Because of the property of such a humor, it is in the nature of yellow bile to have the completion of its generation or actualization of rotting on the third day; but it is the property of phlegm that this happens sooner. This can be varied because of other factors, as will be said. And so we said subtly in our inquiry that in that periodicity—in which the matter of the second paroxysm must be generated or actualized or newly completed and separated during the time of quiet—a disposition of rotting is not acquired of itself; rather, a disposition toward the *form* of such a humor being generated or actualized is acquired of itself, which disposition might not be putrid. And it happens to it that if it is putrid, or if there is rotting, it nonetheless does not cause a fever until the matter has a sufficient quantity, which it does not have except in such a space of time. Nor is there any doubt that phlegm aggregates in a shorter time. Consider this.

<margin>c</margin>
**The matter, therefore.** This is the assignment of the discourse, and he first wants to summarize that the fever—namely the first putrid matter outside the veins—fails because the "matter of the rotting" (that is, the putrid matter) is dissolved. In it, there is the discovery of heat that does not fail to cause rotting until the paroxysm begins and is dissolved, etc. Also, this heat passes to what is neighboring; and in this, he said:

<margin>d</margin>
**Because of the discovery, etc.** This denotes the cause of the return, that is, the periodicity. It can be explained in two ways. First, the text that says "is dissolved" is visited: by "neighboring," he understands the continuous parts of the same humor which are all made into paroxysms. Then "passing to the neighboring" is explained as proceeding successively from part to part until it "cuts off at the third"—that is, the whole quantity of matter moved for one paroxysm. And therefore he adds: "and it exhausts the matter and does not find another neighbor"—namely, a continuous one by which the paroxysm could endure. But it well finds a neighbor for another future paroxysm. Thus he adds: "and it remains"—that is, it ceases for a time, and the fever remains waiting for the matter to be drawn to the place where the first was, or to stand in the place of the first. And this is what he means by "it will attract," etc. Or the fever remains "virtually" in the heat left behind by the humor that is already dissolved, by which heat another mass of matter is expected which will stand in the place of that which receded. 

In the second way, by "neighboring," we can understand the humor that ought to cause the second paroxysm; and then the sense will be that the heat ignited in the first matter, indifferently dissolving the "ash," passes to the neighboring—that is, to the humor that must cause the second paroxysm. This dissolution of ash and passing to the neighbor happens in the entire time in which the first matter is finished and no neighboring continuous matter is found that can provide more for the paroxysm. And this is what he means:

<margin>e</margin>
**Until it cuts off the limit.** That is, the quantity of the matter.

<margin>f</margin>
**And finishes, etc.** That is, this dissolution, putrefaction, and incineration—and also the passing—happens "until" (that is, in the time when) the matter is finished, its quantity having been cut off by dissolution, in which finish no neighboring matter is found by which it could...

<summary>This page explains the medical theory behind why fevers recur in cycles, attributing it to either residual "heat" left in the body or the time it takes for organs like the liver to produce enough "corrupt" humors (like yellow bile or phlegm) to trigger a new attack.</summary>
