# Fen Treatise
### 1 ii
### c 3

...the heat of that <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase in symptoms</term> lasts longer; however, nearby matter can well be found for another paroxysm. And in this, the contradiction is removed: which appears in the speech of <note>original: "auicē"</note> Avicenna. For where he previously spoke of it "passing through to what is nearby," he now says, "it does not find anything nearby." For there are different "nearby" things. And it appears that one should not follow the school of thought which says "not failing," which some wish to be an affirmative statement. For by saying "not failing," Avicenna intends a continuous action and the continuous heat of one paroxysm, in which entire paroxysm the heat unfailingly dissolves the matter.

<insert>
...the fever remains, waiting for other matter, and draws it to its place. But when the <term>putredo: putrefaction or rotting of humors</term> is inside the veins, then it happens that a complete resolution is difficult. And the putrefaction is not resolved through continuity.
</insert>

<margin>a</margin> "But when." Here he proves that putrefaction inside the veins causes a continuous fever, and he argues thus: then the fever is continued when the putrid vapor and putrid matter are not resolved except with difficulty. But this is when the putrid matter is in the veins. And in this, he gives two causes. The first is because the veins are continuous. Hence, the matters that are in the veins are close to one another; therefore, the putrefaction immediately passes from one matter to another, both to that which is part of the matter for one <term>exacerbation: an increase in the severity of a disease</term> and to that which is matter for another exacerbation. And so Avicenna said two things: first, that the "nearby thing" putrefies; second, that it is "resolved toward another nearby thing," or it resolves (meaning it goes or passes through). The second cause of the slow or difficult resolution of vapors and putrid matters is: because these matters are connected to the heart through the middle cavities of the veins. But <term>T.: possibly referring to Thaddeus of Florence (Taddeo Alderotti)</term> says: what does the first cause contribute to the difficulty of complete resolution? For it does not seem to prove anything else except that the matters quickly putrefy after the first matter that rotted; and this is because the matters are close to each other. Furthermore, what does the second cause contribute to the difficulty of complete resolution? Indeed, from this, it seems it might do the opposite: because those locations are hotter, and thus more capable of dissolving the matters. Furthermore, why did he say that this continuity exists "in certain veins"? Indeed, it is in all of them, since they all arise from one trunk. To the first, it must be said that by the "resolution of vapors and matter," I understand their absence or diminution, yet in such a way that they do not cause a fever; rather, it ceases from this fever. Since the first part of the matter has been moved to putrefaction inside the veins, then because other matters are nearby, the putrefaction proceeds by continuing onto the nearby matter: so that before the first is finished, another succeeds it. But when it putrefies outside the veins in the pores and locations where there is no abundance of fluid, the first matter is finished and another is awaited. Some, however, have wished—as we have already explained here—that Avicenna meant this difficulty of resolution is three-fold: one from the density or solidity of the veins; another from the proximity of the matters; and the third from the continuity to the heart. To the second point, it must be said: although greater heat may dissolve, it nevertheless assists putrefaction more. Avicenna means that the putrid smoke in the vein is forced to go toward the heart because the cavities of the veins are continuous with the heart, whether they come from the heart or are continuous via the liver or via the arteries associated with the vents. A doubt might arise here as to where the matters putrefy more vehemently: either in the veins or outside the veins; we have written specifically about this elsewhere. To the third point, it must be said that he said this because he is speaking of veins in which there is putrid matter, so he does not care to speak of the continuity of the veins except insofar as the matters are continued in them. And so it could be explained "on account of continuity"—that is, of the putrid matters which are continuous in certain veins with other putrid matters. It is doubted: if the matters in the veins are close, therefore when a <term>choleric: caused by yellow bile</term> fever begins, it ought to immediately pass into a <term>sanguine: caused by blood</term> or <term>phlegmatic: caused by phlegm</term> one, because these three are mixed together in the veins. And we say that a continuous fever does not always start from matter that putrefies in the veins; we must imagine the whole blood, or according to those locations of the veins, having a disposition according to that humor. For example, <note>original: "vbi gĩa," shorthand for "verbi gratia"</note> when a continuous choleric fever begins, then the blood tends toward "cholericness." And so the succession of putrefaction is more in the <term>cholera: yellow bile</term>. Furthermore, putrid yellow bile is more similar to healthy yellow bile than to phlegm. And because the humors are near each other in the veins, continuous fevers do not last in their simple form without associating with themselves other matters of a different species. And in this, consider many variations that disturb the minds of doctors: when they have seen a patient with one continuous fever whose signs appear uniform enough in the first days—for example, showing yellow bile and that of a non-malignant sort—and they see signs of strength and a praiseworthy pulse, and properly digested excretions, and in the exacerbations, praiseworthy sweats—even in the first <term>creticio: a turning point or "crisis" in a disease</term>—they later see unhealthy urine and many variations in the waste and other things. Thus, previously it was believed the patient would escape, and later the doctors are forced to change their opinion. This frequently happens on account of the movement or "ruin" of different matters toward putrefaction. And it happens more to modern men <margin>b</margin> up to now because bodies are vehemently full, and it happens through much error in the diet of doctors wishing to stuff those suffering from fever. It is doubted whether blood can produce a periodic fever. It seems so, because a period is owed to each humor that befits it, as Avicenna states in the chapter on fevers of abscesses. Furthermore, from the disposition of the parts that send and receive matter, a fever becomes periodic; just as <note>original: "Gal."</note> Galen said. But this can happen to the blood: for the liver could multiply it in a determined time and then send it to some part in a determined time; and this is proved because we see bloody flows according to periods in certain people. To the contrary is Galen in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers*. The opinion (6) is at the end of the book *On the Differences of Fevers*. <margin>c</margin> Because the putrefaction of blood is common in the veins or in the largest vein, not having a specific part sending or attracting it; therefore, its putrefaction kindles one continuous fever from the beginning to the end. And this is Avicenna's reason. <margin>d</margin> <note>original: "Auer."</note> Averroes, in the third book of the *Colliget*, agrees. But just as we argued there against Galen, although this happens frequently, it is not always necessary. Furthermore, if fevers that have periods are exacerbated, they will arise from the dispositions of the parts sending or receiving, or generating, or attracting superfluities—as he himself concedes in book 5—then this can be present in the blood; although as is commonly said, it cannot persevere much in its own form outside the veins. It is the opinion of many on the Commentator's third treatise: they say that blood is not a fourth substance, but is that which is composed of phlegm, yellow bile, and <term>melancolia: black bile</term>. And so when it putrefies, it declines either toward yellow bile, or toward phlegm, or toward black bile. And then the period of blood will only be according to the periods of those humors. And Averroes alludes to this enough in the *Practica* of the *Colliget*, comment 68, when he says: it is more probable that when blood putrefies, three fevers are generated in it, etc. And to summarize the speech of many commentators, their intention is: that if one is forced to say what fever that blood produces when it does not decline toward the other three humors, they respond by saying: first, that it will not have a cycle according to the period of any of those humors, because it does not match any of them. Second, that

<column-break/>

it is truly more likely that it would cycle in the manner of the cycle of phlegm more than yellow bile; as he shows at length from the speech on the second book of *Prognostics* regarding that word: "because if the urine passes to redness." And he proves it because phlegm easily passes into blood; also because such phlegmatic blood is multiplied more in the body of a <term>tertian: a fever recurring every third day</term> which is periodic; therefore, it has the disparity which it receives, because the putrefaction of the first blood moved to putrefaction caused the disparity. And therefore the regeneration of the second blood that ought to go to the "mine" <note>the source or organ</note> will be according to that received disparity; and thus it will become a choleric, phlegmatic, or melancholic period. We do not see fit to proceed against him in this regarding what he said about the nature of blood, since we have discussed those sayings elsewhere. But when he first said that if it putrefies, it will not have the period of any of those [humors], he speaks truly in a way; but nevertheless, he does not declare which period. And when he says secondly: that it will have the period of phlegm more than yellow bile,

<insert>
...which is in certain veins with others: because every thing that is nearby to it putrefies; then it is resolved toward another neighbor. And again, that which is contained in the veins is of a more vehement continuity to the heart.
</insert>

this can be said to be true in a certain way, yet as an absolute statement, it faces opposition. For the nature of a period is seen to be attributed to a humor no less than to that humor into which it is more fit to be transformed. Therefore, the periodicity of a fever will be attributed no less to yellow bile than to phlegm. And when he thirdly suggests that the regeneration of blood will happen according to the received distemper, an adversary would say that this is not true: because if someone's liver is generating blood of good quality, but it is superfluous in quantity alone, it will go outside the veins where, by putrefying, it will cause a fever. And then, although a bad quality might remain in the part in which it putrefies, nevertheless the liver in the intervening time could return to its natural complexion, which will make the same blood; and in an unequal time, it will push it to the part; and thus again from where the period arises. We say therefore in brief: that a "period" is two-fold. One follows the nature or property of the humor. And this is determined and finite, because it follows its own nature; and it is that which we say—that yellow bile moves from third day to third day, and phlegm from day to day, or black bile from fourth day to fourth day, and blood uniformly. And in this way, if the question is whether blood can produce a periodic fever, we say yes, with the period that befits it; I do not say it produces the period of yellow bile, nor of phlegm, nor of black bile, but its own period. Which is for one continuous attack to have a paroxysm, or duration, or motion. Whence Averroes in the 4th book of the *Colliget* says it has only one paroxysm; just as therefore blood by its property has its paroxysm, which is to afflict continuously and not to have "over-growths" like the tertian, nor from day to day, nor from fourth to fourth. So any humor from its property has a certain paroxysm: namely, yellow bile a tertian, etc. And therefore Avicenna said that a period has the period that befits it; and it appears that the "period" of blood is improperly called a period. Rather, it ought to be called the "privation of periodicity." The other type is the periodicity that follows the disposition of the parts sending, attracting, and generating the matter, and in this, it follows the quantity and quality of the matters and the location and disposition of the sending and receiving parts; and such periodicity is variable almost to infinity. And according to this, any humor—not by this specific humoral nature, but on account of the said dispositions—can cycle. And with this, any humor can have any period; this, however, is proven. For it can happen to any humor that by the disposition of some part, it is generated or accumulated in an undetermined time. And it can happen that it is pushed out at a determined time. Therefore, it can happen to any of them that it will cycle; this first appears in the blood. For we see certain people have a flow of blood every day for several days, and some every month; this, however, is only because his liver (to use an example) generates so much blood in such a space of time that can be sent to the nostrils or the anus. Therefore, if that blood were held in the veins at the time it is usually pushed out, or putrefied outside the veins, it would cause a fever. Or it is possible that it produces a proportional fever having a period equal to that period of the blood flow. And thus one must imagine concerning yellow bile, phlegm, and black bile. That any humor can have any period becomes clear when the aforesaid causes are considered. For since it is imaginable and possible in fact that this man's liver does not multiply blood every day, and another's liver multiplies it every month or every year, the blood of any day and the blood of any month can flow out or be retained, whence a fever arises. It is imaginable—indeed, possible and actually occurring—that in whatever space of time or measure (from a day to a year) it can happen to a man, according to different individuals; and so it is for other humors. From which it is clear that a true <term>recidiua: relapse</term> is different from a paroxysm: because to have a paroxysm is for the sickness to return with the order of a tertian or quartan fever. But to relapse is for the sickness to return, yet not necessarily with an order. However, it can coincide with a relapse, and other things can be seen from this. But it is doubted why this does not happen frequently, just as we frequently see continuous periods, and tertians for yellow bile, and quotidians for phlegm, and quartans for black bile. It must be said that it happens more frequently in natural things according to the nature of the form of the natural thing, and that which is according to the "violence" <note>meaning an external force or unnatural state</note> of the form. A period every third day is according to the nature of yellow bile compared to the moving heat; but for yellow bile to be moved every day, or every fourth day, is a certain violence—either because of a greatly superfluous quantity, or a very small one, with much thinness or much thickness, and with little or much heat or sensitivity; according to these, the periods are varied much. Whence it is "violated" from its proper motion, and it either anticipates or postpones it. And thus it appears to you that when [Galen] in book 5 believed he was investigating the causes of periodicity, he investigated nothing but the causes of the recession of fever; and the recessions vary according to the diversity of matters and parts. But the causes of the determined periodicity of yellow bile, or phlegm, or black bile, he did not scrutinize; because he always understood that it was from the nature of the humor, as appears if anyone attentively considers his speeches. And therefore authors, relying on this—wishing to prove that a blood fever has a tertian period—prove it by the fact that blood passes into the nature of yellow bile. And those wishing to prove that irregular fevers turn into quartans prove it because the humors then pass into the nature of black bile. When, therefore, they have the mode of substance and location corresponding to their nature: then it paroxysms from third day to third day; and thus black bile every fourth; and thus phlegm daily; and thus blood with a continuous paroxysm and not a repeating one. But when many foreign variations happen to these humors—from qualities and quantities, modes of substance, and dispositions of parts and locations—they vary greatly in their periods, as you have already seen. It is doubted, however, what is that quantity of yellow bile, and mode of substance, and location which ought to correspond to its property so that it becomes a paroxysm from third day to third day. We say that it cannot be given determinately; but it is argued from the fact that in natural things, quantities and other things correspond to form; so when the effect ought to come from the form—just as from the form of yellow bile it ought to move every third day—when the yellow bile is in that disposition, then it will be moved by our heat in such a quantity and such a time. Because just as natural beings do not act as they ought from their determined form on account of violence done by an external quality—for example, when rhubarb evacuates blood and also disturbs it on account of superfluous quantity or the disposition of the body—so yellow bile, by its substance, quality, quantity, and specific sensitivity, will proceed.

<summary>This page discusses the mechanisms behind continuous and periodic fevers, arguing that while specific humors have natural cycles (like yellow bile every three days), these can be altered by the physical state of the veins, the liver's production rate, and the proximity of the heart.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of how putrid humors (bile, phlegm, and black bile) behave within the venous system. It specifically explores why some fevers follow a predictable cycle (intermittent) while others are constant (continuous), based on the "digestion" or maturation of these fluids.</meta>

# Book 4

...to change its periodic motion. It is doubted because we also find <term>cholera: yellow bile, one of the four humors</term>, and likewise others—namely phlegm and <term>melancholy: black bile</term>—to result in two contradictory dispositions in the same way. For when there is a heap of yellow bile, an <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or fit of fever</term> occurs from every third day to every third day. If none of it is resolved, then after the first attack has receded, it also cycles from every third day to every third day. However, the time in which the yellow bile is not yet generated should change the timing of the attack compared to the yellow bile that is actually found after the first attack has receded.

And we will first state a seemingly confused solution: that because of this, it does not change its mode, but remains within the range of the third day. For the yellow bile persisting after the other attack has receded will gradually dispose and move toward the third day, and the other matter, which did not pre-exist, is gradually generated and moves on the third day. Another solution is: that the first yellow bile—namely, that which is currently ruling—moves again on the same day, or the second, or the third. If what is moved happens on the same day or the next, it becomes a "double tertian" fever. If, however, it is on the third day, it will be a single tertian fever. See this solution in our inquiry concerning the "prolongation of fevers."

Another solution is: that the yellow bile in one common heap is not of the same disposition—or very close to it—as the yellow bile that moved previously. And the reason is that it would have been moved at the same time as the other, or the attack would have continued. It therefore has a diversity from the first. And then, in the middle time, it is prepared; and by its nature, it will be prepared on the third day and ready to be agitated by the heat of <term>putredinal: relating to the decay or rotting of humors</term> and natural heat. In the same way, even if no yellow bile for the second attack pre-exists in the heap, the heat of the body part generates it, and by generating it, disposes and finishes <margin>b</margin> it on the third day. Other depths of this subject I omit here; you may seek them in our aforementioned inquiry.

<margin>a</margin> It is further doubted whether the "bad quality" left in the veins by the putrid matter—which is continually being dissolved—is the cause of the return of another <term>exacerbation: an increase in the severity of symptoms</term>. Just as outside the veins, the quality of the humor is the cause of the return of the attack. And we say that generally, the return of an attack happens in the same way outside the veins as it does inside the veins. For the attack returns intermittently because a "bad quality" remained in the places where the matter putrefied, or because the matter in the act of the attack prepares other matter. In the same way, matter putrefies in the veins, and the bad quality acquired by the walls of the veins is the cause of a re-gathering of matter, even if the first matter proceeds by dissolving entirely. Also, the matter currently putrefying prepares other matter that is not yet putrid, so that putrefaction overtakes it on a determined day. This preparation happens either in uniform and continuous matter (which prolongs the attack) or in matter that needs to be "activated," which exists as a potential in the blood. This causes the return of the exacerbation or attack. Thus the fever returns through newly generated matter.

Regarding how the return of the attack is generally the same for intermittent and continuous fevers, there are special differences that <note>original: "auic."</note> Avicenna points out: for the matter that putrefies in the veins is associated with a great abundance of humors. Thus, the heat can be more continuous by applying itself to one part of the matter after another; hence, the second attack returns before the first matter is dissolved. The matter first moved toward putrefaction is not ready to be "turned to ash" (completely consumed) as it would be if it were outside the veins. And this is what Avicenna says.

<margin>d</margin> "And let the putrefaction not be resolved." Rather, its bodily substance remains under the form of a humor and is transformed through the act of digestion—or its opposite—and runs until its peak, if the fever is not much prolonged. And this is what is usually said: that continuous fevers occur when matter is prepared for a single expulsion when the matter putrefies in the veins. But <gloss>T. d.</gloss> <note>original: "Tamen dicitur" - However, it is said</note> therefore the signs of digestion cannot be continuous, because the new matter moved toward exacerbation will always be at the beginning of its motion, just as the first matter was at the beginning of the first attack.

It must be said that there is no doubt that at the beginning of any exacerbation occurring in a continuous fever, the urine appears <term>crude: "unripe" or undigested, indicating the body hasn't overcome the illness yet</term> compared to that which appears during the time of rest or remission. This crudity is properly caused by a certain "suffocation" of the heat under the matter at that time. Therefore, although in some continuous fevers you previously saw signs of digestion, you should not be disturbed if the sick person passes crude urine at the beginning of their exacerbation. What then is the difference between the matter causing an exacerbation in a healthy state of fever and that causing the first exacerbation when the person began to be feverish? Consider that the difference is seen because the first was entirely crude, with which the disease began. But this matter, which causes the exacerbation of the current state, has the digestion that is due to it, or which it acquired while it stood as an antecedent cause. If all the matter making one true continuous fever stands from the beginning as an antecedent cause, even if one part moves before another for the reasons stated above, then from the beginning, the whole has some unreadiness. But as the fever proceeds and the disease is healthy (heading toward recovery), some digestion and action proceed upon it. And thus, digestion proceeds even over that which putrefies. That which is moved during the increase or peak of a healthy disease has a praiseworthy preparation or digestion before it moves. I do not mean digestion as the opposite of actual putrefaction, but rather that while it actually putrefies, it is then digested with a digestion opposite to its putrefaction.

But <gloss>T. d.</gloss> <note>However, it is said</note> if a continuous fever from matter within the veins does not have all its matter from the beginning as an antecedent cause, but is generated successively, how can the signs of digestion continue? We say that either they will not continue, or if they do, it is because the second matter generated is always more digested than the preceding matter. How this might happen we cannot discuss at present. Consider, however, that you will rarely find continuous fevers that, while going toward health,

<note>original: "gnanter dixit"</note> specifically said.
<margin>b</margin> Of eradication. Regarding intermittent fevers.
<margin>c</margin> And of time. Regarding continuous fevers that repeat if not eradicated. Another version of the text says "of time," namely the affliction or the motion of eradication, that is, of rest.
<margin>d</margin> Which are diversified, etc. This helps because when matter passes from one kind to another (e.g., from yellow bile to black bile), the order of attacks is not changed, because the matter differs only in quantity or thickness. But it would differ if it changed in "species" or "form." And therefore he says that the matters are diversified in their kinds because they are changed in species (specific form). The periodic mode does not change just because matters always change in quantity or substance, but also because they have changed in species. The second cause is a bad regimen (lifestyle), which is a known cause. The third is the weakness of the patient; for when the "virtue" (internal strength) is strong, the motions are ordered, as in the third book on crises, chapter five. Thus, disordered attacks are seen, as in <note>original: "auer. 4. collz."</note> Averroes, *Colliget* book 4. The fourth cause is the "multitude of sense" (high sensitivity); for when there is great sensitivity in the flesh, the internal power is excited by even a small gathering of matter or almost any motion of vapor, and thus disorder occurs. Others say the multitude of sense is a multitude of pain, by which the matter is disturbed, as Avicenna said.

<column-break/>

contain signs of digestion every day and at every hour of the day; where they do continue, they are from a single type of matter. And besides the predicted things, there is another special condition of the matters that putrefy in the veins and within them. For the extreme putridity from matters inside the veins is, as if by violence, forced toward the heart, not having a way as suitable as the pre-causal veins; because the hollow toward the heart is wider and more accessible. But matters outside the veins have many pores toward the skin, through which they are resolved. From this, the solution to the questions appears. Can matters outside the veins cause a continuous fever? It should be shown that yes, because of the quantity or thickness of the matter; thus a second attack arrives before the first is resolved. And can matter inside the veins cause an intermittent fever? It should be said that yes, it is possible, though rare, because if only a little matter is first moved and the second matter is delayed, the first can be resolved before the second reaches putrefaction, and thus the fever will be discontinued. And therefore Avicenna said a complete resolution is difficult; he did not say it is impossible. He says the putrefaction is not resolved—meaning, for the most part—as if to say it does not reach "incineration" (being burnt away) as it does when it is outside the veins.

<margin>e</margin> And indeed, these fevers that have attacks of "eradication" and "time" sometimes lose their order because of the diversity of the matters in quantity (much or little) and thickness (thick or thin). And because of the diversity in their kind, so that some matter is changed and becomes the kind of another matter; these are diversified in their "species," not just in quantity or thickness. And sometimes it happens from the badness of the patient's regimen, or because of their weakness, or because of their great sensitivity. And the attacks that are "eradicated" (cleared) start for the most part with <term>horripilatio: shivering or the hair standing on end</term>, or cold, or <term>rigor: stiffness or shaking</term>, and are resolved through sweat. And they [continuous fevers] do not start with cold or shivering for the most part, except because of the coldness of the humor, or because the humor bites the muscles, or because of the depth of the heat returning to the interior parts, or because of the weakness of the strength, or because of the cold of the air, as happens in winter time. And that which happens from the "biting" of the heat is more worthy to be compared to shivering and cold. And most often what happens from it is like the stinging of needles in every limb. But the resolution of matter with sweat is because the putrefying or putrid heat dissolves the moisture, and a "cinder-like" quality remains. When, therefore, that moisture is not blocked in the veins, its expulsion through the sweat in the pores becomes easy. However, "inseparable" (continuous) attacks are diminished but not cleared by sweat, nor do they begin with cold, except because of the weakness of strength or the deepness of the innate heat; for then the extremities become cold, and that is a bad sign. And in some fevers, cold and shivering are joined because the matter that putrefies is composed of both cold and "biting" qualities. And sometimes certain putrid fevers are composed in such a way that they become inseparable. This happens, for example, when a humor begins to putrefy in a place, and when putrefaction has overtaken it, it is all putrefied and consumed by it; then another humor of its kind or not of its kind begins to putrefy; then it meets...

<margin>g</margin> "And these indeed." Here he investigates certain special differences in putrid fevers: first, those based on the motions of the attacks; second, he compares continuous and intermittent fevers; third, he assigns the causes of certain diversities in the pulse (at the point "the pulse indeed"). The first part is in four points, just as there are four diversities. First, therefore, he assigns the cause of the disorder of the attacks; and there are four kinds. And the first is subdivided. It should be considered that Avicenna...

<margin>e</margin> "And the attacks." Here secondly he assigns the cause of the onset with a "type" (pattern) and the finish with sweat in intermittent fevers. And the reason why this is not so in continuous ones. And the reason they attack with cold and shivering. And finally, he shows how it happens that intermittent fevers become continuous. What he means by "rigor" etc., return to his specific chapter; here he takes rigor as distinct from shivering. Secondly, he takes it for the same thing. It should be considered that two of the causes he posits are specific to intermittent fevers: the coldness of the matter and the "biting"; because places outside the veins are sensitive, but the veins are not so. Three of these causes are common to both intermittent and continuous fevers; indeed, the cause which is the "deepening of the heat" toward the matter happens more in continuous fever. For the heat is deepened because the matter is plenty, or bad, or in a noble organ, as often happens in fevers of internal abscesses. "Weakness of strength" is understood either from age/nature or the badness of the disease dissolving it, from which the exterior parts become cold. Consider that "biting" accidentally chills; and therefore it is properly called shivering or rigor because of the coldness.

<margin>f</margin> "Attacks are diminished." That is, a continuous fever is rarer than an intermittent one. Or "diminished," meaning they do not recede entirely, but lessen. Or "diminished" at the onset with a pattern, because they rarely begin with one, although they sometimes do, as in a continuous phlegmatic fever. Here consider why in continuous fevers cold appears: because of a defect in resolution or suffocation; and both are bad.

<margin>g</margin> "And in some." This is clear.

<margin>h</margin> "And sometimes." Here understand how fevers from matter outside the veins can become continuous; he says: "it begins to putrefy in a place," namely some place outside the veins, and likewise inside. And "periods," that is, the attacks or "rest," namely coldness, or even a slow movement over the limbs, or not biting, or weakness—namely of the expulsive, digestive, or resolving power—or because of the weakness of sense; for limbs that are dull in sensation stand with the matter... and rest.

<margin>a **And paroxysms.** Consider here the cautious way of speaking used by the Author <note>original: "aui." referring to Avicenna</note> when he says "like the matter of a quartan fever," for he does not say it *is* the matter that causes the movement from the fourth day to the fourth day, but he said "like." He also said "like phlegm," not saying the matter is moved much every day, but to show that from the quantity of the matter and the nature of its substance, one can only argue for the speed or slowness of the **paroxysm** <note>a sudden attack or fit of fever</note> within the same species of fever or in different ones; one cannot, however, determinately argue for the specific day of movement. He said: "either it is subtle, like **yellow bile** <note>original: "cholera"</note>," and from this nothing is proven, because it does not hasten by its thinness like phlegm, nor does it delay by its small quantity like **black bile** <note>original: "melancholia"</note>. Yet another text says it sometimes hastens because it is subtle like bile. Consider this, therefore: that movement determined by the number of days—namely, from the third to the third, or the fourth to the fourth, or from day to day—must be attributed not to quantity or substance, but to some specific property. To what the movements of the fifth and sixth day are attributed, and why it is not necessary to multiply specific forms, we have stated in our inquiry on the prolongation of fevers.</margin>

¶ And sometimes putrid fevers are composed in other ways of composition, which I shall distinguish in their own chapters. Indeed, the **paroxysms** of fevers are sometimes prolonged and sometimes shortened. Their prolongation is either due to the thickness and viscosity of the matter and its great quantity, or its resting state, or due to the weakness of the bodily virtue <note>the body's natural healing power</note>, or due to the weakness of the senses, or due to the density of the pores, which prevents the humor from being resolved; and their shortening is due to the opposites of these factors.

<margin>b **And worse.** Here is an association with the fourth part: "whatever fevers," etc. And the cause is not in the whole body, i.e., in the habit of the body toward the skin, but in the internal parts. It is as if he says: "this which I say is in the whole is rather in the parts," namely in the places where the veins exit or in the parts of the heart. This must be joined to the statement above which says "the worse fevers are," etc., or "in the parts," according to the commentary.</margin>

¶ And paroxysms again hasten or are delayed. Their delay is either because the matter causing them is sparse or slow to move toward the site of putrefaction due to its thickness, and this indeed is like the matter of a quartan fever. Their speed is because the matter is plentiful, like phlegm—unless it is "vitreous" <note>thick, glassy phlegm</note>, for then its paroxysms are sometimes delayed—or it is subtle like yellow bile.

<margin>c **And little.** This is a case positioned in the association: "Those who increase the coldness of the temperament," either regarding the species or the degree of heat, and the "smallness," etc., is measured. For external heat is measured according to a measure proportional to natural heat, as we have declared elsewhere, following the mind of Averroes in the seventh book of the *Colliget*.</margin>

And the worse fevers are indeed the "inseparable" <note>continuous</note> ones in which the putrefaction is inside the veins. Then those that are deep-rooted, in which the putrefaction is in the whole body or in the parts of the heart. And it **rarely** <note>original: "paruz" (parvum)</note> happens that elderly people suffer a very burning fever, because of the coldness of their temperament and the scantiness of their flesh.

<margin>d **The pulse in its kinds.** Because one pulse is in the phlegmatic species, another in the choleric, etc. For one tertian fever can be milder than another and have fewer "accidents" <note>symptoms</note>. "In the beginning," i.e., in the extremities, or at the start of the fever's arrival. For example, a fever might be "ephemeral" <note>lasting only one day</note> from cold, as is clear from the differences of pulses; though this is not strictly to the point, because an ephemeral fever is not a putrid one, it can nevertheless transition into a putrid one, or however the cold occurs by which the body of the arteries is clothed.</margin>

The dispositions of the pulse vary in putrid fevers according to the diversity of their types and according to the variation of a single species in its intensity or weakness, and in the strength or weakness of the symptoms. Sometimes hardness occurs in the pulse, either because of a hot abscess of great extension, or because of a hot abscess in a hard limb, or because of extreme dryness, or when cold dominates at the beginning. And sometimes it is soft, because of soft matter like phlegm or blood.

<margin>e **In cleansing.** i.e., by evacuating many vapors, namely by venting through the intake of cold air. Yet the heat makes one feel suffocated and enclosed, like a fire buried under many logs.</margin>

And this is because the "soul" <note>the vital spirit</note> is in a soft organ, such as the liver, or in cases of pneumonia or lethargy; or because of the moisture when the body waits, intending to sweat. And the pulse at the beginning of paroxysms is weak and constricted because of the arrival of the body's virtue over the matter, and its preoccupation **in cleansing** and venting.

<margin>f **They signify.** The discourse on putrefaction and the diversity of fevers according to it has already preceded; next, the signs of putrid fevers are placed. First, this; second, from what signs and symptoms collected together he places a general mode of signifying them; third, he places the cause regarding the symptoms. There: "Know." There the third: "shivering." The first is in two parts: first, he places the signs signifying putrid fevers; second, the signs by which they are distinguished from each other. There: "in the continuous." First he places the collection of signs, and last he places two causes. The first collection is: that a putrid fever arrives without a primary cause for the most part. For sometimes primary causes move antecedent ones, as was said above in the discourse on ephemeral fevers. Therefore, when there are signs of repletion and thickness or viscosity of humors and blockage, and a "semi-fever," a putrid fever should be suspected. The second collection of signs is from the pulse and the breath, in which the "systole" <note>contraction</note> is greater, because there is a greater necessity to expel putrid vapors and others, as Haly Abbas says in the second treatise, commentary 7 and 8, which is in today's reading. The third sign is well known.</margin>

<margin>g **And for the most part.** It must be considered that although some fevers invade suddenly like lightning (as in the book on crises, chapter 17), nevertheless some invade quite suddenly. We should consider what ***almelilotu*** is: it is a certain disposition mixed with a "bad" heat, yet not so much that it is a fever. It is as if he says a man stands between fever and health. However, Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"</note> in the sixteenth book of the *Continens*, second chapter, says that *almelilotu* is a fever, but because of its smallness, it is not felt. He says that sometimes it is before there is a fever, and sometimes after. Therefore, Rhazes understands by *almelilotu* a certain bad heat that can be called a small fever, or can be said not to be a fever properly, because such a slight heat can remain after a fever. Thus *almelilotu* can happen not only before a fever, but after. We also take from the intention of Avicenna and Rhazes in the cited chapter which symptoms are joined to this rising heat of fevers. There are indeed certain symptoms that, for the most part, are joined together immediately.</margin>

When it is prolonged, it causes one to fall into putrid fevers or causes weakness and a yellowing of the complexion. <meta>This page continues the technical differentiation between "ephemeral" fevers (short-lived and non-rotting) and "putrid" fevers (caused by the decomposition of bodily humors). It focuses on clinical diagnostic markers—sweat, heat distribution, pulse quality, and urine—to help the physician determine if a fever is a simple one-day ailment or a dangerous, deep-seated infection.</meta>

Book III
114

the first **paroxysm** <note>a sudden attack or peak of symptoms</note> in which there is neither sweat nor moisture. The **ephemeral fever** <note>original: "ephimera"; a fever lasting only a day, caused by heat or stress rather than infection</note> is quite the opposite, for it recedes with sweat in the first paroxysm. This explanation is similar to or conforms with the opinion of **Rhazes** <note>a famous 9th-century Persian physician</note> in the 16th book of his *Continens*, second chapter. The fact that a putrid fever recedes without sweat in the first paroxysm shows that this is not equally common to every putrid fever. It applies less to a pure **tertian fever** <note>a fever that peaks every three days, often associated with malaria</note> because, since its substance is subtle, light, and prone to being converted into vapor, sweat can occur in the first paroxysm. This is why it is said that although there may be sweat in a tertian fever at the start—that is, in the first paroxysm—due to certain factors, another version of the text says "there is a reduction" in the tertian. This means there is less of it in a tertian fever than in other putrid fevers; namely, that it is less common for the first paroxysm *not* to recede with sweat. This is because the first paroxysm frequently recedes with sweat due to the lightness of the matter.

I explain it otherwise: it is a sign of all putrid fevers that the first paroxysm is evacuated—that is, it recedes—with sweat and moisture, meaning with copious watery sweat. The ephemeral fever does the opposite, as it does not recede with copious sweat, but rather with a dewy sweat, like the sweat of a healthy person. However, the tertian fever has less watery sweat than other putrid fevers because of the subtlety of the matter. Nonetheless, an ephemeral fever does not transform into a putrid one; if you hold the explanation of the tertian, its paroxysm resembles the ephemeral because it recedes with sweat, and not with very watery sweat. Therefore, a distinction is made between the first paroxysm of an ephemeral fever and a tertian, saying that ephemeral does not transform into a putrid one. That is, the ephemeral fever has its own signs that are not signs of putridity. 

Indeed, the signs of a putrid fever are that the "increase" <note>the phase where the fever gets worse</note> of the paroxysm is distinct from the beginning, rather than mixed with it. An increase is said to be "mixed" with the beginning when the quality of the heat at the start and the heat at the increase differ very little. But in a putrid fever, the heat of the increase and the heat of the beginning are different, and therefore the increase is not "mixed." Alternatively, it is called mixed when the heat rises so suddenly that it creates no diversity or delay. Similarly, the increase of a putrid paroxysm is not proportionate, but rather disproportionate. It is called disproportionate for the stated reason: the heat of the increase is much greater than that of the beginning; indeed, cold frequently appears at the beginning, and heat in the increase. Therefore, the increase is also not "similar" to the beginning. It is also not similar because the heat of a putrid fever does not rise uniformly like the heat of an ephemeral fever, because any **humor** <note>bodily fluids like blood or bile</note> is more heterogeneous than **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"; the vital force believed to carry heat through the body</note>. According to this, it is said that a putrid fever is when there is no such uniformity. 

It can be explained another way: it helps the signs of the ephemeral, which are that it does not transition or go toward a putrid state, even though it resembles the first paroxysm of a tertian in the form of the sweat. In an ephemeral fever that does not transition into a putrid one, the increase is not "mixed"—that is, from the disposition of the beginning which was a deep-seated heat—and the preceding heat that exists in putrid fevers. The increase is not proportionate, or rather, it *is* proportionate to its own beginning; for just as the beginning of an ephemeral fever is from heat, so the increase proceeds with heat, and it is not "dissimilar." Rather, it is similar to and conforms with the beginning, which does not happen in a putrid fever. And this is why he says the ephemeral does not transform into a putrid one. 

¶ Therefore, it then appears that an ephemeral fever does not transform into a putrid one when its increase is *not* mixed, when its increase is *not* disproportionate, and when its increase is *not* dissimilar. That negative phrasing should always be repeated; this is the style of **Avicenna** <note>a foundational Persian physician and philosopher</note> in many places. A putrid fever, therefore, has an increase in its paroxysm that is mixed, disproportionate, and dissimilar. But the ephemeral has an increase that is not mixed, is proportionate, and is similar. It also has an increase that is not very long, and therefore he adds: and the "prolixity" <note>length or duration</note>...

**signifying** putridity, although it does not appear in a tertian fever with a very large opening because of the lightness of the matter. ¶ **And concerning the signs:** if it is putrid, there is an evacuation of the first period with sweat and moisture. The ephemeral fever is the opposite of that, even though in the beginning it may be in a tertian fever due to the aforementioned lightness, such that it is similar to the ephemeral, which nonetheless does not transform into a putrid one. ¶ **And when** its increase is not mixed, not proportionate, and not similar. ¶ **And the prolixity** of the increase again signifies that it is putrid.

¶ **And the addition** of the pulse in magnitude according to its progression signifies the increase. ¶ **Furthermore**, it is an interpolated fever beginning with a rigor or a shivering, and it mostly leaves with sweat and moisture; it is resolved with paroxysms, or it is inseparable from the time. It is not like an ephemeral fever in urine, pulse, and the complexion of the whole cleansing, and in its accidents <note>symptoms or side effects</note>. ¶ **And for the most part**, the accidents of putrid fevers are many, consisting of thirst, headache, and blackness of the tongue, especially at the peak; and the heat increases from distress and vehement agitation caused by the struggle between the "matter" <note>the infected humor</note> and the "virtue" <note>the body's natural healing power</note>. For sometimes the matter rises, and sometimes the virtue rises up. ¶ **And the pulse** likewise sometimes tends toward magnitude and strength, and sometimes

<margin>a</margin> ¶ "Furthermore." This is the second collection of signs, where he means that fevers, whether they are continuous or interpolated, have distinct signs from the ephemeral fever over time—that is, they do not separate from it, but if it is continuous, it does not cool down over time.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ "And for the most part." This is the seventh collection.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ "And the pulse." This is the eighth. The pulse is enlarged in the hours when heat is expelled, and in the hours of relief after the evacuations of matter it becomes small; however, it is small in the hours of "suffocation" under the matter, and in the hours when the virtue is dissolving.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ "Hardness." This is the ninth part, in which he means that a hard pulse is not specifically assigned to putrid fever, but happens because of the causes he lists. **Galen** <note>the influential Roman physician</note> lists these in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ "They vary." This is the tenth part. It has already been shown that the diversity of both the pulse and the quality of heat in putrid fevers at the beginning and the increase is due to the movement in the matter from suffocation to the expulsion of heat, or from rawness to digestion.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ "And as long as the pulse is not strong, etc." It is doubted whether he means that in a putrid fever the pulse becomes strong and fast, which seems false; for in an ephemeral fever, the virtue is stronger, therefore the pulse should be stronger. Some make a distinction for the ephemeral and say: when the pulse is stronger but not fast, then it is ephemeral. Hence, above in the signs of ephemeral, he says the pulse is inclined toward strength. Others say that although the virtue is stronger in an ephemeral fever, because it is not under such "necessity" as in a putrid fever, it does not make the pulse so strong. Others say the strength of the pulse in ephemeral fever is true strength, but in putrid fever, it is a "fictional" strength; for a large and fast pulse creates a certain unarticulated appearance of a strong pulse, as Galen posits in his second commentary on pulses.

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> ¶ **"And it is."** This is the 11th collection of signs. See that the "beginning" does not exclude the sign of hidden digestion, as Galen argues in the 18th chapter of his first book *On Crises*. Deception occurs in this regarding the location of the matter: as when the matter of a putrid fever is not in the area of the veins, then even though it is at the beginning, digestion may appear in the urine. Deception also occurs due to the appearance of a "fictional sediment" <note>original: "hypostalis ficte"</note>, which is some digested phlegm or something broken down by heat, which will appear in the urine immediately at the start of some putrid fever. Deception also occurs because of the shortness of the beginning, as we said above. Therefore, when the matter of a putrid fever is in locations that the urine signifies—such as the liver and all the veins—then from the start of its putrefaction it shows "rawness" <note>undigested matter</note>, because the body's virtue has not yet performed the action of digestion upon it, nor has the corruption of digestion occurred.

**to smallness, weakness, and constriction.** ¶ **Hardness** sometimes occurs, though it is not always necessary unless there is a hard **abscess** <note>original: "apostema"</note> with the fever in whatever member it may be. ¶ **Or** an abscess in a hard member, even if the abscess itself is not hard. ¶ **Or** if there has already been the drinking of cold water or something else among those things that harden the pulse, as mentioned in the book of pulses. ¶ **Diversity** in the beginning and the increase is one of the properties of putrid fever. ¶ **And of** its strong significations, although it does not appear much in tertian fever due to the lightness of the matter: as long as the pulse is not strong, and not fast with the aforementioned speed, then the fever is still ephemeral and has not transformed into a putrid one. ¶ **And the urine** in the beginning is undigested or poorly digested, and perhaps it is "acute" <note>original: "acuta"; meaning sharp-smelling or highly colored</note>. ¶ **And know** that from acute, killing fevers, escape is rare except with a **contraction of a limb** <note>here meaning an abscess or localized swelling forming during a crisis</note>. ¶ **And when** the fever is eased after the settling of an abscess in **pleurisy** <note>inflammation of the lungs/chest</note> and similar conditions, then know that something of the matter remained, which the matter moved to the place where pain appears.

### On Inseparable Signs. Book III.

**In continuous fever** there is a diversity of the pulse, which is very apparent according to the fever. In most cases, it has neither order nor "weight," and the fever persists and does not separate after...

<margin>b</margin> ¶ "And perhaps it is acute." This means the urine is very tinted, or sharp in smell, or "acute" in that it quickly designates either health or death.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ "And know." The first point is that if any fever is acute and mortal signs appear, yet the patient survives, this will happen through a crisis resulting in an abscess; this is what he means by "contraction of a member," namely, an abscess. For "contraction" is sometimes used for a spasm, sometimes for the tension of tetanus, and sometimes for an abscess. The cause is this: when a disease is acute and you see signs of death, it is usually because you judged the body's "virtue" to be weak and the matter "raw" (not ready for evacuation), and the virtue unable to dominate due to the sharpness of the disease. If such a person survives, it is only because the virtue, stimulated to its utmost effort, expels that matter to a corner of the body. This expulsion cannot be a perfect evacuation because of the rawness of the matter, so it results in an abscess. It rarely happens otherwise, perhaps in individual miraculous cases where a crisis occurs without digestion through perfect evacuations, but those crises do not happen without terrible symptoms; hence he said "rarely." It appears that after the crisis, there is a "contraction," meaning a shortening or a depositing of the matter in the lowliest member, because it was made of bad matter and it corrupted the small part where it settled.

¶ "And when." This second point some have misunderstood, but we understand it as it stands: that internal abscesses sometimes "quiet down," not because they recede perfectly, but because some part is resolved or moves to another place. According to Avicenna's usage, just as the soul quiets, so the fever is "eased." For example, in pleurisy, the abscess quiets but has not totally receded; therefore, some matter remains where the pleurisy was. Another part has moved to some other member, which you can know if you see pain there. If the pleurisy patient is eased of fever but feels pain in the foot, it is a sign that part of the matter has moved there and is not resolved. 

**"In continuous."** Having given the signs of putrid fevers in general, he now gives the signs by which they are distinctly known from one another. They are generally distinguished as either continuous or interpolated, or as being caused by bile, phlegm, blood, or melancholy. First, he gives four signs to recognize a continuous fever. The first is from the pulse: the diversity is more apparent in a continuous fever. Second, he says "according to the fever," meaning the diversity could come from other causes, but here it is the fever. Third, it has no "order." Fourth, it has no "weight" <note>original: "pondus"; a technical term for the rhythmic proportion of the pulse</note>. Continuous fever makes a person move further away from health than an interpolated one, and thus it moves the pulse further away. Rhazes calls this weight "the scale."

<margin>m</margin> ¶ **"And it persists."** This is the second sign.

<summary>This page discusses the diagnostic differences between ephemeral and putrid fevers, focusing on the timing of sweat, the consistency of the pulse, and the state of the urine. It also explains how "acute" fevers might result in localized abscesses during a survival crisis.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical clinical analysis of putrid fevers, moving from general signs to the specific characteristics that distinguish fevers caused by the four different humors: yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile. It transitions into Chapter 4 of the treatise.</meta>

Fen Treatise

If a fever is considered putrid and has already lasted more than twenty-four hours, it does not seem to be an **intermittent tertian** <note>a fever caused by yellow bile that peaks every third day with a break in between</note>, which lasts three hours during its peak period; nor an **intermittent daily** <note>a fever peaking every day</note>, which lasts seventeen hours; nor a **quartan** <note>a fever peaking every fourth day, associated with black bile</note>, which lasts twenty-four hours. It seems, therefore, that it is a **continuous fever**. This sign provides an estimation rather than a certainty. For a non-pure tertian <note>one mixed with other humors</note> can last beyond twenty-four hours, as will be said later. Therefore, **Avicenna** <note>the 11th-century Persian physician and author of this text</note>, to strengthen this sign of continuous fever, adds a third point, saying:

<margin>a</margin> "And it is not associated," etc. And with others such as the shivering of cold, or others, i.e., deep pulses, etc., evacuation with sweat, and evacuation with a clearing of the fever, etc.

<margin>b</margin> "And of those." This is the fourth sign. It can be divided into two: persistence, i.e., continuity, because it does not recede—this sign and the thing signified are almost the same—or the persistence of its diversity: namely, the intensity of diversity in the pulse or the heat. The diversity of the pulse is persistent and more intense, and this occurs because of the struggle of the **matter** <note>the diseased humor</note>; for the matter [struggles] against the **virtue** <note>the body's natural healing power</note> since it is in less vital places, as is evident.

...twenty-four hours: and it is associated with what we said regarding the disposition **b** of the **radicals** <note>the fundamental life-sustaining heat and moisture of the body</note> following a preceding rigor and other signs. **And among those** things which signify it is its persistence and the intensity of the change in its disposition: for at the **peak** <note>the highest point of the fever's intensity</note> it is sometimes diminished and at another time increased.

### On the things in which putrid fevers differ and in which they share. Chapter 4.
<sig>Chapter 4.</sig>

**F**ever which is due to the rotting of **yellow bile** <note>original: "colere"</note> follows the movement of **tertians**, whether it is the movement of the beginning of the **paroxysm** <note>the sudden onset or peak of symptoms</note> or the beginning of the intensity—except for the species called "scorched" <note>original: "adusta"</note>, whose movement is very hidden and is like an inseparable, enclosed fever. And the pure tertian is indeed **acute** <note>sharp and fast-moving</note> because of the thinness of the matter, and its heat is great and "biting" <note>a stinging sensation on the skin</note> because of the strength of the yellow bile. **But it is health-bringing** <note>original: "salutifera"; meaning it has a predictable, positive outcome</note> because yellow bile is naturally light and because it brings about rest. However, the non-pure tertian is of a longer duration than the pure. **And the pure** indeed rarely exceeds seven periods, except by error. **The continuous** fever sometimes finishes within a week. **e f** And that which is from the rotting of the blood is a continuous, inseparable fever. Its heat is very great and uniform with a certain smoothness, not with the "biting" of yellow bile; and sometimes through...

<margin>c</margin> "Fever which is." Here he sets down general things by which different putrid fevers differ and what they produce. He does this first; second, he sets down certain things in which they share, as the heading says. Third, he sets down the cause. Then the second: and the quartan. Then the third: and know. They are known, however, by the things in which putrid fevers differ when their proper signs are known, or things of whatever kind. First, therefore, he sets down the things proper to **choleric** <note>yellow bile</note> types. Second, the **sanguine** <note>blood</note>. Third, the **phlegmatic** <note>phlegm</note>. Fourth, the **melancholic** <note>black bile</note>. Then the second: and that. Then the third: phlegmatic. Then the fourth: but the quartan. He identifies the choleric fevers by their diversity: and that there are three: namely, the intermittent tertian, the continuous tertian—also called "proportional" according to the vocabulary of **Galen** <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician</note>—and the fever called **causon** <note>a burning fever</note> or scorched. Second, he identifies them by the manner of their movement: because they go from the third [day] to the third; whether it is intermittent or continuous. And the *causon* has that very hidden movement and is likened to the "enclosed" fever, i.e., the sanguine one. Third, he specifically descends to the pure intermittent tertian, of which he says it is acute, i.e., faster in movement or brief and of great heat, i.e., in degree and sharp because of the strength of the yellow bile, i.e., strong heat: because it is added in degree and joined to dryness.

<margin>d</margin> "And health-bringing." Because it is light, etc. And understand that this lightness is due to the thinness and ability for **resolution** <note>the process of the diseased matter breaking down and leaving the body</note>. Regarding the qualities of the matter, blood and phlegm are milder than yellow bile, and thus the contradiction with the speech of Galen in his commentary on the *Prognostics* [book] 2, comment 47, is removed. And here is placed the aphorism of **Hippocrates** <note>the "Father of Medicine"</note> with his edition which says "a true tertian," etc.

<margin>e</margin> "The continuous sometimes finishes within a week." He is referring to the *causon*; because these fevers are very acute. And what the tertian does in a "period" <note>the time between peaks</note>, the continuous does in a day, as Hippocrates says in his commentary on the aphorisms, book 9, aphorism 7. The peak of the sharpness can be terminated within 7 days; he says "sometimes," and indeed sometimes even after the fourth day.

<margin>f</margin> "And that." He identifies the sanguine fever outside the vessels, i.e., by its continuity, the manner of its heat, and the timing of its **status** <note>the stable, peak phase of the illness</note>. He set a term which is a time that has not arrived. But it shares more with it: namely, that in the quartan there is a status in which a **crisis** <note>the turning point of the disease</note> occurs; for a crisis on the fourth day is rarely seen, as [Galen says] in book 3 of *On Crises*.

<margin>g</margin> "Phlegmatic." Here he first sets down the things proper to intermittent phlegmatic fever, and second, the continuous. Four things are attributed to this intermittent phlegmatic fever. First, that it is of milder heat, etc. Second, because it is long due to three causes of movement. Third, because it involves great fear due to two causes. Of these, the first is because it has a small space of time [between attacks]. The second is because it is associated with corruption and weakness at the "mouth of the stomach" <note>the esophagus or upper stomach</note>, from which it is not excused. And the cause is because the stomach is the "mine" of phlegm, and that which is most multiplied in it is phlegm: as Avicenna says in his chapter on specific things, in the chapter on *soda* <note>a medieval term for headache</note>; and Avicenna, Book 3, Fen 13, chapter on diseases of the stomach. And therefore we can say similarly: that choleric fevers harm the liver because of the gallbladder, and melancholic fevers harm the spleen, as **Rhazes** often says in the 16th and 17th books of his *Continens*. From these harms to the stomach, bad **accidents** <note>symptoms</note> follow, which he lists; and in this can be found the fourth thing. How the stomach is the cause of these things appears in book 3.

<margin>h</margin> "And that." The continuous phlegmatic fever, called "milky" <note>original: "lactica"</note> or "hectic" <note>original: "ethice"</note>, is similar in three ways. First, in the form of the heat at the first onset: because it is not sharp. Second, in a certain persistence of heat. Third, in the "thinning" <note>emaciation</note> that quickly follows from the great defect of the stomach. The pulse is not hard as in a true hectic fever; this is because of the softness of the phlegm. **Thadeus** <note>Thadeus of Florence, a 13th-century physician</note> says that a hectic fever is not found with a soft pulse, like that which occurs from much phlegm in the chest; and then it needs another distinction within the phlegmatic. And sometimes the pulse becomes hard for many hardening causes that can happen, which were said above. He says afterwards that the continuous phlegmatic fever is longer to the degree it is less pure, and shorter to the degree it is more pure. And this speech is common to the phlegmatic fever, whether continuous or intermittent, and the cause is because phlegm mixed with yellow bile or blood becomes heated and refined, and is prepared for resolution. And therefore the fever becomes shorter in both universal and particular terms.

<column-break/>

...**g**. But because **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> adds thickness and fixation to the phlegm, therefore when phlegm has a slight mixing of melancholy, it makes the fever longer; whereas if it were pure phlegm, as Avicenna says, there is much ambiguity in those speeches, and many contradictions appear. All of these we have discussed specifically in our question: "Whether a pure phlegmatic fever is longer than an impure one."

...reaches its peak in four days. The **phlegmatic** **i** [fever], which has a paroxysm every day, is of mild heat compared to the choleric. It is long because of the viscosity of the matter and its coldness and its great quantity, and it involves great fear because it has a short interval between attacks, during which it is associated with corruption and weakness at the mouth of the stomach. This cannot be avoided, and it is among those things that attract bad symptoms like **syncope** <note>fainting</note>, heart palpitations, and loss of appetite. And that which is inseparable <note>continuous</note> is the thing most similar to a **hectic fever**, were it not for the softness of the pulse, though sometimes it also becomes hard. And to the extent that it is less pure, the paroxysm is smaller and shorter, unless it declines toward melancholy due to its lack of purity. The **quartan** fever, however, is not acute because of the coldness of its matter; it is long for that reason, and if it is pure, it perhaps extends for one year. If it is not pure, it is of shorter duration, but there is no fear in it because it takes its course over a long time and because it is not of such sharpness as to be followed by violent symptoms. **And the quartan** and the tertian, if they are both intermittent, are resolved through vomiting, resolution of the bowels <note>diarrhea</note>, sweat, or the provocation of urine. In the continuous fever, however, it is resolved through a flow of blood from the nose.

**And know** that the beginning is prolonged...

<margin>i</margin> "Quartan." The things which are proper to the quartan fever, whether intermittent or continuous, are first that it is not acute, i.e., not of sharp heat, or not acute, i.e., not of sharp or fast movement. Second, that it is long; it can indeed extend for a single year, or even years as will be set down below. "Not pure" is of shorter duration—against which one could argue that it could be made non-pure by phlegm, which makes the melancholy sticky and prevents resolution. It should be said first that phlegm does not prevent resolution; rather, by removing it from the "fixation of earth" <note>the heavy, dry quality of melancholy</note> and leading it toward "water" <note>the cold, wet quality of phlegm</note>, it prepares it for resolution. For within the whole genus [of humors], melancholy is more difficult to resolve than phlegm, i.e., of slower resolution. Or it should be said that he speaks of a non-pure quartan, i.e., made of "scorched" melancholy, which can be called non-pure in a certain way. Hence an **aposteme** <note>an internal swelling or abscess</note> made of scorched melancholy is called a composite aposteme, as if it were from another scorched humor; as understood from **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century physician</note> in his commentary on the *Tegni* [of Galen]. Second, that there is no fear in it, and he gives the cause.

<margin>k</margin> "And the quartan." Here he sets down certain things in which some of the putrid fevers share, or most of them. It appears that he says the tertian and quartan share a means of termination. By "burning" or "inflaming" fever we can understand the *causon* fever, which, besides the said modes of crisis, can be terminated by a nosebleed when yellow bile is mixed with blood; hence bloodletting <note>phlebotomy</note> is also suitable for them as will appear below. But Thadeus says the tertian and quartan could also be terminated this way. It should be said that this is true, although not explicitly stated; or it should be said that it happens more often that the matter of the *causon* is mixed with blood, i.e., yellow bile, because of the locations where they dominate, such as the parts of the heart. And by "burning fever" we can understand a blood fever, in which a crisis can occur not only by a nosebleed, but by sweat, urine, vomiting, and stool—evacuating the blood. That sweat can be bloody appears from **Aristotle** in book 3 of *On the Parts of Animals*. Avicenna testifies to urine and vomiting in book 3, Fen 13. He gives us to understand the termination of the phlegmatic fever: for it is in some way between the quartan and tertian in sharpness. And perhaps because in the phlegmatic fever it often happens that it is consumed gradually without a manifest, perfect evacuation. And second, regarding the differences in fevers, the chapter on the quartan says that more [diseases] are in the melancholic humor than in the phlegmatic, which speaks of evacuation according to the paroxysms.

<margin>l</margin> "And know." Here he sets down two causes. And fevers. First, in two parts. First, he sets down the cause; second, he removes a doubt. Doubts are raised about each of these points. First, it seems that the "beginning" <note>original: "principium"; the first stage of the fever's course</note> is prolonged in a tertian: because it is a brief fever in both universal and particular times; therefore, the beginning of both the paroxysm and the whole illness should be brief. Furthermore, choleric humor is quickly ignited like dry wood; therefore it quickly reaches its increase and its peak. Second, he doubts because it says the "status" <note>peak</note> is prolonged in an "enclosed" fever. On the contrary, there is some enclosed fever that proceeds always by declining, and some that proceeds always by increasing; therefore in some, there is a long decline, and in others a long increase. A doubt is raised about the third statement: namely, that the "decline" <note>original: "declinatio"</note> is prolonged in a burning fever. On the contrary, a burning fever is either a *causon* or a continuous tertian; but these fevers are acute, terminating suddenly. Therefore the decline is brief. A doubt is raised about the fourth statement: first, according to one text that says the "status" and "decline" are in the **quotidian** <note>daily fever</note>. Against this, Avicenna later says the longest part of a phlegmatic fever is the "increase" <note>original: "augmentum"</note>. Furthermore, Galen says at the end of book 3 of *On Crises* that when a fever has a long peak, it is of sharp movement; and when it has a brief peak, it is of slow movement. According to this, it seems that a slow-moving illness cannot have a long peak. Another text is also doubted which says both the "status" and "decline" are in the "continuous" fever. Against this, a longer disease has longer stages. But an intermittent fever is longer compared to its continuous counterpart. These speeches of Avicenna, taken from Rhazes, were very strange and exhausted many praiseworthy men. About these, Thadeus first said: that when we say the beginning is prolonged in a tertian, the peak in an enclosed fever, and the decline in a burning fever, it must be understood relative to the other stages of that same fever. For example, in a tertian, the "beginning" stage is longer than the "increase," "peak," or "decline" of that *same* tertian. Assigning the cause, he says that in a tertian, whether intermittent or continuous, the yellow bile rots in places far from the heart; and therefore Nature, not caring much about its rotting, does not quickly bring it to a peak, and thus the beginning is prolonged. He also says that in the "enclosed" fever, the peak is prolonged for three causes: one is the suitability of blood for rotting; because it is hot and moist, it quickly rots. The second cause is the "obedience" of blood to Nature itself; because it is obedient, Nature quickly brings it to its peak. The third cause is the "diligence" of Nature regarding blood; since Nature loves blood, it quickly brings it to its peak to digest it and resolve it from rot. It is like an ignited fire in tow or straw. Thadeus also says that in a burning fever, i.e., *causon*, the decline is prolonged because, due to the extreme heat and burning, the food and drink that are consumed are quickly turned into heat or yellow bile...

It includes deep scholastic commentary on the duration of different stages of a fever—beginning, increase, peak, and decline—and how these vary based on the humor involved.</summary>
