<meta>This page continues the technical clinical analysis of putrid fevers, focusing on why different fevers (tertian, daily, etc.) have varying durations for their four stages: the beginning, the increase, the peak, and the decline. The text reconciles conflicting statements made by Avicenna and Galen by drawing on later commentators like Thaddeus Alderotti and Dino del Garbo.</meta>

Book

# On the Duration of the Stages of Fevers

Wherefore such a body is cleaned slowly of bilious <note>original: "cholericis"</note> excesses, and for this reason the decline <note>term: "declinatio" — the fourth and final stage of a fever's course</note> is long. And if you say that the decline is similarly long in a tertian fever because the food is converted into yellow bile, it must be said that, while that explanation is insufficient, the complete cause is this: a burning fever <note>term: "causon" — a high, burning fever usually attributed to yellow bile</note> is caused by yellow bile putrefied in the primary locations of the heart. From this, inflammation is created in the heart and the parts nearest to it. Because of this inflammation and heat, the body remains in the decline of the disease under a disposition that continues to generate yellow bile. In a true tertian fever, however, the bile does not putrefy next to the heart; therefore, that disposition recedes quickly, and the decline is brief. Finally, he says that in

<margin>In a daily fever, the peak and the decline are prolonged.</margin>
a daily fever <note>original: "quotidiana" — a fever recurring every day, attributed to phlegm</note>, the duration is prolonged because of the cause already mentioned regarding the blood: because phlegm, on account of its humidity, quickly reaches putrefaction. Furthermore, it is "friendly to nature," <note>Medieval physicians believed phlegm was the humor most similar to blood, and thus nature was less likely to expel it violently.</note> wherefore it sometimes takes the place of blood. But the decline is prolonged in it because the humor is viscous; hence it prevents a quick resolution from the body, from which follows a long decline. These are the sayings of Thaddeus <note>Thaddeus Alderotti (d. 1295), a famous professor of medicine at Bologna.</note>. Yet if you consider them, they are rhetorical statements that do not satisfy the intellect, and therefore I omit further refutation.

After him, Dino <note>Dino del Garbo (d. 1327), a celebrated medical commentator.</note> attempted to explain this passage, saying that this discourse can be interpreted in two ways. One way refers to the "particular times" of a paroxysm <note>the individual "fit" or attack of the fever</note>; the other way refers to the "universal times" <note>the entire course of the illness from start to finish</note>. Referring to the particular times, he says that the lengthening or shortening of a stage in any disease can be understood in two ways: one way is "absolute" in respect to the other stages of that same disease. In this way, what Galen says in the third book of *On Crises* is true: that an acute fever moves such that its peak <note>term: "status" — the highest point or plateau of the fever</note> is prolonged. In such a fever, the peak follows continuously from the beginning; such a fever is an acute disease. But a fever whose peak is shortened is of "slow movement," as such a fever does not have vehement symptoms <note>original: "accidentia"</note>, so its peak does not amount to much.

In another way, a prolonged time in a certain fever can be understood not absolutely, but "comparatively" to other fevers. For example, one might say that the beginning in *this* fever is prolonged compared to its other stages, more so than the beginning in *another* fever is prolonged compared to its stages. This is how Guic. <note>likely William of Saliceto</note> understood it here. All of this must be referred to the stages as they are distinguished by their symptoms. The beginning is prolonged in a tertian fever relative to its other stages, more proportionately than in other fevers. The reason is that the "time of the beginning" is the time in which nature is occupied by the matter of the disease. Therefore, it is a time of suffering for nature. But the "time of increase" and the "peak" are times in which the resolution of the matter begins to occur. And because yellow bile causes much "passion"—that is, it inflicts much suffering because of its sharpness and its horribleness to nature—yet it is easily exhaled and resolved. Therefore, the bile itself prolongs the beginning, but not the other stages. In a "conclusa" <note>term: "conclusa" — likely a synocha, a continuous fever where the heat is "enclosed" in the vessels</note>, however, the peak is prolonged, because the fever is almost entirely "peak," reaching its highest point almost suddenly. But in a burning fever—

<margin>In a burning fever, the decline is prolonged.</margin>
that is, a continuous tertian—the decline is prolonged, not absolutely but proportionately more in respect to its other stages than in other fevers. This is because, although the bile itself should be easily expelled and evaporated, the bile in this case is contained in a solid and dense place, such as the veins, from which exhalation is difficult. This is why, in respect to the matter, the decline is said to be proportionately more prolonged than the other stages or than in other fevers. Indeed, this particular decline persists until the time of the next paroxysm, as the fever does not cease before the next fit comes on. This is evident from the beginning of the first paroxysm through a space of 48 hours, including the time of the first fit. It is not prolonged this way in an intermittent tertian, since that ends in a feverless state, nor in a

<margin>In a "conclusa" fever, the peak is prolonged.</margin>
"conclusa," which has only a single paroxysm. In a daily fever, the peak and the decline are prolonged. The peak is long because, since its matter is viscous, the heat that reaches the highest point is retained in it for a long time. Thus it does not decline so quickly. The decline is also long because, due to the viscosity of the phlegm, the heat transpires slowly from it. For this reason, it is rarely found to be a continuous fever of "total eradication," as Avicenna says. Just as a continuous daily fever is rarely found, the discourse of the second book of *On Crises* and the discourse of Avicenna here do not lead to the same conclusion. For according to that understanding, it would not be true that the daily fever has a long peak, since the other stages occupy more time than the peak alone.

From these things, Dino wants the solution to Avicenna's contradictions to appear: both here and below in the chapter on phlegmatic fever. Here he speaks of "particular times," but below he speaks of "universal times." That he speaks of particular times here is evident by his mention of the "continuous quartan" and the "daily fever of total eradication," for that discourse refers to paroxysms. Afterward, Dino explained these discourses by referring to universal times as they are described by symptoms and the alteration of the matter. For the beginning is prolonged in a tertian more than other stages, because as a continuous fever, since it is "horrible" to nature, it begins to be digested with more difficulty than its digestion and expulsion are completed. Thus, "rawness" <note>term: "cruditas" — undigested humors</note> persists in it longer in proportion to other dispositions. Similarly, because it is a very subtle humor in a place where it is quickly resolved, when the difficulty of symptoms begins, it reaches its peak very rapidly. 

But in a daily fever, the peak and decline are prolonged proportionately more because of the humor's viscosity, in which maturation and expulsion are completed with difficulty. Therefore, the symptoms, the vapors <note>original: "flatus"</note>, and the declines are also prolonged. In the "conclusa," the peak is prolonged because, due to its great sharpness, it almost seems to have no beginning, but appears to be in its peak state immediately. This is by reason of the place where the matter is situated. But in the burning or continuous tertian, the decline is prolonged proportionately more for the same reason stated above: namely, that the yellow bile is contained in a solid and dense place. From these points, the contradiction between Avicenna here and Galen in the third book of *On Crises* is removed, because here Avicenna speaks of universal times, but Galen there speaks of the particular times of a paroxysm. 

The contradiction between Avicenna here and below in the chapter on phlegmatic fever is removed in this way: by understanding that here he speaks of universal times. For the peak of a phlegmatic fever is longer, as is the decline, relative to other fevers; specifically, the peak and decline are more prolonged relative to the other stages than they are in other fevers. This is how Avicenna is understood here. But below, in the chapter on phlegmatic fever, he speaks absolutely: namely, that the "increase" <note>original: "augmentum"</note> is longer than the other stages in a phlegmatic fever. This is speaking absolutely, for the "increase" is when the matter begins to be digested and ends when digestion begins to be completed. Now, this matter, because of its viscosity, is digested with the greatest difficulty when it *starts* to be digested; that is, digestion proceeds upon it with the greatest difficulty. Therefore the increase is long. But it does not begin to be digested or altered with such supreme difficulty, so the "beginning" is not long. Nor is its alteration or digestion completed with such supreme difficulty once it has begun; thus the peak is not as long. This is how Avicenna is understood there. These things were written by Dino, nearly in his own form. In these matters, consider how much he labored, and how many points could be challenged, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

After these men, Francis of Piedmont or Bartholomew of Varignana labored on this passage. First, they say the beginning is prolonged in a tertian, understanding this as the "universal beginning" and not the beginning of a paroxysm. For the beginning of a tertian paroxysm is very brief: its chill recedes quickly and the heat rises. But the universal beginning is long—that is, the time for the alteration of the matter—because yellow bile is disobedient to digestion by reason of its great heat and subtlety. Since these qualities are strong from the start, the beginning of a tertian lasts a long time. But after it begins to "obey" <note>Medical metaphor: when the diseased humor starts to respond to the body's natural heat and begins the process of "cooking" or digestion.</note>, it quickly receives correction. He illustrates this rhetorically: for there are some men who at the beginning are very rebellious to a king, but after they begin to obey, they obey 

<column-break/>

<insert>
->[the beginning] is prolonged in a tertian; the peak in a "conclusa"; the decline in a burning fever; the peak and decline in a continuous fever; and the peak and decline in a daily fever.<-
</insert>

totally. Thus, in a tertian, the beginning is prolonged regarding the alteration of the matter. But he says this should be understood regarding the beginning as it stands in relation to the other stages and symptoms. 

Secondly, he says that the peak is prolonged in a "conclusa." First, he posits the causes given by Thaddeus and refutes them. Those causes were: the blood's "readiness" for putrefaction, the "obedience" of blood to nature, and nature's "diligence" regarding the blood. But he says the "aptitude" or "readiness" of blood to putrefy is the cause of the fever's *continuity*, not the cause of the peak being longer. For what is apt to putrefy affects all stages: beginning, increase, decline, and peak. He also says that what is said about the "obedience" and "diligence" of nature toward the blood argues the opposite. For if the blood is favored by nature and is obedient, nature should move the blood with a motion that *shortens* that stage which is most troublesome to nature, and that is the time of the peak. 

Therefore, he says that by "conclusa" we should understand a "homotena" fever <note>term: "homotena" — a fever that maintains a constant level of intensity without much variation</note>. This is properly called a "conclusa" because a "conclusa" fever arises from the uniformity of the affliction. Such uniform affliction occurs most in a "homotena," in which no increase or decrease appears. In this fever, the peak is prolonged; indeed, it is almost entirely "peak," because resolution and putrefaction occur equally due to the matter's aptitude for putrefaction. 

Thirdly, he says that the decline in a burning fever is long. He says that some versions of the text were "corrupted" and that it should instead say: "the peak in a conclusa or burning fever," because Avicenna calls a fever of the blood "burning," and thus it would be the same. Similarly, he says the part that says "peak and decline in a daily fever" is corrupted, and should instead say: "peak and decline in a daily, or else in a continuous fever." He says that if we explain the text as it stands, the reason given by Thaddeus is not good. Thaddeus says the decline is prolonged in a burning fever because food is converted into yellow bile. But one could argue from this that the "peak" or some other stage should be prolonged where the heat is strongest and converts food more to bile. 

Others say the decline is prolonged in a burning fever because of the great weakness of the "virtue in the spiritual parts" <note>The "virtue" or power located in the heart and lungs.</note>, whereby the body's power cannot prevail. But he says this is not valid, because in the decline, the virtue is weak only compared to what it was at the summit or the beginning of the illness; yet compared to the illness itself, it is fortified. We should understand that a burning fever is one that ends gradually. But some say this is very far from the truth of Avicenna's mind. For it rarely happens that a "causon" <note>burning fever</note> ends gradually; it happens more in other fevers, so he should have said it of them. 

Fourthly, he says that in a daily fever, the decline is prolonged, not in respect to the increase—for the increase is longer, as Avicenna will say later—but in respect to the peak and the beginning, which he had mentioned. These men thus order the text as follows: 
**A.** The beginning is prolonged in a tertian. 
**B.** The peak in a "conclusa" or burning fever. 
**C.** The decline in a daily fever, or else a continuous fever. 

However, certain "modern" doctors <note>referring to late 13th/early 14th-century contemporaries</note> have made arrangements not worth remembering. We say that this passage of Avicenna is taken from Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (d. 925), whose massive encyclopedia *Al-Hawi* or *Liber Continens* was a primary source for later physicians.</note>, in the 16th book of the *Continens*, where he establishes that in this form, the durations of the stages of fevers are made diverse. In a tertian, the "principium" <note>beginning</note> or "synocha" <note>continuous blood fever</note> is prolonged. In a "causon" <note>burning fever</note>, the decline is prolonged. But all three stages will be prolonged in a quartan fever. 

And let us say that Avicenna speaks only of three stages, not of the "increase," because it is Avicenna's custom to frequently divide the "increase" into two parts: he joins the first part to the "beginning" and the second part to the "peak," as he did above in the fourth chapter. Whatever is said about the beginning, peak, and decline is true regarding "universal times" and "particular times." These things are true when comparing these illnesses to each other in these stages in this way: In a tertian, the paroxysm's beginning or the universal beginning is long compared to the beginning of a "homotena," whose beginning is hidden. In the "conclusa" (the homotena), the peak is prolonged compared to the said tertian, because it is almost entirely peak. If you say it would be necessary to say that the decline in a tertian is long compared to a homotena, it must be said that this is true, but it did not please him to set down every particular conclusion. 

In a burning fever, the decline is long compared to the decline of a homotena, whether it is a continuous or intermittent tertian. A burning fever is a "causon" in which, after the matter is evacuated through a "crisis" <note>a sudden turning point in the disease</note>, a "flame" remains for a longer time around the spiritual parts than in other bilious fevers. This is due to the internal heat of the burning fever, because it is the heat of other bilious fevers combined with the heat of a blood-based homotena. 

There are thus three proportions that Avicenna took from the text of Rhazes. First: the beginning in a tertian is longer when compared to a synocha. Second: the peak of a homotena is longer when compared to a tertian. Third: the decline of a burning fever is long compared to the aforementioned fevers. He says afterward that the peak and decline in a daily fever are prolonged. It should be considered that the stage of "notable plurality" in a phlegmatic fever is the "increase," as will be seen in the second chapter; for the humor is ignited with difficulty. Therefore, if Avicenna's words here had been about the "increase," it would be distinct from the other stages. But according to Rhazes, he does not speak of it here, but places the peak and increase into two parts. Or perhaps it pleased him to remain silent about it, since he noted that the increase of a daily fever is long compared to other stages as well. 

He chose to say that in a phlegmatic fever, the peak and decline are long relative to the beginning of the phlegmatic fever. For phlegm, when it receives heat, holds it for a long time and declines with difficulty. Indeed, it is like green wood that always emits some smoke. If you wanted to compare a phlegmatic fever in this to a tertian, a blood-synocha, or a burning fever, you could. But it is a waste of effort to distinguish absolute greatness from proportional greatness. Therefore, it is better to say that the peak and decline in a daily fever are notable parts in it and greater than the beginning. 

That which is said—that the peak and decline are greater in a daily fever—must be understood by comparing a continuous fever to an intermittent one. It is true that proportionately, the continuous has a longer peak and decline relative to its intermittent version. For if one continuous bilious fever ends in 7 days and an intermittent one in 12 or 13, the continuous one should have a peak and decline occupying four days. The difficult accidents in a continuous fever occupy much time, and the greater flame recedes more slowly. Meanwhile, the intermittent occupies 5 days for the peak and decline. But 3 in relation to 7 is a greater proportion than 5 in relation to 12. However, this phrasing is not commonly found. 

We have now followed the explanation of Dino, and we added there that the beginning of a tertian is called "longer" because of that "evaporation" which Galen approves of. Many other things which now seem "childish" <note>original: "puerilia"</note> to us we once added. Wherefore it seemed to us that this text should not be treated subtly, but passed over in a "gross" <note>general or broad</note> manner as Rhazes intended. We found in the sayings of Rhazes many contradictions in the 16th, 17th, and 18th books of the *Continens* when he speaks of the length and brevity of stages, which we had intended to solve. But I omit them on account of the length. 

From these sayings, the solution to the contradictions is provided. To the first point, it must be said that the tertian is compared to the homotena. To the second, it must be said that he speaks of the blood-synocha. To the third: although the crisis in a burning fever happens suddenly, the heat persists after the crisis. To the fourth: if he had wanted to speak of all the stages here, he would have said the "increase" is the longest in a daily fever.

<summary>This page analyzes the variable lengths of the four stages of fevers (beginning, increase, peak, and decline) across different types like tertian, daily, and burning fevers. It reconciles conflicting classical authorities by distinguishing between "absolute" duration and "proportional" duration relative to other stages or diseases.</summary>

### Treatise on Fevers

But he wished to speak of the three times <note>The "three times" likely refers to the beginning, middle, and end of a fever's course.</note> specifically: first about each one individually, then about two together, and this is what pleased him. Regarding the fifth point, it must be said that a fever with a long peak <note>term: "status" — the peak or plateau of a disease's intensity</note> is a motion that is acute in respect to it; it has a brief peak, and therefore every continuous fever is more acute than an intermittent <note>original: "interpolata"</note> one compared to it. And a continuous fever, because it has a long peak with respect to its beginning, is more acute than a daily <note>original: "cotidiana"</note> fever, which proportionately does not have this. After all these things they arrive at, and which resolve the heat that others have begun, it seems to us that one wishing to reach an understanding of these proportions and similarities must doubt which time of the fever is most prone to being prolonged according to the nature of any humor, while all other conditions remain equal.

For example: let there be four proportions—one of yellow bile <note>original: "chole"</note>, another of phlegm <note>original: "phlātis"</note>, another of black bile <note>original: "melācolie"</note>, and another of blood—and let all other factors be as equal as possible. Therefore, is the time longer in a paroxysm <note>term: "paroxismus" — a sudden attack or increase in the intensity of a disease</note> of choleric matter, or in a paroxysm of phlegmatic matter, and so on for the others? Indeed, there is no doubt: all periods of a melancholic paroxysm are longer. Then all periods of a phlegmatic one. Then all periods of a choleric paroxysm. If, however, a blood-based fever is entirely of one paroxysm—just as a single paroxysm of a quartan, tertian, or daily fever—its length is also greater than the length of the paroxysms of other fevers. 

Let us say something, therefore, to stir those who come after us. And it is that our authors are in sufficient agreement in saying that in a phlegmatic fever, the time of increase <note>term: "augmentum" — the stage where symptoms intensify</note> is longer than the other stages of phlegm; for phlegm comes to ignition with heat with difficulty; indeed, it has many surges of heat, and sometimes many remissions because of the coldness and viscosity of the humor. In a blood-based fever, however, they are not determined. For in it is found the "homotena" <note>A fever that stays at a constant intensity.</note> in which the peak is longer, and the "epacmastica" <note>A fever that continuously increases in intensity.</note> in which the increase is longer, and the "paracmastica" <note>A fever that gradually decreases in intensity.</note> in which the decline <note>original: "declinatio"</note> is more prolonged; but whether most of these occur from the nature of the blood-based humor has certainly been affirmed by discovery. 

In a choleric fever that lasts 12 hours in paroxysm, it does not seem affirmed that the time in paroxysm is longer due to the nature of the humor. And perhaps this was not found through experience, because it happens that now one time and now another is found. Therefore Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis" — Abu Bakr al-Razi, a famous 9th-century Persian physician.</note> says in the 16th book of the *Continens*: that in a tertian fever the beginning is longer, and in the 18th book, Chapter 9, he says that in a tertian fever the peak is longer. I do not believe it is possible to demonstrate this by reason, because no middle term is found by which it could be necessarily concluded. If, however, anything is persuasive, it is that the beginning of a tertian paroxysm is longer because of the cause previously stated by us and others. 

In a quartan fever, I do not find it determined with certainty which of the times is notably longer; they have a certain equal proportion in length, so that the increase of a quartan does not notably exceed other times, just as the increase of phlegm exceeds other times; but the beginning in it seems shorter than the other times as a rule. And perhaps Rhazes wished this in the 18th book of the *Continens*, chapter one, where he says the times of a quartan are "middle," the times of a tertian are shorter, and the times of a phlegmatic fever are longer. For just as that third point is not corrupted, Rhazes wished that the times of a tertian be uniform in brevity, but the times of a daily fever are very distorted in length because it has a very long increase. The times of a quartan are of a middle sort; consider this. Then he said:

<margin>Because a continuous quartan and a daily fever of complete eradication are rarely found. And fevers that are not cured except little by little, specifically those involving abscesses <note>original: "apostemose"</note>, turn toward wasting <note>original: "arefactionem"</note>; and specifically in acute fevers where it is necessary that the patients eat, yet they do not eat because of the intention that nature should overcome the matter; or it is necessary that cold water be given in drink, yet it is not given so that the matter does not become "raw" <note>term: "cruda" — undigested or unprocessed humor</note> and is not helped by another cooling. For if there is another intention which we shall speak of regarding feeding and giving cold water to drink, the stronger of these two intentions should take precedence over both, and the observation of those two should be set aside.</margin>

### Chapter 5: On the Significance of the Accidents of Fevers.

The understanding of the signs of fevers is taken from the preceding regimen and when it occurred. And from the emerging and present dispositions, and from the regions and times, and from age and complexion; and from the pulse and urine, and vomiting and bowel movements; and from the flow of blood from the nose; and from the state of the fever in shivering and sweat, and the quality of the heat, and from the paroxysms; and from the state of appetite and thirst, and from the state of breathing, and from accompanying symptoms like headache, sleeplessness, and mental

<margin><a> Although Avicenna, naming choleric and phlegmatic fevers, divided them into continuous and intermittent, he did not do so for melancholic fever, but rather for quartan. Therefore he assigns the cause of this: it is that a continuous quartan is rarely found. And thus his speech is verified for both; nevertheless, in the first sense, we understand it as intermittent quartan, which is found more often, as will be said above. Even if the daily fever is divided into continuous and intermittent, that which is called intermittent is usually not entirely eradicated. And therefore intermittent phlegm usually has a rest that is not entirely true.
<margin><b> And fevers that are not etc. Here he posits another case. It should be considered that while an acute fever persists, because of the risk of death, contrary intentions occur in the mind of the physician: one is the intention to feed, because the strength appears weak and the body is prone to wasting; the other is the intention to cool and quench with a drink of cold water or cold compresses, because a strong, melting inflammation appears. Opposite intentions arise in the same fever: one is the intention *not* to feed, because we judge the disease to be short and the matter to be plentiful, so that nature's strength may be free to digest the matter. The other intention is *not* to cool, so that the matter does not become "raw." The physician therefore stands in this ambiguity. And if in truth the intention to feed and quench prevails, yet he omits them, the sick man is consumed by wasting <note>original: "marasmodes"</note>. Therefore, let them be permitted. Avicenna says the remaining harm follows the conflict of intentions, but the omission was known. For what follows is the prolongation of the disease with raw and multiplied matter, or sudden death follows. In these ambiguities, the judgment of a skilled and practiced physician prevails. This is why Galen well said: a physician must be practiced and prudent by nature.</margin>
<margin><e> The understanding. This is the chapter on the general signs of fevers, in which the meanings of the accidents of fevers are placed. Wherefore in the rubric, it speaks of the meanings of the accidental fevers, i.e., those things which are signified</margin>

<column-break/>

confusion <note>original: "alienatione"</note> and restlessness, and others. For there are accidents of fevers from which their dispositions are signified; and there are accidents signifying their magnitude and their smallness, such as the quality of the heat and its quantity. And there is that which is vehemently biting <note>term: "mordicativa" — a sharp, stinging sensation of heat on the skin</note>, from when it first attacks until its end. And there is that which bites at first, then decreases because of the resolution of the matter and becomes mild; and there are those which bite [later]. And there are those whose heat is moist. And there are those whose heat is dry. And there are accidents that signify their genus: such as the accidents proper to a tertian, like the beginning of the paroxysm with stinging and shivering <note>original: "horripilatione"</note> and biting heat in it. And the accidents signifying their malice are such as restlessness, mental confusion, and sleeplessness. And accidents signifying digestion or indigestion are like what we shall say about the states of the urine. And the accidents that signify a crisis <note>term: "crisis" — a turning point in a disease</note>, which we shall speak of. And accidents signifying recovery <note>original: "sospitatem"</note> and its contrary, and we shall say all those things. <insert>And from the appearance</insert> there are many judgments: such as he whose heat turns to a leaden color from whiteness and greenness signifies coldness of the

<margin>in fevers through the accidents of fevers. Since from the preceding chapters you have learned that this fever is putrid, and from the category of choleric ones, for example, you gather all the accidents that are in it and see what they signify. For you will see that the same meaning is not in all accidents in fevers: some signify the malice of the fever or its contrary; some digestion or its contrary; some its nature according to its genus; and so on. And then through the knowledge of this chapter, the knowledge or true cognition will be completed. First, Avicenna enumerates all these accidents, then shows their meanings.
<margin><d> For of fevers. It should be considered regarding the first part that "accident" is taken broadly for everything that can signify something in a fever, whether it follows the fever or not, such as age and region. Avicenna follows this in enumerating: the understanding of the signs of fevers, i.e., we take meanings in fevers from the regimen, etc. "Accident" is therefore taken for any sign or significance. Consider also that all these accidents or signs from which we take a meaning can be reduced to an order: they are either extrinsic or intrinsic. Extrinsic factors include the past general regimen, region, and time. Intrinsic factors include natural things like age, or things contrary to nature, such as changed qualities or actions. He says: "from the preceding dispositions." This can be understood in two ways: first, from the illnesses the patient had in the past. Second, it can be explained as the non-natural and natural things which, though they preceded, are present with the fever, such as region and age. Consider also "accompanying symptoms like headache, sleeplessness, etc." They are called "accompanying" because they are persistent accidents that necessarily follow. But you will say...</margin>
is not blood a necessary following? It must be said that the aforementioned accidents are more following of putrid fevers than the beginnings. For the change of pulse, urine, and bowel movements are more following than headache and mental confusion.

<margin><e> For of fevers. Here he follows and shows the signs which are taken from accidents. And they are eight. The first is the magnitude and smallness of the fever. The second is the genus of the fever, whether it be phlegmatic or choleric. The third is the malice of the fever. The fourth is the digestion of the matter or its opposite. The fifth is its crisis. The sixth is health and death. The seventh is the mode of the matter, i.e., whether thin or thick. The eighth is the goodness of the fever. According to this, there are eight parts. Consider that the magnitude of a fever is its intensity—either the qualitative increase of its heat or its quantity. Therefore he distinguishes the modes of heat: quality (sharpness) and quantity (heat in much humidity, the sign of which is much or little evaporation). The modes of sharp heat are: those which feel biting, as in burning fevers; or those that bite at first and then soften, as in mild tertians; or first feel mild and then bite, as in phlegmatic fevers. A "great" fever is one that has sharp heat always persevering.
<margin><f> And there are. This is the fourth part in which he shows the significance of accidents regarding the genus of fevers, and he gives a known example.
<margin><g> And accidents. This is the third part: the malice of the fever, and by its opposite, its safety.
<margin><h> And accidents. This is the fourth part: digestion and its opposite.
<margin><i> And accidents. This is the fifth part in which he abbreviates the significance of the crisis.
<margin><k> And accidents. This is the sixth part: health or death.
<margin><l> And the appearance. That is, the habit and color of the face. This is the seventh part: the thickness or thinness of the humors. If the color is leaden from white and green, and the habit of the face is cachectic <note>term: "cachectic" — a state of physical wasting and malnutrition</note>, it signifies coldness of the humors: raw phlegm and thick, viscous black bile. Consider that "exercise," as we said according to Avicenna and Rhazes, and a certain kind of cachexia appears around the face, such as frequently appears in those suffering from indigestion from eating too much.</margin>

It should be considered that what he says regarding their movement in itself can be explained in two ways: first, because a rapid resolution occurs due to the width of the pores; second, because of the movement in itself, that is, due to the subtlety of the humors <note>The "subtlety" or thinness of body fluids allows them to move and dissipate more easily.</note>. Hence, they are ready to be resolved within themselves. Second, wasting <note>original: "extenuatio"</note> occurs quickly in fevers because of movement in themselves—that is, because the feverish are moved—that is, they are restless and awake, or they have taken a purgative medicine, or they have had this movement, that is, a spontaneous flux. And of those, there are some whose hour is the beginning, such as shivering <note>term: "horripilatio" — the sensation of hair standing on end, goosebumps</note> and cold, and such as the depth of sleep which follows most beginnings of fevers because of the weakness of the brain and the decline of heat to the interior of the body where the matter is, and the multitude of vapors raised from it by the mixing beginning in the body until...
</margin>

<margin>a</margin> **And of the accidents of fevers.** This is the eighth part, in which he places the eighth significance: namely, time. For he wishes that certain accidents happen in the peak state, and it is well known. It should be considered that the depth of sleep follows most beginnings—that is, most beginnings of intermittent fevers. Regarding the beginnings of exacerbations, its cause is the weakness of the brain; and to this weakness he assigns four causes which weaken the brain with the weakness by which sleep is made. And therefore they are also called the causes of sleep from above. One cause of the weakness of sleepiness is the decline of heat. The second is the multitude of vapors because of commotion—namely, of the putrid heat with the matter, or because of the commotion of the matter by the heat. The third cause is cold, because the brain, since it is cold by nature, is chilled even more when heat is withdrawn. And therefore if a man is of a cold brain by nature, a greater depth of sleep occurs. The fourth cause is the coldness of the matter. And therefore this properly occurs in phlegmatic matter <note>Matter dominated by the humor of phlegm, which was considered cold and moist.</note>. If, therefore, they are awake in fevers, if ever the depth of sleep occurs, it will be solely because of the revocation of heat to the inside.

<margin>b</margin> **And things.** Because Avicenna had briefly passed over the accidents signifying the genus or species of fever, therefore here in a general discourse he more perfectly and summarily places the things from which it is known of what species a fever is; and he takes "species" broadly even for "genus." And he says that from which this is known are: the disposition of the fever in the sharpness of its heat, because it signifies more choleric matter, etc. And this occurs from a primitive cause because it is signified that it is not putrid, and from antecedent causes because it is signified that it is putrid according to the conditions predicted in the first chapter on ephemeral fever; for primitive causes could move antecedent causes.

<margin>c</margin> **And the disposition of fever in adherence.** "Disposition" is understood in two ways. First, because the fever sometimes adheres and is not separated, then it will be known because it is continuous and uniform; sometimes it is eradicated, and we know it because it is intermittent <note>original: "interpolata"</note>; and by time—that is, sometimes it cools, and then it is a proportional continuous fever. And from these we judge the species of fever. For continuous uniform fevers of adherence are sanguine <note>Caused by an excess of blood.</note>. Intermittent fevers are from other humors, and so are proportional continuous fevers. In the second way, the disposition of fever in adherence can be explained: that is, when it has come and adheres to the body; and this because he declared the disposition of the fever in sharpness—that is, from the sharpening and return of the paroxysm <note>term: "paroxismus" — the periodic spike in a fever's intensity</note> with rigor and cold, etc. Because it signifies an intermittent one, and another according to the diversity of these, namely cold and rigor, etc., as will be known from the following chapter. Or its contrary: because it invades without any specific type <note>original: "typo"</note> and signifies a continuous fever. And then it is either proportional or not, according to what he said about cooling—that is, that which is from it, namely rigor and shivering, etc. That, however, which is from this is the depth and smallness of the pulse, and the remaining dispositions known from the fourth chapter of this section.

<margin>d</margin> **And the disposition of fever.** He says this to declare what he said about eradication, proceeding according to it: that which is with much sweat signifies a humoral fever; or little, namely a dewy sweat not from humors, that is, it is signified because it is not humoral. But according to this explanation, what he said about cooling remains declared—that is, the disposition of cooling by which it cools in sweat. And it signifies subtle matter and attests more to a choleric fever or of the times—that is, whether the invasion is from the third day to the third <note>A tertian fever, often associated with yellow bile.</note>, or from day to day, or from the fourth day to the fourth <note>A quartan fever, often associated with black bile.</note>. From these, indeed, we are aided in the knowledge of the species of fevers, as is known, nor did Avicenna care to declare this further.

<margin>e</margin> **Or past disposition.** That is, the things from which the species of fever is known are the disposition, etc. For if his regimen was in choleric foods, and much labor, etc., and the age is of youth, and the form—that is, a lean, choleric habit—and the time is summer and the air is feverish, and the disposition of the pulse is with much speed and frequency, and the urine is highly colored, a fever from choleric matter is signified. When therefore you consider Avicenna in this chapter, he gave you a way to form a habit for the perfect knowledge of putrid fevers. And it is so that you may collect all accidents and things by which you can judge and know anything; and with all those collected, first know: if this fever is great or small. Second, of what genus or species it is. Third, whether it is malignant or safe. Fourth, whether the matter is digested or not. Fifth, know its crisis. Sixth, life or death. Seventh, the motion of the matter. Eighth, the time of the fever. And all these besides the fifth and seventh are taught particularly in the following chapters of this section. The fifth and sixth, however, are taught in the second section of this book. When therefore you have known all these, you will be perfectly knowing of humoral putrid fevers, and this is it, etc.

<margin>f</margin> **Shivering.** Since he has set forth the significations of accidents, here he determines concerning certain accidents which are frequently found in fevers, about which he had not given perfect knowledge in other places, although he spoke of them in general in the first chapter of the second section, the chapter on the causes of non-natural movements, and something in the chapter on putrefaction. These accidents are shivering, cold, etc. First, therefore, he notifies each of these; second, he sets forth their causes and significations.

<column-break/>

inflammation resolves them, and it is aided by that cold of the brain in itself and the cold of the humor which wants to putrefy and becomes heated. And the things from which the disposition of the fever and from what species it is known are the disposition of the fever in its sharpness and its lightness; and the disposition of the fever in this, that it occurs from primitive causes and antecedents according to the predicted condition. And the disposition of the fever in its adherence and its eradication; and the disposition of the fever in its sharpness with rigor and cold, and shivering or its contrary; which is from it, namely... And the disposition of the fever in its dismissal with much sweat, or little. Or the past disposition: regimen and age, and form, and time, and art, and the disposition of the pulse and of the urine.

## Sermon on Rigor, Cold, Shivering, and Exhaustion. Chapter 6.

->Shivering is the disposition in which the body finds diversity in cold and a pricking in the skin and muscles, and laziness precedes it;<-

<margin>
...cold, and not equal over the members, but as if some secondary cold were brought down, as if it were carried and ran over the members around the skin; and this according to the movement of vapor. With this also, a pricking <note>original: "punctio"</note> belongs to shivering, so that it follows the pricking. And according to this definition, shivering properly arises from hot, pricking matter. And it is consistent with the words of Avicenna above in the chapter on putrefaction, when he said that it arises from the biting of heat and more worthily so it may be proportioned to shivering in the fourth book, first section, second chapter on the causes of natural movements, when he said that shivering is when matter harms by pricking. But it is doubted because according to this definition, shivering is not distinguished from the rigor of a tertian fever. It must be said that the rigor of a tertian, in which there is also a sensation of cold, that is, of pricking, differs from the aforementioned shivering: first, because in this shivering these things are milder
</margin>

hence there is not a vehement pricking, and consequently not a vehement flight of heat to the interior, and thus it is not a vehement cold. Second, because in shivering there is no movement of shaking <note>original: "concussionis"</note> as in true rigor, and this is because the matter is not moved so strongly over the sensible members. And he hints at all these things below when he says shivering occurs from fewer causes than the causes of rigor. Third, because these sensations in shivering are around the skin and places near it, namely in the suffering of the muscles toward the skin; but in rigor, they are deeper. And Avicenna hinted at this when he said "in the skin and muscles"—namely, as far as the parts near the skin. Therefore Galen, in the book *On Rigor and Tremor*, in the penultimate chapter, said: "if its surface is moved with an inordinate movement, and it is cut into at the beginning of the paroxysm besides the fact that the whole body is moved, it is simultaneously called shivering and horror; and it is an accident that happens only to the surface of the skin and in the nearby parts; and it relates to the skin as rigor relates to the whole body." And according to this, Aristotle in the seventh part of his *Problems*, the ninth problem, calls shivering a "superficial passion." Galen said, however, that in shivering the skin becomes rough; and this because the hairs stand erect, as Aristotle says in *Problems* 8, problem 21, and 7, problem 14. And the better cause of this is because with the heat fleeing and the skin being chilled, condensation occurs in the flesh; and the flesh having been thus condensed and contracted, the hairs are raised, just as if someone were to fix a nail in the earth and gather the earth around it, it stands more erect. It should also be considered that this happens in rigor, and because such an erection of hairs occurs for the said cause, the disposition of these appears in the skin as it does in **plucked chickens** <note>original: "depilatis pullis" — a vivid medieval medical analogy for "gooseflesh" or "goosebumps."</note>; for with the flesh contracted and gathered further at the root of the hairs, it appears higher in one place and thicker in another. **Second**, it is doubted whether shivering differs from horror, which is an accident of semitertian fever. Some say that horror can be understood under shivering because shivering is a sensation of mild cold and mild pricking, and thus it can also be called horror; however, horror is not necessarily a superficial passion, rather it is deep, because it occurs in an intermittent tertian joined with a continuous phlegmatic fever; as in the second book of *The Differences of Fevers*: that choleric matter therefore also pricks deeply, but not so strongly as if it were pure and not joined with a phlegmatic fever, as below in the chapter on semitertian fever. Now therefore it appears that this definition can be one; second, this definition can be two. For shivering is a lesser disposition than rigor, and a lesser disposition than pure cold, namely valid cold; just as therefore there is some shivering which is nothing other than a small rigor, so there is some shivering which is nothing other than a small cold. And therefore one definition will be made thus: Shivering is the disposition in which the body finds a diversity of chilling in the skin and muscles. Pure cold, however, is that in which a man finds cold even in the depths of the body, and it is a valid cold as in quartan and certain phlegmatic fevers. Another definition is this: Shivering is the disposition in which the body finds pricking in the skin and muscles. Rigor, however, is that in which a man finds pricking deeper and a greater pricking. It should be considered secondly that laziness precedes shivering, because when harm is done to the muscles, a man becomes lazy. And "fraction" (that is, exhaustion/lassitude) immediately precedes it. And by these things Avicenna hints that shivering is a weaker disposition than cold and rigor; for matters which by their scarcity and weakness cause laziness and aches and added exhaustion cause shivering, and added more, they cause rigor. And deservedly so, as we have declared from the intention of Galen in book 5 of *On Accidents and Diseases*.

**It is doubted** whether there is a "bad movement" in shivering. It must be said that there is not in it a bad movement of accidents, but a certain bad movement around the skin from a bad movement of the expulsive faculty; hence also in an itch, Galen imagines a bad movement in book 5 of *On Accidents and Diseases*.

# Fen, Treatise II

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin> **And a kind of shuddering.** <note>original: "fractio"</note> It should be considered that it is difficult to express these conditions precisely because of their characteristics. For "shuddering" is the same as "breadth" <note>This refers to the "width" or expansion of the pulse or the spread of the humor's effect.</note>; how then is breadth a type of shivering? It is said by some that it is a type of shivering because it is like a genus to all these things; hence, in cold, rigor, and shivering, there is a "breadth" of sensation. Others say it is a type of shivering because it arises from the same cause as shivering. Others say it is a type of shivering because it is a disposition that occurs *before* shivering, and therefore it is called a "kind" of shivering. However, we must imagine this "breadth" as that which precedes a fever, which is not a breadth caused by the expulsion of humors, but a breadth arriving from the humor itself. This is the state in which a hidden motion of stinging or hidden cold begins to mix in, as when a tertian <note>term: "tertian" — a fever that recurs every second day, typically associated with yellow bile</note>, quartan <note>term: "quartan" — a fever that recurs every third day, associated with black bile</note>, or phlegmatic fever is about to follow. As it gradually ascends, shivering first occurs, which comes from cold bile or from an obstruction of the blood. Therefore, this "shuddering" is nothing other than a certain hidden shivering joined to a "breadth" of sensation, or a breadth joined to a hidden shivering. And thus he said "a kind of shuddering"—that is, not pure shuddering—or "a kind of type," meaning it is not truly a distinct mode, as "breadth" is not truly a mode of shivering.

<insert>
1. Shuddering: and a kind of shuddering is a type of it. ¶ **Cold**, however, is when a patient feels pure cold in their limbs and in the muscles <note>original: "lacertorum" — referring to the fleshy parts of the muscles</note> of their back. ¶ **Rigor**, truly, is when one cannot keep their limbs still due to the commotion and trembling occurring in them and involuntary motions; and perhaps it is a powerful cold. ¶ And strong rigor does not occur except in phlegmatic and quartan fevers. ¶ And among the causes of this vehemence of rigor is the intensity of the expulsive faculty in the muscles. Because of this, the more viscous the cause of the rigor is, the more intense the rigor will be.
</insert>

<margin>b</margin> **Regarding cold.** It should be considered that he also defines cold: first, for those who have cold in their limbs—that is, in the hands, feet, and other extremities. In this, it differs from shivering <note>original: "horripilatio"</note>, because in shivering, cold is not felt in the extremities in a way that the person seeks to be warmed; rather, shivering is felt only around the skin and almost externally.

<margin>c</margin> **In his limbs.** That is, he feels cold in the whole body. Second, because the man feels the cold...

<margin>d</margin> **In the backs of the muscles.** That is, in the thick parts of the muscles, namely in the fleshy places. That area is called the "back" of the muscle. There they feel it much more than in other parts; and because of this, it is distinguished from shivering.

<margin>e</margin> **Pure.** Cold is called "pure" in four ways. First, because it does not allow for heat; in this way, it is distinguished from the cold of rigor, such as that of a tertian fever patient where heat is felt inside (as noted in the book *On Rigor and Tremor*). Second, it is called pure when it is not mixed with stinging sensations; in this, it differs from shivering and rigor. Third, it is called pure because there is no shaking <note>original: "concussio"</note> in it, as there is in rigor. Fourth, it is called pure because it is very intense; in this too, it differs from shivering and rigor properly so-called, such as occurs in tertian fever. It is questioned which of these includes the "outer-chilling" <note>original: "infrigidatio"</note> of the extremities, which occurs in phlegmatic patients and which Galen discusses in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers* and Avicenna below in the chapter on phlegmatic fever. It must be said that "outer-chilling" is cold, even if it is not entirely intense; therefore, it is included under "cold" regarding his statement: "let him feel pure cold in his limbs"—meaning it does not allow for heat, stinging, or shaking. Or we might say it is included under the first definition of shivering.

<margin>f</margin> **Rigor truly.** Here he first shows what rigor is. It should be considered that the rigor he defines here is nothing other than a shaking motion caused by the movement of matter over the sensitive parts of the body. This is the "inability to hold the limbs still" due to trembling and commotion, which are involuntary motions not correctable by the will. Galen says these motions occur because hot, stinging matter is moved (as in tertian fever) or cold matter is moved (as in certain phlegmatic and quartan fevers). Therefore, the rigor defined here occurs from hot or cold matter. Thus, it appears that for Avicenna, rigor is the shaking motion, cold is the pure coldness felt in the limbs, and shivering is the condition in which the hair stands on end, and its variant is "shuddering."

<margin>g</margin> **And perhaps.** Here he secondly extends the name of "rigor," as it is sometimes used for a powerful cold where no shaking occurs (as used by Galen in the second book of *On Fevers*). Or perhaps Avicenna means that although there is shaking and cold in rigor, rigor should primarily be called "strong cold" rather than "shaking." This is because the shaking motion is caused by or follows that coldness, as Galen clearly explains in the book *On Rigor*. We have discussed this more fully in the fifth book of *On Accidents and Diseases*, and there it says: "Rigor is a powerful coldness suddenly coming upon the body, pulling it from a natural disposition to an unnatural one."

<margin>h</margin> **And it may not be.** Here thirdly he shows in whom there is or is not strong rigor. This can be explained in two ways. First, in phlegmatic and quartan fevers, there is no "strong rigor"—meaning there is no powerful shaking motion. The reason is that unless the matter is moved forcefully over the sensitive limbs, it does not cause this motion. But cold matters cannot be carried forcefully because of their thickness, nor can they reach the same level of subtlety <note>Thinness or lightness of a humor.</note> as yellow bile (as noted in the Greek translation of *On Accidents and Diseases*). Thus Avicenna’s speech is the same as Galen’s when he says: "Such a tremor—that is, such a rigor which is a shaking motion—is not generated from cold humors, which, because of their excessive thickness, move neither quickly nor forcefully." Second, it is explained that there is no rigor as strong in any fever as there is in phlegmatic and quartan fevers; in this case, by "rigor" he means "strong cold." In no other fever is such a powerful coldness felt as in phlegmatic and melancholic fevers, which are cold by their nature. Or we could say he is speaking of rigor as a shaking motion, which is "stronger" in phlegmatic and quartan fevers in terms of *duration*, because it lasts a longer time. It should be noted that these terms—shivering, cold, and rigor—are used very inconsistently by authors. Sometimes "shivering" is used properly as here by Avicenna; sometimes it is used for "rigor" (as in the chapter on putrefaction, where he says shivering occurs from "biting" humors). Sometimes "shivering" is used for "cold" (as Rhazes does in the chapter on phlegmatic fever). "Cold" is sometimes used properly to distinguish it from shivering and rigor, and sometimes it is used for "rigor" (as Galen does when he says "rigor is a strong coldness"). Finally, "rigor" is sometimes used properly for shaking motion, and sometimes for every type of chill, whether it be shivering, cold, or rigor. Physicians should therefore look past the names to the actual physical realities.

<column-break/>

**Regarding the causes.** Here he provides the causes of these conditions: first of rigor and cold, second of shivering. He gives the cause of rigor and cold together because both involve cold, though cold is without shaking. Some have struggled to divide these parts, but let us say what the author intended. There are five or six main rules by which the causes of rigor and cold are investigated.

**The first rule** is that the intensity of the expulsive faculty <note>term: "expulsive faculty" — the body's natural power to push out harmful substances</note> in the muscles is the cause of the intensity of rigor. From this, it is inferred that the more viscous the cause of the rigor is, the more intense the rigor will be. It should be considered first that the intensity of the expulsive faculty—that is, a vehement effort in expelling—is the proper cause of rigor (the shaking motion). Shaking naturally results from such effort and violence of expulsion. It is also the cause of "cold" insofar as this effort involves a bad sensation and the flight of heat to the interior. However, this cause primarily belongs to the shaking motion. Second, he mentions the muscles because these are the sensitive parts where this expulsive effort most occurs. 

A doubt arises: he says the strength of the expulsive faculty is the cause of rigor, but Galen says rigor is due to the *weakness* of the faculty. Galen proves this by saying a strong faculty contains and withstands everything, while a weak faculty reacts against anything. The answer is: if the matter is subtle (thin), a strong faculty does not cause rigor because it expels it invisibly; but a weak faculty causes rigor because it moves it visibly through the sensitive limbs. If, however, the matter is gross (thick), a strong faculty *is* the cause of rigor because it moves it visibly; but a weak faculty, being unable to move it at all, is not the cause of rigor. This is what Avicenna meant here when he said: "the more viscous the cause, the more intense the rigor." 

Another way to say it: there are three faculties involved in rigor—the expulsive, the sensitive, and the vital. Regarding the expulsive faculty: the stronger it is (meaning the faster it carries the humor), the more intense the rigor, because there is a greater sensation and effort. (If it were so strong that it expelled the humor invisibly, there would be no rigor). Regarding the sensitive faculty: the stronger the muscles are (meaning less prone to pain), the less rigor there is. Regarding the vital faculty: if it is strong with plenty of spirit <note>term: "spirit" — the subtle substance that carries life and heat through the body</note> not fleeing inward, there is less rigor.

**A doubt is raised:** which cause produces stronger rigor—a hot cause or a cold cause? That is, hot matter or cold matter? It is argued that cold matter causes stronger rigor, as Avicenna says: "the more viscous the matter, the more intense the rigor," and viscous matters are colder. Averroes also says that rigor from cold humors is stronger for two reasons: 1) cold air makes us shiver more than hot air, and 2) the cause of tremor is the concentration of heat in the interior to expel its opposite (cold). In contrast, Galen says hot matter causes stronger rigor.

**The common solution** is that rigor can be "stronger" in two ways: **intensively** or **extensively** (by duration). 
1. **Intensively:** Rigor is stronger from *hot* matter because hot matter causes more sudden injury and pain, inciting the expulsive faculty to a more violent shaking. Hot matters move faster through the sensitive limbs.
2. **Extensively:** Rigor is stronger from *cold* matter because it lasts longer. Cold matter is thick and moves slowly, taking a long time to be expelled. Thus, in phlegmatic and quartan fevers, we see a long-lasting rigor, whereas in tertian (hot) fever, the rigor is very intense but brief.
