# Book III

...stronger. Whence **Galen**, in his book *On Rigor*, says: that a rigor caused by phlegm is neither strong nor rigid, although it often lasts for several days. And by this, the reasoning of **Avicenna** is resolved, who understands "stronger" to mean "longer lasting"; however, since the material is viscous, it becomes the strongest or greatest of all. It must be said that it is "greater" because it lasts longer, but not because it is more "intense." And the reason is that thick, viscous matter does not stimulate the expulsive force <note>The body's natural faculty for pushing out harmful substances.</note> as strongly as sharp, thin, biting matter, which dissolves continuity <note>A medical term for causing pain or tissue damage.</note> suddenly. If, therefore, some thick viscous matter were joined with as much stimulation of the expulsive force as is joined with hot, thin matter, the viscous thick matter would produce a stronger rigor.

<margin>a</margin>
Regarding the first reason, **Averroes** says that a rigor from an extrinsic cause is not the same as one from an intrinsic cause, since an internal biting cold humor is not found in the same way a hot humor is; but externally, cold air is found to be biting, since it is a thin, penetrating body. And therefore, the coldness of the air can cause a biting and sudden sensation; however, air that is naturally dry and biting is not found inhabiting the internal parts. But hot medicine encountered from the outside is found to be more biting, such as verdigris <note>term: "verdigris" — a green pigment/medicine made from weathered copper, known for its sharp or "biting" quality</note>. To the second point, it should be said regarding the "minor" <note>A term from formal logic referring to the second premise of an argument.</note> that cold, through the variation of heat, shuts the heat inside; no less than positive cold—that is, cold from cold matter—even if both types of cold are "positive." As we have said elsewhere, when the cause producing cold is called "privative," it is a hidden cause. When it is said that cold is more contrary to natural heat than heat is, it should be said that heat "by accident"—that is, through privative cold—is more contrary to natural heat. And the reason is that because of the great "biting" sensation from hot matter, there is a great flight of heat to the interior parts, and thus a great cooling occurs on the outside. Or it should be said that the great coldness of cold humors dulls the senses, and thus it does not stimulate the expulsive force as much as when biting is caused by pale bile <note>original: "cholora falua"</note>; for when the sense is preserved, there remains a greater sensitivity to the stimulating thing. However, the sense is better preserved because with the rigor of bile, a notable heat remains in the interior parts. Whence Galen, in the aforementioned book, says that a person with a tertian fever <note>A fever recurring every second day.</note> is very sensitive and feels the bile in the depths of the body at the hour of the rigor, none of which is found in those with quartan fevers <note>A fever recurring every third day, associated with "heavier" cold humors.</note> at the hour of the rigor. Another way of resolving this contradiction pertains to the "tremor"—that is, a shaking rigor can be produced either by the effort of the expulsive force, as he says in the fifth book of *On Accident and Disease*, and thus a stronger one is produced by hot humors because they stimulate it more with their biting quality; or it can happen because of the "bad motion" in the natural heat besieged by cold, as Galen says in the book *On Rigor*, and thus it becomes stronger from cold humors. When the mind of Averroes is considered, perhaps they are in agreement. They feel that a more intense shaking rigor is produced not by cold humors, but by hot ones; and this is because they stimulate the expulsive force more, making its effort greater due to the resistance of the thick, viscous humor to be expelled. And although it shuts the heat inside more, and although it stimulates more, and cold humors shut the heat in more, they seek cold humors because they are more contrary. For it is not only that which dissolves continuity that excites the expulsive force most strongly, but that which is contrary to us by its quality, such as cold things. And "sour" phlegmatic things, moved in the form of vapor, can move very suddenly through the sensitive members; and these are the "medicinal" humors that produce the strongest rigors. We witness that **Avicenna**, however, saw stronger rigors in quartans from phlegmatic matter than are found in tertians. And perhaps this is because pure, sharp bile is very rarely found due to the many "indigestions" that modern people suffer from excessive overfilling <note>original: "repletione"</note>.

<margin>a</margin>
**And blood.** This is Averroes' second chapter in number, in which the cause is given why everyone shivering is chilled, even if the cause is hot. And it is because the blood "sinks" <note>Retreats from the surface to the core.</note> during the rigor. These things happen when a rigor occurs. Doubts that arise here should be sought in our discussions on the fifth book of *On Accident and Disease*: namely, what is the motor of the blood going inside first? And why does the blood flee inside? Indeed, if the rigor is caused by a stinging matter, it ought to go to the sites of the stinging—that is, to the places of the muscles <note>original: "lacertorum"</note>.

<margin>b</margin>
**And know that the humor.** This is the second principal chapter and the third in number, in which he places the second cause of rigor: and it is a special cause. Either a cold humor causes rigor by its motion, being scattered over the sensitive members; but before it was scattered, it was at rest, creating a flow and waves, and therefore its coldness was not perceived. It should be considered that a cold humor is the cause of rigor (as distinguished from "shivering" as a known cause of rigor)—that is, of the shaking motion. And this happens in two ways: first, because it forces the expulsive power of the muscles to expel it, and Avicenna gives this cause to be understood from what is said in the first *Canon*. Second, because it puts to flight and shuts the heat inside; whence a motion occurs in the "melting" or "bad" heat, as Galen deduces at length in the book *On Rigor*, and as we declared in the fifth book of *On Accident and Disease*. It should be considered second that before the cold humor was moved, no "passion" <note>In this context, a "passion" means a physical reaction or suffering.</note> occurred. But you might say: Avicenna places this first because it is at rest, and harmful things that are locally at rest hurt less, as Galen says in the fifth book of *On Accident and Disease*. And we disputed it there. The second cause is because the body is "accustomed" <note>original: "assuefactus"</note> to it, and from that which is customary, no "passion" arises. But you might say: this humor comes with local motion to where it rests, therefore it ought to have been felt. Furthermore, what kind of "habituation" is this? It should be said that the place in which it rests (where it grows cold before the paroxysms <note>term: "paroxysm" — the sudden onset or intensification of symptoms, such as the shivering fit of a fever</note>) is the place inside the veins, and perhaps sometimes outside. And inside it is not felt because of the dullness of the veins' sensation, or because they do not feel at all, as some say. And then this will be another third cause: whether it be inside the veins or in some place outside before the paroxysm, we will say that it is either gradually congested there or locally carried, and therefore its transport is not felt. And this is its "habituation." And in this habituation, if you consider well, it does not induce as much cold in the part it is accustomed to as it induces afterward in the part to which it moves at the beginning of the paroxysm. For that cold thing and the member it is accustomed to remain under a certain heat, and the coldness lies hidden deep within the member. And even granting the proposition that in habituation—from the gradual arrival at the member it becomes accustomed to—it had induced as much cold as it induces in the members to which it moves suddenly, still, that accustomed cold is not perceived in the same way. It should be considered thirdly that "scattering" much or little can be understood from the quantity of the spirit, and it is known either by its quality—that is, the intensity of the scattering—and the more vehement the scattering, the stronger the rigor. And it can be scattered "ordinarily," making a weak rigor from a separate cause. That is, the thing scattering it is heat, such as from a bath, or from exercise and the like; whence in men filled with phlegm, these heats excite rigors and chills. Or something else, like the expulsive force which begins to be burdened by these humors it was previously accustomed to. It should be considered fourthly that a four-fold reading is found here because of the cause of "diverse repletion" <note>An over-fullness of humors that is different from the usual state.</note>. For when a cold humor that a member was accustomed to is moved swiftly, then it encounters parts of the members which it did not encounter

<column-break/>

before. And if you consider well: even the parts of this humor touch the members—parts that were deep inside and were not touching—and therefore they can chill the part in which they were. And this is as if you held a piece of ice in your hand but never touched it where it was cracked; there you would find a greater coldness not suppressed by the heat of your hand. Here, therefore, this cold humor, carried suddenly and touching members it did not encounter before, causes a sensible cold. This is because this "repletion" is different from the prior one, because this one is unaccustomed, and it will become 

<margin>accustomed. That is, he says "because of the cause of diverse repletion," meaning the cold will be felt because this humor is found suddenly where it was not found before. Indeed, it was resting; and if it had been moved when it came to the member it was accustomed to, that happened gradually. This "finding" is therefore different from that one. And thus the second reading is preserved, which says "because of the cause of diverse repletion," the coldness of this humor is also felt because it chills by its sudden motion. And if the explanation of the cold of the interior humor is that the member it was accustomed to was not being chilled, then the cold is felt because of the cause of a "diverse cold complexion" <note>A change in the body's constitutional balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note>. Thus the third reading is preserved, as this coldness can be called a "diverse bad cold complexion" which causes a bad sensation; therefore that cold is felt because of the cause of a diverse complexion. And thus the fourth reading is preserved; and these are the facts of the second part of my chapter on the causes of pain.</margin>

...scattered in the body, a rigor not leading to a fever; and sometimes it has cycles <note>original: "periodi"</note> and its strength is not the strength of a rigor that leads to a fever. And the matter that causes the "weariness" <note>original: "lassitudinem"</note> of rigor by its small amount, causes rigor by its large amount before it putrefies <note>term: "putrefaction" — the "rotting" or breakdown of humors that medieval doctors believed generated the heat of a fever</note>; for if it does not putrefy, it does not lead to a fever. And sometimes cold and rigor happen because of the sinking of heat into the body because of food and things similar to it. And rigor and cold precede fevers because the "crude" <note>Undigested or unrefined.</note> humor is poured out to the muscles at the beginning: and it harms by its coldness in comparison to the muscles...

<margin>c</margin>
**And many times.** This is the fourth chapter of the *Canon* in order and the second of the "causes" annexed to the second principal chapter. From this: that a cold humor which is difficult to putrefy—such as "glassy" phlegm <note>term: "glassy phlegm" — a very thick, cold, and clear type of phlegm thought to be particularly stubborn</note>—can cause a rigor that is not followed by a fever. We spoke of this in the second book on the *Differences of Fevers* and in the fifth book of *On Accident and Disease*. It should be considered that this rigor can be a rigor that is simply "coldness," as is known; and this happens when only a cold thing, moved gradually, chills. And it can be a rigor that is a "concussion" <note>A shaking fit.</note>; and this happens when it pushes with the vehement effort of the expulsive force. And when, after a sudden cooling, the natural heat is collected inside. And that it can come periodically is well known. It should be considered second that a rigor caused by glassy phlegm is stronger when a fever follows than when a fever does not follow; for when a fever follows, it moves that phlegm faster because of the liquefying heat of the putrefaction that is beginning. And this is what he means by "its strength is not the strength of a rigor leading to a fever."

<margin>d</margin>
**And matter.** This is the fifth chapter in order: and this is a principal chapter because the cause of "shuddering" <note>original: "fractionis"</note> is taught here; however, it is Averroes' discourse on rigor, and it can be called principal because it places the cause of rigor—namely, "much matter"—though it might be better if it were an annexed chapter. We should consider and accept that the cause makes for "lassitude"—that is, shuddering—for those causes that produce rigor also produce shuddering when they are few in number. Therefore, "rigor" is taken broadly here to include "horripilation" <note>term: "horripilation" — goosebumps or the hair standing on end</note>; for the matter causing shuddering, when increased, causes horripilation. However, these things are noted in the fifth book of *On Accident and Disease*. It should be considered second that **Thaddeus** takes from this reading that rigor—and indeed any type of chill—is not part of the "essence" of a fever, nor is the time of the cold part of the fever's duration. And therefore it is not part of the "regime" of the paroxysm; for such a rigor exists before putrefaction, but a fever does not happen except with putrefaction. But he doubts this because rigor *can* happen when matter putrefies; for the heat of putrefaction moves the glassy phlegm, whence a stronger rigor is produced from it, as has been said. Furthermore, when an exacerbation precedes, it sometimes emits things that cause a certain cooling so that they seem to be another part of the paroxysm, as appears in the second book on fevers. It should be said, as Thaddeus says second, that cold and rigor are not "of" the fever, nor "of" the time of the fever—that is, of the time measuring the fever—even though it happens sometimes "with" the fever, and thus at the same time. The reason is that fever is heat, and otherwise there is heat. It should be known, however, that the time of cooling by a cold humor is sometimes distinct from the time of heating. Similarly, sometimes a shaking occurs through putrefaction; and because of this, it does not putrefy. And sometimes the heat of putrefaction begins in the matter and is weak, whence no fever is produced, but only a liquefaction that aids the cooling. When Avicenna says, therefore, that cold matter causes rigor before it putrefies, he means a "pure" rigor—that is, with pure cold and not the first heat. And he means a "great" or "complete" putrefaction—that is, one that touches the whole humor.

<margin>e</margin>
**And sometimes it happens.** This is the sixth chapter in order and the third principal chapter, in which he places the third cause of rigor: which is the sinking of natural heat to the interior because of food and similar things, such as the passions of the soul or the cold of the air. And this "similarity" is broad. It is said, however, that it moves inside because of food so that it may be digested; or it moves—that is, it is almost "suffocated"—by the food. Because upon its first arrival, the food is a contrary thing suffocating the natural heat; afterward, the heat rises again and is strengthened over the food. And this cause is more consistent with the words of Averroes in the fourth book of the *Colliget*.

<margin>f</margin>
**And rigor and cold.** This is the seventh chapter in order and is the fourth annexed chapter. It should be considered that the humor is called "crude"—that is, cold—like phlegm or parts that are cold in comparison to the muscles when it is first poured out. But afterward it harms through heat because it putrefies; and when it begins to putrefy, it begins to grow hot, as is known in the chapter on "what is eaten and drunk" in the first *Canon*. And according to this exposition, the text here is clear and rarely speaks of rigor caused by hot matter. It is as if he were saying that rigor and cold precede fevers either because the matter harms first with the coldness of a cold thing and later harms with heat when it putrefies, or because it harms by biting, etc. This chapter is therefore annexed because he has already said in general that a cold humor causes cold, and "cold" was taken commonly for both coldness and rigor. In another way, a humor is called "crude" with the crudity opposed to putrefaction, which he mentions in the first book, second section, in the chapter on the causes of cooling; and this coldness is common to both secondary humors and those beginning a paroxysm.

<summary>This page analyzes the physiological mechanics of rigor and chills, debating whether they are caused by cold humors, sharp biting humors, or the retreat of natural heat. It reconciles classical authorities to explain why shivering typically precedes the onset of a fever's heat.</summary>

# Fen Treatise

### On the Causes of Rigor

->**Section 11**<-

**Column 1**

That is, a type before they putrefy <note>In medieval medicine, fevers were often thought to be caused by humors "rotting" or putrefying in the body, which then generated unnatural heat.</note>: then the meaning is that the humor, not yet putrefied at the beginning of the paroxysm <note>A paroxysm is the sudden onset or intensification of symptoms, like a fever spike.</note>, having been poured into the muscles, causes harm by its coldness—specifically, a positive coldness, as when the matter itself is cold; or by a privative coldness <note>A "privative" coldness refers to a lack of heat, rather than the presence of an active cold substance.</note>, followed by a stinging sensation. Then, when it begins—that is, the cold—it ceases when the heat of putrefaction arrives. If you study well, I see why the cold ceases in phlegmatic patients when the putrid heat arrives, but it is not apparent why the cold that comes from the stinging of the bile <term>choler: yellow bile, associated with heat and sharpness</term> should cease. I say that putrefaction is not the cause of the stinging from choler ceasing; a sign of this is that when a burning fever <note>original: "causon", a high-intensity, "burning" fever.</note> is ended by sweats preceded by rigor, the putrid choler is expelled onto the sensitive parts of the body, where it stings violently despite being putrid. But I say that as long as the choler is moved strongly over the sensitive parts, then a sensible stinging occurs, by which heat is driven away, even though the choler itself is abundant. If, however, it is not moved strongly, no sensible stinging occurs, and thus no rigor happens. Indeed, all those with jaundice <note>original: "iterici"</note> would otherwise shiver, as **Galen** says in his book *On Rigor*. In the beginning of the paroxysm, therefore, the choler moves strongly; afterwards, it becomes accustomed to the limbs and is moved by the heat making it evaporate. And when this multiplied heat is expanded outward, you should consider this.

**Column 2**

Then, when it begins to putrefy, it begins to grow warm. <insert>And sometimes rigor precedes fevers because of the stinging of the humor and the strength of the expulsive force <note>The body's natural power to drive out harmful substances.</note> that is in the muscles, just as a person is shaken by the pouring of very hot water over the skin, especially when it is salty.</insert> And perhaps harm occurs from that which stings so that the innate heat <note>The vital warmth believed to be present in all living beings.</note> may flee to the interior; and thus cold dominates, which is why cold occurs with the stinging of heat, as if the cold were dominant. <insert>And the stinging of heat indeed occurs at the membrane covering the interior. And sometimes rigor happens because the heat flees to the interior, as happens in internal abscesses <note>original: "apostematibus".</note>. And sometimes...</insert> shivering <note>original: "horripilatio", often translated as goosebumps or the bristling of hair.</note> and rigor signify health in inseparable fevers: because

---

<margin>a</margin> regarding the shaking: it mentions the example of expulsion, to which one is moved by hot water—namely, strongly—from which it stings; and this word "concussion" <note>original: "concussio", meaning a shaking or jarring.</note> is taken from the shaking that a dog or a horse and many animals do. It is doubted because that cause of rigor seems to be included under the first cause, which is the effort of the expulsive force. It must be said that it is included, although this cause is presented as one common to many. For the expulsive force is thought to expel because of something stinging or chilling. Or it must be said more subtly: that although the effort of the expulsive force concurs with the stinging of the matter, **Avicenna** says it is "because of the stinging and the strength of the expulsive force"; these are distinct causes. First, because it is one thing for matter to sting and another for the expulsive force to expel; second, because even if the expulsive force did not attempt to expel, the hot matter would still sting strongly, and rigor would occur because of the flight of heat to the interior out of fear of the great and sudden stinging.

<margin>b</margin> And it was said "when it is salty." It is doubted whether a salty humor <note>original: "humor falsus", referring to phlegm that has become salty or acrid.</note> causes more rigor in **Avicenna’s** sequence, when he says rigor precedes fevers because of the stinging of the humor, especially when it is salty. It must be said that perhaps **Avicenna** intended to mean that rigor more often precedes when it is salty, or that if the stinging precedes, it is when the humor is salty. For salty humor stings with its saltiness no less than choler does, and by its unsuitability for expulsion, it compels the expulsive force to strive more strongly than it does when the matter is choleric; and the sign of this is a bad dysentery with severe straining <note>original: "tenaisimones", or tenesmus.</note> caused by the aforementioned salty humor. If you wish to hold that salty phlegm causes a lesser rigor in intensity, but a greater one in duration, you would say it is "more" when it is salty because the rigor is more prolonged.

<margin>c</margin> "And perhaps." It is doubted why he says "perhaps." It must be said that stinging is sometimes small, and then there is either only a vague soreness or shivering, and no rigor occurs. But when that which stings harms with a strong stinging, then the heat is drawn or flees inward; and thus the person is so strongly cold that he judges himself to be more cold than stinging. This is why he says "as if cold were dominant." And because the membrane <note>original: "panniculus"</note> covering the muscles is the most sensitive part, **Avicenna** expressed more about it, saying: "stinging of heat," that is, stinging of hot matter. It is doubted why it is not said that stinging also comes from cold matter, since even cold can be stinging, as in the fourth book of *On Simple Medicine*. It must be said that matters are not found in us so subtle that, penetrating by their thinness, they could sting. For although acidic matters are found, they are nonetheless thick. Stinging is the effect of a very thin, penetrating thing, like vinegar among cold things, as **Avicenna** says in the second book of the *Canon*, chapter four.

<margin>d</margin> "And sometimes it happens." This is the ninth cause in order, and it is the fourth principal one in which he places the fifth cause of rigor: which is the flight of heat inward because of abscesses. This cause differs from the second cause: because that cause is the drowning of heat due to natural or non-natural causes, such as food and air and the like. But this one is due to a violent cause contrary to nature—namely, a large abscess. **Avicenna** has therefore now placed five principal causes in which he placed the five causes of rigor (or of cold). The first cause is the effort of the expulsive force. The second cause is the coldness of the humor. The third cause is the drowning of heat by food. The fourth cause is the stinging of matter. The fifth cause is the flight of heat to the interior because of a large abscess.

<margin>e</margin> "And sometimes" it can be said first that he places a cause by which he teaches how to prognosticate <note>To predict the outcome of the disease.</note> from rigor, and he hints that rigor is twofold: namely, a "critical" one which is praiseworthy <note>Meaning it signals the "crisis" where the body overcomes the illness.</note>, and another non-critical one which is bad. And this latter one is twofold: one caused by excessive matter, the other caused by the falling of innate heat by way of resolution and consumption; the signs are known and will appear in the second *Fen*. Otherwise, it can be said that this is the tenth cause, regarding those things where he shows that rigor caused by the expulsive force moving matter—of which he spoke—sometimes happens from the expulsive force operating regularly and with order after signs of digestion and on a critical day. And this is good, of which the "Association" <note>likely referring to a group of commentators or a specific text like the *Aphorisms*.</note> speaks regarding burning fever. Sometimes it happens from the expulsive force operating as a "symptomatic" evacuation, because it is stimulated by the multitude and malice of the matter; such rigor is not after signs of digestion nor on a critical day, though it could happen to be on a critical day.

<margin>f</margin> "And concerning rigor." This can be read together with the preceding, as is clear from what was said; and it can be the eleventh cause in order, and the seventh principal cause in which he shows the sixth cause of rigor: which cause is the ultimate failure of natural heat in acute fevers, as in those approaching death. And you see after this rigor the weakness of every power and the fall of heat, which is signified by

<column-break/>

the falling of the pulse.
<margin>5</margin> "And dryness." This appears in the appearance <note>original: "tornalitate", likely referring to the contour or drawn appearance.</note> of the face and the roughness of the body. <insert>Because **Avicenna** says that these things appear after this rigor, yet even before there is a fall of innate heat and consequently a defect of power and the hollowing of the eyes, sharpness of the nose, etc. However, because they are more manifest after this rigor, he therefore said "which follow it." And this is one rigor among those of which the "Association" said: "If rigor falls upon a fever when the body is not yet failing but is weak, it is fatal." How this may be true will appear in the second section of this book, and we have spoken upon that "Association."</insert> It must be considered that this rigor can be cold from the defect of natural heat, and it can be rigor—namely, a concussive motion—which is the motion of the expulsive force in limbs failing near death, as **Avicenna** imagines in the third *Colliget*. And I believe that by "expulsive" he understands the "containment" of the limbs in their natural positions; when this fails, an agitation occurs not properly from an agent acting for a purpose, but from a defect of power, just as in the palpitating motion of a failing flame, and in the motion of falling leaves from trees. And in this agitation, it sometimes happens that matter is expelled. Or he understands "expulsive" properly, which is moved to act because of the [lack of] power to sustain the limbs—that is, because the limbs do not sustain or do not contain the matters. But here would be a place for speculation, which I leave to others who believe **Averroes** understands it so. It is doubted because one cause of cold is missing—namely, the sudden eradication of hot matters, of which he speaks in the second section in the chapter on the narration of good signs, where he says that shivering after an evacuation is among the good signs; and he understands "shivering" as "cold," as appears from what he adds there. It must be said that 

they signify one thing: matter is expelled from the veins and goes out. <insert>But when it is not with digestion <note>In this context, "digestion" refers to the body "cooking" or processing the humors to a healthy state.</note>, nor in a critical hour, and lightness does not follow it, it is a sign that the expulsion of that superfluity is not because the power is overcoming, but rather because much matter is expelled because of its own multitude.</insert> <margin>f</margin> "And concerning rigor": there is that which signifies death, and that which is followed by the weakness of power, and the fall of innate heat and dryness. <margin>i</margin> "Shivering indeed" happens from fewer causes than the causes of rigor. "And the commotion of the soul" <note>Likely referring to psychological disturbances or strong emotions.</note> of the period indicates the period. <margin>k</margin> "And of the elderly" indeed, the fevers are buried <note>term: "buried fever" — a fever that remains internal and hidden, not showing typical outward heat.</note>. And sometimes there is a cause in the length of the fever, a thickness in the viscera, which is why the feverish person lies on their back and extends their feet and touches their own viscera. And sometimes the tongue of the feverish person turns black with the alleviation of the fever: then his fever is buried.

if that cooling is from the surrounding air, it is given to be understood by that which he said in the third principal canon: "and things which are similar to them." Someone might believe they have argued irrefutably when they say that in summer time this chilling occurs. But we omit this.
<margin>b</margin> <insert> "Shivering indeed." Here he assigns the causes of shivering; and he says that it happens from fewer causes—that is, from weaker causes than those of rigor. This is apparent from those things we said in the definition of shivering. But it is doubted whether, when one goes from the "breadth" that is laziness to fever, one passes through all these dispositions: first laziness, then "breaking" (laxity), then shivering, then cold, then rigor, then fever. For such an order is understood by **Galen** in the fifth book of *On Accident and Disease* and by **Avicenna** in the first canon, second section, in the chapter on the causes of non-natural motions. To the contrary, we do not see it happen so in fact. It must be said that some fever sometimes attacks without any "type" <note>The "type" refers to the specific pattern of onset signs like chills.</note>: as will appear concerning phlegmatic fever from sweet phlegm; some attack with all the aforesaid signs, as when some choler begins to dominate. Whence comes a visceral laxity and laziness toward motion; which, when it is greater and moved more, yet does not cause strong shivering. But moved further, it causes cold and trembling. It happens sometimes, however, that these things occur suddenly, because they are not distinguished; as someone might pass to a choleric fever only with manifest rigor, the other dispositions being hidden. Similarly, it happens in cold fevers—namely, in phlegmatic and melancholic ones—because sometimes laziness arrives, then laxity, then weak and superficial cold, then great cold, then trembling, then fever. Sometimes, however, these are confused, though they are less likely to be confused in fevers of cold matter than in those of hot matter because of the slowness of the motions of cold matters.</insert>
<margin>f</margin> <insert> "And commotion of the soul." Here he places the second cause. First, it should stand thus: "Commotion of the soul," that is, the imagination of the paroxysm, indicates the return of another paroxysm. Others say "commotion of the soul," that is, accidents of the soul <note>Emotions or psychological states.</note>, such as when the sick person begins to be angry or saddened, it indicates the manner of the period—that is, the return of the paroxysm. For when the matters begin to move, the patient begins to be ill-disposed in the soul, becoming angry and sad according to the matter and its location; these interpretations are good. We, however, interpret it otherwise. For **Avicenna**, by "soul," sometimes understands the "mouth of the stomach" <note>A common medieval anatomical term for the upper opening of the stomach (the cardia), which was thought to be highly sensitive and connected to the soul's emotions.</note>, as appears in the chapter on quartan fever and the third canon. Therefore, "commotion of the mouth of the stomach" indicates the period—that is, the return of the paroxysm. For it happens in those who have experience of paroxysms that a commotion occurs. In tertian fever, indeed, because of the choler's lightness. In quartan fever, because of the great connection of the spleen to the mouth of the stomach. In phlegmatic fever, because the stomach is the nearby receptacle for phlegm. After this, I found **Dino** <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous medical commentator.</note> giving another explanation: in tertian fever, it is the commotion of the soul—that is, the perturbation that happens in the animated power, for example: depth of sleep and laziness in motions; when these occur according to a period, it indicates the event of paroxysms according to that period. As **Avicenna** says here, for there are some fevers whose paroxysms return without these "types"—such as continuous fevers in which exacerbations or strengthenings occur; and so he wanted to show which accidents occur at the beginning of those exacerbations. In these, there is no "type"—namely, neither rigor, nor cold, nor shivering—and he says that it is the commotion of the soul, that is, perturbation in the power of the soul, namely concerning depth of sleep and laziness.</insert>
<margin>i</margin> <insert> "And of the elderly." This is the second case. It must be considered that the fevers of the elderly lie hidden within due to the nature of their natural heat: because it is weak and not abundant in the extremities; and therefore the accidental heat that is branched off from it (as **Averroes** says in the seventh *Colliget*) does not spread outward. And thus **Hippocrates** understands in the "Association" when he said: "In the elderly, acute fevers do not happen similarly, because they have cold bodies." They also lie hidden within due to the nature of thick humors not suitable for expansion and evaporation. And therefore the letter is preserved which says "long" [duration].</insert>
<margin>k</margin> <insert> "And in length." This is the third case. And he says "sometimes" because there can be other causes, as below in the second section, the chapter on the causes of length: "thickness," that is, of the opposite—that is, the blockage of the hidden matter in the passages is retained and gathered, and the heat is weakened and cannot move freely through the passages to transform the matters; or "thickness," that is, abscesses of thick matters. The patient lies on their back because this is a good position in which, with the muscles relaxed, the liver, stomach, spleen, and the rest can be well felt [palpated].</insert>
<margin>m</margin> <insert> "And sometimes it is blackened." This is the fourth case. In which he notes the "buried" fever, which he says is the kind the elderly have. And the reason for the saying is: because the blackness of the tongue signifies the fever within, and the "alleviation" of the fever—namely, on the outside—signifies that it does not expand outward; therefore, it is buried within.</insert>

<meta>This page continues the medical commentary, moving from the symptoms of rigor (chills) into the practical treatment strategies for putrid fevers—those caused by "corrupt" or decaying humors. It focuses on the prioritization of treatment: whether a doctor should first attack the underlying cause or the fever itself.</meta>

# Book IV

<margin>a</margin> And sometimes this is the fifth rule, which is placed in the first book, the last chapter, although there it speaks of a continuous fever <note>original: "sinochus", a type of non-intermitting fever</note>: because in paralytics, however, the fever is treated first. This is because it is the greater sickness, for quick death is feared from it, but not so in the case of paralysis of some extreme part. If, however, there were universal paralysis, or of the muscles moving the breath <note>the diaphragm and chest muscles</note>, we would attend to that before the fever if possible. Because when these contrary intentions stand together, the physician must attend to both as much as he can. Therefore, Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook</note> allows vinegar syrup <term>oxymel: a mixture of honey and vinegar used to cut through thick humors</term> for the sake of the putrid fever, as will appear in the following chapter, along with rose honey <note>original: "geleniabi", from the Persian 'gul' (rose) and 'angubin' (honey)</note>. Hence in the second book of the "Canon," it says that the rose is nourished with honey etc. And although sugar-rose is also called "gelenia bin," it is taken here as honey-rose because honey is beneficial for paralysis, and there are other benefits here which need not be said.

<margin>b</margin> Chickpea water—specifically of the red chickpea—is beneficial for fever in its own time, as will appear in the first chapter concerning impure tertian fever <note>a fever that spikes every third day, associated with yellow bile</note>. It is also used for paralysis by thinning the humors and provoking their movement. With oil: here he places oil in the place of a seasoning; it is a seasoning which the Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims or Arabs</note> use much, so that they put oil with meat. This is taken from the fifth book of the "Colliget" <note>Averroes' medical encyclopedia</note> and the 26th book of "Foodstuffs" by Al-Zahrawi and the book on dishes by Al-Ghazali.

<margin>c</margin> *If he tolerates it.* This is so that there is not a fever of great inflammation; this refers not only to the oil but to the chickpea water, which we should not use in fevers of great inflammation.

<margin>d</margin> Shaving of the head. This is a rule repeated below in the second section, the chapter on the regimen of those recovering. But there is a doubt about this, because in the third book, in the general rule for the cure of brain illnesses and the chapter on foul cures, shaving is allowed. Furthermore, in the last chapter of the third "Therapeutics," it says: "shaving or shearing—about these operations concerning the hair we have said much." And I say that if hair is removed from a feverish person because it is tedious to them, then you intend to use some remedy for the head. But if you only wish to remove hair, it is better to shear with scissors than to shave with a razor. Avicenna’s reason is that shaving thickens the skin, whereby the vapors are turned back <note>Medical theory held that "vapors" needed to escape through the skin's pores; thickening the skin would trap this heat inside</note>. It thickens because it is a kind of rough friction, and this thickens as seen in the third book of the "Regimen of Health." Others say it thickens because of the coldness of the iron. Dionysius says it thickens because it is done with water, which cools at least afterward. But after the removal of the hair, you ought to use a medicine; because if it is a resolving medicine <term>resolutive: a medicine that "dissolves" or disperses humors</term>, there is no fault to care about, because immediately the thickness is removed by your resolutive washing or ointment. It must be considered if you must use repulsion <note>driving a humor away from a site</note>; we do not care about that blockage, which is small and makes a greater repulsion when we wish to prevent an abscess. In short, it is safer to shear than to shave, but the harm from shaving is small. It should be considered that perhaps Avicenna wished that a feverish person does not lose their hair; and although he said "shaving," he means neither by shaving nor shearing unless the necessity of applying medicines is present. The reason is that hair is the accustomed way; if removed, the air touches the skin more immediately and thickens the pores, which is not suitable.

->**The aim for the universal cures of putrid fevers.**<-

**And sometimes fever is associated with paralysis; therefore, let the fever be treated first. And among those things that suit them is vinegar syrup mixed with rose honey and chickpea water with oil, if the fever tolerates it. (And shaving of the head is among those things which thicken the skin, whereby the vapors are turned back and the fever becomes strong.)**

Know that the aim. General things which are necessary to know about putrid and humoral fevers are their diversity (and he has already spoken of them), and their signs and accidents (and he has also spoken of them). And their cure is known from this chapter and certain following ones. First, therefore, he puts the universal cure of putrid fevers; second, he puts the rule for their feeding; third, the general cure of acute fevers; fourth, he puts the regimen for the "accidents" <note>the secondary symptoms or complications</note>. Consider that although the principal aim of this chapter is the universal cure of putrid fevers, nevertheless it includes the cure of humoral fevers without putrefaction, since mention is made of bloodletting <note>original: "phlobotomie"</note> and cooling with the drinking of cold water. Consider second that since in a putrid fever there are two things which oppose nature—namely the cause <note>the humor</note> and the disposition <note>the fever itself</note>—immediately a double aim arises in the mind of the doctor. One toward the cause, the other toward the disposition. And if these aims are not conflicting, then the physician proceeds with both—namely with things that oppose the cause and things that oppose the disposition. As often as they contradict each other, then the doctor, by good judgment, either turns himself more to the fever or more to the cause. And therefore Avicenna says the aim sometimes turns, etc.

Consider third that it is known that in fever the aim is cooling and moistening, but in the matter <note>the humor</note> it is that it should be matured <term>maturation: the process of bringing a "raw" humor to a state where the body can expel it</term> regarding the matter currently putrid, which maturation is the preparation for expulsion; as it is said, it should be "digested" <note>meaning "processed" by the body's internal heat</note> regarding the cause... either they can be rectified and for these causes he says "let it be digested," or they cannot be rectified but are prepared for expulsion and he says "let them be matured." This is the exposition according to the doctrine of Avicenna. Consider fourth that he says: "or it is necessary that it be evacuated." This mode of speaking is used by Avicenna either because it is not always necessary that it be evacuated by a doctor because nature does it, or because the matter can be so rectified by digestion that it should not be evacuated; rather, by digestion alone the fever perfectly ceases. What we think about these things we have written in our question "On the Greatness of Fevers."

Here three questions are commonly moved. First: whether in a putrid fever the aim toward the cause is prior to the aim toward the fever. It seems first that the aim toward the cause is prior by the word of Galen <note>The most influential Greek physician (129–216 AD)</note>: "it is necessary to cut off every cause first." On the contrary: because the first aim of the doctor is toward that which is most against nature and most infested; this, however, is the fever, since it is the stronger sickness. It must be said briefly that "first aim" is said in two ways. First, "first aim" as the first thing the doctor intends, and thus it is the removal of the fever. In another way, "first aim" as the

<column-break/>

first thing he brings into the mode and act of the cure. And then I say that the cure of putrid fever is twofold: one regular, the other "coactive" <note>forced or necessitated by danger</note>.

### On the aim for the universal cures of putrid fevers. Lesson VII.

**And know that the aim in treating these fevers sometimes turns toward the side of the fever, where it is necessary that they cool and moisten; and sometimes toward the side of the matter, where it is necessary that it be matured or digested, or it is necessary...**

...a cure is called twofold. First, because you cure in another way—that is, you oppose the disease in a different way than its mode of being dictates, or because by curing you manifest harm in order to avoid a greater harm. I say, therefore, that speaking of the "regular cure"—that is, the cure made according to the rule and aim accepted from the mode of the putrid fever's existence—the prior aim is toward the cause (the putrefaction). The reason is that the mode of the putrid fever's existence is a mode of a disposition depending on a cause; therefore, the mode of destroying it is the mode of removing the cause. Regarding this, Galen says in the fourth book of "Therapeutics" that in fevers which have an antecedent cause inside, the first aim is from the cause. If, however, we speak of the "regular cure" in the second way—that is, which is without any harm—then by considering subtly, there is no priority or posteriority of aim in such a cure... but there is a simultaneity. For this regular cure is when, having considered the cause and the disposition, something is indicated to be so beneficial that it harms nothing if it is opposed to both cause and disposition at once. And this Galen says: if the cooling things for the fever and the auxiliary things for the cause agree, that which is shown from both sides should be done immediately. For example, the giving of cold water or violet syrup.

I say secondly that in "coactive" cure, the first thing we intend in the act of curing is sometimes toward the fever. For we are forced to begin from the fever and not the cause when the fever is of such vehemence that by attending to the cause through some digestion, the patient dies; therefore we begin from the disposition (the fever). In the second mode of coactive cure, the doctor sees that if he cuts off the cause, it harms the disposition, and if he treats the disposition, it increases the cause. Then he meditates on which is the lesser harm.

The second doubt is whether digestion belongs to the "joined cause" or the "antecedent cause." <note>Joined cause: the humor already causing the disease; Antecedent cause: the humor still in the veins ready to flow in.</note> It seems it belongs to the joined cause because Avicenna wants a "laudable sediment" in urine to be nothing other than the processing of the things making the sickness. Further, digestion makes putrefaction cease; but the putrid humor is the joined cause. On the contrary, it seems it should belong to the antecedent cause because the joined cause is the humor which is burned through putrefaction; but to this is owed evacuation, not digestion. Thaddeus <note>Thaddaeus Alderotti (1210–1295), a famous medical professor at Bologna</note> wished in his practice to dispute that digestion belongs to the antecedent cause. We say that digestion is suitable for both the joined and the antecedent cause. For we see that nature does so: it digests and repels the putrid humors that make the fever, and similarly it digests and expels the humors which are corrupting. Further, we see in the "rest periods" of intermittent fevers, when there is no fever actually present, that doctors consider the signs of digestion in the urine. For the matter of intermittent fevers evaporates... but in continuous and especially acute fevers, because the matter is kept for one single expulsion, we attend to its digestion.

It also explores specific treatments like oxymel, chickpea water, and the risks of shaving a patient's head during illness.</summary>

# Treatise II

...must be digested before nature [can act]. Or it should be said that the antecedent cause <note>original: "causa antecedens"; the underlying imbalance that predisposes a body to illness</note> creates a potential joined with the act. Nevertheless, in truth, a "digested" substance is that which appears in the judgment [of the illness] and signifies a crisis <term>crisis: a turning point in a disease where the patient either recovers or declines</term>. In a critical stage, it is separated from the joined cause <note>original: "causa conjuncta"; the immediate, active cause of the symptoms</note>, because it is that which is expelled during the crisis through the power of nature, having been pre-digested. For nature fights more against the joined cause—just as it is more affected by it—than against the antecedent cause. How one matter is digested while another is expelled during a crisis is discussed in our work on the severity of disease. To the second point, it should be said that the digestion of the joined cause makes the actual putrefaction <note>the "rotting" or corruption of humors</note> cease; that is, it prevents the matter from becoming putrid. 

<margin>
Just as the digestion of the antecedent cause makes [the illness] cease—that is, it prohibits the affecting matter from passing into the joined cause. Regarding the second reason, that the humor brought forth is said to be evacuated because its digestion is directed toward the end goal, which is evacuation. But because the antecedent cause can be corrected more frequently than the joined cause, the authors commonly say that...
</margin>

> **T**hat it may be evacuated. ¶ And digestion: when it is thickened, its balancing is with thinning. ¶ In thinness, its balancing is with thickening. And sometimes those things which the fever requires regarding cooling are contrary; then that...

to the antecedent cause, strength is owed; but to the joined cause, evacuation is owed. The third doubt is whether the same digestive agent—for instance, the same syrup—digests both the joined cause and the antecedent cause. It must be said that insofar as the affecting cause and the joined cause are in one disposition, one syrup is suitable. For example, non-putrid phlegm, in the form of an affecting cause, is thick and viscous; and putrid phlegm, existing as a joined cause, is also thick and viscous. Therefore, one syrup is suitable for both: namely, a "cutting" or thinning syrup. For example, vinegar of roots <term>syrupus acetosus: a common medicine made of vinegar, honey, and herbal roots</term>, unless something else prohibits it. But insofar as the antecedent and joined causes have different dispositions, the digestive syrup must be varied. For example, non-putrid phlegm is cold, and thus a syrup of roots may be granted with the addition of, say, calamint <note>a mint-like herb used to warm the body</note> or sometimes with honeyed roots. However, putrid phlegm is hot; therefore, it is safer to give sugar syrup <note>original: "si. zuccari"</note> with the two roots and without calamint. If, therefore, you give a syrup to a person suffering from a phlegmatic fever during the hour of rest, you can give a warmer syrup; but if you give the syrup during the hour of affliction <note>when the fever spikes</note>, these matters of heat will be better known in the progression of this chapter and in special cases.

¶ And digestion. Since he [Avicenna] previously set forth a general case in which he places two intentions for the evacuation of putrid fever—and that sometimes the physician turns more to one intention than the other—here he begins to follow the cure of putrid fevers according to these general intentions. First, he declares one of these intentions. Second, he shows why he sometimes returns to one and sometimes the other. Third, he shows with what tools and how they perform these intentions, and how and with what one is done, and how and with what the other is done when we return to it. This begins where it says, "sometimes they are contrary," and "when cooling." Concerning the first part, it should be considered that Avicenna <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was the preeminent medical authority of the Middle Ages</note> says that the intention in treating these fevers sometimes turns to the side of the fever itself, etc. He wished to follow the three aforementioned cures: namely, what the intention is toward the fever, what it is toward the cause, and when it is that we turn more toward one or the other. When these general intentions for curing putrid fevers are fully held, this chapter will be complete. Therefore, everything is founded upon this first rule. Second, it should be considered that Avicenna does not show what the intention toward the fever is—which is cooling, or by which we cool and moisten—because it is well known what cooling and moistening are; for cooling and moistening are alterations made by a cooling and moistening thing. Nor does he show what the intention toward the matter is, which is evacuation, because it is known that evacuation is the extraction of humor from the body. These things are presupposed to be known from the first book. It remained, therefore, for Avicenna to declare to us what "digestion" is. For he already said it is necessary that the matter be digested or matured. So that the diversity of terms does not lead you into error, he says that by digestion he understands the balancing of the humor: namely, so that it becomes fit for expulsion. If it is thin, let it be thickened, and vice versa. That is, that its thinness be lessened by thickening and its thickness by thinning; not that it be moved from one extreme to the other. Thus he says "thickening is a balancing with thinning." Therefore, by digestion he understands the preparation for exiting, whether it is called digestion or maturation. Commonly, they doubt here whether digestion proceeds by thickening, and we have disputed these questions at length and noted them in the *Book of Principles*. The "Consiliator" <note>Pietro d'Abano (1257–1316), a famous medical commentator</note> treats this diffusely. Commonly, practitioners pass over this with the solution that digestion in a restorative sense always proceeds by thickening; they understand that the digestion of humors—which are destined to become part of a limb—always thickens, because limbs are thick relative to humors. But digestion by which humors pass into "spirits" <term>spiritus: a subtle, vaporous substance believed to flow through the nerves and arteries</term> proceeds by thinning, since spirits are thinner than humors. However, digestion of harmful matter—which is the preparation of the harmful for expulsion—sometimes thickens and sometimes thins. We, along with other philosophers, often say that digestion, as it is the perfection of moisture (i.e., watery parts) by the surrounding dry, earthy heat, always thickens. For moisture is thickened by earthy dryness. But as it is the transmutation of earthy dryness so that moisture may terminate it, it always thins; because earthy dryness is thinned by the mixture of moisture. Because of this, some things appear thicker, because in their origin they had much water (like the kernel of an almond when considered in its watery form vs. when complete), or they appear thinner (like things that are initially like stone and bitter and later become succulent). This is a summary of what we have said elsewhere. It should also be considered that, in our opinion, no digestion performed by nature is, in itself, primarily a balancing for expulsion. Rather, it is the induction of suitable dispositions through the act of nutrition, if possible. Nature, using its powers, strives to assimilate whatever can be made healthy; but if it cannot ultimately be made healthy, it expels it, as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine</note> feels in the second book on the *Differences of Fevers*. A sign of this is that nature gives whiteness to putrid matter, from which pus is made; and that alteration is from the digestive power of the solid members. The digestion of harmful matter by the power within us is the acquisition of certain dispositions preceding the act of nutrition, and this happens because the matter is disposed for expulsion, either because it becomes of a more suitable substance or because it becomes a more appropriate object [for expulsion]. For a final declaration of these things, see our question on the severity of disease.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Here is the second part: "and many times." Here is the third. Divide the first part into two: first, he shows that contrariety sometimes occurs—indeed, most often—between that which the matter requires (evacuation and digestion) and that which the fever requires (cooling). This is because the evacuating and digestive agent is hot, and this harms the fever. Second, he shows what contrariety occurs between that which is suitable for cooling and that which we need for the reduction...
</margin>

¶ And sometimes. Here he shows why this intention sometimes turns toward the fever and sometimes toward the other part: namely, toward the matter. The cause of this is the contrariety that sometimes exists in these intentions, because what preserves one harms the other. First, he shows these contrarieties in general; second, he shows how sometimes there is no contrariety, but rather what benefits one also benefits the other; third, declaring the point in general, he shows toward what the physician should turn when contrariety exists.

> **W**hat the humor requires regarding digestion, evacuation, and resolution. ¶ For sometimes the digestive and evacuating agent is hot; indeed, it is so for the most part; and then it is necessary that the more fearful [danger] be observed more carefully.

...of the matter, because cold prohibits the matter from being reduced. Third, he inserts another rule. It should be considered from Avicenna's words when a physician turns his intention toward either the fever or the matter. The cause is the contrariety of those two intentions; if a contrariety exists such that what helps the cause harms the digestion (or vice versa), one must necessarily choose one of these intentions. He chooses that which is "more fearful"—that is, the one which, if omitted, would cause greater fear or danger. If it is observed, there is greater utility and less danger. In this, Avicenna shows a general rule: whether the physician should turn more to the cause or the disposition when these intentions fight against and oppose each other. Second, consider that Avicenna shows a special contrariety between the intention of digestion and evacuation on one side, and cooling on the other, because digestive and evacuating agents are hot. Therefore, they harm the fever. It is doubted whether an evacuant is hot, and it seems not, because cassia, tamarinds, and myrobalans <note>exotic fruits used as laxatives</note> are cold. Furthermore, it will be discussed here regarding evacuation through the bowels and urine; an evacuant through urine is not necessarily hot, such as common seeds. It must be said that light evacuants—those that evacuate by smoothing or licking or compressing—are not hot; but those placed in a stronger grade (evacuating by "resolving") are hot. For the attractive power in them is strong, and this is aided by heat. Avicenna did not say absolutely that every [evacuant] is hot, but that sometimes it is. It is doubted why he says "for the most part." It should be said that this is not because there are more species of things in the world that evacuate by resolving than those that evacuate by smoothing, but because most evacuations of matter in fevers are done with things that evacuate by resolving. I say "appropriate" or "eradicative" evacuation. For common "eradicative" evacuation, which is a certain efficacy called among the Arabs, is done with things that evacuate by smoothing and licking. When Avicenna considered those that evacuate by resolving—even if they are few compared to smoothers—he said "sometimes," because we use them at a determined time. But when he considered them from the perspective of their use for true reduction or eradication, he said "indeed, for the most part." Regarding those that provoke urine, it is well known that they are mostly hot. Indeed, by thinning the watery part of the blood, they do this and thicken it. Some are hot, such as fennel, parsley, and similar things. Those that provoke urine because they are watery—sliding toward the urine like melon water, cucumber water, and watery wine—are not hot, but cold and moist. But you might say: cold common seeds provoke urine and are neither moist nor fluid. It must be said that such seeds (melon, cucumber, etc.) either preserve the wateriness by the power of their fruits, or have hidden hot parts, or have a specific property. It is doubted whether the digestive agent for putrid fever matter is hot; it seems not, because cold water "digests" choleric <note>yellow bile</note> matter, as Avicenna says later. Furthermore, some matters need thickening, which is done by cold. Furthermore, the fever that most often occurs is from bile (*cholera*); therefore, most digestive agents are cold. On the contrary, Avicenna and other authorities like Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (865–925 AD), another titan of Islamic medicine</note> and Pietro d'Abano discuss this. In this question is the solution: digestion is threefold. First, the power itself, which is neither hot nor cold. Second, natural heat. Third, the disposition induced by food and medicines. This third is twofold: one is the opening of the pathways, which is done by hot things (thus the digestive is hot because cold does not dilate); the other is the change of the matter's quality which made it "disobedient" [to nature]. In this case, the digestive can be hot or cold, depending on which quality of the matter needs to be opposed. This opinion is true when well understood. Another solution is from Ruffianus, who is called "more than a commentator." He wishes that the digestive of the joined cause be cold and dry. This is because what has putrefied is hot and moist; therefore, cold and dry are opposed to it. But the digestive of the antecedent cause (the cause of the putrefaction) is hot and dry, because that cause is an obstruction needing "opening." We say the words of this man are true, even if they are not sufficient here. For if it is understood that the digestive of putrefaction—that which opposes the external putrid heat—is cold, he speaks truly; but this is not enough. For not only does the actually putrid humor have the malice of heat which we must oppose, but it has a malice of substance, to which the "digestion" of the physician is more owed. Through such digestion, it is made more ready for expulsion than by mere cooling. One must similarly ask whether the agent preparing the substance of putrid humor for expulsion is hot or cold, and why he says it is "for the most part" hot.
