<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "digestion" (maturation) of diseased humors in fevers, specifically examining whether medicines should be heating or cooling and how to manage the use of fruit-based remedies.</meta>

...becomes hot. That is, an opening medicine <term>aperient: a medicine used to open the pores or internal channels (obstructions) of the body</term> is the opposite of hot. He speaks truly; however, this is not sufficient for us in this investigation. For there may be other dispositions in the humor that causes the fever through which it is prone to putrefaction <note>original: "putredo"; the "rotting" or corruption of the body's humors</note>. These dispositions require cooling: for instance, because the humor is too thin or too inflamed. Furthermore, we have shown in the first [book], fourth treatise [of the *Canon*], that although all putrefaction is in some way connected to impeded or prohibited transpiration <note>original: "transpiratio"; the release of vapors through the skin</note>, not every putrefaction occurs necessarily because of prohibited transpiration. Similarly, not every putrid thing requires a hot opening medicine to remove the obstruction <term>oppilation: a medieval term for a blockage or "stuffing" in the veins or organs</term> that prevents transpiration, as some have said. Let us therefore say what actually happens. First, it is the case that the humoral matters that cause fever—if they are to be digested by the action of the limbs—are digested by heat, because the limbs act with natural heat. Second, if these matters are digested by their own "proper digestion"—which is the mixing of the moist with the dry—they are digested by heat, whatever the matters may be. For such a mixing is the action of heat, as is gathered from the second [book of the *Canon*].

## Of two things. 

And perhaps the opposite is true: that which is suitable for the fever regarding cooling—such as Indian melons <note>original: "meloes indi"; likely watermelons or a similar cooling fruit</note> and other vegetables—is contrary to what is suitable for the matter regarding its reduction. Therefore, it is forbidden to give these in a drink, except where there is no matter. And all...

<margin>4th treatise on Meteorology, chapter 2.</margin>
The agent of this paroxysm <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase in the intensity of a disease</term> can be the natural heat, differing according to the different limbs. The temperate heat of medicines acts to comfort the natural heat; then the medicines digest [the humors], acting either immediately on the matter—of which we have noted many things in the fourth chapter of the second book—or otherwise. Thirdly, let us say that "digestion"—that is, the removal of any bad disposition by which the humor is hindered from evacuation—can be achieved by both hot and cold opening medicines, and by thickening medicines, depending on how the bad dispositions of the matters are managed. And according to this, Avicenna says that digestion is "equation" <note>original: "equatio"; a balancing or leveling of the qualities of the humors</note>. In the second book, in this chapter and the chapter on these dispositions, the changeability of the matter is understood. For although this digestive could be hot (as it thins and opens), it could also be cold (as it thickens). However, it is usually hot, because most febrile matters are found to be thick, and obstructions are usually found joined with putrefactions, thickness, and the viscosity of the matters. And this happens because of excessive gluttony and a lack of exercise. Whence thick and viscous humors are generated, whether they be cold or hot. To the first contrary point, it must be said that treatment by cold water is rarely done, because it is rare that such bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> and other conditions are found. More frequently, however, matters are found whose conditions indicate the giving of a digestive with some degree of heat. To the second statement, it is said that the discourse is quite strange which the commentator [Averroes] placed in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Art of Medicine*</note>... and he says Galen wanted it so that when the blood is hot and bilious, its passage into all the veins is easy. This disposition does not seem to align with the intellect. We shall say that perhaps Galen intended that bilious humor is very prone to becoming inflamed and putrefied, and thus associated with every other fever, such as quartan or quotidian <note>types of recurring fevers associated with different humors</note>... 

<margin>a</margin>
**And perhaps.** He shows that what is suitable for the fever by cooling is sometimes the opposite of what is suitable for the matter by resolution <note>original: "resolutio"; the breaking down or dispersal of a humor</note>. For example, what is sometimes suitable for the fever by cooling with Indian melon water and similar things—such as gourds or cucumbers or citruls <note>a type of melon or gourd</note> and the water of apples or plums—and such cooling is contrary to what is suitable for the matter regarding its reduction. Therefore, these waters of melons and the like are forbidden to be given in a drink except where there is no [morbid] matter. This contradiction of intentions differs from the previous one: because in this case, what suits the fever harms the matter, whereas in the preceding case, what suited the matter harmed the fever. It should be considered that the "Indian melon" is what we call the "green melon." Other "vegetables" are other similar fruits like citruls, gourds, etc. Thus, the term "vegetable" <note>original: "olus"</note> is broader among the Arabs than it is among us. For us, it signifies only herbs, but for them, it also signifies fruits. You will find this often written by Avicenna... and below in the chapter on the cure for tertian fever <note>a fever occurring every third day, traditionally linked to yellow bile</note>. But in all these, let it be noted that the cooling power prevents the matters by "chilling" them. But it is doubted because the melon does not cool so much as to prevent evacuation. Furthermore, it evacuates because it greatly provokes urine. Whence below, in the chapter on the cure for quartan fever, he maintains that lettuce is colder than melon; and where lettuce is forbidden because of cooling, melon is not. He also maintains that in melon there is a powerful provocation of urine. It should be said first that here he speaks of the green melon when it is not ripe, and similarly of young cucumbers and gourds and unripe citruls. But in the chapter on quartan fever, he speaks of the sweet melon. Whence he says: there is nothing found quite like the sweet melon. But the "sweet melon" is the ripe melon, which we call a *pepo* <note>original: "pepon"; a pumpkin or large melon</note>. Because someone might believe we could use the sweet melon because it provokes urine, Avicenna adds a general rule: that all such fruits and their waters should be postponed because they harm feverish patients with their boiling <note>effervescence/heat</note>. We do not wish to be brought into contradictions here about these names: melon, pepo, citrul, cucumber—that is, *anguria* according to the Arabs. For we speak here with these terms because they are from the Arabic language—namely Avicenna, Averroes, and Rabbi Moses [Maimonides]—whose terms for these fruits are the basis for ours... all these said fruits and others like them are cooling. And therefore, they are suitable for the fever. But it is contrary to what is suitable for the matter regarding reduction. This is said, first: because by cooling they prevent it from resolution and make it raw <note>original: "incrudant"; making it harder for the body to process</note>. Second: because of their aptitude for corruption, they multiply bad, putrescible matters... Consider "unless where there is matter": that is, some stronger, hot, thin matter in which there would be more benefit from the cooling of citruls and melons than the other harm that would be done by them. And Haly Abbas, in the third [book] of his *Practice*, immediately at the beginning of tertian fever, allows Indian melons on the day of the attack. Whence Averroes says the juice of the *anguria*—that is, the Saracen cucumber—is contrary to bile with its whole substance... or "unless where there is no matter," as in a hectic fever <note>original: "febris ethica"; a chronic, wasting fever</note> or a true ephemeral fever <note>a fever lasting only one day</note>; then these could be granted with the intention of cooling, as the retention of matters does not prohibit it.

<margin>b</margin>
**And altogether.** There is a doubt about this rule. For the "water of fruits"—that is, the water from the decoction of plums, violets, and jujubes—which Mesue <note>original: "Adefue"; Pseudo-Mesue, a famous medical authority</note> writes about in the seventh distinction of his *Antidotarium*, gently softens the belly and expels bile. But such softening is praised, because just before the seventh day, Avicenna allows violet syrup. Furthermore, physicians commonly give it, and sometimes they give the pulp of cassia before the seventh day. Some correct this text, saying that the water of fruits should *not* be proposed. Others are those who

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin>
say that the "water of fruits" should not be given before the seventh day because such water is "solvent" <note>laxative</note>. Whence Mesue says of it: "it draws out red bile with ease." These people, however, are little practiced in the operations of the art. Haly Abbas, who must be trusted in practice, begins tertian fever with the water of manna, tamarinds, and cassia before digestion appears. Let us say that "water" is used in Arabic books for "juice" or for a "decoction" <note>a liquid made by boiling down medicinal plants</note>. And with this, let us say that the "water of fruits" is twofold. One is the water that softens the belly, which is made from plums, cassia, manna, violets, tamarinds, jujubes, and certain others... This water of fruits is described by Mesue in his *Antidotarium*, and it is for you to compose it according to the matter and proportion that seems right to you, provided the intention is the softening of the belly and the tempering of heat. Of this "water of fruits," Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"</note> speaks in the last chapter of the 18th [book] of the *Continens*, where he says: "If the convalescent is weak and cannot sustain [stronger medicine], give him the water of fruits. And I give him such water every morning and it purges him twice." Avicenna speaks of this above in the chapter on ephemeral fever... This water of fruits is not forbidden from the beginning of putrid fevers; rather, it is commonly permitted for the purpose of softening the belly. Whence Avicenna says immediately that it is the ultimate degree of softening. And you see that the community of doctors gives cassia at the beginning of putrid fevers, and others give violet syrup and dissolve it with a decoction of violets and plums... And the reason for this is that it is most useful at the onset of putrid fevers for the belly to be softened and the sharpness of the fever to be prevented. These are all understood under the term "water of fruits"—that is, softening water—and they settle the heat. This is so because they are mostly made from softening fruits like cassia, plums, tamarinds, and jujubes, along with violets and manna. But you see that many of these evacuate bile by their property; therefore, it is necessary to wait for digestion before their use. It should be said that in these medicines, the power to soften the belly is effective, but the power to dissolve bile is very weak. Therefore, if they find bile ready in the first passages, they draw it out without any trouble. But if they do not find it ready, they do not therefore agitate the remaining bile. This is useful without harm, whatever the fever may be: bilious, sanguine, phlegmatic, or melancholic... although the compositions of these softening medicines must be different according to the different fevers... The second is the water of acidic fruits that resist putrefaction, such as the water—that is, juice—of verjuice <note>sour grape juice</note>, lemon, orange, or sour pomegranate... we can give this water of fruits at the beginning of putrid fevers in which we wish to resist the malignancy of the putrefactions. Whence in pestilential fevers, its use is highly praised. The third is the water of fruits that is named commonly with herbs or vegetables among the Arabs, and these are fruits like cucumbers (called *anguria* or Saracen cucumber) and the green melon... these are what Avicenna intends here, and he forbids it until the week [is out]. It is Avicenna's custom to understand "the week" as up to the seventh day... he intends that the water of citrine melons, cucumbers, and the like should not be given while the matter is undigested. But on the contrary, Haly Abbas allows Indian melon water at the beginning of tertian fever. Furthermore, in the management of acute fevers, for the purpose of cooling, Avicenna gives the water of citrul, melon, and cucumber. But the necessity of extinguishing [the heat] can be even before digestion... Furthermore, Cassius Felix, in [cases of] burning fever <note>original: "causo"</note>, many times used the juice of gourds. Let us say to this that Avicenna's intention is that the water of fruits—that is, Indian melon and cucumber and the like, such as apples and pears—has utility in putrid fevers: it extinguishes [heat], and in this it is good. And regarding this, Avicenna says that Indian melons and other vegetables, like gourds, etc., suit the fever by cooling. But because their "water" is very prone to corruption due to the watery moisture being apt for boiling and putrefaction... he told you to be careful to postpone its use until the week [is out]—that is, until digestion appears in the matter. But you will say: "Will this water of fruits not be just as corruptible after digestion as before?" It should be said that once digestion has occurred, the putrefaction is not so able to be increased as it was before. For it is understood that a reduction of the matter has occurred. Therefore, if it is necessary to extinguish the heat, you will give the water of fruits more safely after digestion and the reduction of the matter. For before that, it adds to the putrefaction... First, because by cooling it thickens the matter and prevents its evaporation by narrowing the paths. Second, because it adds to the putrid matters. Therefore, Avicenna, considering that Indian melon water is harmful in this—that it prevents the reduction of the matter—and this harm is great, he made a rule for melon water and others like it, and said: Care should be taken that the water of fruits be postponed until the week... and then he assigned the cause.

<margin>b</margin>
<margin>Note: "Care should be taken that the water of fruits be postponed until the week": and this is the commentary on barley water. And all fruits harm those with fever with their boiling and their corruption in the stomach. And many times indeed a thing is found which digests and thins...</margin>

# Treatise II
## Page II

Therefore, it is necessary to give them in no way, or at least to postpone them until after all other fruits. For instance, Indian melons, cucumbers, and the like harm a person with a fever by "ebullition" <term>ebullition: a state of "boiling" or fermentation where humors corrupt rapidly in the heat of the stomach</term>, because they boil and are corrupted in the stomach. ¶ It must be considered, however, that sometimes such a great necessity exists—especially for the extinguishing and sharpness of the yellow bile—that we trust it can be done through these types of melons and we begin with them, just as Haly Abbas <note>original: "balyabas"; refers to the 10th-century Persian physician Haly Abbas</note> did. And despite all this, Haly Abbas first recommends softening the belly <note>i.e., using a laxative</note> before giving melon water, as appears in the third book of his *Practice*, in the chapter on the cure of tertian fever.

¶ This is how the words of Avicenna should be understood below. If we can extinguish the heat with another thing, let us not use them or let us postpone them. Avicenna understood all of this in the seventh book of the *Colliget* <note>The *Colliget* was actually written by Averroes, but was often bound or studied alongside Avicenna</note>, where, in establishing the order of cooling medicines, he first puts forward barley water, julep, and syrup with sugar and rose water; then, according to some modern physicians, he places the juice of gourd and melon, etc. This is what Avicenna meant when he says: "afterwards let us use the water of fruits." Thus, he is content with barley water or rice water. Later, we will discuss many things through which these contradictions cease. But a doubt is raised: among these fruits which you said ought to be postponed, you named apples (which among us are called *mala*) and you named pears. But this does not agree with practitioners, who commonly give cooked apples to feverish patients as part of their diet. And we say that this is the diet upon which the Italians have settled because of the exhaustion of those with fever. For cooked apples are less harmful because their watery moisture—which makes them prone to corruption—is evaporated by boiling. Their cooking is done by roasting or boiling, as Galen suggests in the second book of *On Aliments*. I praise roasting in cases of fever more than boiling, with the intention that they be further removed from ebullition and corruption. But if the intention is watery cooling and moistening for the purpose of a faster descent [through the bowels], those cooked in water are more praiseworthy. You may read from the authors about the diversity of these apples and pears—regarding their acidity, sweetness, the thickness or thinness of their flesh—and you will know how to choose what is best to give your feverish patient. It should be noted, however, that it appeared to the wise Arabs that great malice occurs from eating apples. Hence Averroes in the fifth book of the *Colliget*, after praising apples for strengthening the heart, said that apples generate thick flatulence in the "second digestion" <term>second digestion: the metabolic process occurring in the liver and veins</term>. He says it is said by the wise that they can partly generate hectic fever, and that the winds generated from them have a bad quality. ¶ This is the discourse of Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides</note> in the *Aphorisms*, on the authority of Ibn Zuhr <note>Avenzoar</note>: an apple without scent strengthens the heart and brain, and its scent is useful for those with consumption <note>wasting disease</note> and melancholics. But the eating of it is worse than the eating of all other fruits, because by its specific nature it generates windiness in the nerves and muscles which is not resolved except with difficulty. It must be considered that when necessity forces the use of fruit water, the physician ought to try to correct their harm with cooking—just as we cook gourd in barley paste—and by eating other things, as will appear to the prudence of the physician.

<insert>
and it cools with evacuation just like vinegar syrup. **And know** that fever is sometimes of such vehemence and sharpness that it is not permitted to use a causal regimen <note>treating the root cause</note>; rather, it requires extreme cooling, especially if you do not find a strong "virtue" <term>virtue: the patient's innate vital strength or "battery life"</term> resisting and enduring it. **But if you find** it resisting and enduring, cut off the cause and expel the humor and cut off food, and do not cool with a cooling that prohibits resolution <note>the breaking down and removal of the disease matter</note>. **But if** you find the virtue failing, it is sometimes occupied by a contrary complexion; therefore cool it and revive the virtue with food. Once it becomes strong through its revival and overcomes its contrary, return to the cause. And when you cool the heat of the fever, as much as it is reduced on one side by the febrile heat, just as much is regenerated on the other side by the increase of putrefaction. And this is what is added there: "nor in the meantime," etc. But you will ask what kind of cooling would do this? It must be said that this would be with some external cold thing causing a blockage, like cold water, or internal, like cold water drunk without reason, by which the fever would be extinguished immediately, but since much matter is packed down, it would rise up again after an hour into a greater or lesser putrefaction. Galen says this in the seventh chapter of his *Therapeutics* where, speaking of cold water given inappropriately, he says it brings no small relief by extinguishing the fever at first, but finally, with the cause remaining, another fever will happen again, many times more difficult than the first. This is what Galen wants; Avicenna, however, wants you to extinguish the vehemence of the fever, but not in such a way that putrefaction is increased by it.
</insert>

<margin>a</margin> ¶ And many times. Here he shows that sometimes this contradiction is not found, because something is found that can benefit both: such as vinegar syrup <note>oxymel</note>, which cools and digests the matters. It must be considered that by vinegar syrup we should understand the simple kind made from water, vinegar, and sugar, in which there is a cooling power from the water and vinegar, and a subtle power through the vinegar which disposes the matter to move, while the sugar cleanses it. And therefore it is said that it evacuates. Because we have made a separate treatise on vinegar syrup where we spoke of all its varieties and every matter for which it is suitable, we will not pursue this further here. But you should join that treatise to this Canon.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ And know. Since he has already declared why the physician turns more toward one intention than the other—because there is a contradiction in carrying out those intentions—here he shows to which of those two intentions he should turn, although he spoke generally in that word "the more fearful of two things." And therefore this Canon declares that one: namely, which intention is more fearful, and consequently more to be observed. First he shows when the physician's intention turns toward the fever; second, when it returns to the matter; third, he adds the following Canon. ¶ The first Canon is from Galen’s *Therapeutics*, at the beginning of which he says: if the magnitude of the fever is intolerable to the sufferer, one must not increase the fever through those things by which we cut off the cause. For we would intend both at once: the fever and the humor. This is what Avicenna says: sometimes the fever is of such and so sharp a heat that if you wanted to digest it with hot things or provoke evacuation with hot things, the patient would be lost by the small addition made to the heat. Therefore, cool it extremely—that is, with strong cooling by drinking cold water or another extinguishing drink and by poultices. Even if digestive or evacuative medicines are not present at that degree of heat, life could not endure for as long as is required for the operation upon the cause; it is expedient for you to cool, and the regimen of the cause shall be dismissed. Second, it must be considered that the physician is certain he must hasten to cool when he does not find the patient strong enough to resist the "dissolution" <note>the breakdown of the body's tissues</note> caused by the vehemence of the fever's heat, and when he does not find him strong enough to endure it without food. For if the physician finds a patient with a strong fever but finds him strong in pulse and resisting dissolution—which is the case for those with thick humors, dense pores, and similar dispositions—and finds him enduring it without food, he will not care to cool with extreme cooling; rather, by cutting off food, he intends to treat the cause and use gentle extinguishers or digestives.

<column-break/>

...the third member of his division: namely, to intend more toward one while not omitting the other. Others commonly say that Galen does not praise the physician intending toward the disposition while increasing the cause. Whence, if the disposition is increased by this, he says: "if we cure the fever with whatever aids, if these aids always increase the cause for us, they will make it worse," etc. This exposition can be saved if it is understood thus: the physician cooling the fever ought not to cool with something that, while cooling, simultaneously increases putrefaction; for by increasing putrefaction, it increases the febrile heat. As much as it is reduced on one side, just as much is regenerated from that heat through the increase of putrefaction. And this is why it says "nor in the meantime." But you will say, what cooling would do this? It must be said that this would be with an external cold blockage, like cold water, or internal, like cold water drunk irrationally. The fever might be extinguished immediately, but with the matter packed down, a greater fever would arise later. Galen says this in the seventh chapter: cold water given inappropriately confers no small relief at first, but because the cause remains, another fever arises, often harder than the first. Avicenna wants you to extinguish the vehemence without increasing putrefaction. We say that Galen did not mean something so simple, but as a man of better judgment in the particulars of medicine, he wanted to compare the intention of curing the disease (the fever) with the intention of treating the cause.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ **And if you find.** This is the second Canon, in which he shows that sometimes the physician turns his intention toward the cause—that is, to the matter—and neglects the fever or intends toward it only slightly. Digestion is the intention toward the cause; he was silent about this, giving it to be understood that the other intention is evacuation. This is twofold: sensibly through the belly (provocation), which he meant when he said "cut off the cause and expel the humor," and hidden through resolution, which he expressed when he said "cut off the food." If you find the strength resisting the febrile heat—so the patient does not mind the bad sensation or dissolution because the heat is weak or the patient is very strong—you may treat with the regular cure: intending toward the cause and cutting it off.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ **And do not cool.** As if to say: I do not say that if the fever is strong you should in no way cool; but under the stated conditions, you should not be forced to cool with a cooling that prohibits the resolution of the matter, such as cooling with cold water, or with poppy syrup and the like.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ **But if.** Here he places the third Canon. Since two intentions were placed—one for the fever, one for the matter—it appears that the indication taken from the patient's "virtue" (strength) does much here. The first Canon considered the vehemence of the fever and a weak virtue; the second considered a strong virtue. Therefore, the third Canon considers a failing virtue, for which we do everything. Its failure can be from resolving heat, so we give food because the failure can be from the loss of spirits and humors below the necessary quantity. Then, fortify the virtue through food; and this is what he says: "and revival." Fortify it by altering the unnatural heat; this is what he says: "and it overcomes its contrary." Then return to the cause by digesting and evacuating as seems best to you. It is doubted how this third Canon differs from the first. It must be said that the first is taken principally from the vehemence of the fever, while this third is taken from the actual failing of the strength itself.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ **And when you.** Now Avicenna has declared the two curative intentions used in the cure of putrid fevers. Here he shows how and with what these intentions are carried out. First, how cooling is done; second, how evacuation is done. It must be considered that these "troches" <term>troche: a medicinal lozenge or disc</term> are the troches of roses mentioned at the end of the chapter. Troches of camphor, barberry, and spodum <note>burnt ivory or metal ash used as an astringent</note>, by drying and binding, retain and thicken the matters even if they were digested. Therefore, it is necessary that the matters be digested and evacuated first; then their use is safe. For they cool and pull back together the limbs that are exhausted from previous evacuations, whether natural or artificial. If there is any residual matter, they consume it.

<summary>This page outlines clinical "canons" or rules for treating fevers, debating when a physician should prioritize cooling the patient's temperature versus expelling the corrupted humors (the cause). It highlights the dangers of using cold water or certain fruits like melons and apples, which can cause humors to "boil" or ferment in the stomach if not handled correctly.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the cooling properties of medicines, specifically focusing on "rose sugar" and the critical distinction between treating a hectic fever—which requires simple cooling—and a putrid fever, which requires removing the underlying corrupted matter. It also begins a series of "canons" or rules for the timing of medical interventions like bloodletting and purging.</meta>

# Book IV
## IV

Treatment for a hectic fever <note>original: "ethica"; referring to a fever of the "habit" or solid parts of the body</note> is satisfied with providing the opposite of the sickness <note>i.e., cooling the heat</note>. But in a putrid fever, you must strive to cut away the cause. These troches <note>medicated lozenges</note> prevent the cutting away of that cause. Here, Avicenna expands his discourse a little, wishing to show that not only do cooling, astringent <term>astringent: substances that contract tissues, often called "stiptic" in older texts</term> medicines harm a putrid fever on account of the morbid matter, but even feeding and cooling in general can harm it. For cooling "fixes" the matter and prevents it from being dissolved, and feeding increases the amount of matter; this is not the case in a hectic fever. This is why he says that cooling is "suitable to the sickness" but "unsuitable to the feeding." Why? Because cooling restores the temperament and strengthens the vital power, and feeding increases the spirits and humors which nourish that power. Therefore, while these are "friends" to the body's vital power, they are "friends to the enemy" of that power—namely, the morbid matter. Because they help both the body and the disease, we need a specific rule <note>original: "canonem"</note> for feeding those with fevers: we must provide as little food as we possibly can without causing harm. This is the meaning of the seventh aphorism <note>referring to Hippocrates' *Aphorisms*</note>: "The food given to those with fever is strength to the healthy," etc. We explain this according to our interpretation, and not like Benedictus <note>possibly Benedetto Reguardati or another commentator</note>, who misunderstood that aphorism and others following it.

We have doubted elsewhere whether "rose sugar" <term>rose sugar: a medicinal preserve made of rose petals and sugar or honey</term> is appropriate at the beginning of putrid fevers. It seems so, because all physicians commonly give it to infants in cold water. Furthermore, in the chapter on the cure of phlegmatic fever <note>fever caused by an excess of the humor phlegm</note>, before the seventh day, Serapion the Younger <note>original: ".S. infra geleniabi"</note> gives a rose preserve, which is rose sugar or rose honey. Furthermore, Rhazes in the 16th book of the *Continens* <note>Rhazes was a famous 9th-century Persian physician; the *Continens* was his massive encyclopedia</note>, when speaking of melilot, allows rose sugar; therefore, it is even more allowed at the start of a fever. Furthermore, it comforts the stomach, as Mesue says in his book of medicines. Furthermore, Avicenna says in his fourth book, treatise 7, that it helps with fever. Furthermore, it helps by cooling and softening via the roses, which loosen the belly. This is what Mesue says in the chapter on the rose.

On the contrary, Avicenna says here: "do not cool with that in which there is astringency and drying," and rose sugar has these qualities because of the roses. Likewise, Rhazes in the third treatise of the *Al-Mansuri* says that those suffering from heat and burning should in no way eat it, especially in summer, for it heats them and brings on thirst—though Simon of Genoa <note>a 13th-century medical lexicographer</note> says the translator erred, because Rhazes was actually speaking of rose honey. 

First, let us define what rose sugar is: it is a preserve made of fresh roses and sugar mixed together and cooked in the sun, not over a fire (as bad apothecaries do). In the fifth book, it is said that the power of rose sugar is cold in the first degree and dry in the second. There is disagreement whether sugar itself is temperate or hot in the first degree, and whether it is slightly moist or dry. It remains, then, that rose sugar is either roughly temperate or slightly cold, and certainly dry. Variations occur depending on whether white or red roses are used, and whether white or red sugar is used. But the power of rose sugar is somewhat astringent, and yet also somewhat cleansing <term>cleansing: "abstersive," or capable of wiping away impurities</term>.

I say that in no fever of strong inflammation, such as a choleric fever <note>caused by yellow bile</note>, is rose sugar appropriate. First, because it is not proportional to the task of extinguishing the heat. Second, because it "inflames" in the stomach; for if even cucumber water sometimes inflames in such patients, rose sugar will do so much more. And if you say "I will give it with much cold water," we reply that the effect then comes from the water, not the sugar. I also say generally that in putrid fevers, it is not appropriate at the beginning before digestion and evacuation for two general reasons: 

First, it is not for cooling, as Avicenna teaches to cool with barley water, violet syrup, or vinegar syrup, and sometimes melon water, but he says nothing of rose sugar or even rose syrup. Furthermore, Haly Abbas in the third book of his *Practice* lists many drinks for the feverish and mentions nothing of rose sugar or rose syrup. Furthermore, Rhazes in his *Divisions* only moves to rose sugar in the second stage of treatment, not the first. Furthermore, Averroes in the seventh book of the *Colliget* does not much praise syrup made of sugar and rose water, which some "new physicians" of his time were using; he does not praise it because of the astringency of the rose water. Therefore, even less should the substance and body of the rose be used.

Nor is rose sugar appropriate for the second intention, which is the evacuation of the morbid matter. At the beginning, evacuation should not be done with something that brings astringency and drying; this is why myrobalans <note>a dried fruit used as a laxative</note> are prohibited, as will appear later. And so Avicenna commanded here that you should not even cool with a thing that is astringent. From this, the following rule can be formed: at the beginning of fevers, cooling is not appropriate with a thing that "constricts" the morbid matter by its astringency. This is why wormwood is prohibited later in the chapter on *hemitritaeos* <note>a type of semi-tertian fever</note>. Rose sugar does exactly this. This is confirmed by Mesue, who says rose sugar constricts matter in the chest (as seen in the cure for consumption), unless you want to be stubborn and say the astringency goes to the lungs while the cleansing power stays behind. I say the opposite: experience shows the cleansing power travels, but the astringency wins out, especially in older preserves. 

I do not praise the use of rose sugar, neither new nor old, at the beginning of a fever for the two reasons stated. However, it can be appropriate for a special purpose: to comfort the stomach and provide some cleansing, which we need in a phlegmatic fever. In that case, it is better if it is made with honey, unless something else prohibits it, and mixed with other medicines as you see fit. It is also more appropriate at the end of fevers. Thus, the contradictions are resolved. As for Rhazes, it should be said he speaks of a condition that happens at the end of fevers, or one where myrobalans are allowed—but these are not allowed at the start of putrid fevers, as is well known.

## Thus, regarding these fevers: do not cool them with anything in which there is astringency and drying, such as cooling troches, except after purgation and evacuation.

## ¶ And know that the cure for a putrid fever is different from the cure for a hectic fever. For the cure of hectic fever is focused on the opposition of the sickness, but the cure for putrid fever is not focused only on the opposition of the sickness, but rather on the cutting away of its cause. Although that which is suitable for the sickness and for feeding may be

"And know." Avicenna has already given the rule for putrid fever regarding the "intention" of cooling (which looks to the state of the body). Here he gives the rule regarding the "matter" of the disease. First, he gives the rules for the morbid matter: if a physician acts on these at the beginning, he performs a general "lessening" called drying, which is best at the start of fevers. Second, he returns to the completion of cooling. Third, he gives the rules for matter further along in the process. Rule two: "and do not prohibit cold water to him." Rule three: "and when you have administered..."

<column-break/>

...the aforementioned rules. The first rule is in two parts: first, he shows what is necessary for one wishing to cure a fever. Second, he follows with rules for the matter through evacuation and digestion. He says: "if you are ignorant." It must be considered that although no proper cure can be performed if the specific fever is unknown, he means specifically the cure that "cuts the cause," which is the true cure for putrid fevers. Ignorance of the fever here does not mean you don't know it's a fever or that it's putrid (for he presupposes you know that much). It is ignorance of the *mode* of the cause: whether it comes from an abundance of choleric or phlegmatic humors. For we only have a confused knowledge of this at first. As the 16th book of the *Continens* says: when a physician knows a fever is putrid or humoral, but does not know distinctly which cause it is from, he cannot cure it correctly with the "proper" cure, because that cure must involve things that target that specific matter. Therefore, Galen rightly commands in the first book of *To Glaucon on the Method of Healing* that at the start of an acute regimen, one must strive first to know the sickness and its cause, and only then to medicate.

## ...a friend to the vital power on its own part, but an enemy to the vital power in part, because it is a friend to its enemy—which is the matter—and thus helps both of them. For this reason, we need a rule in its regimen. And we shall make a separate chapter for it, if God wills.

## ¶ And know that it is not possible for you to cure a fever unless you have recognized it; but if you are ignorant of it, then lighten the regimen and be careful, and do not let the paroxysm occur unless the belly is empty.

## ¶ And do not move anything on the day of the paroxysm as much as you can.

"But if." Here he follows with the rules for the matter of the fever. First, he gives a general rule. Second, a more specific one. There are three primary rules. The first is a continuation of what preceded: do not proceed with digestion and evacuation—things that target the cause—because it is impossible unless you recognize the cause. If someone asks what to do in the meantime, he answers: "lighten the regimen" <note>original: "subtilia regimen"; i.e., put the patient on a very thin, light diet</note>. Some say this is because when a sickness is unknown, it is better to leave it to nature, for nature will either cure it or make its type manifest to you. If left to nature, she can focus on the sickness without being hindered by food. Others (including myself elsewhere) say that in an unknown fever, one takes the indication from the disease itself, which might forbid feeding.

Let us put it another way: fevers whose causes are "ignored" are those that do not have violent symptoms—neither in the touch, the discharge, nor the pulse. They are mild, and we are in doubt whether this mildness is because the matter is small and benign, or because the matter is thick and hidden. In such a fever, it is best to lighten the regimen. For if the matter is thick, the fever will eventually manifest it as it progresses. But what is this "subtle regimen"? Does it start with barley water, or meal, or a small chicken? And for how many days? A certain rule cannot be given, but is left to your judgment. Rhazes suggests four days. This is how the physician targets the matter through "food-lessening"—he knows the matter is there, but since he doesn't know its type, he doesn't use a specific medicine, but rather prevents the matter from increasing. 

"And if." This is the second rule: that the paroxysm <term>paroxysm: the "fit" or the point at which the fever is most intense</term> should meet an empty belly—meaning a stomach empty of food and bowels empty of waste. This is so the febrile heat does not lift bad vapors from them, which would increase the corrupted matter.

"And do not move." This is the fourth rule: do not evacuate the matter during the paroxysm. **It is doubted** whether we can move matter (evacuate) on the day of the paroxysm. It seems so, because a fever might necessitate bloodletting <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term> or pharmacy <note>drugs/purges</note> or enemas <note>clisters</note>. Furthermore, if the paroxysm must meet an empty belly, you must evacuate with an enema on that day. Furthermore, in a quartan fever <note>a fever that peaks every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>, vomiting is commanded at the hour of the paroxysm. Furthermore, matter is most "mobile" and thus easiest to evacuate during the paroxysm. Furthermore, nature itself performs a "critical evacuation" <note>a "crisis," or sudden turning point in a disease</note> at the hour of the paroxysm. In opposition stands Avicenna. 

We must consider first that by "day of paroxysm" we mean the *time* of the fit, not the 24-hour day. A paroxysm might start in the evening, meaning the morning would be a suitable time to evacuate. Generally, we say that a "regular cure"—which aims to do no harm—should not evacuate during the hour of the paroxysm. Regarding bloodletting, the rule is in the first book. Regarding pharmacy, we should not join two strong movements against the body's vital power: the movement of the paroxysm and the movement of the purge. Second, the matter is already in the "way of expulsion" by nature during a paroxysm; a drug might interfere with this. Therefore, you must not evacuate during the paroxysm because it causes too great a commotion in a body already under the strain of the fit. It is better to wait for the period of quiet.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on feeding patients with fevers, specifically referencing the Hippocratic principle that feeding a body full of "evil humors" only increases the harm. It transitions into specific medical rules (canons) for the sequence of treatment.</meta>

...the more one errs, and the more the patient is nourished, the more harm is done <note>original: "magis peccat"; literally "sins more," here meaning a medical error or worsening of the condition</note>.

->**Rule 1**<-

In every putrid fever, one must first take care to evacuate the putrid matter through vomiting, through the bowels, or through sweat, before proceeding to cooling treatments. The reason is that if you apply cooling first, you constrict the pores, and the morbid matter cannot find a way out.

### On Bloodletting

In a synochal fever <note>original: "synocha"; a continuous fever caused by an excess of blood</note>, if the body is "full" <note>referring to "plethora," or an overabundance of humors</note>, do not hesitate to perform bloodletting. However, be extremely cautious in a hectic fever, lest you withdraw the vital spirit and the body’s natural heat.

<margin>Hippocrates says: In acute diseases, the crisis occurs quickly.</margin>

In tertian fevers <note>fevers that peak every third day, often associated with malaria</note>, if the matter is lodged in the stomach, it is better to induce vomiting. <gloss>by means of vinegar syrup</gloss>

->**Rule 2**<-

Food should not be given during the peak of a paroxysm <term>paroxysm: the period of greatest intensity or a sudden attack of symptoms</term>. This is because nature is currently occupied with the struggle against the disease, and if you add food at that moment, you double the labor that nature must perform.

<column-break/>

### On Cooling Remedies

Rose water and lemon juice are useful, but one must be cautious of their extreme coldness when treating weak patients. <insert>especially in the elderly</insert>

If the patient suffers from an intolerable thirst, give them barley water <note>original: "aquam hordeaceam"; a common medieval cooling drink made from boiled grain</note>.

# Book III
## III

...are trapped; and the vapors heated by the fever are enclosed: by the inflamed matter itself: and therefore it is good to cleanse them. Thirdly, because the materials around the mesenteric veins <note>original: "meseraicas"; the veins carrying nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note> are corrupted by the heat of the fever and flow back toward the intestines. And even if they did not flow back, it is good that they be directed toward them: lest they cause an abscess <term>abscess: "apostemationis," a localized collection of pus or swelling</term> and inflammation of the liver, or the corruption of the chyle <note>the milky fluid of digested food</note> reaching the liver. For these reasons, I praise the softening <note>original: "lenitionē"; refers to mild laxative action</note> of the belly. And specifically with an enema <note>original: "clisteri"</note> as Avicenna says. And it pleases me that a person with a fever should move their bowels at the hours they were accustomed to in health; however, let them use these softenings with enemas and medicinal drinks. We must consider secondly that Avicenna begins this loosening "subtly," that is, gently. For this loosening of the belly is said to be "lenitive" and "cleansing" of the materials it meets in the parts of the intestines; it is not, however, properly "taking away" or "diminishing" the matter which is the cause of the putrid fever itself; though this may happen incidentally, it is not Avicenna's primary intent. He only intends to cleanse the internal parts with something soothing or gently scouring: which might cleanse the intestinal materials and the primary mesenteric parts, and temper the heat of those parts, and prevent the corruption of the materials. ¶ Such softening should be done in phlegmatic and melancholic fevers, but less so in fevers that are more inflammatory, in which dryness of nature occurs more; and therefore he said specifically "if there be dryness there," since in whichever fevers there is dryness of the belly, then we specifically soften it. We must also consider thirdly that Dionysius <note>likely referring to a commentator</note> holds that Avicenna means here a "diminishing" softening, that is, a minor evacuation of materials. For softening should precede bloodletting <note>original: "phlomiā" / phlebotomia</note>; but a general "diminishing" treatment should follow bloodletting in a fever. Concerning which Avicenna spoke: ¶ when the urine appears red and thick. And we say that although it is true that a minor evacuation can be done from the beginning, nevertheless Avicenna's intention here through these medicines is only to "soften," that is, to cleanse the said intestinal parts, although these may have another utility besides this: at least because they temper the febrile heat by altering it. However, Avicenna does not properly intend to "diminish" by the specific evacuation of matter without the reduction of the matter that causes the fever; for these medicines do not target any specific matter. Namely, barley water and vinegar syrup <note>original: "sirupus acetosus"; also known as oxymel, a mixture of honey and vinegar</note>; nor even vinegar syrup with a little manna <note>a sweet plant resin used as a mild laxative</note>. For although manna evacuates yellow bile <term>cholerā: yellow bile, one of the four humors</term>, this is when it is given in a large amount, not a small one, and it evacuates gently; hence it is given before digestion as Averroes says in the chapter on manna: all these things participate in the work of softening, that is, the moving of the belly. This will be asked about at the end of these canons. Consider fourthly that four things are given to soften the belly. The first is barley water. The second is *firacost*, that is, a little manna also with barley water: so that the manna may be dissolved with the barley water. The third is vinegar syrup, namely with common water. It should not be composed exactly as the text says "barley water and vinegar syrup," because later he forbids the mixing of barley water and vinegar syrup. The fourth thing is the aforementioned manna with violet syrup added, for example: two drams of manna and half a dram of violet syrup, or two. And this is when the belly is not moved by any of the three aforementioned things. And this is what he means: ¶ "if nature be gentle," that is, if it is not softened by any of the three things mentioned: give this fourth one, because it is a more softening thing than any of those, as is well known. Or alternatively: ¶ "if nature be gentle," that is, if the feverish person is not by nature constipated <note>original: "stipticus"</note>, then do not give any of those three when they will not be softened by them, but immediately give manna with violet syrup. ¶ This is what he says: ¶ "it is like firacost," that is, adding manna so that it is like violet syrup. ¶ By saying "like firacost," he also understands similar things, like cassia <note>a mild laxative pod</note>. And by "violet syrup" he means fresh violets, as will be declared later. Consider fifthly when he says "let the softening be the ultimate end." Some explain that softening alone should be done when preparing for bloodletting, so that by softening alone the feces are purged. Others say that evacuation immediately after bloodletting should be softening alone. Others say that in the beginning, before digestion, one should only use lenitive medicine. And we say that Avicenna intends that the "ultimate" or final operation intended by these four medicines is the softening of the belly, not a "flow" of the belly which diminishes or eradicates the matter—at least not in a laborious or minorative way. For if you intended a strong, laborious loosening and a flow of the appropriate matter, you would use other medicines to be mentioned later; and this is what he means by "let it be the ultimate," that is, the final intention through these medicines is softening, not a laborious loosening or "flow." For if you intended a flow, it would be necessary to move to other things, for example, scammony or agaric or rhubarb. Consider sixthly that although these softenings are evacuative, they are also digestive, by adapting the matter—like vinegar syrup—and also by preparing the pathways.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ "And more beloved by me": here he teaches how to soften the belly through enemas and lists what these enemas are made of. Consider that enemas are more "beloved" because they weaken the vital power less, and this is what he means when he says "the ultimate need is in the power," that is, according to the final intention he has regarding the body's strength... ¶ The reason in the *Book of Pharmacy*: he commanded the use of enemas when you wish, or according to the limit of what you need in "power," that is, the evacuative potential. The limit in this was softening, not a flow; but for softening, another evacuative might still be used, as will appear later. Also, enemas harm some people more than if they took the softening medicine by mouth. Consider thirdly that in the fourth section of the *Therapeutics*, he gives enemas with honey-water and oil. Rhazes, in the 16th book of the *Continens*, second chapter, makes an enema with this: nine kirats of saffron, two egg yolks, two ounces of oil of roses, three ounces of boiled wine, and enough barley water. But Avicenna’s enema seems better to me, in which there is a scouring effect from the juice of beets <note>original: "blitis"</note>, which he calls *sicla*. ¶ It is the smaller beet which is hot and dry. The other beet is called "Yemeni vegetable" by Avicenna, and it is cold. It is the broad beet; and if you want cooling, you use its juice. Hence he also speaks of the beet in two chapters of the second book of the *Almansor*. In red sugar there is also a scouring effect; in egg yolk and violet oil there is softening; in violet oil there is cooling and softening; in *baurach*, that is, salt, there is a provocation to exit and a kind of scouring. We, however, use an enema made from a decoction <term>decoction: a concentrated liquor resulting from heating or boiling a substance</term> of mallow, pulp of cassia, violet oil, red sugar, and salt. It is doubted whether it is permitted to use sharp <note>original: "acutis"; meaning strong or irritating</note> enemas in acute fevers. It seems so, because in abscesses of the liver, one makes an enema with a decoction of colocynth <note>bitter apple</note> and centaury, as appears in the penultimate chapter of the second book of the *Therapeutics*. Avicenna is here to the contrary. It must be said that in the regular cure at the beginning of putrid fevers, we ought not to use sharp enemas. The reason is that these do not help the fever; rather they harm it because they inflame. Hence in the first book, fourth Fen, Avicenna says regarding things that lead to fever: not even on account of the matter. Because in the beginning, they are "crude" <note>undigested</note>, they are not to be evacuated regularly, as we shall say. Hence also in the use of sharp enemas, Avicenna wished the materials to be "digested" <note>processed by the body's heat</note> as appears in the first chapter of the 16th Fen of the third book of the *Canon* in the cure of cholera. Once the matter is digested, we can use enemas...

<column-break/>

...sharp ones. Just as with other evacuative medicines by dissolving: and specifically when the materials are digested in the parts suited to descend to the lower intestines: just like other materials in the hollow of the liver: and specifically when they are difficult to move—so does a sharp enema act. See the 13th book of the *Therapeutics*, when some part of two abscesses of the liver remained. However, in a "forced" cure <note>an emergency or specialized case</note> arising from some accidental cause, namely a putrid one, we could use sharp enemas: either at the beginning or in the course of it, when that accident turns our intention toward itself. For example, if there were much dryness of the feces in the intestines: and a blockage <term>oppilatio: an obstruction or blockage in the vessels or organs</term> which could not be removed by oily enemas. Hence we would need strong things in this chapter, such as polypody, safflower, turpeth, and similar things added with others, as appears in the third book of the *Canon*, Fen 16. Just as if we feared a case of *subet* <note>a lethargic coma</note> or apoplexy; or if a man had many crude humors in the parts of the lower intestines evaporating thick winds to the head: ¶ through parts of the belly. And there are many other cases in which we are forced to make enemas with a decoction of agaric and similar things in putrid fevers. Avicenna, therefore, wished the canon on enemas to be suitable in the ordinary or regular cure of a putrid fever. And therefore he said "of common benefit": because it commonly helps in every putrid fever, when his intention is softening, not a flow of the belly, nor a laborious loosening.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ "When therefore": here he shows how one must follow up with lenitives. And he means that nature "obeys" through this: because if a man is made "flowable" in the belly by these things, he can finally use milder ones. Consider that this discourse can refer both to medicines and to enemas. First, it can refer to medicines: because at the beginning of a putrid fever you needed to soften it with, for example, manna and violet syrup; when therefore you have given this once or twice, or up to three times, the nature becomes obedient. Because after the sick person moves their bowels well by themselves, it is not expedient that you give this any longer, but a weaker thing suffices you. For example, barley water alone or vinegar syrup alone. And Avicenna implies by this that if the lenitive you gave at the beginning is the weakest among all lenitives—for example, a subtle barley water—and the softening responds to you from it, you can also desist from it if it seems right to you. He said "perhaps" either because you began at the start with a lenitive so weak that a weaker one cannot be found—and then it could not be changed to a weaker one except by a smaller dose—or he says this because of hidden dispositions perceivable only by estimation. For example, although the nature was obedient today after giving the lenitive, the physician's estimation may fall such that if he gave it again after tomorrow, this person would become hard-bellied; and that estimation which seemed to have begun will not proceed. It will stand, therefore, in the judgment of the practiced physician. In the same way, this discourse refers to enemas, in which a change can be made from the more scouring/lenitive to the less; hence you will be able to leave out the juice of beets and salt and red sugar, and be content with barley water and violet oil. It was customary for us to doubt here: whether, when two indications stand—namely bloodletting and medicine—bloodletting or pharmacy should be sent first. And let us say that this question asks about pharmacy which evacuates by dissolving... if you ask about a lenitive like violet syrup and manna and cassia: or even about an enema similar to these whose intention is the removal of feces from the intestines and the corrupted materials there: I say that the softening should be sent first with an enema as the "more beloved" way or with a drink. Because bloodletting ought not to be done while the feces are dry in the intestines, and while such corrupted materials exist, as happens to those who have suffered indigestion (Book I, Fen 4, chapter on bloodletting). Hence Avenzoar <note>original: "3oar"</note> in a "sanguine" fever <note>a fever of the blood</note> sent the softening of the belly first with a drink, even before bloodletting was done; we use these lenitives, although Avenzoar did it perhaps because of some other offending materials mixed with the blood.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ "Then make": this is the canon on evacuation through urine, and it is the second canon. Consider here "then" indicates the order. For before diuretics <term>prouocatiua: substances that "provoke" or induce urine</term> are given, bloodletting must have preceded (if it was expedient) as well as softening. This was proven in the 8th chapter on the cure of ephemeral fever from obstruction; and in the 8th book of the *Therapeutics*. It is well known that it is necessary to soften the belly first. For if diuretics found bad, corrupted, overflowing materials in the intestines, they would move them toward the liver and the veins. Consider secondly that although through these diuretics evacuation occurs, let it be primarily the "digestion" of materials: that is, the division and thinning of thick humors (which are more common), and the opening of the paths both of the veins and the pores. And this is a kind of digestion, namely preparing the ways, as is understood from the commentary on the *Aphorisms*: "cleanse bodies when you want to purge," yet with this they evacuate materials by casting them into the paths of the veins and leading them out through them. Consider thirdly that these diuretics are diverse according to the diversity of the materials. For if the materials are thick and viscous, the diuretics are hot and dry. These are diversified according to the diversity of the materials in that for some, the root of parsley or fennel suffices; for others, with these, the roots of celery, asparagus, and butcher's broom; in some, one must move to *meu* <note>spignel</note> and similar things. But if the materials are "choleric" <note>bilious</note>, we will give a decoction of common cold seeds with simple vinegar syrup, and Avicenna implied all this when he said "and similar things." He said "decoction," meaning with a decoction or that a compound vinegar syrup be made with these roots and similar things. Consider fourthly that regarding Avicenna's intention, it appears—as we said in the treatise on vinegar syrup—that the use of simple vinegar syrup is prior to the softening of the belly, and even to digestion. But the use of compound vinegar syrup—such as that boiled with celery root—is later, after the softenings have been done and after some preparation in the preceding matter. And this is because it is a strong provocative, although compound syrup itself is also a preparer of matter for evacuation, as we said before.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ "Then make him sweat": this is the canon on evacuation through sweat, and it is the fourth. Consider that Avicenna says "then" and intends that the provocation of sweat should not be done unless all the aforementioned things have preceded: starting with bloodletting, if bloodletting is indicated. For if, while a fullness <note>original: "plenitudine"</note> removable by bloodletting remains, a medicine provoking sweat by dissolving were to increase it, and...

<summary>This page details the specific sequence of medical treatments for fevers according to Avicenna, emphasizing that the bowels must be gently softened (using enemas, manna, or syrups) before more aggressive treatments like bloodletting, diuretics, or sudorifics are used to avoid trapping toxins or causing internal abscesses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the sequence of treatments for putrid fevers. It transitions from the general necessity of softening the bowels to the specific methods of inducing sweat (sudorifics), urination (diuretics), and vomiting (emetics), while considering the patient's strength and the "movement" of the disease's underlying matter.</meta>

# Fen I, Treatise II
## Page 1

...would put the body in danger. The softening of the belly must come first; this is almost always necessary so that by inducing sweat, one does not move corrupted intestinal matter into the veins. There is a question of whether a medicine that induces urine <note>original: "prouocans vrinam"; a diuretic</note> should be given before inducing sweat. Here we say briefly that sweat-inducing medicine works in two ways: one is applied from the outside, which works through moderate heat by opening the pores and gently drawing the materials toward the exterior, such as by rubbing with white wine and warm fresh water. If the fever is acute, you will find no relief from anointing or drenching.

<insert>
**But if you find** a swelling <note>original: "tumorem"</note> first moving toward the stomach, you should induce vomiting with substances that do not disrupt the patient's habits. Rather, use things like vinegar syrup <term>vinegar syrup: "syrupus acetosus," also known as oxymel, a mixture of honey and vinegar used to cut through thick phlegm</term> with warm water, since nature is already moving the humors.
</insert>

...accomplished by covering the patient with blankets and anointing with chamomile oil and similar things. The other type of sweat-inducing medicine is applied from within, which works by melting and thinning the materials and moving them toward the skin. According to this, a medicine can be both a diuretic and a sudorific <note>sweat-inducer</note> depending on the different tendencies of the body in the urinary tracts and other organs. For example, fennel root, by thinning the blood and essentially melting it in people whose kidneys are prone to receiving materials and who have a strong "attractive power" in the kidneys, will induce urine. In another person, however, it may create a vaporous melting because of weak kidneys, and by moving through the pores toward the skin, it will induce sweat. You can observe many similar things in this regard. It appears that a medicine to induce sweat taken by mouth is stronger than one for urine when compared to the same natural constitution. For the diuretic thins the humors into a watery state and makes them pass to the kidneys, aided by the kidneys' natural power to draw water from the humors. But the sweat-inducing medicine thins the humors into a vaporous or more subtle wateriness that must penetrate through narrower passages than the urinary paths. Furthermore, it is not aided by the attractive power of the sweating members (the skin and its surroundings) in the same way the urinary medicine is aided by the urinary organs.

We say, therefore, that a medicine that induces sweat by first dilating the passages from the outside may be used immediately after some minor evacuation or softening. However, it is safer if the purging and the induction of urine come first, especially if the materials were already tending toward the urine or if there were blockages in the veins. But when inducing sweat in the second way (from within), it is more appropriate that it follows the diuretic. The induction of urine is given first as a way to move materials to the urinary paths, because moving them to the sweat paths would be difficult. When nature wishes, it can better induce sweat because it distinguishes one material from another more effectively.

Therefore, when Avicenna considered this order in the medical art, he said: "next make him sweat," and he explained mild sweating when he said "open the passages," meaning open the pores. If this mild induction of sweat should follow the aforementioned evacuations, then much more so should a strong induction of sweat. Galen, in his *Therapeutics* <note>original: "S. autem. ri. terapen."; referring to *De Methodo Medendi*</note>, wished for the induction of sweat to be possible only after evacuation. Thus he said: "once the body is evacuated, one may rarify it with a medicine having a temperate heat, such as chamomile oil."

Thirdly, it must be considered that this statement can be explained in two ways. First, that Avicenna wants you to rub the body with a compound of chamomile oil, white wine, and warm water. These, mixed in the proportion you see fit, open the pores and move the materials toward the skin and sweat. This explanation fits the literal text and the intention of Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"</note> in the 16th book of *The Continent*. Alternatively, it can be explained that Avicenna prescribes the induction of sweat and the opening of the pores through three aids. The first is anointing and rubbing with chamomile oil; this is why he says "like anointing with chamomile oil," etc. Rubbing and wiping should be done during this anointing because he fears the viscosity of the oil might cause blockages if rubbing does not thin the oil or wipe it away. This is familiar to those who know Avicenna's style; he often says "let anointing be done by wiping" when he wants to prevent the oil's thickness from blocking the skin. The second aid is the drinking of wine, as Avicenna says "with white wine," meaning drinking a clear wine that seems appropriate. The third aid is a bath or a fomentation <note>a warm, moist medicinal compress</term> with warm fresh water.

This explanation is more in line with the words of Galen in his *Therapeutics*, where he says: "one should not rarify the whole body before it is evacuated; but once evacuated, it may be rarified" through chamomile oil. At this time, a watery (thin white) wine should be drunk to move the "excrements" (the evacuations), along with a bath prepared from fresh water. Avicenna’s teaching is the same as Galen’s, arranged thus: after evacuation, make him sweat and open the passages—that is, rarify him with chamomile oil, a drink of thin white wine, and a warm fresh-water bath.

### And if the fever...
This canon <note>rule</note> is immediately connected to what was said, for anointing with warm things, even temperate ones, should not be done in every fever. Rather, if the fever is acute—meaning it has much "flame" whereby the body dissolves and tends toward death—one should not be anointed with chamomile oil. Instead, use cooling ointments like oil of violets, water lily oil <note>original: "nenufario"</note>, and similar things, and an "embroche" <term>embroche: "embroca," a liquid medicine poured over a body part or applied with a cloth</term> using cooling ingredients like rose water, spodum <note>ash or oxide of zinc</note>, sandalwood, camphor, and cooling juices if appropriate. That "embrocatio" can mean an epithem <note>a topical poultice</note> is found in the first book, fourth chapter on "embroca" in the translation by Gerard of Cremona <note>original: "lĩa Serard di extra"</note>. This rule will appear below in the chapter on the management of acute fevers.

### But if you find...
This is the rule for evacuation through vomiting, and through this, he also speaks by similar judgment about evacuation through the bowels. He means that if the matter is moving toward the stomach, you should make him vomit. If it were not moving there, you should not induce it except for another cause. Thus, Galen in his *Therapeutics* says: "if by chance the impulse is toward the mouth of the stomach, lead it out by vomiting; otherwise, one should not provoke it against nature." If it moves to the intestines, loosen the belly.

Consider first that he does not use the word "then" here, to show that this induction of vomiting or loosening of the belly does not follow the strict order of the others. It may be done before bloodletting <term>bloodletting: "phlobotomiam," the surgical removal of blood to balance the humors</term> or after. If I see an urge to vomit, I provoke it; likewise for the bowels, whether before giving syrup or after, or before or after sweating.

<column-break/>

Consider secondly that the phrase "at first" is explained in two ways. First, as the preparation for vomiting. Second, as "at the very beginning" of the illness, even if no other evacuation has been done. If you see him nauseated, do not stop it; rather, provoke the vomiting. This is even more necessary if the other evacuations have already been performed.

Consider thirdly that he says "things not different from custom." This is because they do not differ from things already in use, like simple vinegar syrup. Sugar water and vinegar are not different from the habits of healthy people; or it is said because they are common to those with fevers. Vinegar syrup is similar to the things we use for feverish patients, such as barley water and pomegranate wine. He said this so that vomiting is not induced with something harsh, but with something mild and familiar.

Consider fourthly that he says "with warm water since nature moves the humors toward vomiting." If nature did not move the humors toward vomiting, there would be no intent to vomit, and then the syrup could be given with cold water. But since he intends to induce vomiting, cold water would prevent it. Even if vomiting occurred with cold water, it would not soothe the stomach as it is helped by warm water. He said this to clarify: "if you find the humor moving toward the stomach in such a way that nature moves it toward vomiting"—that is, moving toward the upper stomach, not the lower—then "do not diversify that nature," meaning do not change its direction. For where nature finds a path to lead the matter out, it should be followed.

Consider fifthly the signs of matter moving to the intestines: "rumbling" (which is well known) and the "descent of feces," meaning the patient feels the matter moving downward or feels a "biting" sensation <note>stinging or irritation</note> near the end of the rectum. Then apply something that loosens the bowels, either by mouth (like cassia or manna) or by enema or suppository.

To understand what has been and will be said, we must ask: did the physician proceed in the cure of putrid fevers with these five rules? These are the rules for how to diminish or evacuate the matter of a putrid fever. It seems so, because all these rules concern evacuation, and evacuation only happens if the matter is led out of the body. Furthermore, in bloodletting, when the matter is blood, bloodletting evacuates that blood. On the contrary, it is argued that some of these rules do not truly evacuate the matter of the fever. First, the second rule is about softening the belly of feces and matter found in the intestines, which are not necessarily the cause of the fever. Furthermore, the induction of urine prescribed here is not for the purpose of purging through the urine, but for the purpose of "digesting" the matter. A diuretic given to evacuate would be prohibited before digestion <note>in medieval medicine, "digestion" meant the thinning and preparing of humors before they could be safely purged</note> because it moves the matter prematurely.

To resolve this question, we will first look at the practice: how a physician uses these rules when arriving at a patient starting a putrid fever. If you see a need for bloodletting, perform it according to the first rule. Keep in mind the rules for bloodletting you must know from the first book. That night or the next morning, soften the belly with cassia and violet syrup or manna. If you see that sufficient softening can be done with an enema, do that instead as it is gentler. If you use vinegar syrup or barley water, it will also soften the belly; this is done by the second rule.

Once these things are done according to the first two rules, a few days will have passed (for example, three). It is then time to proceed to a more digestive syrup, as the intestines are now clean. I will begin giving at dawn a compound syrup made with parsley or fennel root. Do not forget the second rule about softening; I always want the belly to be loose by enema or other means. If it seems right to me, I will open the pores with an ointment of chamomile oil or another sweat-inducer. Thus, I have proceeded with four rules. And at any time I see the matter tending toward vomiting, I will aid nature in that. Whether before or after bloodletting, if I see the patient nauseated and wanting to vomit, I will use vinegar syrup with warm water to induce it. Now your feverish patient is being managed by all five rules.

Secondly, to solve the question, we say: we speak of evacuation through bloodletting according to the first rule. I say that bloodletting done right at the start, if it is a "synocha" <note>a continuous, non-intermittent fever</note>, truly evacuates and diminishes the matter. Indeed, sometimes it eradicates it, and the person is immediately freed. If the fever is from matter other than blood, but mixed with blood, the physician who bleeds the patient accidentally diminishes that matter. The reason is that he directly diminishes the blood, and because the humor causing the fever is mixed with the blood, it follows the blood out during the evacuation.

The question remains: does a physician working with the other four rules evacuate or diminish the matter of a putrid fever? Let us make two distinctions. The first, which the commentators of Avicenna missed, is that the "diminishing" of putrid fever matter is of two types. One is "proper" evacuation, which cuts away and evacuates the specific humor causing the fever, like purging phlegm with turbith <note>a medicinal root</note> in a phlegmatic fever, or using lapis lazuli in a quartan fever. This is called "minorative" (diminishing) evacuation because part of the matter is removed, leaving a portion that can still sustain the fever. When this evacuation leads out all the matter—at least enough to end the fever without fear of relapse—it is called "eradicative."

The other type is "improper" minorative evacuation, which is not the evacuation of the specific humor of the fever, but the evacuation of materials that are commonly and necessarily joined to it. Pay close attention to the second distinction: in putrid fevers, there are necessarily two modes of matter. One is the "appropriate" matter—for example, phlegm in a daily fever <note>quotidiana</note> and bile in a tertian fever. These may be the "joined causes" (like bile actually putrefying) or "antecedent causes" (like phlegm that isn't putrid yet but is so excessive that it will inevitably putrefy if it remains). Evacuation that removes this specific humor is truly minorative or eradicative.

It emphasizes following "nature's lead"—purging through whichever path the body's humors are already moving—and distinguishes between general cleansing and the specific removal of disease-causing humors.</summary>
