# Book III

Strictly speaking, neither the conjunct nor the antecedent causes of a fever are necessarily present at once; however, certain things are necessarily joined or found in those suffering from fever. Indeed, in every **putrid fever**, since there is a distemper of heat throughout the whole body spreading putrid vapors, an inflammation necessarily occurs around the regions of the **intestines** and **stomach**. Due to the wider spread of putrid humors, some corruption or alteration—whatever one chooses to name it—occurs in the feces, the <term>chyle<note>original: "kilo"; the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note></term>, and the mucus found there, as well as in the materials around the <term>mesenteric veins<note>original: "meseraicas"; the veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note></term>. From these, we must imagine that thick and evil vapors arise. Although this corruption of materials around the primary organs of nutrition is necessarily the end result in every putrid fever, there is nevertheless a diversity among them according to the type of fever and the location of the matters within them, and according to the differences in the condition of the parts of the stomach and intestines; and this diversity is not small.

¶ Secondly, in every putrid fever, the serum or watery part of the blood necessarily becomes oily, and the blood receives some infection because of that same heat and the putrid vapors. These parts of the blood are prone to becoming inflamed and infected; I do not wish to be troubled by childish objections. If someone says that in every putrid fever there must be another separate fever caused by that watery, inflamed, and infected part, we would reply that such an infection of the blood—which happens in every fever and necessarily follows it—is not an inflammation sufficient to create a new fever, nor does it remain once the putrid fever is removed. It exists as a dependent state; this will be understood by those who have seen our writings on the first book regarding the *Differences of Fevers*. I say thirdly that in every putrid fever, the vapors—which normally exit the pores of healthy people imperceptibly—necessarily become thickened, multiplied, and malignant. This is because the vapors of the putrid humors scattered at the edges of the body are thicker and worse than those present in a man according to nature. Following this observation, in every putrid fever, a certain **obstruction** <note>original: "oppilario"</note> of the pores and a prohibition of breathing through them <note>transpiration</note> occurs due to the thickness of those vapors. Although these vapors arising from putrid humors have much diversity among themselves in terms of thickness and thinness, and other differences proportional to the humors from which they arise. But you might say: "These vapors ought to be reduced to the 'conjunct cause' <note>the immediate cause</note> of the fever and should not be spoken of as the sum of matters necessarily joined to fevers." To this, we must first say that the vapor reduced to the conjunct cause of the fever is the putrid vapor rising from the putrid humor itself. But besides that vapor, there are other vapors in the feverish patient which rise from other, non-putrid humors; these are evil and thick because, by the strong and unnatural heat, even the thick part is thinned and then thickened again by the mixing of putrid vapors—and it is of these we speak. In a second way, we must say that the vapor rising from the putrid humor which is reduced to the conjunct cause of the fever is the vapor that reaches the **heart**. If that vapor reaches the heart, it can nevertheless exit through the hollows of the veins and arteries—namely, a part of it exits with the breath, and a part can pass through the arteries since the heart drives it into them. But the vapor that rises from a putrid humor which does *not* reach the heart, but is carried to the edges of the body, is not the cause of the fever; rather, it is "necessarily joined" to the fever, or almost necessarily, or at least for the most part. I say this to remove those who would cause trouble and because of certain things we said in the question regarding the *Prolongation of Fever*. If you consider it subtly, the vapor that imprints putrid heat—that is, the putrid fever—upon the heart, if it is gradually driven from the heart into the limbs through the arteries, or through the arteries and veins, or in whatever way it is carried into the limbs after its action on the heart, it is then part of the sum of matters necessarily joined to fevers and is not the cause of the fever itself. For the causation of a putrid fever from the heart to the limbs is not through the putrid vapor itself; rather, it is a certain conveyance through the blood and the <term>spirit<note>the vital force or "pneuma" believed to travel through the arteries</note></term>. Although no putrid vapor that has touched the heart is carried into the limbs, it happens that a part of this vapor is necessarily carried there. These things are declared at length in our question on the *Prolongation of Fever*. Let us conclude, therefore, that in every human suffering from a putrid fever, three modes of "inconvenient matters" are necessarily found besides the proper matter which is the specific cause of the fever:

1. One mode is the matter around the parts of the stomach and intestines and neighboring parts; these matters are fecal, chyle-like, mucous, and the thick vapors found there, and things similar to them.
2. The second mode of matter is the oiliness—that is, the viscosities or wateriness of the blood in all the veins, from which it also happens that the moisture of the limbs is changed.
3. The third mode is the thick vapor of inconvenient quality scattered through the body, flying through the hollows of the veins and arteries and passing through all the pores of the body toward the surface.

Although these matters are not the specific cause of the fever, nor the conjunct cause, nor the necessary antecedent cause, they nevertheless impede and burden the **virtue** <note>the body's vital power</note> by their presence; by their reduction and removal, the virtue is strengthened and relieved. Therefore, I call these "necessary matters"—or those almost necessarily following, found in, or joined to putrid fevers. We shall also say above that some matters are "contingently joined" to putrid fevers; these are the ones not found in every person with a putrid fever, but which happen to be found in some. For example: in some putrid fever—whether choleric, phlegmatic, or melancholic—some **choleric humor** <note>yellow bile</note> is moved toward the stomach, or some phlegmatic matter is inflamed by boiling and also ascends to the stomach, or these humors break out into the intestines. You will be able to find many other particular modes of matters according to all three modes of the said matters, which particular modes will be contingently joined to the putrid fever, though these are more clearly apparent in the stomach and intestines, as you may consider. Since, therefore, it has now appeared to us that there are some matters necessarily joined to putrid fevers (though they are not necessary antecedent causes nor conjunct causes) and others that are contingently joined, we shall say that the evacuation of these matters—assuming it were possible to evacuate them entirely—ought not to be called a truly "eradicative evacuation." This is because the fever is not rooted out by this. For even if it were possible (though it is impossible) that all the corruption or change around the intestines were removed, and the entire infection of the blood depending on putrid vaporization were removed, and all that infected watery or oily part were evacuated, and all the evil vapor scattered to the surface of the body were removed through transpiration—if the putrid humor alone and the vapor that touches the heart alone remained, the patient would still be feverish with putrid fever. Therefore, the reduction of these infected matters should not be called a "proper minorative evacuation," because it is not the reduction of the specific matter of the fever, but the reduction of matters commonly and necessarily (or contingently) joined to putrid fevers. Thus, the proper name is "drying of the body" <note>original: "ericcatiō"</note>. For this reason, **Avicenna** called it "minoration and drying"—that is, a reduction which is a type of drying. It seems that among the Arabs, these words joined together (minoration and drying) signify this minorative evacuation of those matters joined to fevers necessarily or contingently. I, however, used to call this "common evacuation" to distinguish it from "proper minorative evacuation," which reduces the matter specifically assigned to the putrid fever. I call it common because it is the evacuation of matters commonly joined to all putrid fevers. For in all putrid fevers, those matters of the three modes are found, and it happens that contingently joined matters are also found, although in this there is much diversity according to the type of putrid fever, as we have said, and according to the diversity of bodies. With these distinctions and the premises following from them, let us set forth nine propositions. The first is that as long as the putrid fever persists, the intention to purge these matters persists. The reason is that as long as the putrid fever persists, these matters continually return, which

<column-break/>

burdens and hinders the virtue; therefore, the physician's intention remains fixed upon them. The second proposition is that the removal or reduction of **intestinal matters** and those near them is done by "softening the belly" <note>laxatives</note>; for this purpose, **enemas** <note>original: "clisteria"</note> are more effective. The evacuation of infected watery matters in the veins is through the urine, and also they can be led out through sweat. The evacuation of vapors is through transpiration—that is, through the pores—by "rarefaction" <note>opening/thinning</note>, which is what **sudorific** <note>sweat-inducing</note> medicines do. One might argue that in "hectic" fevers <note>original: "ethica," a wasting fever</note> these intentions should be the same, and we could give these medicines and work with them. But we must say that such corruptions of matter do not occur in hectic fevers as they do in putrid fevers, because of the many putrefactions. And even if in hectic fevers there were an infection of the wateriness and oiliness of the blood such as exists in those with putrefaction, and the same curative reason or intention arose, it could not be done so openly. Provocation of urine and sweating in a hectic patient is not like in one with putrefaction; rather, we would fear it in them for fear of "drying them out" <note>over-dehydration</note>. ¶ The third proposition is that the physician should act at the **beginning** of the onset of a putrid fever with a "minorative diet" which cures the matters that are necessarily or contingently joined to the fever. This is clear because it cures those intestinal, watery, or vaporous matters; and I understand "the beginning" as one of the four times of the disease, in which the matter is **crude** <note>undigested/unprocessed</note> or secretly boiling toward digestion, as at the end of the beginning. ¶ The fourth proposition: It happens that a physician in the beginning of a putrid fever also uses **bloodletting** <note>original: "phlomiā"</note> to evacuate matter contingently complicated with that putrid fever, and no other. The reason is that someone may have a putrid fever from some part—for instance, choleric or phlegmatic—and the whole body is habituated to or filled with blood that does not correspond to this part as a conjunct or antecedent cause; yet this blood becomes inflamed and burdened so that it does not allow nature to attend to the management of the diseased part. Then we bleed and reduce that blood. Similarly, it is imaginable in some putrid fever involving a humor other than blood, where bloodletting is performed not for the sake of that humor (to be evacuated or reduced) but to reduce the excess blood that happens to be found with that putrid fever. In that bloodletting, no part of the putrid humor—for example, **cholera** <note>yellow bile</note>—is evacuated, even though bile is the necessary antecedent cause. And if you say "Surely bile would be drawn out by this," we must say it is not true in the case where bloodletting removes a superfluous repletion of blood; the bloodletting evacuates from a superfluous quantity and not from the necessary or innate quantity. ¶ The fifth proposition is that the physician might choose this even if some bile might be stirred or cause harm, rather than the harm that could follow from omitting bloodletting. The sixth proposition is that the physician should be cautious with a patient with putrid fever in the beginning for four reasons... it was not by itself a truly minorative evacuation that cuts away from the conjunct cause or the necessary antecedent cause. The first reason is taken from the **time** in which the action occurs; it is in the beginning when the matter is **indigested**. Since indigested matter is not regularly evacuated nor is it a "minorative" reduction of matter that significantly removes crude humor, it cannot be an "eradicative" evacuation, but only a "lenification" <note>softening</note>, not a laborious evacuation—that is, not a true reduction of nature nor truly eradicative. ¶ The seventh reason is that this evacuation is not done with medicines that are "appropriated" to specific humors, but it evacuates indifferently. This is seen by looking at the types. For softening with enemas, or with barley water, or violet syrup, or honey, or simple medicines is a softening not appropriated to a specific matter; such softening can be done in every fever. Thus, in phlegmatic and choleric fevers, we could soften with barley water and with **manna**. Similarly, provocation with **celery root** <note>original: "radice apij"</note> is not appropriated to the urine, but it thins the wateriness to make it move into the urinary paths. But "rarefying" the pores with **chamomile oil** makes the vapors of any fever transpire, and it does not evacuate a determined humor. Likewise, inducing vomiting with warm water or **vinegar syrup** <note>original: "sirupo acetoso"</note> does not by itself evacuate the specifically assigned matter. Against the aforesaid, one might say: first, that manna evacuates bile by its property; further, that **violet** evacuates bile by its property of dissolving, as is seen in the canon on the violet; second, violet syrup. Against this, the provocation with celery roots is appropriated to humors... just as provocation with... is appropriated to hot humors. To the first, it must be said that manna, **cassia**, and violet syrup are given here only as softening and curing agents by their property; the physician will give these medicines only to soften, and they will not purge by their property, although sometimes they have a property of purging. For example, if manna is given in the quantity of one ounce with a decoction of syrup, it will evacuate bile by resolution, though weakly. But I will give an ounce of it with honey-water <note>original: "aqua ox[ymellis]"</note> or violet syrup; its use will only be to soften. Hence Avicenna says: "When we want to soften, we use cassia..." so it is with violet syrup. Because of this, violet syrup is seen as being for recent illnesses. ¶ The seventh reason of dryness: that is, dry violet has some evacuating power by dissolving, because the consumption of the moist part reveals its heat and bitterness; hence it has the power of evacuating by loosening the water. But you might say every violet syrup evacuates by dissolving because the moisture of the violet will be consumed both by boiling and by time. We must say that violet syrup made from **fresh violets** is more softening; that made from **dry violets** is more curative/evacuating, doing more by loosening than that made from fresh ones. Because boiling and time consume the moisture of the violets, it nevertheless preserves enough to suffice for softening. Thus we say that since violet syrup is made from fresh violets, the lubricating moisture is not entirely consumed; rather, a notable part of it remains and is transferred into the sugar and water. ¶ To the second, I say that the provocative syrups used by Avicenna are not used to provoke this or that matter through urine or sweat because it is the conjunct or necessary matter in putrid fever. Hence he does not want to give a bile-provoker in the beginning of a choleric fever when the matter is crude, nor in a phlegmatic fever to give something that provokes phlegm through urine or sweat. The reason is that these matters in the beginning are indigested and thus "disobedient" to evacuation; so it would be for the urine. But Avicenna uses these provocatives in the beginning for two intentions. One is the leading out through urine or sweat of that watery or serous matter which is commonly found in those suffering from putrid fever; this does not need digestion for evacuation, because it is inherently ready to be evacuated, as it is through sweat. Hence we frequently see nature itself moving many sweats in feverish patients which are not from the specific matter of the fever. We must believe the same of the infected wateriness that goes with the urine. The second intention is the **digestion** of the matter. Therefore, in a phlegmatic fever, he uses celery root, but in a choleric fever, he uses common... or a decoction of endive—not because he wants to specifically approve a diuretic for the matter, but because he wants to appropriate a **digestive**. You, however, would want to appropriate the diuretic once digestion has already occurred. Then, if in a phlegmatic fever he gave celery root in the beginning for digestion and the reduction of common watery matter, he will give the "Syrup of Five Roots" <note>a famous medicinal compound</note> after digestion to reduce the specific, digested phlegmatic matter, because it is stronger. And if in a tertian fever <note>a fever recurring every three days, usually choleric</note> he gave some endive water in the beginning, he will give an emulsion of common seeds once the matter is digested. That which has always been a doubt to me is whether, just as we find medicines that purge through the belly (which we give to digested matters, like **scammony** for bile, or others for phlegm and melancholy), there are also diverse medicines that provoke through...

<summary>This page discusses the nature of the "matters" (corrupted humors and vapors) associated with putrid fevers and the strategies for their evacuation. The author distinguishes between the root cause of the fever and the secondary symptoms (like thick vapors and oily blood), arguing that early treatment should focus on "softening" and reducing these common burdens through specific syrups and light diuretics rather than trying to "uproot" the fever while the matter is still crude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of how to manage the body’s "humors"—the vital fluids like blood, phlegm, and bile—during a fever. It specifically examines the "Canons" or rules for using diuretics, bloodletting, and regulated sleep to assist the body’s natural heat in "digesting" or breaking down the diseased matter.</meta>

# Book II, Treatise II

**Column 1**

The urine shows that digested materials are being separated by the specific form of <term>phlegm<note>One of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture</note></term>, of <term>melancholy<note>Black bile, associated with cold and dryness</note></term>, and of <term>cholera<note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness</note></term>. We do not find this stated extensively by the ancient authors. The **sixth contingent proposition** is that at the beginning of putrid fevers, through the actions taken under this canon, some humoral matter might be evacuated. This is the "proper humor" which could have been the conjoined or antecedent cause of that fever. The reason is that at the start of a putrid choleric fever, it happens that some part of the cholera is driven to the stomach or the intestines; the rest of the cholera was either moving toward putrefaction or was in such a state that if it remained, it could become putrid. Thus, it is imaginable that it can be evacuated through the urine or through sweat. But you might ask: "If nature moves this matter at the beginning before digestion, then why shouldn't the physician also move it?" The answer is that a physician cannot distinguish or separate these humors without causing harm in the way nature does, nor does the physician recognize them as clearly. (Whether the evacuation of the proper matter of the fever should be done at the beginning will be discussed later).

The **seventh contingent proposition** is rare and occurs in those putrid fevers where "strange modes" are given to the physician. By acting at the beginning with one of the four rules, the physician cuts off the entire conjoined cause of the fever and frees the sick person. For example, suppose a putrid fever is caused by worms in the intestines or by putrid feces in the gut, or by some putrid humor floating there. The administration of a <term>solutive<note>A laxative or substance used to "loosen" the bowels</note></term> or a light emetic can free the patient from this fever. Such fevers can be classified among the sum of putrid fevers, as we have said elsewhere. From all this, it appears that a physician proceeding with the four canons at the beginning of putrid fevers does not diminish nor evacuate the proper matter of the fever, except perhaps by accident.

The **eighth proposition** is that the quantity of these "lightenings"—whether by provoking urine or thinning the pores—depends on the duration of the treatment and the strength of the medicines used, according to the physician’s judgment.

The **ninth proposition** is that if the physician proceeds with the said four canons and materials at the start, and continues as the matter is being digested, it sometimes happens that the fever’s own matter is evacuated—not because those treatments have the inherent power to evacuate it, but because the matter, having become ready for evacuation, is expelled by the body’s own moving strength with only a slight nudge. From these points, contradictory opinions should cease. Regarding the first argument—that all these are canons for performing evacuation—the answer is that this is true for the evacuation of those matters joined to the fever (namely the four canons).

Regarding the argument from the opposing side—that the canon for provoking urine is not truly for provoking urine itself—the answer is that it is not for provoking "urine" in a specific sense, but for expelling wateriness and poisonous virulence, which are essentially the byproducts of the "first digestion" <note>The initial stage of digestion occurring in the stomach and intestines</note>.

<margin>a</margin>
**And forbid him.** This is the canon where the physician turns his attention to the matter, so that it may be resolved, and forbids that which prevents such resolution. 

It is doubted, first, whether sleep is harmful at the start of a **paroxysm** <note>The "fit" or sudden increase in the severity of fever symptoms</note>. It seems not, based on the texts in the second section on the signs of sleep in fever. Furthermore, in the treatment of shivering, **Avicenna** administers medicines that induce sleep. 

It is doubted, second, whether sleep helps during the decline of a paroxysm. It seems not, because sleep moves the matter inward and prevents it from being resolved, which is what ought to happen during the decline. 

It is doubted, third, whether it helps during the "status" <note>The peak or plateau phase of a fever spike</note>. It seems it might be harmful, as **Avicenna** says in the second part of this book that sleep at the peak of paroxysms is "worse." 

It is doubted, fourth, whether these sayings hold true for the general stages of the fever as they do for the specific times of the paroxysm. This question could be discussed at great length, but since we have said much about it in the first section of the second part, we will be brief here. We say that at the beginning of paroxysms—specifically when there is a "type" signifying that internal heat is being suffocated—sleep is generally not appropriate. The reason is manifold: first, in sleep, these "types" (cold and shivering) are prolonged because sleep does not allow the heat to occupy and expand through the matter; it is this expansion that stops the cold and shivering. The second reason is that sleep and these shivers at the start of a paroxysm drive the matter toward certain internal organs, namely <term>apostemes<note>Internal abscesses or swellings</note></term> or areas prone to them. Thus, it causes those swellings to grow. This is what **Galen** and **Rhazes** intend in their writings. The third reason is that sleep at the start of a paroxysm prevents digestion, because it does not allow the heat to expand into the matter but suffocates it beneath it. 

However, it must be said that at the start of a paroxysm, sleep is sometimes permitted for those with very sensitive muscles, especially if the matter is thin and very sharp, putting them in danger from the harm of the shivering. In such cases, the physician's care shifts toward this. This resolves the two arguments brought against this conclusion. 

Secondly, we say that during the decline, the body’s "virtue" (strength) is weak due to the resolution of matter, and the matter itself is lessened; through sleep, the natural heat is fortified. Therefore, the little matter that remains is expelled either through sweat or invisible evaporation. To the contrary argument—that sleep prevents resolution—the answer is that while this is true in itself (by drawing heat inward), it nonetheless helps by comforting the body's strength. 

Thirdly, we say that the benefits of sleep at the peak of paroxysms are subjects of ambiguous and varied debate. **Avicenna** speaks hesitantly here, saying: "and perhaps it does not harm at the peak." **Rhazes**, in his sixteenth book, says that sleep occurring at the peak of a paroxysm will be beneficial. Yet **Avicenna**, later in the second section, says that all sleep at the peak of fever paroxysms is "worse." But these differences can be reconciled. Some try to settle the contradiction by saying that sleep is worse at the very beginning of the "status" (peak), but helps toward the end of it. **Dino** and I, however, have said that moderate sleep at the peak is good because it strengthens the vital force and aids in the digestion of the matter. But the sleep condemned by Avicenna at the peak is "prolonged sleep," which is like a <term>subeth<note>original: "subeth"; a state of lethargic, deep, or morbid sleep</note></term>. This deep sleep is bad as a sign, and it is worse at the peak than at the start of the paroxysm. For deep sleep at the start follows the nature of the start itself and is not as blameworthy; but if deep sleep occurs at the peak, it must have a significant cause, since the expansion of heat at that time should make a person disposed to wakefulness, not sleep. Other explanations are given by Dino and others, which you may see there. 

But let us say that at the peak of fever paroxysms, there is a double disposition: one that is harmed by sleep and another that is helped. There is a weakness of strength due to the resolution that occurred during the whole "increase" phase; and in this case,

->centered text<-
->**they prohibit the digestion of humors.**<-
->**At the decline, however, it is**<-
->**highly beneficial; and perhaps it does not harm**<-
->**at the peak. And do not forbid him**<-

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

sleep is beneficial because it prevents further resolution of strength and comforts what remains. There is also a great multitude of vapors in the entire body because the heat has occupied all the matter and is expanded over it; these vapors do not exit the body in a quantity greater than that which rises from the matter. If they are retained inside, it is no longer the "status" but the "decline." Therefore, when sleep is provoked, these numerous vapors are compressed and moved inward. 

It happens, then, that one person is helped more at the peak by the comforting of their strength; once strengthened, they expel those many vapors more copiously than if they had not been comforted by sleep. In such a case, sleep profits the man at the peak—for example, a thin, choleric person whose humors sin more in sharpness than in quantity. It also happens that another person of the opposite disposition is harmed more by the many vapors compressed at the very start of sleep than they are helped by the comforting of their strength; indeed, they did not need such comforting. That person will be harmed by sleep at the peak. Therefore, **Avicenna** spoke prudently when he said: "and perhaps it does not harm at the peak." 

But you might say that the same could be said of the start of a paroxysm (that perhaps it helps) and the decline (that perhaps it harms). The answer is that they are not alike. Sleep in the decline of a paroxysm is more naturally determined toward helping than harming, because the strength is much resolved and the vapors are few. But at the start of a paroxysm, sleep is more naturally determined toward harming, because the matter and vapors are closed within, and sleep closes them further, while the strength is not yet resolved. 

Fourthly, we say that the "increase" phase is a time which, in its early part, is judged like the "start," and in its later part like the "status." This is why **Avicenna** was silent about it, and **Rhazes** understood it so as well. **Moses Maimonides** <note>original: "Rasi moyfes"</note> considered that sleep at the start of a paroxysm harms more than at any other time, and that at all other times it either helps or harms less; he called all this "benefit" in comparison to the greater harm it causes at the start. He says in his commentary that the times when sleep will help are: after the beginning of the paroxysm and the abscess are complete; and much more during the time of the peak; and the most useful sleep is during the time of the decline. We omit the fourth doubt for the sake of brevity. 

However, current speakers give judgment on sleep during the "universal decline" of the disease specifically. We have elsewhere declared, regarding the aphorism "In which disease sleep brings labor, it is mortal," that this is most verified in the "universal decline" of a disease—that is, a deceptive or false decline. For sleep in a true universal decline ought to help. Similarly, they say that at the beginning of a universal fever, the heat is submerged under the matter, and therefore a person should not sleep as much at the start of a universal disease; they should sleep more during the decline, but only a little during the progress or middle stages of the disease. 

Consider that in a **continuous fever**, where the universal stages are distinct from the times of the paroxysm, one expects a digestion in the matter that is different from the digestion expected in the matter of a single, intermittent paroxysm. For the digestion of paroxysmal matter is like a continuous evaporation and expansion of heat over it. In this, the judgment of sleep may differ somewhat between the start of a paroxysm (or exacerbation) and the total start of a continuous fever. And consider that at the peak of acute continuous fevers, there can be various dispositions toward different **crises** in which sleep might help, or perhaps harm in others. Consider that reason.

->**cold water; unless there is a humor**<-
->**in him that is raw and thick; for then**<-

->**know; that when phlebotomy helps.**<-

<margin>b</margin>
**And do not forbid him.** Since **Avicenna** said above that when you cool the patient, do not use something that causes <term>stypticity<note>A contracting or binding effect, like an astringent</note></term> at the start of these fevers, he wanted to give a rule for cooling. A physician turns his attention to the specific stage of the fever. This rule is very general and undetermined; therefore, he wishes to return to speaking of a specific coolant: namely, cold water, which those with fever often crave. It will be shown in which fevers it is appropriate as a drink or an external application. First, he gives the rule for its use in general; second, through the bath. First, he gives a general canon on the granting or not forbidding of cold water. Second, he distinguishes the particular canon: "unless it be the stomach or liver." It must be considered that the use of cold water as a drink could be for the purpose of cleansing or drinking it pure. Avicenna wants you not to forbid cold water to a feverish person unless the humor is thick and raw. He assigns a well-known cause for this. Since this canon is immediately explained by Avicenna, there is no need to dwell on it here.

<margin>c</margin>
**And know.** Here he proves what he said: that cold water should be granted to the feverish person, and he brings two reasons. The first is that sometimes a drink of cold water completes the cure; and if it is not given, the patient will not be cured. He says this: that sometimes a physician, having performed **phlebotomy** <note>Bloodletting</note> and seeing the patient's relief, cares no further for him. The patient is not fully cured; yet if cold water had been given as a drink, he would have been. This is what he means when he says "when phlebotomy helps." Then, by using a "bad path"—that is, by not giving cold water—the patient will not be "purged" (cured). Avicenna says that the fevers in which we can safely use cold water are **Synocha fevers** <note>A type of continuous, high fever</note>, and in these, phlebotomy is the greatest help and brings the most relief. An ignorant physician, seeing the patient much relieved after bloodletting, thinks the cure is done and does not give cold water (which would complete the cure), but instead has the patient return to diluted wine; then the feverish man is not freed but made worse. 

I explain this canon another way: that when a thick humor is present, phlebotomy sometimes helps, and you believe from this that the fever is purely "sanguineous" (caused by blood)—that is, the cause joined to the fever—and you use the "bad path" by giving cold water when you should not. Because cold water further thickens that matter, the matter will not be purged by sweat or any other evacuation; rather, it will be thickened more. This is proved by the previous canons. 

But this explanation is doubted: how is it possible that phlebotomy helps, yet cold water thickens the matter? It should be said that although many explanations could be given, one is understood from the fourth proposition of the question raised above. Let us set the case thus: someone has a fever from thick cholera or phlegm separated from the blood, and along with this, they have a great "repletion" of blood which immediately begins to inflame. When that cholera or phlegm begins to putrefy, we are forced to perform phlebotomy—not only because we fear the inflammation of that blood and suffocation from it, or its rush to the principal organs, but because nature, burdened by this fullness, cannot attend to the digestion of that cholera or phlegm. The cholera is not made worse by the phlebotomy; rather, it is improved, because nature, relieved of the overload, can diligently work to evacuate it. Once the phlebotomy is done and the patient relieved, an ignorant physician believes this to be a "sanguineous" fever because the bloodletting helped. Because there is a strong flame of heat from the deeply putrid cholera or phlegm, the physician is deceived into giving cold water, which only thickens that raw, thick cholera. Thus, it will not be purged.

The third explanation is also mine: that Avicenna encourages you that although phlebotomy helps, you should not fail to do those things after phlebotomy which...

# Book IV.

<margin>They discuss the softening of the belly, its provocation, and its thinning: because if a "bad path" <note>original: "via mala"</note> is chosen, the patient will not be purged and will not be freed from the illness. He says this because of "soothing physicians" who, seeing that a <term>phlebotomy<note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</note></term> has been performed, immediately relax the rest of the commendable regimen. They neglect the laxatives for the feverish patient, failing to provide <term>clysters<note>Enemas used to clear the bowels</note></term> or syrups, or even proper dieting; instead, they allow the patient to eat meat and drink wine. The fourth exposition belongs to Dynus and Francis of Piedmont: they say that Avicenna wants to follow Galen's seventh book <note>original: "Sal. 7. ter." likely referring to Galen's 'Therapeutics'</note>. This means that sometimes in a <term>synochal fever<note>A continuous, high fever often attributed to an excess of blood</note></term> there is a need for bloodletting, but the physician does not perform it, either through error or because of the fear of the patient or those standing by. In such a case, cold water should be used. Therefore, he says he will later describe "another way." It is interpreted thus: When bloodletting would be helpful but the patient is not purged due to the physician's ignorance or the patient's fear, then you shall use the "other way"—that is, you shall give cold water to drink. This is what Galen says in his ninth book: "If you are forced to treat a patient for whom the aid of bloodletting has been abandoned—either because of the ignorance of the physicians or the fear of the patients or their servants—you must resort to the giving of cold water to cool them." Dynus says: if the text says "a bad path," it means that because of some error the patient will not be purged (bloodletted); therefore, you must provide cold water. This interpretation, however, is considered forced.</margin>

<margin>a **On the Humor.** This is the second reason to prove the previously mentioned rule: specifically, when he intends to speak generally and without confusion. Sometimes, in the condition of those with fever, cold water does not act on thick matter but on thin matter. This is proven because if the matter is thin and <term>choleric<note>Related to yellow bile, which is hot and dry</note></term>, cold water is appropriate because it "digests" it, since the digestion of such matter is actually its thickening. Here Avicenna suggests that when a physician turns his intention to the fever and its cause—as in a choleric fever from thin bile—he can fulfill both intentions with a drink of cold water: it both cools the body and thickens the matter, which the strengthened nature of the body then expels.</margin>

Third, what follows from the drinking of cold water when given appropriately. Fourth, what to know when these indications contradict each other. <column-break/>

<margin>Regarding the first part, it should be noted that Avicenna touches upon eight conditions that prohibit the drinking of cold water in fevers. The first is the weakness of some noble or principal organ, such as the stomach, liver, lungs, or kidneys. This weakness may be due to a looseness of the tissues. From drinking cold water, these organs are struck by the cold penetrating them, destroying their functions; as Galen says, one patient could no longer swallow after drinking cold water due to organ weakness. <gloss>The second condition is a cold "bad complexion" in the stomach or liver. Adding cold water to an already cold organ will destroy its function. <gloss>The third condition is an abscess in the viscera. Although Galen says some "erysipelas" <note>An inflammatory skin condition, here applied to internal inflammation</note> can only be cured by cold water, internal abscesses prohibit it for two reasons: first, the organ is already stretched and weak, and the cold water strikes it too violently (unlike external abscesses where the skin is hard and dense). Second, cold water prevents the "reflow" of matter because it constricts the pores. However, if the inflammation is so great that we fear the patient will be consumed by heat, we might be forced to give cold water to prevent the organ from being "burned in the furnace" of the abscess. <gloss>The fourth condition is pain, because the organ becomes more susceptible to the impact of the cold. <gloss>The fifth condition is a lack of blood, whether from illness or nature, leaving the organs "naked" of natural heat and vulnerable to cold. <gloss>The sixth condition is weak innate heat, referring to those who are naturally weak or the elderly. <gloss>The seventh condition is a lack of habit, such as people from hot regions like Ethiopia. One traveler reported that there everyone drinks warm water and thinks they would die if they drank it cold. When they drink cold water, their "rare" (porous) organs, kept open by heat, are suddenly struck and "congealed," leading to spasms or hiccups. <gloss>The eighth condition is extreme emaciation, which is a major prohibition.</gloss></margin>

<margin>c **Where, however.** Here he lists the eight conditions that allow or indicate the giving of cold water. <gloss>First, the matter must be hot and thin, which is indicated by intense heat and the need for thickening. <gloss>Second, if the matter is thick, it must already be "digested" (broken down). Rhazes notes this in his 17th book. We understand "thick digested matter" as that which accompanies a strong, flaming fever, requiring extinction by the strong cold of water; once the heat is extinguished, the body's vital power is comforted and expels the matter it finds already digested. If it were undigested, the cold would only cause more rot. <gloss>Third, the body should be fleshy, because nerves covered by flesh are less struck by the cold. <gloss>Fourth, innate heat should be abundant (the patient is naturally warm). <gloss>Fifth, the vital power <note>original: "virtus," the body's internal strength</note> must be strong. <gloss>Sixth, the viscera must be healthy (no abscesses). <gloss>Seventh, the natural complexion must not be cold, meaning the nerves are not easily shocked. <gloss>Eighth, there must be a habit of drinking cold water. When the fever and heat indicate cold water and nothing prohibits it, it is the best possible remedy.</gloss></margin>

Where, however,<gloss>c</gloss> the matter is hot or thick and already digested, and the body is fleshy, and the innate heat is exuberant, and the power is strong, and the viscera are healthy and their natural complexion is not cold or infected—indeed, if they are accustomed to cold water—then cold water is the best thing. <margin>d **Regarding "Many times."** He proves why it is the "best thing" by showing the benefits. The vital power is strengthened when the "flame" of the fever is dampened, allowing the body to expel matter through whatever route is best (vomit, urine, etc.). If the fever is choleric, bile is expelled. If the fever is from blood, corrupt humors are expelled. Even if blood is not mentioned by name, it can be expelled through the nose, menstruation, or hemorrhoids. Aristotle says a blood-fever can end by the expulsion of matters that no longer look like blood because they have been corrupted.</margin>

<margin>e **Second Consideration.** The quantity of cold water given varies by the intensity of the fever. We do not give everyone the same amount. Some may drink until they reach a state of shivering or a "livid" (bluish/greenish) skin color due to the sudden cooling. <gloss>We do this when the fever's flame is at its peak and the hour is hot. A "mina" (about 18 ounces) is mentioned as a measure, but Galen wisely does not fix a strict measure, saying one should drink as much as the sufferer desires. <gloss>Third consideration: sometimes drinking a large quantity of cold water turns a fever into a "phlegmatic" (cold/damp) fever. A physician might prefer this, as it is better for the fever to become cold and slow than for the patient to die suddenly from the burning heat. Once the vital power is comforted by the drink, it can expel the matter through its proper paths.</gloss></margin>

<margin>f **And sometimes.** Here he advises that when indications conflict, you must follow the stronger one. For example: if someone has a fever and a liver abscess, the abscess says "no cold water" (it might harden the matter), but the intense heat and thirst say "yes cold water" (to prevent death from drying out). In this case, do not withhold the water. It is a "lesser evil" for the abscess to increase slightly or the matter to remain raw than for the patient to die of heat.</margin>

# Fen I Treatise

We do not give it [the water] arbitrarily, for all this remains in the judgment of the estimator <note>The physician’s "estimative" faculty—his professional intuition and judgment</note>. The physician is guided by the quality of his judgment under scientific canons and practical experience.

<margin>Thirdly, it must be considered that when these contrary indications exist, Avicenna wants you to take the better and safer path. For instance, if it is sufficient to give acetous syrup <note>original: "sirupum acetosum"; a vinegar-based medicinal syrup</note> with water, or a julep of many mixtures with water—for a mixture with little water is more nourishing and less extinguishing—giving these with water is safer than giving pure water, because these drinks still extinguish</margin> the heat and soothe the thirst without being as harmful to the **aposteme** <note>original: "apostemati"; an internal swelling, inflammation, or abscess</note>, as is well known. This rule is set down in the eighteenth [book] of the *Continens*, chapter four.

<insert>In this drink, the physician gives a very large quantity of cold water to the sick person, even until his heat turns "green" and he trembles. Perhaps the fever will be converted to a phlegmatic state, and perhaps nature will be comforted and expel the illness through sweat, urine, or a flux of the belly, resulting in health. And sometimes there are certain prohibitions, yet the malice of the heat and thirst is feared, and you estimate that it will lead to dryness or wasting away. In that case, do not prohibit cold water, for even if it adds to the aposteme and its rawness, that is better than wasting away. But you might say: "Shall I give this syrup with cold water or with hot?" It must be said that if your process for giving these syrups occurs when there is a strong indication for cold water due to fear of wasting and thirst, yet an aposteme restrains your boldness—such as some rawness in the matter or a digestive blockage—you should give them with cold water. We give them so that they might diminish the "malice" of that cold water which we intended to give. If, however, it falls within your estimation that all these things could be better accomplished if the water is given with the aforementioned syrups, do not make it cold.

**E**ven when it is not permitted <note>original: "Et cum non licet"</note>, consider here that it is not lawful for him to drink it during a fever in which all things contradict this drink, or do so vehemently. If, therefore, that which prohibits it is the thickness and rawness of the matter, the water adds to that thickness and rawness, and creates another kind of obstruction. It is possible that it might block several parts, and from this, a new putrefaction and a new fever arise because of the renewed matter—either in its disposition or in the act of drinking cold water. The fever is not extinguished but remitted, and then it returns more intense than before. Furthermore, from this chilling, other matters could be generated according to their species from the matter that was causing the fever, and another fever will be created. In short, one should dispatch himself from this as appears in the ninth [book] of the *Therapeutics*.

That cold water may strike the nerves and be a cause of tremors or spasms is known to those who have knowledge of the fourth fen of the third Canon. It must be considered that there is one who is not accustomed to drinking cold water, such that every time he drinks it, he is harmed by it. For these, there is a certain judgment that drinking cold water is harmful. There is another who is unaccustomed to cold water and is accustomed to hot; for him, cold water is certainly harmful. There is another who, although not accustomed to drinking cold water, is nonetheless not harmed by it if he drinks it occasionally. Regarding him, Galen argues in the second [book] of the *Therapeutics* that if he is occasionally forced to drink cold water, he is not harmed; therefore, he is less harmed by drinking it than one who is accustomed to drinking cold water without harm. On this, read the history of **Axon**, the soldier of Mytilene <note>original: "Ax. militinesi"; likely Axon of Mytilene, a figure mentioned by Galen to illustrate the power of custom</note>, who held primacy in all Peripatetic theory, etc. Indeed, he speaks of the use of cold water externally by way of infusion, that is, a bath. And for the sake of this, he speaks of the bath of hot water and things similar to it in power.

It must be considered that by "infusion" we can understand placing the extremities in cold water—as is desired in the chapter on the cure of tertian fever—or that the whole body is placed in cold water. And this is in harmony with the words of Galen in the second [book] of the *Therapeutics*, chapter nine. He touches upon four conditions that are required for this. First, that there be strong inflammation. Second, that the complexion be hot and dry. Third, that he has evacuated—that is, softened—the belly, if it is expedient. Fourth, that it be in the true and manifest decline of the fever. And this is known when signs of digestion have preceded and the evacuation of the matter has occurred through nature or art.

All these conditions are known, except for the one that requires the body to be hot and dry, since he previously taught to give cold water to the hot, moist, and fleshy. It must be said that cold water taken internally is safer for the fleshy man when it meets sparse members. But externally, with the intention of cooling and removing the heat that a putrid fever impresses, it is better granted to a hot and dry body. For perhaps in a fleshy person, one would fear the addition of heat from the trapped internal heat. And thus the corruption of the text that some make here is resolved—those who say he meant a hot and moist complexion. But Galen's text seems contrary to these eyes in the second [book] of the *Therapeutics*, where he says: "If he is well-fleshed and of a hot and dry constitution, and if you plunge him into a cold swimming pool, it will not harm him, because at such a time, by putting them into cold water, they immediately sweat." And their belly is that from which cholera <note>Yellow bile</note> has erupted. We say it is certain from Galen’s principles in the third [book] *On Complexions* and in the commentary on the *Aphorisms*, part five.

However, there is a place in the *Therapeutics* stating that cold water meeting the exterior of fleshy bodies strengthens the heat inside. Therefore, when Galen says "well-fleshed," he means that the person should not be very thin, so that from bathing in cold water the nerves are not struck in such a way that he spasms or is otherwise badly harmed. And perhaps this is because before the fever he was well-fleshed, and the fever has made him so thin that from the use of cold water externally he will not be inflamed, but will be cooled as much as is expedient for him. We can say another way: that from a cold water bath the physician seeks either the extinction of heat—and this he does in a hot and dry body into which it penetrates—but there is a suspicion of superfluous chilling lest it strike the solid particles of the living being. Or, he seeks a certain gathering of natural heat and its revocation to the interior, and its reflection to the exterior, and with this a certain proper cooling, not very deep nor reaching the substance with the cold of the water. And this is more suitable in the fleshy; hence in the second [book] of the *Therapeutics*, Galen says a certain young man,

Galen therefore proceeds with his estimative judgment and bathes a fleshy fever-patient in the state [of the fever]; he wants this to be a strengthening of the natural heat. Avicenna, however, precedes with his estimative judgment that one should bathe a choleric man who is hot and dry, not a fleshy man such as a sanguine or temperate person is. And he bathes with cold water, not in the "state" [of the fever] as Galen did, but in the true decline when the matter is already evacuated, and he cools the residue of the heat that remained. And with this, he also comforts the natural heat. But there is a suspicion for the very thin person that he might spasm from the cold or incur a "hectic" state of old age. We shall stand therefore by the judgment of Avicenna—that is, the prudent physician who considers the quantity of flesh. It is not so little that the said part follows. Therefore, the two men, Avicenna and Galen, do not contradict each other, but say two things, each of which can happen.</margin> 

by a julep of many mixtures. And when it is not permitted for him to drink cold water, and he is bold regarding it, it is feared that it might cause a constriction of the pores, which may be the cause of another fever with the occurrence of another obstruction, and perhaps it will be more vehement than the first. And when it meets a weak member, it corrupts its operation; it often makes swallowing difficult, causes difficulty in breathing, and causes tremors and spasms and weakness of the bladder, or the kidney, or the colon. 

And he who must most of all be prohibited from drinking cold water is he whom it harms in his health. Indeed, when you see strong heating and a hot and dry complexion, and you have evacuated, then you will sometimes concede that an infusion be made in cold water during the decline and the appearance of digestion and evacuation of the humors. And it is not bad to add 

<margin>It should be considered that in our times, physicians do not dare to use the cold water bath in fevers. This is because of the difficulty of a true estimation, and no less because the remedy is criticized by the common people. The physician fears that if something else happens, he will be defamed. Indeed, there is more jealousy among physicians toward each other than among the common people. And they use a bath with hot water; for the drink, we shall speak of anointing with oil or other softening things, such as mallow and others.</margin>

roses or dilating things like chamomile oil, as we have already said. 

There is a doubt concerning the premises: first, whether cold water is suitable in fevers. See that Avicenna, in the third fen, chapter 5, and the 13th chapter on stomach anxiety, says one should not drink anything in a fever except hot water. On the contrary, Avicenna here handles this question, and the Conciliator <note>Pietro d'Abano, a famous 13th-century medical author</note> prolongs it and forms a multitude of arguments, which are outside the purpose in their difficulties. 

We, therefore, shall say that the drinking of cold water is sometimes in a small quantity, as when we mix it with syrup, or in the time of food, or with pomegranate wine, or with wine, or with sugar or vinegar, or otherwise. As happens when giving a drink to the sick person at the hour of food. And when they give a spoonful of rose sugar or violet sugar or some cordial confection which physicians have constructed for the sick person. Regarding such drinks, it is also when we sometimes soothe the patient because of the dryness of the throat and heat, and we allow water to be held in the mouth and drunk in such ways. 

In the exhibition of a small drink of cold water, the physician generally ought to attend to two things. One is that the fever is not of the kind that strongly indicates giving a large quantity. For if a little is given, there is fear of its inflammation, which Avicenna hints at below in the chapter on the cure of pestilential fever, when he says: "Very much cold water suddenly is helpful; but very little, given subsequently, perhaps excites the heat." And these are very inflamed fevers in which water of watermelon and melon are suitable for choler. As Averroes says in the fifth [book] of the *Colliget*, the penultimate chapter. 

In this way, the speech of Hippocrates in the third book of *On Acute Diseases* is saved, when he says that water changes into choler in choleric people. Although the speech of Hippocrates can be verified in many ways, yet one way is that water in a small quantity is ignited and inflamed in itself. In many paroxysms where greater inflammation is required, it is that which can be done by a little water.

The other thing the physician must attend to in giving the small drinks of cold water is to examine the conditions which Avicenna and others put forward. For after he has established that the fever is not of the kind that indicates extinction with a copious and sudden drink of cold water, and he does not doubt that a little cold water might ignite and harm beyond the intention, consider if it is good that it be given with syrup in the morning, and with the drink during food—whether cold or hot water. And you will know from the aforementioned conditions. For example: if it is the summer season, and he is always accustomed in health to drink things actually cold and not be harmed by them, and the matter is sufficiently choleric, and in the stomach there is no thick matter causing anxiety of which we fear greater infusion through cold water—and with many other conditions which you can consider—I say that to this person you could give cold water in the morning with his syrup, and at the hour of food, and in the other aforementioned ways. If, however, things are contrary to the above, you will give hot water with the syrup, etc.

But you say: "I propose a case where some fever has a strong burning, indicating that cold water be given in a large quantity, and if it were given in a small amount it would be ignited; yet it is not the time now for giving that large amount, as it is certified in my judgment that it is necessary first to soften or digest. I ask, what water shall I give with the syrup and in the food?" Not cold, because that little would be ignited, and the large amount is not yet suitable. Not hot, because it would be much more ignited. It must be said that you will give it cold, but associated with vinegar or lemon juice or some thing that prohibits it from ignition. 

And an experienced physician could say that if the postponement of much cold water in this fever is because of some expectation of digestion—because the choler is thick—he will be able to give hot water with the syrup for the digestion of the thick choler, and also with food so that it does not make the matter raw. And it does not follow that because a little cold water is inflamed, therefore a little hot water is. This is for two reasons: First, because cold water is fixed and does not pass quickly. Second, because where it is fixed, it there creates a certain hot congregation, and they are strengthened by the resistance of the contrary. From these things, inflammation occurs. Regarding hot water, this does not happen. These things, therefore, are said about drinking cold or hot water which we use daily with syrups and at the hour of food; and by this, I wish that the meaning of Avicenna in the third Canon, fen 13, the chapter on stomach anxiety, be understood.

Let us say secondly that there is a drinking of cold water in a large quantity, the measure of which large quantity some authors take in no other way than that it be given as much as the sick person wants to drink, so that he is satisfied, as Galen says. And many others with them. And these ask how great such a drink is and whether it causes trembling and lividity of color, as Avicenna said. And whether such a drink of cold water is suitable in putrid or humoral fevers could not be better said than it is said by Galen and Avicenna and others. And it is that, with all indications standing, it should be given boldly. If all things contradict it, do not give it. If some consent and some do not, let the more fearful indication be observed. And concerning all these things, we are now perfectly dispatched. Regarding cold water in ephemeral fevers, it has been said above; in hectic fevers, however...

# Book III

It will be seen below. The second doubt is whether in a fever we ought to wait for **digestion** <note>original: "digestionem"; the process where the body "ripens" or matures harmful humors so they can be expelled</note> before giving cold water. It seems so from the ninth section, which suggests that although **phlomia** <note>An herbal remedy, likely mullein or a similar plant</note> is suitable for a **synocha** <note>original: "synocha"; a continuous, non-intermitting fever often associated with the blood</note> at any time, drinking cold water is only appropriate when signs of digestion appear. Furthermore, Averroes, in the seventh book of his *Colliget*, continuing his discourse on synocha, says the first condition to observe in drinking cold water is that the matter must be digested. On the contrary, the same Averroes in the same place sees that it is better to provide cold water in the beginning without the appearance of signs of digestion, not caring for the sayings of some who argue against this.

We, however, say that the fevers in which a copious drink of cold water is suitable are those of blood and **choler** <note>original: "cholericæ"; yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness</note>; for it is a long way off from being suitable in phlegmatic and melancholic fevers. If, therefore, there is a blood-based fever, it seems doubtful whether a copious drink of cold water should wait for digestion. For the **Conciliator** <note>Pietro d'Abano (1250–1316), a famous physician and philosopher known for reconciling contradictions in medical authorities</note> does not wait for digestion in sanguineous matter, as appears in Distinction 171. Or it seems it should be expected, as appears from other sayings. And it can be said that if the blood is not putrid, the matter is already digested by its very nature, and specifically if the blood has no fault in quantity or quality, cold water can be given without waiting for further digestion. But if the blood is putrid, one must consider: if it is thick in substance, it cannot be penetrated by cold water, and it is better to wait for some digestion. If, however, it is thin, its "digestion" will actually be its thickening by the cold water. As for choler, if it is thin, cold water will be given appropriately before digestion, because its digestion will be achieved by the cold water. But if it is thick, it is better to wait for digestion.

A doubt is raised about what was said first regarding non-putrid sanguineous matter: for we see that Nature, in evacuating it, waits for digestion; thus the **crises** <note>original: "crises"; the turning point of a disease</note> of true synochas happen on determined **critical days** <note>original: "diebus creticis"; days like the 7th or 14th where the disease's outcome is decided</note>. Therefore, in giving cold water, digestion should be expected, so that after the cooling is done, Nature can expel the matter. A second doubt is raised that in a **caufon** <note>original: "caufone/causus"; a very high, burning fever</note>, which is a fever of thin choler, digestion is expected before cold water is given, according to **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "balyabate"; a 10th-century Persian physician</note> and Cassius Felix. They say that after the illness has achieved **pepsim** <note>original: "ppsaim/pepsim"; the Greek term for digestion or ripening of humors</note>, cold water is given along with other conditions.

To the first, it must be said in two ways. First, although it is not entirely necessary in a synocha without putrefaction to wait for digestion to give cold water, it is still useful. If Nature waits, it is because of the injury from the febrile heat; thus it awaits help from the **lunar aspects** <note>The position of the moon, which was believed to govern the movement of bodily fluids and the timing of crises</note>. Once the fever is extinguished by cold water and the **virtue** <note>original: "virtus"; the body's innate healing power or vital force</note> is comforted, it expels whatever is ready at that hour, whether it is a critical day or not. From this, the third doubt is solved: we do not always need to choose a true critical day to give the drink. If it is given on a critical day, it is useful because many things concur at once to help the virtue evacuate the matter: its strengthening through the extinction of heat and its strengthening by the celestial aspect. But if this drink is given on a non-critical day, the sick person can still be freed on that day through proper evacuation. This evacuation will be a kind of crisis brought about by the force of the medicine/water violating the matter and expelling it, rather than by the natural order of the fever's movement. It will be like a crisis caused by a strong purgative medicine, where Nature does not wait for a critical day, and we free the patient from the fever through that evacuation. Consider this well.

To the second doubt, it should be said that the caufon in which digestion is expected is the caufon from thick choleric matter. Sometimes "caufon" is also used to mean a sanguineous fever. However, one must carefully consider that in "burning" fevers which indicate a drink of cold water, and in which digestion seems necessary because of some rawness of the matter, the physician must have a "latitude of good estimation." For if it seems that waiting for digestion will lead to the death of the patient, or if the digestion will take a "bad form"—for example, the corruption of the matter where a mere **hypostasis** <note>original: "hypostasis"; sediment in the urine</note> appears that is not true digestion—it is better to give the cold water. Do not wait for digestion and do not care if the matter remains raw and the fever is prolonged. This must be chosen over the death of the sick person; this was the understanding of Averroes and Avicenna.

A fourth doubt is raised whether a bath of warm fresh water is suitable in putrid fevers before digestion. It seems so, because one interpretation of the text says "with lukewarm fresh water" refers to a bath. These are the rules we use in the beginning. Furthermore, in a **tertian fever** <note>A fever that spikes every third day (every 48 hours), usually caused by yellow bile</note>, it is not entirely denied by Avicenna. Furthermore, a bath "rarefies" <note>Opens the pores and thins the tissues</note>, and rarefaction is allowed before digestion. The contrary is taken from the eleventh section and from **Maimonides** <note>original: "Rabi moyse"</note> in his 19th aphorism, where he says a bath is useful after the digestion of the humors.

We say that we do not intend to speak of all parts of the bath. Galen spoke sufficiently of them, but we wish only to speak of the bath in a tub of warm fresh water. There is no doubt that after digestion and evacuation, it is useful if any residue of matter remains in the body, specifically that which is fit to be drawn out through the pores. If other conditions exist, such as dirtiness of the skin, blockage of the pores, or roughness of the body, and the patient is accustomed to bathing, we can safely use the tub-bath several times. However, if digestion is done but evacuation is not, although we could use it believing the matter could dissolve through the pores, it does not seem entirely safe to me for fear of dissolving the matter and moving it to a part of the body not suitable for its evacuation. If the humors are raw and specifically if they are many, staying in a bath is harmful by dilating and moving matters that are unfit for evacuation.

Yet, although choleric humor may be raw, it is thin and fit for evaporation; it is a "juice" which warm fresh water corrects. Thus, a bath before digestion is less harmful in a tertian fever. I said "a bath in which one stays," because if the bathing were only a kind of pouring or sprinkling of warm water without staying long, it could be suitable in any fever before digestion, because it would aid digestion through temperate heating and moistening—as in melancholic matter—and would not dissolve the humors too much. Thus Avicenna, in the chapter on the cure of **quartan fever** <note>A fever spiking every four days, associated with black bile</note>, allows entering a bath even if there is no digestion, provided it is only an effusion of warm water in an amount that delights the body and moistens it, but stops before the humor is liquefied.

After this, you should know that in our country, men are not accustomed to baths. The evacuation of putrid matters through a bath does not happen without the resolution and evacuation of the **spirits** <note>The subtle substances believed to carry life and sensation through the body</note>. The fever already causes an excessive resolution of spirits, and because it moves the humors—and if they are deep, it is difficult to move them to the skin—I say you will commonly find little utility in the use of baths (that is, tubs of fresh water). Furthermore, it is much labor for the sick person in both body and soul to be positioned, kept there, and removed. Often, mistakes are made in the temperature of the water and the duration of the stay. For all these reasons, I do not care for the use of a fresh-water bath in the cure of putrid fevers unless it is customary. Perhaps for this reason Rhazes did not find great utility in it; he says in the *Continens*: "I have not seen a bath be useful to a feverish person in any condition." To the first and third contrary arguments, it must be said: rarefaction in the beginning of putrid fevers ought to be done with light things, whether by anointing or washing, and not with things of strong dissolution.

<insert>
A bath may be administered, along with a drink of thin mixed wine and anointing with soothing oils. And when you have administered the aforementioned rules at the beginning of the fever's onset, then you must afterwards occupy yourself with digestion and evacuation—not following the path of weakening and drying, as we have already said, but rather the path of cutting off the cause.
</insert>

<column-break/>

The question is whether wine is suitable in putrid habits. It seems so, because in acute fevers, where it seems least appropriate, wine is given according to Hippocrates. Furthermore, wine performs the digestion of matters and comforts the virtue, as all say. Furthermore, wine is given to rarefy and open the pores. On the contrary, section 8 warns against wine while a fever is present.

Here, first, it must be known that a certain wine is found that is cold in its **complexion** <note>original: "complexionis"; the constitutional balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>, such as wine from the vine which in our regions is white or red and tastes sharp and harsh. It has the flavor of sour pomegranate or verjuice. Men feel their heat reduced by it, though if their stomach is not strong, they are harmed by it as by other thin, cold things. Only a few books mention this wine, which is the opposite of other wines in complexion. For while most wines are hot, this wine is cold—not cold in the way we say a white onion is cold compared to a red one (while still being hot compared to a man), but truly cold. We call such wine "harsh" or "burnt." It is as cold as we say lettuce is cold, which does not heat us. This is what is said in the book *On Good and Bad Juices*: that among wines, there is a great difference in flavor. Do not believe that when the text above mentions "watery wine," it always means this specific wine; sometimes it does, sometimes it doesn't, and we cannot always distinguish them by reason. I say this wine can be granted in fevers at the beginning and throughout. One need not fear the usual harm of wine (injury to the head, heating, or the stirring of matter through heat-driven dissolution).

Other wines are hot in complexion, but there is a great difference among them. Some are "watery" and heat only slightly; these are useful for the digestion and distribution of food—these are the thin, white wines with little "substance." Although such watery wines perhaps do not heat every man, we speak here of wines where there is some heating compared to the person drinking them. Other wines are "vinous," clearly heating, and these are of great diversity. Following these, I set down these practical canons:

**First Canon:** Where there is fear of **frenzy** <note>original: "frenesi"; delirium or inflammation of the brain</note>, it is safer to omit all heating wine, both watery and vinous. One must allow matters to evaporate, and for this, watery wine is better than others.

**Second Canon:** Where there is **syncope** <note>original: "sincopis"; fainting or sudden loss of strength</note> or fear of it, one should not fear the great intensity of the fever too much; you can grant wine to comfort the virtue. Thus, it is granted to "Saracens" <note>Muslims, for whom wine was religiously prohibited</note> during syncope, even though it is not normally lawful for them to drink it. The measure of it should be according to the intensity of the fever. In the beginning of fevers caused by cold matter where syncope occurs, give watery wine.

**Third Canon:** In no fever from choleric matter is any wine suitable at the beginning or before digestion. The reason is that it inflames and agitates the choleric matter. Thus, Haly Abbas says wine is not at all suitable for those with fevers from choler. If you wish to "rarefy" at the start of such fevers, do not do it with wine, but with light rubbing, warm water vapor, or oil of chamomile.

**Fourth Canon:** In choleric fevers, once the matter is digested—and much more once it is digested and evacuated—wine can be granted. It helps the matter transpire through the pores and aids its digestion through the urine. Galen says wine moves all "excreations" <note>Excretions or waste products</note>.

**Fifth Canon:** In "cold" fevers (from cold matter), when signs of digestion appear, wine can be safely granted. This is obvious, and thus all authors cry out that wine should be given when digestion appears in the matter.

**Sixth Canon:** In the beginning of cold putrid fevers, wine can be granted with less hesitation than in the beginning of hot fevers. First, because its inflammation is not feared; second, because a wine of weak heat can be chosen which will have a light power to open the passages. It will not cause a harmful agitation in the matter but rather a gentle heating that digests cold humors and dilates the pores. An experienced physician will know how to judge this. In hot matter, this same heat of the wine could cause inflammation if it is very hot.

**Seventh Canon:** In regions where men have a very strong custom of drinking wine from birth, it can be granted more safely to the feverish than in other parts. Thus, the precepts you find in the books of the Saracens are not to be so strictly applied to us regarding the use of wine, because it is not lawful for them to drink it and they are very unaccustomed to it. Likewise, the precepts of the Greeks, who wanted men not to drink wine until age seven (as Maimonides relates), must be considered alongside the diversity of wines according to climate.

To the first argument: in acute fevers, wine should be given when due and the kind that is suitable. To the second: wine helps digestion of raw humors, but it could inflame very hot humors and agitate very raw ones, especially a potent wine. As for the other points, the **Conciliator** treats these two questions differently; take them as you please.

"And when you have administered, etc." Now Avicenna sets down canons for the cure of putrid fevers, intended for the matter, with which the physician works...
