# Fen I, Treatise II

In the beginning of a fever, one performs a common evacuation, which is called drying <note>original: "ericcatio"; a medical process of thinning or drying out harmful fluids in the body</note>. Here he sets down the rule regarding the matter: but the physician working with them intends to cause the "cutting off" <note>original: "abscissionem"; the complete removal of the cause of the disease</note> of the matter. Thus Avicenna continues his own discourse. However, the continuity can be maintained by saying: he first placed the rule for evacuation that is suitable in the beginning; here he places the rule for evacuation that is suitable after the beginning, when the matter has been digested. Therefore, first Avicenna continues his discourse; second, he follows it through, where he says: "And do not evacuate." It is doubted whether at the beginning of the symptoms (that is, the onset of the fever) evacuation should precede, since according to the rule it seems not. First, concerning **bloodletting** <note>original: "phlebotomia"; the practice of drawing blood to balance the humors</note>: even if it were necessary, it should not be done at the beginning, but postponed as will be said later; and it is taken from the first book, fen 4, chapter 8 on bloodletting. Second, concerning the provocation of humors, it seems it should not be done from the beginning: because unless the matter has been evacuated through provocation, they are not suitable, as in the ninth book of the *Therapeutics*, chapter 15 and 16, on the authority of Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler</note> and the famous Rufus <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a renowned physician of the 1st century</note>; and elsewhere it is stated that in the beginning of fevers where bloodletting is not suitable, evacuation is not performed. In the same way, it is proven concerning evacuation through sweat, which was the intention of Rufus and Oribasius. 

On the contrary, according to Avicenna, to solve this one must first consider that the "beginning of symptoms" or the "symptoms of fever" refers to the beginning where there is a distinction regarding all symptoms for which there are signs of crudity <note>original: "cruditatis"; the state of humors being "raw" or undigested by the body's heat</note>. And thus the rules are properly understood in the use of pharmacy. It could also be understood as the beginning of symptoms absolutely in every fever, whether there is vigor in that beginning (as at the end of a **synocha** <note>a continuous, high-grade fever</note>) or not, as in others. Second, it must be considered that Avicenna does not say that you should use these rules at the very start of symptoms, but he says that if you have administered them, you have performed a "minorative" <note>reducing/lessening</note> evacuation, which is drying. And so he wants you to consider how well you use the aforesaid rules and in what way: for if the fever is in the beginning of its onset and the matter is crude, bloodletting is not suitable; or a minorative bloodletting is suitable if there is a bloody fullness, as we said above. Third, it must be considered, as we said above, that evacuation in putrid fevers is twofold: one is common, which is the evacuation of matters commonly and necessarily joined to the fever, which is called drying in Avicenna’s work—as, for example, the cleansing of the intestines and the clearing of various vapors and certain infected watery matters in the urine. The other is proper evacuation, which takes away the humor that causes the fever. Having established these points, let us say: understanding the "beginning" broadly to include bloody fevers and other fevers of other humors, you practiced in the beginning with bloodletting: by reason of which it could be truly minorative, and truly cutting off the cause totally, as said above. But if you practiced with other rules and not with bloodletting, such as in **choleric**, **phlegmatic**, or **melancholic** fevers, in which bloodletting is not suitable (or if it is, only minorative bloodletting is used), I say that if the use of these other rules (aside from bloodletting) is in the beginning, you have not properly reduced the matter brought to it, but you have performed a common evacuation, which is called drying. And therefore by itself it loosens the belly, but gently, not strongly. You provoked neither urine nor sweat, except very lightly. And because the contrary symptoms cease, note that Avicenna in the same way sets you to bloodletting in the beginning: but it is not expedient for him to provoke urine or sweat. If in the beginning it seems right to you, do it with very light things, and after a small cleansing has been done. 

It is doubted secondly whether, as the rule says, we should "cut off" the matter in the progression of fevers; this is generally disputed. It can be considered that, as we said above for the clarity of doctrine and to speak distinctly of the rules of bloodletting and the other rules for lenitives, such as the flow of the belly and the provocation of sweat and urine: We say, therefore, that evacuation by bloodletting can cut off the cause in two ways: sometimes, without a prior step, it cuts off the cause totally in one turn, as in a synocha, in which one bloodletting frees the person; and this happens most especially in the beginning, for when it is postponed it cannot be done so copiously, as will be said later. And sometimes, it can cut it off in repeated turns; as if someone's blood were bad, causing the fever, and a gradual bloodletting performed again and again eventually rectifies the whole blood. <gloss>A certain common evacuation differs, called drying, from the proper evacuation called "cutting off." First, on the part of time: because evacuation which is cutting off happens after the beginning when the matter is digested by regular operation; but evacuation which is drying happens immediately in the beginning, because we immediately provide an enema or, if expedient, we give a lenitive to the patient.</gloss> But it is doubted: can we not use a provoker of sweat or urine at the very beginning of all of them? For there is a certain fever for which evacuation is not suitable at the beginning, neither by bloodletting nor by medicine. Indeed, in no fever is evacuation by resolving medicines regularly suitable in the beginning; but if evacuation has not been made, we cannot use provokers or sweaters, as has been said. <gloss>It is doubted secondly whether we can use this rule in the process after digestion.</gloss> To the first, it should be said that if it be a fever in which a reduction has been made by bloodletting, there is no doubt that we can more safely use it from the beginning

<column-break/>

with given substances or provokers of urine: in which the principal intention is the opening of the passages. Through this, the digestion of the matter follows, as was said above. And in this, it follows that common matters are evacuated. But if the fever is of a specific matter in which no minorative proper evacuation is to be made from the beginning, then we cannot use provokers of sweat, nor urine of any great strength, because an agitation of the matters would occur. I shall, however, cause a dilation and opening of the pores by a light, proper friction with cloths and coverings, and a provocation of the opening of the passages with simple acetous <note>vinegar-based</note> syrup, or with barley water, or with syrup of two roots <note>likely fennel and parsley roots, common in medieval medicine</note>. Perhaps, indeed, the evacuation of humors is multiplied without benefit. 

In a case where the fullness is great, in which neither bloodletting nor medicine is suitable before digestion: I ask whether here you should cause sweating or provoke urine from the beginning. It must be said that nothing should be done that agitates the feverish person, but I will refine the matter, as in **syncopal** <note>fainting</note> fever with rose water; and these can be called provokers and sweaters, and this whole thing stands in your estimation. <margin>a</margin> To the second, it should be said that we also use this rule in the progression of the disease, as appears regarding softening, sweating, and provocation, and this will be more fully declared here. Secondly, these evacuations differ based on the things with which they are done: for the evacuation that is "cutting off" is done with a thing that chooses the matter in the evacuation—that is, which evacuates the proper matter of the fever. How this selection is made by a loosening medicine is well known. But the evacuation called drying is not done by choosing the humors for proper evacuation, but by leading out the available matters; and this is manifest in softening the belly and the beginning of the urines. But "cutting off" evacuation or sweating takes the humors by a "tearing" <note>original: "ripis"; likely referring to a forceful pulling of humors</note>. Second, because a minorative can happen immediately, and then a total cutting off; and the cutting off of a part, which are properly called minorative and eradicative evacuations, differ first: although digestion is exercised in both, minoratives take only a part, while eradicatives take the whole. Second, because a minorative can happen immediately when some part of the matter is digested, if it seems to the physician that he ought to take it, as in phlegmatic fevers, as will be declared later; but the eradicative happens when all the matter is digested, and this regularly. Third, because by the power of the evacuation it can be done with a lighter thing, but the eradicative requires more, and this lightness is by the degree of the strength or by a smaller dose. For example: first you reduced some of the matter with rhubarb; afterward you eradicate with **scammony** <note>a harsh medicinal root used as a strong purgative</note>. A second example: to reduce, you give a small dose of scammony; to eradicate, you give a full dose. It could happen, however, that a certain eradicative was much lighter than the preceding minoratives, because that which remained to be eradicated was very little. From all these things said, it appears that minorative evacuations are like a certain preparation for eradicative evacuation, either in part or in nature; whether that minorative evacuation is called what I, with Avicenna, call "drying," or whether it is called the minorative which is the cutting off of a part: for by both the strength is alleviated and the passages are prepared.

But then it is to be doubted whether a "cutting off" evacuation could be made through sweating or urinary medicines. And it is said to be known of itself that through sweating medicines, the appropriate matter can be evacuated. It is known that by provoking sweat or urine in a melancholic fever, it causes that matter to go out; when the urine is black, it is cutting off the melancholic matter. And in the same way, sweating medicines like old **treacle** <note>original: "tyriaca"; theriac, a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "cure-all"</note> and the medicine of **asa** <note>likely asafoetida</note>, and others which are mentioned in their chapters as moving matters through sweat. And all these are evacuants according to the path of cutting off the matter. Therefore, in the use of these sweaters and provokers, we wait for digestion, just as in the use of loosening medicines, as will be said later in its own chapter. Indeed, as will be declared, the use is safer following other medicines.

<margin>a</margin> **And do not evacuate.** Here he places the rule for this evacuation. Secondly, he sets down four evacuating medicines. The first part has three points: first he gives the rule, second he declares it, third he joins the rule for curing putrid fevers. Consider therefore that in these rules: this one is about evacuation, not about that which is "drying," which only fits in the beginning of symptoms, and consequently while the matter is undigested. And this is reasonable: because that evacuation does not touch the proper matter of the fever except by accident, and in that, digestion is not expected as it is in loosening medicines. Furthermore, softening the belly and provocation and light sweating do not regularly touch the proper matters of fevers, as we have declared. It is left, then, that this rule is about "cutting off" evacuation, whether eradicative or minorative, which is done with combining and resolving medicines or by strongly provoking sweat or urine. 

<margin>a</margin> **Perhaps.** Here he declares the stated rule. First regarding the first precept, which says not to evacuate undigested matter. Second regarding the second precept, which says "unless by necessity." Third he places a certain rule rectifying this evacuation. The first reason is that if matter is evacuated before digestion, the evacuation of humors not reaching their state is multiplied. Dynus <note>Dino del Garbo (d. 1327), a famous commentator on Avicenna</note> explains: that is, whose evacuation is such that nature cannot reach the state of digesting the matter, and this diminishes the strength. Another explanation is our own: that evacuation before digestion is the cause of good humor being evacuated; and then the good humor ought not to come to a state of digestion to be evacuated, but rather to nourish and be converted into **spirits** <note>original: "spūs" (spiritus); the vital forces believed to animate the body</note>. Our third explanation is that by evacuation before digestion, subtle matter is evacuated which of itself would have been resolved and would not have reached the state of digestion. Therefore, it was not expedient for you to evacuate the cause with a resolving medicine.

<summary>This page discusses the precise timing and methods of evacuation in treating fevers, distinguishing between "drying" (minor initial cleansing) and "cutting off" (targeted purging after digestion). It warns against premature purging, which risks depleting the body's vital spirits instead of removing harmful humors.</summary>

# Book III

<margin>a</margin> **And perhaps.** The second reason: that evacuation should not be performed which harms the ripening <note>original: "maturatio"; the process where the body processes a disease-causing humor</note>. But even before digestion this occurs: because it weakens the internal strength and because it evacuates the thin <note>original: "subtile"; thin or watery fluids</note> part of the matter; thus the thick part remains and is not well-digested, as Haly Abbas <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> says in the third book of his *Practical Medicine*, in the chapter on the evacuation of putrid humors.

<margin>b</margin> **And perhaps.** The third reason: that evacuation should not be performed which causes the malignant humor to multiply. However, evacuation before digestion does exactly this because it agitates the matter and mixes it with the good fluids; thus the good is corrupted and the bad is multiplied. This is the discourse of Avicenna in the first book, fourth section, fourth chapter. 
But you might say that this mixing ought to rectify this bad matter because it is touched by the good. It must be said that mixing which occurs through the active power of the rectifying substances is good; but mixing which occurs through the agitation of a bad humor that is distant from the nature of blood is what causes the most harm: for from this, more corruption of the good humors occurs than rectification of the bad. It is doubted why Avicenna used this way of speaking, saying "perhaps." It must be said first that a person does this for the sake of a forced, reducing, or eradicating evacuation in a violent matter <note>original: "materia furiosa"; matter that is acting aggressively or unpredictably in the body</note>: if it is done sometimes before digestion, these harms might not occur; or if they do occur, they are lesser harms than those which would follow from leaving the matter alone. Or it must be said that he said this because of certain estimable cases in which a praised result happens to a physician working against the rules. For example: some presumptuous doctor gave a laxative medicine before digestion in a colicky or flatulent fever, and the matter was not violent, nor was it an irritated flowing matter, yet there was some necessity for reduction before maturity. Therefore, this medicine was given entirely against the rule, and the three predicted harms ought to follow: namely, the evacuation of a humor that should not be evacuated, the hindrance of ripening, and the multitude of bad humors; and perhaps it happens that none of these occur. For it happens that a man may be of a robust nature, whereby his strength defends the good humors from the pull of the laxative medicine, and they help themselves by expelling the bad matter, even though it is undigested, and the medicine will evacuate it all. Thus digestion is not hindered, nor will the bad humor be multiplied, and the sick person will be freed by a doctor who acted badly; and this will be further explained below where he says: "And I think."

<margin>c</margin> **And you.** First he presents the error; second, he refutes it at the point "For the matter." He presents their statement and the reason for the statement; this man was Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; the great Persian physician Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi</note>, as held in the sixth book of the *Continens*, chapter 2. Hence Rhazes, in his *Book for Al-Mansur*, immediately concedes myrobalans <note>A fruit used as a laxative</note> in a tertian fever. And Rhazes was not only the author of the idea that choleric humors should be evacuated before digestion (because in truth he believes their expulsion is not before digestion since they are already "digested" by being thin), but in the case of cold humors, he concedes that evacuation ought to occur before digestion, as appears in the 16th book of the *Continens*; and Averroes saw that passage, as appears in the 7th book of the *Colliget*. What the truth is about this, we shall say later.

<margin>d</margin> **For the matter.** First he argues with reasons against him, and in this the reason of those others is resolved. Second, he argues by authority. Third, he shows what could have been the cause of why they held this opinion and the motives for the opinion, at the point: "And it would be better." Fourth, at "I think." He brings four reasons against him. The first reason can be formed thus: all humor intended for evacuation ought to be digested before evacuation, because digestion is the balancing <note>original: "equatio"; bringing into a manageable state</note> of the substance of the matter so that it may be expelled. But all humor, whether thick or thin, is unfit to be expelled; for the thin is absorbed and the thick is fixed and immobilized. The viscous, however, adheres to the walls of the members by its tenacity or stickiness. Therefore, it is necessary to thicken the thin humor, or to condense it, and to thin the thick humor gradually, lest by a powerful and sudden thinning a collapse occurs. On this passage I would write more, were it not that it was subtly explained in our question on the "Greatness of Disease."

<margin>e</margin> **And if this man.** The second reason. This man would concede that "troublesome" humors <note>original: "humores fyros"; stubborn or difficult fluids</note>—namely thick, viscous ones unfit for expulsion—ought to be digested. Therefore, by this he ought to concede that thin humors ought to be digested. And he holds the strength of the preceding reason, which is what he says: "if this man" (namely Rhazes) "had heard nothing from the ancients about digestion before we said it," and before the dispositions of the troublesome humors were removed (namely through their thickness), he ought to know this through that which he knows about the digestion of the troublesome ones: namely, what concerns those that are thin, etc. It should be considered that he speaks with reproach to this man in this: that if he had never heard anything from anyone before Avicenna about digestion, etc.—as if he says "if from our sayings and before this reminder of ours he had heard nothing"—he should know that thick humors are unfit for expulsion, and through this he should know that thin ones are also unfit because of an entirely opposite disposition. Another text has the word "reminder." 
Alternatively, it could be explained that this is a clarification of the previous reason: and he says this man by himself ought to know something about digestion even if no one told him. And it is known that a "troublesome" humor (that is, unfit for expulsion) ought to be digested; therefore, both the thin and the thick ought to be digested. He ought therefore to know this—namely that thin and thick humor ought to be digested—through that (that is, through the disposition of troublesome humors and those unfit for evacuation). It appears, therefore, that "troublesome" is taken in two ways. In one way, by earthy immobility, as thick troublesome humors are. And in this way, "troublesome" is taken above when he said "fixed thick." And this pertains to the first exposition. In another way, "troublesome" is taken broadly to mean "unfit." And in this way it is taken here as far as the second exposition is concerned.

<margin>f</margin> **Why then, etc.** The third reason. If thin matters were already digested, then in the beginning of acute fevers, which are from thin matter, a praiseworthy sediment <note>original: "hypostafis"; the deposit found in urine used for diagnosis</note> would appear; this is visibly false. The consequence is noted because the sediment in these acute fevers is nothing other than the humor causing the sickness which is now digested. Therefore nature expels it; therefore it is necessary that there be a praiseworthy sediment in the beginning of a blood-based fever. I know this is why Dino <note>Dino del Garbo, a 14th-century physician</note> understands "the beginning" here not as a single moment of time, nor

<column-break/>

to the state through digestion, so that it may be evacuated. **And perhaps**<insert>a</insert> evacuation harms maturation. **And perhaps**<insert>b</insert> the malignant is mixed with the good: because the malignant is moved without its own digestion. **And you** do not listen to the man who thought that the intention in digesting is to thin: for a hot humor is thin, though it is not necessary that it be thinned. **For the matter**<insert>d</insert> is not as he said: rather, the intention in digesting is to balance the substance of the matter, so that it becomes prepared for easy expulsion. For the thin which is absorbed, the thick which is fixed, and the viscous which adheres—all of that is not prepared for easy expulsion; rather, it is necessary that the thin be thickened, and the thick be thinned gradually, and the viscous be cut. **And if this man**<insert>e</insert> had not heard anything in the discourse of the ancients about digestion before we said it, and he remembered the disposition of the digestion of troublesome humors—namely, that the part of them which is thin needs to be thickened and the part which is thick needs to be thinned—it would be necessary that this be known through that. And because it was not fitting that he consider by himself and say: **Why do urines** in acute fevers not have a sediment in their beginning, but afterwards they do? And is a praiseworthy sediment anything other than the humor causing the sickness, which is now digested? **Why therefore**<insert>f</insert> is it not expelled at the beginning of the sickness for the sake of health, if thinness is the ultimate thing intended in digestion? Therefore it would be necessary that there be a praiseworthy sediment at the beginning of fevers of blood and yellow bile. **But if** nature is not able to expel that superfluity except after the hour in which the preparation for expulsion in the urine occurs, then similarly it ought to be known that to evacuate the humor before that hour in which digestion appears in the urine is an inconvenience or a difficult evil. **And perhaps** it moves and does not operate ultimately, and perhaps it mixes the malignant with the good. **And it is better** for this man that he should think well of those who were like Galen and Hippocrates in those things which they wrote about this and should pay great attention; and then he should return to his contradiction, because every contradictor who, in the first place, stands upon the truth is excused. **Truly** it would be better if he did not consider it in his own consideration. **And I think** that rarely...

<column-break/>

as a space of three days, nor a point where it begins; but as an intention common to these as Hippocrates also understands in the first book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, when he says: "one must give to the sick in the beginning, etc." For the discourse of Avicenna is well-verified concerning the "beginning," which is one of the four universal times of a disease. He says this as if asking: why did that man not consider within himself and say, etc. One must consider what he says regarding "praiseworthy urines": because an unpraiseworthy sediment can come from the organs themselves, but a praiseworthy one must come from the matter that is the "joined cause" <note>original: "causa coniuncta"; the immediate cause of the symptoms</note> in acute diseases, in which the matter is saved for a single expulsion; and consequently the whole "antecedent cause" is beneath the "joined cause," or it will be so until the state of the disease. And therefore the digested matter is expelled; and the sign of this digestion is a praiseworthy sediment. In non-continuous fevers, however, the sediment can come from matter that is antecedent; and similarly in continuous tropical fevers. We do not linger on this because of what was said in our question "Whether digestion is owed to the joined cause."

**But if. This is** the fourth reason. Nature in acute fevers does not evacuate the matter except after the signs of digestion that appear in the urine; and this is what he says: **Except after the hour**, etc. Namely, except after the appearance of the signs of digestion in the urine. Therefore, in the same way, the physician ought not to cure except when digestion is achieved; and he repeats what was said above to give vigor to this reason.

**It is doubted** because the consequence does not seem good: "nature does not expel, therefore neither should the physician." Rather, below he commands that if nature does not evacuate, you should evacuate. It must be said that if nature does not expel because of a defect, then you ought to expel; but if nature, acting in an orderly way, does not expel because the humor is unfit, you—also acting in an orderly way—ought to do the same: namely, wait until it is fit.

**And it is better.** Here he argues against that man by authority. And he says that this Rhazes ought to believe Galen and Hippocrates, and this is what he means by "think well of them." That is, he should have a good opinion of them: namely, that they were good men who are to be believed in what they wrote. Namely, both in the first *Aphorism* when he said "digest things to be medicated" and in the *Aphorisms* on acute passions. But if this man does not want to believe Hippocrates and Galen, he ought first to pay great attention and consider much and examine; and then contradict Galen and Hippocrates. For a contradictor, when he stands upon the truth (namely, when it appears to be truth to him after a good discussion, even if it is not the actual truth), is excused. Truly it would be better if he considered it in his own consideration—namely, that of Hippocrates and Galen—or in his own personal consideration. It is as if he says: if he had considered well, he would not have contradicted; otherwise he did not consider, or he should not consider—that is, he should not believe himself, but Galen and Hippocrates. Consider the great praise that Avicenna gives to Galen and Hippocrates in the work of medicine; consider the reproach he says of Rhazes: namely, that if he had considered within himself, the aforementioned truth would have appeared to him: namely, that evacuation ought not to be done except when the matter is digested. Even if it is thin, it is not therefore to be expelled, but rather because of its unfitness; those who look at few things easily pronounce judgment. Avicenna therefore wants this reason to be so evident that Rhazes would have seen it immediately if he had considered it; and if he had not been able to see it, and the contrary had appeared true to him, then he would have been excused. For a man who insists against a truth with a very strong reason that is insoluble to him is excused. It is therefore a reproach that he says of Rhazes: that he did not attend to what he says.

**And I think.** Rhazes was a great practitioner and experimenter. And therefore in his practice, he gave many laxative medicines before the digestion of the matter, and from this, it succeeded well for him. And therefore he acquired this through experience, and he purged the matter in acute fevers immediately in the beginning before digestion, and he continued this way. And this is what he says: "they were useful in this case," namely the cure of putrid fevers before digestion. And Avicenna removes this and says that his experiments, which are against the rule, are worth nothing. Nor is it a sign—namely, that it should be done this way in other sick people. For although in one sick person or in many this might happen, it is not a sign that it ought to be done so, and consequently it is not a sign that a general rule can be made from that work. For this is an accidental occurrence.

**The question is whether** seeing by experience in many sick people that a medicine given before digestion freed the feverish patient, we ought to take this as a general rule: that a laxative drug can be given before digestion. It seems so: first, because many things are believed by experience alone, such as operations from a "specific form" <note>original: "forma specifica"; the unique, often hidden property of a substance</note>; nor do we have anything else by which we make a rule of curing except confirmation through experience, as is taken from the ninth book on *Simple Medicine*, chapter five. Furthermore, from the effect following the operation, our work is confirmed, as is taken from the commentary on the *Aphorisms*, second part, fourth section. **To the contrary**, it must be said to Avicenna first that when an experiment is against true reason, a general rule cannot be made from it, because then it would be a false rule. For either the reason is true (which we know because it has manifest propositions and is confirmed by the judgment of many wise men). And this ceases because the argument is about specific form. For an operation that is from a specific form is understood by the senses, nor does it have an effective contrary reason. Second, I say that an experiment against reason is an occurrence that happens in the minority of cases. And therefore Avicenna said "not even one," speaking in the singular.

**But it is doubted** how it can be that the sense contradicts reason. **I do not say...**

### Treatise II

Now, regarding the observation that those suffering from fevers are helped by a resolving medicine <note>original: "farmaco resoluente"; a drug intended to loosen or break down humors</note> before the matter has ripened <note>original: "digestione"; in medieval medicine, this refers to the body "cooking" or maturing a disease-causing humor so it can be expelled</note>: sometimes this is true, and the physician is not deceived in his judgment. This occurs in two ways. First, because the matter was "raging" <note>original: "furiosa"; referring to humors that are particularly violent, fast-moving, or malignant</note>; thus the cure was achieved before ripening because it was a feverish state. However, this observation does not contradict the medical rule <note>original: "canonem"</note>, but rather aligns with its own rules. There are, therefore, two rules: one is that you should not evacuate raw and non-violent humors before they have ripened. The other is that you should evacuate "raging" humors before ripening. These two rules do not contradict each other in the realm of reason, nor does sensory observation conflict with reason.

In another way, this observation is true because of unique individual conditions <term>individual conditions: the specific, non-generalizable physical traits of a single patient</term> which are made known to us through the practice of this art. These individual conditions are not just a single state, but demonstrate a unique individual whose like has never existed from eternity nor will exist again. In such a person, a singular property might allow a laxative medicine to cure them. Thus, raw matter follows the evacuation without harm. However, these individual conditions include all the hidden

<insert>
Thus, experiments <note>original: "experimenta"; here meaning practical experiences or clinical trials</note> occurred for the man which were beneficial in this chapter, and he accepted them. **And indeed, regarding such experiments that do not follow the medical rules, it happens that not even one is effective.** And it happens that not even one of them serves as a sign, for this is appropriate. **And furthermore, the matter is often highly mobile and changeable from limb to limb, and you judge that there is no time for its ripening.**
</insert>

dispositions occurring rarely, of which the physician cannot reach a certain knowledge through any specific sign. In such a disposition, it can happen that a resolving medicine given before ripening helps. For example: let there be a phlegmatic fever <note>fever caused by an excess of the humor phlegm</note> at the beginning with thin, raw urine, and let this matter be hidden around the primary mesenteric veins <note>veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note>, being thick and viscous within itself, but slippery and, so to speak, oily on its surface. If a laxative medicine like agaric <note>a medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note> is given, the patient will be immediately liberated at the very beginning. And because someone might challenge this case by saying the matter was already ripened or that it was recognizable, you should set up the case such that it cannot be known and is indeed raw, yet the medicine still evacuates it—notwithstanding that the urine appears thin and raw. These benefits from an evacuation performed "against reason" are not truly against reason in reality. Reason established what was true for the majority of cases or for dispositions recognizable to the physician; however, we see these rare dispositions happen often. This benefit belongs to hidden, individual dispositions that occur very rarely. Therefore, they cannot be reduced to a rule, for a general rule cannot be formed from rare individual dispositions. Nor can a particular or individual rule be formed for those individuals: for if we said that in every human having such individual dispositions, raw matter could be evacuated before ripening, and a purging would be done with medicine before the ripening of the matter, this rule would be useless or unscientific to the physician. The form of the rule cannot provide knowledge of these hidden individual dispositions. It appears, then, how this observation—that one is helped by a laxative medicine given before ripening in non-violent matter—does not contradict the truth of the matter in itself. Yet a rule cannot be formed from this as a sufficient sign that we ought to act this way in other men. As Avicenna well says: sometimes this observation is deceptive, because it is understood through reasoning opposite to how it ought to be understood. For example: sometimes, against reason and against what ought to have been done, a person is liberated from a fever by being given medicine before ripening, when in truth it should have been given to ripened matter. The physician then takes this recovery and says the medicine was the cause. But in truth, the cause was the patient's own internal strength <note>original: "virtus"</note>, which was provoked by the medicine; this vigorous strength fought against the medicine and against the fever and obtained the victory. You should not, therefore, attribute this to the medicine; for if the medicine had not been given, the patient would have been liberated more quickly and with milder symptoms, and would have remained in his convalescence and health. He could have recovered in a better way. Therefore, this experiment which does not follow the medical rules is of no value, as Avicenna says. And this error could frequently happen, yet one cannot make a general rule from it. This is what is said in the chapter on quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with black bile</note>: that it is corrected from error. But as to the second argument, it must be said that the benefit which confirms our work is the benefit following your action. But you say: Reason says this man is liberated by the work of purging medicine; therefore I say that Galen and Hippocrates <note>the two most foundational authorities in ancient and medieval medicine</note> would deny this, and we should believe those two men more. And if you say, "Reason could say I have seen in experience that a medicine given at the start of an acute fever to a thousand sick men resulted in many being liberated and few dying; and another five hundred were not purged at the start, of whom more died." Hippocrates and Galen would laugh. This was because all or most of those were sick with an acute fever from "raging matter" properly so called, or from matter offending in its vast quantity; therefore, before ripening, it had to be cleaned out. Thus the operation was not against the rule, but according to it. Wherefore, etc.

<margin>a</margin> **But when, etc.** Now Avicenna has declared the rule or reached that point which was canonical: that you should not evacuate unripened matter. Here he explains this rule in its second part, where he says "unless because of necessity." First, he posits the causes for which you evacuate immediately at the start due to necessity, without waiting for future ripening. Second, he confirms the fewness of these cases. Third, he verifies this through a comparison. The first part is in three sections, as he posits three cases in which we evacuate before future ripening. In the first of these, he posits the cases and touches on the cause. Second, he specifically proves the reasoning. It must be considered that this case in which Avicenna commands evacuation to be done before ripening can be understood solely regarding "raging matter"; then he explains "very mobile," meaning highly unstable, vehemently mobile, vehemently raging, and vehemently bad. And Avicenna assigns two causes why its evacuation is necessary then—that is, immediately at the start before ripening. One cause is that there is no time for its ripening according to your estimated judgment. This is because its malice is not capable of being ripened. The second cause is that even if you judge it could be rectified through ripening, nevertheless, because it is mobile and goes from limb to limb, an abscess <note>original: "apostema"; a swelling or internal collection of humors</note> is feared in the limb to which it goes, or some other danger. Either an abscess or another danger, such as sudden death. And this is because in the whole time it is left alone and its ripening is expected—which is a long time when the matter is depraved—there is fear. He calls it "equal ripening," meaning a ripening that balances its substance; so that if you wanted to do anything else in raging matter, it would take a long time to balance it because its substance is so far from balance. In another way, this case can be understood as "raging matter" properly speaking, and in matter that is very plentiful; although it might not be truly raging, nevertheless

<column-break/>

because of its excessive urgency, we fear it may suffocate the patient before it reaches a steady state, or that the body cannot withstand the ripening process. Because of this, we reduce the matter by cutting it away <note>purging</note> before ripening. He explains: "but when the matter is very plentiful," specifically in its quantity, and when the matter is mobile, meaning raging, even if it is not much. Then this rule includes the cause he specifically posits there: that is, if you are afraid. Then the causes he assigns refer to both types of matter; for when he says "there is no time for ripening," this can be because the matter is plentiful or because it is raging.

<margin>b</margin> **An abscess happens, etc.** Because it is plentiful or because it is raging; certain commentators refer this only to plentiful matter and not to raging matter; it causes the fall, etc., either by its multitude or its raging nature.

<margin>c</margin> **Fear.** Here he brings in three reasons. 1. First adapting them to raging matters. First, he argues thus: the fear in evacuation before the ripening of raging matter is less than the fear of the swelling in that raging matter if it is left alone. Therefore, evacuation of raging matter must occur immediately at the start. Avicenna holds this as a known consequence; for just as we act in life's affairs, choosing the better or the lesser evil, so we act regarding the laboring patient, as he says in the first chapter of his *Therapeutics*. Avicenna has this preceding point as already known to those who hear his words here: there is even fear if raging matter is left alone, specifically the fear of death. But if evacuation is done before ripening, there is only the patient's anxiety and disturbance from the difficulty of the evacuation. Therefore, this is more choice-worthy. 2. Then the reasoning can be applied to plentiful matter where we fear it cannot be ripened unless it is reduced. For if it is left alone, there is fear of death. Second reason: nature itself tries to evacuate raging matter immediately before ripening because of the greatness of its harm; therefore, the physician ought to act according to nature's example. In the same way, this reason can be applied to matter offending by its quantity. But it is doubted: if this reason is true regarding plentiful matter, then every sick person sweating at the start or having a flux of the bowels ought to be evacuated before ripening. We see this because nature works at the start on the evacuation of matter. It must be said that evacuations appearing at the start of fevers signify a great fullness or bad matter, as was explained by us in the second section; then if the physician sees that nature has reduced enough of the matter that the remainder can be expected to ripen, the reducing or "cutting away" evacuation should be left alone. This remains to the judgment of the physician. If, however, after the evacuations, a great fullness remains about which you are in doubt, medicine should be given. This is especially true when the patient has only sweated, and we will not delay on this. Third reason: when the physician helps nature, he ought to help it with the "ultimate help," meaning sufficient help, because the physician is the helper of nature. But in raging matter, there is no help that suffices except evacuation. Therefore, there is no excuse from evacuation. It should be considered that "ultimate" in Avicenna's speeches is sometimes taken for "last in time," just as it is said that in abscesses, resolution is appropriate "ultimately" <note>at the end</note>. Sometimes it is taken for a "vehement remedy" which ought not to be tried unless others have preceded it, just as we say the "ultimate remedy" is surgery with iron. In a third way, "ultimate" is taken for "sufficient"—that is, the appropriate remedy such that no other is effective except this. It is taken in this way here: because in the cure of a disease depending on raging matter, the sufficient help (which is ultimate in its sufficiency) is evacuation, so that no other suffices nor should another be tried. That no other suffices is proved when he says, "and you judge, etc." and therefore this reason holds by virtue of the preceding points, and because of them Avicenna introduces it almost as a conclusion when he says "therefore." It should be considered thirdly that the reason can be adapted to the evacuation of matter occurring before ripening because of excessive quantity: that there is no other sufficient help except to reduce that quantity. 

It is first doubted whether raging matter is hot or cold matter. It seems to be cold, because these matters are properly "raging" when they associate with the motion of windiness <note>original: "ventositas"; gas or vapors within the body</note>. As in the first book on crises, chapter 9, Galen applied this word "raging" to illnesses that move with a raging, swift motion, and specifically when there is a diverse motion in them from humors and windiness. The same is taken from Rhazes in the 16th book of the *Continens*. But windy matters are cold, namely phlegm and melancholy <note>black bile</note>, as is taken in the third book of the *Canon*, first section, in the chapter on the quality of the second symptom from the matters. To the contrary, because the fevers that arise from these matters are acute, as is understood from the aphorism: in very acute cases, use medicine early; but acute fevers are from hot matters.

It must be said that raging matter must have two conditions. One, that it is mobile from limb to limb. Second, that it is of much harm, vehemently disturbing the body's action, as is understood from the commentary on the aphorism "ripened things are to be medicated." And therefore some wise men call it "tumultuous matter," because it makes a tumult now here, now there. Others call it "arrogant" or "raging" for the known cause. This matter can be of much harm for two reasons: either because it is of a very bad quality contrary to life, as is clear in a very acute fever; or because it is of a very bad quantity contrary to life, because it has almost a poisonous nature due to its great malice tending toward universal depravity; or because, even if it is not of a bad quality, nevertheless its sudden motion to the noble or principal limbs causes it to cause bad symptoms. For example: pain and bad sensations in the limb to which it moves. For example, so that the feverish person now suffers in the head, now in the throat, now in the chest; now he feels a harm in breathing because of the motion to the lung; now he suffers in the liver, now in the stomach. And thus there is no rest for the sick person. This can happen even if the matter is not poisonous. But it is doubted: if this matter is so mobile, then the feverish person should appear sometimes with fever and sometimes without. It must be said that it is imaginable for all this matter to be moved, and then wherever it is moved, bad inflamed fumes always rise from it which reach the heart; and thus there is always fever, although with this fever there is a diverse variation. Because now it is hotter and more inflamed in one limb and now in another. And therefore it would be possible for it to be suddenly propelled to some extreme and distant limb like the foot, and the fever would suddenly cease. And just as the matter could suddenly return again, so the fever would suddenly return. In another way, we can imagine this matter staying in the veins as in a common place, and according to its soft parts, one of its fruits might fluctuate now and another fruit then, while its thicker part remains at rest. First, however, it appears that the matter consists of tumors and is not pure vapors or pure windiness; because those would be resolved by nature in such motion, or if they were not resolved by nature, they would have been resolved before, and we would not need laxative medicines. Second, it appears that such matters are hot for the most part, because being mobile from limb to limb testifies to heat, since cold immobilizes and quiets. Third, it appears that these are hot, malignant, choleric <note>related to yellow bile</note> matters, because such are those that are mobile and of a poisonous quality, which poisonousness they acquire because of the bad stench of their property. Fourth, it appears that they are not "eruginous cholera" <note>a specific, rusty-colored, highly toxic form of bile</note> because although that is poisonous, it does not have this agility and mobility, since it partakes of the earthy nature because of the extremity of its combustion. Fifth, it appears that a sudden evil because of the combustion of cholera can...

Seventh, it appears that these raging matters are rarely found, because it is rare for choleric <note>yellow bile</note> raging matters to reach such thinness, extreme mobility, and malice of quality. This does not happen except through great alienation and distance from the nature of the humors and the nature of man. Such things rarely occur in us since they have an external cause; nor is it frequently found that blood is extremely thin and highly mobile through the body, moving now to one limb and now to another; and such poisonous matter as we have described is very rarely found. Therefore, Hippocrates spoke well when he said: "Truly many things are not raging." Regarding Galen: by "windiness," he understands certain vapors that associate with warm limbs and make them mobile; indeed, in their thinness, they are very similar to vapors. Such matters are hot, or this windiness rises from other cold humors and mixes with these hot matters. 

It is debated whether raging matters can cause an abscess <note>original: "apostemare"</note> in a limb. It seems not, because they are mobile and not fixed in a limb; but that which is not fixed does not form an abscess. To the contrary is Avicenna, when he says a pleuritic abscess occurs. And Francesco da Piedimonte <note>a 14th-century physician</note>, in his commentary on the *Aphorisms*, regarding the phrase "medicate what is ripened" <note>original: "digesta medicari"</note>, wishes to argue that raging matter does not cause an abscess, and that the fear it inspires is not fear of an affliction but fear of death without an abscess. Then, when Avicenna is cited, he responds that Avicenna meant "most matter" <note>original: "materia plurima"</note> and did not mean raging matter. Let us say instead that raging matters *can* cause abscesses in limbs. Galen understood this in his commentary on the *Aphorisms* (fourth part), regarding "medication," when he commands that these raging matters be purged lest they move to the principal organs and fill them. If, therefore, he fears the noble organs being filled by raging matter, he fears them forming abscesses. Furthermore, windiness can cause abscesses in limbs; therefore these raging matters can too, because raging matters are no less corporeal than those windy matters, nor are they less mobile. Furthermore, we see an abscess in the brain occur from scorched bile <note>original: "cholera adusta"</note>, which is very hot and wicked, and which can be called raging. To the argument, it must be said that although it is mobile, it can cause a "mobile abscess"—that is, it causes an abscess now in this limb, now in that, through the path of its spreading and movement from limb to limb.

It is debated whether raging matter should be evacuated immediately on the first, second, or third day. It seems not, based on the reasons proved above: that undigested matter, whether hot or cold, should not be evacuated. First, because the healthy part will be evacuated, or the thinner part will be evacuated and the thick part will remain. Second, because it harms the process of ripening. Third, because by agitation it mixes the malignant with the good.

¶ Furthermore, regarding thin matters because they are "soaked in" <note>original: "ibibuntur"</note>, Avicenna commands they be left alone; therefore, also raging matters. To the contrary is the common opinion of physicians. ¶ It must be said that raging matter ought to be evacuated immediately, without waiting for ripening. The reason is that if it is left alone, there is danger of death, as Avicenna declared. In its evacuation, however, there is preservation from the harms that follow in other matters from lack of ripening. For raging matter, by its very "rage"—that is, its mobility—is not as unsuited for evacuation as fixed, stagnant matters. Thus Galen, in the first book of *On Crises*, chapter five, says in these illnesses (namely, those of raging matter) one must use purging medicine at their beginning, because the movement of this matter dominating the body assists the medicine, so that it easily draws them out. But whatever matters are watery and yet fixed and stagnant without being ripened at all, they do not obey purging medicine. Therefore, those three harms which Avicenna says occur in the evacuation of matter before ripening do not follow in the evacuation of raging matter before ripening. For this is evacuated as the nature of the matter desires; and the healthy part is not evacuated, nor is only the thin part evacuated (because the whole thing is thin), nor is ripening hindered (since it is not suited for ripening, nor do we wish it to ripen), nor is the malignant mixed with the good. Indeed, it is drawn out, and if any of the aforementioned occurs, it is very little; and we prefer this over letting a man die from the force of the raging matter. To the second point, it must be said that thin matters that are not mobile but lying quiet and soaked into a limb—which the physician estimates can be ripened in time without danger—should not be moved before ripening. From this it appears that the physician from the very beginning (namely, the acute stage) ought to have a powerful judgment <note>original: "potentem extimationem"</note> by which he judges whether this patient is likely to die from the rage or the quantity of the matter unless it is purged before ripening, or whether this other patient suffering from even hot matter can recover if left without evacuation.

¶ It is debated whether one who evacuates raging matter should do so "eradicatively" <term>eradicative: a complete and forceful purging intended to pull the disease out by its roots</term>. And it must be said, as is commonly stated, that it must be evacuated eradicatively with a purging and loosening drug given in a sufficient dose, provided other factors like strength, age, and similar conditions allow. The reason is that all raging matter is truly unsuited for ripening; therefore, if you leave a part behind, there is no hope that it will ripen. Furthermore, even if the remaining part is small, there is fear of death, because since it is very malignant, even a little of it can kill a man. Others have said this was Avicenna’s command when he says "therefore when..." Eradicative evacuation is the "ultimate help." And for this reason, Rhazes purges in acute cases before ripening using scammony <note>a harsh purgative resin</note>; and the physician must take care lest the purging agent, being hot and dry, causes inflammation, as noted in the 19th book of Rhazes' *Continens* and by Galen in his commentary on the *Aphorisms* regarding "In acute passions [etc]." And he does this by mixing the purging agent with cold, comforting things, as is well known. ¶ It is debated whether we can evacuate raging matter through bloodletting. It seems not, because Galen, in discussing its evacuation, always seems to name "pharmacy" <note>drugs</note>, as appears in his commentary on the *Aphorisms* and in *On Acute Diseases*, and in the phrase "medicate what is ripened," and "medicate in very acute cases." On the contrary: because for pains passing from the back to the kidneys and the hips, bloodletting is appropriate, as Hippocrates says in the sixth part of the *Aphorisms*. But this seems to be raging matter. ¶ Furthermore, in certain cases, bloodletting is commanded by Galen in his *Therapeutics*, and this can be classified as raging matter. It must be said that raging matter is spoken of in two ways: first, properly, because it is mobile and of a poisonous quality, like some very mobile bile; and these are evacuated by pharmacy. The reason is that matter which is of a very bad quality and mobile here and there cannot be blood, nor matter close to the nature of blood, nor much mixed with blood. Rather, it is distant and running outside it. Therefore, it must be evacuated not by bloodletting but by something else that draws it out by its specific property. In a second way, it could be called raging matter not strictly so, but by its mobility alone; thus some blood could be such, and perhaps it could be evacuated by bloodletting. The contradictions cease. However, a doubt would arise as to what gives it this mobility—whether it is a form within it or a vapor. And if it is a vapor, what causes the

¶ "And you should know [etc]." Here begins the second chapter, in which we evacuate before the ripenings that could occur later in the matter. First, he sets forth the case and suggests the reason. Second, he proves it (beginning at "secondly" and "and when it is postponed"). Or it can be said that it has three parts, just as he brings forward three reasons for the belly. ripening. Avicenna suggests this reason: because this bloodletting in this fever—since the matter is blood—aims at the withdrawal of blood. But when we intend to withdraw blood by bloodletting, we do not need to wait for ripening, just as we regularly wait in evacuation with drugs. For ripening is not expected except in humors other than blood; and consequently, in evacuations other than bloodletting. Therefore, one must bloodlet immediately, namely, at the very beginning of the fever. It is debated whether ripening must be awaited for bloodletting to be performed. It seems so, according to Galen in the ninth book of *Therapeutics*, chapter seven, and chapter eleven, and chapter fourteen, where he commands that bloodletting should be done without the lack of ripening that affects the belly. ¶ Furthermore, when thick humors were present, the ancients gave a digestive <note>ripening agent</note> before bloodletting, such as syrup with hyssop, as he says in the first book of the *Canon* in the chapter on bloodletting. ¶ He generally includes eye pains in his commentary on the *Aphorisms*, seventh part. And Galen, in his book *On Bloodletting* (new translation), affirms this. Furthermore, Avicenna in the chapter on bloodletting in blood-related fevers commands that excessive bloodletting be done when maturity <note>ripening</note> is present. Furthermore, blood can be faulty in its thinness or thickness; therefore, all of it must be ripened. To the contrary is Avicenna here, where he says that in "diminishing" bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia minoratiua"; a small amount to reduce volume</note> ripening need not be awaited, but in "eradicative" bloodletting, ripening must be awaited. And this seems to be taken from Avicenna's chapter on bloodletting, where he says that in blood-related fevers, excessive bloodletting should not be done from the start, but when maturity is present, let excessive bloodletting be done, because the multitude of the fever is removed at the hour of bloodletting. This statement can be brought back to a good understanding: and it is that at the beginning of fevers, in which we perform diminishing bloodletting—because there is a fault of other humors in the blood and not a fault in the blood itself—we do it without waiting for any ripening. And in blood-related venous fevers, we nonetheless bloodlet immediately and eradicatively once there is ripening, because the withdrawal of the fault is immediately prevented. Dynus <note>Dino del Garbo</note> truly said that in bloodletting done by reason of "fullness" <note>plethora</note> or the repletion of all humors proportionally in the watery blood, ripening should not be awaited. But if bloodletting is done by reason of a fault in the blood alone (which is a humor distinct from others), ripening can be awaited in that case. Let us say that these statements are conformable to Avicenna's words. They are: that in bloodletting, sometimes the "intention is the blood"—that is, we intend the withdrawal of the blood itself. Sometimes it is the "intention of other humors" besides blood. And in bloodletting, the intention is blood when the fever is from blood abounding in the veins, which exists under the form of blood. This "blood" can be understood in two ways, as Baly <note>likely Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi</note> says in the second treatise of the *Tegni*: either for the mass of all humors in the veins (which the commonality of physicians calls blood), or for the one distinct humor that is blood alone. In the first way, taking blood as the whole mass, an increase in it is an increase in all humors together proportionally. And therefore there is in this a fault of quantity alone. ¶ This could be followed by a fault of quality, as in a synochal fever <term>synochal fever: a continuous fever, often attributed to an excess of blood</term> without putrefaction, from which a synochal fever with putrefaction can arise. But taking blood in the second way, its increase is its overgrowth above the others; if this happens to occur (which perhaps it does not), as Dynus well said. I say, therefore, that if a fever arises from blood alone, faulty in quantity alone in the first way, but in the second way it could be faulty in quality, then bloodletting intends to evacuate only the blood, which alone is at fault. And because this is so, such bloodletting must be done immediately at the beginning of this fever, and ripening should not be awaited as we wait for it with purging drugs. And we declare, therefore, first what ripening is that we wait for in purging drugs: it is that when the intention of the pharmacy is to evacuate a humor having its own forms outside the blood—as in a pure choleric fever, or in pure phlegm or pure melancholy—we ought not, by regular rule, give a purging drug since the intention is the evacuation of those humors; but first we ripen the matter, and afterward we evacuate it. If it is done before proper ripening, it is by necessity, because the matter is raging or abundant, as said above. ¶ We might also say that in a drug where the intention is not those humors, but the intention is to draw them out with it, as when we give cassia from the start. But regarding bloodletting, it is the total opposite of what was said of pharmacy. Because when in bloodletting there is the withdrawal of blood alone, as in a fever from true and abundant blood (such as in a non-putrid synochal fever), bloodletting must be done immediately from the beginning; and as quickly as it can be done. And do not wait for you to ripen the matter. Avicenna proves this by three reasons: namely, that in a blood-related fever, bloodletting must be done immediately from the start. The first is: when bloodletting is for the withdrawal of an abundance of blood—which bloodletting is the "intention of blood"—ripening must not be awaited as in purging. Rather, it must be done immediately in the beginning, if in a blood-related fever the intention of the bloodletting is the withdrawal of blood and it is for the withdrawal of an abundance of blood. Therefore it should be done immediately and not deferred so that ripening might be permitted, as in purging. He takes the first proposition (in which the force of Avicenna's reason stands) as known from the fact that blood, being faulty in quantity but having the form of blood, is of itself most suited for evacuation by bloodletting; hence, when a vein is opened, it immediately runs out. Therefore, ripening must not be awaited, and this is what he says: "And you should know that bloodletting, when the intention [etc.]," is not of that type (namely, evacuation) in which it is restored—that is, to perform it, ripening should not be awaited.

¶ It is debated why blood, faulty in quantity, is so suited for evacuation, while other humors are not suited for their own evacuations in the beginning. It must be said that an increase of blood does not follow from an alien compulsion in the body, nor in its substance, as it possesses the form of true blood; and therefore it is suited for flow. But other humors distinct from blood (which the purging drug regards as distinct and separate things to be pulled out) cannot grow except with a malice of quality in the body, which is the cause of the multiplication of bad humors, or which is associated with their multiplication and follows it. For example: coldness in the overgrowth of phlegm. In this malice of quality, the humor becomes malignant and of an unsuitable substance, even though it possesses the form of a humor...

<summary>This page discusses the medical treatment of "raging matter"—violent, mobile humors that must be purged immediately to prevent death, bypassing the usual rule of waiting for humors to ripen. It also explains why bloodletting is uniquely exempt from the waiting period in cases of blood-based fevers, as blood is naturally ready for evacuation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the timing of medical interventions—specifically bloodletting—based on whether the disease-causing matter is "ripe" (digested) or still "raw" (undigested). It focuses on synocha, a type of continuous fever associated with the blood.</meta>

# Fen I Tractatus II

<column-break/>

nature. For example, phlegm <note>one of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and moisture</note> is often too viscous and therefore resistant to evacuation unless it is first prepared and "ripened" <note>original: "digeratur"; the process of medicinal or natural heat softening the humors</note>. When humors other than blood begin to cause a fever, they have acquired a "malice" through which they succumb to putrefaction and are no longer regulated by nature. This malice of quality makes their substance unsuitable, and this unsuitability is itself a form of malice. However, when blood increases in quantity while maintaining its true form, it cannot become "foreign" in its substance in a way that prevents evacuation. Therefore, the vein is naturally suited for its removal; it is its own proper path and no other.

A second doubt arises: do the statements of Avicenna <note>a 10th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook</note> conclude that this applies to putrid blood fever? It should be said that if the blood is putrid but not far removed from the form of healthy blood—as in the beginning of a putrid *synocha* <term>synocha: a continuous fever caused by an excess or fermentation of blood</term>—one should not wait for ripening. This is because the blood is naturally fit for evacuation. This putrid *synocha* is specifically the type that is close to the non-putrid variety, where a great quantity of blood begins to rot. However, if the putrid blood were far removed from the nature of true blood (such as being too thick or too thin), some ripening might be expected.

It is further doubted whether blood should be let immediately if it is multiplied alone, without other humors, as Honyer states. Here, Dynus <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous 14th-century medical commentator</note> believes that ripening should be expected because this blood is only multiplied through a malice of quality, making it of "bad substance." But Dynus doubts whether blood can ever be increased alone, and he believes it cannot. We, however, say that if it happens that only the blood increases greatly—and the bile, phlegm, and melancholy <note>the other three humors</note> do not multiply but are rather diminished—and that blood remains in its true form, then it is fit for removal by bloodletting, and ripening need not be expected.

For blood that remains in its true form does not suffer great "distemper," as Averroes <note>a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> says in the third book of his *Colliget*. When there is an excess of blood in quality, it remains so for a long time. Thus, Avicenna’s first reason is clear: bloodletting should be done immediately at the start when the intention is to remove blood. One should not wait for the ripening of the blood matter nor its evacuation; for ripening prepares for evacuation, just as one waits for the digestion of food in the stomach. Authorities like Galen <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medieval medicine</note> agree that if digestion is occurring in the stomach, bloodletting should not be performed.

Avicenna's second reason proves the previous point: since bloodletting is intended to evacuate blood, it must be done at the very beginning. ¶ The third reason is that bloodletting must be done at the start because if it is postponed, the patient might die from the onset of weakness. If the intention is to evacuate blood and it is not done at the start, later bloodletting might kill the patient by weakening their "virtue" <term>virtue: the patient's innate life force or strength</term>. These last two reasons will be explained further later.

It appears, therefore, that in bloodletting intended for blood, ripening is not expected. However, if the intention is to remove humors other than blood, bloodletting waits for ripening. This is because bloodletting is sometimes performed because other humors have "offended" the blood; the blood itself has no fault except that the other humors have infected it. In such cases, bloodletting is done so that as the corrupt blood leaves, the other humors mixed with it follow in the evacuation. Therefore, if those humors are very foreign in their substance, they will not follow the evacuation, nor will the infected blood exit well, as it has been made unsuitable by them. If the vein were opened then, only the good blood and the "spirit" <note>the vital breath or pneuma carried in the blood</note> would exhale with it. Therefore, one must prepare them to follow the blood and perform the phlebotomy afterward. This was the path taught by the ancients and also by Galen: when thick humors exist with the blood, or the blood itself is thick, it should first be "ripened" with syrup of hyssop <note>a herb used to thin and clear phlegm</note>, and then the blood should be let.

Under this consideration, Avicenna commands that at the beginning of an illness caused by humors mixed with blood, bloodletting should be omitted and performed later if necessary. Thus, in "plethoric" fever, we omit bloodletting at the start when the urine appears red and thick. But if those humors mixed with the blood are not too foreign in substance, so that there is hope they will follow through the opened vein, then we do not need ripening but perform the bloodletting immediately. It must be considered that there are degrees of mixture; a small bloodletting might be granted at the start, and as the fever proceeds and the matter is ripened and rectified, a more copious bloodletting may become appropriate. By diminishing the "antecedent cause" <term>antecedent cause: a surplus of humors in the body that feeds the localized disease</term>, the patient's strength will dominate and they will be liberated quickly. This explains Avicenna’s chapter on bloodletting: when he commands a small bloodletting at the start of a blood fever (with other humors mixed in) and a larger one as it progresses.
