Dynus weighed the difficulty of this doubt. Since this inquiry asks nothing else but whether the matter is "ripened" at the start of a *synocha* fever, he says for a final answer: it should be called neither ripened nor unripened, but "similar to ripened." He says one should not wait for sediment in the urine because, as Galen says in the *Prognostics*, sediment is that which escapes the operation of nature during the conversion of blood. Now, in a *synocha* fever without putrefaction, since there is no malice of quality in the humors, that "thing" <note>the waste matter</note> is not present. Such humors are naturally fit to nourish the body, as their only fault is their excessive quantity; therefore, in such a state, one need not wait for sediment. Dynus has good intentions in many of his sayings, though he may have explained himself poorly. ¶ We say first that it is self-evident that blood which offends only by quantity, or blood beginning to rot, is fit for evacuation by bloodletting. If it is delayed, it corrupts further and becomes less fit for removal. ¶ Second, as this blood tends toward health during the fever, it can be ripened, and its ripening will be shown in the urine by a red color and a white, cone-shaped sediment. After its appearance, nature will cause a "crisis" <note>a turning point in the disease</note> through a nosebleed or otherwise. But where it is fatal, a black sediment might appear unless suffocation happens first.

The solution to the root of the question—whether the matter is ripened at the start of a blood fever (*synocha*)—is this: it should be called "ripened" with a ripening sufficient for evacuation by bloodletting, and no other is so sufficient if the *synocha* is true and pure. But it is not yet ripened with the ripening it will have in its later stages. But then it is doubted whether, at the start of this *synocha*, the urine shows ripening through any "cloud" or "hypostasis" <term>hypostasis: the sediment or suspension in urine used for diagnosis</term>. It should be said that we have nothing written on this by famous authors. Avicenna does not list urine signs in his chapter on *synocha*. Galen, in his ninth book on therapeutics, considered the urine in the veins of those with non-putrid *synocha* and perceived that its substance and color did not differ much from the natural state. From this, we might suspect it had no sign of ripening, which is shown mostly in the sediment. In another youth with a putrid fever, he saw signs of putrefaction in the urine and other things. From this, one might argue there was no sediment because when putrefaction begins, ripening cannot appear.

¶ We say that all signs, whether in the urine or the pulse, which demonstrate that the offending humor is blood, are signs of this ripening. I say secondly that the sediment created by the action of nature upon the blood matter—since the action begins at the start of the fever—does not appear at the very beginning; otherwise, it would not be the "beginning," just as in other fevers. But it seems this can be resolved: since this blood is benign and nature acted upon it before the fever, it is possible that by the time the fever starts, nature has completed that action, and thus a white sediment exits with the urine at the very start. This would be a place for investigation: whether this is possible. The possibility is confirmed by the benignity of the humor, the continuous action of the veins on this blood, and the nature of the fever itself, which has changed the body very little at its start.

It is doubted second whether nature waits for ripening in the blood and then expels it; if so, art <note>the physician's skill</note> should do the same. Furthermore, if the blood is ripened at the very start, why does nature not expel it? It should be said that nature acts without intellect; therefore, it tries to ripen matter that does not stimulate it and then expels it. If nature used reason and said, "this blood is ready to flow and fit for evacuation, and if it stays longer it will kill the patient or become unfit," then it would expel it immediately. Therefore, a physician, stimulated by the excessive quantity of blood at the start, performs the evacuation without waiting for further ripening than what is present at the beginning. It appears, therefore, that bloodletting in a true *synocha* fever without putrefaction is done before the future ripening of the later stages, but not before ripening sufficient for evacuation.

Regarding the contrary arguments: to the first, it should be said that this case is an exception to the regular rule because this evacuation occurs before the ripening that would come if the matter were left to ripen. To the second, Avicenna does not mean that the sediment made from the alteration of blood starting a fever is "praiseworthy" <note>i.e., a good diagnostic sign</note> at the very start. To the third, it should be said that it has four distinct times or stages, but they are not distinguished by "rawness" and "ripeness" in the same way. The matter is "raw" compared to what it will become, but not "raw" in respect to its fitness for bloodletting.

But a doubt remains: Avicenna's fourth argument against Rhazes <note>Al-Razi, a 9th-century physician</note> does not seem to hold. He argues that when nature liberates a patient from a blood fever, it waits for a ripening that blood fevers do not have at the start; therefore, the physician should do the same. There are many ways to answer this, but I say nature sometimes does not wait, but moves a great hemorrhage <note>original: "emorafagiā"</note> and suddenly liberates a true *synocha* without putridity. It does not act this way in other fevers. This is a great doubt with much to be discussed, which I omit.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ "And when bloodletting is postponed." This is the second reason proving the main conclusion: that bloodletting should occur at the start of a true blood fever. The reason is that when it is postponed, it no longer fulfills its intention. It is doubted whether, if bloodletting was not done at the start, it is still the intention. It seems so, because Avicenna and Galen say that bloodletting should be done whenever there is a necessity for it, whether at the start or on the fortieth day. To the contrary, Avicenna says here that some unrefined physicians said that when bloodletting must be done at the start because of "raging matter" <note>materia furiosa</note> and it is not done, it cannot be done later because the raging matter might kill the patient. Dynus says this can be understood regarding "diminishing bloodletting" <note>bloodletting intended to reduce overall volume</note>, which is needed at the start when the patient's strength is stronger and before distressing symptoms have appeared. Later, it cannot be done properly in diseases where we wait for a "crisis," because we need the strength of the patient, and thus the blood must be saved like a "treasure."

¶ We say that this discussion concerns bloodletting where the intention is the blood itself, as in *synocha* fever. When it is postponed, the original intention is lost. At the start, the intention was to remove blood that still had its true form and was little changed; therefore, it could be done copiously. but after the start, the blood is corrupted and more distant from its true form. Therefore, bloodletting cannot be as copious as at the start, and thus it does not fulfill its intention—neither in its end nor its utility. You should not, therefore, have postponed it. But the contradictions cease here: for at whatever time I see a necessity for bloodletting...

<summary>This page debates the timing of bloodletting in continuous fevers (synocha), arguing that when the blood is the primary cause and remains in its true form, evacuation should be immediate rather than waiting for the humors to "ripen." It contrasts the physician's rational intervention with nature's non-intellectual process of ripening matter before expulsion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the timing of medical evacuations. It specifically addresses when a physician should intervene with bloodletting or purgatives at the very beginning of a disease, rather than waiting for the "matter" (the humors causing the illness) to ripen or "digest" through the body's natural heat.</meta>

# Book IV

...perform bloodletting, <note>original: "phlomīa"</note> which I ought to do at the beginning. Its purpose is the drawing out of blood from those who are only slightly "sinning" <note>the text uses "peccantiu" to describe humors that have become imbalanced or "corrupt"</note> in their humors. If it is postponed, it is not as useful; indeed, it perhaps kills, because the patient is already weakened by the severity of the illness, having lost a great help by waiting. And therefore, bloodletting can add such weakness that the patient dies from it. However, this is not a certainty; for this reason, he said "perhaps." ¶ And similarly for the same reason. Some have spoken of this case as being about the evacuation of "furious" <note>highly toxic or rapidly progressing</note> matter, but Avicenna had already spoken of this. <margin>Against Dinus</margin> Some, like Dinus <note>Dinus del Garbo, a famous 14th-century medical commentator</note>, seem to feel in part that this case is a continuation of the preceding one. Yet, in another way, it differs from the case above: in that it is understood that digested matter should be evacuated. This, therefore, ought not to occur unless nature itself is failing to evacuate it. On the other hand, let us say that this is a third case, in which he proves that in times of necessity, we must not wait for digestion; rather, we must evacuate at the beginning, even if the matter is raw. <margin>Evacuation at the beginning</margin> ¶ In the first case, he sets out the situation; in the second, he explains it where he says "at the state." <margin>The Case</margin> The case is this: someone suffers from a fever caused by such a quantity of matter that, because it is so excessive, you fear nature will be overcome. For example, there is a phlegmatic fever <note>caused by an excess of the cold/moist humor, phlegm</note> of such great abundance that there is no hope the matter can be digested because of its superfluous multitude, and therefore the patient will die. Therefore, immediately at the beginning, you must evacuate and not wait for digestion. And this is what he means: "if you fear the victory of the humor," namely, because of its sheer quantity. <margin>Consideration</margin> The most necessary caution is evacuation, which diminishes that humor. And consider that he said "humor," and by this, he means the victory of humors other than blood. For already in the preceding case, he spoke of a superfluous multitude of blood which was to be evacuated immediately by bloodletting; here, therefore, it was appropriate to say that when a humor other than blood is exuberant, evacuation must be done immediately. And he says it is so. It must be considered that he specified the time in which this evacuation must occur: in the beginning, even if it is not digested. And this is what he says: ¶ "if it is not digested, do not move it etc." <note>a common medical aphorism: do not stir up undigested humors unless absolutely necessary</note>, meaning evacuate at the start, even if it is not digested. ¶ It must be considered that we have three cases so far in which we evacuate immediately from the beginning and do not wait for the matter to be further digested. The first case is if the matter is "furious." The second case is if the matter is blood remaining in the form of blood, but "sinning" in quantity alone. And in these two cases, we evacuate copiously: in the first case with medicine, and in the second with bloodletting. In the second case, the matter is considered digested, although in the first case, the matter might in some way be called digested because furious matter has a certain readiness for evacuation. The third case is when any humor other than blood is of a superfluous quantity, as in choleric, phlegmatic, or melancholic fevers. Whence we do not hope the humor can be digested unless medicine diminishes it. And this evacuation is "minorative" <note>meant to reduce the volume rather than totally purge the body</note>, and the humor that is drawn out is not digested, but the digestion it will have is similar to that which remains. <margin>Doubt</margin> It is doubted whether, when the matter is still raw at the start of a fever, one can give a laxative <note>original: "farmacuz solutiuū"</note> medicine. It seems not, for three reasons which Avicenna assigns above. <margin>Galen against Avicenna and Hippocrates</margin> ¶ Also, Hippocrates said only digested things should be treated with medicine. ¶ In the fourth book of *Acute Diseases*, he says how those suffering from phlegm in the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen, under the ribs</note> should be treated. On the contrary, here are Avicenna and Hippocrates in the second part of the *Aphorisms* when he said: "In the beginning of diseases..." For that is the aphorism he places here. <margin>Note here many opinions of physicians on evacuation at the beginning</margin> Certain presumptuous physicians, in putrid fevers, immediately from the beginning give a laxative syrup, believing they are following the precept of Avicenna in the chapter on phlegmatic fever; however, as will appear there, they do not follow Avicenna, though they operate very presumptuously. For evacuation with a laxative medicine at the beginning of putrid fevers is not the rule, except when forced by necessity; therefore, it should not be done in all cases or every day. ¶ Likewise, through this, an evacuation performed... occurs on the "critical days." <note>the days on which a disease was expected to reach its turning point</note> Some others are the very worst, opposite to the former: they would never give a laxative medicine at the beginning of any putrid fever; indeed, it seems to them a great thing if they give pure pulp of cassia <note>a mild laxative derived from the seeds of the Cassia fistula tree</note>, following Hippocrates, who said that only digested things should be treated with medicine. And what I wonder at more is that the Commentator <note>likely Averroes or another major scholar</note>, a man of much science, did not dare to purge at the beginning of fevers except with clysters <note>enemas</note> and light medicines; by light ones, he means cassia and the like, as appears in the third tractate of the *Tegni*. <margin>Solution to these opinions</margin> To all these, let us say that putrid fevers either occur with an abscess <term>abscess: here "apostemate," meaning an internal swelling or localized inflammation</term> or without an abscess. And let us speak briefly of fevers with abscesses. Because the flow of matter to the site of an abscess is mostly with blood, we therefore mostly perform bloodletting at the beginning. If, however, there is a flow of other matters whose removal cannot be done by bloodletting, <margin>Note the opinion of Avicenna</margin> let us say that at the beginning of these abscesses, we can use evacuating medicines by resolving them, in which there is the power to evacuate the matter that was flowing—that which is in the course or flux—but not the matter which is already fixed in the part. The reason for the first is: that matter which is flowing ought to be diverted; and as is presupposed, this diversion cannot be done by bloodletting. Therefore, medicine must be used. Namely, because it is a humor other than blood that flows, and with this, it is of an exceedingly superfluous quantity. Whence, unless it is diminished, the abscess will become so large that the patient will die; it is therefore necessary for a medicine to diminish the matter and divert it. Thus Galen advises in the 13th book of *Therapeutics* in the chapter on abscesses, and thus Avicenna generally commands in the first book. When he said: the matter of hidden abscesses is to be diminished by bloodletting, or by loosening the bowels, etc. <margin>In abscesses, evacuation must be done at the start</margin> ¶ And although this case is taken from the nature of an abscess, yet with this, the physician must consider the nature of the part affected by the abscess; if he gives medicine to divert and diminish the matter, it must be such that it does not move toward those parts. Therefore, in abscesses of the intestines and the anus, a laxative medicine would not be good; rather, it would be necessary to diminish the matter by vomiting. And you may see this in Galen's 13th book of *Therapeutics*. This evacuation with medicine at the beginning of abscesses is done for the sake of the matter that is flowing or ready to flow, which we intend to diminish and divert. But the matter of the abscess that is already resting in the limb, or wedged into it, we ought not to move with medicine; for such matter, by the very fact that it is resting, is unfit for motion. And therefore, attempting to draw it out with medicine disturbs it and causes it to settle in healthy places. <margin>Against the Conciliator</margin> The Conciliator <note>Peter of Abano, known as "Conciliator"</note> gives an example: that doing this is as if someone tried to uproot a tree from the earth before separating the roots from the sides. And Avicenna, with Hippocrates, stated the same opinion in the first book, when he said: "But when the humor is contained in one place, etc." But it is a doubt how I can give a medicine that diverts and diminishes the flowing matter by evacuating it, yet does not evacuate the matter that is already in the abscess. Furthermore, such medicines sometimes liberate the patient on the day the abscess begins; as Galen says in the 13th book of *Therapeutics*: "Consider how some of those who began to have inflammations in the eyes were cured in one day by purging through the lower bowels." Furthermore, just as it is possible for the flowing matter to be so much that corruption of the limb or rupture of the abscess is feared before maturation, so it is possible for the matter staying in the part to be of such a kind and quantity that these things are feared. Furthermore, in external abscesses, when the matter staying in the part is excessive and suffocating, we diminish it by scarification <note>making small incisions in the skin</note>, not waiting for maturation, as is understood in the first book; why then should we not do the same in internal abscesses with medicine, taking what is in the part of the matter? It should be said that it is manifest in itself that matter which is flowing and ready to flow at the beginning of internal and external abscesses is considered to need reduction and diversion through medicine, though more frequently through bloodletting. It would also be manifest that these matters, by the very fact that they are flowing, are somewhat more fit so that by the violence of the medicine they are directed toward the medicine and the places of evacuation. It is also manifest that matter which rests in a limb is not so fit for movement unless it matures. ¶ What are those matters that rest in an abscessed limb? They are those that were once in flux, but by some delay are now compacted together and settled in their substance. And when they are thus, they are not obedient to medicine. Moreover, they are further removed from the paths through which the medicine must lead them. From the first judgment, therefore, the physician estimates that the matters of abscesses resting in the swelling are unfit for evacuation by medicine. But the matters running and ready to run are more fit. And when the physician stands upon this judgment and wishes to give a laxative medicine—which evacuates by diminishing and diverting and does not agitate the matter that is resting in the part—he must by his good estimation compose a medicine of such power. And he does this himself by knowing the laxatives that evacuate from a distance, like colocynth, hermodactyls, etc., guarding himself from them so as not to mix in a great quantity those medicines that carry the treatment to those specific sites, and avoiding the mixing

<column-break/>

of them. And using medicines whose operation is around the common sites of the veins, like rhubarb and turbith <note>a root used as a purgative</note> in their writing or scent; not by their own vigor through ginger. But whether laxative medicines should be given after the matters resting in the abscesses of internal limbs are matured, we shall not discuss here. But you will learn that Hippocrates, in this evacuation, used hellebore and *sellichino* <note>possibly a regional or corrupt term for a specific plant like scammony</note>, which are medicines that evacuate from a distance, etc. It should be said that perhaps other medicines were not known to Hippocrates, and we ought to believe that he used them in a small quantity and with the necessary comfort. And the diversity of people regarding the intake of medicines in the time of Hippocrates and the past time is a great diversity, as Avicenna says in the fourth book of the *Canon*. To the second point, it should be said that such liberation occurs because that which is in the part is resolved by nature, since that which flows in is not multiplied. Or it should be said that it sometimes happens that the matter in an abscess—namely, the kind fit for evacuation—obeys the movement of the medicines just like that which flows. Hippocrates, therefore, when he said that healthy places are destroyed by evacuation performed with medicine at the beginning of abscesses, meant when those matters are resting and are unfit for motion. And the physician, by his estimative judgment, has to judge them to be unfit unless they mature, and he has to judge those that are in flux to be more ready. To the third point, it should be said that you could posit a case where nothing can be done, as in one where the physician can perform no good. In such a case, the patient necessarily dies. The physician, therefore, in that case, can balance his judgment: which is more dangerous—to agitate the matter existing in the part wishing to diminish it with this agitation, or to leave the matter and evacuate nothing of it, even though there is suspicion of the corruption of the limb because of the multitude that remains? All this is in the head of the physician. To the fourth, it should be said that it is safer to diminish by... <note>unclear: "alpeliair̃"</note> the matters of abscesses than to give medicines for those resting in the internal limbs. The physician must therefore use prior deliberation and balancing; for few things are to be given concerning purging with medicine in the first stage of fevers with abscesses. You will find many particulars written by us in the chapter on frenzy, and the chapter on squinancy <note>tonsillitis or peritonsillar abscess</note> and pneumonia, and on abscesses of the stomach, and on abscesses of the liver. <margin>In putrid fevers, a laxative should not be given</margin> ¶ If, however, the putrid fever is without an abscess, then regularly one should not give a laxative medicine at the beginning, as it says above: hot or raw and undigested matter should not be evacuated. Yet we evacuate if compelled. But that which presumptuous physicians do... we have already experienced. <margin>Why a laxative should not be given at the start</margin> Or in cases of superfluous quantity of matter, we say this is manifest: that in the first stage of hot, phlegmatic, and melancholic fevers, the physician sees that the matter is not much; indeed, it is of such a quantity that he judges nature can process it until the "state" <note>the peak of the illness</note>. And the physician knows that the power of the patient's virtue can sustain itself, either alone or with the help of art, with such small matter. Since he can trust in its successive digestion, then in no way should he give a laxative medicine at the start, because the patient will be saved without it. And this medicine, by agitating the matter, could do more harm than good for the reasons written above. <margin>¶ If however the matter is much, it should be given</margin> But if the physician sees at the beginning of said fevers a superfluous quantity of matter and judges that with such a quantity the patient's strength will not reach the state by digesting it—indeed, foul putrefaction will be added to the matter and the patient will die—then the physician judges that if the matter were of a smaller quantity (for example, one ounce less), the virtue of the patient could overcome it by digesting it successively. Then the physician must necessarily give a laxative medicine to diminish that matter. <margin>Authority of Rhazes</margin> And this is what Rhazes <note>9th-century Persian physician</note> taught us in the 5th book of the *Continens* when he said by his authority: "You must not wait for digestion in a quartan, tertian, or quotidian fever <note>fevers categorized by the frequency of their cycles</note>, but evacuate the body if the matter is much. If it is little, we must not evacuate at all." And he adds: "If the humor is obedient, let us evacuate it, so that we may digest the residue afterward." And this is how Galen understood it in his commentary on the aphorism <margin>Galen in his commentary on the Aphorisms</margin> "In the beginning of diseases, etc." where he wants that if the disease is... and we see a place for strong medicine, we should do it. Indeed, such a strong medicine is sometimes a laxative. Galen therefore wants a purging to be done with strong medicine sometimes at the beginning of a fever, so that the residue, made smaller, can be better digested by nature. And thus Avicenna in his specific chapters... as will appear in all those. For in this our province and in modern times, men are found to be vehemently replete <note>over-full of humors</note> because of the multitude of food and drink and disordered lifestyles. Therefore, much utility has been found among bold practitioners in evacuation performed at the beginning of these putrid fevers. Some generally purge at the beginning with an evacuating medicine; we, however, evacuate some at the beginning and omit others, according to the given case. The solution to the contrary points: when evacuation of raw matter was prohibited by Hippocrates, <margin>A certain solution to the doubt about putrid fevers</margin> it is understood as a regular rule, not one of necessity. For we are compelled sometimes to evacuate without waiting for digestion. Or it is understood "eradicatively" <note>a total purging of the cause</note> unless the matter is furious; yet we can diminish it from the beginning. And therefore, the words of Hippocrates in the fourth book of *Acute Diseases* can be explained thus: that at the beginning, a total, eradicating medicine should not be given to those with pleurisy and hypochondriac issues, though the matter may be diminished, whether it is flowing or ready to flow. And this solution is more manifest to the community of physicians and more acceptable. ¶ Regarding whether a resolving medicine can be given at the start of abscesses of internal limbs: it should be said that it can be given to diminish if the matter is very much and you fear its victory because of the multitude. But to eradicate, a loosening medicine should not be given, unless perhaps the matter were furious. To the reasons given that those three cases assigned above by Avicenna can be brought into this minorative evacuation: it should be said that we prefer these three harms to the harm of death. And we hope that they will be lessened by giving the medicine that will evacuate that bad humor. And thus those three harms will become fewer from this. <margin>Evacuation should be done at the start or during the increase</margin> Secondly, it is doubted whether it is better to perform this evacuation at the beginning or during the "increase" <note>the *augmentum*, the phase where symptoms worsen</note>: as in the increase some matter might be ripe, or the matter could receive some digestion by being diminished. For there is a succession in the digestion of these matters according to the intensive degree of digestion. On the contrary is Hippocrates when he said in the aphorism: "In the beginning of diseases, etc." teaching nothing about the increase. On the contrary also is Avicenna here, who, as if to express his intention well, said "move in the beginning." Because he did not mean "do not move in the increase," but said "do not move except in the beginning." Let us say it is manifest in itself that the physician, when he has judged the matter to be very much in the very beginning of the fevers—whence he fears its victory over nature—should resolve in his soul to give laxative medicine before the "state," because at the state, the patient could not survive. Under this judgment, the physician can have two other mutual judgments: in one of which, with the signs at a different time, he must give this medicine. For the judgment is that the matter is of such great plurality and the disease of such great malice that no digestion can begin in the matter. Rather, corruption and black urine will begin, and then there will be an increase of the disease and death. And then the physician in that time of the beginning should give laxative medicine and not unless in the beginning, because then the patient's strength is stronger. When it has proceeded to a malignant increase, the strength is more weakened and the matter is more foul. And thus he is to be left to the prognosis: that he will die before you can help by diminishing the matter with laxative medicine. And in this way, it is necessary that we use it at the beginning of apoplexy, at least through very sharp clysters, if they cannot be given in a drink; however, they mix laxatives for this with subtleties, as appears in the 7th book of the *Colliget*. And if you should say to me: if I give medicine at the beginning of apoplexy or a fever whose abscess is internal, I move the matter. I see that if you posit a case to me where the patient is endangered at every turn, you should do nothing, as in apoplexy certain authors command that nothing be done in the beginning; whence Galen spoke to this intention...

It outlines specific exceptions where immediate bloodletting or purging is necessary to save a patient from being overwhelmed by a "multitude" of corrupt matter, particularly in fevers and internal abscesses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the timing of medical interventions, focusing on the Hippocratic aphorism regarding treatment at the onset of a disease. It debates whether to intervene immediately in "furious" cases or wait for the "digestion" (ripening) of the humors.</meta>

# Section I, Treatise II

In the aphorism <note>original: "affo."</note> "At the onset of diseases..." <note>Hippocrates, Aphorisms 2.19: "In the beginning of diseases, if any move is to be made, move it..."</note> etc., it is said that those about to die ought not to be medicated, but their future state should be predicted to them. But if there were some possible case in which someone with a fever could be helped more than harmed by a medicine given at the beginning, the most prudent physician must strive to recognize it, even if nature dictates that the person must die. Avicenna proceeded here with this estimative judgment. For when a great amount of matter <note>the "humors" or fluids causing the illness</note> was imagined to be overcoming the body's strength <note>original: "virtute"</note>, he did not want an evacuation to take place except at the beginning. But you might say: "Let us suppose there is a bad increase in the bubbling of the fever, for example, with some blackness or lividity of the urine." Could one still purge then?

It must be said that Avicenna's response is sufficient for the one asking: that an error of over-caution is safer. For it would be more secure to have purged at the beginning, not so much because of a lack of strength, but because the matter was less corrupt at its inception. Secondly, Avicenna says that if you believe the patient will die, you should leave a prognosis <note>a prediction of the outcome</note>; he spoke with this intention in the commentary on the aforementioned aphorism. But if, by your estimation, there is any hope of recovering life through the help of evacuation, then do it. For not everyone in whom lividity or blackness of urine begins will necessarily die, as we have to declare in the second book of this work. Another estimative judgment is that although this matter is abundant and its digestion <note>the process of the body "ripening" the humors for expulsion</note> is not to be hoped for except bit by bit, it is at the beginning entirely crude and resistant to being moved; yet I hope that in time the matter will be prepared somewhat for evacuation—for example, in the space of three days. Then I would begin to give some "minorative" <note>a mild laxative or treatment to slightly reduce the volume of humors</note> without waiting for full digestion. Indeed, some hidden digestion suffices for me, such as the thickening of the urine in a certain phlegmatic fever, where perhaps the heat of putrefaction can bring about that adaptation of the matter, which is its division into deeper parts. Then, by reducing it with turbith <note>original: "turbit," a purgative root</note>, I would do this several times if it seems right to me. Avicenna proceeded in this way and with this estimative judgment in the cure of phlegmatic fever, as will appear later. Averroes, in the 7th book of the *Colliget*, brings an example of this regarding the carrying of a heavy load by dividing it into parts. It is possible that one may proceed with these two estimative judgments in a single fever. And this settles the question of Mundinus of Forlì <note>original: "Mundini de foro iulii," a famous anatomist and professor</note>, who asks whether a purgative medicine is appropriate for thickened urine after its thinning. It must be said that it can be more appropriate than when it remains thin, because that thickening is a sign of some digestion—that is, some preparation—even if the feverish heat produced it. Regarding this, look at the beginning of the chapter on the cure of phlegmatic fever. <margin>a</margin> A third doubt arises: with what medicine should we perform these minorative evacuations? It must be said: with a medicine that has a loosening effect. The reason is that such a reduction is intended for the humor that is in the way. Since it is a great quantity of a dominant humor, it must be reduced to a smaller quantity by cutting away a part of it. But a part of the bile <note>original: "cholere"</note> cannot be cut away except by a medicine appropriated to it, nor can a part of the phlegm, nor a part of the black bile <note>original: "melancolie"</note>. And so, with this intention, at the start of bilious fevers, Rhazes <note>original: "ras̄."</note> purges with scammony <note>original: "scamonea," a harsh purgative</note>; and Avicenna concedes this in the chapter on the cure of tertian fever when he says "unless in the manner we have described." And in phlegmatic fever, he purges with turbith, and in melancholic fever with epithyme <note>original: "epitimo," dodder of thyme</note> or lapis lazuli. Let him remain silent, therefore, who wishes to perform specific minorations with cassia or syrup of violets. If it is said that these draw out bile and phlegm, it must be said that they do so when they are in common places like the stomach and intestines. But if you wish to draw matter from the veins and remote parts, choosing them, you must do this with loosening medicines.

<margin>b</margin> **At the peak** <note>original: "Apud statū"</note> etc. Avicenna had said above that undigested matter should not be evacuated. From this, it was inferred that digested matter could be evacuated. He wants to clarify when we can evacuate digested matter. And he gives three rules <note>original: "can̄."</note> for this. The first is that you should wait until digestion is complete. In the beginning of the "state" <note>the *status* or peak of the illness</note> you are not prepared to evacuate, but as the state proceeds, once the matter is perfectly conquered by digestion. And this is what he means by "at the peak"—that is, when the peak arrives, do not move anything (namely, with a loosening medicine) until nature conquers and digests. That is, until it conquers through complete digestion; for the total completion of digestion occurs during the progress of the peak. But you might say: in the peak, the matter is digested, as it is in the "increase" <note>the stage where symptoms worsen</note>; but in the increase, we can move something by evacuating it part by part, just as we do in phlegmatic fever. Therefore, in the peak, we can move some part, and afterwards the remaining part, even if it is not in the full completion of digestion. It must be said that if Avicenna is speaking of the peak in terms of its symptoms <note>original: "accid̄tia"</note>, in which the difficulty of symptoms occurs, then it is manifest that we evacuate more safely in the increase than in the peak. This all goes back to the aphorism of Hippocrates: "At the onset of diseases..." etc., and that other one: "Around the beginnings and ends, all..." etc. But this discourse is universal in all things. For in the peak, regarding digestion, the difficulty of symptoms does not occur in all fevers, and in some, it is not something to be worried about. And therefore let us say that Avicenna directs his speech to the well-organized and prudent physician who guides the sick person even to the peak with little matter—whether it was little to begin with or whether he made it little—and judges that it can be joined to the body's strength and perfectly digested. Nothing forces him to be preempted in evacuation. And therefore he allows that matter to be most perfectly digested before it is evacuated; nor indeed, after it is most perfectly digested, does he evacuate it unless nature fails in the evacuation. And therefore Avicenna sets down the second rule, saying:

<margin>c</margin> **Move it at the hour of its movement**—that is, at the hour of most perfect digestion. "If nature itself does not move," as if Avicenna were saying: "If you judged that nature could digest this matter by itself or with your help, let it be perfectly digested." And because nature is accustomed to evacuate after perfect digestion, it is to be believed that it will evacuate. But if, due to sluggishness or blockage of the senses or any other cause, it is not evacuated, you evacuate it at that hour of perfect digestion; for that is its proper hour, when it acts naturally. Therefore he does not command that you evacuate at the hour of the crisis <note>original: "cris̄," the turning point of the disease</note> or on the critical day, as some have been accustomed to do. Hence they transposed the third rule, saying "and if nature itself does not move at the hour of its movement," namely, at the hour of the crisis, that is, on the critical day, then you move it. But it is not expedient to transpose the third rule thus. If you know that the hour of nature's movement is twofold: one is the hour of perfect digestion, and at this hour you should move it, for nature does so unless hindered by some cause. The other is the hour of the crisis, and at this hour you should not move it. That matter is sometimes undigested and yet nature expels it appears from Galen in the third book of *On Crises*, chapter 1, and in the second section of this book in the chapter on signs signifying a bad crisis. We do not place the causes of omission here, but we will place them

<column-break/>

in the last chapter of the second section of this fourth book, where it must be disputed whether a physician can do anything on the day of the crisis, and what, and how; however, this is not found here in Avicenna. On the day of the crisis, you should do something regarding evacuation, but if nature does not perform the evacuation of the crisis on its due critical day, you evacuate afterwards on a non-critical day. Therefore the third rule follows: "If it moves or has moved, then leave it alone," because nature has done its work, and leave its operation alone because it is already acting. Similarly, if it is about to act, leave it without food, and leave its operation without evacuation. This is therefore the aphorism of Hippocrates: "Those whose crisis occurs..." etc.
<insert>
And all that we have prolonged in this aphorism, we leave to the second section of this fourth book, to be said with His help.
</insert>

<insert>
It is not in its proper hour, just as necessary feeding is not in its proper hour. And the proportion of that evacuation to stopping the malice of the matter is like the proportion of that feeding to preventing the strength from falling. And when therefore he performs the evacuation, then consider the hour of the interval <note>between fever fits</note>, or the hour of the time itself, or the coldest hour which is in the day. And do not evacuate through a flux of the belly on the day of the period <note>the day the fever is expected to return</note>. Nor perform bloodletting. And do not act with the evacuation of art against the direction of nature's evacuation. And do not diminish.
</insert>

<margin>c</margin> **And this is that** here Avicenna confirms the words of the authority Hippocrates in the aphorism "digested things are to be medicated." It must be considered that three rules are set down, which are three cases in which it is necessary to evacuate from the beginning without waiting for digestion. <margin>First</margin> The first case is when the matter is truly "furious" <note>violent or toxic</note>, because it moves from member to member, etc. <margin>Second</margin> The second case is when bloodletting <note>original: "phlobotomia"</note> is indicated, which is the intention of the blood. The third case is when the victory of the humor is feared because of its great quantity. And in all these cases, the matter can be called "furious"; yet in truth, it would be better if the first and third cases were understood, as appears from what he said. <margin>d</margin> "Let a loosening medicine be administered," etc. He adds: "At the beginning, however, it should not be administered," namely, the loosening medicine, "unless the disease be furious"—that is, because of its mobility and malice, as the first case says, and because of a great quantity that can be reduced by pharmacy, as the third case says. For although the very great quantity of blood at the beginning, of which the second case speaks, could be called "furious" matter, yet we do not evacuate it irregularly and manifestly causing harm while wishing to choose the lesser harm; rather, we evacuate it regularly and causing almost no harm, except when we lead the patient to fainting <note>original: "sincopi"</note>. Similarly, if we evacuate it with a loosening medicine; hence here Avicenna was pleased to explain the aphorism just as Hippocrates understood it. Therefore the confirmation of the regular rule and the exception of the Hippocratic aphorism appears. For he says not to evacuate undigested matter in heat or cold is to say that digested things are to be medicated; and to move what is not crude; and it is said "unless because of necessity" is to say "unless the matter be furious." This, however, which Hippocrates said—"unless the matter be furious"—is that which was said in the first case: when the matter is mobile or changeable from member to member, etc. That is what was said in the third case: if you fear the victory of the humor, namely, because of its great quantity. One might doubt because the Moors <note>referring to Islamic medical authorities like Rhazes or Avicenna himself</note> place another mode of the matter's furiousness, namely, by reason of the nobility of the part, such as the matter of the blood. It must be said that some of our predecessors placed two modes of the furiousness of matters: first, by reason of mobility, malice, or poisonousness, such as they say exists in an anthrax; second, by reason of the quantity of the matter, as in a *synocha* <note>a continuous fever</note> and in any illness of much matter; third, by the importance of the organ <note>original: "principatus membri"</note>, as in phrenitis—that is, the accident of pain, as in colic—and by reason of the mobility of hindered action, as in "ignance" <note>likely a term for loss of consciousness or delirium</note>. We say that Avicenna ought not here to follow the cure of putrid fevers according to all the diversity of particular patients, because that belongs to the third book and the discourse on phrenitis, ignance, and colic. And therefore he spoke of these two or three types of furiousness.
<margin>d</margin> **And** perhaps it is not, etc. He said this because generally, for the most part, the matters taken are not furious; yet in the specific constitution of some years—indeed, in many years and climates—many furious matters can be found in one of the three or two ways described by Avicenna.

<margin>e</margin> **And such is.** Here he proves the statements by a reason taken from a similarity, and he argues thus: just as we sometimes feed at an inconvenient hour and against the rule of regular feeding, and we do this so that we may prevent the strength from falling—as when, at the hour of the "status," we give food, such as wine and meat, during symptoms that dissolve the strength—so we evacuate with a loosening medicine at the hour of the beginning when the matter is not digested, which hour is not the regular hour of evacuation. And we do this so that we may cause the malice of the matter to cease, which malice is that which can be called furiousness—namely, the furiousness of malice and mobility, and the furiousness of superfluous quantity, as has been said. And it appears from these words that Avicenna explains the Hippocratic aphorism more generally than Galen does, although Galen's discourse can also be explained concerning the other two types of furiousness, on which we do not labor at present.

<margin>f</margin> **When therefore** he exercises, etc. From the preceding rules, it is clear that we can evacuate digested matter when nature does not evacuate it; and we can evacuate undigested matter when it is furious; and when in bloodletting there is an "intention" of blood <note>a clinical reason to draw it</note>, then we ought to do it. Here Avicenna places certain rules which are less general than the aforesaid. And the evacuation to be performed is rectified. First, he places rules common to bloodletting and pharmacy. Secondly, rules proper to each of those evacuations—namely, here second: "And do not diminish." The first is in three parts, as he places three rules. The first rule is about the specific hour of evacuation, whether it be by pharmacy or bloodletting. And it is that you should choose the hour of interpolation—that is, the hour in which there is no fever, if it is an intermittent fever; or the hour of the time if it is a proportional continuous fever; or the more remiss hour—that is, in which some remission of the heat is felt, as in a "concluded" fever. Hence, although blood-fever does not have exacerbations of itself, yet it has some remission in the hour of the coldness of the air, namely, in the morning, as is taken from the intention of Isaac's *On Fevers*, book 5; and then bloodletting should be performed regularly. We disputed this above. The second rule follows from that: if, indeed, one ought to choose the hours aforesaid, it is necessary that you do not evacuate nor perform bloodletting on the day of the paroxysm—that is, in the state of the paroxysm. And in truth, that rule proves the first one, and all this was declared above. The third rule is that you should not evacuate through an evacuation opposite to the part through which nature evacuates. He follows the eleventh aphorism: "Where nature tends, there one must lead," etc. And this is verified in evacuation through pharmacy: for instance, if nature tends toward the belly, do not provoke vomiting; and in evacuation through bloodletting: for instance, if nature evacuates blood through the menses, do not perform bloodletting from the arm unless another intention and another necessity should concur; and thus it is verified in other evacuations.

<margin>g</margin> **And not.** Here are placed special rules according to each evacuation: first in evacuation by pharmacy, second by bloodletting, where it says "second and counsel." The first is in two parts, as he places two main rules. There the second: "And know." The first is in two parts: first he places one main rule. The second follows: "and all." The first rule is that you should not give a loosening medicine that brings about the condition of the "movement"—that is, the return of the period, meaning the paroxysm. For there are loosening medicines that dispose the body toward the return of the paroxysm, such as scammony, and therefore you should not purge in a tertian fever with that alone, because it inflames and disposes toward the paroxysm. Therefore, temper it. And if in a fever there were a paroxysm of epilepsy, do not purge with a thing in which there is the power of celery <note>original: "apiū"</note>, because it makes it return. And in a phlegmatic fever, at the beginning, do not purge with chebulic myrobalan <note>original: "kebul'"</note>, because although they evacuate phlegm, yet by constricting the residue, they dispose the body toward the paroxysm.

<summary>This page discusses the precise timing and conditions for medical evacuations (purging and bloodletting), debating when a physician should follow nature's lead and when they must intervene early due to "furious" or overwhelming humors.</summary>
<keywords>evacuation, digestion, humors, paroxysm, bloodletting, pharmacy, Avicenna, Hippocrates, medical timing, purgatives, crisis</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the timing of medicinal interventions at the start of a disease or during its peaks (paroxysms). It specifically addresses whether a patient should be given liquid nourishment like barley water or subjected to bloodletting when a fever is at its most intense.</meta>

### BOOK IV

#### Signature: g iii

Similarly, black myrobalans <note>The dried fruit of the Terminalia tree, used as a gentle laxative to purge "black bile."</note> are used at the beginning of melancholic fevers. Perhaps for this reason, it is said that you should not reduce the dose, because these medicines would not establish the proper pattern of movement for the cycle <note>original: "periodi"</note> at the end of these illnesses as they do at the beginning—which is when we intend to reduce the humors. However, Avicenna prohibited the use of myrobalans at the very start of these fevers.

¶ And it is said: here the rule <note>original: "can." for canon</note> proves what was previously stated. For if during the hour of a paroxysm <note>The period of most intense symptoms or highest fever spike.</note> we ought not to give barley water with sugar, nor julep <note>A sweet medicinal syrup, often rose-water based.</note>, then much less should we give laxative medicines. It is debated whether, while a paroxysm is ongoing, we can give barley water and white sugar, or water and julep.

<margin>a</margin>
It seems that we can, according to common practice.

¶ Furthermore, those with fevers are sometimes plagued by thirst and intense heat. But these drinks are of a nature to temper heat. Furthermore, among the things that mitigate thirst is julep, as Avicenna says in the third book of the *Canon*, sixteenth section, third chapter on the cure of colic, first chapter. Furthermore, how can it be said that those things are a "heavy regimen"—such as barley water and julep—when they are numbered among the "subtle" <note>Light, thin, or easily digested.</note> diets? On the contrary, Avicenna, Mondino, and Francesco de Piedimonte <note>Mondino de' Liuzzi and Francesco di Piedimonte were prominent medieval medical authorities.</note> have said that these things are prohibited during the hour of the period—that is, at the start of the paroxysm—but in other times they are not prohibited. <gloss>Otherwise it must be said: first, by "heavy regimen," he understands a food-based regimen. The meaning is that food should not be given, whether drunk or eaten, during the hour of the paroxysm. This is the aphorism: "In paroxysms, it is necessary to withdraw [food]."</gloss> <note>Hippocrates, Aphorisms 1.11.</note>

¶ Secondly, it must be said that barley water, sugar, and julep are among the most significant of food-like things; therefore, they also should not be given. The reason why they should not be given during a paroxysm is because they break the cycle by constricting the channels <note>original: "meatuum," the pores or internal passages through which humors flow.</note>. That is, because they tighten the pathways. This "breaking" causes an unequal kindling of heat and a delay in the peak, and consequently a delay in the resolution of the matter <note>The "matter" refers to the excess humors causing the fever.</note>. For food given is a cause for nature to act against it, causing it to cease the resolution of the matter. Similarly, it multiplies the matter because it is converted into it. It also happens that these foods are drawn toward the inflamed limbs and block the ways; and if you consider it well, for every occasional cause, they block the ways. For if heat is turned inward so that food may be digested, then the resolution of the paroxysmal matter is prohibited, and a closing of the ways results from this. If the matter and the humors are multiplied, a closing of the ways occurs. Therefore, the harm of a heavy or food-based regimen is that it breaks or ruptures the progress of the cycle by constricting the channels (that is, through blockage), and such a break prolongs the paroxysm. It must be considered, however, that this rule is the general one; but under compulsion, we sometimes give these and other things. The cause of this compulsion is sometimes the temperament and habit of a choleric body, which leads one to feed at the start of a paroxysm... <note>original: "vt. s. r. tera." likely referring to Galen's *Therapeutics*.</note> and in the book on *Urgent Causes* and in the following chapter. Sometimes the cause is also an "accident" of the case, such as a loss of strength or unbearable thirst and a strong flame of heat, because of which one is moved to give those things that suit the aforementioned conditions. Sometimes the cause is a paroxysm so prolonged that there is no hour in which there is no paroxysm; therefore, we choose the least inconvenient hour, distancing ourselves from the start of the paroxysm if we can.

¶ It should be considered that the thicker the barley water, the more inconvenient it is during the hour of the paroxysm, because it is more like food. However, it could be made so subtle <note>Thin or diluted.</note> that there is little nutritional power in it, and it would approach the nature of water in its power. Therefore, it could be granted more safely during the hour of a paroxysm. And for this reason, Avicenna said it should not be placed in barley water and sugar; though he might allow subtle barley water, he does not allow it to become food-like with sugar. But you will say: "Can I give a drink of simple water during the hour of the paroxysm according to Avicenna?" It must be said that you can, unless something else prohibits it. And I say that you can give that in which there is no nutritional substance and which is a subtle thing; it evaporates quickly, descends, and helps the action of heat in the ripening of the humors. However, a large quantity of it drunk could be harmful because it is retained inside and could, by its potential coldness, be a cause of thickness and of thickening the humors. To the contrary arguments, it must be said that the common view of physicians condescends to the whims of the feverish. Therefore, it is better to fill the patient slightly twice and aim for the transpiration of the matter, and so that the paroxysms are finished as quickly as possible, which is done by opening the pores and not impeding the ripening <note>original: "maturam," the cooking/digestion of the disease-causing humor.</note>. For the physician is the helper of nature, as Hippocrates said; he hints at this many times in the *Aphorisms*. Finally, it must be said that although this is a "subtle" diet in respect to the whole disease, in respect to the paroxysm, every food-like thing is a "heavy" thing.

<margin>b</margin>
¶ And you must know: here he states the rule for "diminishing" medicine, which evacuates by removing a piece of the matter, even if it is not digested or not perfectly digested, but has become viscous and difficult to lead out. For the medicine that does this is strong in one way because it evacuates a humor that is difficult to extract—and therefore it is turpeth <note>A heavy purgative root.</note>, or agaric <note>A medicinal fungus.</note>, or colocynth <note>Bitter apple, a violent laxative.</note>—but it is weak because we want it to evacuate only a little of that humor, so that it causes the bowels to move only once or twice. Thus, it is like using a single scruple <note>A small unit of weight.</note> of turpeth, to use an example.

<margin>c</margin>
¶ And the advice: here the rule has a doubt. For Avicenna already said above that when bloodletting <note>original: "phlomia" or "phlobotomia."</note> is postponed from the beginning, it is not his intention. Furthermore, it does not seem it should be divided into several times; rather, we do it copiously in one go, sometimes until fainting <note>original: "sincopim."</note>, as appears below in the chapter on *Synocha* <note>A type of continuous fever.</note>. It must be said that phlebotomy is twofold: one in which the intention is the blood itself—which is done when the blood is at fault in quantity, even if it is little at fault in quality—and he spoke of this phlebotomy above, and does not speak of it here. The other is phlebotomy in which the intention is for humors other than blood; and this is properly when the blood itself is not in excess in quantity, nor is it properly at fault in quality, but other humors within it are at fault. Hence, if phlebotomy is performed, other humors follow it out. Of this phlebotomy, therefore, Avicenna speaks here. Nor does he absolutely command you to abandon it, but to do so if possible. And what moved Avicenna was that, given the case in the mind of the physician, two opposing judgments arise. One is that phlebotomy [is good] because as much as the other humors mixed with the blood are reduced, so too is the blood. The opposing judgment is that phlebotomy should not be done because it harms by evacuating the blood, which is not in excess; and it is impossible for this phlebotomy to take place without doing harm. And because the harm that follows from the evacuation of blood is a great harm, consider if the patient can be freed without phlebotomy; and then Avicenna's advice is that phlebotomy be abandoned. Nor does Avicenna say it should be postponed, but abandoned if possible. If, however, in your judgment it seems it cannot be abandoned, it is better to divide it into turns as you see fit...

<column-break/>

<margin>
...the humor through a thing which immediately creates the pattern of movement for the cycle. ¶ And a heavy regimen should be entirely avoided during the hour of the cycle, so that barley water with sugar is not given in drink, nor julep, so that it does not break the cycle by constricting the channels; for there is fear, rather, help [nature]. For Hippocrates says: the physician is nature's helper, not its hinderer. ¶ And you must know that many times a medicine that is "strong-weak" is needed: its strength is from the fact that it dissolves viscous humor; and its weakness is from the fact that it causes the bowels to move once or twice. ¶ And let it not be evacuated...
</margin>

...rather than performing a copious phlebotomy all at once. And first, Avicenna proves that if phlebotomy (in which the intention is not the blood but other humors) cannot be abandoned, it should not be done copiously in one go, but the number of times should be multiplied. Second, he proves the goodness of his advice—namely, that it should be abandoned if possible (that is, not done if it is possible). There begins the second part: "And it is not..." First he argues thus: a great deal of blood should not be evacuated suddenly, therefore the said phlebotomy should not be done in one go, but it is expedient for it to be evacuated in several turns like food. He already stated the conclusion; he proves the premise because if...

...all at once, so that the strength does not fall. And the advice indeed...

...much blood is evacuated suddenly—that is, evacuated in one turn—one evacuates a lot of that for which evacuation is not necessary, as is known, because this is a phlebotomy in which the intention is not the blood. ¶ It must be considered that Avicenna trusts in good intellects; therefore, he poses brief propositions, all of which are founded upon this: that here the discourse is about phlebotomy in which the intention is for other humors and not principally the blood. ¶ For it is manifest through itself that in a phlebotomy in which the intention is the blood as such, no doubt arises whether it should be done or not; for it must necessarily be done as the opposite to that "repletion" <note>An excess of blood.</note>, and consequently it is indicated by the repletion. But in a phlebotomy in which there is no such intention but an intention for other humors, doubt immediately arises from the very condition of the repletion, because it can partly benefit it and partly manifestly harm it. And therefore, in this phlebotomy, counsel <note>Deliberation.</note> is required. And in this advice, Avicenna does not prohibit phlebotomy as some understand from Avicenna, but he gives conditional advice: which is that, given the case, you should not perform phlebotomy if it is possible to free the patient otherwise.

¶ Therefore, sometimes it is not possible, and consequently, sometimes perform it—not by evacuating in one turn, but in several turns, as reason proves. And consider as the "Conciliator" <note>Pietro d'Abano, author of the *Conciliator Differentiarum Philosophorum et Praecipue Medicorum*.</note> says in Difference 62: <insert>Here they are bolder regarding phlebotomy: because their climate abounds more in blood than the Arabs; and therefore they boldly command phlebotomy in every putrid [fever]. See the *Therapeutics*, which we explained above.</insert> ¶ It must be considered that this text can be explained in two ways. First, that it proves the aforementioned premise as we said. Second, that it proves phlebotomy ought to be abandoned as much as is possible. For such a phlebotomy evacuates much—that is, a manifest quantity of blood whose evacuation is not necessary, because by itself it is not at fault, as is understood from Avicenna.

<margin>d</margin>
¶ "And it is not." Here he proves that the said phlebotomy should be abandoned as much as is possible. It must be considered that the text can be explained in two ways. ¶ First: neither the physician nor the patient can be evacuated without needing blood, so that the strength <note>original: "virtus," vital power.</note> remains strong for the evacuations which the patient will perhaps need. These evacuations are because perhaps it will be necessary to use many clysters <note>Enemas.</note>, many sweats, and other "insensible" <note>Invisible, like perspiration.</note> evacuations. He said "perhaps" because it is possible that health may follow quickly without these. A physician, however, must prepare himself so that where he sees a suspicion of these things, the patient can sustain them. And if that suspicion does not follow, but the patient is freed without it, he should not be blamed but rather praised if he prepared himself for it. He argues thus: we cannot excuse the presence of blood for the evacuations we need; therefore, it is good advice that if possible, phlebotomy should be abandoned. The premise is known because we need strong vital power in evacuations. Therefore, the presence of blood, by which that strength stands, is known by consequence. However, some crude physician, believing he could demonstrate against Avicenna, might say that the blood is infected and corrupt, and with it, the strength will not stand strong against the harm of evacuations. ¶ Avicenna responds that if it is as you say, I do not prohibit phlebotomy, but divide it. ¶ In the second way, the text can be explained: the evacuation of blood through the said phlebotomy does not excuse you from needing to perform other evacuations. Therefore, if you can abandon phlebotomy, abandon it. The consequence is known because even after phlebotomy is performed, it is necessary to give laxative medicines. It is necessary for the vital strength to be strong, as we said. ¶ Furthermore, consider that those pharmacies <note>Medicines.</note> which you will give later will be able to free the man, even though phlebotomy was not performed. The premise is known because this fever in which this advice about phlebotomy is given is from matter other than blood, in which we are mostly forced to use laxative medicines. He said "perhaps," however, because it is possible for a crisis to be made by nature and for the patient to be freed without any laxative drug. ¶ This text could be explained in a third way: that Avicenna wants to perform this phlebotomy for the sake of other humors more malignant than blood. Whence it will be necessary to give more drugs than if we had not performed phlebotomy. And this explanation can remove... and you may consider it from the chapter on phlebotomy in the first book.

<margin>e</margin>
¶ "And it is weakened." This is the third or second reason for proving that the said phlebotomy should be abandoned as much as possible: because it weakens the vital power so that it cannot produce future crises. And the reason is known from what was said before. Therefore, the explanations of certain people should cease—those who say that Avicenna is speaking of phlebotomy in a fever in which a crisis is expected. Others say he is speaking of a prolonged fever. For these are very specific explanations. The arguments made to the contrary are resolved.

<margin>f</margin>
¶ "And know." Here he explains the rule for curing a putrid fever by considering certain "accidents" <note>Symptoms or non-essential conditions.</note>, certain joined dispositions against nature, and also natural ones; and there are four cases. ¶ The first case is that if the headache is light, following the fever in its increase and decrease, the intention is directed toward the fever. And he understands this when he says: when a headache and fever are joined, the fever is more worthy of cure, because the cure of the fever should come first. But if the pain...

<summary>This page discusses the dietary and surgical management of fevers, arguing against feeding patients or performing large-scale bloodletting during the peak of a fever (paroxysm). It emphasizes preserving the patient's "virtus" (vital strength) so nature can successfully resolve the illness through a "crisis."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the treatment of fevers, specifically focusing on complications such as severe headaches, the treatment of infants through their nurses, and the dietary management of jaundice and colic in febrile patients. It references the works of Avicenna and Rhazes to determine the priority of treatment when multiple symptoms occur simultaneously.</meta>

# Fen I, Treatise II

If the pain in the head is so intense that the fever would naturally subside on its own <note>original: "remitteretur"</note>, let it be managed through the inflammation and boiling of the humors; focus your attention principally on the cure of that pain. Therefore, sometimes it is necessary to soothe it with a stupefactive <note>A numbing agent or narcotic, like opium or mandrake.</note>; and for this reason, perhaps, it is said that it should be soothed. However, regarding how he teaches to make the fever return, or what its causes are, and the method of cure, this depends on the knowledge of first principles. The headache is also treated further on in the third book, first section.

<margin>
a
¶ And when an infant. This refers to the master of the canons, Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"</note>, in the 16th book of the *Continens*. For we cannot provide infants with other medicines or substances except for milk, which flows from the breast. This is because of their similarity to the milk; no harm is feared when it is placed in the bones. In the 5th part of the *Aphorisms*, it is said that milk is harmful to those with head pain. Because of this, lest the milk be corrupted in them by the heat of the fever, we rectify that milk through the nurse, giving her lettuce, pomegranate wine, and well-diluted wine; and we manage the rest of the regimen as it seems best to us. Or we make certain adjustments for the infants, tempering the heat in them, and we use them at the hour that seems best to us.
</margin>

Head pain sometimes makes a declining fever return to its peak; therefore, it is necessary that it be soothed. And when a nursing infant has a fever, then the mother's milk must be rectified. ¶ And when the urine is jaundiced <note>original: "icterica"</note> during a fever, it signifies an abscess <term>apostema<gloss>an internal swelling or collection of humors, often inflammatory</gloss></term>; therefore, the treatment is to give barley water to drink, or oxymel <note>original: "syrupum acetosum," a mixture of honey and vinegar.</note>. Does the fever then increase? Let the intention be directed toward the abscess. And sometimes when there is colic with the fever, the path is not opened by giving barley water to drink; rather, give chicken broth <note>original: "ius galli"</note>, and let the broth be mild, and increase its oiliness; then barley water may be given to drink if it is necessary. Concerning laxatives, there is a potion made from tamarinds.

<margin>
b
¶ And when it shall be. This is the third rule <note>original: "cañ." for canon</note> about which there is doubt. For if the urine is jaundiced—that is, intensely colored with yellow foam—it signifies an abscess and
</margin>

therefore we must focus our attention on the abscess, since the fever depends on it. Here Rhazes speaks of "dependents," by which he understands a blockage of the bile duct <note>original: "pori fellei"</note> leading to the intestines; with this blockage, jaundice <term>ictericia<gloss>a yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by bile</gloss></term> occurs and the urine becomes jaundiced. In that case, we must first cure the fever. This statement can be upheld if one were speaking of a blockage in accidental jaundice joined with fever. For example: because someone was previously jaundiced, having been accustomed to it for a long time, and now has a fever not because of the cause of the jaundice but from another cause; since it is so, these are two diseases not depending on one another. Because the fever is a supervening disease while the first blockage is the cause of that jaundice, one must begin with the cure of the fever. But if that fever followed from that bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> which is retained because of the blockage, and the part produced jaundice because of the fever, it would be necessary to focus on the cure of the blockage before the fever. Others say that Avicenna's <note>original: "auic."</note> method here is one of "forced cure," in which, although the fever follows the abscess, we nevertheless focus first on the fever rather than the abscess because of the fever's intensity. Avicenna said this same thing above regarding the things in which putrid fevers differ. However, focusing on the fever, Avicenna focuses with those things which do not specifically harm the abscess, such as barley water and oxymel; for they do not cause harm in the way that pure water would, as was understood earlier in this chapter. Otherwise, we say that Avicenna's speech here is not about an abscess which a fever follows, but is a speech about a certain disposition toward an abscess, which disposition accompanies the fever and the flame by which the liver <note>original: "epar"</note> is inflamed with a strong inflammation signified by the jaundiced urine. Hence, a drawing of humors to the liver and an abscess are feared; therefore, one must begin by cooling the febrile heat. Among the soothing things is the use of barley water given copiously, or the use of oxymel with water as it seems best to you. And then, once the fever is cured or lessened, if any disposition of heat remains in the liver about which you again doubt lest it excite an abscess, focus on that. But you might say: "While the fever persists, can I not place an epithem <note>A topical poultice or medicated cloth.</note> of sandalwood over the liver and be excused from this fear?" It must be said that Avicenna considered here the correct order of cure and, with it, the least deceptive. For since this heat of the liver, by which an abscess is feared, follows the universal flame of the fever itself, its principal and true cure is to lessen that flame, which is like the efficient cause, and afterward to come to that which has happened in the liver. By this lessening, no harm is feared from the prohibition of the resolution of materials, which might be feared from a cooling epithem on the liver.

<margin>
c
¶ And when. This is the fourth rule. It is doubted whether, while fever and colic persist,
</margin>

we can use barley water or chicken broth. It seems that barley water is allowed according to Avicenna in the third book, 16th section, 4th treatise, first chapter, where he says if it is there—namely, with the febrile colic—let the chicken water be exchanged, and in its place let there be barley water. Furthermore, chicken broth has oiliness, and especially if it is increased in it as Avicenna commands; but in this, there is a suspicion of inflammation. To the contrary, Avicenna says that the path—namely, of the intestines—will not be opened, because the colic will not be helped by giving barley water to drink; rather, chicken broth. Furthermore, in the chapter on barley water, Avicenna prohibits giving barley water when dryness is added to the nature; but in colic, there is a dryness of nature, as is well known. Therefore, some have said that in colic, barley water should not be given because it is windy and causes bloating <note>original: "inflatiua"</note>; hence it increases the colic, so chicken broth is given instead. Others have said the opposite: that barley water should be drunk and chicken broth should be placed in a clyster <note>An enema.</note>. Sometimes we say that chicken broth is of two kinds: one is simple, and that can be given while the fever persists, nor is inflammation feared from it because it does not have excessive oiliness. Similarly, the malice of its oiliness is lessened by soothing that broth with a decoction of soothing things, such as violets or prunes or jujubes, if it seems best to you. Avicenna, however, believes that chicken broth is among the cold lubricants, as appears in the chapter on colic from feces; and in this, he intends that its oiliness should not be feared to cause harm through inflammation. The other is a laxative chicken broth, made so by laxative medicines mixed with it, such as polypody <note>A type of fern.</note>, safflower <note>original: "cartamus"</note>, rock salt <note>original: "sal gemma"</note>, and the like; and this is not safe in colic. Avicenna, therefore, in the third book, in place of medicinal chicken broth, gives barley water on the condition that once clysters have been made, barley water suffices for cleansing. Here, in place of clysters, he prefers a soothing, non-medicinal chicken broth, and once the evacuation of feces has been performed, he afterward gives barley water, and either way is sufficient. ¶ We say again that colic is of two types in fever: one is mild, which arises from the common drying of the feces around the intestines by reason of the febrile heat; this drying could induce some mild colic in someone. And that can be cured by tempering the heat with barley water and washing the intestines with barley water; and thus Avicenna speaks in the aforementioned third book. But against this, Avicenna, below in the chapter on barley water,

<column-break/>

prohibits barley water when the feces are dry without dry matter. Let us say that if it seems best to you, you can provide a clyster before giving the barley water. Or it should be said that he speaks of barley water which is a ptisan <note>A medicinal infusion or porridge.</note> that is given in place of food, but before feeding, the intestines must be purged. But in the third book, he speaks of drinkable barley water in which there is the cleansing virtue of the barley, and it is almost no nourishment except for a very little bit. The other is a strong colic from a strong blockage of feces or windiness occurring in the fever; and this would not be moved by barley water, but by a strong medicine such as pure chicken broth, or a medicinal one

</margin>

as it seems best to you, or at least make it soothing and increase its oiliness. This is done either by decocting soothing things in it as we said, or if you increase the oiliness, you make it soothing in this way; its oiliness is increased by taking a fatter rooster or by giving the oilier part of the broth. And Avicenna does all this by focusing on the colic which, when it is strong, takes precedence in the cure; and if we harm the fever a little bit by this, we do not care, considering the malice of the colic. And this is what Avicenna says: "when there is colic with the fever"—namely, a strong one—the path (that is, of the intestines) will not be opened with light things, nor by giving barley water to drink, because its cleansing and soothing are not strong enough to cut through the strong blockage from dried feces and thickened winds; rather, the path is opened by giving chicken broth to drink. And with soothing things—that is, make the broth soothing and increase its oiliness so that the strong dryness of the feces may be removed.
