In this chapter, therefore, he focuses more on the colic than the fever because the colic here is an accident <note>A symptom or secondary condition.</note> that draws the cure to itself, whereas in the chapter on colic, he focuses more on the fever because it is an accident of the colic which diverts the cure to itself. 
and specifically putrid ones. Here he lists the medicines with which we evacuate these febrile patients. And he listed these medicines because the use of laxatives is suspected, and it is safer to receive knowledge of them from others. Although in putrid fever the intention is sometimes to cool the fever and moisten it—since cooling and moistening things are well known, and there is not such great fear in their use—Avicenna is excused from listing those medicines and leaves them as known in the second and fifth rules. And concerning the cooling thing in which there was fear—namely, cold water—he has already set down the rule; and with this, he spoke of syrup of violets, although he placed it for soothing; and although there is an intention to digest the matter, he wants those digestives to be known from the same books and the particular chapters of this book where he places digestives according to the diversity of the materials. However, he has already set down a common or nearly common digestive: namely, oxymel. It remained, therefore, for Avicenna to list the laxative medicines which must be appropriate to the materials; and this part will stand for you in place of an antidotary <note>A collection of medicinal formulas.</note> for this chapter, as far as its first part is concerned. I have labored sometimes in dividing these parts, but it seems to me better to say that it has three parts as it has three laxative medicines. **F**irst, the medicine is made from tamarinds and manna <note>A sweet plant exudate.</note> which is called "tereniabin"; and another is a species of manna called "syracost." And consider that this medicine can be given in a small quantity, and then it is only soothing and causes a "minoration" <note>A gentle reduction of humors.</note> which is called "drying out," and it can be suitable in any fever in which you wish to soothe the intestines; and it can be given in a larger quantity. For example, one ounce of tamarinds and half an ounce of each manna; then it evacuates bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> by its property, and it is suitable in bilious fevers in which you wish to evacuate bile. Therefore, that laxative medicine satisfies the rules which preceded regarding the soothing of the belly and the rules which preceded regarding the evacuation of matter according to the path of "cutting off"—namely, minorative. If, therefore, you want this medicine to be stronger, add "lubleb"; it is one of the species of milky plants, and it is a smaller species. Simon says it is among the easier laxatives and is given in acute fever, and a great deal of it is found in vineyards. We, however, do not trust that we know it. We also strengthen it through cassia, the nature of which is well known.

And it is a medicine which we can use in the cases mentioned above as in the beginning, such as if the matter is "furious" <note>Violent or rapidly progressing.</note> or more mobile.

It must be said that it should not be a true washing, but a washing that is "nourishing"; it should be steeped and nourished and allowed to thicken, and pills should be made. In this nourishment, its malice is rectified, as appears to one who knows the chapter on aloe, endive, and nightshade; therefore, let us not prolong the speech here. And here you can resolve the doubts about washing and not washing.

It must be said that the use of myrobalans is either at the beginning or in the process once digestion is complete. At the beginning, their use could be either to evacuate the matter when it is expedient to minorate it because of its quantity, or to eradicate it because of its "fury." Or their use could be to consolidate other medicines. And indeed, if anyone uses myrobalans at the beginning of a fever in a dose sufficient to eradicate furious materials, such use is not suitable; because since they are weak in loosening, they would not lead out those materials with a copious evacuation. This, as is known, he understood beforehand; nor is their use suitable for minorating materials—for example, bilious ones as the yellow [myrobalans] do—because medicines that minorate those materials (namely, those undigested from the beginning or not yet digested) ought not to be like...

# Book IV

### [Left Column]

<margin>a</margin>
...weak. Rather, they are strong and because of this, they evacuate something of the unsuitable matter. Also, because myrobalans <note>original: "myrobolani"; the fruit of the myrobalan plum, used in medieval medicine as a gentle purgative that also has astringent properties.</note> leave behind traces of wrinkling <note>Refers to the astringent effect that causes tissues to contract.</note>. Hence, they bind the residual matter and tighten the paths of the ducts, making them unsuited for flow. Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037).</note> expressed only this here when he said that the intention by which it should work is not found by him. That is, this man who prescribes myrobalans in the beginning does not find in them an intention by which a useful effect is worked; rather, they cause harm because they constrict the pores after the loosening [of the bowels]. Because of this, the residual matter is narrowed and prevented from evacuation and resolution. They also bloat the viscera, and from this, they render the belly styptic <note>Constipated or tightened.</note> rather than light. But at the beginning and in the progression of a putrid fever, a great and necessary opening of the paths and an intention of softening is required; now, myrobalans do the opposite. It appears from this that they do more harm when given in substance than when their expulsion <note>Likely referring to an infusion or strained preparation.</note> is exhibited. If, however, their use were for the purpose of consolidating other medicines—for instance, scammony <note>original: "scamonea"; a powerful purgative resin derived from the root of Convolvulus scammonia.</note>—because it would be necessary to use them in the beginning, myrobalans could be exhibited, just as Rhazes <note>The Persian physician Al-Razi (865–925).</note> uses them in the 16th book of the *Continens* at the beginning. If there is also another medicine given with them that removes their harshness and constriction, and if he gave their infusion with that, it would not be bad to grant them even in the beginning, just as Rhazes grants their infusion with manna <note>A sweet plant secretion used as a mild laxative.</note> in the first tract of the *Almansor*. But if the discourse is about the use of myrobalans in the progression [of the illness], it must be said that once perfect digestion of the matter has been achieved and it is most fit for evacuation, we can use them. If we are confident in the perfect evacuation of those matters through one dose of myrobalans, you need not fear the residue being constricted, since there is no residue. Therefore, the convenient use of myrobalans is after perfect digestion <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" refers to the ripening or maturation of the diseased humors.</note> and some preceding evacuations. For the residue of the matters can be drawn out by myrobalans, and the members loosened by the preceding fever and the spontaneous and artificial evacuations can be strengthened and re-aggregated. This is what Avicenna understood. However, concerning the use of myrobalans at the beginning of abscesses of the stomach, read what we wrote in the third book, section 13.

Therefore, let him take the knowledge he needs for verification from there. Know after this that among us, we do not commonly use these purgatives in putrid fever; but in choleric patients <note>Those with an excess of yellow bile.</note>, we commonly use rhubarb, tamarinds, and scammony, though not frequently. ¶ And those with fever. This is to say that Avicenna posits three cases here. First canon: some understand that in a summer changed from its nature—which is a cold summer—the feverish person should stay in a windy house <note>A well-ventilated or draughty room.</note>. This is a crude discourse, and we are forced to say "feverish with fever." Otherwise, let us say that those with fever in summer are much delighted by cold air and venting air, and they have the windows opened so the winds blow through the house. This is more tolerable in a hot fever; but in a cold fever—namely, from phlegm or melancholy—it is more harmful, because the many and thick vapors of phlegm and melancholy are prevented from resolution. And therefore, it harms specifically one who sweats, because it prevents that sweat.

...powder camphor and scammony over it. ¶ And let them be preserved so they do not dissolve with vapor; then let it be left until it coagulates by itself with ease. Let its dose be from 2 drachms to 3 and a half. ¶ And it is possible that it be made from turpentine and syracosi and *tabarzet* sugar <note>A high-quality white sugar.</note> into the form of *penidie* <note>A twisted sugar candy or lozenge.</note>. ¶ And scammony and camphor are placed in it according to the quantity that falls into one potion; of camphor up to a *tosugi*, and of scammony up to a sixth of a drachm, so that it does not become horrible to the soul <note>i.e., making it more palatable or less nauseating.</note>. ¶ And a feverish person in summer with a cold fever should not enter a windy house, especially when he sweats, so that the matter is not turned back from its resolution.
¶ And troches are not suitable for the beginnings of these fevers except after digestion and evacuation.
¶ And troches are more suitable for one whose fever is clinging to his stomach, as if it were a hectic fever <note>original: "ethica"; a persistent, wasting fever often associated with consumption.</note>. And by the softening of his habits in his regimen, he feels the fever sometimes; it is not so much noted...

...given in substance do not slip away so easily and work more strongly. They make a strong impression on the stomach. Their use happens because they are commonly abominable; he who takes them once almost never wants to take them again.
¶ Second, consider that the troches we use in hot fevers are cooling, like troches of roses, spodum, violet-tinted barberry, camphor, and the like. But the troches we use in cold fevers are aperient <note>Opening or laxative.</note> and thinning to the matters, such as troches of eupatorium, capers, and rhubarb. In mixed fevers, they are mixed. Third, consider that certain cold troches are also styptic, such as certain troches of roses, some of barberry, some of camphor. But others are also softening, such as some of camphor and violet troches, and those made from seeds of violets, citron, sandalwood, psyllium mucilage, and the like. Cooling troches in cold fevers are sometimes softening and aperient, like those from anise and fenugreek seeds and...

---

...liquorice; and some are strongly aperient, like those of asarum <note>Wild ginger.</note>, madder, and the like. You should consider all these things in the dispensatories <note>Books containing medicinal recipes.</note>; and having set these down, we will place the cold troches we use in hot fevers into four propositions. ¶ The first is that in a hot fever, styptic cold troches, such as those of roses, are not suitable at the beginning because they narrow and constrict the matter, as we saw above. Second, in a hot fever at the beginning, if there is much inflammation in the stomach, cold troches can be suitable, specifically the softening ones, because they can extinguish that heat. And if it seems to you that there is a great necessity for cooling styptic troches, wanting them to linger in the stomach, choose this over the harm of stypticity—do what seems best to you. However, in such strong, intemperate heat of the stomach, if there is a need for a cold troche like one of camphor, they can be given because they are digested and produce this cooling more than decoctions. And then the text of Avicenna is saved, which says troches are more suitable for him whose fever is burning in his stomach, as if it were a hectic fever. ¶ Third canon: if in the fever there is not strong inflammation of the stomach, the giving of syrups and cooling decoctions suffices; then it is suitable to abstain from troches. Fourth canon: cooling troches, in proportion to how styptic they are, are suitable at the end of hot fevers, as they remove the heat that remains after the evacuation of the matters and they strengthen the members. Perhaps they would even remove the residue of the matters, which is why Avicenna says "after digestion and evacuation." Regarding warm troches used in cold fevers, we set four canons. ¶ The first is that in cold fevers at the beginning, strongly aperient warm troches are not suitable. The reason is that they agitate the matter, eject it irregularly, and thicken it; this was the opinion of Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), a Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> in the 5th section of the chapter on the cure of quartan fever <note>A fever occurring every third day, associated with black bile.</note>.

<margin>a</margin>
¶ Second canon: in cold fevers we can use light aperient troches at the beginning, specifically if the matter is in the stomach, requiring a medicine that remains in the stomach, such as in phlegmatic fevers that resemble hectic fevers. And this is what Avicenna says according to this text: that troches are suitable for him whose fever is clinging to his stomach. Third canon: if the matter stays in the veins and remote parts, syrups are better than troches because they penetrate more. Fourth canon: in cold fevers, during the progression and at the end of the beginning, stronger and aperient and strongly educive <note>Drawing out.</note> troches are to be granted because the matters are then ready; this will appear in the special chapters on phlegmatic and quartan fever, and from these, contradictions cease. ¶ Some say that cold troches are absolutely prohibited in the beginning of hot fevers because they cool too strongly, and it is prohibited to cool much and suddenly. But Dynus <note>Dino del Garbo (d. 1327), an Italian physician and commentator.</note> said that the troches prohibited in the beginning of putrid fevers are those given for the sake of diminishing the matter, such as troches of wormwood and roses, which are not suitable in the beginning. By "fever clinging to the stomach," he understands a phlegmatic fever. Hence Avicenna said above concerning that which occurs with injury to the stomach and resembles a hectic fever: in such phlegmatic fevers, the administration of said troches is especially suitable, both for the diminution of the matter and for tightening and strengthening. And we say that even in the beginning, it is not safe to use them.

<margin>b</margin>
¶ And by the softening. This is the third canon, an example of which is if someone accustomed to bathing and exercise should fall into a fever from these recent superfluities <note>Excesses of humors or waste.</note>. This fever is not of great vigor except for two reasons. ¶ First, because it signifies a primitive cause. Second, because by returning to the habit if possible while the fever remains, or to something equivalent, he will be helped. Here, however, is a place for speculation belonging to the theoretical part: which fever is primitive...

Is it the same as the tertian fever that arises from a bodily cause? In this whole chapter, one might doubt whether it is lawful to mix digestive and laxative <note>original: "solutivas"; medicines that loosen the bowels to expel humors.</note> medicines. We spoke of this in the first book, section 4, article 2. When he considered it, the question was not as doubtful as the general community of doctors makes it out to be. <margin>a The comparison about which Avicenna speaks when he says "more convenient" is explained by some as more suitable—namely, for those who are moist rather than dry, as Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler and personal physician to Emperor Julian.</note> says. Others say more convenient than dry foods. Others say more convenient for those suffering from fevers among the moist. ## Chapter on the feeding of feverish patients in general.
### Chapter viii.

Beside the more convenient feedings, when he established universal rules <note>original: "canones universales"; general principles of medical practice.</note> in the cure of putrid fevers, he placed a rule for feeding. And because in both rules, mention was made of barley water and oxymel <note>original: "sirupo acetoso"; a syrup made of honey and vinegar, used to cut through thick humors.</note>, he therefore makes a chapter on this here. Second: Barley water. The first part is in three sections. First, he chooses the quality of food appropriate to the hour. Third, the type of diet, at the second part: "when it happens." At the third: "and you should know." The first discourse is on the aphorism of Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> regarding a liquid diet. You may refer everything we have explained regarding that aphorism here and elsewhere to this place. The opinion, however, is that this food is appropriate because of the fever, which is a "dry" disease. And because the fever is hot, he also gave it to be understood that the diet ought to be cold. Or according to Oribasius, he gave more heat to the dryness of the fever, and therefore opposed it with a moist

---

<margin>b Here he conditions the hour of feeding upon three things. First, that there be no dry feces in the intestines, as in the first book of Avicenna’s *Regimen*, because the fever and its vapors can be a cause of the food's corruption. Second, that the patient not be fed at the hour of the paroxysm <note>original: "paroxismi"; the periodic peak or crisis of a fever.</note>, which is what he means by "should they occur to them"—namely, periodic peaks in intermittent fevers. And if they are strong in the burning or strengthening of continuous fevers, he gives the reason. That rule is an aphorism of Hippocrates: "In the peak of the fever, one must withdraw [food]." Therefore, he postpones it until the decline <note>original: "declinationem"; the period after the peak when the fever begins to subside.</note>, just as Hippocrates does at the end of the first book on the *Regimen of Acute Diseases*. He says, however, in that which follows the peak, that as much as you can distance the food from the strength of the fever and move it toward the hour of rest, do so. But consider the peak or exacerbation that returns, because you must distance yourself from the beginning [of the next peak] except in certain cases. We dispute over that aphorism as to how many hours before a peak we ought to feed the patient, and we held that this judgment is estimative <note>Subjective or based on the physician's experience rather than a fixed rule.</note> and varies according to the species of fever. For in phlegmatic fevers, we ought to feed further from the presence of the peak, and in quartan fevers more than tertian, if we can. It also varies according to whether foods are slow or fast to digest, or prone to causing inflammation. It varies according to whether bodies are stronger or weaker in the stomach; therefore, authors differ among themselves in the measurement of the time for food before a peak. Their diversity is not a contradiction but a difference in estimative judgment.</margin>

<margin>c The third condition he observes in feeding is that the customary hour be chosen if possible. For natures delight in customs, as Hippocrates says.</margin>

diet. We do not care for the discourse of Oribasius. Thaddeus <note>Thaddeus Alderotti (1223–1295), a famous professor of medicine at Bologna.</note> said that he wanted to establish a diet for feverish patients and children, and that it must be moist and not cold. And we say with this that in the use of cold things against fevers, there is a greater fear of the retention of matter than there is in the use of moist things. Nor does it suit the reason of age when he said "moist for infants"—that is, when he spoke of "fleshy and moist" people. Therefore, if a complexion were dry, these things would not be as suitable according to this teaching and the teaching of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 CE), whose medical system dominated the Middle Ages.</note> at the end of the third book of *Therapeutics*. We discussed this there regarding the nature of the fever's matter. It must also be considered that the moist things chosen ought to be moist in virtue <note>Having a moisturizing effect on the body's internal state.</note> as much as possible. For the virtue of barley water—whether it is dry or moist—will be discussed later. They ought to be moist and not prone to putrefaction, which adds to the fever, such as seasonal fruits. Galen says in the second book on *Aliments* that these are easily corrupted. This is the summary of all that was noted on that aphorism.

---

<margin>f And afterward: the barley-water <note>original: "ptisana"; a medicinal gruel or decoction of barley.</note>. This is a barley drink made from pure barley flour, which we speak of in the following chapter, where it says that it is not the thin, strained ptisana properly called "barley water." This ptisana is neither coarse nor thin compared to the extremes placed here. In this, one must stand by the instruction of our fathers, who found this experience through much investigation. And those foods which follow the "side of the acute" are the extremities of the cock and hen. By "cock," he means a small chick, which Rhazes <note>The Persian physician Al-Razi (865–925 CE).</note> calls "gallicolum." Take note here that although we mostly prescribe a female chicken, a small male cock can be given; however, the praise of female chickens is much greater among all the Arabs. Consider that he says "extremities" because they are not of as much nourishment as the fleshy parts of the breast, nor are they as heavy. Another reading has "these are the extremities of the hen." Consider secondly that he begins from the side of the coarse diet of the healthy and proceeds by degrees to the middle diet, passing through it to the other side—the thin diet. He places in the order of the thin diet a certain food which had not been there, because it is also placed on the other side prepared in a different way. For bread made of fine wheat flour <note>original: "simila frumenti"; the highest quality wheat flour.</note> can be prepared—that is, broken or dissolved in water—in two ways. One way is by thin dissolution, where it is washed and refined many times with a sufficient abundance of water so that it is like a drinkable potion. Then it is a thin diet, and thinner than the middle diet which is the ptisana, because it would have less nourishment than the ptisana.</margin>

<margin>g In another way, it can be dissolved by coarse dissolution into coarse pieces, washed little or not at all, leaving it in the water so that it is a chewable food; then it is in the category of a coarse diet and nourishes more than a ptisana does. Therefore, he said that the coarse is a stronger food. Washing, however, removes the parts of the leaven from the bread, whose harm might be feared in a fever. Whence bread is forbidden in internal abscesses <note>original: "apostematibus"; swellings or inflammations.</note> before maturation, as Avenzoar <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), an Andalusian physician.</note> says in his book on specific remedies. What washing does, we shall say in the second book in the chapter on bread. *Lubugi* are partridges <note>likely a Latinization of an Arabic term for partridge species.</note>, which are at the peak of the coarse diet because they nourish much and their nourishment is subtle. Chickens—namely, small ones. But you will say he already spoke of the extremities of small chickens when he said "cock extremities." It must be said that perhaps it is better that the text says "hen's extremity," so that the body of the hen is the coarse diet of the healthy, but the wing-tips are the coarse diet of the feverish. It is not appropriate for the diet of the healthy and the coarse diet of the feverish to be too close. Or it must be said that a small chick is a thin diet—that is, less coarse compared to the extremities of a large, full hen. *Alchanzi* are small birds. Sorbable eggs <note>original: "oua sorbilla"; soft-boiled eggs that can be sipped.</note>, few in quantity but rich in nourishment, are a coarser diet than properly "hard" ones. That is, so sippable that they are very liquid, or thin eggs like those of a hen, not coarse like those of a goose.</margin>

## On the feeding of feverish patients in general. Chapter viii.

Beside the more convenient foods for those with fevers are moist foods. Specifically for one whose complexion is moist, such as infants and the stout, these are appropriate because they resemble the complexion and are contrary to the illness. ¶ Never, when a fever occurs and the nature is dry, should you feed at all until the fever has perfectly departed. ¶ And it is necessary that periodic peaks <note>original: "parorismi piocidi"; likely a corruption of "periodici."</note> and peaks that are strong occur while their bellies are empty, in which there is no food at all. For if they were fed at that hour, nature would be occupied in digesting and would cease to digest and expel [the illness], and the sickness would be confirmed and prolonged. ¶ And because of this, it is necessary that they postpone feeding until the decline and in that period which is after it.

---

¶ And if it happens by chance that the hour of decline is the customary hour for food, then it is the best that can be. ¶ And know that regarding feeding and regimen, there is that which is very thin <note>original: "subtile"; light or easily digested.</note>, and all that which is very coarse <note>original: "grossum"; heavy or highly nutritious.</note>, and therefore that which is between them. Its time of decline tends more toward the thin, and part of it tends more toward the thick. ¶ The ultimate in thinness is the prohibition of food. And the very coarse is the administration of the foods of healthy masters. Those which follow the thin side, which is the middle, is to be content in food with the juice of pomegranates and a very thin julep <note>A sweet medicinal drink, originally from Persian *gulab* (rosewater).</note>. After that, thin barley water, and after that, coarse barley water and cold and moist vegetables such as orach <note>original: "atriplices"; a leafy vegetable used like spinach.</note>, spinach, and blite <note>Another leafy green vegetable.</note>, and similar things. After that, the barley ptisana as it is, which is the middle. Those who follow the coarse side are the extremities of cocks and hens. Thinner than those are partridges and chicks, and thinner than those are small birds and sippable eggs, few in number and thin, and small fish.

Furthermore, in the stationary stage and before the stationary stage of the disease, something must be asserted, as Hippocrates says in the first part of the *Aphorisms*. ¶ Therefore in the disease... To the contrary is Avicenna and Hippocrates. It must be said that when such an acute fever is found which ends on the third day, like a tertian fever, or one of a single peak when the strength is firm and other things agree, feeding then is harmful and hinders nature from its operation, and the patient can stand without food until the crisis <note>original: "crisim"; the turning point of a disease.</note>. It would therefore be bad to feed them. Say, however, that one must attend to customs, climates, and conditions which Galen found...

For pomegranate juice is very little nourishment and very thin, but there is more nourishment in julep and water...</margin>

...of thin barley—namely, much water and a little sugar in the julep or a little barley or barley water. But it is doubted whether orach and spinach are at the summit of the thin diet. You see that they are not, because they are foods of the healthy, and such diets are coarse, as he said. It must be said that these foods are a thin diet because they are of little nourishment and perhaps thin. However, we are not discussing this now. To the contrary, it must be said that a small quantity ought to be given. Or it must be said that not all foods which the healthy use are a coarse diet, for they also use sugar-water and pomegranate wine. But he intends that the food of the healthy, which is a coarse diet, is food by which the healthy are strong in their health, such as types of meat, specifically of quadrupeds, and bread in sufficient quantity. We have already spoken of the diversity of the ptisana above. And similar things like lettuce and borage.

...elaborating by asserting whatever else we have said about that passage. It is, however, a manner of speaking: it aggregates toward conglutination <note>original: "conglutinationem"; a sticking together or healing of tissues</note>, that is, although it may be sticky, it nevertheless aggregates or unites these aids or utilities. It aids digestion because it is quickly digested and also soothes because it smooths out roughness and lubricates, etc. However, how it is moist and provides moisture will appear in the following chapter.

<margin>a And the ancients. Here he compares barley water <note>original: "ptisanam"</note> to honey water. Second, he compares honey water and barley water to oxymel <note>original: "sirupum acetosum"; a syrup made of vinegar and honey</note>. Third, he raises a provocation and sets us aside. There follows "ba." There [is] 3. And let there be sufficiency. It must be considered that honey water, made subtle by a large quantity of water, nourishes less than barley water; yet it is called more "subtle" <note>In medieval medicine, "subtle" means thin, penetrating, or easily processed by the body, as opposed to "gross" or heavy</note> among the ancients. He understood this when he said its nourishment is small, and therefore he adds "small in power." Second, it should be considered that Avicenna praises this honey water, first because it does not linger: rather the water, which is part of it, penetrates, and this is by the power of the honey heating and sweetening it. Second, because its moisturizing effect is great. He does not mean that it moisturizes much by nourishing—for that would contradict him—but that the water remains moisturizing without evaporating before it can act. That it cleanses the passages and opens them by scouring and provoking [excretion] is well known; it should not be understood as "much" in excessive quantity, but "much" meaning "sufficiently," so that in this it is not inferior to barley water. And because someone might fear its heat, he says its hot quality is broken by the water. But it is doubted because we do not commonly use honey water for fear of inflammations. It must be said that we should not use it as Rhazes <note>The 9th-century Persian physician Abu Bakr al-Razi</note> says in the 16th book of the *Continens*. In this country, it happens that choleric humors <note>The yellow bile humor, associated with heat and dryness</note> are much excited in fevers, even if they are not choleric fevers; and therefore perhaps its use has been abandoned. However, Rhazes concedes its use in the 17th book of the *Continens* when acidity is felt in the stomach of the feverish person. Climates must be considered in this, as the author says in the 7th book of the *Colliget*.</margin>

### And more subtle than these are barley gruels <note>original: "kist ordei"; likely derived from the Arabic *kishk*, a preparation of parched barley</note> just as it is. And more subtle than that is bread likewise dissolved in well-chilled water with a good, subtle dissolution. "Gross" <note>heavy or thick</note> food, however, is strong food, *altacugizar* <note>original: "altacugizar"; a Latinization of an Arabic term for a type of twice-baked bread or biscuit</note>; and food stronger than that is gross.

### And barley gruel is indeed a good food, for it brings together glutination and its own digestion, smoothness, leveling, lubrication, scouring, moisturizing, and opposition to fever, the quenching of thirst, speed of penetration, and washing; and there is no "stipticity" <note>astringency or bitterness</note> in it. Wherefore it does not reside nor get fixed in the pores and passages even if they are constricted; and there is no "adherence" in it, since it happens to be pressed out, and perhaps it scours the phlegm itself. And when its boiling is well done, it does not cause bloating at all. And the ancients went as far as where the "thinning" <note>original: "subtiliatio"</note> of a more subtle regimen is necessary: a regimen which is barley gruel and its water; and honey water with very much water, since its nourishment is small. And because it makes the water penetrate, and its moisturizing and scouring and its opening and its provocation are great, and its heat is broken. And it undoubtedly sometimes adds a certain something in strength, although it be small; and oxymel <note>original: "syrupus acetosus"</note> made from honey follows it, but it is grosser and more nourishing and of a stronger "cutting" <note>referring to the ability to break up thick humors</note> and scouring. And there is not in it that heat which causes harm to warm viscera, which is found in honey water. But now—

<margin>b And it follows it. That is, oxymel follows honey water, perhaps in the common use of the ancients; or in a subtle diet, because honey water is a more subtle diet than oxymel. And here was the order, by placing the order of the subtle diet. For he begins from the more subtle and comes to the less subtle. However, oxymel is more nourishing than honey water made with very much subtle water. This is because oxymel receives more honey than honey water, and as if thickened in boiling; but honey water remains subtle and watery. And thus oxymel is grosser. Rhazes, in the 17th book of the *Continens*, gives the proportion for honey water as one part honey and seven parts water. It should be considered that in four properties, oxymel exceeds honey water: first, because it is more nourishing; second, because it is more "cutting"; third, because it is more scouring; fourth, because it is more tempered in heat so that it does not cause inflammation. These things are noted. One might add a fifth: that he calls it "grosser." But you might say oxymel should cause more inflammation than honey water because it has more honey. Some say that because of the vinegar, it does not linger in the passages like honey water, though honey water also lingers little. Otherwise, it must be said that the vinegar tempers the heat of the honey. Or it must be said that he means "cane honey," which is sugar, when he speaks of oxymel made of honey. But when "honey water" is mentioned, it seems by usage to be understood as water of bee honey.</margin>

<margin>c But now. Because he had mentioned oxymel made of honey, he declares which honey: namely, from cane honey, which is sugar. For pure sugar, cleansed of its dregs, is properly called white. This is indeed better than bee honey, because it does not inflame in the same way, nor does it heat as much as honey. And although honey is a sufficiently tempered "manna," nevertheless it is manna collected by bees; and the labor of the bees in the honey causes some "imprinting," namely by heating, as Avicenna understands in the chapter on honey. And similarly, oxymel made from sugar is better than that made from bee honey, although it scours less.</margin>

<margin>d And let there be sufficiency. He makes us take notice because he praises honey water much, and afterwards he praises oxymel, specifically the sugary kind, much. What should be done in fevers regarding their use? He says, therefore, that the use of sugary oxymel should suffice for you; because in it there is sufficiency for those things we need in fevers—digestion, opening, scouring, and provocation—and inflammation is not feared from it as it is from honey water. Even if it is cane honey water, it is more flammable when it does not have vinegar. Because he had made you secure in its use, he reduces his boldness in its excessive use, because "scraping"—that is, the excoriation of the intestines from sharp vinegar—is feared. And this is feared as will appear at the end of the chapter on the regimen of acute fevers. Here can be brought in whatever was said by Hippocrates in the third book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases* regarding these drinks, and whatever Galen and others said, and what we say in the same place.</margin>

<margin>e And to the thinning. When he distinguished the types of feeding and regimen by giving examples of them, he shows in this chapter the things that indicate them. And first, in general, he shows which things indicate "thinning" the diet and which indicate "thickening" it. First in two parts: because first he shows what things indicate thinning the diet, second what things indicate thickening. There is "ba" and "thickening." The first in three, just as he posits three questions.</margin>

<column-break/>

he places first the "strength" <note>original: "virtutem"; the patient's vital force</note> which consents. Where the second: "and more worthy." Where the 3: "And of those." It should be considered that by "thinning of the regimen" he does not understand only a refined diet as opposed to a gross one, but we understand the reduction or rationing of the food itself. For every putrid fever indicates thinning—that is, a reduction of food compared to what is given in health. This is because of the "matter" <note>the diseased humors</note> themselves, for whose digestion and evacuation we want "Nature" <note>the body's internal healing power</note> to be free to work. It should be considered that because of the nature of the matter, some "gross" [thinkers] understand a diversity of matter; we say that some matter is subtle and some is gross, and that the nature of subtle matter indicates thinning. But if we consider well, all matter indicates thinning in the diet, but in this there is a diversity that was not here in the mind of Avicenna speaking generally. Therefore, the nature of the matter must be understood—that is, the matter itself; and for the first part: so that it depends on that, and this is what principally indicates thinning: namely, the matter. But the possibility of the strength [of the patient] consents; since Nature, without food—that is, with thinning—can digest, cleanse, and evaporate. And these discourses are understood in the first book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, commentary 44.

### —specifically cane honey, which is sugar; and properly purified sugar is better than bee honey, although its scouring is less than the scouring of honey; and similarly for oxymel made of sugar.

### And let there be sufficiency in oxymel. But perhaps it will cause one to incur "scraping" <note>original: "rafuram"; abrasion or ulceration</note> of the intestines, and this is indeed fearsome in acute illnesses; and we shall set down the drinking of barley water and a separate discourse on oxymel. And the thinning of the regimen of the sick person is signified by the nature of the matter, and the possibility of Nature in digesting it, resolving it, and evacuating it. And the most "worthy" of hours for thinning is the *status* <note>The peak or plateau stage of a disease</note>; for here is the intensity of Nature's occupation in the "battle" against the matter. And it is not fitting that, by withdrawing from it, Nature be occupied with another thing; and specifically near the *crisis* <note>The turning point of the disease</note>; for before that, the battle is not yet confirmed. And of those things which signify and make thinning relevant is if there be a necessity for phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note>, or a loosening of the belly, or clysters <note>enemas</note>, or the soothing of pain; then it is necessary that you give effort to preserving that necessity; then feed if food is necessary, unless there is something else prohibiting it. And the "thickening" of the regimen is signified or required by the "strength" <note>virtus</note>. And the most worthy of hours for thickening is the hour in which the strength is not greatly occupied with the matter; and this is the beginning of the illness. And it is necessary that the harm of that thickening be aided with "dispersion" <note>original: "sparsione"</note>; since it is—

<margin>f And more worthy. Here is an aphorism: that in the *status*—and he takes *status* here for the stage regarding the symptoms as is commonly seen—it concurs with the *status* regarding the digestion of the matter in diseases that keep the matter for a single expulsion. In this time, therefore, the physician ought to thin the diet more than in any other time; and the reason for it is posited: because all Nature is intent on the battle. And one should not occupy it with food either before the crisis or during the crisis. And you may bring in aphorism 38 to this place, and others upon that aphorism "to those, however, later," as if to say that before the *status*, a grosser diet could be fed. As Hippocrates says, "in the beginning, however, more abundantly refresh, so that the sick person may suffice."</margin>

<margin>g And of those. Here is the discourse of Hippocrates in the first book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases* and Rhazes in the 17th book of the *Continens*, chapter 4. It must be considered that this thinning is "particular": because it respects a determined hour in which it is necessary to bleed, to give an enema, or to loosen the belly; which things should not be done with crude food in the stomach; and this is what he meant by "give effort," etc. Know that the soothing of pain must happen as early as possible. For pain hinders feeding and agitates the food in the stomach; and therefore one must first intend the soothing of that pain. These things being completed, feed if it is necessary. Second, it should be considered "unless something is prohibiting": it can first be understood that you give effort to completing that necessity unless there is a prohibition; because due to a fall in strength and fear of syncope <note>fainting</note>, sometimes we feed before we bleed; just as it happens to those into whose stomach "cholera" <note>bile</note> flows. First, we also feed before we loosen the belly—that is, we first comfort the sick person with food, as in the third book of the *Canon*, section 7, chapter on the cure of syncope. And because the treatment creates a necessity for cleansing and you fear harm to the patient, so that you may comfort the stomach and for drinking, give fragrant wine; and feed with commendable food. Sometimes we are also compelled to feed before we give a clyster, as with certain men who are harmed by clysters by reason of the stomach for a known cause, among whom there is much sensitivity. Since immediately when the intestines are moved and evaporation happens in them, harm is caused in the stomach; and of these there is much sensitivity of the stomach. Under this intention, it is commanded in the book *On Acute Diseases*, 9th book of the *Continens*, first chapter, that a clyster should not be made with a full stomach. Sometimes also great weakness and pain compel feeding before the soothing of pain; here he therefore said "unless it be prohibiting," namely, prohibiting feeding. In another way it can be understood that, these necessities being completed and phlebotomy performed, the beginning of a paroxysm <note>a sudden attack or increase in symptoms</note> could supervene. Whence we are compelled not to feed except in case of need. And similarly, the belly having been loosened and a clyster given and pain soothed, something could supervene that would make food be postponed. Where [is] "g." It should be considered third that the necessity of these things in putrid fevers signifies a "repletion" <note>fullness/excess of humors</note> which indicates fasting and not being filled or fed; and therefore, unless there is a prohibition, one should first intend to complete these necessities.</margin>

<margin>h And the thickening. It should be considered that by "thickening" I do not understand a "gross diet" as opposed to other types of diet, but the feeding itself. For that which is given of food is not given except for the sake of "strength," so that the person may be nourished and not the disease. For the strength itself is the reason why we feed. As he said in the commentary on the Aphorisms. Look at the 3rd book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, Commentary 71. Just as the disease or the matter principally indicates thinning—that is, the removal of food—so the strength indicates thickening, and the disease is like a co-judge or co-consenter. But it is doubted whether Avicenna touched on these two modes of diet, the subtle and the gross. It must be said that he clearly touched on them when he prescribed two examples: namely, to give nothing (which is the ultimate in subtlety) and the food of healthy people; and when he proceeded toward "giving nothing," he called all this thinning; and when he began from "giving nothing" and gradually arrived at barley water...</margin>

<summary>This page details the dietary regimen for fever patients, focusing on the medicinal properties of barley water (ptisana), honey water, and oxymel (vinegar syrup). It establishes the crucial medical principle that food should be withheld or "thinned" during the peak (status) of a disease so that the body's vital force can focus entirely on fighting the illness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of dietary "thickening" and "thinning" in medical treatment, specifically transitioning from the types of food used to the frequency and quantity of meals based on the seasons of the year, following the teachings of Avicenna and Hippocrates.</meta>

Fen I Treatise I

**Column 1**

The whole is made subtle by washing twice, and so proceeding toward the food of healthy people, as was given to be understood. He will call this entire process "thickening." And it is worthier. It must be considered that thickening at the beginning of an illness is appropriately understood in a broad sense for every giving of food which is suitable at the onset, according to the diversity of the illnesses. In some types of thickening, therefore, there would be one of the grains; in another, a julep <note>original: "iuleb"; a sweet medicinal syrup</note>; in another, barley water; in another, chicken; and so on with others. And this gives you faith that Avicenna <note>referred to as "A." throughout</note> understands by "thickening" what we have said.

Here the question would arise whether the regimen <note>original: "regimen"; the prescribed way of life and diet</note> in a fever should proceed by thinning. This is a question we noted at length in the first [book of] Aphorisms, in the first chapter of the Fen, and in the fourth [part of] the *Conciliator* <note>original: "conciliatō"; likely referring to Pietro d'Abano's *Conciliator*, a famous medical text reconciling contradictions</note>; that distinction is discussed diffusely in section 134. And let us say briefly here that in fevers in which we expect a cure and which preserve the matter for expulsion through a crisis <note>original: "expulsionē vā cretica"; the "critical" turning point of a disease</note>, we thicken the regimen from the beginning; we proceed by thinning until the "state" <note>original: "statu"; the peak or plateau of the illness</note>, and this is commonly called the "universal regimen." Therefore, the worthier time for thickening is the beginning, because it is distant from the peak and the struggle of the disease. Hence, the vital power is not much occupied with the matter, as Avicenna says. Sometimes, however, it happens in the form of a "particular regimen" that we thin at the beginning. And in the chapter [it says] that because of a defect of the power, we sometimes thicken at the peak; and this is called a "particular regimen," following the particular dispositions that indicate it. It should be considered that although it is necessary to diet more "grossly" <note>i.e., with heavier food</note> at the start of fevers, this dictation is not entirely free from harm. But our harm is that by which the power is prevented from being sustained for the struggle at the hour of the peak; therefore, it is better to proceed by degrees from the beginning than to give [food] at the peak or near the peak. And because in the beginning food generates harm, Avicenna succors that harm with "scattering" <note>original: "sparsione"</note>, which some have explained as "with gradual evacuation," and sometimes with "friction" and "division" <note>original: "mētū," likely *minutionem* or *partitionem*</note>, that is, with the partitioning of food into several parts, because it will weigh less heavily upon the vital power and distract it less from the digestion of the matter which it must perform. And this is what he means when he says "because it is again lighter upon the power"; by the manner of speaking "again," Avicenna hints that there is another cause than the one he first set down. The first cause, therefore, is that food divided into small amounts given in turn is more easily overcome and multiplies the bad matter less. The second cause is that it weighs too much upon the power, whence nature is removed from the digestion of the matter; and therefore he says "again."

->It is lighter upon the power again. **And summer** indeed, on account of its resolution, requires the addition of feeding and its separation: for the vital power is not sufficient to digest that which is a great deal at one time. And since the resolution in it is through scattering, then it is necessary that the replacement be through scattering.<-

<margin>a</margin> **And summer.** He places the appropriate feeding and the choice of the specific kind of diet in more specific discourses or chapters. 1. First he gives the cause of feeding according to the times of the year. 2. Second, according to the kinds of illness. Third, according to the diverse disposition of the vital power. Fourth, according to the complexion. Fifth, according to age. There [he says] "And when you understand." There the 3rd. "And sometimes," there the 4th. "And concerning bodies," there the 5th. "And the elderly." First he begins with the cause of feedings in summer. And he intends that one should add to the number of feedings according to how frequently one eats, and he gives two causes. The first is because in summer the power is weak because of the resolution <note>original: "resolutionē"; the depletion or thinning of the body's humors and fluids caused by heat</note> caused by the heat, which cannot digest large quantities at one single time; therefore, let one be fed at several times. The second cause is that resolution in summer is almost continuous; and this is what he means by "on account of scattering," therefore it is necessary that the replacement—that is, the restoration—be through scattering, that is, almost continuous. It must be such, however, that one food does not hinder the other food in digestion. Now, from this it would be proved that a person ought to be fed continuously. But because food would hinder food in digestion in the stomach, one cannot eat continuously; but so frequently that there is, as it were, a continuous succession of nourishment to the limb.

->**And in winter** it is the opposite: because on account of the smallness of its resolution, it does not require much replacement in digestion. Furthermore, if one gives much replacement suddenly, [the body] will be tolerant of it and strong in its expulsion.<-

<margin>b</margin> **And in winter.** This is the chapter on feeding in winter. And he intends that the opposite should happen: that a person should be fed rarely and at few times, but more copiously at one time. And this is for causes opposite to the two causes predicted in summer. The first cause is opposed to the second: because in winter resolution is small, as a person is not so continuously depleted; therefore a person does not need much replacement, that is, at many times. The second cause is opposite to the first: because in winter the power is strong to tolerate food given suddenly—that is, in a large quantity and at few times. Indeed, he calls this "suddenly" and says that it is strong in its expulsion, which can be explained in three ways. First, for driving it into the limbs. Second, for expelling its superfluities. Third, because after the food is expelled through all digestions, the power remains strong for a long time because the limbs are not dissolved in that season. 

There is a doubt first about the cause which Avicenna gives to prove that one should be fed frequently in summer, but rarely in winter. For he says that resolution is through "scattering," that is, almost continuous. But it seems to be continuous in winter as well. For the air inhabiting us continuously depletes us. For the air in all dispositions depletes on account of what is in it from the power of the sun and stars, as in the first chapter of the Fen 2. If you should say that it depletes only a little, it suffices for me that it is continuous, and thus that the replacement should be as continuous as possible. Furthermore, it seems that a person is depleted more in winter, because the principal depleter is the natural heat, and this is stronger in winter, as appears in the commentary on the Aphorism "In winter, the bellies [are naturally hottest]." And furthermore, bodies ought more to be prepared for sweat—that is, to artificially open the pores and sweat—less in summer than in winter. For all the ancients said so, as in Aristotle's *Problems*, book 2, the first problem. If resolution were greater in summer, it would not be necessary to add the aids of art to it. 

Let us say, therefore, that these chapters are common to both the healthy and the feverish; indeed, they only prove things about the feverish by a disposition similar to the healthy in these times. Second, let us say that these chapters are true in bodies in which a weakening of power occurs in summer through resolution, and in winter a strengthening of heat through aggregation, or at least not a weakening through dissolution. For a body that would be mortified by cold in winter could not tolerate food at one time; and a body that would be invigorated by heat in summer—such as the body of a cold old man—would tolerate a larger quantity of food in summer than in winter. Let us say, therefore, that the heat of the air continuously alters us. And because in summer it is an active heat, first it immediately dissolves us—that is, it opens the pores and depletes us. Second, by sharpening our own heat, it makes it more depleting. Therefore we are continuously depleted in summer, and thus we need continuous restoration and replacement. And as much as it is possible for nourishment to be carried continuously into the limbs, it is better: first, so that they may continuously succumb to loss; second, so that the burning of the heat may be tempered by the food. And this happens by continuous feeding—that is, frequent, in the possible manner, as has been said. In winter, however, the opposite must be said, as is apparent, nor is it necessary to prolong the discourse. Fourth, we will say that the resolution made in summer is greater in quantity, both the helpful and the superfluous being turned into vapor alike; nor does the heat of the air distinguish

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

between the harmful and the useful in resolution. Nor does the natural heat of foreign things distinguish; it happens therefore that good things are depleted, and so it happens both that bad parts remain and parts of the good things that remain are corrupted and made bad by foreign heat. But in winter, the hidden resolution—by which only superfluities separated from the useful are resolved imperceptibly—is naturally smaller, whence those things which ought to go through the urine to the skin are not drawn out; but only the superfluities of digestion, dissolved or resolved imperceptibly, recede from us. The violence of heat, however, also draws superfluities toward the skin that ought to recede elsewhere; and then these useful things are resolved. 

But as for why it appears that we ought to prepare for sweat more in summer: because one should provoke it with some loosening agent. In winter, however, it is less ready, as someone might say, because in winter there is fear of the striking of the sweating parts by the cold of the air, which is not so in summer. In Aristotle's *Problems*, book 2, problem 34, resumed, where he expresses his intention more clearly, he gives another cause. He says that in winter one ought to prepare for sweat less, because the moist superfluities in us are digested and exhaled by the heat drawn inward. With all such moist things, or most of them, being consumed, the body does not need an "attempted" expulsion—that is, one made through effort, namely by art producing sweat. But in summer, with the natural heat resolved and the flesh made thin, our moist things are not well digested; rather, those that do not remain are corrupted; and therefore such moist things need "haution," that is, the stated extraction. And Hippocrates adds our discourses. And with these the last arguments cease; and you should bring to this place whatever we said on the Aphorisms, part 1, "In winter, the bellies," where we said many things about winter and summer resolutions and explained them in our way. Second, the aforementioned *Problems* of Aristotle. 

To the argument, it must be said that the argument commits a fallacy on account of the question of the continuity of resolution. For, although it is not to the purpose, let us say first with a common foundation that just as nutrition is continuous regarding dispositions, so regarding the induction of form it is discontinuous: because the induction of form happens in an instant, as is commonly believed. Thus resolution, which is the corruption of the moist parts or the limbs that are nourished—or also of some inanimate parts—which having been turned into vapor depart, is a continuous action regarding disposition, and happens in time; but regarding the removal of form, it happens in an instant. And just as with strong natural nutritive heat exiting in the space of one natural day, as in an example, more nourished things arise from its action; so they will be more frequent, and with weak heat fewer, although the action of both is continuous in all time. Thus, with the heat of the air being strong, as in summer, in one natural day there will be more resolved things of flesh and good nourishment than in one natural day of winter, and we need more frequent replacement, as has been said. If you wished to hold that resolution and nutrition, regarding the induction of substantial form, are continuous acts as we held elsewhere, you could also save Avicenna’s opinion in this: that winter resolution is with few parts of the good parts. Whence food given once can suffice for a long reapposition. But let us not prolong this now, because they are very profound.

It is doubted whether the total food which a man takes in summer at several times in one natural day is more than the total food which he takes at few times in the same space of time. And it seems that it is more, according to Avicenna, when he says summer needs "addition and separation." He says "addition" regarding quantity, and "separation" regarding number. Furthermore, in summer there is a greater resolution of both the good and the smoky moisture; therefore we need a greater restoration. To the contrary is Hippocrates in the Aphorisms, when he says "in these times, therefore, more offerings," etc. Francis of Piedmont holds that the total quantity of food which we give in summer is greater than the total quantity which we give in winter. And he proves this through Avicenna here, for through the reason brought forward his opinion is strengthened: for frequent and great resolution indicates a frequent and great amount of replacement, and thus a multiplication of food; but there is great resolution in summer. Therefore without doubt it will not be found [otherwise]. B. [Another] authority is against this opinion, which authority could not be explained. But Maimonides <note>original: "Rabi moyses"</note> in his commentary on the Aphorisms, part 2: "And that food once or twice," where we have seen the translation, says thus to the letter: "Summer is the time in which food ought to be given several times and in smaller quantity of whatever he eats at all times." This seemed to be signaled by the Hebrew letter in all those together, and was not referred to any one of them; for that seemed certain. 

And although demonstrations cannot be brought forward for that opinion of Maimonides, yet it can probably be proved that bodies, from the nature of summer, have in themselves more superfluities corrupted by the nature of winter. Therefore from this the body needs a smaller quantity of total food. The consequence is noted from the commentary on the aforementioned Aphorism. And it is known from the sayings according to the opinion of Aristotle, *Problems* 2, problem 7, in the commentary on the Aphorism "In winter, the bellies." Furthermore, the power that transforms food is much stronger in winter than in summer; therefore it can sustain a greater mass of food. This reason would not be solved by the adversary: because a weak agent in a long time will be able to do as much as a strong one in a short time; and he will take the long time as the space of all the digestions multiplied according to the multiple number of feedings in summer. And to this solution, he will say that the natural heat in summer is called weak: so that in all those times in which one is fed and digests, it cannot digest as much food as it digests in those few winter times. 

And without doubt we have learned this by the experience of certain gluttons known to us: that in winter they eat in the night before day, and before the third hour, and at the third hour, and at the ninth, and in the evening. And when they wanted to eat the same quantity of food as frequently in summer, they could not do so without notable distress. This is an example through experience by which you will know: that in winter a greater quantity of food is tolerated in all feedings than in summer. It should be noted, however, that some drink that is quickly digestible and quickly passing could be tolerated in summer more and in a greater quantity than in winter. And it appears less that a larger quantity of it could be given in summer and at more times than in winter; through experience we see that well-disposed bodies, and even more so the bodies of the feverish, tolerate a greater quantity of drink in summer than in winter. And this Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"</note> seems to feel in the 17th book of the *Continens*, in the chapter on air, when he says: "Then in summer use moist things and wines, used much and well diluted." To the contrary things it must be said that Avicenna, when he says "addition," means "separation"; and when he says "it does not require much replacement in digestion," he means "at many times."

To the other, it is said that it is one thing for it to be indicated to be done, and another for it to be indicated that it *can* be done. There is no doubt that summer imposes the necessity of much food: because much good moisture is consumed; in winter, little, for the opposite cause. But we cannot do this: because in summer the power is weak; in winter, however, the power is strong. Therefore we can do this. And then to the argument, it must be said that summer, on the part of resolution, indicates more food than winter; but on the part of the weak power, it cannot transform it, and thus indicates less. But you would say, if winter indicates giving little food, why then did we give much? It must be said that it indicates little should be given, but the strong power, being able to digest much, indicates much. Also, unless there is copious blood and spirit, it will be overcome by the cold of the air, as in the commentary on the Aphorism "In winter, the bellies."

<margin>c</margin> ->**And autumn.** Here he places the chapter on the appropriate diet in autumn. It must be considered that, as Avicenna wishes in autumn, in his chapter, we consider how we may order the regimen. One<-

<summary>This page discusses the seasonal adjustments required for a patient's diet, contrasting the frequent, small meals needed in summer due to body depletion (resolution) with the larger, less frequent meals tolerated in winter due to stronger internal heat. It navigates conflicting medical opinions from Maimonides and Aristotle regarding whether total food intake should be higher or lower in these seasons.</summary>
