<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of medical "regimen"—the prescribed diet and lifestyle for a patient—focusing on how a physician must balance the "thinning" of food (making it light and easily digestible) against the patient’s "virtue" (vital strength). It specifically addresses the influences of the seasons, particularly autumn and spring, on the body's humors and strength.</meta>

### Book

**Column 1**

...is the weakness of virtue <note>original: "virtutis"; the body's innate vital power or strength</note>. Because autumn is a bad season that weakens virtue, as appears in the first Fen, the second [treatise] on the pulse, in the chapter on the seasons of the year. The second reason is the repletion <note>over-fullness</note> of corrupt humors; because of this, autumn is also a bad time. For it resembles a disease of corruption, as in the commentary on the Aphorisms. And for these reasons, the first [consideration] indicates feeding and adding to the food <insert>thus thickening, that is,</insert> so that the weak virtue may be comforted by food. The second, however, namely the repletion of corrupt humors, indicates the thinning and scarcity of food; because for corruption, cutting away and evacuation are necessary, not repletion, as in the commentary on the Aphorisms. The aforementioned is taken from the Greek translation. It is necessary, therefore, that the diet in this [season] be thinned; but because of the defect of virtue, one shall be fed frequently, though because of the corruption, only a little food shall be given. Therefore, when compared to summer and winter, it will hold a middle way between them, as authors commonly hold or concede. For we do not feed as frequently as in summer, nor as few times as in winter; nor shall we give as much food as in winter, nor as little as in summer. For now the heat begins to gather again and is prohibited from dissolving compared to summer; according to this, the masters hold that virtue is stronger than in summer and weaker than in winter. And this would be the place for consideration; this, therefore, Avicenna <note>referred to as "A."</note> intended when he said "to spread out," that is, frequently, and "little by little," that is, a small amount is better; and then he gave the general cause as noted. It is doubted why he did not speak of spring. It must be said that he gave it to be understood in the same way as autumn. For its disposition is midway between summer and winter; and therefore we give less food in spring than in winter, and more than in summer. But Dynus <note>Dynus del Garbo, a famous 14th-century medical commentator</note> says that from spring and other seasons, an indication can be taken in two ways: in one way as they are the cause of the bodily disposition, namely of repletion, and thus since spring is a cause of repletion—and similarly of a disease of repletion as Galen said in the commentary on the Aphorisms—a little food is appropriate in

### spring. In another way, as it is the cause of the disposition of virtue and the resolution of the body: for the sake of which feeding occurs. And in this way, spring indicates much food just as winter does, though not so much, because virtue is strong and little resolution has occurred. Dynus could have said this more sweetly by saying that the feeding of spring is partly preventative or preservative, of which Avicenna speaks in the first [book of the] Canon, Fen 2, in that chapter "Hot Air," and Rhasis <note>the Persian physician Al-Razi</note> in the 17th [book] of the *Continens* in the chapter on air. And thus in spring we give little food because we perform bloodletting and evacuation. Another feeding is for men already healthy, not those in a neutral state; and this is copious, of which the aphorism "bellies in winter" speaks.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ **And you should know.** This can be inferred from the aforesaid: that in autumn, considering the corruption of humors, we should thin [the diet] greatly; but considering virtue, we cannot, because it would fail greatly. And it could be a certain rule by itself. And I will say that he has already established the cause of feeding according to the seasons of the year; here he places it according to diseases: first in general, then specifically according to the species of diseases. In the first part, he wishes that based on the indication taken from the disease we would give no food; but virtue does not suffer this, but rather fails in many diseases, and when it fails, the cure is of no value. For "the physician is the virtue," etc. As you knew in the preceding chapter and in the beginning of the first book: where the operating virtues are known, and the operations of medicines are known, which act when moved by virtue.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ **And when you have understood.** Here he places the rule for diet according to the types of illness: such as illnesses or fevers, some being very acute, some absolutely acute, and some chronic, as Galen says in the second and third [books] of the *Prognostics* and the third of *Crises*. And first, he sets the rule for the regimen of very acute illnesses; second, for absolutely acute ones; third, for chronic ones. Fourth, he gives the cause in feeding which is from the beginning in comparison to the "state" <note>the peak of the illness</note>. It must be considered what was said about the types of regimen: that unless we respected virtue, we would thin [the diet] to the ultimate degree. It follows that if there is any illness in which we do not care for virtue, the cure which is through food is this: that in that illness all food can be prohibited. Secondly, it must be considered that there are two things which indicate that food should not be given here. One is primary, the nature of the illness: because a very acute illness reaches its peak quickly. The other is a co-indicator or consenting factor: such as a strong virtue, which you estimate will not fail in this time, even if no food is given, or if no thick food is given, but only pomegranate wine or a very thin julep is given. And he says "you shall estimate" because all judgments finalized for action are estimates. Thirdly, it must be considered that he gives the cause or rule: for the physician must, as much as possible, alienate occupation from the virtue and exercise it upon the matter <note>the disease-causing substance</note>. If, therefore, you indicated that the patient can stand without food or at least without thick food until the crisis, it is bad to feed him during the struggle. Fourthly, it must be considered why he said "with the dismissal of food." There is no other thinning than that. It must be said: at least with the dismissal of all thick food. Or he said it might suffice to drink pure water, lukewarm, hot, or cold as it seems to you. Fifthly, it must be considered that "properly on the day of crisis" he said this because if you are in doubt about feeding, and it does not seem to you that anything should be given in a very acute fever, do so from the beginning of the days, so that you are not forced to feed him at the hour of the crisis.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ **And if you see** that the illness is acute and finishes in 14 days: the regimen, therefore, not being thinned in the extreme, can be to give a *ptisana* <note>barley water</note> or something from the category of highly thinned diets toward the ultimate thinning, which is to give nothing, properly on the day of crisis, which is the day of battle, unless for a very great cause, namely because of a collapse of virtue by way of resolution. For when factors that dissolve virtue happen, food must be given immediately, as Galen says.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ **And if you see.** By "chronic illness" or one nearly chronic, he understood a "tropic" or "convertible" acute illness which is long, up to 40 days;

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

...as Galen says in the first of the *Prognostics* and the 60th [chapter] of *Crises*. But take this rhetorical example: Dalyabatis, in the third [book] of *Practice* in the chapter on the regimen of the body through food, who by the authority of the ancients likens the physician to a traveler, the disease to the journey (that is, the length of the road), and the virtue of the sick person to his expenses. Just as a traveler estimates his expenses according to the length or shortness of the road, so the physician does, etc., and it is well known. It must be considered that these species of regimen mentioned above can be adapted to three species of fevers: for the very acute, the most thin diet is appropriate; for the absolutely acute, a middle diet; for the chronic, a thick diet, or one declining toward thick. And here the masters make a multiple distinction of thick and middle fever diets. For first, some such diets are so called because foods are compared to one another in the quantity or scarcity of nutrition, and they call that division of diet taken from the part of the matter; which division they say is the one Avicenna set down above. Secondly, some call them such in respect to the illness: so that what is suitable for the very acute is called thin, for the acute is called middle, and for the chronic is called thick. Thirdly, some are called such in respect to the virtue related to the "state" <note>the peak</note>: so a diet that can lead the sick person to the state is called middle; one that cannot is called thin; one that can lead beyond it is called thick. Fourthly, some say that thin diets are those which proceed toward the food of the healthy. The closer it is to healthy food, the thicker it is; the further away, the thinner. And thus everything given as food, in

### asmuch as it is less or involves some deprivation, is called a thin diet; whereas something substantial that is given is called thick. No more on this, especially since these should be done at the beginning, in the first chapter of Fen 4 of the first Canon.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ **Again.** Here is the rule of feeding from the beginning toward the "state," which wishes that one proceed gradually by thinning in respect to what was given at the beginning. It must be considered that he said "in all species": thus in the beginning [of a very acute fever] you gave a julep, in the increase you will give pomegranate wine, and in the "state" nothing. In absolutely acute fevers, in the beginning you gave *ptisana*, in the progress a julep, and in the state nothing, specifically in the hour of crisis. In chronic ones, if at the beginning you gave chicken, in the progress barley meal, in the state you will give *ptisana*—if the state occupies several or many days. These are said by way of example and estimated judgment. Avicenna assigns the cause of this gradation of diet. It must be considered that when we wish to temper some illness, either because a crisis is not expected or is far from the beginning, we thin the diet. Then again we thicken it, as he wishes where he adds in the chapter on quartan, sextan, and quotidian [fevers].

<margin>f</margin> ¶ **And when you know.** This can be a rule even in the preceding part where he allowed a thin diet or one near to it; and he wishes that all this be done with virtue inspected: because if virtue were strong, the patient can stand for one week with very little food—indeed, a julep alone may suffice. And if you fear that giving a julep would not suffice, but something a little more is required, give barley water; because it would nourish more than a julep, as Avicenna understood above. Truly we believe that Avicenna's mind was that in great collapses of virtue, one should be succored not only with barley water, but even with meat and wine, as appears in the third Canon, Fen 7. But this term is very specific: namely, where the sick person's virtue is sustained by very little food; if a julep is not enough, let barley water or barley *ptisana* be given. This must be considered specifically in fevers involving abscesses <note>original: "apostematum"; internal swellings or inflammations</note>, because in these we must attenuate [the diet] much so that the matter is diverted from its course toward the abscessed part, making the body "greedy" <note>literally "avaricious"</note> through abstinence from food. Hence, in an abscess of the rectum, Avicenna makes the patient fast for two days, as appears in the third Canon, Fen 6.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ **And when you are ambiguous.** This is the second rule annexed to the premises. For someone might say to me, "The type of illness is not immediately known to me from the first day; what then shall I do regarding the diet?" And he says that it is better to thin the regimen than to thicken it, provided the virtue consents. And this is what he means by "observing the virtue," namely, considering and maintaining the virtue and its "tolerance," that is, that the sick person could tolerate it.

<margin>h</margin> ¶ **And from this is solved the question** of whether it is better to thin or thicken the regimen. He says that thinning is better while virtue stands, that is, with virtue consenting. And this solution, although it is "thick" <note>simple or broad</note>, is nonetheless the best possible; although we have prolonged the discourse on this at length along with our predecessors on the first part of the Aphorisms, one must finally arrive at this solution. But you might say "tolerance of virtue" depends on the length of the disease, but we already presuppose that I do not know the type of disease. It must be said that the physician has some greater conjecture about this than a layman; and therefore he forms an opinion about the duration of the disease, and according to that he measures the tolerance of virtue. If you were to say, "Suppose the physician knows nothing," it must be said that in this case no good rule can be given. What therefore will he do? He will act by chance like an old woman. But such an estimation would rarely fail in [actual] cases. Suppose a fever ought to be long, lasting 40 days: which is the greater error—that the physician feeds the patient at the beginning more thinly than necessary, thinking it short; or that he feeds him more thickly than necessary, thinking...

### Fen 1, Treatise

**Column 1**

...that it is more extensive or longer. Second, he posits that some fevers might last 14 days; which is the greater error: for the physician to "thin" <note>to prescribe a very light, watery diet</note> the regimen more than he ought, believing the fever will end in seven days, or to "thicken" <note>to prescribe a heartier diet</note> it more, believing it will end in 30 days? We have spoken of these matters in the first [commentary on the] Aphorisms. Galen gives us a certain principle on this in the first [book] of *On Crises*, chapter 16. And the general cause of this rule is in the preceding chapter, where he said: "If you are ignorant of the [type of] fever, thin the regimen."

<margin>a</margin> **A**nd of that. This is the third rule annexed to the aforementioned; omitting the expositions of others, I will say that Avicenna <note>original: "auic."</note> seems to feel that one of the ancients was of the opinion that in a fever—however acute—arising from "thin choleric matter" <note>yellow bile that is thin in consistency</note>, food ought to be given. This is so that the "virtue" <note>original: "virtus"; the body's innate vital strength</note> may be comforted with food, and this for secondary reasons. First, because that matter of the fever is thin; therefore, the intention is not [to wait for] its digestion. In response: if the virtue digests the food, and does not attend to digesting the [fever-causing] matters, it is of no concern. The second reason is because the intention is not the evacuation of the matter; in response: since you wish it to be done by nature, or you wish to do it yourself if nature does not, yet in the act of evacuation it is necessary for the virtue to be strong; and thus food must be given.

->**R**egarding the addition, you observing the strength and tolerance [of the patient]. And regarding him who thought that feeding in an acute fever is better because there is no intention in the digestion; in response: regarding evacuation, whether you wish nature to do it or not, I know an error has already been made; rather, when you fear a collapse of virtue, then feeding is better.<-

->**A**nd regarding bodies, there are choleric bodies <note>people of a hot and dry temperament</note> which require a regimen different from that which we have described; specifically when they are accustomed to eating a great deal. For when they are not fed, at least in the very beginning of the fever, or rather in the hour which is worse—which is the hour of the "status" <note>the peak or plateau of the fever</note>—their dispositions are not free from two things...<-

<margin>b</margin> **A**nd regarding bodies. Here he posits the rule of feeding according to certain habits or complexions <note>the balance of the four humors</note>; first of the whole body, second of the parts. There he says: "And of those, there are..." The first rule is in three parts, just as he posits three rules in feeding according to three complexions or habits. There he says: "And there are..." and the third: "And every..." Regarding the first rule, it is doubted whether choleric bodies require a contrary regimen to what we said. It seems not, for many such things exist. In response: we would do this in many cases, yet it rarely happens that this is done. Furthermore, a dry complexion needs to be preserved by dry things, just as a moist one by moist things. Hence, a moist diet is suitable for those who are infirm and **F**at; therefore, this person [the choleric] ought not to be moistened by food. Rufus <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a Roman-era physician</note> says that this applies when they are accustomed to eating a great deal. Against this is Galen in the first [book] of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, commentary 44, where, in providing two examples, he posits the one whose regimen he wishes to be thinned is accustomed to eating a great deal. And it seems fitting that eating a great deal is a sign of great "repletion" <note>fullness of the humors</note>; and since where there is great repletion food is not suitable, it is rather more suitable not to be fed. It must be said first that the "choleric bodies" spoken of here are "exuberant" bodies: they are hot, dry, lean, very prone to "resolution" <note>the dissipation of vital heat and fluids</note>, and led a life of much exercise and wakefulness. This is the "young man" of whom Galen speaks in the third chapter of his *Therapeutics* and the second chapter of the book *On Crises*. Therefore, not all choleric bodies are such, but only some; and such was Avicenna's way of speaking, for he did not say "all choleric bodies," but said "And regarding [some] bodies," meaning certain choleric ones. Second, it must be said that the regimen mentioned above by Avicenna was that the "paroxysm" <note>the periodic fit or peak of the fever</note> should occur with an empty stomach; that the patient should not be fed during the hour of the paroxysm, nor while the paroxysm persists. It was also held that while a very acute fever exists, the man should not be fed; indeed, food should be taken away. These choleric bodies, therefore, need a regimen different from this: we can feed them at the beginning of the paroxysm, while the paroxysm persists, and whenever it is about to happen; at whatever hour of the paroxysm we encounter them, if they have not been fed, we feed them. Hence, in the fifth chapter of the *Therapeutics*, Galen says of them that we may feed them harmlessly at any time of the paroxysm, though less harmlessly during its "declination" <note>the period when the fever fit begins to fade</note>. Here, however, Avicenna treats the fact that whether in the beginning, the increase, or at any time, we are compelled to feed these people. And he argues thus: these choleric bodies are either weak in virtue because of the great action of resolution and inflammation—and then, with the fever coming on, a "syncope" <note>fainting or sudden loss of strength</note> overtakes them by way of resolution, and they die suddenly during the paroxysm—or they are strong, with a strength that resists syncope and sudden death during the hour of the paroxysm. In the latter case, since they are dry and inflammable, they fall into "hectic" <note>original: "ethicam"; a wasting fever</note> and "arefaction" <note>drying out</note>; they take on a "pinched face" <note>original: "facies tornatilis"; the hollowed, sharp-featured look of the dying, known as the Hippocratic facies</note> such as Hippocrates describes in the first [book] of *Prognostics*. Thus was the patient mentioned above: because in previous times the fever was still strong, he became parched through fever and abstinence, with a pinched face, and later fainted. If there had been the feeding that Galen performed, he would have died in that syncope; and from this it is known that the man had been in that state until that day. But if you give food to choleric bodies of this kind—whether during the hour of the paroxysm, or immediately before it is about to come, or during the paroxysm itself, or at the beginning of the acute fever—the dryness or the sharpness of the heat is lessened, and its resolution, syncope, and drying out are prevented. Therefore, it is appropriate, contrary to the form of the rules stated above, to feed them. To the first contrary [argument], the solution is clear.

**T**o the second, it will be said that this happens because the fear [of syncope] outweighs the natural complexion. To the third, some say that the text of Galen is false. Otherwise, a man accustomed to much food is in need of it; and such a man is one of "dissolution" and "resolution" of much food, for whom much repletion does not occur from this...

...nor is he attacked by it, nor does he have a great deal of dregs <note>waste matter in the bowels</note>. ...[The text] returns to the day. It is doubted, secondly, whether the hour of the "status" <note>the peak</note> is a worse hour for feeding than the hour of the beginning of the paroxysm. It seems not, according to Galen in the penultimate commentary of the first [book] of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*. To the contrary is Avicenna. Some say that Avicenna speaks here of the "universal" beginning and status—as if he wished to say that if a continuous, very acute fever were occurring in these people, we ought to feed them not only at its beginning but at its peak. Thus the universal peak is "worse." Avicenna presupposes, as is known, that we can feed them from the beginning of the paroxysm and also at the peak. Others say—namely Thaddeus <note>Thaddeus of Florence</note> on that aphorism "In paroxysms"—that this letter is corrupt; he wants to say "rather in the hour which is worse," which is the hour of the status. For the feverish heat is then great.

Others say—namely the Conciliator <note>Peter of Abano</note>—that the harm of feeding at the beginning of the paroxysm is greater than at [the peak?], because it extends through more times. But the harm at the peak is greater "intensively" <note>in terms of intensity</note>; it hurts more at the peak of the paroxysm since it is more vehement than the fever. And Thaddeus suggests this same solution. Another is the explanation of Dino [del Garbo] and Mundinus: it is that he speaks here of the beginning and peak of the paroxysm when he says that the hour of the peak is "worse," yet he does not say it is worse "for feeding." Rather, he understood that it is worse regarding the "accidents of arefaction" <note>symptoms of drying out</note>; because consumption and drying out happen more at the peak of the paroxysm than at the beginning. And we shall state this exposition by expanding it: that he speaks here of the universal times of an acute fever when it happens to these choleric bodies; or even of the particular times of the paroxysm when an "interpellation" <note>an interruption or interval</note> comes to them, as was in Galen's example. And let us say that in the very beginning of an acute fever one ought not to feed, but give a "julep" <note>a sweet medicinal drink</note>; but rather "farre" <note>spelt or grain</note> of barley or "ptisan" <note>barley water</note> according to what seems best to you. And similarly at the beginning of a paroxysm: not only at the beginning, but at the universal or particular peak we can feed. For the peak is the worse hour for making all "accidents" <note>symptoms</note> happen that are apt to occur to these people by way of resolution: such as syncope, sudden death, and drying out. Indeed, even the "declination" <note>fading</note> of the paroxysm is worse than the beginning of the paroxysm in causing death by way of resolution, as appears in the second chapter of the third book *On Crises*; and below in Fen 2, regarding the hour and times of death, when the times are "depressed" <note>low or weakened</note>. It should be considered that there is a triple [regimen]... It should be considered that a double mode of syncope <note>fainting/collapse</note> can happen to these cholerics. One is by way of the resolution of heat; this happens more as the paroxysm proceeds than at the beginning. The other is by way of the "flux of bile" to the stomach itself; and this happens much at the beginning of the paroxysm, because that is the hour of agitation in the internal parts. When, therefore, Avicenna had understood the first [kind], regarding syncope by way of resolution, he said [what he said]; perhaps because it can overtake certain people. It is doubted, given the aforementioned case for those with fevers: what is better—to anticipate the paroxysm immediately with food, or to feed at the beginning of the paroxysm, or in the "augmentation" <note>increase</note>, or at the peak? It must be said that in these people, it is necessary that the fever does not find the stomach empty of food. Therefore, [feeding] before the paroxysm, yet very close to it, is less bad, so that the food has begun some digestion. And if an error is made, at whatever time you encounter him, feed him. Thus did Galen in the second book of *Therapeutics* and in the book *On Causes* for those with "catarrhs." Otherwise, it could be said that in these people there could be refreshment to [block] the path of the descent of bile to the stomach; then it is necessary to feed a short time before the paroxysm or at the very beginning of the paroxysm, so that the bile flowing to the stomach does not find the stomach bare, but finds food with which it may be mixed, by which it may be evacuated, and by which same food the stomach may be comforted.
</gloss>

**I**f, however, the fear is by way of "resolution" and drying out, one must feed immediately before the paroxysm so that the feverish heat finds the body moistened by the nearby vapors of the food and the food in the stomach. Then the physician should consider, as the paroxysm comes on: if he sees dryness and weakness being added, it is a sign that the food given before the paroxysm is not sufficient. Therefore, let him give food again at that hour when he sees the necessity; and such necessity will be more apparent at the "status" <note>the peak</note>. However, if it could be deferred without danger to the "inclination" <note>the waning of the fever fit</note>, that would be a more suitable hour, as Galen said in the *Therapeutics*.

<margin>c</margin> **A**nd there are. It is doubted concerning this rule: since these are hot and moist bodies, they should be able to tolerate being without food, as Galen said in the 8th book of *Therapeutics*. It must be said that bodies of "exuberant flesh" <note>plump or muscular bodies</note> are either "rare" <note>porous</note> and prone to resolution—and of these Avicenna speaks here—or they are dense in their pores, and these tolerate hunger. There could also be in some fleshy people some special disposition of the stomach or an aptitude for resolution and weakness. Hence, in such a person, he would not tolerate being without food.

<margin>d</margin> **A**nd every. It is doubted concerning this rule, because regimens should be contrary to the dispositions [of the patient]. If, therefore, one person could not tolerate being without food, the other [opposite type] ought to tolerate it. Furthermore, weak "innate heat" <note>the natural vital heat of the body</note> resolves very little; therefore, [such a person] should tolerate being without food. Furthermore, the elderly easily bear fasting, and yet they have weak heat. Again, much heat shows that much blood is being "cooked" <note>metabolized</note>; and such a person tolerates being without food.

**I**t must be said that Avicenna understands by these people "children" and the "decrepit." Children, whose heat is strong—either in "quality" <note>intensity</note> or "quantity" <note>abundance</note>. He says this because of the diversity of opinions regarding the complexion of a child versus a youth. Or, by "strong," he understands choleric bodies. Or he says "strong" in action and "abundant" in form. Or he says "strong" in regard to youths, and "abundant" in regard to children. It seems, however, that he means the same thing by "stronger" and "more abundant," because he opposes it to "weak." Whichever way our speech is explained, it is known to him. By saying "or the innate heat is very weak," he understood the "decrepit" <note>the very aged</note> and not just the "elderly"; thus the penultimate argument ceases. Let us say, therefore, that children, who have much heat prone to resolution, cannot go without food, as the Aphorism of Hippocrates says. The decrepit, however, are like a lamp ready to be extinguished; and therefore they cannot go without food. But in both, there is a difference in the ability to go without food: for the decrepit need a little food frequently, but children need more food and also need it frequently. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion regarding the administration of food and drink to feverish patients. It specifically addresses how the body’s "innate heat" and "humors" (like yellow bile) dictate when a patient should eat, focusing on children, the elderly, and those prone to fainting. It transitions into a detailed recipe and rationale for barley water and oxymel.</meta>

**Column 1**

...contrary dispositions in that which contains contraries in the digestive regimen. For a great amount of heat—because it is able to digest more—calls for more food, just as a small amount does. ¶ Thus, children and youths call for and receive more food. But in the way they agree, they also agree in their regimen. For each is prepared for "extinction" <note>the total loss of life-force</note> as well as "consumption" <note>the wasting away of the body</note>. For the great heat of a child [fails] through "resolution" <note>original: "resolutionem"; the rapid evaporation of bodily fluids</note>, while the small heat of the decrepit man fails by way of extinction. Therefore, each must be quickly assisted with food. Regarding the elderly, it should be said that although the weak heat of a decrepit man resolves little, it still requires a small amount of food so that it is not extinguished, as he lacks the internal, oily moisture to sustain him. This, however, is a place for speculation. Finally, it must be said that a large amount of resolvable blood indicates that food should be given.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ **A**nd of these. This is the rule for feeding according to a certain disposition of the stomach. It must be considered that some men are "unfortunate by birth," in whom yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> flows to the mouth of the stomach for any slight cause every day. Physicians speak of these in the second treatise of the *Regimen* <note>likely referring to Galen's *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases*</note> and the second chapter on complexions. When there is a man in whom yellow bile flows to the mouth of the stomach immediately as a fever fit <note>term: "parorismo"; the peak or onset of a fever attack</note> begins, stomach pain, headache, and frequent fainting <note>term: "sincopis"; a sudden loss of strength or consciousness</note> follow. This is what is said of them—that is, the "choleric" types. They are of the kind who cannot tolerate being without food, or whose bodies require a regimen different from what we have described. Thus, we are forced to feed them before the fever fit, or at its beginning, or at some hour during the fit. Secondly, it must be considered that the disposition of these bodies differs from those previously mentioned: those are in danger by way of evaporation and drying out, though some might still suffer from bile flowing to the stomach and causing fainting. But those spoken of here are ill-disposed because of the onset of headache and similar stomach accidents due to the effusion of bile, and the cause is not weakness through evaporation. Therefore, they do not have to be extremely choleric in habit. If fainting occurs, it is not from a "vehemence of weakness" <note>extreme exhaustion of vital power</note> but rather the flow of bile to the mouth of the stomach. However, fainting could happen to such a person through weakness and evaporation as well. From this it appears that the feeding differs. It was said above that they should be fed with nourishing and moistening food, such as barley water <note>original: "ptisana ordei"</note>. Wine can also be given before the fit. But those who suffer these accidents solely from the bile reaching the stomach are fed before the fit with medicinal foods that restrain the abundance of bile and comfort the mouth of the stomach, such as pomegranate wine or oxymel <note>original: "syrupo acetoso"; a syrup made of vinegar and sugar or honey</note>. When they have finished these, we comfort them afterward with something "styptic" <note>original: "stiptico"; a substance that contracts tissues to stop flow</note> such as verjuice <note>original: "rob de agresta"; a tart juice of unripe grapes</note>. And when the disposition is mixed—where bodies are choleric, dry, and prone to evaporation, and one fears the bile flowing to the stomach—we give food of a mixed virtue: nourishing, comforting, and repressive of the sharpness of the bile. Avicenna <note>original: "auic."</note> suggests this same thing when he says: sometimes barley water suffices, sometimes pomegranate wine should be administered, sometimes oxymel, and sometimes oxymel mixed with much water. Know these things.

### Innate heat is very weak and cannot let go of food. ¶ And among these are those to whom pain and injury happen in the stomach and headache because of their common connection, and these are of this kind. ¶ And for these, perhaps barley water suffices, and perhaps they need to mix in pomegranate juice and similar things so that the mouth of the stomach may be comforted.

### ¶ And sometimes it is necessary for us to make them vomit with ease before food. And in many of these there is fainting; the cause is not a vehemence of weakness, but rather the effusion of matter into the stomach. When they take oxymel mixed with much warm water in drink, or wine mixed with much water, they also bring up choleric humors in vomit; and their virtue becomes strong. They are never fed with any styptic "rob" <note>a thickened fruit juice or syrup</note> unless they are settled. ¶ And the elderly, the weak, and infants are of the kind who do not tolerate hunger. ¶ Of the first group of old men, there are those who do not have a strong tolerance for hunger, and adolescents follow them—specifically those having solid limbs and wide veins in cold air. ¶ And many times the physician errs in dividing the diet for the sick in another way because he prohibits food for them in the beginning of the matter, and when the end approaches—

<margin>b</margin> ¶ **A**nd the elderly. Here he sets down the rule of feeding according to age. First, he teaches that errors should be avoided. Although a rule was placed above regarding age, this rule is more expressive. Perhaps those statements could be adapted to the dispositions of ages and similar dispositions when they arise not from age but from illness. It is said that anyone whose natural heat is very weak (like the decrepit) or very great (like children) cannot go without food. Thus, this rule written here is either only about ages or is most manifest regarding ages. He expanded the rule when he said "the weak"—that is, those similar to the decrepit, such as those recovering from a very "resolving" <note>draining/evaporating</note> disease. Regarding the first group of old men, there is an aphorism: "Old men [bear fasting] most easily." And adolescents follow the elderly in this ability to tolerate hunger. Contrarily, it is said youths [do]. It must be said that by "adolescents" <note>original: "adolescentes"; in the medieval sense, those in the prime of life, roughly ages 20–35</note> he means both youths and adolescents. For adolescence signifies youth, as the *Conciliator* <note>Pietro d'Abano, a famous 13th-century medical commentator</note> says. Specifically, the "first old men" who most easily bear fasting are those with solid limbs (because dense limbs prevent evaporation) and wide veins (from containing much matter, yet without much resolving heat) in cold air. Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"</note> says those who are of weak virtue like the decrepit, and of much "dissolution" <note>fluid loss</note> like children, cannot abstain from food. After these come those in the end of youth, especially when their bodies are hard to the touch and they are accustomed to cold air and a "gross" <note>heavy or thick</note> regimen before the illness.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ **A**nd many times. Here he posits the error that happens so that you may avoid it. Secondly, he shows the harms that come from that error. It must be considered that this error

<column-break/>

comes to physicians much and frequently. For from the very beginning, they follow the rule placed above. And with an ambiguous matter, they "thin" <note>prescribe a light diet</note> the regimen more than is appropriate; thus, they are forced to "thicken" it <note>prescribe heavier food</note> when the disease is at its peak or near it. This happens all day long. It must be considered that he said "in another way." For error can fall into feeding in many ways besides this one. One was feeding in an acute fever; this is another. Similarly, it was an error not to feed the very choleric before a fit. Thirdly, it should be noted they erred in two ways: one was that they should have fed more heavily in the beginning and did not; the other is that they should have fed more lightly at the peak and instead fed more heavily.

### —the peak <note>original: "status"; the stage where the disease is most intense</note>, and they know that the "virtue" <note>strength</note> is falling, they necessarily feed them at that hour. ¶ Now they have erred in two ways: if they fed them in the beginning, it would be an error; and there is ignorance in this error. ¶ And it happens to these sick people that they suffer from "nauseating catarrhs" <note>drainage that causes gagging</note>, both choleric and wakeful, because of the "resolution" <note>evaporation of fluids</note> and the lack of digestion. They become restless, and their "matters" <note>humors</note> and "virtues" <note>vital powers</note> are constricted, and their vapors are multiplied; therefore they hear things that are not there, and they tremble, or they twitch or jump and turn in their beds, and they imagine what is not there, and their lower lips tremble or jump because of the pain at the mouth of the stomach, and their souls are saddened because of the heaviness of the matter.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ **A**nd these. Conversely, feeding them in the beginning would not have been an error. It must be said that every feeding in a "material fever" <note>a fever caused by a physical humor like bile or phlegm</note> induces the error of "thickening" <note>making the humors harder to clear</note>. The food that those with fever take provides strength, but in the beginning, the error is smaller than at the peak. Or it should be said that if they fed them "gross" <note>heavy</note> foods which they ought to have in the beginning, the error of thickening would be more tolerable in the beginning than at the peak of the whole disease.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ **A**nd it happens to these. Because they are not fed in the beginning, they are afterward suddenly filled at the peak, such that they suffer catarrhs, etc. All this talk is about acute fevers. The commentator there perfectly assigns the cause of these accidents—namely, the catarrh, which is the "acute course of hot matters." This happens during a time of superfluous abstinence because of inflammation, and also during a time of superfluous repletion <note>over-fullness</note> at the peak, because the food is corrupted by the matters falling and flowing into the stomach, which causes nausea. They are "wakeful" because they are wakeful both when empty and when filled, due to many vapors rising to the head. Out of the deprivation of food, they become restless. They "alienate" <note>suffer delusions/hallucinations</note> because of vapors rising to the head. Matters are constricted during the time of repletion because Nature is not free to digest and expel them; and during the time of hunger, they should be fed, yet their virtues are constricted due to weakness from evaporation. When they are weakened by evaporation or weighed down, [the vapors] are multiplied. The rest is known; you may add the words of Galen <note>original: "Galte."</note> from the aforementioned commentary. ¶ Rule for giving barley water and oxymel in drink.

### ¶ Rule for giving barley water and oxymel <note>original: "syrupum acetosum"</note> in drink. Book IX.

### Barley water is of a kind in which there is none of the body of the barley, but only its "virtue" <note>medicinal power</note> and form. It has no place in a cure nor any trust in its help unless it is of "complete decoction" <note>thoroughly boiled</note>. The best kind is where the quantity of water is 15 parts to 1 part of barley <note>original: "rr. 15... 1"</note>—that is, when it has been reduced properly to a fifth. That which is red and "subtle" <note>thin/fine</note> should be taken; for this is the subtle kind whose nourishment is less, but whose moistening, cleansing, and extraction—

<margin>H</margin> ¶ **B**arley water, etc. He promised in the preceding chapter to set down specific words on barley water and oxymel because he frequently mentions them in previous chapters.
¶ First, regarding the ways of composing these drinks; second, he sets the rule for their use. First, he gives the method of composing barley water, then oxymel. Note that this is the barley water we commonly use as a drink for the feverish, where the "body" of the barley does not pass into the water, but only its "virtue." This is done by putting the whole barley to boil with water—not using barley flour. Because "subtle" <note>thin</note> things should transmit their virtue in decoction, they must be boiled a long time. As in the second book, chapter five, this water must be "completely decocted" <note>boiled down</note>; otherwise, it neither cures nor is useful because it neither cleanses nor nourishes. Secondly, consider that this water is not so free of the barley's body that nothing passes through, but it is very little and nourishes little. However, the superficial virtue of the barley, which is "abstersive" <note>cleansing/scouring</note>, does pass through; therefore, it cleanses and opens [the pores/vessels] more. Thus it digests with a "light digestion" because it does not make a strong impression by cooling or opening. Moistening and washing are properly done by the water, but the extraction of "superfluities" <note>waste humors</note> is properly done by the cleansing and washing which draws them out through the stool and also the urine. Thus, he allows it to be more medicinal and less nourishing. Let it sit and discard the dregs. The ratio is 15 to 1. Others say it is different, but we do not labor over this, as no great error can fall here. What we call "barley water" is not the same as "ptisana" <note>a thicker barley porridge</note>. ¶ It is doubted whether barley water is a suitable drink for every feverish person. It seems so, because fevers are hot and cold—

# Second Treatise

<page-num>1</page-num>

<margin>a</margin> **F**or whatever is praised in the 80th Canon, in the chapter on barley: Furthermore, barley ptisan <note>original: "ptisana"; a medicinal porridge or decoction</note> is generally eaten above every other food made of grain in these acute sufferings. Why? Because barley water is medicinal. Furthermore, barley water cools and moistens because barley is cold and moist; hence barley is more moist than wheat, as stated in the first book of Aristotle's *Problems*, problem 36. On the contrary, some say barley water excites because it is dry in its power, as noted in the 80th Canon. Furthermore, it heats, as in the 16th book of the *Continens* <note>The "Continens" is the vast medical encyclopedia by Al-Razi, known as Rhazes</note>, where it is said it should be used...

<insert>
...of the superfluities from it, and the digestion made from it is very equal. And there is a decoction in which there is something of the body of the barley and its flour. And what is more pleasing to me in such matters is that it should not be boiled too much; rather, it should be according to a measure that removes bloating and does not reach the point of making it excessively viscous. And regarding this indeed...
</insert>

...that which heats, such as barley water and honey water. It must first be said that barley water—which is a certain drink, not the ptisan itself—can be made more cleansing <term>abstersive<gloss>cleansing or purging of waste</gloss></term> and less cooling and less moistening, and this is done by discarding the outer husk <note>original: "cortex"</note> of the barley but not the inner part. There is another kind made from barley with its husk removed, and that one cleanses less but moistens more and nourishes more; for there is a cleansing power in the husk of the barley. Mesue <note>A famous Persian physician</note> set down these two modes of barley water.

<margin>b</margin> **S**econdly, it must be said that the question here is not whether it is suitable as a food for those suffering from fever, because it is well known that it would not be suitable except in a very acute fever, in which the most subtle diet is appropriate—though not in the final stage where nothing is given, or only pomegranate wine or julep <note>a sweet medicinal syrup</note> is given—though these things are known from what was said before.

<margin>b</margin> **B**ut the doubt is whether barley water is suitable for them to use as a daily and extraordinary drink. For those with fevers cannot be restrained from wanting to drink often. And it must be said that in hot fevers, such as acute choleric <note>caused by yellow bile</note> and sanguine <note>caused by blood</note> fevers, this drink can be granted well enough. The reason is because it washes, cleanses, and tempers the heat. It also exits the stomach quickly, as is understood from Haly Abbas <note>original: "Alyabate"; the Latinized name of the Persian physician Al-Majusi</note> in the ninth book of the *Theoretical* <note>The "Liber Regalis" or "Royal Book"</note>, in the chapter on barley. But whether it should be made more cleansing and medicinal or less so depends on what appears from the patient's condition. In cold, phlegmatic, and melancholic fevers, however, and especially when they are intermittent—in which such great cooling is not sought—perhaps the drink should not be used so constantly. In those cases where it ought to be cleansing, it is perhaps mixed with parsley and fennel, as Avicenna teaches in the 60th chapter. But you will ask: what daily drink shall I give to those having cold fevers? It must be said: barley water prepared as we described, or water with a little sugar and nothing else if you wish it to cleanse more. In strong and acute fevers, we use pomegranate wine as a constant drink, unless we wish to cool them.

<margin>c</margin> **R**egarding the contradictions, it must be said to the first that Avicenna does not grant barley water alone in cold fevers, but with parsley and fennel. To the second, it must be said that he argues it is a good drink in acute fevers. To the third, regarding the comparison of the temperament <term>complexion<gloss>the balance of the four humors/qualities in a substance</gloss></term> of barley to dry or hard barley: it must be said that barley in its temperament is dry in power, yet it has certain moist parts not well digested; and this water is windy and causes gas. It is just as we say of this water and of ginger: in dried ginger, it is virtually dry, yet with this, it has a certain accidental moisture, a sign of superfluity, just as in fresh rue because it is windy, and in ginger; and thus its powers change quickly in it. Therefore, those who say barley is moist understand it in the aforementioned way; however, that gas-producing moisture is digested through boiling. And although barley is dry—indeed, according to Haly Abbas, it is dry because it is cold—its dryness is tempered by the moisture of the water. Therefore, barley water remains cooling and somewhat moistening, especially when the barley is perfectly cleansed of all outer husk. To the other argument, I believe that text is corrupt and intended to say it should be used because it does *not* heat. Or it should be said that barley water "heats" in the sense that it cools less than pure water. Or it speaks of the barley water that is more cleansing, which cools less, and that which is more washing and moistening is less cleansing; each of these is apparent from what has been said.

<margin>d</margin> **I**t is doubted secondly whether there should be twenty parts water to one part barley. It seems not, because Haly Abbas in the fifth book of the *Therapeutics* teaches taking one part barley to fifteen of water. Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli, a prominent Jewish physician</note>, however, in his *Particular Diets*, says seven parts water to one of barley. Avenzoar <note>original: "3oar"; the Andalusian physician Ibn Zuhr</note>, in the 16th treatise of the *Teisir*, in the chapter on the cure of chest abscesses, says two parts water to one of barley. Avicenna and Mesue agree. It is doubted thirdly to what quantity they should reach in boiling. For Avicenna teaches reducing it to a fifth part. Mesue, however, to a half or a third part. Isaac to one part. All these questions are resolved because we make barley water more cooling, moistening, and washing by using a large quantity of water and a little barley with little boiling; and this is what is done today for the washing of the feverish. However, we make barley water having more of the barley's power, being more cleansing and nourishing, by using much barley and much boiling. And sometimes it is boiled so much that much of the barley's power and body passes into the water and makes a residue which is like a ptisan. Our authors, therefore, proceeded with different professional judgments according to the diversity of fevers and climates; thus, few agree on the composition of barley water, yet each speaks the truth.

<margin>e</margin> **A**nd concerning the decoction: here is the second mode of barley water, which is that in which there is something of the body of the barley and its flour. First he proposes this, and secondly he gives the rules <note>original: "canones"</note> concerning it. It should be considered that barley water in which there is something of the body of the barley and its flour can be made in three ways. First, by boiling whole barley that has been previously husked and rubbed, with such a long boiling that a little of its internal parts break out into the water by cracking; the thin part of this water is more medicinal, and the thick part is more nourishing. Therefore, some who do not want any of the barley's body to pass through tie the barley in a cloth. Second, it is made by breaking the barley, which among us is called barley grits <note>original: "far ordei"</note>. Third, it is made by taking barley flour and boiling it in the proportion that seems best to us; this is called barley ptisan.

<margin>f</margin> **A**nd what is more: the first rule is to remove error. For many, considering that Galen <note>The foundational Greek physician</note> prescribes much boiling of barley ptisan, might overdo the boiling. Therefore, he wants its boiling to be appropriate—neither excessive nor insufficient; and this stands by the judgment of an expert cook. Among us, however, perfect boiling is recognized by the smell.

<margin>g** **A**nd it happens: here is the second rule. It should be considered that by us...

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin> ...it has been declared at length how acidity <note>original: "acetositas"</note> of food occurs in the stomach, and how it happens from heat and how from cold. For the stomach is naturally hot and accidentally cold. As in a choleric person or a feverish youth, a conversion of things to "smokiness" occurs. But when the stomach is cold by nature—even if it is heated accidentally—it causes in watery, cold things like milk and barley water a bubbling and a kind of putrefaction; hence such things turn sour in such a stomach. And therefore infants having a burning fever <term>causon<gloss>an acute, high fever with intense thirst</gloss></term> because the heat is dulled by moisture, where it does not burn but causes bubbling, the milk turns sour in their stomachs, as will appear in the chapter on burning fever.

<margin>b</margin> **A**nd barley water: here he sets down the mode of barley water, but with a diversity of barley. It should be considered that barley itself could be understood as barley cleansed of no husk; and this mode is not in use, nor does it seem suitable according to Avenzoar in the 16th book, first chapter, where he says that if any of the outer husk remains in the barley, it provokes coughing and windiness. In another way, by "barley" we mean barley cleansed of the thick outer husk, and by "dehusked barley" we mean barley cleansed of every husk—that is, both outer and inner. And this seems to be the intent of our authors regarding how those barley waters differ, as appears from what has been said. If you wish "barley" itself, not dehusked, to be understood as dry barley cleansed of no husk, I do not forbid it. And that barley water will be of stronger cleansing. Hence Avenzoar says of it that it washes the belly. It is doubted whether the barley from which barley water is made should be large or small. It seems it should be large according to Avenzoar. It seems it should be small according to Mesue in the chapter on barley water, where he says it is made from "subtle" barley. It must be said that large barley seems to be more moist in temperament than small barley; for its very size and the extension of its body show its greater moisture. Therefore, if you want a more moistening water for fevers, it is appropriate to make it from large barley, as is commonly done in our regions. If you want it not so moistening, make it from small barley, if the contrary qualities are required. Or it should be said that by "subtle" barley, he means barley which we call "large," which is long and not cramped in its thickness.

<margin>c</margin> **B**ut it is doubted whether the barley with which barley water is made should be whole when it is put to boil, or crushed. It seems it should be crushed according to Isaac in his *Particular Diets*, where he says "let the barley be broken," and Avenzoar in his 36th book, first chapter, where he says "let it be ground or pounded in a stone mortar," and Haly Abbas in the fifth book of *Therapeutics*, where he says "let it be rubbed moderately." On the contrary is Avenzoar in the first book of the *Teisir*, where he maintains that those who break the barley are far from the path of truth, because in every seed there is a natural power before it is destroyed and broken; it alters things through that power which follows its integrity, through which it draws water to itself. In short, Avenzoar maintains that whole barley has a power that follows its integrity, by which it draws water when it stands in infusion; and before it boils, its pores are opened. And this water has the power of the barley, as Avicenna and Mesue say. But if the barley is broken, the power in it dies. It is the same as with barley which, if sown whole, grows and draws moisture to itself from the earth, but if broken, it does not grow. Averroes <note>The Cordoban philosopher and physician</note> took this reasoning in the fifth book of his *Colliget*, in the chapter on barley, on the authority of Avenzoar. This contradiction is easily resolved: for if you want a more nourishing barley water, so that something of the flour or marrow of the grain passes into the water, it is necessary to crush the barley. If, however, you want a more medicinal, altering, and cleansing barley water without nutrition, let the whole barley be boiled. However, the older authors, when they prescribe the barley to be crushed, do not mean it should be smashed, but that it should be pounded so that the husk is separated from it; and thus Isaac understood it.

<margin>e</margin> **A**nd better. It should be considered that in this oxymel <term>syrupus acetosus<gloss>a syrup made of vinegar, water, and sugar or honey</gloss></term> there is cooling from the water and the vinegar. There is also moistening from the water, and also somewhat from the sugar—if it is not old—and it "cuts" <note>original: "incidit"; breaks down thick humors</note> and acts through the vinegar, and cleanses through the sugar, and also "opens" <note>the pores or vessels</note>; and this is a suitable drink in fever. And regarding this syrup, we have already made a unique treatise. He called it "vinegar made from wine," as this is more "incisive" and penetrates more deeply. It should be considered that although the quantity of vinegar to be infused is set down here, and the sugar remains uncovered, nevertheless in the composition of this syrup one must consider the quality of natures, as stated in the 6th treatise of the Canon. For just as men differ in the use of wine—where some can take pure wine and some cannot—so it is with the use of vinegar and sour things. And therefore one must make oxymel differing in acidity according to the diversity of men. This is the intention of Galen in the fourth book of *The Regimen of Health* and of Serapion. This syrup, therefore, which is set down here, is for common use and of standard composition. And when you use it, you can add more or less water, so that the power of the vinegar is more or less broken; and we wrote of those things regarding the fifth Canon.

<margin>f** **A**nd to aggregate. Here he sets down a rule in the use of these drinks. It is doubted whether it is suitable to mix oxymel with barley water. It seems so, according to Avicenna in the third book, first fen, in the chapter on phrenitis <note>inflammation of the brain/delirium</note>, where he allows barley water with honeyed vinegar <term>oxymel<gloss>original: "oxymelle"</gloss></term>. Furthermore, immediately below he teaches mixing a little vinegar with the barley water; but if he allows vinegar with it, then much more sugar and water. But oxymel is nothing else but those three. Furthermore, below in the chapter on phlegmatic fever, he allows this mixture. Furthermore, Galen in the first book of *Aliments* teaches that vinegar be mixed with ptisan. On the contrary, in Avicenna, there are multiple ways of speaking; some have said that these should not be mixed. Because they are different drinks, just as we should not mix different foods—as in the first book, third fen—because they are not well digested; thus neither different drinks. This solution is not satisfying, because all day long we mix more diverse syrups than barley water and oxymel. And when it is said that we should not mix different foods, it must be said that this is true of *very* different ones, where digestion might be corrupted. But barley water and oxymel agree well enough in cleansing, opening, provoking <note>urination or sweat</note>, and cooling. Others have said that a little oxymel can be mixed with barley water, but not much. The Conciliator <note>Pietro d'Abano, whose famous work "Conciliator Differentiarum" sought to reconcile medical contradictions</note>, in Difference 169, confirming the aforementioned solution and beginning from it, gives the reason why we should not mix these: because their operations are confused. For oxymel divides and sequesters matters and prepares them for expulsion, while barley water washes away what has been "cut," cleanses, and leads it out through sweat and provocation, as Avicenna will soon state. This solution does not please me because, although the releasing of matters could be done before the leading out, nevertheless they can be mixed at the same time. For preparation does not hinder the leading out. Hence we see that our authors make compound medicines that are subtle-making, dividing, and thinning of matters, as appears in the syrup of eupatorium and epithyme. Haly Abbas, however, in the third...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of medicinal drinks from the previous page, specifically focusing on the interactions between vinegar syrup and barley water, and transitioning into the general treatment of acute fevers. ### Book

In the preceding chapter on the care of tertian fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day, typically associated with malaria</note>, it says that vinegar syrup <note>original: "syrupus acetosus"; likely oxymel, a mixture of honey or sugar and vinegar</note> and barley water should not be mixed if one drinks them; indeed, barley water should not be given immediately after the syrup before it is digested. For the syrup makes the barley water descend too quickly from the stomach, and thus the body is not properly nourished by it. This is the solution given by Dynus <note>Dino del Garbo (d. 1327), a famous Italian physician and commentator</note>. For he says that barley water is either a food—that is, the kind containing the body of the barley—and this should not be mixed with vinegar syrup because the syrup causes it to pass through undigested and fail to nourish. He says this was the intention of Galen in the third book of *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases*. Alternatively, barley water is solely a medicinal drink—an "alterative" drink <term>alterative<gloss>a medicine that gradually restores healthy bodily functions</gloss></term>—and such a drink can be mixed with vinegar syrup. In this case, there is no impropriety in mixing them, which is why Dynus says Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"; the Persian physician Al-Razi</note> commanded in the 9th book of the *Liber ad Almansorem*, in the chapter on liver pain, to give the syrup with barley water. But if you want distinct effects and operations from the barley water, the vinegar syrup should precede it, and the barley water should be given afterward. We have already provided two solutions here.

The first is like Dynus’s solution: if barley water is given as food, vinegar syrup should not be mixed into it in a full dose, lest it cause it to descend too quickly. If Galen says to mix vinegar with the ptisan <note>A medicinal porridge or decoction</note>, it should be understood as a small amount to act as a stimulant or to prevent inflammation, but not so much as to cause it to descend. If, however, the barley water is given as an alterative medicine, vinegar syrup can be mixed with it, or it can be given separately, as will be seen. Our other solution is this: if there is a fear of "acetosity" <note>sourness or acidity</note> in the barley water—and therefore a fear of harm—the vinegar syrup should not be mixed with it, as the syrup makes it more prone to souring. This is hinted at below in the chapter on the care of phlegmatic fever. Because the general population today has stomachs full of matter and stifled in heat due to the many vices of the modern regimen <note>A common medieval complaint that "modern" lifestyles were unhealthier than those of antiquity</note>, this souring is greatly feared, as it is a "bad acetosity." Therefore, we avoid mixing them. This is what Avicenna meant when he said that vinegar syrup corrupts barley water for the most part—meaning it makes it turn sour. He says "for the most part" because in some people with a "fiery stomach," this would not happen; hence, below, for a hot stomach, he suggests mixing a little vinegar with the barley water.

> The syrup is that in which sugar is placed in a vessel, then strong wine vinegar is poured over it until it rises above the sugar; indeed, let it be left uncovered. Then, quiet coals and hot ash are placed under the vessel until the sugar liquefies in the vinegar without boiling. Then the foam is skimmed, and it is left for one hour with great heat until the sugar mixes with the vinegar. Then a quantity of water "two fingers deep" is poured over it, and it boils until thick. Mixing vinegar syrup and barley water together is unpraiseworthy, as it corrupts the barley water in most cases. And barley water should not be given as a drink when natural dryness is present; rather, an enema <note>original: "clistere"</note> should be administered before it. If it turns sour in the stomach, give the thinnest part of it as a drink. If it turns sour, let celery root and similar things be cooked with it. If it turns sour again, then it is necessary to mix some pepper with it, specifically when the matter is not excessively thin or hot. When bloating increases, then a little wine vinegar should be mixed with it for those who are overheated. Again, when vinegar syrup is given as a drink, it cuts through the humors and prepares waste products for expulsion. And you, consequently, after two hours, give—

<margin>a</margin>
"And it should not..." This can be understood regarding the ptisan which is called barley water, as verified at the start of the previous chapter. This was said by Hippocrates in the first book of *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases*. It can also be understood as the barley water that is a medicinal drink. For it has the power of scouring and washing away the waste products it carries. If waste is blocking the way, then vapors will cause harm or move toward the veins; therefore, an enema should be sent first.

<margin>b</margin>
"If it..." This is the third case, where he teaches how to counter the conversion of barley water into vinegar (souring). For it is prone to this by its substance and temperament, if you recall the science of sour flavors. First, he chooses the thinner part, which penetrates more quickly and has more cleansing power. Second, he adds hot things to it to increase heat in the stomach, whereby this sourness becomes less hot—as celery and pepper are beneficial if the fever-matter is not thin and hot, but rather thick.

<margin>c</margin>
"And when..." This is the fourth case. Some believe he should say a little wine—namely, to resolve windiness <note>gas or bloating</note>—and they interpret "for the overheated" to mean "for those with fever." That third point stands as in the chapter on blood fever, at the end, on the authority of Megethius: when you want the bloating of barley water to cease, put some wine vinegar in it, specifically for the overheated. For it happens that strong heat causes it to evaporate, which causes bloating. Vinegar—specifically wine vinegar—prevents it from evaporating by blocking the tendency to bloat. It also makes it penetrate quickly to the urine, sweat, or bowels. In some other bodies that are not "overheated," vinegar might increase bloating; hence in the third book of the *Canon*, chapter on priapism, sour things sometimes cause bloating.

<margin>d</margin>
"Nevertheless..." This is the fifth case. Take from this that barley water, which is a drink, is called "thin alkitf water," etc. It soothes the belly—which he means when he says "it washes"—and it scours and provokes urine and sweat. From this, also take the order: vinegar syrup then barley water; it appears from what was said above that the time for its operation is after two hours.

<margin>e</margin>
"And it is not..." This is the sixth case, where it is held that "at dinner"—meaning after dinner, once digestion is complete—vinegar syrup can be given, so that it does not make undigested food descend too early. Others interpret "at dinner" to mean before dinner when the food is separated—and this is also a true statement.

<margin>f</margin>
"And sometimes..." This is the seventh case. It should be considered that one should follow an order: first give a julep <note>A sweet medicinal drink, often rose water and sugar</note> to soften the matter and the dryness of the body, and afterward give the cleansing and provocative barley water. Therefore, vinegar syrup is among those things that prepare the way for the barley water's operation in cases where moistening is not sought, but rather the "cutting" <note>breaking down</note> of matters. He does not specify how long after the julep the barley water should be given, as he did with the vinegar syrup, perhaps leaving this to your judgment. And perhaps also

<column-break/>

after two hours or a little more. Sometimes he may suggest a preference—namely, that a julep be given and not barley water—because a julep moistens much more, since sugar is moist and barley is dry.
"And sometimes..." This is the eighth case, concerning the necessity of what he mentioned before: the enema. But since everyone should first give a laxative to soothe the upper parts and cleanse them of matters that barley water could not have removed, nor even an enema, you shall give tamarinds. We, however, use the pulp of cassia more often in this case. It is debated whether we should first give simple vinegar syrup in the morning or an enema. It seems we should give the syrup first, because with vinegar syrup there is a fear of "excoriation" <note>stripping or irritation of the intestinal lining</note>. But the fear is less if it is given before an enema is performed; for an enema weakens the intestines, cleanses them, and makes them prepared for the impact of the vinegar syrup to be excoriated. Furthermore, vinegar syrup prepares matters for evacuation, so the enema should follow it. On the contrary, in the *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, it is commanded that if bloodletting <term>phlebotomy<gloss>the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</gloss></term> or an enema is needed, the ptisan should not be given, but those things should be done first, as Avicenna also said above. Thus it seems the same for vinegar syrup. Furthermore, Avicenna places the enema before the barley water, so much more so before the vinegar syrup. It must be said that the talk here is of a soothing enema, as mentioned in the chapter on putrid fevers. I say that if there is a simultaneous need for both—the syrup and the enema—due to the presence of waste, the enema must be given first. The reason is that if you give the enema immediately after the syrup is drunk, it causes agitation of the syrup in the stomach and makes it descend undigested. Or if you give the enema one or two hours later, the vinegar syrup might move matters which, having no exit, will cause harm. Thus one could prove that compound vinegar syrup should not be given before an enema

> The subtle "alkitf" barley water mentioned before: let it wash, cut, scour, and extract the matter through sweat and provocation <note>stimulation of bodily exits</note>. And it is no harm if vinegar syrup is given as a drink at dinner, since the food is already separated from the stomach. And sometimes it is necessary that a julep be given before barley water to add moisture; this is when you see dryness dominating the body and tongue. And sometimes it is necessary that some tamarinds be given two hours before that.

> ### On the treatments of acute fevers. ——— Book 1.
>
> <margin>a</margin>
> What has been said about the regimen of soothing, provocation, sweating, and digestion, followed by evacuation with medicine. And what has been said about feeding afterward is what we needed to remember here. But the ways of extinguishing the intensity of heat are by cooling the air and cooling the food. And with epithems <note>Poultices or liquid applications</note> and plasters. And with medicines. And by holding things in the mouth like psyllium mucilage, quince seed mucilage, purslane juice, and licorice juice to settle thirst; for by constantly applying something to the throat of a patient with a hot sickness, the mouth remains moist.

because it could cause the matters it finds in the intestines to penetrate the veins. It is better, therefore, that early in the morning, an enema be performed in a timely manner, and once the intestines are cleansed, the vinegar syrup (simple or compound) be given. Thus, the matters moved by the syrup find the intestines soothed and ready for passage, and are not retained above the waste for any length of time. Similarly, compound vinegar syrup will not find bad matters needing purging by an enema, but will find the intestines as clean as possible. If, however, some physician is of such good judgment that he knows the exact time when vinegar syrup prepares the matters and has already scoured some of them into the intestines, he may intervene with an enema at that time so there is no danger from the delay of moved superfluities. I say such a physician could give the syrup before the enema.
To the contrary, it must be said: first, it is not good to save someone from the harm of excoriation by the harm of retaining superfluities over the waste. Alternatively, it can be said that performing an enema before vinegar syrup protects against excoriation more than if it were not done, as it leaves the intestines smooth—for example, by using violet oil and cassia—and ensures that the bad matters and the vinegar syrup do not linger there. Second, it must be said that the matters prepared for evacuation by the vinegar syrup are led out by nature, or barley water, or some enema that will be done another way according to the matters which the vinegar syrup scours down to the intestines; it will lead them out with the help of the enema that preceded it. For if they stayed in the intestines above dry waste during the whole time in which the enema was not leading them out, they could harm by quick return or evaporation. However, I leave this order to your judgment.

<margin>b</margin>
"What has been said..." Because acute fevers are very fearsome, he sets down their general regimen. First regarding the matter, second regarding the fever itself. He says "But the ways..." It should be considered that just as he wants to remind us of the regimen of soothing, etc., so also the regimen for bloodletting; and perhaps he omitted it because the acute fevers discussed are those of much bloating, and these are mostly "choleric" <note>caused by yellow bile</note>, in which bloodletting is rarely appropriate and does not suit them by itself.
"But the ways..." This is Avicenna's goal for the treatment of acute fevers, regarding the intention of cooling. This is because in acute cases, one must focus much on this, and in this it is completed—which seems diminished in the general chapter on putrid fevers. First, he sets down six ways of extinguishing the heat of acute fevers, and he explains two of them, later explaining the others by example. "And it is necessary..." It should be considered that there is a question about whether licorice is of a hot or cold temperament. However, in the third book of the *Canon*, chapter on paralysis, licorice juice...
