### Treatise on the Section

It is placed among things having a certain cooling quality: and there is no doubt that also because of its moisture it can repress the sharpness of bile <note>original: "cholere"; yellow bile, one of the four humors associated with heat and dryness</note>: however, its sweetness makes it loathsome to those with acute fevers. ¶ Regarding the inflammation that sometimes occurs in the heat of a fever, Avicenna <note>the Latinized name for the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> also in the 10th Section, in the chapter on medicines for soothing the chest, in the treatise, places licorice juice among the cold medicines. It must be considered that the throat is the part in which the breath <note>original: "spūalis," likely spiritualis/respiratory</note> and the digestive systems meet. Thus, many vapors come to the parts of the throat, and much inflammation occurs in them: and therefore, moistening is good for them so that ulcers do not form, nor does roughness develop on the tongue. ¶ So that "limosities" <note>slimy or mucous buildups</note> do not form, which are harmful, as will appear below in its own chapter. ¶ To temper its heat and dryness is useful so that the heat of the lung and stomach may be tempered. For this reason, it is very helpful. The rest of the points are noted elsewhere.

<margin>a</margin>
**And it is necessary** this part has four sections, just as four methods of cooling and quenching the heat of acute fevers remained. ¶ First, therefore, he teaches how to cool by cooling the air. Second, by cooling the food. Third, with epithems <term>epithems<gloss>medicated compresses applied to the body</gloss></term> and with plasters. ¶ Fourth, with cold medicines. There, he discusses the regimen of food. There, he discusses epithems. There, the fourth section. And sometimes it is... Consider the prohibition of frequency. Certain unrefined people have explained this to mean that frequent breathing should be prohibited. But Avicenna wants the person who frequently visits the sick person to be prohibited. For they themselves heat up the air. And this is what he says in the fourth section of the *Therapeutics* <note>likely referring to a work by Galen</note> in that chapter we are passing through: where he says, prohibiting a multitude of people from entering, for they heat the house. Consider that the Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims/Arabs</note> in [certain] parts soothe houses with mud made with straw: just as we do with cement made from lime: and such houses newly smeared with lime are not good; indeed, they are criticized by Galen in the fifth chapter of the book *On the Usefulness of Breathing*. However, those which are smeared with mud are much better, and especially those smeared recently, because that mud is moist and cold in its virtue: for that mud is a certain tenacious, cold earth: and it does not dry out in cares <note>treatment</note>, which is very helpful. ¶ And sometimes they are helped by the administration of clysters <term>clyster<gloss>an enema</gloss></term> made from the juice of Indian melon and cucumber and gourd and purslane with rose oil and with a little bit of camphor, which is of the greatest help.

¶ And it is necessary that the air be cooled as much as possible. And its cooling is achieved by the prohibition of frequency <note>limiting visitors</note>: and by the hanging of many fans: and by the placement of plenty of snow. ¶ And if the house has been recently smeared with mud, and specifically that in which a "cotton of paper" <note>original: "cotum papiri"; likely a fiber used for binding</note> is placed instead of straw: then it is better. ¶ And sometimes flows from fountains and sprinklings are prepared in it: and sweet water runs in it. ¶ Or bedding is laid over a pool covered with a net: and the bedding on which one sleeps is made of *tabari* <note>a type of fine linen or cloth, possibly from Tabaristan</note> and similar things: and the rest of the bedding is made from the tips of willows and quinces and myrtle sprinkled with rose water and violets and water lilies <note>original: "nenu-faris"</note> and roses. ¶ And sometimes baskets are placed in which there are rows of fruits of good scent and cold nature: such as sour apples: and quinces and smaller pears of good scent sprinkled with rose water and water lilies and willows upon which sandalwood and roses and camphor have been powdered: and upon which a little fragrant wine has already been distilled: then that is the ultimate [remedy]. ¶ This, therefore, is the regimen of the air. ¶ As for the regimen of food, you already know it; and if the wish is present that there be soothing along with the cooling, then give gourd water: and the water of Indian melon specifically and cucumber water; and lettuce with vinegar is the ultimate [remedy]. ¶ And what is convenient to this...

<margin>a</margin> A gloss on complexions: and if that mud is made with "cotton of paper," that is, with the cotton of an aquatic rope, it is better. This is what grows at the top of a rush <note>original: "iunci"</note>. It is called this because from that rush were made the papers called "papyrus papers," although now papers are called by this name. That cotton of the rush is of a cold complexion <term>complexion<gloss>the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in a substance</gloss></term>: and therefore mud mixed with it is better than with straw, which is not of a cold complexion. Consider that he orders many layers of bedding. One that will be over water, and another layer he orders from *tabari* cloth, that is, linen, for it heats less than wool, as in the third book of *Almansor* and the first of the *Canticles*. Others explain *tabari* as leather, which is placed over that net, and from similar things, that is, things that do not cause heating: and these beds are known among them. Or from similar things, that is, uniform and equal positions: because the bedding should not lie in folded sheets or be wrinkled and unequal.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ And the remaining bedding. Here is another layer over a spread-out hide: or as it is matured among us. The sick person could be placed there to rest, and it is a bed made of the tips of willows, etc. *Calathi* is a type of nightshade. But it seems that *calathi* is some vessel like a basket or a type of wide board where these things are placed: and they stay in the sick person's chamber. Moreover, he places fragrant rushes so that they may carry the virtue of those cold scents to the heart: and this is the ultimate in goodness. And it is first to be known that it is bad to make those with acute fevers lie on a feather mattress, because they inflame much. It is doubted whether poplar leaves should be strewn in the chamber of one with acute fever. It is said yes: because it is a tree of a cold complexion. The sign is that it grows near water, and because the buds of the poplar are placed in the ointment *populeon* <note>an ointment made from poplar buds used for cooling</note>, whose virtue is cold. ¶ On the contrary, because the poplar is a tree of a hot complexion. The sign is the stench or hot scent with sharpness which is in its bud: and the yellow color in it. This question asks what the complexion of the poplar is. ¶ It appears from the second book of the *Canon* that it is of a hot and dry complexion. For the poplar is found under a double name: because it is called Roman gold and Roman nut, although it is found as "gold" absolutely. 

<column-break/>

Perhaps he is speaking then of amber <note>original: "karabe"</note>, as we said there in the second book. Therefore, its leaves ought not to be placed in the chamber of those with fever. Regarding the contrary signs, it must be said that although cold herbs like willows grow near water for the most part, yet they are not always found to be cold. For sometimes hot plants can grow there, such as sweet flag <note>original: "acorus"</note> and the herb called "dog ginger" <note>original: "zinziber caninum"</note>. ¶ "The pupil of the eye," that is, healings and many other similar things.

¶ To the second point, it must be said that those buds are placed in *populeon* to temper the coldness of other medicines: just as opium is sometimes placed in hot medicines to temper their heat. Some, however, wished to argue that the ointment *populeon* is of some heating virtue: because when the belly is anointed with it, as around the navel, it provokes sweat: as Nicolaus writes about it.

<margin>c</margin> **Regimen.** Here he sets down the method of extinguishing the heat of acute fevers through food. You already know this, namely in the chapter on the feeding of those with fever, where he gives all the rules of feeding; return there. But if you wish to cool, behold the foods are placed here. It must be considered that although these fruits were prohibited above before the seventh day with the intention of [ripening] the matter, yet they are granted because of the necessity of extinction, which takes precedence as we said above. Their soothing by actual moisture as a wash is known. And along with this, they also provoke [relief]: lettuce with vinegar is the ultimate. It should not be understood as the ultimate in soothing, because lettuce is neither styptic <term>styptic<gloss>tending to contract tissues or stop bleeding</gloss></term> nor laxative, as in the second book of the *Canon*; but "ultimate" means most suitable in reducing the sharpness of the heat of one with an acute fever. *Foca* is a drink made from barley water and other things sometimes, as sometimes bread is mixed and milk-water or cheese-water, that is, whey. ¶ *Dogo* <note>original: "dogo"; likely a dialect or technical term for a dairy byproduct</note>, that is, sour milk with the butter extracted, because it is not inflamed. We do not use these drinks: however, it is said the sum of them is a drink called *ficera* or *fuchalis* or *cerusia* <note>ale or beer</note>. And there are many types of this drink which is called *foca*: and you have another way in the third book, first section, in the chapter on the rules of curing diseases of the brain in the letter of Gerard.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ And if it is present. He doubts how pomegranate juice retains the belly <note>acts as an astringent/constipates</note> when above it is placed as a laxative in the chapter on the cure of pulmonary fever in general. It must be said that pomegranate juice here is understood as the wine of pomegranates which cools. But when he says "retention," he speaks improperly, because it is comparative in respect to the cucumber and melon mentioned: in which there is more of the soothing quality which is not in the wine of pomegranates. Or it must be said that by provoking urine it acts as a styptic. But as for why it provokes [urine], read the second book of the *Canon*. And he does not say this of the sweet pomegranate because it does not cool in this way. Above, however, he was speaking of pomegranates...

---

...that have been pressed with their pulps in which some laxative power is seen, perhaps by compressing. And if it were so, they would be prohibited at the beginning of a fever just like myrobalans <term>myrobalans<gloss>dried plum-like fruits used as a laxative</gloss></term>. Although perhaps in that pressing of pomegranates with pulps there is not such a deep reach to the veins as there is in myrobalans; consider this. Water, that is, the juice of wild grapes, etc. Mulberries <note>original: "mora"</note>, namely not completely ripe, from that region. Lemon not salted: because they do not cool in that way. What he says of barberries and of others is known.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ Regarding the epithem. Here he cools with a plaster and epithems. And first he sets down from what they are made. Second, he sets down the rules. There: "And embrocate"; and this part has three sections. First, he sets down the rules for the embrocation <term>embrocation<gloss>the application of liquid medicinal preparations to the body</gloss></term> of the liver: and thus it is understood for the heart. Second, for the head. Third, again for the liver. There: "And when there." There, third: "And cool the liver." It must be considered that just as embrocation, that is, an epithem or similar cooling of the liver, rectifies the urine: because its cooling reaches the veins. Similarly, an epithem for the heart could rectify the pulse, because its cooling reaches the arteries: he says moreover of the liver that bile and acute matters [gather] there by its power.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ And when children with fever. Here first he sets down the conditions in which we ought not to embrocate the head: and in which we ought to: and he teaches how to recognize them. There, second: "And it is known." It must be considered that while much fullness remains in the head, to embrocate—and similarly the ointments by which cooling of the fever is sought—restricts the matters and causes the formation of abscesses. Wherefore it is more convenient to use some light resolutive <term>resolutive<gloss>a medicine that disperses inflammation or morbid matter</gloss></term> and opener of the pores as the condition makes it necessary. Because according to whether the matter in the head is much or little, thick or thin, entirely flowing or still in flux, and according to whether there is fullness in the rest of the whole body or not, one must vary this opening resolutive: or sometimes we must be content with the vapor of pure hot water alone, and sometimes we decoct chamomile with it, and sometimes other things. If however there is not [fullness], etc., so that there is no specific fullness in the head: and one desires in the head the thickness of extinguishing the flame of the head. Administer then the embrocation and epithems that you wish.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ And more notable, etc. Because milk becomes sticky and makes a crust. Whence it blocks and retains the matters whose evaporation is sought. We have already dissolved the question...

It references the systematic teachings of Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine.</meta>

### On the application of milk to the head according to the summary of the third book.
And regarding the preservation of the hours. It must be considered that the sharp choleric vapor <note>original: "vapor cholericus acutus"; in medieval medicine, "choleric" refers to the humor of yellow bile, which was thought to be hot and dry</note> could be plentiful. Thus, although a mixture with oil of roses, or violets, or water-lily, or an embrocation <term>embrocation<gloss>a liquid medicine rubbed into the body to relieve pain or inflammation</gloss></term> of similar power, helps by removing that sharpness or malice, nevertheless, by retaining its large quantity, it could do harm. Therefore, he said "perhaps it will help you," which we discussed in the section of the third book, in the chapter on the cure for <term>soda<gloss>a medieval medical term for a persistent, heavy headache, often caused by rising vapors</gloss></term> in fevers and the chapter on the cure for soda in general.

<margin>a</margin> **And it is recognized.** What is said here is well known. Let the complete account of this knowledge be sought below in the chapter on headache.

And it is recognized by the state of sleep and wakefulness, and by the moisture of the upper parts of the nostrils and their dryness. When, therefore, you see sleep, or a depth of sleep, or moisture in the upper parts of the nostrils, then beware of embrocations and ointments. Instead, strive to draw the matter to the lower parts of the body. And when you see a powerful redness in the nose and face, then it will not be a bad thing if you cause blood to flow from the nostrils.

<margin>b</margin> **And cool it.** Here he returns to the chapter on cooling the liver to complete the knowledge on that subject, following the rules laid down there. **And it is necessary.** It must be considered that the time for an embrocation of the liver is twofold. One is chosen: and this is when the matter is in the process of resolving—indeed, when it is already evaporating; for example, when the sick person is sweating. The other is forced: and that is at whatever hour you see a necessity for extinguishing strong heat. This is what we previously chose when the sick person was becoming parched. By this, the question is solved about which physicians frequently chatter: whether in a putrid fever we ought to apply epithems <term>epithems<gloss>topical compresses or poultices applied to the heart or liver</gloss></term> to the liver and heart with cooling agents before evacuations have been made. In this, physicians bite one another <note>original: "seise modẽt" (seise mordent); a common medieval metaphor for academic disagreement</note>. It should be said that regularly they ought not to be applied, because these epithems prevent evaporation. However, if the disturbance of heat is so great that we care more that the patient not be consumed by it, or become "hectic" <note>wasting away from chronic fever</note>, or be prepared for dropsy <note>edema or fluid swelling</note>, then we apply the epithem even if evacuation has not preceded it, and even if it is the hour when the matter is resolving. This is because the harm that follows from this is merely the prolongation of the illness, whereas we would rather have that than have the patient die. Sometimes the utility of cold epithems is also the rectification and digestion of thin, hot matters.

And cool it with plasters. And when you cool it, beware that you do not encounter a time of sweating and resolution with vehement cooling; rather, it is necessary that you observe this, for perhaps it may cause the lengthening of the sickness—though sometimes the length of the sickness is safer than its sharpness. And it is necessary that you beware in acute fevers of the "falling of the hair" <note>original: "casum rasure," likely referring to the weakening of the scalp's grip or general debility</note>, since it adds to the weakness of the life-force, and nature is terrified of receiving wastes into the intestines or expelling them because of the victory of those wastes. Perhaps the wastes return to the upper parts and hurt the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen below the ribs</note>, inflating them and hurting the head. And sometimes in a drink of poppy there is a wonderful help in thickening thin matter, which it digests by inducing sleep.

<margin>c</margin> **And it is necessary, etc.** This rule is well known. However, two versions of the text are found. One says "because of victory," meaning because they conquer and settle the matter. The other says "not because of victory," meaning nature does not expel wastes to the intestines when they are raw and painful, unless they greatly overflow and conquer—just as one having sores on the penis does not urinate unless he is overcome by a great quantity of urine and urinates involuntarily.

<margin>d</margin> **And sometimes.** Here he cools those with acute fevers through medicinal drinks. This is the 17th rule of the *Continens* <note>The "Continens" refers to the *Al-Hawi*, a massive medical encyclopedia by the Persian physician Rhazes</note>, in the fourth chapter, on the authority of Philaretus. This discussion concerns simple syrup of poppy—that is, without beans—from which we also give one and a half ounces with cold water for sleep if it seems right to us.

<margin>e</margin> **Let us speak therefore in the first place.** After the general cure for putrid and acute fevers, and after the chapter on feeding them, he speaks of the removal of the "accidents" <note>symptoms or secondary complications</note> which happen more in acute cases, though they can happen in other fevers as well. These symptoms can follow most fevers, indeed all of them, though most of them follow acute ones. Therefore, the determination of the cure for accidents is in a way common to the specific treatments of fevers. Galen <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note>, when he considered that the accidents come after the fevers, placed the cures after them. From these things many "childish questions" are solved which we have occasionally raised here.

### A recollection of the accidents that are difficult in acute fevers. Chapter 11.

Let us speak therefore in the first place of the accidents that have been violent in fevers, and of their cure, and let us hasten to distinguish the acute fevers. These accidents are such as shivering, cold, and horripilation <note>shivering or goosebumps</note>; and such as excessive sweating; and such as an overabundance of nosebleeds; and such as laborious vomiting; and a weakening flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>; and such as a thirst that cannot be tolerated; and such as excessive depth of sleep; and such as inseparable wakefulness; and such as roughness of the tongue; and darkening of the mouth; and such as continual sneezing; and a wicked headache; and frequent coughing; and such as the loss of appetite; and <term>bulimus<gloss>an intense, morbid hunger</gloss></term>; and such as a canine appetite; and hiccups.

<margin>f</margin> **Which is.** The reason there are so many symptoms is for a purpose. There are 22 symptoms that he enumerates. He begins with the management of shivering and sets down the cure. First, he states that there is a shivering that should not be focused on: which is the shivering after sweating and the "critical" shivering <note>shivering associated with a 'crisis' or turning point in a disease</note>. A critical shivering neither 3...

### On the management of shivering and horripilation when they are excessive. Chapter 12.

That which follows sweating is rectified quickly and does not need a regime. And in a critical shivering, it is not necessary that the opposite be done by removal, for it is not among those things that weaken or do anything else. Sometimes they are settled by the binding of the extremities and easy rubbing, and with the warmth of a

<column-break/>

covering and with an ointment of oil of dill and of chamomile, if it is needed.

<margin>...debilitates nor does anything else. But concerning the distress or the addition of the disease: rather it ceases. Understand this as referring to a critical crisis, because it has wicked symptoms, even though it leads to health. But it is doubted: because shivering after sweating seems bad, as Hippocrates says in the 7th part of the Aphorisms: "in sweating, shivering is bad," therefore it ought to be managed. For Franciscus de Pedemontium believes that this shivering during sweating should not be managed because it lasts for a short time, even if it is bad. We say that the shivering of which Avicenna speaks here is not the one Hippocrates speaks of, because that one is during the sweat and is bad and needs management; but the shivering Avicenna speaks of here is the shivering when the sweat is finished. Of this he speaks below in the chapter on the narration of good signs when he says: "horripilation occurring after evacuation is among the good signs." We have said above that horripilation can be called shivering.</margin>

In a severe case, however, when it persists—whether it be in fevers or in other things—it is necessary that the extremities be bound in many places, and the anointing be done with oil of chamomile and lily root. There are some men who strengthen it with these things: which are like cardamom, castor <note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, rue, *sceba* <note>likely a species of wormwood</note>, calamint, saltpeter, pepper, and pellitory. And sometimes it passes by administering liniments made of mustard and other solid things. And sometimes these medicines are boiled in water; then some oil is boiled in it; and the water itself is strong in this chapter on its own, or with some oil that is boiled with it. And similarly, a decoction of oxymel <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note> and its water.

<margin>g</margin> **And sometimes.** Here he sets down the regime for shivering that needs management or cure. First, he sets down the light cure for light cases. Then the stronger cure for stronger cases. **In a severe case.** It should be considered that in some sensitive bodies, shivering is a very distressing accident. There are three distressing types: sometimes for some there is a strong coldness; sometimes for some there is a strong shaking; and sometimes for some there is a bad sensation of pricking. Rubbing and covering, by moving the heat outward, often settle these. And sometimes it is necessary to anoint with the oils he mentions.

### The making of a good oil.

Let dried dill, myrrh, rue, calamint, pepper, and pellitory be taken and boiled in wine in a final decoction; then let it be strained and boiled in half as much sesame oil until the water is consumed and only the oil remains; and let it be administered by anointing.

<margin>h</margin> **In a severe case.** First he sets down the methods of settling shivering with external things. Second, with things taken internally. **And all medicines of strong provocation.** The first has as many helps as he lists, and it is not broad. *Sceba* some say is *ficados*, others that it is a species of wormwood, as it is thought to be "Santonic" <note>Santonica, or Levant wormwood</note> named from that town, as Galen says in the 6th book of *On Simple Medicine* in the chapter on southernwood at the end. It should be considered that the spine and the places most distressed by shivering should be anointed with these oils and ointments.

And of the strong oils for them in such a case—such as the shivering of a quartan fever <note>a fever, like malaria, that recurs every fourth day</note>—there is oil of costus, and oil of *sceba*, and oil of southernwood, and oil of lily, and oil of myrrh. Let there be placed in one ounce of oil three drachms of pepper and one drachm of crushed pellitory. Let wormwood decocted in some oil be administered, or olive oil in which celery has been boiled. And entering into oil of light warmth is very helpful. And perhaps potions are necessary. Many times it is settled with warm water of light heat, and with treatment over its vapor. And when it is not settled by that, if the matter is thick, let anise, calamint, celery seed, mastic, rocket, dill, and similar things be boiled in water. And let the patient be bathed in water in which things like *sceba*, southernwood, calamint, dill, camel grass, rue, marjoram, costus, and hot seeds have been boiled. And all medicines of strong provocation settle shivering.

<margin>i</margin> **And all medicines of strong provocation.** That is, drinking those that provoke urine or sweat. This is well known. This is the part in which he begins to place medicines taken internally. First, the simples. One may doubt why he allows agaric <term>agaric<gloss>a medicinal fungus used to purge thick humors</gloss></term> at the start of a paroxysm <note>the sudden onset or worsening of symptoms</note>, since it is among the loosening medicines. Also, how opium causes one to sweat. To the first, we say we do not use agaric in a quantity that loosens, but we give, for example, half a drachm; for it heats and thins thick matters. And the urge to vomit which it causes is useful, specifically at the start of a quartan fever. To the second, it should be said that opium by itself does not cause sweating, but by provoking sleep, or by relaxing the pricking sensation by which the life-force was terrified of evacuation. Or it should be said that this compound of agaric and opium provokes sweat through the agaric and causes sleep through the opium, and prevents other harms that could follow from the violence of the shivering, such as fainting.

And of the medicines settling the greatest shivering in a quartan fever and things similar to it: let one drink "golden costus"—that is, with warm water—and as much agaric as is needed in warm water. And in agaric there is help. And sometimes he places with it a piece of opium because it causes sleep, and causes sweating, and prohibits the violence of the shivering and other things. And again...

### Treatise II
I

<margin>a</margin> **On** the arrangement. He discusses compound medicines, first the alterative <note>original: "alterantes"; medicines intended to alter the body's state or the quality of the humors without immediate evacuation</note> ones, and secondly those that evacuate. This occurs when the patient is upright or standing; this is done so we may see if they are strong, because if they were weak, opiate medicine could not be granted, or it is done so that the pills may descend better. Aniudem <note>Likely *Anagallis* or pimpernel</note> is a herb from which another is made, and is called *filium* by some, and sometimes it is called *fiseLeos*, as in the third book of the *Canon*, fen 3, the chapter on the cure for dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note> at the end. Regarding the "shaving" <note>likely a reference to a specific pharmaceutical preparation technique</note> in the book of medicines for the head: Some say *Darmelis* is hemlock; others say it is a species of rue; others that it is wild rue, as noted below in fen 6, the chapter on the cure for viper bites. Consider, however, in these hot medicines, the effects of thinning the matter and the retraction of heat to the exterior parts, and the dulling of the senses through opium. Perhaps it is prohibited during the onset of shivering <note>original: "rigoris"</note>, though sometimes necessity compels us, namely the failing of strength along with it.

<margin>b</margin> **And** the evacuation <note>original: "solutio"; referring to the loosening of the bowels</note>. It must be considered that this loosening can be understood to occur once the shivering has settled, and not during the act of shivering itself, which is certain. These medicines are well known, for there are many descriptions of them in the 5th book of the *Canon*, second treatise; choose whichever fits the matter. Diacytonicon <note>a quince-based medicine</note> is for loosening; it is written in the 5th book of the *Canon*, 3rd treatise. Diaphoenicon <note>a date-based medicine</note> is also written there, and by Mesue <note>A famous Persian physician</note>. This is from *afinichio*, that is, the date. It can also be understood that these evacuants are given while shivering persists, and this would be when great danger is imminent; there would be no other way except the evacuation of the matter. This would be done more safely if it were not a "hot" condition, but rather shivering that is not warmed because of "glassy phlegm" <note>original: "phlegmate vitreo"; a thick, cold, transparent humor</note>; therefore it requires strong medicine such as the well-known "fetid pills," which are written of in the 9th book of Almansor <note>Rhazes’ *Liber ad Almansorem*</note> in the chapter on paralysis. And consider that if the matter of this shivering were in the primary veins and around the stomach and intestines, the labor of evacuating them with the usual laxatives mentioned—like Hiera, Diacytonicon, and Diaphoenicon—would not be great and would be more convenient. We have no other proven remedies for vehement shivering except what is written here. Some, however, use "water of the vine" <note>original: "aqua vitis"; likely distilled wine or brandy</note> for this.

### Regimen for superfluous sweat in fevers. Chapter 63.

**It is necessary** that a critical sweat <note>original: "sudor creticus"; a sweat that occurs at the "crisis" or turning point of a disease, signaling recovery</note> should not be restricted as much as possible. However, when necessity arises and it exceeds the proper limit, then the place must be aired and cooled. If this does not suffice, then the patient should be placed on an instrument in which children or youths are accustomed to be shaken in the air <note>perhaps a swing or rocking device</note> and moved in a cold place. One should not be occupied in wiping away <note>original: "eruccando"</note> that which comes out as dew, doing so repeatedly after drying; for that is an occasion to provoke and multiply it, and perhaps it draws on a fainting spell <note>original: "sincopim"</note>. For its wiping away increases it, and leaving it alone restricts it. And it is necessary to anoint him with strong oil of roses and myrtle oil, or with oil of willows, or with oil of pomegranate flowers; or let an oil be made with the waters in which quinces are cooked. <meta>catchword: pon (referring to the next word 'ponibus' or 'ponderibus')</meta>

<column-break/>

for nine continuous days. Other things which he says are well known, as is their cause, etc.

<margin>d</margin> **It is necessary** that one hurries. First, he does this; second, he places a certain rule there. And sometimes it must be considered that one cures the superfluity first by friction <note>rubbing the skin</note> to divert the humors, and by cupping glasses <term>ventosas<gloss>glass cups used in bloodletting or to draw humors to the surface using suction</gloss></term> on the side—namely, of the liver or the spleen. It follows that if the bleed is from the right nostril, place it over the liver. We have found help in this and we apply large cupping glasses; this is praised below in the second section of this regimen of the place, namely the nostril, by placing what they perceive in fen 3 of the third book of the *Canon*. And perhaps it is possible for you to cool the areas of the head as well as the areas of the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen</note>; and this would be the regimen for that place. Do not place cupping glasses directly above, which is explained in two ways: first, although you do not place cupping glasses over the hypochondria, you should only cool those places and thicken the blood. Thus the flow can be cured. If he wanted this, it was because he was suspicious of harm to the spleen or liver if the matters were drawn there. In a second way it can be explained: that he prohibits cupping glasses being placed above, namely around the parts of the head or neck, which draw the matter from below to the head. And when there is nothing prohibiting it—namely, catarrh <note>excessive mucus</note> or superfluous blood which would be sharp in that part—then the cooling of the head is harmful for a flow of blood from the nostrils, as Galen said in the 5th book of *On the Method of Healing*, chapter 6. It must be considered that a quartan fever <note>a fever recurring every fourth day, often malaria</note> from bloody melancholy—that is, mixed with blood—can be cured by a flow of blood from the left nostril, because it regards the spleen more. We know our father cured a certain person of such a superfluous flow with a drink of wine, the covering of cloths, and the provocation of sweat. However, this cure should not be attempted except by a man of good reputation, such as we believe him to have been.

### Regimen for superfluous flow of blood from the nostrils. Chapter 64.

**To** prohibit that which is critical as much as possible. However, when it is necessary to prohibit the flow of blood from the nostrils in acute fevers, then tie the extremities and place cupping glasses on the side that corresponds to the side of the nosebleed. Then consequently apply the regimen for that place; for perhaps it will be possible for you to cool it, and it may be restricted by that; and before, or do not place cupping glasses above. And drop into the nose some of the distillations mentioned in the chapter on nosebleeds; and when nothing prohibits it, cool the head with the coolants mentioned for it. And whenever a flow of blood from the nostrils occurs in those suffering from quartan fever, you must help it with those things known to make blood flow from the nostrils; for in this itself is the healing of the quartan fever. If, however, we fear superfluity, we shall do as we have done.

### Regimen for vomiting which happens to them. Chapter 65.

<margin>c</margin> **Again**, do not cut off a critical vomit. First, by premising that they should not be cured. First he places a certain common regimen, then a special one. If the humor is as first described, it is verified by this: that "vomit cures vomit and flow," as in Avicenna, the third book of the *Canon*, fen 16, chapter 5 on the cure of colic. It must be considered that if the matter is suitable for being led out, a simple vinegar syrup with warm water suffices for the completion of the evacuation by vomit, as is well known. But if the matter is thick, needing stronger division and thinning, then vinegar syrup with seeds of anise, fennel, and the like should be given. And consider that this is the cure for nausea which does not stop because of the matter which must be expelled by vomit.

<margin>f</margin> **And if.** This is a small part and is divided into four: first, he positions the cure when the humor is "imbued" <note>absorbed into the tissues</note> and thick. Second, when it is imbued but not thick. Third, when it is not imbued. Fourth, he specifically positions the regimen for choleric <note>yellow bile</note> and melancholic <note>black bile</note> vomiting. Consider first regarding the first part: that this thick imbued humor can be of a phlegmatic nature or a choleric nature. For these two humors abound in the stomach; yet more of either, when the matter is phlegmatic, requires Hiera and Aloe—at least because there is no suspicion of harm from heating. He mentions Aloe and Hiera because they are similar. Aloe alone does not suffice for the extraction of thick humors, but it is necessary to invigorate it with the "Alexandrian" species <note>specific medicinal ingredients</note> which are in Hiera. And thus Hiera, through the Aloe, evacuates that place, as we understood from the 7th book of *Therapeutics*, the 6th book of *On the Preservation of Health*, and from the chapters on Aloe. But why did he say Aloe when it would suffice to say Hiera, since Aloe is an ingredient in Hiera?

<margin>e</margin> **It must be said** that he said this so that a notable quantity should be of Aloe, and he put Hiera and Aloe so that its dominance would be great. But when the humor is not imbued, even if it is thick, such a quantity of Aloe is not required. And thus he said Hiera and then Aloe, putting Aloe second; the quantity is called "aloe" or a diminution according to the measurement estimated by the physician based on the condition of the humors. By these "Hieras," understand the Hiera of Galen and those which he calls "common" or "universal" in the fifth book. He said "perhaps," because it is possible to lead it out with something lighter, such as honey water or oxymel <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note>.

**And if it were.** Here he positions the cure when the humor is imbued but not thick. It must be considered that this humor is to be understood as choleric, because it is mostly such. However, it can be...

**Book IV**

<margin>a</margin> Because thin phlegm <note>original: "phlegma subtile"; one of the four bodily humors, traditionally associated with cold and moisture</note> requires thin [treatment]. Avicenna <note>A 10th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe</note> therefore aims at two goals: first, the extraction of that humor. This is done through induced vomiting using vinegar syrup given with warm water to wash and open the "pores" <note>original: "pozoś/poros"; the pathways through which humors move</note> without constricting them; since the humor is thin, it follows during evacuation. Second, he aims for the balancing of the humor itself or the stomach. This balancing, if the humor is biliary <note>original: "cholericus"; relating to yellow bile</note>, involves cooling and strengthening the stomach after evacuation so it does not receive more. This is done with water or pomegranate juice—specifically the sour kind—repeated if necessary. If it is phlegmatic, syrup of mint with pomegranate is used. Read a good description of this in the "Antidotary" by <term>Mesue</term> <note>Johannes Mesue, an influential figure in medieval pharmacology</note>. I use this and have found it useful for both biliary and phlegmatic materials. Perhaps cooling from the outside, or rather using cold substances like cold water, is best when there is thin, boiling bile. Indeed, some stomach ailments are cured by drinking it, as noted in the first book, fen 13, in the chapter on the weakness of the stomach.

<margin>a</margin> And it is not necessary. It must be considered that those styptics <note>original: "stiptica"; substances that shrink or constrict body tissues to stop secretions</note> are extremely harmful when taken internally in the aforementioned case, because they close the pores of the stomach and further soak and drive the matter into the stomach. Therefore, if the matter were not soaked in, strengthening the stomach would help with evacuation. And this is perhaps true, for it is possible it might not happen that way. If, however, these styptics are applied as a plaster from the outside, such harm is not suspected; rather, it is possible they push those materials into the depths of the stomach. It is also possible they simultaneously constrict that matter into the parts of the stomach. This requires careful consideration. <term>Dynus</term> <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous 14th-century medical commentator</note>, in his commentary on the fourth part of the first book, chapter 23, seems to apply this text strictly to things taken internally, if one considers it carefully.

<margin>b</margin> And when. This section seems to imply that when the humor is biliary but not "soaked in" <note>original: "imbibito"; absorbed into the stomach lining</note>, the styptics we use are specifically in the form of a plaster. For they raise no suspicion of soaking in, whereas styptics taken internally—even if the humor is not soaked in—can cause that soaking via wine or vinegar. This is because the materials require weakening, and vinegar provides that, while the stomach requires strengthening via wine.

[The text continues:] ...with warm water; then he balances it afterward with pomegranate water to be drunk. If it moves the matter, he should drink it another time until it is balanced and quieted. Similarly, syrup of mint with pomegranate seeds. And perhaps cooling the stomach will settle it. It is necessary to approach with "pontic" <note>original: "ponticis"; astringent or harsh-tasting substances</note> things that settle vomiting with their astringency and acidity—specifically for one whose vomiting comes from soaked-in humor. Because this condition is bad and adds to the soaking, but for those where it is not soaked in, it might perhaps cause it to be cast downward, as it becomes thick; perhaps it will aid the strength of the stomach to expel it through the upper parts. And when the vomiting of bile becomes constant and is not of the "soaked-in" type, then use styptics, and specifically helpful plasters made from pomegranate rinds, galls <note>growths on oak trees used for their high tannin content</note>, and similar things mixed with wine or vinegar. For the vomiting of black bile, it is advised to soak a sponge in vinegar and place it over the stomach. If something stronger is necessary, administer the medicines described in the chapter on the retention of vomiting.

### Management of the flux of the belly occurring in them. Cap. LXII.

<margin>c</margin> **N**amely, we have spoken specifically on this intent in the chapter on the flux of the belly <note>original: "fluxus ventris"; diarrhea or loose bowels</note>. **E**rgo, let us return to that. Among those things that help by way of food are roasted pulses <note>original: "almes"; likely a type of legume like chickpeas or beans</note>, roasted lentils, and coriander. Whichever of these two is used, let it be boiled and the water drained from it; this is especially good when it is acidic with pomegranate seeds.

### Management of their excessive thirst. Cap. LXIII.

<margin>d</margin> **I**t is necessary to bathe the head with very cold oil, which is poured over it and placed on the head if nothing prohibits it (and with cooling waters). Also, a mixture of quince seeds with rose oil, or finally, an infusion of plums, cucumber pulp, alkekengi <note>winter cherry</note>, gourd, black lettuce seeds, and licorice roots, and the pills described in the antidotary for thirst. Among things to be chewed are *almosolat* <note>an Arabic-derived term for acidic syrups or fruits</note> and tamarinds. Thirst sometimes comes from cold, and sleep cuts it off; sometimes it comes from heat, and wakefulness cuts it off.

### On the depth of sleep occurring in them. Cap. LXVIII.

**I**t is necessary that they be removed from deep sleep <note>lethargy or coma-like states during fever</note> with fables...

<column-break/>

...either indigestion causes thirst because of vapors and parts of food which, although they are naturally cold due to the lack of heat, are nevertheless inflamed and heated by accidental heat. From this, the first argument ceases: thirst from heat is caused by hot foods whose vapors are retained around the stomach. The areas of the throat cause thirst, and wakefulness helps in this by evaporating them, though sometimes it is not enough; their heat and dryness must be extinguished by drink. <term>Dynus</term> understood this exposition.

<margin>e</margin> **I**t is necessary that they be removed. A fable <note>original: "fabula"</note> is a narrative composed of changeable and impossible things; in this, it is distinguished from history. Therefore, he says regarding these and similar things: histories. For they are similar to fables in the form of narration by voices, because they are told by calling out or speaking loudly. But it is doubted, since fables usually cause sleep, as appears to be the case and will be stated shortly by Avicenna. It must be said that fabulous and historical narratives sometimes make some people sleep and sometimes keep others awake, as is seen in the reading of books. For some, as soon as they begin to read, immediately sleep; and some, wanting to sleep, begin to read and stay awake. This is understood from <term>Aristotle</term> in the *Problems*, book 18, problems 1 and 7. The cause of this diversity is sometimes on the part of the nature of those reading or hearing, and this is twofold. First, because some have raw, phlegmatic, or cold melancholic humors in the brain, prone to evaporation and windiness. Therefore, while they are awake and not thinking, the heat distracted outward does not cause those materials to evaporate. But when, by reading or hearing fables, there is movement in the spirit and heat of the ventricles of the brain, evaporation of those humors occurs, the spirits thicken, and sleep happens because the spirit is cooled by this and becomes unfit for outward expansion (which is necessary for wakefulness). Conversely, if someone has other biliary, sharp humors prone to evaporate through movement made in the brain during the act of thinking, then beginning to read or hear will make them more awake. Second, this happens due to diversity in the intellect—that is, the "cogitative" faculty. For men are either of poor intellect, or if they are of good intellect, when they do not understand what they read, they are prone to sleep. Similarly, when they hear histories and fables which they do not understand. The cause is first because when they do not understand, they become sad; and sadness <note>original: "tristitia"</note> is a cause of cooling and the retreat of heat to the interior, and such a disposition is the disposition of heat during sleep. The second cause is because in these people there is a double movement, as in every act of understanding. One is spiritual, which is thought; the other is corporeal, which is the movement of vapors and thin humors through the parts of the head. This movement happens when there is movement of the spirits in the act of thinking. We disputed whether this movement is local and how it occurs in the first fen of the third book. Therefore, when a man is of dull intellect, the spiritual movement fails. Then those vapors and moved humors thicken and soften the spirits, and thus the man sleeps; the spirits then cease from their movement and rest. But men of good and sharp intellect, when they read or hear things they understand well, stay awake due to joy <note>original: "leticia"</note>. For they recognize they are in the disposition in which they ought to be according to nature; and according to nature, a man in his proper state stays awake, as Aristotle says. Furthermore, the spiritual movement of the cogitative faculty is the reason why the spirit remains in motion and is not overcome by the moved vapors, as it is overcome in a man of dull intellect. It should be considered, however, that by accident, a man of coarse intellect sometimes stays awake when beginning to read or hear; for although he is sad because he does not understand, he nevertheless uses effort, fearing disgrace. In this, he is troubled by anxiety, which is sadness regarding the future—namely, the disgrace that follows if he is ignorant, or the honor if he knows. Such sadness causes wakefulness, just as sadness about the past causes sleep, as is understood in the first book of the *Canon*. And if you consider it well, this man is not of dull intellect in this regard; rather, he is of good intellect in that he distinguishes possible future honor and disgrace, which is an act of prudence. But he is dull in that which he does not understand—for example, he does not grasp the demonstration that every triangle has three angles equal to two right angles. Similarly, a man of subtle intellect hearing or reading is sometimes provoked to sleep for two reasons: because he has already reached the end since he understood, and therefore he rests; second, because due to the discourse on many intelligible things, it is possible that a great resolution <note>depletion</note> of spirits occurs, and thus sleep is sought for their restoration. However, this will not happen immediately when he begins to read or hear. The cause of this diversity on the part of fables, histories, or other scientific things read is more manifest. For if the narrative—be it fable or lecture—is uniform, both in the manner of delivery and in what it signifies, it provokes sleep, just as a uniform sound does. The reason is that in this, there is a certain disposition similar to rest and a lack of anxiety; hence, one is prone to sleep from this. If you consider it, it results in the disposition called *psigitie* <note>likely a corruption of a Greek term related to cooling or psychological stillness</note>. But if the fable...

<margin>e</margin> And for vomiting. This section is placed in the first book, fen 4, chapter 2, on the rules of vomiting, and in the third book, fen 13, on the cure of bad complexions of the stomach with matter and its obstructions. <term>Dynus</term> above, on the first fen of the first book, imagines that this black bile is "burnt" <note>original: "adusta"; scorched by excessive heat</note>. Vinegar strengthens the stomach by its stypticity; it is also drying and thinning, and it resists external heat. He places it with a sponge because it weighs less and because it should be applied while actually hot. We say that we have never placed great faith in this section, and we wish to test it; though sometimes we have found it useful even in "fecal melancholy" <note>severe constipation or bowel obstruction attributed to black bile</note>. We have applied felt with sharp or strongly heated vinegar. But because other known remedies are more useful, we have set aside its use. Perhaps Avicenna understood this when he said "if necessary." It seems this remedy is for retaining [stopping] that vomiting, and without doubt, vinegar is powerful in this.

<margin>f</margin> Namely, specifically. He refers us to the third book, fen 16, and the first book, fen 4. And thirst. *Ames* is a legume called pea or *robilie*; among others, it is the kidney bean. Others say it is a certain legume used by the Saracens, found in the dietary books as *prisomila*. A chapter on it is found in the second section, chapter 7; it is called *meyse*. In short, it does not appear that they should be roasted, but that he adds stypticity by boiling the water so the residue is more astringent.

<margin>g</margin> It is necessary to bathe. It is doubted how this cooling helps in thirst. It must be said that when the head is cooled, the "mouth of the stomach" <note>the upper opening of the stomach</note> is cooled through the community of the nerves; because of the inflammation of the head communicated to the stomach, thirst could be caused. "If nothing prohibits it," such as excessive fullness or catarrh <note>excessive mucus</note>, as we said above. "Black lettuce"—that is, dark green, because it is colder and moister; or "black" in its seed, because its seed is black and is cold like the poppy. *Almosolat* is a common name for acidic things. <term>Simon</term> <note>likely Simon of Genoa, a medical lexicographer</note>, however, wants it to be tamarind, and the text should read *almosat*.

<margin>f</margin> And thirst. It is doubted how thirst comes from cold, since thirst is an appetite for the cold and moist. Furthermore, how does wakefulness cut off thirst caused by heat, since wakefulness inflames? One person says that cold causes thirst because it congeals moisture; hence, moistening cannot occur, and from this, heat is intensified and thus thirst. Heat, therefore, because it melts that moisture, removes that thirst. He also says that excessive wakefulness, because of excessive resolution, causes cooling and therefore removes thirst from heat. These statements are so crude they do not deserve to be refuted. We say first that this is the statement of <term>Hippocrates</term> in the fourth book of the "Epidemics": just as in wakefulness, thirst is on the surface, sleep is its medicine; but from sleep, there is an "erection" <note>waking up/rising</note>. The cause of this statement is given by the Alexandrian commentator in the same place; he says that by frequent wakefulness, the mouth and throat are dried out, and thirst becomes "on the surface"—that is, moderate and superficial—and it is not thirst from the heat and drying of the mouth of the stomach or the lung. Sleep removes this superficial thirst because, in sleep, the moistening of the members occurs. This thirst is so light that only talkativeness <note>original: "garresima"</note> removes it. In sleep, however, thirst often occurs because hot fumes ascend to the upper parts—for example, to the mouth and throat—and cause thirst. Waking up removes this thirst; that is, the sleeper should rise and wake from sleep so the fumes evaporate to the surface. Our other exposition, which we wrote in the 13th part of the third book, is that Avicenna's statement concerns the heat or coldness of foods or drinks. For thirst arises from cold foods—that is, from indigestion—whether they are cold by nature or not, since undigested food can be called cold, because digested things are hot (since digestion is from heat). When, therefore, thirst arises through the indigestion of food, sleep removes it by completing digestion. This is the thirst of which the aphorism of Hippocrates in the fifth part speaks: "To those who have a desire to drink at night, if they sleep on it, it is good."

It also provides a fascinating psychological and physiological analysis of why storytelling (fables) can either wake a lethargic patient or induce sleep based on their intellectual temperament and the nature of their humors.</summary>

**Book 4, Part 2, Treatise 2**

Whether a story or history is varied in tone—sometimes speaking loudly, sometimes softly—the fables <note>original: "fabulas"; storytelling was a recognized therapeutic tool in medieval medicine to regulate the patient's emotional state</note> or histories contain elements that provoke anger, laughter, or compassion. In such cases, the person’s soul is distracted, moving from one emotion to another. Because of this, the person stays awake. However, such storytelling could accidentally cause sleep; because of the intense focus on these stories—diverting the mind now to anger, now to mercy, now to joy—fatigue and the "resolution of the spirits" <note>original: "spirituū resolutio"; the dispersal of the vital vapors thought to power the body's functions</note> can occur, leading to a desire for sleep.

<margin>a These sayings should be well considered: they are as useful for understanding the aforementioned problems of Aristotle as the sayings of the Conciliator <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous physician and philosopher known as "The Conciliator" for harmonizing Greek and Arabic medicine</note>. These opposites cease by turns: for fables can provoke the wakeful to sleep and excite the sleeper. This is seen later. Furthermore, regarding another reading: we make a sharp, long eye-salve <term>collyrium</term> <note>a topical medicinal preparation for the eyes</note> for him from powder, agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note>, and honey; sometimes we add rock salt or colocynth <note>bitter apple, a potent purgative</note> if appropriate—specifically during the hour of rest or during a "paroxysm" <note>the peak intensity of a disease or fever fit</note> or exacerbation rather than during constant illness. Through this, Avicenna <note>original: "auic."; the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> intends that one should not be weak in mind when taking eye-salves at the peak of a paroxysm. This was explained differently before: that is, it should be done regularly if the necessity appears, to divert the vaporous materials from the head.</margin>

### On the heaviness of their heads. Chapter 19.

<margin>b It is necessary to avoid. This heaviness signifies a material that causes "repletion" <note>an overfilling of the body's vessels or tissues with humors</note>. These are harmful because they block the pores and prevent evaporation, such as an emulsion of milk; for when milk is applied, it clogs the pores. However, according to Haly Abbas <note>original: "baliabate"; a 10th-century Persian physician</note> in the third part of his "Practica" on the cure of symptoms, another cause can be taken. He believes milk is harmful when there is much material present, because it causes a strong "dissolution" of the material—meaning a commotion and liquefaction—but not its evacuation. There is doubt where he first denies "embrocas" <note>liquid medicinal compresses or washes</note> but later allows them. He first denies cold and moist compresses, or anything that blocks the pores, such as a decoction of poppy heads. But later he allows a compress that opens the pores, such as one made from chamomile, or a cleansing one made from bran. Violets are added to temper the heat, though not as the primary intent.</margin>

**I**t is necessary to avoid the use of milk emulsions on their heads, or the pouring of oil over them, or compresses, or "head-cleansers" <term>caputpurgium</term> <note>remedies intended to purge the brain of excess humors</note>. Instead, let them be content with the vapors produced by compresses made of chamomile; and let there be violets in them, and bran, and similar things.

### On the restlessness of those with fevers and others. Chapter 20.

<margin>c Making violet oil. Here he sets down the cure for restlessness; it is the cure for excessive wakefulness. First, he lists many remedies that induce sleep. Second, he sets down the cure for a specific kind of wakefulness. The first part contains as many methods as there are types of "stupefying" <note>original: "stupefaciētiū"; narcotic or sedative</note> medicines, such as opium or henbane <note>original: "iusquiamū"</note>. Some say it is the water lily <note>original: "nenu far"</note>. Others say it is opium. Others say it is certain unripe dates; they are effective if dissolved in water. These things are known from the third book of the *Canon*, first part, and above in the chapter on the regime for acute diseases; namely, in which conditions they can be administered if there is nothing to prohibit it—such as thick material constricted in the chest.</margin>

**T**o make violet oil with oil of lettuce seed, and oil of water lily, and oil of gourd. And apply some of the famous stupefying agents over the temples, and bend the head over moistening vapors, and smell water lilies and mandrake apples, and "asseheseb" <note>possibly an Arabic medicinal term for a specific sedative preparation</note> sprinkled from a distance, and moistening compresses, and other things you know. Likewise, if there is no prohibition, let him be given a drink of syrup of poppy and its "lohoch" <term>linctus</term> <note>a thick, syrupy medicine licked from a spoon</note>. Then, let candles be multiplied in his hands, and let voices be raised with stories; let his extremities be tied with these, using a slightly painful binding with bands that may be quickly loosened. Then command him to sleep and close his eyes; sometimes while he sleeps a little, let the candles be extinguished, the voices cease, and the bindings be loosened when he sleeps. And when he finds lightness and rest from the paroxysm or its intensity, let him regularly wash his face with water in which black poppy has been cooked with a little mandrake and its root. And when there is a "borax-like" <note>original: "baurachius"; referring to salty or alkaline humors</note> humor there, water in which water-mint, sweet clover, "albracuē" <note>likely an Arabic plant name</note>, and poppy have been boiled is beneficial for washing the face and bending over its vapor.

### On the stomach pain that happens to them.

> Then. Avicenna prescribes this regimen in the third book, part 13. The cause of this [sleepiness] is that from all these things a certain fatigue is produced according to the common sense. When the cause of this is suddenly stopped, the "fetuses" <note>likely a metaphor for the internal movements or vapors</note> are moved to the interior and sleep occurs. However, this remedy is fearful, and we wish to omit it lest common people speak against us if we do not achieve the end result. When he finds that these things prevent the resolution of the material, they are more suitable during the rest from a paroxysm. When the materials are thick, phlegmatic, and sharp, water-mint, sweet clover, and "allamen" <note>possibly alum or a specific herb</note> contribute to their thinning and resolution. But to reduce the sharpness, poppy is beneficial, and for inducing sleep. "Allachoen" is feverfew <term>matricaria</term> according to Simon. Avicenna, in the third book of the *Canon*, part 16, in the chapter on the cure of intestinal excoriation, believes it is crowfoot. Others believe it is stinking chamomile.

The third goal is the lessening of their sharpness, which is done with moistening things. The fourth is the calming of the senses, which is done through sleep and the smell of "sauich" <term>roasted barley</term> <note>original: "sauich"; an Arabic term for parched barley flour used as a cooling agent</note>. All of this can be understood under the intention of lessening sharpness. Let him rub: rubbing is done to resolve those vapors. Rubbing around the eyes is beneficial, as noted in Aristotle's *Problems*, book 34, problem 2, although he gives another reason which you may read; that reason can be reduced to this one. Let the palates be rubbed so that some phlegm is drawn out to the "strainer" <note>the ethmoid bone or nasal passages thought to filter the brain</note>. Let them be stretched: that is, rubbed, or rather pulled and moved here and there. Let the extremities be pressed: that is, with strong rubbing. Let things be poured into the ears, etc., such as chamomile for the resolution of those vapors. All these things are beneficial if the sneezing comes from some chilling. Let the "lacerti" <note>the muscles or fleshy parts of the arms</note> be moistened: that is, anointed or bathed with a compress, so that the vapors are resolved through the skin; or it is done because of a hidden evil known to communicate with them in sneezing, along with a minor epilepsy. Let them not be woken from sleep. Immediately he lists contrary views that reduce sleep. Some say they should not be woken from a sleep that is suitable for them, but not from excessive sleep. Others say they should not be woken from sleep suddenly, yet they should be allowed to sleep because sleep retains evaporation. Others say sleep helps by calming the sharpness of the vapors and the sensation, and therefore they should not be woken; but sleep hurts by retaining them, and therefore sleep should be reduced. What should be done is in your judgment. Let it be reduced from dust and sleep or sound, and let them smell "sauich," which is parched unripe barley that strengthens the brain by repressing the sharpness of those vapors; Simon says the same, that it represses bile. "Lutum alnotabi" <note>a medicinal earth or clay</note> is a species of clay like sealed earth or Armenian bole. This sponge resolves those vapors, but with the clay...

<column-break/>

<margin>d That is, by the effusion of bile. It should be considered that there are many causes of stomach pain besides those which Avicenna lists in the third book of the *Canon*, part 13, treatise 2, first chapter. But the cause Avicenna gives here happens much in acute fevers. It should also be considered that this cure he gives here is "preventative" <note>original: "p̄uisiua"</note> because it defends the stomach from receiving bile through syrup of apples—namely pomegranates or quinces. But if the bile were already in the stomach, it would be necessary to evacuate it, first through vomiting. The things with which we strengthen the stomach from the outside are oil of "omphacinum" roses <note>oil made from unripe olives and roses</note> and wine of quinces; sometimes we add mastic and wormwood oil. Note, however, that in our country, most stomach pains in fevers are due to repletion and wind because of people's gluttony; and therefore we cure them with other common things that are well known.</margin>

### Chapter 21.

**O**n the effusion of bile to the stomach: if it happens at the beginning of its "period" <note>the cycle of the fever</note>, give him to drink a little syrup of apples with vinegar syrup.

### On the roughness of their tongues. Chapter 22.

<margin>e In its essence, a certain viscosity. There is a kind of tongue roughness that is nothing other than sliminess. He rubs this away with a cold piece of butcher's broom <note>original: "brusci"</note> or willow wood, and softens and wipes it with known things. Another kind of roughness is dryness, and that is moistened with the pits of plums. We soften dry plums in "julep" syrup according to the teaching of Haly Abbas, and make them hold them in their mouths, and also eat other pits of fruits with salt, etc.—that is, "candy" among us. It should be noted that pillows heat the head a lot; also, sometimes the head is poorly positioned when many are piled up, causing bad breath, and thus they make the tongue rough. Lying on the back also causes dryness: first, because the "superfluities" <note>excess humors</note> that should be expelled through the nose go to the throat and tongue and dry there, and can even harm breathing. Second, because they heat the kidneys. Third, because breathing becomes more difficult from that lying position; other things are obvious.</margin>

**I**n the case of an essence of viscosity, let him rub it with butcher's broom or with willow twigs with almond oil and "tabarzet" sugar <note>a high-quality, refined white sugar</note> until it is clean; or with a sponge and a little salt and rose oil. In this, there is much relief for the sick. After that, when the roughness is not because of viscosity but rather from dryness, it is necessary that he hold in his mouth "sebesten" <note>a type of plum-like fruit</note> or plum pits, or at least those brought from India. It has the color of salt and the sweetness of honey. Let him take of it, as Archigenes <note>a 1st-century Greek physician</note> said, the quantity of one bean. Quince seeds are among those things that moisten the tongue and prevent it from darkening. And it is necessary that many pillows not be used, nor should the sleeper lie on his back, for these two things dry the tongue.

### On the constant sneezing that happens to them. Chapter 23.

<margin>f</margin>
**S**ometimes the harm of constant sneezing is magnified in them; for it hurts them and fills their heads and weakens their powers, and perhaps causes a flow of blood from the nose. Therefore, it is necessary that their forehead, neck, and nose be rubbed, and their mouths opened, and their palates rubbed with force; let their heads be tapped and turned, and their extremities pressed; let warm oils, slightly leaning toward heat, be poured into their ears; let their arms and jaws be moistened; and let heated pillows be placed upon their necks. Let them not be woken from their sleep suddenly, and let them be kept away from dust, and sleep, and everything in whose scent there is sharpness; let them smell "sauich," and "alnatacbi" clay, and sea sponge.

<margin>g **S**ometimes the harm is magnified. First, he lists the harms that come from sneezing, which are three. One is the filling of the head, because by such movement materials are drawn there—though sometimes it is digested material, and in the end, they contribute to the evacuation of materials from the head, as in the third book of the *Canon*, part 5, and in the second commentary on the *Prognostics* [of Hippocrates] regarding that word "if sneezing," etc. The second harm is weakness because of the excessive bad movement; hence sneezing is called a "minor epilepsy" <note>original: "parua epilepsia"</note> as in the third book of the *Canon*, part one. The third harm is the exit of blood from the nose, which can happen at the wrong time and in a sickness where it is not appropriate.</margin>

Therefore it is necessary. Here, second, he sets down the regimen. It must be considered that this sneezing mostly happens from bad, sharp vapors ascending to the head. Therefore, the cure for sneezing is comprised of four intentions. One is the diversion of them from the head, which is done by rubbings. Another is their resolution, which is done by applying heated pillows. Third is...
