### Book 3

...they defile them.
**Bind** the extremities. This happens often in fevers: and many times it diverts a great deal of the cure from itself; and it happens mostly from vapors ascending to the head. First, he <note>the author is likely referencing Avicenna here</note> provides the more general rules: and he aims here at diversion through bindings, frictions, and medicinal inserts <term>collyria</term> <note>While often meaning eye-salves, here it refers to medicinal preparations inserted into the body to draw fluids away from the head</note>. Second, he aims at the strengthening of the head so it does not receive these vapors. And this is done with known cooling agents: such as oil of rose, violet, or similar. And a lotion <term>embrocha</term> <note>a liquid medicine applied to the body, often poured over the head</note> from a decoction of roses, violets, etc. And that is what we commonly use unless there is something that forbids it: such as a cough or a head cold <term>coryza</term>. <margin>Third, he aims</margin> partly at the dissolving of matter and partly at driving it back with chamomile: which softens or eases the matter. Sometimes indeed, softening or easing things are what open and dilate the pores of the limb: as we said regarding the second rule. And perhaps Avicenna intends through this the numbing effect of the poppy, and he placed chamomile to remove their harmful effects. As in the third Book of the Canon, the first Fen, the chapter on the rules for curing illnesses of the brain. It is doubted whether, when someone with a fever has a vehement pain in the head, and with this is coughing and has a discharge through the nostrils, we can from the beginning apply oils to the head and use lotions that are cooling in their potency: like those which Avicenna prescribes. It seems that we can: because this person could become "frenetic" <note>suffering from phrenitis, a medieval term for inflammation of the brain accompanied by delirium</note>; indeed, that pain is sometimes the beginning of it. On the contrary, Avicenna says here and above regarding the regimen of acute diseases: "The foolishness of doctors allows many people suffering from head pain and coughing to turn toward phrenitis because they are unwilling to help with local repelling remedies." <margin>Let us</margin> say that the cough could be on account of a bad hot and dry temperament resulting from the fever. And this will not prohibit the use of those cooling agents on the head. And it could also be from matter falling from the head to the chest and the throat, part of which can also be driven through the nose. And there will be a cough and a cold. And such a cough, in two cases, prohibits the use of those cooling and moistening agents on the head. One case is: if the fear for the throat and the lungs is greater than the fear of the headache. And we have explained this subtly in this third book, first Fen, the chapter on general rules of curing; therefore, take it from there. The other case is if these are signs of much matter standing in the head and filling it: in which case we do not need medicines that block the pores, nor repelling ones, but rather those that dilate the pores, if you do not doubt the further movement of the materials. It is necessary, along with frictions and subtractions and evacuations, to aim in this case—while the cough, catarrh, and cold persist—to follow Avicenna’s prohibition on the use of moistening and cooling agents; if one considers carefully those things he said above and here. Therefore, there can be a case in which a person has a headache and a cough from matter falling from the head, and yet it will be necessary to use these cooling agents on the head. This will be when some matter is at the beginning of a flow to the head, and along with this, some of the matter distills through the "strainer" <note>the ethmoid bone or nasal passages</note> and causes a cough. Or someone with a fever begins to become "lethargic" <note>suffering from *litargia*, a condition of pathological drowsiness</note> whence he begins with a certain heaviness of the head and sleep. And it is possible for then that some rheum is thinned and he coughs. And we should not doubt because of this any harm to the throat or the lung. I say that it is necessary to begin with rose oil on the head: for generally, at the beginning of lethargy, repulsion is prescribed. As in the third Canon, first Fen, chapter 13, on therapeutics. Another case is one that happens much in practice. And it is when someone begins to become truly frenetic with a "true phrenitis" in a continuous choleric fever: whence head pain begins; and at the start of the flow of choleric matter to the brain, some phlegmatic humors begin to be dissolved and thinned: so that immediately as the phrenitis starts, he begins to cough. I say that it is a mistake not to help that beginning of phrenitis with repelling agents applied to the head. This, however, requires a very practiced doctor who knows how to distinguish between a cough caused by "repletion" <note>excessive fullness of humors</note>—which could happen to be joined to the beginning of lethargy and phrenitis—and with this, knows how to measure the danger that is in that cough regarding injury to the lungs or throat: if it is equal to or of less danger than what is in the headache. <margin>And we have seen ways close to this estimative judgment. Know these things then.</margin>

### On the headache that happens to them, Chapter 24.

<margin>a</margin>
**Bind** their extremities and specifically the temples; and bind them with a linen strip: and rub their feet: and let there be placed for them medicinal inserts <term>collyria</term> that draw the matter to the lower parts: and strengthen their heads with known cooling agents. <margin>And if there is not something that</margin> prohibits it, such as a cold or a cough: let their heads be bathed with a lotion <term>embrocha</term> of a decoction of roses and violets and barley or willow leaves and things similar to these: and likewise with rose oil and oil of willows. <margin>And when this does not suffice: then</margin> mix the cooling lotions with soothing things like chamomile and stupefying things like the poppy. <margin>And do not</margin> apply <note>literally "milk" or "press"</note> milk unless the fever is removed. <margin>If however the strength is</margin> strong, apply goat's milk: and if it is weak, apply woman's milk. <margin>And beware of milk during a moist</margin> rheum making a depth of sleep: and likewise beware of moistening agents. And you should not administer moistening agents unless where there is a smoky vapor and the head is dry and there is little sleep: and when repletion is multiplied in the head from a moist vapor: draw it to the lower parts with medicinal inserts and enemas: and bind the lower limbs, even the testicles.

### On their cough. Chapter 25.

<margin>a</margin>
**A cough** very often happens to them from heat <note>original: "colore," likely a scribal error for "calore"</note> or dryness: for which it is necessary that they hold in their mouths "Bechian pills" <note>pills specifically for coughing</note> or lozenges <term>alloboc</term> made of poppy with the pulp of cold fruits and starch and things similar to these: and let them use cooling ointments made from rose oil and from mucilage of psyllium and the juice of purslane and others.

### On the destruction of their appetite

<column-break/>

### Chapter 26.

<margin>a</margin>
**Sometimes** the cause of it is a humor in the mouth of the stomach which causes the destruction of appetite: and it is evacuated through vomiting or loosening of the belly. <margin>And many times it helps with the</margin> insertion of fingers into the throat: and the moving of the stomach: and specifically when he expels through vomiting a choleric or acidic thing. And sometimes it is from the intensity of weakness: therefore let the compulsion that causes it be cured with what is known. <margin>And it is necessary that you bring near to them</margin> good odors exciting the appetite, such as the smell of parched grain <term>sauich</term> <note>Arabic: *sawīq*</note> infused with water and vinegar: and let there be given to them an electuary suitable for those with fever: and a little wine: and the juice of tart fruits of good odor: and let them lick something of the vinegar from fish jelly or *bedi* <note>a savory condiment or relish</note> and similar things; and let there be placed upon the stomach after the first days plasters made from fruits. And let there be in them wormwood and aloes according to what you know: and anointing it with good oils is helpful.

### On their bulimia <note>original: "bolismo"</note>. Chapter 27.

<margin>a</margin>
**Let it be prayed** that it be cured with perfumes and with "Alnatacbi" earth <note>a type of medicinal clay</note> and Armenian bole infused with vinegar: and let them smell *almofolat* <note>possibly tamarinds or a similar sour fruit</note> and clean hot bread and roasted meats: and bind their extremities. <margin>And</margin> pull their ears: and their hair; and strengthen their brains with cooling and moistening lotions. For most of their bulimia is on account of the destruction of the mouth of the stomach: on account of causes communicating with the branches <note>the nerves</note> which come to them with sensation; and it is a hard body: and it is hardened: but the sensation is not perfected with it.

<margin>b</margin>
**Sometimes** it is the cause of it. Here he first sets down the cure according to every variety. Second, he sets it down for exciting the appetite, there: "And it is necessary." The cause of the destruction of appetite could be a humor in the stomach. And the cure for that is a known evacuation. And it could be weakness of the limbs or the liver or the stomach, and the cure is the removal of the cause, etc. And all these things said here are divinely inspired: and they need the completion of the 13th Fen of the third Canon, the chapter on the destruction of appetite. "Or acidic." It is doubted when he ought to be of greater appetite. For acidic things excite the appetite: as gathered in the third book. It is said that acidic things at the beginning of their action help the appetite: but by continuing the action they destroy it: because an immoderate quality destroys the action of its own power. Others say that acidic things can have another corrupt quality because of which they destroy the appetite. All these things said are good. We, however, in the completion of our treatise on appetite, declared that one humor, by a change of place, can destroy the appetite and increase it.

<margin>c</margin>
**And** it is necessary. Here he excites the appetite and teaches a proportionate electuary pertaining to fevers, strengthening the appetite; it is *diacitoten* <note>a quince-based medicine</note> specifically with sugar and specifically without spices. The rest are well known. <margin>Note, however,</margin> we cook quinces or pears in vinegar or water and vinegar: and we grind those and add roses and myrtles, and sometimes calamint, and sometimes other things according to our judgment, and we apply it to the stomach. And it helps both in the flow, and remember what Avicenna says in the third Canon, 13th Fen, in the chapter on the destruction of appetite: that to a person with fever, the appetite sometimes returns with the taking of bread soaked in cold water.

<margin>a</margin>
**Let it be prayed** that they be cured, etc. Bulimia <note>original: *bolisinus*</note> is a hunger of the limbs with a fullness of the stomach. Although it could happen from the coldness of the air: as Avicenna says in the third Canon, 15th Fen, and Aristotle in the *Problems*. Here, however, the talk is about bulimia caused by heat dissolving the limbs: and putting in them a necessity for food: and destroying the appetite of the stomach. And there happens in this bulimia, and in others, a disposition toward fainting <term>syncope</term> and a fall of strength. Therefore, the cure of bulimia is comprised of four intentions. <margin>One is the excitation of the appetite of the stomach: and that</margin> is done with perfumes that are styptic and sharp, like Armenian bole or tamarinds <note>original: *Almosusat*</note>. <margin>The second intention is the strengthening of power. And that is done with perfumes</margin> for the heart and for food: like the smell of roasted meats, etc., even if these excite the appetite. <margin>The third intention is excitation as a caution against the depth of heat: lest they</margin> sleep. <margin>For those suffering from fainting are ordered to stay awake: as in the third Canon, 11th Fen, and</margin> so he says: "bind the extremities," etc. <margin>The fourth intention is to remove the inflammatory heat</margin> of the mouth of the stomach. And he does this with cooling lotions: not so they induce sleep: but so that by cooling the brain, the nerves are cooled, which for the most part come to the stomach. This is what he says: that the primary cause of bulimia is on account of the destruction of the "mouth" <note>of the stomach</note>. Namely, as far as the sensing power is concerned: on account of a cause communicating with the "branches," that is, the nerves that come to give sensation to the mouth of the stomach: and then Avicenna declares that this cause is the febrile heat exciting those nerves. Whence by the excitation they harden, and with nerves thus hardened by dryness, the "perfection of sensation" does not stand—that is, the ultimate goodness of sense. And this is what he says. And it is, namely, the nerve or the mouth of the stomach. Through the nerve, it is a "hard body"—that is, having some moderate quantity naturally with which the goodness of sense stands. And it is hardened, namely, on account of the fever drying it and hardening it more. Truly, the sense is not "perfected"—that is, not at its ultimate goodness with it, namely, the nerve or the mouth of the stomach being excessively hardened. And it should be considered that we use cooling things on the head.

<margin>b</margin>
**And** not. It should be considered that milk, by its actual moisture in a weakened power, reduces the sharpness and the stinging of smoky vapors, namely, the hot, dry, and sharp ones. And therefore its application to the head is sleep-inducing when done properly. Therefore, in two cases it is prohibited. <margin>First, if there is moist matter inducing sleep. Second,</margin> if the matter needs evaporation and resolution. For by blocking the pores, it retains that matter. Therefore, the more convenient hour for its application to the head is in the quiet or the cessation of the fever. Al-Razi <note>original: *Aliah*, referring to Rhazes</note> indeed, in the third book of his *Practice*, in the chapter on the remedy for wakefulness, said: that in milk there is a strong dissolving power; and when it finds matter—namely, a large quantity—it dissolves and disperses it. <margin>You, however, understand that the dissolution is not only through the power</margin> of the milk in itself, but on account of the blockage of the pores: and the harms that follow from this. "If however"—that is, if it is a case in which milk applied to the head is suitable. For example, because...

### On the blackness of their tongue. Cap. xxviii.
It is necessary that the blackness should not be allowed to remain upon the tongue: rather, let it be rubbed with what you know: otherwise, malignant vapors will rise to the head and cause the patient to fall into <term>sirsen</term> <note>delirium</note>.

### On the fainting that happens to them. Cap. xxx.
<margin>d When fainting <term>syncope</term> happens to them at the beginning of fevers because of the pouring out of bile <term>cholera</term> into their stomachs: therefore it is necessary that they be given, before the peak of the fever or at the peak itself, a piece of bread made of <term>simila</term> <note>fine white flour</note> with pomegranate water and <term>verjuice</term> <note>original: "aqua agreste"; the sour juice of unripened grapes</note>. And know that when fainting and fever occur together, then the fainting is more worthy of treatment: and if it requires a little wine, give it mixed with three parts water and old wine: or if not that, a syrup of old apples from which the excess has been removed. And bloodletting indeed often increases the fainting. A light enema <term>clyster</term> is more suitable, and vomiting is helpful to them. Also, the binding of the legs, and placing the hands and feet in hot water. And when they escape the crisis: then care must be taken that they are fed with cooled barley meal, in which there are pomegranate seeds.</margin>

<margin>e "When fainting happens to them." Here, as a reminder and example, he places the cure for fainting occurring in fevers from the effusion of bile into the stomach. And this cure is completed because he turns first to the fainting before it arrives, using things that prevent that bile from coming to the stomach, such as the piece of bread, etc. Since the movement of this bile is at the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>the peak or "fit"</note> of the fever—that is, at the beginning of the paroxysm—it can be prevented. And if it cannot be prevented, let it be given during the paroxysm itself. The benefit of that bread with pomegranate wine or verjuice is the strengthening of the stomach and the lessening of the heat in it, so that the bile is not drawn there; and with this, if the bile does come, it will be weakened and soaked up into that bread, and so it will not cause as much harm, and vomiting it up will be easier. Under this first intention, light enemas are given to prevent this movement, and vomiting is induced. Second, the cure turns to the fainting when it has almost begun, and choice cordial wine is given. Third, see the third book of the Canon, Fen 11 and 12, land 3: because it is not permitted for the Saracens <note>the Muslims, referring to the culture of the author Avicenna</note> to drink wine, and since they sometimes refuse it, he gives syrup of apples, either quinces or <term>matian</term> apples <note>a specific variety of prized Roman apples</note>.</margin>

### On the constriction of their breath. Cap. xxxi.
<margin>g "Bloodletting," etc. It excites that bile because it weakens, etc. "Constriction of breath." First, he sets forth the causes of constriction of breath, which are three causes that frequently happen in fevers; however, seek the full explanation of these in the third book of the Canon, Fen 5.</margin>

Constriction of breath happens to them: either because of a dry spasm which happens in the muscles of breathing: or because of suffocating matter descending to their throat: or because of the weakness that arises in the nerves coming to the organs of breathing. The first of these is cured with moistening ointments or plasters. The second with those things that prevent strangulation. And the third with the balancing of the temperament in the brain and the anointing of the neck with those things that cool and moisten, and also over the stomach with things such as gourd shavings, purslane, and sandalwood with rose oil and similar things.

### On the intensity of their sadness. Cap. xxxii.
<margin>h "And the second." Namely, that it is from suffocating matter causing various types of <term>sanguantia</term> <note>likely a reference to inflammatory swelling or throat issues</note>; this cure is known from the third book of the Canon, Fen 4. Certain unrefined teachers say this text ought to be placed at the end of the preceding chapter because it is a cure for fainting; but their error is manifest, because it appears that the anointing of the neck does not act upon fainting. Furthermore, the author would be very forgetful here if he did not provide a cure for the constriction of breath. But we say this: that the weakness which occurs in the nerves coming to the organs of breathing happens most often in acute fever from the heat that dissolves the spirits from the brain, the nape of the neck, and the nerves. And therefore, Avicenna directed his attention to that heat at its source—that is, in the brain—and in the path of its travel—namely, in the neck—and in the organs themselves, when he says...</margin>

<margin>i "Over the stomach." And in this, he wishes to temper the diaphragm and also include the chest, etc.</margin>

When sadness increases along with the mouth of the stomach, and the arrival of an irritating humor in it: then cool their stomachs with those things you know from foods, and let them be anointed, and let them sleep in a place near the movement of water, on a bed with cold-scented things: water lilies, roses, cold infusions, cold-scented fruits, and sandalwood. And many times indeed, cold enemas made from gourd and cucumber water, and the juice of purslane and houseleek with rose oil, are beneficial for their sadness.

### On the difficulty of swallowing that happens to them. Cap. xxxiii.
<margin>k "Difficulty of swallowing." It must be considered that for the difficulty of swallowing—which the author first says is cured by much bloodletting—this is because of the fullness of blood around the parts of the <term>meri</term> <note>the esophagus or gullet</note>... and therefore he performs bloodletting as is done in material <term>sanguantia</term> and other types where repeated bloodletting is required, and this we declared in Fen 2. And this is why he said "gradually" to repeat it, or perhaps he said it to make you secure: for if you have bled the sick person before this accident comes to him, do not fear to perform bloodletting again in small amounts when this accident occurs. A suppository is better because medicine is not easily swallowed and could excite vomiting, in which there would be danger because of the movement of matter upward; although sometimes vomiting is the cure for difficulty in swallowing. You, however, complete that chapter with the knowledge of the third book of the Canon, Fen 13, where many other causes are placed for difficulty in swallowing and their cure is provided.</margin>

The difficulty of swallowing that happens to them: if the fever is <term>elodes</term> <note>a marshy, sweating fever</note>, then let bloodletting be done gradually: and let a balancing be done to draw it away. And a suppository is better, which is very effective in loosening things from above.

### On the coldness of the extremities that happens to them. Cap. xxxiiii.
<margin>l "Often the heat is submerged."</margin>
Often their heat is submerged <note>sinks deep into the interior of the body</note> and their extremities become cold, and the heat tends to submerge toward the head. Therefore, let the extremities be placed in hot water and let them not drink cold water.

### Discourse on bilious fever. Cap. xxxv.
<margin>m "Often the heat is submerged."</margin>
<margin>n "Choleric fevers." Since he has placed the cure or regimen for the accidents <note>symptoms</note>, he hastens here to distinguish the acute fevers, for he speaks of the continuous type as he promised above in that chapter. And after the acute ones, which are bilious <term>choleric</term> and sanguine, he treats the others; therefore, it has four parts, just as there are four kinds of fevers: namely, bilious, sanguine, phlegmatic, and melancholic. The parts are clear. First, he determines bilious fevers in general. Second, in specific, at "the second."</margin>

Bilious fevers are of three types: the continuous <term>tertian</term>, the periodic <term>tertian</term>, and the <term>causon</term> <note>a burning, inflammatory fever</note>. The periodic tertian is either pure—and it is made from pure bile—or not pure. It is made with the putrefaction of thick bile because of a mixture with the phlegm of the bile, united in some compositional mixture: and by this it is distinguished from the <term>hemitritaeus</term> <note>a semitertian fever</note>. For two separate matters cause the semitertian, but one matter causes this [impure tertian], which is in itself mixed, so that with its heat some of this coldness is mixed, which weighs down its putrefaction, its dissolution, and its digestion: and because of that indeed, there are two paroxysms in the semitertian. And in the impure tertian, there is one paroxysm. And this impure type is sometimes prolonged for a long time: even around half a year. And sometimes it leads to softness and wasting...

<margin>o "A paroxysm of tertian." The first part in two: first, in general, he places its species; second, the signs. And "the intensity." The first in two: first, he sets forth the species; second, he declares them. And "the tertian." He says first, etc.</margin>

<margin>p He doubts first because Galen, in the first distinction, distinguishes fevers in any of three ways into intermittent and continuous, as appears in the book on crises, and second in the book on the differences of fevers. It must be said that bilious fevers are of two types in the first division: namely, intermittent and continuous. The continuous are of two modes: some are called "proportional continuous" because they have manifest increases or exacerbations and manifest remissions. Others are "uniform continuous," not having manifest exacerbations; and these among the bilious fevers are called <term>causones</term> <note>burning fevers</note>. But you will say: can a continuous fever of one mode, not having manifest exacerbations, be made from humors other than bile, such as from phlegm or melancholy? It must be said that yes, as was said above in the chapter on putrefaction. For even in this, the putrefaction is near the heart, therefore we believe a phlegmatic fever can be found which in its continuity is certainly similar to a <term>causon</term>; for the reason why that continuity exists in a <term>causon</term> is that the matter is near the heart, as Avicenna indicates there; but it happens sometimes that phlegm putrefies there. However, such a phlegmatic fever is not called a <term>causon</term> because it is not with the intensity of heat that is in a <term>causon</term>, as its name shows. But a fever from melancholic humor that would be similar to a <term>causon</term> in continuity is far-fetched... because melancholic humor is not apt to multiply and putrefy in nearby parts...</margin>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of fevers from the previous page, specifically focusing on the differentiation between types of bilious fevers (tertian and burning fevers) and how they interact with other humors like phlegm or black bile.</meta>

...which is to the heart, just like the bilious and the phlegmatic. From which it appears why it responds more under a continuous fever, not having excretion or a manifest relief concerning the bilious humor than the phlegmatic or the melancholic humor, because that humor is more fit to be found in the veins near the heart, namely the pulmonary veins, more than the other two humors, since the lung is nourished by bilious blood—that is, a substance prone to turning into bile. These things were declared above. And regarding the <term>tertian fever</term> <note>a fever that returns every third day, typical of yellow bile</note>, this section has three parts: first, it describes the periodic tertian; second, the burning fever (<term>causon</term>); third, the continuous tertian.

<margin>a Burning fever. Here is the third part.</margin>
<margin>b</margin> In the tertian. Regarding the first, it is doubted why he made no mention of the "non-pure" tertian fever caused by a mixture of <term>melancholy</term> <note>black bile</note>. It should be said that: first, it is rare that black bile overflows in the body in the same way as yellow bile and phlegm; second, because these humors are not as easily miscible as yellow bile and phlegm are. Secondly, it should be considered that <term>Avicenna</term> <note>the famous 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> intends this division because the mixture of phlegm with yellow bile is twofold. One is a "unifiable" mixture in which the mixed humors arrive at a single form, and from such a mixture—specifically when yellow bile dominates—a tertian fever is produced. The other is a "non-unified" mixture in which each humor preserves its own form and even has its own <term>paroxysmal</term> <note>the period of the fever's greatest intensity</note> movement, and such a fever is called <term>hemitritaeos</term> <note>original: "emittritea"; a semitertian fever</note>, and therefore the semitertian consists of two fevers. But the non-pure tertian is one fever, because it is one humor made by a mixture uniting into a single form. Thirdly, it should be considered that this would be a place for speculation if two humors dominate equally, into which fever that one would be classified. And let us say briefly that when two humors dominate equally, one humor cannot be made according to a single form, just as two contraries dominating equally cannot become one, as is said in the *Metaphysics* and the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*. It will therefore be a double fever. Fourthly, it should be considered that when a single humor is made from yellow bile and a little phlegm—either through a mixture resulting in a third thing or through the corruption of phlegm into yellow bile—and perhaps because these are close in nature and thus become one fever, so we can imagine that when yellow bile and phlegm abound equally, one humor is made. For from them, thus equally mixed, one putrid fever is made which will neither afflict from third day to third day, nor day by day; but if the forms of these two humors are preserved, one can imagine a non-pure tertian fever being made, which the physician does not call a semitertian of two paroxysms. And this will be when the yellow bile and phlegm are so mixed together that the yellow bile does not move toward a paroxysm unless the phlegm also moves, because they are mixed; not because they are one, but because one does not move without the other. An opponent, however, says that this does not happen unless they have become one humor according to their form; yet he cannot prove this, nor does it seem necessary, and we speak of this in our question regarding the prolongation of fevers. Fifthly, it should be considered that he mentioned "a little coldness." For this coldness and this phlegm ought to be minor in respect to the yellow bile, since that humor is predominately bilious. He also says that this coldness "burdens" the putrefaction of the yellow bile—that is, in the process of the putrefactive heat acting upon the humor—so that it does not become putrid quickly. Heat completes the inflammation later in time because of the phlegm than it would with pure yellow bile, and this is because of that coldness which resists the heat and thus "burdens" it—that is, it makes its resolution slower, as is well known. But it is doubted whether this phlegm or this coldness seems to delay—that is, burden—its "digestion" <note>the medical process of a humor ripening or being processed by body heat</note>, namely the digestion of the yellow bile. On the contrary, it seems to accelerate it, because when yellow bile is cooled and moistened, it is digested; and it seems from this that it does not burden the putrefaction but rather accelerates it, because dryness is contrary to putrefaction, and since yellow bile returns to a moist state, it makes it more fit for putrefaction. Furthermore, phlegm putrefies faster (day by day) than yellow bile (every third day). To the first objection, it should be answered in two ways. First, that the digestion of the bilious humor is twofold. One is the preparation for its evaporation and resolution into vapor, and the thickening and cooling phlegm delays this. The other resolution is its turning into vapor, which does not happen so quickly, and it is of this digestion (which is in the humor during the actual paroxysm) that Avicenna speaks; and the same can be understood of the humor ready for the paroxysm. The other "digestion" is the lessening of the heat and dryness of the yellow bile, and phlegm does this; and so it stands that through the admixture of phlegm, the yellow bile becomes less hot and dry, and yet by itself, it is much more unfit for resolution. Alternatively, we agree to say that digestion is twofold: "true" digestion, which is the proper mixture of the moist with the dry (and phlegm does not do this for yellow bile when mixed with it); and "improper" digestion, which is the removal of its exceeding heat, and this phlegm can do to the yellow bile, and the bile can also do to the phlegm, as noted by <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>original: "Aliab."; a 10th-century Persian physician</note> in the third book of the *Pantegni*, in the chapter on non-pure tertian fever. To the second point, it should be said that to "burden the putrefaction" is to make it so that the putrefactive heat proceeds "heavily"—that is, slowly—upon the matter, and its cooling and thickening do this, for the moist is not easily separated from the dry because the heat cannot penetrate deeply into the matter when resisted by cold and thickness. To the third point, it should be said that phlegm causes more harm in this—that is, it causes more "heaviness" or slowness of putrefaction through cooling and thickening or viscosity—than it helps its speed through moisture or moistening. Another solution could be given, but it would draw us into another science. To the third main point, it should be answered in two ways. First, that phlegm mixed with yellow bile causes the entire paroxysm to accelerate relative to the whole cycle. For example: the paroxysm of a pure tertian attacks every third day at the ninth hour; but the paroxysm of a non-pure tertian from phlegm attacks every third day at the seventh hour, or it is tertian, and yet the parts of the paroxysm follow each other more slowly in a non-pure tertian fever and more quickly in a pure tertian. Alternatively, it could be said that although phlegm makes a paroxysm every day primarily through its "specific form," when it is mixed with yellow bile, that specific form (which follows the substantial form) is broken, just as the substantial form of the phlegm is corrupted. And therefore, it does not make the yellow bile hasten toward putrefaction; but because the thickness remains, even if not that of the specific form, the movement of the yellow bile becomes slow. Therefore, if there is a bilious fever that is not pure due to phlegm not reduced to a single form with the bile, it will have a paroxysm that is faster in its total cycle but slower in its individual parts. And from these things said, the force of the evidence will be apparent to you. For you will see someone having a non-pure tertian whose paroxysms are faster than the pure one that preceded it, and someone else whose paroxysms are slower. I speak regarding the comparison of the movement of the whole paroxysm to the entire cycle. And these things are mentioned before. I will ask the question about prolongation here: because a non-pure tertian is prolonged for about half a year, whereas a pure phlegmatic fever is not so prolonged. Sometimes it leads to "softness." Some say this means <term>paralysis</term> <note>original: "paraloſim"</note>, because liquefied phlegm can run to the nerves. Others say "softness" refers to <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydro-piſſim"; edema or swelling</note>

<column-break/>

or <term>cachexia</term> <note>original: "cacetta"; a wasting syndrome</note> due to injury to the liver. Also, from this, one becomes a dropsical person with <term>ascites</term> <note>fluid in the abdomen</note> when there is <term>hyposarca</term> <note>a type of generalized swelling under the skin</note>, in which there is specifically a softening. Regarding the enlargement of the spleen: because prolonged fevers generate many humors through excessive burning, and since these are drawn with the melancholic matter to their receptacle, the spleen is thereby enlarged. <margin>Burning fever.</margin> It should be considered that he describes the burning fever (<term>causon</term>) based on three things. First, by its mode of movement. Second, by its symptoms. Third, by the causes of the symptoms and the continuity of its movement. For the symptoms concern strong inflammation and others following from it, and the continuity of movement was because the matter is sharp and very close to the heart, etc. In the tertian. He speaks so that he may identify the proportional continuous fever; he identifies the intermittent one by the location of the matter. For the declaration of these things, you should return to what we said in the chapter on putrefaction. And the "intensity." The cause of the multiplication of all these symptoms is the heat, sharpness, and inflammation of the yellow bile, as is known.
<margin>c</margin> Cracking of the lips. This is a sign very common to bilious fevers, as <term>Rhazes</term> <note>original: "Ras."; the 9th-century physician Al-Razi</note> posits in the 16th book of the *Continens*, and the cause is that yellow bile is prone to ascending to the higher parts and is received in the lips, which are fleshy places, and it causes those cracks by its sharpness. And sometimes much drying and cracking happens in the lips by way of a <term>crisis</term> <note>a turning point in a disease</note>. And therefore the common people judge this to be a good sign. It is inclined toward dryness, etc. Because of the causes which Avicenna posits: because those fevers greatly dry out the internal organs. And when you see excessive dryness of the belly in bilious fevers, then judge it to be <term>phrenitis</term> <note>delirium or brain inflammation</note> according to Rhazes in the 16th book of the *Continens*; other things are clear.

The first summary. The last order of signs is from the form of its shivering; here it is useful to know about shivering and "horripilation" <note>the sensation of hair standing on end or skin crawling</note> as presupposed from what was said above in the chapter on the discourse of shivering, etc. It should be considered that <term>Dino</term> <note>Dino del Garbo, a 14th-century physician</note> imagines... then. More difficult, etc. This was disputed above. <margin>According to the second.</margin> This "second" cold is the shivering of the "recalling of heat," and he calls this "a little cold"; but in phlegmatic and quartan fevers, there is cold because of the quality of the cold matter. <margin>According to speed.</margin> Speed of relief, because of the subtlety of the matter and its aptitude for movement, etc. And its shivering occurs. The cause is what is stated in the 6th book of the *Practica*, chapter 3, on tertian fever, and by the <term>Alexandrian commentator</term> <note>likely John of Alexandria</note> on the first book of the *Epidemics* on that paragraph "Those in shivering." For the bilious matters in the first paroxysms are subtle, and therefore quickly and rapidly cause stronger shivering; but later, through "digestion," they are thickened and behave conversely. In the quartan fever, however, the cause is phlegmatic, because the matter from the beginning is very continuous: raw, moved slowly, causing weaker shivers; but in paroxysms near the end, having become subtle, it causes stronger ones, and thus the unlearned person is troubled, but the artist rejoices, as <term>Alexander</term> says in the aforementioned commentary.
<margin>e</margin> And again. The same cause is assigned to the shivering, as is known. And sweating. Hatred of speaking. Some say this is because the spirit and this movement in the brain evacuate the yellow bile. Or it should be said that these patients have the organ of hearing very much "purged," and therefore the audible sound impresses upon it very strongly and literally, and it "tympanizes" <note>rings or vibrates like a drum</note> strongly, and therefore a kind of pain is caused in hearing, just as in the organ of touch (the nerve) when it is exposed.
<margin>f</margin> And the pulse. This is the sixth order of signs... Avicenna's movement toward saying this was because of what was said above in the chapter on the signs of putrid fevers in general, where bilious matter is posited to be light... understand that it is not so light that it causes diversity in the pulse, and because the humor is putrid. And this is what he says: "When the humor weakens it"—that is, the pulse, namely the pulsatile power—and this weakness is of some aggravation... and variability through putrefaction. And he adds to it—namely, to the pulse—diversity at the "status" <note>the peak or plateau of the disease</note>. It is doubted whether in their status, the pulse in the tertian...

# Fen Treatise II

...fever is more diverse than in preceding times. And as responded to by the author: here in the **peak state**, there is a greater weakness of the faculty just as there is greater heat. In the third book, <note>original: "In 3.riu."</note> **Galen** <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note> in the second part of his third book on fevers, in the chapter on the signs of tertian, says to the letter: In that very state, a great sign is putrefaction, and much more so as the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>the sudden attack or spike of the fever; original: "porisimo"</note> invades, and much more as it ascends into the peak state. In this state, it is less so than during the ascent, that is, the increase. He states the same generally in the first book, in the chapter on the signs of putrid fevers; let the signs be observed subtly. We have already extended the discourse on this in the book on the differences of fevers. And here let us abbreviate the response.

What shall I say? First, according to **Dino** <note>Dino del Garbo, a prominent 14th-century medical commentator</note>, he solves this contradiction here by explaining the "third" state. He adds diversity at the **peak state**, that is, up to the state inclusive; and even in the state itself, there is not such great diversity in the pulse because of the greater evaporation of the matter and its diversion to the external parts. This happens most especially in a tertian fever because of the thinness of the matter. Second, here it is to be doubted in the words of **Dino** how the pulse proceeds, adding to the diversity up to the peak, yet in the peak state itself, there is no greater diversity. To save this for ourselves is easy: for we hold that three things can be extended simultaneously. And I believe that **Dino** did not know how to well explain what he wanted to say. For he wanted to say that the pulse is diverse up to the peak state inclusive, and that tertian fever adds this diversity to itself. We shall say that all know from the science of **Enchiphorus** <note>likely a reference to a specific medical authority or text</note> that the heaviness in the matter and the constriction in the internal parts cause some diversity, as does the diversity in the disposition of the matter. From this, diversity arises in the manner of the heat. And this diversity is greater in the **beginning** and the **increase**; indeed, it is greatest of all in the increase than at any other time. For in the beginning, the heat is of a single disposition.

Faster in comparison to other fevers, and it is not of a common constriction because the humor weakens it and adds diversity to it at the **peak state**; and the diversity in it is less than that found in others with hardness, and the pulse is stronger in it. Indeed, the diversity in it is not according to the majority, except for the diversity proper to the fever and another. And in the beginning, it is indeed necessary that the pulse be constricted until the hour of the fever's dilation; and then it is strengthened and becomes fast and frequent. And its diversity is not very excessive. And sometimes it is indicated by the age, habit, region, art, form, time, and the multitude of occurrences of the tertian at that hour. Now, if two tertian fevers are compounded, there are paroxysms occurring every day. He who considers a tertian fever solely by the paroxysm errs in it; rather, it is necessary that other signs which we shall mention be observed. And in those suffering from tertian, wakefulness and a love of anxiety occur; and in many of the elderly, an "ebullition" <note>a boiling or bubbling sensation</note> at the liver.

### The Difference between Pure and Non-pure Tertian. Chapter 37.

**Pure** is thinner and light, whose **paroxysm** is consumed from four hours up to twelve hours; and it does not add much beyond them. And if it adds to the feeling of suffocation in the peak state, it is then expanded; and in the increase, it is as if a battle between both dispositions. And therefore this diversity is greater in the increase than in the peak state or in the beginning. And there is another diversity which arises from the weakness of the faculty following the degree and quantity of resolution. And that is greater in the peak state than at another time, as is known. But why is it even greater? Because in the **decline**, the spirits are more resolved. It must be said that if the decline is toward the good, by that very fact—as the heat remits—there occurs a certain strengthening of the faculty. This must be said subtly and manifested according to one who has understood the writings of **Galen** in the commentary on pulses: that the fall of the faculty itself by way of resolution or bad disposition does not cause diversity in the pulse which is properly called diversity, unless some other battle joins in. **Avicenna** understood this in a few words. Likewise, in the sense of the "feeling," when he said: The diversity of the pulse with the weakness of the faculty is the battle of the cause and the sickness. In the state of the paroxysm, therefore, there is a greater excitation of the matter than in the decline; and if they are near death, such excitation and violence of the battle does not occur. Instead, it succumbs little by little. And therefore it eventually fails, and the pulse returns to a **vermicular** <note>worm-like</note> and **formicant** <note>ant-like/crawling</note> state, having the order of a "mouse-tail" <note>a pulse that tapers off</note> ending, yet it is not diverse because of this. If, however, the decline is toward the good, it is certain that it is not diverse for the reason stated. And the diversity etc. This is known because of the lightness of the bile and the uniformity in its motion of putrefaction and the expansion of heat. With hardness, because the heat and dryness harden it. It was said, however, whether more or less than in a **quartan fever** <note>a fever recurring every four days</note> the pulse is hard, which can happen to both, unless there is a diversity proper to the fever. In the pulse, it has a diversity that the fever owes to the putridity, as in putrid fever. And it does not have diversity just as **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> and **phlegm** do in fevers where there is diversity because of the fever. Because of the matter of the humors, which are heavy, thick, viscous, and suffocating to the heat, and which proceed unevenly in putrefaction, diversity arises in the heat and pulse. And another according to material diseases or accidents which diversify the pulse, such as pain and accidents of the soul; if these are joined to a tertian fever, they can make the pulse diverse. And this then will not be because of the tertian itself but because of other things. Or another, as in natural dispositions. For there are men who by nature have a diverse pulse. And its diversity is not very excessive: this is explained in two ways. First, in respect to that which is in other putrid fevers; and this has already been declared. Or its diversity is not very excessive, that is, when the heat is dilated; and this is in the peak state and has already been declared. And this statement conforms to the words of the fathers above. And sometimes: this is the seventh collection of signs. **Age**, namely youth. **Habit**, namely of having tertian, or habit in hot and dry foods, etc. **Form**, that is, the physical constitution. Now, therefore: this discourse is known, but what is hidden in it depends on the question of periodicity. **Love of anxiety**: because they seem anxious and mobile due to the sharpness of the bile. **Ebullition**, that is, inflammation, as if something were boiling there. And this is a discourse in which other authors agree. And the cause is the fervor of the bile in the gallbladder where the liver "boils."

**Pure is subtle.** Here he places the signs by which a pure tertian differs from a non-pure one. And first, he places the signs of the pure, understanding—and sometimes stating—that those do not apply to the non-pure. Second, he places the signs of the non-pure tertian. First, it can be divided into as many parts as there are signs. The **first sign** is that a pure tertian is subtle. Some say "subtle" refers to the humor. Others interpret "subtle" as being of sharp heat, and the touch judges this. The **second sign** is that its heat is light. Some say "light" refers to the humor being easy to digest, but it is better to say "light" refers to the heat; and its lightness is that it is not a malignant heat like that of other putrid humors, but it is intense in degree, though not because of a malice of putrefactive disposition. For the putrefaction of bile is, so to speak, a "scorching," while the putrefaction of other humors is a rotting. Because of this, certain statements about the heat of tertian—namely about its lightness—which seem to exist among doctors, cease. The **third sign** is that the paroxysm lasts from four hours up to twelve; and this measure of time cannot be given a fixed cause, but that it lasts a short time is known, because

<column-break/>

it is due to the substantiality of the matter, which moves quickly, inflames quickly, and evaporates quickly. And if a paroxysm lasts a long time—for example, if it lasts twenty hours—it is not pure, which indicates a thickness of the bile, which is thickened by either melancholy or phlegm. **To the contrary:** it can be thickened by addition, like "vitelline" bile <note>bile resembling egg yolk</note> according to **Galen** in the second book on natural faculties, and **Averroes** <note>12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> in the second book of his *Colliget*. It should be said that it more often happens that the bile from which the fever arises becomes thick through a phlegmatic mixture than through scorching. Or it should be said that bile thickened by scorching is called "non-pure" bile because it takes on a certain nature of melancholy, not by admixture, but from it.

When the condition is mixed, then it is non-pure. And it is according to the majority coming at seven hours, and such a body becomes hot quickly; and you see the heat proceed from the body while the extremities are still cold. And similarly, a pure fever does not increase when no error occurred beyond seven periods. And sometimes it is presumed because of the subtlety of its matter in one paroxysm in which vomiting occurs, or a cleansing of the belly alone. And digestion appears in the urine on the first day, or on the third, or the fourth, or the seventh. If, however, it adds beyond seven periods, then it is of the non-pure genus. And similarly, if the space of its shivering is prolonged and there is an addition of its paroxysms. And their occurrence with each other according to an order preserving similar proportions; and in the non-pure, that is diverse and not right. And similarly, when the paroxysms are assimilated according to one term, and the remaining signs of the fever's elongation are all that you know. And when you see the beginning with shivering, but which we determined into the state with exuberant sweat, then do not doubt that it is pure. And in the pure, indeed, it is when the patient drinks barley water <note>original: "aquam hordei"</note>; it proceeds into his body with a humid vapor as if he wished to sweat, and sometimes he does sweat. And when it is non-pure, a very great heaviness is found in the head.

through an alteration that thickens the bile more than is owed to bile, and makes it pass into the thickness that is owed to melancholy; therefore, it is called non-pure bile by the power of melancholy. **To seven hours.** Because this is a common limit or a common time for the duration of a paroxysm, but four hours etc. are more extreme times. And bile is more retrievable with a common disposition than with extreme dispositions; and I say "pure bile," I do not say bile absolutely. **And it becomes hot.** The **fourth sign** is the speed of the body heating up because the matter inflames and expands quickly. And it gives a sign of this: because immediately with the extremities cold and the rest of the body, I see heat proceed—that is, from the internal part to the external parts. But you will say this is not a sufficient sign because in phlegmatic and melancholic fevers we find cold extremities at the increase of the paroxysm and yet a hot belly. First, it should be said that this sign is sufficient in a pure tertian, for the cold in it is not because there is a cold humor in the extremities, but because the heat is suffocated within; and soon the bile heats up inside, and when it is inflamed throughout the whole body, the natural heat can expand with it to the extremities in a short time. In that time, the whole body is internally heated. Or it should be said that in other fevers the body appears hot while the extremities are cold, yet not so that vapors are openly expelled; rather, the heating occurs by alteration of the limbs because the vapors are constricted within by their thickness. But in

a pure tertian, the heat of the body is with a manifest evaporation. And **Avicenna** hinted at this when he said "you see the heat proceed from the body," and he said "proceed," that is, evaporate. The **fifth sign** is that a pure tertian lasts at most seven paroxysms. Sometimes sooner: it is consumed sometimes in one paroxysm. As **Hippocrates** says: A tertian fever etc. And the cause is what he comments on there: because he places it in the third book of *Prognostics*. Because it makes an intermittent fever in one paroxysm as much as in one continuous day. But continuous pure colics <note>bilious fevers</note>, since they are very acute, presently exceed the limit of seven periods.

<margin>b</margin> **And sometimes it is consumed.** This is placed as the **sixth sign**. It can be a determination of the saying that it does not add beyond seven periods, for this is not always true that it lasts seven periods; because sometimes it is finished in one paroxysm by vomiting or resolution. And the cause in this is noted: it is possible for a man to have only that bile in that paroxysm which is rectified in the evacuation of that matter, and it can be that the bad composition of the limbs does not remain a bad quality. Why will it not be generated after that? Unless the bilious humor is evacuated otherwise so that it could make a paroxysm. In one paroxysm, that tertian finished its crisis. But this possibility is not so in phlegmatic and melancholic humors; for those humors are of slow aggregation. I do not say that phlegm is of slow aggregation when it goes from the disposition of an antecedent cause to a conjoined one. But I say it is of slow aggregation when it goes from a disposition of health to a disposition of sickness, which disposition is the antecedent cause; this happens slowly in phlegm and melancholy. Similarly, these humors are slowly resolved, and the disposition which is the antecedent cause of those fevers slowly ceases. Therefore, there is not just one paroxysm of a phlegmatic or melancholic fever without another happening after it in its period; this is because of the disposition that was before the first paroxysm, which does not easily cease, and because of the disposition which is left behind from the first paroxysm. Although it is remote that one quartan or one quotidian of a single paroxysm could be found, I do not believe it is impossible. And a case happening upon this remote possibility is this: suppose someone has a thick spleen full of melancholy, and nature is moved to the evacuation of that melancholy, which directs it to the intestines, and through those paths it escapes this evacuation and is carried to the places of the veins. There it putrefies and makes a new paroxysm which finishes with all the matter evacuated so that no quality remains which might attract matter. That man with that quartan will have nothing but one paroxysm of a quartan fever, and we testify to having seen this. **And it appears.** This is the **sixth sign**. It should be considered that in a pure tertian, digestion could appear on the first day, not yet at the very beginning, just as in an **ephemeral fever** <note>a fever lasting only one day</note> as we said above in the chapter on the signs of ephemerals. It should be considered that he said on the first, third, fourth, or second; this is understood concerning the sixth day. Or it was said "first" because of those that terminate in one paroxysm. And he said "third," etc., wanting it to be understood according to the critical and indicative days in which the signs of digestion appearing are more certain. Just as all good signs are more certain in their goodness, and bad in their malice, when they appear on a critical day, as **Galen** says in the second or third book of *Prognostics*. If, however: he applies the statements to signify a non-pure tertian. Although he speaks of two signs which are found in a pure tertian and not in a non-pure one, he gives others to be understood. For example, the heat of a non-pure tertian is not a subtle or light heat, and so on through the other signs. And so etc., it is non-pure if the space of its shivering is prolonged, because that signifies thick bile. **And there is an addition.** This is the **seventh sign**. Addition. And "anticipation" <note>original: "antecessio"</note>, and similarly "postponement," because as much as the second adds to the first, so much the third adds to the second. Or "addition," meaning an increase, and "anticipation," meaning coming earlier. And the cause of these is the uniformity of the matter. **And similarly.** This is the **eighth sign**, and it is of a non-pure tertian fever, namely the quality of the invasion of the paroxysms. Because it signifies a feverish sickness, as in the aphorisms of **Hippocrates**: "Certain exacerbations or paroxysms etc." But a pure tertian cannot be long. And the remaining signs from the time of year and others; therefore, the opposite of this sign is a sign of a pure tertian, namely that paroxysms anticipate or postpone and do not invade at the same hour. **And when.** This is the **ninth sign**. **And in the pure.** This is the **tenth sign**. In the pure, the bilious matter is subtly rectified by the drinking of cold water, whence it is prepared for digestion and the paths are not blocked. Whence it can penetrate toward the veins and the skin and be heated, and vapor can be raised, and the matter itself cooled, and it will re-temper the bad composition. From which a man is disposed to sweat. In a non-pure tertian, however, the matter is more thickened by the drinking of cold water, and it cannot penetrate because of blockages. And it is possible that the inflation becomes greater than that which is touched. And when you do not find...

## Cure of Pure Tertian. Chapter 39.
**I**t is necessary to remember that which is said according to his own roots <note>fundamental principles</note> in the cure of fevers regarding the loosening of the bowels and food and in all the chapters, and build upon that. And then indeed, do not listen to his speech which concedes strong laxatives <note>original: "solutia fortia"</note> in the beginning, such as <term>myrobalans</term> <note>astringent fruit used as a purge</note> and the like, except in that which we mentioned. Rather, it is necessary that you prepare first and soften with certain mild things among those we mentioned there, such as **tamarinds** in the quantity of 40 drams <note>original: "3." used as abbreviation for drachma</note> infused in warm water overnight, then strained, and throw upon it...

...it may be necessary to say "perhaps." And it is imaginable that in some non-pure tertian no rigor occurs—neither a shivering nor a true chill nor a rigor—but only a certain inequality of the pulse and a "sinking" at the beginning of the paroxysm. And this is due to the slowness of the movement of the matter and the weakness of the movement, which does not move uniformly. And then it appears why he said: **perhaps and there is no heat**. The eighth sign: the heat is not so intense. **Nor is it**. The ninth sign, which is the thickness and deformity of the matter. Then when the heat begins to appear in one part of the matter, it is believed to proceed by adding and diminishing, and it is suffocated because of the other moved matter. **And the harsh accidents**. The tenth sign: the accidents are called "harsh" in intensity, such as vehement thirst, sleeplessness, the sensation of heat, and the like. And these are lessened in a non-pure tertian. It is said, however, that the accidents are harsh because of their malice, such as the malice of the pulse; and these are worse in a non-pure tertian. And these are of the worse kind that are not settleable by any bloodletting; indeed, sometimes they lead even to those.

**It is recognized.** Here he places the signs of the continuous fever through the violence of the paroxysms and exacerbations and the violence in the tension, because the tension is inflammation in the continuous fever, whereas in the intermittent it is only during the duration, because the paroxysm or exacerbation of the continuous is longer than the paroxysm of the intermittent, other things being equal. Moreover, the signs of purity and impurity of the continuous fever are understood from the aforementioned signs. And here, Avicenna <note>indicated by 'A.'</note> hastened to set down the opinion of Galen, who was somewhat impugning him.

**It is necessary.** First, he sets down the cure for the pure tertian, second for the non-pure. There, the first part is in two sections. First, he sets down the cure for the intermittent tertian, which cure can be applied to the continuous. Second, he specifically explains the cure for the continuous. There, he says "And you should know." The first is in three parts. First, he sets down the cure for the fever; second for the accidents; third for the heat that remains. There, the second part is "And if it should be." There, the third is "And when." The first of these is in three: first he sets down the cure which mostly happens from the beginning up to the peak state; second in the state when signs of digestion appear; third in the decline. There, the second is "What if it follows." There, the third is "The bath." First, he sets down the cause in evacuation; second in feeding and provocation <note>stimulating urine</note> and digestion and the alteration of heat; third the cause of the feeding taken as to the intention in it. There, the second is "And do not feed." There, the third is "And know that the intention." The first is in three: first, he sets down the cause in evacuation through medicines; second through clysters <note>enemas</note>; third through phlebotomy. There, the second is "or clysters." There, the third is "And sometimes possible." First, he refers us to the general rules upon which he builds not only in this chapter, but in every chapter below. Second, he rebukes **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasim"</note> who in the 17th tract of the *Almansor* and in the *Continens* teaches from the beginning to give scammony and myrobalans and strong laxatives. And it should not be understood that myrobalans are a strong laxative, but Rhazes places them to temper the scammony. But understand other strong laxatives, like rhubarb, which is strong in respect to tamarinds and violets; and it can be said that it is necessary to evacuate by loosening: as such, it is strong in respect to those which soften while evacuating. Myrobalan, however, evacuates by loosening; but then he falls into the speech by which he condemns himself along with Rhazes when he says: "Rhazes in the way that we mentioned." Unless the matter be furious or very plentiful. Whence in the beginning of a pure tertian, lest the matter pass into a continuous or a burning fever <note>original: "causonez"</note> or kill by a furious movement of the cholera <note>yellow bile</note>, then from the beginning—that is, before digestion—we can purge with scammony and strong laxatives. And under this intention, we shall say that Rhazes gave scammony at the beginning. Third, Avicenna shows that in your intention there ought to be a softening, not a flux, not a laborious loosening. And therefore, building upon the foundations set above, he says "soften," etc.

<column-break/>

...he sets down softening medicines of which the first is made of tamarinds, over whose strained liquid is thrown another species in the morning, or the juice of two pomegranates. And all of this was declared above in the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers. The second medicine is a decoction. **Julep** <note>a sweet medicinal drink</note>; and it is a versatile kind, as we said there, with manna, etc. The third kind is an infusion of plums with another kind of manna. The fourth is syrup of violets and violets preserved with sugar; the fourth is mucilage, etc. The quantities of these things you should read from the medical authorities in their chapters. **Or clysters.** Know well from the general chapter when necessity leads, etc. He sets down the cause; clysters can be of many types, but one necessity is the giving of food, whether it be of thin substances; if the world <note>the body</note> be not thin because it does not benefit from a dry belly unless it is softened; and this is what he adds. **For the rectum also**, etc., and if the belly... here is the second cause; and here it is added, the cause of which is that the matter of pure cholera <note>yellow bile</note>, although it be undigested at the beginning, yet from the beginning it has an aptitude for evacuation, since it does not have phlegm or melancholy at the beginning since those are undigested and therefore it has a greater malice in loosening the belly at the beginning of a pure tertian: as appears from the general chapter, the malice will be less than in its likes, that is, according to a similar evacuation in the beginning of other fevers, such as the phlegmatic and melancholic.

<margin>
...or manna or the water of two pomegranates: and just as the decoction of julep with manna and seeded raisins: or an infusion of plums with manna or syrup of manna or syrup of violets and preserved violets. And perhaps he makes a mucilage of psyllium with certain syrups just as is the syrup of plums for lubrication and softening and with a decoction of lentils with julep. Or mild clysters just as is a clyster with a decoction of marshmallow and jujubes and sebesten and lily root and violet oil and fig juice and borax in the manner that you know. And that which necessity touches upon, for the rectum is [used] lest it be lacking in drink, which is like a barley-draught; nor should it be stopped nor given food unless nature is already softened. And if the loosening of the belly at the beginning of a pure tertian fever is of less malice than its like in others, yet its malice is again great. And when it is possible that you perform phlebotomy up to three periods, do so, and similarly when you fear it may become a furious sickness and you do that: it will be that which happens from error, if it happens, is less than in others. And that you do not move anything on the day of the paroxysm unless for necessity, and do not feed except after the aforementioned digestions, or provoke urine with an emulsion of seeds. And that the paroxysm should come upon him while he is hungry; and there is nothing in his stomach; rather, it is necessary that he take in drink oxymel <note>vinegar and honey syrup; original: "sirupū acetosū"</note> every morning; and after two hours, barley water on the day in which there is no paroxysm. And indeed the oxymel...
</margin>

<margin>
<paragraph>
**And when possible.** It is doubted whether after three paroxysms phlebotomy is appropriate in a tertian. I say that yes, from the general rule in the first chapter on phlebotomy, where it says at the beginning phlebotomy should be entirely omitted, and below it says that in a fever when it is necessary to bleed, do not listen to those who say that after four it is not good; rather, after 40 days it is contrary. Avicenna says here: It must be said that in a pure tertian, phlebotomy is not done by reason of the conjunct cause, but it is done sometimes by reason of the disposition in the blood because of the antecedent cause, and this is, as when abundant cholera in the blood and the pure [blood] is disposed so that it follows that motion, or because the blood itself is plentiful and thin; then the blood...
</paragraph>
</margin>

...form. Whence according to the periods, a part is inflamed, and it becomes active cholera when there is a paroxysm. Since therefore these things are from the beginning of the tertian, then you must perform phlebotomy, because if phlebotomy is delayed because of the febrile inflammation, it can happen that the bilious blood becomes more sharp and passes in great part into actual cholera. Or the cholera which was previously mixed with the blood will become sharper and separated; and then at that time phlebotomy will not be convenient, whereas then it can be convenient. And thus at that time in which phlebotomy is appropriate, Avicenna has judged, namely the space of three paroxysms or periods. And from which it appears that if a pure tertian begins with cholera which is the cause of the act mixed with the blood, in the progress of the tertian it happens the blood is inflamed by that cholera and becomes mixed, and phlebotomy ought not to be done before but could be done in the progress. To this, however, it must be said that the statement here only refers to whether it be a tertian or whatever sickness, then phlebotomy should be done; and the necessity of it even if the months have passed. But here in a tertian, it is possible that you perform phlebotomy from the beginning; do that and do not delay, because afterward it is possible that a continuous fever might occur with a worsening of the patient because of the omission of the phlebotomy. These speeches, therefore, are mutually consistent and not [contradictory]. And similarly: here the cause can be referred to a phlebotomy performed with thin bilious blood; if you perform phlebotomy, injury can happen from this, because that part which [is] blood and remains will pass into cholera and make a stronger paroxysm, although this injury is not necessarily happening, as is known; but if it happens, it is a lesser evil than the other evil which is feared from the fury of the remaining blood, which could, for instance, cause an <term>aposteme</term> <note>an internal abscess or swelling</note> of some noble or principal organ. And this which he says, "And doing that," etc., that is, you will perform phlebotomy; or it can be referred by a lighter rule to pharmacy <note>medicine</note>, and it is that if the matter be furious and you do that, namely evacuation with a loosening drug at the beginning, the error which happens from this—if it happens—if any injury follows, it will be less than the other, that is, less than the error or injury from the omission of evacuations; and this is known in the general chapter on all things, for all those are built upon that. And it is necessary that necessity forces you why it was said above in the question regarding this in the general rule [not to bleed] on the day of the paroxysm. **And do not feed.** These are rules much aggregated in the feeding and provocation of urine and the digestion of matter and the alteration of febrile heat, and they are about 11 rules. The first is that you do not feed except under the aforementioned conditions, namely concerning the softening of the belly, so that food does not encounter the beginning of the paroxysm. The second rule: or provoke, namely urine, under the conditions aforementioned in the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers in general, where it was suggested that the provocation should be preceded by the softening of the belly and phlebotomy if it is expedient. The third, that the paroxysm should not come upon an empty belly, and yet it is not sufficient to say "while he is hungry," which means desiring with a "canine appetite" or a full belly; and therefore he said: "And while there is nothing in his stomach." The fourth rule, that oxymel should be given in the morning; and this is the common hour for giving syrup because commonly bilious fevers come from... but if the paroxysm occupied the whole night, it would be necessary to give the syrup in the day some hours before the paroxysm according to your judgment and estimation; and after two hours, barley water so that it washes what the oxymel started, as was said above in the chapter on barley water. On the day in which there is no paroxysm, because since barley water is a certain food, then the paroxysm would not encounter an empty belly; and this speech is more true if by barley water we understand ptisan. The fifth rule is that if...
