<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for treating tertian fevers, moving from the definition of symptoms to specific dietary and medicinal interventions used during and after the fever's peak.</meta>

Fen Treatise II

<margin>
**A**
**Syrup of vinegar** <note>original: "sirupus acetosus"; a common medicinal oxymel</note> is appropriate and useful if given after the **paroxysm** <note>original: "porismum"; the periodic peak of the fever</note> because it settles the remains of the heat and rectifies the residue of the matter. The seventh rule is that it is useful to place the feet in cold water after the paroxysm to draw out—that is, to remove—the residual heat. It also happens that even when the paroxysm has receded, some heat may remain in the extremities, such as the feet; placing the feet in cold water removes this and prevents the **vital spirits** from evaporating. Similarly, if one feels a residual inflammation in the hands after the paroxysm, they can be washed with cold water. But if the vision fails because of certain fears—some say the use of this cold water is not suitable, but **Avicenna** <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> understands "cold water" here to mean water that is cold in its potential, but actually warm, such as water in which roses and violets have been boiled.
The seventh rule is that in the final stages—that is, once the matter is digested—an emulsion of **cold seeds** should be given with syrup of vinegar; for example, seeds of melon, water-melon, cucumber, and gourd. For instance: one and a half ounces each of syrup of vinegar and the milk of these common seeds.
</margin>

<margin>
**B**
Consider that Avicenna believes common seeds are sufficiently powerful to provoke <note>stimulate movement of</note> **choleric matter** <note>yellow bile</note>, just as **calamus** <note>original: "accorus"</note> or **asparagus** is used for **phlegmatic matter**. However, in their use, one expects digestion in a tertian fever, just as one does with strong provocatives in phlegmatic or melancholic cases. Alternatively, it can be understood that a laxative of syrup of vinegar is given before the paroxysm, while after the paroxysm, this emulsion of seeds is given so that the residual matter may be moved toward the urine. A physician of good judgment can give this provocative before the paroxysm if he knows the matter is prepared through digestion.
</margin>

<margin>
**C**
"And before the paroxysm." This rule is not independent, but part of the rule above where it continues: syrup of vinegar would be suitable after the paroxysm, or three or four hours before the paroxysm. Therefore, what is the interval in which we should give it before the paroxysm? Either three or four hours, so that the paroxysm does not occur while this syrup is still in the stomach; for it also has a certain quality of food, as we said above. Its effect would be lost if the patient vomits, as is common at the beginning of a tertian paroxysm, and its action would not work well on the matter because it would be consumed by the febrile heat. But he did not give a timeframe for when we should give the syrup of vinegar after the paroxysm, because the fever ceases immediately. Indeed, while the residual heat remains, one can give the syrup of vinegar without needing to wait an hour.
The eighth rule is that after the paroxysm, **barley water** should be given, whether syrup of vinegar was given beforehand or not; its utility is manifest.
The ninth rule—though many points could be made about it—is that if we require a **refined regimen** <note>original: "subtilitate regiminis"</note>, give **pomegranate wine**, which is a refined life-sustainer, as was said above. Such refining can be partial, as in every paroxysm, or it can be universal: as if on the final day you judged by estimation that the tertian fever would not pass the third paroxysm; then Avicenna teaches how to grade the regimen, which is well known.
</margin>

# After the paroxysm is appropriate; and similarly to place the feet in cold water to draw out the residual heat. <gloss>a</gloss> And I prefer that near the end, an emulsion of the aforementioned cold seeds be given in syrup of vinegar, and before the paroxysm by three or four hours, and then again after the paroxysm give barley water. And when a refined regimen is necessary, give in the drink pomegranate water and **melon water**. <gloss>b</gloss> In these similar cases, the regimen is graduated and has the method mentioned before; as the state [of the illness] approaches, let it be refined. On the first days, let the patient be fed with **barley kisk** <note>original: "kist ordei"; a traditional dish of cracked grain and soured milk</note> and bread rubbed with cold water, or like the mixture made from sour milk and lentils. And when food is accepted in the stomach, if it is given in a drink of barley water which is not very refined; and if it should be necessary, give it in a drink of strong pap <note>a soft cereal</note> with a decoction of parsley root. If the stomach is weak and the fever is not great and is pure, give a mixture of pap with similar things. <gloss>c</gloss>

### On the Crisis

Now, if the signs indicate that the **crisis** <note>the turning point of the disease</note> is near, then barley water, sweet pomegranate water, **plantains** <note>original: "muza"</note>, and syrup of vinegar are sufficient. The fruits preferred for them are sweet pomegranates, plantains, and ripe plums. **Melon**, however—that is, the fruit—is of the greatest help because it loosens, provokes, and breaks the intensity of the heat and causes sweating; perhaps it does no harm unless it causes indigestion. Among vegetables, give gourd, cucumber, **winter cherry** <note>original: "alkbebedi"; likely alkekengi</note>, and lettuce. And know <gloss>d</gloss> that the discovery in feeding tertian patients is either **moistening**, such as giving them the "extremities" <note>original: "alkhalegit"; likely from the Arabic for trotters or extremities</note> at the end—chicken testicles and brains of kids <note>young goats</note> for those who have no nausea—and egg yolks; or it is cooling and moistening together, as in barley kisk. And do not exceed this in cases of much bloating, especially at the beginning, unless you find intense inflammation or fear its conversion into a **burning fever** <note>original: "causonide"</note> or a continuous fever. Now, if the crisis follows and you see digestion in the urine and it is according to the praiseworthy signs you recognized: then if nature clears it, all is well; if not, then treat it with that which assists nature through the provocation of urine, loosening of the bowels, vomiting, or the flow of blood. And do not act against these things. Now if you do not find...

**d**
"And not the last." Here it is noted what movement of fruit made you secure in introducing melons and gourd. And do not cool too much at the beginning—that is, the paroxysm—because that is a cause for its prolongation. The intention then should be the movement of heat at the beginning, or generally when there is no great flame and the matter is raw.
</margin>

<margin>
**B**
"And know." What is said here is well known.

"Alhalegi." What this is, is explained as "extremities," others say "joints," like the feet of lambs or pigs. Hence **Galen** <note>the Greek physician</note> allows the extremities of pigs in his *Therapeutics* to **Glaucon** for those who have no nausea, because brains cause nausea, as stated in the third book of *On Aliments* and the second Canon; they should not be given to those with nausea. Alternatively, it can be explained that they should be given with spices or things that prevent nausea. Egg yolks are more digestible, as Galen says to Glaucon.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
**e**
...excused from vomiting, but if nature does not excuse it, then it is because it moves imperfectly toward the crisis. Hence evacuate; all this is built upon the **Aphorisms** and the general Canons above. If the nature itself does not produce a crisis, evacuate with a laxative medicine. One medicine is **scammony** <note>a powerful resinous purgative</note> in **julep**; a second medicine is a decoction of **myrobalans** <note>astringent plum-like fruits</note>, etc., which you can strengthen with **fumitory**, **senna**, and scammony. Consider here the use of senna. A third medicine is **troches of spodio** <note>medicinal lozenges made with zinc oxide or burnt ivory</note>, etc. The fourth is a description of a certain laxative medicine. Perhaps Avicenna wants this to be added to the description of the troches of spodio, and then it would be a description of laxative troches of spodio; see the fifth Canon. "With cold water": against which **Avenzoar** <note>the Andalusian physician Ibn Zuhr</note> commands laxatives to be given with warm water. It must be said that regularly it is given with warm water to assist their operation; however, in inflammatory fevers, for fear that the medicine might be corrupted by the heat, it can be given with cold water.
</margin>

# ...it can be retained more by excessive bloating and become more and more encrusted. However, when the matter is digested, because of the intense heat, cooling can safely be done both during the decline and at any time you see inflammation suspicious of a continuous or burning fever or wasting. Here falls the question: in which place should the speculative position be set, given that they require cooling drinks and **epithemata** <note>topical applications or compresses</note>? One is at the beginning and the other at the height of the tertian fever; which cools more safely? You should consider that Avicenna believes it is not as safe at the beginning. <gloss>e</gloss>

### Question

Now he presents the cure of tertian fever in its steady state, and he intends that if nature produces a perfect crisis, you [should assist].

<margin>
**F**
"And after that." Consider here that Avicenna wants the provocation of urine after the loosening of the bowels. Consider also that when nature attempts some crisis, he assists it; hence nature itself does it. But where it attempts no crisis, he chooses evacuation through the belly.
</margin>

<margin>
**G**
"And if there were." Here he uses cooling drinks and compresses equally; because without doubt, their use is safer, as he said in the [section on] the regimen of acute diseases.
</margin>

...manifest decline, then evacuate by loosening the belly. One such is six parts of scammony in julep; or a decoction of myrobalans with **tamarinds**, **manna** <note>original: "tereniachin"</note>, raisins, roots, and **cassia fistula**. Strengthen them with fumitory, senna, and scammony; and among those things suitable for them are laxative troches of spodio.
**Description:** Take 4 drams of pitted yellow myrobalans, 2 drams of fine sugar <note>original: "tabarzet"</note>, and 1 dram of scammony. Let it be drunk with cold water. After that, let them be treated with provocation [of urine]. And if there should be excessive heat and maximum inflammation there, once you have evacuated, it will not be bad to give something from the strong cooling drinks used in the regimen of acute diseases; perhaps apply a plaster from them. As for the **bath** <gloss>g</gloss>, do not let him approach it except after digestion. After digestion and at the decline, it is better for them and brings relief; although the error of entering the bath before digestion is safer here than with other fevers. The bath should be temperate, with good air, and moist, in which they may sweat with ease so as not to inflame their bodies. Let them be anointed with oil of violets and roses mixed with water. They should not stay long in it but leave quickly; indeed, repetition is more beneficial for them than a long stay. If after exiting they are bathed in lukewarm water, let them stay in it according to the time of decline. Then, when they exit, it is beneficial for them to drink a light white wine mixed with much water and be covered in their places; for they will sweat profusely. If anything remains, it will be digested. After that, let them be fed with cooling and moistening foods and vegetables of that sort. Do not fear to let them drink wine mixed with much water after the decline. For they say that wine "broken" by mixing benefits the quantity of the residue by resolving it; and it assists the penetrating water with its strength and its small amount of heat. Therefore, it cools the intensity and moistens. And if there are accidents of thirst and headache... <gloss>h</gloss>

---

<margin>
**h**
"As for the bath." Here he sets the cure for digested matter, specifically during the decline. The cure is by bath and wine; he understands a bath of fresh water, as Galen says in the *Therapeutics*. Cholerica matter, when undigested, if refined, would be more suitable for evaporation; the moisture of the water restrains its dryness. Therefore, the bath harms in sciatic and melancholic fevers before digestion, in which the matter is liquefied and moved. It should be considered that the bath should be "temperate" to the sense of touch, but the air should be good—not foul—but moist air from the splashing of temperate water, so they evaporate moist vapor and sweat easily. This happens if the bath is temperate and anointing is done. This is done to temper the heat and retain the water in the pores, which remains to cool and moisten. Some understood "lukewarm water" to be less hot than "temperate." We say this is a dispute over words.
</margin>

<margin>
He calls "temperate water" that which has a suitable heat so the pores open and the matter evaporates, and they sweat well. Secondly, he can then be placed in water that is less hot; I call this lukewarm or temperate as you please. This is done to settle the heat. Perhaps the anointing with oils should not have preceded but followed the use of lukewarm water. It can be said that this lukewarm water is hotter than the temperate water, as there is a progression from less hot to more hot water as is done in the bath when moving from one room to another.
</margin>

<margin>
**i**
"Then when they exit." But not immediately, because wine immediately after a bath is forbidden, as declared in the *Regimen of Acute Diseases*. Rather, let him rest a little after the bath and then drink. They will sweat by the power of the preceding bath which moved the matter to the exterior, and by the power of the wine-water which penetrates and strengthens the heat to moisture. What little choleric matter remains is rectified by the moistening of the pores.
</margin>

<margin>
**k**
"And do not fear, etc." He gives the reason why wine "broken" by mixing benefits: with the water changed, a little wine benefits the remaining quantity of the matter by resolving it—that is, evacuating it by sweat or evaporation with the heat strengthened. The wine helps the penetrating water with its strength—that is, with its specific form, wine penetrates to the members. And by its mixture—that is, by its heat. Here two things assist penetration. Therefore it cools, because the water dominates there. Another reading says it "cools the residue." Avicenna means that in this mixture of a little wine and much water, there is a "breaking" of the wine, not its destruction. The quantity of residual heat of the wine does two things: one, it assists in resolving; two, it helps the water to penetrate with strength—that is, with a strong quality of cold.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the technical discourse on treating tertian fevers, specifically focusing on the management of residual heat in the liver and the distinction between "pure" and "mixed" fevers according to the authorities of Avicenna and medieval commentators.</meta>

Book III

density and humidity: to which water is mixed with a little heat. And at this time it follows that it should cool and moisten. Likewise, we shall state the proportion as being two parts water to one part wine. However, the physician varies this according to the types of wine and the nature of the bodies, according to his own judgment. And thus it is clear.

<margin>
A. And when after the crisis.
</margin>
**A**nd when after the crisis. One must consider whether, once the tertian crisis has ceased either by art or by nature, heat still remains. For example, in the liver, which may cease after one paroxysm <note>the peak or "fit" of the fever</note> because it does not have a fixed cause retaining it. Sometimes the heat is not prepared for by such inflammations: and this is because there is some **obstruction** <note>original: "oppilatio"; a blockage in the vessels or organs</note> in the liver which sustains that heat. And these obstructions often occur through the excessive use of cooling agents during the fervor of the tertian heat. Therefore, the remedies for that hot **dyscrasia** <note>original: "distemperantie"; an imbalance of the bodily humors</note> cannot be effective unless those obstructions are opened with diuretic seeds and roots. And this case is subject to the principal rule in the second chapter, where it is said that for heat with obstructions, the physician must be careful of excessive cooling. Look there, see the "vesica" <note>bladder</note>, and complete it. We do not intend here to declare how an obstruction acts as an efficient or conserving cause of unnatural heat, or how it does not. However, if it is joined to a hot imbalance, one must first intend to remove the obstruction. For these things are known at the beginning of the science.

**B**ile and others: their cure has already been passed to you. And when some inseparable heat remains after the crisis, then proceed as above: namely, that you administer syrup of vinegar with diuretic juices, or in which diuretic seeds and roots have been decocted. And know that the cure for continuous tertian fever is similar to the cure for intermittent tertian: namely, it consists of thinning the matter from the obstruction, disposing it for digestion, and cooling it. This is done with syrup of vinegar combined with seeds such as citron seeds and endive seeds, properly crushed; and specifically, two hours before, give it in a drink of barley water. And for the refinement of the food...

<margin>
b. And know. They doubt whether the cure for continuous tertian is more inclined [to digestion].
</margin>
**B**ut know. They doubt whether the cure for continuous tertian is more inclined toward observing the **digestion** <note>original: "digõe"; in medieval medicine, this refers to the 'ripening' or maturation of a harmful humor so it can be expelled</note> of the matter. **Dinus** <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous 14th-century physician</note> and **Francis of Piedmont** <note>Franciscus de Pedemontium, another major medical authority</note> respond that this is because the matter of continuous tertian is more undigested. It is therefore necessary to digest it more. But why is it more undigested—that is, more unfit for expulsion? First, because it is more thoroughly mixed with the humors in the veins—that is, the blood. Second, because this matter, by the nature of the place in which it resides, is not as fit for evacuation as the matter of intermittent tertian fevers. But these arguments are not well understood by me. First: because **choleric** <note>yellow bile</note> matter, the more it is mixed with the humors in the veins (the blood), the more benign and "digested" it is. The further it is from the blood, the cruder it is, as can be understood regarding tertian fever, which is the truth. But [the authority] in Book VII wants this bile to be mixed. For that which is mixed with blood cannot be separated from the blood by pharmacy <note>drugs</note>. For it is said that if this mixture is such that pharmacy does not suffice, then **phlebotomy** <note>bloodletting</note> is required, and we will not need "digestion." Or it should be said: assuming some bile exists in its proper form and is mixed with blood in a way that does not warrant phlebotomy but is evacuable by pharmacy: it will be better evacuated by a drug if it is in its proper form, separated from the blood, because separated bile is more wicked and more absorbed. And this is a matter of consideration. You will, however, find our words to be true if you compare these two types of bile in a proper comparison. The second argument of Dinus does not appear true, for the bile we evacuate in intermittent tertian is also in the veins—namely, the bile that precedes the cause—though not always necessarily so. And thus, regarding the location of both matters, there is equal ease in evacuation by a drug. We say that all the intentions mentioned for intermittent tertian also apply to continuous tertian; yet in five things, there are greater increases in the continuous than the intermittent. First, one must focus more on the digestion of the matter. Second, one must focus more on cooling. Third, we focus more on the refinement of the regimen. Fourth, more on the provocation [of urine/sweat]. Fifth, one must focus more on the loosening of the belly, and less on the use of purging drugs before the digestion of the matter. The reason for the first—why we cool more and refine the regimen more—is a known cause. But the specific reason why we observe digestion more—that is, digest more—is because the matter is more unfit and more disobedient to the regimen, not for the reasons Dinus gave, but for another reason that Avicenna judged: which is that the matter of continuous choleric fever and the matter of intermittent tertian that we evacuate are both in the veins—in the continuous fever, the matter is joined and antecedent; in the intermittent, it is only the antecedent matter. But the matter of continuous fever is unfit in both substance and quality; hence it could not be repelled and evacuated by nature, but remained in the cavities. The matter of intermittent fever is more fit for evacuation in substance and quality; hence nature expels it to the veins when it is provoked. And consider that Avicenna said that in continuous fever we observe more "digestion of digestion"—that is, we focus more on digestion. But it will be doubted how much more we focus. It should be said that this is done either by giving simple syrup of vinegar more times (for example, in one day), or by giving a larger dose, or by giving a more digestive form—for instance, making the water more acidic with more vinegar. Later, another interpretation is given: A. wants the matter of continuous bile to be cruder than intermittent matter. But he wanted to observe digestion more—that is, to wait longer for digestion in it before wishing to evacuate—so that the evacuation occurs with more digested matter, because the fever is continuous. But in intermittent fever, even if it is not so digested, it can be evacuated more safely. For purging medicines having violence, such as **scammony** <note>a harsh plant-based purgative</note>, are what evacuate these matters. In intermittent fever, we can use these medicines more safely, because we have a greater degree of rectification and we do not fear the inflammation of the body and the weakness that we fear in continuous fever. And thus, although the humor may not be much digested, it is possible to draw it out of the body with a more violent drug in intermittent matter. In continuous fever, therefore, whether the matter is more fit or more benign by nature than intermittent matter, or more unfit, we still observe the state of digestion more in evacuating through the bowels, or vomiting, or provocation, or sweating, than in intermittent fever. The reason for the greater intention in continuous fever—namely, the provocation of urine—is known. For continuous matters are in the larger veins where there is a greater connection to the urinary paths. But since the cause of intermittent fever can be in the same places, another reason must be given (though the aforementioned is good): because that happens more often. And another reason is: in continuous choleric fever, there is a greater injection of the wateriness of the blood, for the evacuation of which one must focus more on urine or the provocation of sweat, as appears from the declaration above in the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers in general. And this greater provocation of urine shall be done with the frequent use of thin barley water, and in its time, with the frequent use of an emulsion of cold, provoking seeds. Later, one might imagine that there is a greater quantity of matter requiring greater provocation in continuous fever; but this alone does not necessitate greater provocation, but also evacuation through the belly, always observing the state of digestion more in continuous than in intermittent fever, as was said.

<margin>
c. And it is necessary that it be refined.
</margin>
**A**nd it is necessary that it be refined—namely, the regimen, or that the care of continuous fever be more refined than intermittent, as is noted. Regarding the type of intention—namely, focusing more on loosening the belly in continuous fever—this is due to the greater dryness of the belly and the greater fear of **phrenitis** <note>delirium or brain inflammation</note>. But it is doubted because at the beginning of continuous fever, purging drugs (solutives) are not granted; rather, lenitives <note>mild softeners</note> such as violet syrup and fruit waters—namely, solutive ones like tamarinds and mild enemas (clysters) only, and not sharp enemas. But in the discourse, it seems that in continuous fever we should use strong purgatives before digestion, because the use of purgatives before digestion is due to the fury of the matter or its excessive quantity, as we said above in the chapter on the general cure of putrid fevers. But in continuous fever, especially...

<column-break/>

III

...it is less; the use of strong drugs is more to be suspected in continuous fever. And therefore, as much as we can, we ought to make the matter more fit, so that the degree of weakness and the readiness of the matter for evacuation matches the degree of weakness and the reduction of the vigor of the purging drug in dose, quality, and virtue; for in continuous fever, we need weaker ones more than in intermittent, as is clear from what has been said. Besides this, it happens that sometimes we are forced to give purging drugs before digestion due to the "fury" and quantity [of the humors]; and this compulsion and irregular gathering happens more—that is, more often—in continuous fevers

<margin>
than in intermittent ones, as has been argued. But these discourses do not contradict each other; know this.
</margin>
than in intermittent fevers, and for administering mild enemas in the beginning and for provocation: and because it should be refined, and purging drugs should not be allowed in the drink at the beginning, nor anything approaching them, except those which are like violet syrup and fruit water; and they should use only mild enemas.

<margin>
d. And they should not use sharp... here, exclude every oral lenitive.
</margin>
**A**nd they should not use sharp... here, exclude every lenitive given by mouth. And only enemas should be made that are mild. And he says to him who said: either violet syrup or fruit water. But perhaps he said this because you ought to use mild enemas and mild drinks more. And he built this upon the rule set down above when he said: "And more beloved to me is the use of enemas." He can also exclude sharp enemas, meaning you should make enemas that are mild, not sharp; because in [continuous fevers]

**T**hey inflame and agitate the matter and cause fear of **phrenitis** <note>delirium or "frenzy"</note>. And for this reason, sharp enemas would be less suspect in intermittent fever. And I believe this is what Avicenna means.

<margin>
On the cure of non-pure tertian. Ch. 40.
</margin>
**T**he things in which the cure of non-pure tertian fever differs are the things in which it shares with "cold fevers" by the "second license." And perhaps this is approached by those having the pure type: namely, that they should not wait...

**R**egarding the things which etc. After the cure of pure tertian, he places the cure of non-pure tertian. And first, he places the difference between the cure of pure and non-pure tertian, and from this, he sets down several rules with reasoning. Second, in general, he takes up the cure according to their diversity. Third, specifically the cure of non-pure tertian in particular. There, "and it is necessary to consider." Then the third part, "And when you see." The first part is in two: first, he places this difference in general; second, he declares it in particular. There, "and perhaps." Third: the first distinction is refined; and the exposition of **Thaddeus** <note>Thaddeus of Florence, a 13th-century medical authority</note> is found, which says: that fevers are twofold. Some are of the "first license," like quotidian fever. Some are fevers of the "second license," like **epiala** and **liparia** <note>types of mixed fevers involving both cold and hot sensations</note>. Now, in whichever fevers of the first and second license occur, in those the cure of pure tertian differs from the cure of non-pure. But although the exposition can be saved, it is nevertheless not clear: because there are some things in which those fevers can agree, in which the cure of pure and non-pure tertian does not differ (for example, in cooling, focusing on the fever). And so Thaddeus ought to have declared himself. And another exposition is that which Dynus seems to have understood: that some fevers are cold of the "first license," like pure **phlegmatic** fevers; some are of the "second license," like non-pure phlegmatic fevers. Those things, therefore, in which these fevers occur, are those in which the cure of pure and non-pure tertian differs. This exposition can be sustained, but it is not clear and an objection can be made against Thaddeus. There are many other expositions which are not worthy of memory. We shall say: because we have always spoken upon this passage, and up to now this error runs. And it is first to be known that by "cold fevers" he understands fevers from "cold matter"—for example, in this context, fevers from phlegmatic matter. Second, it is to be known that for Avicenna, "license" is the same as "indication" <note>original: "iudicatio"; a medical indicator for treatment</note>. Hence it is his custom to sometimes say "license," as appears in the third book of the Canon, fen 14, on the cure of hot abscesses of the liver. In "indication" or "license" regarding cold fevers, therefore, there is a double type. One is primary, and this is cooling and moistening. And the other is secondary: and this is the indication taken from the cause and the disposition as it depends on the cause, and the diversities according to that. And these things ought to be presupposed here. For example: the first thing the physician intends in a fever is cooling and moistening; the second is the removal of the cause, which varies as the cause varies; and also the rectification of the disposition, which varies as the cause varies. Avicenna therefore wishes to say that the things in which the cure of non-pure tertian differs from pure tertian are those which come from the "second license" or "intention" regarding cold fevers, in which (namely, the licenses or intentions) mixed cold fevers share; consequently, those in which they differ from choleric fevers. For example: in the example of cold fevers, from the "second license" or intention toward the cause, a syrup that thins thick, viscous matter is appropriate, because all phlegmatic things have some viscosity and thickness. And in this, pure tertian differs from non-pure tertian, because for non-pure tertian a thinning syrup is appropriate, which is not appropriate in pure tertian. But non-pure tertian does not differ from pure tertian in that in which cold fevers share from the "first license," because that is cooling. But the cure of pure and non-pure tertian does not differ in the intention of absolute cooling, because cooling is appropriate to both, though there is a difference in the degree of cooling. This is what Avicenna says: "The things by which the cure of non-pure tertian is diversified" (namely, from the cure of pure tertian) are the things in which "cold fevers share" (namely, fevers of cold matter). I speak of "things from the second license"—that is, the intention held toward the cause mediately and immediately. In those things, therefore, in which cold fevers share among themselves regarding the license held from the cause, in those the cure of non-pure tertian differs from pure tertian. And the reason for this general statement is that non-pure tertian shares with cold fevers in its cause from that part where phlegm is mixed with bile, and consequently from that part which is non-pure tertian fever. Therefore, non-pure tertian fever will share or agree in treatment as far as the causes are concerned with cold fevers, and this is "sharing with them in the second license." For the cure of cold fevers differs from the cure of pure tertian as far as those things that regard the cause, and consequently as far as those things that are appropriate to cold fevers from the "second license." That which cold fevers share from the second license is that in which the cure of non-pure tertian differs from the cure of pure tertian. And the syllogism Avicenna intends shall be formed thus: That in which cold fevers properly share with one another is that in which cold fevers differ from hot fevers (for example, pure tertian). But that which is appropriate to cold fevers from the second license is properly that in which they share. Therefore, that which is appropriate to cold fevers from the second license is that in which cold fevers differ from hot fevers. And then it is presupposed that that in which cold fevers share is the second license belonging to non-pure tertians. But in that, cold fevers differ from hot ones, such as pure tertian; therefore, in that, non-pure tertian differs from pure tertian. And there would be other ways of forming these syllogisms. "And perhaps..." Here, he places these differences specifically, and for me, there is a new protection just as there are nine differences. Then there is the third part, "And what feeding." The parts will appear. For the first understanding, consider: that the first part can be explained in two ways. First, by making one out of the previous virtues; and that Avicenna wants to place a difference between pure and non-pure tertian as far as the "license of bathing" is concerned. For sometimes in pure tertian, a bath can be granted before perfect digestion, and specifically to one accustomed to it, as Altab. says in the third part of his practice; but in non-pure tertian, it cannot be granted unless the matter is most perfectly digested.

### Treatise II

<margin>a</margin>
This is what he says. And perhaps it is granted to those who have the pure fever, namely, that one should not wait for the height of the decline <note>original: "declinationis"; the stage where the fever begins to subside</note> to provide a bath. But sometimes one waits for digestion, that is, when one waits for digestion for the sake of using a bath: it is not necessary to wait for the total or final digestion, such as that which occurs in the decline. For in those possessing a non-pure tertian fever, the bath is prohibited before digestion, and this is for three reasons as has appeared. Another exposition is made by dividing this part into two: and the second part begins there: "Since it is prohibited." In the first part, Avicenna <note>a 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon" was the standard medical textbook in Europe</note> intends to compare the non-pure tertian fever to the pure one regarding cure by evacuation. This cure ought to be done by the "second permission," which is the permission according to the cause <note>medical logic allowing a treatment because it addresses the underlying root cause</note>. He means to say: that in those having a pure tertian fever, it is granted that one should not wait for the fullest digestion for evacuation, just as they wait for digestion although they can evacuate before perfect and complete digestion and before complete decline. But in the non-pure tertian, it is necessary to wait longer for digestion for the evacuation to be performed. And this is what he previously said: that they should wait longer for digestion in the loosening of both humors <note>original: "col."; likely referring to the choleric and phlegmatic humors</note>. Consider therefore that Avicenna identifies the time of truly complete digestion by the time of the greatest decline: because the matter has been so digested that a great decline of the fever can follow. If therefore you wait for digestion to perform an evacuation, do not wait for the greatest digestion in a pure tertian; but wait for this in a non-pure tertian since the matter is thick <note>original: "grossa"</note> and more unfit for evacuation. <gloss>it is said</gloss> In another way, this part can be explained by speaking of evacuation: that Avicenna wants to say the complete opposite of what was said here. And it is that in phlegmatic fevers and non-pure tertian fevers, we do not wait for the peak of decline, that is, of digestion. But when we wait for digestion so that we may evacuate: indeed, always for the most part before the decline and before perfect digestion, we give many solutive medicines <note>laxatives or substances that "loosen" the humors</note>. In pure tertians, however, we wait for total digestion and decline to give a solutive drug, except perhaps rarely. And this is what he means when he says "perhaps." And this is what he says by distinguishing the tertian from the part previously mentioned, thus: The circumstances in which phlegmatic fevers agree in intention or permission from the cause or toward the cause are also the circumstances that suit non-pure tertian fevers. Consequently, these are the ways in which non-pure tertians differ from pure tertians. And among these things is evacuation. For in these fevers—namely, phlegmatic and non-pure tertian—one does not wait for the final or greatest digestion and decline when waiting for digestion to perform evacuation. Instead, they evacuate before this completion of digestion. In pure tertians, however, perhaps this same thing will happen or occur, but it happens rarely. In non-pure tertian fevers, however, it happens without a "perhaps," because we almost always evacuate with solutive drugs without waiting for the peak of digestion or decline. It must be considered that these two expositions compare these fevers in evacuation by drug: since the same rule applies to these by the second permission. Nor is there anything which more pertains to the second permission in fevers than evacuation, since it leads the matter causing the fever out of the body; and therefore by reason Avicenna began with this evacuation. And these two last expositions in which a comparison is made regarding the evacuation of these fevers seem contrary to one another, yet they are not, as will appear.

...the peak of the decline: but sometimes digestion is awaited. <gloss>and so forth</gloss> But the bath is prohibited in them: for the bath <note>original: "balneū"</note> makes the undigested phlegm descend because of that which it pours out to the site of the putrefaction, and it mixes the bad humor with the putridity; and it resolves the subtle parts and makes the thick remain. <gloss>and so forth</gloss> And feeding: every day again; or near the feeding is one of those things that harms them: indeed, they should be fed one day and not the other. And let there be in the foods that which cleanses and warms a little <unclear>bit</unclear>. And let the feeding be thicker in the beginnings of the sickness than in the beginnings of a pure fever; then gradually it should be adjusted.

<margin>b</margin>
**For the bath.** Here he assigns three causes. **The first cause** is that it moves crude phlegm, which being agitated and stirred by liquefaction and not evacuated, harms many members and corrupts and infects more humors. For harmful things induce more harm while they are being moved. This is what he says: it makes the undigested phlegm descend. For the liquefied phlegm flowing from its swelling descends and mixes the bad humor. **The second cause** is that the bath before digestion mixes the bad phlegm, which is the antecedent cause, with the putrid phlegm, which is worse. And this is because the putridity pours into it, which it finds by mixing, and in this is a great evil: because that phlegm which was not putrid becomes putrid, and perhaps it would have been possible to defend it from putrefaction. And because the fever can be doubled in this at one time. And this is what he says: "And it mixes," etc., "because of that which it pours out." And this third exposition is made for the unlearned, because a good intellect does not need it. **It resolves the subtle.** The third cause is noted.

<margin>c</margin>
**And that feeding.** This is the third difference in cure between the non-pure tertian and the pure. Regarding which he doubts, because it seems from this that a more refined diet <note>original: "subtilior"</note> suits the non-pure tertian; since in the pure cure he posits the opposite. We shall say that the feeding is a sufficiently copious feeding; but "near the feeding" is a diminished feeding. After this, we shall say as they commonly say: that one kind of feeding is universal, which is a deliberate feeding established in the physician's mind from the beginning of the fever until its standing point <note>the "status" or peak of the illness</note>. And this is thicker or more copious in non-pure tertians, since the non-pure tertian is longer-lasting. And therefore, in a non-pure tertian, from the beginning and before the peak, we will give chicken; because it must be prolonged, for example, for five days or months. But in a pure tertian which ought to terminate on the 13th day, you would not give it except sparingly. This is a more subtle diet than giving chicken. Another kind is the particular feeding which is done according to what the present disposition indicates at the moment. And we prefer the latter, that in fact these two feedings agree according to the specific cases. And in this feeding on the day of the paroxysm <note>the peak of the fever fit</note>, a more refined diet is used in a non-pure tertian than in a pure one, because the feverishness occupies that whole day; whence we cannot feed them, nor even nearby. Galen, however, in his *Therapeutics to Glaucon*, grants this feeding on the day before the determined day occurs. And this in non-pure tertians: because one must intend to digest the matter, which is done by not feeding, and for the length of the sickness so that the strength may suffice.

<column-break/>

Whence we feed more appropriately, or on the day of the paroxysm, we do not feed. This is what Avicenna says. And again the cures of the non-pure tertian differ: since feeding every day or near feeding—which is a reduced feeding—is among those things, etc. The physician, however, has the power to judge in this, and if strength does not suffice, it is necessary to give some food every day.

<margin>d</margin>
**And let it be in the foods.** This is the fourth rule. He says that in the foods of those having a non-pure tertian, there should be that which cleanses and warms a little, because of the thickness and viscosity and the slight coldness which the bile has from the phlegm mixed with it. And therefore, let there be in the foods chickpea water, hyssop, etc.

<margin>e</margin>
<gloss>And let there be feeding. This is the fifth rule, and it is noted. As if the refinement of the tertian was similar to the refinement of the pure tertian.</gloss>
Toward a strong refinement, perhaps, just as is the refinement of the tertian. And let there be less cooling. And let it be clysterized <note>given an enema</note> in the beginning with sharper clysters. And let digestion be expected more in the loosening of their bowels. And let there be in their barley water digestive and solutive virtues <note>properties</note>, just as that which we said regarding the one in whose stomach barley water becomes acidic; indeed, stronger than in that one. For perhaps it is necessary that hyssop and oregano and calamint and spikenard be decocted in it according to the complexion <note>the patient's specific bodily balance</note>. And beet is helpful to them. And the mixing of chickpea water with barley water; and in the end, chickpea is helpful also.

<margin>f</margin>
**And let there be cooling.** This is the sixth rule. It is doubted why he says these things in which the non-pure tertian differs in cure from the pure tertian are matters of the "second permission," which suit phlegmatic fever; but cooling is a matter in which things of the "first permission" agree. It must be said that the permission of greater cooling in a pure tertian and less in a non-pure tertian, insofar as they are compared from the disposition to the cause—namely, here to bile and there to phlegm or to bile thickened by phlegm—is the second permission. Therefore he said above that the second permission is permission from the cause itself to be digested or evacuated, and from the disposition as it varies from the cause. From which it appears: that all these different types by which the non-pure tertian is distinguished from the pure are indications taken from things appropriate to non-pure tertians regarding the second permission. <gloss>and</gloss> The **first rule** is evacuation which suits the non-pure tertian. The **second** is bathing after digestion is completed. The **third** is feeding every other day. The **fourth** is to put cleansing and warming things in the foods. The **fifth** is a more ample thickening at the beginning. The **sixth** is less cooling because of the thickness of the humor. The **seventh** is clysterization with sharper things in the beginning. The **eighth** is the expectation of the perfection of digestion. The **ninth** is the placement of warm medicines in barley water. <gloss>it is said</gloss> Otherwise, it can be answered to the doubt by saying that less cooling in a non-pure tertian and more in a pure are things that are owed to them or suit them from the "first permission." And then we will say that although things of the "second permission" in which cold fevers agree with each other—just as things in which the cure of a non-pure tertian differs from the cure of a pure tertian—are not nevertheless things of the "first permission" in which cold fevers agree. For example, less cooling and less moistening are things in which the cure of a non-pure tertian and the cure of a pure tertian agree; indeed, even in those they can differ by degree: because we cool and moisten less in non-pure tertians. Just as you might ask why Avicenna said these things differ as being things of the "second permission" suiting cold fevers, when they also differ in things common to cold fevers from the "first permission"? It is because he made these rules more numerous and more technical <note>original: "artificiales"</note>.

<margin>g</margin>
**And let it be clysterized.** This is the seventh rule. The cause is the multitude and thickness of the matter, and the abundance in the entry of the stomach and intestines where the source of those phlegms is, which is mixed with bile. And these clysters are made sharp in respect to the clysters of a pure tertian by adding a little mercurialis, carthamus, turbith <note>original: "turbit"; a purgative root</note>, and other things as it seems to you.

<margin>h</margin>
**And let it wait.** This is the eighth rule. It is doubted whether in giving a solutive drug that evacuates by loosening, such as turbith in a non-pure tertian—generally in fevers—we ought to wait more for the digestion of the matter and the perfection of digestion than when giving a proportional drug such as scammony <note>original: "scamonea"; a powerful purgative resin</note> in a pure tertian. It is answered that in a non-pure tertian we ought to wait more for digestion according to Avicenna here and above, according to the first of the two later expositions. Furthermore, the matter of a non-pure tertian is thicker and more unfit for evacuation; therefore digestion must occur. To the contrary is the final exposition made previously. On the opposing side are those commonly practicing and one who practices: because in non-pure tertians they give many solutive medicines before all perfect digestion and before the decline. Furthermore, Avicenna allows sharp clysters at the beginning. Furthermore, turbith is used. Again, he teaches in this fever to compose a medicine whose part may evacuate the evil. And this is done so that we may frequently purge those having a non-pure tertian before perfect digestion. Furthermore, in the cure of a phlegmatic fever, he does not diligently wait for digestion; indeed, he frequently evacuates with turbith even before the completion of digestion. Therefore it is so in a non-pure tertian, because it participates in the nature of the phlegmatic; and insofar as it participates in it, it differs from a pure tertian in disposition and cure. Here is a twofold solution. One with which the common opinion has passed, namely, that evacuation is twofold. One "rooting out" <note>eradicating</note> the matter, and because this is a stronger evacuation and the thick matter is unfit for it, it waits for a more perfect digestion in a non-pure tertian. The other is a "lessening" <note>minorative</note> evacuation, and this does not wait for perfect digestion in a non-pure tertian and in fevers because of the multitude of the matter; indeed, before digestion we frequently lessen with turbith in non-pure tertians and in cold fevers. For then such a lessening evacuation is done in non-pure tertians. And thus the contradiction that appears in Avicenna's text is solved according to our exposition. When he wanted to evacuate by eradicating in non-pure tertians, he said: "wait more for digestion in the loosening of their bowels." But when he wanted to lessen, he said that it is granted by necessity or always or for the most part to those having a non-pure [fever] that they should not wait for the peak of the decline, that is, of digestion. But sometimes they wait for perfect digestion, but this is perhaps granted to those having a pure [fever], because it is not so granted. But sometimes and perhaps this happens, as it is granted. But the second solution is truer and for those having more of the habit of medicine, although the preceding solution is true insofar as it is reduced to this one. Let us posit here three propositions which are three causes for evacuation in these fevers. **The first proposition** is this: that in every cure which is done by loosening thick and viscous matters—whether they be phlegmatic, melancholic, or choleric purely thickened by phlegm or melancholy—we ought to wait more for digestion, i.e., make the matter more digested, than in evacuating by loosening purely subtle choleric matters. The reason is: because thick, viscous matters are more unfit for movement by a drug, and therefore they ought to be made more digested. **The second proposition** is: that it more frequently happens that we evacuate by loosening from the beginning and before perfect digestion in fevers with abundant thick matter—of which the non-pure tertian is one—than in pure tertian fevers. The authors and the reasons mentioned above prove this: that there are illustrious physicians. For in one having a non-pure tertian or a cold fever, physicians from the beginning and before perfect digestion give many solutive medicines; indeed, whenever the matter begins to be digested somewhat, they begin to evacuate with turbith or agaric; and thus they proceed frequently by digesting or evacuating. And this never fails unless it is prohibited by the patient's condition. But in one having a most pure tertian, although we see some small sign of digestion, we do not evacuate in the beginning; but we wait until the peak of the fever in it; and if nature does not evacuate and bloodletting does not evacuate, we evacuate then the digested matter, as Avicenna commanded above. It rarely happens, however, that from the beginning and before perfect digestion we evacuate by loosening. And the cause of these things is: because in non-pure tertian fevers and other related fevers there is much matter, whence it is indicated that it should be consumed little by little and one should not wait for the whole digestion and evacuation. But in most pure tertian fevers this is not the case, since in pure tertians we evacuate before digestion and in the beginning only because of the fury <note>the intense heat or activity</note> of the matter; and rarely is the matter of a pure tertian furious with true fury. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the treatment of mixed (non-pure) tertian fevers, specifically focusing on the timing of "digestion"—the process by which harmful humors are ripened for expulsion—and the various methods of evacuation like bloodletting and purging.</meta>

### Book III

What our last exposition says about the final steps. And perhaps it happens that you consider it as pure.

<margin>a</margin>The third proposition: that which happens rarely is the evacuation of our digestion, or rather the completion of digestion in a pure tertian fever. It is not helpful for it to be so digested; indeed, it can be evacuated more while raw <note>original: "crudo"; refers to humors that have not yet been "cooked" or processed by the body’s heat</note> when it breaks out frequently in a non-pure tertian fever, where, for example, in a pure tertian where the fury of the bile <note>original: "cholere"</note> or a great multitude of it indicates a laxative medicine <note>term: <term>farmacu solutiuū</term> (laxative medicine), a drug used to purge specific humors</note>, such as scammony, which does not happen frequently, but rarely. I say that immediately you should act without caring about any hidden or apparent digestion: because the bile has a certain mobility. But if it is a non-pure tertian fever or a phlegmatic fever that is prolonged, it indicates only that the matter should be diminished according to the nature of custom or the multitude of those humors. I say that you should not act while it is entirely raw, but regarding the matter, you can give turbith <note>original: "turbit"; a root used as a potent purgative</note>; but we expect at least some hidden digestion: just as it begins to be digested, so you will begin to evacuate. However, what should be done regarding the gravity threatening apoplexy was said above in the general cure for putrid fevers. And if you consider two expositions: those which seem contrary are saved: for they were placed upon that passage, "and perhaps it is granted." And if you also consider the cause of the third proposition, it is the same as the cause of the first proposition.

**And** so that they may be. This last part is a note, and it is noted that they are stronger, at least in a larger quantity. For it is not surpassable in degree beyond pepper. And consider that in a pure tertian, pepper in water is granted by accident: because it is the acidification of food, which is not from the first license nor from the second. But in a non-pure tertian, it is granted from the second license, namely on account of the matter according to the complexion <note>the specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—in a person's body</note>. That is, according to the diversity of complexions needing more or less quality: which is more or less aromatic, in which these simple medicines are made digestible. Some say according to the complexion, that is, if the complexions and mixtures are combined. It should be considered that from the beginning, he does not give pure chickpea water <note>original: "aquā cicerū"</note>, namely of the black or red varieties.

<margin>a</margin>And because it is an opening and provocative agent because it agitates raw matter; but with somewhat digested matter or perfectly digested matter: chickpeas, that is, chickpea water, helps, which can be called "chickpea," that is, the body of the chickpea, whose nourishment is hot, having hot vapors moving toward the heart, as said in the second book of the *Canon*, in the chapter on chickpeas. And therefore, at the end, when the fever ceases, it can be granted in food.

<margin>b</margin>And then. Here he places the cure of the non-pure tertian in comparison to the pure one. It should be considered that this diversification is in the foods mentioned. And I place the error at the last point. Let there be a non-pure tertian slightly distant from a pure one because of the small amount of bile mixed with a little phlegm. I say that in its barley water, from the beginning, chickpea water shall not be placed, nor celery <note>original: "apū"</note>, but maidenhair fern <note>original: "capilli veneris"</note> and endive.

<margin>c</margin>And when you see. He distinguishes the threshold of the cure for the non-pure tertian from the cure of the pure tertian; and since so many rules of healing are known, just as there are governing forces. He will place specifically the cure for the non-pure tertian. And first by evacuation. Second by digestion and evacuation again. Third, he places the reception of certain medicines. Some say "in it," there he acts. Aids. There the things. And concerning all of them, the first is in four, although he places four rules in four evacuations. And the first rule is in phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note>: which is if you see thick and very red urine, it indicates phlebotomy. For it signifies matter sinning in the blood, as we said above in the general chapter.

<margin>d</margin>Also, if you have performed phlebotomy, you will not need a clyster <note>term: <term>clisteri</term> (enema), used to clear the bowels and draw humors downward</note>. Some of our peers say that one ought not to have a clyster and phlebotomy on the same morning; but regarding the mention of time: I say before the fever, the permission of a clyster; in the morning, phlebotomy: because thus you will not need a clyster: because Avicenna confirmed this in the third book of the *Canon*, in the chapter on the cure of spitting blood. There he says that a clyster should be administered unless or when there has not been phlebotomy. On account of the prohibition, that is: because phlebotomy is prohibited to all. And we say there: that where in a case in which there would be great weakness, he does not prohibit a clyster cleansing the intestines from feces before phlebotomy; indeed, let him be clysterized with a lenient clyster in a timely manner; then let phlebotomy follow: if that is required, then you will not need a clyster: because that was permitted to cleanse the intestines from the dregs of the last food. <gloss>To</gloss> this, we respond to Avicenna in the third book of the *Canon*: that he is speaking there of an acrid clyster, which ought not to occur on the same day as phlebotomy. And so he says there that an acrid clyster should be administered to draw matter from the parts of the head when there has been no phlebotomy. <gloss>And</gloss> by this, another exposition appears: that the clyster is twofold. One is cleansing of the feces; and you will need this on the day of phlebotomy, either before or after as it seems best to you. The other is the acrid clyster, and let that not be done on the day of phlebotomy. And you will not need this on the day of phlebotomy.

**The third** exposition is from Avicenna: that phlebotomy sometimes so sufficiently diminishes the matter that you will not need a clyster, namely an acrid one, nor another minor evacuation; however, it is most often the case that we need an acrid clyster, because of the many repletive matters in the parts of the stomach and intestines; which the sharpness of the clyster ought to evacuate. As is taken from the third book of the *Practica* by Haly Abbas <note>original: "Ali abate"; a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note>. And know that it is not a secret. <gloss>Second</gloss>, the rule is to praise vomiting. And in this, Galen <note>the most influential Greek physician of antiquity</note> agrees in the third book of *Therapeutics to Glaucon*, and Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"; a major Persian physician</note> in the seventh book of the *Continens*. And all agree. And the reason is: because in vomiting, both matters are evacuated cleanly. For this mixed fever is phlegmatic and a non-pure double tertian and is associated with multiple obstructions, involving the stomach and heat in the liver; and regarding those made hot by bad movements, that vomit will be extirpating both matters after food because it is easier, as Haly Abbas says: for the expulsion of many things is gentler than that of a few, as he says. But let the vomit be done with oxymel <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note> or warm water or something else.

**The third** rule is concerning laxatives; first, the cleansing ones, which solve only by wiping away, such as "algeniab" water, that is, rose sugar or honey water: and we use syrup of fresh roses. It is called water because it dissolves when the substance is water. Or it is called water, that is, the subtle part of those things, not the thick part of the decoction, namely to complete the cooling. Or they solve with this by cutting into it, like simple acetous syrup; afterward, it passes to cassia; but at the last, it will be for the strength. Turbith, that is, a decoction or infusion or an eruption or a pure quantity. Behold that in the beginning, he grants strong and hot things, namely turbith, even with some hidden digestion in the matter. For hidden digestion is not excluded in the beginning, as is understood in the first book of the *De Septimanis*, seventh chapter: because these things have been declared above. <gloss>As much as</gloss> Haly Abbas does not grant evacuation before digestion in this fever, unless the matter is tumultuous, that is, humorous or furious.

<column-break/>

And all these things are known from the general chapter. Partially in this one, that clysters are for the beginning. The fourth rule is in clysters: which are more favored than other drugs; thus the rule is built upon the general rule, and there it is declared. "Alafek" is tribulus, but "lialafek" is bile; and either reading is good. Consider that these clysters have a sharpness as was prescribed above in the seventh rule, when he said: "And let him be clysterized in the beginning with sharper clysters." However, these are the clysters which are understood to be composed of these three orders. A certain lenient one in which neither turbith nor safflower <note>original: "carthamu"</note> is placed.

**With** them. And it is necessary that the proximity of the non-pure to the pure fever be considered, and its distance from it; and according to that, let it be diversified between its cure and the cure of the pure one. For if it is very close to the pure, then diversify between them with a small variation. And when you see their urine is thick, then perform phlebotomy: and when you have performed phlebotomy, you will not need a clyster. And know that there is nothing more helpful for them than vomiting after food. And concerning laxatives in its beginnings, those which are closer to being equalized are "algeniab" water of the decoction and acetous syrup. And perhaps we will put cassia fistula in it; and the strength is such that you place in it the virtue of turbith. And clysters in the beginning are more favored than other laxatives, and they are clysters in which there is mallow, chamomile, beet, safflower, violet, and "febelte" and figs and the scent of turbith. And from them is "casicti" and sesame oil and borax <note>original: "baurac"</note>. And perhaps it needs one of these according to the distance of the fever from the pure type.

<margin>One happens in which safflower would be placed. Another sharper one in which turbith or safflower and turbith are placed. Needing, however, one of these clysters according to the distance of the fever from the pure: because the further it is from it, the sharper the clyster you need. And he said "perhaps," because in one fever one might need not just one, but perhaps all the said clysters, namely of the three mentioned orders. Otherwise, it can be said "one of these," that is, either a lenient clyster. For if the fever is far from pure, I need a laxative with turbith. But if it is not so far, a clyster can suffice.</margin>

**Therefore**, when you know that digestion has now arrived, then evacuate and provoke; and do not worry. And of the good evacuations for them is that they take Hiera Picra <note>a traditional bitter medicine composed of aloes and other herbs</note>, 5 drams; juice of lettuce and eupatorium, 3 and a half drams each; celery, citrine and chebulic myrobalans <note>types of astringent fruit from India</note>, 5 drams each; turbith, 7 drams. Let pills be made from these with celery water. And let its dose be 2 drams. And of those, there is a decoction of my own good invention: namely of eupatorium, wormwood, chebulic myrobalans, 5 and a half drams each; melon, cucumber, and watermelon seeds, 10 drams each; celery, polypody <note>a type of fern</note>, "sucbaba," "bedeoard" <note>likely bezoar or a specific thistle</note>, 10 drams each; turbith, 1 ounce; cassia, 6 drams; stoned raisins, 20 drams; figs, a certain number.

**Aids.** Here are the rules for digestives and evacuations rectifying the malice of the nutritive organs and trying to help nature in digesting with acetous syrup. For example, let one ounce of simple acetous syrup be given in the morning for a digestive, and half an ounce of "geleniab," that is, rose sugar or honey. And in place of this, we use half an ounce of rose syrup made from fresh roses. And let this be when the tertian is not far removed from the pure. For if the matter is further and thicker, let acetous syrup of the roots be given, namely of fennel and parsley. Or from the beginning let simple acetous syrup be given, and toward the end of the beginning, let the one of the roots be given.

<margin>e</margin>And after the seventh day, that is, after the opening of digestion; and so it is understood. For so Haly Abbas wishes in this chapter. For wormwood <note>original: "absinthiū"</note> before digestion is harmful, as below in the chapter on semitertian fever <note>original: "emitriteo"</note>. Namely, he proceeds to more provocative things as is known. And if 14 days have passed, that is, evacuations having already been made and the fever being in decline: give the lesser rose troches <note>small medicinal lozenges</note> which the fifth rule mentions, like troches of roses; and perhaps by "lesser" he means those which do not contain scammony; and they are of a short description in which there is cooling and strengthening on account of a certain simplicity; because they do not evacuate except after digestion, as appeared above at the end of the general chapter.

<margin>f</margin>If however the illness is prolonged. Here Avicenna makes us imagine a very long non-pure tertian. For that which preceded has already ended after the 14th day, or not much beyond. But he imagines this one to be greatly extended, for example, to two or three months. And because such a thing harms the nutritive organs by obstructing them and making them flabby and weak and gathering many matters in them—whence a man can become hydropic <note>original: "hydropicus"; suffering from dropsy or edema</note>—therefore he should attend to troches, namely of eupatorium, and with plasters and fomentations of the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen, where the liver and spleen are located</note>. We will give troches of eupatorium. He says that we see fit to add to the syrup of roots things suitable for this intention. For example, we add eupatorium, scolopendria <note>hart's-tongue fern</note>, tamarisk, "cuenta," and sometimes camel grass <note>original: "fquinarum"</note> and the like.

<margin>g</margin>And heating. That is, light and gentle: as with oil of spica <note>lavender oil</note> and wormwood. They soften by dilating the pores and transpiring the matters, such as chamomile with a little wormwood and spica; and sometimes camel grass, calamint, and similar things. And you should understand that another cure ought to be done besides this one, which provides for the malice of the nutritive organs. Therefore, perform phlebotomy where appropriate, and vomiting, and clysters, and this medicine which diminishes the matter. And let the digestive syrup be given. When you therefore know that perfect digestion has now occurred, then evacuate, namely with an expelling and despoiling drug; and provoke, namely the urine with stronger provocatives, and do not worry. Some explain "do not worry" as: do not intend to alter the humors further but focus more on evacuating. Others: And do not worry about other intentions; but primarily intend to evacuate. We say with this exposition this other: do not worry, that is, act without hesitation after the matter has been digested with perfect digestion. For in the time before this: if you evacuated with a drug or provoked urine, you did this with hesitation because the matter was not prepared. But once the matter is digested, evacuation and provocation are granted more safely, because no harm can follow from the state of the matter's indisposition.

<margin>h</margin>And concerning evacuations. First he places certain laxative medicines. Second he places a certain rule, and according to its end, he places certain other laxative medicines. He makes two descriptions. Hiera is taken as the common "pigra" <note>Hiera Pigra, the "sacred bitter" laxative</note>, which Avicenna gives so absolutely. And Galen in the seventh book of the *Therapeutics* was known.

<margin>i</margin>And of those. "Sucbaba" is one species of thorn; "bedequar" is another; but they are very close in virtue. And we use only one of them, namely the white thorn; which is sugar, or among others, it is "bedequar." "Rose pfice" are a variety of rose. A "ladus" is a large measure of four ounces; among others three ounces. A "siliqua" is four grains. And we do not intend to verify these recipes. For the general method was written by us upon the fifth book of the *Canon*, and if you have knowledge of the simples <note>individual herbs/ingredients</note>, it is easy for you. And there we wrote the method of invention for compound laxative medicines.

<margin>k</margin>And perhaps. He said "perhaps" because the necessity of these laxative medicines is when the non-true tertian is greatly prolonged. In that which is very...
