# Treatise on Fevers

<margin>
The Solution <note>original: "Solutio"; here meaning the evacuation or purging of the illness.</note>
</margin>
is near when we do not purge purely with an evacuating and dissolving drug before perfect digestion is achieved. And if we do purge, we purge with the power of the drug and not its physical substance. Franciscus <note>likely a reference to a specific medical commentator like Francesco di Bartolo</note> doubts how they can evacuate a viscous humor if it is already digested. It must be said that before perfect digestion, we evacuate in small, diminishing amounts <note>original: "minorative"</note>; at that time, it is viscous with as much viscosity as it has reduction in digestion, but for a thick, viscous humor that is already digested, it possesses the viscosity proper to its species, even if it is digested. Thus, the "parts" of viscous humors still retain viscosity—insofar as they are parts—which bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> does not have, and it can be called a viscous humor primarily. It must be considered that the necessity of this medicine arose because of the great amount of matter and the difficulty of its removal, as well as the need to preserve the patient's vitality <note>original: "virtutem"</note>. For the medicine could not be given in a single dose to draw out the entire humor, because the patient's strength would not have sustained it. It must, therefore, be given in several doses so that the vitality is not destroyed. And this is what he means: it is possible for a gradation to be made in it—that is, it should be given in several turns. He says afterward that this medicine is one that can "subtleize" <note>term: <term>subtiliare</term> (to thin or refine thick humors to make them easier to move)</note> and "aggregate" <note>term: <term>aggregare</term> (here meaning to tonify or strengthen the organs)</note>. Some misunderstand this, thinking it means it can be given separately in many parts or all at once. Let us say otherwise: this laxative medicine of which Avicenna speaks is one that receives the "bodies" <note>the raw physical materials</note> of the medicines, such as the aforementioned medicine that contained *hiera pigra* <note>a traditional bitter purgative made with aloes</note>, etc., and such as the medicines he describes at the end of this chapter.

<margin>
Thirty sebestens <note>a type of plum used as a mild laxative</note>, rose-honey <note>original: "geleniabin"</note> made with roses, five drachms weight of peaches; let them all be boiled according to this description. And let a large jar be taken from it in which scammony <note>original: "siliqua .i. scamonee"</note> has been placed. Perhaps a strong medicine is necessary in one way and a weak one in another. Its strength is according to how it evacuates the viscous humor, but its weakness is according to how it does not evacuate a great deal at one time; rather, it is possible for a gradation to occur so that it evacuates the matter whose removal is necessary in many stages, so as not to destroy the vitality. And this medicine is that which can thin and strengthen, and it may purge a little of it, or it may purge a great deal; a little of the bad matter, or a great deal of the bad matter. Regarding decoctions <note>liquid extracts made by boiling</note>, perhaps it does very little. Of this medicine, let a quantity of five drachms of turbith <note>a purgative root</note> be taken—that is, more according to necessity—and scammony properly ground, and let it be prepared with the aforementioned rose-honey and drunk; or let agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note> and scammony be taken according to this composition, prepared with the aforementioned rose-honey, and drunk. Or let it be placed in one ounce of fresh rose juice and drunk with rose syrup.
</margin>

But if you consider these medicines, some elements enter into them that loosen the belly, and some that thin the thick matters, such as celery seeds, turbith, agaric, and scammony. Along with the fact that they purge, they thin the humors. Myrobalans <note>astringent fruit used to balance purgatives</note> and rose-honey, however, "aggregate"—that is, they comfort the limbs with their stypticity <note>the quality of contracting tissues to stop flow</note>. This is what Avicenna intended: these artificially composed medicines can thin the matter and strengthen the limbs, and with this, purge the matter that is difficult to lead out. He says afterward:

<margin>
Recipe.
</margin>

And let it purge a little of it. He wants to make a comparison for you between medicines that receive the physical "bodies" of the drugs and those that receive only the "virtue" and the decoction. Because if you compose a medicine from the physical bodies of the laxatives, then a little of it purges a little, and a lot of it purges a lot of the bad humor. For example, let such a medicine be made: Take one drachm of turbith, six grains of scammony; let them be prepared with rose syrup of fresh roses... [discussion of dosage and effects on the bowels follows]. If you give a little, it purges a little, causing a bowel movement three or four times of thick and bad matter. Such a medicine is one where a little evacuates a little of the evil, and a lot evacuates a lot of the evil. But if you make a decoction from the same laxatives, a little of it does not do that. Hence, a jar of it purges little and will not draw out the matter that is difficult to evacuate; it is known that laxative medicines are not as powerful in a decoction as they are in their substance. Furthermore, a large quantity of decoction is abominable and causes "repletion" <note>over-filling the stomach</note>. From this, Avicenna wants you to know that if you wish to compose a medicine that is both strong and weak—as he said, where a little evacuates a little of the bad, viscous, difficult-to-move humor, and a lot evacuates a lot—you should compose it from the bodies of the medicines and not make a decoction of them. And according to this rule, he composes three medicines from the bodies of the drugs. The first is turbith and scammony (about 52 grains), as this can be one dose; perhaps you need a larger dose, or you might add turbith and decrease the scammony. The second medicine uses agaric and is like the first; these two medicines are most suitable in a non-pure tertian fever that is far removed from a pure one. The third medicine is placed in juice, etc., and that is suitable for a non-pure tertian that is close to a pure one.

<margin>
Avicenna [...]
</margin>

Avicenna, etc. He has placed his discourse on the intermittent and continuous tertian fever; now follows the discourse on "causon" <note>term: <term>causon</term> (from the Greek 'kauma', meaning heat or burning; a highly acute, dangerous fever)</note>, so called from *caumate*, meaning a burning fire. In the first chapter, he first identifies its species; second, its duration; third, the bodies fit and unfit for falling into causon; fourth, he places the saying of Hippocrates. Hippocrates doubts what he says—that causon is made from bile in the veins of the whole body—since he did not say this above when he identified causon. Furthermore, this fever would be continuous. It must be said that when bile abounds and putrefies not only in the veins near the heart but also in those far away, then a person suffers a "burning" properly so called, and it is called causon. This discourse completes the one placed above. But when the bile is in the veins not 

<column-break/>

near the heart, then it is a continuous fever distinct from causon. Galen seems to have known this mode of causon—that is, from bile dominating in the veins of the whole body—in the fourth book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*. It is doubted why causon might not be from bile mixed with a little phlegm, like a non-pure tertian. We say it is made from "false phlegm" <note>original: "phlegmate falso"; phlegm that has become salty or sharp through mixture with bile or heat</note>. It should be said that perhaps it is understood from what has been said: that just as intermittent and continuous tertian fevers can be made from pure and mixed bile, so can causon; specifically from bile mixed with a little phlegm. Or it should be said that causon is named from

<margin>
On the causon fever, which is called *saricos*. Ch. 61.
</margin>

-> <insert>C</insert> <- the burning signified by intense thirst; and this symptom is caused more by false phlegm, and this helps the existence of causon because the movement of phlegm is more uniform and closer to an inseparable continuous fever that has no manifest rest.

<margin>
c
</margin>

Avicenna says there are two modes: either causon is bilious, and the cause in it is a multitude of putrefaction, either within the veins of the whole body, or in the veins following the parts of the heart specifically, or in the veins of the parts of the mouth of the stomach, or in the liver; or it is phlegmatic and arises from false phlegm putrefied in the veins following the heart, as Hippocrates said in the *Epidemics*. And it does not arise from false phlegm, as you know, except from the wateriness of the phlegm with sharp bile. It is therefore bile that putrefies the wateriness mixed with much wateriness. Since causon has more vehement accidents <note>symptoms</note> than tertian, it must be of shorter duration than it. In the elderly, causon fevers rarely occur, and when they do occur, they perish because they do not occur in them except from a very strong cause. Furthermore, their vital powers are weak. In youths and children, they occur most frequently; and in infants, it is milder because of their moisture. And sometimes it is in them with a deep sleep because of the rising of vapors to the head. And Hippocrates said that if a tremor occurs to someone in a causon fever, then a "mental alienation" <note>delirium</note> follows...

<margin>
d
</margin>

It must be considered that he identifies only one species of false phlegm, and from this, causon specifically arises. This is the sharpest false phlegm, which is produced by the paths of putrefaction or "combustion" <note>original: "adustionis"</note> leading to "ashes" remaining in the phlegm itself. Or we shall say that both species of false phlegm are touched upon, and then he explains it with sharp bile—that is, with a sharp humor, whether it be bile or some part of the phlegm that has been burned. He says "from wateriness" because a salty taste arises from a watery liquid mixed with earthy matter, as was declared in the first and second books.

<margin>
e
</margin>

This he says to show that if causon arises from false phlegm, it is primarily through that which includes the power of bile. Whence sharpness comes to that phlegm. He wants to show that it is from false phlegm according to the mixture of bile, not just the putrefaction of phlegm. Therefore he says "bile that putrefies," meaning the bile that is part of the false phlegm... because in quantity, the phlegm wins out, just as in a salty taste, the watery dominates over the bitter.

<margin>
f
</margin>

And the cause is that nature cannot endure strong symptoms for a long time.

<margin>
g
</margin>

What he first says about the elderly is clear from the causes he has given.

<margin>
h
</margin>

Milder in infants. It is argued that it should not be from a strong cause in them since they have a moist complexion. It should be said that if an infant and a youth reached an equal dryness in causon, it would be worse in the infant. Or otherwise: causon is principally a "hot" disease, and an old person resists this more than an infant. Therefore, if it happens in an old person, it is dangerous; if in a child, the infant is apt to be inflamed but their moisture sustains the "blunt" heat. When it is said causon does not occur in infants except from a strong cause, that is false, because causon is not necessarily a dry fever, but a hot one.

<margin>
i
</margin>

Although causon usually causes wakefulness, when it happens to infants (who have much subtle watery moisture), much evaporation ascends to the head, and then sleep occurs.

<margin>
s
</margin>

Hippocrates's Aphorism: "In those whom tremors occur in a causon fever, delirium <note>original: "alienatio"</note> solves it." Galen condemns this aphorism, saying that if the matter that causes the causon (which is in the veins) is sent to the nerves, it causes a tremor, and the brain suffering from this nerve affliction causes delirium. Thus the causon is "dissolved," but this is a worse condition (the tremor and delirium) than the causon itself. But Hippocrates was not accustomed to speak this way regarding the "solution" of illnesses. When Avicenna considered Galen's objection, they did not seem sufficient to him; it seemed to him that Hippocrates's word could be true. He promised to verify this aphorism. One way it is plausible is when the brain and nerves become very hot. Avicenna makes us imagine that with causon there is a tremor—a bad movement of the animal vitality caused by phlegmatic matter. It could be that a person already had this tremor, and through the use of hot things, the matter multiplied into a causon. Or a man with a hot liver but a cold, moist brain gets a causon that melts the moist matters of the brain and makes them flow to the nerves, causing a tremor or even paralysis. When the febrile heat "inflames" the tremor and nerves, it can consume that matter, and thus the tremor is cured. The sign of this cure is delirium, which signifies the brain and nerves are thoroughly heated. Thus Hippocrates's word can be true in a specific possible case.

It features a technical debate between the theories of Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna regarding whether tremors and delirium in such a fever represent a healing "solution" or a worsening of the patient's condition.</summary>

<margin>a</margin> However, that third commentator explains it differently: so that it is said to be similar to how it happens, namely, concerning the resolution <note>original: "solutio"; the breaking or ending of the fever</note> from the source in which there is shivering <note>original: "tremor"</note> and delirium <note>original: "alienatio"</note>: when the brain is heated and the nerves are heated, specifically through the expulsion of bilious matter <note>original: "materie cholerice"</note> to the nerves and the sensory organs, and through the evaporation of bile to the head during such movement. Therefore, Aristoteles <note>marked as 'A.'</note> imagines that the burning fever <term>causon<gloss>an acute, inflammatory fever characterized by intense internal heat and great thirst</gloss></term> is resolved when shivering (that is, rigor) follows, even though delirium also follows; so that delirium alone is not the sign of resolution, but if, once the burning fever is held, shivering follows (that is, rigor) and delirium (that is, even if delirium follows, the burning fever is resolved). Since Galen did not concede this, Hippocrates <note>marked as 'ampho. hypo.'</note> imagined that this delirium results from pure matter remaining around the brain. But Avicenna imagines that the bile is driven to the nerves through the sensory organs, causing shivering (that is, rigor), and when the vapors are moved to the brain by this motion, delirium occurs. When, after this, sweat, vomiting, or diarrhea follows (though sweat follows more frequently), the cure for the burning fever is achieved.

<margin>b</margin> And it is similar. Here he gives the second way of the truth of Aphorism 10, arranging it by transposing the letters. In those for whom delirium occurs in a burning fever, shivering resolves it. And I believe that in their language, the third part could be constructed this way without blame. For among us, this does not sound right unless the parts of the text are transposed. Here, therefore, is what he says: it is similar, as when a burning fever occurs, and thus a confusion of the mind (namely, in him) and it is resolved (namely, the burning fever is cured), and that confusion occurs through shivering (that is, rigor), signifying the expulsion of the matter to the nerves (that is, through the nervous and sensory organs). And this aphorism is the same as that one: "Aristotle says that when shivering follows a burning fever, resolution occurs," except that here delirium is added. That delirium can be simultaneous with the burning fever and not be a sign of the <term>crisis<gloss>the turning point of a disease when the patient either begins to recover or declines</gloss></term>, and the meaning will be: that the burning fever may exist with delirium, yet when shivering follows, resolution occurs. And that delirium can follow with the critical event (namely, with shivering). And we have sometimes seen this. And this is what the second explanation above says. And for the most part, the cause is noted.

<margin>a</margin> namely, the remission of the fever; otherwise, the "hiding of the stages" means it does not have distinct stages; rather, in all its intensity, it seems to be in a steady state <note>original: "status"</note>, as Galen felt. If anyone considers those divided fevers, they have a division like a <term>synocha<gloss>a continuous fever</gloss></term> because it is either uniform, increasing, or intensely increasing; and thus it has a "hiding of stages" because it is either entirely in the steady state, or entirely in decline, or entirely in increase. "Retention of sweat" because the matter is not moved to the outside of the veins as happens in any paroxysm of a <term>tertian fever<gloss>a fever that returns every third day</gloss></term>. And therefore, it is saved for the sweat of a single crisis. Other signs are noted.

<margin>c</margin> **Hippocrates says.** Because someone might say there is intense thirst in a burning fever, he shows how sometimes, by an external means, the thirst is mitigated; and he cites Hippocrates' aphorism from the fourth section: "For those with dry coughs," etc. He posits what Galen seems to say in the commentary on that aphorism: "from the soft flesh," namely from neighboring places; we do not declare this here. Furthermore, he says "small" because a great cough would add to the thirst because of the great commotion. "Accidental," namely from whatever accidental cause, as Galen says in the same place. For if it were a cough that one was previously accustomed to having, perhaps it would not sooth the thirst in this way.

<margin>d</margin> **And the heat.** It should be considered that in an intermittent fever at the time of its peak <note>status</note>, the heat is proportionally stronger in the external parts—that is, it is very strong outside, considering the internal strength. But in a burning fever, the cause is far more internal than external. "Exhaustion," namely a certain lighter weariness because the matter is not around the locations of the muscles, and it is not abundant there, nor heavy. And in the flow of blood—not the critical kind, but the bad kind—it is sharpened and opens the orifices of the veins in the nostrils; and this frequently occurs in others. And "looseness of the belly with pure bile." Dynus says that the bile of a burning fever is not "purer" (meaning less mixed) than the matter of continuous fevers, as he says is Galen's intention in the second book on crises; but he says it is "worse" <note>original: "prauior"</note>—take his words if you please. The bile of a burning fever is more scorched and tends more toward the nature of the element [fire]. "Loss of appetite," namely for food.

<margin>e</margin> **And when.** It is doubted how milk turns sour <note>original: "acetat"</note> in the stomachs of these people. On the contrary, it ought to turn into something smoky <note>original: "fumosum"</note> according to the opinion of the aphorism: "to give milk to those with headaches is bad." Dynus argues that if an infant's stomach is naturally hot, if they have a burning fever, the milk is converted into something smoky; and so it goes for other foods. But if the stomach is naturally cold, even if it becomes hot through the burning fever, the milk is converted into something sour. And he wished, I believe, to make us remember the discourse of Aristotle above in the chapter on barley water: when he said it happens that it turns sour in a stomach that is cold in its substance (that is, naturally), even if there is much external heat in it from the malice of the temperament. For milk in this naturally cold stomach, by the accidentally hot fever, putrefies; because it suffers a lack of natural heat (that is, the digesting heat), since a cold stomach cannot give it perfect digestion. And it has external heat because of the external feverish heat; and therefore milk in these people is converted into vinegar more than if it did not have a hot

<margin>g</margin> "If the cure of a tertian." ¶ First he posits the cure up to the decline. Second, in the decline, there: "And perhaps." ¶ The first rules <note>original: "cañ." for canons</note> extend themselves to the matter and to the fever, and also to some symptom. ¶ The first rule is noted because pure tertian, and properly continuous fever, and burning fever [causon] share [the same treatment].

<margin>h</margin> **And since.** This is the second rule: whether you ought to soothe or to evacuate by loosening because of the fury of the matter, it is better to hasten: because the brevity of the disease does not give you space for completion, because complete evacuation is done when the matter is perfectly digested.

<margin>i</margin> **And not.** The third rule, in which he solves the question of whether bloodletting is appropriate in burning fever: and he wants that if the matter be mixed with blood—the sign of which is that there is turbidity and redness in the urine—bloodletting can be done. But if not, the bloodletting makes the bile rage and will inflame it. And all these rules are built upon general rules.

<margin>k</margin> **Again.** The fourth rule is the rule on the "thinning" <note>subtiliatione</note>, namely of the regimen or the cure. **And since.** The fifth rule is in that [case] in which many things are resolved, such as the porous bilious bodies about which we have made a long discourse in the chapter on the feeding of feverish patients because of the loss of sensation (namely, of the mouth of the stomach), as was said above in the chapter on the cure of bulisimus.

<margin>l</margin> **And needs.** This is the sixth rule, the cause of which is: that in them there is a stronger dryness of the intestines. And therefore you will give the gentlest laxatives you can, and in a larger dose; for example, two ounces of syrup of violets with a little psyllium mucilage and similar things. "According to all species," because you also need a more intense cooling... narrated through the species in the cooling chapter on the regimen of acute [fevers].

<margin>m</margin> **And sometimes.** This is the seventh rule, in which he soothes with tamarinds in the hour of "small warmth"; because in a burning fever there is no manifest warmth but a small warmth, and this without doubt is better: because the medicine is less scorched and soothes more. And consider here that he teaches [the patient] to sleep over the water of the dissolution or decoction of tamarinds, which is a light medicine. And he does this so that agitation does not destroy its power. And we have spoken of sleep over stronger and weaker medicine in the first rule, fen 4. ¶ Also on the third rule, fen 1, the chapter on the general rules of illnesses of the head. ¶ "A little camphor" for cooling, although this camphor causes wakefulness. And although Isaac makes us suspicious of camphor in his book of fevers.

But it is doubted why Galen, in the third book on the *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, in the last commentary, does not allow a bath in a burning fever caused by false phlegm; Avicenna says the opposite. It should be said first, according to Dynus, that a bath is understood as lukewarm, and this is not suitable for false phlegm. But hot above lukewarm, so that the material, which is more difficult to dissolve, does not rot through a lukewarm bath but is dissolved by a hot one, as has already been said about this. Others say that a bath before digestion can be more safely allowed in burning fever if the matter is <term>choleric<gloss>related to yellow bile</gloss></term>, although it is not entirely perfectly digested. But in false phlegm it cannot be allowed. And so Galen seems to understand it in the same place: this will be the opinion: that in choleric matter, although the digestion is not entirely perfect, it can be allowed; but in false phlegm one must wait for the final completion of digestion, and also that much evacuation has preceded, and the matter is very little.

Here is the discussion. In the first part, he assigns two reasons on behalf of Galen as to why a "blood fever" does not come from the putrefaction of blood. First, because when blood putrefies, it becomes <term>cholera<gloss>yellow bile</gloss></term> and is no longer blood. Therefore, a fever from the putrefaction of blood is not "sanguine" but "choleric." And Galen puts forth this reason in his second book *On Crises* and his second book *On the Differences of Fevers*. The second reason is because a blood fever is treated with the cure for choleric fever or the cure for tertian fever—that is, the cure for choleric fevers. And this appears because he does not distinguish fevers of much heat or acute fevers in treatment, but puts them all under the treatment for blood fever, if anyone diligently attends to the sayings of Galen in *Therapeutics to Glaucon*, book 9, and book 1 of the *Therapeutics*. Something must be considered: indeed, almost all commentators, among whom is the Reconciler <note>Peter of Abano</note>, hold that this was never Galen's opinion, but rather the opposite: namely, that a sanguine fever arises from the putrefaction of blood. And this is first because Alcabitius <note>an astrologer/physician</note> following him said this, as did Johannitius. Furthermore, in the 9th book of *Therapeutics*, he places a putrid <term>sinocha<gloss>a continuous fever</gloss></term> from putrid blood, in which a paroxysm has not been made every third day in the form of a choleric fever. And these men say: that when Galen says blood is converted into bile when it putrefies, he understands it as blood constricted in some one place which, because of prohibited transpiration and putrefaction, is converted into bile as far as its subtle part is concerned. <insert>However, if it putrefies in the veins, since it does not have such great compression, it is not so quickly converted into putrefaction; and they say Galen understood this, as did Averroes who also understood this from Galen, as appears in the fourth book of the *Colliget*. <margin>a</margin>
In this, Galen seems to contradict himself. And this is what Averroes courteously brings forward concerning him when he says that Galen's words are varied in this fever. If therefore he does not contradict himself, it is because in certain places he speaks according to his own intention. At other times when he speaks according to a commonly accepted opinion, and thus he is excused from contradiction. But it has seemed to us that when Galen's intention is pushed to the limit, he himself wanted it to be that from putrid blood comes bile and not a sanguine fever. And this is because when blood putrefies, it becomes bile. And that which gives much faith to this is that several illustrious men of the past charge Galen with this, such as Rhazes in the 16th book of the *Continens*, the second chapter at the beginning; and in the fourth book of the *Colliget*, Averroes disproves Galen regarding this; and also in the *Practice of the Canticles*, in the chapter on the cure of cold disease, and it is commentary 68. Also Johannes Damascenus, in the second chapter of *On Consolation*, says: "Galen says regarding blood to which it happens that it putrefies: you ought to know that its subtle part passes into yellow bile and its thick part into melancholy." Averroes, however, if one does not pretend, charges him with this: and beyond this, he makes a contradiction in his own sayings. Alcabitius, however, turning his reins back to Galen, and also Serapio with many others, told the truth in this and omitted to see what Galen might have wanted, lest being forced by the truth they should refute him. Furthermore, in the second book *On the Differences of Fevers*, Avicenna moved that this had been his intention. For in the second chapter he did not enumerate the fever of blood. And in the chapter on <term>emittrittea<gloss>semitertian fever</gloss></term>, Galen concluded the genera of fevers; and never up to that place had he made mention of putrid fever, after he had begun to speak of the species of fevers in the second book. Galen was therefore keeping in mind the desire to give a new opinion on blood fever and therefore returned in the eighth chapter to the investigation of sanguine fever; he says that none was worse—that is, a stronger investigation.

### On Blood Fever. Chapter 44.
<insert>Galen’s opinion was that a sanguine fever does not arise from the putrefaction of blood. For blood, when it putrefies, becomes bile, and is no longer blood. Let there be then a choleric fever, not a sanguine one; and let it be the aforementioned burning fever and tertian fever, and treat it with that cure.</insert>

This discourse of his is contrary to the discourse of Hippocrates and contrary to that which is suitable; and a great part of his error is in his statement that when blood putrefies, it becomes bile. For this statement causes two intentions to be thought of, one of which is that when it putrefies, it reaches the point that after the putrefaction it becomes bile. And the second is that while they are putrefying, then it becomes bile. Just as it is said that wood, when it is heated, becomes ash. Let us consider thus in each of the two propositions. But the first understanding is a distribution of corrupt acceptance. But it would be a wonder if Galen had wanted a sanguine fever to be made while the blood was putrefying: because this would have been a worse and stronger investigation; indeed, it would have been much easier. And therefore Galen proves demonstratively: First, that a fever is made from putrid blood. Second, he proves that we place this fever in a period and in the nature of choleric fevers: because blood, when it putrefies, becomes bile. And the fever consists in the species of humors into which the blood is transmuted. And the examples of the conversions of blood into bile in <term>apostemes<gloss>swells or abscesses</gloss></term> are examples of its conversion into bile wherever it putrefies, whether in apostemes or in the veins. And he wants this in the second book *On Crises* and in the *Therapeutics to Glaucon*, where he blends the cure of continuous fever and the cure of burning fever in one chapter. And Cassius Felix follows Galen in the 9th book of the *Therapeutics*. Either he spoke according to the truth, being forced by it, or according to common opinion. Or we shall say that although Galen posited that a fever from putrid blood was not sanguine but choleric, he nevertheless posited that some of them have manifest exacerbations, and some are closer to being "concluded" and have no manifest exacerbation, as in the second book *On Fevers*. And therefore Galen waited in that case to see if a paroxysm would occur every third day and it would have been a choleric continuous exacerbation. But because that paroxysm did not come, it was not a choleric burning fever, but a <term>peraugmastic<gloss>a fever that continues to increase in intensity</gloss></term> one. Whether it be so or not, let us posit that someone has said this: that from putrid blood a fever is not made in the genus of sanguine but of choleric. And let the reason for the conclusion be this: that blood, when it putrefies, becomes bile and is not blood.
<margin>e</margin>
**This discourse.** First he introduces the authority of Hippocrates, which we do not have manifested, unless he wanted to take this opinion from the end of the first book of *Epidemics*. And some things from the sayings of the fourth book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases* follow. There: "And a great part." Here he first shows that this discourse is contrary to that which is suitable—that is, the truth. Second, that it is contrary to the discourse of Hippocrates. There: "Truly the truth." First he puts the understanding of the proposition upon which Galen's opinion is founded. Second, he follows the refutation of both understandings. There: "But the understanding." It should be considered that he says "a great part of the error" because the root of that error is in that proposition, since it is the foundation of the opinion. And perhaps Avicenna includes other errors in Galen's sayings which he did not explain to us but only mentioned the error that seemed greatest to him. It should be considered that a twofold understanding is known in the example: for if someone were to say wood when it is heated becomes ash, it can only be understood in two ways: either that the measure of heating and incineration is the same, or that incineration is the effect/limit of the heating. In the same way is the understanding of the assumed proposition.

**The Understanding.** First he refutes Galen by understanding his proposition in the first way. Second, by understanding it in the second way. There: "That which indeed." He says first the first understanding is corrupt. And consider that Avicenna does not say the first understanding...

# Book III

<sig>m</sig>

<margin>a</margin>
...to be false. On the contrary, he says that it is of a false or corrupt interpretation. For a proposition under that understanding is true: namely, that blood, after rotting, is or becomes <term>yellow bile<gloss>Latin: cholera</gloss></term>; so that being yellow bile is the end-point of that transformation, just as generation is the end-point of an alteration. Although the proposition is true, it is interpreted "corruptly" because once granted, Galen’s conclusion does not follow. And he proves this by three reasons, always granting the proposition under the stated understanding—indeed, he always places it in a <term>syllogism<gloss>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</gloss></term>. First, he argues thus: When blood putrefies (that is, at the end of the rotting process), it is yellow bile in its thin part and <term>black bile<gloss>Latin: melancolia</gloss></term> in its thick or dense part. Therefore, the whole of the blood does not become, nor is it, yellow bile; and consequently, it should not be called a "choleric fever" any more than a "melancholic" one, as he says later. The consequence is well-known; the <term>antecedent<gloss>the first part of a logical proposition</gloss></term> regarding the first part is Galen’s proposition under the first interpretation. Regarding the other part, the proposition is necessary: because just as the thin part of the blood has become yellow bile at the end of the transformation, so it must necessarily be that the thick part of it has become black bile. <term>It should be considered<gloss>Latin: Considerandum</gloss></term> that Galen anticipated this argument which was to be made against him. But he solves it in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers* and the second book of *On Crisis*, saying that for the conversion of the thin part of the blood into yellow bile, a small transformation is sufficient and it happens easily; but for the conversion of the thick part into black bile, much transformation is required, and it does not happen so quickly. Therefore, when the thin part of the blood has become yellow bile, its thick part has not yet become black bile, but is positioned in a "middle term"—that is, in the middle of the motion from blood into black bile. Galen hints at this secretly in the second book of *On Crisis*, chapter twelve, where, although he had frequently said before that there are three types of fevers and had given the reason that blood, when it rots, does not remain blood but becomes yellow bile. Lest anyone should say it also becomes black bile, he said: "yellow bile is generated when heat overflows in a thing more than is proper." Of black bile, however, he said: "black bile is generated when heat overflows greatly." He wanted to solve this argument more clearly in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers*, where he says: "If indeed it is over-cooked, the thinnest and fatty part of it is transformed into yellow bile; but that which is thicker into black bile, as when coals are ignited." For in both cases, while the blood is boiling, a transition into the melancholic humor occurs; and then Galen shows that this is somewhat of a melancholic humor because it is not *truly* black bile, but is on the way to becoming black bile. This must be understood as a melancholic humor that has not most certainly become black bile, but is positioned in the middle term—that is, in the motion where a middle point is given; for while a mobile object is moved, it is partly in the point from which it starts and partly in the point toward which it goes. But when Galen defends himself thus with the understanding of his own assumed proposition, he binds himself. For once yellow bile is made, either the remaining part is under the form of blood (and thus the fever should be called "sanguine" because that is the humor upon which the transformation, which is rotting, acts), or it is under the form of black bile (and thus he has his second point). And if speculation were to fall here, according to Galen, it would be speculation about the "middle of motion," and it would not help him. And already in our youth, we formed this syllogism of mine in the "first figure" and "second mode" thus: Nothing converted into black bile in one part and yellow bile in another part should be said to be "converted into yellow bile" according to its totality. But all blood after rotting is, according to one part, converted into black bile and, according to another part, into yellow bile. Therefore, no blood should be said to be converted into yellow bile according to its totality. Other masters, however, say Avicenna's reasoning should be solved by the fact that the part of black bile is small; but without doubt, it is not so small that it cannot cause a fever—and it causes none except a melancholic one if it is black bile. Or at least it will be a choleric fever that is not pure, but mixed with black bile, which Galen never intended.

->There are three modes: the first of which is that blood, when it rots, its thin part is converted to bad yellow bile and its thick part to black bile; therefore it does not become yellow bile in its totality. 
And the second is: that this happens *after* rotting, and our consideration is in the state of rotting itself. And the third is: since after that it becomes yellow bile, we do not know whether there is rotting in it or not. For many things rot, and the thin and thick are separated from them; and there is no rotting in the thick, nor in the thin: because it is not necessary that what is generated from something rotten be rotten itself; for there arises from rotting that which is not rotten. And<-

<margin>a</margin>
**And the second.** He shows the second mode of corrupt interpretation. And it is the second argument against Galen, and he argues thus: The conversion of putrefying blood into yellow bile is *after* the rotting. Therefore, a fever from rotten blood is not a choleric fever but a sanguine one. The premise is Galen’s proposition under the first interpretation. The consequence is proved because our consideration, when we say "rotten blood causes fever," is a consideration of blood when it is disposed through rotting, so that rotting is its form. A syllogism can be formed in many ways, but it is formed in the "second figure" thus: Every blood causing fever is in the state of rotting. No blood that has become yellow bile is in the state of rotting; therefore, no blood that has become yellow bile is a blood that causes fever. This syllogism fits the second reason better, but for the third reason, it is more suitable in the first mode of the second figure, thus: No blood that has become yellow bile is in the state of rotting. Every blood causing fever is in the state of rotting. Therefore, no blood causing fever is blood that has become yellow bile.

<margin>b</margin>
**And the third.** He shows the third mode of corrupt interpretation. It is the third argument against Galen. First, he makes the argument; second, he strengthens it. First, he argues thus: Yellow bile generated from the rotting of blood can be non-putrid; therefore, it can cause "non-fever" <note>meaning, a state without fever</note>; and this is against Galen, because that fever will not be choleric. The consequence is well-known. It is proved because from a rotten thing, there do not always result things that are themselves rotten; for neither the thin nor the thick must necessarily be rotten. For non-rotten things are made from rotting. Avicenna wanted us to understand this through the examples of vinegar and worms, which are made from rotting. A syllogism can be formed against Galen in the aforesaid way and another way thus: Nothing generated after rotting is necessarily rotten. All yellow bile generated from the rotting of blood is generated after rotting. Therefore, no such thing is necessarily rotten; and this is in the second mode of the first figure.

<margin>c</margin>
**And if generation.** Avicenna wishes to grant to his adversary that what is generated from rotting is rotten; and then he argues that from this, it follows that a fever from rotten blood would be both choleric and melancholic; and then he concludes, and it is evident. It seems to me that Galen wanted to solve this reason thus: yellow bile which is made from rotten blood is not always rotten, and therefore it does not cause a choleric fever. Therefore, the solution by Galen is nothing, because it follows that a fever from rotten blood is therefore not always choleric.

<margin>d</margin>
**As for what.** Here he proceeds to refute Galen by understanding his proposition in the second sense. This second understanding is: when blood

<column-break/>

rots, it then becomes yellow bile; so that in no measure of time is it true to say "the blood is rotting" for which it is not also true to say "the blood is becoming yellow bile." And he says first that this is a lie, and he introduces three reasons. To understand these, it should be considered that Avicenna presupposes Galen to mean by "yellow bile" the humor which is *actually* yellow bile—that is, having the form and species of yellow bile; so that when we say "while blood rots, it becomes yellow bile," it is understood as actually yellow bile. And that such was Avicenna’s understanding of Galen appears in the third reason. It also appears from the fact that if they understood "while blood rots, it becomes yellow bile" to mean "it is disposed so that it *may* become yellow bile," but it does not yet have the being and form of yellow bile, it would not follow from this that the fever from the blood was choleric—which Galen nevertheless wanted to conclude. Similarly, this would be Galen's first proper understanding, and it would not be a pure lie. Therefore, it must be that the second understanding is such: when blood rots (that is, while it is in the process of becoming rotten), it is *actually* yellow bile; so that there is no time or instant of rotting to be designated in which it is not true to say the blood is yellow bile according to its thin part. This being understood, it is argued thus: that which is on the path to corruption is not yet corrupted; but blood, while it rots, is on the path to corruption; therefore, it is not yet corrupted. And then it is further argued: Blood is not corrupted; therefore, it has not become yellow bile, because the generation of this yellow bile is through the corruption of the blood. He then provides proof for the <term>minor premise<gloss>the second statement in a syllogism</gloss></term> when he says: rotting is on the path to corruption; and this is a well-known proposition. And if you wish to expand on this, consider the words in the fourth book of *Meteorology* and see <term>Trusianus<gloss>Pietro Torrigiano de' Torrigiani, a 14th-century commentator on Galen</gloss></term> in the third treatise of the book *Tegni*, who disputes this.

<margin>If its generation from rotting made its rotting necessary, it would be required that the thick, ash-like part were also rotten. There would then be a melancholic fever there as well; this, therefore, is what makes the explanation necessary: that a broader understanding is reached. And indeed, what is understood in the second place is a lie, since rotting is the path of corruption. And rotting indeed does not have a single moment. And the conversion of blood into yellow bile does not happen except over time. And rotting indeed is a corruption happening to the blood, and it is blood just as it happens to <term>phlegm<gloss>one of the four humors</gloss></term>, and it is phlegm and not yellow bile nor black bile, except when...</margin>

<margin>e</margin>
**And furthermore.** This is the fourth reason, which many people misunderstand. For some believe the text is transposed, and they want to say: rotting does not happen except at a certain time, and the conversion of blood into yellow bile does not have a duration of time but happens in an instant. But this transposition is a corruption of Avicenna's text, because it would not be a different reason in essence from the preceding one. Therefore, Avicenna intends otherwise and argues thus: The conversion of blood into yellow bile happens over time; but the rotting of blood does not happen over time—rather, in an instant. Therefore, the rotting of blood is not the conversion of blood to yellow bile. To understand this reason, it must be considered that generation happens over time, not because time is the true measure of generation (as is transformation in substance, for that happens in an instant), but it is said to happen over time because alteration necessarily precedes generation. And therefore, generation in substance is the end of motion. Whence, in the eighth book of the *Physics*, comment 54, the Commentator says: that generation is either alteration or the end of alteration. Besides this, it should be known: that putrefaction does not have a "starting time," but begins from an "instant in potentiality." And these things must be understood according to the text of the *Physics*. From which it appears that Avicenna argues very well against Galen thus: it was said that while blood rots, it is then yellow bile. But this is false, because it is true to say of blood that it "rots" in an instant, but the conversion into yellow bile does not happen in an instant. On the contrary, time must pass in which this conversion into blood happens. But you will say, I claim that in the first initiating instant of rotting, the blood is yellow bile through some preceding heating before the rotting. It must be said: either all of it is yellow bile (and this is impossible, because then the blood never rots, as it would not be blood before that instant nor after), or some part of the blood in the first initiating instant of rotting has become yellow bile, and then some part becomes yellow bile through rotting *after* that instant; but it does not happen in the first instant after it, because "instants" are not immediate. Therefore, the point follows: because one must grant an initiating instant of the rotting of blood in which the blood is not yellow bile. And if this reason is well considered, the first one stands as a dividing path thus: For when it is said that "when blood rots, it becomes yellow bile," then it has the being of yellow bile. Either putrefaction is taken for the whole disposition up to the first instant of the generated being of yellow bile, or it is taken for the first instant of rotting; and in this way, let it be granted that in motion, there is a first "changed-being," at least in potentiality. If indeed rotting is taken for the whole disposition up to the final "having-been-rotted," which is the beginning of the "having-been-generated" as yellow bile, then Galen’s proposition is false: because blood, while it is on the path of corruption, is not yet corrupted; but while it is in "rotting" as a disposition, it is then on the path of corruption. Therefore, it is not corrupted, and consequently, it has not become yellow bile. If, however, rotting is taken for the first instant of the initiation of rotting—before which instant there was no rotting—then Galen’s proposition is false: because for blood to become yellow bile, time is necessarily required; but for rotting to have that initiating being, time is not required, because as such, rotting does not have a duration of time. Therefore, at that moment, the rotten blood is not yellow bile. Thus, this reason is more elegant and effective. For the proposition about which there was no small doubt was granted by the adversary—namely, that putrefaction does not have time—and it is argued by the second reason. Or it was denied, and then it is argued by the first reason. And many years after the first explanation was made, we found that <term>the Saint<gloss>likely referring to Thomas Aquinas or another high authority</gloss></term> understood this passage just as we have said. But you might say Galen could argue that "putrefaction" is taken for "having been putrefied," which is the first "having been incinerated," which is also the first "having been generated" as yellow bile. It must be said that those first three reasons proceed in that way: because that is the first understanding of the proposition against which Avicenna has already argued, if you consider it. Or it must be said that then Avicenna argues thus: The conversion of blood into yellow bile happens over time; therefore, that "having been putrefied" state was preceded by some disposition in time. But that was rotting, which is in the time before the final instant of "having been putrefied"; therefore, the prior time before that instant was a fever, and yet it was not yellow bile. And in this way, it could be formed...

<meta>This page continues a dense scholastic debate regarding the nature of fevers, specifically focusing on whether a fever caused by "corrupt blood" should be classified as a blood fever or a bile-based fever. It moves from logical proofs into a reconciliation of the views of Galen and Avicenna, eventually categorizing different types of continuous fevers.</meta>

# Or Treatise II

...sea: the second reasoning is this. And rotting. This is the third or second reasoning. And he argues thus: As it stands with the rotting of the <term>phlegmatic humor<gloss>phlegm</gloss></term>, so it stands with the rotting of the blood. But when phlegm rots, it remains phlegm and is not <term>yellow bile<gloss>Latin: cholera</gloss></term> nor <term>black bile<gloss>Latin: melancholia</gloss></term>, except when it has been converted by the completion of the rotting process. Therefore, when blood rots, it is not bile, but blood. Some unrefined thinkers wish to solve this reasoning by denying the similarity because phlegm is a humor unfit for transformation into bile, whereas blood is fit. But this contributes nothing to Avicenna’s reasoning; for it is concluded that for a certain measure of time after the blood has become rotten, it is not yet bile. This suffices to show that the proposition "blood while rotting is bile" is false. It is not only enough to disprove it by saying there is some span of time in which blood is rotten but not yet bile, but even that there is a single instant, as the preceding reasoning shows; and this is sufficient for Avicenna. However, if you wish to dispute with him and speak of bile created *from* rotting *after* the rotting has occurred, then turn to his arguments against the first interpretation of Galen’s proposition, which is why these reasonings proceed.

> ...it may be converted after that with the completion 
> of the rotting. ¶ **Again**, the truth 
> is healthy as the word of **Hippocrates**, that 
> rotten bloods generate fevers. ¶ **Let us** 
> **say** therefore now that the fever of blood

<margin>a</margin> ¶ **Again, etc.** A fever is generated—specifically a blood-based one, not a choleric one. But then it is doubted whether there is a way of harmony between Galen and Avicenna on this question. And I say that although <note>Thaddaeus Alderotti (c. 1210–1295), a famous medical professor at Bologna.</note> Thaddaeus, in his commentary on <note>The Isagoge of Johannitius, a standard introductory medical text.</note> Johannitius, took a middle path between these men, they can nonetheless be reconciled. For this reason, it should be considered that Galen’s discourse on fever from rotten blood places it in the genus of choleric fevers; it is a fever from blood in which rotting happens due to an excessive amount of "suffocation" <note>This refers to internal heat being trapped or "choked" by blockages.</note>. When this rotting happens to it, the fever, when considered according to the judgment of a **natural philosopher**, is called a blood fever from rotten blood and is not called choleric. This is the path Avicenna followed. Hence, all these propositions by which he argues belong to the natural philosopher. It appears that Avicenna is content to hold against Galen that in the very first instant of the initiation of rotting, there is rotting in the blood, and yet it has not yet become bile. Whether this is an instant or an imperceptible measure of time is something a physician does not consider. Galen, however, considers the defect of the fever according to the judgment of a **physician** working toward the cure of fevers; he says this fever from rotten blood is "choleric." Hence, it is most often found to have an analogy to the fits of a <term>tertian fever<gloss>a fever that spikes every third day, typically associated with yellow bile</gloss></term>. The reason is that the aforementioned blood has much of an "oily" quality. Therefore, when rotting begins in it, it immediately declines toward a choleric nature, so that although one might grant a certain measure of time in which no part of that blood has been made into bile, that time is very brief and not considered by the physician. Therefore, because rotten blood, almost from the very beginning of its rotting, associates with itself hot, boiling, and evil bile—granting it might not be *truly* rotten—it is nonetheless evil and inflamed. Therefore, this blood fever ought to be called "choleric" in this way; and this does not happen in other fevers. For when <term>black bile<gloss>melancholia</gloss></term> or phlegm becomes rotten, it does not immediately associate with itself bile through the rotting of a part of those humors. Therefore, those can be called purely phlegmatic or melancholic fevers. But a fever from rotten blood can be called a choleric fever right from the start, and it must even be cured by that same treatment—using <term>alteratives<gloss>medicines that change the condition of the humors</gloss></term> and evacuatives—to reduce the sharpness of the bile. Therefore, <note>Avenzoar (Ibn Zuhr), a famous 12th-century Andalusian physician.</note> Avenzoar, in the chapter on blood fever, advises giving some medicine that evacuates bile before performing <term>phlebotomy<gloss>bloodletting</gloss></term>. And without a doubt, if I see that the bile has multiplied before the bloodletting, it is necessary to do what Avenzoar commands. But if it is not much multiplied, or is still in the blood, one must begin with bloodletting. In this way, therefore, these two men can be reconciled.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ **Let us say therefore.** After Galen's opinion, he places his own judgment. And first, he divides the blood fever into its primary species; second, he compares those to other fevers; third, he gives its causes; fourth, he gives its two species; fifth, he gives the <term>crisis<gloss>the turning point of a disease</gloss></term> and symptoms of the blood fever. In the first part, he presents this division of blood fever: one kind is "putrid" (from rotting) and another is not; the latter is a fever only of heating and boiling, and it is without rotting. This is called a <term>synocha<gloss>original: "sinocha", a continuous fever</gloss></term> without rotting. And he says that Hippocrates gave it the name "concluded" <note>Latin: "conclusam".</note>, applying this name and no other. For this "synocha" is the same as a fever from non-putrefied blood. But if the term synocha means "from putrefied blood," as <note>Simon of Genoa, a 13th-century medical lexicographer.</note> Simon of Genoa says, "concluded" means a cause that is uniform in its motion, having no <term>exacerbations<gloss>sudden worsenings</gloss></term> such as other fevers have. Now, a synochus with rotting of the blood can have "efforts" <note>spikes or surges</note> as said above. It should be considered that this whole discourse can be referred to both types of synocha, namely with and without rotting, because both are continuous and "concluded" without other fevers; and this applies properly to them and not to other fevers. Here another doubt might arise: whether a fever could be made from a humor other than blood through heating alone without rotting; we have noted this at length in the second book on the *Differences of Fevers*.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ **And the greatest part.** In this part, he gives certain causes for the boiling of the blood, such as "oppilation" (blockage), etc., because this prohibits evacuation, leading to inflammation. It appears that a "suffocating oppilation"—that is, one that prohibits evacuation—can be the cause of boiling with or without putrefaction, depending on the diversity of bodies and the order of events. For first it causes only boiling, and then rotting may follow, although such an order is not always necessary. For a "putrid synocha" can occur without being preceded by a synocha without rotting. Consider this.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ **And sometimes it happens from other causes.** Such as anger, labor, and other heating causes. Considering the disposition of the spirits as greater, the disposition of the blood 

<column-break/>

follows. I say a general disposition. The causes that inflame the blood must be more vehement than the causes that produce an ephemeral fever—namely, those that inflame the <term>spirit<gloss>the vital breath or pneuma</gloss></term>. And this is what he says: "Which become vehement above the vehemence of an ephemeral fever," meaning above the strength of the causes that produce an ephemeral fever.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ **And it is named deep sleep.** Many names are found among the authors for this fever; but the "depth of sleep" occurs in it because many humid vapors rise to the head. And a synocha without rotting happens more often when its vapors are mild. "Strong," namely of sleep, is the same as "deep sleep." And this strength also arises from the blockage of the "subetic" veins <note>A medieval term likely referring to the jugular or carotid vessels.</note>.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ **And it is.** He compares the fever: first, the synocha without rotting to other fevers; second, the synocha with rotting. It should be considered that Avicenna hints that this fever has the nature of a "middle" through negation. For since it is not an ephemeral fever—because the first thing heated in an ephemeral fever is the spirit, but in a synocha without rotting it is a humor—similarly, it is not a putrid fever because in putrid fevers the humor is rotten, but in this fever, the blood is not rotten. From this, it appears that this fever is a "middle" through participation; for it participates in the nature of ephemeral fevers in that it is a kind of simple heat in the vapors of the blood, but it participates in the nature of putrid fevers in that it resides in the humors. All these things were understood by Galen in the ninth book of the *Therapeutics*.

> ...the first thing heated in it is the 
> humor; and it differs from the fevers of 
> rotting because it has no rotting, and 
> it is an acute fever and not an ephemeral 
> fever, nor a <term>hectic fever<gloss>a fever of the solid parts of the body</gloss></term>, nor 
> a fever of rotting. ¶ **And many times** 
> indeed it changes into a fever of 
> rotting or a hectic fever. ¶ **And** 
> **many times** indeed **Galen** makes it 
> run the course of "day fevers." ¶ **And**

> is common to every humor; and in

<margin>g</margin> ¶ **And it is an acute fever.** As if to say, although it agrees with the ephemeral, it is nonetheless "acute," meaning it is vehement—one in which there is fear due to the speed of the outcome. But an ephemeral fever is not acute, even though it is short, as held above in the third chapter. These things are understood from the end of the book *On Crises*.

<margin>h</margin> ¶ **Nor hectic.** This is clear. And since it is not putrid, it can change into a putrid fever; and although it is not hectic, it can nonetheless change into a hectic fever or a hectic fever can follow it. All these things are known.

<margin>i</margin> ¶ **And many times, etc.** Galen, in the ninth book of the *Therapeutics* and the eighth book of the *Course of Day Fevers*, places it among the ephemeral fevers.

<margin>k</margin> ¶ **And it seems.** I do not find this statement in Galen unless Avicenna took it from the second book of the *Differences of Fevers*, where he said that the fever in rotten blood is "simpler" than those in other humors. And perhaps when translated into the Arabic language, that discourse signified this; but our commentators commonly explain "simpler" as "milder." What we understand of that text, we omit here. It is doubted how it follows that "rotting of the blood is common to every humor; therefore the blood fever is not composed with other fevers." ¶ **It must be said** that blood can be putrefied sometimes through the dominance of black bile in it (and this because the blood is converted to cold and dry) or phlegm (because it is converted to cold and moist). According to this, there are three fevers of the blood. Avenzoar deduces these in the commentary on the *Practice of Canons*. In this way, the rotting of blood can be said to be "common to every humor" by way of alteration, because it can be converted now to the nature of one, now to the nature of another. According to this, when the rotting of the blood is in the blood of the whole body or the great vessels, it makes a simple fever, not composed with another fever from that same blood, because it is impossible for the whole blood to decline except toward one <term>complexion<gloss>the balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry)</gloss></term> or combination of qualities—namely, toward the dominance of one humor. For if the whole declines toward the cold and dry of black bile, it is impossible that the whole should decline toward the hot and dry or cold and moist. Perhaps Avicenna understood Galen in this way. But then Avicenna rebukes Galen because there is a contradiction in this. For Avicenna will say that in the veins, along with the blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm can be found in addition to those into which the blood declines through its own <term>distemperance<gloss>imbalance</gloss></term>. And then a phlegmatic-blood fever could occur because the blood declines toward the cold and moist, and with this, a choleric or melancholic fever could arise from those humors found mixed with the blood, as Galen understands in the *Book of Elements*. Avicenna will also say that a fever from melancholic blood can be composed with a fever from the black bile into which that melancholic blood has been transmuted: so that there will be one fever from the melancholic blood while it remains in the form of blood, and another fever from the melancholic humor into which that blood has been transmuted. It appears, then, how Galen’s consequence is deduced and how it is attacked by assuming rotting happens through the blood’s decline into the matter of some humor. In another way, blood can rot from a fault of quantity alone. And when blood in the veins rots from quantity alone, then a fever from it cannot be composed with another fever; for in such blood, every humor is contained in "power" and rots, and none is contained in "act"—that is, before the rotting. For then it would not have been a fault of quantity alone, but of quality, due to the fault of another humor mixed with it. From these things it appears that by understanding Galen thus, he meant that in the veins with the blood, no humor exists "in act." And if any is there, immediately the blood is said to be faulty in quality. From this, it is taken that a fever with blood is not composed with another fever—namely, one made from a humor that had previously been with the blood before the rotting. But this contradicts certain of Galen’s sayings in the *Book of Elements*, where he grants that other distinct humors exist with the blood. This is the more common opinion of physicians, though the philosophers' opinion is different and perhaps more true. And then he says he does not wish to prolong the discourse because the physician is not helped by it—that is, there is no utility in prolonging the speech. Alternatively, a better explanation is that the physician is not helped by the fundamental point of this controversy: whether distinct humors exist in the veins in their own form, or whether all are under the form of blood and are only discovered by separation from it. However, <note>Peter of Abano (1250–1316), known as "The Conciliator" for his attempts to reconcile Greek, Arabic, and Latin medical traditions.</note> the Conciliator, in Difference 90, assigns this contradiction in Galen’s sayings differently. For first, Galen says in the book *On the Differences of Fevers* that this blood fever is "simpler"—that is, not able to be composed with another fever. Galen says the opposite of this in the penultimate chapter of the same book, where he says: "If indeed it becomes weak at some point, and this power is the cause, not only of superfluity, but the blood itself is also corrupted and rots and causes a fever." If the predicted heat is still preserved, there are two species of fevers complicated with each other. The Conciliator believes this contradiction resolves itself because a putrid fever from blood *inside the veins* is not composed with another fever.
