# BOOK I

And this is what he says first: that the fever itself is simpler; but it is easily combined with another fever when the blood rots within an <term>aposteme<gloss>an internal swelling or abscess</gloss></term>; and he states this second. We have already disputed this question and written against him, where we held that a fever from rotten blood, called <term>sinocha</term> <note>original: "sinocha" - a continuous fever thought to be caused by an excess or corruption of blood</note>, can be combined with other types of "rotten" fevers, even though its own heat might overshadow the heat of the others, as Isaac says in section 5. And if anyone carefully considers the true text of Galen in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers*, he will understand well, as we explained in that place; here we omit those details.

<margin>n</margin> **And the cause.** Here he places the causes that Galen lists in the ninth book of *The Method of Medicine*. And he says that the cause is <term>repletion<gloss>an overabundance of humors</gloss></term>, specifically <term>plethora</term> and <term>oppilation<gloss>a blockage or "plugging up" of the vessels</gloss></term>. This prevents <term>transpiration<gloss>the release of vapors through the skin</gloss></term>, which leads to inflammation. Because it prevents the exit of vapors, it causes a multiplication—that is, a lack of reduction—in the blood. Exercise also inflames and expands the matter that fills the body; these are the common causes of both types of *sinocha*.

<margin>a</margin> **And the cause** of this fever is indeed repletion, blockage, a high amount of exercise, the sudden stopping of customary exercise or evacuation, and then the performance of laborious exercise. And sometimes the wateriness of the blood causes a great deal of rotting due to the mixing of watery fruits; for this reason, it turns to rot. A high amount of <term>crude humor<gloss>undigested or "raw" fluids</gloss></term> in the blood is also a nearby cause, as it prepares the blood for rotting—such as that generated from eating cucumbers, <term>wild melons<gloss>original: alcethed</gloss></term>, pears, and similar things. This fever is continuous and does not remit because of the "commonality" of its matter <note>meaning it affects the blood throughout the entire venous system</note> and its persistence until either a crisis or death. Its species are: the <term>epaugmasticus<gloss>a fever that is gradually decreasing</gloss></term>, which is the safest, because the resolution of the matter is greater than the rotting that began with difficulty and does not stop diminishing. Next is the <term>homotenus<gloss>an "equal" fever</gloss></term>, which perhaps remains the same for seven days. The worst of these is the <term>augmasticus<gloss>an increasing fever</gloss></term>, because the resolution of matter in it is less than the rotting. Its <term>crisis<gloss>the turning point of the disease</gloss></term> usually occurs by the seventh day, and its resolution comes with an evacuation that is either felt or unfelt by the patient. Sometimes it changes into a <term>burning fever<gloss>original: causonidem</gloss></term> or into <term>brain inflammation<gloss>original: sirsen</gloss></term>. Occasionally, with excessive cooling, it changes into <term>lethargy<gloss>a coma-like state</gloss></term>, and sometimes it changes into <term>smallpox<gloss>variola</gloss></term> and <term>measles<gloss>morbillum</gloss></term>. Sometimes there occurs in it a profound sleep and a bloating of the belly which sounds like a drum <note>tympanites</note>, and a loosening of the bowels does not relieve it. When the loosening of the bowels is not effective, and then a wide, green stool <note>original: asafuiridis</note> is passed, this is specifically a sign of death.

<margin>b</margin> **And sometimes.** The difference between the wateriness of the blood and a crude humor (that is, crude phlegm) is well known. The "nearby" cause of rotting is that when blood is indisposed, it causes blockage.

<margin>c</margin> **And its indeed.** It must be considered that the "commonality of matter" means it is shared among all the veins; blood creates such a repletion. The cause of this, as Dynus assigns it, is that the multiplication of blood—which keeps the nature of blood—follows the general property of blood. But such multiplication is common to all veins because blood is a balanced humor. Therefore, its multiplication does not follow the distemper of a specific organ (as other humors do, which exist in states of imbalance); thus, the multiplication of blood follows the multiplication of the matter that holds the form of blood. From this, it appears that the rotting of blood is common to all veins. However, if a fault occurs in the blood by itself and not as a result of overall multiplication, this only happens through a fault in a specific organ that multiplies a humor other than blood within the blood; then it becomes a <term>periodic fever<gloss>a fever that comes and goes in cycles, like malaria</gloss></term>. We, however, in the general science of humors, have already spoken against Dynus, saying that the multiplication of true blood can happen from an "agent" (like a hot and moist liver) and from "matter" (like blood-producing foods), just as the multiplication of phlegm happens from an agent (like a cold and moist liver) and phlegmatic foods. Furthermore, even if we grant what Dynus says, the objection remains: why does the blood, even when filling all the veins or principal matters, not have rotting phases according to periods, where the unnatural heat occupies one part of the blood at one time and another part at another? Let us therefore propose three points. First: just as phlegm has the property of being collected every day to cause a fever, and bile every third day, so blood has the property of making a fever continuous until recovery or death. Hence it is said below by A. <note>likely Avicenna</note> that every humor has a "period" that suits it. The second proposition is that this continuity is helped by the sheer volume of blood in all the veins. Because of its volume in the whole body and its fitness for heat, the whole is inflamed. There is no sensible part that is expected to be gathered or activated to be heated again; but in bile, phlegm, or melancholy, the whole does not rot at once, but only a part; as that part is resolved, it is possible for another part to be gathered again. And because this cause is not entirely sufficient without the first, A. immediately added: "and its adherence," etc. It is as if he said: a blood fever is not periodic because blood is a matter common to all veins. The sign of this is that it is not periodic, but a uniform continuous fever until the crisis—that is, until recovery or death. The third proposition is that it is not impossible for a fever with a period to be made from blood. The reason is that blood can be gathered and rot within the veins or outside the veins. Therefore, a blood fever *can* be periodic; the conclusion is clear. The premise is proven because every day or every third day, or according to some other period, the body can emit a certain quantity of blood through the nose or the belly. Therefore, if blood is retained in the veins or pushed outside the veins and corrupted, it can cause a fever. It appears from what has been said that an "interpolated" (periodic) fever can be made from blood when the matter is outside the veins. For blood can be pushed outside the veins in a certain measure of time against nature. The reason is: to whatever part of the body blood can be pushed naturally, it can be pushed unnaturally. Since it can be pushed gradually to places outside the veins by turning into fluids, it can also be pushed there non-gradually due to certain causes. Hence, a man has been seen who sweated blood in his sweat. However, it should be considered that these modes of blood are perhaps not as "true" as the blood that is multiplied in the whole body, from which the true continuous blood fever (sinocha) arises. And without doubt, it is so in most cases. With blood abounding in the whole body, it is imaginable that nature might overcome it and expel one pound today and another tomorrow; thus it is imaginable that today one pound is retained (not evacuated) and rots, and is resolved before another pound rots. In these sayings, we wish to satisfy the question of whether a blood fever is periodic; we have spoken at length about this in the book *On the Differences of Fevers*.

<margin>d</margin> **And its species.** It should be considered that here we accept the three famous species of *sinocha*. Although Avicenna and Al-Zahrawi adapt these to a *sinocha* involving rot, they can also be adapted to a *sinocha* without rot, as understood from Galen’s ninth book of *The Method of Medicine*. Second, consider that although in a "peraugmastic" (declining) fever only the decline is apparent, all four stages of the disease <note>onset, increase, peak, and decline</note> are present but hidden; and the same is true for the other species. First, there is a doubt about the cause given by Avicenna. For if the amount of vapor being resolved is more than what is being elevated by rotting, then the fever should stop. We have given two other solutions elsewhere, which are essentially one. The first is that the quantity of vapor reaching the heart is twofold: one by which the vapor causes fever (and if there is a decrease from this, no fever will occur); the other is that by which the vapor causes a fever that can become smaller or larger. Comparison is made to this quantity: if the resolving vapor is less than that which begins the fever, the fever proceeds by diminishing; if it is less [than the resolution], it 

<column-break/>

proceeds by increasing; if equal, it will stay the same. The second solution is that the quantity of blood vapor causing the fever has a "latitude" (a range), such that both a smaller and larger amount can cause the fever. When the fever begins from a vapor of a certain quantity, if a smaller vapor follows because more is being resolved than before, it becomes "epaugmastic" (declining). If a larger vapor follows, it is "augmastic" (increasing). But you might say: suppose a fever starts from a vapor so small that nothing smaller could cause a fever, and then the succeeding vapor is even smaller; then this fever would have nothing but an onset. It must be said that in such a case, this follows necessarily; and we sometimes see in men certain sudden heats that recede immediately. If they persisted, they would be a true and manifest fever. We could expand on many things here. A second doubt is why paroxysms <note>fits or peaks of fever</note> having these three differences do not occur with humors other than blood. The cause of this doubt is that a tertian fever or its paroxysms are similar to a single *sinocha* fever. Why then, when bile is rotting, can it not be said that in one body the quantity of vapor is greater than what is resolved, in another smaller, and in another equal? Then one paroxysm of a tertian fever would be "augmastic," another "epaugmastic," and another "homotenus." It must be said that in a blood fever, since its matter is common and there is no specific "suffering place" in the veins, the multitude of vapors immediately seeks the heart. From this multitude, in the first part of time, there can be a decrease, an addition, or equality; these are the three species of *sinocha*. But in periodic (interpolated) fevers, because the humor has a specific place, it begins with a "typus" <note>the periodic pattern</note> and small evaporation due to the "suffocation" of the heat. Afterward, the heat rises and spreads through the matter, and a greater evaporation occurs until the heat is equally expanded, after which it ends. Therefore, in every such paroxysm, the four stages are manifest and distinct. To the contrary, it must be said that the reasoning only argues that one paroxysm of a tertian fever can be greater in its "increase" compared to another tertian paroxysm; in one the "status" (peak) will be greater, and in another the "declination." But despite this, the other stages are clearly manifest. And what we have said of the tertian fever, we say also of phlegm and melancholy.

<margin>e</margin> **The worst of them is the augmastic.** It should be considered that a fever can proceed with an increase over the quantity of the "equal" (homotenus) heat, and this is worse, as is well known. It can also proceed by increasing toward the quantity of the equal fever, and this is less bad than the equal fever; although if one considers the cause—which is more rotting and evaporation than resolution—the "augmastic" (increasing) can absolutely be called worse than the others.

<margin>f</margin> **Crisis at the seventh.** There is a doubt because a continuous tertian fever ends on the seventh day, while the periodic (interpolated) one ends at the seventh paroxysm, as Galen says in his commentary on "The true tertian," etc., and in the third book of *Prognostics*. Therefore, since blood fever is from thicker matter, it should have a later ending. It must be said that since blood fever can be "peracute" (very sharp/fast), it can end at the seventh day; even on the fourth, as per Galen's third book *On Crises*. To the reasoning, it should be said that although blood is thicker, a blood fever can reach the same level of sharpness as a bilious fever.

<margin>g</margin> **Its consumption.** It should be considered that he did not say it is consumed by digestion alone, as the commentator [Averroes] wished in the third tract of the *Regimen*; Galen seems to feel this at the end of the book *On the Differences of Fevers*, and we wrote about this in our question on the "times of disease."

<margin>a</margin> **They are changed to burning fever.** This is because of the "burning" and the conversion into bile, which, if it abscesses the brain, will cause *sirsen* (phrenitis). However, with cooling—such as by drinking cold water or cold compresses—the blood, turned to the likeness of phlegm and squeezed into the brain, can abscess and cause lethargy. Other things are well known: what he says about the greatness and depth of sleep. He says afterward that in a blood fever "tympanites" (drum-like bloating) may occur, which is not stopped by a flow of the belly or by "resolving" (that is, resolving plasters applied around the belly). If it appears with green spots (measles), it is a sign of death. The reason is that the aforementioned condition signifies a failure of natural heat; thus there is evaporation without resolution, and a continuous regeneration of windiness occurs. Green measles signifies matter turned to a poisonous nature. Its "width" signifies the subversion of the matter and a failure of the body's power to push it outward.

<margin>b</margin> **Signs.** First, he lists its signs. Second, signs of its change (permutation). Third, signs of its prolongation. Specifically, "Signs of permutation," then the third, "Signs of length." The first part can be divided into as many parts as there are signs: "Complete repletion" (common to the whole body) without shivering, because the matter is between the veins and is hot and moist. There is no sweat—that is, not every day or every other day as in paroxysmal fevers—but it occurs at the crisis on the critical day. "Itching in the evil" occurs for one who is accustomed to bleeding from the nose, and similarly for one accustomed to "cupping" at the site where the cups are placed. "Constriction of breath" comes from the great filling of the deep veins. Hence, one must suspect <term>apoplexy<gloss>a sudden loss of consciousness or "stroke"</gloss></term> in them, which comes from the blockage of those veins, as Hippocrates says in the fourth book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, and Avicenna in the third book. Therefore he says: "it is an evil; an abscess of the throat," etc. These things are from the great repletion in the veins around [the neck]...

<summary>This page analyzes the causes and classifications of blood-based fevers (sinocha), debating whether they can follow periodic cycles and describing dangerous complications like brain inflammation, lethargy, and drum-like abdominal bloating.</summary>

II
Tractate

<margin>
a Regarding the epiglottis <note>original: "epiglottis"</note>: that is, around the windpipe and the tongue. The flow of tears is caused by an abundance of blood around the eyes, through the mouth, or from the tear ducts; we have examined these modes subtly in our commentary on the third book. Its heat is very great because it has dried in much vapor rising from a "warm pool"—therefore he called it "lacunal" <note>original: "lacunale," referring to a hollow or pool</note> or otherwise "lachrymal" <note>original: "lachrymale," relating to tears</note>, meaning it is prone to large, dark tears. While the patient's <term>vital power<gloss>virtus; the body's innate ability to function and heal</gloss></term> is still strong, the obedience of the bodily instruments is a necessity, though not with excessive variation. Why is the <term>yellow bile<gloss>cholera</gloss></term> less burdensome than the blood? It must be said that <term>burning fever<gloss>causon</gloss></term> and a strong <term>tertian fever<gloss>a fever recurring every third day, associated with yellow bile</gloss></term> have greater malice and greater heat at their peak than the heat of a blood-based fever. Therefore, although the pulse should be less varied in burning fever due to the thinness of the matter, it is actually more varied because the malice of the heat casts down the pulse's strength more. We spoke of this above in the chapter on tertian fever.
</margin>

### On the signs. Chapter 45

<margin>
b And this: first, he places the signs of a <term>putrid sanguine fever<gloss>a fever where the excess blood has begun to "rot" or decompose</gloss></term>, adding notes on the thickness and likeness of the blood. Second, he discusses the non-putrid type, adding something about the putrid. There, he notes that putrid *sinocha* is more "causal" <note>original: "causalis"</note> compared to other putrid fevers. But compared to "fervid" *sinocha* (the non-putrid kind), it is not causal; rather, the blood recedes from its natural state through putrefaction, and the fever returns to an inequality of heat—specifically, a stinging or "gnawing" sensation <note>original: "mordacitatem"</note> and the manner of a specific fever-cycle or period.
</margin>

The signs of a sanguine fever are the persistence of the fever, redness of the face and eyes, and a swelling of the veins in the temples. There is a complete <term>repletion<gloss>an overfilling of the vessels with blood</gloss></term> without shivering, and there is no sweat except during the <term>crisis<gloss>the critical turning point of the disease</gloss></term>. Often, it is accompanied by itching in the nose and in the area of the neck where <term>cupping glasses<gloss>ventose</gloss></term> are placed. There is a constriction of the breath, and frequently these patients fall into a deep sleep and have difficulty speaking; this is a bad sign. Similarly, an <term>aposteme<gloss>an internal swelling or abscess</gloss></term> of the throat, or of one or both tonsils, and a flow of tears are signs. Its heat is very high due to the vaporous and tear-like moisture that has not been dried out as it is in burning fevers. Its pulse is large, light, full, fast, and very frequent; it is varied, but not excessively so. It is less varied and fast than in a burning fever. Its heat does not reach the peak of a burning fever or a strong tertian fever, nor that <margin>b</margin> which comes from putridity; in those cases, the symptoms are more violent, the cure more difficult, and they are more similar to burning fever. Indeed, the thinness or thickness of the blood may be known by this <margin>c</margin> and what comes out of it. Fervid *sinocha* is more like an <term>ephemeral fever<gloss>a one-day fever caused by external factors like heat or exhaustion</gloss></term> in its beginning, but its heat has a small stinging and harmful quality, causing inflammation and a sense of distance; its greatest effect is felt near the heart. The putrid type is steady and remains the same according to many. The signs of it changing into something else are those of whatever it turns into, such as suffocation or abscesses of the throat and tonsils—you already know these. You will also know the signs of smallpox, the signs of <term>phrenitis<gloss>sirsen; inflammation of the brain</gloss></term>, headache, mental confusion, and others you have already learned.

<margin>
c The signs are clear. You already know the signs of duration from the chapter on recognizing the hours. Regarding <term>digestion<gloss>the process of the body "cooking" or maturing the harmful humors</gloss></term>: it is slow, and if it appears late, the illness is longer. Regarding "turnability": if it is slow, it signifies a long illness; if fast, a short one. The "diversity of disposition" refers to the variation in the mode of heat over its duration—that is, the time it lasts. If it is an "additive" *sinocha*, like the <term>angmatic<gloss>a specific sub-type of continuous fever</gloss></term>, the heat does not increase uniformly but sluggishly. At its "station" (peak), if it is "homotene" <note>original: "homotena," a fever that maintains a constant level</note>, it does not stay uniformly. In its "diminution" (decline), it does not decline uniformly; rather, it proceeds lukewarmly or sluggishly through these stages. This whole discussion could refer to a single fever that proceeds unevenly with lukewarm heat throughout its duration, so that one sees it increase, then stand still, then decline, and it varies in whatever way it is understood. This diversity signifies that the blood is <term>crude<gloss>undigested or raw humors</gloss></term> and the duration is clear. Regarding signs from the urine: he does not list a third, because the urine is simply red. For more on thickness and thinness, see Serapion in the 6th book of *Practica*, and Rhazes in the 4th book of *Almansor*, etc.
</margin>

The signs of its duration, as you have already learned, come from the delay of the signs of digestion and the "turning" of the face, and the variation of its state during its course—during its increase, its peak, and its decline—so that it seems as if the fever itself is lukewarm. For this signifies that the blood is full of raw hu-

<column-break/>

-mors <margin>e Here he first sets out the cure for these objectives up until the decline. Then he discusses the decline at the end. The first part has four points. First, he sets out the cure by evacuation. Second, by thickening and thinning the blood. Third, by cooling. Fourth, by cleansing. He omits the cure by "binding," which is understood through thickening and thinning. For when the blood is corrected in its substance with things that have properties against putrefaction, it then digests. The cure through "resolution"—the opening of the pores and perspiration—is also known from many things said in the chapter on ephemeral fevers and the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers in general. The first section has three parts: first, he shows the most suitable evacuation; second, he shows the evacuation that must be done before this; third, he shows what must be done if the aforementioned evacuations cannot be performed. Consider that he prescribes three things. 1. That bloodletting be done from the hand in the arm. From which vein you should know from the chapter on bloodletting, provided one does not wait for the peak strength; this was declared above in the general cure of putrid fevers. 2. "Unless there is repletion," etc., lest undigested and corrupt matter be carried to the veins. Note that if you perform bloodletting, remove the excess first. 3. That you bleed until "syncope" (fainting). It is doubted whether bloodletting should occur after the start of a sanguine fever. Albucasis <note>original: "Azarauium"</note> seems to say no in this chapter, where he says: if he was deprived of bloodletting at the beginning, let him be entirely careful about drawing it during the increase of the sickness, except at its peak, and if the man is strong. And he says this is similar to the case of *sinocha* without putrefaction. The same seems to be the view of Isaac in the chapter on *sinocha* with putrefaction. On the contrary, Galen says that if the fever persists, etc. It must be said with Galen that in *sinocha*, if the strength is preserved, one should bleed not only during the first seven days but also on the following days, such as the 9th and 10th. The reason is that evacuation opposes repletion. Albucasis is to be wondered at, though perhaps for his own reasons. We must say that in the later course, we cannot perform such a copious bloodletting as in the beginning, as we declared above; and this is what Albucasis means.</margin>. The timing of its crisis is signaled by the appearance of the signs of digestion; if these are delayed until after the third and fourth day, there will be no crisis on the seventh. And indeed, the crisis often occurs on the fourth day.

### On the cure of sanguine fever. Chapter 46.

<margin>
d The intention in the treatment, etc. First, he sets out the intentions of the treatment. Second, he executes them. Third, he lists the foods. Fourth, he does not neglect the cure of the symptoms. Consider that these intentions are seven. 1. Evacuation. 2. Correction of the substance of the blood (thickening or thinning). 3. Cooling. 4. Cleansing. 5. Digestion. 6. Resolution. Evacuation and resolution differ: evacuation is the manifest drawing out through bloodletting, but resolution is specifically the drawing out of vapors. Regarding digestion and substance correction: this is understood from the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers. Then they return specifically to the correction of the humor and the prevention of putrefaction; thus, it is opposed to putrefaction. But thinning and thickening are specifically opposed to the state of the humors. Therefore, thinning is a specific intention in putrid *sinocha*. The intention of thinning and thickening is common to all *sinocha*. Evacuation and cleansing also differ: evacuation is specifically of the offending humor which is the cause of the sickness; cleansing is of another added or joined humor. Thus, when the bile into which part of the blood has turned, or other associated matter, is drawn out, it is called "cleansing of the blood." Consider that these intentions arise from the matter in the state of sanguine fever. They are always in it. 1. Repletion, which is opposed by evacuation. 2. The thickness or thinness of the overabundant blood, which is opposed by equalization through thickening or thinning. 3. Heat in the limbs, which is the fever or the blood, opposed by cooling. 4. Humidity or corrupt matters that infect the blood, opposed by cleansing. 5. The rotting blood, opposed by digestion. 6. The multitude of vapors and the blockage of retained things, opposed by resolution, which also includes the opening of blockages.
</margin>

The intention in the treatment of a sanguine fever is the evacuation of most of the blood, even unto <term>syncope<gloss>fainting</gloss></term>, and the thickening of the substance of the blood if it is very thin, watery, and choleric. Also, its cooling and cleansing; and the thinning of it if it is too thick, or if the patient previously took things that generate thick blood or raw humors; and the digestion of the matter causing the fever and its resolution. There is no evacuation like bloodletting from the hand, regardless of the hour it happens. One does not wait for the crisis or digestion unless there is a nauseating repletion—in that case, be careful and remove it first. If the fever persists, then perform bloodletting, and do not stop bleeding until the patient approaches fainting or falls into a faint, if the body is strong. For fainting cools a strong <term>complexion<gloss>the balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a person</gloss></term>. <margin>f Sincopis. He brings three reasons from Galen's 9th book of *The Method*. 1. Sudden bloodletting until fainting sometimes removes the fever by extinguishing the strong febrile heat. Therefore, it is suitable for a strong complexion, i.e., a man strong in power.</margin> And know that bloodletting and taking cold water to drink sometimes excuse the need for other cooling. <margin>g And know that bloodletting. The second reason: this bloodletting and the drinking of cold water excuse other cures. Therefore, it should be done, because providing the drink of water and other cooling while a superfluous repletion remains is not safe.</margin> And indeed, dividing the bloodletting into parts is better if there is no necessity for haste; <margin>h And dividing. Because he made us sure about bloodletting, he now says it is more convenient to divide this bloodletting into several sessions, as it is safer for the patient's strength and can suffice for the cure.</margin> for perhaps in that division there will be the approach of fainting and the finality <margin>i If there is no necessity. This could refer to a superfluous, suffocating repletion that cannot be helped by a divided bloodletting, but only by a copious bloodletting leading to fainting. Here, Albucasis might include a reason proving that one must sometimes bleed unto fainting: for a suffocating repletion can sometimes occur in *sinocha* where death is feared unless there is a copious bloodletting; therefore, such a bleeding must be done.</margin>. And perhaps the final bloodletting will be followed immediately by a choleric flux of the belly and sweat, which must be wiped away every hour until it stops, for perhaps the patient will be saved by it <margin>k And perhaps. This is the third or fourth reason why evacuation should be done: because nature, being strengthened, expels the bad matters and the residue through its proper channels. Thus the sick person is healed; when bloodletting is done unto fainting, this occurs. Therefore, one must believe the cited authors, Galen and Avicenna, regarding these evacuations.</margin>. And let the resulting weakness and fainting be helped with light food and rest. <margin>l And let it be helped. Here he removes an objection that might be made. Someone might say that fainting is a bad accident which we should not cause. He responds that such fainting is mild and is removed by light food and rest. By "light food," understand food of quick penetration and digestion, the strength of which is of the degree you see fit—such as wine, <term>julep<gloss>a sweet medicinal drink</gloss></term>, pomegranate juice, or meat broth.</margin> And it is necessary that the softening of the bowels be done first with those things that are known, such as the water of two pomegranates (namely the sweet and the <term>moxi<gloss>a sour or bitter variety</gloss></term>) until the end, and <term>syracost<gloss>a medicinal syrup</gloss></term>, and tamarinds, and light <term>collyria<gloss>medicated washes or suppositories</gloss></term> of which we have spoken. <margin>m And it is necessary. Consider that the corrupt matters which are associated with sanguine fever...</margin> And sometimes it is necessary, upon digestion, to evacuate with things like <term>myrobalans<gloss>dried, plum-like medicinal fruits</gloss></term>, <term>fumitory<gloss>fumi terre; a bitter herb</gloss></term>, <term>cassia<gloss>casiafistula; a mild laxative</gloss></term>, and similar things.

Book III

<margin>
The humors <note>original: "guinee," likely a transcription error for "humores" or "materiae"</note> are sometimes located around the regions of the stomach and intestines, and around the <term>mesaraic veins<gloss>the veins draining the intestines</gloss></term>; in such cases, nature is softened with those things he mentioned before bloodletting, so that the matter is not drawn back into the veins. It is possible that the bile from a clyster <note>an enema</note> sometimes causes a suffocating effect in the veins; once these are digested, they can be evacuated. This is done after bloodletting. If it must happen before bloodletting, it should be done until the "neutral point"—that is, until the flavor is no longer passing into sweetness—or until the proper quantity is reached, such as a dose of four or six ounces, or until a determined time, so that this cleansing is not delayed too much.
</margin>

<margin>
**a** Regarding the disposition: it may be that a vein cannot be found in the arm, or the physician does not wish it—for instance, if it seems to you that the patient’s strength is insufficient for bloodletting. If bloodletting from the arm is not permitted, yet required, it can be performed from the forehead, as noted in the third book of the *Canon* <note>referring to Avicenna's Canon of Medicine</note> in the chapter on frenzy. If none of these can be prepared because of complications, one must rely on nature; if the patient's strength is lacking, then use gentle means, such as with tamarinds, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
**b** And the regimen, etc. This concerns the pores: use proper rubbing or syrups made with water after bloodletting, such as simple acetous syrup, or with endive, maidenhair fern, or if helpful, with fennel and parsley roots.
</margin>

<margin>
**c** And if the physician doubts why nature prohibits fainting during a natural flow of blood, yet does not prohibit it during bloodletting: he says that in a natural flow, fainting does not occur unless the evacuation is extremely excessive, since nature chooses what to evacuate. But in the medical art, it can happen with even a smaller evacuation.
</margin>

<margin>
**d** Truly the blood: here he places the cure by thickening the blood if it is too thin; he also implies that thinning should occur if it is too thick.
</margin>

<margin>
**e** Regarding the cooling: He places the cure through cooling, according to the *Canon*. What he says first is known from the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers in general. The intent in curing a sanguine fever is cooling with rose <term>troches<gloss>medicinal lozenges</gloss></term>, especially during the decline of the fever after evacuations have been made. This was the practice of the ancients, such as Rhazes in the 17th book of the *Continens*. I do not know the moderns' view, but it should be done with the "solemnity of nature"—since its dryness prohibits barley water, as explained above in the chapter on barley water. Otherwise, if the belly is not soft, the dryness of the belly may be relieved by washing and cleansing with barley water. Thus, barley water is conceded even when the belly is dry, provided it is thin and cold.
</margin>

<margin>
**f** And know: here he references Galen's *Therapeutics*, book 9, regarding the remaining disposition—that is, the later stage—until another putrid disposition is acquired from the first.
</margin>

<margin>
**g** Cleansing: here he treats the cure through cleansing. Since in a continuous fever the humor polluting the blood is mostly bile, in which the blood’s oiliness is easily drawn, he manages the evacuation of the bile. If it becomes impure through undigested matter, he orders it to be digested. Sometimes it is enough that the raw blood can be brought back to a good state through digestion, and thus evacuation is not required. And as he said, let the bile be evacuated and the raw humor be digested. He also understood that it should be cleared of whatever matter makes it impure.
</margin>

<margin>
**h** And at its end: he places the cure in the "declination" <note>the final stage of a fever</note> by removing the residue of heat and strengthening the limbs that were dissolved and weakened. These are the well-known troches.
</margin>

<margin>
**i** Truly the book. Blessed herb: that is, purslane. Other things are well-known. It is doubted whether bloodletting should be performed until fainting in a continuous fever. Rhazes says in the 17th book of the *Continens* that it is a mark of great wisdom not to withdraw blood suddenly until fainting, but to draw it in two parts: half the first time and half the second. Averroes proves this in the 7th book of the *Colliget*, where he argues against Galen. First: bloodletting to the point of fainting is not a "skillful" evacuation because art imitates nature, and nature never performs a healthy evacuation that leads to fainting. Rather, this happens in "bad crises" where the body expels more than is convenient. Second: the goal of evacuation is to remove the superfluous while preserving the natural quantity; fainting diminishes the natural quantity. Third: cooling through fainting is "accidental medicine" and is dangerous. Fourth: it is better for a little foreign heat to remain than for the natural heat to be diminished. Fifth: in a body with this fever, there is a heat whose separation leads to rot. Therefore, bloodletting to fainting should not be done.
</margin>

from those things you have learned. If the patient's condition does not tolerate bloodletting from the arm, let the vein in the corner of the forehead be bled, or let cupping glasses be applied. If none of these can be prepared due to some complication, then provide a loosening of the belly in the manner used for <term>burning fever<gloss>causon</gloss></term>. Let the regimen consist of those things that open the pores, cut through thick humors, and settle the boiling of the blood. And if fainting occurs from the bloodletting, feed them with bread and <term>verjuice<gloss>sour grape juice; "aqua acreste"</gloss></term>. If a natural flow of blood occurs on its own, it should not be stopped unless fainting is imminent. For thickening the blood, use things like "rob" of jujubes <note>a thickened fruit juice or syrup</note>; this is made by boiling jujubes in five pounds of water until a third remains, then thickening it with sugar—the less sugar used, the better. Lentils prepared with strong vinegar are also of this kind. But beware of giving the syrup of jujubes or the body of the lentils if the matter is already thick. Cooling is achieved with things like cooled water of gentle herbs, cooled lettuce water, or by drinking cold water if nothing prohibits it; perhaps it is drunk until it causes shivering, for this may occasionally heal him. Sometimes the fever changes to a phlegmatic type and is cured with rose troches and the like. This indeed is the cure of some of the ancients, and some of the moderns have followed it. Giving barley water to drink is a helpful treatment, but only when the belly is soft. The best time for this is during the hour of intense boiling, distress, inflammation, and frequent pulse.

And know that being content with cooling alone while neglecting bloodletting and loosening the belly increases blockages and tightness. Therefore, rot and heat are added to the remaining disposition. Cleansing

<column-break/>

<margin>
By bloodletting to fainting, the natural heat is diminished and the strength is weakened, causing the humors to become corrupted, and there will be nothing to correct this. To the contrary is Galen in his *Therapeutics*, book 9. Many have tried to reconcile Averroes and Galen. Some say Averroes prohibits fainting that is "irrecoverable," while Galen allows "recoverable" fainting; this is a crude argument. Others say Averroes forbids bloodletting to the point of fainting inclusive, while Galen orders it exclusive. This is also crude. Whoever wishes to reconcile these men should take the words of Avicenna when he said: "Partitioning the dose is better." And let him say that when the fever is present, if it is not necessary to act in haste, then partitioning the bloodletting is better. But if it is necessary to act quickly, then it may be done until fainting, if other factors allow. Galen saw two men die from fainting during bloodletting because he did not consider what was necessary. We have already written much on this. Let us say briefly that Avicenna wished to agree with Galen, but he believed the best physicians who preceded him in the art were Albucasis <note>Azarauius</note> and Avenzoar. These two men are against Averroes on this point, especially Avenzoar. Furthermore, it is more fitting to avoid a greater danger with a lesser one. By bloodletting to fainting, we avoid the greater danger of death; once the "danger" of fainting has occurred, a man is revived by splashing cold water on his face and thin food. The death we avoid is sometimes by suffocation, and sometimes the death that comes in bad crises. For by bloodletting to fainting, a continuous fever without rot is sometimes removed. If you bleed less, the fever remains and can become putrid, in which case one must wait for digestion and "critical movements," which could lead to death. Furthermore, in the other view, there is no less fear than in the evacuation, as Averroes understands. But the ultimate change, like ultimate cooling, kills, just as cold water can change a state to static coldness. Therefore, he can concede the ultimate evacuation. It is doubted whether in a fever with rot, bloodletting should ever be done to fainting. It must be said that we bleed less in a putrid fever—drawing a smaller quantity—because the strength is weaker and the blood is not so fit for evacuation, since the fever cannot cease through this bloodletting; the rot cannot suddenly cease as it can in a fever without rot. We preserve the strength for the remaining crises. To Rhazes, it must be said that he does not deny that bloodletting, but says it is a matter of wisdom to know where it should and should not be done. To Averroes' first reason: art imitates nature sometimes, and sometimes supplies its defects, as seen in the amputation of flesh. As Averroes experienced in himself when he became gouty. To the second reason: in evacuation, one preserves the natural quantity as much as possible; Averroes even concedes giving <term>colocynth<gloss>a powerful purgative</gloss></term> with which such preservation of "spirits" is impossible. To the third: Averroes does not deny accidental benefits, like the benefit of scammony in a tertian fever. To the fourth: the proposition is false, because a defect of natural heat can be immediately corrected with white wine or other gentle things after fainting, but a residual fever forces one to wait for crises. To the fifth: Galen says those humors are expelled by vomiting or sweating once the strength is relieved. These are two new reasons why you argued against that opinion: first, no one is recorded as dying when bled without fainting, while some are recorded as dying from it; I speak of the sanguine fever. Therefore, all dangers of abscesses and suffocation can be avoided by repeated bloodletting without fainting.
</margin>

should be done with things that dissolve bile according to the requirements of the patient's strength and weakness, because perhaps the bile itself is the cause of the blood's putrefaction. At the end of the fever, give him drinks such as camphor troches and spodium troches. These troches are also good: **k.** <note>Recipe</note> Spodium, 3 drams; purslane seed, 5 drams; cucumber seed, 4 drams; gourd seed, 6 drams; gum tragacanth and starch, 3 drams each; licorice juice, 7 drams' weight. Let them be made into troches.

Another description, especially for weakness of the liver: **k.** Roses, 3 drams; barberry juice, 2 drams; cucumber, melon, citron, and purslane seeds, and spodium, 1 dram's weight each; gum, tragacanth, and starch, 0.5 drams each; rhubarb, saffron, and camphor, a quarter of a dram each. Let troches be made. For food, use those made from jujubes and lentils with vinegar, pomegranate, and sumac. If there is fear of constipation from these, break it with <term>syracost<gloss>a digestive syrup</gloss></term>, prunes, gourd, or sorrel. For fruit, use Damascene pears, pomegranates, and Damascene apples. For vegetables: cucumbers, gourds, spinach <note>alkebetbed</note>, endive, purslane <note>bolus benedictum</note>, sorrel, coriander, and similar things. If headache, heart palpitations, sleeplessness, deep sleep, or excessive nosebleeds occur—which destroy the strength—or other complications, treat them as we have taught you in their proper place.

### On Phlegmatic Fever. Chapter 47.

The "leuiti" <note>likely a specific type of mild fever</note> and the fever of putrefied phlegm is sometimes paroxysmal <note>recurring in fits</note> and sometimes inseparable <note>continuous</note>. You have learned the cause of this. It has its hours like other fevers, and the shortest of its starting periods is usually 18 days.

<margin>
**k** Final note: He places the bilious and sanguine fevers first, followed by the "static" fevers—first in general, then specifically, then he provides the cure.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature and duration of fevers, specifically transitioning from general continuous fevers to the classification and symptoms of phlegmatic fevers (those caused by an excess of the humor phlegm). It references common medieval authorities such as Avicenna, Galen, and Rhazes.</meta>

Fen 1 1 Treatise II

<margin>a</margin> In that first part, he first provides a general division of phlegmatic fevers: whether a phlegmatic fever is periodic <note>original: "porisalis," likely a corruption of "periodica"</note> or continuous. The cause of this was explained above in the chapter on the causes of putrefaction. Here he indicates the cause in terms of time; he intends that its universal beginning lasts, for the most part, 18 days and recedes within a light period—otherwise 53 days. <margin>b</margin> It is doubted because if the beginning lasts 18 days, then the beginning is the longest part of the phlegmatic fever. For if the remainder is divided into three parts according to the three stages after the beginning, each would be smaller; the opposite of this is stated by Avicenna when he says that the longest part is the increase <term>augmentum<gloss>the stage where the fever's intensity grows</gloss></term>. <margin>c</margin> It must be said that the "beginning" spoken of here in phlegmatic fever is long because the cold and viscous humor delays the "kindling" <note>the onset of the fever's heat</note> and the opening of maturation. But that this length is exactly 18 days cannot be proven; it stands by experience and the testimony of the author without doubt. Therefore, in phlegmatic fevers, both continuous and intermittent, "rawness" <note>original: "cruditas," referring to undigested humors</note> persists in the urine for a long time before the truth of digestion <note>signs that the body is processing the humor</note> appears, and thus the beginning is long. To the contrary, he first says that by "beginning" we do not mean the beginning properly distinguished from the whole increase, but that which concludes the part of the increase—namely, up to the appearance of manifest signs of digestion. If these begin to appear at 18 or 15 days, the end will be around 40 or 44 days according to general discourses. If we follow the commentary on the *Aphorisms* <note>of Hippocrates</note>, part 7, where it is terminated, etc. However, to Thaddeus <note>Thaddeus Alderotti, a famous 13th-century physician</note> it seemed that the text should say: Eradication is within 60 days because phlegmatic fever is chronic, and the limit of chronic illnesses is beyond 44 days, extending to 60. And because perhaps this is a true statement for intermittent phlegmatic fever, but in continuous fever it can terminate in 44 days or less; for when you weigh all these statements, they are matters of judgment. In a second way, it can be said that here he means the universal beginning, but in the following passage he means the particular increase. <margin>d</margin> Or we say the reasoning does not conclude if we hold to the text that says "light days," for if the beginning occupies 18 days, the increase can occupy 22, and the remaining time is divided into the peak <term>status<gloss>the plateau of the fever</gloss></term> and the decline, assigning for example 8 days to the peak and 16 to the decline, which in total are 60. Or by dividing otherwise as it appears to you, so that it falls on 59.

<margin>a</margin> And safer. Here thirdly he shows that the phlegmatic fever is "safer" when it is of "clean times"—that is, those that have clearer intervals. Since a phlegmatic fever never fully recedes, it always has some smoky vapor of putrefaction <note>original: "effumationem"</note> during its hour of rest, just like the burning of green wood; thus, the one that is cleaner is safer, signifying phlegm that is less raw and less viscous. That much sweat signifies the subtlety <note>thinness</note> of the matter and the porosity of the body is well known. But it does not seem to signify a small amount of matter; rather, much sweat signifies much matter. <margin>b</margin> We say that the cleansing of the fever signifies little matter; sweat signifies much matter—that is, it is being made less. Or it should be said that it signifies little in respect to much, because the humor, by weighing down the virtue <note>the body's natural power</note>, prevents sweating. Consider that Thaddeus said "of clean times," meaning distinct and not confused with one another; and this is praised because it signifies uniform matter.

<margin>b</margin> Longer. He infers from this that he understands the matter of this fever to be thick, viscous, raw, and slow in kindling. Therefore it follows that the increase of the periodic fever is slightly longer than the decline, and it is much longer than the decline of a tertian fever <note>a fever that peaks every third day, usually caused by yellow bile</note>. And this is noted. And we have already prolonged the discourse on this above in the chapter on the things by which certain putrid fevers differ, etc.

<margin>c</margin> For the most part. i.e., in most cases. <margin>d</margin> For a certain tertian fever can have a longer decline than a certain phlegmatic one.

<margin>d</margin> And phlegm. Here fourthly he shows the types of phlegm from which this fever arises. It is doubted because besides these there is raw phlegm, mucilaginous phlegm, tasteless phlegm, likewise watery, harsh <term>ponticum<gloss>astringent or sour like unripe fruit</gloss></term>, and "gypsous" <note>plaster-like or chalky</note> phlegm. <margin>e</margin> We say gypsous phlegm does not cause fever. Raw and mucilaginous can be understood as "glassy" phlegm <note>original: "vitreu," thick and transparent like molten glass</note>, but tasteless and watery are comprised under "sweet" phlegm, and harsh under "vinegary" <term>acetofum<gloss>acidic or sour</gloss></term>. And you should return to the science of principles for this.

<margin>e</margin> And mostly. Here fifthly he shows the bodies fit for this fever; they are those in whom phlegm multiplies. Whence Galen in *Therapeutics to Glaucon*: "I have not seen a choleric youth" <note>meaning one dominated by yellow bile</note> with this. You should return to the science of principles for this.

<margin>f</margin> And little. It can become a [text unclear] for the reason stated: that the stomach is the mine of phlegm; therefore, phlegmatic fever harms the stomach, just as tertian harms the gall and liver, and quartan harms the spleen. As Rhazes says in the 7th book of the *Continens*.

<margin>g</margin> And know. He wishes therefore from this chapter that since in phlegmatic fever there is cold, the pulse is restricted in one dimension and small in all, following the words of [text unclear] in the book on the *Distinction of Pulses*. However, it can be explained otherwise. And you should consider this.

<column-break/>

<margin>b</margin> and its eradication in most cases is within 60 days. <margin>a</margin> And the safer of them is that which is of clean times: and especially that which has much sweat; for it signifies the subtlety of the matter and its small amount and the porosity of the body. <margin>b</margin> The longer of the parts of this sickness is the increase, although its decline is generally longer than the decline of a tertian fever. <margin>d</margin> And indeed putrid phlegm is sometimes "glassy": and sometimes "vinegary": and sometimes it is sweet and sometimes it is salty, and you already know how a burning fever <term>causon<gloss>a high, acute fever</gloss></term> arises from salty phlegm. <margin>e</margin> And this phlegmatic fever mostly happens to those of moisture and rest: and to the elderly and infants: and to those suffering from nauseating satiety <note>overeating to the point of sickness</note>: and those exercising and bathing after repletion <note>eating a full meal</note>: and those having vinegary evacuation and those having repletion and those suffering from a descent of humor: and catarrh occurs to the stomach which putrefies in it. <margin>f</margin> And there is little evacuation from the lesion in the mouth of the stomach. <margin>g</margin> And know <margin>h</margin> that with every fever with which there is cold, the pulse is constricted and diminished.

<margin>l</margin> With the return of cold. Because after the heat begins to appear and is believed to proceed to the increase, the cold returns again. And this is because of the diversity of the parts of the matter moved to putrefaction.

<margin>m</margin> And perhaps rigor is mixed with the cold. i.e., shivering <term>horripilatio<gloss>the sensation of hair standing on end</gloss></term> as appears from the following discourse.

<margin>n</margin> And greater, etc. The reason is that then the matter is more refined <note>original: "subtiliata"</note> and therefore moved more strongly. And this is the cause of a greater type <note>of shivering</note>. As in the 3rd book of *Accident and Disease* and above; and it appears why he said cold and rigor. For cold either follows the quality of the matter—and this is not the case here, that it should be greater in the peak, when the matter is more heated by digestion and putrefaction—or it follows the movement of heat to the inside. And this happens more in the peak, because the matter is moved more suddenly. And therefore it more suddenly induces a bad sensation. Whence the heat is moved more inside. And he speaks of this cold. Rigor indeed is taken either for a shaking or for shivering. And both happen more in the peak: because from the sudden movement a greater shaking or some shaking can follow, if there was none before, but only a small cold. And from the sharpness of putrefaction some shivering can follow, or a greater shivering. Dino <note>Dino del Garbo, another medieval medical commentator</note> labors in vain when he asks whether a daily fever begins with shivering, and whether it begins with rigor. These words are very equivocal, as we declared above in their own chapter. Understand therefore the nature of the type which the matter produced: and call that rigor or cold or shivering. And this appears because Avicenna immediately said that rigor in glassy phlegm is more vehement: and immediately states that phlegmatic fever does not cause rigor. Therefore these questions and contradictions are of words, if you have understood those things we wrote above in the chapter on these types.

<margin>o</margin> And this. Here he puts many signs of phlegmatic fever, whether it be from glassy or raw or mucilaginous or natural phlegm. This discourse is widely applied. <margin>q</margin> Secondly, he first says the cause he proposes is clear.

<margin>p</margin> Or by heaviness. i.e., of the members, depth, etc.

<margin>q</margin> By depth, etc. i.e., heavy, deep sleep because of many cold and moist vapors seeking the head.

<margin>r</margin> It begins more mildly. Because in the first paroxysms <note>original: "prmorū," for "primorum"</note> the matter is sometimes sweeter and lightly moved, and therefore there will be neither cold nor rigor, i.e., no shaking movement.

<margin>s</margin> It is postponed until the time. Because in later paroxysms, such as those of the increase or peak, there could be cold and rigor.

<margin>t</margin> And perhaps there will be cold and not rigor. This can be understood of the first paroxysms in which it is possible that there is pure cold and not the shaking movement which he calls rigor; and this because the matter is carried slowly. It can also be understood of the later ones, as if he wished to say that sometimes the first paroxysms are not with cold, nor even with shaking: and later paroxysms happen with cold, though it may not happen with shaking; even these things can occur as is clear.

<margin>u</margin> And many times it begins with syncope <note>fainting</note> and it is not—namely, the syncope is not completed, or it does not happen in all, but it happens in many. The cause why it happens many times in this fever is noted.

<margin>x</margin> That one. Clear.

<margin>y</margin> The other. The cause is what he immediately puts: because putrefaction begins from the sweeter part.

<margin>z</margin> And most. Here he puts signs of phlegmatic fever absolutely or common signs. And it has 7 parts according to the 7 orders or sums of signs which he puts. The first sign is in the timing of the syncope. And as it appears, the second is taken from the manner of the heat. And it has parts, just as the modes of signs are from heat. This second part is an aggregation of signs from the manner of heat. And its first sign is this: that in the beginning of the paroxysm the heat is more vehement, and in the later ones the heat is less; he gives a likely cause for this. It must first be considered that although the discourse can refer to the heat in a single paroxysm, if one considers it subtly, it is more aptly referred to the heat of the first paroxysms compared to the heat of the later paroxysms. # Book III

...for those in whom the heat is less: it is neither determined nor can it be limited. This is because the heat depends on the quantity of the matter—whether it is sweeter <note>In medieval medicine, "sweet" phlegm was considered more liable to transform or putrefy than "natural" or "salty" phlegm.</note>, thinner, thicker, or colder—and these various quantities differ from person to person. Consider second: that this statement is true regarding fever attacks <term>paroxysms<gloss>the periodic spikes in fever intensity</gloss></term> that have a preceding cause—a single accumulation of matter sufficient for several attacks. In such a case, the more mobile part of that accumulation will move first: namely, the sweeter, saltier, or thinner part. For this reason, the first fever attacks will have greater heat. Later, however, the thicker part will move, which is slower to stir; thus, the later attacks have less heat. Indeed, when the attacks are not caused by the original accumulation of matter, but by matter newly generated from scratch, the heat of the attack will be whatever the newly generated matter produces. This matter did not exist before, neither as an antecedent cause nor a conjoined one—I speak here of the cause in the form of a <term>humor<gloss>one of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that governed health</gloss></term>, which was already present as a cause related to the body's complexion.

It is questioned why this statement seems to contradict what was said above in the chapter on tertian fever <note>A fever that spikes every third day, usually associated with yellow bile.</note>. There, it was stated—following the opinion of the commentator on the first book of *Epidemics* <note>Referring to Galen's commentary on Hippocrates.</note>—that in fevers arising from cold matter, the peak attacks are made of thinner matter and are more active because of this. Consequently, the shivering fits <term>rigors<gloss>violent shaking or chills preceding the heat of a fever</gloss></term> in the peak of a quartan fever <note>A fever that spikes every fourth day, associated with black bile/melancholy.</note> will be stronger. Conversely, in tertian fever, Avicenna says here that the matter causing the later attacks is thicker phlegm. Therefore, the solution is this: because this caused me some distress before I moved on, I have omitted many of my other solutions to provide these.

First, I offer one: the thicker matter moved in later attacks is thicker in its substance when compared to the sweet part moved earlier; yet, despite this, it is "thinner" due to <term>digestion<gloss>the process by which the body's internal heat "cooks" or ripens a raw humor so it can be expelled</gloss></term>. Because it is more digested, it is thinner than that "thin" part moved in the first attack. Conversely, the thinner matter that caused the first attacks, although thinner in substance, is "rawer" <note>original: "crudior," meaning undigested or unprepared by the body's heat</note> despite that thinness. It follows from this that the thinner, rawer matter moves more sluggishly, while the thicker, more digested matter in the peak attacks moves more strongly and swiftly. You should consider this based on the principle given in the question regarding the "stages of disease." Alternatively, it can be said that these attacks—whether from sweeter or thicker matter—are common at the beginning or around the start of the illness. Thirdly, it can be said that the statement of the commentator on *Epidemics* and Avicenna above is verified when dealing with a single type of matter, and not when the matters are diverse, as is the case in this true discourse.

...that is settled. And it is similar in that the cause is this: because putrefaction <note>The breakdown of humors that leads to fever.</note> reaches the sweeter matter first, then the saltier and thinner, and finally the thicker and colder. 

The heat felt by touch is weak and "vapory" at first; then, when the hand is held on the limb for a long time, the hand feels sharpness and a biting sensation <note>original: "mordicationem," a stinging heat often associated with putrid humors</note>. <margin>a</margin> However, it is not similar or equal in all parts upon which the hand falls; rather, it is diverse, for in one place it finds a certain roughness, <margin>c</margin> and in another place smoothness. <margin>d</margin> It is like the heat of <term>cholera<gloss>yellow bile</gloss></term> after it has passed through a sieve <note>original: "cribellatam"</note>; because phlegm is viscous, its effect is diversified by heat, just as happens with other viscous things when they boil: they break apart in some places and do not break apart in others. Whatever its heat may be, it is mostly too small to cause a flaming inflammation or great distress; <margin>e</margin> it is greatly relieved by cold air and cold water, <margin>f</margin> by thickening <margin>g</margin> and thinning, <margin>h</margin> and by deep breathing and exhaling. Often <margin>i</margin> it happens that its heat settles for a period of one or two hours; because of this, it is thought to have reached its peak when it is actually still increasing.

<margin>a</margin> **And touch.** This is the second sign based on the type of heat, the cause of which is the thickness of the vapor. Thus, it does not penetrate immediately.

<margin>b</margin> **However.** This is the third sign from the type of heat. It is a statement from Galen's book *On the Differences of Fevers*, chapter 10 or 12.

<margin>c</margin> **Roughness.** That is, a harsh heat in the place where it shows itself—for example, in the holes of a sieve.

<margin>d</margin> **Smoothness.** That is, a mild, agreeable heat in another place—for example, on the solid part of the sieve.

<margin>e</margin> **Whatever it may be.** This is the fourth sign: as if to say, whether it is this way or not. For it is possible it might not be so. Although the parts of viscous phlegm may differ in evaporation, these vapors coming toward the skin can be dispersed uniformly regardless. However, phlegmatic heat does not reach the point of inflammation and restlessness from a strong burning. This is what he means by saying it is "mostly smaller"; though sometimes, from strong putrefaction, it can cause an inflammation close to that of bilious fevers.

<margin>f</margin> **And thickening.** Specifically, of the breath.

<margin>g</margin> **And thinning.** Specifically, of the breath, because it does not necessitate frequent exhaling of the breath as a bilious fever does. In bilious fever, frequent exhalation is appropriate; here it is rare, interrupted by fatigue, or the thickening and thinning of the skin due to uncovering the blankets. Those with a strong fever heat, as in a tertian fever, uncover themselves, and then the pores thicken and they are greatly distressed; then they cover themselves again so the pores thin, and they remain in that state of anxiety.

<margin>h</margin> **And often.** This is the fifth sign.

<margin>i</margin> **That it settles.** That is, it remains equal. All of this happens because of the diversity of the matter. Thus, "plateaus" occur during the increase and the decline. Regarding the increase, it appears that time explains it. But in the decline, it happens to reach a lower heat than was at the peak. And when you believe it is continuously descending, it will stay there because of the delay of the phlegm and the slowness of its expulsion; it is even possible that more heat could be added to it.

<margin>k</margin> **And fevers.** This is the third summary or third order of signs from the cause.

<margin>l</margin> **Little sweat.** That is, they produce little sweat, or the text contains "the vapor of little sweat," meaning vapors that are not easily turned into sweat or cannot pass freely through the pores.

<margin>l</margin> **Consider** that these obstructions <note>original: "oppilationes"</note> do not all appear in the urine, because only those in the urinary paths—the liver and nearby parts—show there. Thus, the urine might not be thin, yet the paths in the limbs, the pores of the vein branches, and the openings from the veins into the limbs will be obstructed.

<margin>m</margin> **And thirst.** This is the fourth order of signs, and it is clear.

<margin>n</margin> **And inflammation.** This is the fifth order, referring to a state of <term>cachexia<gloss>bodily wasting and decline</gloss></term> due to obstructions and thick vapors. Thus, it can lead to dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, in which the skin becomes thinner with tension.

<margin>o</margin> **The color, however.** This is the sixth order of signs from the heat.

<margin>p</margin> **Toward greenness.** Due to the coldness of the phlegm and the "mortification" <note>loss of vitality</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>q</margin> **And yellowness.** Due to some burning from the fever.

<margin>r</margin> **Leaden-hued.** Because it is joined with the whiteness of the phlegm; this is the color of lead. Note that Avicenna had subtle theories regarding colors, as appears in Book 6 of *On Natural Things*, part three, or in the first book, the chapter on the complexions of wood.

<margin>s</margin> **Of the other fevers.** Namely, the hot ones.

<margin>t</margin> **Of this.** This is the seventh order of signs from the pulse. First, he gives the differences of this pulse; then he compares it to other fevers and gives the cause at "And frequency"; thirdly, he completes these distinctions of the pulse at "And more vehement." He says first that it is made small: the pulse is small and "lowered," meaning submerged, because the heat is suffocated by coldness, viscosity, and the sheer amount of matter, which is weak from these same causes. It is "rare" <note>slow or infrequent</note> due to the coldness of the humor. "At first," meaning at the start of the fever attack while the coldness remains, because then the heat arrives afterward. "In the end," meaning in the progression or the final stage, it becomes more frequent and very frequent. It should be considered whether "at first" can only be paired with "rare," which would mean that the pulse is submerged and small throughout the phlegmatic fever, but only rare at the start. However, it can be paired with every difference he mentioned: meaning the phlegmatic pulse at the start of the attack is small, submerged, and rare, but later becomes frequent. This returns to the same meaning.

...you will see it already beginning to increase, and similarly, it has plateaus during its decline. <margin>k</margin> Phlegmatic fevers <margin>l</margin> indeed have many obstructions due to the abundance of moisture, and their vapor produces little sweat because of the viscosity of the humor. And when it does produce sweat, it is not abundant; among its more specific signs are the lack or absence of sweat. Thirst <margin>m</margin> is indeed lessened in phlegmatic fevers, unless it is due to a "false" cause or a cause of vehement putrefaction; even then, it is less than the thirst in other fevers. <margin>n</margin> Inflammation <margin>n</margin> of the sides is increased in them, and sometimes it happens that the skin of the side becomes thin with tension. <margin>o</margin> The color <margin>p</margin> of patients with phlegmatic fever inclines toward greenness and yellowness <margin>q</margin> running <margin>r</margin> into whiteness, so that the result is like the color of lead, even until the peak. Rarely does the color turn red in a way that matches the redness seen in the stages of other fevers <margin>s</margin>. <margin>t</margin> Its pulse <margin>t</margin> is small, submerged, weak, and rare at first; then it becomes frequent at the end. Its frequency <margin>u</margin> and its smallness are more vehement than the frequency of quartan and tertian fevers; its smallness and the vehemence of its frequency are due to the vehemence of the smallness of the phlegmatic fever itself <margin>v</margin>. The vehemence of the frequency of the phlegmatic pulse is greater than that of the tertian and quartan pulse. Because the smallness of the phlegmatic pulse is greater than the tertian or quartan, this is what he means by "than its smallness." 

Then Avicenna presupposes a known fact: namely, that the pulse in this phlegmatic fever becomes smaller than in quartan or tertian. He then argues that it is therefore more frequent than in tertian fever, because it compensates <note>original: "restaurat"</note> for what it lacks in magnitude. This is what he means: the vehemence of its frequency is due to the vehemence of its smallness. 

However, it is doubted whether the phlegmatic pulse is smaller than the melancholic one. That it is smaller than the pulse of a bilious fever is not doubted. It seems that the melancholic pulse is smaller according to Galen in his book *On Crises*, the chapter on tertian fever, where he says: "Quartan fever at the start of the attack places the pulse in a state of smallness that no other illness follows." Therefore, phlegmatic fever does not reach a smallness of pulse as great as quartan. One might ask this in the fourth chapter on quartan fever: he says the pulse of this quartan fever is smaller, more so than in phlegmatic fever. Avicenna in the *Al-Tabari* <note>Referring to the *Liber Regalis* of Haly Abbas</note>, Book 8, Treatise 5, says the opposite in the signs of phlegmatic fever: "The pulse here is smaller than the pulse of quartan fever, etc., because phlegm weakens its power with its dissolving coldness and chills it by its abundance." Rhazes states the same in the *Continens*, the chapter on phlegmatic fever at the end. 

Let us say that authors are found to be in great disagreement regarding the differences between phlegmatic and quartan pulses. For those who judged the comparison of these pulses and their reasoning relied on the cause which, in their estimation, seemed more likely to be the cause. He who says the pulse is smaller in phlegmatic fever points to the coldness and abundance, suggesting this does more than the causes found in melancholic humor. However, he who says the pulse is smaller in melancholic fever believes that the coldness of melancholy is greatly aided by dryness, so that the organ [the artery] becomes disobedient to dilation, and in this, it surpasses phlegm. But those who judge by experience can disagree because the differences in pulses can be very deceptive, and variations occur according to the species of phlegm and other factors that coincide. Thus, one author could find the phlegmatic pulse smaller, and another the melancholic pulse smaller. 

Therefore, if we take two fevers—one from natural phlegm and another from natural melancholy—at the same time, in the same climate, and in the same balanced man (or one in winter as a phlegmatic fever in a phlegmatic body, and another in autumn in a melancholic body), then the question is regarding their humors: which motion toward putrefaction makes the pulse smaller, the phlegmatic or the melancholic? Although neither question can be strictly demonstrated, I believe the phlegmatic humor makes the pulse smaller because it is colder, viscous, and abundant, as Haly Abbas said. As for the contrary opinions, it must be said that they proceeded with their estimated judgment according to what they found through experience in many cases they encountered, in which the absolute truth did not appear to them. For the sake of more scholarly judgments, it can be said that the pulse in phlegmatic fever is smaller *intensively* [in depth], but in melancholic fever it is smaller *extensively* [in duration], because the quartan "type" and paroxysm last longer than the phlegmatic.
