**Fen. I. Tractatus II.**

**Column 1**

It becomes more frequent than the pulse in a quartan fever <note>original: "pulsu quartane"</note>. And in this, there does not seem to be much disagreement: for authors agree that the pulse of a phlegmatic person is denser than that of a melancholic person so that, through this density, it may restore the defect in magnitude <term>magnitude<gloss>the physical size or volume of the artery's expansion</gloss></term> which it has over the quartan fever. <margin>§. Truly, with his imagined proportions <note>original: "fantastiis proportionibus"; likely referring to theoretical pulse rhythms</note></margin> as he imagined proportions in the *Therapeutics to Glaucon*: that the pulse of a quartan fever is just as much rarer than the pulse of a phlegmatic fever as the pulse of a phlegmatic fever is rarer than the pulse of a tertian fever. However, it is difficult to find this through touch: yet he asserts these differences can be comprehended through touch, as his imagination shows in the *Book of Differences of Pulses*. And we have prolonged our intention on these matters in the first book.

The third doubt is whether the pulse of a phlegmatic fever is more frequent than the pulse of a tertian fever. It seems not according to Galen in the *Therapeutics to Glaucon*. It appears through Averroes’ *Colliget*, the fourth chapter on phlegmatic fever, where he says the pulse of this fever is consistently rarer than the pulse of a tertian fever in any of the four stages of the fever. Rhazes wants the same in the fourth book of the *Almansor*, the chapter on continuous fever; and many authors agree on this. Reason seems to confirm this because the choleric <term>humor<gloss>yellow bile, which was believed to be hot and dry</gloss></term> is very hot and highly inflaming, and the heat creates distress; I know much more by the greater necessity for cold air, as Avicenna says above; therefore frequency adds more to the pulse. Furthermore, the reasoning of Avicenna, which is also the reasoning of Haly Abbas <note>original: "Alisb."; likely Haly Abbas (Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi)</note>, does not seem to conclude the matter. For when it is said: that when the magnitude of the pulse is lacking, restoration is made through frequency.

## The pulse: truly* it is not faster than the pulse of a quartan fever, and sometimes it is slower than it, or similar to it, especially in the beginning; and it is of great diversity with a loss of order; and the small and weak pulses among them are more diverse. ¶ And indeed the signs of the pulse regarding this are among the more certain signs. ¶ The urine, however, is at first white and thin because of the multitude of blockages <term>oppilations<gloss>blockages in the vessels or organs caused by thick humors</gloss></term> and cold; then it becomes red because of putrefaction <term>putredinez<gloss>the "cooking" or decay of humors that produces feverish heat</gloss></term>; and it is disturbed because of poor digestion; and sometimes the condition is altered at one time; and sometimes it will be cleansed of thick matter, and the putrid part is resolved; and the blockages will return and it will be whitened at one hour and another; when it remains within the thick matter and the state of putrefaction; and at the hour of blockages it is white, then when the matter putrefies after that, it is expelled; and as it opens the blockages it becomes red, until it comes back over the blockages, so that it blocks them another time from that same humor.

<margin>a</margin> We shall say first that restoration occurs through velocity. Therefore the reasoning argues more that it is faster than it is frequent. Second, we shall say that the reasoning would conclude if the heat of the tertian and the heat of the phlegmatic were of the same intensity. Then, if a small pulse were joined to one heat and a large one to another, it could be argued: therefore it is faster and more frequent, or at least more frequent. But since the heats are unequal in degree, the smallness of the pulse in the phlegmatic is such that as much as the heat of the phlegmatic is diminished from the heat of the choleric, so much is the phlegmatic pulse diminished from the choleric pulse; therefore it will not be necessary for the pulse to become frequent. On the contrary is Avicenna when he says: And its frequency indeed and its smallness are more vehement than the frequency of the quartan or tertian. Haly Abbas feels the same when he gives the cause that Avicenna provides, although he does not explain it regarding tertian fever, but only regarding quartan. Shall we say that the text of Avicenna is suspected to be corrupt? And he wants to say: And its frequency indeed and its smallness are more vehement than the frequency or the smallness of the tertian, and thus I suspect the text ought to stand. Alternatively, it can be said: that in some part of the paroxysm <term>paroxysm<gloss>the peak or "fit" of a fever</gloss></term>, as happens in the beginning, many times the pulse in the phlegmatic is more frequent than in the choleric. And the reason is: that many times it begins with a state of fainting <term>syncopis<gloss>a temporary loss of consciousness or strength</gloss></term>, and many times fainting occurs in it. And in this state, because of the great diminution of magnitude, the pulse becomes very frequent. But against this: in a fainting fever, the pulse becomes rare. It must be said that this is true while the coldness of the humor lasts; and even while the heat lasts it may not be frequent, as in choleric people because that phlegm is not heated much. If in a phlegmatic fever from other phlegm already much heated by putrefaction, fainting comes on or its magnitude fails greatly, it will become more frequent than in a choleric fever. But when the steady state has come and the heat is expanded, and there is no fainting—because then fainting does not happen, though it might—the pulse becomes less frequent than in a choleric fever. Let this then be the summary of the solution: that this frequency is because of the fainting; and if this idea pleases you, resolve it by the reasoning that although there are different degrees of heat, nevertheless with a great smallness of pulse and a lesser degree of heat, a greater frequency can occur than with a higher degree. Hence the pulse of women is more frequent than the pulse of men. Regarding the other point, the solution will appear in the following part. Thirdly, it can be said that the pulse of the phlegmatic is not absolutely more frequent than the choleric pulse, but proportionally to its smallness: because in no fever, neither choleric nor melancholic, is there as much addition in frequency due to smallness as there is in the phlegmatic.
<margin>a</margin> Truly. Alternatively, that although the pulse of the phlegmatic may be more frequent than the pulse of the quartan, it is not however faster than it. And the reason is that the power which restores the defect of magnitude through velocity must be strong in some way. But in this fever, power fails greatly. Whence Haly Abbas said that the power in this fever is dissolved and chilled.
<margin>b</margin> Or similar: to it in the first stages. Because of the great brokenness. Whence it becomes small and slow; yet it becomes dense. For density is the offspring of a failing or weak power. As Galen says in the *Commentary on Pulses*, the chapter on the phrenetic pulse.
<margin>c</margin> Or similar: to it in the first stages, namely, similar to it in slowness when in the beginning of the fever fit the body has not reached much chilling. And here a question would fall where many imaginative things could be said.
<margin>d</margin> And it is of great diversity with a loss of order. He wants the phlegmatic pulse to be diverse and disordered. And the cause is the aggravation and suffocation of power by the thick, viscous, and plentiful humor. And because through the defect power causes smallness and weakness of the pulse, it follows that in the diversity of the pulse many small, weak, and diverse beats fall in this because of the battle between the mat-

And it is good, which is when that state remains, that is, stays or is retained within the thick matter, etc., that is, within the thick matter: and is disposed toward putrefaction, and is not yet putrid. It appears therefore that in the phlegmatic patient, the state can be found in a double condition. One is the condition in which the putrid part is evacuated. The other is the condition of the standing thick matter, which is disposed toward putrefaction. And this is the condition of the blockage: because then it is disposed. And therefore with these things having been premised, Avicenna subjoins the clear speech saying at the hour of blockages the urine is white, namely thin: and the urine of putrefaction and expulsion is colored and thick. And again after this, thinness and whiteness will return when the thick matters are moved to cause blockage. This speech was of a Jew <note>possibly referring to Isaac Judaeus, a famous physician</note>, as appears in the 16th book of the *Continens*, first chapter.

And its remission is not a clean remission* since the matter with its thickness and viscosity is plentiful. Age, habit, the season, and the preceding things from nauseating satiety signify it: and the aforesaid form and the color of the face and the swelling and the smoothness of touch signify* it. ...differ etc. And it happens. This text is difficult and has two interpretations. The first is the common one, which Dynus <note>Dino del Garbo (c. 1280–1327), a famous Italian physician and commentator</note> seems to have favored over others: that the rigor—that is, the cold occurring at the start of a flare-up—continues for 6 hours in a continuous fever, or roughly that amount. This cold is greater in a continuous fever than in an intermittent one. This is what he says regarding the following point: for the periodic phlegmatic fever—that is, the intermittent one—does not empty out the residue of the cold; rather, the shivering and cold endure within it. However, it is hidden and not apparent—that is, not lasting as long as in the continuous type. Therefore, the summary of the opinion is: the cold at the beginning of continuous phlegmatic flare-ups is more manifest and lasts longer than the cold at the start of intermittent phlegmatic paroxysms <term>paroxysm<gloss>the period of a fever where symptoms are at their most intense</gloss></term>. He says the cause for this is that under the phlegmatic matter of continuous fevers, the innate heat is more "suffocated," as it occurs within the veins. But if experience does not deceive us, we have seen the total contrary: namely, that the cold in the paroxysms of intermittent phlegmatic fevers was stronger and lasted longer. The cold at the beginning of those arising from phlegm seems reasonable, because intermittent phlegm is "purer" and is in locations where it can become warm less easily and more slowly, as it is not reached by as much heat. But the phlegm in a continuous fever is not so pure or cold, and it is more besieged and penetrated by powerful heat; therefore, it ought to retreat more quickly and be more remiss. Forced by these facts, we have made another interpretation. One single word makes the whole text difficult: "rigor" <note>original: "rigor"; usually meaning a cold shiver, but here debated</note>. For perhaps "rigor" is used here differently than it is used elsewhere by Avicenna or another author; for it is used to mean a "lukewarm heat" that appears during the quiet hours of a flare-up. And Avicenna means that just as in an intermittent phlegmatic fever the paroxysm lasts 18 hours and the rest lasts six, so in a continuous fever the flare-up lasts 18 hours, but the "tepidity" of the heat lasts six hours, or roughly that—perhaps even less than 6 hours. Or it is increased, and the text is clear. "Overcoming"—namely, this heat of rest or remission in a continuous fever overcomes that which occurs in a periodic fever—that is, the heat in the rest period of an intermittent fever. For the periodic fever is not emptied—that is, not cleansed—of the residue of heat, yet it is hidden and not apparent, just as in the continuous type. He means nothing else than that although in both continuous and intermittent phlegmatic fevers a remiss heat (which he calls "rigor") lasts for six hours, the heat in the continuous type is nevertheless more manifest. In the intermittent type, it is more hidden. And therefore, one can still be called intermittent and the other continuous.

# On the fevers that are mostly of the phlegmatic kind, though sometimes from bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>, and are not of the type that arise from black bile <note>original: "melancholia"</note>, categorized by names and judgments. Chapter 50.

These are the *epialos* and *lipparia* fevers: both are from the highest category of fevers in which the locations of heat and cold differ internally and externally. This is due to the diversity and the location of that which decays <term>putrefies<gloss>medieval medicine held that fevers were caused by the "rotting" or decay of bodily humors</gloss></term> and that which does not. There are three divisions: the "humoral fainting" fever <note>original: "syncopalis humorosa"</note>, the "minute subtle" fainting fever, and the "long-lasting and nocturnal" fever.

### The fever in which cold is hidden and heat appears, which is called *epialos*. Chapter 51.

This fever arises from "glassy" phlegm <note>original: "phlegmate vitreo"; a thick, cold, transparent humor</note>, but it is trapped in a hidden and deep place where it becomes cold. The matter has already begun to decay, and the vapor from what has decayed is scattered; as it decays and spreads, it becomes inflamed in the external parts of the body. That part which is not decayed remains cold in the internal parts. And indeed, the cold does not appear at that time because it is settled and associated with the limb in which it resides; it does not suffer from what happens to it. After the decay begins, however, it is moved and becomes cold in a certain "cooling," though this does not reach the point of affecting the whole body. Chapter 52.

<a> **On these fevers.** Here he determines which fevers are reducible to the phlegmatic types: because they mostly arise from phlegm, although they occasionally arise from bile, such as the *lipparia* (called *taburoe*) and the *minute fainting fever*. They do not arise from black bile, as will appear. That is, they arise from pure phlegm tending toward its nature or having its mixture, just as Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician</note> posits regarding the *lipparia*. This is what the **Rubric** says. First, he lists these fevers; second, he examines them where it says "This fever." He says first that these fevers are *epialos* and *lipparia*, both of which belong to the class of fevers where the locations of heat and cold differ internally and externally, setting aside the diversity of the matter and the locations where these substances are purely formed. Second, he says some are called "minute fainting fevers," some "long-lasting," and some "nocturnal." It should be known, however, that besides these, one might find another fever where heat and cold are found in the same location, which will be explained in the *ekthesis* <note>a detailed explanation or layout</note>. How the locations of decay differ in them will appear in their own chapters. Then he lists three other species when he says "and there are," meaning besides the aforementioned species, there are three other divisions into three species. In total, there are six species.

<b> **This fever.** Here he examines these fevers. It has six parts, just as there are six fevers. First, he examines the *epialos*. Second, the *lipparia*, and so on; the parts are noted. The first part is in two: first, he gives the cause of *epialos* and how it arises from that cause. Second, he gives the signs at "The signs of it." The first is in two: first he does this, and second he removes a doubt at "And indeed his..." Avicenna's idea is that in *epialos*, cold appears inside and heat appears outside, and the cause is "glassy" phlegm trapped in a hidden place—that is, in the interior parts. It becomes cold where it is—that is, it appears cold there. But the vapor of decay rising from it when it rots, and the part that rots, is scattered outside and becomes inflamed—that is, it appears hot in the external parts. The part of this phlegm that has not decayed is what appears cold in the interior parts. Some doubt whether in *epialos* heat is felt outside and cold inside, as Avicenna thought. We do not intend to argue about this, for it is a question of names. But we will say that our authors use these names, *epialos* and *lipparia*, in different ways. For the name *epialos* signifies a certain fever in which heat and cold are felt simultaneously in the same part. Galen uses the word this way in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers*, and in the book *On the Malice of a Diverse Complexion*, and in the commentary on the seventh part of the *Aphorisms*. Also Haly Abbas <note>original: "Aliah."; 10th-century Persian physician</note> in the 6th chapter of the 6th book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, and Rhazes <note>original: "Ratio"; 9th-century Persian physician</note> in the 3rd chapter of the 16th book of the *Continens*. Some also use the name *epialos* to mean a fever where cold appears outside and heat inside, such as Isaac in the second book on fevers, the chapter on *epialos*, and in the *Problems* (17, problem 2). Others use the name *epialos* in the opposite way to signify a fever where cold appears inside and heat outside, which is how Avicenna uses the term here, and Serapion <note>9th-century Christian physician from Syria</note> in the sixth book of his *Breviary*. It is called *epialos* from *epi* (above) and *alia* (other), because the heat is above the cold—that is, outside the cold. Therefore, let us not argue about this, but describe a fever where there is cold inside and heat outside, and call it whatever you like, and assign the cause for why it appears so. Consider that Isaac imagines the cause of this fever (which he calls *lipparia*) to be matter composed of melancholic and phlegmatic humors: because thick phlegm lies inside, and thick bile decays and inflames the exterior. His imagination can be tolerated. There is doubt about what this "hidden and deep place" is. Second, it is doubted how the feverish person feels cold inside. To the first, it must be said that by hidden, deep places we can understand the stomach and intestines and the parts immediately adjacent to them. Or we can understand the locations of the internal veins and the deep parts of the muscles. By "external places," we mean the extremities—namely, the hands and feet. From this, the solution to whether this fever is continuous or intermittent appears: if the matter is in the veins, it is placed among the continuous fevers; if outside, it is placed among the intermittent. To the second, it must be said that although cold is perceived around the stomach and intestines or around the deep veins of the deep muscles, one must imagine that the hot, decayed vapor comes to the heart and warms it, causing the fever. Hence, the person does not say they feel cold in the depths—that is, in or around the heart—but feels cold around the stomach, intestines, and back—namely, around the internal muscles of the back and belly—and feels heat in the feet and hands. Regarding this, there can be many variations concerning the diversity of internal locations where cold is felt and external locations where heat is felt; you should consider this. It is doubted thirdly that there can be specific internal locations of certain veins where this cooling happens; therefore, the external locations must necessarily be cold, because the cooling of internal parts is followed by cold in the external parts, as appears with the cold in the extremities during the flare-ups of a continuous phlegmatic fever. It must be said without doubt that the external parts ought to be cold, but the presence of hot, decayed vapor makes them hot by force. Or it must be said that the locations of the internal veins where cold can be perceived are not the veins near the heart...

**Signs.** The signs are the same as those mentioned before. The matter, due to its thickness, sometimes decays in a quartan or tertian pattern, because such matter in the body is small and of a small, fiery decay. This small amount is one of the causes for the lengthening of the period <term>period<gloss>the interval between fever attacks</gloss></term>. And therefore...

<c> **And indeed his.** Someone might ask why this phlegm is felt inside now, but was not felt before it moved toward decay. He responds that the cold of that phlegm does not appear inside at that time—namely, when it is not moving toward decay—because it was standing still and "associated" with the limb in which it resides; therefore, the parts it encounters do not suffer from it. After it begins to rot, it is moved, and it "becomes cold"—that is, its cooling becomes apparent. This is a certain kind of coldness because it is not pure cold, but rather a certain weak heat that ought to be called so; nevertheless, it is judged as coldness. However, this cooling does not "reach"—that is, such cooling does not reach the heart, because then it would not be called a fever, or it would be a type of fainting fever. We do not intend here to philosophize about how something that is weakly hot can be felt as cold, like urine to someone urinating in a bath, as Galen says in the third book of *On Simple Medicine*. Consider that he says "it becomes cold" because the appearance of such cooling occurs through a certain internal unfolding of the cold humor. These things were explained above in the chapter on the discourse of rigor and cold. It is doubted because the heat felt outside comes from hot, decayed vapor; but this vapor rises from decaying phlegm standing inside; but that phlegm is actually decaying—therefore it is actually hot—therefore heat should be felt in the interior. It must be said that we must imagine the decaying parts of this phlegm to be few compared to the non-decaying parts; yet they are enough that the vapor is sufficient to inflame and extinguish the potent heat. But the cold parts in the locations where they are overcome the hot parts by cooling the locations where they are situated. Even if such an imagination is not used, we will not deny that this fever is *epialos*, since it is a fever in which heat and cold are perceived in the same part.

<d> **The signs of it.** He first gives the signs. Second, he explains something. Third, he gives the signs again at "Second: Alexander," and thirdly at "The space." He says first that they are the same as those mentioned—namely, above in the chapter on the signs of intermittent phlegmatic fever, which are the signs of phlegm in general. Or they are the same as mentioned—namely, concerning the nature of this fever—that the person is cold inside and hot outside. **The urine, etc.** The reason is that because this phlegm is "glassy," it cools the interior more than in other phlegmatic fevers.

<e> **The pulse, etc.** Supplement: with respect to other phlegmatic fevers; however, with respect to a healthy person, it is fast and frequent because he is feverish.

<f> **It increases every day.** That is, it flares up or paroxysms every day. Consider that perhaps at the beginning of the paroxysm of this fever, the disposition is similar to other phlegmatic fevers from glassy phlegm, because there is cold in the extremities; but when the decayed vapor already begins to expand outside, as in its increase, then specifically the cold is felt inside and the heat is felt outside. And if someone wishes, they can imagine that in the very beginning, heat occurs outside and cold inside. Consider this: and it occurs "most often." He says it occurs "most often"—namely, the daily paroxysm—because it does not always happen this way; rather, it sometimes paroxysms every fourth day or every third day. The cause of this is that the matter is of a small quantity and small decay because of its thickness, coldness, and viscosity; and when it does decay, it is a small, fiery decay.

<g> **The small amount of matter is the cause of lengthening.** That is, the delay or postponement of the period. He responds that this paroxysm every third or fourth day is not a reason for it not to be a daily fever; for a fever is "daily" when its decay is like daily decay, and the decay of this fever is of that kind. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the classification of phlegmatic fevers. The previous page discussed how the duration and nature of the initial cold (rigor) distinguish continuous from intermittent phlegmatic fevers. Here, the author examines specific subtypes like "glassy" phlegm fevers and the paradoxical "Lipparia" fever, where the patient's internal and external temperatures seem to contradict each other.</meta>

**Treatise II**

**Column 1:**

It should not, therefore, be called non-phlegmatic; as if to say that the classification of fevers is not based on the timing of the paroxysm <term>paroxysm<gloss>the period of a fever where symptoms are at their most intense</gloss></term>, but rather on the nature of the matter. It must be considered that some have argued from this text against our opinion—the one we hold, that the form of the fever follows the humors according to the nature of their specific form. For they say that if the specific form accompanied the substantial form (for example, of phlegm), then such a paroxysm would always follow. Therefore, phlegm would never cause a paroxysm every third day or every fourth day. Yet Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was the standard text in Europe.</note> says the contrary. We reply that the effect which follows specific and substantial forms follows them in a determined measure and by accident, unless something prohibits it. For instance, the herb turbith <note>A medicinal root used as a purgative.</note> evacuates phlegm by its property and in a measured amount; yet if it is given beyond the quantity that its form requires, it will even evacuate blood. Therefore, it is possible for this to happen alongside the phlegm, or without it. Similarly, a magnet will not attract iron if it is smeared with garlic <note>A common medieval belief about the properties of magnets.</note>; there are many such examples. Phlegm, therefore, moves from day to day by its own property when it possesses a determined quantity and consistency of substance. However, when it becomes thin or thick, even if its specific form dictates a certain paroxysm, it is hindered by these accidents. Thus, the movement will become sluggish and delayed until the third or fourth day. We have written more on this in the section on generation.

Second, it must be considered that this "glassy" phlegm <term>glassy phlegm<gloss>phlegma vitreum; a cold, thick, transparent type of phlegm resembling molten glass</gloss></term>, with its coldness, thickness, and viscosity, is not fit to receive a putrefaction <term>putrefaction<gloss>putredo; the process of a humor "spoiling" or decaying, which medieval doctors believed generated the heat of a fever</gloss></term> that is truly putrid. For substances fit for this are those that are hot and moist. Therefore, it will receive a very violent heating, and its putrefaction is a kind of violent "ignition" or something similar. This is what is meant by "the fire of small putrefaction"—that is, such putrefaction is not true putrefaction, but rather an ignition. 

Third, it should be considered that the scarcity of matter and of putrefaction are among the causes for the lengthening or retardation of the period. For as was declared in the question regarding periodicity: the matter to be moved during a paroxysm has two "movers." One is nature, or the natural heat; when nature is not stimulated, it does not move the matter. A scarcity of matter is a cause of slow stimulation, because it takes longer to reach the quantity required to stimulate nature. The other mover is external heat; when the matter is thick and difficult to affect, and poorly receptive to putrefaction, then it also moves slowly. This is Avicenna's meaning.

<insert>
**Regarding the paroxysm not returning every day: this fever does not cease to be phlegmatic. Rather, it is phlegmatic because its putrefaction is the putrefaction of phlegm. This does not exclude it from being phlegmatic; it is phlegmatic because the putrefaction belongs to phlegm, not because the paroxysm fails to return every day. Indeed, the duration of its paroxysm is from 14 hours up to 23 hours, and for the most part, it is consumed before then, because this matter is not present in great abundance.**

# On the fever in which heat is hidden and cold appears, which is called lipparia.

### Chapter IV.

**This fever is for the most part phlegmatic, and sometimes it is...**

<insert>
**The duration. Here he provides another sign: the duration of time. It must be considered that this can be explained in two ways. One way is that the paroxysm of the fever, by which it is distinguished from others, lasts from the 4th hour until the 24th, such that the first four hours are not part of this fever. This differs from others, for in the first four hours the patient feels only internal heat because the phlegm begins to move, but the vapor has not yet reached the outside to heat the exterior parts. One might imagine, then, that around the fourth hour the hot vapor comes outside and heats the exterior; then it becomes "empiala" <note>A fever where the patient feels hot and cold at the same time.</note> and lasts until the 24th hour, or usually less, as Avicenna says. Although this explanation does not please many, even though it is mine, I have put it forward because it prompts many ideas regarding the nature of this fever. The second way it can be explained is that Avicenna means the paroxysm of this fever lasts at least 14 hours and at most 24, and for the most part is finished before 24. He assigns the cause as follows: since this matter is scarce, it is not of such quantity that it could last 14 hours. It must be considered that in Avicenna’s view, the phlegmatic matter that becomes "ignited" and putrid in empiala is scarce, and therefore the paroxysm ends quickly—much faster than the periodic fever commonly occurring. Thus it can end in four hours, even if it is glassy matter, or it can last up to 24. This was the opinion of Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (c. 865–925), another foundational authority in medieval medicine.</note> in the 16th book of the *Continens*, third chapter. He wonders if, after the resolution of a small amount of putrid phlegm, a person remains with a sense of cold in the interior because the part of the raw and cold phlegm that was not putrid could be substantial. It is not to be expected that this would be resolved in a short time. It must be said that it is possible to remain with a sensation of cold if that phlegm remained in motion; it is also possible that nature has become accustomed to it and it remains quiet, so the patient does not suffer from its cold. Consider this.**
</insert>

<insert>
**This fever. Here he determines the nature of the fever in which the interior parts are heated and cold appears on the exterior, which has been given the name "lipparia." First, he premises its cause; second, he explains it. The second part starts at "And when." First, consider that every paroxysmal fever starting with cold can be called "lipparia" at that starting time, because the internal heat exists while the extremities are still cold. But this is not the type of fever discussed here; rather, we speak of the one that by its nature remains in this state throughout the entire paroxysm. Second, consider that what was said of "empiala" should also be said of "lipparia." Some authors use the name "lipparia" to signify a fever where there is cold inside and heat outside, as in the fifth book on fevers. Others use the name to signify a fever where the interior feels hot and the exterior cold. It is called "lipparia," that is, a "fat" fever, because fat people feel heat inside and cold outside, as noted by Aristotle in his work on phlegm. Avicenna uses this term for such a fever, as does Galen <note>The Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose system of humors dominated medicine.</note> in the third book on simple medicine and in the *Aphorisms*. In fevers that do not fail, the exterior parts are cold. This is also mentioned in the commentary on the *Prognostics*. Third, it should be considered that thick yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> is rarely found in the thickness required for this fever, as that movement is foreign to that bile. However, thick phlegm is frequently found in the interior; therefore, this fever is more frequently found to come from phlegm.**

<insert>
**The manner. The first part is in two: first he premises, then declares. Since it is not resolved: he says first that the fever arises from phlegm because the phlegm putrefies inside at times and heats only that place. It is doubted what kind of phlegm that is. It must be said that it is either glassy or raw phlegm. But you might ask why it is not cooled inside as in empiala. It must be said that if putrefaction comes to this phlegm in all its parts, then it only heats and does not cool the interior; this is what happens in lipparia. However, if only a certain part putrefies and the greater part remains cold and not so putrid, then the interior is cooled as in empiala. Both can happen due to the diversity of people, places, and the diversity of matters within the same species, and due to the diversity of the acting causes.**
</insert>

<insert>
**choleric [fever] from very thick bile**
**The way it is phlegmatic is that when the phlegm inside is inflamed and putrefies, it heats that place. It is not resolved unless the putrefaction heats the exterior of the body with a spirit of vapor from its great heating. Since the power <term>power<gloss>virtus; the body's natural defensive or metabolic force</gloss></term> pours out to the place where the injury is, then the exterior parts are emptied of heat; therefore they are specifically cooled when there is raw, glassy, and cold phlegm in the exterior. And again, because a vapor is often resolved from it that did not putrefy but is raised up, it creates heat and heat stays with it for a short space, then it separates from it as the vapor of heated water separates. Does it then separate from it as it was in the root before the actual putrefaction?**
</insert>

<insert>
**Since. Here he explains: first, why when that phlegm putrefies inside, the exterior parts are not heated; second, why the exterior parts are cooled. He says first that the putrid phlegm in the interior heats only that place because the putrid phlegmatic matter in the interior is not then resolved through the pores, except that the putrefaction, because of the great heating in that putrid matter, heats the exterior parts toward the skin and extremities with the vapors of that matter spread outward. And under this proposition, one understands that it is possible for the phlegm putrid in the interior...**
</insert>

...not to be heated by a great enough heating to move the vapors to the outside. Therefore, it heats only that internal place and not the external place or places. To deny this possibility is not possible, but it is not easy to posit it. Now it appears that the putrid phlegm in the interior in this "lipparia" fever differs in two ways from the putrid phlegm in "empiala," which is also in the interior. First, in empiala, it is not all heated, but in lipparia, all or the greatest part of it is heated; both are possible in different people. Second, because the putrefaction in the phlegm of lipparia is not strong and of great heat such that it can move vapors outward; but in empiala, those few parts that are putrid have a strong fiery heat that gives the vapors motion toward the exterior, which is why the exterior becomes heated.

"And when the power." He has already proven that it is possible for the exterior not to be heated, but only the interior place. Here he wishes to prove that it is possible for the exterior to be cooled, and he gives three causes. The first is because that vital power <note>original: "virtus"</note> tends toward that internal place where the putrefaction occurs. It is doubted why in empiala the heat and spirit are not poured toward the internal place where the injury (the putrefaction) is, as happens in lipparia. There are many ways to explain this. First, the cause of this diversity could be the diversity of individuals in their sensitivity and aptitude for internal suffering. He who has great sensitivity in the interior where the phlegm putrefies will have a "flight of heat" to the inside, and it will become lipparia. Another who is not like this will not have that, but could have empiala. A second cause could be the nature of the putrefaction—whether it is malignant or not. It may be that the putrefaction and heat in the whole of the phlegm in lipparia is milder in degree, and yet becomes more malignant, forcing the vital power to flee inward. A third cause could be given: the diversity of the heating of these matters. Let us imagine that in lipparia there occurs a certain "ignition" and roasting of the entire phlegm; thus, with the parts of the phlegm being pressed down, no evaporation occurs. Because of the harm of the fiery roasting heat, the heat flees inward. In that case, it must be said that the action of the heat in the phlegm and its putrefaction is stronger in lipparia than in empiala. This is the opposite of what was said before, and would be another mode of lipparia. Fourth, it can be said that in both cases the heat returns inward, but in empiala, the hot vapors move outside, and they move in a way that forces the movement of the heat from the inside, drawing it out as if by force. This method seems well-suited, although I have said something about it above; if it pleases anyone, let them accept it.

<margin>It is doubted</margin> It is doubted whence the coldness in the exterior parts is caused when the heat flees inward. It must be said, as was said above, that it is either from the air or from the cold element within us, which does not intend to be pushed out in this way.

<margin>Specifically.</margin> Here he gives the second cause of the cooling, and it is clear. Although he seems to place this cause alongside the first, it is a sufficient cause on its own for the exterior parts to be cooled. For even if the heat does not flee inward, the glassy phlegms in the exterior will cool the exterior if they have some mode of motion that vapors coming from within can provide. It appears to you from this that if a few vapors come to the exterior from the phlegmatic matter heating the interior, those few vapors melt or agitate the many glassy phlegms standing outside; their cold is felt, and the heat of the vapors is not felt—thus lipparia is created.

<margin>Avicenna.</margin> But because Avicenna saw that hot vapors, along with that phlegm, are more likely to cause a sensation of heat and cold in the same parts, he omits saying this, because such a fever belongs rather to the following chapter. Because of this, Avicenna joins this cause to the preceding one to show that the mover of this glassy phlegm toward cooling is the heat fleeing inward, from which its coldness appears. I understand "mover" here in a broad sense.

<margin>Again.</margin> Again, here he gives the third cause of this cooling in the exterior and heating in the interior. He maintains that the cause is that from that putrid phlegm inside, a vapor flees and creates heat in the act of rising, and that heat lasts only a little while with it, etc.

<margin>It is doubted</margin> It is doubted because this vapor ought to be raised much more easily in empiala fever, because one part is putrid and that will raise a watery, cold, and non-putrid vapor from the non-putrid part. In lipparia, however, since the putrefaction is over the whole phlegm, a non-putrid vapor cannot be raised; rather, it will necessarily be putrid and hold heat.

<margin>It must be considered</margin> It must be considered that according to a sound understanding, Avicenna hints at this division: that of the vapor rising from the external phlegm, some is non-putrid and consequently does not preserve heat because it does not have it deeply and intrinsically; whereas another is a non-putrid vapor which is nothing other than the putrid body of the humor itself, refined and raised into vapor. We can therefore imagine that in empiala, the vapor that comes outside is putrid, because it rises from the putrid part whose putrefaction has a strong heat giving that vapor a strong outward motion. But from the remaining non-putrid parts, no vapor rises because those are many parts and are only meltable by the heat of the putrid parts, which cannot make them evaporate to the outside; rather, they only melt and cool the interior. And if a vapor rising from the non-putrid parts came to the outside mixed with...

# Book III

**Column 1:**

...of putrid vapor, then in this fever heat is felt [internally], and cold is felt in the external parts. This is because of two vapors: it is the fever discussed in the following chapter. Or, only heat would be felt in the external parts if the putrid vapor with its heat were to prevail and did not allow the non-putrid vapor to return to its natural coldness; this would be <term>Empialla<gloss>a fever where the patient feels internal burning heat but external chilling cold</gloss></term>. Alternatively, cold would be felt both inside and outside if the non-putrid vapor prevailed in this: namely, returning to its natural coldness, and thereby overcoming the heat of the putrid vapor; this belongs to the category of <term>Lipparia<gloss>a fever where the patient feels internal cold but external heat</gloss></term>, insofar as there must be an external heat around the heart in every fever; or perhaps it would be an unusual type of fever. Consider this well. Let us therefore conclude our reasoning on this: in *Empialla*, a putrid vapor rises from the putrid parts of the <note>original: "pblatis," likely a contraction for "phlegmatis" or "pleuritis" depending on context, here referring to the phlegmatic matter</note> phlegm. From the non-putrid parts that cause the sensation of cold, no non-putrid vapor rises; or if it does rise, it cannot return to its radical coldness because the heat of the putrid vapor opposes it.

In *Lipparia*, however, one must imagine that every formal part of the phlegm possesses heat, or at least possesses no coldness capable of inducing a sensation of cold. Therefore, in the internal parts, a pure heat is felt; although every part is hot, we can imagine that not every part is putrid. Then, from the putrid parts—due to a weak motion of putrefaction within them—a putrid vapor rises, but without enough strength to penetrate to the outside. Instead, it only seeks the heart, because the internal passages are wider. From the non-putrid parts, however, one must imagine many non-putrid vapors rising and coming to the outside; when these lose their [initial] heat, they become cold. 

But it is rightly doubted here: what is the "separator" of these vapors, so that the putrid one goes to the heart and the non-putrid one tends toward the exterior where it cools? We must say that this happens due to the coincidence of their causes. For as we proposed, since that putrid vapor cannot be expelled to the outside, it follows that it must go to the heart. But one might doubt: suppose that non-putrid vapor also goes to the heart; what would follow? We say that the non-putrid vapor goes with the putrid vapor and will not return to its coldness in the heart, both because of the heart's own heat and because of its companion, the putrid vapor. And if it pleases your imagination that it *could* return to coldness, then that would be a mode of <term>syncopal fever<gloss>a fever causing fainting or loss of strength</gloss></term>. 

But again, it is doubted: suppose the putrid vapor is so scant that it can only reach the heart, while the non-putrid vapor—actually hot—is plentiful, going to the heart and heating the heart with its active heat so that it harms the heart's functions; when does this fever occur? This doubt would lead us back to the difficult speculations about fevers from which we have already freed ourselves in our [other] questions. I will say that you can call that an <term>ephemera<gloss>a fever lasting only one day</gloss></term>. You should no more be troubled by calling this an "ephemera" than you are by calling that which arises from the vapor of undigested food in the stomach an "ephemera." You have other ways of explaining this in our *Questions*. 

This, then, is the way of understanding these *Lipparia* and *Empialla* fevers regarding these vapors: by positing that the putrid vapor rises from the putrid part and the non-putrid from the non-putrid part. We can also imagine a non-putrid vapor rising from a putrid part, and even a putrid vapor [rising from the same], and this according to the diversity of putrefactions. For when putrefaction sinks deeper into the matter and divides the body of the phlegm, it refines one part which becomes a true "flame" of putrefaction, rising high as it is thinned out; that which is nearby is then putrid vapor. If, however, the putrefaction does not sink so deep, and the thin wateriness in the phlegm is raised up—which is not called "flame" but "phlegmatic vapor"—then from the putrid part there rises a vapor that is not putrid. 

In *Empialla* fever, therefore, because the putrefaction in the matter is deeper and stronger according to one of the ways mentioned above, something putrid rises. In *Lipparia*, however, something watery rises which is radically not putrid but hot; hence it later loses its heat when it reaches the exterior, a place of lesser heat. One might be moved to ask: why is the vapor that rises from the putrid part in *Lipparia* not putrid? If so, how can this fever be among the "sum of putrid fevers"? We shall say that it is not truly putrid in the sense of the *vapor* being putrid, but insofar as the "source" <note>original: "minera," literally "the mine" or "ore," referring to the site of the diseased humor</note> is putrid, the fever is called putrid. A similar thing can be imagined in the putrefactions of other humors. One could also add to all the above that every vapor rising from putrid matter is in some way putrid, but when it is not deeply putrid, it can shed its accidental heat, as in *Lipparia*. When it has deep putrefaction, it does not shed it, as appears in *Empialla*. By these points, many questions are solved, for the solution to the earlier question now appears. 

Finally, it must be considered that we presuppose here that "cataract water" <note>likely referring to a chilled or condensed fluid</note> can return to its coldness, and vapor can return to coldness—returning in the manner of a substance. We do not provide the cause here, but we saw it in the second Canon, second chapter. It should also be considered that a twofold nature is found here. One is said to have been "in the root," meaning that this vapor in the non-putrid watery vapor is separated from that [other] vapor by a separation, etc., just as heat is separated from the vapor of hot water, as is seen on the <note>original: "manubrio lebetis"</note> handle of a kettle. Therefore, when this accidental heat is separated from that vapor, it is "in the root"—that is, radically—from the perfection it has by nature; before putrefaction arrived, it was of intense coldness; it returns, and it chills the body.

**M**ode: previously, regarding how it may be choleraic <note>caused by yellow bile</note>: when the choler is scant and internal, and it putrefies and heats the place, and nothing is resolved from it, there occurs what we said in the comparison with phlegm. 

**E**ndorsement is given to this choleraic fever under the name "taburos" <note>Possibly a corrupted term or local name for a specific bilious fever</note>. But *Lipparia* is a generic name and is of longer duration than <term>hemitritaeus<gloss>a semitertian fever, combining features of a daily and every-other-day fever</gloss></term>. And someone might ask how it can be a fever if heat does not proceed from the heart into the whole body. For that which is narrated is of the genus in which heat does not proceed from the heart into the whole body. 

**R**esponse: thus, in the definitions of these things, one condition is observed: that there be nothing that prohibits it, just as we define cold water.

**A** Mode: Here he shows how *Lipparia* arises from choler, and the mode in which a small amount of choler putrefies in the internal parts—additionally, in the thick internal parts—and heats them. But because of its scantiness or thickness, nothing of it is released to spread to the outside. From this, there occurs what occurs in *Lipparia* made from phlegm, according to the first mode; for *Lipparia* from phlegm is in this 

<column-break/>

comparable or similar to this *Lipparia* from choler. It must be considered that just as in *Lipparia* from phlegm, a chilling of the external parts could occur if "glassy phlegm" was in them, so it is imaginable that something in the internal parts could be choler and [something else] from phlegm. But this would be difficult, just as in the phlegmatic cause of internal chilling, there can be a "flight of heat" to the place of putrefaction; this is much more likely in the choleraic type. A third cause is excluded from choleraic fever: for it is not imaginable that an aqueous vapor which could be chilled should rise from choler; or it is difficult to imagine.

<margin>b "Endorsement... name, etc." This name has no explanation among us.</margin>

**I**ts [the body's] moisture: when it is disposed according to its nature, and there is nothing to prohibit it. And we define a "heavy thing" as that which tends downward when it is left to its own nature. In all these [fevers], heat reaches the heart, proceeds into the arteries, and is scattered. But truly, a prohibition of this occurs in certain places, just as it happens to one upon whom <term>pruine<gloss>This term caused much confusion; it can mean hoar-frost (pruina) or burning coals (pruna). The author clarifies below.</gloss></term> are placed. It is necessary that the evidence of these be in actual effect.

<margin>c "It is of longer duration than hemitritaeus," that is, in a single paroxysm. And this is because of the thickness of the matter, the sign of which is scant evaporation. It would please me more to say it is of longer duration than a "pure tertian." And perhaps Avicenna wishes to mean that it is of longer duration in its periodicity; that it does not recur every day, nor is it necessary that it recur every third day, because it can recur every fourth day. And it is not denied that it is a choleraic fever, as can be understood here from the things said in the chapter on *Empialla*. Therefore, when he said "hemitritaeus," he understood it through the phlegmatic and the choleraic tertian.</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'H' surrounded by a thick red circular border containing rubricated text.</image-desc>

**H**ad this fever existed, it would only be where there are two cold matters moved because of putrefaction: one of which is in the internal parts and the other in the external parts; and there is no other...

<margin>d "And someone has..." here he first raises a doubt, then solves it.</margin>

It is a doubt how *Lipparia* fevers can be called "fevers" when they do not fit the definition of a fever, which says it is an "extraneous heat," etc., "spread throughout," etc. He responds that in the "intermediates"—that is, in the definitions of those things, namely fevers, which are natural entities defined by certain effects or accidents—one condition is observed through which the final predicates are true in those definitions, unless there is something prohibiting them. For example: when we define water, we say it is a "cold and moist body," and this is from its nature and unless there is a prohibitor; yet hot water is found, and thus the contrary appears in the definition, and so in all things. 

He adapts this to the present case and understands that it is so here: because a fever is heat kindled in the heart which spreads to the other members unless there is a prohibitor. In all these fevers, therefore—namely, whichever are *Lipparia* or not *Lipparia*—heat comes to the heart and proceeds of itself into the arteries and is scattered over the members. But sometimes it is prohibited from being scattered to certain places, just as happens to a man or a place upon which <term>pruine<gloss>hoar-frost</gloss></term> are placed. "Pruina" consists of aqueous vapors congealed by strong cold, as in the second book of *Meteors*; therefore, it strongly chills. Where we have "hoar-frost" (pruina), the Jew has <term>nir<gloss>possibly referring to the Hebrew word for "light" or a transliteration of a term for snow/frost used in Hebrew medical translations of the time</gloss></term>. And he says: just as it happens to one upon whom *nir* is placed—that is, cold upon the extremities of the feverish person—or if *nir* or frost or ice be placed upon another spot, that place will be chilled, and the fever will not be able to spread into that place; and yet that man is said to be "feverish." In a similar way, for many causes, the spreading of the fever over the members can be prohibited. And the cause is nothing else but the "glassy phlegm" chilling the external parts.

**D**ocumentation: if someone should ask whether the members upon which these fevers are prohibited from spreading are sick and impaired in their functions, he says that they are. It is necessary that the documentation of these—namely, the fevers—be present in the whole [body] in actual effect. But it is doubted: if the hand of a feverish person is prohibited from receiving the fever, how then would its function be harmed by the fever which is in the heart? Furthermore, since there is a prohibition here due to actual cold killing [the heat] like snow, how then is the function harmed by the fever, since it is harmed and dies from the cold? We have already properly declared this in our question concerning the *Subject of Fever*. We declared that a part so chilled has a "cold disease," which is its form; and thus its functions are harmed by the coldness. Along with this, it has the fever "by community"—that is, because the heart is feverish, the hand cannot exercise its functions. For it presupposes for its functions the temperament of the heart. And either one of these is sufficient for the hand to be unable to exercise its functions. 

It can be explained in another way, and less subtly: if one says that snow or frost should prohibit the fever over the members to which they are applied, it is necessary that they be of such great coldness that they induce a "cold disease" harming the functions; otherwise they would not prohibit it. In our *Questions on Fevers*, this text was explained differently because of the reading that was accepted, which says <term>prune<gloss>burning coals</gloss></term>, meaning fire. For just as the heat of a burning coal is a heat that does not evaporate and is not spreadable, but burns the place in which the coal is placed without evaporation, so certain humors putrefying within heat the internal places without evaporation to the exterior. Yet despite this, they are called "actual functions of the whole."

"Of this fever it has," etc. This is the third type of fever in which each of the two is found—namely, heat and cold—in each of the two places: namely, inside and outside. Therefore, there is no part in which one does not feel both heat and cold. Avicenna gives such a mode: that we should imagine two phlegmatic, cold, "glassy" matters, one of which is inside and the other outside. And let each be moved by putrid heat in such a way that their coldness appears; and from this, the patient will feel cold inside and outside. But along with this, he imagines that some part of both matters putrefies, and the internal putrid matter emits a hot putrid vapor reaching those places which are being chilled. Therefore, that vapor will heat, while the cold matter will chill. In the same way, from the part of the external putrid matter, a putrid vapor goes inward where the cold vapor is contained, and it reaches those parts; therefore, he will feel heat and cold. 

And if you imagine what Avicenna wants, it will be seen that there are two matters of two *Empialla* fevers. For internal matter alone, without the external, would cause *Empialla*. And another mode of *Lipparia* made from phlegm appears, which he did not pose above: namely, that the matter making this *Empialla* is placed within... so that if he feels the putrefaction as cold in the external parts, the putrid vapor is carried within and heats the internal parts. And it is a wonder why Avicenna made no mention of that. Perhaps the reason was that he expected us to understand it through the things being said in this chapter. It must be considered that Avicenna says "if it existed," because it is a doubt whether heat and cold can exist in the same part. One way of saying this is that these qualities are not in the same "formal part," but in different formal parts so close together that the sense is deceived in judging the location of the parts, and judges the whole to be hot and cold—just as he gives the example of the neck of a dove <note>a common medieval example of iridescence where colors seem to mix</note> and of many red and white pictures in one space, where because of this they are judged to be different colors in the same [place].

fen Tractatus 11

<margin>a Add this: he speaks of movement toward the outside. And there is no doubt that it is known that vapors are sent inward. The dilation of the arteries assists in this.</margin>
<margin>b And you. Because someone might ask how phlegm putrefies and becomes cold, and was not cold before. He says that you already know the cause of this above in the chapter on *empyema* <note>original: "empiada"</note>.</margin>
<margin>c In the management of cold humor in the arrangement of motion: that is, that the regimen causes cold when it is moved because it cools, whereas previously while resting it did not cool. It must be considered that Galen <note>original: "Gal."</note> seems to feel, in the cause of this fever according to the common exposition of the second book on the differences of fevers—namely, that the diversity of the parts of phlegm placed next to each other results in one part putrefying and becoming hot, while another part near it does not putrefy and remains cold.</margin>

...part. And that which confirms this way of speaking is: because if heat and cold were impressed upon one and the same part in this fever, then the feverish person would perceive "tepidity" <note>lukewarmness</note>, which is the form between these contraries. And he would not perceive those two contraries; and we pass over this here. For we have already written about this above in the second book on accident and disease. One must also consider that part. And there is no cause for a great deal of harm, namely through universal putrefaction, because then these materials would not grow cold. Therefore, only a small part of them putrefies, as we said regarding empyema. Or there is no great harm, namely because of a malignant putrefaction; because if this were the case, then the <term>virtue<gloss>the body's natural vital power or strength</gloss></term> would flee violently to the interior parts, and the exterior would grow cold, which causes the most harm. Then, when they begin to putrefy, each of them sends out a hot vapor including its own parts, and where it is cold. And you indeed already know the cause in the management of cold humor in the arrangement of motion.

### On Humoral Syncopal Fever. Chapter 55.

This is mostly due to a raw, repletional <term>phlegm<gloss>one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture; "repletional" refers to an excess of this fluid</gloss></term> which causes a highly uneven fever, because it now overcomes the virtue. And for the most part, the weakness of the mouth of the stomach aids in this; and when it moves and begins to putrefy, it overcomes the virtue more and causes hesitation, so that if it is left alone with the matter, it will not be able to struggle against it. And when an effort is made in its evacuation, it becomes disobedient if done with ease; or it moves with a motion that suffocates the virtue. And when one is occupied in its evacuation with a loosening of the belly or <term>bloodletting<gloss>original: "pblebotōia"</gloss></term> with labor, the virtue cannot tolerate it. For how will it be tolerated when <term>syncope<gloss>fainting or sudden loss of consciousness due to the heart being overwhelmed</gloss></term> occurs there with its own arrival? And with all this, they are in great need of evacuation. And again, they are in great need of food because in their humors there is nothing to nourish the body or give it life, and the body is deprived of nourishment. Yet if you strive to feed them, the matter is increased.

"This for the most part..." After he determined fevers in which there is heat and cold, and most of them are phlegmatic, he determines other matters regarding fevers. And first concerning humoral syncopal fever: it is called syncopal because syncope occurs in it, and it is called humoral because it occurs with a multitude of humors. And first he places that which arises from phlegm, which is most common; second, that which arises from <term>cholera<gloss>yellow bile, the humor associated with heat and dryness</gloss></term>. (See below: "And when it happens"). The first part has three sections: first, he makes it known from the cause and somewhat from the accident; second, from the method of cure; third, from its accidents. (See below: "Which if left alone" and "And it happens"). It must be considered that raw phlegm is more often found in a "repletional" substance (of great quantity) than repletional cholera. And therefore he says "mostly" or "repletional," because through many repletions and nauseating satieties all this is gathered; this conforms to the words of Galen <note>original: "Gal. 12. tera." referring to book 12 of the Methodus Medendi</note>. It causes a highly uneven fever. This is explained in many ways. First: that is, very different from other phlegmatic fevers as will appear from its method of cure and accidents. Second, uneven: that is, interpolated; because perhaps it is more interpolated or frequent than continuous, because perhaps nature could not sustain such malice continuously. Third, uneven: that is, separate and distinct or distant between one <term>paroxysm<gloss>the period of greatest intensity or fit of a fever</gloss></term> and another. For although the matter is plentiful, it is thick, viscous, cold, and unfit for putrefaction. Therefore, it more often happens that paroxysm follows paroxysm. It "aids upon it," namely the syncopal fever, because syncope is to be produced in it on account of its proximity to the heart, as appears in the third book of Avicenna's <note>original: "can. fen. xi."</note> *Canon*. Or it aids upon it, namely multiplying the cold phlegmatic matter. It must be considered that it "overcomes the virtue": because the delay harms more and causes the virtue to hesitate; for the virtue does not know what it is doing. For if it ceases from the movement of the matter, it is suffocated under it; if it moves it, it is also suffocated under it, as will appear. "Which virtue if it were left alone." It must also be considered that in this difficulty of cure, the hesitation of the virtue appears. Avicenna <note>original: "auic."</note> shows the difficulty of the cure: first through the act of evacuation. For either you will not evacuate them and they are suffocated, or you will evacuate and then it does not obey the movement because the matter is raw. Or it agitates and suffocates. Or you will evacuate with a strong pharmacy or a copious bloodletting. And this is what he says: "with a loosening of the belly with labor," that is, a strong, laborious one, or "bloodletting with labor," as both refer to the same, that is, a copious bloodletting is not tolerated etc. For these laborious evacuations will strongly move that matter beforehand, which, before it is drawn out, will kill [the patient] since the evacuations themselves cause syncope. It appears therefore that they cannot be evacuated, and yet they strongly need evacuation because there is a great repletion. Consider however that in bloodletting there is a special harm; hence it is entirely forbidden in book 12 of the *Therapeutics* and book 16 of the *Continens*. Second, he shows the difficulty of cure through feeding. For they need food and cannot be fed, because the matter is increased and the [existing] matter is diminished—that is, it would be diminished through abstinence; or "diminished" means existing as a small amount in comparison to itself when multiplied by food. For these patients have a weak stomach that does not digest food, but rather multiplies raw materials. But I say what must be done in such hesitations. It must be said that the cure can hardly be performed, and for the most part it is fatal; this suffering is as we have seen by experience. It should be known what stands in the place of these, namely in place of feeding and evacuation, as he seeks in the chapter on cure. It is doubted because he says that in this syncopal fever there is nothing in the humors to nourish and give life to the body through the multiplication of spirits. On the contrary, Galen <note>original: "Gal. ix. tera."</note> in the second chapter of book 9 of *Therapeutics*, speaking of this fever, says that those who are so disposed can endure the longest fasting because they have raw, undigested humors from which the body is nourished. The same is said by Rhazes <note>original: "Rab." usually refers to Rhazes in this context; "16 continētis" points to his Liber Continens</note> in the 16th book of the *Continens*. It must be said, as Rhazes and Galen suggest, that these phlegmatic humors are sometimes not very raw or very...

<column-break/>

...bad. And people then do not have a bad color nor sunken eyes, and such people can be nourished, and they happen to escape from these fevers. Sometimes they are very bad, raw, and indigestible, and with them a man's face takes on the color and habit as if he were <term>cachectic<gloss>suffering from a state of physical wasting and malnutrition</gloss></term>; and from such humors he cannot be nourished. And a man dies from this syncopal fever. Galen says the same there. For if they should happen to be not only raw but have reached such a point of corruption that they cannot finally be digested, it is impossible for one who is so sick to be saved.

<margin>a And it happens. There he places the signs and accidents of this fever: first from the pulse. It must be considered that this causes one to imagine this fever to be continuous, because the fuming of the matter to the heart appears to happen through the internal parts. Yet in an interpolated fever, such a fuming can occur just as we imagine a putrid smoke coming to the heart from materials outside the veins. It is doubted whether a man then suffers from fever when the cold thing is poured out to the heart. It must be said that then, through the harm of cold in the heart, one should not imagine that the man has a fever; but when he begins to fall into the harm of heat, then he begins to fever. For the sake of escaping the harm of cold, he says it happens through heating which nature performs, namely by moving the spirit and that "adrenal" putrefaction; and then when the parts of the phlegm are heated, the pulse becomes frequent and fast, since it cannot be "great" in the proper sense during <term>systole<gloss>the contraction of the heart</gloss></term> because of the multitude of vapors—more so than the speed or frequency of others. It is doubted whether regarding this, Galen <note>original: "Gal. 12. tera."</note> in the second chapter, speaking of the pulse of these patients, says at other times, namely from the first paroxysm, the arteries of these pulse more rarely and slowly than all others suffering from fever. Furthermore, it was said above that in phlegmatic fevers the pulses are more frequent than in others, but not faster, and this is because of the weakness of the virtue. Therefore, this will be much more so in the syncopal fever. It must be said in two ways: first, that the pulse in these is slower and rarer because of the mortification of heat under the raw, viscous matter even if the spirit putrefies. And this happens in comparison to other fevers. However, the systole compared to the diastole is faster and more frequent because of the great multitude of vapors around the heart. Second, that here he compares the pulse when the heart already yields to the harm of heat, to the pulse that was there before when the harm of cold stood; hence he says "more than the speed of others," namely the pulses preceding during the time of the harm of cold, but not of other feverish people. And therefore he adds: "although it overcomes them," namely in respect to other fevers, let there be smallness, etc.</margin>

diminished; and if he is not fed, the virtue falls. And it happens at its inception that a cold thing is poured out to the heart, causing syncope to occur; and the pulse is diminished, and slowed, and becomes rare. Furthermore, nature is diligent in the heating of the matter and its thinning. And the putrefaction that is moved in certain of its parts aids upon it; therefore the heart escapes from the harm and its coldness and falls into the harm of its heat, so that the pulse becomes fast and particularly in its contraction: more than the speed of others, although that which overcomes [it] is smallness, slowness, and rarity. And its period is the period of a phlegmatic [fever], and it does not differ from it; and with it there is a swelling of the face and a softness of the body. And the colors of those having the cause are not fixed upon one disposition; rather, sometimes the matter is ashy and leaden; and sometimes it becomes yellow <note>often meaning greenish in this context</note>; and sometimes it becomes black; and sometimes their lips become like the lips of one eating mulberries. Their eyes are dark green, protruding greatly during the commotion of the illness, so that it becomes like one who is <term>maniacal<gloss>suffering from a frantic or frenzied state</gloss></term>; and that which is under their <term>hypochondria<gloss>the upper regions of the abdomen, below the ribs</gloss></term> is of a violent swelling, and likewise their viscera. And sometimes they vomit something acid. And when they have an <term>abscess<gloss>original: "apostema," a localized collection of pus or a swelling</gloss></term> in certain viscera, then there is no hope at all. And sometimes it happens to them in...

¶ And the period. Because he says that this phlegm is not intensely foreign to the nature of phlegmatic fever, just as "glassy" phlegm is. For it is not believable that such could be found around the parts of the heart unless it were monstrous; but it is raw repletional phlegm, which is plentiful even if it were very bad. Therefore the paroxysm of a phlegmatic fever is preserved. ¶ And with it there is swelling of the face, as in <term>cachexia<gloss>wasting syndrome</gloss></term> on account of the thick vapors of raw phlegms and the malice of digestion. To softness on account of the mastery of phlegm in the heart. And the colors, etc. They are not fixed because of the struggle of the resisting virtue, rather sometimes its matter, that is, the skin: and it is the matter, i.e., the subject; or the matter, i.e., the color; or the matter, i.e., the coloring humor. Citrine <note>yellow</note>, i.e., green: for frequently one is taken for the other, as in the second commentary on the *Prognostics* and the 21st commentary on the second book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*. However, this diversity occurs according to the different degree of the struggle and the suffocation of heat under the matter: as when it is less suffocated, it appears ashen or leaden, but when more, it becomes green or black. And from this depraved suffocation the lips become black, as in one who eats mulberries. Dark eyes, etc., by the mortification of heat which is suffocated by the matter. Protruding, that is, preeminent because of many phlegmatic vapors; and it is possible that it is because of some manner of suffocation. At the commotion, i.e., the victory of the sickness, namely at the intensity of the illness. Moreover, we have declared what "commotion" signifies in the speeches of Avicenna on the 6th section in the chapter on the causes of the "bite" or motion or commotion, that is, the beginning of the paroxysm. And he becomes like one who is maniacal on account of the restlessness and anxiety in the virtue, and on account of the distress of the stomach from its repletion, whence it does not rest in its place. Thaddeus <note>original: "Tbadcus," likely Thaddaeus Alderotti</note> however says that he becomes maniacal only as far as the face, because he has it terribly and vehemently inflamed on account of thick windiness. Viscera: because they are also the higher places toward the flanks and the navel.

<margin>b ¶ And sometimes they vomit something acid. Because in their stomachs this phlegm is prone to be generated because of the coldness.</margin>
<margin>c ¶ And sometimes. Everyone agrees on this because the virtue cannot tolerate the malice of an abscess and its fever. And the one common safety of an abscess in the internal parts is the strength of the virtue, as in book 5, chapter 5 of the *Therapeutics*. Furthermore, we cannot feed these people for fear of the abscess, and they need food for the sake of the virtue, not having anything that nourishes and gives life, as is understood from Galen in the same place in part and in book 12 of the *Therapeutics*.</margin>

It must be considered that the dominant <term>cholera<gloss>bile</gloss></term>, namely a large quantity of thick bile, like yolk-colored bile according to Avicenna, through that which he says "dominates in the internal parts," can in its motion cause syncope by suffocating the heat. Therefore it is called syncopal. ¶ It is called humoral because of the multitude of this humor; a burning occurs because of the heat of the humor when the heat occupies it. Whence a greater burning occurs than in the aforementioned pure phlegmatic fever; they vomit bile, because this yolk-like bile is made from phlegm, and bile is found in many parts of the stomach. ¶ And they are to him. This can be explained in two ways. First, concerning the phlegmatic syncopal fever, and he had already said this; but he adds "for the most part" to show that it can be changed from that order. Second, "to him," i.e., the syncopal fever made from this bile. And I believe this was Avicenna's intention. For this bile is thick on account of the phlegm, and it has much exuberance, and therefore it can cause a paroxysm every day. And mostly...

The text highlights the extreme difficulty of treatment, as both evacuation (like bloodletting) and feeding the patient can lead to a fatal collapse of the "virtue" or life force.</summary>
