<meta>This page continues the technical classification of fevers, moving from the internal sensations of temperature to specific diagnostic categories: "syncopal" fevers (associated with fainting) and "diurnal/nocturnal" fevers (occurring by day or night). It transitions into the practical "Cure" or treatment section for phlegmatic fevers, following the teachings of Avicenna and Isaac Israeli.</meta>

Book III

**Column 1**

...it does so. Whether it should truly be called a "tertian" fever <note>a fever recurring every three days</note> or not is merely a question of naming.

<margin>a</margin>
**N**either fever, etc. This "syncopal" fever is named after the *syncope* <note>fainting or loss of strength</note> that occurs during it. It is called "diminished" to distinguish it from a "repletional" fever <note>a fever caused by an excess or "fullness" of humors</note>. For so, I believe, it signifies in Arabic: because that matter is not repletional, but is called "subtle" <note>thin or refined</note> because there is little of it, and it arises from subtle choler <note>yellow bile</note>; or because it happens to choleric people of a subtle habit. Or, among the Arabs, this "small, subtle fever" is called a "hectic" fever <note>original: "ethica," a wasting fever</note> such as occurs in "phthisics" <note>those suffering from wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note>, as is said in the treatise—not on phthisis itself, but because this syncopal fever is similar to those consumed by it, appearing like phthisics.

### Chapter 56. On the Small, Subtle Syncopal Fever.

<margin>b</margin>
**I**t is "acute" because it is intense and ends quickly: because in this fever, the "natural virtue" and "animal virtue" <note>the body's internal vital forces and cognitive/sensory powers</note> fail. And the pulse is at its weakest in a single paroxysm <note>the peak of a fever fit</note>: because in the first or second paroxysm, the strength falls with "addition"—that is, much more. Or it happens in the body—namely, this fever or this loss of strength—with speed, because it occurs suddenly due to the rapid movement of the material.

<margin>c</margin>
**A**nd sometimes. When there is great wickedness in the material, it does not suffice then. Mostly in the "fourth" <note>referring to a quartan cycle</note>. For the most part, this material is choleric, which could be subtle, poisonous, or "melancholic"—that is, made from burnt choler. The conditions of this material are that it be "subtle deep bile" in the limbs, such that the limbs cannot shake that material off. Either it is of a poisonous substance, or it is putrid. As such, it causes fever in a body of a hot and dry complexion, for this is the type of body in which these subtle choleric materials are found. Or, according to the sixteenth book of the *Continens* <note>a major medical encyclopedia by Al-Razi</note>, this material is prepared more for syncope through the process of "dissolution" <note>the breaking down of tissues or humors</note>.

...or in the first two with addition, or occurring in the body with speed. And sometimes it does not suffice with it until the fourth. Or it is made from subtle "chymes" <note>humors/juices</note>, mostly of which the choleric is of intense subtlety, or by the refinement of a wicked poisonous substance which has already undergone putrefaction in bodies of a very hot and dry complexion. Or more paroxysms of this fever are like those of a tertian fever.

### Chapter 57. On Diurnal and Nocturnal Fever from Phlegm.

<margin>d</margin>
**A**nd more paroxysms. Because for the most part, they are choleric paroxysms. But if this material is poisonous and melancholic, it has the nature of a paroxysm in the "fourth" <note>recurring every four days</note>. Or perhaps because this type of wicked choler is "leek-green" <note>original: "prazina"</note> or "rusty" <note>original: "eruginosa"</note>. Thus Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli</note> in the chapter on tertian fever: he does not like the idea that a fever should be made from leek-green or rusty bile, since the body's strength could not sustain it long enough to putrefy. We, however, believe this is not impossible. And if you prefer the opinion of Isaac, you may give this poisonous choler whatever name you wish.

A "diurnal" fever is one whose paroxysm happens in the day and its relief <note>original: "lepor"</note> in the night; a "nocturnal" fever is the reverse. Both are bad, but the diurnal is longer and worse, frequently turning into a "hectic" <note>wasting</note> fever because of its length and its occurrence in the heat of the day. And if it does not...

<margin>e</margin>
**B**ecause, etc. First, he describes the mode of these fevers and compares them to one another. Second, he proves it. One must consider that this fever is no different from an "interposed phlegmatic" fever <note>a fever caused by phlegm that comes and goes</note>; rather, it is the same as that, but is given this name by "accident" <note>circumstances</note>. For when a continuous fever invades every day during the day—specifically at the start of the day or midday—and cools down at night, so that even though a change occurs at the start of night or day, it nevertheless follows the movement of the day and the rest of the night, it is called "diurnal." If, however, the paroxysm begins as night approaches and cools during the day, in the same way, it is called "nocturnal." Because it is characteristic of phlegmatic fever to have a paroxysm every day, this fever is phlegmatic. Therefore, Avicenna <note>original: "Auic."</note> does not care to treat it differently below. If you consider it well, this fever could be choleric—such as a "double tertian" or a single tertian—and it differs from other tertians because it happens to change in its paroxysms, such as when it happens not to follow the movement of day or night. In a certain way, this is imaginable regarding "quartan" fever, which could be called diurnal if its movement is for the most part and most strongly in the day, and its rest is for the most part in the night. But because this cannot be properly adapted to melancholic fevers, Avicenna did not want this fever to be among the sum of the melancholic ones, since he said above that these fevers do not arise from melancholy. Perhaps the reason that moved Avicenna to speak of this fever was to show which is worse: for materials to be moved to a paroxysm in the day and cool at night, or the opposite. And the speech of Avicenna in these things he says is verified regarding any material that might be moved, whether it be phlegmatic, choleric, or melancholic; yet, such a mode of movement—called diurnal or nocturnal—is best adapted to phlegmatic fever.

<margin>f</margin>
**A**nd it makes. He proves that the diurnal is worse than the nocturnal. The first reason is because it causes one to fall into a "hectic" fever. The reason is twofold: first, because it is longer, being from more material, as he proves immediately; second, because it happens in the heat of the day. As if to say that the heat of the day and the heat of the fever join together in drying out the body and causing a hectic state.

<margin>g</margin>
**A**nd if itself. The second reason: that fever is more severe which happens at the hour most fit for the pores to open and for material to resolve into vapors. But the diurnal fever is of this kind. This is noted because it would not happen at that hour unless the material were abundant; for despite the opening of the pores and the resolution of the material, it still causes fever. This therefore signifies the multitude and strength of the material—specifically in its quality and movement—by which it can move against the body's strength despite the "resolution" <note>sweating out/evaporation</note> that takes place.

<margin>h</margin>
**A**nd it is necessary. The third reason: that fever is worse in which it is necessary for the patient to be fed at night and, similarly, to stay awake at night. But in diurnal fever, this is the case. This is noted because it is human custom to sleep at night. The minor point is noted: the patient should be fed in the hour of cooling, which is at night. But immediately after being fed, they must not sleep; for those having a "repletional" fever, such as phlegmatic ones, must not sleep immediately upon "repletion"—that is, upon taking food—unless the food has settled to the lower parts of the stomach. For otherwise, catarrhs evaporating to the head follow, which harm the stomach. A certain "suffocation" of heat in the stomach also follows. Therefore, it is necessary that they stay awake, and this weakens them. If you say: "When I am forced, and food is given to you at night, what shall I do about their sleep?" It must be said that you should do what seems the lesser evil. For you shall make them stay awake for one or two hours after food, and afterward, you allow them sleep. In this third reason, many comparisons could be made regarding feeding and sleep in the times of paroxysm for diurnal and nocturnal fever, which I omit.

<margin>i</margin>
**A**nd tolerance. This is the fourth reason, and it is mentioned with the first. He argues thus: a fever is worse in which there are two causes for falling into a hectic state; but in diurnal fever, there are two causes. One is the tolerance of the fever in the heat of the day, and this greatly dries and consumes the body. The other is wakefulness in the cold of night; that is, during the night, even though it is cold, wakefulness "resolves" and dries the body when a man ought to be resting and attending to digestion and the restoration of what was lost in the heat of the day.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

<margin>k</margin>
And to the highest degree, etc. Because it is from material that is abundant and strong.

<margin>l</margin>
**T**he Cure, etc. Having described these fevers, he sets down the cure here. First, of those that occur as phlegmatic fevers; second, of those that do not occur so, which are "phlegmatic-like" <note>original: "annepe phlegmatici"</note>. First, he presents the cure for a "periodic" <note>original: "p'todice"</note> phlegmatic fever. Second, he adapts it to the cure of a continuous fever. The first part has two sections: first, he sets down the cure owed by reason of the cause; second, he teaches how to aid the "accidents" <note>symptoms</note>. In the first part, he wants the cure to be diversified according to the diversity of the "times" <note>stages of the disease</note>, the "disposition" of the material, and the "species" of the materials. One might wonder why he says the cure is diversified by times, since the appearance or hiding of "digestion" <note>the process of the humors ripening/breaking down</note> already includes the diversity of times. It must be said that this cure is common to continuous and intermittent phlegmatic fevers, which Avicenna wanted in the following chapter. And here, when he says in the heading "The Cure of Phlegmatic Fever," although in this chapter they first seem to be applied to intermittent ones. The distinction of the stages of the disease is based on the symptoms, and this distinction happens more in continuous phlegmatic fever; it is a distinction regarding the "digestion" of the materials and suits both. As for the first distinction, he says it is diversified by the "hours"; as for the second, he says "according to the appearance." The diversification of the cure according to times (as the symptoms are distinct) is especially in comparison to the "state" <note>the peak</note>, in which the difficulty of symptoms lies; and it is a diversification in the order of feeding, which we have arranged for that state. But the diversification of the cure according to times distinguished by the alteration of the material is a diversification in the use of medicines that promote "digestion" and "evacuation," which medicines address the material according to how it is disposed. Or it could be answered otherwise: that the cure of phlegmatic fever would not be diversified by time except by the diversity of the disposition of the material, because perhaps these occur simultaneously. But he says this for greater clarity: the cure is diversified by times, and diversity by times is diversity by the appearance or hiding of digestion; for we properly attend to this distinction of times in phlegm. And Avicenna says this because it often happens in phlegmatic fever that the "times" are broken; for when signs of digestion clearly appear, as if the fever were at its peak, the signs of "rawness" <note>undigested humors</note> return. And then, when signs of rawness appear, one should not use the cure for the "increase" stage, but the cure for the "beginning." Therefore, so that no error falls in the speech saying the cure is by times, he adds that by "times" I mean those things distinguished by the disposition of the material, so that at whatever time rawness or the hiding of digestion appears in the material, it should then be treated with the cure for the beginning.

### Chapter 58. On the Cure of Phlegmatic Fever.

The cure of this sickness is diversified according to its "hours"—namely, the beginning, the increase, the peak <note>original: "statū"</note>, and the decline—and according to the appearance of "digestion" in it or its hiding, and it is diversified according to its materials: namely, "vinegary" phlegm, "glassy" phlegm, "salty" phlegm, and "sweet" phlegm. And all its species share three things in the hour of the beginning: the necessity of "equal lenification" <note>mild purging</note> or vomiting; and the necessity of administering "subtiliating" <note>thinning</note>, "incising" <note>cutting/breaking up</note>, and "diuretic" <note>urine-promoting</note> medicines.

<margin>m</margin>
**A**nd all. Here he follows the matter: first, according to the different intention by times and the disposition of the material; second, according to the diversity of the species of phlegm; third, he sets down the medicines and things suitable according to those intentions. The first part has three sections: first, he sets down the curative intentions required in the beginning; second, what is done in the "increase"; third, he orders the regimen in comparison to the "state," giving understanding of the "decline." In the first, he says all species of phlegmatic fever agree on three things for the cure in the beginning: first, "lenifying" <note>softening the bowels</note> equally through the belly or vomiting; second, in "subtiliation" <note>thinning</note> through "incision"; third, in diuretics. One might wonder how Avicenna does these three. It must be said that lenification of the belly is one; vomiting is the second; thinning, incising, and provoking urine are the third. Or otherwise: lenification and vomiting are the first (to evacuate the proper and more manifest paths); incision and subtiliation are the second; but the provoking of urine is the third. It should be considered that "lenification" is taken in two ways. First, properly for a "lenitive evacuation"—for example, with violets or cassia—by which nothing of the phlegmatic material is evacuated except by chance, but the parts of the intestines are cleansed. And this is called "equal" because it is a light lenification. In another way, lenification is called "evacuation through the belly" that takes something of the material which is the joined cause or near others, such as that which is done with a turbid odor, and it is a "minorative" <note>reducing</note> evacuation. And this lenification is called "equal" because it is light compared to the stronger ones that are done later. It can be understood in both ways, as will appear. Similarly, vomiting is of two types according to "equality": one light, and one taking something of the material. It should also be considered that in phlegmatic fever we recognize it is "repletional," in which there are "dregs" <note>original: "feces"</note> of material and others around the parts of the stomach and intestines; and regarding this, the intention arises in the beginning for "equal lenification" and "equal vomiting." Second, we consider that the material is thick and viscous, and "incision" and "subtiliation" are appropriate. And we consider that it can be driven into the "emulgent" veins <note>veins leading to the kidneys</note>, and we use diuretics by which we [expel] it through the veins.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "Cure" or treatment phase for phlegmatic fevers. It moves from general definitions of the fever types into the specific timing and application of "digestive" medicines—those intended to thin and break down the cold, thick humor of phlegm—before evacuation can be attempted. It draws heavily on the authorities of Avicenna, Serapion, Galen, and Rhazes.</meta>

### Treatise II
Folio 3

<margin>a</margin>
**A**nd when he declares what he has said: he intends that although the things previously mentioned are suitable at the beginning of phlegmatic fevers, nevertheless, according to Serapion <note>Serapion the Elder, a 9th-century Syrian Christian physician</note>, if you move the matter before three or four days with the aforementioned softening, "cutting," thinning, and diuretic medicines, you will cause harm; you will achieve nothing. But after three days, one can use them, because the heat of the fever already begins to thin the matter and "digest" it <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" refers to the process where the body's heat acts upon a raw humor to prepare it for expulsion</note> to some extent. From this, it is understood that external heat digests the matter.

It is first doubted whether we can use an equal softening treatment before the first day. It must be said, as a general rule for all such cases, that for the time before the third day, or up to the third or fourth, I understand this as the time of "crudity" in the matter <note>the state of the humor being raw and unprocessed by the body’s heat</note>. I recognize this because the matter is discolored and thin. However, by the time after three days, I understand a time of some hidden, initiated digestion—whether it begins through medical art or from within the body—and whether the heat of the fever performs this. This is the time of some thinning and digestion of the phlegmatic matter. Consequently, some of it will begin to mix with the urine. I recognize this because the urine begins to be somewhat colored, or becomes turbulent, or thickens. 

And although Avicenna <note>the 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> and also Serapion begin this time after three or four days, it is nonetheless possible that in some individuals it does not begin until six or seven days; this depends on the diversity of bodies and materials. Therefore, take Avicenna's command as an example: the meaning is that you should not "move" the humors with the aforementioned medicines until some appearance of digestion occurs. From this, the previous doubt is resolved. For if by "softening" you understand that which is done with enemas, then those with cassia or syrup of violets and the like are not effective. I say that this can be done before the third day to purge fecal matters, as was said in the general causes. If, however, by "softening" you understand a light and slight softening of the matter, I say that it cannot be done before the third day because the matter is "crude" <note>unrefined</note>. All these things were known above in the general cure of putrid fevers.

In the same way, the question of vomiting is resolved—whether it is appropriate in a phlegmatic fever before the third day. If it is a light vomiting—for example, with warm water—and it is for cleansing certain matters not yet attached to the stomach but ready to be vomited, then it is a good custom; because all or most factors agree, vomiting can be induced before the third day. But if the vomit is stronger, intended for the nature of a matter difficult to move, it requires some preparation so that it is not done before the third day. 

It is then doubted whether before the third day we can use "cutting," thinning, and diuretic syrups. It seems so according to Avicenna, for in a fever he begins and proceeds until the seventh day with *julep* <note>original: "genellabin," a sweet medicinal drink</note> such as fennel water and parsley water; but these are thinning and urine-provoking. Furthermore, Al-Habbas in the third book of his *Practice* and Rhazes <note>the 9th-century Persian physician al-Razi</note> in the tenth book immediately proceed with honeyed vinegar syrup <note>original: "sirupum acetosum mellinus," similar to oxymel</note>, which is "cutting" <note>original: "incisiuus," a medicine that breaks down thick humors</note>. On the opposing side is Avicenna here in the 7th chapter and the 6th chapter of his *Breviary*, where he says that the treatment of this phlegmatic fever universally, at its inception after three or four days, is with things that thin and "cut," such as *sekanjabin* <note>original: "secaniabin," a Persian syrup of honey and vinegar</note> and things that provoke urine. And Galen <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician</note>, in his *Therapeutics to Glaucon*, says that oxymel <note>honey and vinegar</note> should be used after the first few days; Rhazes also wants the same in the 16th book of the *Continens*. Furthermore, these medicines are of strong virtue, which disturb and move the matter and prevent it from being digested. Avicenna leans toward this reasoning.

To solve these points, it must be considered that "cutting" and thinning things are those that only prepare the matter for evacuation, but diuretics are those that evacuate the matter through the urine. Therefore, everything that thins phlegmatic matter is of a weaker operation than that which leads that matter out through the urine. An example of thinning and "cutting" agents for phlegm is simple honeyed vinegar syrup, or with fennel root or parsley. But an example of diuretics is the "syrup of five roots," or one in which *asarabacca* <note>original: "assarus," a plant used as a purgative</note> and similar things are placed. We do not intend here to return to the principles by showing by what virtue thinning, cutting, or the provocation of urine occurs. For we have already noted this in the second book of the *Canon*. Although the substances and virtues are distinct, it happens due to the diversity of patients that a provocative medicine is also "cutting" and thinning. For instance, if the phlegmatic matter is very thick and viscous, honeyed vinegar syrup does not suffice for its digestion (that is, for its division and thinning). Instead, a syrup with hyssop and two or five roots would be needed, which would be sufficient for provoking urine in sweet phlegmatic matter that is not very thick or viscous. A syrup for provoking urine in very thick matter would be one with roots, asarabacca, and capers.

This same effect also occurs from differences in dosage. For a small dose of the syrup of roots would thin and divide the matters, while a larger dose would provoke, or could provoke, the urine. Third, the same occurs from the diversity of the disposition of the intestines and urinary paths. For the broth of chickpeas <note>original: "jus cicerum"</note> given to men with open paths loosens the belly; it does not move to urine but thins and wipes away the matter of the stomach and intestines. It softens the belly by its "nitrosity," especially that of black chickpeas. In another person, however, it will take its course to the urine and provoke it, as we said in the second book in the chapter on chickpeas. Fourth, the same occurs from the mixing of things that restrain the motion of thinning and provoking medicines, keeping them in the first parts of the stomach and intestines. This happens when one mixes rose sugar or rose syrup with the syrup of roots; thus its provocative power is lessened, and it remains as an agent that divides and thins the matters. And if a diuretic substance, such as a decoction of gromwell <note>original: "granorum solis," literally "seeds of the sun"</note>, is mixed with a laxative syrup, it causes that syrup to prepare for the urinary paths and to operate in them to provoke urination.

Second, it must be considered that "cutting" and thinning agents are of two kinds. Some are light, not stirring or agitating the matter, such as honeyed or simple sugar vinegar syrup—specifically with vinegar that is not very sharp or used in great quantity. Others are stronger "cutting" and thinning agents that can agitate the matters, such as compound vinegar syrup with certain roots, or with hyssop or thyme, and where the vinegar is very sharp. We say that a "diuretic" is properly so called when it leads a sensible part of the matter out through the urine, such as the syrup of five roots and seeds and the like. And in these syrups and medicines, there are also many degrees. Another type is a "diuretic" properly speaking which casts itself into the urine and does not move the matter of the fever; but it can cause certain virulent humors in the veins, which are ready for evacuation and joined to the fever, to be urinated out. We spoke of this at length above in the general rules of every cure. An example is a thin *julep* and thin barley water.

Having established these points, we say that before the third day—that is, while "crudity" persists in the phlegmatic matter—we must in no way use strong thinning, "cutting," or provoking agents. The reason is that all of these agitate and stir the matter; they resolve the thin part or provoke it and leave the thick part behind. Hence Galen, in the fourth book of his *Regimen*, says specifically regarding strong diuretics: "I do not praise diuretics now," etc. For it is not good to digest with such great disturbance or commotion; it is not necessary at all. And thus, because it agitates much matter (of which there is a lot), it hinders digestion. When the matters are digested, we can then use stronger ones and increase the strength of the medicines according to the degree of digestion. 

But you will say that once the matter is digested, we do not need thinning or "cutting" agents, whether strong or weak. It must be said first that we do not need them for *digesting*, but for *provoking*, so that strong thinning agents then become provocative agents. Or it should be said that we do not need this for the digestion of the part that is already digested, but for the other parts. Thus, at the beginning, because of the multitude of the matter, we cannot use strong laxatives or thinning agents lest they agitate and corrupt the healthy parts and cause thickening. But after the beginning—that is, after some digestion and evacuation of the matter—we can use stronger thinning agents to complete the digestion. For once the matter has been "cleansed" <note>original: "mundificatione," a purification process</note>, there is not so much fear concerning the agitation of the remaining matter which is not yet digested, nor the "earthification" <note>turning into a dry, hard, earthy state</note> of that which is digested.

<margin>Know therefore from this that Avicenna adds to the strength of thinning and diuretic agents as one proceeds by digesting and diminishing the humor. Consider that increasing the degree of these medicines in the process helps because the parts of the stomach and intestines are cleansed of the bulk of the matter. Therefore, there is not such great suspicion regarding the penetration of these matters into the veins through diuretics and thinning agents intended to penetrate the veins and provoke urination. I say secondly that before the third day we can use a weak provocative agent, which is called "provoking" only in an equivocal sense, such as thin *julep* and thin barley water. But we do not use a "provocative" properly so called, as we said. We can also use a light thinning and "cutting" agent that is not agitating, such as simple oxymel or with a decoction of maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillorum veneris"</note> or some root, according to what your judgment dictates so that no commotion occurs in the matter. 

From these points, Avicenna's primary intention appears. For he says that if the matter is thinned, one can use these—that is, those that are strong and moving in some degree. But "before that"—that is, while the matter remains crude—will you move the matter with a "softener" (that is, a diminisher that works by resolving) and with strong thinning and "cutting" agents that move the matter, and then with true diuretics? No, because all these move and agitate, and therefore you will cause harm and achieve nothing. 

It appears second from Avicenna's intention that if the matter is thick and crude, and it does not appear that it is being digested in any way, you should lead it to the beginning of its digestion with light thinning and "cutting" agents, such as simple vinegar syrup or others that do not agitate the matter. When that thinning begins to appear, you will then begin to move to stronger syrups, such as adding to one ounce of simple syrup three ounces of fennel water, or giving one ounce of compound syrup with one or two roots and three ounces of liquid honey of roses, or as it seems best to you. And as the matter proceeds by diminishing, so you can increase the degree of these. 

It appears third that the contradiction between the authors is settled: those who allow "cutting" and thinning agents immediately from the beginning and those who deny them are referring to different things. It is doubted what the order between these is. It must be said that first, it is necessary to soften the belly with enemas or another softener; then, if expedient, to induce a light vomiting. Second, one must use digestive, "cutting," and thinning agents. Third, one must diminish the matter with a laxative or a provocative of urine, according to what appears best to you. If, however, by "softening" we mean "diminishing," then the matter must first be somewhat digested—either by nature, or the fever, or light medicines—afterward diminished, then strong "cutting" and thinning agents used, and afterward provoked through the urine. This seems to be the opinion of Rhazes in the 16th book of the *Continens*.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>b</margin>
**A**nd in the increase. One must consider this according to "equality"—that is, according to what is appropriate for each specific matter. Or according to "equality" because it is not thick (as at the beginning) nor thin (as at the peak); or according to "equality" because it is not thin like in a tertian fever nor thick like in a quartan fever. It is doubted why he made no mention of the regimen through medicines. It must be said that Avicenna clearly understood this from the preceding rules. For if at the beginning, after some thinning of the matter, it is allowed that you "move" it with "cutting," thinning, provocative, and diminishing agents, then it is allowed much more in the "increase" phase <note>original: "augmento," the phase where the fever's intensity grows</note>, in which the digested matter can be diminished and provoked, and the remainder more safely digested.

<margin>c</margin>
**A**nd perhaps. Here he organizes the regimen of the beginning and the increase in comparison to the "status" <note>original: "statum," the peak or plateau of the fever</note>. First, when the peak is near; second, when it is far off. Third, he declares certain things there. If it is certain, he says in the third part: "If however..." It should be considered that by "barley water" we understand *ptisana* <note>a medicinal barley broth</note>. If, therefore, one is content with that in the first three days, and if this fever does not pass into the fourth day, then Avicenna’s statement above—that the beginning of a phlegmatic fever lasts fifteen days—was true in most cases.

<margin>d</margin>
**I**f it is certain. Here consider that in a phlegmatic fever, when the indication is taken from the matter, abstinence from food is appropriate. Also, sleep is used upon it to digest and consume the matter, and exercise to resolve it; there is no fear concerning the potential of exercise nor of inflammation in this fever as there is in "hot" fevers. And insofar as these things would weaken the patient, they are not appropriate. But if the peak is far off, abstinence would weaken them. Therefore, when the peak is far off, this is not appropriate. Rather, at the beginning, we incline toward "thickening" the regimen; and when the increase arrives at first, it requires at its own beginning to be thinned in respect to the regimen of the start. And thus, it proceeds with thinning. These things are written in the 18th book of the *Continens*. 

It should also be considered according to the "dynamic" power <note>original: "dynam," referring to vital force</note> that he assumes here that a "crisis" <note>the turning point of a disease</note> can occur in intermittent fevers. For this is the cure of intermittent fevers no less than continuous ones, in which he organizes the cure with respect to the nearness or distance of the peak. And this is according to whether a crisis can occur in it. He also says the same above in the chapter on the cure of tertian fever: "For if a crisis follows," etc. Galen holds the contrary in the third book of *On Crises*, first chapter. He has already shown this where he says that the solution of a sickness happens suddenly when the sicknesses remain continuous and not intermittent. We, however, considered this doubt trivial and not applicable here.

<margin>e</margin>
**I**f, however, the peak... Because he had persuaded that at the beginning one could thin the matter with consideration given to the material, and also when we want to temper it if the fever is brief and from little, thin matter, he therefore declares here in which phlegmatic fevers a more excessive thinning of the regimen is allowed. He intends that the longer the peak is delayed, the more safely you could thin at the beginning for several days. Because in the following days you will be able to help more with a "thickening" of the regimen for some days, and afterward proceed gradually toward the peak by thinning. For a long time is sufficient for this in a prolonged sickness, but it would not suffice in an acute one. And because in prolonged phlegmatic fevers, having considered the matter at the beginning, you can thin the regimen for some days—for example, giving only barley water or *julep* if it is going to last.

It debates the timing for using thinning syrups and diuretics, concluding that treatments must be scaled according to the stage of the fever and the thickness of the patient's phlegm.</summary>

### Book
# III

four days. Nevertheless, in the proper order, you ought to provide a small chicken from the beginning of the state of the illness. And therefore, he wishes that you do not stay for a long time at that beginning with this subtle regimen <note>A "subtle regimen" refers to a diet of very light, thin foods intended to avoid adding more "bulk" to the body's humors</note>, whether it be experimental or looking only at the matter. But when seven days have passed, you shall no longer continue upon it: because it weakens, and it can weaken the power of the mouth of the stomach if there were much subtlety of diet, drawing corrupt materials toward the stomach.

<margin>a</margin> **And how often.** It is clear that after much thinning of the diet, one will return to "thickening" <note>Moving from thin broths to more substantial foods like bread and meat</note>. Therefore, he intends that you should not return to a very abundant regimen [all at once], such as whole chickens—that is, complete with bread.

<margin>b</margin> **And muzaguarach.** This is a method of preparing a certain sauce <note>original: "saporis"</note>; or it is a food made from chickens, sour grape juice <term>agresta - the tart juice of unripened grapes</term>, and vinegar, which was previously called *malabach*. Therefore, let a small boiling of chicken or a little meat suffice, or let barley meal suffice, as it seems best to you. And perhaps that is a case in itself: namely, that although you thin the diet at the beginning, you should not persist in that thinning; likewise, if you provide "thickening" food at the beginning, it should not be too heavy.

<margin>c</margin> **Or let the decline appear.** Here he hints at the regimen for the "decline" <note>the "declinatio" is the phase of a disease where the symptoms begin to fade and the patient recovers</note>. He intends that you can more safely thicken the regimen and give chickens during the decline than at the beginning.

<margin>d</margin> **Further.** Here he differentiates the cure according to the type of matter. He intends first that when "sweet" or "salty" phlegm is present—and generally when it is less thick, less viscous, and less cold—the softening <note>original: "lenitio" - loosening of the bowels</note>, which is the reduction of the matter, should be done with a milder medicine. For example, using only the scent of turbith <note>a purgative root</note> or the pith of safflower. But for "vinegary" or "glassy" phlegm <note>terms used for extremely cold, thick, and congealed humors</note>, and generally for thicker, more viscous, and colder phlegm, the reduction should be done with a more laborious medicine because it must be more powerful, such as with the body of turbith or agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note>. Further, knowing that in sweet and salty phlegm, a certain "cooling"—that is, a reduction of heat—is necessary; but in glassy and vinegary phlegm, neither cooling nor reduction of heat is necessary. And this is understood thirdly: in sweet and salty phlegm, we need "digestive" medicines <note>medicines that "ripen" or process the humor</note> that are thinning and "cutting" <term>incisiuis - medicines that "cut" through thick, sticky humors like a knife through grease</term> in which there is no strong heating, such as honeyed or sugary syrup of vinegar. But in glassy or vinegary phlegm, etc. 

One might doubt how he allows thinning and cutting medicines for salty phlegm, since they might be very drying, and salty phlegm is already dry. It must be said first that this statement refers only to medicines that process the phlegm. Or otherwise, that both sweet and salty phlegm are viscous and thick, needing thinning and cutting; and this cannot be done without something "dry," though it does not primarily need heating. He intends, therefore, that in this sweet phlegm one should focus on thinning and cutting primarily; although the medicine doing this is dry in the category of "cutters," provided it is not hot, it is suitable, just as wine vinegar is suitable here.

<margin>e</margin> **And more suitable.** After the causes of the cure according to the times and according to the materials, he here gives the medicines suitable according to the times and according to the states of the illness, since the time allows this in this sickness, whereas it would not be allowed in an acute fever. 

Once the seventh day has passed, do not persist in thinning the diet, because that weakens and adds to the weakness of the mouth of the stomach. And as often as he feels a greater length of illness, thin the diet less, although thinning it is altogether more necessary in this than in a quartan fever <note>a fever that returns every fourth day, usually linked to "melancholy"</note>. And similarly, you must not hasten to feed him with things like chicken and bread with *muzaguarach* unless weakness is feared, or the decline of the disease appears. 

Further, the cure is varied for the one whose cause is salty or sweet phlegm, and the one whose phlegm is glassy and vinegary, which produces excessive cold in which the body does not warm up. Nevertheless, in the first two types, a softening with mild medicine and a certain cooling is necessary. And in these [latter] two, a more laborious medicine is needed. In the first two, "cutting" is needed with thinning agents that do not have much heat, though they have much drying power. And in these [latter] two, it is necessary to use that which thins with cutting and heating with sharpness; and specifically when the phlegm is mixed with melancholy <note>black bile</note>. For in such cases, things like "diacyminum" <note>a cumin-based preparation</note>, a confection of sulfur, and the administration of salty things are necessary. 

And the more suitable medicines administered at the beginning are "geleniabin" <note>a conserve of roses and honey</note> up to the seventh day. And it is not bad if fennel water, endive water, and parsley water are administered again with the geleniabin according to necessity. And syrup of vinegar is of vehement necessity again, along with honey-water with hyssop. And it is possible that through this, that which is sought regarding the softening of nature <note>bowel movements</note> may be achieved, specifically with a solution made of rose sugar and the red roses called "Persian" <note>original: "persicis"</note>, since both are laxative and softening.

<column-break/>

whether it be endive water or parsley water, and whether these be simple or mixed. And the use of syrup of vinegar and honey-water at the beginning is well known. You should begin, therefore, with whichever you wish according to your judgment gathered from many factors. For example, if a man has a very weak stomach, easily upset by vinegar, and along with this a liver that is becoming hot while the matter is quite viscous: you will give for digestion in the morning this: an ounce each of liquid honey-roses, endive water, and parsley water. Or give a syrup made by art having these virtues or intentions.

<margin>f</margin> **And it is possible.** Here can be placed the second rule, or part of the preceding rule, in which he shows: that although the aforesaid things tend to thin and cut the materials, nevertheless from them we also seek the softening of the belly; and specifically when the *geleniabin* is made of Persian roses, because it purges gently and softens. And we ought to understand that purging the upper parts of the belly softens it. These "Persian roses" are not known to me, but our red roses do this sufficiently.

<margin>g</margin> **And although it is necessary that his softening be strengthened.** And it should be rubbed in *lueleb* water <note>possibly a preparation of hops or a similar climbing plant</note>; and let it be mixed, if he wishes, with *castafi* <note>a medicinal ingredient, possibly a typo for a gum or seed</note> and penidium <term>penidium - a twisted sugar-candy used as a pectoral or vehicle for medicine</term>. And again, *geleniabin* taken with honey and turpentine mixed with *lueleb* water: but let there not be a constant persistence in using laxatives at the beginning and afterward, especially when the matter is mixed with choler <note>yellow bile</note>. For that leads to corruption and pain <note>original: "prolapsionis" - likely a reference to exhaustion or prolapse</note>. 

And many men indeed give in a drink at the beginning a medicine of turbith every night; and likewise a mastic pill twice a week; and likewise pills of diuretic seeds. 

**Description of the turbith medicine:** Take: ginger and mastic, a dram each; and turbith ground like a fine powder <note>original: "alcohol"</note>, a dram; and four drams of "tabarzēt" sugar <note>a very pure, hard white sugar</note>. Mix them all, and let it be given to him in a drink every night in the amount of one *aureus* <note>a weight roughly equal to a gold coin</note>. This should be done when nature is not soft <note>when the patient is constipated</note>.

<margin>i</margin> **If indeed he responds.** If he responds twice every day, he does not need this. I indeed do not like waiting for digestion and softening with the things we said before; rather, it is necessary that some of the matter be evacuated, and the rest be waited for until it is digested. And let that be done with ease, little by little, without excess; then let it proceed to diuretics. 

And I also abhor it when it is like the water of prunes and tamarinds and such; those things which weaken and dissolve the "subtle" parts. And if the matter is inclined toward the addition of cold: let the pith of safflower be mixed with it. 

**And if the matter is inclined toward the choleric:** let it be mixed with syrup of violets, or violets preserved with *siracoft* <note>an unidentified medicinal preparation</note>, or crushed dry violets. And you should help with light clysters <note>enemas</term> made of honey and salt and fig water and sesame oil. 

And vomiting should be induced with radish water, and radishes infused in syrup of vinegar with seeds, and such like. **And if much vomiting is necessary** because of the multitude of what happens to him regarding nausea and the alteration of the taste of the mouth, let them administer grains...

<margin>g h</margin> **To follow.** This is the second or third rule regarding the logic of softening with *lueleb*. It is a type of minor milky substance <note>original: "lactitinii"</note> that we wrote about above in the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers. It must be considered that these softening agents have a degree of "attraction" <note>the power to pull humors toward the bowels</note>, and *lueleb* ought to be given when three days have already passed according to the true rule: when the matter is choleric—that is, mixed phlegm and choler. But you will ask why this persistence in softening should not be done. He says because those things soften the mouth of the stomach; therefore, the stomach is then weakened. And this is the cause of the corruption of the complexion of the whole body. Nor is there no cause: for it is not specifically assigned in phlegmatic cases where there is some choler. It must be said, therefore, that the aforesaid softening agents draw out the thin matter and leave the thick; and specifically when the matter is choleric, because the "tereniabin" <note>manna/honey-dew</note> and *lueleb* draw out some of that. It happens, therefore, that the thick phlegm remains, causing more blockage <term>oppilans - obstructing the vessels or organs</term>, and a disposition toward dropsy and cachexia <note>a wasting syndrome</note> occurs. Also, they are harmful because they soften [the stomach]. 

**And many.** This is another rule placed according to certain people and the opinion of Rhazes in the *Book of Almansor*, Treatise 7, Chapter 18. He first puts that rule, and second his own opinion where he says "I indeed." It must be considered that Rhazes intends three things. First, the gradual reduction of the materials with a laxative drug. Second, strengthening with mastic pills, which have a "stiptic" <note>astringent</note> quality; he does not continue their use. Third, to provoke the matter through urine. This, however, can be a suitable cure if it is appropriate to give the turbith medicine when some digestion appears; but before this, it is not suitable to be given. And every night is not a rule that must necessarily be observed; rather, one must consider the strength of the patient. Diuretics, however, must be given after some reduction of the matter has been done, as we said above. Turbith "like alcohol"—that is, ground. Wherefore Rhazes in the same place orders it to be sifted through a cloth called an *orale* <note>a veil or mouthpiece cloth</note>.

<margin>i</margin> **I indeed.** It should be noted first that Avicenna did not say he does not like softening and digestion, for he likes both; but he does not like "staying" in them and waiting for them—that is, being content to soften for a long time and digest and do nothing else or do too little. Rather, as soon as something of digestion appears, do not wait longer, but evacuate something, then digest the remainder. Do not wait, but evacuate again so that this happens little by little. And this is what he says: "I indeed do not like the waiting for digestion"—that is, that digestion should be waited for after something of it has appeared. Softening in the same way, so that the digestives and softeners perform their effects. And the cause of this is: that this is a disease of "repletion" <note>an excess of bodily fluids</note> from much thick, viscous matter not fit for movement. Therefore, it is to be digested and evacuated little by little according to the rules of the first book. Then proceed to diuretics. Diuretics, however, need preceding digestion so the matter can be evacuated; they need a reduction of the matter, lest if there be much, it be stirred up [harmfully]. And the stronger the diuretics are, the more they need these preceding steps. 

And "similarly I abhor"—that is, that it should be continued. They should not be continued because they weaken the stomach by softening it. And "if the matter," etc., "let there be mixed with it" the softening medicine and pith of safflower because it evacuates phlegm.

<margin>k</margin> **And you should help.** This is the rule regarding the clyster. **And vomiting.** This is the rule regarding vomiting.

# Part I, Treatise II

...together with seeds. Take: anise, fennel, Bishop’s weed <note>original: 'ameos'</note>, and similar things that divide the phlegm and provide substance to the seeds. Take: radish with cold water—that is, slightly warm or cold so that it stays in the stomach—and let it not pass through quickly otherwise than with water.

<margin>a</margin> ¶ And vomiting: take this, for it is a more powerful aid because the stomach is the "mine" of phlegms <note>Medieval doctors called the stomach the 'minera' or source where phlegm was produced by poor digestion</note>, as we have often said. Therefore, one must take it because vomiting is permitted at the beginning, as Avicenna <note>original: '.A.'</note> says at the start of the chapter. It should be said that the seventh day does not exclude the "beginning" <note>Physicians divided illnesses into stages: beginning, increase (augmentation), peak (state), and decline</note>. Or it should be said that this statement follows the authority of Serapio regarding the second case of containment, and is understood as we said above: that a light vomiting can be done immediately and with light remedies. But vomiting with stronger ones—for example, with agaric <note>a type of medicinal mushroom used as a laxative or emetic</note>—requires some digestion of the matter. Therefore, one ought to wait until the seventh day so that the stomach, weakened by a strong commotion, does not become apostemated <note>inflamed or abscessed</note> by the matter moved toward it.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ And if it happens. Here is a rule regarding vomiting in the sedation of a headache, and it is well known.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ And if one requires barley water because of thirst or something else that occurs to you, use it with roots—namely, fennel or celery—so that it helps with the digestion of the matter and prevents it from turning sour <note>original: 'acetosare'</note> in equal quantity—that is, twenty-fold. ¶ We usually put one ounce each of parsley, fennel, or celery root for two pounds of barley water. Or let a sour syrup <note>original: 'sirupus acetosus', likely oxymel, a mix of honey and vinegar</note> be mixed in if you want greater sedation of thirst and you want "incision" <note>Technical term for breaking up thick, sticky humors</note>, provided it does not turn to vinegar; for if it were to turn to vinegar, the sour syrup should not be mixed, but rather honey water, which prevents it from turning sour.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ And the best hour to take the other—that is, barley water—or the other—that is, sour syrup—is if the water—that is, the urine—is tinted at the beginning of the matter—that is, from the start of this fever. For it signifies that with the phlegm there is some hot matter; then indeed it is necessary to give *geleniabin* <note>a medicinal syrup or preserve, possibly a variant of julep or oxymel</note> in the drink first; Serapio wants to say *secamabin*—that is, sour syrup. Then give barley water after two hours. And this is the rule placed above in the case of barley water. *Geleniabin* can also vary: sometimes it wipes away and thins the matters of the stomach, which the barley water will then wash away.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ And it is not necessary. This rule concerning anointing and embrocation <note>the application of medicinal liquids to the skin</note> should be read continuously: let it be said that no inunction or embrocation should be made when the illness is in its beginning and the humor is "walking" in the body—that is, it is spreading and unstable. These inunctions and embrocations are those we make to the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen</note> and the belly, just as was prescribed in a non-true tertian fever. And the rule gives this because these things soften the viscera: because they relax them with moist heating, both by actual moisture and because with this measure of heat they melt the raw matters and make them "walk" more and spread through the body. However, placing the hands and feet in hot water to divert vapors from the head is not forbidden in this way; indeed, we allowed it above, and without doubt this placing of the extremities in hot water is more appropriately done when the matter is digested and lessened, although it may be allowed even before this. Furthermore, the rubbing of the hands and feet is also allowed because it does not cause the harm that embrocation and anointing do to the belly. On the contrary, since it is a certain opening heating of the pores, it is suitable, even though the phlegm is thick and raw, because it is opposed to it. From these things, the contradictions that seem to appear here in the text of Avicenna cease.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ And let cold water be avoided. ¶ This is evident.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ And how often. Because whether at the beginning or in the process [of the illness]. For such urine signifies bloody phlegm or phlegm mixed with blood. Beware, however, lest such a tint occurs because of the depth of the rot <note>original: 'putredia'</note> at the site of the phlegm and some provocation of the choler <note>yellow bile</note>. ¶ For we have seen those who, when such urines appeared, were disturbed by taking blood—the retention of which was necessary—because the urines were thinned by a sudden defect of natural heat and actual heat with it; about which ignorant doctors have boasted. And from this has come death or the worsening of the illness; know these things.

<margin>h</margin> ¶ And Serapio says: take Avicenna in the second rule, the case regarding the spider. They say it is useful in tertian fever; but if in phlegmatic fever, perhaps it is an impropriety; see what Rhazes <note>original: 'Rasis'</note> says in the *Book of Animals*, in the chapter on the spider.

<margin>i</margin> ¶ And when. It seemed to Dino <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous 14th-century medical commentator</note> that the cure for phlegmatic fever is placed here as far as the end of the beginning, so that this is part of the beginning. And Dino’s speech can be true, and we can understand "augmentation" <note>the worsening phase</note> as distinct from the beginning. As we say, here the cure of the phlegmatic fever begins when it is in augmentation. And it is divided into three parts. ¶ First, he gives one rule. Second, he places certain others. Third, he completes the cure when it is in augmentation. There, often. There, the third part: "with." It must be considered first that in this rule, he intends to comfort the stomach, which is more intended as the fever increases, because the stomach is weakened more. Second, he intends toward vomiting. Third, toward provocation <note>stimulating the discharge of humors</note>. ¶ It must be considered second that Avicenna left out what was known from the aforesaid: that you should intend toward gradual evacuation...

<column-break/>

[Column 2]

...if it is expedient: toward digestion—namely, "incision" and thinning. Nor was it necessary for him to repeat everything in every place. It must be considered third: with the reduction of food, otherwise a decrease because of the augmentation; or a reduction because with food the vomiting may be light. ¶ It is doubted whether there is much provocation in that which is mixed with *geleniabin*. To the contrary—because much provocation is not granted except after evacuations and digestion; and here he gives it in the beginning. This is Dino’s way of speaking, for he is forced to say that these things precede since he places the cure of phlegmatic fever which is in the beginning—that is, at the end of the beginning.

<insert>
Avicenna calls this "augmentation"; therefore he says that these strong provocative medicines are not granted by reason of the illness, because such diuretics are given by reason of this in the decline or at the time of the peak; but strong provocatives are granted in the beginning by reason of an accident—namely, the cold or the shivering that happens at the beginning in the beginnings of the paroxysms <note>fits or spikes in fever</note>. For above, in the chapter on the regimen of shivering and horripilation <note>goosebumps/chills</note>, he said all medicines of strong provocation sedate the shivering. ¶ We, however, say that if Avicenna here places the cure of phlegmatic fever which is in the beginning when he speaks of the beginning (more truly the end of it), then strong provocatives are suitable, because they are stronger than at the absolute beginning. If, however, he speaks here of the cure made in augmentation, then "at the beginning"—that is, of the augmentation—after the seventh day—that is, after the movement of digestion. For in this way Avicenna is accustomed to speak, as we said above in the general rules of the cure. Or otherwise: with *geleniabin* which was given in the beginning. Thirdly, after the seventh day, when some hidden digestion has appeared, let it now be mixed in the augmentation. Therefore Avicenna does not grant these at the beginning. But to that which was given at the beginning, he now adds stronger provocatives, and let it be done with hot water. This aid is added here. And he extinguishes thirst with this, although there is a burning heat. Dino, following his exposition, says that *geleniabin* with strong provocatives extinguishes the thirst—not the thirst that comes from inflammation, but the thirst that occurs at the beginning of the vigor of the cold; which thirst comes from the gathering of heat toward the internal parts. Therefore, that which takes away these chills takes away that gathering of heat within which is the cause of the thirst. And following this, it takes away the thirst. ¶ We, however, following the other exposition, will say that Avicenna referred that speech to hot water, which is given for this reason with them: because it sedates thirst from phlegmatic matter; as in the third book, section 13, the chapter on the signs of the dispositions of the stomach.
</insert>

The more viscous and thicker the phlegm, the more beneficial the rubbing will be. ¶ And it is said that rubbing with a spider's web with oil is very helpful. And when the illness begins to increase after that: then let there be care for the mouth of the stomach: because it comforts it. And there are chewable medicines <note>original: 'masticationes'</note> made from mint, mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree</note>, and anise; and let vomiting be administered with radish <note>original: 'raphano'</note> according to what we said, with the reduction of food. And let it be with *geleniabin*, not given in a drink at the beginning, but mixed after the seventh day, so that it may comfort the mouth of the stomach; and let there be much provocation in it, such as anise and mastic. And let it be with hot water properly at the beginning of the period; for at first it resists the shivering and the cold, and it extinguishes with this the thirst which is a burning heat. And many times because evacuation of the phlegm and the raw humor is permitted at this hour; but it is better that one should wait in it for the completion of digestion. And when the illness begins with heat, it is continually helped with lozenges <note>original: 'trociscis'</note> of this kind. Take: yellow myrobalans <note>an astringent fruit</note>, aloes, juice of hemp-agrimony <note>original: 'eupatorii'</note>, juice of wormwood <note>original: 'absintii'</note>, five drams of each; saffron and mastic, six drams of each. Let lozenges be formed, and let him take from them every day the weight of one dram, and every night the weight of half a dram. ¶ And when you see that digestion appears, help it with those things that are like celery and fennel leaves, and roots of camel grass <note>original: 'squinanti'</note>, and maidenhair fern <note>original: 'capillus veneris'</note>. If, however, you know that the matter is very thick, it is not bad to use a little pepper or to use it in a little thin wine, not much. ¶ And sometimes resolving ointments help toward digestion and resolution with strong power: and they are more suitable in this illness than in the remaining fevers. And it is necessary that one considers in this...

<margin>k</margin> ¶ And many times. Dino, continuing his exposition, says "at this hour"—namely, the hour of the beginning; he says this because of Rhazes, about whom it was said above. And if Avicenna’s speech is still about the cure that is suitable in the augmentation, then there is a doubt: how can phlegm be raw at this hour—namely, the hour of augmentation? It is also doubted because, whatever the case may be, he says that the completion of digestion should be expected, when he said above: "I truly do not love the expectation of digestion." It should be said to the first that augmentation can be raw phlegm in many extensive parts and in many degrees, although there is some digestion in it or some parts are digested. Therefore, in the raw part, the completion should be expected absolutely, but that which suffices for evacuation. And by this the second doubt is solved. And perhaps through the mind of Avicenna this went: when some evacuation has been made before and the matter is somewhat lessened, then in manifest augmentation it is better that you wait for digestion if you wish to evacuate, or you should evacuate first. For the evacuations that preceded were more forced than this one. Otherwise we can say that here he speaks of raw phlegm by species: under which it can be understood to be phlegm by its nature very thick and cold and viscous, such as glassy phlegm, or sour phlegm, or raw phlegm, which is called raw by its proper name. And all these phlegms are distinguished against sweet, or tasteless, or salty phlegm. Therefore these phlegms in augmentation and windiness, although they have some digestion, are nonetheless called "raw" by the name of their species. And because these are of more difficult evacuation than sweet phlegm, it is necessary to wait longer for digestion in their evacuation. And this is what he understands: "it is better that in it"—namely, in raw phlegm—"the completion of digestion be expected"—that is, a more complete digestion than in non-raw, sweet phlegm.

<margin>l</margin> ¶ And when the illness. Here a rule is added: "with heat," because of some choler <note>yellow bile</note>. Whence he grants yellow myrobalans, but not alone, because that would be against the rules said above in the general chapter; indeed he grants aloe, and it is the basis here. However, myrobalans are granted more safely if this cure is in the augmentation of the fever.

<margin>m</margin> ¶ And when you see. Here he resumes the cure of the augmentation to complete it. Or he places the cure of the augmentation: and it has as many parts as the rule places. "When digestion appears"—that is, appearing manifest. And then we truly know that it is the augmentation, as in the first book on crises. Take: leaves, etc., decoctions of these things. Resolving ointments. Consider that resolving ointments "with strong power"—that is, strong in power, such as rue oil—for example, or "with strong power"—that is, because the body should be strong in power, lest the resolution weaken it. These ointments indeed and those things drunk in the beginning while this matter is raw and abundant. But here they are granted in the augmentation, the matter existing as somewhat digested and with a reduction having been made.

<margin>n</margin> ¶ And they are more suitable. In the remaining [fevers]: because they are rightly opposed to the coldness and moisture of the phlegm, but they are not so contrary to choler or melancholy. But if the power were, etc. [supply: "and the shivering were strong"], add, etc., because these are strong in power for rubbing...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for treating phlegmatic fevers, focusing on the transition from the early stages of the illness to the "period of increase" and the "state" of the disease. It provides specific recipes for decoctions and troches meant to digest and evacuate phlegm.</meta>

# Book

...so that it penetrates, either by rubbing or by wiping away—that is, by cleansing: so that the actual softening is removed. And if the strength is not sufficient—meaning if the vital power is weak—then use remedies to bring balance, such as chamomile oil.

<margin>a</margin>
**And when it passes the 14th day.** By this time, Avicenna <note>original: 'A.'</note> also understands the "period of increase" <note>the phase where symptoms worsen before reaching their peak</note>, which he previously noted through the signs of appearing digestion, and this is measured by an estimable measure of time. And if anyone considers it, Avicenna seems to have in mind a phlegmatic fever whose hidden digestion begins after the third day, whose manifest digestion begins after the seventh, and whose process of non-digestion ends after the 14th, so that perhaps around the 20th day it reaches its "state" <note>the peak or plateau of the illness</note>, where it may be thinned more, etc. Consider here what we said above: that in the progress of the matter, the material is digested; however, we use more "thinning" remedies <note>medicines that break down thick humors</note>, and thus we digest it more. The cause of this is threefold, as stated above. First, because these provocative medicines are what require digestion, and the more the matter is digested, the more we provoke it. Second, because there is no fear of agitating much matter when part is already digested and part is diminished. Third, because these thinning agents are also sharp, and thus they putrefy raw matter. A fourth cause is added: because the more phlegmatic matter proceeds by digesting, the more it proceeds by becoming "earthy," just as digested phlegm sinks more in water, while raw phlegm floats. This is a sign you take from Averroes in his commentary on the *Canticles*, third treatise, the chapter on hypostasis, commentary 11. It stands, therefore, that what is moist in the phlegm is more changed into dry when it is digested, and yet the whole is more earthy. Therefore, to counteract that earthiness and to move it toward an "airy" state with the proper mixture, we use more thinning agents when it is more digested. This fourth cause, however, is not comprehensible to every intellect.

<margin>b</margin>
**Administration of troches** of roses: specifically after the administration of diuretics and evacuants.

<margin>c</margin>
**And wine.** At this hour—that is, after the 14th day—when digestion is very manifest; and he assigns the known causes.

<margin>d</margin>
**And when you see digestion** and strength: that is, in digestion, because it has been perfectly digested. He therefore places the cure in the "state" <note>the peak of the illness</note> regarding the digestion of the matter. And if you consider it well, it is possible that it is in the "decline" if the matter was first diminished gradually, just as it was gradually being digested. Thus it becomes diminished by art or by nature, and this happens for the most part. And the difficulty of accidents can also concur with this, though it happens more rarely. And first he briefly sets this down; second, he sets down many medicines that are suitable for phlegmatic fever at other times besides the beginning. There is the second part: "And when you see." It should be considered regarding the first part that Avicenna is silent about the use of thinning agents and diuretics and the use of laxatives <note>original: 'solutivorum'</note>, because it is known that one ought properly to use laxatives and those things that provoke urine when the matter is digested. And if this matter must remain in the body, because he does not trust that it will be finished quickly with evacuation, you should use the aforementioned thinning agents lest it be ignored too much. For after that, you will give what is suitable for evacuation: troches of wormwood <note>original: 'absinthio'</note>, which are strongly active and provocative, as in the fifth book, eighth treatise. And in summary, wormwood is only suitable after digestion, as was said above in the chapter on the cure of impure tertian fever.

<margin>e</margin>
**And when you see.** That is, he first sets down medicines that are suitable for "rigor" <note>the shivering or chills accompanying the fever</note>, and second, those that are evacuants and also digestive. There is the second part: "And let it be given to him every night." It should be considered that these medicines would not be suitable at all while the matter remains raw, as appears from what was said above; and therefore he said "and the illness is not in the beginning." And because after the beginning, the rigors become stronger in this fever.

<margin>f</margin>
**According to the description.** That is, just as they are described in order elsewhere, "by half"—that is, until the consumption of half the liquid.

<margin>g</margin>
**And when you see phlegm.** Dinus says: that is, clearly exiting through the outlets.

<column-break/>

...strength and fever and rigor. If the strength is strong and the fever is not very severe, add those things to the joints by rubbing; and if not, let subtle oils be administered which are inclined toward a balance. And when 14 days have passed, then it is necessary to administer what thins more, such as fennel and celery; and perhaps we need the seed of both, and anise, and that which is like oxymel <note>original: 'sirupus acetosus'</note> with seeds, in which hyssop and mullein <note>original: 'albasce'</note> are placed, and the administration of troches of roses. And perhaps it is necessary to add to them, for the sake of the stomach, frankincense, mastic, cypress, wormwood, and similar things, because the present situation requires it. And subtle wine benefits them at this hour with its thinning quality, and because it strengthens the innate heat and provokes [humors] and causes sweating. And when you see digestion and strength, you shall give him to drink, after that, troches of wormwood. And when you see cold at the beginning of paroxysms <note>fits of fever</note> it is harmful and the illness is not in its beginning: give as a drink warm water in which those things have been boiled that are dry, such as celery seed, anise, and basil; and you shall again administer such things and stronger ones by embrocation <note>liquid medicine rubbed into the skin</note> and by steaming; and sometimes it is given as a drink for a vehement rigor. The decoction follows this manner: Take: ginger, oregano, and bishop's weed, 3 drams of each; coriander, 4 drams; roses and calamint, 3 drams of each; raisins, 7 drams. Let them be boiled according to the description and let the dose be 3 drams. And when you see phlegm, you shall give theriac <note>a famous universal antidote and panacea</note> in a drink, and let large rose troches be given again in a drink with fennel water. And give him every night a medicine of turbith <note>a purgative root</note> and pills made of aloe with spices that are like pepper. And for that purpose, a decoction of this kind: Take: Hiera picra <note>a bitter purgative</note>, 8 drams; turbith, 10 drams; black myrobalans, 5 drams; eupatorium, 5 drams; Indian salt, 3 drams; bedeguar <note>the gall of a wild rose</note> and zedoary <note>an aromatic root</note>, 4 drams of each; anise, 3 drams. Let them be cooked with celery water and let it be taken in a drink according to the amount of necessity. (And stronger than that is this: Take: the two roots <note>parsley and fennel</note> and lily root, 10 drams of each; Hiera picra, 8 drams; eupatorium juice, 5 drams; celery and fennel seed, 4 drams of each; nard <note>original: 'spice'</note> and mint, 8 drams of each. Let troches be made from them and administered.) A good decoction: Take: the two roots, 10 drams of each; pitted raisins, 7 drams; anise and mastic, 3 drams of each; bedeguar, zedoary, and eupatorium, 4 drams of each. Let them be boiled in three pounds of water until it returns...

<column-break/>

...to one pound; then it indicates to us the necessity of evacuation, evaporation, and resolution. Another way it can be said: "and when you see phlegm"—that is, abounding as the cause of the rigor; and if you do not see it in the exits, use theriac—namely, the old kind. But whether theriac ought to be given before the digestion of the phlegmatic matter—namely, while it remains raw—we do not say much here; however, we believe it is safer that some digestion has preceded it. And although in paralysis it is conceded by many before digestion, the matter of paralysis is further removed from the veins than that of phlegmatic fevers.

<margin>b</margin>
**Large troches of** roses. Avicenna describes no "large troche of roses" in the fifth book, which I would give when the matter of the fevers is not diminished. Because this is the cure after the beginning, it ought to be understood that after that digestion, the phlegm is diminished with fennel water, because they become more provocative from this.

<margin>i</margin>
**And every night. Here he sets down** evacuating medicines that rectify the members and the matter. And first, the weaker evacuants; second, the stronger ones, there where it speaks of evacuants. First, he notes how many medicines he sets down. It should be considered that Avicenna here gives a sound understanding by quoting Rhazes <note>original: 'Rasio'</note> in conceding turbith pills every night, which is understood to be after the beginning—namely, because when there is some digestion in the matter, those which are like pepper—that is, which species are like pepper, such as galangal, cinnamon, and others which are called by the general name "Alefangi"—or like pepper, meaning in the form of pepper, because small pills, being quickly dissolved, quickly pass to the members.

<margin>h</margin>
**...to one pound of water and let it be taken as a drink for several** days while fasting. Good troches for chronic fevers and the vehemence of rigor: Take: Hiera picra, eupatorium juice, wormwood, zedoary, bedeguar, 5 drams of each; celery and fennel seed and anise, 3 drams of each; Naphtic salt, 4 drams; dodder seed, 10 drams; Chebulic myrobalans, 10 drams of each; agaric <note>a medicinal mushroom</note>, 15 drams; rose troches, 20 drams; of turbith, 30 drams. Let troches be made from them and they are laxative. And again: aloes, yellow myrobalans, 7 drams; rhubarb, mastic, eupatorium juice, wormwood, one part of each; let them be ground through half and administered. And again: Hiera, Chebulic myrobalans, and salt, 4 drams of each; celery and fennel seeds and anise, 1.5 drams of each; wormwood, 5 drams; rose troches, 3 drams; zedoary and bedeguar, 2 drams of each. Let them be ground and formed into pills. A good decoction: Take: eupatorium, 5 drams; lily root and licorice root, 3 drams; bishop's weed, 3 drams of each; celery and fennel seed, 4 drams of each; roses, 5 drams. Let all be boiled and let the dose be 10 drams of all. Again: the three roots, 4 drams of each; zedoary, bedeguar, eupatorium, and wormwood, 5 drams of each; centaury, 4 drams. Let them be boiled and let 4 drams be drunk. And again: the herbs eupatorium, fumitory, bedeguar, zedoary, and wormwood, 5 drams of each; raisins, 10 drams; yellow myrobalans, 10 drams. And this particular cure is false, and is more suitable for one in whom cholera <note>yellow bile</note> prevails.

<margin>k</margin>
**And for that. This is** the first description, the virtue of which you may see from the simples. Bedeguar: that is, white thorn. Zedoary <note>original: 'sucbahum'</note>: thorns similar to that in virtue. See Serapion.

<margin>l</margin>
**And stronger. This is another** of the "two roots"—namely, parsley and fennel. It should be considered that this medicine is stronger only because it is a solid substance, whereas the preceding one is given as a decoction. However, as for the virtue of the simples, the preceding one is stronger because of the turbith.

<margin>m</margin>
**Decoction. This is** the third medicine, and in summary, they are compositions of known medicines. But the Hiera which is placed in many of them is understood as the true Hiera <note>original: 'yera'</note>. Galen, in the 7th book of *Therapeutics*, whether it be the "Universal Hiera" or the "Common Hiera," which is composed in the fifth book of the *Canon*. Here, therefore, we do not discuss the virtue of these medicines, because it is known from the simples. If, however, there is anything to know from the composite form, experience will show. We have discussed these things concerning the defining of doses and composite laxatives in the fifth book of the *Canon*, and it is in the *Viaticum*.

<margin>n</margin>
**And this particular cure.** Namely, by the medicine just mentioned into which yellow myrobalans enter. It is for bile, etc., and also others from the aforementioned are suitable for this.

<margin>o</margin>
**And agaric. The** virtue of agaric is magnified, as experience teaches. And many authors use it not only in the evacuation of phlegm but also in digesting it, as we shall see in continuous fevers—namely, every day or even frequently according to your estimation.

<margin>p</margin>
**Nettle seed.** Because it provokes the matter through the urine and digests it, and it is possible that they are laxative. And therefore it is suitable after digestion, otherwise called conversion; and then they enter into it to help the digestion of food and of the phlegms of the stomach. But let there be added in it—namely, with what has been said of the aforementioned medicines—a composition of dodder seed <note>original: 'semen cuscute'</note> for the weakness of obstruction. Alternatively, turbith and dodder seed if there were much phlegm with this. Or with it—namely, agaric—dodder seed, or with it—namely, the seed...
