### Treatise Section

### Column 1

<margin>
Seed of nettle and dodder; because of the spleen itself; fenugreek. And consider this with them, namely that these are sufficiently warming.
</margin>
<margin>
Furthermore, he proceeds to the third point, where he places medicines that strongly evacuate <note>expel humors from the body</note>, and these are noted. In the first description, the pills could be of one volume; they must be large and stronger because of the colocynth <note>a powerful, bitter purgative</note>.
</margin>
<margin>
The second is stronger because of the scammony <note>a resinous plant used as a harsh laxative</note>.
</margin>

One requires these in this illness at the time of digestion: that the dose of turbith <note>an oriental leadwort used as a purgative</note> pills be increased and strong enemas be administered. <meta>This page continues the medical instructions for specific types of fevers, moving from general phlegmatic fevers to complex conditions like empialos, lipparia, and fevers accompanied by fainting or syncope. It compares the opinions of major medical authorities like Galen, Avicenna, and Alexander of Tralles.</meta>

### Book III

<margin>a</margin> Their cure. He describes the care of fevers caused by the humors, specifically phlegmatic fevers. First, *empiale* and *lipparia* <note>original: 'empiale' and 'lipparie'; 'empiale' is a fever where the patient feels cold and hot simultaneously, while 'lipparia' is a malignant continuous fever with high internal heat</note>. He includes in this category any fever where heat and cold are felt at the very same time, because it matches *empiala* in its underlying matter.
<margin>b</margin> "Associated with one path," meaning they are treated in the same way simultaneously; along with the aforementioned, use daily syrups and honeyed or sugar-based syrups. These include myrtle or others as you see fit, using both simple and compound medicines as established in the previous rules.
<margin>c</margin> And he also prescribes, occasionally for the strengthening of the stomach, a gradual progression: moving from digestive and thinning medicines to infusions of aloe, then to laxatives that provoke urine, and also those that strengthen the stomach and provide nourishment. He intends all these through the substances he lists.
<margin>d</margin> And diuretics should be given.
<margin>e</margin> And regarding helpful laxatives, if there is "melancholy" <note>black bile</note> thickening the phlegm, use those; use yellow ones if there is any "choler" <note>yellow bile</note>.
<margin>f</margin> Enemas, etc., if there is thick phlegm present.
<margin>g</margin> The regimen for *lipparia* requires more thinning ("subtiliation") than others; since there is internal heat in *lipparia*, we cannot safely use hot thinning agents as we do in *empiala*. Or, because *lipparia* can arise from choler (such as the type called *taburos*), an error might occur if it were treated with the cure for phlegm; its cure should be understood from the chapter on choleric fevers.
<margin>h</margin> This fever. First, he sets down its cure when caused by phlegm; second, when caused by choler. He says, "But if it were..." The first part has two sections: first, the cure in general; second, specifically. Galen notes that Avicenna focuses on the materials in the veins near the intestines and in the intestines themselves, starting with mild enemas and moving to stronger ones. First, an enema should be used, and then for the materials past the liver, use friction <note>massage</note> to thin them and cause them to evaporate. This friction must also be gradual. Note that we can also understand gradual evacuation through laxative drugs, starting mild and becoming stronger. This is the precept of Rhazes in the 6th book of the *Continens* in the chapter on the cure of syncopal fever <note>fever involving fainting</note>, confirming this with the authority of Alexander.
<margin>i</margin> And Galen here sets down the cure in detail; everything he says is from Galen’s *On the Method of Healing*, Book VII. It seems to me the best division of the text is into parts matching the "canons" or rules. The first rule is that if evacuation with drugs is omitted, focus on friction. He says: "He fails in evacuation... with friction," meaning if evacuation is skipped, use friction. Whence Galen asks: "How then should such people be healed who need evacuation but cannot bear the help of evacuatives?" I have found no other evacuation for them except through friction; the method of friction is well known. He doubts whether a laxative medicine can be given to these people. It seems so according to Rhazes, where he quotes Alexander: "Give a laxative drink to alleviate that phlegm so the nature is not weighed down; if the patient seems strengthened by the result, it is good; if not, give the laxative again." Against this are Avicenna and Galen. Their reasoning is: these humors cause syncope <note>fainting</note> when they are still, because they lack strong movement. Therefore, they will do so much more when moved by a strong or even weak drug. In this disagreement, there is no way to reconcile them except as we often do: each of these men proceeded with his own judgment, and both are practically possible. Alexander judged that a drug reduces thick, viscous matter that friction cannot draw out, provided the person is strong enough in vitality to endure the movement of the medicine. But Galen and Avicenna judged the opposite. Neither side can definitively silence the other; both may be appropriate. It can also be said Alexander speaks of syncopal fever where the phlegm is "benign" and close to blood. He then adds regarding bloodletting: if the physician sees the person is strong enough, they can endure the drug. Avicenna and Galen speak of syncopal fever where bloodletting is forbidden. Whence, in *Method of Healing* VII: "In none of these is the removal of blood usually done without the greatest harm."
<margin>k</margin> And to the highest degree. Here he sets the second rule: the thinning of the phlegm. Not too much heating, as that would thicken it. It is doubted whether the physician should be content with friction and a thin diet (namely, only honey-water with hyssop) for several days. It seems so from Galen and Avicenna, because feeding increases the matter. Against this is Alexander in the chapter on fainting—

### Chapter 54

Their cure is close to the cure we have already described. Both are "associated with one path." It is necessary to begin first with honeyed and sugar-based oxymel <note>original: 'syrupo acetoso'; a syrup of vinegar and honey</note>. In both cases, it is prescribed that "wild rob" <note>fruit preserve</note> cooked with honey and rose syrup be administered. Then, create a gradation in the way of taking drinks, from seeds and their waters to an infusion of aloe and rose troches with mastic, and pills of aloe, *hiera picra* <note>a traditional bitter purgative</note>, and eupatorium pills. In both cases, care must be taken for the stomach; a vomit should be administered with bean-water, radish, anise, calamint, and diuretics.
Helpful laxatives include those made from black and yellow myrobalans, turbith, and sugar. Among those providing great relief are sharp enemas, in which are placed safflower pith, lesser centaury, dill, chamomile, mallow, melilot, brine, and honey. The regimen for *lipparia* needs more refinement than the regimen for the other.

—fainting with fullness, where he proceeds against Galen’s intention, saying: "I do not know what Galen suffered from to ordain this," and he shows that for some subsequent doctors, Galen’s cure was unsuccessful, and they could not save the man from death. He argues by reason: Alexander says it does not seem that vitality can be strong enough to endure immoderate friction and stay without food. Therefore, he advises moderate friction (as Galen prescribes) but not such a thin diet. This contradiction is resolved like the first: each man proceeded by his own judgment. It can be said: either the humors are so bad the body cannot be nourished by them (in which case they should not be on a thin diet, for they cannot bear a long fast, and honey-water will not suffice, but you must give barley water or chicken broth); or, the humors can be digested and converted, in which case they can tolerate the fast and the very thin regimen of only honey-water until the seventh day, according to Galen’s judgment.

->On the cure of fever with syncope and humors.<-
### Chapter 55

This fever is difficult to cure. The method in its treatment is a gradation from mild to strong, especially when nature does not respond on its own. Then, clean with enemas that which is in the intestines and the veins near them from superfluity, and for the rest, administer thinning with friction <note>massage</note>. Galen said he fails to evacuate most of them except through friction. The best method for their friction is to begin with the hands and legs, descending from the upper to the lower. Administer this with a rough cloth to scrape the skin. Then change to the hands, descending from the shoulder to the shoulder blade, so that the skin becomes warm; then to the back and chest; then return to the legs and the first order. Devote half their time to friction and half their time to sleep if possible. To the highest degree, the rule of their cure is thinning, not intense heating. Among the things that help them are thinning agents, such as honey-water with the strength of hyssop and celery seed in the mornings and similar times.
But if there is an excessive flow from the bowels, cook the honey more intensely; it will not loosen unless it is a mild, helpful mixture. Honeyed oxymel is also helpful, specifically in summer and with the habit of drinking cold water mixed with cold water; in winter, one should not take it as a drink at all, and taking it warm is better for them, unless necessitated by the heat of summer and extreme warmth. The most suitable thing to drink for thirst is honeyed oxymel. Wine helps in the beginning, specifically if their fevers are sanguine. But they are few, and specifically in the elderly. Wine after food is necessary for them, and it is necessary for you to consider the pulse of one having this sickness always; whenever you see him begin to weaken and fall suddenly, feed him bread soaked in wine, provided there is no blockage in the internal organs. When this kind of illness is associated with him, there is no way for cure or confidence for three or four days, until the matter begins to thin as Avicenna said above in the general rule, or from the beginning because it starts from the first day. I intend this more for the accident of syncope <note>fainting</note> than anything else. It therefore addresses the cause of the syncope, and thus the first argument is solved. This wine should be watery, not "winey," so as not to inflame. The physician's judgment should measure the degree of its potency and the weight of the water. Avicenna said "if the fevers are sanguine," whereas some texts have "if they are *not* sanguine," meaning inflammatory. Or, Avicenna says this because sanguine phlegm is not as raw in the beginning as non-sanguine phlegm; thus, by reason of its disposition, wine can be granted more safely, though from the side of the "flame" (heat) it might be granted less; and in this rests the quality of judgment. And "specifically in the elderly," meaning wine is given, or "specifically in the elderly" syncopal sanguine fevers are rare.

<margin>q</margin> Wine after food. That is, they should drink wine not only when they are fed, but also outside of mealtimes because of their weakness. Or, this is the Saracen manner <note>referring to Arab physicians like Avicenna</note> to drink after digestion is complete to aid the movement of food; and thus contradictions cease.
<margin>r</margin> "And for you." This is the seventh rule. Note that Avicenna provides two types of food. One for the syncope, namely bread in wine. The other is food regarding the body's strength in relation to the disease, such as barley water, after which the patient sleeps; for the food given for syncope is not followed by sleep, as one suffering from syncope is commanded to stay awake.
<margin>s</margin> "When therefore." The cause of this was stated above. Whether that (the syncope) should be prohibited, or whether that food should be given when there is no syncope, as he immediately adds.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on fevers, transitioning from general phlegmatic conditions to more complex cases involving syncope (fainting) and the specific nature of quartan fever—a fever that recurs every four days, historically associated with "melancholy" or black bile.</meta>

# Treatise Section

<margin>a</margin> ¶ **And the bath.** This is the eighth case. The reason is that it weakens and dissolves the matter <note>the "matter" refers to the excess humors causing the illness</note>.
<margin>b</margin> ¶ **And heat.** This is the ninth rule.
<margin>c</margin> ¶ **And if there should be.** He describes the cure for a fever with syncope <note>fainting caused by a sudden loss of strength</note> resulting from an overabundance of choler <note>yellow bile</note>, which he mentioned above. Vomiting is easy because of the nature of the choler and its location, for much of that choler is found in the stomach, as we have said.
<margin>d</margin> ¶ **And it may soften.** That is, the belly should be softened, or a light vomiting should be induced. For vomiting or softening the belly is very helpful; this specific matter moves more easily toward evacuation than phlegm does.
<margin>e</margin> ¶ **And finally.** In short, it is better and more effective in this fever than in daily fevers to sometimes act with this light softening and an even lighter friction <note>medical massage</note> than is used in phlegmatic cases. One must monitor the patient's "virtue" <note>vital strength or energy</note> as we said. For a daily fever, the best progress is made through daily softening of the belly and light vomiting, so that we are not forced to evacuate a large amount suddenly in a single day.
<margin>f</margin> ¶ **It is necessary, etc.** Here he describes the cure for fever with syncope, specifically the one called "minute and subtle." First, he uses topical applications <term>epithymata<gloss>poultices or medicinal compresses applied to the body</gloss></term> which help the fever and the corrupt "subtle" matter; this gives strength and comfort. It is also useful to apply <term>spodium<gloss>ashes or mineral residues, often used as a drying agent</gloss></term>. The patient should be revived with juice through foods that restrain the choler and provide some comfort. Water of fruits—that is, apples or pears—or water of melon seeds. I do not believe they mean "fruit water" in the sense of cassia or tamarind; however, at the end of the day when the patient is resting, these laxatives are given and are useful for gently drawing out that choler, specifically tamarind, as appears in the *Canon* in the chapter on tamarinds.
<margin>g</margin> ¶ **If however.** He lists foods useful for syncope, such as *Almufufat* <note>original: 'Almufufat'; an acidic dish, likely a chicken broth or stew prepared with vinegar</note>, which are certain sour foods made from chicken.
<margin>h</margin> ¶ **Regimen.** This is clear from what we said above regarding these fevers, etc.
<margin>k</margin> ¶ **And they thought, etc.** All humoral moisture, etc. The reason is that it can neglect its own heat's regulation and be occupied by external heat, which is the cause of "putrefaction" <note>the rotting or morbid alteration of humors</note>, as Galen says in book II of *On the Differences of Fevers* and book XI of *Therapeutics*.
<margin>m</margin> ¶ **How much it may thin.** That is, how it varies in preparation: because some moistures are preparations for others. Or "it may thin" might mean it happens rarely: this putrefaction of melancholy <note>black bile</note> happens due to a lack of preparation.
<margin>n</margin> ¶ **And healthier, etc.** Meaning safer from an <term>aposteme<gloss>an internal swelling or abscess</gloss></term> of the spleen and other bad afflictions of the spleen, such as hardening and obstructions.
<margin>o</margin> ¶ **To dropsy.** See this in the third book of the *Canon*, section 14.
<margin>p</margin> ¶ **And in it there is security from spasm.** This is an aphorism from the fifth section, where it is said: "Those held by quartan fevers are not greatly seized by spasms." One reason given here is that the humor is dry—namely, "hedgehog phlegm" <note>a metaphorical term for thickened, irritating phlegm</note>—which is the cause of spasm. Or because the humor is dry and earthy, it is not

prone to flow to the nerves. Another cause is given by Avicenna in the third book, second section, in the chapter on spasms, which is "concussion" <note>violent shaking or tremors</note>: for where there is an evacuation of matter, other signs are known.
¶ **The signs are, etc.** ¶ First, he presents the common signs of quartan fever. Second, he presents signs according to the diversity of causes. Third, he presents special signs from the pulse, urine, and certain others. In the first part, he lays out four modes of signs, and at the end, he provides two causes. He places the rule there. ¶ The general summary of the signs of quartan fever is taken from the nature of its cycle. Observations are made first at the very beginning of the <term>paroxysm<gloss>the sudden onset or worsening of fever symptoms</gloss></term>. Then, as the paroxysm proceeds, at its "state" <note>the peak of the illness</note>, it is felt that the cold in this fever has a maximum beginning, increase, peak, and decline. This is due to the slowness of the movement of the melancholy humor, just as in phlegmatic fever. This indicates that the cold from this humor is due to its own coldness and not from a lack of heat due to the biting nature of the matter, but is like cold induced by cold air. It is the same in phlegmatic fever, though the cold of phlegm is greater, as phlegm is colder than melancholy—though there is some debate on this. ¶ These statements can, however, be referred to the beginning of the whole disease: he says the cold in the first paroxysms is small because the matter moves slowly, being "raw" <note>undigested or unprocessed by the body</note>. Then, in the increase and peak, it begins to add up because, being more "digested," it moves more suddenly. Later it lingers at the peak, then declines because the matter is diminished. These things were said above in the chapter on tertian fever. I understand that this cold does not increase in the peak because cold is added to the matter; rather, because it is more digested, it is actually less cold, but it *seems* to increase because it moves more suddenly. This is better described as an increase in "concussion" or trembling rather than an increase in the quality of the cold itself.

alteration in the pulse. This feeding is among the necessary things: when the syncope becomes severe, it must be prevented. The liquid upon which the patient sleeps should be barley water, to which nothing should be added unless the strength fails; if something is added, let it be bread soaked in julep or honey water. And the bath is indeed among the most notable things, along with heat and very fresh air. For if there is a running of the humors to the lung, heart, and brain, the freshness prevents its "digestion" <note>the metabolic processing of the humors</note>. But if there should be choleric humor in it at some point, then if vomiting is easy and the belly is softened, it is very helpful; and ultimately, it is better to proceed continuously in this way.

### On the cure of fever with subtle fainting. Ch. 61.

-> **I**t is necessary to fill the patient's chest with food little by little. Let the food be bread or similar things soaked in cold pomegranate water if the patient desires it; and likewise in fruit water. If strength is needed, *almosofat* made from chicken with vinegar and verjuice <note>original: 'agresta'; sour juice of unripened grapes</note> and fresh herbs, especially coriander, will be helpful if administered. <-

### Night and day regimen. Cap. 62.

-> **T**he regimen for these is the same as the regimen for phlegmatic fevers; there is no difference between them. <-

### On periodic quartan fever. Ch. 63.

-> **M**ost quartan fever is periodic, and cases of inseparable <note>continuous</note> quartan are fewer. The causes of quartan are those things that generate melancholy <note>black bile</note> and afterwards cause it to rot; you already know all of that. And you know that one type of melancholy is the dregs of blood, and another is the "burning" of blood and the ash of the humors. You know that one comes from blood, one from phlegm, one from choler, and one is the burning of natural melancholy itself. ¶ And some have thought that quartan fever is not generated from natural melancholy because it does not rot. <-

<column-break/>

Indeed, this argument should not be listened to; rather, it is a property of all humoral moisture that it may rot whenever it is thinned in its preparation. Most often it occurs in a succession of different putrid fevers because of the diversity of the humors from which they are generated; when these are added and not evacuated, melancholy increases, and when it rots, quartan fever begins. Often it happens following a condition of the spleen, and with this, the spleen does not evacuate due to pain or hardness. A "healthier" quartan is one that does not happen because of a spleen abscess or other spleen conditions. For quartan that comes from a spleen abscess often leads to <term>dropsy<gloss>edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</gloss></term> and ruin. However, a "safe" quartan frees the patient from many bad illnesses, such as melancholy and epilepsy, and in it, there is security from spasms because the humor is dry. For the most part, it is safe as long as no error occurs in the treatment; sometimes it lasts for twelve years, and when it is that long, it leads to dropsy.

### And know that autumn is the enemy of quartan.
### Ch. 64.

-> **T**he signs are that quartan begins in everyone with a small chill; then the cold begins to increase; afterwards, it lessens at the peak. Sometimes the body becomes hot, but it is not a violent heat, though it is greater and more apparent than that in phlegmatic fever. For melancholy, the matter in question, burns like fire in thick logs: it does not flare up with a flame that can be easily cured, and it does not seize the whole body suddenly. Rather, there is heat in the interior with <term>horripilation<gloss>goosebumps or shivering</gloss></term> and cold in the extremities; this is due to the thickness of the humor. There is cold and some pain, like the breaking of bones, and there is a contraction because of which the teeth chatter; however, it is not like in phlegmatic fever, where it leads to extreme weakness. <-

<margin>q</margin> ¶ Although it becomes hot, it is not a violent heat, such as that of a tertian fever <note>a fever that peaks every three days</note>.
<margin>r</margin> ¶ Although it is greater. Because the matter more strongly resists inflammation, it seeks coldness and superfluous moisture, which chokes the heat.
<margin>s</margin> ¶ For the matter itself. He wants to declare that heat in the melancholy matter does not become violent. Melancholy burns like fire in "thick logs"—that is, earthy ones—because not much flame rises from them, unlike a clear fire. It does not seize the whole body suddenly; rather, there is internal heat with shivering in the extremities. The process from cold to heat happens over a noticeable time because of the thickness of the humor; it is heated and inflamed with difficulty.
<margin>u</margin> ¶ And it is with cold. That is, in this fever, just as in phlegmatic fever, true cold is felt. "With some pain," meaning pain as if the bones were being crushed. It is believed that because the nourishment is "melancholic," a commotion occurs there due to the properties of the melancholy humor or its heat. The thick, dry vapors rising from the melancholy cause a bad sensation in the membranes around the bones and muscles, leading to contraction, which the light vapor of phlegm does not do. This is the sensation of "bone-breaking."
<margin>x</margin> ¶ And there is contraction in quartan, specifically in the muscles of the jaws, which causes the teeth to chatter. Chattering of the teeth occurs from the contraction or spasm of the jaw muscles, as we explained in the first book of *Prognostics*. Thus, thick, dry vapors cause this. "However, not as in phlegmatic fever." There is doubt as to why teeth chattering does not happen in phlegmatic fever. It must be said first that the text might be corrupted. Or, it could be that this does not refer to the trembling and concussion of other members and the jaws, because such trembling is seen more in quartan fever. Reason and experience show this; it refers to the cold mentioned above. He said that in quartan there is cold just as in phlegmatic fever, because the matter of phlegm is colder. But it is doubtful which of the two humors causes greater trembling: melancholy or phlegm. We wrote about this same question in the third book, first section, in the chapter on epilepsy. Thirdly, it can be said that in both phlegmatic and melancholic cases, a certain trembling, teeth chattering, and jaw concussion can occur, as happens in tertian fever. But true chattering, which is a specific contraction from the compression made in the jaw muscles, happens properly in quartan and phlegmatic fevers.

### [Column 1]

...is of such a kind as occurs in a phlegmatic fever. For the earthy and dry, stinging vapor of the melancholic humors <note>In medieval medicine, "melancholy" or black bile was associated with the element of earth—cold and dry.</note> moves the membranes of the muscles and nerves toward a certain thickening and compression or stiffness. This lasts for a notable time, which the vapor of another humor does not do unless it shares in a melancholic nature. Therefore, there occurs a clenching of the jaws; and this is not merely a striking of them together <note>chattering</note> as happens in a phlegmatic fever when a shaking occurs, but it also happens in a tertian fever <note>a fever recurring every three days</note>. I consider, therefore, that such grinding of the teeth—that is, its cause, which is a disordered movement in the temporal muscles—leads to a weakening of sight due to their connection to the brain and the optic nerves, or because of the jarring of the upper jaw and the teeth which communicate with the parts of the eye.

<margin>a</margin>
**¶ Or gentle.** That is, strict during digestion—meaning, when the matter is "digested" <term>digested<gloss>in medieval medicine, this refers to the "ripening" or maturation of a diseased humor so it can be expelled</gloss></term>. This is confirmed regarding the coldness following the quality of the matter, not the coldness following the movement, as has already appeared. Or "lightly," meaning the grinding of the teeth. For when melancholic matter is digested, it is not as "stiptic" <note>astringent or binding</note> or earthy, and therefore it does not cause such a true grinding. This is what he means when he says the "malice is delayed"—that is, the malice of its coldness, its binding nature, and its earthiness is as it was at the beginning. ¶ To clarify: the digestion of melancholy does not entirely remove its earthiness and binding nature, but only slightly, or it remains as it was at the beginning. The coldness of a quartan fever is similarly digested matter; but at the beginning, the coldness was slight because of the slow movement of the matter, whereas the digested matter is slight for another reason: the weakening of the coldness through digestion. Or at the beginning, the grinding of the teeth was slight, not because the matter was not more "pontic" <note>sharply astringent</note> or earthy than when digested, but because it did not move in the beginning as it does during the "increase" <note>the worsening stage of a fever</note>.

<margin>b</margin>
**¶ And concerning the signs.** Either pain—namely, of the spleen. And from the signs it is clear.
<margin>c</margin>
**¶ And the period.** That is, the cycle or interval.
<margin>d</margin>
**¶ And quartan fever occurs in winter.** Because the humors scorched in summer are constricted in winter by the arriving cold and are prevented from dissolving and being evacuated, hence they putrefy.
<margin>e</margin>
**¶ And many times.** This is from Hippocrates, in the third book of *Prognostics*, regarding disordered fevers, etc. ¶ The commentator there says fevers are diverse: first they are continuous, then they become intermittent, leading to mixed fevers, etc.—that is, to various disordered fevers.
<margin>f</margin>
**¶ Therefore, of the mother.** <note>original: "mris" likely referring to "materis" or matter</note> These fevers stand through the addition of "ashiness"—that is, the conversion of blood into this ash-colored melancholic matter. Or when it becomes certain, those superfluities, etc. This is the speech of Galen in the same place when he says: "Therefore the sickness is equalized in all the veins with the victory of black bile; then the quartan fever takes hold."

<margin>g</margin>
**¶ And of that.** ¶ He does not list the signs of quartan fever from melancholy separately—that is, natural melancholy—because the aforementioned signs of quartan fever apply to it absolutely. The paroxysms <note>sudden attacks or peaks of fever</note> are longer because the matter has thickness through its melancholic nature and viscosity from phlegm; thus melancholy is formed by a continuous succession of phlegm. After it begins to heat up, the cold begins again, as was said regarding phlegmatic fever; due to the viscosity of the humor, the urine is thicker. On the contrary, because melancholy is a thicker humor than phlegm, it must be said that after melancholy has become phlegmatic, it is more prone to melting and dissolving in water than when it is pure melancholy; thus the urine is thicker, for although melancholy is thicker, it sinks to the bottom of the vessel, etc.

<margin>h</margin>
**¶ And that which is.** ¶ He lists the signs of "sanguine" melancholy <note>black bile derived from "burnt" or overheated blood</note> following blood fevers. He says "perhaps" because melancholic blood can be generated by gradual "adustion" <term>adustion<gloss>the "scorching" or overheating of a humor, making it thick, dark, and toxic</gloss></term> without a fever, as we generally say in the third book of *Prognostics*; and so it is with other types of melancholy produced by the adustion of other humors.

<margin>i</margin>
**¶ And that, etc.** ¶ He lists the signs of "choleric" melancholy <note>derived from yellow bile</note> with "horripilation" <note>goosebumps or shivering</note> because of the stinging nature of the choler.
<margin>k</margin>
**¶ And the pulse.** Here he lists certain special signs taken from specific things: first from the pulse, second from the urine, third from sweat, and fourth from thirst, though some are mixed. The parts are clear. "Serinus"—that is, hard, diverse, or harsh.

<margin>m</margin>
**¶ And to equality.** While it is not moving—that is, while it is not at the beginning of the paroxysm. For when it is already manifestly heating up, melancholy does not heat up as unevenly as phlegm. Or while it is not moving—that is, when it is not a paroxysm during the "tepor" <note>the quiet or lukewarm period between attacks</note>. And it is a sign regarding the quartan fever in which complete cleansing does not occur.

<margin>n</margin>
**¶ And many times.** It should be considered that although in every putrid fever the "systole" <note>contraction of the pulse</note> may be faster or of greater diversity than the "diastole" <note>expansion of the pulse</note>, as we said above in the general signs, nevertheless in a quartan fever compared to a tertian, this happens more because the humor is much thicker, inciting the systole more than the diastole; whereas in a tertian fever, because the humor is burning and subtle, it is the opposite. ¶ This is what he means: many times an unequal diastole occurs, and a systole of vehement necessity, according to the opposite of the tertian, etc.

<margin>p</margin>
**¶ And the pulse of the quartan is better, etc.** That is, it is not so small nor so frequent as the pulse of a phlegmatic fever; and this was clearly explained above in the chapter on phlegmatic fever. They are...

...vision; but gentle during digestion, since the malice is diminished, as it was a little at the beginning. And concerning the signs of quartan fever, they are its preceding causes from fevers that have been prolonged, and from the spleen or pain; and the signs of quartan fever are also the disposition of the complexion and the significance of the melancholy, and age, and time <note>season</note>, and food, and form, and habit, which are similar to these. And its period is twenty-three hours. And many times it is a tertian fever in summer, and becomes a quartan in winter. And many times diverse fevers lead to mixed fevers, in which there is no order because of the diversity of the residue of the humors remaining after the fevers. When, therefore, the state is confirmed by the addition of ashiness, they confirm the quartan fever. And of that which is from adust phlegm, the paroxysms are longer, and cold happens to them following a greater succession of persistence; and the sweat is slower, and the urine thicker, and the hardness of the veins is less, and it happens mostly following a succession of phlegmatic fevers. And that which is from adust blood is preceded by signs of blood and its fever, and redness of the urine; and it is indicated by form, age, and time. And perhaps it will be after blood fevers. And in that which is from adust choler, the pulse is of more vehement speed and frequency; and it begins with horripilation and cold in the flesh, and thirst and sweat. And sometimes it happens so, with sweat and inflammation; and the season and age indicate them more strongly. And sometimes they indicate it because it happens in succession to choleric fevers. And the pulse in a quartan fever is inclined toward hardness because of the dryness of the humor. ¶ For it is drawn toward the...

<column-break/>

### [Column 2]

...and slowness. And it is also said that it can be said that just as weakness of the "virtue" <note>vital strength</note> makes the pulse slow in a phlegmatic fever—where it recovers only because of frequency—so a smaller "smallness" makes the pulse slow in a quartan. That is, the pulse is not as small as in a phlegmatic fever; hence it can exist with a better "smallness" so that it is not forced to speed up the pulse.
¶ **And at.** This speech is understood to mean that at the beginning of the paroxysm, that is, the "type" <note>the characteristic onset</note>, slowness is added because of the addition of cold, and frequency...

<margin>q</margin>
...it adds according to some proportion; because once the pulse has been made small, frequency is added in some way. ¶ Dinus says frequency and rarity are added; and he says he means this because according to Galen in the second book on crises, just as slowness is added in a quartan, so also rarity is added. But if the text says frequency is added, Dinus says it should be interpreted as an increase in frequency in the quartan pulse compared to the phlegmatic pulse. For in a quartan, frequency exceeds that of the phlegmatic; that is, it is "rarer" <note>slower/less frequent</note> in a quartan fever than in a phlegmatic one. And if you consider this, it is a corruption of the text. Then Avicenna means that as cold precedes, it becomes slower and rarer than before, since it becomes slower than it is rare; because the failure of the second is compensated more by frequency—that is, by speed. Similarly, as heat precedes, it becomes proportionally frequent—that is, fast. Therefore it is more slow and rare. And this is how he understands it. And Avicenna follows this. ¶ Galen's fantasies.

<margin>q</margin>
**¶ And its diversity.**
...interior; as if the pulse itself were harsh; and it remains equal while not moving. And if it moves, the pulse is greatly diversified because of the thickness of the superfluity. And its "cleansing" <note>relief of symptoms</note> becomes apparent during the "tepor" <note>the interval</note>; and it is a complete sign of quartan fever. And many times an unequal diastole and a systole of vehement necessity occur in it, according to its opposite, which is in tertian fever. And the pulse of a quartan is better than the pulse of a phlegmatic fever in its smallness and frequency, but it is similar to it in slowness; and at the beginning of the paroxysm, its slowness and frequency increase; and its diversity is greater than the diversity of other fevers; then it begins to grow larger and become frequent and fast. And the urine in quartan fever is similar at all hours in its lack of digestion <note>meaning it stays consistently "crude" or unchanged</note>, because of the coldness of the matter and its thickness, except at the "status" <note>the peak</note> of these. The conditions of the air and its colors also vary, and for this reason: because melancholy is generated from diverse humors. And among the signs of digestion in a quartan is the lightness of the tremor. The urine at the beginning is white, inclining toward green; crude, having no digestion. And after the beginning, its condition varies because melancholy is mostly generated from diverse humors; and it is black during the "declination" <note>the fading of the fever</note>; and sweat in a quartan is very much in comparison to a phlegmatic fever, but not much in comparison to others; and thirst is lessened in this fever, unless it is from choleric melancholy.

<margin>r</margin>
¶ **And the urine, etc.** "Similar at all hours": because it is not now thin and now thick, as was said regarding phlegmatic fever; because the humor is not of such quantity nor so viscous. ¶ Therefore it does not move so unevenly toward the blocking and opening of obstructions; or "similar at all hours," etc., meaning the lack of digestion lasts for a long time; and the truth of it is that melancholy is varied and many.

<margin>s</margin>
¶ **And among the signs of digestion.** Consider that in the state of the "type," the cold in a quartan is greater, as was said in the third case of tertian fever from the intention of the commentators on the first book of *Epidemics*. ¶ Rabbi [Moses Maimonides], in the 18th chapter on quartan fever, says near the end that after many days the melancholic humor will become subtle; and it will be scattered through the sensitive members; and then the rigor <note>shaking/shivering</note> will be vehement. And this is a good sign in this fever. For it signifies that digestion is taking place; often, because melancholy arises from phlegm, the rigor or tremor or blood following the quality of the matter is lessened, but following the movement, it increases more vehemently. And either of these can fail: so that sometimes in the state of digestion there is less rigor, and sometimes more; you consider this. The rest of what he says is noted. From the Prognostics: white urine—that is, subtle and translucent; but properly in "natural" melancholy. To those attending closely, it seems that all melancholic diseases share a common sign of "crudity" <note>being undigested</note> in the common disposition of the urine; consider if there is some sign of digestion common to all.

¶ **Let it be considered.** Here he places the cure, first generally or commonly for intermittent fevers within continuous ones, though it clearly applies to the intermittent quartan. Second, he applies this cure specifically to the continuous fever. According to Avicenna, he first places the cure through medicines and diet; second, he specifically lists the appropriate foods. First, he gives the cure more generally; second, more specifically. Where he says "And if the melancholy is sanguine," he gives the source of the diversity in the cure of quartan fever. When he says "of it," it is because in a disease depending on a great cause, the great consideration in the cure is the consideration of the cause. Whence Galen said in the *Techni*: "It is necessary first to cut off each cause." One might doubt why he did not list the diversity of the cure according to the stages of the disease. It should be said that he intended this to be understood from what was said in the chapter on phlegmatic fever: because the cure for daily and quartan fevers share this: that the use of strong "subtiliating" <note>thinning</note> and provocative medicines should not occur unless some digestion has preceded in the matter; and so too the use of evacuants. And he speaks of this in the process. He explained the cure as being more diversified according to the types of melancholy, because melancholy receives a great diversity of treatment in its species. Here he follows the cure; and here the division made above could occur: that first he gives the cure in general, second in special, etc. First, he gives the cure by intending to the cause and disposition; second to the "accidents" <note>symptoms</note>. First, he gives the cure through medicines, also touching on diet. Second, he gives the cure through diet or food items, also touching on medicines.

# Second Treatise of the Fen

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> Secondly, he takes the indication from the time of year: there. And you should know that when a quartan fever begins in winter. First, in three parts, he presents the cure: first through **bloodletting**, second through **loosening the belly**, and third through **digestive medicines**, touching upon the regime of food. Secondly, he presents the cure through vomiting or a general rule. There, the second part: "And vomiting." There, the third part. ¶ First: The first part is in three. First, he presents the cure that is more applicable to "sanguine melancholy" <note>A mixture of black bile and blood.</note>; for it could also be applied to "fecal melancholy" <note>A thick, waste-like form of the humor.</note>. Second, he presents the cure for "choleric melancholy." Third, for "phlegmatic melancholy."

And you. Indeed. There, the third part: "And if." Then he adds a note: "And you should know." First: The first part is in three. First, he presents the cure through medicines. Second, he touches on the regime through food. Third, through altering medicines. There, the second: "And it is necessary that they drink." There, the third: "And medicine." There, one method should be known by which things are commonly done; however, the better way is to say that the entire chapter has as many parts as he sets down rules. 1. One is general: because one rule is suitable for all types of quartan fever at the beginning for the reduction of the matter. Under this general rule is then the rule for reducing matter through **bloodletting**; 2. reduction through **pharmacy** <note>Medicinal purging or drugs.</note>, which he sets down. One must first consider that the reason why it is reduced in the beginning is so that preparation may be made to evacuate and digest the residue. Secondly, it must be considered that here "the beginning" is not taken as a single distinct time opposed to the "increase" and "state" <note>The peak of the illness.</note>, but for the whole time that is before the state. Or let it be said "in the beginning," that is, before the stronger evacuations are made, or before the illness has progressed much. Thirdly, it should be considered that he identifies three harms in bloodletting when it is performed where it should not be—namely, where the matter is not sanguine or mixed with blood. One is that it weakens, which is obvious. The second is that it intensifies melancholy; and it is harmful because evacuating the blood rectifies the melancholy, since the opposite is beneath it. Third, that it causes restlessness. Regarding this, he first doubts: it does not seem that bloodletting moves humors to the exterior. ¶ First, because **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> in the chapter on the cure of smallpox, where after the fourth day he does not permit bloodletting, fearing lest the matter be drawn back inside. Further, in the 6th Fen of this third treatise, the first rule does not allow bloodletting to be done when poison is on its way to the interior. And this is for no other reason than that bloodletting draws poison inward. Further, bloodletting evacuates from the veins, and the emptied veins draw to themselves, and thus they draw inward. ¶ Again, it is doubted, for it is confessed that bloodletting draws to the exterior; it does not seem that this is a harm, but rather a help, because the matter is distanced from the heart, which is the primary subject of the fever. **Dynus** <note>Dino del Garbo (c. 1280–1327), an influential Italian physician and commentator.</note> says that bloodletting moves to the exterior for two reasons. ¶ First, because it causes boiling and commotion in the humors, and boiling moves to the exterior. Second, because the veins that are bled are on the outside, and therefore they move the humors outward. ¶ This harm, however, is specific to intermittent fevers, because it moves the matter toward the "mine" of putrefaction <note>The localized site where the diseased humor is decaying.</note>; because they move toward the exterior veins, since those are near the places outside the veins, the matter moves to those places. ¶ Therefore, although the heart is the subject of the fever, the place from which the cause of putrefaction begins is not the heart, but the places outside the veins, toward which bloodletting moves and attracts the matter. ¶ But near those places. There, the speeches of Dynus, if anyone considers them well, are not very clear. Let us therefore speak more clearly: that the veins which are bled (for example, in the arms) have two connections and ties: namely, a connection toward the skin, and a connection toward the depth of the heart. And therefore the opening of those veins can suck or draw matter from two places toward the parts of the veins near the opening. For they can draw from the places around the skin, and then the matters are moved inward; and therefore bloodletting is prohibited in poisonous diseases and bites, lest the poison which is around the skin and those nearby parts be moved inward. ¶ Concerning these evacuations with bloodletting and pharmacy in diseases and punctures, many things were noted by us on the 6th Fen; look for them there. Secondly, bloodletting can draw from the interior places toward the same parts, namely of the veins and the site of bloodletting. And therefore it diverts from internal abscesses and the flow of internal members. And thus the solution appears to the first question, whether bloodletting draws inward or outward. It must be said that it draws interior matters outward (namely to the veins around the site of bloodletting) and exterior matters (namely the matters of the flesh around the skin) it draws inward to the sites of bloodletting. Secondly, it appears why it is harmful in a tertian fever: when the melancholy is separated from the blood and not fit to follow the blood in evacuation. ¶ For such melancholy lies around the internal veins of the spleen and liver. Bloodletting, therefore, moves that melancholy further away from the places fit for its evacuation—namely, from the mesenteric veins and the places of the intestines, which are the more appropriate sites for its evacuation. And from this, the third harm of inappropriate bloodletting in quartan fever appears. And thus the contradictions cease.

**And if it is necessary.** It must be considered that from Avicenna's way of speaking, it appears that "beginning" here is not taken properly for a single distinct time against the "increase," but "beginning" is taken for the start and part of the increase, or for the time before the state. For he himself says that this is a "diminishing evacuation," which cleanses the body of some part of the bad matter. ¶ It alleviates it so that it may be subjected to **digestion** <term>digestion<gloss>the process of ripening or preparing humors for expulsion</gloss></term>. But digestion does not happen in the beginning, unless by digestion you mean "hidden digestion," which in my judgment is not sufficient for the digestion of melancholy. Indeed, we wait for digestion beyond that. It must be considered...
<meta>catchword: Considerandum</meta>

<column-break/>

...is appropriate concerning those things which we shall say. **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a celebrated Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> says of all its species there are judgments in which they share: and that is that they are diminished in the beginning. Therefore it is necessary to attend to whether there is blood dominating in it, and specifically when the quartan fever is from "sanguine melancholy." Then, indeed, let it be bled and the blood extracted according to the quantity of necessity; and perhaps the multitude of it requires that a very great amount be extracted from it. And when bloodletting is not necessary, then bloodletting is continually harmful, for it both weakens and continually draws out the opposite of melancholy, and continually moves the humors to the exterior. And if it is necessary, let something be evacuated at the beginning of the humor making the fever, for the purpose of alleviating and cleansing. That indeed happens at the time of digestion, according to how it helps it. And if afterwards, it should be the day after the paroxysm <note>The peak or fit of the fever.</note>. ¶ And it is not necessary that the "provocation" <note>The use of a purgative or medicine to stir the humors.</note> be done in the beginning with strength; and it is necessary that "softeners" <term>mollificantia<gloss>gentle laxatives or stool softeners</gloss></term> be administered. And if, where it does not seem good to use potions, administer in their place suitable enemas; but it is necessary

that they be light. Their strengthening is not allowed except when the illness follows the state. And if a doctor has already presumed and by loosening has drawn out the melancholy in the beginning sometimes with a strong solution and has prohibited the illness entirely, it is a "success by error" <note>The right result reached through a wrong method.</note>. And it is necessary that the patient be prohibited from eating on the day of the paroxysm and fasting be commanded, and cold water be prohibited on that day. And it is necessary to understand that on these days one should use the meat of small birds <note>original: "taiegi," likely partridges</note> or chicken in the first periods—the small birds until three or four periods, then chicken, for then the chicken is better. And if medicine is used on the day of the paroxysm, let it be **geleniabin** <note>A rose-sugar preparation, often used as a mild digestive or sweetener in syrups.</note> rubbed with warm water twice or three times in the day. Let it be geleniabin with 3 parts of oxymel <note>original: "sirupi acetosi," a syrup of honey and vinegar.</note>. And you indeed know that when the melancholy is choleric, then it is necessary that what is administered in it be that which loosens from the category of **myrabolans** <note>A dried plum-like fruit used as a staple purgative in medieval medicine.</note> and violets. And if it is phlegmatic, that there be administered in it something at the beginning in which there is the virtue of polypody, epithyme, and fumitory. And know that **whey** <note>original: "aqua casei"</note> is good where...

<margin>a</margin> ...diminishing: and a greater digestion should be expected: and that which is in the distinct beginning against the other three times. For melancholy is a humor most unfit for movement, nor is it a humor of great "repletion" <note>over-fullness</note> like phlegm; and therefore in the beginning and more quickly we can evacuate in a phlegmatic fever than in a quartan. But you may take whichever of these expositions you wish.

<margin>b</margin> **And third, how is this solved?** For it can be asked: which is better in a quartan fever—to give the laxative on the day before the paroxysm, or on the day after the paroxysm? And Avicenna seems to want it to be given the day before the paroxysm, because he says "let it be the day after," and does not say "if it be in the day after." Therefore he places one day between the paroxysm and the medicine. And consequently it is given on that day before the paroxysm; and although several causes can be given for this, two seem primary: one, because the strength is greater and fortified; second, because the melancholic matter is more accumulated and sharpened; and therefore certain places in which it is begin to have some movement, not to other places, but within the places themselves. And this helps with evacuation. ¶ Many things could be said here, because many factors can concur from which we choose a different hour to give the pharmacy between paroxysm and paroxysm.

<margin>c</margin> **And it is not necessary.** Thus let "provocation" be explained: that is, it is made by laxatives like lapis lazuli and hellebore, which is known; if "provocatives" are explained as things provoking urine, that is also known. Because these agitate the raw matter and draw out its subtle parts.

<margin>d</margin> **And it is necessary that softeners be administered.** That is, things that ease the belly, like cassia or manna, to cleanse the feces and the corruptions of the intestinal matter. ¶ If it seems to you that these softeners should not be made with dew <note>unclear reference, possibly a specific prep</note>, make enemas as said above; the use of enemas is more pleasing to me. ¶ Consider also that sharp enemas require prior digestion, as is known. And it is set down in the third rule of the 16th Fen in the chapter on the cure of choleric fever. Or explain "softeners" as things that "moisten" the melancholic humor, because they are its digestives.

<margin>e</margin> **And if the doctors.** It must be considered that Avicenna prohibited giving a laxative drug at the beginning of the paroxysm, and also in the general beginning. And he did not want them to be given except when the matter is digested; but some doctors are found who give strong medicines at the beginning of the paroxysm and at the beginning of the disease, and the sick were liberated. He says, however, that it is "right by error." That is, that doctor conducted himself erroneously, or that a right and good end proceeded from error; just as a bad leader of an army might succeed despite acting badly. And as such, he should not be praised, nor should such action be a rule for others. But you might say, O stubborn doctor, since this quartan-fever patient was liberated, why did I do wrong? It must be said that it was an individual case, and another such is not found among fifty thousand men. ¶ Therefore, if one proceeds thus in the cure of others, there will be danger. Or it must be said that he who was liberated from the quartan fever with an erroneous cure has from this some bad disposition which he would not have if he had been cured rationally.

<margin>f</margin> **And it is necessary.** It is doubted why he first gives small birds <note>original: "taiegi"</note> and afterwards chickens; indeed, on the contrary, because a diet should proceed by becoming more subtle. A certain man says that it is a "testing diet"; otherwise, because when the diet is not ordered toward the state of the illness, or if it is ordered toward the state but is very distant, we can begin to subtilize the diet for a few days, so that the strength may be free against the matter and the harm of digestion can be corrected, as was said above in the cure of phlegmatic fever.

<margin>g</margin> **And let it be done.** It is doubted how he allows here geleniabin and oxymel with water, when above in the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers in general he prohibited sugar and juleps <note>sweet medicinal drinks</note> at the hour of the paroxysm. It must be said first that this drink is what should be given on the *day* of the paroxysm, not *in* the hour of the paroxysm. Or it should be said, more better: that this drink is more medicinal and less nutritious than barley water or sugar or julep. Know also that although vinegar causes an increase in melancholy (as is gathered in the third of the *Regimen in Acute Diseases*), nevertheless its malice is rectified by the sugar. And this drink is also a good digestive for some days, and specifically in the beginning. And when you wish to use a more powerful subtilizing agent, you have a wealth of other syrups for this.

<margin>h</margin> **And you.** Yellow myrabolans and violets are on account of the sharpness of the bile; but at what time you should use the myrabolans, I ought to know from the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers.

<margin>i</margin> **And if it is.** Because they evacuate phlegmatic matter.

<margin>k</margin> **And know.** Whey <note>original: "aqua casei"</note> is a good material for infusions, as **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Assyrian physician.</note> said, when there is violent and sharp heat, because it eases the matters and evacuates. Avicenna thought, however, that although the liquid part of milk is hot and dry through its sharp nitrous parts through which it loosens, it nevertheless has much of the watery, cold, and moist, through which it washes, as we have already said on the second rule in the chapter on cheese. And therefore Avicenna does not safely use whey in a weak or blocked or softened stomach, nor even when a cold humor is present. But in its place he uses water in which rose-honey is boiled with a strong boiling, so that he may obtain this result. And this can be the material for infusions of whatever medicines you wish. **And vomiting.** It is doubted whether vomiting on the day of the paroxysm before the start of the paroxysm is suitable. It seems not: because above, laxative medicine was prohibited on the day of the paroxysm. Therefore emetics as well, since they are stronger. Further, in the fourth section of the *Aphorisms*, it is commanded that melancholics be evacuated through the lower parts. On the contrary are all others; wherefore Avicenna commands it to be done because it alleviates or eradicates. As he will say later. General things about vomiting at the beginning of the paroxysm we have already said above in the general cure; here let us say how much it is expedient in quartan fever: because vomiting with a strong thing like...
<sig>k</sig>

<column-break/>

¶ In my younger years, I explained this passage thus: but it is necessary that it be evacuated in the beginning etc. for the purpose of alleviating and cleansing: supplement this by saying "let it be done in the beginning itself." However, not in the absolute beginning, but when some subtilization of the matter appears; and this does not exclude the reason for the "beginning." For that is—that is, that evacuation—when it is not a "diminishing" or "alleviating" one, but an "eradicating" one at the time of digestion—that is, when the matter is digested—and not in the beginning. It is according to what I shall indicate. The other exposition which I have already hinted at pleases me more: that all this refers to the diminishing evacuation...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "quartan" fever (a recurring four-day fever), specifically detailing the protocols for therapeutic vomiting and the dietary regime required to manage the melancholic humor associated with the disease.</meta>

# Book

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin> Evacuation should not be performed with hellebore <note>original: "eleboro"; a toxic plant used as a powerful purgative</note> or lapis lazuli <note>original: "lapide lazuli"; powdered blue stone used medicinally to purge black bile</note> because of the reasons stated above, for which we have prohibited laxative medicines. Instead, vomiting can be induced with a decoction of radish or its seeds; indeed, it ought to be done. The first reason is that it cleanses the corrupt materials in the stomach which "quartaners" <note>those suffering from quartan fever</note> aggregate due to the impairment of stomach digestion caused by the fever and the proximity of the fever to the stomach. The second reason is that most melancholic matters have their root around the area of the spleen, and those areas communicate with the stomach through many large veins. Therefore, on the day of the paroxysm <note>the onset of the fever fit</note>, before its arrival, the humor already begins to move in those places and must be expelled to locations outside the veins. Vomiting, therefore, draws it out and diverts it toward the cavities of the stomach and the intestines. And this is what Haly Abbas <note>original: "Aliab."; referring to the 10th-century Persian physician Haly Abbas</note> intended in this chapter: that since the humor is tumultuous and ready for motion on the day of the paroxysm, vomiting ought to be performed. In this vomiting, either some of the matter is diverted to the hollows of the stomach and various intestines and distracted from its motion through the sensitive members—and then the paroxysm is alleviated and can be removed—or, if that quantity is great, none of this humor is distracted from its course. Even then, the paroxysm is alleviated because the materials which are badly placed in the stomach are not the cause of the continuous fever; rather, they add heat and anxiety when they undergo corruption by the febrile heat. But you might say: "By this reasoning, I could give a laxative drug such as senna or epithymum." It must be said that you cannot time your drug to the moment of evacuation—that is to say, you cannot ensure it acts just before the paroxysm comes—nor can you command it to act only upon the humor that has been moved and not on others. Instead, it acts upon everything, and a very great commotion will occur which ought not to coincide with the motion of the paroxysm. It is safer to act on the day of rest. It is doubted whether these words seem to contradict our statements in the general cure of putrid fevers, where the reasoning of Thaddeus <note>original: "Thadei"; likely Taddeo Alderotti, a famous 13th-century medical professor</note> was praised, arguing that evacuation should not occur on the day of the paroxysm because the matter is moved by a motion contrary to the motion of the drug. Yet here it is said that in quartan fever, vomiting is done to divert the matter from its path toward the stomach and intestines. It must be said that materials which are in the regions beyond the liver and in remote places should not and cannot be diverted, for that could not happen without a strong, debilitating motion that would coincide with the motion of the paroxysm. However, the motion of materials around the stomach can be diverted by vomiting without using a strong drug. And if the melancholy is "phlegmatic"—that is, having phlegm as the matter of melancholy around the stomach—this vomiting is much more appropriate. This is what Avicenna says, especially when the melancholy is phlegmatic. The hour for this vomiting should be near the paroxysm only, so that some commotion begins in the matter; this is either one hour before the paroxysm, or a half-hour, or at the very beginning of the fit, according to what seems best to you. The solution to the first argument is now apparent. To the second, it must be said that if you wish to evacuate with hellebore or lapis lazuli, you must choose the day of rest. But if you wish to evacuate with a light vomiting, it is done at the beginning—not only at the universal beginning <note>the start of the disease</note> or the beginning of the paroxysm, but at other times of the paroxysm, and this requires consideration. For such vomiting is not done for the sake of the matter that is already spread toward the skin and flesh, but for other matters stirred up around the stomach, which you can draw out through vomiting at any hour if nature has moved them there, or if you believe they are ready to be drawn out by vomiting, as happens at the beginning of the paroxysm.

The administration of it [radish decoction] is perhaps preferred over others when there is violent heat. For *geleniabin* <note>a medicinal syrup made of roses and honey or sugar</note> and its strained water with its strong decoction takes its place, especially when there is weakness in the stomach or when the cold humor prevails. And vomiting again, especially before and after food, is more convenient, particularly on the day of the paroxysm and before the shivering fit. Especially when the melancholy is phlegmatic, it is among the things that help; and not only at the beginning, but indeed at every hour.

**It is necessary, therefore,** that one does not labor at the beginning or at the start of digestion until the completion of digestion is reached, in evacuating superfluity with that which heats with strength, nor with that which dries with strength among medicines and the skipping of meals, nor with that which debilitates through loosening the belly, nor again with that which debilitates at the beginning through an overly refined regime.

**And you should know** that when a quartan fever begins in summer or winter, it is necessary that the first drink be barley water and *secheniabin* <note>original: "secaniabi"; oxymel, a syrup of vinegar and honey</note>, so that it may open the obstructed passages for the sake of provocation <note>stimulating the humors</note> and be consumed quickly; and that is three or four hours after the preceding period. And when the quartan fever occurs in winter, then there is no way that troches <note>original: "trocisci"; medicinal lozenges</note> should be given in the drink.

**And you should know** that cold and moist things that are easy to digest and good food are not suitable for this sickness because it is a "black" fever and because they are contrary to one of the qualities of melancholy, which is dryness. Therefore, they must be administered again where no harm to digestion is feared, and let the quantity not be such that harm to digestion is feared, or let something be mixed with them that tempers their coldness and does not diminish their moisture: that is, things that are moderately warm. And let him avoid everything cold and dry. And the moist and cold things suitable for this sickness are such as endive, lettuce, melon, and peaches. And it is not 

---

<margin>h</margin> **It is necessary, therefore.** Here the author states the circumstances in which you should not attempt evacuation (that is, hidden or manifest consumption) while the matter is still raw at the beginning, nor even when it begins to be digested. There are five such things: first, with that which heats, like pepper or garlic—note that. The second is that which dries, nor should one dry vehemently with a medicine like sulfur, for example. The third is that which dries vehemently through the regime, such as skipping food, because the patient should not be entirely deprived of food for several days, or even on the day of rest. Fourth is the strong loosening of the belly which debilitates, as with lapis lazuli and similar things. He intends that the loosening of the belly should be weak and gentle, or with things that evacuate by loosening lightly, such as polypody and senna. Evacuation can be done when digestion begins, even if not complete, and perhaps with lapis lazuli and similar things but in a smaller dose. The fifth is much refining of the regime; hence he is not deprived of food, yet very little and of little nourishment is given to him. Whence Avicenna begins with small birds. Others have a text here that says: "unless with that which debilitates through loosening... [text cut off]"

<column-break/>

<margin>b</margin> **And you should know.** Consider that *secheniabin*—that is, vinegar syrup—is made with sugar in summer and with honey in winter. With much barley water in summer and less in winter, it is a drink suitable for both summer and winter quartan fever. In winter, indeed, because obstructions occur then, as seen in the second part of the first book in the chapter on the causes of obstructions, and the materials are thicker; such a drink opens, thins, and provokes because of this. In summer also, the opening of passages is useful, and it tempers the heat.

necessary to avoid these, except perhaps because of the intensity of the cold, which is found in lettuce, but not in sweet melon; or because of the intensity of provocation leading to the thickening of the blood, which is found in sweet melon; or because they are prone to putrefaction, which is found in peaches; and you must observe these things. Foods that are moderately warm with added moisture are very helpful, especially when they reach a balance of heat where it is needed, so that they aid digestion alongside cold and moist things, such as mixing figs with endive. And it is not bad at first to take those things in which there is saltiness, sharpness, and cutting <note>original: "incisio"; the ability of a medicine to break up thick humors</note>, when you do not fear an increase in heat. At the end of the sickness, however, there is no excuse for this. And troches of wormwood are helpful until the end of the sickness. Among those things that help is sitting in warm, sweet water before food every day: a bath that moistens and does not cause sweating nor excite heat; and a continuation of comforts and rest, and the avoidance of exercise and bodily or mental motions. And all these fevers require moistening things and vary in the quantity of cooling and heating.

**And the necessity** for drying things is because of the power of cutting, cleansing, and loosening they possess, and not for the sake of drying itself.

**And it is necessary** that the stomach be observed with good, strengthening plasters that are between the power of heat and its subtlety, according to what the condition requires. And let the spleen and liver be observed and managed so that they do not harden or develop abscesses. And perhaps it is necessary to induce vomiting using radish water with its seed, mixed with vinegar syrup.

**And perhaps** it is helped by first eating figs and that which is salted...

<margin>c</margin> **And be consumed quickly.** That is, once the opening and provocation have been achieved, the quartan fever would otherwise quickly return. And "it smokes quickly" <note>likely meaning the humors disperse</note>: that is, immediately when the paroxysm ceases, he should begin his routine to rectify the remaining materials from the paroxysm, and this should continue until the next paroxysm at those hours the physician deems fit.

<margin>d</margin> **Troches.** That is, constricting or drying ones, like those of roses. This is because we do not need much extinguishing [of heat], but rather the opening of pores and obstructions more.

<margin>e</margin> **And you should know.** This is about the diet. First with cold and moist things. He means that lettuce can be granted if you do not fear its coldness. Therefore, in summer, in a "choleric melancholy," it can be given, or mixed with something warm like a little parsley; or similarly a ripe melon. And with its seeds it can be granted if you do not fear its provocation. Therefore, it can be granted when the matter is already digested and diminished. Similarly, peaches can be granted if you do not fear easy putrefaction. Therefore, they can be given to those accustomed to digesting peaches well, or with things that rectify them, such as a little pure wine and those things discussed in the chapter on peaches and apricots.

<margin>f</margin> **Warm foods.** He means that if I do not need cold foods for digestion because the matter is "fecal melancholy," then warm things should be given in moderation. And this is clear.

<margin>g</margin> **And it is not bad.** Since he had praised moderately warm things, he shows that we can use strongly warm, salty, sharp, and "cutting" things. These are like salt-brine, mustard, sharp sorrel, and calamint. This is when you do not fear the heat because it is "melic" melancholy <note>a type of melancholy mixed with honey-like/thick humor</note>, especially at the beginning of the sickness with some digestion appearing. And this should be in a small quantity. For these things rectify the materials and prepare the stomach; we even use them sometimes for vomiting. However, when the matter is digested and diminished, they are more useful. I see he says "at the end," not otherwise.

<margin>i</margin> **And among those.** It should be considered that this washing and bathing is granted before digestion to moisten, because it is for a short duration. Therefore, the matter is not moved, but the body acquires some moisture contrary to the dryness of melancholy. And Avicenna teaches this immediately after, saying: "bodily and mental motions," which are drying.

<margin>k</margin> **And all.** This is clear.

<margin>l</margin> **And it is necessary.** Here he intends to address the accidents that can come from stomach weakness and the obstruction and thickening of the liver and spleen. It is known that he aims for a balance between the "power of heat" (its potency or vigor) and its "subtlety" (its weakness or remission). For some require a more powerful operation and some a weaker one. Let the spleen be observed with strengthening and obstructing [agents].

<margin>m</margin> **And perhaps.** Because sometimes the decoction of radish alone is sufficient without the radish seed. For its seed is stronger, as noted in the second book.

<margin>n</margin> **And perhaps it is helped.** Namely, toward vomiting. It should be considered that he suggests a variety of ways to induce vomiting. For sometimes, after many things have been taken, it is vomited up with vinegar syrup; sometimes vomiting is achieved by taking the vinegar syrup itself on the day of the paroxysm, because then we do not fill the stomach with other things like soup or such, lest if anything remains it might cause harm when the paroxysm arrives.
