# Book I, Division I, Tractate II

...because of the coldness, the shivering, and its sharpness. That is, because of the cold and shivering that occurs with the chills, etc. Consider also that if you are certain that what is given to induce vomiting will indeed be vomited back up, you may give figs and such things as a way to provoke it. But if you suspect retention, then do not. And sometimes food is taken five hours before. Avicenna considered that if it is retained, it is not necessarily a bad thing.

<margin>a</margin>
**O**ne should enter the bath on the second day—that is, the day following the day of the paroxysm <note>the onset of the fever fit</note>—so that the remnants of the materials may be resolved and the complexion <note>the body's balance of humors</note> rectified. Consider Avicenna's distinction: if the matter is "digested"—that is, diminished through vomiting so that it is in decline—let him enter the bath according to the description ordered above, passing through the heated rooms as described in the first book of the therapeutic section. This is so that the person may sweat well and the pores become open. Or, according to the disposition—that is, as the condition requires: if the condition of the digested matter requires it, let the man sweat. If, however, the matter is not digested, as in the universal beginning or the increase of the illness, let there be only a simple pouring of water and not a long-lasting bath, lest the "crude" <note>unprocessed or thick</note> humor be liquefied. In such a case, it would corrupt the good humors and cause more blockages.

<margin>b</margin>
**O**n the third day, which is the day before the paroxysm, vomiting should be performed. It is to be suspected that the stomach sometimes holds fluctuating food which, due to weakness, it could not well digest. Perhaps that washing or bathing moved some materials around the stomach. This is what he means when he says that the bath "resolves"—that is, dissolves. This is the precept of Rabbi Isaac <note>original: "Rab. Is."; referring to Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> in his book on the cure of quartan fever, citing the authority of the "Continens" <note>a major medical encyclopedia by Rhazes</note>. Thus, after he ordered the bath to be taken on the second day, he says: because the bath scatters superfluities toward the stomach and thins the humors, vomiting is necessary on the third day. However, Avicenna does not mean that because vomiting was done on the third day, one is excused from vomiting on the fourth day, which is the day of the paroxysm. Therefore he says "although," etc.

<margin>c</margin>
**I**f the melancholy, etc. Here he specifically sets down the cure according to each type of matter. Second, he sets down the care that must be done after the evacuations following digestion. Third, he describes many medicines there. Then, "take counsel." For the first part, there are four points. For the first: it is called "sanguine melancholy" because it is mixed with blood, or made from blood; yet it is close to it in nature and in its subtle—that is, light—mixture.

<margin>d</margin>
**A**nd if it is choleric, etc. This is the last type in respect to other quartan fevers, because this melancholy is very "burnt" <note>inflamed or agitated</note>. A complete solution—that is, eradicating the matter—should appear upon digestion. Because the matter is less thick and has less of a sharp nature. Then, after the evacuations are performed, let there be a "gradation" <note>a step-by-step increase in medicine strength</note>, etc., which they concede more safely at this time. For the matter itself is prone to catch fire from the mixture. Therefore, I judge that vinegar syrup with endive and fennel water would suffice.

<margin>e</margin>
**A**nd fasting is most important until the time of the period <note>the fever fit</note>; because on the day of the paroxysm, food is not suitable, as the patients are dry, parched, and flammable. And if so, etc.—that is, figs and mustard and similar things before it. And let it be aided after that with a drink of much water. Then let there be a succession with vinegar syrup and let him vomit. Among the things that benefit him is to take it on the day of the paroxysm. Then let him vomit after taking it; for safety, this protects from the harm of the fever, which is due to the cold and shivering and the sharpness of the fever. If he takes other things, such as honey, and drinks honeyed vinegar syrup and fills himself with food, then let him take warm water and vomit. When the paroxysm is consumed <note>finished</note>, let him eat a little supper and bathe in the morning. And if he takes food five hours before the paroxysm so that he may vomit, perhaps it will help him even if he does not vomit. Vomiting before the paroxysm, whatever the humor may be, either alleviates the paroxysm or eradicates it. It is part of a good regimen that he fast on the day of the paroxysm if nothing prohibits it, and let him not take food until the paroxysm is over. And let him enter the bath on that day if there has been digestion according to the description. If there has not been digestion, let there be nothing but a pouring of warm water in an amount that delights the body and moistens it, so that it reaches the point where the humor is liquefied by it. And on the third day, vomiting should be administered because of the surplus of food and what the bath resolved, although it is necessary that vomiting be administered on the day of the paroxysm again. If the melancholy is sanguine <note>mixed with blood</note>, it will be helped by bloodletting from the basilic vein <note>a major vein in the arm</note>; then a subtle evacuation with those things which are put in to cleanse the blood, such as the virtues of *fucbaba* and *bedoard* and polypody and fumitory and chebulic myrobalans. This type indeed receives a cure quickly. And if the melancholy is choleric <note>mixed with yellow bile</note>, then it is up to you to administer the ultimate cooling and moistening from medicines and foods; and administer tempered water for sitting in and washing. And let there be a softening of the nature at the beginning with those things that are like this: what is made from violets, and what is made from whey with the virtue of polypody; or vinegar syrup with epithyme and syrup of "rob" <note>a thickened fruit juice</note>, and julep water and cassia. But let its complete solution be made after many days when digestion appears in it—that is, when the matter is choleric. Then let there be a gradation to that which thins and cuts. And if rectification of the stomach is necessary, then let it be done with oily ointments and poultices <note>original: "epithiathib."; compresses</note> which do not exceed the strength of chamomile, wormwood, melilot, and similar things. And fasting should be prolonged until the day of the period. And sometimes again it is one of those things that is not suitable for him, and if it is on the day of the period, let a very little food suffice them. Among the helpful cleansers are those in which there is a decoction of myrobalans and epithyme and fennel in vinegar syrup in which violets have been boiled. And perhaps it is taken in a drink containing asafetida...

<column-break/>

...he should not abstain from food, but let something else be given to him. 

<margin>f</margin>
**A**nd perhaps—if you do not fear overheating and you hope that the benefit of thinning the matter through asafetida and provoking sweat will be great—it should be used before the fever, provided the matter is perfectly digested. "Asafetida" <note>original: "afsa"</note> perhaps refers here to the sweet kind, which is not found among us. "Anima" here refers to the stomach <note>original: "Anima. i. stomachus"; meaning the "spirit" or appetite of the stomach</note>.

<margin>g</margin>
**A**nd if the melancholy is phlegmatic <note>mixed with phlegm</note>. And similar things like parsley and asparagus. The "dissolving virtue at the beginning," etc.—here it appears that in phlegmatic matter and matter similar to it, Avicenna intends for us to use dissolvents more boldly from the beginning. I understand "from the beginning" to mean when some thinning of the matter has started, as we have often taught above. "Small gradation" means a small step from turbith to agaric. And perhaps turbith is stronger? Then understand the "grade" in terms of doses, until it begins to be digested; for then he will be able to vomit with more strength. "Hellebore with its disposition"—that is, in its proper preparation. Other things are well known.

...in fasting because of the day of the paroxysm; and let him vomit it up if he feels nausea in his "soul" <note>stomach</note>. And if it is phlegmatic melancholy, return to honeyed vinegar syrup with water of celery and fennel and the like. And if softening is necessary, let there be mixed with it at the beginning a common dissolving virtue from the virtues of turbith and polypody; and let there be a small gradation to the strength of agaric. Let it be done so that he vomits with honeyed vinegar syrup of seeds and such things until it begins to be digested. And if your operation is on the stomach and its plastering with that which is stronger—such as with dates and figs and the like—likewise anoint it with warm oils, proceeding even to oil of costus. And perhaps it is necessary in this case to provoke vomiting with vinegar syrup, and let there be in it the strength of mustard and white hellebore; indeed, perhaps it is necessary that hellebore be given in a drink with its proper preparation when weakness of the body's strength is not feared. And if the melancholy is "pure," of the nature of the dregs of blood, then it is rectified first with julep water and sugar-penids <note>pulled sugar sticks</note>; and the administration of honeyed and sugary *geleniabin* <note>a conserve of roses</note> is suitable. In the end, evacuate them with things such as a decoction of yellow and black myrobalans, fumitory, and raisins. When the sickness is therefore digested, then bloodletting from the basilic vein is good. And let vomiting be administered after food, either strongly or lightly according to the hour and necessity. It must be done continually, since it is the root of the evacuation, along with medicines and strong enemas. The medicines administered at such a time are epithyme, polypody, agaric, stoechas, Armenian stone, and lapis lazuli (both washed and unwashed), and the juice of centaury leaves with honeyed syrup. And perhaps black hellebore is necessary; and perhaps they infuse fennel and fumitory with epithyme in vinegar syrup for the "colic." Then take counsel regarding the vomiting and give in a drink for the phlegmatic and melancholic: theriac <note>original: "tyriacaz"; a famous compound medicine</note>, mithridat, and the medicine made from asafetida, sulfur, and pepper; let him drink it only in water. Among these is mustard, which should not be administered continually but rather every three days, and at first a longer time before it. Similarly *diapiperon* <note>a pepper-based confection</note> and similar electuaries. And do not hasten with any of these before digestion; for if you give theriac and similar things in a drink at the beginning, you will "propose a quartan with a quartan"—that is, you will double the fever—and perhaps you will attract other illnesses, especially in winter. And at the end of it, if bloodletting is necessary, dare to perform it. Galen says: "I have cured many people from quartan fever thus: I gave them a dissolvent drink after digestion, then I gave them a drink of wormwood juice, then I gave them theriac." And I say that asafetida and pepper are uniquely helpful when digestion appears and the state of the illness arrives. Feed him...

<margin>h</margin>
**A**nd if it be in the beginning—that is, when the matter is not digested—if you wish to soften the belly: *Lubleb*—that is, a type of milk-product <note>original: "spēs lacticinij"; though often used for scammony, the author here interprets it as a dairy preparation</note>, as we have often explained. It is not given to evacuate the melancholy, but to move the feces and the thick, superfluous materials of the stomach and intestines and entirely for softening and moistening. Other things should be given with julep water—that is, with julep and sugar-penids for softening and moistening. "And in the end"—that is, when the materials are digested. Regarding "yellow myrobalans": it would be better to say "chebulic," for then Avicenna believes that the yellow ones sometimes evacuate the phlegm, the increase of which occurs under the dominance of the "fecal" melancholy; therefore he spoke of the yellow ones.

<margin>i</margin>
**W**hen therefore it is digested, etc. That is, in such a way that it is close to blood, and the urine appears red and thick. But at this "hour," there are many hours if you consider them, and many degrees of necessity. "It is the root"—that is, the root of the cure, because this melancholy has its "mine" near the spleen and near places close to the stomach at such a time—that is, the time of digestion. Regarding "choleric": here he returns to the previous topic. "Then take counsel"—that is, let the rules mentioned above be in your mind "during the vomiting"—that is, after the evacuation. That is, performed after digestion, because that evacuation is stronger; and usually it is not just one, but many evacuations are repeated. "Theriac"—that is, fermented; in my judgment, it should be older than six years. However, Avicenna fears inflammation in the choleric and sanguine types, and he follows his own knowledge. "Mustard at first"—that is, earlier and before the medicine of asafetida and sulfur. For the use of it—that is, prepared mustard—is safer, just as we make it in "mustarda," which is the use of the said medicines. And therefore you can use it a longer space of time before. And if mustard is not given continually, much less those other things. The use of all these is for the consumption, drying, and resolution of the materials. Therefore, before the digestion of the matter, they are harmful, as they sometimes multiply the matter and make it more malignant. Wherefore they can double the quartan fever and cause other melancholic illnesses, specifically in winter, when there is greater fullness and materials are not prone to resolution but to sickness. Whence in the new "Prognostics" of Galen to Epigenes, chapter 2, when Galen is asked why theriac doubled the quartan fever in the philosopher Endinus, he replied that the illness was still undigested. For the medicine contains an undigested "bad juice" <note>original: "chachochinnā"; cachexia/bad humor</note>, and especially in winter—at the beginning—it is capable of disturbing what is offered, but not of digesting or causing it to sweat out. And hence it happens in the fever of quartans that the necessity of bloodletting arises from many possible causes, one of which is inflammation produced in the blood from the use of hot medicines, and then a more copious feeding.

<margin>k</margin>
**G**alen says in the "Therapeutics to Glaucon," chapter 2: *Sabane* is a food made from salted fish and nuts and spices, of which he writes in the second book of the Canon, and its virtue is drying. *Elbuue* is another kind...

# Book I, Division I, Tractate II

<margin>a</margin> A food of a similar kind: and "remich" <note>original: *remich*; a medicinal preserve of fruit</note> made of pickled capers. These things were explained in the preceding treatment for phlegmatic conditions. Feed him with those things in which there is a thinning and drying power, such as garlic.
¶ And perhaps, if a "digestion" <note>the maturation of the humors</note> appears, and the *abaca* <note>a specific measurement or weight</note> is not of great weight or measure—namely, the size of one bean or four grains—it should not be of a choleric nature, for inflammation is feared. Where it is not feared, it can be allowed. And as he said above in the treatment of quartan fever regarding choleric melancholy: "And perhaps it is taken in a drink," etc. These statements do not contradict each other; rather, one helps the other. For when I say "perhaps it is given or taken," it is understood that perhaps it is *not* given or taken.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ And regarding the lozenges <note>term: *trocisci*; medicinal tablets or lozenges</note>. Here, nine composite medicines are first described. He says first that it helps at this hour—that is, after digestion and evacuation—and that it helps in many ways: by opening and strengthening the liver and spleen and all digestive organs, and by provoking and resolving the matter. Consider that these other things [work] from the power of the simples and are "digested"—that is, the digestion appears in the matter—because this medicine dries the matter, resolves it, and provokes it somewhat. It is more appropriate for phlegmatic cases. "Adelle," etc.; for us, this would be a decoction of ginger thickened with honey.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ "And sometimes." This is the third medicine, used when there is little harm, occurring in the decline [of the fever] and when there is much heat. Because this quartan fever is in decline, much disparity remains in the liver and the digestive system, along with a "subtiliation" <note>thinning</note> of the matter—that is, the matter is thin or thinned, and not very thick. A *siliqua* <note>a unit of weight, about 4 grains</note> is four grains; others say 8 grains. This medicine tempers the heat because of the *biuszaz* and mandrake, and it consumes by roasting, which also corrects their harmful qualities; it belongs to this class—namely, those things which are suitable in the decline when the matter is digested.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ "And from them." This is a medicine made of "semi," or others are names of places. Or *alochen*, which is feverfew <note>original: *matricaria*</note>. This is a medicine that resolves the matter; myrobalans <note>term: *myrabolani*; astringent plum-like fruits used as a laxative</note> are added for some strengthening of the limbs.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ "And again." This is the sixth medicine, and it is evident.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ "And of that." This is the seventh medicine. It also requires the digestion and lessening of the matter. It is a medicine made of asafetida <note>original: *assa*</note>, just as a preceding one could be called a medicine of garlic or cassia bark.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ Lozenges of this kind. This is the eighth medicine, and it is a medicine that is quite effective at digesting the matter.

<margin>h</margin> ¶ "And again." This is the ninth medicine, which can be made in the form of lozenges; it also requires some digestion and lessening of the matter.

<margin>i</margin> ¶ "And when." It pleased Avicenna to set down the regimen for shivering <note>original: *rigor*</note> in quartan fever, first through vomiting. If its powers—the shivering's—do not obey the treatment of vomiting because vomiting does not calm that shivering, then treat the shivering with those things said above in the chapter on the regimen of shivering. Or thus: if the powers of the feverish person do not obey vomiting with warm water, then provoke vomiting with those things, such as radish, and specifically radish seed according to the *borax* <note>likely a reference to a specific dosage or salt</note> of the shivering. And evaporation—that is, treating it with a warm soak <note>term: *embroca*; a liquid application or warm compress</note> in water; for one could soak it. *Scbea* is a species of wormwood, southernwood, or thyme. And it is clear.

### ¶ On the recounting of laxatives which are needed after digestion. Chapter 66.

<margin>B</margin> Six drachms of chebulic myrobalans, five drachms each of epithymum <note>dodder of thyme</note> and wormwood, three and a half drachms each of yellow myrobalans and agrimony juice and emblic myrobalans. Two drachms each of celery seed, anise, and a half-measure of fennel. Let a decoction be made of them, and let it move the bowels with ease. Or let there be taken: half a drachm of wormwood, eight drachms each of chebulic myrobalans and epithymum, and seven drachms of fumitory, six drachms each of *suchaba* and greater centaury, five drachms each of agrimony and camel-grass root. **Light pills.** These are administered every five days; they are helpful in this case and have been tested. Take half a drachm each of epithymum and turbith, six and a half drachms each of caraway and anise, eight drachms of bishop's weed, eight drachms each of celery and fennel seed, six drachms of polypody, eight drachms of white agaric <note>a type of medicinal mushroom</note> which is easily ground, five drachms of Indian salt, and fifteen drachms of *hiera picra* <note>term: *hiera picra*; "holy bitter," a traditional purgative powder</note>. Let pills be made with mint water; let the dose be one and a half drachms. When the matter is phlegmatic, these pills are preferred. The dose is two and a half drachms. And since there is pain in the spleen, this medicine helps and moves the bowels with ease. Take fifteen drachms of hart's tongue fern, seven drachms of agaric, half a drachm each of black myrobalans and *hiera*, eight drachms each of chebulic myrobalans and wormwood, seven and a half drachms each of *suchaba*, *bedeard*, ground-pine, and agrimony juice; five and a half drachms each of tamarisk fruit and caper roots; three drachms each of celery, anise, and fennel seed. Let a confection or pills be made.

### ¶ On the feeding of patients with quartan fever. Chapter 67.

<margin>R</margin> It is more correct that their regimen be inclined toward a certain thinning in the first weeks, up to three weeks, except for that which obstructs the strength. This means they should abstain from meat and *alz-umet* <note>original: *alz-umet*; rich meat dishes or gravies</note>. This diminishes their humors, relieves them, and shortens the duration of their illness. After this, it is necessary to revive the strength...

<column-break/>

¶ Or let wormwood be taken. This is the second medicine and can be given in a large dose from two to four ounces. The rest is clear. But consider that Avicenna did not set down any composition of a powerful laxative. For he had already spoken about medicinal stones and hellebore. And therefore, if you need them, you may use that power as it seems best to you. However, for quartan fever, we have no secret experiment, but a cure according to the rules and precautions aforesaid.

¶ Aetius is [cited]. There, he first sets the order of feeding. Second, he states what the conditions of the food for those with quartan fever are.
"And you should know." Third, he sets down certain canons.
"And you already." It must be considered <margin>1</margin> first: that the regimen is ordered from the beginning until the "state" <note>the peak of the illness</note> because of the struggle expected in that state; then we begin with a thicker regimen and move toward a thinner one. However, we temper this if the illness is perhaps short; we begin with thinning. This is called a "tentative regimen," about which we spoke above in the chapter on the treatment of phlegmatic conditions.
¶ When the regimen is not ordered for the "state" <note>peak</note>, it is because the illness is taken up gradually, as most often happens in quartan fever, or the state is very distant. Therefore, regarding what is currently present—the fullness and thickness of the matter—we order the diet. Then we can begin with a thinner <margin>2</margin> diet first and afterwards thicken it, as Avicenna does here and taught above in this chapter. It must be considered second that he begins the thin regimen without meats, and afterwards gives meats when he thickens the diet. Either he began the thin diet with autumn fruits and proceeded by thickening toward young chickens, and in this there is no contradiction, since either gradation is possible in different men and different dispositions, and likewise in one man. And when a person with quartan fever changes from abstinence from meat to eating meat, he first begins with the meat of small birds, and afterwards proceeds to young chickens, and from chickens to kids and rams—namely, *asales* and *abimezec* <note>local or Arabic names for types of meat preparations</note>. It must be considered <margin>3</margin> third that *alz-umet* is a way of preparing meat dishes that are oily—namely, with bacon or lard among us, or oil and fatty meats among the Saracens. You have many ways of preparing these fatty meats of chicken, kid, and ram with oil from Al-Zahrawi in book 26 and in book 6 regarding dishes. However, I find that sometimes *alz-umet* is breadcrumbs upon which the fat of a roast falls. That word *alz-umet* is placed here twice. First, when he says they should abstain from meat—namely, boiled or roasted—and *alz-umet*—namely, types of oily foods made from meats cut into pieces and prepared with honey, oil, and garlic as the aforesaid state, although I believe these types of *alz-umet* can also be made from fish. Secondly, it is placed when he says, "when therefore the time arrives in which it follows"—namely, the fever—"the *alz-umet*"—namely, oily foods of this kind, because it is the safest time in which to give them...

...twenty drachms of saffron and parsley; five drachms each of spikenard and castor; three drachms each of anise, celery seed, and caraway; two and one-third drachms each of amomum, cassia bark, and storax; and one and two-thirds drachms of the confection of Adrian. And when the shivering is vehement, vomit with warm water and oxymel <note>original: *sirupo acetoso*; vinegar and honey syrup</note> to help it. But if its powers do not obey, then use those things whose mention preceded according to the *borax*. And let an evaporation be made with a soak in which wormwood, chamomile, and similar things have been boiled, with the person covered with woolen cloths to collect the heat.

Fen II Tractatus | 130

It returns and does not diminish. Thus, the one who interpreted **alzūmet** <note>original: *alzūmet*; a medicinal meat broth or juice, often from chicken</note> as "difficult accidents" erred greatly. Fourthly, it must be considered that the entire order of the regimen which Avicenna <note>original: *Auic.*</note> establishes here is based on a temperate clinical judgment: that the quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days, associated with "black bile"</note> should be expected to last for a month. Therefore, in the first three weeks, the patient should abstain from meat and **alzūmet**, and a light diet should be used, though not excessively so. For this reason, he is not satisfied with only julep, but uses a light chickpea water with almond milk and similar things. By this regimen, the body's strength is freed to deal with the diseased materials.

> After three weeks, begin to give more nourishing things, which are a heavier diet than the preceding one. Start with **alduragi** fish <note>original: *piscib⁹ alduragi*; likely a type of rock-fish or stone-fish</note>, i.e., those found among rocks, etc. Then move to chickens and small birds. This is what the **altaragi** says <note>original: *altaragi*; likely a reference to a specific medical authority or preparation</note>, for he did not care to establish an order here between chickens and birds. And if it seems right to you, move to general foods, as Avicenna understood. For it is certain that this regimen continues for six weeks. Then he began to give **alzūmet**. And if you see that the quartan fever is not diminishing—rather, it is now at its beginning—it is certain that it will extend for nearly a year. Therefore, you should then begin your "heavy" regimen, which is very nourishing. For example, where you gave small birds and chickens, give **alzūmet** or hens, full-grown chickens, young goats, rams, and birds with soft flesh, namely young pigeons.

<margin>a</margin> **Alduragi**. Some say this means a turtledove. Others say it refers to meat prepared by boiling or roasting, which is more nourishing than the **alzūmet** made from them. Avicenna understands, therefore, that with this heavy regimen on days of rest, after some days you should return to a light regimen, according to what seems best to you.

<margin>b</margin> **And you should know**. Regarding the four properties, these are the signs found in "praiseworthy" meats prepared in good ways.

<margin>c</margin> **Pure wine**. This is especially used when some "digestion" <note>the maturation or breaking down of humors</note> is apparent in the diseased matter.

<margin>d</margin> **Disposition**. In these three things, he places the difference between the treatment of intermittent and continuous quartan fever. First, a shift toward warming agents is better in the intermittent type. Second, I say "equal" warming agents—that is, properly proportioned according to the matter and the condition. But in the continuous type, a shift toward cooling is better—that is, a milder warming.

along with those things which are here: **alcadradrie** fish and soft-boiled eggs, chickens, and **albatagi**. Therefore, when it reaches the time in which you know the **alzūmet** is needed, and the sickness does not decrease, then it is necessary to maintain the strength with food using the stronger meats of hens, chickens, rams, and young goats, and birds with soft flesh. These are chickens, **alduragi**, and good fish that are not large. And know that the condition of the food for one who has quartan fever is that it should combine several properties: one is that it should not be raw, but rather should resolve the "rawness" <note>undigested humors</note> caused by the sickness. The second is that it should not be "gross" <note>heavy/thick</note>, but rather should thin out what is thick. The third is that it should not be constricting, but rather should loosen the bowels. The fourth is that the blood generated from it should be "praiseworthy" <note>healthy</note>. Most of all, food should have the qualities of heat and moisture. You already know what should be eaten before a paroxysm <note>the onset of the fever fit</note>, how many hours before, and why. You also know that food is sometimes necessary during a paroxysm, specifically in the first stage, for the reasons mentioned before. However, it is preferred that the fever arrives on an empty stomach, so that nature is not occupied with other matter, but only with the matter of the sickness until it expels it. And the wine should be pure and light.

### On the Cure of Continuous Quartan Fever. Chapter 68.

**I**f your patient has the fever we described before, the rule for it is similar to the rule for intermittent quartan fever. It does not differ except in a few things. One of these is that the shift in this fever is toward balance in warming agents, because cooling in this case is better due to the persistence of the fever. Therefore, it is ordered that in its cure, those things should be administered which are here: vinegar syrup with seeds, **geleniabin** <note>a preserve of roses and honey</note>, water of equal roots, and suppositories with honey. Another difference is bloodletting, which is more necessary in this case because the matter is more contained in the veins. And among these differences is that the allowance of meat in this sickness is less; therefore, beware of this.

<column-break/>

the density can be burnt and become "melancholy" <note>black bile</note>, which causes quartan fever. And if it is burnt further and becomes "earthy" so as to cause a five-day or six-day fever, it still has moisture that can putrefy and, by evaporating, carry the feverish heat—just as coals made from green wood emit more flame than those from dry wood.

<margin>b</margin> **Sextana** <note>a fever recurring every six days</note>. Here first he places the opinion of Hippocrates, and Galen in the third part discusses them. The second part is there: "And therefore." The first part is in three. First, he places the words of Hippocrates; second (b), third, he completes the discourse. Galen said there in the third part: "Truly Hippocrates said first," etc. Hippocrates spoke, namely, in the *Book of Epidemics*.

i **And Galen**. First he places the opinion of Galen; second, he takes up his intention. Although (b) he spoke first about the differences of fevers in the fourth chapter, he spoke more at length in the *Commentary on the Epidemics*. A "strong quintan" <note>five-day fever</note>—that is, pure and distinct. But there was for Galen one quartan fever delaying until the end of the fourth day, which, being extended into the fifth day, seemed to be a quintan fever. Therefore it is a "hidden" fever. Galen says, namely, in the *Book of Epidemics*: it should be considered that Avicenna, following Galen’s intention, assigns the cause in seven-day and nine-day fevers. Because the cause he gave for the five-day fever cannot be applied to these. He says the cause is in the "regimen" <note>lifestyle/diet</note>; for the malice of the regimen makes the fever, and its correction makes the fever cease. Therefore, the repetition of the bad regimen causes the periodic movement and return of the paroxysms.

k **And its periods**. He shows that the cause of these fevers is not from their periodization and return. He says that the periods and returns of these fevers are not the periods of the "matter" <note>humor</note> being poured out to the sites of putrefaction—as we said in tertian, quotidian, and quartan fevers—or the return of the matter. Galen says in the said commentary that it must be observed in experience, etc.—that is, if anyone through experience finds this seven-day fever and those similar to it. This is the intention: that the cause is not "matter" that has an outpouring and return, but the cause is an error in the regimen which is maintained. Thus, no error should happen in the regimen or cure or experience—that is, the cure—because the cure will be to ensure no error occurs. However, the first explanation is better.

l **Although**. Here in sum is placed the intention of Galen. It is that Galen essentially denies these fevers. The reason is that if these fevers existed, then there would have to be another "root"—that is, another humor besides the four humors. But this is false, as is well known. For the humor making these fevers cannot be black bile (because that moves on the fourth day), nor yellow bile, nor phlegm for a similar reason, nor blood (because that makes a continuous motion). Therefore, there would necessarily be another root—that is, another humor distinct from these. This is what the reason states.

### On Sextan, Septan, and Similar Fevers. Chapter 69.

**T**hey are named **pbitanos** <note>original: *pbitanos*; a term for a specific fever type</note>, and some call such fevers "resolvable." These are generated from matter similar to the matter of quartan fever, but it is less and thicker. And for the most part, they are made from the aforementioned matter. Regarding sextan and septan fevers and when they occur, Hippocrates and Galen spoke. I have not seen any of them in my life, nor have I seen a "strong, naked" quintan fever; it is only a hidden fever. He says it is not far-fetched that the cause in a septan <note>seven-day</note> or nonan <note>nine-day</note> fever is the regimen. For when a certain regimen is administered and followed, it causes the fever. For the repetition of it at such an hour necessarily causes that fever. If it were stopped and corrected, it would not happen. The cause is therefore in its periods, or rather in its repetitions—the repetition of the regimen and its periods. These are not the periods of matter being poured out and returning. He says it must therefore be observed in the experience of this sickness this intention: so that an error does not occur. Although Galen essentially denies the arrival of these fevers, as if it were necessary for such a fever to have another root. Truly Hippocrates verified the discourse in the finding of the septan and nonan fever; and that is not a manifest wonder or a manifest impossibility, such that it would be necessary to return to investigating it. And the words which Hippocrates spoke regarding these fevers are that the septan is long-lasting but not deadly, and the nonan is longer than it and is not deadly. And he said that the quintan is worse.

<insert>
In the last chapter of the *Continent* <note>original: *cōtinentis*; likely Rhazes' *Liber Continens*</note>, Galen said in the *Book of Epidemics*: "I have not seen a quartan fever except one that lasts until the fifth day," which seems to contradict Hippocrates' statement. For it would be impossible, as he says of the quintan. It does not appear to be a quartan fever based on which humor it is. Avicenna said that Galen's denial is not a total denial of these fevers, but he denies they depend on a determined humor; he says they arise from an error in regimen. He doubts it because it seems impossible for any fever to periodize from seventh day to seventh day, or similarly, without having "matter" that pours out at the hour of the paroxysm and is afterwards resolved and then pours out again. Furthermore, this matter would be some humoral matter and not outside the genus of the four humors. It must be said that Galen hypothesized that these periodic fevers arise from the movements of humors which are under humoral forms, moving in a certain period by the nature of the humors and the determined disposition of the body. This is seen in one having a tertian fever whose paroxysm returns every third day, no matter how well he is managed. Regarding the sum of these fevers, Galen could not imagine quintan and sextan fevers existing after them. The reason is that it would mean providing humors of other kinds. One must therefore say that the continuation of an error in regimen is the cause of this; for example, an error in something "gross" <note>heavy food</note>. Often you see someone recovering from a long fever who eats figs every morning; on every seventh day, from the bad digestion of those figs and dairy, something is gathered around the mesenteric or other parts which does not have the true form of the humors. That corrupted thing causes a fever every seventh day. If it had the true form of some humor, it would not make a septan fever; if it were yellow bile it would make a tertian, and so on. This was Galen's intention without a doubt in the *Commentary on the Epidemics*, although he does not follow this matter much; rather, he postpones it out of reverence for Hippocrates, whom he is forced to contradict. But if one understands it, this appears to be the solution to the contrary arguments.

### Column 2

...indeed, that periodicity follows the specific form of the humors. But Avicenna seems to say the contrary when he says melancholy causes a quartan not insofar as it is melancholy; but let us explain: not insofar as it is melancholy alone, but insofar as it is melancholy with a determined thickness and smallness. To understand this, therefore, it must be considered that Avicenna and Galen both saw that periodicity generally and in most cases found follows the specific form of the humors. For from the quantity and thickness of the humors, it is impossible to find these undetermined periods found for the most part, since those dispositions are varied almost to infinity, as we have declared elsewhere. And Avicenna saw this more clearly, as appeared to us for some time—namely, after we saw the commentary on the *Epidemics*. We found that Galen firmly saw this. However, this is the difference between these men: because after Galen grants that periodicity follows the specific form of the humors, he could not grant that there would be a quintan, a septan, and such fevers, because it would follow that there would be another humor besides those four. For if a continuous period is of blood, a daily of phlegm, a tertian of choler <term>choler: yellow bile</term>, and a quartan of melancholy, therefore a quintan will be of a fifth humor. Avicenna did not see that although periodicity follows forms or specific natures, yet this is also the case with other natural accidents. For they follow forms with determined natural accidents, just as the attraction of iron follows a magnet of a determined quantity and quality. Whence if it is anointed with oil, it does not attract, as in the seventh and eighth books of the *Physics* by Averroes. Although therefore melancholy is principally moved in the fourth [day] by its property, yet it requires a determined quantity and mode of refinement; if these are changed, it will be able to cycle without keeping its usual motion, since it can in another quantity be putrefied, corrupted, and suffer. Therefore, it can be moved at another time. What this property is, and between which things this habit of delay <note>original: "mor⁶" likely for "morae"</note> exists, we have said in our inquiry.

<margin>c</margin> "Furthermore, there is no disposition." This is the highest praise; and it was given to Hippocrates when he says that neither to concede that which is not seen, nor to concede that which is not heard, nor to concede that which some expert would say, nor to concede that which some philosopher says, is such a concession as to concede that which Hippocrates says, or that which Hippocrates testifies. To concede therefore what Hippocrates says is to concede a thing seen, a thing heard, a thing experienced, and a thing physically proven. For he himself was a philosopher and an expert who would not have written if he had not seen and heard what he wrote. Another reading, however, says that there is no contradiction. And he wants that to concede what Hippocrates said is not to contradict things seen, etc. He also brings in testimony and repeats the motive for removal. Galen says: "I confess, however, that I have seen a quintan and a sextan; and it always invaded from the 15th day to the 15th day." And this was in Berardinus de Burinaris of Gualdo. That which invades once a month is affirmed by Rhazes <note>original: "Raſis"</note> in the 16th book of the *Continens*. Although he mentions the genera, we are encouraged to understand that. Master Jacobus of Firmo, however, for several years on one day and hour, suffered one paroxysm of fever once a year.

# Book

All distinct moistures in the body parts should first be understood under a two-fold division. For the moistures that exist in the body parts—but are not yet the body part itself—are either prepared for nourishment, which are the first and third moistures (that is, the "exchange" moisture <note>original: "cambium"</note>), or they are prepared for moistening (that is, the joints and other parts when some cause of vigorous movement has dried them out).
¶ This moisture is of the nature of "dew" <note>original: "ros"</note>. The purpose of dew, therefore, is principally to moisten the joints and members, and not to nourish them unless nourishment is lacking. This we declared in the first chapter according to our opinion: that when the first moisture becomes "exchange" <note>original: "cambium"</note>, it does not necessarily become "dew" first. Rather, in the transformation of the first moisture into "exchange," dew is generated, just as phlegm is generated in the transformation of chyle into blood. Alternatively, the text can be explained as first establishing the moistures—namely the first and the others—when it speaks of those moistures prepared for nourishment (which refers to the first moisture) and for moistening the joints (which refers to the second moistures, called "dew"). Regarding these, therefore, this distinction of terms makes known these four moistures according to the sum of the chapter.
¶ How he identifies the first moisture, then the second of the secondaries, then the first, then the third, then the fourth. There he says: "And of those it is that..." and there for the third: "And of those..." and there for the fourth: "And of those are the moistures..." What he says first is the preface. The second part has two divisions: first, he explains the second moisture, which is like dew; second, he returns to the first. There he says: "And the first..." He returns, however, to show that from the inflammation of heat in the first moisture, which is in the small veins, a putrid fever is created if it is a putrefactive inflammation. Or, a "synocha" fever <term>synocha: a continuous, non-putrid fever caused by boiling blood</term> is created when it is an ebullient <note>boiling</note> inflammation without putrefaction, as you learned in the chapter on synocha. For since this moisture is still true blood, and differing only slightly from the nature of blood, it can become putrid and inflamed. With the nourishment...

This letter is explained in two ways. ¶ First, according to Dino <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous 14th-century physician</note>: as he himself seems to understand it to be said: that when that nourishment which is to be expanded and stored or retained in the members is not expanded, but rather remains inside in the small veins: then it putrefies because since it does not receive digestion from nature, it must putrefy and cause a putrid fever. The cause, however, why it remains inside in the small veins is the blockage of the orifices, or a defect in the expulsive power of the veins, or a defect in the attractive power of the members. And although this explanation is good, it can nonetheless be explained another way which includes the previous explanation. And it is that Avicenna <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> proves by this that the first moisture causes humoral fever. And it is argued thus: That which has a humoral form not far removed from the dispositions of the humors can easily cause a putrid fever. But the nourishment in the small veins is of this kind; therefore, etc. ¶ For regarding the nourishment outside the veins, one part is that which is stored, like the "exchange" <note>cambium</note>, and another is that which is expanded, like the "dew" <note>ros</note>. And these nourishments are very far removed from the humoral form. But the nourishment that stays in the veins—namely the first moisture—is not expanded like dew, but is in the path of expansion; nor is it stored like exchange, but is on the way or path to being stored. Therefore, that moisture which is like the matter of those two is not far from the form of a humor and the dispositions of humors. It will therefore cause a humoral fever. It must be considered, therefore, that from Avicenna’s speech it is understood that the first moisture is like the immediate matter of dew and exchange; for part of it is stored as exchange, and part is expanded as dew. Nor do I imagine the entire first moisture first becomes dew, and dew becomes exchange. But since by nature’s intention exchange is principally made from the first moisture, there arises in this transformation a first byproduct, just like phlegm in the generation of blood, as we said in the first book. This is what he says: "since nourishment..." It is well said that the first moisture is the matter of putrid and boiling fever. Since... because: the nourishment is not entirely expanded when it is under the form of the first moisture. That is, this nourishment is not expanded outside the veins, but rather remains. It is doubted of which fever it is the matter, since Avicenna says nothing of "dew" <note>ros</note>. It must be said that according to the consumption of dew, one species of hectic fever is placed. However, if putrefaction happens to the dew being poured to the heart, it will cause a putrid fever reducible to a species of putrid fever, toward whose nature that dew most inclines when it putrefies. For if the dew is intensely hot like yellow bile, then this is reduced to a choleric fever. And Averroes <note>the Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> perhaps understood this in the third book of the *Colliget*. And similarly, if the exchange moisture putrefies, it can cause a putrid fever; even from the putrefaction of the flesh a putrid vapor could arise and cause a putrid fever, or from the putrefaction of chyle. In the commentary on the book *On the Differences of Fevers*, we reduced all these fevers to putrid fevers. But Avicenna later saw that the first moisture was like true blood, and having changed little from the nature of blood, he reduced its inflammation to the class of blood-fevers. He could not do this for the other moistures, as they are further from humoral nature and closer to the nature of the body parts. He understood, therefore, from this that the putrefaction of dew and exchange and body parts would cause a fever of an unusual mode, though reducible. And specifically our opinion feels this way, which we hold: that the moistures—namely dew and exchange—differ in species from the humors and the body parts. There would be a doubt, however, whether just as from inflammation without putrefaction of the first moisture a boiling fever can occur, so too could a fever occur from inflammation of the dew and exchange without putrefaction. And let us say that if it could happen, it would be reduced to ephemeral fevers or hectic fevers. For those parts could be inflamed and the heart distempered without putrefaction; it does not seem to be among impossible things. ¶ These things are said in our general commentaries. Next, he identifies the third moisture called exchange <note>cambium</note>. And he says: "And of those..."—namely the moistures existing in the members as actual nourishment. Not that they are actually "animated" <note>possessing the soul/life of the organism</note>, but that they are actually in the place where they will immediately be animated: at the pores and places where dissolution occurs. Namely, "nourishment is the exchange..." etc. And they are joined—namely these moistures which are called actual nourishment and are called exchange. "Addition"—that is, the application or something added in it—namely the member. "Similar"—that is, similar to that which was dissolved. From all these, therefore, he has identified for us the moisture which is called exchange.

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin> In this part. Avicenna says this for one of two reasons. First, to show that although "exchange" is now in the place where it is to be animated—so that between its surface and the surface of the member there is no medium—yet for some time it stays there before it is animated. For it does not yet have the coagulation and solidity required for the form of a body part; and the cause is that it has been a short or near time since it flowed from the veins into the pores. ¶ Furthermore, the details of those courses and transformations are unknown to men in this life. Or he said this to show that exchange receives the form of the member. However, afterward it is made flesh, and each of the similar parts still needs action by which it may become harder. ¶ It is clear.
<margin>b</margin> "And of those." Here he identifies the fourth moisture, and we have not delayed here because we completed our knowledge of these moistures according to our ability in the first book.
<margin>c</margin> "And the likeness." This likeness is not a perfect likeness, because oil does not replace the parts of the wick that are consumed, though it delays their consumption and passes into the form of fire. "Exchange" <note>cambium</note>, however, does replace the parts of the member. ¶ This says more than the commentator on the signs of the liver. It is doubted because the example is deficient, as it does not provide a likeness for the first moisture, which is in the small veins; its likeness is oil contained in the small vessels with which we refill the lamps. The example of "dew" <note>ros</note> is the poured-out oil. The example of "exchange" is the soaked-in oil. The example of the "glue" or "binding moisture" is the moisture joining the parts together. It must be answered in two ways: First, that according to some, he had already set aside the first moisture from the consideration of one looking at the chapter on hectic fevers, because that becomes a fever of putrefaction and boiling. Therefore, three moistures remain—namely dew, exchange, and glue—to be considered in the chapter on hectic fever. ¶ Of these three, he provided a likeness. Second, it must be said that Avicenna listed the first and second moisture together when he said they were "prepared for nourishment" regarding the first and "moistening the joints" regarding the second, which is called dew. In the second place, he put the third moisture, called exchange. Third, he put the fourth. Therefore, he organized those four moistures into three orders. In the first order, he put the first—namely the first and second. In the second, he put exchange; in the third, glue. ¶ This example continues: let the poured-out oil be the likeness of the first and second. And this is what he says first. Let the soaked oil be the likeness—that is, of the secondaries—that is, exchange. Why he spoke of the first and second together and called them "primary" will appear later.
<margin>d</margin> "And when." Here, having preceded with the distinction of moistures, he shows what hectic fever is first. ¶ Second, the modes of hectic fever, which are called species, are distinguished. There, at "Truly while." It must be considered that by "radical members" we understand the "spermatic" parts <note>the foundational tissues formed from the original seed, according to medieval embryology</note>, yet in hectic fever, not only the radical parts but also the fleshy parts are inflamed—that is, they have an inflamed state. This does not depend on a cause specifically in the heart, which is the primary subject of fever, and that inflammation is formally called "hectic fever." Just as unnatural heat from the vapor of a putrid humor is called a putrid fever, and from an inflamed spirit <note>pneuma</note> it is called ephemeral; and although the liver may have unnatural heat in itself from a putrid humor and spread it to the whole, and could impede the whole operation, yet that heat is not called a fever. ¶ He does not say that its heat is a fever, but he speaks of others, as all these things were demonstrated in the question of the subject of fever.
<margin>e</margin> "While it." First, he provides one distinction. Second, regarding it, he removes an error. Third, he provides the distinction of others. There, at "And this indeed sickness." There, third, "Some..." It is doubted first whether these are true species of hectic fever. It is doubted second why he did not establish four: one for the consumption of the first moisture, a second for the consumption of dew as well. To the first, it must be said as is commonly said: that hectic fever divided by the consumption of moistures is not divided into true species. The reason is: because then hectic fever would not be a fever made in the members, but a fever and something depending on a cause as far as many species are concerned. The consequence is noted: because the first species of hectic fever would be that in which the first moistures were in a heated state, and consequently the members in a heated state from them; otherwise it would not be a fever, as those moistures are inanimate parts. And it follows from this that this hectic fever would be from a cause. And thus the second species of hectic fever would be that in which exchange is in a heated state and the members are becoming heated. Therefore, it is necessary to imagine the species of hectic fever another way: namely, by the state of one heat according to its degree in the body parts. First, it begins to consume the first moistures, and then it is the first species of hectic fever; with the same heat remaining, the consumption is manifested in the exchange moisture, and it is the second species. Finally, the consumption appears in the binding moisture—namely in the substance of the members—and then it is the third species. To remain, therefore, in one heat of the same degree. All these things can happen, just as with one fire and one flame remaining in a wick, the consumption of the poured oil, the soaked oil, and the binding moisture can occur. And this is the distinction of the mode of heat from moisture to moisture. It must be considered, however, that when I say the degree of heat of hectic fever does not vary, I do not deny that it *can*. And perhaps in the third species the type of heat is much varied, either within the range of the degree or outside the degree. And this is because of the great defect of moisture. Just as it varies in old age from youth. Yet it is posited as possible that no variation of heat would occur either in the degree or in the duration of the degree; still, a graded consumption of those moistures can occur. It must also be considered that when we say the first moistures are consumed in the first species, and the second in the second, and the third in the third, I do not mean that in the first species only the first moisture is consumed and not the second, but that in every species...

<summary>This page explains the medieval medical theory of 'hectic fever' using the analogy of a lamp. It categorizes the body's moistures into four types (primary, dew, exchange, and radical) and describes how the fever progressively consumes each, leading to the three stages of wasting.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical exploration of "hectic fever" (febris ethica), specifically debating the number of species or stages of the disease based on which bodily moistures are being consumed. It draws heavily on Avicenna’s Canon and Galen’s therapeutics.</meta>

# or Treatise

<margin>
Regarding the hectic <note>original: "ethicã"</note>: unless an ephemeral fever precedes it, in certain remote or near reasons it seems to pertain to the dryness of the humors.
</margin>
The nature of hectic fever is the consumption of all moisture. I say "consumption beyond nature," and the reason is that in every type of hectic fever, a heat that consumes beyond nature is present in a moisture that is capable of being consumed. In the first species, the "first moisture" <note>The most fluid, immediate moisture used for nourishment</note> is consumed, as is clearly manifest. Indeed, more of this moisture is consumed than any other. This is most evident when the first moisture is consumed in great or majority part; the same is to be understood regarding the third species. Regarding the second doubt, I will speak briefly here of what we have settled elsewhere at length. First, it seems imaginable at first glance that the species of hectic fever are distinguished into four or five. One in which the **blood** is consumed. Another in which the **moisture** is consumed which is **youthful** <note>original: "iuvenis"</note>. A third in which **dew** <note>original: "ros"</note> is consumed. A fourth in which **exchange** <note>original: "cambium," moisture transitioning into tissue</note> is consumed. Fifth, in which **glue** <note>original: "gluten," the moisture that binds the solid parts together</note> is consumed. But it seems that Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> and other authors did not distinguish the hectic fever except by three species. This is because they treated the consumption of the first moisture and the consumption of "dew" together; for dew is a foolish, fluid moisture, easily consumed and evaporated in the same way as the first and youthful moisture are consumed. Therefore, since they are consumed together and do not have a separate order in the process of consumption, their consumption falls under the first species. Or perhaps Avicenna understood this first because he numbered these two moistures together—namely the first and the second—and thus spoke of them as they first appear. He said, according to the second exposition, that these are moistures prepared for nourishing and moistening. And when he said these are two divisions, he nevertheless provided one comparison for both of them: namely, **oil poured into a lamp**. It also appears in this that he said the first species, though it has the name of the genus among the Arabs, nonetheless

**Paroxysms** <note>original: "Parorismos"</note> nor the hours of the paroxysms. And some have said that hectic fevers either depend on humors of a proximate time with coagulation, or with those things which are like flesh, or with the hard radical members such as **bones and nerves**. And if by this speech it is understood that they depend according to the path by which they finish the radical moisture continued within them, this will be so. And the first intention is equal: if it signifies that the first thing the hectic fever finishes is the moistures of proximate time with coagulation, the speech will not be sound. And indeed, the hectic fever sometimes happens after an ephemeral fever <note>A fever lasting only one day</note>. And sometimes it happens after putrid fevers and abscesses <note>original: "apatum," likely from the Greek "apostema"</note>. It is rare <note>original: "longinquum," literally "distant" or "unlikely"</note> for hectic fever to happen by beginning with the radical members already inflamed, for the humor is not inflamed, nor is the spirit before that; rather, those members are heated first, then following the procession of days, the others are heated. This is unless a very strong cause occurs. And indeed, one cause is sometimes the cause of hectic fever, and sometimes the cause of ephemeral fever, according to the vehemence of its change and the weakness—

in Greek it is called *ethikos* <note>original: "ethicos"</note>, that is, as if concerning the beginning of rarefaction; since it does not have a specific name among its own species. Although the first species could be distinguished into two—one being the consumption of the first moisture and the other the consumption of "dew"—nonetheless these species do not have distinct names. This is because they happen at the same time and do not follow one another in time. And then we shall say that "consumption" is also understood by the consumption of the first moisture, since that is blood only slightly changed. Let us say secondly that perhaps the authors began to distinguish the modes of hectic fever from the consumption of dew and the consumption of the first moisture (or both together). The reason is that hectic is a "member-fever" <note>A fever fixed in the solid parts of the body</note> which is fixed in the members and because it consumes the members. Therefore, that consumption of moistures will vary the hectic heat: those which are "member-moistures." But these are the ones that have already flowed into the veins—the veins being common places—and finally flowed into the large common vessels; they are in the small and final vessels. When the member composes two moistures, the habit of the body and the moisture opposed to rarefaction remain. It is not, however, by a bloody abundance; for the veins can be swollen while the flesh withers. Therefore, the distinction of the heat of consumption is according to the moistures around which the consumption and rarefaction of the body appear. And these, without doubt, are **dew, exchange, and glue**. The first moisture is in some way in this, insofar as it is more of a member-moisture (that is, appropriated) than blood is. And then its consumption—namely of the first moisture and the dew—constitutes one species, as we said above. It remains, therefore, that since blood, distinguished against these moistures, is not a member-moisture (that is, it is not appropriated, but rather common in respect to the appropriation of these moistures, and is common for the nourishment and generation of the spirit), I say that by that consumption and reduction to small amounts, a distinction of the mode of consuming heat—namely, hectic—is not made. And from what has been said, many things said by the authors in the distinctions of hectic and other fevers are understood. And it is now known what those say who claim it is according to the first moisture: this is not the species of hectic, because that is the matter of putrid fever. For although that moisture makes a putrid fever when it putrefies, one must still ask when it evaporates and causes hectic fever because of the heat of the members. And Galen's words in the seventh book of the *Therapeutics* <note>original: "terrapeutice"</note> regarding the distinction of these moistures. And he names the *oybulent* <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek term for wasting</note>, that is, a manifest and great diminution as to the heat, because the natural heat is greatly diminished due to the great consumption of the moisture; so also the accidental heat must be consumed. And according to this, the heat of the hectic does not remain in the same measure as it was in the first species of hectic fever, but either changes degree or the duration of the degrees. Whatever it may be, we do not care about this. And this is indeed the sickness. Because someone could believe that the distinction of hectic according to these moistures was a truly specific distinction, he removes this: for if the first or second moisture were the subject of the heat produced, whereby heat would be made in the members, then the hectic could have paroxysms. Or otherwise, he wants to show that hectic is not a fever depending on the humor. And it is clear.

**And certain** (that is, Galen in the last chapter of the *Therapeutics*): either it depends on the humors of proximate time by coagulation (that is, moistures recently coagulated are consumed), and he means new fat <note>original: "pinguedinem nouam"</note>.

**And if from the speech.** He gives two understandings to this distinction of the species of first hectic. The first is this: that in the first species of hectic fever, the moistures which are continuous with the members (that is, inside the members) are finished and consumed. And since they are much softer and more vaporous, they consume the moisture more. And this speech seems to be the same: that they consume "dew" more from the beginning, and afterwards "exchange," just as new fat is consumed more than flesh, and flesh more than bones from the beginning. **And if it signifies.** The second understanding is this: that hectic fevers entirely consume the recently coagulated moistures as

<column-break/>

new fats; and then nothing is consumed from the bones: because then that statement is false, as is well known. Others labor much over this passage and confuse themselves, but we understand it as we have settled: that the sum of it is this—the heat of hectic fever never consumes new fat without also consuming the "dewy" moisture of the flesh and members at that same time.

**And indeed the hectic.** Here he posits the cause of hectic fever: which are causes in the making. And first, certain causes, namely other fevers. This shows how three kinds of fevers can have one common cause. Or he declares the statement and completes the narrative of the causes of hectic and the mode of its arrival. There at the section "And the cause," and there thirdly, namely the fever which—

<margin>
—is from putrefaction. Fourth, he posits certain causes. It should be considered that in the first part, Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> wants the arrival of hectic fever to be mostly because of ephemeral fevers, or putrid abscesses. And this follows because it is rarely found "by beginning" (that is, that no other fever precedes it). He doubts, therefore, in what physicians labor in vain: whether hectic can be made "by beginning" <note>meaning spontaneously or as a primary disease</note>. He solves it thus: it is very rare and far from the event that it should happen by beginning. And Avicenna's reason is: if hectic frequently happened by beginning, then some external flaming cause occurring to us—for example, the heat of the sun—would first inflame the radical members before it would inflame the spirits and humors. But this is false: because spirits and humors are more apt to be heated than members. Therefore they will be heated first, and afterwards, over the course of days, the members are heated. The consequence is well known. However, Avicenna says that although it is very rare, it is not impossible. For it is possible from some strong cause for the members to be put into a heated state before the spirits and humors. Therefore, it is possible for hectic to "begin" (that is, to come before it follows other fevers). It is doubted what he means by a "very strong cause." And it is said that he understands a "preparation" in the members, by which they are made apt by some agent to be put into a heated state. However, the spirits and humors are not put into a heated state by that cause. For example, a great dryness of the members from preceding triumphs <note>possibly "struggles" or "excesses"</note>, vigils <note>staying awake</note>, and abstinence. Whence they are made quickly inflammable by the occurrence of—
</margin>
—the time of its suspension, like fire. For it encounters wood in two ways: one is according to the way it heats them and finishes within them, and that is its path of inflammation. And the fever of putrid abscesses very often changes into hectic because of the vehemence of the fever, and the vehemence of the thinning of the food in it, and the prohibition of cold water, and the lack of observation of the side of the heart with ointments, plasters, and epithems <note>medicated cloths</note>; and especially in sicknesses of the members near the heart, such as the diaphragm. And very often the necessity of physicians causes a fall into this because of the cause of strength and the frequency of fainting <note>original: "sincopis"</note>, giving wine and meat broth <note>original: "aquam carnis"</note> and medicine made of musk and similar things to drink. And sometimes hectic is compounded with putrid fevers and abscesses. And indeed, hectic fever in the beginning of the matter is difficult to recognize and easy to cure; at its end, it is easy to recognize and difficult to cure. And the end, *aldubul* <note>Arabic: atrophy/wasting</note>, does not receive a cure at all.

### On the signs. Chapter 2.

<margin>
—as it is said that heat can produce hectic and not putrid—
</margin>
—the heat of the extremities. But spirits and humors are not so. And because this preparation is very strange, it very rarely happens; therefore do not worry about this speculation since they cannot see how the members come to such a preparation in "pre-habituation" or reception; on the contrary, they see the spirit come to it, since it is impossible for bones and flesh to be made rare as quickly as the spirit. And therefore this is not an aptitude from rarity and absolute possibility. But from this mode of the substance determined to this agent; we cannot go further beyond this except that experience finds hectic fever "beginning" now, because [otherwise] the reason would not have been confirmed nor believed. I, for one, have never seen hectic "begin"; thus every hectic seen by me followed other fevers.

**And the cause.** Here he posits the line comparing three kinds of fevers to one cause, showing how they can come from it: and it is believed that Avicenna wants to say that some external cause is sometimes so strong that it causes hectic and ephemeral fever to happen at the same time. And then the hectic is made "by beginning," because no other fever precedes it (that is, if it happens simultaneously with it). And similarly, he would say it should be understood that sometimes a cause is powerful enough to make hectic and putrid fever. But in saying these propositions, let us say Avicenna here declares what he says: "unless a very strong cause occurs." He wants to show what is impossible: that one heating cause is sometimes the cause of hectic and not ephemeral, and sometimes the cause of ephemeral and not hectic. It should be considered first that it was not so doubtful how one heating cause can make hectic and not putrid, just as it was doubtful how it could make hectic and not ephemeral. Because the heat of a putrid fever is a "putrefying" heat, and not every cause that inflames most strongly is putrefying. For putrefaction is a suffering of a determined mode; therefore, when some heat comes from outside, a man who is in some way apt for "drying out" <note>original: "arefactioni"</note> will become hectic and will not incur a putrid fever. But it is very difficult to see how he becomes hectic and does not first incur an ephemeral fever, since both are only inflammation; it is ephemeral in the spirits or blood (namely, *synocha* <note>a continuous fever</note>, which can be reduced to ephemeral). However, Avicenna tries to give a cause for this when he says that one inflaming cause—namely, the heat of the sun or anger or similar things—is sometimes the cause of hectic and not ephemeral, and sometimes the cause of ephemeral and not hectic, according to the vehemence. It should be considered secondly that he says the cause of this is the vehemence of its change and the weakness of its suspension. One should know that, as was declared in the questions before and in the first chapter of this treatise, febrile heat is not only governed by being excessive or unnatural, but that it is retained in some matter. In such a way that even when the external agent is removed, the heat is retained in the spirit beyond nature, or in the members. For a heat that only stays during the presence of hot air is not called a fever, just as a bound hand is not called a "fellowship of the members." Therefore, some heat can encounter the spirits and members simultaneously and inflame them strongly upon encounter. But because the spirits are rare and not resistant, that flame will not remain; thus it will not be retained or suspended, but only the presence of the inflamer will be said to inflame the spirits, just as air is bright only in the presence of illumination. But that flame received in a solid, hard body will be retained and suspended within that body, and thus it will be a hectic fever without an ephemeral one preceding it. A clear example is what is said in the second book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "metbaurorū"</note> concerning the heat of a lightning bolt, which does not burn or cause flax or cloth to smoke, yet it melts and burns iron or gold. And it should be imagined that flax or loose cloth has, at the arrival of the lightning, a heat that is the absence of hot vapors; yet they do not have a heat that can be suspended or retained in them, because they are not proportionate recipients of that heat. Avicenna's example is that fire sometimes encounters wood such that it heats them, and the heat remains in them so that when the fire that acted on them is removed, they smoke because of the retained heat; at other times, the wood is inflamed only in the presence of the inflamer and the fire is not retained. These [examples] are well-known and common, yet here they require investigation. And indeed, Avicenna says one cause is sometimes the cause of hectic according to the vehemence of the change (namely, made in the spirit) and the weakness of the suspension (namely, the retention of that heat in the spirit). And he also understands the vehemence of the change and the strength of the suspension made in the members, whence hectic is made. And perhaps the third [point] of Avicenna here was diminished: he wants to say according to the vehemence of change and weakness of suspension, according to the vehemence of change and strength of suspension, just as fire etc. heats and smokes; and then there is inflammation and retention of the flame, the sign of which is the smoking. The second is the path of inflammation (namely, of the sun) and not of smoking, whence the heat immediately recedes from the wood. It is doubted, therefore, because from this cause it can be argued that whenever there is some external heating cause, hectic is made and not ephemeral, since the members are apt to retain heat—
