<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "hectic fever" (febris ethica), specifically moving from the definition of the disease to its diagnostic signs—chiefly the pulse and the reaction to food—and the theoretical debates surrounding these signs among Galen, Avicenna, and Averroes.</meta>

# Book III

...not the spirits. I also say that the spirits are suited to receive and retain heat from an agent proportioned to them in strength. But when the heat vastly exceeds them, it heats them most strongly. This is not proportioned to the spirits, but indeed to the members; therefore, the members then receive and retain it. However, agents that cause such immoderate heating are found very rarely; whereas agents that heat moderately are found frequently. Therefore, most frequently an ephemeral fever <note>A short-lived, one-day fever</note> precedes a hectic fever, and rarely does a hectic fever begin on its own. Alternatively, we have elsewhere explained this text thus: sometimes one thing is the cause of hectic fever, sometimes of ephemeral, and sometimes of putrid fever <note>A fever involving the "rotting" or corruption of humors</note>, according to the reality—that is, according to the diversity of the way it enters the body.

**...of ephemeral and hectic. And fever.**
Here he means that hectic fever sometimes follows a putrid fever, not from abscesses <note>original: "apofteomasas"</note>, but from the intensity of the fevers and the negligence of doctors, or through error. Sometimes hectic fever occurs because of the addition of inflammation, which the doctor is forced to cause with <term>dianusco: a warming medicine</term> and similar remedies on account of fainting <note>original: "sincopim"</note>.

**And sometimes.** Here he posits three cases. The first is well-known. Here fall subtle speculations regarding the composition of hectic and putrid fever, in which speculation there are subtle reasons which we wrote in our question concerning the composition of fever.

**And hectic.** The second case is well-known because hectic fever in the beginning does not change the body much, and therefore it is recognized with difficulty. And the cooling <note>original: "infritidatiōē"</note>, which is its cure, the body tolerates well in the end—that is, in the process. It follows that the impression is greater, and thus the body cannot regenerate the consumed moistures.

**And the end.**
The third case is that the end of this species is not cured because of the great consumption <note>wasting away of the body</note>.

**Another.** First, he posits the signs absolutely, but much...

<image-desc>Decorative red ornamental drop cap "P" beginning the word "Pulsus".</image-desc>

The pulse is indeed small <term>minutus: small or thin</term>, hard, frequent, weak, and of a uniform nature. In touch, it is that which feels less heat than the heat of a synochal fever <note>original: "finochi"; a continuous inflammatory fever</note> and similar fevers inflamed in the matter. In the beginning, when it is touched, it is more gentle; but when the hand remains upon it for a while, the heat appears with strength and a "biting" quality <note>original: "mordicatione"</note>. It does not cease to increase, and the hottest place in it is the location of the veins and arteries. But their heat is uniform; for it does not decrease, but rather when food is taken, it increases quickly, and the pulse becomes very strong and begins to grow large. Because of this, it happens to foolish doctors that they prohibit food to them because of what happens to them from the symptoms, and thus they destroy them. If they adapt to the first species... Secondly, he posits the signs of the second species. The first in three parts: first, he posits the signs of hectic fever in itself; second, the signs of the transition from ephemeral fever; third, the signs of it when compounded with putrid fever. The first sign is taken from the pulse: it is "minute," meaning small, because of the weakness of the power. "Hard" because of the action of the artery. In these, there is a degree according to the degree of weakness and hardness. Indeed, the hardness and the defect of the powers are more manifest in the process of the disease than in the beginning. It is "frequent" so that it may recover the defect of its magnitude.

<margin>b</margin> **Weak, etc.** Fixed according to one habit—that is, disposition—because it does not have paroxysms <note>sudden peaks of fever</note>. Yet it is not so fixed that it does not change with food, drink, sleep, waking, and the rest.

<margin>c</margin> **In touch.** It must be considered that doctors differ on whether the heat is greater in hectic fever, where it is intense in the members, or the heat of a putrid fever, specifically of synochal and similar burning fevers <note>original: "causonū"</note>. It can be held that in hectic fever it is greater than in putrid fever. I do not believe it is inconsistent that in a certain putrid fever there is more intense heat than in a certain hectic fever. Hence, in the first book it is said that in some hectic cases the heat is more intense than in some synochal fevers. All these are determined in our questions on all fevers through certain propositions. However, the heat of synochal and burning fevers represents more to the touch because of the abundance of smoky vapors. Hence, it is said that synochal fever has a flame that meets the hands of those touching it. But in a hectic fever, the multitude of heat does not "meet" the hand immediately. Thus it appears that in hectic fever, if the hand remains for a long time, more heat appears, which did not appear immediately due to the lack of many vapors.

<margin>d</margin> **And it is hot.** It is doubted whether the heart is hotter than the rest of the parts in a putrid fever; the locations of the arteries ought to appear hotter in it. We have distinguished the primary reasons for this in the questions on the origin of fevers. First, we say that the locations of the arteries in the extremities—namely, the hands and feet—are the locations of the veins which associate with them. Second, we say that this happens in some other dispositions, as in spasm and lethargy, as in the commentary on the pulse of the lethargic. Therefore, Galen <note>original: "Gal."</note> spoke cautiously, saying this happens in hectic fever and not in other fevers, but he did not say "not in other sicknesses." Third, we say that Galen seems to feel that the cause of this is the dry heat in the body of the heart. Therefore, Galen promised this when he said: "The greatest knowledge of hectic fevers is from the arteries." Galen makes us imagine two causes from this: one is that in hectic patients, the heat is drier and sharper—or stronger—in the heart than in other fevers. Therefore, it will be so in the arteries of hectic patients more than in the arteries of others with fever. There is experience in this: that vapors included in other places besides the arteries, being sharp, cannot give this indication. He teaches to bathe and let the body transpire in this experience. The other cause he makes us imagine is that when the dry heat in the heart is extinguished, that heat will most strongly be felt by the touch in the places where moisture is introduced. These are the locations of the arteries and veins. Take these causes if they please you. To the contrary, it must be said that although in a putrid fever the heart is hotter, nevertheless the heat of the putrid fever is felt throughout because of the putrid fumes in both the arterial locations and other places.

<margin>e</margin> **And it is uniform.** That is, not having paroxysms or peaks.

<margin>f</margin> **Truly.** First, he posits the sign and declares it with an example. Second, to remove doubt, he gives the cause. The first thing he says is well-known.

<margin>g</margin> **And food.** Here he removes a doubt. Someone might say that food ought to cause an intensification and change of the pulse as it does in other fevers. To this, he responds and posits four propositions. The first is that the intensification and "inflammation" <note>a flare-up of heat</note> caused by food in other fevers is not like the inflammation caused by food in hectic fever. Consider that Avicenna <note>original: "Auic."</note>, by his way of speaking, concedes that food in other fevers kindles a different sort of intensification. But it does not kindle this specific intensification found in the hectic patient after eating. The second proposition is that food in other fevers necessarily causes some diversity on account of the motions of nature—that is, natural heat—which, when food is first taken, is as if suffocated, but afterwards is dilated and expanded. At the very least, from the food taken, some comfort is given to the heat, unless the body is in a very strange state near death. This change of disposition is common to putrid, ephemeral, and hectic fevers if they are fed while the fever persists. The third proposition is that this inflammation in the hectic patient from food is not like the paroxysmal inflammation in putrid fevers, in which first a constriction of the pulse occurs and then the heat rises at a determined hour. Rather, this inflammation occurs whenever they eat, at any hour. The fourth proposition is where the truth appears: if food inflames in other fevers, why do we not say that other feverish patients are "heated by food," but only say this of the hectic patient? To solve this, he posits this: the hectic patient has a sickness that is "not vehement"—meaning he has a fever that is established <note>original: "facta"</note> and not "in the making" <note>original: "fieri"</note>. Therefore, that quality which is "in the making" is called vehement because it 

<column-break/>

is in motion or impression from an agent; but an established quality is called "not vehement" due to the cessation of that movement. Because the hectic patient has a febrile heat that is not vehement—that is, it is already established—he does not "feel" that heat, as is said in the first book in the chapter on the causes of pain. It has become "fitting" <note>habitual</note> to the member. Therefore, the heat of the hectic patient is not felt of itself; but when he is inflamed by food, then that inflammation from the food is felt. Thus, the hectic patient is changed by food to the point of feeling heat. And therefore it is said that the hectic patient "is heated by food," but one having a putrid fever feels his own heat already, so he is not said to "be heated by food" in the same way, because he was already hot and feeling the heat. This is what Avicenna means: the hectic patient has a sickness that is not vehemently discerned. 

**discerning.** That is, so that he may discern it, etc. And that statement is negative. For the hectic patient indeed has a bad and very hot sickness; but it is not of such a kind that he feels its vehemence without a new cause. This is why he says "discerning the vehemence," meaning the vehemence he *would* discern if it were still "in the making." When, therefore, food inflames the members, then there is vehement heat—that is, heat "in the making" from motion—on account of which vehemence it is felt. **He doubts** how hectic fever can become "fitting" to a member. I say, according to the common way, that it is called "fitting" because it is in all the material parts... until that form which is acquired and that which is in the subject become one form, it is a false and "extraneous" complexion. But when the acquired form and the subject form make one form, then this extraneous heat is made "fitting" because it has become one in number with that which was natural. **He doubts** why the hectic patient becomes "super-heated" when food is taken. Even if the food is cold, it heats him. He tries to give the cause: for all dry heat, once moisture is removed, is more ready to show heat. A sign of this is lime sprinkled with water <note>Quicklime reacts violently with water, releasing heat</note>. The heat of hectic patients is dry. When the hectic patient is "sprinkled" with the moisture of food, such sensible heat will appear which was not felt before. Averroes <note>original: "Auer."</note>, however, in the fourth book of the *Colliget*, derides this cause, arguing it is impossible for the nutritional power of the members of a hectic patient to be so distant from the nutriment that it destroys it, as cold water is contrary to heat. Averroes imagines that while life lasts, we should not believe the members become so "extraneous" that nutriment entering them inflames and evaporates like water on hot lime. Averroes surely speaks the truth. However, it suffices to say that the heat of hectic fever is manifested by the watery part of the food being inflamed. Thus, not all the food, but a certain part is inflamed—not totally destroyed, but heated so as to be felt by the touch. 

**I will therefore state a brief opinion:** regarding what we have already written at length. First, in every fever in which we eat while the fever persists, as in continuous and hectic fevers, the food taken heats the patient. The reason is that in all such fevers, the members are under an extraneous heat, and therefore they will heat the food, and the patient will feel hotter than before. I say, second, that this heating is not as "sensible" <note>perceptible to the senses</note> in other fevers as it is in hectic fever. In the hectic patient, it is clearly and distinctly perceivable by both the patient and the doctor. The reason is that the patient did not feel his own heat before. When the hectic patient takes food, he changes from "not feeling heat" to "feeling actual heat," and this is very perceptible. Similarly, the hectic heat felt by the doctor is uniform outside of meal times. When the doctor touches him after a meal, he perceives a "disformity" or change in the heat. But one having a continuous putrid fever always feels his own heat and feels it as "disform" even outside of meal times. Thus, even if he is heated after taking food, it is not as distinguishable since he was already feeling heat and had irregular sensations of heat due to the motion of putrid vapors. Therefore, this addition of heat is not as distinguishable or perceptible in a putrid fever as it is in a hectic one. This sensation in hectic fever is also aided by the quick distribution of food to the members. For in the hectic patient, there is no "matter" <note>blockage or excess humor</note> to prohibit the attraction or passage of food; therefore, going suddenly, it is suddenly inflamed. But in those having a putrid fever, there is a sluggishness...

# Treatise III

...then the food is in transit because of the matter: which stands in the way both because of the laziness of the drawing faculty and the [faculties] serving the food when they are occupied with the digestion of the matter. And it appears to some that the heat [stems from] water and food in a putrid fever. However, it is not necessary for the pulse to be greatly enlarged in this way, as in a hectic fever: because on account of the vapors and putrid humors, it happens to be much shortened and overwhelmed more than in a hectic fever—at least in the first species. Therefore, Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> understood this cause. If anyone considers his third point, the opinion of Galen <note>original: "G"</note> can then be reduced to an understanding. Galen only intends that in hectic fever, the heat which previously did not appear now becomes apparent, just as in lime <note>A common medieval analogy: lime stays cool until water is added, then it burns</note>. But in a severe putrid fever, the heat did not appear before, but now appears from the consumed food; whereas in hectic fever, the heat appeared earlier. However, youthful concepts can be troubled by this: as if they might say that in hectic fever, heat never appears that was not appearing before, because that heat which exists now is not what was there before, but rather it is a new heat being produced. But even if this is granted, nothing is said against this statement: namely, that a hectic patient who did not feel the heat before now feels it. Concerning identity and otherness, we do not intend to dispute. To this our opinion, the opinion of Averroes <note>original: "Auer."</note> can be reduced. For we ought not to imagine Averroes to have been so unrefined as to believe that the heat which is in the members in a putrid fever could not heat the food; rather, he means that because the heat in hectic fever is fixed—that is, established and imperceptible in the radical members <term>Radical members: The primary, fundamental organs like the heart and liver</term>—it has to act upon the food: it transforms it into the heat that is felt afterward. But because the heat in a putrid fever is not fixed, one feels it, and it does not heat the food with the heat that is felt, just as if there had been no sensible heat before. To the same end, it must be said that in the food entering the stomach, there are two parts. One is the subtle, dewy part <note>original: "roralem"</note> which quickly passes to the members—namely, two hours after food, or thereabouts—and it is this part that the hectic patient feels as heat. And because the movement of this part varies at different times, some authors have written that this heating is felt two hours after food. Others say three hours; some, one hour. The other part of the food is thick; its stay in the stomach is for more hours than two, and it goes to the liver gradually and becomes blood. Afterward, it becomes the primary moisture and nourishes. And all this is seen to happen in the space of twelve hours, as Averroes collects at the end of his commentary on the *Canticle* <note>Referring to the *Poem on Medicine* by Avicenna with Averroes' commentary</note>. And whether this food heats the hectic patient requires consideration, which is not positioned here. Along with this, it truly ought to be considered whether that dewy part of the food which passes truly increases and becomes <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food</term> like blood, or whether it does not truly nourish; and concerning these things we have written much in our treatise *On Appetite*.

<margin>A.</margin>
And concerning the signs of the changing of the fever, it is estimated that the transition to hectic fever is by the intensity of the strength of the heat—that is, in the third stage, very much so—for according to the first stage, the fever begins to decline after twelve hours. When, therefore, the fever passes twelve hours and no signs of decline appear, but instead it continues until the third day every day and becomes strong, then that is hectic. And concerning the signs of the composition of hectic with putrid fevers, there is a remission of dry heat after the end of the decline, and after exuberant sweating, and an increase in parching and thinning according to what that illness makes necessary: and an oiliness in the urine and excrement. And if it is <term>ebrica: a type of fever associated with specific humors</term>, that which appears and another which is hidden signifies this: a constriction occurring in the pores; for this sort of thing is not found in *ebrica* at all. And know that sometimes hectic fever begins alongside the stomach; whereby it corrupts the complexion of the liver through proximity.

<margin>L. iiij.</margin>
### On the signs of aldubul. <note>original: "alduburen/aldubul", referring to the Arabic term *ad-dubul*, meaning the final wasting stage of a disease or marasmus</note>

<margin>I.</margin>
The signs of *aldubul* are that when the fever drives out *aldubul*, there becomes a vehement hardness of the pulse, along with its weakness, smallness, and frequency. This is especially true when the cause of the fall into hectic is an abscess <note>original: "apa" for "apostema"</note> that does not resolve. For that—namely, the frequency—increases greatly, and likewise the speed. And its pulse is of the kind named "mouse-tail" <term>Mouse-tail pulse: A pulse that starts strong/thick and gradually tapers off into a thin, weak beat</term>. Now, if it comes from the drinking of hot wine, the pulse will be "needle-like" <note>original: "acualis"</note> instead of "mouse-tail." And there will not be very vehement symptoms of the abscess, if indeed it gives it space up to this point. And oiliness and "petals" <note>Flake-like sediments</note> appear in the urine, and the eye begins to sink deep. When, therefore, the *aldubul* reaches its peak, the sinking of both eyes becomes stronger, and dry <term>lippitudo: inflammation or crustiness of the eyes</term> multiplies. The ends of the bones of every member and in the face grow [more prominent], the temples flatten, and the skin of the forehead is strained. The color of the skin is destroyed and becomes as if covered in dust from the burning of the sun. It leads to a heaviness in lifting the eyebrows, and the eye becomes sleepy and closed without sleep. The nose becomes thin, the hair grows long, and lice appear. The belly <note>original: "ueter" for "venter"</note> seems to diminish and adhere to the back, because the skin becomes dry and has already been drawn in, and it draws the skin of the chest with it. While, therefore, the nails are curved and bowed...

<margin>E.</margin>
And if it were some other [fever], that is, a putrid one, the hidden part signifies it—namely, the hidden putrefaction which that illness has to produce of itself.

<margin>D.</margin>
And know: it must be considered that hectic fever remains with the stomach, either because it begins from it—namely, from a bad dry complexion of the stomach, which is followed by aridity, and from that follows hectic fever—and that such a defect of the stomach harms the liver, which is known; or it remains with the stomach because the stomach's defect is joined to the hectic, and this harms the liver.

<margin>f.</margin>
The signs indeed follow the species and the hectic fever, and from them can be understood the signs of the first species when remitted, and the signs of the third species when intense in vice. "Drives out"—that is, it goes to *aldubul*, that is, to the second species. "Increases greatly" because the pulse becomes very small on account of the great fall in strength and from the abscess; because the strength is recovered through much frequency.

<margin>f.</margin>
"Mouse-tail"—namely, bordering on moving from small to smaller, and frequent...

<column-break/>

...to more frequent until it kills.

<margin>G.</margin>
¶ But if it were a change in the pulse from the drinking of hot wine, let it be assumed that the pulse is "needle-like"—namely, called "spindle-like" <note>original: "fusualis"</note>. Because on account of the heat and the moistening from the wine, after small strokes, some large ones occur, and then it returns to small; and this pulse is called "spindle-like" or "needle-like" because of its resemblance to a needle, which is thin. Whether, therefore, hectic fever comes from wine, or the change of the pulse comes from wine, one must imagine that the change in the pulse comes from the wine drunk at that time.

<margin>b.</margin>
¶ "And there will not be," etc. This text can be explained in two ways. First, that there will not be [vehement symptoms] when the fall into hectic fever comes from an abscess, whether a hidden or ruptured *dubelati* <note>abscess</note>; there will not be very vehement accidents, for it does not reach this point—namely, the hectic stage or such a pulse in hectic fever—because it kills before then. Although it makes the hectic fever, the pulse with this progression causes it to kill earlier. In another way it can be explained: "and there will not be," etc., meaning when the fall into hectic is from drinking hot wine, there do not appear very vehement symptoms of an abscess, in which there are pulses like the "mouse-tail." For they do not appear because if very vehement symptoms appeared, they would not give space for a needle-like pulse to form.

...then it has already come to its peak and begins to tend toward its decline; and when it begins to tend toward its decline, the cartilages liquefy.

### On the cure of hectic fever. L. iiii.

The intention in the curing of hectic fever is cooling and moistening. And each of these is completed with the application of its causes and the expulsion of the causes of its contrary. And perhaps the cause of one is the cause of the contrary of the other, just as the cause of cooling itself: for it is sometimes the cause of drying, which is the contrary of moistening—such as cooling with camphor lozenges and those things which are made of <term>podio: likely spodion, or burnt bone/ivory</term> and similar things. And perhaps moistening is also the cause of heating, which is contrary to cooling—such as wine, for it moistens but it heats, wherefore it is necessary that this be observed. And if necessity calls for strong cooling, it will not be unless it is joined with a certain thing, or preceded by, or followed by something in which there is the power of moistening. And similarly, when necessity calls for strong moistening—it is faster with things like meat water <note>broth</note> and wine—then it is necessary that cooling be joined to it, or precede it, or follow it. And if the cause of the hectic is an abscess or a lesion in a member, then it is necessary to cure that first. And he who wishes to compose a regimen from different modes suitable for it, in which the fever is very vehement, then it is necessary that he begins and gives camphor lozenges in a drink, and those things which run their course, with diluted vinegar syrup <note>original: "siropo acetoso", likely oxymel</note> at sunrise, such as barley water in cases of cancer—if he does not abhor them—and with <term>julep: a sweet medicinal drink</term> and pomegranate water and the mixing of psyllium mucilage, if there is nothing prohibiting it on account of the stomach or other things. And the cooling regimen is that which you know of cooling drinks, cooling vegetables, and lozenges, such as lozenges of camphor and <unclear>templis</unclear> and ointments and similar things; and the cooling of their air, even in winter. But if he cannot tolerate it, let the fire be lightened from him. For the cooling of their air is the best thing, as is dressing with sandalwood and camphor and making him smell that in which there are roses and camphor and sandalwood and cold fruits and <term>sebezebran: possibly a variation of "sebesten," a type of plum</term> and lily with rose water. And evaporation through sweat and the bath.

<margin>L.</margin>
¶ "And they appear"—namely, in hectic fever when it passes into *aldubul*. The oiliness, etc., are evident.

<margin>k.</margin>
¶ "When therefore," etc. "To its peak"—that is, consequently when it is in its increase. "And they grow"—that is, the ends of the bones appear more, etc. "Sleepy eye without sleep." Avicenna means what he says in the first book on the differences of fevers: it is not sleep for them, but potential wakefulness. "The hair grows long"—that is, it appears longer because the flesh is consumed, and it stands out from the skin. The wrinkling or constriction of the skin contributes to this, whereby the hairs are raised and appear more. A similar point is made by Aristotle in Book 8 of the *Problems*, problem 11, when he assigns the cause of why the hairs of those shivering are raised. Otherwise, we might imagine that the hair grows long because in these patients, from the parching heat, the smoky matter multiplies, which is suitable for the growth of hair. However, the first cause is better.

<margin>l.</margin>
¶ "Lice appear" on account of the corruption of nourishment under the skin. For it is said that the generation of lice comes from within and then they exit under the skin.

<margin>m.</margin>
¶ "When therefore," etc. It has already arrived here; it has reached the decline because it leads to death and to the third species of hectic fever.

<margin>n.</margin>
¶ "Intention." Here he first treats hectic fever. Secondly, he succors the accidents or dispositions following hectic fever. The first part is in two: first, he posits the intentions to be held in the cure of hectic fever and removes error that can occur; second, he posits certain medicines and their use. The first is in two: first, he posits the cure of hectic in itself; second, when it is joined to another disease. The cause of the aforesaid is that the curative intention is founded upon contrariety, as in the third treatise of the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>. Other things said are well known.

<margin>o.</margin>
¶ And here he wishes to posit medicines and the things they use. First, he posits a cooling and moistening regimen, positing the things by which this is done. Second, he posits the regimen and cooling things. Third, moistening things. It must be considered that first he teaches to give camphor lozenges in a diluted place, then at sunrise barley water, etc. Third, he teaches to give after noon and before evening psyllium mucilage, and all these during the hours when the sun or the day is stationed. This is the way of speaking elsewhere, as in the third *Sextus*, chapter 19, on the cure of the dripping of urine. Therefore, this regimen is composed of different modes because it is from a cooling and also a moistening regimen, and from the use of various medicines which suit the hectic patient in whom there is strong inflammation, for these are strongly extinguishing. Consider, therefore, that hectic patients can differ among themselves by degrees of heat: for someone can be hectic with one measure of heat, and someone can be hectic with a second degree of heat relative to that. The reason for this is that every degree of heat produced in the heart, which is from the first degree of sickly heat up to the last degree, can be hectic heat. In this, however, there is great breadth and diversity. "On account of the stomach"—namely, in which cooling and softening might be feared on account of the psyllium mucilage, or because of excessive slipperiness of the intestines.

<margin>p.</margin>
¶ "And the regimen." Here he posits the cooling regimen and cooling things, and posits rules in the use of some of them. "Sebezebran": some explain this as wild pomegranate. I [disagree]...

# Book III

<margin>
From whatever point he descends here in a more temporal discourse to the care [of the patient] rather than to many things: by which we cool and moisten. First, he sets down cooling medicines. Second, moistening ones. Third, the regimen in food and drink. There he says: "But medicines." There in the third part: "It is necessary that often." The first part is in two. First, he sets down cooling medicines that are also moistening. Second, he sets down cooling medicines that do not moisten. There he says: "But cooling medicines." The first part has seven [points] just as there are these seven medicines. 1st: he gives a general statement, which is that medicines that cool and moisten are nutritious: or nutritiveness prevails in them, more so than in those that do not moisten. And this is because moisture is the matter of nourishment. 2nd: the first medicine is barley water <note>original: "aqua ordei"</note>, of [barley] well-peeled and cleaned, with crabs. I, in one pound of barley water, have two ounces of well-washed crabs cooked down.
</margin>

...indeed, not being found, explain [the one] in which I trust: vaporization with sweat through a bath. I believe this text may be corrupted by the fault of the translator: for it ought not to lead to sweat, as he posits later. Therefore we are compelled to posit "vaporization with sweat," that is, in such a way that it approaches sweat: moving the nourishment to the members, yet not so that they produce sweat. Or "with sweat," that is, with air so moist that it is full of watery vapors, so that from their application to the skin a person seems to sweat. That is, in a bath. That is, the vaporization of the suffering limb, which I [call] "warming" <note>original: "lantefico"</note>, which does not greatly disturb the people, namely the tranquility of the body and the soul. It prohibits the medicine from penetrating deeply, because this happens when a styptic <note>term: "styptic" — a substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</note> prayer occurs, whence it closes the pores. But when the thing is a styptic peace: it reaches through subtle, gliding parts, then that stypticity does not hinder the operation or penetration; rather, it helps the penetration, as is apparent concerning oil of roses according to Galen in the third [book] of *Simple Medicine*. "Rob" <note>term: "rob" — a thickened fruit juice or syrup</note> of fruits, not "rob" absolutely, which is the sapa <note>original: "sapa" — boiled wine must</note> of wine. All other things he says are well-known.

<margin>
b And it is necessary that the extremities be pulled off. Because that which is in the extremities is not of a moist virtue, as it is in the body. Let them be washed three times. According to Rhazes <note>original: "Rasim"</note> in the 17th [book] of the *Continens*, washing in narrow turns. Because this rests with the washer: that as often as he washes, so often he cleanses the sugar, that is, dissolved in water: because thus it is white sugar. If you fear heating, then the argument that was considered difficult is solved. However, he says it does not seem that milk should be given to a hectic patient <note>original: "ethico"</note> because milk is corrupted in a choleric stomach, namely one that is hot and dry. It must be said that this is not true unless there is a very great excess. On the contrary, milk is suitable for hot and dry bodies unless there is superfluous cholera <note>term: "cholera" — here referring to yellow bile, the hot/dry humor</note> in the stomach, as is understood in the second [book] of the *Canon*, in the chapter on milk. In total, it is not suitable for every hectic patient, but for the hectic patient who is not greatly inflamed. Whence Rhazes in his treatise to Al-Mansur <note>original: "almasoris"</note>: if anyone suffering from this illness has a body strongly and vehemently thin, and there is no strong heat in him, warm milk as it is drawn from the breasts benefits him. A hectic patient can, through a mild degree of heat, not corrupt the milk. And the sign of this is because a choleric person multiplies more cholera from one food than a hectic person multiplies from it.
</margin>

<margin>
c But medicines. Here he sets down many medicines that are taken, and anointed, and plastered. "Arasen" is the name of a place, but in Rhazes in the *Continens* it is a hospital. Other things are known through themselves.
</margin>

<margin>
d Of those indeed. First he sets down...
</margin>

<column-break/>

And it is necessary that the retention of cooling plasters <note>original: "emplastrorum infrantiūm"</note> not be prolonged too long over the members very close to the organs of breath <note>original: "membris anhelitus"</note>. For perhaps it brings "breath" <note>likely referring to a chill or heaviness</note> to them, which is a great harm to the voice. And it is necessary that he incline toward rest and sleep, which [bring] tranquility and joy. And let the sick man be guarded from that which makes him angry, and that which makes him sad, and that which makes him anxious, and from hunger and long thirst. The cooling plasters which it is necessary for them to use are aromatic, for they are a very fat help, especially over the chest: because of that which follows it; and let them be cooling so that there is no stypticity in them. For stypticity, along with the fact that it causes dryness to happen, prohibits the power of the medicine from penetrating deep. And it is necessary that the changing [of the plaster] be constant so the medicine does not remain but warms up, while observing the vehemence of its cooling: for when it cools vehemently, it is not long before it weakens the limb. Therefore, because of the organs of breath: it is not far-fetched that it might hinder the diaphragm and other things from the emission of breath with ease. And concerning the moistening regimen, there are light foods and fruits and fruit-syrups <note>original: "robub"</note> and ointments and plasters and scents and head-purges and rest and tranquility, and that no violence be brought upon him in hunger or thirst.

### On the recollection of medicines that cool them. Ch. V.

**O**thers indeed among them are cooling or moistening; all are nutritious or nutritiveness prevails in them, like barley water cooked with crabs, on account of the crab. And it is necessary that the extremities of the crabs be pulled from their feet and their bodies: and let them be washed with cold water and good salt with ash three times and more until they are cleansed and purged of the gravity of their odor; then let them be cooked in barley water; and like the water of cow's milk from which the butter has been extracted, and like the juices of the aforementioned boiled pot-herbs in the chapters on acute fevers, like the mucilage of psyllium. In vinegar there is either vehement drying or a resolving power, wherefore it is necessary that it be drunk with that which resists two properties, namely by the mixing of much water or with certain moistening and softening things. And the first indeed is that donkey's milk <note>original: "lac asine"</note> be cooling along with its moistening, so that some make its cooling better than the cooling of cow's milk from which the butter has been extracted: truly it reaches him who has no periodic fever, nor matter nor humor prepared for putrefaction. And it is necessary that thick milk be avoided; and among those things that benefit them is sugar: and when you feel putrefaction happening from the milk, then dissolve it with ease, and if you fear heating, then abstain from it for some days and treat it with troches <note>term: "trochisci" — medicinal lozenges</note> and fruit waters; then repeat the milk.

**B**ut cooling medicines that do not have moistening are such as these troches:

<column-break/>

the well-known told [ones], namely camphorated troches and troches of dates and cold juices, which are troches of this kind: Take <note>original: "r." for "recipe"</note> spodium <note>term: "spodium" — ash of ivory or bone</note>, Armenian bole, of each 3 drachmas; of roses 6 drachmas; seed of purslane and citron and gourd and amber, of all 3 drachmas each. Let troches be made from them and let the dose be 2 drachmas in weight, and they are very good. And again others for them: Take plantain, starch, and gum tragacanth, of all 3 drachmas each; Armenian bole, spodium, of both 4 drachmas each; of poppy 5 drachmas; roses and seeds of gourd and citron and purslane, of all 6 drachmas each; peeled quince seeds and seeds of melon and cucumber, of all 7 drachmas each; juice of licorice 10 drachmas in weight; let them be prepared with mucilage of psyllium. Cooling ointments, epithems <note>term: "epithema" — a liquid poultice or compress</note>, plasters, scents, and head-purges are those which you already know. And the best ointments are with oil of gourd and poppy and water-lily <note>original: "nenufare"</note> and willow and violets. Cooling and moistening beds are those that are very flat, made of hides sprinkled with rose water, or of linen of its kind: which is made in Tabaristan <note>original: "tabrasten"</note> and let its filling be that which does not heat; rather let it be of the kind of combed linen and let it be renewed constantly. Or let the bed be of hides which are already filled with water after there are rectifications upon them which flatten the water well and prohibit its inequality; and let the beds be near waters and their courses, and under them leaves of cold and moist trees, namely of willow and often rue <note>original: "ryue"</note> and moist, fragrant, cold pot-herbs like roses and leaves of cold trees and vine tendrils and similar things.

### On the recollection of medicines that moisten them. Ch. VI.

**T**he recollection of others which are with cooling has already passed. And it remains now to consider the quality of giving in drink types of milk and milk from which butter has been extracted, and the quality of administering the tub <note>original: "tine"</note> and the bath: from the administration of ointments and pot-herbs and epithems and the rest of the regimen. And we have indeed already taught the manner of giving in drink the types of milk in the chapter on phthisis <note>term: "phthisis" — a progressive wasting of the body, especially from tuberculosis</note> and dryness of the stomach: wherefore it is necessary that that be the rule. And there is no milk like woman's milk, [then] like donkey's milk, then goat's milk whose pasture must be from herbs and moist pot-herbs as you know; for it, and especially donkey's milk, eradicates the hectic [fever] if it is an eradicator for it, and there is no choice above it unless putrefaction happening or the expectation of contained matter prohibits it. And milk indeed is a benefit to them from the beginning of the hectic fever until its end. And woman's milk taken by sucking is suitable for all. And the rule in giving the milk from which butter has been extracted in drink is the first for that again. And the best is that you begin from 10 drachmas up to 30 drachmas; because that which is above them would be a helping power, and where it is possible, you should mix it...

...that which he intends, secondly he carries it out. There he says: "And we indeed." And this is in three parts. First, he gives the regimen through milk. Second, through the tub. Third, through the bath. And between these he places [the section] on ointments and plasters. The rest of the regimen, namely through food and drink, he places last. There he says: "Let him fear." There in the third part: "The entering of the bath." It is doubted in the first small part whether human or donkey's milk is better for a hectic patient. Whence it seems human is better through Galen in the 7th [book] of *Therapeutics*, and Avicenna here. To the contrary is Avicenna here: "there is no choice above it," that is, nothing is chosen that is better than it. But first he specifically said "donkey's milk." As for the manner, when Avicenna wants to praise something poorly, it is the aforementioned manner. Just as immediately below he uses this way of speaking: and in the third book according to the first chapter on the common rules of head ailments. Furthermore, goat's milk seems better: because Galen posits that it is a middle or equal milk in the book on *Good and Bad Juices* in the fourth chapter. Let us say first that the repeated discourses of Avicenna are not uniform in his books: just as we showed something of this in the second book of the *Canon* in the chapter on milk, and Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Maimonides</note> depended on something of this. But we do not have to discuss these things here. Second, we will say that human milk is better for the hectic patient: because it is more conforming and closer to human nature. But donkey's milk is better: because it is more subtle and colder and moister. Goat's milk, however, is middle or equal, namely in substance compared to donkey's milk. For the complexion of the donkey seems to decline toward coldness and moisture, which the softness of its flesh and its whiteness shows much; others, however, will have it that it is a cold and dry animal. It must be considered that Avicenna not only prohibits milk because of actual putrefaction of the matter, but also because of expected putrefaction of the contained matter which is in the form of an antecedent cause. As for the tub <note>original: "Tina"</note>: First, he sets down the regimen through a lukewarm tub, speaking of a cold one. Second, he returns to the use of the lukewarm tub and tempered heat. Third, he sets the order of the tub to the use of barley water. Fourth, he sets the order of the use of the tub and also the bath to ointments and to the cold tub and to the emulsion of milk. There is the second: "That however." There is the third: "And if he takes." There is the fourth: "And let them be administered." In the first part, he wants to say that in the beginning of hectic fever, before the patient has become thin or very dried out or weakened: immersion in cold water heals. And because someone might speak against this: because that cooling weakens and leaves behind a bad cold complexion. Re...

# Book 1, Treatise II

<margin>
a. This promises that the specific cooling and weakness is slight and can be removed in the time following. This is what he means: "Again, the weakness of the body," namely in the state mentioned from cooling, he cures it with a little cooling. Because the cooling is slight, from which this weakness follows, because the body was not yet consumed, nor was it greatly susceptible to being struck by cold water.
</margin>
<margin>
a. "But if it should be," etc. That is, if the hectic patient is already much weakened and thinned, he is "dyed" <note>likely meaning "affected" or "stained" in a medical sense</note> if he is placed in a cold tub of water, so that he falls into the "senile hectic" <note>the wasting fever typical of old age or end-stage consumption</note>.
</margin>
<margin>
b. "And that according to the least," that is, at the very least this is feared. Again, however, what he says about falling into the senile hectic is because he can live longer with that cause than with a febrile hectic fever. All these things were said by Galen in the second book of *Therapeutics* <note>original: "terapeutice," referring to Methodus Medendi</note>.
</margin>
<margin>
c. "That," etc. "And he tolerates with it," namely with tenderness, the cold water. As if he were to say: let the porous person become rare <note>let the skin's pores open</note> and let him be made tender by warm water; nevertheless, he tolerates cold water better.
</margin>
<margin>
d. "And if he has taken," namely if he first gives, etc. "After," that is, after the tub, let him milk <note>apply</note> milk over the body. Consider therefore that here he administers the tub three times: 1. First he gives barley water, although afterward he administers the tub. 2. Secondly, he again gives barley water and after that the tub, so that the food may be distributed, and this is good. And understand that if you can place him in the tub a third time, that is, it verifies what he said: if the tub is repeated three times in a day. Or you can understand it differently: whether you give barley water before the tub, or first provide the tub and then give barley water, both are good.
</margin>
<margin>
e. "And let it be administered." The anointing after the tub and the bath keeps water in the pores, which cools by returning to its own coldness, as is known from Book 1, Treatise 2. And this is "according to tolerance," that is, if he tolerates it. The milk emulsion [is used] if he is not weak, because a weak person cannot tolerate so much being done.
</margin>
<margin>
f. "Entry into the bath." This is called a "stove" <note>original: "stufa," a heated steam room</note> among us. It has three chambers as described above in Book 1.
</margin>

...with it some cooling lozenges <term>trochisci</term>. And it is for you to add to the aforementioned total in the drink the final amount, if the strength is capable of digestion. That soaking tub <term>tina</term> is best which is lukewarm, in which there is not much heat, and it should also contain the virtues of cooling and moistening vegetables and herbs. It should not be such that it causes sweating, for it is not permitted that the vapor of the tub be hot. If it were not for the fact that it prohibits the administration of the cold tub, one would not choose anything over it; however, what prohibits this is the weakness of their bodies and their emaciation. In the initial stages, this perhaps heals them, but it heals the weakness of the body with that slight cooling which it produces in completing what is possible to be cured. But if the patient is weak, it is feared that they may fall into "senile hectic," and that at the very least. However, with that, death is delayed longer, and perhaps he lives with it for a significant amount of time. And many times, indeed, his change to that hectic state is more correct.

Regarding the procedure for the tub, it is more correct to begin with water that is warm to the limit, and then make a gradation to cold, and then to a tolerable temperate cold. For this gradation makes the body receptive to cold water, since injury does not occur except through the sudden arrival of an opposite in the temperament. And again, the body acquires from the warm water a great deal of tenderness and tolerates the cold along with it. If the tub is repeated three times in a day, it will be correct. It must be administered with ease so that the patient's strength does not fail. And if he takes barley water two hours before the tub, it will be suitable; and if he precedes the tub with an emulsion of milk over his body—as we shall say, so that the tub may dilate the pathways of the food—then let him receive barley water. And for similar things afterward, let him wait, and then let the tub water be administered; so that the food may be distributed, it will be good.

After the tub and the bathhouse <term>balneum</term>, let an anointing be administered with cooling and moistening oils, such as violet oil, especially when it is made from pumpkin oil, and similarly water-lily oil and pumpkin oil. And if after the tub he is moved to that which is slightly cold but tolerable, let him then be anointed. And if the anointing comes first and he hurries to then enter the cold water, it will be slightly correct; this is according to tolerance, and it is not bad to proceed by degrees in this.

**Indeed, the best of hours for this action is after the digestion of food. If it is possible for him to submerge in cold water suddenly without gradation after the warm tub, it is the most extreme part of the cure, but it is also the strongest in terms of fear. Pouring water with ease is less fearful than sudden submersion of the sick person in it, but it provides less benefit. The cold should be according to the quantity of standing cold water, which is between lukewarm and that which is intensely cold. If a milk emulsion is first applied over his limbs:**

<column-break/>

...if he is not weak, or if it is mixed with water if he is weak; then if the tub is administered, it will be correct. For the emulsion of milk over the body is intensely moistening. The types of milk that are good for this are those mentioned before. It is best that they be milked directly from the breast. It is worth focusing on the joints by rubbing the aforementioned medicines onto the whole body and the joints. Entry into the bathhouse is not granted to him unless it is done so as not to cause sweating, nor to inflame him, nor to alter his breathing; the water should be less hot than the air of the room. The heat of the water should be such that it delights and does not harm, and does not cause sweating. This is when there is no matter in his body prepared for rot <note>putrefaction or sepsis</note>, and especially when the food is not yet digested. Indeed, it ought to be when the desire is for the digested food to be expanded into the body; he should not prolong his stay in the bath, but rather depart from it quickly. When he departs, let him take some moistening things and drinks that do not harm him, known to be made from barley and milk. When thirst happens to him in the bath, let him quench it with barley water, and "alraib" <term>sour milk or buttermilk</term>, and the milk should be ass's milk. Entry into the bath and the exit from it should be done in a way that involves no labor at all. We have already announced this in other places and will repeat the conditions for it.

<margin>
Second [point] 1. Galen says in the *Therapeutics*: "In our homeland, we would not place a hectic patient in that, but we use the tub in its place, because we can more easily moderate it." Afterward he says the water should be less hot than the air. This is because the same degree of heat placed in water and in air heats more when in water than in air because of the thinness of air.
</margin>
<margin>
g. And otherwise, let us say that Avicenna said this to show that the hectic patient needs water and to be placed in it, and does not need air. He says "let it be hot," etc., meaning: put him in water and care for its quality, and do not keep him in the air. This is especially so when there is matter ready for rot and his food is not digested. He must not enter the bath. "Arabi" <note>likely referring to al-raib</note> is sour milk from which the butter has been extracted.
</margin>
<margin>
h. "And it is necessary." This is a precept from Galen's 5th book of *Therapeutics*, and we have already announced it in Book 1 and Book 3. He says below in the text that a "sabana" <note>sheet</note> is a type of bed, which he said is called *pedetolene* <note>original: "pedeto lene," a Greek term for a stretcher or linen litter</note> in Greek. It was placed in the first room so that while standing in it, he might be stripped of his clothes. "Let the sweat be dried." Because if it happens that he sweats, you should not strive to make him sweat. Or "sweat" refers to the moisture of the water, because otherwise the oil would not be applied to him. The rest are well-known.
</margin>

**He should be carried to the bath in a portable bed in which the bedding is cleverly arranged so that he arrives at the first room with it. He should be moved to that which is made of two cloths full of wool or cotton, called in Greek *pedetolene*, which is suitable for the bath. Let him be stripped of his clothes in that room, or in the middle room if it is not hot. He should not linger in any of them except for the time it takes to change and for a few breaths while stripped of clothing. Then let him enter the second and third rooms, provided they are not of intense heat, and let it be done in the amount that he can tolerate the tub. This is what has been said, and what is most pleasing to me is that his tub should be in the temperate middle room. When he is removed from the cold tub, let him be covered with a towel and his sheet, and let his sweat be dried with a towel, and let him be anointed and fed.**

### On the Feeding of those having Hectic Fever. Chapter 7.

<margin>
<note>Note on the decorative initial O: The commentary identifies specific foods.</note>
"It is necessary," etc. *Almes* are fish. Among others, *robille*. *Debogeti* is a way of preparing food. *Aduragi* are St. Peter's fish <note>Tilapia or John Dory</note> used there. *Adugi* are small birds. Some wine for strengthening. *Morsos* is a jelly called galantine among us. *Aduragi* is a turtle-dove; others say it is a species of partridge. *Lulagezi* and *alrobugi* are types of partridges. *Pullio* refers to small chicks. *Gulmen* is a type of sour food. Generally, know that among the Saracens <note>Arabic speakers</note> there are many ways of preparing foods, which they vary in flavors and colors, as appears in their books mentioned above. "Meat water" <note>meat juice</note> differs from broth, as Avicenna says in the book *On the Powers of the Heart* in the chapter on meats. "And no sign of digestion appears": although in hectic fever no sign of digestion appears, cold water can still be given because it is not a material fever <note>a fever caused by humors</note>. Therefore Galen wanted in the 3rd book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, commentary 15 at the end, that a sign of digestion is the "spark of life" in melting fevers for giving cold water as a drink. However, if digestion appears, it is suspected that there are some matters in the hectic patient that need rectification; it is better for giving cold water as a drink, even if the natural heat is strengthened. *Sirfen* is an abscess of the brain. *Sirfen* is also an abscess of the chest. Avicenna perfectly assigns the cause of his statement.
</margin>

**It is necessary that food be separated in them; they should not be fed to fullness all at once. Furthermore, the best thing they are fed is barley water, and barley, and washed wheat bread soaked in cold water. And types of milk—nothing we have said prohibits any of them—and cow's milk from which butter has been extracted, since it is of the greatest nourishment. Also *almes* and pumpkin, and of fruits, Palestinian melons, which are named *alraki* among us Indians. And when he feels a recovery of strength, then food is not bad.**

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "hectic" (ethica), a category of wasting fever. The previous page detailed the cooling baths and initial diet. # Book I

<column-break/>

**Lillis.** <note>original: "Lillis," likely a specific chapter heading or person’s name</note> Barley water made from roasted barley: it possesses a specific quality due to the roasting; namely, gum arabic and boiled lentils. It should be prepared with water boiled several times—namely, in a decoction. Because water that has been boiled again and again is well known for these qualities.

**The dispute** <note>original: "Lis," likely a variant of "Litis," here used to describe a medical debate</note> concerns the condition of old age; as Haly Abbas <note>original: "balyab," referring to the Persian physician Haly Abbas</note> says in the second book of his *Theory*, and Avicenna in this chapter. First, he gives the reason why he determines it here: because it is the custom of the ancients to speak of it after the *Ethics* <note>meaning the study of the hectic fever, 'ethica'</note>, and Serapion did this in the sixth book of his *Breviary*, as did Rhazes in the sixteenth book of the *Continens*. This is the custom of the ancients to speak of it after the hectic because it is contrary to the hectic fever. While the hectic fever is a hot disease of the heart and the whole body, science shows that the contrary can occur in the same subject and be shared. The second reason was that the hectic of old age in all its species is a dryness of the heart and the entire body. In this, it shares a trait with the febrile hectic, which, although primarily a heat, is nevertheless associated with dryness of the heart and the whole body in any of its species. Therefore, he says above: because the hectic of old age shares dryness with the febrile hectic, he defines it thus: they differ in heat and cold. Namely, heat is associated with febrile hectic, but cold is associated with the hectic of old age. The third cause is that certain ancients named the hectic of old age a "fever," among whom was Haly Abbas in the eighth book of his *Theory*, and Serapion in his sixth treatise, who divided the hectic fever into "hot" and "cold" (or the hectic of old age). Thus, his science on the matter fell under the chapter on fevers. However, this naming is improper, since "fever" is named after "fervor" <note>boiling heat</note>, or from fire and heat. Whence in the first book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, in commentary 43, it says that a fever occurs when natural heat is changed into a fiery heat. Whence Rhazes, in the sixteenth book of the *Continens*, in the last chapter, says: "Whenever a harmful heat dominates the whole body, it will be a fever and is called a fever; but if there is coldness in the whole body, then by law it should not be called a fever." Nevertheless, by way of similarity, it is called a fever, because just as a fever is an affliction of the whole body originating from the heart, so the hectic of old age is a coldness and dryness of the whole body originating from the heart. **Intent:** Here he proceeds, and first gives the modes of this hectic; second, the bodies susceptible; third, the causes. 

**And old men...** <note>original: "Et senes"</note> It must be considered that because all hectic of old age is dry, yet not every such affliction is cold (as will soon appear), he therefore characterized it by the dominance of dryness. And if you consider that every hectic of old age is a cold affliction, yet because the coldness in it arises from dryness—that is, the consumption of moisture—this is truly the hectic of old age. I say "in most cases," because there is a certain hectic of old age in which the coldness does not depend entirely on dryness, such as that which occurs from drinking cold water or bathing in it. It must be considered that he seems to posit two species of hectic: one in which there is a balance of heat and cold, and another in which there is coldness; and both share the trait of being without fever. It is first doubted whether heat can be joined with this dryness. Second, whether dryness with heat is the same as the hectic. It is doubted thirdly whether it is possible for the hectic of old age to exist with both heat and cold. To the first, it seems that with the hectic of old age, which is dryness, the heat of the whole cannot be joined, because then it would be a fever, the contrary of which Avicenna says: "without fever." To the contrary is what is said in the first chapter of the book *On Wasting* <note>original: "de tabe"</note>. It should be said that when this question of names is well considered, there is no doubt in the matter itself that a dryness as great as that found in any old age can be joined to a fever—namely, a bad hot complexion in the heart and the whole body. But whether that dryness with fever can be called "senile hectic" or "febrile hectic" is a question of words and not of the reality. It must be considered here that dryness to such a degree as is found in any "wasting" <note>original: "tabe"</note> or in any senile hectic—where there is a great dryness that is the consumption and lack of the glue-like moisture of the members—can be joined to heat. Namely, either to a heat that is its cause, or to a heat accidentally joined to that dryness and not as its cause. If indeed such dryness of the solid members is joined to a heat that is its cause, then either that heat is a fever or it is "made" <note>artificial/accidental</note>. If it is a fever, then such dryness is called *tabes* or *marasmus* <note>terms for severe wasting</note> joined with "melting" fevers, because that heat is called a melting fever joined to marasmus or wasting. Whence Galen, in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*, says that the "burning fevers" <note>original: "causones"</note> which have consumed all the moisture of the heart are not only hectics, but are *marasmodes* <note>wasting-like</note> and wasting. If, however, such heat is "made," then this aggregate—namely, such dryness and such heat—is the third species of hectic, because they share the same definition. For the hectic of the third species is a heat beyond nature made in the heart and members with a manifest consumption of the ultimate moisture. This definition is also the definition of the presupposed dryness. And this solves the second question, whether the dryness of the moisture of the members joined to febrile heat is the same as the hectic. It should be said that if that dryness is joined to a "made" heat, it is the third species of hectic. For if the definition of marasmus is taken from this—which is to be a dryness of the ultimate moisture...

->it is sufficient to rub it with moist cheese that is not salted.<-

**And** if he is further weakened, it is not bad if he is fed with a broth of *isidabegi* <note>likely an Arabic medicinal plant or preparation</note> with moist coriander boiled with it, for those who are thus [afflicted], such as *alduragi* <note>Francolin/Partridge</note> and *altaciugi* <note>another type of game bird</note>. **And** perhaps it is necessary that he be given some light wine to drink mixed with much water; and perhaps it is necessary that you feed him with a *mosos* <note>a type of dish or paste</note> made from the meat of francolin and partridge and *alcubugi* <note>another bird, likely a lark</note> and chickens; and a sour *hosule* <note>a broth or dish</note> or a sour jelly made from the meat of a kid <note>young goat</note> or beef, when there is strength of digestion there. And the vinegar of the *almosos* and the jelly is helpful to them and strengthening in this condition. And perhaps there is no excuse for meat-water <note>broth</note> mixed with syrup of cold, sour fruits, or swallowed egg yolks. And when weakness leading to fainting <note>term: "sincopi"</note> is prolonged with it, it is necessary that they be fed with meat broth taken from the sides of a kid with a little salt, which should be strained and poured over it. A portion of it should be of apple water and a tenth part of it of fragrant wine, and it should be drunk warm. Indeed, cold water that is not of very intense cold is not bad if given to them to drink, if the patient is not weak, or if nothing prohibits it. And that which prohibits it will either be an aposteme <note>an internal swelling or abscess</note> under the hypochondria, or there will be putrid humors or raw humors in the whole body which all require digestion; and no sign of digestion appears, for if it should appear, the fear will be less. And so, if it were a hectic changed from *sisyen* or *busen* <note>Arabic medical terms for types of wasting</note>, for with this it is better that the drinking of cold water be forbidden than with others. For when the hectic follows upon destructive diseases which soften the body while drying out the bones and flesh, it follows upon weakness. When, therefore, it is joined to weakness after the taking of cold water, it does not delay in falling into the genus of another hectic, which shares with this genus in dryness but differs in heat and cold, and is named the hectic of old age and the hectic of senility. And...

<column-break/>

...without any other moisture remaining with it; then marasmus is not hectic. But if marasmus is the ultimate dryness, whether it be with heat or with cold, then any marasmus is a hectic of the third species, as has been declared. And just as we compare the hectic of old age (in which the fourth moisture—namely, that of the members—is consumed) to the third species of hectic, so the hectic of old age (in which the third moisture is taken away) can be compared to the second species of hectic. If, however, such dryness called senile hectic is joined to heat that is accidentally joined to it—for instance, from anger or the sun or another heat—then it is a double disease; each has its own name, and one does not depend on the other. To the contrary arguments, it should be said that when Avicenna says "without fever," he does not mean that fever cannot be joined to it, but he meant that this hectic is properly the senile hectic, distinct from the febrile hectic; which in the beginning of old age is without fever acting as its cause. To the third question, it is argued that it is impossible for the hectic of old age to exist with a balance of heat and cold, because such is the condition of senile hectic when it is the condition of an old man. But old men are cold and dry. To the contrary is Avicenna, when he says: "because sometimes it exists with equality in heat or cold." To the contrary indeed is Galen, in the seventh book of *Therapeutics* and in the first chapter of the book *On Wasting*. To understand this, it must first be known that this hectic of old age has many names. For it is called senile hectic; it is also called *tabes* (wasting); it is also called *marasimus*; it is called *marcor* <note>decay/fading</note> by Galen in the eighth book of *Therapeutics*; it is called *phthisis* <note>consumption</note> by Maimonides <note>original: "Rabbi moyse"</note> and in the fifth section of the *Aphorisms*. Second, it must be known that whatever the name, the nature of this affliction is consumption proceeding from dryness, occurring first in the heart and then in the other members. If, however, this should be first in another member than the heart—such as dryness of the whole proceeding from the stomach—it is not truly noted as marasmus or wasting. Third, it must be said regarding the question that it is not well understood how senile hectic could occur without a distemper in the active qualities—namely, in coldness. The reason is taken from the seventh book of *Therapeutics*: for in this condition, they are not nourished as parts; but when parts are not nourished, they become cold. Whence it says in the sixth book: "for most certainly in the act of nutrition..."

...that which would be a second disease in which the innate heat is already destroyed. And similarly, water of extreme cold hurts them very much in every condition and corrupts the innate heat of their radical members. And perhaps it hastens their end or changes them into another mode of hectic.

<margin>
On succoring the conditions following the hectic. Chapter VII.
</margin>

**Ellis** <note>original: "Ellis," likely a shorthand for "Another [affliction]" or a chapter marker</note> is syncope <note>fainting</note>: and we have already given the regimen for this many times. And among those [afflictions] is the flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>. And it is necessary that he be cured and succored in this, for in this there is great fear. And among the cures for it, first is that there be barley water or *faufel* water. And roasted millet and gum should be put in their barley water, or lentils boiled repeatedly, or milk boiled with stones or with fire alone until its "aquosity" <note>watery part</note> is consumed; and especially with millet. And let them take these troches <note>lozenges</note>: Take 5 drams <note>original: "3.v."</note> of Armenian bole, roasted chestnuts, and roses, 4 drams of each; spodion <note>ash or metallic oxide</note> and amber, 3 drams of each; sour seeds, husked barberries, 6 drams of each. Let troches be made with the juice of quinces, and give them to drink in pear water in the morning and at bedtime. And let roasted psyllium be given to drink, and similarly a powder of spodion in which there is Mecca balsam is very helpful. And if it reaches the point of excoriation <note>raw/ulcerated skin or bowel</note>, let the excoriation be cured with clysters <note>enemas</note> which you know to be suitable.

On the hectic of old age. Chapter IX.

**Larrit** <note>likely "it is common" or a corruption of "Apparet"</note> custom allows that they call the hectic of old age a hectic fever. And let us also proceed in the accustomed way: the definition of the hectic of old age is the dominance of dryness over the complexion without fever. And sometimes it exists with equality in heat and cold, and that is according to the least. And sometimes it exists with cold, and this condition is named old age and the hectic of senility, for that which happens to the body in the hour of old age is that which happens in that hour...

# Part 1, Treatise 4
