# Fen <note>A section or division of a book in Avicenna’s Canon</note> Treatise III

...and that it is full of fire. A second doubt is raised regarding at what time this pestilence is said to occur: whether in autumn or in the following winter. A third doubt is raised as to how these signs are also causes. For fires falling or standing in the highest part of the air <note>meteorological phenomena like shooting stars or comets</note> do not cause anything in our bodily moisture, even if they signify it. In this matter, the meteorologist and the astrologer can say much. I will speak according to what suffices for us. First, I say that these fires do not signify a true pestilence, but only the malice of autumn: they signify its excessive dryness. But a dry autumn is a wicked thing, producing wicked illnesses.

<margin>a</margin>
Because these dry, hot vapors which become fires above make the air dry down here; they are of the same species. The reason is that these fires run the course of causes: not that those which are high up near the outer edge of the fire cause this specifically, but those which are in this space of the same species as them. And this is what Avicenna says lastly: it indicates by an indication of the cause, for they indicate those things which are the cause. Secondly, we can say that a hot and dry exhalation does not make a pestilence. But when many vapors rise in the air, then a pestilence occurs. Hence, in the first problem of the *Problems*, Aristotle says that when a great vapor is emitted from the earth, then a time of pestilence occurs. These fires, therefore, are to be understood as fires indicating great evaporation by their appearance, although Avicenna places this later. Or we could imagine that a multitude of vapors in the air cannot be refined but are mixed with the air; a part of these can be heated and dried, although at the beginning of their elevation they were not like that; or there was a hidden hot and dry vapor within the humid vapors. Because of this multitude of humid vapors, with the hot and dry ones remaining mixed in the air and raised upward, pestilence arises from them. Thirdly, those fires which were not raised upward, but only began to ascend mixed in, can signify pestilence according to this mode and run the course of causes because they indicate the said cause. Here, the third discourse from the principles of the meteorologists might be troubled, but we do not care. Thirdly, we can say that these many fires, not only moving but also stationary—of which the comet is one—arise from the lordship of Mars, whose lordship is the cause of death and pestilence in the air. They run, therefore, the course of the cause because they signify the cause, namely, the impression of Mars. Therefore, Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a renowned 10th-century physician</note> on the *Prognostication of Fevers* said: when the appearance of stars like many and diverse lamps in autumn signifies pestilence. He adds that some here ask the intention of this reason; we will say that these things cannot be understood unless one first observes the many movements of the stars and the knowledge of their conjunctions with one another, which happens in their circle according to the quality of each of the stars, which is according to their places. Now, therefore, the solution to the first and third doubt appears. As to the second doubt, it must be said according to the first way of speaking: that this pestilence will be in autumn itself, for there will be fevers from corrupted materials, and other certainties like scabs, leprosy, and cancers; and it can extend into winter, in which these materials are constricted. But according to the second and third ways of speaking, this pestilence could be in the coming winter, spring, and summer.

### **When the south wind and the east wind are multiplied for several days. And whenever you see a turbidity of the air and its cloudiness, and you expect rain but find the air empty and dry, and it does not rain, then know that the complexion of winter will be corrupt. Moreover, a malignancy signifies a bad summer pestilence when there is a scarcity of rain in spring with cold; then the south wind is multiplied and the air is disturbed for some days, then it clears after one week, not more, and cold occurs in the night and in the day the heat is vehement, with a suffocating feeling, disturbance, and heat: then the pestilence has already arrived and pestilential fevers, smallpox, and things similar to these are expected. And similarly, when the summer is not of vehement heat but of vehement disturbance, having altered mornings, and "asubub" <note>likely "al-shihub," Arabic for shooting stars</note> and fires and "rebiziz" <note>another Arabic-derived term for meteorological phenomena</note> and others have already passed in autumn, it is a sign of pestilence and other things. And similarly, when you see the air altered many times in one day: and the air clears on some day, and the sun rises bright, and it is disturbed on another day, and it rises in veils of mist which is like dust, then judge that a pestilence will happen. Signs, however, which are according to the path of the cause of dryness are, for example: you see frogs already multiplying, and you see creeping things generated from putrefaction already multiplying. And among those things that sign this is: that you see mice and animals that live under the earth flee to the surface of the earth and come out miserably. And you see animals of an evil nature like "qlalakibi" <note>unclear; likely an Arabic term for a type of venomous insect or reptile</note> and similar things flee from their nests and go away from them and perhaps leave their eggs.**

"And when the south winds are multiplied." It must be considered that the multiplication of the south wind <term>Auster; the hot, humid wind from the south</term> makes the air humid and it is hot. The east wind <term>Subsolanus; the wind from the east</term> however, adds to the heat in the air. In "Thenis" <note>likely the Hebrew month Tevet, corresponding to Dec/Jan</note>, namely the month of December, in which many say winter is, you see these winds blow and you see the air cloudy then. The release of many vapors signifies humidity and heat disturbing and mixed in the air. If it rains through the ascent of these vapors and their conversion into water, then the air would not remain thoroughly mixed with those vapors, and thus putrefaction would not occur. But because there is no rain, but instead you find the air empty of rain and dry (that is, deprived of rain), the air is corrupted; for those vapors with heat become putrid or they putrefy the air. Because not only in winter, but there can be vapors and such corruption that it will dominate the whole year. And this is a problem from Aristotle's *Problems*, in the first and third problem. For he says: why are south winds dry and not watery? And he solves it by saying that they create foreign heat and humidity in the air; for they are humid and hot. It must be considered, however, if the east wind is together with the south wind, it adds heat to that excessive humidity, because of which it putrefies more quickly, so that the heat of spring or summer is not awaited.

<margin>b</margin>
¶ "Pestilence." It is doubted why little rain and cold in spring contribute to this pestilence. Furthermore, how cold in the night and heat can happen. It must be said that a cold spring with little rain holds the material until summer. Then, that is, after spring, the south wind is multiplied: and this is the cause of many vapors in the air; the sign of which is the turbidity of the air. And when these vapors are thoroughly mixed with the air, as they are somewhat thinned, the air becomes clearer than it was before. And this clarity ought not to last long; it suffices for about a week. And again the air is disturbed by the arrival of many vapors. For if that clarity lasted beyond a week, it could signify the consumption of those vapors. And from this dominance we suspect that the air is putrid from those many vapors; for they bring heat in them and cold happens at night. It must be considered that this cold and this heat can be understood to be in the air. For these vapors are humid and watery by nature. Therefore, as the sun recedes, they tend toward coldness; but with heat trapped in them, putrefaction occurs, because heat wins and internally heat appears in them. According to this imagination, first in the evening coldness will appear in the air, and at some other hour of the night heat will appear. Conversely, we could imagine that the thick air made from these vapors retains the heat which it acquired in the day from the first evening until some part of the night; afterward, however, it changes to cold. You, however, consider this. But this cold and heat can be

<column-break/>

understood to be in the bodies. For this putrid air, being inhaled, harms the heart, even if it does not yet cause a fever. Therefore, the heat is drawn from the exterior parts to the interior. Cold, therefore, occurs in the night around the extremities, and heat in the internal parts. We could say otherwise that this thick, humid air, in the absence of the sun, cools down at night, and from this, heat is trapped inside; because one feels the heat less, although it harms the spiritual parts <term>spiritual parts; the organs involved in breathing and vital spirit, like the heart and lungs</term>. Whatever the truth is, this air disturbs us: and by harming the spiritual parts, it is the cause of a kind of suffocation. For the heart is harmed in its attraction of air, and from this, it seems as if the person is not being relieved by it. This, however, appears more at night: either because in the day there is ventilation from the west and north winds (as in Aristotle's *Problems* 25.13); or because heat is trapped inside; or because in the day, due to attention to other things, men do not so much observe these changes in themselves. This happened to the philosopher Brita with an abscess <note>original: "apostema"; a swelling or abscess</note> in the hip, which bothered him more at night than in the day, as appears from Galen in his book on the *Differentiation of Diseases*. This pestilence, therefore, is evil and great: for it is a true pestilence from much putrefaction in the air.

<margin>c</margin>
¶ "And things similar to these," such as measles <note>original: "morbilli"</note> and carbuncles <note>original: "carbuculi"; plague boils</note>, i.e., abscesses from poisonous material, corruptions of the limbs, and similar dispositions to those which this pestilence makes. And we testify to having seen this. The cause of these is similar. This is another sign of this pestilence in which we signify a hidden and malignant putrid material in the air, the sign of which is that people are greatly disturbed, so that they cannot rest in the nights of this summer; although they do not specifically indicate a strong heat, it is therefore from the malice of the putrefaction.

<margin>d</margin>
## On the Treatments of Pestilential Fevers. Chapter IV.

The summary of their treatment is drying. And that with bloodletting <term>phlebotomia; the therapeutic draining of blood to balance the humors</term> and loosening of the belly <note>purging</note>, and it is necessary that it be begun with evacuation: if, however, the material is overcoming...

<margin>e</margin>
"Having altered mornings," namely from heat proceeding to cold and vice versa as we said above. Commonly, however, it happens that around dawn the cold appears more, the closer the sun is to us, as in *Problems* book 15, problem 5. "Fires," namely of diverse modes. "Alezein," i.e., descending fires. And Avicenna used this word to signify the diverse modes of fire which are diversified in form, motion, and rest: and in motion there is great diversity. Therefore he said: "and others," i.e., other and diverse modes of these fires. As for example, that some comet appears with this, Avicenna says. "They have passed in autumn," to indicate that the cause of these is the dominance of some malevolent planet, whose impression in the air begins to appear at the time when these fires are more apt to be made, namely, in autumn. "And of others," namely of the circles and the beginning of death.

<margin>f</margin>
¶ "And similarly." This alteration is from heat to cold. Whence the strength is weakened, from turbidity to clarity. Not only in one year, but from day to day. Whence it signifies a multitude of scattered vapors in the air. And the rising of the sun with a humid mist scattered in the air signifies the same. Whence the air appears as if it is dusty; a pestilence happens, namely, quickly. This sign, however, is theirs whenever it happens: for if it happens in winter, it could signify a pestilence in spring or in that very winter, according to the quantity of the vapors and their violence and malice.

<margin>g</margin>
¶ "The signs, however." It must be considered that these signs are said to be according to the association of the cause, because they themselves are not the causes; but they are associated with the cause, just as a multitude of small frogs signifies excessive humidity, from which they are made, as is also taken from Aristotle's *Problems*, book 1, problem 17, where this problem is asked. We, however, saw before a certain pestilence such a great multitude of these frogs that they covered the earth in many places. And they were small frogs with a certain tail. And these frogs Aristotle calls "crinoidas" frogs; others, however, say that their faces have red markings.

<margin>h</margin>
"Alarbuki," i.e., certain serpents. For these signs signify great putrefaction in the caverns of the earth. It must be considered that these can be called signs like the causes, such as flying fires: for although they are not the causes, they nonetheless signify the cause. Yet the signs which in truth are the causes are the multiplication of the south wind, the turbidity of the air, the appearance of dusty air, and similar things.

"The summary of the treatment." First, he gives the rule of treatment. Second, he gives the rule of preservation. The first rule has two parts: first, he gives the cure by evacuation; second, by cooling and the rectification of the air. It must be considered that, as we have already said, pestilential fevers can be different in different people: as in one person they are choleric <note>yellow bile</note>, in another phlegmatic, in another melancholic <note>black bile</note>, and in another sanguine <note>blood</note>; because of this, there is a diversity of them. Nevertheless, it happens that humidity putrefies around the heart, and this is the true pestilential fever. And some pestilential fever can be that in which the humors putrefy around certain veins, and this is because of their disposition. Evacuation, therefore, should be done either by bloodletting or by pharmacy <note>medicinal drugs</note>, as is appropriate. And take note that to perform bloodletting in a pestilential fever in which it is not appropriate is a great error, and greater than a similar error in others. Secondly, it must be considered that since in a pestilential fever there is not a great imbalance in the degree of heat (as in a burning fever <term>causone; a high, acute fever</term> and similar things), but the presence of bad material indicates evacuation rather and before any alteration. And therefore he said that the summary of the treatment is drying, i.e., evacuation. Where, however, there is great alteration or inflammation along with the pestilential fever—as when it is a hectic fever of many and acute heats—we boldly cool it down. Thirdly, it must be considered that since this material is putrid with a malignant putrefaction, we must strive as much as we can for its evacuation, and quickly. For we always hope more for the corruption of its material than for its digestion. And this is because of the thickness of the present corrupted air and the aptitude of the material; because of this, we begin with evacuation. And I have seen colleagues, expert men, who in a wicked pestilence gave evacuating drugs on the first, second, third, or fourth day—in short, as quickly as they could—loosening the materials: such as rhubarb for some, and agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note> for others with turbith <note>a purgative root</note>. And some gave these medicines strengthened with a little scammony <note>a strong laxative resin</note>. And we saw more people escape through the hands of these men than through the hands of those who did not purge except with light enemas and sometimes only cassia <note>a mild laxative</note>. And those solemn men said they wanted what Avicenna meant when he said: "And it is necessary that it be begun with evacuation." And they said that if in furious diseases it is commanded to evacuate before digestion, much more is this evacuation appropriate in material making a pestilential fever. For it can be called more furious than all furious material. Fourthly, it must be considered that regarding this evacuation of water, Avicenna...

# Book III

...hurries to call the process in a pestilential fever "drying." Whence he says the sum of the cure is drying <note>Latin: *exsiccatio*; in medieval medicine, moisture was associated with decay and putrefaction, so "drying" was the intended remedy</note>. For Avicenna calls evacuation—when it is not a minor reduction—"drying": whether it be a reduction of materials that are not the immediate cause or the preceding cause. But these are complicated matters, or rather matters joined with the fever. And thus he named it above in the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers in general when he says: "when you have administered the aforementioned canons, and it proceeds according to the path of reduction and drying," etc. Whether these materials are the immediate cause or the preceding cause, in this way he calls reductive evacuation "drying." And so too in the chapter on the cure of smallpox, when he says the patient should be bled <note>original: *flobothometur*</note>.

<margin>a</margin>
And the fourth way is by drying, that is, by reducing the matter. And this reduction is also called the "cutting off of the cause," namely, a privative cutting. Therefore, this drying—that is, the reductive evacuation—is taken when there is a conjoined cause making the fever; and Avicenna begins to do this. But you might say: if that matter is as wicked as "furious" matter <note>matter so corrupted it causes violent symptoms</note>, why then do we not evacuate by eradicating the matter? It must be said that this is because of the "falling of strength" <note>the patient's physical exhaustion</note>. For this fever begins from a malignancy of the spirits. If anyone wished to hold that in the beginning of pestilential putrid fevers, a medicine that evacuates by dissolving would not be suitable, but only one that flows gently, like cassia and violets, he bases himself on this word "drying." For Avicenna was accustomed to call evacuation "drying" when it is done with medicines that do not evacuate by dissolving <note>gentle laxatives vs. harsh purges</note>. And this discord returns to the uncertainties we discussed above in the cure of putrid fevers in general. However, I believe that in pestilential cases, one must hurry to purge with a medicine that evacuates by dissolving, as the reasoning of the aforementioned men proves; however, the determination of the time and the quantity of the medicine remains in the judgment of the physician.

<margin>b</margin>
**And it is necessary.** It should be considered that cooling lessens the putrefaction and tempers the heat which these patients feel around the heart. Cooling is done: first, by cooling their houses; second, by cooling them through things they consume; third, he sets down the regimen for a specific pestilential fever; fourth, he sets the regimen through food; fifth, he rectifies the air as he mentions before and after. There he stands. And let it be administered. There is the third part. "What if." There is the fourth. "And sometimes it happens." There is the fifth part: of rectification. What he says first is well known. "Liniment" and "ointment" <note>original: *delibutio*</note> are the same thing, though an ointment is like a more flowing liniment.

<margin>c</margin>
**And let it be administered.** It seems that Dinus <note>Dinus del Garbo, a famous medical commentator</note> was in doubt here, since in a pestilential fever there is a double intention: namely, the evacuation of matter and cooling. Why does he not list evacuating medicines, but instead cooling ones to be taken beforehand? Such as camphor troches <note>term: *trocifici*; medicinal lozenges</note> and cold fruit syrups <note>term: *rob*; a thickened, tart fruit juice used as a syrup</note>, like syrup of verjuice <note>unripe grape juice</note> and syrup of redcurrants and such. He responds that the medicines for evacuating matter were stated above; and they are the same as those that evacuate the matter of both pestilential and non-pestilential fevers. In this, Dinus spoke well. But later he says that cooling and drying medicines of this sort, like camphor troches and fruit syrups, oppose putrefaction itself. For putrefaction consists of heat and moisture, and therefore camphor troches are suitable for every pestilence considered as a pestilence. Because that is a certain fire to the putrefaction, although by reason of the matter of the putrefaction they may be more suitable in one pestilential fever, like a choleric one <note>caused by yellow bile</note>, and less in another, like a phlegmatic one. Yet even in a phlegmatic fever they are suitable by reason of the putrefaction caused by the corrupted air, whereas in another phlegmatic fever (one that is not pestilential) they would not be suitable. These sayings of Dinus need clarification. For the camphor troches we use in a choleric or bloody pestilential fever do not need mixing with other things to temper the coldness of the camphor; but I believe that when the pestilential fever is sluggish and the matter is cold and phlegmatic, then it is good to give something of musk or medicines made from musk, like *dyamuscum* <note>a musk-based cordial</note>, etc. And I believe Galen held this in his *Technē* <note>his "Art of Medicine"</note> when he says—and after Galen and Dioscorides found herbs of great help and swift value—just as camphor is valuable in hot pestilential illnesses, so musk is valuable in cold pestilential illnesses. It is doubted whether we can use Theriac <note>term: *tyriaca*; a famous universal antidote with dozens of ingredients</note> in a pestilential fever. It must be said that where the fever appears very sluggish with much low heat and poisonous putrefaction, some Theriac can be given. And I believe Galen wished this in his book on the benefits of Theriac. I also praise a medicine of rose water, wine, and Armenian bole <note>term: *bolo armeno*; a medicinal red clay used as an astringent</note> in pestilential fevers. Avicenna writes this in the second book in the chapter on Armenian bole. I have made this composition: take one pound of rose water, two ounces of wine, and two drams of Armenian bole; let them be mixed. Give it in the morning with a dissolved syrup, and give it at night and at midday for those whom it seems appropriate. And if you fear its binding effect <note>constipation</note>, help with a gentle reduction and add much syrup of citron or oranges, or verjuice, or pomegranate wine.

<margin>d</margin>
**And water.** This is the saying of Johannicius <note>original: *Joannis positi*; likely referring to Hunayn ibn Ishaq</note> in the 16th book of the *Continens* in the chapter on air. The reason for his saying is this: for there can be an inflammatory pestilential fever in which a copious drink of cold water would be suitable according to general causes. If, therefore, only a little were drunk, it could subsequently be ignited, and it will be ignited so that it sometimes turns into cholera, as Hippocrates says in the second book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*.

<margin>e</margin>
**What if this pestilential fever is wicked.** In which the heat is hidden within; whence the extremities are cold, and because of the retention of vapors the abdomen <note>original: *hypocundria*</note> is distended and it evaporates toward the head. Because of their malice, there is no sleep, but wakefulness and delirium. And because of the great fire, the chest is much elevated, and because of the multitude of vapors to be squeezed out, there is a great constriction of it. It is necessary, therefore, to draw the heat outward with rubbing and the steaming of the extremities. And support the natural heat with suitable heart-strengthening cordials.

¶ **And when.** It should be considered, according to Dinus, that the appetite fails in a pestilential fever because of the stomach's proximity to the heart. Whence the spirit with which the stomach performs its operation is corrupted, and therefore it does not desire food. And so they are "restored to eating," that is, they should be forced to eat, so that those spirits may be rectified and their malice corrected. It should be considered that to restore them with food is to feed them frequently and in small amounts, so that the weak strength can digest the food given in many instances, which it cannot do all at once. If, therefore, there is a prostration of the strength of appetite or not, feeding is praised; yet in most cases, the appetite fails. The cause of the failure is that the spirits of the heart in these people are infected, and are continually infected by the air. And therefore they need, as it were, a continual restoration or renewal of the heart and comfort, which is done through foods contrary to these: namely, cold, acidic vapors. For praiseworthy vapors raised from food, which pass quickly, rectify the spirits by mixing with them and materially increasing them. For many eat, even violently, and though their appetite is destroyed, they are freed from the fever and they vomit if you consider the poisonous aerial contamination of the man. Therefore, it is very necessary to restore him with food—that is, to compel them or to feed them frequently. Otherwise, they give this exposition: let them be restored, namely, so that what is lacking from food is supplied by cordial electuaries <note>medicinal pastes</note>.

...if it be of blood, let phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> be performed; and if there be other humors, let them be evacuated. And in every way, you should cool their houses and rectify the air of the houses themselves, either by cooling or by placing around them fragrant, cold fruits and the ends of cold tree branches, and with liniments and sprinklings taken from cold, fragrant fruits, and from camphor and rose water and sandalwood. And let their house be sprinkled every day several times, and especially with rose water, and with willow and water-lily water; and if there are flowing waters and spray in the house, it will be better. I will speak of the rectification of the air: let camphor troches be administered to them, and cold syrups, and the water of sour milk, and sour milk with the butter removed, and rose water in which good sour juice is dissolved, and vinegar with water again. And very much cold water suddenly given is very helpful; but a little given subsequently perhaps excites the heat. But if the matter is prolonged so that the abdomen distends, and the extremities are cooled, and wakefulness and mental confusion are prolonged, and you see the chest—that what is upon it rises and falls—then it is necessary to administer a regimen that draws the heat outward. And when the appetite falls, let them be restored to eating, for many of those who act manfully upon this and eat by force are delivered and live; and it is necessary to restore them with food, and it is necessary that their foods be from acidic and drying things, and they should be of small quantity. For their foods are again bad. For their large quantity hurts insofar as it adds matter, and they hurt insofar as they are bad. A part of the rectification of the pestilence is for the healthy who are in it; for a part of it is for the healthy and the sick. In that which is for the healthy, the intention is that the air be dried and made of good odor, and its putrefaction be prohibited with whatever thing it may be, and let it be renewed with raw aloeswood, and ambergris, and frankincense, and musk, and sweet costus, and storax, and sandarac, and asafetida <note>original: *asla*</note>, and cloves, and mastic, and terebinth resin <note>original: *albotin*</note>, and laudanum, and honey, and saffron, and *bonki* <note>unclear resin</note>, and cypress, and juniper, and *alufne* <note>possibly a type of absinthe or artemisia</note>, and laurel, and cyperus, and lemongrass <note>original: *lqnanto*</note>, and *fauina*, and sweet flag <note>original: *acoro*</note>, and civet <note>original: *galia*</note>, and bitter almonds, and asarabacca <note>original: *allaro*</note>. And sometimes compounds are made from these. And let the house be sprinkled with vinegar and asafetida. But for the healthy and again those with fever and the sick, there is fumigation with sandalwood and camphor and pomegranate peels and myrtle and apples and quinces and ebony and *afsegi* <note>vitriol or similar mineral</note> and tamarisk and redcurrants, and in every way let the fumigation be multiplied.

### On Preservation from Pestilence. ###
### Chapter V. ###

<margin>a</margin>
It is necessary that superfluous humors be extracted from the body; and its regimen should be inclined toward drying in every way and by the reduction of food, except through exercise. For it is necessary that neither baths nor travel be administered, nor should thirst be tolerated; and let the air be rectified with those things we said, and let the food decline toward acidic things, and let it be reduced. And let the meat that is administered be boiled in acidic liquids, and let it be taken with *albeluen* and *alcaris* and *almosos* <note>Arabic-derived terms for specific stews or preserves</note> made with vinegar and without vinegar, with sumac and verjuice, and lemon water and pomegranate water. And those things preserved in vinegar are helpful, and specifically capers preserved in vinegar. And *algeleniabin* <note>a conserve of roses or honey</note> is among those things which benefit and prohibit putrefaction from them. And...

<margin>§</margin>
**For their foods.** First, their foods can be explained as: the foods that are found then are bad, that is, they are infected even by the corruption of the air. Therefore, their large quantity hurts, that is, a large amount of them hurts, insofar as there is an addition, namely, in bad matter. Therefore, let a little of them be given. And they hurt insofar as they are bad, that is, of bad quality, because they are corrupted by the air. And therefore let them be made acidic. Here, therefore, Avicenna proves that a large quantity of food should not be given, but they should be fed frequently. For acidic, cold foods benefit. In the second way, it can be explained: "their foods," that is, the foods which they use in time of health, etc. And Avicenna proves that cold, acidic foods should be given to them, and not in large quantity. Because if these were not given, those would be given which they used in time of health, namely, in large quantity and not acidic but fatty and seasoned, as is the common custom of men. But it is manifest that to give in a large quantity is bad, because it adds to the matter; and to give in the accustomed quality is bad, because such foods are bad in quality, since they do not rectify the malice. Therefore, it is necessary that they be of small quantity and that they be acidic.

<margin>b</margin>
**Rectification.** Here he rectifies the pestilential air, as mentioned before and after. And he places the rectification made for the healthy with hot and cold things, such as vinegar. However, in the bodies of the healthy, we use hot things more safely for the rectification of pestilence than in those with fever. "With whatever thing," namely, it must be said: or with whatever thing, hot or cold. But hot things are safer in the healthy. **Sandarac**, that is, some explain it as varnish or *bonka*, i.e., asphodel. However, in the second Canon, it is held to be given, as it is a thing that has not reached us. **Alufne**, you have the chapter in the second Canon; it is known. "With vinegar and asafetida," namely, separately or in a composition of them. Moreover, vinegar in a pestilence strengthens everyone; for although a certain vinegar arises from putrefaction, yet by its coldness and dryness with a subtle substance, it resists putrefaction in a wonderful way.

<margin>c</margin>
**For the healthy etc.** [and] those sick with other illnesses, although they might not be fevers, but are putrid ulcers and pustules. Or even the "sick," that is, those with fever, for which "the sick" is a superfluous term. For it is clear that these things are cold, which are beneficial for fevers. **Alkekengi** <note>Winter cherry</note> is known to be a species of nightshade. Another text has *afsegi* and it is not found what it is, etc.

**It is necessary that [they] be extracted.** Thus, namely, bodies are preserved, first regarding the difference of fevers. "Where exercise" <note>original: *ubi exercitio*</note>, that is, do not dry the humors with exercise. For strong exercise which dries the humors causes inflammation and necessitates the attraction of much air. And this is very harmful when the air is corrupted. And therefore he says, "it is necessary that it not be administered," namely, exercise...

# Fourth Treatise

...a drying agent for excess moisture. And this was the precept of Isaac <note>likely Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note>, as it appears in the book *The Containment*, in the chapter on air: for he says that a bath should not be administered, or at least very rarely. Nor should one indulge in much drink, which causes inflammation. The people of our region, however, do not believe they can escape the pestilence unless they drink much wine. I believe, however, that in a time of pestilence, drink should be moderate and suitable for them—specifically for those accustomed to it, as the people of our region are. For habit and the inability to tolerate the absence of wine make it necessary, not only in a suitable quantity, but even in an abundant quantity. For they pass...

<margin>
*Alcuen*, *aleatum*, etc., are methods of preparing food, just as we would say "folded" or "gelatinous." *Algeniabin*, that is, sugar of roses or honey of roses, taken before the fever. The medicine he proposes was that of Rufus <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a Greek physician of the 1st century AD</note>. And it is written in this proportion: Take 2 parts aloes, 1 part each of myrrh and saffron; let them be ground. Let a little of it be taken with one ounce of fragrant wine. Rufus says: "I have never seen anyone drinking this medicine who was not delivered and preserved from the epidemic." And no medicine was ever found to be its equal, as stated in the 17th book of *The Containment*, in the chapter on air. On this chapter, however, we have debated other matters—whether a specifically pestilential fever can be found, and whether a pestilential "hectic" fever is possible—which we will omit for now.
</margin>

<margin>
Among those things by which an escape from the disease is achieved is the administration of theriac <note>an ancient "universal" herbal jam used as an antidote</note> and mithridate <note>a complex semi-mythical herbal remedy</note> before the fever, along with the rest of the royal regimen. And regarding the medicine made from aloe, saffron, and myrrh: let about 1 drachm <note>original: ʒ. j.</note> be taken every day, as it is helpful.
</margin>

### On Smallpox. Chapter 6

Sometimes there occurs in the blood a "boiling" <note>original: *ebullitio*; the text views the disease as a process of fermentation or bubbling up of impurities</note> following the path of a certain putrefaction of the kind of boiling that happens to juices; and such accidents happen through them internally so that their parts are distinguished from one another. And of this, the cause is a somewhat natural thing making the blood boil, whereby that which is mixed into it is putrefied by it.

<margin>a</margin>
Sometimes it occurs—it is called among us *mascalozzi*, and by some *reuuelboni*. *Adozbiim* <note>possibly a corruption of an Arabic term</note> is called among us *rosaria* <note>meaning "the rose-like disease," a common name for rashes</note>. He determines these things after the discussion on pestilential fevers because they are of the same nature as them and follow closely upon the disposition of the air. First, he determines the mode of generation of smallpox; second, the differences and signs; third, the regimen. The first part is in two: first, he determines smallpox, although it can also be applied to measles; second, he specifically determines measles, where he says: "Know that measles..." The first is in two parts: first, the mode of generation and causes; second, the signs. The first part: first, he proposes the mode of generation of smallpox; second, the causes and types. First: first, he previews the mode of generation; second, he explains it. He says first that sometimes a boiling occurs in the blood following the path of putrefaction, which boiling is of the kind that happens to juices. When that boiling of the blood occurs, such accidents happen, namely smallpox, where its parts—the blood and the juices—are distinguished from each other, i.e., separated. Consider first that no author has been found who speaks so deeply and subtly about the generation of smallpox and measles as Avicenna, though Avenzoar, Isaac, Rhazes, and Albucasis preceded him. What we have from other famous authors is nothing compared to how deeply he explores this. Consider second that although the heading is "On Smallpox," it should be understood to include measles, as they share the same generation through that boiling; however, the blood in smallpox is of greater quantity and humidity, so the boiling is greater. Consider third that Avicenna, wishing to investigate the generation of smallpox and measles, did so by way of "boiling." In every generation of these diseases, some boiling occurs in the blood, and the sign of this is the fever that follows. Secondly, most smallpox and measles occur as a way of separating and purifying the blood. For most of them come because of an infection from the womb, but such purification and rectification cannot happen without a strong movement in the blood, just as is seen in grape juice <term>must|unfermented grape juice</term> when it is purified and becomes wine. Therefore Avenzoar says at the end of his third book: smallpox and measles grow with a very impetuous and malignant fever. Just as you see that those who extract butter from milk do so only with great and strong labor and laborious motion, so it is believed that in the motion and expulsion of smallpox and measles, the same must occur. Consider fourth that this text can be explained in two ways. There are two kinds of boiling: one by which the thing boiling is purified, like the boiling of grape juice to make wine. The other by which the boiling thing is corrupted and putrefied, like a melancholic effect, where it becomes vinegar and the blood boils through decay. Avicenna understood both these boilings in this chapter. It can be said that what Avicenna says here is a general discourse on these boilings; by either boiling, the blood can bubble up. And therefore he said, "sometimes a boiling occurs." Similarly in either case, there is boiling or putrefaction. For in the boiling that purifies, although it is not strictly a putrefaction of the juice or blood being perfected, there is a putrefaction of the part that is separated as a superfluity—for example, the dregs and foam of wine. In that boiling, they certainly putrefy. That boiling is a putrefaction, though it varies by degree. When he said "following the path of putrefaction," he meant that whether the blood boils by a perfecting boiling or a corrupting boiling, smallpox and measles can occur. And he said "such accidents" happen because of it, i.e., the boiling. And because in every boiling some separation of parts occurs: in the perfecting boiling, there is a separation of good from bad; in the corrupting boiling, a separation of the liquid from the dry. Thus the end result of putrefaction is "turning to ash." And so he said below: "so that their parts are separated from one another." I say secondly that this discourse can specifically refer to the "perfecting" boiling. For the event of smallpox is usually from such a perfecting boiling. Such a boiling is not entirely a process of decay, for a heat that is entirely decaying is purely destructive. But it is "putrefactive" in that such heat has something foreign in it; hence it is feverish. Third, because such boiling...

<column-break/>

...is directed toward the perfection of the superfluous parts, through which separation the blood is purified and the good part remains. And so he said, "following the path of a certain putrefaction," and did not say "according to putrefaction." For that boiling follows the path of putrefaction in the blood; just as the blood that remains is purified like wine because of the boiling of the grape juice. It inflames in this boiling, yet it was not corrupted. But if that boiling and heating had proceeded excessively, it could have corrupted the good blood, just as if boiling grape juice were to happen in a way that it did not remain good wine but was corrupted. Similarly, that boiling does not lead directly to the putrefaction of the wine's essence, but because the separated superfluous parts are left behind by the governance of natural heat—not being suitable for the body—they are taken over by putrefactive heat. Therefore Avicenna said well when he said "following the path of a certain putrefaction," etc. What he adds below, "so that the parts..." etc., shows he is speaking of this boiling, because through it, the good parts are properly distinguished from the bad.

<margin>b</margin>
"And of this..." If the previous discourse was common to both boilings, we will say that here he clearly distinguishes them. First, the boiling that separates and purifies. Second, the one that is corruptive. If, however, the previous discourse was only about the purifying boiling, we will say: first, he explains that one; second, he explains the other boiling which is not purifying.

...from the remains of its menstrual nourishment, which is from pregnancy; or it is generated in it after that from drossy and bad foods that "rectify" <note>meaning to process or change state</note> its substance and make it boil until it becomes a purified substance, stronger than the first and more apparent, like that which nature effects in the juice of grapes: so that it purifies it by making wine of a similar substance, once the airy foam and the earthy dregs have already putrefied. And of this, the cause is a thing arriving from the outside, making the hidden things boil, which mixes the humors with the blood in a mixture that is in a state of boiling and standing under...

<margin>
He says first that "of this," i.e., of this boiling whose cause is, etc. Consider that wishing to make this boiling of the blood and juices known, he said its cause is a "natural thing." It is doubted, therefore, what kind of heat it is: the heat that makes the blood boil with a separating boiling—like the boiling of grape juice—is called "quasi-natural." Secondly, it is doubted whether this boiling is a species of digestion. And we will say that this is known from the fourth book on *Simple Medicine*, or from the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. For this, take these principles: juices having a middle maturation or incomplete digestion of watery moisture will boil and be perfected in this cooking. Just as the heat that perfects those fruits is twofold—its own internal heat and solar heat, as understood by Aristotle—so that heat saved in the juice expressed from fruits makes those juices boil, bringing the completion of maturation. And just as the digestion of fruits is called *pepansis* <note>Greek for ripening/digestion</note>, so the digestion of the juice of those fruits can be reduced to the same *pepansis*, though this requires speculation. This heat, by which juices boil, since it is their complexion, is called "natural" both intrinsically and extrinsically; or "unnatural" because of the surrounding heat that aids in this, or because of a burning or inflammation added in a degree beyond that which is in the perfected juice. For perfected wine does not actually hold that degree of heat it had when the boiling occurred. Similarly, we imagined that the heat which makes the blood boil with a purifying boiling is called both natural and unnatural in these ways. And so he said "quasi-innatural."
</margin>

<margin>c</margin>
"Making it boil." Secondly, he touches upon the act or action by which the agent induces the effect when he says "making it boil." For the aforementioned heat acts toward the maturation of crude or incomplete watery moisture, whether it be blood or grape juice; and in this action, a conversion of some watery parts into vapors occurs, which, penetrating through the body of the juice, rise to the top; and this is called boiling. Thirdly, he touches upon the effect of this agent and action. First, he touches upon the effect primarily intended when he says "making the natural malice of the blood." For the heat of boiling in grape juice better mixes certain dry earthy parts with the watery moisture, and moist parts with the dry. And in this, the completion of maturation occurs; and some superfluous watery parts evaporate or are separated, and thus dregs remain—therefore, good wine remains. Also, good blood.

<margin>d</margin>
"Whereby it is putrefied." He touches upon the secondary and accidental effect when he says "and that which is mixed in it is putrefied by it," i.e., the parts that were mixed are now separated by the boiling and they putrefy, which is manifest in the superfluous parts separated from the blood, as we said above.

<margin>e</margin>
"Of those things that are thinned." Fourthly, he touches upon the matter in which the boiling occurs, which is blood that can be purified through boiling; the matter of this boiling is twofold. One is from the mother's womb. and this is what he says: "And of... etc.," i.e., that same boiling occurs in the remains of nourishment or menstrual fluids, i.e., in the blood left behind in the fetus from the menses of women during pregnancy—the menses collected in the matrix at the time of impregnation. And the smallpox that occurs in the boiling of this blood accompanies every human being, and that infection accompanies every man, although there is great diversity in this, as will be said later. Other blood suitable for boiling and purification through boiling is gathered from bad food, such as from the excessive and unusual use of milk—for example, camel's milk, as will be said. For it is not unfitting that there be generated in us some blood similar to the menstrual blood of women, having thick drossy parts and bad, crude watery parts; whence by boiling or purification, the smallpox that occurs from this blood happens to certain people, and according to this, someone can have smallpox twice. He said, however, "of those things that rectify," i.e., thin, and make it soft and crude or fluid. Below, Avicenna uses this word in the second chapter, and in the third chapter when he says "Thinned, it is composed." And in the third book, fourth fen, treatise on coughing up blood, when he says that which is spat out from a vein is "thinner." Avicenna says this because not just any blood is suitable for purifying boiling, but only that which is drossy and very watery and fluid; otherwise, it would not boil. And so he says "and they make it boil."

<margin>f</margin>
"Until." Here he repeats for clarity and states the end goal intended in this boiling. For through boiling, it becomes a "rectified substance," i.e., purified, with the drossy and watery superfluity excluded. "Stronger," i.e., in its mixture; as in wine, a stronger composition of watery moisture with dry earth is made. "More apparent," because previously the wine was hidden in the grape juice and did not appear. And let it be understood so regarding the blood. And this is what Avicenna says, seeming to understand that grape juice and completed wine do not differ in species, but differ in being complete or incomplete; and wine is, as it were, "hidden" in the grape juice. And we believe this to be true. However, there is a question here that belongs to the study of nature. Avicenna explains his words with an example, wanting to show that just as there is boiling in grape juice, so there is sometimes boiling in the blood in the stated manner. Consider that we have imagined the vessel like the human body, and the wine made of similar good substance, which was previously deformed by dross and water. And we imagined that the vessel does not need the dregs or the foam—indeed, it hates them and does not require them. Then we have imagined that once the separation is made, the foam putrefied, etc.

# Book IV

...always happens in fact that the froth of one putrefies in spring: and even then we do not care to discuss the dregs from here: but by applying it to the blood, a similar boiling appears: and the parts that are separated from the blood putrefy. And regarding this, the same author <note>Avicenna</note> declares another boiling of the blood, in which **smallpox** <note>original: "variole"</note> occurs, and he says: regarding this—that is, regarding this boiling and what its cause might be. It must be considered that Avicenna touches upon this knowledge of the "evil of boiling." He touches upon the primary acting cause when he says that its cause is an external arrival—that is, an acting cause and an external heat which comes from the outside. This is a rotting corruption and heat that spoils the blood, or a heat proceeding in any way that is putrid, yet causing a boiling: just as in a **continuous fever** <note>original: "sinocha"</note> without putrefaction. 

It is doubted whether, if that heat is putrid, it can therefore be called internal: because putrid heat made internally is [actually] external, as understood in the *Meteorology* <note>original: "metthauroz"; referring to Aristotle’s work on natural phenomena</note>. It should be said that the boiling heat which corrupts the liquid might be putrid; not that it is internal [in origin], but it is the efficient cause: just as the heat that makes **must** <note>unfermented grape juice</note> boil. This can be called "internal" with respect to the arriving heat, as declared in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. 

Secondly, he touches upon the action which causes the boiling, and this is well known. Thirdly, he touches upon the matter when he says "hidden"—that is, the hidden humors within us. It must be considered, therefore, that the blood in us [exists] up to the point of a perfecting aptitude: and he does not call this "hidden"; rather, it is manifest to them: because it will necessarily cause boiling if the blood was contracted from the womb, or from the use of foods that generate blood similar to it, which desires to boil and be rectified <note>purified or corrected</note>: although in this there can be much diversity. Some blood is not fit for this boiling: either it is good of itself and cannot be rectified by any boiling, nor does it need it. And that blood is "hidden" in us: since it never boils of itself except through external acting causes, such as the heat of the sun or other heat. It can, however, be prepared for this due to great age, so that some quality or quantity will not necessarily make it boil. 

Whatever the case, he explains "hidden" as the humors contained within us. This can also be explained another way: that the external arriving cause is hidden, or some hidden disposition or some wicked pestilential constitution, the cause of which is hidden, as Avicenna says above. And from this pestilential disposition of the air, it often happens that smallpox is multiplied. And we have seen this in a wicked pestilence... and it is called the third cause of **smallpox** and **measles** <note>original: "variol' variole et blage. i. morbilli"</note>. They are of the disease which he says [occurs] mostly: they are moved by the corruption of the air brought on by carcasses, etc., which mixes the humors. 

Fourthly, he touches upon the effect of this boiling: that it mixes the humors with the blood. This boiling, therefore, of which he spoke before, separates and leaves the blood rectified; but this [other boiling] mixes it and in the end leaves the blood scorched and corrupted. But it is doubted in what way this boiling mixes things. It must be said that in the act of boiling, the blood becomes agitated; and those humors that are with it in this agitation are mixed with it. And you might say this can likewise happen in a "perfecting" boiling, which does not release [the blood] from agitation and mixing. It must be said that this is true: yet the end is the division of the complete and good blood, and it is named from that. But because in a "bad" boiling the completion of the blood does not follow, but only mixing and finally corruption occurs, it is just like mixing itself through boiling. 

It is doubted again: since this bad boiling ends in the boiling and corruption of the blood, why does he not say that it corrupts it? It should be said first that he gave this to be understood, or subtly [suggested] that blood boiling with a corruptive boiling does not wait until it is finally corrupted before it produces smallpox. Instead, it can be expelled before this; indeed, this happens more because it is expelled before it is fully corrupted. And he identified such boiling through mixing; but in "separative" boiling, it must follow the end, and some part of the blood must be purified and completed—though it is not considered unfitting that some part of that boiling blood can be pushed out and cause smallpox before it is finished. For if it had remained, it would have been completed; but since this boiling happens to all the blood, a part necessarily remains which is rectified. And this is the end even in the order of the human body, since this heat causing the boiling is, as it were, natural. 

**And of standing under the sun.** Fifthly, he touches upon the example of external causes inflaming and causing this boiling. One cause is standing under the sun. For if a man exposes himself to a strong sun, the blood boils; and such boiling is not perfecting but corrupting and mixing. A second cause is a spring that is changed in its qualities, such as when it becomes very hot and humid, changed in its order—namely, in relation to winter, because a hot and humid winter preceded it; or in its parts, so that the beginning of spring is hot and humid and the end is milder. And this is what he means by "it mixes the humors with the blood while the mixing continues"—that is, it goes into a state of boiling. 

Consider Avicenna's subtle way of speaking; for he says the blood "goes mixed into the state of boiling"—that is, when it boils or when it is disposed through boiling. For when it has finished boiling, it would not be mixed but rather separated, like something reduced to ash. Otherwise, we might offer another subtle explanation: that corruptive boiling is similar to perfecting or separative boiling. For even in perfecting boiling, a greater mixing appears until the end, when separation begins. Hence, must <note>grape juice</note> boiling from the start appears more turbid than before boiling; and therefore I said "going into the state and likeness of boiling." He likens this [bad] boiling to that [good] one. 

"Going and mixed in disposition"—that is, in the likeness of standing under the sun. For just as it happens when blood boils under the sun, he makes a distinction between this boiling (which comes from an external cause like external heat) and that which comes from internal heat, because the latter finishes its action for the good. It should be considered, however, that it is not impossible for these two boilings to concur at once: for example, a child who is ready for smallpox from the residue of **menstrual nourishment**, and a pestilential air occurs making a boiling similar to that which happens from standing under the sun; this child will incur smallpox. Whichever cause predominates in corrupting or separating and perfecting, the judgment of the victory of the disposition will be given to it. 

We have spoken enough about the action of contrary agents in the generalities, in the question concerning the times of diseases. But concerning what has been said, it is first doubted whether smallpox and measles can be formed from the residue of menstrual matter. It seems first that they cannot: because an infant in the womb is not nourished by the menses, nor generated from them, but rather from the best blood of the woman, as **Avicenzor** <note>likely Avenzoar, the 12th-century physician</note> testifies at the end, and we believe this was the intention of Galen in the first book on sperm, chapter 8. Furthermore, we see this smallpox is sometimes delayed for seven or fifteen years or more. But it seems impossible that blood taken from the womb could remain until that time. Also, menstrual blood passes into the limbs of the child, and the limbs do not boil; therefore, no boiling will occur from that residue. Furthermore, ask why it does not boil immediately when the infant is outside the womb, but is delayed until the time of boiling and rectification of the blood. If it boils now and did not boil for many years prior, ask in what state it was before and what new state it has now acquired. 

It is doubted secondly whether this smallpox is made from all the blood boiling, or from the watery and airy parts, or from the dregs and grainy parts that are separated. It seems it is from all the blood: because all authors posit that smallpox is made from bloody matter. Whence Avicenna says: "The cause in smallpox is a bloody fullness," etc.

<column-break/>

...therefore it could be expelled bit by bit to the skin, and make small pustules <note>original: "apostēmata"</note> around it and under it, and these will be smallpox. Furthermore, if boiling were required, it would be most significant in the generation of smallpox which occurs when "bad" blood is rectified—which was the remnant of menstrual nourishment. This boiling is not required to rectify the blood. For that rectification is the separation of watery and earthy parts that make it unclean. This sort of separation can happen without boiling—namely, through the action of the attractive, retentive, and repulsive powers <note>the four "natural virtues" of medieval medicine</note>, just as melancholy, bile, and wateriness are separated from the blood. 

To the contrary are Avicenna and **Rasis** <note>Rhazes</note> in the 18th book of *The Continent*, in the chapter on smallpox, and other authors. To the first doubt, it should be said that from the residue of menstrual nourishment, smallpox and measles are formed for the most part—that is, in most cases, their arrival is from that cause. The reason is: because we find that this effect cannot be traced back to anything except that cause. For it is known by the senses that almost no human can be found who escapes this suffering, though it varies in age and manner. It is known to most—indeed, almost all—that few escape without becoming "menstrual" in the first age, happening up to the 5th, 6th, or 7th year. Therefore, some common cause exists for them. It does not seem to be shared except in the case of using milk, and that is not the cause, because human milk is suitable for many. Therefore, the cause is from the womb—namely, the menstrual nourishment that is continuously administered. 

These accidents, therefore, arise from the menses. This is the way of it: menstrual blood, which is expelled from month to month, is a certain superfluous, watery blood, not well-matured. And this is apt to boil. If, therefore, this infant is nourished [by it], then it stays in the veins and begins [to affect] the blood generated in the child outside the womb, making it like itself. Similarly, if the limbs of the child are made or increased from that humor or menses, it disposes the blood that is continuously generated in the child to be watery, raw, and apt for boiling. 

Regarding how this previously mentioned menstrual blood is expelled, I say that it does not become the nourishment of the fetus, nor the matter of its nourishment, nor its growth, nor its generation, as Avicenzor rightly says and as we declared in the third chapter. And then we shall say that this blood, which is retained during the time of pregnancy, infects the fetus and its limbs with its quality. Whence the blood becomes watery and raw and in need of boiling so that it may be rectified—or it becomes a boiling by which it is rectified, just like must. 

And this appears as the solution to the first argument: it is not necessary that the fetus be nourished from the menses for this, so that its blood is disposed and affected by the menses in such a way that it boils later. Rather, the qualitative infection alone suffices. Avicenzor gives a beautiful example: for we see that vessels, through long soaking and infusion of liquid things placed in them, receive an infection and soaking from the ferment even after a long time. If it continues there for a long time, then after much washing, if you place unleavened dough there, it will ferment without any [new] ferment being added—which would not happen in a new vessel. 

To the second doubt, it should be said that no doubt in medicine appears to me for which I do not believe the authors have said something, except this doubt—namely, for how long a time a humor can remain in the body, whether it be a natural moisture or one contrary to nature. We find in the book on chemistry and "chao-chemistry" <note>likely alchemy or humoral chemistry</note> that a bad regimen practiced in youth appears in old age: and this can be through the remaining of the quality without the remaining of the same humor. We find also that aged bile <note>cholera</note> can be found in early old age, as understood from **Galen** in his commentary on the *Aphorisms*, part three. Beyond this age, Avicenna says in the chapter on signs... though it does not appear how long the bile found in early old age lasted from the end of youth. For the extremes of these ages are continuous, and no probable way appears to me by which the duration of a humor's stay in the human body can be well understood in its breadth. But I believe either this is a knowable thing not yet known, or it is not knowable at all, just as irrational proportions are not knowable, as appears in the third commentary of the fifth book of **Euclid**. 

To the argument, it should be said that it is not necessary for that menstrual blood which passed into the fetus, or that blood of the fetus which was in contact with the menses, to remain with its physical body until the arrival of smallpox; rather, it suffices that the infection remains successively. Just as if someone conceives on the first day a woman begins to menstruate, they will become a leper in the 7th year. If conceived on the second day, they will become a leper in the 14th year or up to 15. If conceived on the third day, they will become a leper from the 26th to the 27th year. And if on the fourth day of menstruation, they will become a leper from the 36th year up to 48, as **Azarauius** <note>Albucasis</note> says in the chapter on leprosy. And yet one must not imagine that the physical body of the menses remains for all that time. Rather, the infection remains, which induces that effect at such a time. 

But concerning the aforesaid, it is doubted: if the raw, bad menstrual blood infects the child, whence comes the boiling of that blood? When the menses of a woman are retained, they do not go to the womb but are scattered through the woman's veins. Why then does it not boil and cause smallpox in women? For we ought to see women who do not menstruate suffering from smallpox. It should be said that when a woman’s menses do not flow to the womb—for example, because of a blockage of the uterine veins—then, being scattered through the body, they are corrupted and putrefy; nor does nature suffice for it to boil and be rectified. 

But to one considering this subtly, this does not suffice. It seems, therefore, that the blood which is apt for boiling and rectification is not the menses itself, even if it passed in its form into the fetus's veins; but it is some blood produced by the limbs. That is, in the child's age, the blood is qualitatively infected by the menses, and this blood stays in the child's veins; for those veins and the flesh of the child and all the limbs are infected with that infection. And when all these things are joined, then the blood becomes apt for boiling, especially when it happens from the nature of certain foods that blood is made similar to this. 

Secondly, it is doubted how the menstrual infection which is the cause of leprosy differs from the menstrual infection which is the cause of smallpox and measles. 

<margin>

</margin>

For you will see some children with smallpox who look as if they have leprosy: and it appears that the infection by which smallpox is made is not so wicked and is rectifiable through boiling. And yet, in what appears of the state of the conceiving woman, there is no difference more subtle than this: namely, that a leper is conceived from the womb during the actual act of menstruation; but from a conception outside the time of menstruation comes the infection by which smallpox and measles are made. 

This doubt I leave to others to discuss. For here I would be too long-winded, as I would need to say many and difficult things about leprosy. I also leave aside at what time a conceived fetus is most infected for the generation of smallpox—whether it is conceived immediately after the departure of the menses, or before their arrival, or at a time equally distant from both extremes. And it is imaginable that a fetus is better disposed and suffers less from smallpox later if it is conceived some days after the menstrual purgation, so that the hollows of the womb and its parts are clean, and the blood of the woman's veins is pure, and nothing sensible has yet re-aggregated for any future menstruation. It must be said there is no doubt that the limbs of the child are infected with the quality of the menstrual blood: and that the successive remnants of this infection are perhaps rooted through the successive remnants of these qualities in the limbs. Therefore, although the limbs do not boil, nevertheless, through the boiling in the blood, they themselves are also rectified <note>In medieval medicine, "rectification" refers to the purification or balancing of a substance, like refining a liquid.</note>: and the hidden [infection] ceases within them: and the purified blood improves the limbs: and the limbs, having been made good, improve the blood: and if this happens, it is not possible for a person to suffer from smallpox more than once from this infection.

He solves the final argument of the first question. **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Auenzoar"; a famous 12th-century Andalusian physician</note> says: that after the infant is outside the womb, the natural heat in him is aided: it is increased and strengthens nature, and it strives to digest and refine the said bad and harmful humor and expel it to the outside. **Isaac** <note>original: "Isaac"; likely Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century physician</note> truly seems to suggest in this chapter: that the menstrual matter which is drawn from the womb is that which causes smallpox and measles; that our nature did not move that matter toward this expulsion for as long as [the child had] smallpox, unless that matter is moved of its own accord—namely, through those causes that move the matter—so that Isaac intends that the movement of that matter is not because a [natural] power begins to move it, but rather some causes dispose that matter in such a way that it stimulates nature, and therefore it is moved. These causes, according to Isaac, are some external causes: for example, bad food generating bad humors, or corrupt air. For by these causes that matter becomes malignant and moves: and nature then expells it. And therefore he holds that smallpox occurs in early childhood and adolescence: because people are greedy and consume food immoderately, nor do they beware the influence of the air and other things, whereby from these things that matter is moved, and nature moves against it; but in decrepit old age, smallpox never

occurs; because it is impossible for that matter to remain until a decrepit age without being moved earlier by causes occurring with the change of age, food, and the like. And if it remained, it would have become habituated; this was the opinion of Isaac, though he speaks confusingly, for the brevity of Isaac's words might cause many to err in many things, especially when he says it is impossible that that matter should remain in the body until a decrepit age. It seems, therefore, that he intends this because that matter could remain until some age before decrepitude in which smallpox occurs. And because some smallpox [occurs] up to 15 years and beyond, therefore some matter would endure until that time, having been drawn from the womb. But in truth, Isaac does not mean this. Rather, he means that the matter which is apt for boiling and smallpox—whether it is that which was contracted from the womb, or some matter having an infection according to the likeness of that—cannot be but that it is moved before decrepit age on account of occurring causes. Whence nature expels it, as we have said. And if any matter having that infection should pass through to a decrepit age, and so that in decrepit age infected matter were found with that infection, then on account of the successive remaining of the infection, it would be so habituated to the decrepit man and natural to him that it would not cause smallpox. I myself, however, testify that I have seen smallpox in a sixty-year-old man.

Setting these things aside, I will say what is possible for us according to natural principles: and it is that the blood of the child infected from the womb does not boil unless it has acquired for itself a determined mode and degree of heat, just as **must** <note>original: "mustū"; unfermented grape juice</note> does not boil immediately when it is pressed. But this mode of activating heat is not in the child immediately when he leaves the womb. For the heat lies hidden, suffocated and enclosed and obstructed with much moisture. When, therefore, through the passage of age, such a mode is acquired in the heat—whether the agent of this is an internal cause or an external cause—then the boiling and rectification happen, and smallpox and measles occur. And because the acquisition of this kind of disposition in the heat is diversified according to the diversity of the infants' complexions, and according to the diversity of their regimen and the air, therefore the time of the acquisition of this heat is diversified, and consequently the time of the appearance of smallpox and measles.

From this question, the problem is solved as to why these accidents happen more in boys than in youths, and in males more than in females. Whence in the 18th [book] of the *Continens*, **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; a foundational Persian physician</note> says that this passion happens more to boys and girls in certain places, etc. The cause, however, is because the menstrual infection is more contrary to males than females: and males are hotter. Therefore, a greater boiling occurs in males: because with this, it requires greater boiling and concoction <note>The process of "cooking" or ripening humors in the body.</note> so that the blood may be rectified. To the second question, it must be said that smallpox and measles can be made from those superfluities <note>Waste products or excess humors.</note> that are separated, which superfluities in different men can be very different. They can also be made from that purified blood when it happens to be in superfluous quantity, or when in the boiling it was greatly heated, from which it happens to be expelled; and here we do not proceed [further], because its solution is very well known. To the third doubt, it must be said that it is possible, but very rare, that smallpox and measles occur without a preceding manifest boiling. And this appears from

<margin>d</margin> ¶ *And very often* [it occurs] unless on account of strong causes, such as a very hot and moist complexion whose remnants are still strong in old age, or on account of a strong hot and moist constitution. *After spring at the end of autumn.* The reason is that the moistures in the preceding time being powerful and apt are ready to break out. Not in the constriction of winter, but with some external heat, they boil: especially when a hot and dry summer precedes. If a hot and moist summer had preceded, it would not have delayed until autumn, but the smallpox and measles would have been made in the summer itself. *And it was autumn.* Because despite a preceding hot and dry summer, even if autumn is hot and dry, at the end of autumn, with the heat enclosed within and suddenly vaporizing, a boiling will occur. And I believe that this boiling is conformed to the generation of measles and smallpox. **Rhazes**, however, in the 18th of the *Continens*, wants these smallpox cases to happen at the end of winter. Whence he says thus: *When I see an autumn of intense heat and dryness, expect smallpox without fail in the winter or spring.*

<margin>e</margin> ¶ *And smallpox.* In this cause, the locations are noted. Where it should be known that although nature distances this matter from the principal [organs] as much as it can, as Isaac says, nevertheless not only the skin but also other places can suffer smallpox where that matter boils. But the more powerful nature is, the more the matter is pushed toward the skin, and the smallpox is safer because of the location; but the more the matter remains in the interior parts, the more dangerous they are. Whence it is not impossible to imagine some dying on account of smallpox beginning in the heart, just as sometimes certain abscesses are begun in the heart. Whence, therefore, it is to be wondered if membranes and coverings and nerves can suffer smallpox when the veins vomit the boiling, abscess-forming blood into them.

<margin>f</margin> ¶ *And when they appear.* In this cause, the times are noted when the itching begins. And like millet grains, sharp; then it is the beginning—the "heads of pins," namely in sharpness because they prick. But when they come out, then is the increase. When they are filled with pus, then is the "state" <note>The peak or plateau of a disease.</note>. When they come out and are scabs, etc., then is the declination of various colors. This diversity of colors is caused on account of the diversity of time in drying out. Or it can be imagined that there were different colors on account of the diversity of matters which were separated in the boiling, which did not appear thus when they were hidden under the skin. Now, however, when they are broken, they are more manifest. *And perhaps they are changed to a phlegmon.* For one smallpox [pustule] is bloody: a small phlegmon. When, therefore, much matter is moved at once to one place, a large abscess will be made; and the **essere** <note>term: <term>Essere</term> A medieval term for a skin rash or hives, often associated with choleric humors.</note> is a small pustule made from subtle, vaporous matter raised from choleric blood. When, therefore, the blood boils, it is possible that the thick part is expelled through the windiness, and the subtle choleric part is turned to the skin, and "essere" is made, and it "dubelets"—that is, a breakout which collects pus; namely, one large breakout as we said. It can also be interpreted that "dubelet" is phlegmatic. This is when the smallpox is from matter declining toward the phlegmatic.

<margin>g</margin> ¶ *And very often.* From this diversity, the question is solved as to from what matter smallpox is made. It should be said that it is mostly from the blood that boils. And therefore, for the most part, they have the color of a phlegmon; nevertheless, in this boiling, sometimes bad matters arise through the corruption of the blood; whence something phlegmatic can occur, and they will be white.
</margin>
