<meta>This page continues the medical analysis of smallpox and measles, specifically looking at the "judicial canons"—the diagnostic rules—used by medieval physicians to predict the outcome of the disease based on the color, shape, and timing of the pustules.</meta>

### Book IV

or something burnt and cold, which makes it melancholic, becoming black or violet or green, as is well known. And regarding the green ones: here begin the **judicial canons** <note>These are "rules of judgment" or diagnostic guidelines used by physicians to provide a prognosis.</note> based on color, although for the certainty of judgment, other factors are added. First, he presents the judicial canons based on color; second, based on the manner of emergence; third, by their order; and fourth, by the signs of accidents and other factors. 

In the first part, he presents four canons, though more could be made. The **first canon** is that green pustules, etc., are significant because they indicate poisonous matter. The **second canon** concerns those that are white, meaning those tending toward whiteness.

<margin>a</margin> This signifies either phlegmatic blood or a rapid conversion to pus, which indicates a "healing" or maturation. This is a good sign if they are few in number but large in size, because it shows the matter is not excessive and the body's **expulsive power** <note>The vital force responsible for pushing disease out of the body.</note> is strong. Thus, it expels the matter to one place at once. 

But you might ask: wouldn't it be better if they were few in number and small in size? It must be said that this would be true if we were certain it was not due to the retention of matter caused by a failure of the body's power. Alternatively, "large size" can be interpreted to mean that although they are large, it would be better if they were easily resolved; for then they would heal quickly and without difficult complications. Hence he adds, "what distress," meaning the suffering during the duration of the illness. 

The **third canon** concerns the timing, which should be near the first or second day and not delayed to the seventh or beyond. This counting begins from the day the symptoms start, which will be discussed below—for example, the day the fever, back pain, and nose itching begin. For in some cases, the emergence of the smallpox is greatly delayed, for instance to the 7th day or after the signs appear; this signifies an inability of the vital power to move the matter, whether the cause is in the power itself or in the matter. Consider the **critical days** <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, "critical days" were specific points in an illness (like day 7, 14, or 21) where the patient would either begin to recover or take a turn for the worse.</note> in the eruption; it is better if the smallpox begins on the 7th day than the 6th. 

The **fourth canon** follows these. He means that white pustules in small numbers are preferred. When they are numerous, they are not as good. "Proximity" follows from there being many; though if there are few, it does not necessarily follow that they are distant. Pustules that merge without a break are a bad sign, as they signify a great deal of matter. Those that join to form a single large smallpox bump, appearing oblong or round, are bad, for a round shape 

signifies excessive matter. Likewise, it is bad if the smallpox bumps are "double"—that is, one appearing inside another.

<column-break/>

<margin>h</margin> Smallpox does not occur only on the skin, but also in the depths of the body. Therefore, some matter might be thick and cold, and in its slow movement, it may not putrefy. Thus, the separation—that is, the expulsion—happens without "boiling" <note>Medieval doctors viewed these diseases as a "boiling" or fermentation of the blood.</note>. When it comes time for the body to form an **aposteme** <note>An internal or external swelling or abscess.</note> or smallpox, a putrefaction occurs, which causes a putrid fever. 

It is better, therefore, for a man to have smallpox followed by a putrid fever, because we do not know how it will end if he had a fever that already receded and produced a successful **crisis** <note>The turning point where the body expels the disease.</note> through smallpox. To have a putrid fever and then develop swellings in the armpits or extremities—even if the fever receded—is worse than having swellings followed by a mild "one-day" fever. In the former case, the person is already weakened by the preceding putrid fever and is in a poor state, so such a crisis will not be entirely safe. There are other ways of explaining this which I leave to others.

<margin>d</margin> **And that.** Here are the judicial canons based on signs and accidents. Consider that if the **breath** and the **voice** remain good, it signifies that the matter has been expelled from the principal organs and the "spiritual" parts <note>The heart and lungs.</note> are healthy; therefore, the person is generally safe. "Frequent" [distress] means the loss of power or an internal swelling, for such frequency arises from these two causes. Intense thirst comes from strong inflammation or the enclosure of matter inside. This hastens death because it signifies a failure of the vital power.

<margin>e</margin> **And most.** This is the second canon. Many who die from smallpox die because they are "suffocated" in the throat. Death by "loss of power" happens due to the wickedness of the matter. "Scraping" refers to **dysentery** <note>original: "disinteria"</note>. This happens either because the intestines themselves develop smallpox pustules, or because the matter flows down and excoriates the lining.

<margin>f</margin> **And with.** This is the third canon. It signifies that the poisonous matter is returning to the inside.

<margin>g</margin> **And when.** This is the fourth canon. The cause is that whoever urines blood in an acute fever dies. It signifies an intense blood-repletion and the sharpness of the "boiling"; there is a fear of suffocation from this. When it reaches the point of suffocation, one urines black urine because the [natural] heat has been extinguished. This is confirmed by the loss of vital power; for if the urine were a sign of recovery, the vital power would be strong.

<margin>b</margin> **And the flux.** This is the fifth canon. **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicē."; the famous 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note> notes that these signs appear in both smallpox and measles. They can happen without a loss of power. Due to the "boiling," matter can become green near the digestive organs, and blood can flow from an abundance of heat making the blood watery. If you do not see a loss of vital power, do not judge it as death.

<margin>i</margin> **And many times.** This is the sixth canon. **Averroes** <note>original: "Auer."; the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> says this sickness only happens once. Avicenna says it can happen twice. Others say twice or three times. I say that smallpox from "menstrual infection" <note>The medieval theory that smallpox was caused by a child being "contaminated" by menstrual blood in the womb.</note> only happens once. If it happens twice, it is very strange and means the first boiling did not fully purify the body. But smallpox from "bad food or air" can happen twice, three times, or more, I believe.

<margin>k</margin> **And of the color.** This is the seventh canon. A leaden [bluish-grey] color signifies cold, thick matter with some melancholy. Since nature cannot push it to the extremities, it pushes it to a nearby part.

### On the signs of the appearance of smallpox. Ch. VII.

<margin>l</margin> **Sometimes** the appearance of smallpox is preceded by back pain, itching of the nose, fear in sleep, intense pricking in the limbs, general heaviness, redness in the face and eyes, tears, inflammation, and a "leaping" [pulse] with constriction of breath, hoarseness of voice, thick spit, heaviness of the head, headache, coughing <note>original: "casacaz"</note>, dryness of the mouth, distress, pain in the throat and chest, and trembling of the feet when lying down or turning. And with all this, a concentrated fever.

### On measles. Ch. VIII.

**Sometimes**, etc. These are the signs before they appear on the skin, occurring when the "boiling" begins inside. Back pain occurs because there is a large vein there which is stretched by the abundance and boiling of the blood. Itching of the nose [in children] usually signifies worms. Fear in sleep is caused by vapors moving to the head. Pricking in the limbs occurs as the matter penetrates to form the <term>bothor</term> <note>A term used in translations of Avicenna for pustules or skin eruptions.</note>, that is, the smallpox. General heaviness is due to the abundance of blood. Redness is due to the...

Fen III, Treatise III

...itself by the boiling blood in those parts due to hot vapors. <margin>a</margin> Tears, as well as the fullness and liquefaction of moisture, cause inflammation because the sick person feels themselves being inflated and burned. A multitude [of pustules] occurs in some because of many vapors. A "leap"—that is, a tossing and turning—is also caused by these same vapors. Likewise, there is a constriction of breath and great fullness. For perhaps he means that the sick do not rest in bed because it seems to them that they are suffocating. Hoarseness of the voice arises from injury to the throat and the windpipe of the lung due to many vapors, because it arises from that very boiling. There is a thickness of sputum because the matter <note>The diseased humor or "materia."</note> is liquefied by the heat from the head to the throat. By that same heat, it is thickened and dried. A heaviness of the head occurs from the multitude of blood; for this is one cause of it, as is understood in the first Fen of the third [book] of the Canon <note>Referring to Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*.</note>. A headache results from many vapors stretching the membranes. How headache and heaviness differ is understood in the first Fen of the third [book] of the Canon; for heaviness is a certain movement of pain. *Lasaran* <note>original: "Lasaran", a Latinized Arabic term for palpitations.</note>, that is, a tremor or pulse of the heart, is caused by much boiling blood around the spiritual organs <note>The heart and lungs.</note>. Dryness and so forth are evident. Tremor of the foot. I find all the aforementioned signs in [book] 18 of the *Continens* <note>The *Al-Hawi* or *Continens* by Rhazes.</note> from Al-Zahrawi <note>original: "Azarauio", referring to the surgeon and physician Albucasis.</note> in this chapter; but I find nothing from him regarding the patient lying on their back. I believe that by this "tremor" he understands a tossing and turning, which appears more when a person lies on their back. And therefore he says: "And the decline of the body," that is, with the legs extended. The fever is concluded because it is of the blood.

<margin>a</margin> You should know that measles is essentially a choleric smallpox, and there is no difference between the two in most of their characteristics: except that measles is choleric <note>Associated with yellow bile, which was considered hot and dry.</note>; it is of smaller quantity; it almost does not penetrate the skin; and there is no depth to it that one need worry about, specifically in its beginning. Truly, smallpox in the beginning of its appearance has eminence and height, while measles is smaller than smallpox and occurs more hidden than smallpox. And its first signs of appearance are like the signs of the appearance of smallpox, but tears are more numerous in it, and the distress and inflation are more vehement; however, the back pain is less than in smallpox. In smallpox there is a fullness of blood, stretching the vein positioned over the back, for the generation of smallpox is due to a multitude of corrupt blood, and measles is due to the vehemence of the malice of a small amount of corrupt blood. And measles, for the most part, emerges suddenly, while smallpox comes out little by little.

## On the Signs of its Health <note>Prognosis.</note>. Chapter IX.

<margin>b</margin> These are like the signs of health in smallpox, for that which is of fast progression, appearance, and maturation is safe. But that which is hard, green, or violet is bad; and that which is of slow maturity, with frequent fainting and distress, is pernicious. And that which is hidden again suddenly is bad, causing fainting.

<margin>c</margin> In smallpox, it is necessary that one begins by extracting blood <note>Bloodletting or phlebotomy.</note> sufficiently when the conditions are met; and similarly if it is measles with a fullness of blood. And the time for this is up to the...

...I find that women do not agree: some say smallpox happens first, and others say that by chance measles occurs first; and I could not note an excess in this priority. But when we consider that the matter of measles is sharper and more mobile, it is predicted that measles happens [first], and this is when the matter from within strongly directs this disposition. But when we consider that in the beginning the heat is more moist, and later becomes sharper, smallpox seems to happen first, and later measles. For the movement of these matters follows the disposition of the air much, which happens sometimes to be sharper and sometimes more moist. And therefore, in many children, contrary experiences have been seen, because sometimes smallpox preceded, and sometimes measles.

<margin>a</margin> And the first signs, which are of the first matter: the boiling of both is similar. But the tears in it—namely, in measles—are more numerous because the matter is moved more and is more ready for exit. The habit, however, of the multitude and paucity of tears in all diversity we have already subtly examined in the third book, the 3rd Fen, 1st tractate. The distress, restlessness, and inflammation are more vehement because the matter is hotter and sharper. The back pain and stretching are less because the matter is less. And this is what he adds... [the pain] in smallpox, etc. Therefore it follows from this: that measles emerges suddenly because of the thinness and heat of the matter.

<margin>b</margin> "It is necessary." First he places the cure; second, the preventative regimen for certain members; third, he eradicates the marks <note>Scars or pits left by the disease.</note>... In this first part, he treats two intentions: first, bloodletting; second, the extinguishing and soothing of the "boiling." Regarding bloodletting, it is certain that it is appropriate. "Sufficiently": it is expedient for him even to the point of fainting, as is written in the 18th [book] of the *Continens*. contrary is the saying of Avicenna and Rhazes in their divisions, and all authors concur. He says then that when the signs of smallpox are appearing, but the pustules have not yet begun to emerge, bloodletting is appropriate; because there is much matter in the veins and it is boiling, which bloodletting evacuates and tempers. And similarly one must understand regarding measles: if the signs are felt, because the matter becomes bloody and filling, or mixed with blood. However, when the smallpox begins to appear or come out, bloodletting is not appropriate; because they themselves are a certain kind of crisis <note>A "crisis" in medieval medicine was the turning point where nature expelled the disease.</note>. Bloodletting, however, hinders their exit and makes the matter return inside. Before, therefore, this exit begins, bloodletting is appropriate; for the matter is lessened, and it makes nature powerful over the residue. It must be considered that the time for that bloodletting is up to the fourth day, namely inclusive or exclusive; because commonly they are accustomed to begin to appear by the fourth day, namely on the third or fourth. This time, therefore, Avicenna placed as a general rule; because if they began to appear on the second day, bloodletting would not be appropriate on that day. And similarly, if their appearance were delayed until the seventh, bloodletting could be done after the fourth, as on the fifth or sixth.

Know that when smallpox precedes, bloodletting should not be administered unless a vehemence of fullness and a dominion of the matter are found; then, indeed, bloodletting [is done] in a quantity that draws it out. And the most convenient thing that is administered in this sickness is bloodletting; and if the bloodletting is of the nose vein <note>Likely the angular vein near the nose.</note>, it brings the benefit of a flow of blood from the nostrils and protects the upper parts from the malice of smallpox; it is easy regarding inflammations. And when bloodletting is necessary and he is not bled again completely, a corruption of the extremities is feared for him; and similarly a similar thing is sometimes feared over him for whom "extinguishing" <note>The use of cooling medicines.</note> is constant, and the belly is loosened. And it is necessary that feeding be done first with those things in which there is comfort with "repercussion" <note>Driving the humors back or away from a site.</note> and extinguishing without constriction of nature and thickening of the blood, such as what is made of jujubes with tamarinds and cassia; and with that which is made from immature dates and from prepared lentils and *issidabegi* <note>A type of cooling syrup or preserve.</note> and a vehement softening. The intention in them should be those things by which it is softened, like tamarind. <margin>e</margin> Know that it precedes. It must be considered that this can apply to a case where, even if the smallpox begins to appear, bloodletting can be done: and that is when there is a more rapid vehemence of fullness and dominion of matter. That is, in the exit of the matter, the corruption of the members is feared. Then, indeed, notwithstanding that they begin to appear, bloodletting can be done. Because that bloodletting does not divert the matter which has already exited the veins; for there is such fullness in the veins that, because of this "diminishing" bloodletting, the emptying of the veins does not occur. Whence the matters are chased out; but only the superfluous fullness will be diminished. And this is what he says: "in a quantity that draws out," that is, it lessens the matter, and not "in a quantity that diverts." And another doctor of the veins would say that although it might draw some matter back into the veins, nevertheless this harm would be less than the benefit. To the contrary reason, it must be said that after four days bloodletting can be done if some greater [danger] does not precede, notwithstanding the same sickness. And it is easier on infants, namely bloodletting of the nose; because since bloodletting of the arm cannot be done on them, bloodletting of the nose can be done. Whether, however, bloodletting of the nose can be done without another bloodletting being permitted first—when it is indicated, etc.—we have disputed in the first Fen of the third [book] of the Canon, in the chapter on phrensy. Or it is easy on infants—namely, the malice of smallpox in the parts of the face—and this is because of their tenderness.

...whence we see some are blinded, and some are greatly disfigured.

"And similarly," etc. Because from much "extinguishing" <note>Over-cooling the body.</note> the matters are constricted. Whence the interior parts are corrupted; and therefore he says "similar to that," because just as in that case the exterior parts are corrupted, so in this one the interior parts are corrupted. For it is moved by the matter and becomes malignant; whence, being pushed to the outside, it corrupts the extremities. "And it is necessary [feeding]": that is, let it be given to him by mouth.

He says this because although it is commanded that the members be strengthened by something styptic, I do not want the belly to be bound up by this. "And thickening": that is, and with thickening. "And a vehement softening": that is, with that in which there is vehement softening. Therefore, this whole speech ought to be joined thus: let the feeding be done in the beginning with those foods in which there is comfort with repercussion and with extinguishing and with the thickening of the blood; and with those foods in which there is vehement softening. He says "vehement," however, because since these foods are styptic, let the vehemence of the softening thing repress their stypticity, and the stypticity repress their softening. From this mixture, therefore, the constriction of nature does not happen, as he commands, but rather nature remains soft.

<meta>This page continues the medical discourse on the stages of smallpox and measles, focusing on the critical transition between the initial "boiling" of the blood and the physical eruption of pustules on the skin. It addresses the debate over using cooling remedies and laxatives during these different phases.</meta>

### Book IV

<margin>
That is, the beginning of the preceding symptoms, such as fever and others, which is the "beginning of the boiling" <note>Medieval doctors believed smallpox was caused by the blood "boiling" like fermenting wine to expel impurities.</note>. And there is another beginning: namely, the "beginning of the appearance" of the smallpox, when they just begin to be scattered through the skin and emerge. I say, therefore, that in the beginning of the smallpox—that is, the appearance on the skin—those cooling remedies are not suitable. As Avicenna says, they hinder the exit; thus, the matter rubbed in the parts near the veins, which is ready to be expelled and activated, is instead constricted inside the veins and corrupts the organs. However, in the "beginning of the signs"—that is, the beginning of the boiling—those cooling remedies are suitable. For boiling is either "separative," in which case cooling things do not entirely stop the boiling but moderate it so that the healthy part of the blood is not corrupted by the boiling; or the boiling is "corruptive," in which case they are not suitable. And it appears that milder things can be used to settle the "separative boiling" than those used to settle the boiling of smallpox and measles.
</margin>

On the contrary, all authors agree. It must be said that the beginning of smallpox is twofold: namely, the beginning of the preceding symptoms—that is, the fever and others—which is the "beginning of the boiling." And there is another beginning: namely, the "beginning of the appearance" of the smallpox, when they just begin to be scattered through the skin and emerge. I say, therefore, that in the beginning of the smallpox—that is, the appearance on the skin—those cooling remedies are not suitable. As Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the most influential physician of the Middle Ages.</note> says, they hinder the exit; thus, the matter <note>The diseased humors or "materia."</note> rubbed in the parts near the veins, which is ready to be expelled and activated, is instead constricted inside the veins and corrupts the organs. However, in the beginning of the signs—that is, the beginning of the boiling—those cooling remedies are suitable. For boiling is either separative, and then cooling things do not entirely stop the boiling but moderate it so that the healthy part is not corrupted by the boiling; if, however, the boiling is corruptive, they are not suitable. And it appears that milder things can be used to settle the separative boiling than those used to settle the boiling of smallpox and measles.

<margin>
To the contrary arguments, it must be said: when authors forbid cooling "extinguishing" remedies in the beginning of smallpox, they mean in the beginning of the appearance, not in the beginning of the boiling and the signs. To the second point, it must be said that such "extinguishing" does not entirely take away the boiling but rectifies it if the boiling is separative. Secondly, it is doubted whether a "loosening" medicine <note>A laxative or purgative.</note> is suitable from the beginning. It seems so, because the matter may need to be diminished. On the contrary are all other authors. It must be said that a loosening medicine that acts by "softening" is suitable from the beginning. The reason is that it eases intestinal virulences and cleanses those primary veins. However, in their use, there must be caution, because these "softeners" must also be cooling things that settle the boiling. Likewise, they should not be given in large quantities for two reasons. First, because generally in those having smallpox, a "flow of the belly" <note>Diarrhea.</note> is feared; hence Avicenna said above that the flow of the belly is part of the smallpox illness and is apt to happen to them. Therefore, pure softeners in large quantities can cause a harmful flow of the belly. Second, because certain softeners have a weak power of evacuating and dissolving, such as "manna," as was mentioned above regarding the treatment of putrid fevers in general. Therefore, through a large dose, it can draw out by dissolving and cause a harmful flow. This is what Avicenna meant: if the body does not respond to tamarinds, let *syracosu* <note>original: "syracosu", likely a variant of "syrup" or "shir-khusht" (a type of manna).</note> be added—that is, a certain manna—with skill and caution, by using a small quantity. I say secondly that a loosening medicine that evacuates by dissolving is not suitable from the beginning. The reason is that the matter is mixed with the blood, and also because there is a fear of excessive flow. In short, in the whole treatment and its observation, you must be suspicious of excessive flow of the belly in this sickness, as seen by our authors. Therefore, when nature responds to itself with softness, do not increase the loosening medicine. And when it does not respond, use it with caution. Hence Avenzoar <note>An influential 12th-century Andalusian physician.</note> held that for the most part, you should not need tamarinds. The solution to the contrary arguments is evident.
</margin>

<margin>a</margin>
# a When therefore.
Here he sets down the treatment: first, when they begin to appear; second, he sets down the medicines suitable in the beginning of the symptoms (at the section "The medicines however"). The first part is in four sections. First, he gives instructions for those things taken internally and lists the medicines. Second, for those things occurring externally. Third, regarding bloodletting. Fourth, he gives certain other special instructions (at the section "And it is necessary that he does not come near"). There is the third (at "And perhaps bloodletting"). There is the fourth (at "And when it happens"). He says first: "When therefore," etc., the sickness—that is, this fever—which precedes the appearance. "The second day": It should be considered that this is given as an example. But therefore he said immediately "and they begin," etc., because if they did not begin to appear, you could still use cooling. "Perhaps": he says well because of hidden dispositions; for it can begin to come out and cooling might help more in one part than it would hurt the boiling—namely, slightly. "Smelled": that is, just as the odor is presented to him, because it aromatizes him with some of these decoctions. Or it is smelled, namely through the nostrils, so that its heating draws the matter outward to the parts of the face, just as a sign because they generate lice in some.

...of vehement benefit in this hour. When therefore the sickness has passed the second day and the smallpox begins to appear, then perhaps cooling will be a cause of error, more so because it retains the superfluity <note>Waste products or excess humors.</note> inside and delays its movement over the principal organs; and perhaps it might not be possible for them to proceed and appear, and restlessness and anguish happen, and perhaps nausea happens. Indeed, it is best to help the superfluities in this disposition with those things that cause boiling and open blockages, such as fennel and celery, and with sugar and their juice or a decoction of the roots and seeds; and perhaps something of saffron may be smelled, and fig water is very good. For figs are of vehement expulsion to the exterior, and that is one of the causes of escaping their harm. And among those things that contribute greatly at this time is to take washed lac <note>original: "lacca", a resinous secretion.</note> 3 drachms, peeled lentils 7 drachms, tragacanth 2 drachms; then let it be cooked with 5 lbs of water until a quarter lb remains; let it be strained and given as a drink. And among those things that are of vehement benefit to make the smallpox appear is to take yellow figs 7 drachms, peeled lentils 3 drachms, lac 3 drachms, tragacanth and fennel seeds 2 drachms each; let them be boiled with 5 lbs of water until nearly a third remains, and let it be strained and given as a drink. For it expels the "oppression" <note>original: "castitatem", here used medically for a feeling of constriction or tightness.</note> from the regions of the heart and prevents [abnormal] pulse of the heart. And it is necessary that no oil at all be applied to him at this hour. And it is necessary that he be governed and kept away from cold air, especially in winter, and let that be done with him which is done with one who is sweating; for cold blocks the pores and makes the matter return backward. And a multitude of drinking of water made with snow and entering a "windy house" <note>A drafty room.</note> are very bad. And perhaps bloodletting is bad because it repels and turns back that which is proceeding, if it is done after two or three days. And when it happens from covering and heating that there is a kind of fainting, or fainting occurs, then a regimen of air that attracts is necessary; and return to the odors of camphor and sandals <note>Sandalwood.</note>. And if there is no excuse, let the body be uncovered to the windy house, or the help is with heating or the cessation of cooling. And when they begin to come out, and relief is not found with their exit, but instead a spreading oppression is found and the tongue leans toward blackness, then beware—

<margin>b</margin>
# b And of those.
These medicines are taken in their own form from Rhazes, book 18 of the *Continens* <note>The *Al-Hawi* or *Comprehensive Book* by the Persian physician Rhazes (c. 865–925).</note>...

<column-break/>

...containing: and from there lac is placed in these medicines to strengthen the liver. "Tragacanth": that is, gum tragacanth, has some cooling property and breaks the sharpness of hot things, as Serapio said; and therefore it is put in this decoction.

<margin>
That is, "And it is necessary," etc. "In this hour": namely, the exit of the smallpox. "Oil," etc., because it closes the pores. "That which is done with a sweating person": that is, just as is done for a man who sweats, for he should be wary of cold air. Hence, if those who sweat are cooled from the outside, they feel nausea—as in Avicenna, second of the Problems, 19th problem. "And a multitude of drinking": namely, in this hour, because in the beginning, before they start to appear, a cold drink of water is allowed, as in book 18 of the *Continens*. "Bloodletting is bad": namely, at this hour, because they are just beginning to appear. "But after two days or three," he says; and here it is explained, because this time varies in different people. Hence, above at the beginning of the chapter, it says that the window for bloodletting is up to the fourth day. He said "perhaps" because of what he said above at the beginning of the chapter where he said, "unless there be found," etc.
</margin>

<margin>c</margin>
# c And it is necessary, etc.
In this hour, namely the exit of the smallpox, oil, etc., because it closes the pores. That which is done with a sweating person—that is, just as is done for a man who sweats, for he should be wary of cold air. Hence, if those who sweat are cooled from the outside, they feel nausea. Do not heat [him]. And it is necessary that you keep those having smallpox and measles away from "plastering of the belly" <note>Applying medicinal pastes/poultices to the stomach.</note>; for in this, there is a fear of sudden constriction of breath and that a bad flow of the belly and mixed blood happens. And in the end of it, it is necessary that nature be preserved; and he should be fed in place of lentils things like lentils "eliriated" <note>Boiled and then drained to remove certain properties.</note> with two boilings and a change of water; and in place of lentils, "almadid" <note>likely a barley-based dish.</note> with tamarinds and cold, acidic lentils, and pomegranate water, sumac, verjuice <note>Sour juice of unripened grapes.</note>, and similar things. "The medicines however" in gross... and infants, preventing it from boiling, which are prescribed in the beginning, are such as "rob ribes" <note>Redcurrant preserve.</note>, and verjuice, and the water of *sfofum* <note>unclear, possibly a fruit.</note> fruits, and wild palm syrup especially, and *altelea* syrup, and syrup of *zumar*. And indeed, wild palm syrup has several descriptions, which we give in the Antidotary; and we will give here a truly marvelous description: and it is that which is made with the water of repeated sour milk, and its power is very vehement.

<margin>d</margin>
# d And when it happens
That is, here he sets down the fourth instruction. "Regimen of air": that is, through cooling. "The house of wind": because the air is windy with the windows open. "And similarly," etc.: let it be done gradually, and not suddenly. "And when": beware not to heat, because it signifies a bad boiling.
</margin>

<margin>e</margin>
# e And it is necessary, etc.
"Plastering of the belly": namely, with cooling things or things that block the pores; [beware] of this in the hour of the exit to the exterior, because it hinders and constricts the matter. It should be considered that physicians often go against this instruction. For in children, worms are associated with smallpox and measles, or they are feared; and therefore one plasters the belly.
</margin>

<margin>f</margin>
# f And in the end.
It should be considered that "in the end"—that is, in the progress or in the decline—dysentery and bad flows are feared in these cases because of the weakness of the intestines; hence Albucasis <note>Azarauius.</note> made a principal chapter on this. And Serapio, in the sixth book of his *Practice*, also doubts regarding this flow. And therefore nature should be preserved—namely, so it does not become too "flowy," so to speak, but is reserved. And it is preferred by using "stiptic" <note>Astringent.</note> things that were not loosening before. Therefore, if you previously gave boiled lentils without throwing away the water, give now lentils boiled twice, always throwing away the boiling water, because they will be more astringent. Or even in place of lentils—namely, as they are without the throwing away of the water—feed "alke makic" with tamarinds—that is, with food made from barley flour and lac, with the butter removed, and tamarinds—which food does not loosen the belly as much as lentils with their boiling water, at least when there is no superficial saltiness of the lentils. Feed also in place of lentils, etc., with lentils made acidic.
</margin>

✝ Not with sharp vinegar but with acidic verjuice.
✝ "The medicines however." *Rob ribes*: that is, from wood sorrel. *Wild palm syrup*: that is, of wild palms. And *altelea* syrup: some say this is of pears, others of agrimony, others of the fruit of palms. And syrup of *minar*: some explain it as being from flowers; but *minar* is the bud or sprout of the wild palm, of which it is written in the second book. But wild palm syrup is placed in the Antidotary in the sixth treatise, where it is called syrup of *alcorir*. It should be repeated in acidity. The description of this syrup is noted, and its power is cooling and settling the boiling. And therefore neither sugar nor honey is added...

Fen III, Treatise III

<margin>
This is either used for the comfort of the stomach, or because they add spikenard <note>original: "spicam"</note> to somewhat rectify the coldness of these things. "Upon the root of the gourd" means upon the bottom of the vessel in which this final light decoction is made; or at least in another vessel.
a. And when they emerge. Use gold, because an incision made with gold <note>original: "auro"</note> heals more easily than one made with iron, as Rhazes <note>original: "Az." referring to Abu Bakr al-Razi</note> says in the first part, 34th problem. What he says about salting is well known, but we do not use this. For although salting matures, a maturation has already been made previously. It should be said that by the power of saffron, if anything is not entirely mature, it completes the maturation.
b. And concerning the management of small ones—that is, because they are not completely mature. And "large," etc., because they are very moist. This text is written thus: "Let the patient suffering from smallpox with much moisture have a thin cloth full of millet flour placed over the maturing pustules," etc. And "bad oil," because common oil or any oil at the hour of drying—that is, when we wish to dry—is harmful. Therefore, to clarify this, he said at the end: "And the administration of some oil after drying."
</margin>

...of unripe apricots <note>original: "chrysomilorum"</note> and sour things, and the juice of verjuice, and the juice of currants, and the juice of vine shoots, and the juice of peach roses, and the juice of water lilies, and the juice of violets, each a third part; and the juice of the acidity of citron and the juice of the acidity of bitter orange, each two-thirds of a part; juice of coriander, lettuce, fresh poppy leaves, endive, and purslane, each a quarter part; juice of willow leaves, apple leaves, pear leaves, medlar <note>original: "alzarur"</note> leaves, rose leaves, and shepherd’s rod <note>original: "virge pastoris"</note> leaves, each a quarter part; juice of goatsbeard <note>original: "herbe birci"</note>, dried roses, dried water lily, and the juice of dried barberry <note>original: "biberis"</note>, and the seeds of endive and lettuce; and pomegranate flowers <note>original: "balaustiarum"</note> and water lily, each half of a tenth part; and juice of fresh mint, a sixth part; and juice of fresh barberries, half a part. Let the medicines and juices be gathered and set over the fire; and place in them four parts of lentils, and two parts of hulled barley, and three parts of sumac, and three parts of pomegranate seeds. Let all be cooked over the fire until half of the liquid remains; then let it be strained and rubbed vigorously. And let it be filtered, and take of camphor <note>original: "cafora"</note> for every weight of 300, one weight of gold <note>original: "pondus aure."</note>. And let the camphor be pulverized and put upon the base of the gourd vessel <note>original: "radicem cucurbite"</note> or another vessel, and pour the medicine over it with ease. Then let its head be tied with extreme strength; then place it over coals until it is known to have boiled strongly. Let it be shaken and placed in a glass vessel, and let its head be tightened so that the camphor is not lost, and seal it with clay <note>original: "lutet"</note>. Let its dose be up to three drams. And there are some who put in it spikenard, ginger, fennel seed, anise, cyperus, and pepper in equal parts according to the quantity that seems right.

And when the smallpox pustules emerge fully and the seventh day has passed, and maturation appears in them, then it is necessary that they be ruptured with gold needles. And let the moisture be removed with cotton. Salting <note>washing with a saline solution</note> is necessary; and when you wish to salt, keep the salt away from the large pustules you have erupted from nearby, for that causes pain. Rather, salt those that are beside them, and leave the salt to close the path of their openings until they expel their own salt. Do not salt before the completion of maturation, for that might perhaps cause vehement pain and abscesses. And salting is indeed a necessary thing after they mature, and that is done with salt water in which there is the power of saffron. And if that water is rose water, it is better. And the water in which tamarisk, lentils, and roses are cooked: then salting is the last step, especially if this salting matures and dries, and makes the scabs fall off with speed. And fumigation with tamarisk is very helpful. In winter, the patient should be applied to a fire made from tamarisk wood.

And when the smallpox pustules are of vehement moisture, then it is necessary to

<column-break/>

fumigate with myrtle and its leaves.
And regarding the good management during the maturation of small and large smallpox pustules, the desire to dry them is such that the patient should sleep upon the flour of rice, millet, barley, and beans; it is more beneficial to place this as the filling of the mattress, which should be of thin fabric through which the drying power can penetrate. Cypress leaves are also good for this. "Bad oil" <note>common or unprocessed oil</note> is avoided at this hour because it prevents drying; but when the pustules begin to dry, then it is necessary to smear them with the aforementioned medicines containing saffron. And when ulcers occur from the smallpox, white ointment <note>original: "unguentum album"</note> is helpful, especially mixed with a little camphor and the scrapings of cane roots with rose water, or the scrapings of the veins of the willow tree or the medlar tree. And sometimes an ointment of ceruse <note>lead white</note> and litharge <note>lead oxide</note> is helpful. And when there are crusts in the nose, a wax salve made with pure rose oil, ceruse, and calamine <note>original: "climia"</note> is helpful. The administration of some oil after drying and during ulceration is good; during drying, it makes the scabs fall off with speed, and during ulceration specifically because oil itself is the base for plasters and ointments. Red ointment is indeed good for smallpox ulcers.

# On the observation of the limbs, and their defense from the harm of smallpox and measles. Chapter 11.

<margin>
c. And during ulceration, etc. As if to say, some ointment like the "red ointment" is suitable for an ulcerated smallpox pustule; but oil is the base material of ointments. For red ointment, see Book IV, Fen III, Tractatus 11.
d. Members. First, he enumerates the members that one ought to guard. Second, he perhaps shows the harms that can happen to them. These members are quite tender and soft, and therefore easy to harm, and the harm must be treated. Third, he teaches the method of preserving them from the occurrence of harm. There are five parts here, just as there are five members. For "almuri" of barley, see the second Book of the Canon, the chapter on "muri." These things that Avicenna says here are for remembrance, for you must recur to the third Fen of the third Book of the Canon.
e. But when they appear. Because now it is the beginning of the smallpox. The treatment is like the beginning of ophthalmia, in the beginning of which styptics are taken—not just any, but cold styptics are praised; therefore, he praises rose water with camphor. We have spoken more on this matter in the third Fen of the third Book. The rest of what he says is well known. One must recur to the third book, Fens 9, 5, 4, 6, and 17, etc.
</margin>

<margin>c</margin> Once the crust has formed, because it makes the crust fall off. For the crust is soaked in oil, swells, and falls away.

<margin>d</margin> The limbs that must be guarded from the harm of smallpox are the throat, the eyes, the upper passages of the nostrils, the lungs, and the intestines. These limbs are the ones that perhaps become ulcerated. For perhaps the eye is destroyed, or a white spot <note>original: "albugo"</note> occurs in it. In the throat, suffocation perhaps occurs, or ulcers occur which prevent swallowing into the esophagus <note>original: "meri"</note>; and perhaps they reach the point where there is a pernicious corrosion there. In the upper parts of the nostrils, ulcers perhaps occur which constrict the passages of smell. In the lungs, there perhaps occurs the "rumbling" <note>original: "borthor"</note> of smallpox and measles, a vehement constriction of breath, and perhaps they cause the patient to fall into phthisis <note>original: "pthisim," a wasting disease</note> when they are ulcerated. In the intestines, excoriation perhaps occurs, which is difficult to help. The preservation of the eye is best achieved by applying an eye-salve <note>original: "alcohol"</note> made with *almuri* <note>a salty liquid or brine</note>, coriander water, and rose water in which sumac and camphor have been placed; and especially on the first day, with *almuri* alone. Similarly, let an eye-salve be made with a prepared powder <note>original: "alcohol nutrito"</note> of coriander water and sumac water with camphor placed in it; and the juice of pomegranate pulp is good again in the beginning. <margin>e</margin> When the pustules appear, then making an eye-salve with rose water and camphor is more suitable, and it is said that making an eye-salve with white mustard water <note>original: "napia alba"</note> is good for this. Pistachio oil is among those things used by women in our region after smallpox and the occurrence of harm in the eye...

<meta>This page continues the medical discourse from Book III, specifically transitioning from the treatment of active smallpox pustules to the removal of their scarring and the broader pathological theory of fevers caused by internal and external abscesses. # Book III

->Book<-

**Column 1**

<margin>b</margin> In this indeed: "Thin clay" <note>original: "lutum rarum"</note> is common clay from which vessels are made. "In the hoof of a camel" <note>original: "in ungula cameli"</note>: likewise for a continuous fever, take the hooves of a ram when they are roasted and anoint the place, and certainly the scars will disappear. "Pepper stone" <note>original: "lapis pipis"</note> is not available. *Alkubuzi*, that is, *alduragi* or *aduray*, are the same thing, as it is said of the turtle dove. *Sumera* is a liquid medicinal mixture used for smoothing the face.

<margin>c</margin> When he had known: I have been accustomed to divide this chapter before "the woods" in two ways. First, because Avicenna <note>the 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> first shows the outcome of ephemeral fevers <note>one-day fevers usually caused by heat or emotion</note> from abscesses; second, those of putrid fevers; third, of hectic <note>original: "ethicarum," referring to fevers affecting the solid parts of the body</note> fevers. There the third begins: "And this indeed." In the second way: first he shows which fevers follow external abscesses, and second, internal abscesses. In the first part, according to this division, he argues that external abscesses are mostly followed by an ephemeral fever, and he gives the reason for this. Sometimes a putrid fever can follow because of the size or proximity of the abscess, such as when the abscess is in the armpit or the breast.

<margin>c</margin> **And that they are for the most part.** It must be considered that "for the most part" is explained in two ways. First, the majority of ephemeral fevers—whether they come from heat reaching the heart without putrification—arise from "primitive causes" <note>external triggers like sun exposure or fatigue</note>. It is as if he said that most ephemeral fevers are caused by primitive factors, though they can also arise from external abscesses which do not alter the heart except by simple heating, much like primitive causes like the sun do. Second, he explains that these external abscesses arise from a primitive cause like a blow or similar things, without "corporeal causes" <note>internal imbalances</note> being present. This is because the abscess is not naturally inclined to generate putrification in the body; therefore, a simple heating follows, remaining within the limits of an ephemeral fever and not likely to turn putrid. This is taken from Avicenna's third book of the *Canon*, the third chapter on ophthalmia. He says "mostly" because even some external abscesses causing ephemeral fevers can occur without a primitive cause.

<margin>d</margin> **But when.** Because he had said that fevers following external abscesses are mostly ephemeral, he clarifies that they can sometimes be putrid in essence when the putrification reaches the heart by "fuming" <note>the medieval idea of toxic vapors traveling through the veins</note>. This happens because the abscesses are large or nearby. Perhaps this adverb "perhaps" should not be linked with what he says "happens," but with what he previously stated: namely, "it reaches," etc.

<margin>e</margin> **And mostly indeed.** This text can be explained in two ways like the one above. First, the majority of these—that is, the majority of external abscesses causing putrid fevers—do not occur except from "antecedent causes" <note>internal conditions already present in the body</note> of raw, repletive humors. For when external abscesses occur in bodies filled with bad humors, even without a primitive cause, they are prone to cause putrid fevers because of the tendency of those bodies toward the putrefaction of humors and the enlargement of the abscess. He said "similar to these" because external abscesses caused by antecedent corporeal factors and those caused by primitive causes without antecedents look alike. He spoke of "antecedent corporeal causes" to show that these causes are humors that "sin" <note>meaning they are pathological or imbalanced</note> in quantity or quality. Thus he meant "repletive" regarding the quantity and "raw" regarding the quality. Or he meant "corporeal" as in the complexion <note>the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> and "repletive" as in the humors. This knowledge depends on what we wrote at length in the second section of the first Canon.

<margin>f</margin> **And sometimes they occur.** Namely, external abscesses that cause or are capable of causing putrid fevers and ulcers. For example, from an ulcer or pain in a toe, someone may incur an abscess in the groin. This is because the matter moving toward the foot finds soft flesh in the groin and is retained there. Avicenna said this to show that primitive causes...

## On the Eradication of the Marks of Smallpox. Chapter 12.

<margin>a</margin> In this part we speak at another time when we discuss beautification <note>original: "decoratione"</note>, but now we will say what is more convenient and pertinent. Among those things that eradicate the marks of smallpox are reed roots, *sarcocolla* <note>a herbal resin used to "glue" flesh</note>, melon seed and its dried rinds, washed rice, barley water, egg white, "rare clay" <note>porous clay</note>, or common mud, litharge <note>lead monoxide</note>, *tabarzet* sugar <note>a highly refined white sugar</note>, starch, sweet almonds, and bitter almonds. Of oils: lily oil, pistachio oil, and donkey fat with rose oil and similar things. The water found in a camel's hoof that has been roasted is the ultimate remedy. Of those things which are stronger: sea foam <note>cuttlebone</note>, pepper stone <note>likely pumice</note>, costus, *ammonia* with [unclear], soap with *baurach* <note>borax or soda</note>, burnt old bones, radish seed, dried radish flour, birthwort <note>original: "aristologia"</note>, and lupin. Of foods that rectify a leaden complexion: sweet grains, chickpeas, good wine, the yolks of soft-boiled eggs, chicken broth, and fattened *alcubugi* and *alduragi* <note>likely types of fowl</note>. It is necessary for the patient to bathe frequently. Of composite medicines: take burnt bones, old sheep dung, new shells, starch, melon seeds, washed rice, and parched chickpeas, 50 parts each; and *alben* grains, lupins, costus, and birthwort...

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

...are sent: just as pains move the antecedent causes. Alternatively, it can be explained as: they occur, namely the ephemeral or putrid fevers, etc.

<margin>f</margin> **But the fevers.** First he shows which fevers follow internal abscesses. Second, he notes their diversity. There the second part: "And the more violent." It must be considered that internal abscesses collect much matter, and the veins there are wide; therefore, putrid smoke <note>vapors</note> can travel continuously to the heart, and thus putrid fevers occur. He said "perhaps" because of many contingencies. For Avicenna imagines it is not impossible for a fever following an internal abscess to be ephemeral, such as when it is far from the heart, like near the rectum.

<margin>b</margin> **And the more violent.** He sets out the diversities of these fevers. The first is according to the diversity of the types of abscesses, and this is clear. "And these abscesses" (III) is the second diversity according to the abscessed organs; and he wants you then to refer to the third book. The third diversity is due to the proximity or distance from the heart.

<margin>f</margin> **And the fevers of those in the members.** The fourth diversity is according to the nature of the member's substance, whether it is fleshy, membraneous <note>original: "panniculare"</note>, or nervous.

<margin>f</margin> **It is doubted** because he says that the fever of an abscess of the membranes and similar things (namely, nerves) is weaker. He states the opposite in the first book, second section, in the chapter on the signs of abscesses. It must be said that fevers are called "more violent" in heat; thus the fever of an abscess in a fleshy member is more violent because those abscesses collect more matter, and matter in a fleshy member heats up more, so there is a fever of greater heat in it. In another way, a fever is called "violent" due to certain common symptoms, such as pain, sleeplessness, spasm, and the like; and thus fevers following abscesses of the nerves, membranes, and similar parts are more violent.

<margin>k</margin> **And note those in the vicinity of the arteries.** The fifth diversity is by the nature of the member, whether it is nervous or arterial. Consider that although a fever following an abscess of an arterial member may be more violent because it is near the arteries (as the heart communicates more through the arteries), it can also be for another cause, like proximity. For instance, an abscess in the hollow of the liver causes a more violent fever than an abscess of the spleen, yet the spleen is more "arterial" than the hollow of the liver. This is even more true of the "hump" <note>the convex part</note> of the liver, since no artery comes to the hump, yet the whole part is close to the great artery.

<margin>l</margin> **And not the same.** This is the diversity of these long fevers... [The text here breaks into a recipe]: ...take 5 parts of everything, and 20 parts of dry reed root. Let a paste <note>original: "gummera"</note> be made of them with melon water, or with wild cucumber water, or with barley water, or with bean water. Let the member be smoothed with it, and washed in the morning with a decoction of violets. Another: new shells, old [unclear], reed root, starch, melon seeds, washed rice, costus grains in equal parts; let a paste be made. Also lupin and black chickpea should be smeared with them.

## On Fevers [from Abscesses]. Chapter 13.

<margin>i</margin> Since he had known the dispositions of fevers that follow apparent <note>external</note> abscesses—which are for the most part said to be of the genus of ephemeral fevers since these abscesses for the most part do not reach the heart except by their heating, without their putrefaction, and for the most part these are from primitive causes—when, however, their putrefaction reaches the heart due to their size or proximity, it becomes a fever perhaps not of the genus of ephemeral fevers. And for the most part, similar cases do not happen except from antecedent corporeal causes of raw, repletive humors; and sometimes they arise from ulcers to which malignant matters are attracted and retained in soft flesh. But fevers that follow internal abscesses perhaps do not occur from the application of heat to the heart without putrification. And indeed, more violent fevers arise from internal abscesses, for they are of the genus of *erysipelas* <note>a skin infection, here used for internal inflammation</note> in certain viscera, and pain, thirst, and swelling spread. They are marked by signs of a great mixture of bile with blood. These internal abscesses are like abscesses of the brain and its membranes, and the *simach* <note>a medieval term for a membrane, often the peritoneum or pleura</note> of the ear, and sometimes the throat. And in the membrane that separates the chest <note>the pleura</note>, and the liver, and kidneys, and bladder, and matrix <note>uterus</note>, and intestines, and things similar to them. Their fevers vary in violence and weakness according to the proximity or distance of the heart. Furthermore, the fever of those in fleshy members is more violent, and the fever of those in the vicinity of arteries is more violent, while the fever of those in the vicinity of veins alone is weaker. And these fevers are not evacuated by periods according to the matters that are poured out to the abscesses; for their periods follow other cycles according to various matters. Let us pass over this briefly, as we have said much about periodicity in the general questions. I say therefore that for abscess fevers to be periodic in a determined measure, and to be strengthened or return after they have subsided, it is necessary for matter to be moved toward putrefaction now, with the previous matter having evaporated before. But this only happens because matter is generated at a set time and moves to the member at a set time. These are causes on the part of the "sending member" <note>the organ shedding the excess humors</note>. And thus he said "according to the matters that are poured out."

# Part I, Treatise III

For these are according to the generation of the humors and according to their movement—namely, the regulation of the matters—even if there concurs with this an attraction made by an abscessed member drawing by heat and pain. And therefore it is said that the attraction is caused by heat and pain, that is, an attraction made by heat and pain. Therefore, these are the causes of the periods <note>the intervals or cycles of a fever</note>. Thus, the nature of each humor is determined with determined periods. For the nature of yellow bile <note>original: "cholere"</note>, which is different from black bile <note>original: "melancolia"</note>, has another determined time of regeneration in quantity by which it can cause a fever. It also has a determined time in which it moves toward the abscessed member, and the abscess itself has a determined attractive heat and a determined heat. It follows, therefore, that in every humor there is an inherent period that is suitable to it, because in each there is generation, movement, heat, and pain that are appropriate to it. Blood, however, seems suited to afflict continuously. Therefore, its period is properly not to "periodize" <note>to have intervals</note>, but to have one paroxysm <note>the peak of a fever fit</note> or attack.

They are according to their generation and according to their movement and according to the attraction of heat and pain toward them; for to every humor there is a period that happens to it. And you should know that many times the abscesses appear to be healed and yet the fever remains, which signifies then that a cleansing <note>original: "mundificatio"</note> has not occurred. And these fevers sometimes prolong and lead to a hectic state <note>original: "eticaz," referring to a wasting fever affecting the body's solid tissues</note>; and properly so when the abscesses are in the liver <note>original: "etie," likely a corruption of "epate"</note>. Those, however, which are in the membranes, when they are established, do not wait until the hectic state.

### On their signs and their judgments. Chapter XIII.

**W**hen there are fevers and internal abscesses, three kinds of signs and accidents <note>symptoms</note> are found: namely, signs and symptoms signifying the sick member, signs and symptoms signifying the matter, and signs and symptoms signifying the disposition of the sick person. The first kind of signs are such as the hollow pulse, and a stabbing pain of the abscess in the parts of the chest, and this dry cough in the beginning and moist afterward, which are similar to those. Regarding the signs present signifying an abscess in the parts of the chest: at the highest, there is pain and heaviness in the member, and it is hotter than the other members with an added heat that is not customary. And thus a spasm, for it is many times associated with hot abscesses in nervous members. The second species is like the signaling of the intensity of a tertian fever <note>a fever recurring every three days</note>, which signifies that

<margin>a</margin> And know: here is one canon <note>rule</note>, and another variation can be placed. It is doubted if the fever is an accident of the abscess, whereby the abscess might be removed and the fever remain. It must first be said that this fever which remains is not that one; but the abscess is gone, yet another fever from the putrefaction of the humor remains besides the abscess. And therefore it signifies that although he is cured of the abscess, yet a cleansing has not occurred—that is, another associated condition remains. Alternatively, it can be said that it is often "healed," meaning it *appears* to be healed because the pain and the heaviness in the place and the cough cease (for example, in pleurisy), because the matter is mostly resolved. Yet something of it remained in the place or around the place of the abscess, sufficient to maintain the fever. Therefore, it is a sign that a perfect cleansing of the abscess has not been made. And this case is like the case of the "porismos" <note>an anatomical or pathological discovery</note> written in the commentary on the Aphorisms <note>Hippocrates' Aphorisms</note>.

<margin>b</margin> In the ancient text also: pleurisy remained and the fever ceased. Here, however, the fever remained and the pleurisy nearly ceased. And these are the fevers of internal abscesses.

<margin>c</margin> It is doubted because properly abscesses of the lungs ought to lead to a hectic state since it is a member close to the heart. To the contrary is Avicenna here and Galen in the *Art of Therapeutics* <note>original: "arto terapeitice"</note> in that chapter "Let us pass through," where Galen seems to have defended, and Dino <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous medical commentator</note> with him, that the hectic state called marasmus <note>wasting away</note> or dryness is more likely to occur from an abscess existing in the liver. And this is because of a defect of nutrition originating from the liver and not from the lung. But the hectic state which is an inflammation, or from inflammation and boiling, more likely occurs from an abscess in the lung because the heart cannot be vented. Consider this yourself.

<margin>d</margin> Those indeed: that is, those abscesses or those fevers following abscesses that are in the membranes, namely of the diaphragm, when they are established (namely, in black bile), because they are not resolved. They "do not wait," because they kill first. Whence Galen, speaking in the same place about an abscess of the diaphragm, says: "Many times have I seen them killing before the most certain difficulty of breathing and delirium are completed." But in those in whom such dispositions are present, they mostly die before a hectic state is generated.

<margin>e</margin> With the fevers. First, he places a certain division of signs and symptoms and explains it. Second, he places a certain diversity of signs based on that division. Third, he places certain other signs (at "And the members" and "the third" and "heat"). It must be considered that he said there are certain signs and symptoms that signify the member in which the abscess is; he wants you to return to the third book, in which you have the signs of an abscess of each interior member. By saying there are signs signifying the matter making the abscess, he wants you to return to the third book somewhat, and to the third section of this fourth book. And by saying there are signs signifying health or death, he wants you to go to the second section of this fourth book. And therefore he abbreviated everything here and gave some things as examples.

<margin>f</margin> And it is hotter than the rest: because an abscessed member is like a glowing furnace, as in the eleventh book of the *Therapeutics*, the last chapter.

<column-break/>

the matter is bilious. These symptoms indeed are the dispositions which indicate his health or judge his death. And the hidden members indeed vary in causing fevers and receiving them, both by their duration and by their periods, according to their own size and the size of their veins. And according to their members: for in the internal members there are those which are near the heart and of powerful community <note>connection</note>, such as the membrane <note>the diaphragm</note> and the lung. And among them are those which are far from the heart and of weak community, such as the kidneys <note>original: "rnes"</note>; these indeed do not always cause strong or continuous fevers on account of their abscesses, and many times they are interpolated <note>intermittent</note> and are of the genus of mixed fevers: tertian, quartan, quintan, and sextan. And there are with them shivering and trembling, and their status is ambiguous; and they are signaled by heaviness in the place of the loins and in the parts of the *alchati* <note>the pelvis or hips</note>, and pain, and a specific heat in the member greater than usual. When, however, matter is gathered in a member so that it is a primary organ, or of strong community with the heart, or of intense sensation, and it is nervous: then with the intensity of the fevers accompanying its abscesses, there happen to it great restlessness and spasm, and perhaps strange symptoms accompany it; just as with abscesses of the uterus <note>original: "matricis"</note>, for it is associated with a fever, a headache <note>original: "soda"</note>, and pain in the neck. And the heat indeed, although it burns in those abscesses, yet it is not

the second point by which abscesses vary in causing fever is according to the size of the veins—namely, the pulsing <note>arteries</note> and the quiet ones <note>veins</note>—and in this he touches upon the greater or lesser connection with the heart. The third is according to their members—that is, other than the heart—with which the abscessed member causing the fever communicates. For example, the matter communicates with the head and the lining of the brain, and therefore in an abscess of the uterus, a fever will occur with a headache.

<margin>g</margin> **For.** Here he follows up on what he ought to show: that abscessed members, varied according to size, are varied in prolonging and shortening fevers and in how they periodize. He ought also to show secondarily how members varied according to the size of the veins are varied in intensifying fevers. But because he knows all this from the one who knows the third canon and what preceded in the fourth book, therefore Avicenna passed over it very briefly. And what he said in the third book, he tries to place here cursively. Therefore, passing on, Avicenna first shows how members varied in distance, proximity, and connection of sensation vary in causing fever and in their periods. Second, he shows how abscesses varied according to their own members vary in causing fevers (at "The second" and "And perhaps"). That the diaphragm is near and of intense proximity to the heart—which is noble and very sensitive—is known. That the lung is also near, communicating, mobile, and bound to the veins and arteries is also known. The kidneys, however, in respect to those mentioned, are far through members that are not noble, and also less noble

which are little bound and little sensitive in respect to the diaphragm, and also less noble than those. Therefore, the matters do not flow so copiously to them; it varies the vapor. Therefore, it is not necessary for strong or continuous fevers to occur. And because many and diverse matters can gather in them, which tolerate much harm, and diverse occurrences can happen in them, therefore fevers can occur which are not interpolated—that is, which are not ordered but are diversely mixed tertians, etc. And "their status is ambiguous" because the physician, seeing such ambiguity of the fevers, is uncertain of what it is and marvels or is ambiguous about health or death. And this signifies the fevers of abscesses of the kidneys. Concerning this, Casis writes in the 18th [book] of the *Continens*, the fourth chapter at the beginning, which I have seen in its proper form where he speaks of Raynaldo de Monte Melino.

<margin>b</margin> "When, however, it is gathered." Dino doubts whether a continuous fever follows from abscesses of the viscera. It seems not, because the matter of the fever ought to be inside the veins (as above in the chapter on putridity), but the matter of abscesses is outside the veins, in the pores. Furthermore, it is characteristic of continuous fevers not to have shivering (as Galen says in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers*); but certain abscesses of some viscera, like the kidneys, cause a fever with shivering as here. Galen understood the opposite in the fourth [book] of the *Aphorisms* on that word "fevers which do not." Here he argues at length that the fevers which run to abscesses of the viscera are continuous because of the matter which is in the veins of the abscesses; or because they are interpolated, they are because of matter that has left the veins. And we say that matter outside the veins so near the heart can cause a continuous fever, as was done with the lungs—namely, the illnesses of the chest—and the demonstration for this is known. Therefore, fevers following abscesses of the viscera are mostly continuous for the reasons we wrote above in the chapter on ephemeral fever from an abscess. Afterward, they can nonetheless sometimes be interpolated, as Avicenna says here and gives the cause. To the contrary, it must be said that that speech is true for the most part. Or it must be said that if the matter is within the veins it causes a continuous fever, and with this it stands that some matter contained outside the veins can cause a continuous fever. To the second, it must be said that that of which Avicenna speaks here is interpolated because it sometimes follows an abscess of the kidneys. To the contrary, it must be said that interpolated fevers for the most part do not arise from abscesses of the viscera. And perhaps since the uterus is situated near the rectum and is not "nervous"—meaning of nerves originating from the brain—it seems strange that a fever with a pain of the whole head should follow from its abscess; and this is what he calls *soda* and pain of the neck, that is, of the back of the head, or *soda* as pain of the head (the back) and the neck. Yet the uterus communicates with the breasts and the chest and the "nut" <note>the nucha or spinal cord</note> by connection to the posterior parts. Therefore, these accidents can happen from it, although they seem strange. And this is a clear explanation in the example of the diversity of fever following members varied by their own connections—namely, those with which they communicate other than the heart. And you can have many other examples, but Avicenna took the most unusual example.

<margin>f</margin> And the heat. Here he places certain other signs of abscess fevers, and they are two. The first is from the manner of the heat. And it is specific: only if it is a great thing because there is putrefaction of the abscess and with this in the veins. And regarding the pulse. The second sign is from the pulse: the pulse of putrid abscesses is diverse. Its "systole" <note>contraction</note> is greater, and such is the case in fevers of internal abscesses: small in the beginning because of the suffocation of the heat under the matter that is moved. Of swift constriction—that is, the systole—at the peak <note>original: "statum"</note>, at the time of expression or expulsion. Then it becomes "magnified"—that is, the expulsion being made and the virtue <note>strength</note> invigorated. Alternatively, it can be explained so that "then" does not indicate the order of time but of the speech: so that it is said "then," that is, besides this, the pulse is large, swift, and frequent according to the member.
