# Book

<margin>a</margin> Digestion <note>the process of "ripening" or maturing the bodily humors so they can be expelled</note> can be delayed in respect to phlegm and can happen in the semitertian fever longer than in the phlegmatic fever. And regarding vomiting, such is the matter that dominates. Here, understand that vomiting in which something else is mixed is worse than vomiting pure bile: because it is purified from bile, and phlegm falls into the signs of semitertian fever. But vomiting pure bile falls into the signs of pure tertian fever <note>a fever that recurs every three days, usually associated with yellow bile</note>, which is a healthier fever; we have written about these things in the second book of the *Prognostics*. And regarding bowel movements: they are improper. Regarding disposition: here he speaks summarily of other things, which he says he has spoken of elsewhere; for he has already spoken of the mode of heating and cooling and the return of shivering in semitertian fevers: and regarding thirst when he says "few of the accidents," etc. And he does not wait. That is, when the first part of the chapter where he first places the signs of semitertian fever is dominated by phlegm. And he promises that it does not wait for the "status" <note>the peak or stable period of an illness</note> in judgment. For the term "status" is taken differently here than above when he spoke of the status which it produces, namely: the longer duration of the pores <note>original: "porismi," referring to the channels through which humors move</note>: because phlegm prolongs the illness more and delays resolution. The shivering is less, because it returns more to the internal cooling. There is a constriction of the vessels <note>original: "fistulis," literally pipes or tubes, referring to vessels or ducts</note> due to many vapors raised by the phlegm, specifically in the pulse: because the putrefied vapor moves much through the arteries; since in semitertian fever, the phlegm is in the veins, which are associated with the arteries. The complexion of the body inclines toward the phlegmatic, and more so the habit: namely, the habit of having phlegmatic fevers, or a habit of phlegmatic foods. And those things which run together: namely, art and service, etc.

<margin>a</margin> And if bile dominates, it is clear from the opposite of what was said. And when the signs are equally frequent: namely, mixed. Because there is a great appearance of middle signs: or the signs are frequent: namely, the return of shivering when the paroxysms <note>the sudden onset or attack of a fever</note> invade together: and this is because of the noble struggle. And the shivering: namely, because it is a true terror as in the second book on fevers. And therefore it is neither a "rigor" <note>a severe chill with shivering</note> nor approaching a rigor: that is, neither declining toward a rigor, nor toward a surrounding coldness: but toward a middle state.

<margin>b</margin> And when first. This is the fourth part of the chapter in which he first places the signs: when the semitertian is pure or true: because the continuous part is phlegmatic and the intermittent part is choleric <note>caused by bile</note>. He says that this is a rigor, though weaker. Now he proves that there is a rigor in this semitertian because the bile is outside the vein: and it does not have a contradiction in the struggle when producing a rigor on the part of the phlegm: because the phlegm is inside the veins. And it is not mixed outside with the bile: but it is weaker because while the phlegm is inside, the bile is outside through alteration: and because of the vaporous phlegm being dulled: so that it produces a pure rigor: just as the bile moves out from the hollow of the veins and is expelled outward onto the sensitive members: which therefore is dulled by the phlegm with which it is mixed inside: or in some way is altered and infected inside: and because of this, such a rigor is still called "horror" <note>a less intense, bristling coldness</note>, that is, not a pure rigor. From which it appears that the "horrid" semitertian is that which is made from two intermittent fevers—choleric and phlegmatic—attacking at the same time in the pores.

<gloss>a</gloss> ...is smaller and <gloss>b</gloss> Vomiting of bile is less, and the urine is of a more vehement whiteness and crudity: and sweat is less, and the age is childhood or old age, and the complexion of the body signifies them: and similarly the habit and those things that run with it. And if bile dominates, the paroxysms are shorter and the extremities reach heat faster, and there is thirst and more vomiting of bile and more erupting sweat and perhaps it declines to shivering: which is like a rigor: and the urine becomes more vehemently colored: and the age is youth: and the complexion of the body sometimes signifies it: and similarly the habit that runs with it. And when the two humors are equal, the signs are frequent, and there is a pure, complete shivering, not a rigor, nor approaching a rigor. And when the proposition is more manifest in the periodic and continuous parts, which most men designate with the name of pure semitertian, and it is continuous: the phlegmatic part itself is a weaker rigor: because the extrinsic matter is choleric: and there is no contrary to it on the part of the extrinsic phlegm with it; in that which is necessary regarding rigor: but it is weaker and perhaps cold and shivering repeat in it so as to cause an error in the "status" as you know: and <gloss>d</gloss> the heat of the viscera and belly is multiplied with coldness of the extremities, and the pulse becomes of more vehement purity and rarity. <gloss>e</gloss> If however the continuous part is choleric, there is no rigor nor great shivering: and the pulse becomes larger and faster and the distress more vehement. <gloss>f</gloss> And if two continuous fevers are composed, there will be no rigor at all. And it happens to the continuous tertian that it is relieved before the phlegmatic reliefs.

<margin>c</margin> And perhaps etc. so that it produces a rigor in the "status": as you know because it is estimated: because of the expanded heat which now becomes the status: and it is not similar, for shivering and cold return again sometimes.
<margin>d</margin> And it is multiplied, etc. This is because certain members are already heated above with a fixed shivering, although that saying can be understood more broadly as we hinted above. And the pulse etc. because of the phlegm which putrefies inside, which is slower compared to the bile.
<margin>e</margin> If however. Here he puts the signs of the semitertian when the continuous part is choleric and the intermittent part is phlegmatic: no rigor occurs: because the bile is inside. Nor is there great shivering: that is, nor true shivering because there is a surrounding coldness, though weak: because the phlegm is outside the veins. It does not have a contradiction from the bile mixed with it: but it has some contradiction from the bile which is inside the veins, as is understood from what has been said. And the pulse etc. is clear.
<margin>f</margin> And if they are composed. Here he puts the signs when both are continuous; there is no rigor at all: because the bile is inside. and perhaps he does not say "no cooling at all": because although phlegm is not in the veins, it is not prohibited from causing a cooling: as above in the chapter on the phlegmatic fever, and it happens to the continuous tertian: that it is relieved, namely from that exacerbation before etc. so that it does not return etc. because the phlegmatic returns sooner since it returns every day, and the choleric on the third day. It should be considered that he omits the signs of the semitertian composed of bile and phlegm when both are intermittent: because they are already understood from what has been said and specifically there. And when they are composed etc. and also above when he spoke of the return of shivering.
<margin>g</margin> Necessary in the semitertian. After the knowledge of the semitertian, he puts the cure and abbreviates it because it is understood from the chapter on the cure of putrid fever in general: and from the chapter on the cure of an impure tertian fever. And first he promises the chapter: and compares the cure through evacuation to the cure through alteration. Secondly, he declares that. Thirdly, he puts the medicines suitable in this cure at the determined time. There: "And when." There the third: "The medicines." The first point is very much to be considered: that as much as we can, we should diminish the matter in semitertians. And therefore I frequently use laxatives in them. For it is a fever of great repletion: there is more of an inflated heat. And therefore one must be more concerned with evacuation than with extinction <note>cooling or quenching the heat</note>.
<margin>a</margin> And when. Here he declares the point regarding what he prescribed about evacuation with laxatives. Secondly with vomiting. Thirdly with the provocation of urine and sweat. There: "And vomiting." There the third: "and provocation." The first precept is that the laxative medicine ought to follow the digestion of the matter: because the matter ought to have digestion: unless it is a soothing medicine: such as cassia. Unless it is a laxative that does not cause distress, such as *lubleb* <note>original: "lubleb," possibly a specific herbal preparation or milk-based remedy</note>: that is, a certain species of milk-food of which he spoke above in the chapter on the cure of putrid fever in general. *Terebiabin*: that is, manna. *Siracost*: that is, another species of manna. It should be considered that a few soothing medicines do not require digestion, as is noted. Laxatives also that do not cause distress do not require that digestion: such as manna, whose property is to loosen bile. For it is such a light laxative for bile: that if it does not find it ready, it does not agitate it: and therefore there remains for it a collection of loosening...

<column-break/>

...soothing. And these things are declared in the aforementioned chapter, and from this understand that *lubleb* is more appropriate for phlegm than for bile.
<margin>i</margin> And after the appearance. Consider diligently that he does not say "after perfect digestion": but "after the appearance of digestion": because immediately when digestion appears or when digestion becomes apparent: although it is not perfectly digested, evacuate with strong medicines: as was said in the chapter on phlegm. And afterward again regarding the residue. He says it "passes through" <note>original: "pertransit"</note>: because such evacuations with strong medicines, as with turbith and agaric and similar things, when perfect digestion has not occurred, are not without some harm: but when after perfect digestion: a regular evacuation would not be said of it, that it "passes through" etc. but A. <note>likely referring to Avicenna</note> says that it is according to rightness and suitability.
<margin>k</margin> And vomiting. It is clear from radish water etc. or this radish water etc. is for phlegm or with oxymel <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, supplement: if bile is dominant, although this is suitable even when phlegm dominates: but vomiting from radish is stronger.
<margin>l</margin> And provocation. Here he puts the rule for evacuation through sweat and urine. And first he shows what their quality ought to be. Secondly the time for using those provocatives. There: "And when they hasten." It should be considered that provocation is taken in two ways: as above at the beginning of this chapter. Sometimes for the provocation of urine and sweat, as here, and perhaps in the second rule of the fourth chapter at the beginning. But the medicines that provoke urine and sweat are of a hot and subtle substance. And therefore we ought not to use strong and more equal ones: where we can use better ones: about which we have written extensively in the chapter on the cure of putrid fevers in general: where we also declare when and with what strong ones and with what weak ones we can use them. And when unlearned expositors believe that he understands here laxative medicines through "decoctions." These people err in two ways. First because: he had already given complete rules for laxatives. Secondly because: the knowledge of Avicenna would be lacking in the rule regarding the time of using provocatives. We say therefore that by decoctions he understands provocatives for urine and sweat: such as fennel roots, parsley, and similar things, or *affari* <note>possibly a corruption or local name for a botanical ingredient</note> and...

That it does not return before its restitution.
### On the treatment of the semitertian fever. Chapter xii.

It is necessary in the semitertian that you have great concern in evacuating the matter according to the species of evacuation: from loosening the belly, and vomiting, and provocation, and sweating: more than the intensity which is through cooling. And with laxatives, all should be according to the digestion, unless they are of the kind that soothe the nature: and loosen: and do not cause distress: such as *lubleb* water with *geleniabi* <note>a compound medicine, likely containing sugar or honey</note>: if it be that which overcomes phlegm: and such as *terebiabin* and *siracost* and infusion of tamarind and syrup of violets: if bile be dominant: and such as is composed of these if the two humors are nearly equal. And after the <gloss>i</gloss> appearance of digestion, if the evacuation of the humor is done with strong medicines, it "passes through": and <gloss>k</gloss> vomiting should be according to the dominant humor, either from radish water with warm oxymel, or oxymel with warm water: and <gloss>l</gloss> provocation should be done with those things in which there is heat: and when they hasten in drinking decoctions before digestion, they fear *siffen* <note>an Arabic-derived term for an internal inflammation, often of the pleura or abdomen</note>. <gloss>m</gloss> But the medicines helpful in the way leading to the "status" to rectify the matter and mature it and to aid its harms: among the singular medicines is wormwood, but after the seventh day and the appearance of digestion, such that it be "Roman" <note>referring to *Artemisia pontica*, considered milder and better for medicine</note>, which is good; and when you hasten with it, it moves the humors: and does not evacuate them: and when it is taken, it causes distress and sadness and nausea, then it returns upon them with its heat: and it erodes them and with its astringency it makes them...

...dyed with the grains of the sun and similar things. And he called them decoctions: because those provocative medicines are suitably given in the form of a decoction: so that they may flow into the veins and members. But laxative medicines, whose purpose is to evacuate through the lower parts, are most often given more suitably in substance and not in decoction: as he said above in the chapter on the impure tertian. When therefore these provocative medicines having some strength are given before digestion, it is feared: that is, an abscess of the chest or *sirfen* <note>an Arabic term for an inflammation of the brain or its membranes, similar to meningitis</note>: that is, an abscess of the head. For they agitate the matter and make it flow to the head or to the chest or to other parts: but he spoke only of these parts above the nutritive organs because these provocatives, by agitating, inflate: and sharpen the matter: which, ascending, will cause *birfen* or *sirfen*.

<margin>m</margin> But the medicines. Here he puts the medicines, first one simple one: namely, wormwood. Secondly, another medicine: namely, barley water with hyssop. Thirdly, he puts more compound medicines. There: "And Galen": there the third: "Compounded." It should be considered that Avicenna touches on four things. First, the time of administering wormwood: namely, its juice or decoction or its substance in lozenges or powder, and he touches on two times: namely, generally in the way leading to the status: that is, in the increase, and particularly after the seventh day. But here the seventh is not taken for the measure of time alone: because if the matter after the seventh were crude <note>undigested</note>, wormwood would not be suitable: but A. trusts that in the semitertian after the seventh day some digestion appears. And therefore he adds "and the appearance of digestion," as if to say, I understand "after the seventh" in such a way that digestion appears. And this is the intention of Galen in his *Therapeutics to Glaucon* and Ali Abbas and Serapion in this chapter: that wormwood should not be given except after the appearance of digestion. Secondly, he touches on the utility because it rectifies the matter because it matures it. And this is because by diminishing it, it aids maturation. And aiding those things which are signs of appearance and others which are known. Thirdly, he chooses wormwood when it is Roman, and this is because it is not foul-smelling. However, as much as you want it to be laxative and digestive: choose that which is more bitter. Fourthly, he touches on the symptoms which follow when it is taken or drunk before digestion and you hasten with it: namely, before digestion. Where it is doubted whether wormwood can be given in a semitertian when digestion appears: and it seems not: because it does not evacuate phlegm. Furthermore, when some digestion appears, some part of the matter is not digested. Therefore, it will move that undigested part: and will not evacuate it. Similarly, it will erode it: and make it sluggish. On the contrary are all the authors. Let us say that when digestion appears: although it is not perfect: syrups in which wormwood is placed are suitable: and we use it at this time when we can: however, men often refuse wormwood. But of its own...

<meta>This page continues the technical medical commentary on Avicenna’s Canon, specifically addressing the treatment of semitertian fever (hemitritaeus). The previous page discussed the diagnosis of these fevers based on the dominance of phlegm or bile. This page transitions into the debate over specific ingredients like pepper and barley water, provides medicinal recipes, and concludes with a discussion on relapses.</meta>

[...evacua]tion is that which, by its own power, evacuates the more significant part and opens obstructions. Its action ends when it evacuates that part; and if it is mixed with that matter, it can achieve its effect. If, therefore, no part of the matter were digested <note>ripened or matured for expulsion</note>, then its commotion would be within the matter itself. Thus, it would cause distress, sadness, and nausea from the movement of the matter, until it returns to a stable state. Secondly, it performs its effects of heating, extinguishing, and astringency, by which it contains the matter and makes it sluggish. He says "it returns" because the principle intended by it is something vital. When it does not act, it moves the matter and initiates the effects of heating and drying.

From these things, only the second article is apparent. Regarding the first, it must be said that he does not deny the evacuation of some phlegm, but rather that it does not evacuate "viscous" phlegm, as is understood from the chapter on wormwood in the second book of the *Canon*. We also declare many things in the second book, in the chapter on wormwood, and in the third book, fen 15. We also dispute concerning a certain kind of wormwood, taking from Galen’s *Therapeutics to Glaucon* in the chapter on impure tertian fevers. And those who came before them, perhaps Hippocrates and others, and Rhazes <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi, a foundational Persian physician</note>.

<margin>a</margin> And he said. He first puts forward the opinion of the critique and the motive. Secondly, he removes it, there where he says "This Galen." The one who spoke against Galen was Alexander <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias or Alexander of Tralles</note>, as Rhazes notes in the 18th book of the *Continens*, in the third chapter: "he transgressed," etc., meaning he was alienated from the truth. And "he stood," etc., as Gerard <note>Gerard of Cremona, the translator</note> glosses: as when someone was present but did not know what to say. It is a wonder that he would say such a thing about such a drying agent. And "he did not know": here is the motive, that pepper harms the fever by producing phlegm, and barley water harms the phlegmatic matter by its coldness, making it sluggish; therefore, barley water with pepper should not be given in semitertian fever.

<margin>b</margin> And this certain [man]. Here he removes that opinion. First, it is shown that this man's error is a general error, and he removes his motive by disparaging him. Secondly, he removes a specific error of his by arguing against him from his own words. Thirdly, to the praise of Galen, he wonders about what was said regarding contradiction. First, he says that this man's error is not unique to this intention, namely, in the cure of semitertian fever, but is common to all cases where there are contrary matters and intentions. In these diseases, we mix contrary medicines, trusting that nature will discern between them. An adversary might say: "this medicine composed of contraries is not good." Yet we trust that nature will discern, etc. And this is what he says: the rule given is also in aid of nature, when the natural medical heat is prepared to resist such contraries—that is, diverse matters and diseases composed of contraries. With composite medicines, etc., which he best adds: that semitertian fever cannot be evacuated otherwise. And because someone might say nature cannot distinguish these medicines composed of contraries, Avicenna responds that if the vital power is so defective, then the cure is of no value regardless of how it is done. This is because curing is a power, as we said above. Disputing about this power and the separation performed does not belong to this place; we have already written about this in our treatise *On the Heart* and in many places. And the man erred.

<margin>c</margin> And this. Here he argues against him thus: This man allows celery and dill in semitertian fever, in which there is no strong heating and which thins the matter. Therefore, he must allow pepper in a small quantity: because from this it is "cooled," that is, heated only mildly, since its heating is diminished, and it thins the matter no less than a larger quantity of celery would. And then Avicenna declares here that pepper is mixed with barley water. This is done for three reasons. One is the water: barley water, by its slipperiness, makes its power reach the veins. The second cause is that it destroys, that is, diminishes its power—namely, the excessive heat of the pepper. Third, because it makes the matter run toward it, namely, the pepper; it makes the humors flow, moistens them, and digests them. Thus, the pepper is more easily digested and penetrates into them because of the penetration provided by the barley water. And if you consider these, Avicenna solves the reason for this contradiction: for Avicenna denies that pepper inflames the
<column-break/>
fever, because nature directs the pepper toward the phlegmatic matter. And he denies that barley water

makes the matter sluggish, because nature directs it toward the heart. And if the barley water acts on the matter, it prepares it for the operation of the pepper and provides those two benefits mentioned.

<margin>d</margin> Furthermore. Here he praises Galen in the practice of this science with the highest praise ever given to him. For Galen's contradictor had said that Galen stood like one who forgets what he ought to say because he does not know what to say. Avicenna says it is quite wonderful that Galen would forget this, which he ought to say, and that he was alive to judge this. That is, where he speaks, it was his judgment that it be so; to say otherwise of Galen is a vice.

<margin>e</margin> And compounds. Here he provides the description of composite medicines, all of which are beneficial once digestion—at least manifest digestion—is achieved. In all of them, there is a rectification and some reduction of the matter according to the proportion of the members. We shall not linger in verifying these recipes, as it is already known how one must act in the cure of putrid fevers generally, as when we spoke of troches <note>medicinal lozenges</note>. And we have written of this above in the fifth book: at this hour, namely, arriving at the "status," which is the hour of the fever's increase.

<margin>f</margin> Troches, etc. For semitertian fever, namely, at the hour of increase or in the decline, the benefits having been achieved. Troches, etc., for phlegmatic cases, that is, for semitertian fever in which bile dominates. Gum: namely, Arabic. Chalk: namely, of Crete <note>likely lithomarge or a medicinal clay</note>; Armenian bole or "sealed earth" is used in its place. For proper digestion: namely, perfect digestion. Whence the outer line is better, which is said for proper digestion. It should be considered that, in my judgment, all said troches and pills are more beneficial once digestion is done and some evacuations made at any other time; even in the increase of the fever, they can be suitable because vigor has appeared in the matter, and the cause of this is known from frequent experience, etc.

> **B** Relapse: is properly attributed to it <note>the fever</note>, because while it is possible for many other diseases to relapse, this term is usually applied to common relapses in fevers. Therefore, he provides a caution regarding it and a caution in the cure. The judgment is that a relapse from an intrinsic cause is worse than its "root" <note>the original onset</note>. The reason, as he states in the second part, is that the malice is vehement: because some intrinsic cause and the state and strength of the body is weakened by the preceding illness. They ask whether the relapse and the root are one single illness, and they linger long on this; we also join them in lingering over the "second dangers" of the Aphorisms, specifically the aphorism: "Those things which are left behind." However, we omit that here because we believe it to be crude; also, at the start of this work, we promised to omit childish matters. The caution he gives by his counsel is this: that one should not begin evacuation until the movement of the illness is manifest. For if it is not manifest to you whether it is from an extrinsic cause (where the fault lies in the patient’s regimen) or from an intrinsic one, you cannot cure it correctly. Furthermore, a relapse can be weak at the start and bad with a hidden wickedness. If you multiply remedies and perhaps give a laxative medicine, its malice is uncovered, and the patient may die without it being your fault; yet you will follow with infamy. May almighty God deliver us from such infamy and other dangers, and grant us eternal glory, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

Whereby the cooling agent is occupied with the fever and the parts of the heart, and the heating agent with the matter; and who is he who would cure semitertian fever without this? <meta>This page transitions from the specific treatment of fevers to the broader theory of medical prognosis and the "crisis"—the critical turning point of an illness. It establishes the definitions and structural framework for the following treatises on how a physician can predict the outcome of a disease.</meta>

# First Treatise of the First Fen.

<margin>a</margin>
**W**e say that Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians."</note>, in the preceding *fen* <note>A division of the text, from the Arabic word 'fann' meaning a branch of science.</note>, determined the nature of fevers according to all their diversity. In this second *fen*, he determines the prognostic signs and the crisis, setting down the various modes and species of the crisis itself. The reason is that a crisis most greatly occurs in fevers; as is evident in the second book on crises, a crisis is a vehement and rapid movement of a disease. Since the vehement movement of disease happens more in fevers, Avicenna immediately follows his determination on fevers with this determination on the crisis. First, he puts forward his intention for what is to be said; second, he carries it out. The second part begins at: "The meaning of Crisis." The first part is in two sections, because first he does this for a second time, mentioning prognosis and showing what prognosis is; the second section begins at: "And prognosis." It should be noted that Avicenna identifies four things: signs of crisis, signs of digestion, judgment, and the process of judging.

<margin>b</margin>
These are the matters upon which the outcome is resolved. It should further be noted that there are several dispositions. The first is whether a crisis is coming or not. The second is its mode, whether it happens suddenly or gradually. The third is the manner of the crisis: that is, whether it leads to health or to death. The fourth is the universal time: that is, whether it happens early or late. The fifth is the particular time: on which specific day it will come. The sixth is the cause of the crisis: whether it occurs by way of evacuation <note>expelling harmful fluids</note> or by permutation <note>a change in the nature of the disease</note>. The seventh is by what means it should happen, such as through sweat, etc.

### Second Fen on the Prognosis and Judgments of Crisis. Chapter 1.

**W**e shall speak in this *fen* about the dispositions of the crisis and its days, its signs, the signs of digestion <note>The "ripening" of the bodily humors so they can be expelled.</note>, and what is appropriate to each of the significations regarding judgment, and concerning good and bad signs. These indeed are the matters upon which the case is resolved in this prognosis. Prognosis is when a physician speaks regarding signs found concerning a future event, reaching a conclusion on the disposition of the illness as to whether it will end in escape <note>recovery</note> or perdition <note>death</note>, based on what is known of the body's strength and its firmness, or its decline, and the knowledge of its duration and the mode it will take—for example, whether it will happen. **First Treatise on the crisis and the intentions of its significations, and the goodness and malice in a crisis, and what constitutes its divisions and its judgments of crisis. Chapter 2.**

<margin>c</margin>
**T**he intention of "Crisis" <note>Original Latin: 'crisis,' derived from the Greek 'krisis,' meaning judgment or decision.</note> is "separation" in spoken terms. Its explanation is an alteration that happens suddenly, either toward the side of health or toward the side of sickness. It has significations by which the physician reaches an understanding of what is happening. The declaration of this is that an illness in the body is like an external enemy of a city, and Nature <note>The body's internal healing power.</note> is like the lord preserving it. Between the two of them, light skirmishes have already run their course, which are not cared for until a vehement battle arises between them both. Because of the signs of the battle's vehemence, certain dispositions and causes occur, such as a strong pulse, or rumbling and shouting <note>likely referring to internal bodily noises or the patient's distress</note>, and the rushing of blood. Then a separation occurs in a time of imperceptible quantity, almost in a single moment: either the lord overcomes the outsider, or the external enemy overcomes the ruler. A victory will be complete when there is a total overcoming of one of the two parties. A surrender of the city occurs when it is not a complete victory—in which there is an overcoming that does not prohibit a return or a reversal—so that it happens

<margin>c</margin>
And the prognosis is clear. But it is doubted whether prognosis is a science. And it seems not: because there is no science of that which does not yet exist. Secondly, because it is contradicted by the astrologer. To the contrary is Avicenna here; it must be said that prognosis is a present science, which appears to us when judging future things concerning the sick. To the first point, it must be said that prognosis is not entirely about non-existence. To the second, it must be said that the physician gathers prognosis from various signs of the illness, whereas the astrologer does so from the various movements of the heavens.

<margin>d</margin>
He now carries out the discussion of the crisis from those things he promised. First, he declares the nature of the crisis; second, the critical days. The second part begins at: "Concerning men." The first part is in two sections: first he does as said; second, because he had not made mention of the regimen of convalescents, he determines the reason for them. The second part begins: "It is necessary that convalescents..." The first is in four parts, just as four things remain besides the critical days. First, he determines the dispositions of the crisis; second, the signs of the crisis; third, the signs of digestion and indigestion; fourth, the judgment or prognosis regarding signs of death. The second begins: "The crisis is preceded by..." The third: "Having now spoken..." The fourth: "Death will occur." Alternatively, it can be divided into three parts: thirdly determining signs of digestion, and fourthly the judgment appropriate to each signification of good and bad signs. The third begins: "Digestion is known." The fourth: "For every alteration." Thus it appears from many of these chapters. Below, for the sake of the first evidence, it must be known that the rubric <note>A title or introductory heading, traditionally written in red ink.</note> Avicenna places here is the rubric for this entire treatise. And it is in the rubric of this chapter: because what is placed generally in this whole chapter is placed specifically below. And therefore, as the rubric hints, Avicenna declares three things in this chapter: first, the demonstrations and significations of the crisis; second, its malice, goodness, and its divisions; third, the judgments of the crisis; fourth, he joins a canon <note>A rule or standard procedure.</note> to what was said. The second begins: "And every illness..." The third: "And indeed the signification..." The fourth: "And know that the crisis does not..." The first is in two parts: first he puts forward the intentions of the crisis; second, he declares them. Notedly, he defines the crisis according to the name by which it is called "separation."

<column-break/>

<margin>e</margin>
¶ Separation in spoken terms: for when a judicial sentence is given between those who have a dispute among themselves, then a "separation" of the dispute occurs, and they no longer litigate. "In spoken terms" means in the divisions. He hints at this at the end of this chapter. Also Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note>, in the third book on crises, chapter 2, etc. Secondly, he defines the crisis according to the thing itself when he says "and its explanation." In this way, Galen defines it in his commentary on the second section of the Aphorisms <note>Referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates.</note>. To whomever a crisis occurs, he says that a crisis is a rapid and vehement movement of a disease. But it does not seem that Avicenna sufficiently defines the crisis as an alteration—

<margin>f</margin>
—because he takes it from Galen in the first book on crises, the last chapter. In a crisis, we consider two things: namely, the preceding commotion which is first called the crisis, and the alteration that follows that commotion, whether the alteration is for good or for evil. Therefore, it should not only be called a crisis of alteration, but also the commotion preceding the alteration.

that a battle happens another time or multiple times; therefore, there will then be a separation of the crisis at their end. And just as when a lord overcomes the invader and puts him to flight and expels him, either so that he expels him by a total expulsion so the city rests from him and its neighbors and the other borders joined with it, or he expels him by a non-universal expulsion, but rather puts him to flight from the city though he cannot put him to flight from the other borders continued with the city. Similarly, the power <note>The body's vital force.</note> which comes with a good crisis either expels the harmful matter from the foundation of the body, which is the heart and the principal members, and from its borders, which are the extremities; or it expels it from the foundation but cannot expel it from the extremities, but rather it reaches them, and it is called a "crisis of permutation." And every illness that is removed is removed either according to the path of crisis or according to the path of resolution <note>A gradual breaking down of the disease-causing material.</note>, so that the matter is resolved little by little until it is finished gradually. And this kind happens most in chronic illnesses and cold matters, which are not preceded by fearful signs and wicked movements. And similarly, every illness that kills does so either according to the path of crisis or according to the path of "arefaction" <note>A wasting away or drying out of the body's moisture.</note>, which is a gradual resolution. And the better crisis is indeed the complete one, which offers manifest confidence and has safe "accidents" <note>Symptoms or secondary conditions.</note>, which indicate on one of the critical days that a fall <note>the resolution of the disease</note> will occur on a praiseworthy critical day. And every crisis is either praiseworthy or bad, and each is either complete or diminished. A complete one is either such that Nature expels the matter by a total expulsion, or by permutation. And regarding the diminished crisis, there is one which is sometimes followed by a good resolution, and in a bad case, by arefaction. The day of a diminished crisis indicates the day of a complete crisis falling in illnesses of subtle, hot matters while the strength is strong. And a crisis of permutation is expected where the strength is weaker and on the day of indication, and that—

¶ And the declaration determines the meaning of crisis through an example. It should be noted that in this example, Avicenna declares the crisis: because just as between the lord of a city and an enemy there are several small battles, and finally afterward the ultimate war, so between Nature and the disease in the days of indication <note>Days when signs appear showing how the disease will turn.</note> some battles run; then the final battle will occur, which is the crisis, etc. Secondly, he declares two diversities of the crisis. The second begins: "victory indeed." The first diversity: because a certain crisis is perfect, and another diminished. This is declared because just as an enemy conquers the lord or vice versa so perfectly that he no longer returns to battle, so too, etc. The second diversity is because some crises are by evacuations, and some by permutation. He declares this by saying that the lord sometimes expels the enemy from the city to the borders.

<margin>g</margin>
¶ "And every illness"—here he distinguishes the alteration which is a crisis from that which is not a crisis. Note that Galen, in the third chapter on crises and in his commentary on the Aphorisms ("Those for whom a crisis occurs"), posits six species of crisis. Note that in every crisis, there must be a victory either of Nature over the matter, or of the matter over Nature. But victory does not happen without a battle; therefore, in every crisis, there must be a struggle and a fight, and where there is no fight, there is no crisis.

<margin>g</margin>
¶ "And every illness" determines the divisions of the crisis. For a crisis receives division chiefly from three things: from the mode of its event, from its manner, and from its cause. According to this, he does three things: first, the first division; second, the second; third, the third. The second begins: "And the better crisis." The third: "And diminished indeed." It should be noted that "every" is held here divisively and not collectively, as if to say that for all illnesses, some are converted, etc. Further, it should be noted here that the sudden consumption of an illness, whether for health or for death, is called a crisis. But a gradual consumption toward death is called [wasting].

<margin>h</margin>
¶ "And the better crisis"—here he sets down the conditions that are observed in a good and praiseworthy crisis.

<margin>h</margin>
¶ "And the better" sets down the diversity or division on the part of the matter. And first, he puts forward the divisions of a praiseworthy crisis. Second, the said division. The second begins: "And every crisis." It should be noted that he posits four conditions for a good crisis: first, that it be complete through the perfect expulsion of the harmful humor; second, that there be confidence in it, etc., from the preceding signs of digestion; third, that it be safe; fourth, etc., since these four can be reduced to the common ones which Galen posits in his commentary on the Aphorisms of the first section ("Those for whom a crisis occurs").

<margin>i</margin>
¶ "And every crisis" sets down the division of the chapter. It should be noted that if he does not give an example of a complete bad crisis, it is when strength fails in the expulsion, whence death follows—though also from suffocation. Two other members are to be understood from the diminished crises which Avicenna implies: namely, a diminished good crisis followed by a complete good crisis, and a diminished bad crisis as is immediately taken.

<margin>k</margin>
¶ "And diminished" sets down the division on the part of the cause of the crisis. For a crisis is either evacuation or permutation. First, therefore, he shows in what modes a crisis by evacuation happens, and in which cases a crisis is permuted. Second, he distinguishes these crises. The second begins: "And know that..." The first is in two parts: first he does as said; second, he subdivides them differently. The second begins: "And the first indeed..." It should be noted that this part serves Avicenna's point that a diminished crisis in a good case is sometimes followed by resolution. Someone might believe that it is always so for all...

# Book III

<sig>m</sig>

<margin>You move this. Avicenna says that sometimes a diminished crisis <note>original: "crisīs diminutā"</note> follows a complete crisis, and that from a diminished crisis, one can judge the day of a complete crisis, etc. Secondly, this serves Avicenna's point, as it shows in which diseases a crisis of evacuation <term>evacuation: the total removal of harmful fluids from the body</term> occurs: namely, in those where the matter is hot and thin, and in which the vital power is strong. And in which a crisis of transformation <term>transformation: when the disease moves to a different part of the body or changes form rather than leaving entirely</term> occurs, because the vital power is weak—that is, in comparison to the power required for a crisis of evacuation. He does not say "weak" in an absolute sense, because such a power would produce no good crisis at all, but rather in cases where the matter is thick and where the indicative signs are weak. Indeed, the indicative day can be called weak either because it is among the later days (i.e., beyond the 20th day) or because it is diminished in strength.</margin>

<margin>Urine and weak signs of crisis.</margin>
...both good and bad signs at once. And a crisis is expected when the matter is thicker. And first, the disposition is diversified again, for when the matter is extremely hot, it produces a crisis and sweat; if it is slightly less than that, even if it is still very hot, it produces a crisis with a flow of blood from the nostrils; and if not that, then through a flow of urine; and if not that, through a flow of the bowels and vomiting. And you should know that mucus and ear-pus and bleary eyes and tears are among the crises of ailments of the head, and sputum is among the crises of ailments of the chest, and the opening of the blood of hemorrhoids is a good crisis for many ailments, though it usually only happens in those for whom it is a habit.

<margin>a ¶ And first indeed the disposition. Since Avicenna had said that the matter of a total evacuation was hotter than the matter of a crisis of transformation, and since this heat has a range <note>original: "latitudinem"</note>, Avicenna here determines the range of that hot matter, assigning that matter to certain evacuations according to their differences.
a ¶ And first indeed: that is, the crisis which occurs through strong power and hot matter, etc. The reason is that the more the matters are thin and hot, the more they are expelled through narrower paths and toward the extremities; and the less they are so, the more they move toward closer parts and cannot be expelled to the extremities, etc.</margin>
And indeed, the sharpest crisis and the one closest to the liver <note>original: "hepatioez"</note> is the flow of blood from the nostrils, because it follows the expulsion of matter all at once; then there is the flow of the bowels, then vomiting, then urine, then sweat, then there will be a breakout <term>breakout: an abscess or skin eruption (Latin: eritura)</term>.

<margin>b ¶ And you should know that mucus. Here he determines the evacuations of the crisis which are assigned to specific members.
b ¶ And you should know. He distinguishes these crises: first, the crisis of evacuation; second, the crisis of transformation. The second starts at: "There will be indeed." The first is in two parts: first he does this, second he compares them to each other.</margin>

Therefore, it would be by reason of the disease, not the evacuation. No, because a flow of the bowels can happen suddenly, just like a nosebleed. On the contrary, here is Avicenna, and Galen mentions this in the commentary on the *Aphorisms*, fourth part: "To those for whom there is a movement toward the joints." For the knowledge of this, one must first know that a crisis mostly happens in acute fevers because the matter is inside the veins. Second, it should be known that a crisis is fast and close to separation when it is finished quickly; and all these things are more present in a nosebleed than in any other evacuation. Because when the matter is in the veins, it can immediately break out through the veins and finish quickly, which is a continuous and great evacuation... and because the matter existing in the veins can be expelled more slowly to the exterior parts, that is an evacuation; and so on for the others.</margin>

Note that "transformation" <note>original: "permutatio"</note> is a general name for breakouts. For there can be a transformation and not a breakout, just as if there were scabies, pustules, or "anthrax" <term>anthrax: a severe, burning boil or carbuncle</term>; carbuncles are species of breakouts.

The first is clear, etc. "Tuayrum" is an abscess in soft flesh, like a bubo. Whence Haly <note>Haly Abbas (930–994), another famous Persian physician.</note>, in the second treatise, commentary 194, says it is an abscess of soft flesh.</margin>
And sometimes a crisis occurs, or something related to it, by which the muscles and nerves are congealed, and sometimes through scabies and its species, into warmth, and cancer, and "albaras" <note>a skin condition involving white patches, similar to vitiligo or leprosy</note>, and glands, and ruptures, and varicose veins, and inflation of the extremities, and other things like these.

<margin>e ¶ And a crisis occurs. He has composed the varieties of evacuations and crises that happen often; he now sets down the evacuations that happen rarely.</margin>
And of the species of transformation are those which do not lead to a breakout, but instead produce things like twisting and spasm, and softening, and pains of the hip and back and testicles and knee, and jaundice, and elephantiasis <note>a chronic thickening of the skin and underlying tissues</note>, and varicose veins.

<margin>f ¶ And of the species. Here he determines what sort of transformation crisis occurs without a breakout.
g ¶ And know that the crisis. Here he sets down the diversity of these transformation crises according to whether they are more or less praiseworthy, and regarding health or lack of health.
g ¶ And know. He sets down the rule: as long as it does not happen, health does not happen. It should occur on a certain day or after digestion. Some interpret the text thus: "And know that health does not happen until the crisis of transformation occurs." That is a meaningless thing to say.</margin>
And know that a crisis made from transformation which becomes a good crisis, if it happens, health occurs. A change of transformation that occurs toward the lower parts is more praiseworthy, and a breakout is more praiseworthy.

It should be noted finally: Avicenna uses this metaphor, that just as an enemy in the city starts a war before he takes strength, etc., so if a disease begins the fight before digestion—whence those accidents which are mentioned occur—it is consequently before nature takes up its matter. Then it signifies a universal breakout, because of the length of the disease or death, because it is a bad crisis, as Galen says in the commentary on the *Aphorisms*, second part. -positions signifying a good crisis and a bad crisis. And just as when an enemy attacks a city and triumphs in the fight, and presses hard and heightens the strife, and displays the signs of a vehement victory while the defending lord is far away, not taking up his arms nor able to use his instruments—these are signs to testify that the victory will belong to the defender or the victory to the attacking enemy, and it signifies the malice of the lord's disposition from the testifying signs. And if the disposition is the opposite, then the judgment will be the opposite.

Similarly, when the disease moves the signs of crisis—which I shall speak of—before the occurrence of digestion, it signifies a breakout in a limb or some other thing, and perhaps it will be after apparent health. And the more praiseworthy of the transformations signifies a bad crisis, and if there is some digestion there, it signifies a diminished crisis. And if there is complete digestion there, it signifies a good, complete crisis. And indeed, a complete crisis occurs at the "state" <term>state: the peak or plateau of a disease (Latin: status)</term> and perhaps it arrives when the decline begins. And for this reason, vehement cold hinders a complete crisis, because the "state" of the disease and the crisis itself become difficult. How then shall its decline be? And many times it is necessary for the physician to help the harm of the cold by warming the place and pouring warm oil upon the belly of the sick person until he sees sweat begin, then he should stop the pouring and wipe away the sweat and keep the place in balance.

<margin>k ¶ And the more praiseworthy, which is not so praiseworthy, a crisis of transformation when it is a bad crisis, etc. But it is doubted whether every crisis of transformation is bad. It seems not: above he said in that part, "And every indeed praiseworthy crisis is a complete crisis of transformation." Likewise, Avicenna immediately says that if there is good and complete digestion there, it signifies a complete crisis, etc. On the contrary is Avicenna. It should be said that a crisis of transformation can be complete because, for instance, the whole matter of the disease is gathered in the breakout. But every crisis of transformation is "bad" in comparison to a crisis of evacuation, because in it the enemy is not expelled outside the body, etc.

¶ And complete indeed. Here he notes the crisis according to the time of the disease in which it ought to occur.

l ¶ Complete indeed the crisis. First he says this; the second part begins: "And for this reason." But it is doubted whether a crisis can happen in the decline. It seems not, according to Avicenna below in the second chapter, where he says: "In the decline a crisis never occurs." Likewise, a crisis is a fast movement, etc. But a fast and vehement movement, etc., cannot happen in the decline, because the sick person would happen to die; which is contrary to Galen in the third book on crises, chapter four, and Avicenna above on the hours of disease and below on the types of death. The consequence holds: because a crisis is a fast and vehement movement, etc., in which the sick person is led to death or to health. On the contrary is Avicenna here. It should be said that in the decline a third thing happens, as is taken from Galen in the first book on crises, the last chapter: first after the commotion, second after the following changes, third when the matter arrives. Now, a crisis regarding the commotion cannot happen except in the "state" (peak); because it cannot happen except in the vehemence of the disease, for which reason a crisis is defined as a fast and vehement movement, etc. But regarding the following change and evacuation, it can happen when the decline arrives. And so Avicenna speaks here, and the contradictions are reconciled.

m ¶ And for this reason. Now he infers what he had added to the words. Or he declares what he had said: because he had said that a crisis occurs at the peak and in the decline. Now he wants to declare this by a sign: for the sign of this is that cold hinders a complete crisis, because it makes the peak difficult. How then shall its decline be? Above, it much more hinders the movement of matter from the right side, which was in the decline; therefore he adds "with the decline."

n ¶ And know: here Avicenna teaches in general how to judge a crisis. And first he does this, second he explains and assumes it, third he removes a doubt or assigns a cause to what he had said. The second begins at: "And similarly." The third at: "And at the last." It should be noted that Avicenna finds three signs through which we can have confidence in a crisis: one, that it happens on the days in which it is customary, such as on the critical days. Second, that nature chooses to start the war, not being stirred up by the matter. Third, that it chooses for itself a disposition...</margin>
And know that the movements of the crisis which happen on the days and hours in which the custom of nature runs to fight the disease through purgation—which happens when there is an appearance of nature in choosing the hour or choosing the disposition with the help of God—are those in which trust is held. If, however, the fight happens with the disease inciting it and with restlessness, that is among the things that signify the vehemence of the oppression of the disease and the transformation of the matter, because of that which always tends toward the mouth of the stomach during the decline of the humor, whereby it is moved by vomiting, or toward its bottom, whereby it is moved by a flow of the bowels...

Sen II Tractatus I
O ii

...positions in the matter: because of the digestion <term>digestion: the process where the body "cooks" or matures the harmful humors so they can be expelled</term>. But you might say, therefore, it seems that nature <note>Nature refers to the body’s innate healing power.</note> uses weak reasoning regarding future events; the contrary of which is stated in the fourth book of the *Regimen of Acute Diseases* by Galen. Likewise, Galen states in the third book of *On Natural Faculties*, and the sixth book of *On Accidents and Disease*, and the third book of *On Internal Parts*, that nature does not move unless a harm is perceived; therefore, it moves of itself to fight. It is answered that nature does not act out of weakness, but only acts according to what happens to it prejudicially; for its action in disease is proportional to the action of the diseased matter against nature. Since the diseased matter does not all move to act against nature at the beginning of the illness, nature does not move in its full strength at the beginning, but rather during the "increase" phase, because then the diseased matter is more active. Therefore, nature acts more against the disease during the "state" <term>state: the peak or plateau of an illness</term>, because the diseased matter is then moving entirely against nature. Thus, nature moves against the disease with all its effort. Therefore, nature chooses this hour for the crisis and the expulsion of matter more than any other hour; it should be said that nature moves more in this hour because it is innate to the body from the celestial heavens and is stimulated by the diseased matter, etc.

<margin>a</margin> And similarly, regarding what they were. He explains by example but signifies the assistance and the opposition from the disease in its own expression. It is as if they said, "My enemy invited me to take revenge because of the provocation he does to me," etc. These are the words of Galen in the third book of *On Crisis*, chapter five.

<margin>b</margin> And to the last point. Here he takes up the judgment regarding the crisis. It can be said that he makes mention of the anticipation of the crisis before the determined time. And he would say that the cause was the provocation made by the disease; now, because someone might believe that this is always the case, he wishes to inquire into its cause in summary. First, he does this. Second, he explains a certain thing that was mentioned. Third, he attaches the canons <term>canons: fundamental rules or principles of medicine</term>. The second part begins at "For the accidents." The third at "And when it precedes." He points out two causes in general: intrinsic ones, which are the powers of the sickness regarding the matter and the vehement movement of nature regarding the strong movement. The other cause is extrinsic, such as food and drink. For example, sometimes after drinking much wine, a crisis occurs before it ought to. "For the accidents": he had said that through accidental psychological factors <note>original: "accidēs aiale"</note>, etc., he now wishes to teach this, saying how certain accidents act in the reasoning of the disease's crisis: because it moves the skin and the humors to the outer parts; hence it causes a crisis, etc. Joy moves things outward; therefore, etc.

<margin>c</margin> "And when it precedes." Now he attaches the canon, etc., and it is clear.

<margin>d</margin> "And you should know." Here, Avicenna attaches a certain canon regarding what was said; there are four canons which will be clear upon reading. And it should be noted that these are the words of Galen in the third book of *On Crisis*, chapter four.

<margin>p</margin> Where "fourth" is understood as the fourth day; as is clear in the same place in Galen. See the cause from Galen in the place cited above, etc.

<margin>e</margin> "And better." The second canon is attached before the "bad" one. "Compressive" is taken in one place, and this is a crisis through an abscess or "compressive," that is, oppressive, namely of the vital power.

<margin>f</margin> "In the beginning." Because the matter which nature produces in the beginning, according to the course of nature, is an evacuation; as Galen states in the commentary on the *Aphorisms*: "In whatever diseases," etc.

<margin>g</margin> "And to the last." The third canon regarding individual numbers, that is, individually numbered, namely in a "synochal" fever <term>synochal: a type of continuous fever</term>; when it is praiseworthy, namely the disposition of the increase, through the comparison of digestion in the decline, etc. Here he has what I was saying.

<margin>h</margin> "Later we shall say." Namely in the chapter on the types of death.

<margin>i</margin> "And you should know." The fourth canon: for nature, not having been attacked—that is, submerged by the matter—

<column-break/>

...and similarly, it is a disposition that causes coughing and sneezing to happen. And similarly, how there are signs indicating that a crisis may occur on a day such as the fourteenth, because it precedes it, and the beginning of the crisis is found to move before the day itself is "critical," such as on the eleventh. Now this signifies that the crisis will not be complete and sometimes not good, but it signifies that nature was assisted in the struggle. But if the illness is "fraudulent" <term>fraudulent: a disease that hides its true severity or mimics other conditions</term>, then it is not hoped that the crisis will be good; and if the illness is "safe," then it is not hoped that the crisis will be complete. And finally, the anticipation of the movements of the crisis before the state which that illness deserves happens either because of the strength of the illness, or because of the vehemence of its movement and its sharpness, or because of an exciting extrinsic cause. What usually happens regarding this is due to an error in food or drink, or through exercise, or because of a psychological accident <note>original: "accidens aiale" referring to strong emotions</note>. For in psychological accidents, there is an entry into the movement of the crisis and in the alteration of its parts; for anger triggers a crisis so that it happens through a flow of the bowels or vomiting or urine, and joy causes it to happen through sweat. And that happens through the movement of the spirit to the interior and the exterior. And when they precede the struggle in such a way that the vital power is not fixed with it until the "state," it is a sign of death; and perhaps some residue remains for the power until the "state," and it is safe. And you should know that a crisis does not fall on a day and hour of rest and tranquility, nor in a time removed from vehemence except rarely and slightly, and the sum of both is less. And Archigenes did not see this in crises except twice, and Galen once. And the better crisis is that which is in the hour of the "state"; in the case that precedes it, there is no confidence; rather, it is either diminished or a bad compressive one. In the beginning, a crisis never happens unless it is pernicious. And finally, the accidents of the signs of crisis in the first days of sickness signify a pernicious state, and in its increase, it signifies a diminished crisis is praiseworthy; in the decline, however, a crisis never happens. How death or a disposition that is not of a good crisis happens in it, we shall say later. And you should know that the crisis in safe illnesses is postponed. For nature has not been overcome, and it is possible for it to wait until it finds the completion of digestion; and in deadly illnesses, it precedes. And the sick person does not leave the struggle with his illness suddenly, and there is no path...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "crisis"—the critical turning point of an illness—focusing on how the physician can distinguish between a "natural" movement of the disease (leading to recovery) and a "violent" movement (leading to further injury). It connects the physical symptoms (signs) to the specific organs involved.</meta>

### Book III

...he sends: secondly he declares. The second part begins at "And it is diversified." This is divided into two: first he investigates how the matter is diversified; secondly, from which part the movement comes. The second part begins at "The cause, however."

<margin>
It should be noted that Avicenna shows from these points how the crisis is diversified based on the diversity of the matter, which follows as a consequence. For if you see that the matter tends upward, you cannot distinguish whether the crisis will occur through a nosebleed or by vomiting except through signs that indicate the nature of the matter; if it appears that the matter is bloody, etc. <note>original: "sanguinea"</note>
</margin>

**The cause of the parts**, however, tells how the accidents <term>accidents: secondary symptoms or occurrences that are not the primary cause of the disease</term> of the crisis are diversified based on the diversity of the parts. First he does this; secondly, concerning the designation of the various modes of crisis toward different parts. The second part begins at "unless the figure." The first part is the entire sequence, etc. To understand the other part, it should be noted that Avicenna suggests one type of digestion of the matter which moves symptomatically and violently upon the principal members <term>principal members: vital organs, usually the heart, brain, and liver</term>. And this has many accidents; for if it moves toward the brain, it causes a confusion of the senses, etc. And what we distinguish with them, namely, the accidents of the brain. And here at the beginning of the chapter: but if it moves toward the parts of the heart, then a pounding of the heart occurs, etc. Alternatively, the matter is moved by nature operating naturally. And he means this when he says: "Or it is moved toward expulsion," that is, toward the sites of expulsion, because it is naturally expelled. For when the matter moves violently, it does not move toward the site of expulsion, but toward the principal organs as its destination. And then this is what he says: "either it moves from every side to the surrounding part," because it then moves toward the whole body, and it cannot be that it does not pass through the principal sites, since it was previously prevailing violently. And he means this when he says: "unless there is an excess upon the principal members." Just as in the other part—namely, the division mentioned previously—it was said that the matter moves violently, etc. And then, invading the principal members, it must induce bad accidents, just as when it moves violently upon the head. And he means this when he says: "when accidents occur similar to its accidents." If it were not on the side of nature—that is, from nature by way of a crisis—it is instead there violently, remaining around the principal members. For as was said, when the matter moves violently toward a principal part from the direction of either hemorrhoids or a flux of the belly <note>original: "fluxus ventris," likely diarrhea</note>, and these signs indicate its manner, it goes to the opposite part. And the nocturnal signs are more vehement than the diurnal signs from the cause in this—without a doubt, as is known—because the matter causing the sickness increases the accidents and the signs because of its movement. And it is diversified either because of the diversity of the matter or because of the diversity of the movement. And the diversity caused by the diversity of the matter is, for example, when the movement of the matter is toward the upper parts. Then the figures signify the species of the sickness, the age, the complexion, and other things. If the matter is bloody, the physician then expects a flow of blood from the nostrils; and if it is gathered that the matter is choleric <term>choleric: related to yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness</term>, he expects vomiting, but mostly unless other appropriate signs indicate a flow of blood from the nostrils. For a nosebleed is a common crisis, and it is preceded by choleric imaginations. And a flow of blood from the nostrils sometimes consumes the matter of furious illnesses, and health occurs immediately.

The cause, however, of the movement is that it moves so that it goes violently upon the principal members and those that follow them in the viscera, and it causes harm to occur in their operations and an impediment to the senses. These things happen on the part of the brain as a confusion of the sense and a headache, and what we distinguish with them; and on the part of the heart, a pounding of the heart and a badness of breath, and what we distinguish with both of them. Or it moves toward expulsion, and that happens in these two ways: for either it begins by expelling from every part and length, and that is toward the whole, which is apparent with sweat; or it begins to tend toward one part. And that which begins is from every part; perhaps there is a part such that when it proceeds, there is no excuse when the passage is made through the principal members, as in the other part. For in tending toward it, it passes over the boundaries of the members, wherefore shortness of breath occurs, and over the boundaries of the brain, again with accidents similar to its accidents as if it were not expelled but rather remained there violently. And perhaps there is a part toward the members that are less principal, such as the mouth of the stomach, where the intention of the matter to be expelled by crisis is that it be expelled by vomiting. Or it is from the principal organs, yet it is a tolerable common office if it arrives quickly at the corruption, just as it arrives at the boundaries of the liver and is expelled by way of the bladder or the gall, and from every part of the site of the expulsion of the crisis, just as in the stomach by vomiting; and if to the boundaries of the head, by a flow of blood from the nostrils and things similar to it; and to the boundaries of the liver by urine; and to the parts of the intestines by a flux of the belly. And when this form is in deterioration, or then it moves toward some member that is minor and not principal, such as toward the stomach when it is said to be expelled by vomiting. Or it moves toward some principal organ that has some common office, namely, in expelling matter from the whole, just as it is then expelled in the way of the bladder or gall; or it is expelled from every part, that is, from whichever part is the site of expulsion. To which place, namely, a readiness to expel is made. Or it is expelled toward the parts of the head, etc., which is clear. And by this appears the reason why bad accidents occur both in the movement of matter and in natural occurrences. But they differ because in a symptomatic movement <note>original: "syngatomatico," referring to symptoms of disease rather than healing</note>, bad accidents occur because the matter moves to the principal organs as if to stay there. But in a natural movement, these accidents occur because the matter moves through the principal organs as if passing through. And from this is seen the verification of the saying of Avicenna in the first book of the *Canon*, the fourth fen: "Take care that the passage does not occur over the principal organs," etc., because the passage ought not to be made as if to a destination, but as if by a path, because nature makes this passage as a precursor.

Now someone might ask: "If there is a sign by which I can know natural movement, etc.?" He responds, etc. But you will say: Avicenna does not state what is signified. **And sometimes.** But you will say: Avicenna, giving an example of a crisis that is said to be good, occurring through the upper parts... when the crisis that is expected has been good; or the sign signifying badness is the first from its arrival, impeding that member if the crisis was bad. And perhaps there is one good sign for this, so that it signifies three parts, just as a pounding of the heart sometimes signifies that the matter is expelled to the mouth of the stomach. And it signifies that the matter is violently attacking the heart. And perhaps there is one sign signifying a common thing coming to the movement toward one part, and other signs are expected which signify the manner in which it is expelled from that part, such as a headache and tightness of breath and tension of the hypochondria <term>hypochondria: the upper part of the abdomen, just below the ribs</term> toward the upper parts; for these signify that the matter moves to the upper parts. Then it is not judged whether it is expelled by way of vomiting or by way of a flow of blood from the nostrils except by other signs. And sometimes it is signified that the crisis falling from another part is a retention of that which usually runs and is separated from its opposite; just as the retention of nature with signs of a good crisis signifies that the critical movement is upward, not downward. Either by a flow of urine, or by sweat, or by vomiting, or by a flow of blood from the nostrils. 

And sometimes the species of the sickness is signified by the crisis, such as an abscess of the liver <note>original: "apostema hepatis"</note> which is said to be on its rounded <note>original: "gibboso"</note> side; then the crisis is either by a flow of blood from the right nostril, or by a laudable sweat, or by urine. And if it is on the hollow <note>original: "concavo"</note> side, it is by a flux of the belly, or by sweat, or by vomiting. And just as in a burning fever <term>burning fever: "causon," a severe, dehydrating fever</term>, its crisis is either by a flow of blood from the nostrils or by sweat, and it is preceded by a tremor; and sometimes it occurs by vomiting and a flux of the belly, especially as in a tertian fever <term>tertian fever: a fever that spikes every third day, typically malaria</term>. And similarly, the fever of an abscess of the head: the crisis never occurs by a flow of blood from the nostrils, nor in pneumonia, nor in lethargy. Pleurisy, however, is between this and that. And many sicknesses have crises in stages, by the aggregation of which the crisis is completed, just as a burning fever when it occurs; first by a flow of blood from the nostrils, then it is completed by an abundant sweat. And a pregnant woman has a crisis with a miscarriage <note>original: "abortu"</note>. 

And know that not whenever the signs of a crisis exist do they necessarily cause a good or bad crisis; rather, sometimes the crisis does not follow at all in that hour, although there is no excuse when the crisis follows them—without a doubt good or bad—in another hour than that hour in which the signs continue. For not every time you see sweat and vomiting and a flux of the belly and headache and disturbance of the senses or badness of breath or depth of sleep or...

**Or through a laudable sweat**: because in an abscess of the head, a crisis by a flow of blood from the left nostril would not be laudable.

**And many times**, etc. **And many times indeed.** Here Avicenna shows how one completed crisis can be completed through several alterations of the crisis, and how a pregnant woman has a crisis through miscarriage.

**And know that not every time.** After Avicenna has placed the signs of the crisis which are only signs, he can now place those which are signs and causes. And first he does this alone... judging the crisis from signs. The second is at "And of those." The first is in two parts: first he does this, secondly he declares it. The second is at "And sometimes." It could be divided: first he does this; secondly, concerning what was said, he places a rule or removes a doubt. The second is at "And when they appear." These are the sayings of Galen in many places: first in *On Crises* book 9, chapter 14, and book 11, and the commentary on that aphorism "Paroxysms," etc.

**And know that not.** Here he shows what follows from the signs of the crisis with them.

**For not every time.** It is with these crises, namely, completed, thus he explains. But it is doubted whether whenever signs of a crisis appear, a crisis follows. And it seems so: since one corollary is placed, the other is placed, etc. To the contrary is Avicenna here, and Galen in the places previously cited. The solution is that regarding the signs of a crisis which are only signs, a crisis does not necessarily follow; because, as Avicenna posits, these accidents can be caused by some cause other than a crisis. But to the signs of a crisis which are signs and causes, a completed crisis necessarily follows, not a diminished one; or a completed one necessarily always follows these. Avicenna understands this well as he was explaining. And Avicenna will place the cause, or remove the doubt, because he said that a crisis does not always follow the accidents of a crisis. Now someone might ask what signifies this. It should be noted that when the crisis is seen, Hippocrates... as Galen posits in the first book of *On Crises*, chapter 4, where he posits this opinion. And the cause is: because when the accidents of a crisis appear and the crisis does not occur, then a difficulty of the crisis is signified; or it signifies that the symptomatic matter was moved against nature, and then death is signified.

**And sometimes it is.** He declares what he had said: it is sworn that a crisis does not always follow the signs...

It specifically addresses how to distinguish between signs that truly belong to the crisis and those caused by other factors, as well as the symptoms that indicate where the "matter" of the disease is being expelled.</meta>
