Book 2, Treatise 1

<column-break/>

<margin>
a The well-being of the sick. He teaches first regarding the patient raising themselves into a sitting position.
b And when they are weighted down, he provides a sign based on the heaviness of the limbs.
c And it is a tremor. According to the physician.
d Often. Note <note>original: "Mo."/Nota</note> that there are three types of dreams: psychological <note>original: "animale," relating to the soul or mind</note>, revealed <note>prophetic or divine</note>, and natural. The psychological dream occurs when a person desires a thing intensely and thus dreams of it. The revealed dream is sometimes true and sometimes false. The natural dream, however, is that which occurs according to the process of the internal humors; the author here refers specifically and only to this type.
e Destruction. He provides a sign from the loss <note>original: "destructione"</note> of appetite.
f And when it is destroyed. He provides a sign from the loss of thirst. A contrary view is held by Hippocrates in his *Prognostics*, where he said that those whom the fever leaves on the day of the crisis <note>original: "rupture"</note> will escape, and you will twice announce they will desire food and not be thirsty; thus he shows that the loss of thirst in a fever is a good sign. However, when there is a cause present that should produce thirst and the patient does not feel it, then it is a bad sign, because it signifies that the sensory faculty has been destroyed and does not feel the irritation of the cause that ought to produce thirst. Avicenna shows this by the blackness of the tongue. Indeed, blackness of the tongue during a fever indicates causes that should produce thirst; therefore, if it does not, it is a bad sign.
g And it is according to. That is, it must be considered whether the majority of the matter causing the jaundice <note>original: "ictericiã"</note> is expelled through a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, which is a good sign, or whether the greater part goes to the skin and the lesser through the belly, which is a bad sign.
</margin>

### Signs derived from movements. Chapter 54.

An abundance of agitation and restlessness is not a good sign and signifies a great amount of vapor rising to the head. <a>The sudden health <note>apparent strength</note> of the patient at any hour or their sitting up is a bad sign; it occurs because of anguish, or because of a confusion of reason, or a constriction of the breath and suffocation. In pneumonia <note>original: "peripneumonia"</note> this is worse, as it is mostly due to suffocation and constriction of the breath, even if it might occur for other reasons. <b>And when the limbs are weighted down and difficult to move, it is also a bad sign. When the fingernails grow dark, then death is present. A tremor <c> is a bad sign when it is not part of a healthy crisis <note>the turning point of a disease</note>.

### Signs derived from the patient’s estimation. Chapter 55.

When there is an extreme fear of death, then there is cause for fear.

### Judgments derived from twitching and "alices." Chapter 56.

Twitching <note>original: "saltus"</note> and "alices" <note>a specific form of shuddering or restless movement</note> occur because nature moves the muscular limbs to expel superfluities <note>waste products</note> from them. While the limb remains clear and the matter is small and obedient, nature does not need this movement; rather, it is necessary to nature because of its opposite. If this occurs with a natural alternation of heat and cold, then it is not a bad sign. It often signifies <d> that nature cannot achieve a resolution <note>the dissolving of harmful humors</note> except with the help of the fibers <note>original: "villorum"</note>, either because of the quantity of the matter or the weakness of the patient's strength.

### Signs derived from dreams. Chapter 57.

Often the sick person sees a dream related to the nature of the coming crisis; for example, one about to undergo a crisis with sweating might dream that they are entering a bath prepared for them.

### Signs derived from appetite. Chapter 58.

The loss of appetite in chronic illnesses is bad.

<column-break/>

<margin>
h And it signifies malice. He provides signs distinguishing between good and bad jaundice.
i When the fever is acute. He provides the difference between an abscess <note>original: "apostẽa"</note> preceding the fever and one following it. But it is asked: Avicenna suggests that an abscess following a fever is worse than one preceding it, which does not seem true, for an abscess following a fever signifies a transformation of the feverish matter and thus a lessening of that matter. However, a fever following an abscess does not just follow an abscess of the extremities, but follows an abscess of the internal organs, especially in an acute fever, as Hippocrates said in his *Aphorisms* regarding buboes. Say then: if the abscess following the fever occurred by way of a critical expulsion, it would be better than one preceding it; however, when the abscess follows the fever and the fever is not diminished, then it is a sign of an abundance of matter and its malice <note>severity</note>, and therefore signifies a worse state than one preceding it.
k Abscesses which. He teaches prognosis through abscesses that occur at the root of the ear compared to evacuation. But against this, Galen in the first book of the *Prognostics* establishes a fourfold determination of an abscess: through resolution, through rotting, through hardening <note>original: "lapideitatem," turning to stone</note>, and through pus. Among these, he places resolution as the first and best. Therefore, these abscesses can be resolved by something other than resolution and still be good. Say then: these abscesses are made of thick matter that cannot be resolved nor determined by resolution. If they could be, it would be good—specifically when the abscess is not followed by any strong evacuations, such as diarrhea or sweating. Or say: by strong evacuations, such as evacuation through resolution, and then the first question is resolved. Evacuation through resolution is "strong" because it signifies that nature dominates the thick matter of the abscess so much that it refined it and sent it out through resolution.
l And if it is necessary. He provides a sign taken from the abscess because...
</margin>

And in acute illnesses, even if it is within that timeframe, at its height it signifies corrupted humors or the death of the psychological and natural powers. <e>And when thirst is lost during burning fevers, it is a bad sign, especially when accompanied by a blackening of the tongue.

### Judgments and meanings of jaundice. Chapter 59.

<f>Jaundice appearing before the seventh day and before digestion <note>of the humors</note> is a bad sign, unless it is relieved by a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, as some have thought. <g>And this depends on further consideration. Ultimately, jaundice before the seventh day is not praiseworthy. If jaundice occurs after the seventh day, it is again not very healthy as long as other signs are not joined to it. But if jaundice happens on the seventh, ninth, or fourteenth day with favorable signs and without harm to the liver or any hardness or abscess, then it is praiseworthy. Indeed, such a thing often happens because of a complete crisis, and it signifies a good outcome and a feeling of lightness found afterward. <h>The opposite of this lightness signifies the severity of the condition. Among the things that signify its severity is when the jaundice is accompanied by a heavy, boiling, choleric <note>yellow-bile-based</note> flux of the belly and the passing of burning, frothy matter; in such cases, one fears for the patient unless they are relieved by a great cleansing flux of the belly or a general sweat, and if their strength is still robust, for then lightness of the body follows quickly.

### Meanings derived from abscesses. Chapter 60.

<i>When an acute fever leads to abscesses <note>swelling or inflammation</note> in the armpits <note>original: "titillicorum"</note> and extremities, it is worse than if those abscesses had existed first and the fever followed them due to rot <note>putrefaction</note>, although the latter is also bad. <k>Abscesses that occur at the root of the ear and do not mature with pus are bad; or those which are not followed by any strong evacuations <note>cleansing of the body</note> are a bad sign. Again, one should not place trust in the "maturation" <note>coming to a head</note> of an abscess when a sore <note>original: "exitura"</note> appears while the remaining humors are still undigested; for that is insufficient, and such things often happen when a recovery is thought to be near, yet the patient dies.

<meta>This page continues the diagnostic classification within the second book of the medical manual. Having previously discussed patient positioning and behavioral signs, it now moves into specific physical manifestations of disease: pustules (blisters), abscesses, vascular changes, shivering, the "crisis" of evacuation, and the nature of sweating as a diagnostic tool.</meta>

Book 2

<margin>
a **Every pustule.** He provides a sign taken from an abscess <note>original: "apāte"/apostemate</note> that appears and then recedes. Note that if an abscess appears and then returns inward, it can be a good sign; because of this, namely, nature, after it has transmitted the matter to the skin, sensing itself perhaps stronger and more capable of digesting the matter of the abscess within the veins and viscera near the skin, pulls that transmitted matter back. In this way, it can signify the strength of nature, although this is a most unusual manner and very rarely occurs.
b **Pustule.** In this chapter, he provides a sign taken from a clear or black pustule. He teaches the prognosis regarding the final change toward various colors.
c **It is said that if it appears.** He provides signs from what are called "empirical" pustules; as if to say, it is said by experience but cannot be explained by reason.
d **When it appears.** He provides a sign taken from the appearance of a pustule in the throat.
e **It is said if it were.** He provides an empirical sign taken from a pustule appearing on the hand.
</margin>

Every pustule and every abscess <term>apostema; a localized collection of pus or a swelling</term> that appears and then recedes is bad. Nevertheless, it sometimes signifies the strength of nature, and perhaps this appearance and deepening is customary for someone of that particular nature, and therefore it is not a sign of extreme malice.

### Signs regarding pustules that resemble chickpeas. Lesson 61.

**A** black chickpea-like pustule <note>original: "pustula ciceralis," a common medieval description for plague-like sores or anthrax</note> in acute fevers is very bad. And when it comes at the end or is delayed, the one who has it frequently dies. The turning of ulcers on the body toward greenness, blackness, a celestial <note>sky blue or leaden</note> color, or yellowness is a bad sign. Of these, yellowness is the least severe. It is said that if something black like a black grape appears on the knee of the sick, and there is redness around it, they will die quickly. But if the illness lasts until the fiftieth day, then the sign of their death is that they break out in a cold sweat. When something like an *alkerna* grain <note>likely referring to the seed of the henna plant or a similar dark berry</note> appears over the vein in the throat along with a large white pock-mark <note>original: "variola"</note>, and the patient feels a desire for hot things, they will die on the twentieth day. We have already spoken of those deadly pustules that happen on the tongues of youths. It is said that if there is any fever and a black abscess appears on the fingers of both hands at once, like a grain of barley <note>original: "berbi"</note>, accompanied by intense pain, the patient will die on the fourth day and will experience a heavy and deep sleep. If nature is constricted with this, pleurisy will occur. And sometimes it is constricted so much until it becomes like stone.

### Signs taken from the form of the veins. Chapter 62.

**H**ippocrates said: if small veins appear on the forehead, the eyelids, and the hollow of the neck <note>original: "furcula," the 'little fork' at the base of the throat</note>, it is bad. An alteration in the heat of the visible veins from their normal state—with a "peacock-like" shimmering <note>original: "calore pauonis," likely referring to an iridescent or mottled appearance of the skin over the veins</note>—and the appearance of veins that were not visible before, is a bad sign.

<margin>
f **Shivering frequently.** Note that this chapter is founded upon that aphorism: "If shivering occurs in a fever while strength is not failing," and upon the commentary of that text.
</margin>

### Signs taken from shivering. Chapter 63.

**S**hivering <term>rigor; a sudden feeling of cold with shivering, often preceding a fever</term> that returns frequently in a severe fever with weakness of strength is mortal. Even when strength is firm, if the fever is not removed by it, it is not good. The worst of all is when an unhelpful evacuation <note>diarrhea or vomiting that provides no relief</note> follows the shivering, and the patient is not calmed by it because the matter cannot be expelled; this is bad. When it happens only once, perhaps the aphorism is not verified, as one must judge whether it is due to an excessive weakness of strength or something else.

<margin>
g **Evacuation.** Here he describes helpful evacuation by its types and properties.
h **And regarding.** He provides a sign of evacuation in quantity.
i **Black blood.** Conversely, it is not always the case that the change of evacuation to black blood is bad. Unless it flows when the black blood itself is evil, then its evacuation is not bad. Say that the evacuation is bad because medicine ought not to evacuate black blood; therefore, if it does, it is bad. Or, as some say, that blackness signifies that nature has fought against the matter, or that the medicine has stripped the matter away.
k **Or fetid humor.** Conversely, a fetid humor is bad while staying inside the limbs and nature, therefore its evacuation should be good. Say, as is told in the commentary on the *Prognostics*, that nothing is so fetid as that which evacuates the very substance of the limbs; this is also seen in those with "ethics" <note>likely "hectics" or consumptive fevers</note> who are in the final stage of wasting away.
</margin>

### Judgment of evacuation. Lesson 64.

**A** helpful evacuation through a flow of the bowels, vomiting, or other means is that which occurs after digestion <term>coction; the process where the body 'cooks' or matures the disease-causing humors</term>, which evacuates the humor that ought to be expelled, happens with ease, and is followed by a feeling of lightness. And regarding the si-

<column-break/>

<margin>
m **And when.** He notes when we ought to help nature in evacuating and when not.
n **And evacuation.** He teaches how to interpret the quantity of the evacuation.
</margin>

-gns of the evacuation of the humor—whether by medicine or not—the rule is that it should begin with the evacuation of the specific humor intended; it is worse if the end result changes to a cured discharge, or to black blood, or a fetid humor, or a pure humor. The same applies to vomiting. When the evacuation is cut short after it has done what it should, it ought to be assisted. But when the evacuation is excessive and digestion has not yet begun, then it is not something to be relied upon for help. A weak and meager evacuation—whether by nosebleed, sweat, or otherwise—signifies that nature moved but was not strong enough. If other bad signs appear, they signify death; if no bad signs appear, they signify a long illness.

<margin>
o **Sweat is a good crisis.** Here he objects: since a crisis through sweat occurs in fevers of intense heat, as found in the 3rd book, chapter 1; but a phlegmatic illness is from cold matter. Furthermore, the second book's chapter on sweat says that sweat is the wateriness of blood mixed with choleric pus. Therefore, in a phlegmatic illness, sweat does not happen by way of a good crisis. To this, authorities say that a crisis through sweat is better and more suitable in acute fevers than in chronic ones, yet it is still good in chronic ones because nature has moistened and refined the matter so that it expels it through sweats.
p **And again.** He calls "fearful abscesses" those which occur in the internal organs from "furious" <note>violent or toxic</note> matter.
</margin>

### Judgments of sweat. Lesson 65.

**S**weat is a good crisis <term>turning point in a disease</term> in acute and phlegmatic illnesses, and also in types of fearful abscesses and abscesses of the internal organs <note>original: "viscerum"</note>.

### The cause of excessive sweat. Chapter 66.

**S**weat increases either because of the matter—due to its abundance or its thinness—or because of the strength of the expulsive power, or the softening of the retentive power, or because the pores are dilated. Sweat decreases due to the opposites of these causes. When sweat is wiped away, it tends to overflow, but when the body is moved, it is cut off.

### Diversity of the limbs in sweating. Chapter 67.

**T**he limbs that sweat the most are those in which the matter causing the illness is most present. Those that do not sweat are the limbs in which there is no such matter, or those where factors causing the constriction of the pores dominate. Among these is the fact that the side upon which the sick person sleeps rarely sweats, since it is compressed, having dry passages, and moisture neither flows to it nor from it. Sweat increases in the posterior parts, such as the back, more than in the anterior parts like the chest; and it increases in the upper parts more than the lower parts, and specifically in the head.

<margin>
q **Sleep more.** Here he provides the specific cause for why more sweating occurs in sleep than in waking.
r **Hippocrates says.** He provides the second aphorism of Hippocrates, and explains it further there.
</margin>

### Diversity of dispositions in sweating and other things. Lesson 68.

**S**leep causes more sweating than waking because the innate heat acts more upon the humors during sleep, and because the hindrance of breath is lessened, which moves matter toward the outer parts. Hippocrates says: excessive sweat in sleep without an obvious cause signifies that the person is taking more food into his body than he can process. But if this happens regardless of how much food he takes, then know that he requires evacuation. The cause of this is that excessive sweat while the patient's strength is healthy only occurs because of a multitude of matter which nature feels compelled to expel; and that multitude is either caused by an immediate cause, which is immediate repletion <note>over-fullness</note>, and...

Fen II, Treatise I

<margin>
a **And it does not excuse.** But judges say that hunger and exercise will not expel those things, as mentioned previously. He says that hunger and exercise are not suitable for humors that are ready to putrefy.
b **And you should know.** Here he shows how sweat happens because of the weakness of nature <note>The "nature" of the body refers to its innate healing power or vital force.</note> and not because of another cause of sweating.
c **Sweat.** In this chapter, he determines the nature of sweat, even in relation to critical days.
d **And rarely.** A doubt is raised: why does he say that acute diseases rarely cause a crisis on the fourth day? And yet he shows that it sometimes happens. This seems to contradict Galen, who says in the third book of *On Crises* that he never saw a crisis on the fourth day except once, and Archideus twice. The answer is that Galen understood this regarding diseases that proceed by an uneven movement <note>original: "motu impari"</note>, such as those that proceed by a "concluded" movement. In diseases that proceed by an uneven movement, there is no crisis on the fourth day, or at least it is the worst hour of the entire period. Diseases proceeding by an even movement are all "critical," as Galen says, and therefore a crisis does not happen to them on the fourth day. Those that proceed by a "concluded" movement can have a crisis on the fourth day because they are acute and do not have clear distinctions between their feverish attacks <note>original: "paroxismorū"</note>, which afflict the patient continuously.
</margin>

Immediate repletion <term>an overfullness of the body's vessels or systems</term> comes from foods recently taken, and this repletion is expelled by hunger, exercise, and sweat. Sweat that is expelled by nature either occurs through a distant antecedent cause—which comes from pre-existing superfluities—and in such cases, nothing excuses the patient except a cleansing evacuation that purifies the body of them. Through sweat, however, perhaps nothing leaves the body except that which is subtle, thin, and small, leaving the corrupt matter behind; it is the nature of the body to desire to expel the corrupt humor, and this is one of the things that weakens it. ¶ And you should know that the stronger the innate heat <note>original: "caliditas innata"; the vital heat believed to drive digestion and life</note>, the more hidden the resolution of fluids is; therefore, sweat does not occur unless there are other causes. Because of this, sweat occurs either from nature, or from repletion and a great volume of fluid, and the intense dilation of the pores, or due to a failure of the body's power to achieve good digestion, or due to the intensity of movement.

### Days in which sweat is increased or decreased. Chapter 69.

Sweat in acute diseases occurs most often on the third and fifth days, and is decreased on the fourth; indeed, it rarely happens that these diseases reach a crisis on the fourth day. ¶ And it rarely happens—as experienced practitioners believe—that a patient sweats on the twenty-seventh, thirty-first, or thirty-fourth days.

### The ways sweat provides signs. Chapter 70.

Sweat signifies through its touch, whether it is hot or cold. It signifies through its color, whether it is clear or declining toward lemon-yellow or green. It signifies through its taste, whether it is bitter, sweet, or declining toward acidity. ¶ It signifies through its odor, whether it is foul, acidic, sweet, or something else. It signifies through its substance, such as whether it is thin or viscous. ¶ It signifies through its quantity, whether it is little or much. It signifies by its location, whether it is common to the whole body or localized; whichever member it comes from, the disease is in that place. It signifies through its timing, whether it is at the beginning, the peak <note>original: "statu"</note>, or the decline of the illness. And it signifies by what follows it, such as whether distress, relief, rigor <note>shivering</note>, "goosebumps" <note>original: "horripilatio"</note>, or something else follows.

### Signs taken from the nature of sweat. Chapter 71.

Cold sweat during the heat of a fever is a very bad sign, especially that which is localized to the head and neck. ¶ It signifies syncope <term>a sudden loss of consciousness or fainting</term>; if sweat that is not cold signifies this, how much more so when it is cold? It is the worst of the types of sweat

<margin>
e **Sweat signifies.** Here he provides the ways according to which significations are taken from sweat.
f **Cold sweat.** ¶ Here he determines the signs taken from cold sweat and makes two points: first, he shows what cold sweat signifies. Second, he provides the manner of significance and the generation of cold sweat; the second part begins at "And sweat does not occur."
g **And sweat.** ¶ He provides a sign taken from the quantity of sweat.
h **And when after.** ¶ He provides a comparison between the distribution of sweat over the body and its benefits.

n **And finally.** He determines the significance of sweat according to its specific properties.

Note that above he was speaking of a person currently in a fever; here he speaks of one who is convalescing <note>recovering</note>.

q **Formicating.** That is, very weak with diversity. *Scribnus* is a diverse pulse with hardness. *Undosus* is "wavy."

because it signifies a thing that has already happened, not a thing that will be. ¶ If the fever is great, then death is near. ¶ And cold sweat does not occur unless the innate heat has already failed, which is why it no longer preserves the moistures; instead, it is separated from them, causing them to be set apart, and the "extrinsic" heat evaporates. Then that heat is separated from them because of its foreign nature, by which they are cooled. Interrupted sweat is bad. ¶ And profuse sweat signifies a long duration of illness because of the large amount of matter; bloodletting <note>original: "phlobotomia"</note> and purging of the belly are not suitable for one having this because of their weakness; rather, use light enemas <note>original: "clisteria"</note>. And when relief is not found after sweating, it is not a good sign. ¶ But if it causes an increase in distress, then it will be a bad sign even if it is common to the whole body. ¶ And sweat that comes too early at the beginning of an illness is bad. ¶ It signifies a multitude of matter <note>excess humors</note> unless the cause is the moisture of the air due to much rain, for then the malice will be less. ¶ And often an illness begins with sweat, followed by fever, and it is prolonged. ¶ And when shivering follows sweat, it is not good, but rather bad, because shivering signifies the spreading of a bad, harmful humor in the body; this signifies that the sweat is not cleansing the body, but rather moving the bad humors whose sharpness has been broken, mixing them with the moistures being resolved through sweat. It signifies that most of the matter is not being resolved by the evacuation of sweat. And when the strength and the pulse are weakened and the forehead sweats a little, it is a bad sign. If the pulse fails, then it is death. For a good sweat—which is suitable for a complete crisis—is that which occurs on a critical day, is common to the whole body, is abundant, and the sick person is relieved by it. ¶ Next best is that which is not common to the whole body but is followed by relief. ¶ And finally, consider the sweat itself in its heat and coldness, its color, its odor and taste, and its quantity (whether much or little), and the time of its exit (whether at the beginning, peak, or decline). Also consider what is associated with it regarding the fever's strength or weakness, and what follows it in terms of relief or heaviness. ¶ And you should know that in convalescence, a person's sweat increases because of the remains of the humors, and therefore it is not bad to perform a small bloodletting <note>original: "minutionem"</note>.

### Signs taken from the pulse. Chapter 72.

A hammer-like <term>martellinus; a pulse that feels like a double-beat or a hammer strike</term>, formicating <term>formicans; a tiny, rapid pulse like ants crawling</term>, extremely fragile, or wavy <term>undosus</term> pulse is bad. And a gazelle-like <term>gazellinus; a pulse that jumps or double-beats like a leaping gazelle</term> pulse with weakness is bad. And a diversity in which there is a strong interruption and weak movements, followed by a single strong beat that provides no lasting help but only momentary strength, is very bad.

Fourth: "and better." The first judgment is taken from the illnesses that are terminated by a nosebleed. It should be noted that the text says "just like pleurisy," but it ought to say "just like phrenitis" <note>original: "phrenesis," a term for inflammation of the brain or brain fever</note>, and so the Jewish text <note>Likely referring to a Hebrew translation or commentary</note> holds it. And he says that pleurisy is between these two dispositions. Avicenna says that the first abscess from whichever nostril makes a crisis; however, this does not happen in pleurisy because it occurs either on the right side (and then the crisis is through the right nostril) or on the left side (and the crisis is through the left). Phrenitis, however, involves both nostrils.

There are some illnesses, like pleurisy and acute or hot abscesses of the liver and those under the hypochondria, that are terminated by a complete crisis through a flow of blood from the nose. Philaretus says the 13th is the essential day, but the 14th is the accidental critical day; these words are understood to mean that the 13th is essentially critical regarding the movement of the illness, but the 14th is critical regarding the completion of the crisis through celestial help. Avicenna says clearly below regarding critical days, and Galen in his final word on critical days, that the 15th day is midway between a critical and non-critical day.

### Signs taken from the excretion. 77.

A diversity of color in that which comes out in the excretion is praiseworthy in two instances (excluding white): one is a critical diversity after digestion on a critical day and with a critical sign. The other is after taking a strong laxative potion, and in these two dispositions, it signifies the expected cleansing of the body. In other cases, however, it signifies "burning" <note>original: "adustio," a state where humors are over-cooked or charred by fever</note>, liquefaction, and a multitude of corrupt humors. A fetid excretion, similar to the excretion of children or of a rotting nature, is bad. A bilious <note>original: "cholerica"</note> excretion at the beginning of an illness signifies the dominion of yellow bile and is not good; but at the end of the illness, during its decline, it signifies that the body is being cleansed and is a good sign. But when a great bilious excretion separates and the illness is not relieved, then that is a bad sign. And a great flux of the belly after bad signs signifies a collapse of the vital force; and unless lightness follows, it is a sign of death, even if the fever seems to have been uprooted. A flux of the belly upon which there is an oily film from the intake of oily things signifies the liquefaction of the radical members <note>The "radical members" were the primary organs like the heart, liver, and brain.</note>, and is a bad sign, but not always fatal; perhaps the oiliness is from the flesh. And when there is a pus-like substance on it, and it flows out yellow and a stench dominates, that is fatal in acute fevers. Excretion upon which a thin substance sits signifies that there is poison from the liver; it is biting and causes the excretion to exit with speed, and perhaps it exits alone, which is bad. When there are things like the husks of lupine seeds in the excretion in any illness, it is a fatal sign.

### Judgments of vomit. 80.

There has already been a place for discussion in the first book concerning vomit. It is necessary that we state something here about it and other things, as the explanation is more appropriate in this place. I say, therefore, that the most helpful vomit is that which is "phlegmatic" and "choleric" <note>A mix of phlegm and bile.</note>, in which there is a strong mixing in the matter vomited or poured out, and it is not of extreme thickness. And the "purer" the vomit is, the worse it is. For pure bilious vomit signifies extreme heat, and pure phlegm signifies extreme cold.

q ¶ And when it is converted: and it multiplies in the hour of total exacerbation, or in the hour of the increase or the "status" <note>The peak of the disease.</note>, it signifies raw, thick matter.
</margin>

### Judgments of urine. 80.

Universal words concerning urine have already been set forth by us in Fen 1, in which there are accidents in the first book, and we shall state here about that and others what is more convenient to this place. I say, therefore, that not everything that does not show a sign of digestion in the urine should be judged as death; for perhaps the patient will be freed from this through an evacuation falling from some part with the power of expelling the digested and undigested matter. Or perhaps the humors will be resolved according to the length of tolerance, or a crisis will occur through an abscess <note>original: "exitura"</note>, especially when the humors were not of extreme malice. It signifies the strength of the sick person, and the minor sign in it is concerning the length of the illness. And similarly, urine that remains according to the color of healthy urine in all hours of the illness: if it begins to be altered with the heightening of the illness, then it is more safe. And sometimes in pestilential illnesses, the urine is "naturally good" in its substance, color, and sediment, yet the one to whom it belongs is going toward death. And you should know that many times a sick person passes bad urine in substance and color, yet that is a critical expulsion, especially in acute illnesses whose cause is the liver and the parts of the urine.

### Bad signs taken from the scarcity and abundance of urine. 81.

Urine that is passed sometimes little and sometimes much, and that which is retained and not passed, is a bad sign in acute fevers, signifying a fierce battle between the illness and nature. It signifies the labor of nature and the thickness of the matter, and that it accepts digestion with difficulty. If, however, the fevers are quiet, it indicates a long duration because of the thickness of the humor.

# Book III

<margin>As Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (980–1037 AD) whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard medical textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> used to state in the chapter on the signs of crisis via an abscess: then the urine appears thin, etc. Whence through the urine one knows [the state] by the fourth [day]. Either through a flow of blood from the nostrils or through urine; because the thicker matter is expelled through urine and the thinner through the nostrils.</margin>
<margin>White urine in illnesses provides signs based on color. First from the color white; second from black; third from red; fourth from pale or yellow. Note there: "You should know." The third [part] there: "Red urine." The fourth there: "In acute fever." The first in two [parts] because burnt urine universally signifies the diversion of matter from the urinary vessels. Then, therefore, either some bad signs appear: and then, as the matter is thin, it signifies a headache; or it is thick: and then it means it is fixed in some member and becomes an abscess <note>original: "apostemat"; a swelling or internal collection of pus.</note>; or good signs appear: because the signs of the crisis itself signify vomiting, etc.</margin>

and with it there is a constant thirst, a frequency in rising to urinate, and an ease of passage. And sometimes it happens because of rawness and a blockage preventing the exit of the matter; and sometimes it happens because of a weakness in the transformative power <note>The body's internal ability to process or "cook" the humors.</note> and not with ease of passage, and it is of less malice than diabetes. And when thin urine is passed in acute illnesses for several days, it signifies a mixing [of humors]. If this mixing occurs and the thinness persists, it signifies rapid death because the matter moves into the brain and the soul is taken away. And when it turns to thickness without any relief, it is perhaps due to the liquefaction of the members <note>The medieval belief that internal tissues were literally melting due to excessive fever heat.</note>. If watery urine is multiplied at the hour of the total fever's exacerbation, it signifies that the soul <note>original: "aia" (anima); referring here to the vital spirit or life force.</note> has moved into the lower parts. And consider the substance mixed with color in the chapters that follow. And know that thinness is such that it should not be joined to blackness or redness. If it is, then know the cause in this is a staining thing or the intensity of the power of the diseased quality imprinting itself into the water.

### Signs taken from the thickness of the substance and its disturbance. Ch. 83.

**W**hen thin urine is converted into thick in a continuous fever and there are good signs, it signifies a crisis accompanied by sweat. If, however, there are no good signs, or there is a fever of intense burning, it signifies inflammation in the heart or in the liver. And the clearing of thick urine before a crisis is not a good sign; for that signifies the retention of the matter and a failure of nature in expelling it. Thick, turbulent urine in which nothing settles and which does not clear signifies a boiling of the humors because of the intensity of external heat and a weakness of the innate digestive power, which is why it is bad. When the urine is thick, and specifically on the fourth [day], it multiplies the crisis of fevers caused by exhaustion, especially if it is associated with a flow of blood from the nostrils.

### Signs taken from white urine. Ch. 84.

**W**hite urine in acute illnesses signifies a declination of the matter away from the veins and the urinary organs; perhaps it declines toward the brain and there will be a headache or phrenitis <note>original: "phrenesis"; a state of delirium or brain fever.</note>, and perhaps it declines toward certain viscera and signifies an abscess <note>original: "a p̃a" (apostema).</note>. And if there are signs toward recovery, these declinations signify that it will be discharged mostly through vomiting, specifically when there is no sign of a bowel movement followed by an excoriation of the intestines. And when the urine is thin and white in an acute fever, and then a disturbance and thickness occurs along with its whiteness, it signifies a spasm and death.

### Signs taken from color in black urine in acute fevers. Ch. 85.

**K**now that a judgment of death is not entirely confirmed by the blackness of the urine's color in acute illnesses, although in itself it is a bad sign; even if other bad signs are associated with it, when you see the vital force <note>original: "virtutem"; the patient's internal strength.</note> is strong and capable of producing various evacuations of every kind, recovery follows. This happens to women when they are purged of bad humors with their menses; for this reason, these women are healthier because perhaps for some reason they are accustomed to being evacuated of such matter by way of the menses. And know that black urine is worse the scantier it is, signifying the consumption of moisture; and again, the thicker it is, the worse it is in acute illnesses.

<column-break/>

And when the black [urine] tends toward being fine and thin, and there is a suspended sediment in it, and it has a sharp odor in acute fevers, it indicates a headache and a mixing [of humors]; the most certain of its dispositions is that it signifies a flow of black blood from the nostrils because the matter is sharp and dominant. Perhaps there will be sweat with it because of the heat, when it neither overflows nor diminishes, and it expels toward the superfluities and precedes the sweat and the bristling of the hair. And when black urine (in which there is a suspended sediment) is associated with a black, round, aggregated mass accompanied by a bad odor, tension in the sides, an abscess under the hypochondria <note>The region of the abdomen just under the lower ribs.</note>, and sweat, it signifies death; and indeed, tension under the hypochondria signifies a spasm. This kind of sweat arises from weakness. Thin, watery urine tending toward blackness signifies by its thinness the length of the illness, and by its blackness its malice. And it is said regarding thin black urine that when the one who passes it desires food, they shall die. And when thin black urine converts to a whitish or yellow color and becomes thick, and no rest is associated with it, it signifies a declining illness; in the liver, it signifies jaundice <note>original: "icteritia".</note>, for this conversion from thinness to thickness and from blackness to whitishness signifies a diminution of heat and a failure of digestion. And that is among those things which are associated with or followed by a lightness [of spirit]. If it is not because of that, it signifies matter already stuck in the liver and not because of a cleansing; it has already caused an obstruction; indeed, if there is heat, then it will suddenly cause abscesses to occur. Thin black urine that is passed little by little in acute fevers over a long time, when it is accompanied by pain in the head and neck, signifies the gradual destruction of reason; this is more survivable in women.

### Signs taken from red urine. Ch. 86.

**R**ed urine in acute illnesses, when it is thin with its redness, signifies—with favorable signs—a rapid crisis; with contrary signs, it signifies a rapid death and, overall, intense inflammation. Thinness with redness in acute illnesses signifies headache and a mixing [of humors]. And thick red urine in acute illnesses, when its passage occurs little by little and frequently and with a foul odor, signifies fear, for it signifies intense heat, illness, and a failure of nature. But when there is an abundant exit of much sediment, it signifies a separation [of humors], especially in burning fevers. And one who passes pure blood in acute illness dies, for it signifies an intense fullness of blood with sharp boiling; there is fear of suffocation of the heart's ventricles if it moves toward the heart, or apoplexy if it moves toward the brain. Very red urine, if it turns thick in fevers caused by exhaustion and then much sediment appears that does not sink, and there is a headache, it signifies a long illness because the matter is disobedient; therefore it does not thicken early, and after it thickens, it does not settle quickly; indeed, its crisis occurs through sweat because the matter has moved toward the veins. This kind of urine resembles the urine of jaundice, but differs from it in that it does not stain cloth. Finally, the substance of red urine and red sediment signifies appetite and rawness; it signifies a long duration when the redness is not intense and is that which tends toward turbulence.

### Signs taken from yellow urine. Ch. 87.

**Y**ellow urine in an acute fever is bad when it turns toward white or black: through whiteness, it signifies the rising of matter to the head, and through blackness, the sharpness of the illness's quality.

### Signs taken from the sediment. Ch. 88.

**S**ediment that is diverse in substance and color, signifying a multitude of different humors, is bad; and worse than that is sediment made of smaller parts, for it signifies that nature cannot expel it except after the parts are diminished. Light and white sediment is often more indicative of goodness. And often he whose sediment tends toward redness but is light survives. But he whose sediment tends toward whiteness but is of a diverse appearance dies. For the goodness of the substance is more powerful and ready to undergo expulsion than the goodness of color; it also signifies that the humors are not suffering much from the illness. Just as good sediment, when its parts are diminished, signifies that nature has already worked upon it greatly and the illness has not acted upon it. Foamy sediment, full of bubbles, whose whiteness is due to the mixing of air with it, is very bad, departing from nature; and raw [sediment] is bad. And it is better for the upper parts [of the urine] to be round and moving than for the sediment to be sufficiently congealed on the top.

### Fen II, Treatise I
**Page p ii**

it is more significant that the illness is of a fast and acute state. And sediment that is not preceded by thinness and a small amount of excess, but rather is found right at the beginning, signifies that the humor is very abundant rather than digested; indeed, it is expected that the sediment should turn red after digestion arrives, and after the urine has been thin at first and after the sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"; the bottom-most layer of urine sediment.</note> was sparse. When it is not so, it signifies that the matter is heavy, thick, and abundant, and that the illness is lethal; likewise, an intense color <note>original: "tincture"; the depth of the urine's pigment.</note> without even a little sediment is a bad sign. When it is not so, it does not signify good, though sometimes it signifies good and maturity <note>original: "maturitatem"; the "cooking" or processing of humors by the body.</note>. Sometimes this happens because of pain, or because of the intensity of heat and hunger; for the color of the urine is increased by fasting, while its sediment is diminished. Red sediment signifies a multitude of blood and a delay in digestion, and in burning fevers, it is joined by distress and sadness; if it lasts until the fortieth day, the illness is prolonged, and perhaps a crisis is not hoped for until the fortieth. Again, red sediment that is suspended—where there is a shifting toward the upper parts—when it is in thin urine, signifies a confusion of the mind <note>original: "permistionem rationis"; delirium or mental disturbance.</note> in acute illnesses; if it persists, death is feared. But if the substance of the urine begins to reach a thickness, and the suspended matter begins to sink and turns white, it signifies health. Sediment that is shaped like a scrap of meat <note>original: "frusti carnis"</note> in acute fevers without signs of digestion signifies that it comes from the scraping of the limbs and not from the kidneys; when there is digestion there, or if there is no fever, it signifies what you already know about the condition of the kidneys. That which is like fish scales, where there is no sign of digestion and the fever is acute, comes from the "scraping" caused by the fever in the nerves, bones, and veins; in other cases, it comes from the bladder. Bran-like <note>original: "furfureum"</note> sediment signifies something similar, indicating that the fever is beginning to "scrape" from the depths; one distinguishes between this and that which comes from the bladder because the bladder sediment is accompanied by signs of injury to the bladder, along with digestion and thickness. Signs taken from combined conditions due to the diverse significations of color and substance, the first of which is in oily urines. L.lxxxix

Oily urine is that whose color and substance resemble the color and substance of oil; although it is bad, nevertheless, when other signs indicate health, there is no evil in it. But sediment, when it is oily, is very bad; and entirely pure oily urine is bad, which makes you see the color of oil with yellow and green tints. When oily urine occurs after black urine, it is a good sign, as Rufus the Wise <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a 1st-century Greek physician.</note> testifies. The worst oily urine is that which appears at the beginning of an illness. When the signs indicate malice and the patient passes oily urine on the fourth day, it indicates the death of the sick person on the sixth. Urine that changes suddenly from praiseworthy signs to blameworthy signs signifies death in acute illnesses, for it signifies a sudden fall of strength <note>original: "uirtutis"; the body's vital faculty.</note> due to the wickedness of the symptoms. Oily urine sometimes signifies mental confusion because it is caused by drying out. Urine in which there are pieces of clotted blood in an acute fever, when the tongue is dry, is a bad sign; if it is black with this, then it is worse. Blood does not run in the urine in an acute fever except because of the intensity of its sharpness, which breaks the vessels and its paths; its clotting is due to the intensity of the heat. Thin white urine in which there is foam and yellow clouds signifies great fear because of what it indicates regarding the exacerbation and intensity of the sharpness of the matter. We have already spoken sufficiently regarding thin black urine. Thin yellow urine at the start of acute fevers, when it turns to thickness and whiteness and then remains dreggy and turbid like the urine of a donkey, and begins to exit involuntarily while there is wakefulness and restlessness, signifies a spasm of both sides, which is followed by death when there are no good signs to overcome them. For urine with a yellow color is not thinned except due to the dominance of the hot choleric humor, and it does not thicken and densify except due to the exacerbation of the illness and the commotion in the conditions of the matter. They have said of scanty urine that is the color of blood that it is bad, especially when the patient has a poisonous passion <note>original: "passio venenosa"; likely a toxic or malignant condition.</note>.

### Bad signs regarding the quality of urine separation. L.xc.

When a patient suffering from an acute fever cannot urinate except for a little with pain, without a wound or abscess in the urinary instruments, and with a frequent and weak pulse, it is a bad sign. When urine is retained in a continuous fever and there is intense headache and much sweating, it signifies a persistent headache <note>original: "cuzegi"; a medieval term derived from Arabic meaning a severe, chronic headache.</note>. Urine that drips drop by drop in a continuous fever with intense headache and much sweating signifies a persistent headache. And urine that drips <meta>catchword: drips</meta>

<column-break/>

drop by drop in a quiet fever signifies a flow of blood from the nostrils. But if the fever is acute and burning, it signifies a bad condition coming to the brain. And if it is quiet, it signifies a great fullness <note>original: "repletionis"; an excess of humors.</note> and a weakness of nature in expelling it. When urine exits involuntarily in acute fevers, there is a weakness of the vital power or an injury in the brain; this only happens because of the ascent of sharp, heated matter to the brain, because the muscular members communicate with it.

### Numbering of bad signs in urine. L.xci.

Watery, preceding, foul-smelling, black, and thick urine is bad. And that in which a vapor like smoke rises from its inner part to its surface is a sign of near death. Again, fatty urine whose color is the color of meat-water with a dominant stench is mortal.

### Bad signs in the sick of various types whose malice is due to their aggregation in feverish patients and others. L.xcii.

<margin>
a. When they are aggregated. He presents a prognostic sign combined from bad conditions of the stomach and brain; for the movement and piercing pain signify a lesion of the brain; and because of the thing that is... of the stinging matter or because of the compassion that the brain feels for the hot matter of the brain.
</margin>
When vomiting, piercing pain, and mental confusion are aggregated, it is a mortal sign.
<margin>
b. Mental confusion signifies a lesion of the brain due to a hot abscess of the brain or due to compassion for the stomach; for in the stomach there is a hot abscess whose vapors ascend to the head and cause confusion; hence, when these happen together, it signifies either an abscess of the stomach only, or of both, and for that reason, they signify death.
</margin>
<margin>
c. When they are aggregated. He presents a prognostic sign combined from the diversity of things felt and seen and that which is evacuated.
</margin>
When the alteration of the body varies in touch, color, and in what is vomited and evacuated, it signifies that nature is ambiguous with diverse humors and illnesses, all of which it is necessary to resist; it is undoubtedly among those things that fail the body.
<margin>
d. When they are aggregated. He presents a prognostic sign combined from apparent coldness and burning of the lower parts and intense thirst. This is from the fourth particle. In those not failing, i.e., if the extremities are cold.
</margin>
When, in an inseparable fever, the coldness of what is external and the burning of the interior parts are aggregated with intense thirst, then it is mortal.
<margin>
e. When they are aggregated. Here he presents a prognostic sign combined from the cold appearance of the teeth and mental confusion. And this is the prognosis of the first book of Hippocrates' Prognostics: "If they grind their teeth in madness, death is near."
</margin>
When mental confusion is aggregated with the percussion <note>original: "percussione"; grinding or chattering.</note> of the teeth, the sick person approaches death.
<margin>
f. When they occur. A sign aggregated from a bad condition of the belly and heart; suddenly through this, it is shown if there is a movement of the crisis.
</margin>
When a black flow of the bowels suddenly happens to the sick person with burning, stinging, and parching pain in the belly, along with a racing heart and fainting, it is a sign of death.
<margin>
g. When they sweat. A prognosis of Hippocrates in the first book of Prognostics when he says: a cold sweat is bad if on the neck, chest, and head alone, for in acute fever it signifies death; in a slow fever, however, it signifies a plurality. Hippocrates in the second book of Prognostics: If a livid color mixed with green appears in the fingernails, it signifies impending death.
</margin>
When the two corners of the forehead sweat with cold sweat, and the nails turn yellow and green and are altered, and the tongue is swollen <note>original: "apatu"; from "apostema", an abscess or swelling.</note> and a strange pustule appears on it and on the body, then death is near. And if there is a throbbing and jumping in the parts of the hypochondria <note>The upper abdomen below the ribs.</note> with fever, and then the eye moves with a bad movement, then a wicked condition must be expected; for this condition signifies an accumulation of wind and the throbbing that happens because of a powerful abscess and the intense constriction of the great vein. A continuous, very large pulse of intense throbbing is associated with mania, and it must be considered. For perhaps the throbbing and jumping are not submerged in the viscera, but rather appear in the abdominal wall <note>original: "mirac"; an Arabic-derived term for the abdominal muscles/wall.</note>; this is not harmful when an abscess is with it unless it exceeds greatly in size. If this condition persists for twenty days and the abscess and fever do not subside, it signifies that it will open, and then perhaps the sick person will be saved; that will be through exuberant urine or a shift of the matter to the extremities, especially to the feet. Those who are weakened by illnesses, when frequent gasping and fainting happen to them, they are already approaching death and will not last more than four hours. When a person has a burning fever and finds a sudden relief and quiet from the heat without a manifest crisis through evacuation or shift, and without ultimate extinction and without shift...

### Signs of the Length of Illness. L. xciii.

<image-desc>A circular emblem containing a cross-like symbol.</image-desc>
<margin>p</margin> Know that the length <margin>x</margin> of an illness happens because of thickness in the viscera or because of a mixing in the regions, for every disposition is weakened in it. When the slowness <margin>o</margin> of digestion touches it, and an even digestion <margin>q</margin> signifies it, or the slowness of the hanging sediment, or the persistence of red sediment (though a small amount of sediment signifies length of illness), it indicates a long disease. <margin>p</margin> And similarly <margin>r</margin> when there is a large pulse along with the sharpness of the illness, and the face is "fat" <note>swollen or puffy</note>, and <margin>t</margin> the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>The upper abdominal region.</note> are inflated and do not subside, it signifies a lack of resolution and a long illness. <margin>q</margin> When the <margin>q</margin> signs of a <term>crisis</term> <note>The turning point of a disease where the patient either recovers or declines.</note> arrive before digestion is complete, and the patient's strength does not fall and signs of death do not appear, then the illness is prolonged. And know <margin>s</margin> that the terrifying nature of a crisis, when it neither helps nor harms and the dispositions remain in their own way, means the illness is long. And a multitude <margin>r</margin> of "jumping" <note>twitching or palpitations</note> in an illness signifies its length, <margin>z</margin> especially when it is violent from the start of the matter. At the end, however, it is more favorable. And when <margin>u</margin> it is associated with a few evacuations, it signifies that nature has moved the matter but failed in expelling it—whether it be a flow of blood from the nose or other good signs—or the absence of bad signs signifies length. And when red sediment remains up to forty days, it indicates the length of a fever, so that a crisis and separation are not hoped for until sixty days. Pollution <margin>u</margin> at the beginning of an illness signifies length. When you see <margin>x</margin> signs of the length of an illness in the preceding days, then their significance is not as strong as the significance of those same signs after that time. And when you see <margin>y</margin> that which is contrary to those

### Signs that an Illness will be Consumed by Crisis or Resolution. L. xciiii.

When the vitality is very strong and the <term>paroxysms</term> <note>The periodic attacks or peaks of a fever.</note> increase in quality and quantity, and the age, complexion, and time incline toward movement and not toward rest, and the signs of digestion and its contrary are rapid, then the illness will be consumed with a crisis. And if the matter is the opposite, and signs of slowness are joined to it, then the illness is prolonged. And it kills <margin>1</margin> with a "resolution" <note>A slow fading or dissolving of the body's forces, rather than a sharp turning point.</note> or it is removed; and if it varies, the crises will be diminished, delayed, and with change. But the attacks <margin>2</margin> are signified by the dispositions of the vitality and the signs of alteration of each of the two things and its contrary.

<margin>3 This chapter has four sayings: 1. It shows what makes a bad relapse. 2. It compares a relapse that happens of itself vs. by error. 3. It identifies that error. 4. It compares the relapse to the root illness.</margin>

### Judgments on Relapse. L. xcv.

The worst <term>recidivatio</term> <note>A relapse or the return of an illness.</note> is that which is faster and occurs with weaker vitality; and without a doubt, these signs of relapse are associated with it. And a relapse may happen through an error of the regimen <note>original: "regis salut9"; the management of health/diet.</note>, or it may happen by itself despite a correct regimen. And the error in this is giving heating things to drink and medicines with which someone wants to improve the appetite, such as honeyed galingale <note>original: "geleniabim mellinum"</note>, rose troches <note>medicated lozenges</note>, and similar things. And the remains that stay after a crisis attract a relapse quickly unless help is given. And a relapse is more violent than the "root" <note>the original onset of the illness</note> because its malice is coming while the state of the body is already weak.

<margin>
4 In the present chapter he places the signs and judgments of relapse. In this chapter he specifically places the signs signifying relapse which are taken from the crisis.
5 He places signs taken from the digestive and appetitive faculties.
</margin>

### Signs of Relapse. L. xcvi.

When in that case the fever does not grow quiet through a complete crisis, and on its day a relapse is feared. And if there was a quiet period without any crisis at all, there is no excuse for a relapse; <margin>5</margin> especially when the crisis is with those things that are like smallpox, or jaundice, or scabies, and at most with that which happens in the skin. And it is signified sometimes that there will be a relapse from the weakness of the vitality and appetite, and nausea, and "malice of the soul" <note>distress or depression</note>, and lack of digestion, and corruption of food in the stomach tending toward acidity and fumosity, and inflation of the hypochondria and the parts of the liver and spleen, and corruption of sleep, and long wakefulness, and violent thirst. And the violence of inflation in the face is especially a bad sign, particularly in the upper eyelid, and especially its swelling <note>original: "apostematio"</note> and its shortening, and similarly with the resolution of the inflation of the face. And among those things that signify it is when the body receives food well but the "thinness" <note>emaciation</note> is not removed by it, especially when these bad accidents appear and become more violent in the hours of the paroxysms of the illness that was. And sometimes a relapse is signified by the pulse when thickness and speed remain in it. And from the deepening of "cretic" <note>critical</note> abscesses and their hiding. And from the urine when a great deal of yellow, orange, or red tint remains in it, or it is among those in which sediment neither hangs nor settles, and when the urine of the sick person is not similar to their natural urine. And certain times are more significant of relapse than others, such as autumn, for in it more relapses fall than in other times. And the type of illness again helps to signify a relapse, such as "apostematous" <note>abscess-forming</note> fevers when they leave behind heat and inflation in the viscera, and like epilepsy, and <term>scotomia</term> <note>dizziness with dimmed vision</note>, and pains of the kidneys, liver, and spleen, and migraines, headaches, and catarrh, and those things generated from it such as *almate* <note>likely a corruption of a Greek term for a specific fluid discharge</note> and other things, and illnesses of the breath.

### Causes of Death. L. xcvii.

Death happens either because of a cause by which the <term>complexion</term> of the heart is corrupted, or because of a cause by which the vitality is "resolved" <note>dissolved or faded away</note> so that it is extinguished. And that which happens because of the corruption of the heart's complexion is either violent pain, or an excess of the known qualities <note>heat, cold, moisture, dryness</note>, or it is an external poisonous quality, or it is the retention of the matter of breath; and because of this, it is necessary that they not be left lying on their backs and their throats not be allowed to dry out. The species of death that happens in the mouths of fevers and the sign of the quality...

# Concerning those whose death occurs at the beginning of a fever's attack and its increase, or its revolution. For in the true decline it is strengthened, and in the false it is softened; in the true it is equal, and in the false it is diversified and departs from order. In a total decline, however, no one dies except because of laborious causes from without which overcome the sick person when they are weak, such as movement, or lifting, or anger; and sometimes these things also happen at the start. ### Regimen of the convalescent. Lesson 101.

# It is advised that for the convalescent, relief should be provided in all things, and nothing heavy should be brought to him in terms of food, nor any movement, nor heating things, nor causes of pressure, until he regains his voice and other things, and is gradually led to equal and easy exercise, for this is very helpful. And you should occupy yourself with that which increases his blood. And it is necessary to act so that he rests and is joyful and glad, and he should be prohibited from evacuations, and specifically from sexual intercourse. And wine with tempering is helpful to him, specifically a subtle, thin wine. And among convalescents, the one for whom it is most fitting to forbid excess is the convalescent whose crisis was hidden, since he is exposed to relapse, and such a person perhaps needs evacuation. And a subtle flowing of the belly is more suitable for him, especially when you see a choleric <note>Related to yellow bile.</note> stool or one declining toward the color of the humor from which the fever came, and you see a defect in appetite. And when you desire that, then make the convalescent rest and comfort his strength, then evacuate. And perhaps it is necessary for you to evacuate and comfort simultaneously with feeding; prepare for him then medicinal foods that are loosening, or mix with them the virtues of suitable loosening medicines, such as plums, and *siracost* <note>original: "siracost"; a type of medicinal manna.</note>, and *terebiabin* <note>original: "terebiabin"; another medicinal manna or resin.</note>, and similar things for those having <term>cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile humor.</note>. And sometimes they are helped by diuretics, and their veins are cleansed by them; and sometimes those known diuretics do that, just as mixed wine does. Concerning phlebotomy (bloodletting), however, it should be known that the convalescent has little need for the extraction of blood; yet perhaps he does need it, and the form and signs of the blood signify this, especially when you find a hidden fever in the veins and see a pustule on the lip; and perhaps it forces you to bloodletting while...

The opposite happens with the opposite condition. If the recovering person has no appetite, then there is an accumulation <note>original: "repto," likely "repletio" or a filling up of humors</note> within him.

And if he has an appetite but does not gain weight after eating, then he is taking in more than his strength and the power of his nature can handle; he cannot digest it and distribute it through the body. Either there are many humors in his body with which his nature is occupied, or the strength of his stomach is greatly suppressed, or the strength of his whole body and his innate heat are so suppressed that the food is not altered with the proper change so that nature can be restored by it.

g. And perhaps. He determines the caution for those recovering from acidic things.
</margin>

### Feeding the recovering patient. Lesson 102.

<margin>
o. And know. He treats the loss of appetite and the cause of that loss, and teaches how to manage this defect in the recovering person.
</margin>
It is necessary that his food be of good quality and easily digestible. He should not endure hunger or thirst, and perhaps it is necessary that the quality of the food be the opposite of the previous illness out of fear of a relapse and as a caution. And know that

<column-break/>

moist and fluid foods nourish more quickly and are less "bold" <note>aggressive or difficult to process</note>, while thick and heavy food or drink is the opposite. He should not take cold things unless the remnants of heat demand it, so that he is managed with what is tempered. He should have a "subtle" <note>refined/light</note> heat with complete moisture that quickly receives digestion. And let his food be in a quantity and measure by which a good digestion occurs. There should be a separation and addition by degrees, so that you do not see heaviness, nor rumbling, nor a quick descent <note>diarrhea</note>, nor a slow retention <note>constipation</note>. Reduce the food if you do not see what ought to be seen; when the stomach is suddenly filled and stretched, he may perhaps become feverish. Similarly, he should not drink suddenly, for fear may arise from that. The hour of his food should be during the cool of the evening in the summer, and in the afternoon in the winter, unless something urgent interferes. The quantity should be divided into portions less than what would fully satiate him. Very cold water is among the things from which a recovering person should stay away; for sometimes it kills, perhaps by damaging certain viscera, or perhaps causing a spasm. We have known people who died because of this. And know that the appetite of a recovering person is sometimes diminished because of weakness or because of humors in the stomach, and this is usually associated with fainting <note>original: "sincopis"</note>. Sometimes it is diminished because of the liver and a lack of "attraction" <note>the liver's ability to draw nutrients</note>, which appears in the color of the skin and in thin, white stool. Sometimes it is diminished because of humors in the whole body and a nauseating fullness. And sometimes because of the weakness of the body's strength and innate heat, or specifically in the stomach. Manage each case with what you know of its routine, doing as much as is required. And know that *sekānjabīn* <note>original: "secammabim"; a Persian medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar</note> is a good medicine specifically for recovering persons when their appetite is suppressed due to weakness in their stomachs, and it provides safety from the scraping of the intestines. Regarding things that comfort the stomach which are warmer than this, such as rose lozenges <note>original: "trocisci rosa"</note> and similar things, these may perhaps be the cause of a relapse.

### On the beginning of the illness and the first calculation of the crisis. Lesson 1.

<margin>
p. Regarding the hours. In this chapter, he speaks of the beginning and the hour in which we ought to begin the calculation so that we may know which day is the critical day. q. And the cause of a sudden change from health to illness is the multitude of matter gathered in the body, and the heat, and the subtlety, and the weakness of strength. For when the strength is weak and the matter is plentiful, hot, and subtle, then it moves suddenly. And if it finds resistance in the strength, it suddenly induces illness in the body. The cause of a slow movement from health to illness, preceded by labors and pains, is the opposite of those things mentioned above.
</margin>
Among men, there are those who say that the "beginning" of the illness, from which the calculation of the critical days is numbered, is the very end of the hour in which the sick person first feels a trace of the illness. And there are those who say: no, rather it is the end of the hour in which he throws himself down <note>takes to his bed</note> and the harm to his functioning appears. This disagreement only arises in fevers that do not happen suddenly; in those that happen suddenly, there is no "beginning hour" <note>as the onset and the peak are nearly simultaneous</note>. This is what happens to some feverish people: the fever begins with a visible onset, while the man was just before...
