Fen II Treatise I

<margin>
a **Many.** Here he posits the causes of the days of crisis and the periods, and how they are determined by the position of the moon. This has two parts: first, he presents this according to the opinion of some; second, he provides the reason why they prove this through "moistures," which is the cause of the aforementioned changes. The second part begins at "And they signify."
b **And it becomes.** He distinguishes the operations of the bodily state, whether they are stronger or weaker.
c **They said.** He touches upon the operation of the moon by reason of its effects through its movement in the circle of the zodiac. Against Galen, in the third book of *On Critical Days*, he posited that the "medicinal month" consists of 26 days and 22 hours. Note that this author set the medicinal month according to the signs of the moon, whereas Galen set it by the month of vision and manifest appearance.
d **There are therefore.** In the upper part of the division of the moon into the times of crisis, he now shows that the predicted times are necessarily verified and vary according to the different types of matter of the disease.
e **And when.** That is, some time among those into which the predicted lunar month is divided. Otherwise: when the illness has begun under a sign of good fortune; and "corrupt dispositions" means the illness began under an unfortunate sign and had a bad beginning. This is Galen's exposition in the third book.
</margin>

One does not consider an illness to have begun when a person is sleeping, or entering a bath, or working, and suddenly develops a fever. However, in fevers preceded by constriction, headache, and similar symptoms, and then both things occur, they are distinguished. It is important to consider the hour of the onset of the fever itself, for that is the manifest opening of the departure from the natural state in the body's complexion <note>the balance of humors</note>. The onset of the headache and the feeling of being "broken" does not count toward the calculation. Likewise, when one lies down in bed or sleeps are not factors to be looked at; for perhaps the sick person did not lie down, yet the fever had already begun. Furthermore, if a woman has given birth and then a fever happens to her, if it is not calculated as a fever but only as part of the childbirth, that is an error. Regarding this, some have said it most often happens after the second or third day.

#### On critical days according to their periods. Book II.

Many men have placed the cause of the measurement of the times of crises in acute illnesses on the part of the moon, because its power is a power that enters into moistures, purifying them through types of alteration and helping to bring them to maturity and digestion <note>the "cooking" or processing of humors by the body's heat</note>, or the opposite, depending on the preparation of the matter. It signifies this through the state of expansion and contraction, the growth of brains <note>original: "cerebellorum"; it was an ancient belief that brains and bone marrow grew and shrank with the lunar cycle</note> as the light in the moon increases, and the speed of ripening of the fruits of trees and herbs with its appearance. They say that the moistures of cities are affected by the moon when their dispositions vary according to the different states of the moon. And the appearance of diversity becomes more vehement with the vehemence of the change in the moon's state; this is most vehement when the moon is in opposition <note>Full Moon</note> to the state in which it began, then according to the quadrature <note>the quarter phases</note>, and this is done by dividing its revolution into halves, and then into halves of halves. 

They said, therefore, that the revolution of the moon is in twenty-nine days and nearly a third, with the days of conjunction <note>the New Moon/dark moon</note> subtracted from them. Because the moon has no operation during those roughly two days and a half and a third, twenty-six days remain. Half of that will be thirteen days and a quarter of a day; a fourth of it will be six days, a half-day, and an eighth of a day; an eighth of it will be three days, a quarter-day, and half of an eighth of a day. This is its minor revolution. Perhaps they extract it by other ways that vary these computations slightly and add a little to them, but there is a transgression in this because they say they ought not to speak so. 

There are, therefore, these times that necessarily cause great changes to appear in them, and they are the days of the "small periods." When it begins and the matter is good, a manifest alteration tending toward wellness appears at that stage. But when the time begins and the dispositions are corrupt, there is an alteration appearing at the completion of the time toward corruption. The crisis of illnesses that proceed over time and are counted beyond a month are measured by the Sun, and in this measurement and experience there is ambiguity. In them are places of such a sort that the preoccupation with supernatural things is multiplied; but this does not hinder the physician. The physician only needs to know when the patient recovers through various crises, and it does not pertain to him to know the underlying cause <note>the astronomical or physical cause</note>, as pursuing that cause would draw him away into another art. Rather, the discourse on the days of crisis should be a discourse spoken according to the path of experience or according to the way of established position and observed timing. And know that many of them name

<column-break/>

<margin>
f **Crisis.** Here he shows which star's motion is considered in the crises of chronic illnesses <note>the Sun</note>.
g **And know.** He describes the "critical revolution" by its genus, i.e., from the genus of its critical points; for by doubling the middle of them, the discovery always arrives at a critical day.
h **And revolutions.** Here he distinguishes the radical revolutions of critical days. But "the revolution of tens" [decenorum]—this text intends to say "twenties" [vicenorum], which is proved by Galen in the second book on critical days; for he says that the radical revolutions are the revolutions of the fourths, sevenths, and twenties, as is clear in the third book of Avicenna when he says the 40th, 60th, 80th, etc., always proceeding by twenties.
i **And praiseworthy.** He sets the method of computing the radical critical days according to Galen and Hippocrates.
k **Others however.** Others set the method of computation according to Archigenes.
l **And consider.** He teaches how to consider his opinion by showing up to which day the four-day cycles (quartans) are stronger than the seven-day cycles (septans).
m **And according to Archigenes.** On the position of the two opinions regarding critical days, namely Dioscorides and Archigenes; he sets a way of composing a middle ground between those two opinions.
n **And know.** After the numbering of crises that proceed by days, he enumerates crises that proceed by months and years.
</margin>

the revolution as that from which the multiplication does not depart from its genus <note>meaning the cycle stays within the pattern of critical days</note>. His intention is that the multiplication does not result in a non-critical day. An example of these is the <term>quartan</term> <note>a four-day cycle</note> and the <term>septan</term> <note>a seven-day cycle</note>. For their middle always arrives at a critical day according to the experience of the days of crisis that happen in illnesses suited to these four-day and seven-day cycles. 

And the revolutions that are good "radicals" are three: the revolution of the fourths, the revolution of the sevenths (which is complete), but the revolution of the twenties <note>original: "decenorum" (tens), corrected to "vicenorum" (twenties) in margin</note> is more complete than all. For the 40th, 60th, and 80th, and all those days, are critical. However, the first two revolutions are diminished because of the "fraction" <note>remainder or decimal</note> which must be observed, through which there are [about] 27 days. The first quartan is the 4th day; the second quartan is that in which the fraction is restored. Because of that, it is on the 7th day, since there are six days and a large portion of the seventh; because of that, it falls "continuously." The third quartan falls on the 11th. There one reaches the hour of the doubling of the seventh, which is followed by the sixth seventh, which is on the 14th. When we have restored the fraction, the third seventh falls on the 20th day. 

So the matter has run in quartans according to this: the first and sixth quartans are continuous, the sixth and third are separate, and the third and fourth are continuous. When the 14th day has passed, then the diversity begins. Those who are praiseworthy, like <term>Hippocrates</term> and <term>Galen</term>, began from the continuous days. Thus the order of days was: the 7th, the 14th, and the 20th (which is continuous with the 14th). Therefore, the multiples of 20 are multiples of the sevenths according to their intention. When we find the sixths and sevenths separated, they are followed by the continuous third which completes the 20th; thereafter it separates from the 20th and is the 24th, then the 27th (continuous), then the 31st (separated by four sevenths), and the 34th (continuous). Then the continuous seventh, which is the 40th, thereafter the multiplication runs on three sevenths as if they themselves were 20, so that the continuation is the 60th, 80th, 100th, and 120th. There is not much consideration for what lies between them in those days. 

Others, however, like <term>Archigenes</term> <note>a Greek physician of the 1st/2nd century AD</note>, said that after the 14th is the 18th (which is a day of crisis), and the 21st, and the 28th, then the 32nd, and then the 38th with the continuation of the seventh. And some counted the 42nd, 45th, and 48th as days of crisis, and they have already overstepped in this. Consider for yourself how the distinction they made between quartans and septans falls. For in quartans, a strong power exists in the days of crisis up to 20 days; thereafter the power comes to the septans up to 30 days. Therefore, when a patient in a chronic illness passes 20 days, then pay attention to the septans. According to Archigenes, the 21st day is much more critical than the 20th, because it is a "disjointed" septan after the 18th, where the diversity runs in the 27th and 28th. Archigenes saw something different from the opinion of both and made the 28th better, and similarly is the disposition of the 31st with the 32nd, the 34th with the 35th, and the 42nd with the 48th. And know that of illnesses, there are those whose crisis is in seven months...

<margin>a Hippocrates says: he posits the division of critical days into even and odd ones.</margin>
<margin>b Further, Galen follows this: if sweats begin, it signifies the contrary in the sequence, because a crisis that is judged by distributed times and "friendly" conversion <note>original: "amica conversio"</note>—Galen condemned this and said it was not so.</margin>
<margin>c And you should know: he posits a composition between good critical days and good signs which appear on a day of crisis that is not itself "good," because if you were to help with soothing remedies, it would not be etc.</margin>
<margin>d Of the critical days: he posits the "root" critical days, promising that he will set these days apart, also showing that the 4th day is the first among the radical critical days, but a crisis rarely falls upon it.</margin>
<margin>e However, the day: he shows the truth and the relationship of the preceding critical days by the 4th and the 7th, and by common, predicted, and separated days; all radical critical days proceed according to this mode.</margin>
<margin>f And you should know: he posits a comparison between the critical day and the movements of illnesses.</margin>
<margin>g From these: for the seventh day most powerfully and ultimately comes on the third day <note>This refers to the calculation of cycles where the end of one period is the start of the next</note>.</margin>
<margin>h Those who: here he posits the order of critical days and calls those days "very strong" above. And on the contrary, he himself prefers the 11th to the 14th, and then the 14th is stronger. Respond that the 11th is stronger in illnesses that proceed by an odd movement, or he prefers them not because it is stronger, but because it is more "indicative." For the indicative day precedes the critical one.</margin>
<margin>i And sometimes: he shows how the proportion is found in itself: in interpolated illnesses and illnesses that terminate in days, months, and years, by reason of their termination and by reason of the indication of their revolution—that is, the periods are convenient and proportional to the number seven.</margin>

...in the same way, indeed in seven years, and fourteen years, and twenty-one years. And there are some who think that after forty <note>likely referring to the 40th day of an illness</note> a crisis does not occur with a strong evacuation, but the matter is not so. And it is not even necessary that the illness be altered to an acute state, or that there be a relapse in it, or a composition of illnesses. And it is not forbidden in a chronic illness that nature should cease to digest it, and then be strengthened over it once more and expel it, even if it be a small amount. However <note>original: "Aeruz," likely a scribal error for "Verum"</note>, for the most part, what has been said is true: that there is a separation in it either with a diminished crisis, or through the exit of a slow movement, or through resolution. Hippocrates says that of the critical days <term>dies cretici</term> <note>Days when the "judgment" or turning point of a disease occurs</note> some are even and others are odd. And the even ones are indeed stronger in crises for the most part and in the first number. Examples of even days are the 4th, 6th, 8th, 10th, 14th, 20th, 24th, and others which we have numbered as even in two lines. And the odd ones are indeed such as the 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th, 11th, 15th, 17th, 21st, 27th, and 31st. Furthermore, Galen denied what was said in this aphorism regarding the 8th and 10th days being critical, and found that to be different from the "roots" of Hippocrates. And perhaps this speech of Hippocrates was made before he well knew the existence of the days of crisis and it has an explanation. And you should know that sometimes days continue and are like a single day for the crisis; and that happens more often after twenty days, whether it be an evacuation or whether it be an eruption <note>original: "erituna," likely "erythrema" or "eruptio"</note>. And you should know that on a day of a good crisis, when bad signs appear, then that is worse and signifies death for the most part, just as if something should happen to them on the 7th or 14th.

->On the proportionality of the days of crisis added to their nobility and their proportion to illnesses. Chapter III<-

**O**f the critical days, some are strong in the highest degree, in which a crisis perhaps always occurs; and others are very weak, and others are in the middle. And I shall speak of them distinctly after I have said that the first day of crisis is the 4th day, and yet a crisis does not often fall on it, and it is indicative of the 7th. But the 7th day is a very strong day, and the 4th day indicates it; and it is right that the 7th be placed in the first, superior order. And the 11th day is not equal in power to the 14th. However, in illnesses in which their paroxysms <term>paroxismi</term> <note>The period of greatest intensity in a fever or disease</note> begin on odd days—as in a tertian fever <note>A fever that returns every third day, typical of some types of malaria</note>—it is very strong and stronger than the 14th. And the 14th day is a very strong day, and it is part of its strength that no day is found to which the 14th is not proportional, being the ultimate in strength in the judgments of crisis and the patient's health, even unto its completion. The 17th day is strong, and that which is proportioned to it from the days is stronger. And its proportionality to the 20th is the proportionality of the 11th to the 14th. The 18th is among the critical days that kill, and more so; and the 27th day is pernicious, and it is as if it were not a critical day at all. The 40th day is stronger than the 34th, although the 34th is of good virtue and stronger than the 31st. And you should know that illnesses which produce a paroxysm on odd days, such as tertian fever and most acute illnesses, have a faster crisis, and their crisis occurs on even days <note>This likely refers to the counting method where the crisis falls on the "even" interval from the start</note>; wherefore in a tertian fever the 11th is expected, and the 14th is not expected except a little, although for the most part the paroxysm of the 7th declines from the 14th a little. And those which produce paroxysms on even days are slower, and their crisis is more often on even days.

<column-break/>

<margin>k Standing days: here he posits the causes of the "interceding" radical days, which are critical because of the root movement of the moon. But on the contrary, Galen in the third book on critical days only posited two causes for these critical days, and Avicenna here posits more. Respond: that Avicenna posited all of them, while Galen posited only the secondary ones.</margin>
<margin>l And if: note that "antecedent" is understood as perhaps not absolute, because thus he makes the crisis antecedent; but it is perhaps in respect to those causes which produce no crisis, for example, heat generating windiness <note>gas</term>.</margin>

**T**hose which are in the superior order are like the 7th, 11th, 14th, 17th, and 20th. And sometimes there are revolutions in illnesses that agree, for the most part, with the number of the days of crises; therefore, seven revolutions of a tertian fever are like the seven days of a burning fever <term>causonis</term>. And sometimes the arrangement of the number of months and years in chronic illnesses is according to the arrangement of the number of days in acute ones; whereby a quartan fever <note>A fever recurring every fourth day</note> lasts seven months, for example, and its indications run according to the consideration of the indications of the days, and there falls among them a matter of precedence or postponement according to the consideration which falls in the days as I shall say.

->On the days falling in the middle. Chapter V<-

**T**hese days which we have mentioned are the radical critical days. However, it sometimes happens to critical days because of some external accidental cause, or from the illness itself in the speed of its movement or its slowness, or from the disposition of the body in its strength or weakness, or from the accidents that occur—such as intense wakefulness from external causes, or things falling from bodily or animal causes when they overflow vehemently—that a hastening or a delay falls before them, although the station of the necessary crisis is not lifted in its hour, but rather diminished by it. And if there were no strong accidental cause, the crisis would be verified and would not precede nor delay. However, when that accident happens and is strong, the hour declines and is delayed or precedes; and if it should be weak, the crisis becomes difficult. And it prevents it from being complete, and the days in which this reflection falls are called "days falling in the middle," and they have the judgments of critical days in part. And these days are like the 3rd, 5th, 6th, and like the 9th and the 13th. For the 3rd and 5th contain the 4th; and the 9th commonly contains the 7th and 11th; and perhaps the falling day will be more convenient to one of the two days which are on its two sides, or it will be a critical day which is between those falling on the other side more pertaining to it: for the hastening of the 11th to the 9th is more than the delay of the 7th to the 9th, although each of them may be for the most part.

->On the power of the days falling in the middle and their weakness. Chapter VI<-

**K**now that the 9th is a strong day, preferred among them, then the 5th, then the 3rd; and it is not shortened from the 4th, which is the root, by a manifest shortening. And the 13th, as if because of its weakness, is not among those in which a crisis occurs. But the 6th is a day in which a crisis falls, but truly that crisis is bad. For if it should come not bad, it will be difficult, hidden, diminished, and not safe from fear; and because of the smallness of the occurrence of the crisis in it—whether it be bad or not bad—it is as if it were the contrary to the 7th, and the 4th day indicates it in its malice. And indeed, the indication of the 4th is rarely completed with good, except with difficulty; wherefore fearful signs happen in it, such as deep sleep and fainting <term>sincopis</term>, and specifically if there was an evacuation, then fainting will happen with vomiting; and in it will happen a fall of strength, and shivering, and tremors, and the destruction of the pulse. If, however, sweat should appear in it, it will not be equal, and perhaps the crisis is diminished in it with an evacuation. Wherefore its completion will be with bad urine <note>original: "erituria," red or bloody urine</note> and jaundice; and there will be bad urine of a bad sediment—this is when the patient is saved, and if not, then in whatever way...

<summary>This page details the classification of "critical days" in medical prognosis, distinguishing between radical (strong) days like the 7th and 14th, and "interceding" days that fall in between. It explains how external factors or the nature of the fever (tertian or quartan) can shift these turning points, and warns of the dangers of a crisis occurring on the 6th day.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of critical days in medical prognosis. While the previous page established the general theory of cycles and the importance of the fourth and seventh days as "roots," this page moves into the specific signs seen on "indicatory days" that predict when a crisis (the turning point of an illness) will occur. It contrasts different types of fevers—such as the "causon" or burning fever versus the "tertian" fever—based on where the diseased "matter" is located in the body.</meta>

Fen II 11 Treatise II

<margin>
a **Of them.** 
In this chapter, Avicenna says that the strongest days of crisis and the strongest falling in the middle are those above. But concerning this, he posits that the 14th is stronger than the 7th, which is in the 14th. <note>original: "Avē. i. 3. .g." referring to Avicenna and likely Galen</note> says further that they are stronger regarding the "matter" <note>The physical substance or humor causing the illness</note> if they have hotter matter, yet they are not stronger regarding the quality and frequency of the crisis.
</margin>
The best are the seventh and the fourteenth. And after them are the ninth and the seventeenth. And you should know that the days of a crisis of stronger judgment, and the strongest days falling among the "indicatory days" <note>Days when signs appear that predict a future crisis</note>, are those which are in the preceding days; and the further they proceed, the more their judgment is weakened.

<margin>
b **Days.** In this chapter, he determines the judicial <note>indicatory</note> days. And first, he shows what signs ought to appear in all indicated things so that those days may be indicatory. Second, he concludes from what was said above. First, he gives the distinction of those signs in general. Second, he explains the predicted distinction.
</margin>
**On the days which are not critical, neither by the first intention nor the second.** L.viii.

These are the first, second, third, twelfth, nineteenth, and fifteenth days, and others like them. And it is a marvel that many of them follow a critical day.

<margin>
c **And it will be.** Here he enumerates the indicatory days of the "root" critical days, but he doubts how the 4th becomes indicative of a crisis on the 7th in a "Causon" <note>A continuous, high-burning fever</note>. However, in a tertian fever, there is an indicative crisis sometimes up to the 11th. Since the matter of a burning fever (cholera) is the same as the matter of a tertian fever, why does such a diversity in the crisis occur? He responds that the matter of the burning fever is in the smaller veins closer to the heart, liver, and stomach. The matter of the tertian fever, although it is the same as the burning fever, is not so close and is outside the veins in the spongy parts of the organs; therefore, their crises are more delayed, and the matter of the burning fever causes stronger symptoms by reason of the location of the matter.
</margin>
**On the indicatory days.** L.viiii.

Indicatory days are those in which traces are seen that signify an alteration of the matter, or signify the victory of one of two things: the alteration of the sickness or the strength of the patient. Or they signify the beginning of a light struggle that runs between nature and the sickness—not for the sake of separation, but because of the intensity of the struggle. The first signs are like the signs of "digestion" <note>In medieval medicine, 'digestion' or 'coction' refers to the maturing or ripening of the humors causing the illness</note> and its contrary. The signs of digestion are like a red cloud in the urine, or one tending toward whiteness. The signs of "indigestion" <note>unripe humors</note> are also well known. The second signs are like the appearance of the strength of appetite or its fall, and the lightness or heaviness of the patient's movement. The third are like headache, anguish, shortness of breath, tremors, unusual sweating, and incomplete evacuation. When these traces appear in these days, there will be a crisis in the known days following them. And the 4th will be the indicator, and the crisis will be on the 7th if the sign was good; or the 6th if the sign was bad. And specifically in a burning fever, it is fixed that it happens on the 7th, and less so on the 6th, or on the 11th, or always on the 14th, 20th, or 21st. And again, the 17th indicates the 20th or 21st. And the 18th indicates the 21st, 20th, and 40th. And among the days falling in the middle, the 3rd indicates the 5th; if it was bad, then the 6th. And the 5th indicates the 9th; if it was bad, then the 8th. And know that the signs of indication sometimes deviate from their days for the reason predicted in the deviations of the crisis from their proper days, to those which are before or after them. And know that on the second day following the indicatory days, something follows from the same nature of what was on the indicatory day when the sickness is moving quickly. And consider the signs that hasten or delay, and judge on the indicatory days whether they hasten or are delayed by this.

<margin>
d **And of the days.** After he determined the indicatory days absolutely, he divides the time of sickness by the middle, such as the 4th in respect to the 7th. And afterwards, he determines the days falling...
</margin>
<margin>
f **Knowledge.** Here he shows for what purpose the knowledge of critical days is useful.
</margin>
**Knowledge of the days of crisis when there is doubt.** L.x.

Knowledge of the days of crisis is necessary for many purposes. For it is necessary, when the crisis is near, that the sick person be managed by a certain regimen, and when it is far off, by another regimen. And it is necessary that during the indication of the crisis and that which is closest to it, the sick person be managed by a specific regimen. Therefore, let him not be moved

<margin>
g **And perhaps.** Since nature perhaps is performing the crisis through sweat, and you evacuate through the bowels and such things, it causes harm.
</margin>
at all with medicine, for perhaps nature will assist in the evacuation, whereby it would flow out excessively. And perhaps medicine will cause a conflict in its part, which will produce labor but not a crisis, and no evacuation will occur; and in this lies the danger.

<margin>
h **And all.** He gives a certain rule in observing the condition of the soul in knowing the critical days. It should be noted that by "natural things" he perhaps understands the natures of the indicatory days, whose nature it is to certify the critical days. Or he understands the nature of the sickness in respect to the heavenly bodies, as appears above in many places.
</margin>
And it is necessary in the knowledge of the days of crisis that you observe again the natural things that alter the known days of crisis.

<margin>
i **And we.** Here Avicenna teaches how to know the critical days about which there is doubt, and in this he posits two modes by which they are known.
</margin>
And we find that knowledge is divided into two modes: one of which is in the crisis of the sickness absolutely, and the other is in the day of the crisis itself from the perspective of the time in which the crisis occurs. For perhaps the dispositions of the crisis are prolonged by two or three days, whereby it is doubted to which of them it should be proportioned.

<margin>
k **Mode.** Here he follows with the first mode which is taken from the time of the sickness. First, he subdivides this mode... the signs of the nature of the illness.
</margin>
The first mode is signified in two ways: from the signs of the shortening of the sickness and its length, and from the natures of the sicknesses and their strengths. The signification from the signs of length and shortening is because perhaps it will be according to the consumption of the sickness; for example, if the sickness is not one of those possible to be consumed on the 4th and those following it, but is possible to be consumed on the 7th and those following it. For if signs of digestion appear with a good appearance in those following the 4th, it is hoped that the crisis will be on the 7th. And if signs of the length of the sickness appear as predicted in their own chapter, know that its crisis will be delayed, and its succession will be without a crisis. And if none of these appear, it is hoped that the sickness will be consumed between the 7th and the 14th. The signification from the natures of the sicknesses is as follows, for example: an odd day is better, as you have known from the fact that acute illnesses with heat move on an odd day, and an even day is for those that differ from them.

<margin>
l **The mode truly.** Here he follows with the second way of knowing critical days, taken from the side where the crisis occurs. This has six points. First, he subdivides this mode... second, he explains the first member of this division, namely what he says regarding the consideration of revolutions. Third, he explains the second member, the time of the crisis. Fourth, he explains the verification of days.
</margin>
The second mode is signified by the consideration of "revolutions" <note>The cyclic returns of symptoms or planetary alignments</note> and from the number of the crisis, and the time of the crisis, and the verifications of the days and their strengths. Signification from the consideration of revolutions is, for example, as you know that an even day is better for a certain sickness and an odd one is better for another sickness. But from the time of the crisis, it is so that you consider and know in which of the two days the longer labor <note>The peak of the symptom or struggle</note> occurs, and let the crisis be placed there, unless it follows that it is of a stronger judgment than the judgment of this signification. And concerning this second chapter, it is that which makes it necessary that the crisis be placed on the middle day out of three days with the predicted condition. The signification from the strength of the days and their natures is such as if a sweat begins in the night of the 7th and does not stop sweating throughout the whole 8th day; then the crisis will be on the 7th, not the 8th, because the fever is eradicated on the 8th. And if it was according to a difference from this, and the sweat begins on the 13th and does not stop sweating internally until the 14th, and the fever is eradicated on the 14th, then the crisis will not be proportioned except to the 14th. And that is because the 8th and 13th are not in the strength of the other two days in terms of goodness. And death is more fitting to occur with the 6th than the 7th, and more fitting with the 10th than the 9th.

<margin>
m **Again.** In the first statement he says from the consideration of judgments, one ought to understand that these judgments are three: namely the preceding commotion, the sudden alteration, and the following evacuation. Thus, when it is doubted to which day a crisis should be attributed, let it be seen to which of these the majority of the judgments are attributed, for the crisis is to be attributed to that one.
</margin>
Signification from the gathering of judgments is like that whose narrative has passed; for example, on the 14th, in what we said, the sweat and the eradication of the fever are gathered together. Signification from the indicatory days is that you consider whether you find indication in the predicted examples.

<margin>
e **And know.** Here he says what signifies the shortness of the sickness before the critical day.
</margin>
...on indicatory days with the intention of the signs appearing in them, as the 11th with respect to the 14th, or with remission as the 4th with respect to the 14th. Here he enumerates the intervening indicatory days with the signification of the indications, just like the days falling in the middle.

a Now you have learned. Here he determines which critical days correspond to which illnesses.
And for "burning fever" <note>original: "incensua," likely referring to causon or a high-intensity burning fever</note>, here he shows to which days they are proportioned. But there is a doubt when it is not according to the sign of evil, because a burning fever is a vehement evil on odd days. The reason is that although burning fever afflicts contrarily, it is nonetheless of yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>, which afflicts from third to third day. It seems that he says it happens on even days and not odd days, for he himself exemplifies this by saying it often kills on the sixth day and judges on the fourth. Or, if you wish to maintain it occurs on odd days after the crisis, it is confirmed by the commentary on that aphorism: "dangerous fourths." ## On the decline of the proportion of days of crisis to several illnesses. Chapter 11.

<margin>
The commentary of Gentilis of Foligno <note>A famous 14th-century Italian physician known as "The Soul of Commentators"</note>, a most illustrious doctor, on the third Fen of the fourth book <note>The Latin says "3.ª quinti cañ." but the context suggests the 4th book of the Canon</note> of Avicenna, happily begins.
</margin>

Now you have learned that the crisis of very acute illnesses happens toward the seventh day, and the crisis of those that follow them in acuteness happens toward the fourteenth and twentieth, and those that follow those toward the fortieth. After that, chronic illnesses absolutely make their crisis. Since a vehement burning fever occurs on odd days, that is an evil sign, and it often kills on the sixth day and is judged on the fourth, and in it occurs a cold sweat and similar things. And because "phrenitis" <note>original: "sirsen," a brain inflammation or delirium</note> will have its crisis according to the common opinion on the eleventh day due to its acuteness, because the beginning of its magnification happens according to the common opinion after the third and fourth days; then it makes a crisis on the seventh. You should therefore know this.

<margin>
c Now we have spoken above. [Part] A determined fevers and the crisis. Here he determines regarding the "aposteme" <note>A general term for an inflammation, swelling, or tumor caused by humors</note>, which is called a common illness; and it has two parts. First, he continues the discourse from the first book. Second, he carries it out at the point "know, I say therefore." It is doubted how this differs here and in the third book "knowledge of apostemes." I respond: there it is determined according to each specific member (organ), such as the liver, stomach, brain, etc. Here, however, they are treated indeterminately or as they happen primarily in the likeness of the whole body, although he also determines regarding internal ones. Therefore, this knowledge belongs to the fourth book, which considers common illnesses that are not proper to one member alone but are more general. Also, it is doubted why he considers apostemes before the "solution of continuity" <note>term: <term>solution of continuity</term> refers to a physical break in tissue, like a wound or fracture</note>, because Avicenna in the first book, second section, third [tract] on ingenuity, began with the solution of continuity. Also, the simple precedes the composite; but the solution of continuity is simpler. It is responded that these can be considered in two ways: through the scientific and theoretical path, and thus the solution of continuity precedes, because a simple disease and the knowledge of simple things precedes the knowledge of composites by the nature of the thing. In another way, the operative and practical path; and thus the knowledge of an aposteme precedes the knowledge of the solution of continuity. First, because an aposteme frequently follows a fever by way of a crisis. Second, because an aposteme frequently causes manifest ulcers; hence the causes of ulcers are apostemes. Third, because after the care of apostemes follows the care of ulcers. For apostemes are treated until their final generation or opening. Fourth, because an aposteme can be called a common disease.
</margin>

### The second Fen is completed, the third Fen on apostemes and pustules begins.
## First treatise on those which are hot and corrupt.
### General discourse on apostemes. Lesson 1.

We have already spoken in the first book about apostemes and their types and cures in a general discourse, to which one who wishes to hear what we are now saying must return. In this book, however, we speak of them in a particular discourse. I say that every aposteme and pustule is either hot or not hot. And a hot aposteme is either from blood and what runs its course, or from yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> and what runs its course. And that which is from blood is either from...

<column-break/>

...laudable blood or from bad blood. And laudable blood is either thick or thin. And that which is made from thick laudable blood is a "phlegmon" <note>term: <term>phlegmon</term> refers to a hot, red, painful swelling caused by blood</note> that involves the flesh and the skin together and is accompanied by a pulsation. And from thin [blood] comes a phlegmon that involves the skin alone and is like a "thorn" <note>stinging sensation</note> and is not accompanied by a pulsation. But indeed, from thick bad blood are made types of evil "erysipelas" <note>term: <term>erysipelas</term> is a skin infection known as St. Anthony's Fire, usually caused by yellow bile but here described as a blood variation</note>. For if its malice becomes vehement and its burning occurs, erysipelas will happen and there will be a burning and a crust, and worse than that is "Persian fire" <note>term: <term>Persian fire</term> refers to a severe, necrotic skin condition like anthrax or shingles</note>. And from thin bad blood happens a phlegmon that declines toward erysipelas with malice and fraudulence. If it is thinner, it will be a "phlegmonous erysipelas," and when its malice is greater, it will be an erysipelas having inflammations and blisters and burning and a crust. 

The bilious <note>original: "cholericum"</note> type, however, is either from a very thin yellow bile that does not contain more within it than what appears on the skin and is acute; and from it comes "formica" <note>term: <term>formica</term> (literally "the ant") refers to creeping skin lesions or herpes, named for the crawling sensation</note> that is merely "wandering," being thinner; or "wandering and corrosive," which is evil. Or it is from a thicker yellow bile of less heat, which contains more within the skin than the first, and is that which becomes a "pustule" <note>original: "pbla," abbreviation for pustula</note>, and from it comes "miliary formica" <note>a rash resembling millet seeds</note>, which is of less inflammation and slower resolution. And if the matter is thicker and worse, "corrosive formica" will occur. And if it is drawn out in its thickness unto the substance of blood and becomes evil, an "evil erysipelas" will occur. And in all these, the matter is thin, although it is diversified after that; it happens because of its thinness that nature expels it and it is not retained in anything except the skin and what is near it. And sometimes the matter of a hot aposteme is multiplied when the aposteme is magnified; it is of the highest degree of acute, mortifying apostemes.

<margin>
e
**And a hot aposteme.** 
This part has three parts. First, on hot ones. Second, on non-hot ones. Third, on leprosy, according to the three types: namely, cold humors and leprosy. The first is in section D, in general; then in special. He does three things: first on simple ones, second on composite ones, third he adds "and you should know." He differentiates regarding species and manner. It is to be considered what "runs its course" means: that is, from laudable blood or non-laudable. It is doubted whether a hot aposteme is made only from blood and yellow bile. I respond: essentially it is made only from blood and yellow bile. It is doubted whether an aposteme is made from yellow bile, as some say it cannot be. To the contrary, Avicenna says it is made, for it can flow and be retained in a member.
</margin>

<margin>
f
**The bilious [aposteme] however.** 
First this, second he removes a doubt at "and in all these." He treats first of those made from thin yellow bile, second from thick. It is asked if true erysipelas can be made from "laudable" yellow bile. It seems so. To the contrary, Avicenna says it cannot properly be made from pure laudable yellow bile like it can from laudable blood, or only rarely. For if yellow bile "sins" in quantity, it becomes foreign and is burned or putrefied. Why does he not mention erysipelas that is neither wandering nor corrosive nor miliary? He says it is rarely found. Or, he already spoke of it when he mentioned "phlegmonous erysipelas." Thin, heated blood converted to a bilious nature makes that erysipelas; but pure bile makes this "wandering" or "corrosive" formica. It is called "formica" (ant) by similarity to an ant running hither and thither.
</margin>

<margin>
g
**Or from thicker yellow bile.** 
It is conceded that from thicker yellow bile two types of "formica" are made: "miliary" (resembling millet) and "corrosive." If it is very thick, like burnt blood, it will be evil because the corrosion is worse when the matter is thicker.
</margin>

<margin>
h
**It is to be noted** that a member is corrupted by much hot matter.
</margin>

# Book III Treatise I

...is corrupted by poisonous matter. This is what the **anthrax** <note>original: "anthoma," likely referring to anthrax or a malignant pustule</note> says. It is corrupted by a burnt corrosive matter: this is what **haurachis** <note>a Latinization of an Arabic medical term for a corrosive condition</note> says. And concerning **apostemes** <term>Aposteme: A general term for a swelling or internal abscess.</term>, they come out or tend toward a point. And you should know that many are compound, for a pure **humor** <term>Humor: One of the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that ancient doctors believed governed health.</term> is rarely found, as seen in the first book on accidents and diseases, chapter 2, and in the second and third commentaries on the *Prognostics*. And you should know: It is to be noted that a "boiling" <note>original: "ebullitio," describing the internal heat and bubbling of the blood</note> occurs around the formation of **pus** <note>original: "saniei"</note>, as in the commentary on the second part of the *Aphorisms*. Following this boiling, there is an inflammation of the arteries of the limb and an inflammation of the vapors. Indeed, a collision <note>original: "islisio," referring to the impact of the pulsing blood</note> occurs, and if it does not cease, pus is not formed. However, throbbing does not always follow. Therefore, it happens because there could be throbbing from the beginning of the **phlegmon** <term>Phlegmon: A specific type of hot, red inflammation traditionally attributed to an excess of blood.</term> due to the inflammation, and then the matter is resolved. Also, it should be noted according to **Dino** <note>Dino del Garbo, a famous 14th-century medical commentator</note> that **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> shows here that he intends to determine the nature of apostemes and the "threefold" types <note>original: "trifecis," likely referring to classifications of skin conditions</note>. For internal ones, it is different. Or, according to Avicenna, one should know that in the formation of pus around apostemes and the "threefold" types—that is, around the skin—throbbing necessarily occurs because there are arteries there. Therefore, he puts it among the signs of external swellings. But in the formation of pus in internal parts, throbbing does not necessarily occur in that way, such as in the flesh of the liver and similar organs. Therefore, he will not list it among the signs of external swellings; neither does throbbing happen in hot apostemes of the liver, as the author states in book 3, chapter 14, regarding hot liver apostemes. 
<margin>a</margin> As you already know: First concerning phlegmon; second concerning **erysipelas** <term>Erysipelas: A skin infection causing a bright red rash, often called "St. Anthony's Fire."</term>, there he says "Already you have known." The first part is in two sections: first on signs and causes, second on the cure. The first part is in six sections: first he gives the signs. Thus he distinguishes: note the signs of phlegmon; third he shows with what...

And from the summary of the aforementioned things is what is called **baraschien** <note>original: "baraschien," derived from the Arabic "baras," referring to a white skin condition like leukoderma or a form of leprosy</note>. These evil species and those similar to them multiply in a year of **pestilence**. And of the hot apostemes, those are evil which are not moved toward a "decline" <note>the stage where a swelling goes down</note> which is followed by lightness and the reduction of the swelling, nor toward the gathering of matter, but rather toward the corruption of the limb. And this does not always happen from the size of the aposteme or the quantity of the matter, but rather it happens sometimes from the malignancy of the matter. And you should know that small apostemes are sometimes singular and pure, but many of them are compound. And you should know that every aposteme on the exterior with which there is no throbbing does not produce pus; regarding internal ones, we have already spoken.
L.ii.

### On Phlegmon.

<margin>a</margin> Already you know the phlegmon and its signs: from heat, and inflammation, and the increase in size, and tension, and the driving force or throbbing—if it is deep-seated or if it is near the arteries, and the limb in which it is located is such that nerves come to it, to which nothing is served more than sensibility, just as you knew its disposition. And the larger and greater the arteries are, the more there will be throbbing, and its pain will be more vehement, and its resolution or its collection [of pus] will be swifter. And when a phlegmon is in a sensitive limb, vehement pain follows it in whatever way it exists, and it causes the small veins of that limb, which were hidden, to appear. And you should know <margin>q</margin> that the name "phlegmon" in the language of the **Greeks** is used generally for everything that is inflamed; then it is said of every hot aposteme; afterwards it is said of that which is from a hot aposteme with the aforementioned property, and it does not lack inflammation because of the narrowing of the blood and the blockage of the passages. <margin>b</margin> And it happens rarely that a phlegmon is simple, but usually erysipelas, or hardness, or "furiosity" <note>extreme, rapid spreading</note> is associated with it. And it has causes, among which are the **antecedent** bodily causes from repletion <note>over-fullness of humors</note> or the malice of the humors...

<margin>a</margin> ...mostly it is replaced. Fourth, he gives the causes. Fifth, the times. Sixth, the termination. And there he says: "you know the contrary." Hence, second, all signs have a bloody cause, and in this, it differs from erysipelas. Not additional pulse or throbbing, and where it exists in others whom it senses no more than sensibility... <margin>q</margin> Now, however, he gives the secondary signs of phlegmon, which are not just that external apostemes are revealed by the senses, as he first posits, but the secondary signs by which the apostemes are distinguished by species. Although they have sensible signs, the intellect can still trace the signs back to the causes. Hence **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> in the fourth book of the *Colliget* on universal signs of disease says that external diseases have demonstrative signs that reveal their causes.

<margin>b</margin> And you should know that "phlegmon" is said... and it should be noted that with blood, **yellow bile** <note>original: "chola"</note> can flow, or it can be converted to the nature of yellow bile, and thus erysipelas is associated. Or **black bile** <note>original: "melia"</note> can be mixed with it, or the associated blood can be thickened. Hardness can be associated with corrosive yellow bile, or it can be intensely burnt and will associate with "corrosive ants" <note>original: "formica corrosiva," a term for a creeping skin ulcer</note> or "Persian fire" <note>original: "ignis persicus," often referring to anthrax or herpes zoster</note> or furiosity.

<margin>c</margin> And it has causes. First he gives the antecedent causes, second the primitive causes. He does not list "conjunct" <note>immediate/internal</note> causes. It must be said that he understood from what was said that it is blood contained in the part, or the humor which is the antecedent cause is the same as the first conjunct cause. Also, it is doubted whether it can happen without repletion. The answer is no, because the matter is necessary... whether much or little. It can occur from a primitive cause without any repletion due to the weakness of the part. One must consider if they are antecedent corporal causes... Avicenna invites this in the first book... here he abbreviates... the strength of the expelling force, the weakness of the receiving part, the quantity of the matter, the lack of digestion, the wideness of the passages.

<margin>d</margin> And of these. It is doubted why ulcers are a primitive cause when they are also antecedent, being corporal things. Also, he can teach the primitive cause and above he placed the antecedent. To the first, it must be said that ulcers in themselves are corporal things, but they are also primitive like **cantharides** <note>blister beetles used in medicine</note> or nettles. These things were discussed at length in the first part. To the second, it must be said that a thing which is a primitive cause can act through the mediation of a corporal cause, just as pain is a primitive cause in itself, but its cause is corporal...

<column-break/>

...namely, bad. Second, also, a primitive cause can act through the mediation of a corporal cause, like pain in a due mind. Also, it must be considered that a primitive cause can be the cause of an aposteme through its antecedent cause, which is repletion. 
<margin>e</margin> And the increase. First he gives the "times" <note>stages of the disease</note>. Second, he shows that some phlegmons are evil. And evil: it is doubted why he did not give the signs of the beginning. It is answered that they were noted: because when these accidents begin, it is doubted what distinction is in these apostemes. Dino answers that the times are distinguished in three ways in an aposteme. First, from its essence, namely from the swelling and quantity; thus Avicenna distinguishes here. In another way, according to digestion and indigestion... In another way, according to accidents... Avicenna, however, distinguishes the times in the first way because it is the more general distinction. But it is distinguished in the third way... as is clear from the text when he says "and the decline toward lightness," namely of the swelling and tension and pain.
<margin>f</margin> Namely, of other accidents. 
And you: Here he gives the signs of the modes of termination. First by **resolution** <term>Resolution: The disappearing of a swelling without forming pus.</term>. Second by **suppuration** <term>Suppuration: The formation of pus.</term>. Third by corruption. And you know in two ways: that if it is resolved, throbbing begins in tension... Rhasis <note>The 9th-century physician Al-Razi</note> concerning hot apostemes says this is a sign of healing. Also, when the matter is resolved, the throbbing ceases because its presence was the cause. Also, the standing inflammation begins to be removed when the matter resolves, therefore the throbbing. To the first, that throbbing is twofold. One is "iectigatio" <note>a twitching or jerking sensation</note> from vapors that rise, and this is with some itching and begins to increase because the matter is thinned and expelled...

...with the weakness of the receiving limb, even if there is no repletion or malice of humors. And among these causes are the primitive ones, such as a bruise, or a cut, or a fracture, or a dislocation, or ulcers which multiply in the limb; whereby the matter flows toward it because of the pain and weakness. And perhaps the matters flow to it and are retained in the passages which are weaker, just as apostemes occur in empty places along with ulcers and **scabies** <note>a contagious skin disease</note>. And its increase <margin>e</margin> is declared by the addition of size and tension, and its "state" <note>the peak of the disease</note> is known by its end, and there the matter gathers if it ought to gather, and the decline begins to tend toward lightness and weakness. And that one is evil which does not tend toward decline nor gather pus, and this kind indeed proceeds to the death of the limb and putrefies it. And many times this happens because of the size of the aposteme and the quantity of its matter. And many times it happens because of the malignancy of the matter, even if the aposteme was small. And you <margin>f</margin> indeed know that which is thinned because the throbbing begins in tension and the inflammation begins to subside. And you know <margin>g</margin> that which gathers [pus] by the increase of throbbing and heat and the fixing of both. And you know that <margin>h</margin> which putrefies because of the difficulty of digestion, and the darkness, and the vehemence of tension. And you should know <margin>i</margin> that as long as nature does not submerge the matter, an aposteme does not reach its point from it, but breathes through its fire which appears externally. And you should know <margin>k</margin> when **milliary pustules** <note>original: "pustule demenuliati," small, millet-sized sores</note> are near each other, they indicate a malignant condition, and it is necessary that those having internal apostemes be given water of **endive** and water of **nightshade** <note>original: "solatri"</note> with the pulp of **cassia fistula** <note>a flowering plant used as a mild laxative</note>.

### The Cure of Phlegmon. L.iii.

When a phlegmon occurs from a primitive cause, one should not...

...the other is throbbing, that is, the pain of throbbing; and these diminish once the matter is resolved according to Dino, because in the pulse there is "diastole" <note>expansion</note> and as much as... there is "systole" <note>contraction</note>... and it says it is similar to the text in the third treatise on swellings where it says that pus signifies a weak and throbbing pain, that is, a strong expulsion. Otherwise, in resolution there is control when the matter begins to thin, then it is expelled, and then throbbing begins...

<margin>g</margin> And you know. The cause is that concerning the formation of pus... It should be considered where he said "gathers" and did not say "gathers and is healed."

<margin>h</margin> And you know that which putrefies. Either nature conquers perfectly and then the limb putrefies and is corrupted, or it conquers perfectly and then there would be resolution, or imperfectly and then it tends toward suppuration or another form. Avicenna intends this to be understood from what was said in the first and third books.

<margin>i</margin> And you should know. First explanation by Dino: he wants to show how an aposteme corrupts a limb... nature does not "submerge" <note>overpower</note> the matter in the limb... pus does not come from it. And when it does not "breathe," that is, it is not dissolved by its fire, that is, by the hot matter placed externally. Nature can be said to be submerged, namely the nature of the receiving limb, and it could not resist... therefore all matter of an aposteme must be putrid, therefore it is submerged and suffocated. Avicenna answers that "breathes" means "ventilation," even if bad, through fire, that is, through the emptiness which is external... Avicenna calls the vacuum "fire"... 

<margin>k</margin> And you should know he says that milliary pustules, that is, malignant carbuncle-like ones, are near... they indicate a malignant aposteme.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of phlegmonous inflammations (phlegmons), specifically focusing on the differentiation between causes and the timing of various treatments like bloodletting, softening agents, and repercussives.</meta>

# Book III

<margin>
Part 3, Fen 3 <note>Fen is a division in Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine</note>. According to this, he places the care. Consider that the primitive cause of the injury itself concurs in the act; and its trace leads to the impression that remains when the cause itself recedes, which impression is not the primary sickness. It is doubted whether one should place the cure for a **phlegmon** <term>Phlegmon: A red, painful swelling caused by an excess of blood.</term> according to the primitive cause or not. It is answered: no. Because neither Galen (Therapeutics, Book 13, Question 14) nor Rhazes (Almanzor, Book 7) place this diversity in the cure when they speak of hot **apostemes** <term>Aposteme: A general term for a swelling, tumor, or abscess.</term>. According to him, the cure should not be diversified because nothing indicates the cause; rather, the primitive cause indicates nothing regarding the cure (On the Method of Healing, Book 4, Chapter 3). The reason is that it is nothing; it indicates nothing because the primitive cause is no longer there, as it has already receded. To the contrary, Avicenna says here and in the first book of the Canon (Fen 4, doctrine on bathing) and in the Practice (Chapter 1) that we should speak of the variety of the primitive cause. This is twofold: first, directly by itself, and thus it is a phlegmon, and because the cause has receded and is not present. In another way, indirectly: and thus we signify a different disposition of the sick body, and thus the curative indication and the intensity of the cure are taken. And first, concerning the bite of a rabid dog and a non-rabid one. So also in the present case, a phlegmon either happens without a primitive cause when the body is full, or from a primitive cause when it is possible the body is not full. For a phlegmon does not happen in a pure body unless from a primitive cause, though it can happen from the intrinsic weakness of the part itself, even if it is from a primitive cause with much matter gathered in the part. Therefore, for a phlegmon, it would be from a primary cause.
</margin>

<margin>
**a** First we accept that the body can be pure. Thus, one cannot use **repercussives** <term>Repercussive: A medicine intended to drive "bad humors" back from a swelling into the body to be processed.</term> as it is said. Second, because the matter is enclosed in the part. Thus also we do not use repercussives. To the contrary, it is said that two authors spoke more perfectly than others.
</margin>

First, he puts forward a certain distinction. Second, according to him, he sets down the cure, there where it says "since according to."

The trace indicates either a cleansing of the body or a repletion <note>original: "repletio," meaning an over-fullness of bodily fluids or humors</note>. If the cleansing meets it, it is not necessary unless the cure of the aposteme is for the aposteme itself. And the extraction of the foreign matter that caused the aposteme to happen, and that is done through **mollifying** <term>Mollifying: Softening or soothing agents used to ease the tension of a swelling.</term> and light **resolutive** <term>Resolutive: A treatment intended to "resolve" or disperse the matter causing a swelling.</term> agents, such as a poultice of wheat flour cooked with water and oil; and sometimes **scarification** <term>Scarification: Making small incisions in the skin to release fluid or blood.</term> spares the distress when the aposteme contains much matter. However, when you find a repletion of the body, then you must not touch the aposteme with mollifying agents, because it will draw to itself more than it resolves from it; rather, it is necessary to evacuate the matter through **phlebotomy** <term>Phlebotomy: The medical practice of opening a vein to let blood.</term> and perhaps it needs only a loosening of the bowels; and when you have done that, administer the mollifying agents. And its cure is indeed the primary cure for one whose primitive cause finds the body cleansed. And it differs from it in this: that it does not need a treatment with many repercussives in the beginning as that one needs; rather, it needs them less. But when the cause is **antecedent** <term>Antecedent cause: An internal cause, like a systemic imbalance of humors, rather than an external injury.</term> and not primitive, then you must begin with evacuation and complete what is required by phlebotomy and by loosening the bowels if it needs it. And the necessity of it is either because the body is impure or because the sickness

<margin>
**b** In a body that is clean by itself or through phlebotomy or another evacuation performed: it needs repercussion by itself. The reason: because in the beginning, the matter must clearly be removed by a removal opposite to the flow; this is done through repercussion. I say "by itself": for if it occurs in the **emunctories** <term>Emunctories: Organs or passages that carry off waste, such as the armpits or groin.</term>, or if it is venomous matter, or if it is expelled by a **crisis** <note>original: "crisim," the turning point of a disease</note>, or if it is thick and viscous, or if it is gathered in a part as happens in the present case, just as in contusions matter is gathered in a part, so in a phlegmon from a primitive cause like a blow or a wound, matter is immediately gathered in the part. Repercussion, therefore, binds the matter and is the cause of its corruption and also that of the limb. It must be considered as a starting point. In which the physician encounters a state: suddenly, for matter is gathered in the part due to a primitive cause. And therefore the matter should not be driven back (repercussed), but one must hasten to resolution lest the putrefied matter corrupt the limb; but if the aposteme is not from a primary cause but an antecedent one, it is not gathered in the part in the beginning, and therefore you can use repercussion. To the contrary: in this aposteme, if there is a flow of matter, then we cannot prohibit it with repercussives because the harm from constriction is greater than the benefit of prohibiting the flow; or it should be said that we resist the flow by diversion to the opposite side and evacuation without repercussives. To the second: regarding a phlegmon without a primary cause. To the third: it should be said as will appear. It should be noted that if repercussives are suitable in a phlegmon from a primary cause, it should be a small amount and for a short time, only so that the limb is comforted, such as with Rose Oil, etc.
</margin>

**a** Regarding "But if." First, when the body is clean. Second, when it is full, at the words "When however." Whether the extraction of matter through the part is the cure of the aposteme as an aposteme. Because no: for the cure of the aposteme as an aposteme is repercussion (Book 1, Fen 4 of Avicenna). Also Galen in the *Tegni*. Also the cure of an aposteme as an aposteme is to remove the matter of the part through pressure or drawing it out, as taken from the *Tegni*. Therefore, attraction to the contrary is not the only way. Avicenna is here to the contrary. To which: the cure of an aposteme as such is twofold: one simple and more comprehensive, involving resolution, scarification, or incision. The other is more composite, and that is with repercussion; because although it does not evacuate the matter from the part, yet there is an opposition to the "river" or flow; and this is suitable when it is in flux, and thus there is a drawing to the contrary, although it does not evacuate matter from the part; yet it diverts it. "Mollifying" means softening. "Opening the pores." "Resolutives" are those that thin the matter. "Light" agents are those not strong enough to putrefy the matter or inflame it, but rather to mitigate the pain. Scarification spares the distress because a long cure would otherwise be needed through resolution, or because the limb might come to corruption because of much matter gathered and corrupted there. It is said: after scarification, you must again use resolutives. It is doubted whether we should evacuate when a phlegmon is from a primitive cause with a clean body. It seems so, because Galen (Therapeutics, Book 13, Ch 3) and Avicenna (Canon, Book 1, Fen 4, chapter on phlebotomy) say we evacuate for magnitude or repletion. To the contrary, Avicenna says that evacuation through the part occurs with the flow; but diversion is done through evacuation of the body via phlebotomy, which is not done for evacuation's sake but for diversion. Galen speaks of this. This is the "flight." Otherwise: then the primitive cause meets a clean body, and with its cleanliness, the matter does not flow disruptively, and then evacuation is not suitable. For if it flowed disruptively, then its cure would be evacuation like others that happen with repletion of the body.

**b** "When however." First this, second he compares. But there: "And its indeed." It should be considered that the order is first to cure with mollifying agents. It is doubted whether in a phlegmon we should use repercussives coming from a primitive cause, having performed evacuation through phlebotomy if it is expedient, and where there is repletion of the body. For in a forming phlegmon we intend two things: to prohibit what is about to happen, and this through repercussives; and second, to delete what exists. Avicenna says the use of mollifying agents in the beginning is fearful. Also Avicenna says that it does not need treatment with many repercussives in the beginning; therefore he concedes repercussion. To the contrary, Avicenna and Haly Abbas (Practice, Book 3) say it can be a hot aposteme.

**c** "And its." He compares first according to agreement. Second according to difference, at "and it differs." The first exposition is that the cure of that aposteme from a primitive cause when it finds the body full and after pre-cleansing is the primary cure of an aposteme from a primitive cause that finds the body clean: because as the body is clean, it had the help of phlebotomy and was clean by itself.

**d** "And it differs." He sets down the differences. First, the cure of an aposteme when it finds the body full from a primitive cause differs (before evacuation is done) from that phlegmon which occurs from a primitive cause that finds the body clean: in this, that it does not need treatment with many repercussives in the

<column-break/>

beginning. Namely, the one from a primitive cause with repletion: and before cleansing, just as that one does. Namely, just as that phlegmon whose primitive cause finds the body clean needs it, or rather even less. Namely, it needs repercussion. But although repercussion may be suitable, it is less suitable for the one with repletion before evacuation because a full body does not receive it; but that which is without repletion can be repercussed more. It is doubted because, according to this exposition, Avicenna concedes repercussives in that which is from a primitive cause without repletion. And above he only placed mollifying and resolutive agents because this is its cure insofar

<margin>
as it is an aposteme. Likewise say: "less than that," therefore in an aposteme from a primitive cause with a full body, he seems to concede some repercussion before evacuation, the contrary of which is in Galen (*Tegni*), because a full body does not receive it; indeed, in no aposteme do they concede it before evacuation. It is answered: the above exposition does not please him much. It is said that in an aposteme from a primitive cause with cleansing of the body, we can repercuss something from the beginning, and properly it is an aposteme and a limb, because one fears the malice of the flow of matter to the place. And if Avicenna does not...
</margin>

is not great, which is why evacuation and the lessening of matter and attraction to the contrary are necessary. And although the body may not have many superfluities, yet in the limb it sometimes happens that the limb itself is weakened, which is why the matters of the body are attracted to it even if they are not superfluous matters. And you must observe the predicted conditions in this: age, season, region, and others. And "begin with repercussives" except in the places we conditioned in the first book. Then oppose the increase with the introduction of mollifying and moisturizing agents with restraining agents; and as it proceeds in the increase, proceed in the addition of mollifiers gradually. And at the end and the "state" <note>original: "statū," the peak or plateau of a disease</note> and the ultimate magnitude and the addition of its finality, make the mollifiers prevail, make them pure. And "drying agents" are those that heal at the end. For these are contrary: and mollifiers are for dilating the pores and for soothing the pain. And a drying agent is that which heals and prohibits anything from remaining that might become **pus** <note>original: "sanies," an unhealthy discharge</note>. If however it does not heal entirely and leaves something behind, it leaves only a small thing which he placed there as resolved. He says that here he speaks more distinctly than he said above: to show that resolutives and mollifiers confer more than repercussives; because repercussion is suitable for each, namely when the aposteme is large, and they are suitable only a little because they should stay for a short time and be light; because perhaps they flow around the site of the aposteme. But in an aposteme from a primitive cause with repletion of the body before cleansing, repercussives are not suitable: and therefore that comparison is held everywhere. Or otherwise, that before cleansing, "untrue" ones can be suitable, but others that are comforting, like rose oil, etc. And therefore it will not be a repercussive because a full body is not repercussed; but it will be to comfort some small part. Namely, in an aposteme from a primitive cause without repletion we can repercuss more strongly than with repletion and before evacuation; and this is what he wants. Another exposition is that the cure of a phlegmon from a primitive cause without repletion differs from its cure from a primitive cause with repletion and before cleansing: because it does not need repercussion because it is from a primitive cause and the body is clean, just as that one needs it. Namely, that which is from a primitive cause and the body is full after evacuation; or rather even less. And therefore the difference is that after cleansing in a phlegmon from a primitive cause and in repletion we can repercuss, and so Avicenna wants in Book 1, Fen 4. But in a phlegmon from a primitive cause that finds the body clean, we cannot repercuss. Therefore that is less abusive, or if we can, it would be very slight. Therefore the primitive cause that meets repletion—if you perform phlebotomy—then we ought to resist the flow of matter more and fear regarding it that it is not contained if the body is clean.

**e** "When however the cause is antecedent." He sets down the cure from an antecedent cause: and first he sets down the cause of the cure or the curative intention. Second he sets down the medicines. The second part at "medicines however." He does first regarding the universal cure, second regarding the special one or the location, at "begin etc." It should be said that this phlebotomy sometimes must be from the cephalic vein, sometimes from the basilic, sometimes from the common vein, but freely. Second, from the opposite part. It is doubted whether evacuation is suitable for a clean body. It seems so: and above in a phlegmon from a primitive cause he did not prescribe it. Also, can a clean body become weakened without a primitive cause? It seems not: because nothing else can be; to the contrary is Avicenna, because thus it is with a phlegmon not from a primitive cause. Also, that a great sickness can come to a clean body and not be from a primitive cause. To the first he says that evacuation is not done in a body that is similarly clean, except when there are many superfluities. Or it is said that even if the body is clean, evacuation is suitable by reason of diversion when the aposteme is large and the matter flows disruptively. It should be noted according to this: just as in a phlegmon from a primitive cause when the body is clean, repercussion is less useful; but when a primitive cause finds it full, after evacuation we can use it more; so when a phlegmon is from an antecedent cause and the body has few superfluities, we can never use or ought to use a repercussive. But if the body is full, it is more useful. Also in a phlegmon from an antecedent cause without much repletion, we can use a repercussive more than in a phlegmon from a primitive cause that finds the body clean. To the second he says there can be weakness in a clean body from the beginning, from generation, or from a preceding sickness. To the third he says a great sickness can happen from nature or time which will be great by reason of the limb in which it is, or by reason of its essence, or by reason of the harm induced, as follows in Galen.

**f** "And begin." First he sets down the local cure according to each stage of time. Second, the harms that can arrive there. And "sometimes it happens." First in the beginning, second in the increase, third in the peak, and fourth in the end. At "drying agents": consider the conditions mentioned above. It is doubted whether a phlegmon from an antecedent cause in the beginning should be repercussed. It seems not: because matter should not be driven to the noble organs <note>the "noble" or vital organs like the heart, liver, or brain</note>. Also corrupted blood should not be repercussed; but a phlegmon is such. But regarding the discovery of blood, it is so. To which: it must be repercussed after evacuation is done; the reason is that the cure of a forming phlegmon and one already formed: just as forming precedes being formed, so the cure of the forming precedes the cure of the formed. To the contrary: it is said that some limbs are ignoble simply, like the emunctories; and in these repercussion is not allowed. Some are not ignoble simply, but in respect to the principal ones, such as external limbs that have noble functions, like the hand, the foot, the eye, etc. And for these we can repercuss. If you say the matter is evil: to this it is said that if the matter be venomous or evil as in "cretic" **erysipelas** <term>Erysipelas: A skin infection characterized by a red, spreading rash, here categorized by its severity or "cretic" nature.</term>, it either fixes or rectifies and annihilates, i.e., resolves the dispersed parts. To the second: it is said that if it be much corrupted it should not be driven back. Or that it cannot be by reason of that part itself; but with flux continuously to the part.

**g** "Then oppose." The authors teach to mix with...
