<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for treating hot inflammations (phlegmons), specifically detailing the transition between different types of topical remedies—repelling, softening, and drying—depending on the stage of the swelling.</meta>

### Fen III, Treatise I

<margin>
Between repelling <note>original: "repercussivis"</note> and dissolving agents <note>original: "resolutiva"</note>: dissolving agents are drying, not softening. In the stage of "augmentation" <term>Augmentation: The phase where a swelling is still growing.</term> there is a double intent: the internal sensation and the physical fact; therefore, one must mix remedies, etc. Also, it should be considered that these repelling agents, when compared to softening agents, should not be too strong lest they constrict the area, but light so they do not dissolve the subtle matter that was compacted and hardened by the initial repulsion; and this is why he mentions softeners, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
**b** And toward the end: that is, every period of time is divided into three parts. Therefore, at the "state" <term>State: The peak or plateau of the illness's intensity.</term> the softening agents should prevail, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
**t** And drying agents <note>original: "exiccantia"</note>. They show what must be done at the end or during the "decline" <term>Decline: The phase where the swelling begins to subside.</term>. And first here, Oribasius <note>original: "fo"</note> compares softening medicines to drying ones; see the section on humectants. It must be considered that by "drying agents" he means pure dissolving agents without softeners, or at least not those used during the "state" of the disease, such as fenugreek, cumin, and the like.
</margin>

<margin>
**k** Again, concerning humectants. This is against those who distinguish between softening and drying or "desiccating." Because softening agents open the pores, dilate them, and soothe pain, whereas desiccants dissolve the matter. Therefore, the task of the softener will be to dilate, dissolve, and soothe pain, but the task of the desiccant will be to heal by consuming the matter with strong heat. Therefore, we can use them during the "decline," where there is no fear of heat or pain. And if that desiccant leaves anything behind that it cannot dissolve—which might induce a new problem—we can use strong, sharp medicines; Oribasius says these include *diagion* <note>a type of plaster</note> and *dia palma* <note>a palm-oil based plaster</note>, an absorbent plaster of honey, and barley flour, and things similar to these.
</margin>

...in which there is sharpness. And sometimes a vehemence of pain happens due to the cooling <note>original: "refrenatione"</note> because of the "suffocation" of the matter and the hardness of the limb. And sometimes it happens that because of this, the matter returns to the principal organs; and sometimes it happens that the **aposteme** <term>Aposteme: A general term for a swelling or abscess.</term> hardens. And it sometimes happens that the limb begins to turn green and black <note>signs of gangrene</note>, especially when it is treated with these at the end of the matter and specifically during the "state" <note>the peak of the inflammation</note>. And you should know that the vehemence of pain makes you need softening medicines without "attraction" <term>Attraction: The process of drawing humors toward a specific spot.</term>, and perhaps there will be cooling with them that does not hinder the softening. Indeed, regarding the return of the matter to the principal organs, he is safe from it unless that which comes from them follows the path of expulsion from them, and the organs receiving from them become the evacuators of those things; for there is no way to repel and expel them entirely. We have already verified these things in their proper place. And when it is feared that the swelling will decline into hardness, administer softening agents in which there is heat and moistening with strength. Repelling medicines <note>original: "repercussive"</note> are those of a middle nature, such as the juices of cold herbs which we often mention in other places, such as the juice of purslane, gourd, endive, and shepherd’s purse, and others; and specifically the juice of nightshade <note>original: "solatri"</note> and their crushed bodies prepared as a plaster; and the juice of psyllium <note>flea-wort</note> also in a wax-salve <note>original: "ceratum"</note> with cold water. Perhaps a sponge soaked in vinegar and cold water spares the labor; and winter cherry <note>original: "kenkengi"</note> is strong at the beginning, as are pomegranate flowers, sempervivum, and a strong decoction of sage, especially mixed with vinegar, or sumac and "tibul" is good again. And if a stronger one is needed, add to them sandalwood, acacia, myrrh, camphor, and white henbane. And the herb called "herb of apostemes" is very good at the beginning. And sometimes its drying and astringency helps when mixed with saffron; but moistening at the beginning is dangerous. And when there is an excess of cooling, it perhaps leads to the corruption of the limb and the corruption of the humor collected in the aposteme, and the aposteme tends toward greenness and blackness. If, therefore, you fear any of this, apply a plaster to the place with barley flour and bindweed <note>original: "volubili"</note> in which there is softening. But if any of this [gangrene] appears, then scarify the place <term>Scarify: To make small incisions in the skin to drain fluid or blood.</term> and skin it, and do not wait for the collection of pus nor for maturation; and do that when you see that which has been poured out...

<margin>
**a** And sometimes: showing the harm that can come from repelling agents, etc.
</margin>
<margin>
**b** And you should know: first he teaches how to aid the vehemence of pain; second, the return of matter to the principal organs; third, the "mordification" <note>corrosion or biting pain</note> and greenness. See the section "and from the return," etc., and "when it is feared," etc. Regarding the first, consider that if the matter is constricted by the repelling agent, causing pain, the cure will be to soften it, as with linseed and chamomile, even if there is cooling in them—that is, a little heat or tempered cold without attraction—such as decocted mallow and barley flour with rose oil. And this is when it is at the beginning; for softening can coexist with their coldness. He mentions another case: in the "augmentation," we mix fenugreek, linseed, and chamomile flowers.
</margin>
<margin>
**c** Indeed, from the return: regarding the matter, the evacuation is safe; for if you repel it before evacuation, there is fear of it returning to the principal organs; but if it is after evacuation, there is no fear that the matter will spread through the body and be destroyed.
</margin>
<margin>
**d** And when heat is feared: that is, tempered heat, because strong heat would harden it. And "moistening with strength" according to Oribasius: marshmallow, fenugreek flour, and *diaquilon* <note>a lead-based plaster</note>, or strong heating and moistening, because the repelling agent has cooled it too much.
</margin>
<margin>
**e** Medicines: he lists the medicines as they are appropriate at the beginning. Second, those in the "augmentation." Third, he gives a certain rule for curing a flow when it tends toward "exiture" <term>Exiture: The point where an abscess is ready to burst.</term>. Fourth, he lists certain medicines appropriate for the "state." Fifth, those for the "decline." Sixth, he gives another rule. First, he enumerates certain medicines that are suitable at the beginning. Second, he teaches how to remove the harm that could happen from their improper use. Third, he...
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
...gives a certain rule regarding dissolving and repelling. Fourth, he shows the caution for removing pain. Fifth, "And when it falls." Third, "And you should know." Fourth, "If therefore." It is doubted whether repelling matters should be cold and dry, or cold and moist. It seems they should be hot, because they are "blate" <note>unclear technical term, possibly related to poultices</note>. First, they seem cold because Avicenna says so here, and Oribasius gives a rule that they should be moist because of the mucilage. They seem dry because they are astringent. He says that generally they should be cold—contrary to the "attraction" of humors—so they cause coldness to arrive, thicken the humors, and break the heat that attracts them. And they should be astringent because they prevent the flow; for they repel by strengthening the vessels with astringent pharmacy.
</margin>

...is very much, and perhaps the limb dies. And of scarification, one type is more superficial and another more deep, and that is according to the location of the aposteme and the disposition of the limb. And when you have scarified, then bathe it <note>original: "ebroca" from embrocation</note> with seawater and other salt waters, and apply a plaster with something in which there is softening. And if you do not need the moistening and bathing, be content with softeners. And know that the administration of those things that repel strongly at the first, and those that dissolve strongly at the end, is bad; therefore, avoid it as much as you can. For intense cooling leads to that which you already know [gangrene]; and cold water is similarly among those things to be avoided, except in cases like **erysipelas** <term>Erysipelas: A hot, red skin infection also known as St. Anthony's Fire.</term>. In cases of intense dissolution, pain occurs. If therefore you wish to manage the beginning with the soothing of pain, do not bring hot water near them, but rather softening oils and plasters made from such medicines; for these are strongly contrary to what is necessary for prohibiting the "effusion" <note>outpouring of humors</note>. You should return to **Armenian bole** <term>Armenian Bole: A medicinal red clay used as an astringent.</term> dissolved in cold water or with rose oil. And the best of all bathing liquids is that made from roses and oil; for oil is specifically a certain dissolver. Or use lentils decocted with roses, or **litharge** <note>original: "merdasengi," lead monoxide</note> with rose oil. If indeed these do not work, and those things that run their course, administer bindweed <note>original: "volubilem"</note>, as this is of great help in the beginning and at the peak; and *assirengi*, *albaafech*, celery, and *albedarungi* similarly. And many times sweet wine mixed with rose oil soothes pain; indeed, a "congealing of the grape" <note>possibly a syrup or thick extract</note> up to 50 drachms. And apply it upon wool, or "hyssop-wool" cooled in summer and warmed in winter, or a sponge soaked in astringent wine or vinegar and cold water; and saffron is included for the soothing of pain. Now, if you see the beginning of the aposteme proceeding on the path toward becoming an "exiture" <note>bursting abscess</note>, then leave off the cooling and proceed on the path of that which ripens and opens. When the aposteme has reached its "state" <note>plateau</note>, then such things as dill, chamomile, marshmallow, linseed, and the like are necessary; indeed, the plasters called *basilicon* and those called *diaquilon*. And the plaster of **colcotar** <term>Colcotar: A byproduct of heating vitriol, used as a dry, astringent powder.</term> dries without pain, and for that reason its administration is convenient when it is in the "instant" of the phlegmon. And it is convenient when there is no fear of a collection of pus; and it is better that you place over it wool soaked in astringent wine. And flesh needs drying less than a nerve does.

<margin>
**s** Salt in the covering. Third, although they should be cold, yet in cold apostemes they are mixed with hot and dry medicines. Fourth, in a cold phlegmon, they are astringent but not much. Fifth, in erysipelas, they are cold and moist, and more astringent, as will be declared below. Sixth, in the eyes, they are cold but not astringent, as has been proven, etc. And "humectation"—that is, softening and dissolving. Therefore we ought to repel. A repelling medicine ought not be moist at the beginning of a phlegmon; but at the "state," it is not enough for it to be cold and moist, but rather hot and dry; therefore saffron is mixed in.
</margin>

<margin>
**f** And when: he teaches how to remove the harm. First, before it happens; second, after it has happened (see "if indeed it appears"). Third, that heat is a mitigator of pain and spasms according to Hippocrates, Fifth Particle. Also Galen, Book 5 of *On the Method of Healing*, uses hot water to mitigate pain. Also Avicenna: softening humectants are for soothing pain, etc. He says that pain at the beginning can either follow a "bad complexion" <note>imbalance of humors</note> and a break in continuity, or it can follow from the constriction of matter in a part or place due to its multitude or due to strong constriction. In the first way, softening is not appropriate. The reason is from Avicenna: that it is contrary to what is necessary for prohibiting the outpouring of humors; and therefore such pain is soothed with repulsion at the beginning. In the second way, then softening agents are appropriate. And this is why Avicenna speaks above, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
**S** If indeed: he placed the medicines that help in the "augmentation." Second, the consideration of bindweed <note>volubilis</note>, because it is balanced, declining toward heat, which helps in the augmentation by dissolving, and in the "state" at the beginning—that is, the beginning of the
</margin>

augmentation: or in the beginning—that is, what is mixed with repelling agents. However, the text can be introduced thus: that after he taught how to remove the pain happening from the flow of matter, then it is done by repelling. He teaches how to remove the pain that occurs because of the "construction" <note>constriction</note>, secondarily because of the improper use of these repelling agents; and this is done with softening agents. It can be said that then the aposteme is in the beginning of the augmentation. Or, after he taught how to soothe pain with strong and pure repelling agents, here he does it with those that are weak and somewhat dissolving. "Congealing of the grape" up to 50 drachms: cooked wine; and he says that it does not just dry like wine, but rather it softens more and is less hot, as Oribasius says. "Wool, etc. cooled": that is, in summer, except in the nerves and the head. "Sponge": it should be understood that it helps more in the beginning than in the augmentation. Whence Avicenna places it above for repelling. "Therefore on the path to becoming an exiture": that is, of healing. It ripens and opens—that is, it dissolves or opens—namely, with the iron <note>a surgical knife</note>, etc.

**b** When however: it must be granted that in the "state," as far as the "accidents" <term>Accidents: The secondary symptoms or signs of a disease.</term> and the matter that flows are concerned, then those things that dissolve are appropriate. And if they do not dissolve, they ripen, and such things are softeners, etc. For Oribasius praises *diaquilon* when the subtle part of the phlegmon comes to maturation; whence the aposteme breaks, and there will be a certain thing like the "thrombus of Sanicius," and a thick part is left in the circuit which did not reach maturation.

**i** The plaster of colcotar: he lists medicines that are appropriate in the "decline." Plasters of **colcotar** <note>calcined vitriol</note> are all medicines in which there is the redness of vitriol, like *diapalma*. And because it dries strongly, it is not appropriate when it is in the [active] phlegmon. Whence he says it is inconvenient when it is, etc.; otherwise it is convenient—that is, although there is inflammation and heat there, it is appropriate. Namely, the medicine of colcotar.

Above, he determined the treatment for sanguineous abscesses; here he discusses those caused by choler <term>Choler: Also known as yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with heat and dryness.</term> and those running through the body. The first part of the section provides the species and signs. The second provides the cure. Note that erysipelas has a difference: it attracts more efficiently because it is sharper and hotter; but for a putrid phlegmon, there is greater fullness. And the more the addition of blood over the choleric humor is multiplied, the more the swelling appears, and the pain and throbbing are more vehement. And erysipelas draws a fever more vehemently than a phlegmon. And sometimes it follows from the heat of erysipelas that the skin is disturbed, wherefore it is changed by that which is named erysipelas, and a phlegmon is not so: therefore the inflammation of erysipelas is not less than the inflammation of a phlegmon, but rather more. Truly the tension of a phlegmon and its pain is because of the stretching, and sometimes it may be greater than the pain of erysipelas, which is lesser. And where* erysipelas most often occurs is in the face; it begins at the bridge of the nose, and the swelling increases and spreads across the whole face. And when erysipelas occurs from a fracture of a bone under the skin, then that is a bad sign.

Regarding the parts: the reason it is bad is because it hinders the cure, a sign that signifies a defect of virtue <term>Virtue: In this context, the body's natural healing power or vitality.</term>. ### The Cure of Erysipelas. Lesson 5.

It is necessary that you evacuate* the body of it with a laxative for choler and by performing phlebotomy; yet phlebotomy indeed does not confer much benefit except when the matter is between two skins. If however it should be deep, then its benefit is diminished and perhaps it attracts more matter. And if you require a repetition of loosening the belly after phlebotomy, do it according to how it is heated from the two matters. Then change* your course to cooling it with strong cooling agents mentioned in the chapter on phlegmons, and with the pouring on of cold water; do this until the color is altered. For pure erysipelas is destroyed with the alteration of color and the diminution of itself. And in the end, cooling in erysipelas is more necessary because the flame and the inflammatory pain in it are greater; and evacuation in a phlegmon is more necessary because the matter in it is more disobedient and thicker. And it is necessary that its cooling in the beginning be stronger in astringency <note>original: "stipticitatis"</note> so that perhaps its astringency is increased over the cold itself. Around the "state" <term>State: The peak of the illness.</term> of the illness, let the cold be more vehement than its astringency; and beware with this that you do not cause the matter to return to an internal limb or to a noble limb. And beware⁴ again lest the limb be blackened and become dark and begin to go the way of corruption. And when anything of this appears, move in the opposite direction of astringency and cooling. And if* the erysipelas should be upon the skin, let it be treated with dross of lead <note>original: "coria plũbi"</note> with harsh wine boiled with leaves of "sicia" boiled with wine, and let it be treated with that in which there is resolution and strong drying along with cooling. And that is like the smoke of old burnt wool, not washed, weight 12 drachms; and of charcoal from the bark of a pine tree, the same amount; of wax, 20 drachms; of dross of lead, 4 drachms; of old goat suet washed with water, 15 drachms; of myrtle oil, 5 drachms. And again, a lighter plaster than that may be made from dross of lead with juice of rue and rose oil and wax.

# Fen III Treatise

<margin>
...medicines that are suitable in the state [of the disease]. But here he places medicines that are suitable for ulcerated erysipelas, which are of very strong desiccation <note>Drying power</note>. It is doubted why he does not provide the cure for erysipelas in its growth and decline. To which it is understood that the cure for the growth is given through the cure for the beginning and the state, but the cure for the decline through the cure for the state. For just as in the state we dry and resolve, and with this we cool, so in the decline, by drying, resolving, and cooling, those cures are affected. This was not previously explained. In erysipelas, we cool in the decline and the state, and we do not fear the congealing of the matter as we do in a phlegmon, in which the matter is thicker and more abundant, indicating a greater need for evacuation and resolution, as he said. The medicines he places are noted, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
Previously [he spoke] about large abscesses; here he speaks about pustules or small abscesses, either from blood or choler <note>Yellow bile</note>. Here he deals with those that "run" in their course and their companions, and he has as many parts here as there are types of those abscesses, namely *Formica* <note>original: "formica"; literally "the ant," likely referring to shingles or herpes due to its stinging, crawling sensation</note>, etc. First, he gives notification, then he provides the cure. First, he shows what it is, then he provides the signs. It should be considered that it is called "formica" because of its likeness to an ant: on account of its smallness, its crawling movement, and its stinging manner of puncturing. Also, it is a pustule, that is, a small abscess and a small prominence. And they differ from large abscesses not only in this, but because for the most part, pustules emit a certain moisture with some ulceration, and so pustules require drying. Any of these can be called formica. It should be considered that every formica is "ambulatory" <note>wandering or spreading</note>, but some are more so, being from thin matter; some are less so, being from thick matter, which is called *miliaris* <note>original: "miliaris"; millet-like</note>; and some are corrosive, while some are not. There are therefore three species: absolutely ambulatory formica, ambulatory miliaris, and the corrosive type. The ambulatory comes from thin choler; the miliaris from thick; and the corrosive from burnt choler. Therefore, any type can become corrosive if it becomes burnt and thickens.
</margin>

**F**ormica is a pustule or pustules that emerge and cause a pure abscess to occur, and they "walk" <note>spread across the skin</note> and perhaps ulcerate, and perhaps resolve, and you already know the cause of each of these. The color of formica is indeed inclined toward yellow <note>original: "citrinitatem"</note> and is inflamed, with a wart-like substance, round in shape, and most have a broad root, except for a certain species called *acrubaurod* <note>A transliteration of an Arabic term for a specific virulent pustule</note> which has a small root like a worm; and in every formica, a sensation like the sting of an ant is felt. In summary, every abscess walking upon the skin that does not have depth <note>original: "latitudinem"; refers to deep tissue involvement</note> is formica. Furthermore, one type is miliaris and another is corrosive, as you have known. That which is an ulcer and becomes putrid is properly called "putrid."

### The Cure of Formica and those things that run in its course. Chapter VII.

**W**hen you do not begin with the evacuation of the humor as is required, but rather treat the ulcer with that which heals it, it returns in another place with harm, and from that very place it does not cease to perform corrosion after corrosion. Whey <note>original: "aqua casci"</note> with scammony is helpful for the evacuation of the matter of formica and similar things. The way in which formica is cured is that when it is corrosive, it should be kept away from the moistening treatments that you have already administered in erysipelas, for moistening is not suitable for ulcers. In its beginnings, administer things like lettuce, water lily, sempervivum <note>Houseleek</note>, bindweed, and purslane. And if it should be necessary, then use things like nightshade, especially dried and crushed, for in it there is desiccation; also plantain, blackberry, and lentils, and after these, barley meal, pomegranate rinds, and vine branches. And when they fear corrosion and ulcers upon it, administer with these cooling things a bit of honey and similar items, or frankincense flour with vinegar. Also, the liquid that runs from moist vine wood when it is burnt, and sheep dung with vinegar, and cow dung with vinegar. When corrosion and ulceration appear, then administer *Andron* troches <term>Troches: Medicinal lozenges or tablets, here used topically.</term> with astringent wine or mixed vinegar, or the juice of squirting cucumber and salt, and ox gall rubbed with nitre <note>Saltpeter or native soda</note>, and pepper and nitre with the urine of a boy. And regarding salt, he said it is suitable to take something like a probe <note>original: "embuba"</note> or the tip of a quill or another thing whose tip is sharp, which can "swallow" the formica; then let it penetrate around it to the depth with its sharpness, and then let those formicae be eradicated with their root. The formicae of those who are children are destroyed if they are put into a bath, although the air of the bath harms them; then let them exit quickly and be anointed with rose oil and rose water.

<margin>
**a** And the color. He provides three or four signs. Dionysius says this is not a distinct species of formica, but another of these types; it differs however in the manner of its shape, but the distinction of shape is not essential.

**c** And in summary. Consider that he hints at three species. It is doubted because there seem to be two species according to Haly Abbas: corrosive and non-corrosive. Likewise, Avicenna says here that in the first division there are two species, namely ambulatory and corrosive. But of the non-corrosive, one is absolutely ambulatory and the other is miliaris, which is from thicker matter with an admixture of "windiness" <note>gas or vapors</note>. It appears that miliaris and absolutely ambulatory are similar because both move by "walking." Therefore, Rhazes says of miliaris formica that both are included under it; but the absolutely ambulatory is more similar to the corrosive than to the miliaris, because the matter of the absolutely ambulatory is hotter though thin, and therefore apt to be ignited and burnt and thickened so that it becomes corrosive. Therefore, the cure of the absolutely ambulatory and the corrosive is listed as similar, but the distinction of the miliaris is clear in its time.

### The Cure of Miliaris. Chapter VIII.

**M**iliaris is similar to formica in its cure; however, it is better in its resolution that there be in its purgative the virtue of something like turbith <note>A medicinal root</note> with that which dissolves choler. And if epithymum <term>Epithymum: Dodder of thyme, used to purge melancholy.</term> is included, it is better, since it is necessary that there be some melancholy and phlegm mixed with the choler. Then let galls, tamarisk fruit, pomegranate rinds, and Armenian bole be taken; let all those be gathered in vinegar and rose water in such quantity that they do not sting, and let them be anointed over it with a quill. And sweet milk is vehemently suitable for the cure of this sickness. And when it passes the beginning, it should then be cured with those things that are like the burnt head of a salted fish with astringent wine. And stronger than that, when ultimate desiccation is necessary, is to take the leaves of *albedarungi* <note>Possibly a type of stinking iris or similar herb</note> and let heat be placed in them and let them be administered. And stronger still is to take the flower of copper <note>original: "flos eris"; verdigris or copper flakes</note> and burnt yellow sulfur, and let a liniment be made of them with wine or the vine-wood water that flows from its burning.

### On Pruna and Persian Fire. Chapter IX.

**T**hese two names are perhaps applied generally to every corrosive and blistering pustule that burns and causes an eschar to occur, such as that caused by a burn...

<margin>
**m** Miliaris. First through evacuation. Second through local treatments. First you must evacuate. Secondly, consider that Avicenna completes the manner of being. He said above that here "windiness" is mixed, because anything pure thickens the choler. Then: first regarding the beginning; second when it passes the beginning. Consider that here very drying medicines are placed: for in miliaris, drying is more suitable than in ambulatory formica. If it is miliaris from choler with windiness, it will indicate desiccation. And therefore if miliaris passes into the corrosive, it vehemently requires very drying things. Milk is given as a drink; it confers against the itch of scabies and *bothor* <note>pustules</note>; it can confer benefit in other species of formica. Otherwise, it should be said that other dry things must be mixed with the milk.
</margin>

<margin>
**n** And when. He provides medicines that dry more than the first. When you see the moisture remaining while the formica remains, use a stronger medicine.
</margin>

<margin>
**o** These two names. Here he determines concerning Persian fire. First regarding its cause, signs, and diversity. Second, he provides the cure. First, he shows what can be understood by the name *pruna* <note>plum or burning coal</note> and *ignis persicus* <note>Persian fire</note>. Second, he provides the differences between pruna and Persian fire through their proper signs. Third, he provides their causes. Fourth, he compares them regarding their names. Fifth, he provides certain judgments. Regarding the first part, Dionysius strongly praises desiccation in the cure of such pustules, such as white ointment. Note what is understood by these two names... and here the causes and signs of these passions.

<summary>This page details the classification and treatment of small, stinging, or corrosive skin eruptions known as Formica, Miliaris, and Persian Fire. The text emphasizes using highly drying (desiccating) botanical and mineral topicals to stop the "crawling" spread and prevent the formation of putrid ulcers.</summary>
<keywords>formica, shingles, miliaris, Persian fire, dermatology, medieval pharmacology, Avicenna, Galen, desiccation, choler, pustules</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the detailed classification of malignant skin conditions, specifically distinguishing between "Persian Fire" and "The Coal" (carbuncles). It moves from defining their physical characteristics—such as color, depth, and the sensation of "crawling"—to providing specific surgical and herbal interventions like bloodletting and drying plasters.</meta>

Second: blistering. Third: burning. Fourth: making a crust <note>original: "escaram"; a dry scab or slough caused by burning or infection</note>. The first part is divided into two. First, it shows what it is in general. Second, in specific. There: And sometimes it is named "pruna" or "carbo" <note>The Coal</note>; Persian fire or sacred [fire].
¶ <term>And sometimes.</term> First he shows what the name "Persian fire" signifies. Second, what the name "pruna" signifies. There: it is released. Second: from this he wants the name of Persian fire to be released, that is, declared, when it can be called a certain "ant" <note>original: "formica"; referring to a stinging, spreading rash like shingles or herpes</note>. According to Rhazes <note>A famous 9th-century Persian physician</note>, Book 12 of the *Continens*, Chapter 7: he places "sacred fire" and "the ant" together. This "ant" however is that which is conditioned by 9 or 10 conditions: namely, eating away, burning, crawling, blistering, emitting humidity, yellow bile-like [matter]. Through the authority of blackness: because it is more citron-colored: of little putrefaction because of dryness. With pustules, etc. And let there be humor there, which is not humor but virulence. And a stench of many boilings, because it is like smoke. But he does not say "most stench," but he says of the highest elevation, because of the material's thinness and boiling, namely, its heat, etc.
¶ <term>And it is released, etc.</term> Consider that the carbuncle or coal is from a darker yellow bile <note>original: "chola ovriori"; likely burnt or dark yellow bile</note> mixed with redness. And therefore the name "coal" etc. blackens. Second, it has the color of a coal because of the redness with it. Third, without humidity. Fourth, the highest blackness. Fifth, submerged, because of the thickness of the matter. Protruding because of the quantity, because it is held to be thick like a lupin bean beneath. Because in the quantity of a lupin. But perhaps the coal begins because a pustule does not precede it, but immediately it is combustible, like the soul of fire or a coal. And it begins with an itch, and no other name [applies]? Through itching it makes a crust which however is caused by the burning from the coal.
¶ <term>Furthermore.</term> He places the accidents or signs of these passions. And through [them] the good. Second, he places certain diversities. There: And through them. First, second, third. First he places certain accidents in which sometimes the coal and Persian fire communicate. Second, he places the proper signs of the coal, and the proper signs of the fire and also the coal. There: and therefore. Third: there: therefore in consider[ation]. Sometimes, because the coal ought not to emit humidity, or it ought to emit little. Wherefore it is said: without humidity. Second, contrary to Avicenna. Wherefore they sometimes communicate in location: because the location in the middle, because of much burning, is at the beginning dried out because it is ash-colored or leaden. But both have redness with blackness.
¶ <term>And that which is named.</term> Namely, by its proper name: because that is named the coal or carbuncle: black roots. Namely, in the middle place.
</margin>

...burning and cautery. And sometimes the name "Persian fire" is released <note>used independently</note> for those things upon which there is a pustule of the genus of the "ant" <note>shingles-like rash</note>, mixed, burning, and blistering, in which there is something "crawling" and the humidity is of yellow bile matter, with little blackness and little putrefaction; that is, it is with many altered pustules as if there were humor there and the stench of the highest boiling and elevation. And the name "coal" <note>original: "pruna"; a carbuncle</note> is released for that which blackens the place and makes the limb have the color of a coal without humidity, and it is of the deepest blackness, submerged. And its protrusion is of small size, like a lupin bean, and perhaps there will be no pustule there at all; rather, the "coal" begins at the very start; it all begins with itching and creates scarifications <note>original: "scarificationes"; here meaning crusts or skin breaks</note>. Furthermore, sometimes Persian fire or the coal blisters, and something runs out from it just as it runs from a site cauterized with burning, and the place is of an ash color, black, and sometimes it is leaden, and in this, the pain is vehement around it without a true redness, but rather with a decline toward blackness. And that which is specifically called by the name of "coal" has black, fiery roots, and it has the splendor of a burning coal. And of both of these, Persian fire is of faster appearance and death, while the coal is slower and deeper, and its matter is like the matter of a pustule and "impetigo" <note>a skin infection</note>, but it is sharper in Persian fire, and what happens from them in the flesh is of faster resolution. And what happens from them in the nerves is more fixed and of slower resolution. And each of the two is from burning yellow bile mixed with [other] matter. And because of that, a black crust <note>original: "escara"</note> happens from both of them, and it is more intensely yellow bile-like when it is Persian fire, and more intensely melancholic <note>black bile-like</note> when it is the coal. And it is for you indeed to name each of the two with the intention that groups both as "coals," then divide them; and if you wish to name them both "Persian fire" for that same reason, then divide them. And if you wish to give each intention its own name, they have already done all that, and there is no dominant preference in it. And sometimes they are with types of "ants" <note>shingles</note> and millet-rashes, with bad fevers of vehement heat and danger. And sometimes these happen during pestilence. And many times they resemble dreams <note>perhaps referring to the visual appearance or delirious state</note> and tend toward blackness in the beginning of the matter, and specifically in its peak stage.

Because the thick matter is difficult to resolve. And styptics make the resolution difficult. Resolutives also in the beginning are not pure in the end also because of the quality of the matter because the sharp heat is intense.
¶ <term>Rather.</term> It should be considered that that medicine ought to have four virtues: desiccation because of the virulence and blistering: and this is why and sometimes it is ulcerated: from which it is not released; cooling because of the quality of the matter; and "pulsive" that is, repercussive, because [there is] some stypticity and not much: because it is poisonous matter: whether the matter flows to the place being disrupted. It must be somewhat styptic and resolutive because of the thickness. It should be considered that these are the medicines of the beginning, however, according to Dino, in every time they ought to be such, having more or less as is clear.

There: And it is necessary that you succor it: do not administer desiccants as much as you can. Contrary: above he said the opposite. It should be said that desiccants, that is, styptics, or as much as you can, that is, ultimately desiccating. As also Avicenna would make in dry [cases] for safety. Therefore, not ultimately dry application in the matter of the coal because it is dry or according to Dino if it is not ulcerated do not administer.
¶ <term>Inflations. Are</term> small abscesses and they run a choleric course: and of the blood. Therefore first he places the cause. Second the cure. There: therefore... modification. Consider two modes of inflation. The first is from thin matter from the boiling of yellow bile. The second from thicker matter from the wateriness of the blood. Therefore it is more underneath.

bad blood constricted in it, which is in the nature of poison, may go out. And let it not be done when the matter is declining toward yellow bile. The local cure, however, is necessary so that it be like the cure of erysipelas. However, it is not necessary that it be a liniment of vehement cooling as in erysipelas, since the matter is declining toward thickness, since it is such that it does not allow for it to return from there to the interior parts, since the matter is poisonous. And it is not allowed that those things which are of vehement stypticity <note>astringency</note> be administered; again, that matter is of slow resolution. And it is not allowed that resolutives be administered, neither in the beginning of the matter when it appears, nor at the height of the inflammation, since it adds to the [heat] quality of the matter. And sometimes it falls to doctors to use fresh nut <note>walnut</note> and its leaves with "savich" <note>likely a phonetic spelling of a traditional preparation, possibly 'savy' or 'sage' or a grain-based paste</note> and raisins and figs in wine and oil of black poppy, and it is better, and from all of these let a plaster be made. And medicines of this kind, if they are placed, let them be only upon that which is not ulcerated. In that truly which from it is ulcerated, it is necessary [to use] that which strongly dries, such as the medicine of Aaron, and Sarapion, and the troches of Ramich, and the medicine of Keisiz with sweet wine and with fruit syrup and the rest which are said in the cure of ulcerated erysipelas and millet-ants. And it is necessary that it be filled over with a plaster twice in the day and twice in the night. And again, do not administer desiccants as much as you can <note>meaning: do not use the most extreme ones</note> because they add to the malice of the sickness. And it is necessary that you succor it, that you protect the place and the locations of administration with Armenian bole <note>a medicinal clay</note> and vinegar and water and the rest which break [the heat] and repel; and that which is proper in that is the wool of hyssop soaked in wine. When therefore the inflation grows and the [virulent] traits remain, let them be cured with those things which are... such as a plaster of dung... and the plaster "diachylon" and with the rest of the medicines for corroding ulcers previously mentioned in the Antidotary. And the nut before it is oily is convenient for Persian fire in this hour. Regarding "Yelice" <note>possibly a corruption of 'helice' or 'vesicles'</note> and inflations. Lesson 11.

<summary>This page defines two severe inflammatory skin conditions—"Persian Fire" (blistering rashes) and "The Coal" (necrotic carbuncles)—detailing their symptoms like itching, blackening, and "crawling" sensations. It prescribes specific medical interventions including deep bloodletting, scarification, and the application of drying plasters made from ingredients like oak galls, lentils, and pomegranate rind.</summary>
<keywords>Persian fire, carbuncle, shingles, bloodletting, yellow bile, medical botany, Avicenna, Dino del Garbo, dermatology, medieval medicine, plasters, scarification</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of malignant skin conditions and their remedies. While the previous page focused on the classification of "Persian Fire" and carbuncles, this section moves into the treatment of these conditions and introduces "Essere" (a term for hives or urticaria) and the more severe "Esthiomenus" (corrosive ulcers or gangrene).</meta>

# Third Fen, Treatise

<margin>
Purification. First through evacuation. Second through local remedies. The second part is there: "let it be applied."
</margin>
<margin>
In the first part, it is said...
</margin>
<margin>
Let it be explained. First, he describes the care when they begin. Second, when they are fully formed. Third, when they are ulcerated. This continues similarly. The third part is there: "if it is noted..." Regarding the second part, which...
</margin>
There are modes [of these conditions]; one is due to a wateriness that is expelled from the boiling of the humors, with which the matter suddenly rises to the area beneath the skin. It finds the skin thicker than the matter beneath it, and so it does not penetrate it; instead, a watery swelling remains. The second mode occurs when blood takes the place of that wateriness, which is why pus is formed beneath. Regarding the cure of these, Lesson 12.

<margin>
Auicenna <note>referring to the author, Avicenna</note> touches on the cure for the two aforementioned types: namely, the bloody type, when he speaks of "thicker skin," and the subtle watery type, when he says "the thing." And if: first when a corrupt flesh is made with ulceration; second when it is there: "And when it falls." And first when the flesh has fallen; second before it falls, teaching that
</margin>
<margin>
bad flesh
</margin>
<margin>
is to be removed before it putrefies. There: "it is healthy
</margin>
<margin>
to fall." It should be considered that he first wants the fall of the <term>eschar</term> <note>a dry slough or crust of dead tissue</note> and the corrupt flesh to occur; then you should care for it with the treatment for simple wounds: namely, by promoting scarring. However, he understands that if the flesh has already been cut and is falling, then the current advice applies.
</margin>

### On the treatment of Essere. Lesson 13.

The purification <note>original: "undificatio"</note> of the body with <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>bloodletting</note> and food is as you have known, and let the regimen and food be administered according to the method that was stated. In the beginning, when they appear, let there be placed upon them something like <term>socotrine aloes</term> with water, or pomegranate rinds, or the bark of their branches decocted with water; let all of that be placed, according to what you know in its place, through decoction and gentle warmth. If, however, blisters should break out and you wish to treat them—since those occurring in thicker skin are painful—it is necessary that they be opened with needles so that what is in them may flow out. Whatever subtle matter is in them will open on its own. And it is not necessary to delay; rather, let it be opened and let what is in them be expressed gradually with ease. Then, they should not yet be healed or brought to life. And if they are ulcerated, let them be treated with <term>epithems</term> <note>topical lotions or poultices</note> made of <term>ceruse</term> <note>white lead</note>, and let it be from <term>litharge</term> <note>original: "merdaśengi"; lead oxide</note> and similar things, and especially when something like <term>iris</term> <note>original: "ireos"</note> falls into them, and the plaster for <term>erysipelas</term> <note>a bacterial skin infection</note> when it wanders and corrodes, and for "the ants" <note>spreading rashes</note> and the rest of which we have spoken. A compound medicine is also: Take <note>original: "R."</note> litharge, one pound; old oil, one pound; arsenic, one drachm. When the litharge is boiled with the oil, it should not stick; then pour the arsenic over it. Also, a medicine suitable for that which happens on the testicles and lips and similar parts is, finally, for members that vehemently require drying. Take <note>original: "R."</note> <term>colcothar</term> <note>iron oxide</note> and <term>chalcitis</term> <note>original: "calcadiis"; a mineral vitriol</note>, eight ounces of each; rose leaves, one pound; grind with water and let it be administered, and let there be goat's fat with honey. And when the eschars and corrupt flesh fall and healthy flesh appears, then let it be treated with the cure for simple wounds. Medicines applied at night cause the eschars and bad flesh to fall. And in Alexandria, they make them fall with a herb named <term>fericiēs</term>, and again <term>tarbebaśis</term> and the oil of <term>albacuen</term> is good for casting them down. Finally, the administration of the falling of the eschar and the treatment of the remainder with the treatment of healthy wounds is very appropriate. A good medicine tested by the ancients, which some of the moderns have granted: Take <note>original: "R."</note> <term>sarcocolla</term> <note>a tree resin</note>, aloes, frankincense, ceruse, and <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "ziniar"</note>, all in equal parts, and let the whole be taken from <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>a medicinal clay</note>; let shapes like hazelnuts be made from them, let them be taken and dissolved with vinegar and water, and let the place be smeared with them, placing epithem upon epithem until a strong contraction occurs and an eschar is formed. Then it will either fall on its own if there was humidity beneath it, or it is necessary that you scrape it and make it fall, and do not cease doing this until the whole falls.

<margin>
Essere. They speak of a certain pustule which he previously called "essere": for which he provides the causes, then the cure. There: "if blood." The first part in four: first he identifies it. Second, he provides the cause. Third, the signs. Fourth, he teaches how to prevent fever. There: "And cause." Third there: "bloody." Fourth there: "and with essere." It should be considered that this pustule is small like a blister; however, for the most part, it does not emit humidity like a blister. Instead, they emit a little bit... like a wasp sting. It happens sometimes because of the flesh... because the matter is porous at night... because vapors are emitted and constricted.
</margin>
<margin>
And the cause is: it is a vapor in man; it differs from a blister because the matter of a blister is wateriness... it will not be an entirely sharp pustule, but stands flat.
</margin>

### On Essere. Lesson 13.

<term>Essere</term> <note>Hives or urticaria</note> is a small, broad pustule like a blister, tending somewhat toward redness and causing itching and distress, appearing suddenly throughout the body. And it happens sometimes that humidity flows from it, and perhaps it is bloody, and for the most part it is intense at night, and its distress is more vehement in that time, as is its sadness. And its cause is a hot vapor elevated suddenly in the body, either from <term>choleric</term> blood or from <term>borax-like phlegm</term>. The bloody type is indeed of more vehement redness and heat, and of more vehement and rapid appearance; the phlegmatic type is lesser in all these things, and the vehemence of the phlegmatic type is at night... more vehement...

<meta>catchword: phlegmatic <note>original: "maticē"</note></meta>

<column-break/>

...phlegmatic. There: "If however." and all that he says is clear.

> This discourse on these matters previously determined some of the hotter swellings; because from hot swellings, gangrene, <term>aschachilos</term> <note>sphacelus or total tissue death</note>, and <term>esthiomenus</term> <note>corrosive or eating ulcers</note> sometimes follow. He determines these things, and first investigates the cause, second the gangrenes. The first part is in three: first he introduces the sequence of the discourse. Second, he seeks the investigation of causes. Third, he places the difference between these. There: "I say." There: "third, what about this." It should be considered that this is explained in two ways. First, proportionally: that is, consecutively, because to the aforementioned swellings, these sometimes...

<margin>
...follow. He said "in a certain way" for two reasons. First, because it does not [always] follow these, but sometimes follows others. It is not necessary that these swellings always precede. Second, because they are ulcers and fall into the chapter on ulcers, not the chapter on swellings. In another way, "proportionally": that is, similar, because in gangrene and esthiomenus and aschachilos there are diverse passions; however, they are placed in the same chapter just like "pruna" <note>burning ulcers</note> and "Persian fire."
</margin>
<margin>
And bloody. Here he places the distinguishing signs of the species themselves.
</margin>
...of the bloody type. And when <term>essere</term> invades a wide area, then if bloodletting is not performed, a <term>tertian fever</term> <note>a fever recurring every three days</note> is feared. And it is necessary that bloodletting be performed in the space that is between that and the... Lesson 14.

<margin>
And with essere. Consider that they invade a wide area when they occupy much space in many parts of the body: and it is signified from this that the matter is much, along with the blood: and therefore it requires bloodletting; for if not, the blood will be inflamed and become choleric and a tertian fever will occur, and this before it inflames, so that it occurs before the peak.
</margin>

### On the treatment of Essere. Lesson 14.

<margin>
If blood. He places the cure first for the bloody type, second for the phlegmatic.
</margin>
If the blood is indeed prevailing, then it will be necessary that you first proceed to bloodletting, then subsequently apply a laxative if the strength permits, which may be from two parts of <term>myrobalans</term> <note>medicinal fruit</note> to one part of <term>hieralogodion</term> <note>a purgative compound</note>; let the potion be 3 drachms in acetous syrup, and soothe it with those things that are such as tamarinds and the water of two pomegranates with their rinds, or the water of an acetous pomegranate with its rind, and an infusion of <term>apricots</term> <note>original: "chrysomilorum"</note> with acetous milk-water and <term>troches</term> <note>lozenges</note> of <term>spodium</term> <note>burnt ivory or zinc oxide</note> with pomegranate water; and hot water is given as a drink many times in the day; it is among the things that benefit it and soften the nature of this cause. And among those things that soothe it is a strained infusion of <term>suacb</term> <note>possibly a variant of an herbal infusion</note> from which they may take 3 drachms. And from foods, <term>tabsil</term> <note>a medicinal preparation</note> and vinegar with oil of almonds and sesame, and oil with the water of bitter grapes and acetous milk. If, however, the humor is "borax-like," purge the body with myrobalans and with <term>turbith</term> <note>a purgative root</note>, of which let there be half as much as the myrobalans, and let his potion be 3 drachms. And let the sick person be given 1 drachm of moist cypress nut with 1 drachm of aloes. And let garden saffron be taken, ground and shaken with vinegar, and taken in a drink. Or let "thin water" <note>whey or light broth</note> be given in a drink, or water from a new jar. And for the phlegmatic type, let them take 1 drachm of <term>cubebs</term> with 3 drachms of sugar, and 3 drachms of the weight of <term>chasteberry</term> <note>original: "agni casti"</note> in sweet milk. And of that which is tested and suitable in every species is this: 2 drachms of <term>calamint</term>, 2 drachms of spodium, 5 drachms of red roses, and a <term>kirat</term> <note>a small weight measure</note> of camphor. In these, errors occur, such as failing to pour oil in deep ulcers, whereby the flesh putrefies. And sometimes it happens because of a corporeal obstruction, such as a bad hot swelling located in a large mass of thick matter obstructing the passages and the internal breathing by which it lives, breaking the complexion. And when it is so confirmed that it destroys the sense of that which has sense, and it also destroys the flesh and that which follows it even to the bone—whether it is beginning or succeeding a swelling—it is named **aschachilos** <note>sphacelus; complete necrosis</note>. ## On Altboboin, Lesson 17.

<margin>k</margin> **T**he most ancient of the ancients named it by a name which is translated into Arabic as <term>altboboin</term> <note>from Arabic *al-dubbuya*, meaning a bubo or glandular swelling</note>: every swelling existing in the members of glandular flesh or elsewhere. Then we say after this of that which is with this: a hot swelling that is destructive. Then it is called a pernicious swelling because of the conversion of its matter into a poisonous substance which corrupts the member and alters its color which follows it. And sometimes it pours out blood and virus <note>foul-smelling discharge</note> and things similar to them, and it brings a bad quality to the heart by way of the arteries, whereby vomiting and heart palpitations and syncope <note>fainting</note> occur; and when its symptoms become vehement, it kills. And it seems that the first people called this last stage <term>carmara</term>. And it is necessary that the worst of them is that which happens for the most part in the armpits and groins and behind the ear because of its proximity to the members which are most vehemently principal <note>vital organs</note>. And the safest of the mortal <term>altboboin</term> is that which is red, then yellow. <meta>This page continues the discussion of malignant skin conditions from the previous page, moving from the general classification of gangrene and "Persian fire" into specific diagnoses of anthrax, carbuncles, and buboes (althoboi). It details the surgical and dietary treatments necessary to prevent these "poisonous" humors from reaching the heart.</meta>

# Section III, Treatise I

It must be considered that there were three types of matter: bloody matter, burnt yellow bile, and a poisonous, excessively burnt yellow bile; the blackness of the skin does not escape this, according to experience. Regarding the first point according to Dionysius <note>likely Dionysius the Carthusian or another medieval commentator</note>, the region is hot. No, it does not escape there. Or as it is said concerning those things which are under the "fires" and behind the ears; indeed, from those black sores, no one escapes. Other surgeons would say it inclines toward blackness—that is, not purely black, but with some greenness, which is mortal. And for buboes <term>althoboi</term> <note>a medieval Latin transliteration of an Arabic term for buboes or pestilential swellings</note> also. And they find [the symptoms], which we do not care for here. Dionysius notes that whether a sore precedes or follows a fever, it is a sign of death. For it signifies a most wicked and poisonous matter found in the body. Hence, in the first book of the *Prognostics* <note>a work by Hippocrates</note>, it is said that if an **anthrax** <note>original: "antrar"; a malignant, necrotic sore</note> or **carbuncle** appears, and if it be dry and emits nothing, nor swells up, one might doubt how an anthrax differs from a carbuncle. Some say there is no difference; but according to William <note>likely William of Saliceto, a 13th-century surgeon</note> in Book 1, Chapter 5, they differ by degree. A carbuncle is made of bad, burnt matter. But an anthrax is more burnt and more poisonous. And therefore, in a carbuncle, there is a protrusion and redness, and it sometimes produces pus, but not so with an anthrax. Hence, the carbuncle precedes the anthrax. It should be known that "carbuncle" is sometimes taken to mean a "coal" or "burning ember," of which Galen speaks in book 14 of *Therapeutics*, and in the first chapter concerning the essence of fevers.

<margin>a. This refers to the pestilential nature. And there are found Greek names for things which are likened to buboes, such as *tursios*, *carmata*, *carmakile*, and *furios*; among us, there is no great distinction between these names.</margin>

<margin>e. On the Treatment. Lesson 18.</margin>
The evacuation which is called **bloodletting (phlebotomy)**, along with that which the time or the hour allows, is necessary from among those things that draw out the putrefied humor. One must decide how to help the heart by defending and strengthening it with things that provide cooling and pleasant scents, such as the acidity of citrus, mint, the syrup of apples and quinces, and very sour pomegranates. Smelling scents like roses, camphor, and sandalwood is also helpful. Let the food be such as lentils with vinegar, and meats prepared with much vinegar, such as the flesh of **arabengi** <note>possibly a type of partridge or forest bird mentioned in Arabic medicine</note> and **bedorum**. And it is necessary to moisten the patient's dwelling with much vinegar and the leaves of willow, violets, roses, water lilies, and the like. And let cooling and strengthening **poultices** (epithemata) be placed over the heart, made from medicines known to improve a hot pulse and to resist pestilence. Finally, let them be managed by the regimen for those in a pestilential air. As for the buboes themselves, and those things that follow the same course, let them be treated in the beginning with things that constrict and cool, such as a sponge soaked in water and vinegar, or in rose oil, or oil of apples and mastic, or myrtle oil; let these be done in the beginning. But in the stable state of the disease, let it be treated with **scarification** <note>original: "scapellatiōe"; making small incisions in the skin</note> if possible, so that what is inside may flow out, and do not allow it to become dark when its "windiness" or swelling increases; and if it requires cupping glasses to draw it out...

<margin>b. Therefore you should apply [treatment]. At the end, he says it is made from heated blood and blood turned to melancholy through burning.</margin>
Concerning "a certain evacuation": First he provides the universal cure through evacuation and defense of the heart; then through local treatments regarding the swelling itself—that is, the bubo, in the fourth sense of the word. Here he addresses the buboes. First, he teaches how to evacuate, then how to rectify the heart, etc. He doubts whether bloodletting is appropriate, as Azaravi <note>the Latinized name for Al-Zahrawi, the great Andalusian surgeon</note> says it is not for anthrax. He also fears it might pull the poisonous matter back toward the heart. It must be said that it is appropriate. First, according to Galen in book 14 of *Therapeutics*, although he speaks of the carbuncle as a "coal," it is understood as a type of anthrax. Also, because it is made of burnt blood, it is suitable. Also, because it is a most acute passion, it is appropriate, as the commentator says, to let blood until the patient faints. It should be known that it is properly appropriate when it is in the body at the beginning, as Rasis says in book 7 of the *Almansor*. However, it is appropriate either at the start when the symptoms are first revealed, or when the pulse falls. And so Rasis is understood. And so Galen, though some say he prohibits bloodletting, and Avicenna with him, adds "as the time allows"—meaning the hour of the disease or the year. To the reasoning, it should be said that it does not pull the poison inward because it has not yet reached such a state of ignition; rather, bloodletting prevents the flow of putrefaction to the part. It is doubted whether it is appropriate to use a **purgative drug** (pharmacy): some say no, because it draws poison inward, as Avicenna says in book 4, chapter 6 on the bite of a rabid dog. In contrast, others say a strong, violent purgative like scammony or agaric is not appropriate, but light things that cleanse the interior are—such as yellow myrobalans, fumitory, senna, plums, tamarind, or cassia, which Rasis mentions; these are suitable. For fumitory evacuates burnt humors, as Mesue says. One must consider the difference between a poison that comes from within and one from without, like an animal bite. When it comes from within, it signifies that there are corrupt matters inside the body that must be deleted; when it comes from without, we do not evacuate.

<margin>c. Then it is necessary. The reason is that poisonous matter seeks the heart; therefore one must defend the heart. Since these matters are hot and putrefied, they must be met with cold things.</margin>
<margin>d. And let the food be. He doubts whether the food should be blood-thickening or blood-thinning. In "coal" and carbuncle, thinning food is given, as Azaravi and Rasis say. But here, Avicenna and Azaravi say the food should be **thickening**. The reason is: in these cases, we fear the arrival of poisonous vapors at the heart. Thickening foods prevent vapors from penetrating by blocking and quieting them. One might say that ptisans and cucumbers are thinning in substance but cooling in quality, so they quiet the matter. Meat of a young goat is subtle in substance but, because it is cold and vinegary, it thickens and quiets the blood.</margin>

<column-break/>

is not appropriate, etc. Also, which foods are blood-thickening in these cases, unless a strong fever prohibits it.

<margin>e. And at the last. As in the sources for pestilential air and fever, we aim for the strengthening of the heart and the prohibition of putrefaction, strengthening them with foods and correcting them. Whereas it is managed differently in other fevers, here it is necessary that no new food be noted near the heart. He doubts whether we can give any **treacle** (tyriaca), which is a remedy against poison. In contrast, it is hot. Dionysius says it is by no means appropriate because it thins the blood and makes it flow more. I say that if there is not great inflammation, treacle is appropriate because it is for poisons. Also, Galen in his book on the benefits of treacle says it is useful in pestilential diseases. Also, William gives it. It helps more by repelling poison than it harms by heating; or it should be said that it has contrary effects: it constricts where there is flow and makes constricted things flow, as Galen says.</margin>

<margin>g. Buboes (Althoboin). First, he places the local treatment for buboes. Some teach two ways: first, when it is not on the path to becoming an ulcer; second, when it is. First, in the beginning; then in the stable state. He doubts whether we should use **repellents**. Azaravi and Rasis say no, because it makes the matter return to the principal organs. It should be said, as Bruno distinguishes, that repellents can be placed around the site so the corruption does not spread, but over the site itself, one must place things that resolve and break the matter, like figs with honey and mustard. Or, if it begins from inflamed blood, repellents are necessary.</margin>

Scarification should be done with precision. And in that sore which has the substance of an ulcer, it is necessary that treatment be administered at its peak or around its stable state with the formation of an abscess. And when there is a fever there, you will delay cooling treatments so that you do not drive the matter back. And the opening indeed is done with things like an **embrocation** <note>a liquid medicine rubbed on the skin</note> with chamomile water and dill and other subtle openers which we will discuss in the chapters on wounds. They called these "carmata" and "sciros." A plaster of maidenhair fern, orach, bindweed, and marshmallow root is beneficial, with a little pine resin and honey with wine, or glue with pine resin and a wax salve, or the dross from beehives, or lupins soaked in vinegar, or squirting cucumber root with **albotin** <note>possibly a type of turpentine or resin</note> glue, or soda with figs or with leaven.

<margin>e. On abscesses occurring in the glands. Lesson 19.</margin>
**Glandular abscesses** that do not proceed by the way of pestilence sometimes occur in a place by chance during a "crisis" (a turning point in illness), and sometimes they occur as the body expells matter from the radical members. Perhaps other ulcers and abscesses on the extremities draw them out, to which the matters run through the pathways where the flesh is found, such as happens in the groin and under the armpits, and the swelling of both in one who has scabies or ulcers on the feet and hands. And sometimes they are with a fullness of the body, and sometimes not...

<margin>b. In the stable state. It should be considered that we should perform this scarification not only in the stable state but in the beginning and growth; as soon as possible, the poisonous matter should be extracted—not only by scarification and cupping, but even with fire. Avicenna touches on the order: first we scarify so the blood runs, sometimes with a warm wash; then we apply cupping glasses. "With subtlety" means through the small holes of the scarification. Also, things that are subtle and rose-like are better for breaking it open.</margin>

<margin>i. And in that one. It should be considered that because of the malice of the matter, it rarely happens that ulcers form; but if it happens, it should be admitted to treatment with opening and resolving things. In the 7th book, it is said that purely ripening things are viscous and might add to the corruption. Note that there is a greater fear of the matter returning when there is fever. Therefore, let cooling things be applied all around, but here you will delay so the matter does not return anywhere but comes out entirely.</margin>

<margin>g. They said. He provides the treatment of some. Note that among these medicines some are ripening and some are resolving. Sleep is also mentioned; some say it helps in digesting the matter. Dionysius says that if the matter moves toward the heart or brain—signs of which are fainting, a falling pulse, coldness of the limbs, or alienation of the mind—then sleep is not appropriate because it throws the virtues inward. Also, in poisonous matter, one must stay awake, as one who has taken poison is told to stay awake. Also, sleep helps movement toward the brain. But if no such movement is seen, one should not stay awake excessively. Much wakefulness heats the body and hurts the anthrax; it also weakens the brain. Moderate sleep is sometimes beneficial. If they must stay awake, they should stay in the house, for the wind inflames them and cold air might repel the matter from the site of the anthrax.</margin>

<margin>a. Abscesses. Having dealt with buboes, he here speaks of swellings in the glandular places. These are mostly from hot matter in the armpits. We should not use repellents here. The treatment of these swellings differs from the treatment of simple hot ones.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of glandular swellings (apostemes) and their causes, specifically focusing on whether they arise from a "crisis" in the body or a general excess of fluids.
