# Book III

...a common disease. <note>original: "morbus cois"</note> 1. 5. It is also determined concerning a swelling <term>aposteme</term> <note>a general term for any inflammatory swelling or tumor</note> of the soft flesh behind the ears, as noted in Canon 5. Here, the author wonders from what matter they are mostly made. He concludes that because they tend toward heat, these swellings are formed by a "flux" <note>a flowing of excess humors from one part of the body to another</note>. Swellings formed by flux are mostly hot, because hot humors are prone to flow. First, he doubts whether the swellings are from a hotter matter, or from frequent drainage of the <term>emunctories</term> <note>natural drainage points of the body, like the armpits or groin</note>, or from the heart, or the liver, or the brain—citing Galen's commentary on the *Prognostics*, section 34. On the contrary, the brain possesses cold superfluities. To this, it is said that they occur during a "crisis" <note>a turning point in a disease where nature attempts to expel the cause of illness</note>, and thus the hotter matter flows, etc. So says Galen in the same place, and Avicenna in the section on the signs of expulsion from a principal organ.

<margin>a</margin>
<margin>And their cure. First, the cure of those that occur in the glandular emunctories; second, in the noble glandular parts. First, those that occur during a crisis and by expulsion from the principal organs; second, when they occur with a repletion of the whole body. He first sets down the general cure, then the local or specific cure. One must consider that a <term>phlegmon</term> <note>a hot, red swelling caused by blood</note> and a pharmacy differ, which we do not count as the same. He doubts from which vein bloodletting <term>phlebotomy</term> should be performed. It must be said that if the swelling is in the neck, use the <term>cephalic vein</term> <note>the "head vein" of the arm</note>; if in the armpit, use the <term>basilica</term> <note>the "royal vein" of the arm</note> or the common vein. If in the groin, use the basilica and the common vein of the foot. This agrees with the general rule of Rasis: for groin swellings, use the basilica and the foot vein. He also doubts whether to bleed on the same side or the opposite side. It must be considered whether the matter is currently flowing or has already gathered, and whether there is much "repletion" <note>an excess of humors</note> in the body. If the matter is flowing and there is much repletion, one must first reduce that repletion with bloodletting from the opposite vein—either across one diameter or two—provided the vein is suitable for evacuating that repletion. For example: if there is a swelling on the right side of the neck and the matter is flowing with much repletion, first bleed the left common vein or the left basilica vein. If the repletion is in the area of the spleen, it may be necessary to bleed the <term>saphenous vein</term> <note>the large vein of the leg</note> on the right or left if the repletion comes from the womb. For example: if he has a swelling in the right armpit and it is flowing with much repletion, bleed from the basilica or left common vein, or the saphenous vein. For example: if he has a swelling in the right groin that is flowing with much repletion, bleed from the right basilica or common vein, and we can also use the left side to diminish the total repletion. If the matter is flowing but there is not much repletion, the goal is "diversion" <note>pulling the humor in the opposite direction</note>. If a swelling is in the right side of the neck and the body is not overly full, perform bloodletting from the opposite cephalic vein. Some do this for head injuries. Avenzoar <note>original: "zoar"</note> in Chapter 3 on cranial fractures reprimands those who do not bleed the feet, especially the left, when there is no repletion; for it would take too long for the effect to divert the matter and would greatly weaken the patient. For example: if there is a swelling in the right armpit and the body is not too full, bleed in the left arm from the common or basilica vein, and then in the foot of the same side (the right), which diverts the matter sufficiently. Rasis says for those with swellings in the armpits, bloodletting in the opposite saphenous vein is helpful to pull the flow downward. If it is in the right armpit, use the right saphenous. The physician’s judgment in creating a diversion from the armpit through the arm or foot vein will be based on the nature of the blood. If it is heavy, pull from below; if light, pull from above. For example: if there is a swelling in the right groin and the body is not full, bleed the right basilica vein of the arm. Thus, two diversions take the place of one sufficient one. But it is asked: if there is a swelling in the right groin, can we bleed from the right basilica of the arm and the right saphenous of the foot? The answer is no, because the right foot and right groin are only separated vertically, whereas the arm is also separated horizontally from the chest; humors are pulled upward with difficulty but flow downward easily. Therefore, if you use the right foot vein, the superior humors will fall downward and move into the groin, just as a wound in the foot causes a swelling in the groin. However, if the matter has already flowed and evacuations have preceded it, then bleed from the vein of the same side. In that case, you may perform three bloodlettings.</margin>

**And their** cure is different from the cure of other swellings in the beginning because of the "eruption" <note>the breaking out of the swelling</note>. One does not administer the same treatment, but rather uses bloodletting and loosening the bowels as is necessary. The other part of the cure should be delayed until the condition declares itself. For if it follows the path of a "crisis" <note>a natural healing peak</note> or the path of expulsion from a principal organ, then it should not be prohibited at all; rather, it should be drawn to the limb by any possible attraction, even with cupping glasses. But if it is caused by an abundance of repletion, then evacuation is the "root" of the cure, along with a reduction of food through "subtiliation" <note>making the diet lighter and thinner</note>. Do not administer expulsive medicines, but rather softening <term>mollificative</term> ones; however, do not use softening agents without evacuation. For perhaps a great attraction of matter toward the limb will occur; rather, when administering softening agents, evacuate at the same time and draw the matter in a different direction. For the fear with expulsive medicines is that the matter will return to the internal organs and principal members. The fear with softening agents is the attraction of too much matter. Thus, evacuation and the diversion of matter secure the patient from the harm of softening agents. And when the pain becomes vehement, then it is necessary to soothe it with things like wool soaked in warm oil; later, add salt toward the end until the pain is immediately calmed. Perhaps at first, one adds more for the pain. And when the body is clean or has been purified, then resolve the swelling and do not worry further. Sometimes wheat flour is useful for resolving it, and also barley flour. Perhaps a strong resolution will enlarge the swelling, so it should not be administered unless it is necessary to expel matter from the principal organs and draw it toward the swelling out of fear for those principal organs.

<margin>b</margin> <margin>The other cure, namely the local one, is used until it is declared whether it occurs by way of crisis or expulsion from principal organs, or by way of repletion; for the cure differs based on this.</margin>

<margin>c</margin> <margin>"But if..." He sets down the cure for a swelling caused by a multitude of repletion. First the universal cure, second the local. Note: when there is repletion, then evacuation—which diminishes the repletion—is the "root" of the cure. But if it is only to divert from the principal organs, it is doubted whether bloodletting should be done on the opposite side in a case of crisis. The answer is that because the matter is being expelled during a crisis, one should not do it unless there is fear of corrupting the heart or bowels. However, if the remaining humors of the body are agitated, one could reduce them. Prohibition of wine is mentioned for armpit swellings for fear of "inflaming" the heart.</margin>

<column-break/>

Many times, what heals them in the beginning is simply warm oil poured over them. However, when the swelling is soft in its quantity and substance and in a noble limb, such as the breast or testicle, and no harm is feared from prohibiting its growth, then prohibit and repel it. But when you feel it declining toward hardness, then use a liniment <note>a medicinal rub</note> wherever it may be.

<margin>d</margin> <margin>"And do not..." First, before the body is evacuated, this should not be done. Second, what should be done after evacuation and purification. First, he does this; second, he calls for soothing the pain. And what is first useful.</margin>

<margin>e</margin> <margin>"And when..." This is clear. And do not worry, namely if the resolution enlarges the swelling. It must be considered that from this text a distinction is made between the cure when matter is driven from the principal organs and when it occurs during a crisis. In those cases, it is strongly resolved and drawn out. But when it is due to a repletion of the whole body, you do not resolve it so strongly because the principal organs are expelling the waste; in that case, barley flour is safer as it draws less, but not repeatedly, as it could return to the principal organs.</margin>

<margin>f</margin> <margin>"However..." He sets down the cure for swellings in the noble glandular parts. First, the difference between the cure of these and the aforementioned; second, their similarity. He says first: if the swelling is in noble glandular flesh, this is what he calls "soft in quantity and substance." It must be considered that the cure is similar to other swellings unless they are "prohibiting" agents—because poisonous or "critical" matter etc. is thrown back to the members. These are noble members or have a noble position. But if the swellings are in ignoble parts, they are made to receive superfluities.</margin>

## On Hot Outbreaks. Chapter 20.

An **outbreak** <term>exitura</term> <note>an abscess or a gathering of pus that is about to break through the skin</note> is a type of "deep abscess" <term>dubellet</term> <note>from the Arabic 'dubayla', a suppurating internal swelling</note> that creates a collection of matter from hot swellings. The name *aludubellati* <note>the Latinized Arabic term for an abscessed condition</note> applies to every ulcerated swelling in the interior, which has a space where matter is poured and remains, whatever that matter may be. An "outbreak" which is hot by its nature then gathers matter. Sometimes a hot swelling begins with a gathering that causes an internal break in continuity. Other times it does not begin that way, but starts as a healthy hot swelling and then converts into an "outbreak" condition as it begins to gather matter. In later sections, we will discuss "cold deep abscesses" which contain viscous, gypsum-like, stony, sandy, or hair-like humors, and others. There are some who restrict the name *aludubellat* to that which contains those types of humors. However, we are speaking now of that which gathers matter. Note that an outbreak begins because of the matter which Nature expels; it is not possible for it to penetrate the skin or the surface of the flesh, but rather it separates the continuity of the flesh by its thickness. Once separated, it rests in the vacuum it has created, so that a sharp "head" appears, especially if the matter was sharp. These outbreaks therefore begin and gather "corrupt matter" <term>sanies</term> <note>pus or discharge</note>, and then they are ripened.

<margin>g</margin> <margin>"But when..." It is appropriate then: because if they are hardened, we soften them. Even if they are ripened, we act accordingly.</margin>

**Outbreak.** Having previously dealt with swellings, he now deals with outbreaks. 2nd: He explains what they are and their various types. 3rd: The signs. 4th: The cure. First, he explains that an "outbreak" has different names and times. 2nd: He compares them. 3rd: He investigates certain causes. 4th: He names the varieties. It must be considered that there are swellings, deep abscesses, and outbreaks. "Swelling" is the general name for every hot or cold humor. "Deep abscess" <note>dubellet</note> is a swelling that has a top and a cavity in which matter is contained, whether hot, cold, or phlegmatic. Avicenna says the name *aludubellati* falls upon every internal ulcerated swelling where there is a place for matter to pour. An "outbreak" is a swelling having a sinus and a cavity, with a tendency toward "corrupt matter" <note>sanies</note>, so that the matter is on the path to becoming pus. If the matter collected in the cavity does not become pus but is retained, it becomes like gypsum, honey, or hair, and is not called an "outbreak" but simply a "deep abscess." But if the matter is prone to becoming pus, it is called an "outbreak." Because the matters that properly become pus are hot, either by themselves or by boiling, an outbreak is properly from hot matter. Matters that become pus are blood or yellow bile mixed with blood, because these "boil," and pus is made from that boiling. Cold humors do not become pus unless they acquire putrefaction and boiling. Thus, Avicenna below does not speak of outbreaks except in cold swellings when they convert to pus—because when cold swellings become pus, their matter must "boil," and thus it takes on the nature of a hot swelling. It appears therefore that outbreaks mostly arise from hot swellings, as these are more prone to becoming pus than cold ones. If an outbreak follows or is made from cold humors, it is because those humors have become heated. Therefore, Avicenna says an outbreak is from a type of deep abscess that makes a collection. An outbreak is the species, and "deep abscess" is the genus.

<margin>h</margin> <margin>"And sometimes..." He describes two ways they are formed: either they begin immediately as an outbreak, or they begin as "healthy" swellings that could have been resolved but instead turn into an outbreak.</margin>

<margin>i</margin> <margin>"And we..." Here he refers us or excuses himself. Note that some believe a *dubellet* is a swelling gathering cold, non-furious matter. Avicenna says that in the definition given above, he is not speaking of that, but of that which gathers matter absolutely, whatever it may be.</margin>

It also defines and distinguishes between general swellings (apostemes), deep-seated abscesses (dubellet), and maturing outbreaks (exitura) that form pus.</summary>

# Fen III Treatise I <note>original: "fen III Tractatus I"; A "Fen" is a major division of Avicenna's Canon of Medicine.</note>

<margin>
a. It clarifies where the abscess will emerge by its beginning: and first it does this. Secondly, it declares the mode of its process. Therefore, it considers the causes that begin to appear in an emerging abscess: when it is not resolved, it comes to the surface of the skin. Indeed, it separates the continuity of the flesh. It appears manifest because of the thickness—that is, the capacity which the matter requires. It rests in emptiness.
b. And how much more. Here he speaks of these kinds of abscesses and their suffering, and he has five comparisons that he posits. Firstly, the comparison of goodness and malice by reason of the matter. We argue from various accidents for various kinds of matter. In the case of heat, the pain is greater because it alters and moves the senses more suddenly.
c. And worse. Here he compares them by reason of eruption.
d. And finally. Here he compares the impending abscesses to their suitability and beginnings. He posits three causes why they do not easily occur in the joints: 1. Because mucilaginous humors <note>sticky or slimy bodily fluids</note> are not prone to forming pus. 2. Large locations do not "suffocate" <note>trap the heat of</note> the matter, whereas forming pus requires the path of "suffocation" and enclosure. Nor do they retain the putrid egress—that is, the heat of putrefaction.
e. And worse. Here he compares by reason of the goodness or malice of the organs in which they appear.
f. And the abscess. He posits certain diversities of abscesses and certain comparisons. Here he posits another diversity: that some ripen quickly and some slowly, and he posits the causes. First, he introduces them in general; second, he declares them specifically.
</margin>

...afterward the pus <note>original: "sanies"</note> breaks out. And perhaps it needs assistance in ripening <term>maturation</term> <note>the process of an abscess coming to a "head"</note> and eruption, and perhaps it does not. And the more an abscess <note>original: "exitura"</note> is of a vehement elevation, with a sharp head and redness, the more the humor is attracted and of vehement heat, and it is of faster maturation, resolution, and eruption—specifically those that project outward. But that which is wide, deep, and of little redness is of thick matter, bad, declining toward the interior, causing little pain but heavy movement. And worse than this is that whose corruption is toward the interior and which corrupts that over which it passes. And there is that which expels to both sides. And its most praiseworthy eruption is toward the proper cavity of the organ which has a path running to the outside, just as an abscess of the stomach: it is better that it erupt into its own cavity than that it erupt toward the exterior and the "mirac" <note>the outer abdominal wall or peritoneum</note>. Just as an eruption in the brain into the two anterior ventricles is more praiseworthy because both have passages such as the nose and ears. But when it breaks into the space containing the brain or into the posterior ventricle, it finds no passage to the outside and causes vehement harm. And not every member is suitable for an abscess to occur in it; in the joints, for instance, the emergence of an abscess is diminished because in them are mucilaginous humors, and their locations are large and do not "suffocate" the matter nor retain the putrid egress. If an abscess should emerge there, it will be due to a very great cause. And the worst and most malignant of abscesses is that which emerges upon the ends of the muscles, and specifically the muscles of the nerves. And abscesses are diversified by the time of the ripening of the pus, according to the humor’s thinness or thickness, its composition of heat and cold, and its balance, as well as according to the time, the age of the patient, and the substance of the limb. And it does not happen that an abscess fails to ripen or that what is in it fails to turn into pus, except because of a lack of innate heat in the limb or because of the thickness of the matter's substance. And sometimes it happens from this that pus is made in its interior part and does not appear to the senses because of the depth of the pus and the thickness of what is above it. Sometimes one can quickly determine the ripeness of the pus, and sometimes not, according to its substance in thickness; for when it matures and thins, its substance becomes light quickly. This depends on whether there is much or little flesh, and the causes of the abscess, and the falling away into pus due to "repletion" <note>an overabundance of humors</note> and the multitude of matter and its corruption. And the causes include nausea, bad exercise, and illnesses that do not reach a "crisis"; along with apparent vomiting and mental harms from anguish and anxieties which corrupt the blood. And among abscesses, there is a species called "tumulios" <note>swellings or small tumors</note>, which is an abscess that breaks and which is...

<margin>
g. And sometimes. Here is an aphorism from the sixth section regarding pus being made. It refers to an abscess or a defect of heat.
h. And it is determined. This is explained by the ripening, etc.—that is, it is quickly recognized. And "sometimes it is not determined"—that is, not quickly recognized. Alternatively: it ripens quickly. And when it does not "stay"—that is, it does not ripen quickly according to the thickness of its substance. If it matures, the cause will appear light. He posits the causes here: 1. Diversity in the thickness and thinness of the matter. 2. Whether there is much or little flesh over the matter; much flesh is a cause of fast pus formation. 3. Concurrent causes that make an abscess, such as "repletion" <note>excess fluid</note>.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
i. And abscesses. Here he says that in some abscesses, the matter is not fit to turn into pus but turns into a certain flesh like the flesh of an ox or bull. Alternatively, pus collects in one part and another, and between the two is flesh.
k. When you see. First, signs of external abscesses; second, internal. First, signs that an abscess is forming; second, that it is ripening; third, the judgments of good pus. All these signs signify that the matter is matured and cannot be resolved, but boils up.
l. When you see. Concerning the generation of pus.
m. Pus. First he shows what is "laudable" <note>healthy/ideal</note> pus, second what is unlaudable, and third the modes of termination. First, he sets down the conditions of laudable pus, then declares them. The action of heat is sometimes simple and natural, sometimes against nature.
n. And not. It has three parts: 1. It is smooth. 2. It does not have a horrible odor. 3. It is white. Laudable pus must be equal in color and substance so that all parts are continuous and uniform. This signifies that the matter has entirely "obeyed" the heat of the body. If it is unequal, some parts have obeyed and others have not.
</margin>

...one of these causes is repletion—that is, of the stomach and liver. Because great repletion in the stomach and liver is the cause of great repletion in the part, and from this the heat is suffocated, and maturation happens slowly. And a multitude of matter in the part can exist without repletion in the whole body. This corruption of the matter matures slowly.

### Signs that an Abscess is Forming. Lesson XXI.

When you see a throbbing <note>original: "pulsatione"</note> of the parts or a prolonged hardness and heat, then estimate that a swelling is on the way to becoming an abscess.

### Signs of Maturation and Its Mark. Chapter XXII.

When you see a certain softness and a calming of the pain, then know that it is on the way to maturation.

### Judgments of Pus. Lesson XXIII.

Laudable pus is that which is white, smooth, and has no horrible odor, and in which nothing has operated except the innate heat <note>the body's natural life-force/temperature</note>, though it is not entirely free from external heat. And its smoothness is added only so that it may be known that it has been prepared by the "digestive virtue" <note>the body's ability to process and transform humors</note> and its preparation does not vary. And it must not have an odor of vehement horribleness, so that it may be far from putrefaction. They have said it is required to be white because the color of the "radical members" <note>the primary, foundational parts of the body</note> is white, and it does not take that color unless nature is powerful over it. And bad pus is stinking, signifying putrefaction (which is the contrary of maturation) and signifying the dominion of external heat. And when pus of diverse parts, colors, and substances emerges, it is also of a different kind than the good. And it is necessary for all pus to cause either putrefaction, maturation, or diminution in the body, or to be altered in some other way.

### Signs of an Internal Abscess. Lesson XXIV.

When a hot swelling occurs in the viscera <note>internal organs</note>, and there occur "horripilations" <note>chills or shivering</note> and fevers, and there is no order to them, but the pain becomes more vehement; and there is a shivering in the beginning of longer duration, and thereafter the space between them does not cease to shorten, and the heaviness of the swelling increases—then know that the swelling is becoming an abscess and has reached its collection. And these pains are not most vehement in the beginning, and the closer they get to the "status" <note>the peak of the disease</note>, the more they are diminished, except that the eruption occurs in the beginning through a break in continuity. The pain comes from that which is collected. When the matter becomes pus, the strong heating and inflammation also rest, whereby the fever coming from the involvement of the heart also rests. And know that the hardness of the pulse is a great testimony. And when a sign of an abscess appears in the viscera, if the pulse is not hardened, do not judge entirely that an internal abscess is forming. For in such a case, perhaps it will not be in the viscera, but in the "siphac" <note>the peritoneum/lining of the abdomen</note> which contains the viscera. And you indeed already know the side on which the abscess is by the heaviness that hangs from it because of the pain.

<margin>
o. It must not have a stench.
p. They said—namely Galen. He says white because flesh makes white pus.
q. And pus.
r. It is necessary for all pus—that is, all bad matter that makes a swelling—to cause putrefaction (corruption of the limb), or maturation (conversion to pus), or diminution (resolution), or hardening.
s. When it happens. Here he posits signs of internal abscesses.
t. And know. Hardness of the pulse follows internal swellings by reason of the tension of the place.
</margin>

...great hardness: that is, great tension. This is because the matter is in the way of healing. For when the pus has been formed, the place becomes less swollen and softens, and then the hardness softens. Consider that if an internal abscess occurs in the belly <note>original: "mirac," referring to the abdominal wall</note>, it will have symptoms similar to an abscess of the internal organs, but it does not have a hard pulse; therefore, do not judge it to be an internal abscess because of this.

<margin>a. When it happens. He doubts whether internal abscesses should be determined here, since they belong in the third book. He answers: he determines external abscesses here so that he might complete the doctrine. Also, because external ones are terminated and ruptured more [easily] than internal ones.</margin>
<margin>b. Question 3. That is, in this [book] he speaks more generally, but in the third book, more specifically.</margin>
<margin>c. When they return. Similarly, they feign other fevers. That is, they are like fevers if they occur with shivering, or they are simulated because they are not disordered as when an abscess is forming; then, because [the body] was occupied with the digestion of the matter, the fever was disordered.</margin>
<margin>d. Evacuations. He posits the regimen for abscesses. For an internal one is used there. First, he posits the regimen of abscesses more generally, and then specifically. There, "Of Medicines." First, he posits the cure in which an abscess communicates with a hot phlegmon <note>a type of inflammation</note>, and then he posits the cure which is suitable for an abscess by itself. There, "That indeed is to be considered," where he indicates two things in which "repulsion" <note>driving the humors back away from the site</note> and "dispersion" agree. Just as in hot phlegmons we first disperse and later repel when they are in the beginning, unless there is fear etc., so it is in the beginning of an abscess. It is doubted whether repulsion is appropriate in the beginning of an abscess. It seems not, because an abscess can begin during the increase of a phlegmon, but then repulsion is not appropriate. It is doubted whether dispersion [is appropriate]. It seems not, because the body is already emptied at the beginning of the phlegmon. Response: some abscesses are just starting, and in these, repulsion and dispersion are appropriate just as in other hot phlegmons. Others follow a phlegmon that began in the manner of healthy phlegmons, and in these, repulsion is not appropriate for the stated reason. Otherwise, I believe: that in every beginning hot abscess—whether it is just starting or not—repulsion is appropriate at its very commencement, and dispersion can be appropriate. Reason: the physician must, as much as he can, prohibit matter from collecting in a cavity which makes the limbs more wasted; but through repulsive [medicine] this is done. Consider that in the beginning, we say that if the matter has already clearly taken up a cavity, ripening <note>maturation</note> is appropriate. Consider also: that these repulsives should not be so strong in the beginning of an abscess, whether it is just starting or following another, as they are in the beginning of hot phlegmons that are not abscess-forming. The reason is: that for the most part, there is much matter, and also because as soon as an abscess begins, it has some cavity, though it be hidden. And so he wants repulsion to be done with balanced [medicines]. 3. Consider that dispersion is mostly done from the same or the proper part, and it could be done from the opposite part. To the reason, add: that even in the increase of phlegmons or at the end of the beginning, repulsion is appropriate, though not strong. And so when it goes toward resolution, we do not repel except when an abscess is formed.</margin>
<margin>e. That indeed. He posits the regimen which is appropriate for an abscess as an abscess. First he promises, then he declares. There, "Of which." Consider that a "great abscess" refers to matter that stands in a cavity and has crossed the pores; and therefore, nothing is owed to it except extraction through that very part. And this is done by cutting the skin. And therefore resolution—that is, extraction—is explained. It is doubted whether, after the matter has entered a cavity and made an abscess, it can be resolved imperceptibly through the pores. Some say no, because Avicenna does not posit it. On the contrary, it is said that scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes, often tubercular</note> is sometimes resolved. To which [we say] that for the most part they are not resolved, but are clearly extracted. The reason is: these matters tend toward pus and are thick; and if [resolution] were done, they would corrupt the limb. And therefore it is not similar to glands and nodes, which can stay in a limb for a long time without danger. Sometimes, however, an abscess can be resolved, as experience says.</margin>
<margin>f. Of which. First he shows one mode of regimen; secondly, another. Consider that Avicenna indicates that there is a "right regimen"—that is, one that is regular and without failure. This right regimen of Avicenna regards the ripening of the matter and its eruption; and it regards the vital strength, to comfort it and preserve it so it does not weaken. Together with what you know, thirdly, comfort is required for the accidents of the abscess when it occurs, because pain dissolves [strength] and when it is opened, many have died from fainting <note>syncope</note>. Therefore, feed the citizen [patient] copiously enough.</margin>

### The Sign of Internal Maturation. Ch. XXV.

When the signs of an internal abscess occur, and then the symptoms <note>accidents</note> which are from fever and shivering cease, and the pain is completely soothed, and a heaviness remains; then know that the pus is now confirmed and ripening <note>maturation</note> is present.

### The Signs of the Proximity of Internal Eruption. Ch. XXVI.

When the pains return and there are prickings and gnawing sensations, and the heaviness becomes more vehement, and similarly the fevers, then the eruption is now approaching. When, therefore, a sudden chill occurs, and the heaviness and pain are soothed, then the eruption has already occurred, and especially when the evacuated pus appears, gnawing at that which it passes through. And it is necessary that there be a "drying out" of the vital strength and a drying weakness. And when an internal abscess erupts suddenly and the contents go out all at once, then perhaps a palpitation of the heart and a bad fainting <note>syncope</note> occur, and perhaps death occurs due to the dissolution of the vital strength. And perhaps vomiting occurs, and a loosening of the belly, and perhaps an abundance of pus is suddenly spat up when the abscess is in the chest, and perhaps suffocation occurs when many things erupt to the chest suddenly.

### The Cures of Approaching Abscesses. Ch. XXVII.

Evacuations are indeed those by which they treat phlegmons in their beginnings, unless there is a fear of the matter returning to a noble organ <note>a vital organ like the heart or liver</note>, as we have declared; for just as they err in this, so do the foolish in things where hot abscesses and hot phlegmons (which are not abscesses) communicate. That indeed which is appropriate for it regarding the regimen is the resolution of that which is gathered in it. And that is according to two modes of regimen. One of which is the regimen running according to the right path, when the sickness does not depart from that which is most common. And it is so that the ripening of the matter is managed so that pus is formed, and in its eruption after that, you should observe the vital strength and preserve it, lest pain and sudden eruption overthrow it. For many men have died from fainting <note>syncope</note> due to the drying out of the vital strength; rather, the physician must observe how he may comfort the vital strength and preserve it with what you know. Wherefore the patient should be fed with good foods unless it is an abscess in the bowels, for then it is necessarily required that the food be made subtle <note>liquid or light</note>. And the second is the regimen departing from the right path because of the necessity of the condition...

<column-break/>

...with meat. Unless it is an internal phlegmon, because then one must use subtle foods because the suffering is more acute, and because great matters run there. Whence Avicenna: Fourth [book], Chapter 50. A symptom comes because of extraction, etc.

<margin>f. And the second. He posits the second mode of treatment for an abscess. First he introduces that mode and its cause; second, he declares it; third, he teaches how to help the symptoms following that mode of treatment, adding certain things there. Consider that the first regimen is more "right," because this one is "not right"—that is, not simply, but according to necessity, etc.</margin>
<margin>g. And it is. First he shows what the necessity is for this "not right" regimen, and he shows what that regimen is: which is the incision of the abscess before ripening <note>maturation</note>. Secondly, he completes the narration or declaration of the causes necessitating this incision. Thirdly, he shows the manner of incision, and he contains it here. And that is... in such things therefore.</margin>
<margin>h. And if. First he declares those causes. First he removes an error. If there is trust... he says that it is a corruption to open before maturation. "Grossness" [is used] not only for thickness but broadly for a multitude. Consider that he posits four causes for shortening [the wait]: namely, in phlegmonous sufferings where the matter is not truly ripening, but rather is malignant.</margin>
<margin>i. And if there is trust. Consider he might say: "Although the heat is weak and the matter incomplete, I will apply ripening agents <note>maturatives</note> and they have some stickiness, whence they prohibit the heat from dispersing." He responds that these maturatives are harmful here only in the indication that they prohibit ventilation <note>evaporation</note>. Inasmuch as they are maturatives, they move the weak heat; that is, they move the natural heat to act upon the matter, and that natural heat is weak and so it is excited to act but cannot; or they move the weak heat—that is, it generates a certain weak heat which moves the matter and putrefies it more, and all that, etc.</margin>
<margin>k. In such things. Here he concludes that an incision should be made; and he gives the method. First, giving a certain mode; second, he shows what should be done after the incision; third, he gives the specific mode of cutting. There, "Then." Third, it must be deep, so that it reaches and breaks through the matter—that is, the abscess.</margin>
<margin>l. Then follow. The reason is: because here we fear putrefaction and fistulas <note>abnormal tunnels in the flesh</note>. Here, strong dispersing and drying agents are used, as were found in the third chapter concerning "formica" <note>an erosive skin disease</note> and "sacred fire" <note>erysipelas</note>.</margin>
<margin>m. And it must be. He gives the mode of cutting in particular. Second, he shows what is not to be applied. Sometimes because of necessity—namely, the fear of a spasm—we are compelled to cut a nerve <note>or tendon</note> entirely across its width... "ligature"—that is, the folding.</margin>
<margin>n. To if. He teaches how to help the symptoms. First he does this; second, he enumerates the harms that follow this perfection <note>completion</note>; third, he adds the cause. Consider that after incision before maturation, it can happen that the matter is led out and bad symptoms do not follow; and then one must proceed to "incarnatives" <note>medicines that promote the growth of new flesh</note>... or consider that the opening is increased and inflammation and virulence will be there; then it is necessary to disperse and dry. Let evaporation be done with decoctions of lentils. Consider that these drying and dispersing agents should be mixed with some maturatives. The reason is that in this incision before maturation, the lips of the wound are hardened by reason of the undigested matter retained there.</margin>

...and it is because when the sickness is great and the abscess exceeds in its size that which is common, and a haste is feared in the expectation of maturation in it, and it is known that the vital strength is not sufficient for the maturation of all of it. And if maturatives are administered, it will lead to a trace of immaturity; then a perforation is necessary with caution, lest the iron <note>the scalpel</note> touch those noble members following the abscess, of which there is fear of the iron's touch. And that is when you have felt that the matter is of such thickness that it will not ripen, and that the innate heat in the limb is of such smallness that it will not ripen, or you have feared that because of its abbreviation it is such that it will be altered by an alteration that is not true maturation; or the abscess is near the joints and principal members, wherefore it is feared that it will corrupt them. And if trust is had in medicines that cause stickiness and maturation, it will not be long before the stickiness prohibits the breath of life <note>inspiration/ventilation</note> from penetrating the space, and the maturatives move the weak heat. And all that helps toward the putrefaction of the limb. In such cases, therefore, a deep incision and a breaking perforation are necessary; then let those medicines follow which are in the highest degree of resolution <note>dispersion</note> and drying.

And it is necessary that the perforation and section be made according to the length of the fibers of the nerves and the limb, unless it is the intention that the operation of that limb be destroyed for fear of a spasm occurring; for then, cut the fibers across the width, and you will save him from that which you feared. And for the most part, the length of the fibers follows the length of the body, except in specific limbs; for in the veins, the length of the fibers for the most part follows the folds and wrinkles, except in specific limbs such as the forehead. And it is necessary that neither water, nor oil, nor anything in which there is fat, be applied to the perforation or section. If there is no excuse but that it must be washed, then let it be done with water and honey, or water with wine, or with vinegar. But if the abscesses and inflammation become more vehement after the perforation, let it be steamed <note>vaporeť</note> with lentils; and if that is not necessary, you shall administer incarnatives and plasters. And know that this perforation [before maturation] is generative of virus <note>foul pus</note>, filth, and fistulas; truly, when you find no excuse...

fen III Treatise I

<margin>
By reason of virulence, there are generated things that are erictive <note>possibly "eroding" or "irritating"</note> and resolutive <note>substances that disperse swelling</note>. But by reason of the undigested matter, they also require ripening <note>original: "digestiuã," here meaning the maturation of the pus</note>. And such ripening agents should not be cooked in water, which moistens and rots specifically virulent ulcers, but rather with lye or honey-water.

And you should know:
Undigested and crude matter moves in the "lips" <note>edges</note> of the ulcer, which are turned into pus and filth and make the ulcers difficult; thus they are called fistulous.

And the locations:
He adds two rules. Consider that fleshy places are warm, and in them there is hope that the completion of maturation may occur; let the incision be delayed until after maturation. It must be considered that the year should be excepted <note>meaning a specific timeframe or condition</note> in which we perforate before maturation. Avicenna did not say this, but it is understood from the third Canon.

And you should know:
The part which says: that these open by themselves.

Of Medicines:
Here specifically he places the regimen for abscesses: first by maturation, second by extraction <note>lancing</note>. There: "secondly in vessels." First he shows what the power of ripening medicines is; second he enumerates those medicines. There "of those." It is doubted whether a ripening medicine is next to the heat of the body; it seems not. First, Averroes in the 5th book of the *Colliget* does not praise the definition by which Galen defined ripening matter. Likewise, Albucasis <note>original: "albeguesit"</note> in his 3rd book on simples: he posits that all things should be equal to the blood which is in the limb. But superfluities are imbalanced; therefore... Also, in the 3rd chapter it is said concerning pigeon dung, etc. He teaches to ripen with pigeon dung. Likewise here, Avicenna.

...maturation, then there is no other technique. And the more suitable places to wait for them to ripen in are fleshy places, far from nerves and veins. And you should know that pineal <note>cone-shaped</note> elevations with sharp heads require little perforation, neither before maturity nor after it.

### The regimen for maturation in the technique for producing pus in visible abscesses. Chapter 28.

The heat of ripening **M**edicines should be close to the heat of the body, and they should have a certain stickiness <note>original: "inuiscatio," refers to a coating that traps heat</note>. Among those in the first degrees are drenching with warm water and poultices with wheat or barley flour; and wheat, when it is chewed, is better for this; and bread with pitch or wax, and saffron, and frankincense powder, and pitch with rose oil, or pork fat, or a poultice of marshmallow and flaxseed. There shall also be a poultice of dry, sweet, thick, fatty figs, either with barley flour—and barley flour again—and specifically if hyssop and wild oregano are put in it, or if it is gathered with water in which they were boiled with a little salt, not in excess. And sometimes fat or oil is put in it, or especially those two parts of white garden glue. And compound medicines are made from raisins, storax, galbanum, myrrh, ladanum, resin, butter, mastic, moist hyssop, root of squirting cucumber, and dragon's blood root. And Galen's poultice with one part oil of *kerua* <note>castor oil</note> without wax, and specifically when this poultice is dissolved in oil; and similarly the *didimos* poultice and the *basilicon* poultice. And among the good things for this is the medicine of marcasite stone with ammonia, which is placed on top until it falls off by itself.

### The regimen for abscesses when they are ripe. Chapter 29.

**W**hen you find an abscess of thick skin with maturation, whose own bursting is not hoped for—and there are veins, cords, and nerves there—then you must perforate it; for if you leave the sanies <note>bloody pus</note>, it will be corrupted and will corrupt and erode the veins and the fibers of the nerves. And that will indeed be more severe when it is near the joints. And you indeed seek with your perforation the place of the pus. And be careful that the gate of the perforation falls lower down, unless where it is not possible. And if that which is above the abscess is thick and you cut it, then cut only the "gate" <note>opening</note>, for the thickness will adhere to that which is after it; but if it has been thinned out, then cut the whole of it lengthwise. And know that the place in which the pus is located is declared by touch, specifically when it is touched with a finger; and you observe with other fingers, at least of the other hand, whether it expels anything in response. And the place of the pus indeed appears from the turning of the color toward whiteness; while it is not mature, it is inclined toward redness. And sometimes the place of the pus is inclined toward blackness and yellowness when the pus is not good; sustain this by touch without sight, yet sight is helpful. It is necessary, therefore, that in the incision you follow the natural lines of the ligatures <note>referring to skin tension lines</note>, except what is done at the joint unless by necessity; and in limbs where the position of the fibers differs in their length, follow the place of the ligature. For if you followed that in the perforation of an abscess which is on the forehead—namely, the ligatures—the skin of the forehead would fall over the face; rather, it is necessary that you vary the ligatures. In those which are like the groins, you must go with the ligature in the width of the skin. And when you have perforated the abscesses and extracted what is in them, then it is necessary that you provide help to glue the skin to the flesh so that it is not broken and hardened, and becomes such that it is not glued, whereby a cavity <note>original: "sinus"</note> is made which does not cease to be filled and returns like the first abscess. And as often as you have cleansed it, do not delay again until it is filled and becomes in truth a type of fistula. And before you make it...

<column-break/>

<margin>
He enumerates medicines that are cold and hot in excess. Furthermore, it seems similar concerning the maturation of humors in winds and appetites. First of use, etc. It is doubted whether stickiness [is needed]. It seems not, by the reason taken from the words of Avicenna, because it prohibits transpiration. Again because it concludes with vapors and putrid things, etc. To the contrary, Avicenna here and above, in the fifth chapter on simples. Galen, Serapion with others. To the first: certain ripening medicines indeed act directly toward maturation, others indirectly. Direct is that which comforts the natural heat, because that is what digests the matter; and because heat is seen to be with moisture, therefore such matter is hot and moist in a tempered way, that is, proportional to the heat of the limb. And therefore the heat of the hand is ripening, and the heat of an oven. And because heat is diverse according to the diversity of complexions and limbs, therefore ripening medicines vary in heat, etc. Indirectly ripening is that which removes the indisposition through which nature does not obey maturation; and this is quantity, quality, or multitude. Above, if the quality is indisposed, either primary or secondary, or the specific form. If it is the substance: either thick or thin or viscous. To the second, it must be said that it ought to be sticky; the reason is because it reflects the heat back and also because it prohibits drying out, etc.
</margin>

...be glued together, in that hour you must cleanse it. And if it is necessary for you to insert into it a probe <note>term: "radiū" - a surgical rod</note>, on the head of which is a rough cloth with which you may cleanse it and rub it; then make it adhere and preserve it with a ligature; what we say regarding the ligatures of caverns and deep ulcers will be very suitable. And you must observe in the perforation that which we said about the conditions; then perforate in the more mature place and the part furthest from the veins, arteries, and cords. Antyllus <note>a famous 2nd-century Greek surgeon</note> says: if there is an abscess on the head, then let its incision be a straight incision and let it be with the root of the hair growth, so that it is not transverse to it, so that the hair may cover it and it is not shown when it has been healed. He says when its place is hidden, then its perforation should be wide; and if it happens in the nose, we shall perforate it straight with the length of the nose. And if it is near the eye, we shall perforate it with a perforation like the head of a new moon <note>a crescent-shaped incision</note>, and we shall make the curvature downwards. If however it happens in the jaws, we shall cut it with a straight incision because the composition of the muscles there is straight, and you know that from the bodies of the elderly. Behind the ears, indeed, we perforate it straight. Arms, however, and elbows and hands and fingers and groins, we perforate all in their length. He says: and if it is near the pupils, we shall perforate it with a round perforation; and a round perforation is that which takes in some of its width along with the length of the body. He says: for when this place is not perforated roundly, it is possible for matter to gather in them and they become fistulas. And similarly also it is perforated near the anus because of the place of moisture which gathers in it. And in the side and ribs, it is perforated by opening <note>likely meaning crosswise</note>. In the testicles, however, and the penis, straight. He says: and let us be prompt always so that the suture follows the shape of the place as much as we are able. The hips and the upper arms are cut in their length, and take care that you do not hurt the nerves. And know that the perforation varies according to the locations; for when it is at the eye, then its perforation is wide, similar to the position of the eye; and in the nose it is according to the length of the nose; and in the jaw it is with the length of the jaw; and near the ear it is cut straight, because the composition of this place is straight, and that is known from the bodies of the elderly. Behind the ears, however, it is perforated straight; and in the arms and legs and hip and penis, all is done straight in length; and similarly in the muscles of the belly and in the back and in the groins and under the armpits, you shall place a perforation taking from the width also, lest a cavity be made in it that becomes a fistula. And similarly in that which is near the anus, take from the width also lest a cavity come forth and it become a fistula; and the testicles and penis straight and in length; and in the side and ribs take in width also so that it is transverse, because the position of the ribs is similar, and the flesh which is over them. He says: always consider the position of the flesh and the fibers of the muscles, for we are not instructed except for this: that we perforate with imitation of the location so that the incision does not come upon a joint or a nerve or the fibers of a muscle; and the perforation should have the size of the abscess. If it is small and what is in it runs out from one place, then cut it in one place. And if it is large, then perforate it from the beginning, then insert your left index finger into it and perforate it where its head reaches; then insert it also in the second hole and do this until you have reached over it. And if there is a sufficient place from which what is in the abscess can come out, we shall perforate it in that place; and if it is round or has a shape so that what is in it does not go out from one perforation, we shall perforate it in several...

Book III

<margin>
a. "And you." He notes what must be observed in the conclusion. Thus he declares that the third part completes the discourse. All these things have been noted at the end of the chapter. It is doubted because it seems that no internal swelling should be opened by force, as all can be opened with medicines. It should be said that we open without iron <note>a surgical blade</note> for two reasons: firstly, out of fear for the patient's state; secondly, if the patient is very weak, a large caustic <note>a chemical that burns the skin</note> terrifies them. However, in hot abscesses, it is much better to use iron. I say therefore that Avicenna says: if we hope etc., to achieve it through medicines. This is understood to be through mild medicines.
</margin>

<margin>
f. Adubetlet <note>original: "Adubetlet," from the Arabic "al-dubaylat," meaning internal abscesses or tumors</note>. He speaks of the cure of internal abscesses, which does not primarily belong to this place but to the third book. He treats it briefly here. Consider that in this, internal tumors and abscesses share common traits, as was said above. That is, in common, bile <note>original: "cholera," one of the four humors</note>, or matter, or red bile which is feared may dissipate. Or in a putrid or evil discharge <note>sanies</note>. To avoid dangers, we accept that everyone for whom it is good [to drain] is lucky. And after the evacuation, we use equal parts. Fourth, that it is matured at last beyond which it does not pass. And this is because the matter is difficult to mature. There are cinnamon etc. with a drink of wine, which leads to the location. One thing is certain: it comforts the heat. Therefore, what wheat flour does on the outside, this wine does on the inside.
</margin>

**A**dubetlet <note>internal abscesses</note>: concerning the cure of internal abscesses, I have spoken in two or three places according to the quantity you know; for everything that aggregates in it runs in an hour. He says: unless it is an abscess near a joint, or a noble member <note>a vital organ like the heart or liver</note>, or a member near a bone or a membrane <note>panniculo</note>, we shall hasten in its conclusion before it is confirmed and before the maturation of the pus corrupts any of these members. I say therefore, this is the regimen for which we find no excuse for delaying the opening. If, however, we hope that it will break by itself, we shall not perforate it; and similarly, if we hope that it will be burst by medicines that cause eruption. For perhaps we find in medicines that cause eruption something that takes the place of lancing. And many times the skin is perforated by a small opening or something is taken from it, and afterwards a bursting medicine is placed over it to prepare the way.

## On the bursting of abscesses. Chapter XXX.

**A**bscesses that are safe, in which there is no great malice <note>virulence</note>, are opened by hot water, which bursts them. However, putrefied ones are vehemently harmed by this because of that which is attracted to them from the matter. And when you see an abscess that hot water rectifies, then have confidence in its goodness.

## On the cure. Chapter XXXI.

**A**nd you should know that a plaster with narcissus root bursts every small swelling, especially when boiled with water and honey; or boil all of that with oil of lily or iris; or use fresh cane root with honey; or dry pitch with the dross of beehives <note>propolis or waste wax</note>; or the "arbofilos" plaster. Or take 1 pound each of wax, resin, and butter; and half a pound each of dry pitch and honey; and 3 drams of flower of copper <note>verdigris</note> and as much oil as suffices. And the medicine made of garlic is very good. Or take 6 parts ammonia, 4 wax, 3 tree glue, 3 yellow sulfur, 3 nitre, and make a plaster of them. And among those things we have experienced is to take the marrow of grain seeds, rancid nut, leaven, cooked cabbage, cooked onions, mustard, and dove dung, and make a plaster of them; for it bursts [the abscess] quickly. And again, wild rue dissolved in mustard mucilage and soap associated with figs. And among the bursting medicines that stand in place of perforation is to administer a plaster made of cashew honey <note>original: "melle anacardo," likely the caustic oil from the marking nut</note> and liquid pitch; let these two be joined by equal heat, then placed over the abscess for half a day, after which it will be burst. And among those that are strong is to take alkali <note>lye</note> and unslaked lime; let them be submerged in half their weight of water, then strained after they have boiled. Let the alkali and lime be in that water; then let them be taken and placed in a copper cauldron over coals and congealed into salt. Take some of this salt, and a fourth part as much of sal ammoniac, and put it in mucilage of watercress in which there is some cashew honey, and let it be administered. Or take Spanish flies <note>cantharides</note>, grind them, and put them in old oil; place them over a light fire, namely the fire of coals, until the whole is coagulated; then let it be ground like a plaster and cashew honey placed upon it, especially if hawk dung, sparrow dung, or duck dung is added. And some have already spoken of "alkebi" <note>likely a specific Arabic remedy</note> with the thinning of the member and its rarefaction through vapors that cause it, using those things in which there is warm humidity; and the more it is resolved, the more the place should be plastered and bathed <note>embrocated</note>. And the regimen must not be void of soothing medicines until its hardness is softened, because it is necessary that

<margin>
h. Ademenul <note>original: "Ademenul," from Arabic "al-dumanal," small boils or pustules</note>. Above he spoke of abscesses; here of Ademenul, that is, of "little cords." The reason is that they mostly turn into abscesses. First he shows what it is and gives the causes. Then the cure: "when they appear." It should be considered that they are of the genus of abscesses, because they either begin as abscesses or quickly turn into them. Consider that we accept this because the cause is corrupt blood mixed with bile or melancholy, like "azaram" <note>possibly a corruption of "anthrax" or "as-sartan"</note>, a malice of digestion—that is, corrupted. The first cause is too much illness, a soft bed, or drinking thick wine as mentioned by Rhazes, etc. Thirdly, consider that the deeper ones are of thick, evil matter, wherefore they pertain to carbuncles <note>anthrax</note>. "When they appear": first he sets the cure more generally, second specifically. There: "secondly." And when the first part is in two: first he sets the cure with local remedies, second with evacuation. There: "secondly." And his cure: consider that the cure of hot abscesses was with repellents...
</margin>

<column-break/>

only soothing remedies be administered. And those resolving medicines are from the highest quality of borax <note>baurach</note>, mustard, bird dung, arsenic, lime, and "cozduwen" <note>likely an herb</note>; and let them be mixed with things like frankincense, glue, turpentine, mastic, and "aldibic" <note>possibly a resin</note>; and let them be joined with vinegar and old oil, and the medicine made with garlic, or from "albacuen" <note>possibly white hellebore</note>, or from pellitory and stavesacre, and borax with honey. And before all these, let the place be bathed with hot water. And the medicine of marcasite, the description of which is: Take 12 drams of marcasite stone, the same of ammonia, 6 drams of bean flour; let it be mixed with liquid resin and smeared over the skin and placed over the discharge until it falls off by itself; and it must be administered immediately because they dry out quickly. And the medicine made from one part of sal ammoniac, a quarter part of "bezabard" <note>possibly a herb or mineral</note>, one and a third parts of litharge <note>lead oxide</note>, and one and two-thirds parts of old oil; let an ointment be made from it. And when medicines do not help as we have said, it is necessary to perforate or cauterize.

<margin>
e. And the cure. Here however consider that they are not of the nature of a carbuncle. It is resolved for the most part because the matter immediately begins to take a head, because it is mostly thick blood.
</margin>

## Regimen of internal abscesses. Chapter XXII.

**A**dubetlet <note>internal abscesses</note> indeed must be ruled by evacuation, especially when bile is exiting in the stool and urine. This signifies that the entire blood is bad. When, however, the physician's estimate is verified that the blood is good because of what it expels to the abscess and after evacuation, then it must be matured with equal medicines, such as thin wine for fever when drunk little by little. And those things which are intended for the most exquisite maturation are the thinning and drying medicines such as myrrh, cinnamon, and other spices; let them be followed by a drink of thin wine that leans toward whiteness; and of the compounds, there are theriac, mithridat, and "homorusia."

<margin>
f. "And when it was." Here in specific. Because they are mostly matured, he teaches first to mature, second to open through maturation. There: "secondly." And when they are matured: first he sets the signs etc. Second he sets a certain cause. Third, the maturatives. There: "secondly." And that one. There: "third." And of. Consider that he sets two signs of maturation or of the base of the root, i.e., it has a base with a pine-like prominence.
</margin>

## On Ademenul <note>boils</note>. Chapter XXXIII.

**A**demenul <note>boils/pustules</note> are likewise of the genus of abscesses. Most of them arise from poor digestion and from movement after overfilling <note>repletion</note>, and those things which follow that course; the worst boils are those which are deeper.

## On the cure of Ademenul. Chapter XXXIV.

**W**hen the boils appear, their cure for about three days is the cure for hot abscesses; then for that, one's occupation must be in resolving and maturing. For perhaps they will be resolved, and that is for the smaller ones, or perhaps they will be matured. And not everything was due to negligence in the treatment of boils; for many times it turns into a large abscess. Its cure is fasting according to the quantity of necessity, bloodletting <note>phlebotomy</note>, and loosening of the belly. And when there is a pulse in the boil and a base at the root, then maturation is necessary; therefore, assist it. And that person who has suffered a multitude of emerging boils is liberated by the loosening of the belly and the rarefaction of the skin with baths administered always after exercise. And of the maturatives: ground "almaru" <note>possibly a seed or herb</note> with milk or figs and honey; and figs with honey itself; and chewed wheat is good for their maturation; and "filtr passe" <note>likely raisins</note> prepared with borax, or figs with mustard mixed with lily oil, and the known boil-medicine, and the known medicine of leaven. And the medicine in which this method exists matures: Take 1 dram of butter, 1 dram of sour leaven, 1 dram of ground "almaru" and psyllium; of all, 1 dram each. 3 drams of fig milk, 5 drams each of fenugreek and celery. Let it boil in milk and be administered.

<margin>
h. Note. Here he speaks of a certain abscess called "morum" <note>mulberry-like</note>, because it is similar to a mulberry in shape and color. It is an abscess improperly called an abscess, because it is rather a soft fleshy addition; because soft flesh in the anus is called "ficus" <note>figs/hemorrhoids</note>, and further it is called condylomata. Sometimes it is called "emoris" <note>hemorrhoids</note>, and it occurs in the eye as Avicenna says, etc. If it is of a good color, it is safe; if it is bad and painful, it is malicious because sometimes it is cancerous. He does not set a cure, because it requires incision if it is not cancerous. Whence Haly Abbas <note>original: "balyb"</note> wished to cure it with regimens. 4. drams. page 179 of the *Continens*.
</margin>

# Book III Treatise II

<margin>a. And the abscesses. First, according to the number of humors, he lists the number of cold abscesses. Second, he discusses phlegmatic <note>original: "pblatica," referring to the humor phlegm</note> abscesses. It is questioned why Avicenna seems to omit watery swellings when he did not speak of them specifically; it seems redundant since he did not treat them separately from the composite ones. To this, it must be said that they are understood to be included here.</margin>
**Cold Humors.** Previously, he determined the nature of hot abscesses that follow their own course; here he discusses cold ones and their course. First in general, and second in specific detail. The first part is divided: first, he lists certain cold humors; second, he describes the cold abscesses. **It should be considered** that the cold humors are phlegm and melancholy, which follow a course of "windiness" <note>original: "ventositas," referring to gas or air trapped in tissues</note> because these humors are mostly cold, and due to a lack of heat, gas is generated or they are composed of them. When composed of cold and hot humors, the cold ones dominate. These three categories are helpful to understand. And when a tumor comes to pus with difficulty and with a heavy quality of heat, then a "windy" <note>original: "pbloma venā," likely referring to a pneumatosis or gas-filled swelling</note> condition occurs. If you treat this at the beginning, poisoned blood <note>original: "san. virulentus"</note> will emerge, and the thick matter will remain, forming a hard ulcer. And when it matures and does not open on its own, perforate it either with medicines or with iron <note>a surgical knife</note>, as was said regarding boils. Among the good agents for breaking them open are linseed, pigeon dung, and leaven. **On the Mulberry-like Growth. Chapter XXXV.**

<margin>c. On the "Morus" <note>original: "Moro," meaning mulberry-shaped growth</note>. This is a soft abscess consisting of added flesh that occurs in porous flesh, especially in the anus and the vulva. Sometimes it is benign and sometimes it is malignant and painful.</margin>
**On the soft abscess made of added flesh** which occurs in porous flesh, especially in the anus and the vulva; sometimes it is benign and sometimes it is malignant and painful.

->Second Treatise on Rigid Abscesses and those that follow their course. Chapter I.<-

<margin>b. And the abscesses. Here he declares, first, the phlegmatic ones; second, the melancholic ones; third, the windy ones; fourth, the composite ones. **It should be considered** that in general there are four simple phlegmatic abscesses: some are called soft, second are watery, third are "dubelet" <note>original: "dubelet," from the Arabic "al-dubaylat," meaning an internal tumor or cyst</note>—namely smooth and phlegmatic abscesses—and hard ones. They are called "simple" not because others are not simple, but because they are "loose" or "pure" phlegmatic swellings made of true phlegm. It is doubted why in the first book he placed "nodes" <note>lumps</note> and glands among the melancholic abscesses. To this, it is said that they are radically phlegmatic, as their root is phlegm, but because that phlegm has turned to hardness, they are called melancholic. They differ from scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes, often tubercular</note> and nodes, though those differ from cancer and scirrhus <note>a hard, cancerous tumor</note>. Both cancer and scirrhus are within the substance of the limb, whereas scrofula and nodes are separate; nodes are even more separate from the flesh than scrofula, which are somewhat retained on the surface of the flesh. It is doubted among which abscesses the "gland" is placed; a soft gland is placed among phlegmatic abscesses, understood here as "smooth nodes." Hard glands are placed among melancholic ones. "Duballet" is a general term for anything in which phlegm gathers in one place. Also, he says there are two types of hardness: one is extremely hard, which is melancholic or hardened phlegm, called scrofula or a hardened node. The other is a hard gland that does not have that ultimate hardness but is harder than soft nodes and glands, and less hard than scrofula; this is simply called a "gland."</margin>
**Cold Humors** and those that follow their course in the body are phlegmatic, melancholic, windy, or a composition of these; and you already know their types. Abscesses are either phlegmatic, melancholic, windy, or composite.

Phlegmatic abscesses are either simple—called soft abscesses—or watery, as happens in a limb when water gathers, like in dropsy <note>edema/swelling</note>. Or they are "dubelet," in which there are smooth nodes, or hard ones like scrofula and hard nodes—namely melancholic ones—or "sephiros" <note>a hard, insensitive tumor</note> or cancer, and you will know the difference between them. Windy ones are either "elevations" or "inflations." An elevation is when windiness is mixed with the substance of the limb. An inflation is when the windiness is gathered in a single space within it. Sometimes these abscesses are composed with each other and with heat.

->On the soft phlegmatic abscess which is called "undimia." Chapter II.<-

This is a soft, white abscess in which there is no heat. The thinner and more watery the matter, the more pronounced the softening; a finger easily penetrates it and leaves a depression <note>pitting edema</note>, which does not happen in a "windy" elevation. The thicker the matter, the more it leans toward hardness and cold. Most of it comes from a phlegmatic vapor and is of the "elevation" type. **Undimia** <note>original: "yndimia," medieval Latin for edema</note> differs from melancholic abscesses by its lack of hardness and lack of dark color. When it happens from a blow or similar cause, and no matter comes to the site except phlegm, it does not form an abscess except a phlegmatic one, which has little pain and does not discharge much.

->Cure of the soft abscess. Chapter III.<-

The cure is through loosening the bowels <note>using laxatives</note> and abstinence from things that generate phlegm.

<margin>d. And melancholic. Namely, those which Avicenna enumerates among the melancholic in the first book, but here among the phlegmatic.</margin>
<margin>f. And windy. Elevation, also called "caccha" <note>unclear; likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic medical term for swelling</note> in the first book, second section, etc.</margin>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Circular diagram at the top of the second column consisting of an outer circle with numbered and lettered sections and an inner circle with radial connections, possibly a classification of tumors or humors. To its left is a decorative rubricated initial 'E'.</image-desc>
<insert>It appears differently in manner, as Avicenna says above, and in its location.</insert>

This is the abscess: first of phlegm, second of melancholy, third of windiness, fourth a composition. See the second part: hard abscesses. See the third: on windy abscesses. The fourth occurs as follows. First, on the soft abscess; second, on smooth nodes; third, on hard nodes; then on scrofula. **It should be considered** that he does not treat watery swellings like dropsy or those in the skull here. First, he determines the nature of the phlegmatic abscess, namely "undimia," regarding its cause and signs; second, its cure. Regarding the evacuation, he first gives the signs, then the cause. Third, he compares it to melancholic abscesses. He says first it is a white abscess, because phlegm is white. If the finger easily penetrates, it leaves a mark <note>original: "vestigio," a footprint or trace</note> in the pressed limb, which does not happen in a windy elevation.

<margin>g. And mostly. Phlegmatic vapor, namely from thinned phlegm; and thus it is of the "elevation" type. Though some say the opposite, mostly it means this "undimia" is the same as an elevation. Or, it is made more from thinned phlegm than hard phlegm. Phlegmatic swellings range from "elevation" at one extreme to "inflation" at the other.</margin>
And those things which are necessary. What should be done is "repercussion" <note>cooling and driving back the humor</note> in the beginning, using things that gather, dry, and resolve. The place should be rubbed with a rough cloth, then drying agents should be applied. One must not touch it with water. What is good in the beginning is to apply a new sponge soaked in vinegar mixed with or infused in "baurach" <note>natron or borax</note> water and ashes. In its substance, the sponge is drying and resolving. The more the illness increases, the stronger the vinegar should be. At the "status" <note>the peak of the disease</note>, use the strongest sharp vinegar, and apply the sponge mixed with oils of powerful resolution. At that time, apply the sponge soaked in ash-water, such as from grapevines, holm oak, or metal filings. The sponge must cover all sides so the matter does not shift to another side. Sometimes, instead of a sponge, if one is not found, use a cloth doubled twice with ash-water. Lime water is even stronger. Other helpful things include rose oil with vinegar, salt, and burnt sulfur; sulfur itself is good. Ash with cabbage water is a miraculous help. At the beginning, use it alone or with certain hot drying agents. Bandaging helps if the matter is not too thick. The bandaging should start from the bottom and go upwards. Myrtle juice is also good. If medicines do not work and the abscess is in a nervous or ligamentous part, mix in things that "cut" <note>break down thick matter</note> while also softening.

<margin>h. And they differ. This is evident.</margin>
<margin>i. And when. We take this first, though it rarely happens from a primary cause like a blow.</margin>
<margin>k. Evacuation. First, he gives the cure by evacuation; second, by local applications. Note that he says nothing of bloodletting <note>original: "phlobotoma"</note>, because it is not appropriate here.</margin>
<margin>l. And with. First, he gives the cure by local agents for the illness itself. Second, as it follows another condition. Sometimes it is with pain. It differs according to the limb. For abscesses at the beginning, at the increase, and at the peak. **It should be considered** that although "repercussion" is appropriate for a cold abscess, for "undimia" one must mix drying and resolving agents, because pure cold agents would congeal the matter in place. Salt water or sharp wine vinegar is used because vinegar has both repercussive and resolving properties.</margin>
And most of it comes from phlegmatic vapor and is of the "elevation" type.

And **undimia** differs from melancholic abscesses by its lack of hardness and lack of dark color.

And when it happens from a blow, it is rarely from a primary cause.

And with local treatments, as it is an illness in itself.

<margin>m. And as often. "Stronger" means more acute or sharp, which is more resolving.</margin>
And as often as it increases, use a sharper or more resolving agent.

<margin>n. And at the peak. He gives the cure for the "status" or peak of the illness. With strong, sharp vinegar, because it is more resolving.</margin>
And at the peak, he provides the treatment for that stage.

<margin>o. And with. This refers to an abscess in a nervous limb. Sharp vinegar can harm nerves because the matter there is not easily resolved and might harden from the dryness of the vinegar. In fleshy parts, it is not a problem. Or, use it with something soothing.</margin>
And when the abscess is in a nervous limb.

<margin>p. And when there is. Note that the cure for undimia differs if there is a primary cause, particularly in sedating the pain.</margin>
And when it follows a primary cause, the treatment varies.

# Book III
