The flow of blood from the lung is fearful in both a large and a small exit.</margin>
We now say that the nature of the flow of blood from the organs differs when they are ruptured, such as the liver and the lung. And there are those from which little blood proceeds; and in each of these two conditions, if it is fearful, it is that which is without fear <note>meaning even small amounts can be dangerous</note>, such as the flow of blood from the lung in which there is fear, and from both of these very much blood flows; and there are those like the bladder, the womb, and the kidneys. From these indeed very much blood does not flow all at once, but sometimes it increases over a long period and leads to undesirable results. And the nature of blood flow from the arteries differs because in some of them it is very difficult and fearful, such as from the large arteries that are in the hands and feet, and these for the most part kill and cannot be restrained; and in some it is easy, such as in the arteries of the skull, for the retention of their blood flow is easy and simple constriction suffices for them. And many times indeed blood flows from small arteries and then is retained by itself. And the difference between arterial blood and other blood is recognized because arterial blood exits with a leap and a pulse, and it is of a more intense purple color, and it does not decline toward the blackness of venous blood and its essence. And know that for one to whom an evacuation occurs, especially of blood and specifically arterial, if it is excessive and a spasm follows, it is a bad sign. # Book III

<margin>
It is necessary <note>original: "Oportet"</note>. He sets down the cure for the flow of blood: and although certain things placed here can be adapted to a flow of blood from wherever it may be, and he likewise speaks in general terms; nevertheless, his principal intention concerns the flow of blood from external members, especially with a wound. He accomplishes this after certain medicines. There he says "And those." First, in this section, he shows from where one must begin when the flow of blood and a wound coincide. Second, he follows through there: "I say." The first part is in two sections: first he shows a wound in which there is no corrosion <note>erosion of tissue</note>, second where there is, there he says "and not."
</margin>

**I**<gloss>a</gloss>t is necessary in the treatment of a flow of blood that one begins by restraining it, and then you may cure its wound if there was one. And it is not possible for you to do so in a case where the cause is fixed by a corroding agent or similar things, except by removing the cause. And if it cannot be tolerated that the cause be removed, it is necessary that it be restrained with its own restraints, which are among the causes that cut off running blood; and those causes are known from the first book. However, I will recount them in a summarized manner.

<margin>
b I say. First he sets down the causes [or means] for restraining the flow of blood. Second, he explains these, there he says "Furthermore." This is in three parts. First, he does this. Second, he shows which of those causes is suitable when there is a swelling <note>original: "apostema"; an inflammatory swelling</note> with the wound, and which is not. Third, he shows how many intentions a physician should have regarding a wound when there is a swelling from which blood will come. There he says "And it is necessary that you know." The third part is there; first he provides the division. Second, he subdivides, there "and the division." First, he says that the causes prohibiting the flow of blood either prohibit it from exiting by diverting it, or by gathering a thing or things at the place, from which there will be no blood.
</margin>

<insert>b</insert> I say, therefore, that these causes are either those prohibiting the exit of that which comes out, or they are those gathering something or things [at the site]. And the first division is the diversion to another part, which is either done with attraction to the opposite side without another exit being made—such as when cupping glasses are placed over the liver and the flow of blood from the right nostril is removed—or such that another exit occurs, just as bloodletting <term>phlebotomy|the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term> for a patient suffering a flow of blood from the nostrils is done from the hand corresponding to the nostril, using a narrow opening.

Restraining without an exit, however, is that which prohibits the movement of the blood and its penetration. And this is either through a cauterizing <note>original: "ignientem," literally "setting on fire"</note> cause or through a numbing <note>original: "stupefacientem"</note> cause. And the numbing agent is either a medicine or a disposition of the body, such as fainting <note>original: "sincopis"</note>, for in the first instance it often restrains the blood. The cause restraining blood in specific places is that which blocks the exit, either with a bandage, or with repulsion from a plug <note>original: "buccellatione"; a small wad or compress</note>, or with repulsion without a plug; or an eschar <note>a dry scab</note> with a cautery; or a cauterizing medicine; or with the freezing of the thing being restrained; or by making it sticky; or by drying; or by the growth of new flesh; or by the tightening of the flesh surrounding the veins, whereby it blocks the vein itself and closes it with a forceful closure.

<margin>
c Division. First he subdivides the first member, second the second. There "The cause however." It is doubted, because he teaches to perform bloodletting from the same hand. And this from another or at a distance. To which [it is said] that in the beginning of the flow when the body is full, it ought to be done at a long distance so the fullness is evacuated. And these things suddenly hold back the body; or if the flow has already proceeded and the strength is weak, then it is the same narrow [opening], because it better preserves the strength.
</margin>

<insert>c</insert> And you must know that when a swelling is associated with a wound in a very large amount, it is not possible to tie it with threads, nor to insert lint, nor to use a laborious tightening; and it is not possible then except to administer gluing, stypticity <note>agents that contract tissues to stop bleeding</note>, numbing agents, and the thickening of the blood. And if there is a cure from tightening or an incision or the proximity of medicine when there is pain, it is very bad; and every painful preparation is bad.

<margin>
d Furthermore. First he declares the causes and modes of restricting the flow which are diverting. Second, those that work around the location, a thing or things. There "The mode however," etc.
</margin>

<insert>d</insert> And it is necessary that the preparation brings together two things: one is the absence of pain, and the other is the checking of that part of the blood's course so that it is not aided by hanging or suspension, and the flow of blood and its exit are made difficult. And when two intentions are prohibited, one should decline toward the lighter one according to what is present and nearer to being tolerated in the disposition. And it is necessary that we recount the manner of it after you have learned that the first thing which must be considered is to know whether the vessel is an artery or a vein by its signs, so that you may act with the artery and be more diligent than you would be when acting with a vein. Furthermore, we say that concerning true attraction to the opposite side (not toward an exit), it is necessary for the member to have friction or binding and tightening, or cupping glasses. And it is necessary that a communicating member be placed from a known member upon the extremity of a single line of continuity between them both, in length and breadth; and from what is varied in the position of length and breadth, whichever of the two is distant is chosen, and that which is near is dismissed, just as

<column-break/>

it would be in the two sides of the head or the two sides of the hands; the length between these two is nearer than that from which a complete harm must be feared; and this matter requires that we remember what we said about it where we spoke in the first book concerning the canons of evacuation. And it is necessary that there be extension and friction and similar constant things from that which is nearer to the second member, then let it descend from it. And it is necessary that one does not wait in the ruptures of arteries and similar things until there is a sufficient technique for restraining the flow of blood and aiding it; and likewise is the judgment in the bloodletting of the distant common side.

One of the two divided modes of the second [intent] is the numbing cause. For example: let the person whose flow of nasal blood is multiplied, or another besides him, be fed with thick foods that thicken the blood, such as lentils and jujubes and similar things. The second mode is, for example, that numbing things are given in drink, or they expose the body to cold, and perhaps fainting occurs and the flow of blood is restrained.

The aforementioned mode in the other division is that one point must be observed in it: that perhaps the artery is not one of the two that continue to the heart, but rather of its two sides, so that when you have constricted it, you find it firmer. Indeed, perhaps a branch of another artery is continued with the other side, which happens in it and brings blood to it aside from the path which you constricted; therefore you need two constrictions. And before that, you must know the part which is the beginning of the vein; for in some places it is lower and in some it is from above. In those where it is higher, it is like in the neck; and in those where they are from above, they are like in the thigh and foot. And when you have known the part, administer the binding and tightening upon it.

And regarding the regime in that case, it is that you should manage to extract the vein with a hook and with the incision of a little flesh that veils and hides it; then wrap it, and afterwards administer the medicines which we shall speak of. But if it is pulsating [an artery], then it is better that you bind it with linen threads. And a thread, even if it is not pulsating, nevertheless many times raises its blood. When therefore you have done that, then apply medicines to it; then leave the binding until the third and fourth day. Then if you see the medicine making a glue-like bond adhering to its place, do not pull it off entirely, but place something of its own kind around it that may moisten it a little.

But if a flow happens of its own accord when you remove that which is over it, then hold that which is under the place in the path of the vein's journey with a primary pressure, by which security from the leaping of blood may be achieved, and remove that which rises from it in its place and change it for another. And let your preparation which you make for the member at this hour be according to what is necessary: and that is that its opening should be more upright than the beginning, so that when it is, for example, in the lower intestines or the womb, then spread some bedding that raises the lower parts and lowers the upper parts according to the greatest elongation from pain; then leave it for three days, then continue this manner until the blood is raised [stops].

Checking with a plug <note>original: "buccellatione"</note> is not possible except in large arteries; make therefore a lint-plug from rabbit hair or from a spider's web or a fine cooked ... <note>text unclear</note> or an old linen cloth; then sprinkle over it medicines that prohibit blood. And put it into the artery itself like a plug, then tighten a bandage over it; and perhaps administer this lint-plug from rabbit hair alone, and it excuses the need for [further] diligence. And you must tighten the adhering bandage so that it is not separated until new flesh grows <note>original: "incarnetur"</note>. Regarding the lint-plug, nature truly rules in its gradual extraction and its expulsion or by other means.

Filling without a plug, however, is when that thing is placed, for example, into its orifice and bound from above without penetrating its veins; and that it should restrain them with things such as little pads and a sponge, and with strong bands of tightening that constrict it with a diversion of the tightening that is attractive. The first tightening must be near the orifice, then let it be wrapped going backward, and loosen the tightening gradually. And know that the tightening of pads and bands, when it is weak, results in the harm of tightening and is an attraction, and no help of tightening or restraint comes from it. And in a full [body], one must be subtle in this chapter. When therefore a good tightening is bound, and it is bound again from the opposite side, the matter is diverted and this tightening resists attraction. And one must not proceed with tightening through prohibition unless it causes pain, unless that was necessary in the first instances, then soften it gradually. And many times indeed one must use a stitching of the flesh and gather its lips and cover it with bands; for many times the collection of the lips and the placement of pads suffices to preserve them by gathering their veins. Furthermore, press upon the medicines...

It is that which is a corruption of the spirit of the limb and the humidity so that it cannot be an instrument [of the soul], and to this happens an alienation of the innate heat and a victory of [external] humidity; therefore putrefaction does not travel by itself. **Corrosive** is that which, by ulcerating, consumes the substance of the flesh; and therefore the fleshy part has sensation, but the putrefied part does not; and therefore corrosive matter travels. Now if it be "wandering": because putrid and corrosive matter travels; yet not everything that travels is corroding, because putrefactive matter is wandering and yet not corrosive; but it could be said that putrefaction is a certain corrosion; or if it be corrosion or putrefaction. **And ulcers indeed** are divided into species of divisions, and it is said that some ulcers are painful and some are deprived of pain; and some are accompanied by **abscesses** <note>swelling or tumors</note> and some are deprived of abscesses; and some are clean and some are unclean; and the unclean indeed are those in which there is an excess of humor and copious humidity, even if they are not "evil" [malignant]; and of these some are foul, and some are diminished, and some of the ulcers are putrid. 

And among the things more harmful to them are midday and sharp humidity with heat. And **Galen** <note>the influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> indeed named such corrosive ulcers "Persic fire" <note>often identified as shingles or erysipelas</note> and "wandering ant" <note>original: "formica ambulatoria"; a type of spreading skin lesion</note>, and after that the putrefied ulcer is a composite of the ulcer and the putrefied sickness, and for each of these there is a disposition. And indeed hard ulcers beginning to turn toward greenness are bad, and cold ulcers are soft, white, and "begging" for heating medicines, and hot ones declining toward redness delight in cold. 

And when a bad body color is associated with bad ulcers, such as lead-white or citron-yellow, then that is a sign of the corruption of the "complexion" <note>the balance of humors</note> of the liver and corruption of the blood that comes to the ulcer, which is why consolidation becomes difficult. 

And indeed those ulcers whose roots are sharp and with which there is itching, the superfluities are sharp; and those whose roots are wide and white with little itching, their complexions are cold. And ulcers generated by a succession of sicknesses are bad, because nature expels to them the residue of the corruption of superfluities. And ulcers that take away the hair from the area following them are bad. 

And the **best signs** signifying the health of ulcers and wounds are when their succeeding declivities turn toward **discharge** <note>original: "sanies"</note>. And it is said among the signs of rapid death when there are good abscesses and light ulcers, but the patient's reason is destroyed, they die. And indeed the causes of malignant ulcers are sometimes wounds meeting with malignant superfluities of the body or a corrupt regimen, and sometimes they follow bad **pustules**, which is why they become prone to ulceration after the pustules. 

And the putrefaction and its wandering and the corruption of what is in its circuit and the difficulty of healing in itself (even with the rectification of the treatment exhibited to it) signify the malignancy of the ulcer. And the best signs signifying the health of ulcers and wounds are when in their succession there is discharge, which is brought about by medicine that makes pus and by the operation of nature. For that operation of nature is according to the natural course, and discharge is not generated except by natural digestion. And it is not associated with the evil from the accidents of bad ulcers, and specifically "praiseworthy discharge" <note>the ideal sign of healing</note> which is white, smooth, even, and which has followed the completion of digestion. Neither is foulness associated with it, since there is no putrefaction in it; and perhaps it is not freed from a small foulness, the discharge which happens with the help of innate heat and another external heat. And we indeed have already spoken of discharge in other places. 

But the ulcers that happen and cause **spasms**, and putrefied scrofulous ulcers, and "algeronati" <note>likely a transliterated Arabic medical term for a specific type of ulcer</note>, and corrosive and cancerous ulcers, and those that run in their course, are those in which discharge is not generated; rather, when discharge appears in an ulcer, it is a good sign with which a spasm is not feared, nor a confusion of reason <note>delirium</note> and things similar to these, unless they be in a place that makes it necessary, such as the posterior and anterior members, unless the matter has passed the limit. Now if the swelling is hidden suddenly and returns, it will not be resolved through pus or similar things. 

Furthermore, those [ulcers] near **nervous members** <note>areas rich in tendons and nerves</note>, such as dorsal ulcers, because they are in the vicinity of the back and the nucha <note>the spinal cord or nape of the neck</note>, and ulcers that fall in the anterior part of the hip and knee, because these again are like nervous muscles in which the matter turns to spasm and confusion of reason. And if it happens in nervous members, in the most part of those in the ascending extension of the body, it is feared; or the course of blood if it falls immediately in the lower extension; and similarly, sometimes confusion of reason is feared from them, and it is feared that it falls [heavily] and discharge follows after it, or that the spitting of blood occurs if it falls immediately above it; and you already know the intention of discharge in the chest from Book III. And sometimes confusion of reason is feared in them again. 

And among the good signs in ulcers is that in their circuit the hairs that fell out grow back. And bodies more susceptible to the cure of ulcers are those of a better complexion and less superfluous humidity, along with the presence of good blood in them. Those indeed that have much humidity or dryness are slow to receive the rectification of ulcers; although moist ones, like those of children, are more susceptible, and dry ones like those of the elderly; and specifically when the complexion is radically dry and deprived of clean blood, and happens to be moist and soft as in the elderly again. And because of that, again, the cure of ulcers becomes difficult in those with **dropsy** <note>edema or swelling</note>; in pregnant women again because of the retention of their superfluities because their menses are retained. 

But yet in the elderly, their ulcers are not healed because of that and because of the scarcity of their good blood. And sometimes ulcers are healed and then they "break open" <note>original: "rescinduntur"</note> because flesh was not generated in them except before "cleansing" <note>original: "mundificationem"</note>; because therefore an unclean superfluity is retained in them, it must follow from there that the continuity reached is corrupted. And sometimes a fistula is "crusted over" because there happens to them a disposition of drying and retention that prevents "breathing" <note>drainage</note>, so that they seem healed because their disposition is similar to what we said; then they break open again because of any movement and commotion and cough and offense and bad lying [position] and others. 

And regarding ulcers in which flesh grows: some are those in which "added flesh" <note>excessive granulation tissue or "proud flesh"</note> grows, and some in which that does not grow. And those in which added flesh is generated are those in which there is a hastening of the growth of flesh before cleansing. And those in which that does not grow are those in which flesh does not grow except after cleansing. 

When therefore the space of the ulcer is prolonged and it is corroded and putrefies and much of its substance is destroyed, then its consolidation is not expected except from the depths. And therefore when an ulcer is old, remaining for the space of a year, and specifically when it is disrupted and disruption—namely, a fistula—begins from it; and being old, it is necessary that it draw out bone from the bones, because they are its foundation. And indeed malignant ulcers are not healed unless all their corruption is removed from them, down to the healthy flesh and bone. 

And the causes which, when they occur, corrupt ulcers are the weakness of the power of the limb, so that it receives all matter, and the malice of the complexion of the limb, and the malice of that which comes to it from the blood, either in quality or in quantity. In quality indeed... </margin>
e. **And sometimes they are healed.** Here he sets the causes of certain accidents, and it has four [parts] just as he sets four causes. There the second: "And regarding ulcers." There the third: "When therefore." The fourth there: "And the causes which." The first in two, just as he sets the causes. There the second: "And sometimes." It is doubted in what the second cause differs from the first. It must be said that the first is absolutely in ulcers; the second in fistulas; and the first is by the remaining of bad matter; but the second is made from drying and preventing the exit of matter while the quality remains, even though the matter from which weak, loose flesh is generated did not remain, which is broken in any way.

# Book 4, Treatise 3
### t ii

<margin>
This section first presents the various methods, then sets the treatment for accidents. The second part: "The treatment after those things, etc." In the first part, he sets the general cause of treatment. In the second, he specifies it: "It is necessary..." Then he sets the general rules of treatment. Then he sets the rules for those already mentioned: "And it is necessary that you know." Then he sets general rules for the causes that coincide. Namely, those that tend toward the causes to be avoided: "And concerning those things that are right in treatment." Then he sets the rules of treatment by reason of those things that are composed with the ulcer, which are dispositions indicating other things. Namely, according to the diversity of the limbs: "and when there is nothing there except..." Then he sets the treatment as it pertains to one diversity. Namely, as it pertains to others: "and the more..." Concerning the first part, he proceeds in two ways. First, that the indication is taken from the ulcer according to what the ulcer is: the purification by reason of the fact that in a wound and an ulcer, superfluities are gathered, without the removal of which healing does not occur. But it is said that the intention of drying is not the direct goal, because the direct goal is unification <note>the closing of the wound</note>; but it is that without which healing cannot be immediately perfected. Namely, because there is no "bad habit" <note>original: "mala abuvia," likely meaning a systemic condition</note> but rather the presence of moisture. It is doubted why he did not say "cleansing" since there is a solution there: by God's gift, drying communicates both subtle and gross humidity; therefore, he proposed this as the common treatment intention for wounds and ulcers, and both communicate in drying. Because in a simple wound there is no need to cleanse, but because there is a loss of flesh...
</margin>

...and an inclination toward alteration, freckling, and spots, because of which there is a malice of all the humors in the body. And of this kind, beyond the fact that nothing is acquired from it to be converted into flesh, it is harmed by that which is converted to it from the superfluities <note>waste products or excess fluids</note>. In quantity, truly, because it adds or diminishes, for which reason the substance with which the flesh of the ulcer is generated is not found. And there is the "clear world" ulcer <note>a clean, red wound bed</note> hurrying toward a scab. And it is not known if it is a clean body with little blood, or if it is because of the "bony-ness" <note>original: "ostrafositatē," referring to the hardness or exposure of bone</note> that happens to its wall or its margins; or because of the dilation of the veins that come to it; or because of the corruption that follows it from the bone; or because of its corruption beginning toward darkness, greenness, and blackness; or because of a limb of bad composition that is near it. And indeed, ulcers of wicked treatment, such as the round ones and those similar to them, are those that kill infants who cannot tolerate the vehemence of the pains and the ulcers, and the difficulty of their treatment, and their own wickedness.

### The Rule for the Treatment of Ulcers. Chapter 2.

<image-desc>Decorative initial S containing leafy and floral motifs.</image-desc>
**K**now that all ulcers require **drying** <note>original: "exiccatiōe," desiccation</note>, except those made from the wearing away of the muscles and their contusion <note>bruising</note>. For these first require that they be softened and moistened. And along with this, although ulcers in their dominant disposition require drying, they sometimes require five other dispositions: purification, cleansing, and other things following the ulcers themselves. And the more the ulcer is larger and deeper, the more it requires stronger drying, and that its lips be gathered by more vehement searching, and perhaps it will be necessary for you to sew them. And consider from the necessary dispositions for searching in that and similar cases what we said in the chapter on wounds. And know that ulcers perhaps require in their treatments the administration of certain medicines that are running and penetrating, and which are injected deeply, and then it is necessary that they be ointments and similar things. For which reason it is then necessary that what appears moist should be hidden and dry; and in those things that lead to a **fistula** <note>a narrow passage or tunnel under the skin</note>, it is necessary that the dryness of its orifices be vehemently overcoming the humidity of its substance. And it is indeed sometimes necessary that their medicines be mixed with that which runs so that they become viscous and adhering; know this again in these cases. And know that ulcers require bandages and tightening for three reasons, one of which is so that the filth <note>drainage/pus</note> may run out, for which reason the strength of its tightening should be from the end of the tightening toward the softening of the tightening itself at its orifice, so that a good expression <note>squeezing out of fluids</note> of it may be made. And the second is so that the flesh-making medicine may be preserved upon the ulcer, and it does not require vehement tightening. And the third is for the incarnation <note>regrowth of flesh</note> of the labors <note>the wound site</note>, and it is necessary that the tightening in it not be soft at the two lips, but rather folded with a vehement complication; and it is not necessary that with the bandage one arrives at an injury so that it swells. And it is necessary that it be helpful in preventing swelling <note>original: "ap̄a," for apostema</note>, since it is not possible for an ulcer to be cured while there is swelling. And if it is not possible for you to prevent it and swelling appears, be occupied with the swelling and the treatment of whatever swelling it may be, with the observation of the ulcer itself, until you have finished the treatment of the swelling, and then only the observation of the ulcer will remain. And similarly, when that which is in the circuit of the ulcer is corrupted and turns green and black, treat it by scarifying and the extraction of blood, and let it be done with cupping; then apply a dry sponge to it, and afterwards drying medicines. And when the ulcer is separated or you find a pure ulcer, then you must first observe whether anything from the body is poured out into the ulcer or not, or rather if it is already localized. For if nothing is poured out to it, let your intention be in medicating it; and if something is poured out...

<column-break/>

<margin>
Flesh generation cannot happen because first the "sanies" <note>thin, bloody pus</note> is generated; so it must be cleansed. And if the gloss says in the 3rd [part] that in every wound a double superfluity is generated, gross and subtle. generated, i.e., apt to be generated. Namely, certain things which: diverse but matching ulcers: which is on the part of the ulcers or wounds in themselves. Namely, he sets down how it ought to be proceeded in the cure when with the ulcer another disposition is composed which indicates another thing; these other things sometimes indicate the contrary, such as a "wearing away" <note>attrition</note> which, by reason of the worn flesh and constricted blood and pain, indicates softness, which is contrary to the ulcer; and concerning this we ought to begin: not entirely dismissing the ulcer; whence it ought to be a remollient, moderately. Sometimes they indicate a different but not contrary thing, thus they require cleansing: and sometimes to be heated or cooled: and this which he says "with this": that ulcers require drying for their dominant dispositions. i.e., along with this that ulcers currently require dryness: nevertheless they require purification: and the cleansing of ulcers. Namely, that in the dominant, etc. it can be referred to contusions which also for a long time require drying: but not unless the contusion has ceased. It is doubted how cleansing is a different intention from the ulcer, since it is an ulcer. Rather, it is in the intentions of the same. Because it is different from a common wound, which is drying: or it speaks of the cleansing of gross corrupted humidities gathered beyond the common manner of ulcers.
</margin>
...to it, be diligent in that which is poured out to it, [treating it] by phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> or loosening of the belly <note>laxatives</note> or vomiting; since vomiting sometimes helps also in this and in the upper parts. He testifies concerning it, and if in the ulcers there should be fragments of bone and membranes <note>original: "panniculi"</note> or other things, do not hurry in extracting them, but do that which we said in the chapter on bones. And indeed the first thing you ought to prepare regarding the being of the ulcer is the opening with its medicines, then purification with its medicines, then the birth of flesh, and consolidation <note>final healing/closing</note>. And if you find the ulcer to be clean and light, having no depth, then let the consolidation be done with that which has no "bite" <note>stinging quality</note>. In foul ulcers, however, a biting cleanser is necessary. And at first when they are treated, they require a stinging medicine because the sense does not feel it; then by degrees one arrives at that which is of a lighter sting until the time of the birth of the flesh is felt. And beware that you do not cause pain with those things, because you are able to, and specifically because there is heat and inflammation there. And it is necessary that you remove the causes preventing consolidation, and they are the causes we numbered and spoke of which decline with the ulcer toward malice. For if you treat those first, you will not be free for the treatment of ulcers as is necessary; rather it will not be possible for you. And many times indeed the composition of the limb is rectified, which suffices in the rectification of the ulcer. And many times on the same, soft flesh arises which is bad flesh <note>proud flesh</note>, which is in itself prone to redness and heat; therefore let it be treated with cooling **epithemata** <note>topical applications or plasters</note> applied to the flesh surrounding it, such as the juice of Nightshade with Armenian bole and vinegar, and cooling plasters of Sandalwood and Camphor cooled with snow, by which the wound does not cease to be consolidated and constricted. And it is necessary that in painful ulcers, which are of vehement pain, you be occupied first in soothing the pain, and that with the softeners that you know. Without doubt, even though they are contrary to the ulcer, nevertheless, since the pain is not soothed, it is not prepared for us to cure; therefore, when we have soothed it, we shall follow up. And indeed, foul ulcers require that they be cleaned, and those are they whose humidity that runs from them is like dregs. And perhaps they are cleansed with honey, and perhaps they are cleansed with powders and ointments; and when they are not cleansed, it is not possible for a pure medicine to reach their body, and specifically powders; for which reason they must be cleansed, then the flesh may be born; and in cleansing, there is more "wiping" as you knew before. And perhaps bad flesh arises, for which reason it is necessary that it be corroded with a sharp medicine and smeared from the outside with cooling things, then eradicated with that by which a scab is eradicated; then let it be cured. And a medicine that for some bodies makes flesh grow, for some of them is corrosive by reason of vehement cleansing when those bodies are very light; or for some of them it is neither cleansing nor making flesh grow; and for that reason the medicine needs to be strengthened, either by breaking its mixture or by diminishing its oiliness, or by adding another medicine to it in which there is commonality and cleansing; and in another body it is, by comparison to it, corrosive, needing to be diminished in its weight or increased in its oiliness, or some styptics joined to it. Those ulcers more worthy that their medicine be strengthened are those whose consolidation is difficult. And concerning those things that are necessary, it is required that the medicine be left upon the ulcer for three days, then dissolved; for if it has not worked then, it will not perform its operation. And it is necessary that you stay far from oil, which is avoided in ulcers; but if it should be necessary, then use oil of **Kerua** <note>original: "kerua," Castor oil</note> and myrtle oil and mastic oil. And when there is nothing there but the ulcer, then it is necessary that you alternate [treatments] insensibly for limbs not tolerating it, and let pain be avoided.

# Book III

<margin>
Necessary. Previously, he established the rationale for curing ulcers according to a certain disposition joined to them that makes consolidation difficult; here he sets down special causes for each of these dispositions. This section has as many parts as the chapters he presents. First, he sets the cause for curing an ulcer that has much subtle moisture, namely "virulence" <note>the discharge of pus or foul matter</note>; for which reason it does not have a cause. Second, he sets the medicines, there in the second part: "And you should know." Third, in which he first sets the cause of the cure, then the cause of recognizing the melancholy <note>referring to the "black bile" humor</note> that is applied there in the second part: "And when you."
</margin>

By reason of this, use a strong medicine. In a patient who has little sensation, do not abstain from necessary medication. Internal and "sublime" <note>highly significant or vital</note> parts are precious and of great benefit, but they receive damage quickly; these belong to the category of sensitive parts and their judgment. Their opposites belong to the category of insensible parts, or those whose sensation is weak. For this reason, it is not sufficient to use only internal remedies like the flower of copper <note>original: "flos eris," likely verdigris or copper acetate</note> and similar things. For those things that are drunk and require things that produce "gluting" <note>adhesion or closing of the wound</note>, use more tragacanth and gum. Those for whom an enema is used require something that is between two things.

Concerning what is correct in the treatment of ulcers, their limbs should be kept still and not moved; if they are moved at the beginning with small movement, it is less harmful than if they are moved after the beginning with laborious movement, especially in a body of "bad humors." One must use medication in ulcers that fall near each other so that "incarnation" <note>the growth of new flesh</note> occurs between two neighboring parts, such as the adhesions that happen between the eyelid and the eye, or between two eyelids, or between two fingers.

Tears and cuts are prone to turning quickly into fistulas <note>deep, pipe-like sores</note>. Ulcers that are near large arteries and veins bring to the soul <note>the vital spirit or life force</note> that which is near them in soft flesh, such as the testicles, the armpits, and the area behind the ear; thus it produces "scabies" <note>here meaning a rough, itchy skin condition</note> and the like. This occurs in those which break open due to a certain cause when the body is full of bad superfluity; then indeed there is vehement pain and it reaches the ulcer. Therefore, one must cure this by cleansing the body and with what is said in the chapter. While the soul <note>the patient's vital force</note> is being cleansed, do not hope for a cure yet. It is necessary in such cases to protect the ulcer from harm with basilicon <note>a "kingly" ointment made of pitch, resin, and wax</note> and similar things if the body has been cleansed; place it between the medicine and the limb to distinguish and prevent harm from reaching the ulcer in any disposition.

You must hear the common discourse: among those things that are necessary, that with which an ulcer is cured should be either suitable or unsuitable. Even if a suitable medicine does not help the disposition, it is still used if it carries no harm. The variation of an unsuitable medicine is either because it is too weak—indicated by it doing the opposite of the expected drying or cleansing—or there is variation for other reasons, such as it heating more than is necessary, causing redness and inflammation. In that case, its strength must be diminished and its inflammation extinguished with a cooling plaster. Or, if it tends toward blackness and darkness, it is known that it cools or does not heat in the measure required. Therefore, one must add to its heating power. Or, it softens the tissue, in which case one must add to the power of styptics <note>substances that shrink tissue</note> and desiccatives <note>drying agents</note> such as balaustines <note>wild pomegranate flowers</note>, galls, and similar things that dry, to assist with their drying power. Or, if it corrodes and "sweats" like bone, one must break the strength of its "abstergence" <note>cleansing power</note>. Often a medicine does not suit because the patient's temperament is superfluous <note>unbalanced</note> in that respect where the medicine should be stronger, or it is weak in the category suitable for it.

## The Treatment of Virulent Ulcers. Chapter III.

It is necessary to administer drying medicines to them so that the "virus" <note>pus or poisonous discharge</note> is cleansed, and then focus on the growth of flesh. If the tissues are soft, then administer medicines to them to make them grow, and for the sweating of their margins due to the weakness of the body of those ulcers; but they must be dried first, and then administered. And when you have administered a medicine and do not find it doing good, or see the condition increasing, then know that the medicine

<column-break/>

is not drying the body; therefore add to its drying power and help it with a little cleansing, such as with honey, for example, and styptic medicines such as balaustines and alum, and less of the strength of oil, or use an oil in which there is drying power. But if you see the ulcer is now becoming too dry, then diminish all the powers: drying, cleansing, and stypticity. Observe this precept in medicines that make the flesh of ulcers grow.

Do not let one thing deceive you: it may be that a medicine is more cleansing than it should be, whereby it corrodes the limb and dissolves its fleshiness into a running moisture which you might mistake for "virus" <note>pus</note>, causing you to add to the cleansing power. Such a medicine makes the ulcer deep and hot, and more like an "aposteme" <note>an abscess or swelling</note>, and the patient feels manifest stinging.

Know that among the medicines that dry ulcers, some are vehemently cooling, such as white henbane, opium, and mandrake root. Some are vehemently heating, such as resin and pitch; therefore, you should temper one with the other according to the opinion of someone's particular temperament. The medicines that cleanse "virus" are these drying medicines: alum, galls, pomegranate peels, frankincense bark, litharge <note>lead oxide; original: "merdasengi"</note>, barley flour and its "savich" <note>original: "sauich," a parched barley meal</note>, red poppy flowers, and the leaves of the "gnat tree" <note>possibly the elm or a tree associated with insects</note>. When a plaster is made with fresh walnut leaves, or a plaster with walnuts—as when they are decocted with wine—it helps greatly and dries moistures without harm.

**A good plaster:** Take litharge and soak it once in vinegar and another time in oil until it turns white; then take antimony, burnt copper <note>original: "calcucecaumenon"</note>, "renarum" <note>unclear; possibly a mineral or plant resin</note>, galls, balaustines, dragon's blood <note>a red plant resin</note>, alum, and silver "climia" <note>metallic dross or oxide</note>. Take equal parts of all, grind them well, and let each be a sixth part of the prepared litharge. Mix them all and administer the medicines we shall name in the *Antidotary* for deep ulcers; among these is sea water. Alum water washes, repels, and dries. All these aforementioned medicines are harmful if there is an abscess with the ulcer. The water in which they are decocted is good for drying. And the decoction of myrobalans (citrine, belleric, and emblic), and the decoction of ceterach <note>a type of fern</note>, and the leaves of "asedre" <note>likely the jujube or neem tree</note> are good for this.

Second, because in these it is necessary to generate flesh, he sets the cause and the medicines in the book, there in the second part: "namely that not..." The first part is in three: first he does this; second, because worms sometimes grow in these, he sets the treatment there in the second part: "concerning things..." First he does this in general, second in special, there in the second part: "And it is necessary that the site..."

## The Treatment of Foul Ulcers. Chapter IV.

One must administer cleansing medicines to them, starting first with those of strong stinging power according to what we said in the *Canon*; then gradually reach those like thapsia and birthwort with honey and a little vinegar. Again, white "glue" <note>likely egg white</note> with an equal measure of rose oil or butter, and again lily root with honey. Again, "herbilet" flour and the herb opopanax. Among compound remedies are the "Indian plaster" and all green ointments with flower of copper, and simple ones like frankincense with ammoniac and similar things, and bark plasters, and plasters made with "herbi" flour, and the salt plaster. Also the black troche <note>medicated lozenge</note> and the green troche. Among drying medicines, take the dregs of oil and honey and alum in equal parts. Take ceruse <note>white lead</note> and "polium" <note>a medicinal herb</note> in equal parts. When the strength must be vehement, take "prasium" <note>horehound</note> with honey. Among the good plasters are salted olives. If a necessity arises here to again administer something liquid for washing, as we will say in the chapter on deep ulcers; all these things harm them if there is an abscess.

Second by the melancholies, there in the second part: "And that it is not possible for you." And here he first sets these drying medicines. Second, he shows the mode of their application. ## The Cure of Deep Ulcers, Caverns, and Hidden Sores. Chapter V.

In their treatment, these require that they be filled with flesh. This indeed does not happen except with an abundance of food and blood. In this case, medicines of vehement drying and cleansing are necessary together. The site of these must be such that the "virus" <note>pus</note> is not retained in them but rather flows out. If you find this site convenient—meaning the "root" of the ulcer is at the upper part and its opening at the lower part—then this is it. But if it is otherwise, and it is possible to alter the site of the depth through natural preparation or alteration, let it be done. If it is not possible, there is no excuse but to cut the ulcer down to its root with a most exquisite incision that leaves no cavern; or let it be made so that a course or passage happens at its root, other than its opening, such that it may receive healing. Observe the disposition of the limb in this, and whether fear arises from it. When this has been done, the ulcer should be tightened with a ligature <note>bandage</note>, starting from its opening and reaching the root where the detection was made. In the beginning, do the opposite, and place the binding in the upper part in both ways similarly. The ligature must not reach the point of pain. ### Treatise III

### The Growth of Flesh in Ulcers. Chapter VII.

Flesh should not be allowed to grow until the wound is cleansed, or until nourishment is drawn to it if it is diminished and nourishment does not reach it. Therefore, when it has been cleansed, then remove everything that is biting and abrasive with strength, whatever kind of ulcers they are and wherever they may be. And it is necessary that in the administration of medicines that make flesh grow, the aforementioned precepts should be observed regarding whether there is an excess of moisture or an excess of dryness. Therefore, do as we said in the chapter on virulent ulcers <note>ulcers discharging pus</note>; not so far as the ulcers remain moist or are dried with intense dehydration, but rather according to the flesh being created, which is of intense moisture or little dryness. Among those things that decrease its drying is the addition of wax and oil to it, if it is a plaster. And among those things that increase its drying is that it be thickened and made dense, and its oiliness and the quantity of medicines be decreased, or that things like honey be added to them. Indeed, the creation of flesh in them is more suitable and slower with plasters, and more difficult and faster with powders. And when the flesh is hardened: it is then proper for the rectification of the wound that powders be sprinkled, and it should be surrounded with plasters and a wine that is somewhat styptic <note>original: "stiptico," an astringent that constricts tissue</note>. This is a good medication for all ulcers as it heals and dries. We have already mentioned the medicines that create flesh in the chapter on wounds. And perhaps we shall remember some of the chosen ones here which are more worthy of this place: burnt antimony, and sarcocolla <note>a tree resin used to "glue" wounds</note>, and fish glue, and burnt vitriols <note>original: "itarie," likely vitriolic minerals</note>, and dross of lead, and burnt lead, and sweet flag <note>original: "acorus"</note>, and beremasis <note>unclear: "beremasis," likely a botanical term from the Arabic source</note>, and dragon's blood <note>a bright red resin</note>, and cypress; and especially for foul wounds, polium <note>a medicinal herb</note> is strong, and centaury, and rhythm <note>unclear: "ritima"</note>, and burnt nitre is wonderful in drying them and in their consolidation.

### The Treatment of Corroding Ulcers. Chapter VIII.

The rule to use in the treatment of corrosive and "fraudulent" <note>deceptive or slow-healing</note> ulcers is that the body and the limb should be cleansed. If the body was already clean, use cupping and the application of leeches upon the site, and the change of its temperament with compresses <note>original: "epitubimatib'" / "epithimatibus"</note> and the rectification of food without slowness or delay. For delay in this matter is among the things that increase their malice. And sometimes it becomes necessary to remove the corrosion by cutting the limb. It is helpful for corrosive ulcers where there is no rot to use an embrocation <note>a liquid medicine rubbed on the body</note> with cold water, myrtle water, rose water, shepherd's purse water, and styptic wine if there is no heat; or vinegar mixed with rose water, and plenty of pure water if there is heat, and similar cooling and drying waters. And if there is rot there, then use sea water and the rest of those things we shall mention in the chapter on putrid wounds. Furthermore, the best treatment for them is the administration of styptic, drying, and cooling things, such as pomegranate rinds, lentils, mastic leaves, rose seeds, Egyptian thorn <note>acacia</note>, and myrtle berries, and embrocations of these medicines. And let such things be strengthened with alum and similar things, or by plastering with sorrel leaves and its branches boiled with wine. And plastering with Armenian bole <note>a medicinal red clay</note> prepared either with vinegar syrup, or burnt dry gourd, or plantain with barley meal <note>original: "fauich"</note>, or 

<column-break/>

olive leaves.

### The Treatment of Putrid and Evil Ulcers. Chapter IX.

The best treatment for these evil ulcers is the cleansing of the body or the limb itself, if the body was clean, with that which cleanses it alone through cupping, leeches, and compresses that rectify the temperament according to what we have said many times, and with similar things and food. And there should be no delay in their treatment, for their rot increases their malice. And they must be prohibited from hot water. Among those things that soothe them is the seed of white henbane with barley meal. And again, when such ulcers exceed in corruption, it becomes necessary that they be plucked out with a cautery of fire, or with a sharp medicine, or with an incision, so that nothing remains except healthy flesh, known by the goodness of its blood or its color, or healthy white clean bone. A sharp medicine takes all the broken tissue <note>original: "ofractaitē"</note> and extracts it, and helps its completion with butter being placed over it one time after another. For these, even if they are not fistulas or broken parts, are evil and deceptive. And perhaps it becomes necessary to cut the limb to save it from its rot. And the embrocations that are suitable for them are like sea water and the waters mentioned in the chapter on fistulas. And when medicines are administered over these and other ulcers, they should be left for several days and not undone. And the medicines which should be administered in these are such as barley flour and vetch flour with a little alum, or dry salted fish flesh with a little marrow, and birthwort <note>original: "aristologia"</note>, and cabbage root, and beet root, and wild cucumber root, and flaxseed crushed with copperas <note>original: "calcadis," iron or copper sulfate</note>, and "basce" <note>unclear</note> with raisins or figs with honey, or a plaster with mouse-ear <note>an herb</note> boiled with honey, or cabbage, or burnt dry gourd, and fresh olive leaves. **A compound medicine:** Take birthwort, and the juice of the leaves of the castor oil plant <note>original: "alkerua"</note>, one part of each; flower of copper <note>verdigris</note>, half a part; let a liniment be made from it with water to the thickness of honey. And perhaps it is necessary to strengthen it with the juice of wild cucumber and "assure" <note>unclear mineral or herb</note>, and let dry cloths be placed over it. And again: take birthwort, galls, and oil in equal parts; let a liniment be made for the ulcer and its surrounding area. Or lime and colcothar <note>iron oxide</note> in equal parts, arsenic half a part. And again: "alsurie" <note>unclear</note> twelve parts, colcothar, and tragacanth four parts; let a liniment be made from them, let them be boiled in half a pint of strong vinegar until the vinegar is consumed; then let it be taken once cooled and the ulcer smeared with them. And again: take colcothar and tragacanth, of each an equal amount; iron scales sixteen parts, perforated galls [some amount]. Or take salt, one part; burnt alum, one part; burnt copper bark or burnt southernwood, half a part. A good plaster: sarcocolla, burnt lime, galls, flower of copper, and birthwort gathered with a little glue, so that it may be a medicine and a binding, and let it be administered after the cleansing of the ulcer. A final medicine, proven: red tragacanth eighteen parts, quicklime sixteen parts, alum sixteen parts, pomegranate rinds sixteen parts, frankincense and galls, thirty-two parts of each; wax one hundred and twenty parts, one pint of old oil. Another good one: burnt lead with sulfur, burnt copper, ceruse <note>lead white</note>, lead, frankincense, litharge <note>original: "merdasegi"</note>, cadmium <note>original: "climie"</note>, ammoniacum, opopanax, mastic, two drams of each; fat from cow kidneys, resin, glue, [unclear], myrtle oil, wax, three drams of each; let those that are to be dissolved be dissolved in a quantity of water, and let those that are to be ground be ground, and let it be prepared. A helpful medicine which Galen and others gathered: Take dross of copper, one dram; rubbed flower of copper, one dram; wax, half a pound; a little litharge, one dram and a half; let a plaster be made from them according to its description; let those that are to be dissolved be dissolved, and those that are to be ground be ground, and let wax be added or subtracted according to the quantity of necessity, and they like it to be mixed with it. # Book

...if there should be ulcers of difficult healing, there shall be applied to them burnt papers, the "Andronicus" medicament <note>original: "medicamē ādrōniū," a specific multi-ingredient recipe named after a Greek physician</note>, dried burnt gourd, or dirty burnt wool, or a plaster made of cypress leaves or the leaves of fully grown holm-oaks.

<margin>Law 100</margin>
### Treatment of those wounds that are difficult to close and others that are at the height of malice.

Strictly speaking, ulcers that are difficult to close are those that are not corrosive or putrid, as is common, but have their own particular nature. For both of those types are "ambulatory" <note>spreading across the surface of the body</note> and sometimes they do not resolve but remain in their state for some time. These are distinct from fistulas <note>deep, tube-like sores that often reach the bone</note>, because those must be cut into. Ultimately, corrosive, putrid ulcers and fistulas are among the most difficult to consolidate <note>to heal or close</note> without a total transformation. Indeed, they are the most alienated in their corruption and in their distance from healing.

The rule in treating these ulcers is that if the cause is a "bad complexion" <note>an imbalance of the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, it must be rectified. If the cause is "bad blood," a diet should be established that generates good blood to counter it; if there is too little blood, it must be increased, or if there is too much, it must be thinned with good food. If the cause is softness or "sordidness" <note>the presence of pus or filth</note>, then treat it with a cleansing regimen. If the cause is excessive dryness and there are no fistulas yet, then treat it with balanced moistening. One good method is to make the limb sweat with hot water until the limb is softened and turns red; then stop, and do not over-cleanse that amount, for you might attract too much "matter" <note>excess fluids or humors</note> and cause great harm to the limb. Afterward, apply a medicament that is less drying; perhaps it is helpful to apply cloths soaked in warm water. 

Sometimes it is necessary to rub the ulcer and the surrounding limb and to administer "attractive" <note>drawing</note> plasters made of pitch. If the cause is a "bad disposition" in the flesh surrounding the wound, treat it as you have learned by "capping" <note>likely scarification or cupping</note>, drawing blood, and aiding it with drying agents. If the cause is a spreading vice, cut into it and let the blood flow, or remove it entirely, for this often brings rest to the area. If there is "repletion" <note>an excess of humors</note>, begin with phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> and the evacuation of the humors. Then, encounter the wound with heat and let as much blood run as possible, so that your intervention does not cause a swelling that is worse than the original ulcer; then treat the wound caused by the burning, and finally the difficult ulcer. 

If the cause is weakness of the limb due to a bad complexion—not just any kind, but an excessive imbalance of heat and cold, or the resulting rarity <note>thinness</note> or extreme thickness of the tissues—one must first address the heat and moisture, then the cold and dryness, using their opposites. Often it happens that the cause is heat attracting and sending matter to the site, in which case cooling, "styptic" <note>contracting</note> treatments are necessary. If the cause is a fistula, treat it as a fistula. If the cause is bone corruption, we must cut in and expose the bone. If it is possible to remove the surface corruption by rubbing, we shall do so with great care; if not, we shall cut it as explained in the chapter on bone corruption.

Galen says: There was a youth who had a fistula in his chest that had already reached the bone in the middle of his torso. We stripped away from the chest bone everything containing the sore and found that corruption had already set in. It was necessary for us to cut the bone, and the corrupted place was directly over the "suspensory of the heart" <note>the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart</note>. After we saw this, we stood in great concern during the removal of the corrupted bone; our goal was to leave the inner membrane covering the heart intact and to keep it healthy. That part of the membrane which was attached to the putrefied chest bone was also affected. He says again: We looked upon the heart with a clear view, just as we see it when we perform a dissection by choice. He says: That youth was healed, and flesh grew in that limb where we had cut the chest until it was filled and joined together, standing between the heart-veil and the outer layer as it was before. He says: This is no greater than wounds where the chest "breathes" <note>referring to a sucking chest wound or open thorax</note>. And he said this: when veins putrefy and grow old, it is proper for blood to run from them in a permitted quantity.

Medicines prepared for difficult consolidation and dominant conditions include copper dross, burnt copper flowers (both burnt and unburnt), iron dross, and "gold glue" <note>original: "conglutinano auri," likely chrysocolla used as a solder or flux</note>. These should be made into wax salves with *colcotar* <note>original: "colcotar," iron oxide or vitriol</note>, tragacanth, and similar things, along with substances that prevent the attraction of fluids to the limb, such as alum and galls <note>oak apples</note>. 

Among the remedies for difficult consolidation is the following: 8 parts each of *climia* <note>zinc oxide or metallic dross</note>, gold-solder, and other items; 1 part each of copper flowers and copper bark; 4 parts cypress gum; and as much wax and oil as needed. Alternatively, take 7 parts each of wax and pine gum; 3 parts *climia*; 6 parts *colcotar*; and enough myrtle oil. Again, boil *colcotar* and *climia* in seawater, or "wild water" <note>possibly verjuice or acidic juice</note>, or water in which

<column-break/>

alkali <note>original: "alkali," potash or soda ash</note> has been boiled. Let it boil a little, mixing it in the sun in summer, then strain it; afterward, let sea salt or alkali-water be added on top. Again, take 2 parts each of burnt copper, resin, and rock salt; and enough wax and myrtle oil. 

Fistula medicines also help, which are dried and ground; these include bitter vetch <note>original: "berbi"</note>, iris, burnt aristolochia <note>birthwort</note>, burnt copper, and frankincense-earth, according to the variety required by the body part. A good medicament: take copper filings and iron filings, mix them with water, coat them with red clay, and burn them in a furnace. Then take them out, grind them, and administer them as a powder, or make a plaster from them and *merdasengi* <note>original: "merdaſegi," a corruption of litharge/lead oxide</note>.

### Method for a good Golden Plaster.

Take good golden litharge <note>lead oxide</note>, less one part of wax; 36 gold-weights each of mezereum root <note>a toxic, blistering shrub</note>; 18 gold-weights of copper flowers; 40 gold-weights each of ground gold filings and ground litharge; and 3 pounds of old oil. First, put the litharge, gold, and copper flowers into it, then the remaining medicines. Again, take furnace-scale, "vein ash," and burnt lead; make a plaster from them with myrtle oil. This oil should be thickened with litharge—for example, 1 dram of litharge to triple the amount of sharp vinegar, and 1 dram of oil (either myrtle or dill oil). Stir them gently until the litharge dissolves and thickens, but do not burn it. Other options include copper bark or washed copper flowers; make a powder of them and first coat the area with honey, then sprinkle this powder over it. Or: 2 parts burnt copper and 10 parts wax; dissolve them in the sun and apply. Or: 8 parts each of white lead and other items; 2 parts each of copper bark, rock salt, frankincense, copper flowers, and pomegranate peels; 1 part lime; 10 parts wax; and enough myrtle oil. Again: 1 pound each of litharge and oil; 1 dram each of unperforated galls and aristolochia; 1 dram of ammoniac; 2 drams of fine frankincense. Make a liniment of these over the fire, stirring with a reed root.

<margin>Law 111</margin>
### Treatment of fistulas and hides <note>tissues</note> that do not bond together.

### Regarding fistulas, their judgment and their types have already been discussed.

That which is necessary regarding the management of the flow of "virus" <note>poisonous discharge or foul pus</note> and corrupt fluids from them, through preparation or perforation, we have already declared in previous sections. The treatment of fistulas varies. Some fistulas are straight and running; others are "antique" <note>chronic/old</note>, whose cavities are deeply rooted in the flesh. These latter ones are difficult to treat. It is necessary to take the entire cavity and excise it, rooting it out from the sides with a razor or other tools, or by cauterizing it with fire, or with caustic medicine. However, medicine is "wicked" and dangerous if the fistula is near a nerve or a vital organ. 

Perhaps the patient is more inclined to let the fistula remain than to endure the cure. It may be possible to dry it out and eat away the "oily, fraudulent" flesh <note>unhealthy, fatty, or necrotic tissue</note> within it, drying the rest of the dead flesh so it closes and remains quiet for a long time, even if it is not fully healed. He who wants this must cleanse the fistula of the "fraudulent, oily" flesh within it, then fill it with drying medicines. It will remain stable as long as there is no fear of "repletion" <note>fluid buildup</note>, humidity of the complexion, contact with water, lying on it in a harmful way, injury, a blow, a cough, or a tremor. 

Regarding the treatment by total eradication and uprooting: know that when a fistula is fraudulent, putrid, and old, there is no remedy except cutting it out with burning, or cauterizing it with fire as we have shown. One must probe the twisting passages to ensure the cautery reaches the bottom until it is "cooked" or burnt away and cut out. 

Cauterizing with sharp medicines—such as sal ammoniac, arsenic, sulfur, copper flowers, and "living silver" <note>mercury</note>—is the height of these treatments. The "living silver" should be "extinguished" <note>made into an amalgam or killed with other substances</note> and mixed with an equal amount of iron filings, half as much alkali, and half as much lime. Let it be sublimated in an *aludel* <note>a pear-shaped chemical pot</note> or suffocated in a "kumia" <note>likely a chemical furnace or vessel</note> as those who work with this chapter do; let it be sublimated like salt. When this is placed upon the fistula, it inflames and scorches it, separating the diseased flesh from the healthy. Then it should be taken with forceps and pulled out. Apply butter to the limb every hour afterward to quiet the pain, then treat it as a regular ulcer. 

For a recent fistula, wash it with strong medicines like *kitran* <note>cedar resin or tar</note>, ash-water, seawater, brine, and soap-water mixed with arsenic, sal ammoniac, and water sublimated from *calcuccauemento* <note>likely a mineral salt or vitriol</note> and sal ammoniac.

**On the Nerves.** He previously determined the treatment for the "solution of continuity" <note>a medical term for a wound or break in bodily tissue</note> that occurs in the fleshier members. Here he asks: why is an accident <note>a symptom or complication</note> in wounded nerves different? ## On excess flesh growing over wounds. Chapter xii.

In the treatment of this, cleansing and drying medicines are necessary; and the less they cause "biting" <note>stinging or irritation</note>, the better they are. And one must not expect this from the aid of nature as is expected in the natural growth of flesh, for the growth of flesh is the work of nature. And everything that nature does not cause to grow, whether with the help of medicine or without it, is contrary to the operation of nature; for that reason, one must rely mostly on medicine. And know that the *trochisci* <note>medicated lozenges or troches</note> made for this do not help old growths, but rather recent ones. If copper should be necessary, then it will be necessary to preserve the troches and store them in a place where the air will not corrupt them. Vinegar dregs have already been praised for this, but that is not entirely sound to me. Making these troches into shapes like hazelnuts preserves their strength better. As for what is said—that it requires warm water of arsenic and other things to be drunk—that is what prepares it for the resolution of its strength and helps the air to corrupt it. The medicament of *gossafie subule* is stronger, but because its suffering from the air and mixed humors is a source of fear, its fury is greater given its condition. These medicines are like copper bark, burnt oyster shells, and two types of burnt *eritioum* <note>likely a mineral or shellfish</note> with their flesh; but the *eritium* remains and constricts the flesh more than is proper, and more strongly than

In the second part, he sets down the conditions in which it is difficult to heal compared to other fleshy members. This begins: "And sometimes the power that is wounded is..." The first is in two parts. First, he does what was said. Second, he adapts it to wounds of the cords <note>tendons</note> and muscles. This begins: "And similarly." The first is in two sections. First, he shows which symptoms are more grave. Second, which are less grave. This begins: "And easier." Another is a break of continuity from a piercing or falling object, which is discussed here. This is the last rubric, in which Avicenna hints at the "accidents": pains and spasms. Everything that comes is troublesome, as appears in the discussion. Second, he hints at the causes: for because of the intensity of sensation, pain can more strongly cause a spasm, from which the body flees; and from which it is also drawn <note>contracted</note>, not permitted because of the defect of power from the pain, whereby the spirit is violently resolved through the way of drying. This creates the condition, as is clear from Hippocrates in the *Aphorisms*, regarding the path of spasms and the deception of evil things. These accidents occur in the break of the nerves because of their continuity; for when nerves are broken, because they communicate with the brain, these evil accidents occur. It is doubted because there seems to be a double contradiction. First, he says it leads to a spasm without a preceding injury. And he says there is an abscess there. Also, if there is an abscess, there is pain, yet he says: "without great pain." Note that a spasm can occur in four ways in nerve wounds. First, by simple commonality of pain, whereby the brain is contracted. Second, by the communication of some malignant vapor from virulence or other poisonous matter, from which the brain also flees. Third, from other matter that has gathered: for example, the place swelled from the skin and afterwards diminished, causing a spasm. Fourth, from common repletion of humors in the body due to pain, which, going to the brain, cause a spasm. From which it appears that some of these spasms do not come from repletion or inanition <note>emptiness</note>, like the first and second; and some do come from repletion, like the third and fourth—that is, from repletion at least in the place where the nerves originate. Tragacanth tempers their power and their stinging, and adds to their refinement. Flower of copper is strong, but it is not like *ziniar* <note>verdigris/acetate of copper</note>, especially that made from copper bark. Among those things that corrode excess flesh: take alkali and unslaked lime, and let it sit in a vessel of its own water in the sun for seven days; let them be moved every hour until they thicken and become like mud. Let troches be made from them and administered. Similarly, the "earthenware" troche and "green ointment" are wonderful, as is the green made with rock salt. And the ointment called *alescore* corrodes flesh without stinging, as do the *duduen* medicament, the *dianor* medicament, and the medicament made from copper horns and ground frankincense; these are suitable for bad flesh, as they take away moisture like a cooked thing, as do all medicines made to be put into the nose.

## Regimen for ulcers that break open after healing. Chapter xiii.

The treatment after they break open is to remove the bad flesh—and indeed the bone follows it—then occupy yourself in drying it according to what you know. Displaced bones are perhaps treated with attractive <note>drawing</note> medicines, such as black poppy leaves plastered with fig leaves and *fauich* <note>possibly a pulse or bean</note>, or white henbane seed and vitriol in equal parts, applied as a plaster.

## Eradication of the traces of ulcers and wounds. Chapter xiiii.

The eradication of the traces <note>scars</note> of ulcers and wounds requires cleansing medicines of strong purification, and their powers should be suited to the nature of what they are cleansing; therefore, treat the strong with the strong, and that which is less so with the less. Cleansing medicines of strong power are, for example, *lamenti*, egg white, arsenic, and "pepper stone" with it. Light, soothing medicines are beans, chickpea flour, radish seed, rare soft mud, and melon rinds. Donkey fat is very good, especially when certain medicines are joined to it. For the traces of ulceration or beating <note>bruising</note>, cleansing with oil of lily relieves it quickly. Furthermore, there are the troches which I shall mention in the chapter on "decoration" <note>cosmetics/aesthetics</note>.

### Fourth Treatise: On the break of continuity in the nerves, and that which does not depend on the restoration of the break of continuity in the nerves.

## Chapter i. On wounds of the nerves and those that follow their course.

**N**amely, because of the intensity of their sensation and their continuity with the brain, very intense pains and very great injuries occur from wounds, such as spasms and "mixing of the reason" <note>mental confusion or delirium</note>. Many times they lead to a spasm without a preceding grave injury, and there is no excuse for there not being a great abscess without great pain.

Nerves and bones are made by heat, but in their finished state, the heat has evaporated the moisture, leaving them firm through coldness; thus, coldness is required for their completion.

The material of the nerves should not be biting. If a nerve is uncovered all around, use oil. If it is covered in a puncture wound, it opens and mitigates the injury.

**E**t their more manageable conditions are fevers and many abscesses that appear in places other than the wounds themselves, along with thirst, wakefulness, and a drying of the tongue, especially when an abscess occurs there.
