And when the dislocation is toward the back, then it is not necessary that the patient be extended downward or raised above the ground; rather, he must be placed upon something hard so that he is stable. When his hip is separated toward the outside, as I said regarding the curvature <term>gibbositas; a hump or protrusion</term>, it is therefore necessary that the patient be extended upon a wooden board or foot-board upon his face, and let the bandages be tight—not over the hip, but rather over the leg as we recently described. And it is necessary again to apply compression with a board and over the **groin** and the place from which the joint has emerged. This is our discourse on the types of dislocation that happen to the hip from a manifest preceding cause. However, since sometimes the hip is dislocated because of an abundance of moisture occurring in it, just as the shoulder is dislocated, it is then clear that one should apply the **cautery** <note>a hot iron used to scar the tissue and "dry" the joint</note> as we described in the place where we discussed this cautery.

<margin>¶ On dislocation of the knee. L. xxvii.</margin>
The knee is subject to rapid dislocation. For perhaps it is dislocated without cause except for fast walking or a slight slip, just as a fleshy person often suffers a dislocation without cause except for a jump. And the knee indeed dislocates toward every side except the front, because of the **kneecap** <term>rotula; the patella</term> and its supporting structures. On the cure: L. xxviii.

<margin>¶ On the dislocation of its supports. On the cure. L. xxviii.</margin>
Let the patient sit upon a seat close to the ground and let his feet be raised slightly. Then let a strong man extend his hand from above and from below with a strong extension, and let the restorer return the joint to its proper arrangement according to the judgment of that dislocation, and let him bind it.

<margin>¶ On the dislocation of the "arresting bone," which is the kneecap. L. xxix.</margin>
When a dislocation happens to it, it is necessary that the foot be placed flat on the ground and the kneecap be reduced. Then let the curvature of the knee be filled with cloths that prevent it from folding, and let splints <term>astelle</term> be placed over it, resisting it in the direction toward which it inclines. Now, therefore, it is tightened and held fast; let the knee not be folded with haste, but gradually until it is eased.

<margin>¶ On the dislocation of the ankle joint at the heel. L. xxx.</margin>
The heel dislocates; if it is dislocated, it therefore requires strong extension and vigorous treatment and a forceful push so that it may return. Then it is necessary that he be kept from walking for about 40 days so that it does not dislocate again. In a partial separation, however, any slight extension is sufficient, then let it be reduced. And when it is completely dislocated, then it must be reduced as some say; they say the patient should be extended upon his back on the ground, and from that which is between his hips at the **groin**, let a peg of equal length enter into the depth of the earth, not permitting his body to move when his foot is pulled downward; indeed, it is necessary that this peg be fixed before the patient is laid back. But if there is a large piece of wood available to you, in the middle of which we said there is another fixed wood, then it will be necessary for the extension to be made upon this wood. And there must be an assistant holding the hip with his hands or a bandage, but in the opposite direction of the first assistant’s extension, and let the physician level the separation with his hand, and let another assistant hold the other foot downward. And after the leveling, it must be bound with strong bandages, and let it go with part of the bandage to the top of the foot and with another part to the heel, and let it be tied there. And care must be taken regarding the nerves <note>original: "neruis," often referring to tendons or ligaments</note> which are above the wide part of the back [of the heel], so that there is no excessively tight binding over them, and the patient must be prohibited from walking for 40 days; and if they try to walk before this, they are not fully healed, and the limb becomes weakened in them and the cure is ruined. But if the ankle bone is separated by a jump—for that happens many times—or if a hot swelling <term>apostema; an abscess or inflammatory swelling</term> occurs in this limb, then this limb must be prepared by laying the patient on his face and extending the limb and leveling it with **fomentations** <term>embrochis; warm liquid applications</term> that soothe hot swellings, and by applying strong bandages so that the patient may rest and not move until the limb is entirely rectified. And the binding of the ankle indeed should be toward the toes, and the ankle itself should be left open.

<column-break/>

<margin>¶ On the dislocation of the bone of the foot. L. xxxi.</margin>
Its treatment is primarily like the treatment for the dislocation of the heel bone; and perhaps it is sufficient that you level it so that you press with your own heel upon it, with a cloth being between them, until it is leveled; then apply plasters and tighten it in the manner you know.

### Second Treatise on the general roots of fractures.
### A universal discourse on fractures. L. i.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'F' showing a scholar or doctor in profile, seated at a desk or lectern, wearing a robe and cap.</image-desc>
**Fracture** is the "solution of continuity" <note>the medical definition of a break in an otherwise continuous tissue</note> proper to bones. And it happens sometimes scattered, and sometimes it is not scattered; and sometimes it happens even, and sometimes it happens split. An even one sometimes happens in width, and sometimes it happens in length. And that falling in width sometimes happens divided, and sometimes it happens undivided. And that falling in length is a division and a **fissure** <note>original: "alscalum"</note> which does not happen separately. And some have named the types of fracture by their own names: calling a fracture in width and depth *mangede*, *rhabhanale*, *astale*, and *arundinale*; and calling a fracture proceeding in length *lineale*; and calling one proceeding in width with length *lunale* and *neruale*. And there is that which is of small parts, one called *sauchbie* and another *alierusie* with *albuberien* <note>these are Latinized Arabic medical terms for specific fracture patterns</note>. And when a fracture is complete, it is not possible for the two bones to remain [aligned], because it is necessary that there be an opposition between them according to the preparation of natural continuity; rather, they are necessarily separated from alignment. And similarly, the separation necessarily causes a piercing because of what it contains of membranes and flesh, whereby pain follows it. And when there is a rounded leveling without fragments, the limb is turned with ease. And for the fracture to incline toward the outside, as Hippocrates said, is better than for it to incline toward the inside, because there are more nerves it encounters there, whereby it causes more harm. And when a fracture falls near a joint and is restored, difficult movement remains because of the hardness and the **callus** <note>original: "rasbadii"</note> that occurs in the ripening until it clears. And that indeed happens worse in the joints of small bones; and it is also worse where the joint is naturally tighter, such as the ankle joint. And the fracture of the worst healing and uniting is that which is according to the roundness [transverse], and then that which is slanted. For it does not adhere except upon itself. Extend the binding, having a wondrous construction for a very long time, and let him take from foods and medicines and from that which sends blood to that part, as we shall say. And the worse fracture of the bones is toward the inside, not toward the outside, according to what is said regarding the cutting of the marrow, and it kills, and it is a situation in which there is no utility. For the marrow has softness and viscosity and is not [easily] cut. And sometimes accidents occur with the fracture, such as wounds and the flow of blood and swelling and the rubbing of that which surrounds it of the flesh; if it is not prepared with the prohibition of putrefaction or if it is not splinted, corrosion will happen from it. And the location of a fracture of the large bones is known by pain and by the fall. But fractures of small children appear by pain and swelling, for in them many signs of restoration appear. And when these bones return to their places, it is possible in infants and those who are close to them that the limb be restored by its primary power in them. But in the age of adolescence and those who follow them, it is not [identically] restored; rather, a healing from cartilaginous material runs over it, joining between the two bones, of the kind that is used to join two pieces of lead or other metals together. And the bones most disobedient to being restored are the upper arm <term>adiutorium; here likely the humerus</term>, then the forearm <term>brachium</term>. Furthermore, when the collarbone <term>furcula</term> is broken toward the inside, its cure becomes difficult. And the more unsightly fracture in the two bones of the leg is the fracture of the lower bone <term>focilis inferioris; the fibula</term>, as was said in dislocations. But the matter of the hip and the thigh is easier because the restoration does not prohibit them from delay [in healing]. And limbs indeed differ in the time of restoration. For example: because the jaw is restored in what is said to be 10 days, and a rib in 20, and the forearm in that which approximates 25 up to 40, and the hip in 50, and perhaps it is extended for a long time until the hip is restored, even up to three or four months. And that which is toward the belly is better than that which declines toward the back when there is a declination in the side of the urine [the bladder area]. And the causes for which a bone is not restored are: a multitude of water fomentations, a multitude of loosening and binding of the bandages, or haste in movement, or an absolute lack of blood, or a lack of viscosity in the body; and because of this, the restoration of a fracture is diminished in choleric people and those in convalescence. And among those things that signify restoration is the appearance of blood which is seen as if it were the superfluity which nature expels from its multitude with effort toward the fracture. On the roots of restoration and binding. L. ii.

<margin>¶ On the roots of restoration and binding. L. ii.</margin>
The basis of restoration is the extension of the limb with the quantity that is necessary. For an excess in it causes spasms and injury, and sometimes fevers come from it; sometimes softening of the body occurs from it.

# Book IV

In moist bodies, there is less harm because of their compliance to extension; however, a lack of extension hinders the quality of consolidation and proper alignment, which is equally important in both dislocations and fractures. One should not believe that bone setting consists solely of preparing the two bones to be straight and positioning pads and bandages, but rather one must cover them with **splints** <term>astellas; small pieces of wood or bark used as stabilizers</term> and secure those splints with further bandages. It is necessary that the limb be kept as still as possible, provided it is done in a quantity the patient can tolerate and does not cause harm or an **abscess** <term>apa; from "apostema," a swelling or collection of fluid</term>, so that the natural vitality of the limb does not die. One must also beware of extreme pain during extension and tightness in both fractures and dislocations. Similarly, one must avoid excessive tightness and delaying the loosening of bandages, as this leads to the death of the limb and putrefaction, making amputation necessary. The goal in most restoration is for the **callus** <term>alrosboth; a Latinization of the Arabic term for the bony healing tissue</term> to form in those areas that are not like the bones of the head; for upon the skull, no such callus arises. Therefore, one must prepare the site so that the callus is neither too dry nor too sparse, nor too thick beyond measure. Regarding the "dryness" of the bone, its size varies according to the limb and the magnitude of the fracture—whether it is large, multiple, or the opposite. You will know through divine-like insight what must be done by considering the patient's diet and the nature of the fracture. When the callus is forming, it is necessary to prevent the patient from compressing movements, sexual intercourse, anger, and rage, as these "burn" the blood. The patient should avoid hot places, as the blood seeks coolness, and healing is aided by strong, **styptic** <term>stiptic; astringent or blood-contracting</term> plasters that possess a certain warmth and glue-like quality. In these, ingredients like **cypress nuts** <note>original: "nur cupsi"</note> and **tragacanth** <note>original: "dragagantū"</note> should be placed, along with medicines that assist with ruptures. When a fracture occurs and does not heal through standard restoration, then something similar to the "friction" used on non-healing ulcers should be performed: the site should be rubbed with both hands until the thin, weak, and viscous matter—which is as if it were nothing—is removed. This is done so that the area is elevated and good, fresh blood is driven into it, allowing a strong callus to coagulate over it. Often, the color of the bone changes and scales off like bark, and blood appears due to the friction; upon such cases, splints should not be placed; rather, if necessary, a good bandaging is sufficient. When a fracture and a wound occur together, it is not possible to delay the restoration until the wounds are healed; for the bone will harden and will not accept restoration except with deformity, violent extension, and great difficulty. Furthermore, when pain and swelling occur with a wound, creating a fear that the limb might be distorted, it is better for the distortion to occur than for a greater danger to arise; therefore, in such a fracture, one should not push the restoration to its absolute limit. If there is crushing with the fracture, there is a fear of the limb's **corrosion** <term>corrosio; gangrene or necrosis</term>; therefore, the location should be scarified so that blood may exit, for otherwise there is fear the limb will die. However, if blood flows too freely, it must be restrained. Often, it becomes necessary because of the tumor-like swelling and the damage of the wound to perform other necessary treatments for the limb, such as **bloodletting** <term>pblomas; phlebotomy</term>, loosening the bowels, and thinning the diet.
<margin>And Hippocrates indeed instructs the one being restored to avoid bandages of **hellebore** <note>a medicinal plant often used as a purgative</note> at that hour, and he knows his intention is to draw the humors to the internal parts.</margin>
<margin>And Galen forbids this; instead, he instructs that **agaric** <note>a type of medicinal fungus</note> be drunk. If it should be necessary, then some **oxymel** <note>original: "sirupo acetoso," a syrup of vinegar and honey</note> should be given, which has a sharp power; it is said this was used in the time of Hippocrates. The abundance of knowledge between these two eras is marvelous.</margin>
And whenever itching occurs from the tightness, it is necessary to loosen it or bathe the limb with warm water until the biting humors are dissolved. If you wish to perform the restoration and it then causes pain and restlessness, it is more correct to stop and remove what you have tried to set; for perhaps by doing so, you will remove the pains from the sick person. In a longitudinal fracture, it is sufficient for the limb to be held together with a tight bandage—tighter than in other cases—where the compression is directed toward the front. In a bone fracture, it is necessary that the two bones stand in a straight line to the greatest extent possible, observing this by comparing it to the healthy side. Consider whether this bone's position matches its fellow on the other side, then restore and observe. For between these parts are things like fragments and protrusions, and others are hollows; truly, when fragments are not decently composed, they create a gap between the bone and the restoration. If it is broken again and fragments remain between the two cracks of the bone, they do not permit one side to adhere to the other and they keep them separated; thus an ulcer forms in which pus always collects, which leads to the bone itself rotting and the limb becoming putrefied. Furthermore, the union will not be strong; for it only becomes strong when the fragments and protrusions are decently continued in their proper opposition. Therefore, extension is necessary after the opposition between the two bones, the protrusions, and the channels that "swallow" them has been verified. When you have extended and opposed them, it is right—once you find the opposition verified—to soften the extension gradually and watch the alignment so it does not decline during the pull; observe with your hand the state of what is being composed. If you find a protrusion or something else, rectify it with your hand. Then, a bandage is necessary to keep the limb at rest—not too hard, for that causes great pain, nor too loose, for that fails to preserve the setting. A middle ground between these is best. And it is necessary that

<column-break/>

the bandage be placed more firmly toward the direction of the lean. If the fracture is complete, it must be leveled with an equalizing pressure from all sides. If the fracture is only on one side, more tightness will be required there. And if there are any small fragments or bones with the fracture, if they are harmful and causing pain, deal with them during the rectification. If they are not harmful, do not worry about them or touch them. If, for example, their **crepitation** <note>the grating sound of bone fragments rubbing together</note> is heard, then there is hope that the callus will flow over them. When you have finished with that, one must not rush the matter.
And when a tearing of the flesh occurs from the fragments, it is not correct to be preoccupied with the width of the tear at the expense of solid alignment; rather, it is necessary to extend the two bones to both sides to the ultimate end of straightness, so there is no crookedness in them, for in crookedness lies the corruption of the bone. When you have extended it, return to the fragment and reduce it and secure it; if it returns to its place, do not widen the tear; instead, as you know, see the measure you need and perforate it according to the size so the fragment may enter. Place over the fragment a piece of smooth skin upon which there can be a thick hole, and let the fragment itself penetrate it; press upon the skin and the hand with a heavy compression on both, and the bone will proceed into the hole back to its root. Then it should be **sawed** <note>original: "seref," from "serrare"</note> with an opposing saw; this is a tiny, subtle, sharp saw like those used by comb-makers. Perhaps the root must be perforated with a **trepan** <term>tripano; a surgical drill</term> by making continuous holes at the site where the fracture is sought. This does not remove the fear of injury when there is a "noble body" <note>a nerve, major vessel, or organ</note> behind the bone, although the instruments might be safe as they move by their own motion, collection, or incision. Sometimes a trepan is cleverly designed and placed upon the width of the substance so that it cannot penetrate except by a helpful amount, which causes less harm than other moving instruments. For this reason, it is necessary that those who restore bones have many types of these trepans prepared. Perhaps a fragment does not appear, but it is necessary to reach inside to dry and retain it, then do what is required. If there is a fragment or a piece of bone separated that is piercing the area and causing pain, then it is necessary to cut and use a regimen to extract what is protruding; often it is necessary to saw it. When the part that is broken is a large continuous piece and there is much crushing and shattering, then it will be necessary to extract the whole thing. If, however, the fracture is not shattered, but there is a dislocation and a fissure of the head of the bone, then cut at the weakest place and leave the rest; for there is no harm in that, whereas the harm in cutting away the whole thing is great.

### On the Warning of Restoration
<insert>1</insert>
It is necessary for the restorer to consider the lean of the bone; for when he finds a **hump** <term>gibbositatē; convexity or protrusion</term> at the part toward which it leans, and a concavity at the part from which it leans, he understands this through touch. Furthermore, intense pain in the part toward which it leans and crepitation also signify this. Upon this, he should build his treatment. It is necessary for the restorer to extend his hand over the site of the fracture, moving upward and downward with ease and subtlety, until—if he sees a separation, a protrusion, or a fragment—he recognizes it. He must not bandage it in any other way than what is required, for otherwise bruising or pain will occur. One should not trust a visual leveling by hand before health is complete, for often swelling hides a distortion or a twist. When the restorer reaches the fracture and finds it, if he does not work with exquisite skill, the limb will be disfigured; if he works too forcefully, it leads to **spasms** <term>spasmū; convulsions or tetanus</term> and a wicked fever. Therefore, it is better that he leave it and not touch it. When he begins to restore the part of the bone and it does not penetrate, it is necessary that he does not use force or make it enter with difficulty in every state; for the damage that will enter the sick person is greater than if the bone remained unaligned. If returning and rectifying it causes great pain, and it is possible for the physician to bring it to the state of the fracture, then it is a relief and a great desire for the patient. One must restore it on the same day, for the longer it is delayed, the more difficult its entry becomes and the harms within it multiply—especially in bones surrounded by muscle and many nerves, such as the **hip** <note>original: "coxa"</note>. One must assist in the speed of restoration by avoiding the causes of the opposite conditions mentioned before; and the first of these is the coagulation of viscous blood.

### On the Preparation for Restoration
One must provide every limb that you restore with a suitable preparation that prevents pain. The best preparation alongside this is that which is natural to it. For example, use...

the hand at the **clavicle** <note>original: "furculam"; the collarbone or hollow of the throat</note> and let it be at the foot toward that which impels it, observing the habit of the patient in this. Just as a limb that ought to be suspended must be suspended according to a balanced alignment, similarly, a limb whose condition indicates it should not be suspended must have its reclining position and its place upon a flat surface, so that no part of it hangs or is constricted. Indeed, suspension is bad for any restoration, just as pushing toward the upper parts is suitable for it, provided no obstruction prevents it. ### On the quality of bandages and splints.
<margin>Chapter 5</margin>

**It is necessary** that the cloths of the bandages be clean, for a dirty cloth is hard and causes pain. It should be thin so that medications may penetrate if they are smeared upon it, and it should be light so as not to weigh heavily upon the infirm limb. It is necessary that the bandages take hold of some of the healthy area to act as an anchor; for that which holds the restored parts is more effective than that which would allow them to separate. Although it is necessary that there be no excess in this, as it would cause the limb to have constricted passages that cannot receive nourishment. Furthermore, that which we advised regarding tightness is primarily to expel the flowing moisture from the infirm limb toward that which is further away from it, and to better prevent that which attracts fluid to itself. A wide bandage is better for this purpose because it adheres more effectively and spreads pressure more widely, as far as is possible for each limb. For what is possible in this regard on the chest is not the same as what is possible on the hand or on limbs that are not wide; for a wide bandage is not possible there. Indeed, because a ribbon is wide, its arrangement on a limb similar to it does not result in a good fit; rather, it becomes unsightly. Therefore, one should be content with a width of three to four fingers for such cases. These are like the **forearm** <term>focile; referring to the radius or ulna</term> and the **clavicle** and similar parts. For it is not possible to use wide bandages on them; indeed, if they are not bound with a thin bandage, it is not possible at all. For a wide one is not suitable for the clavicle. In such cases, it is necessary to multiply the turns of the bandage so they stand in place of a wider wrapping; and the ribbon that is wound should be sufficient if its width is three or four fingers and its length is three cubits. The firmness of the **pads** <term>puluillorum; small cushions or compresses</term> is sometimes very helpful to the bandages in creating adherence. There are two types of pads: one type is intended to even out the concavity of the limb, and care should be taken so that no gap falls between them, nor should they be placed in overlapping layers, and the soft parts should be cushioned with them. The other type is intended to work with the bandage and even it out in a second application, so that the bandage may be wound and adhere with equality, whereby no place will be tighter or softer than another, which causes the splints to adhere with a good grip. First, therefore, are the bandages and ribbons, and second are the splints; the lower bandage prevents materials from flowing and prevents twisting. It is necessary that the margins of the pads be placed where possible, and that quantity requires a certain number of pads. And perhaps it is necessary to manage the pads so that one pad covers and levels them across the length of the bandage falling over the site. The bandage that is called "having two faces" or "two bands" and having two heads is that which is managed so that the middle of the cloth is placed where the alignment of the infirm place is preserved upon its own site; and let that be in the middle of the **application** <note>original: "albadacati"; a technical term for the central point of a double-headed bandage wrap</note>. Then it should be taken with each of the two halves toward different sides, and let it be wound with both hands simultaneously according to the famous method which we do not need to explain.

### On the quality of bandaging with explanation and distinction.
<margin>Chapter 6</margin>

**It is necessary** to begin the bandaging at the fractured site and from where it deviates toward the bone; there it should be more tightly constricted. Where the fracture is more severe, the bandage must be stronger. Finally, the site of the fracture is the place from which it is necessary to expel fluids and to preserve the proper position. This practice secures it against **swelling** <term>apostematione; an abscess or inflammatory mass</term>, and perhaps even resolves the condition. It also provides security against inflammation and the putrefaction of the bone; furthermore, it prevents **infection** <term>uirus; literally "poison" or "slime"</term> if it is generated in the bone itself, reaching the marrow and corrupting both marrow and bone. It is necessary that if the bone is broken, it should be uncovered from that infection, and that paths be made for the pus to exit. It is the best of procedures to defend against that which comes from it, so that the lower limb sometimes expels its superfluity to the upper, because the upper part is weak. One must not reach the limit of tightness in the constriction of bandages and splints such that it prevents the arrival of nourishment and blood; for that is among those things that prevent restoration. Hippocrates says that what helps the bandages in their effort to expel inflammation is the use of **cerates** <term>wax-based ointments</term> that are restrictive, made with omphacine oil <note>oil from unripe olives</note> and wax. Perhaps it is necessary to soothe the inflammation with things like chamomile 

<column-break/>

and like with styptic wine, for it resolves the abscess and strengthens the limb; and where there is an ulcer, the cerate should not come near it. Perhaps that which has strength and resolution is necessary, such as oil, mastic, and ammoniac. Finally, when the bandage is managed and the fracture is fresh and not yet swollen, then it should be made of linen, cooled and restrictive. Perhaps it is enough to smear it with water and vinegar, and perhaps it is managed with cerate and similar things we have described. If it is managed after swelling, then it is better that the bandage be made of wool infused in oil that resolves the abscess and soothes it. Every arrangement in the bandage upon which the cerate is placed underneath provides security from the disturbance of pain, especially when the physician is not present. When pain occurs, it is relieved by loosening and re-binding. Cerate should not be managed especially when there is an ulcer, for it may perhaps attract putrefaction to the limb; instead, black wine should be used in its place. Because an ulcer is often associated with a fracture, the cerate must be kept away, and styptic wine in which a long pad has been infused should suffice. We shall place a single chapter on the dressings of fractures. When you have begun the bandage at the required site, then wind it in turns which you increase according to the size of the fracture; part of them according to its diminution and part according to the abscess if it is visible; then it is brought back to that site. Then it should go as far as the healthy area. This is the first bandage. Then prepare the second bandage and wind it over the fracture two or three times, then make it descend to the lower parts, loosening it gradually. Afterward, prepare the third bandage and do the same toward the upper parts. Thus you will make the bandages equal to expel superfluities from the limb and to straighten it according to the intention in the preparation of these bandages. Again, do not be excessive in extending the tightness on both sides, for the limb may become one of blocked veins, not receiving nourishment, and perhaps it will wither. Sometimes it is not done this way; instead, one begins with the bandage ascending, then follows with the bandage descending, then with a bandage beginning from the lower part of the bottom bandage to the upper part of the ascending bandage, as if it were preserving those two bandages, and let its tighter constriction be placed at the fracture. The intention in one of the two bandages is contrary to the intention in the bandage where the attraction of matter to the limb is sought, whereby it constricts below the limb at a distance from it and does not cease to be loosened in the winding; this is a diversifying bandage. These, therefore, are the bandages that are under the splints, and these are the bandages that are above the splints. The upper bandage must be such that it makes the limb like a single piece that has no movement and prevents twisting. Where the fracture is completely wide, it is necessary that the bandage be of equal mixture and tightness. If the fracture leans to one side, more vigorous care must be given to the side where the fracture is greater. You should not vary the patterns of the bandage upon it by making figure after figure, for that destroys what the restoration has strengthened; and the pain caused by twisting, which perhaps happens from it, and the tightness of the bandage causes spasms; for when it is tightened it causes pain, and when loosened it twists. Hippocrates says it is right that the bandage be loosened every other day; for that is better so the patient does not become agitated and does not approach it with his own touching and rubbing, because of the need for the subtle moisture to reach the limb, which might otherwise turn into infection. It is most suitable to check the goodness of the bandage and its preservation according to the predicted conditions twenty days after the fracture. For that is the time of the beginning of the red **callus** <term>alrosboth; the healing tissue of the bone</term>. Then, when the bone adheres, it should not be constricted too much, and its constricted site should breathe so it is not cramped and the callus is not hindered, or its generation hindered in sufficient quantity, so that only a weak, thin callus occurs. When the callus has already occurred and begins to adhere in a size that is not needed and tends toward excess, then one of the benefits is a very tight constriction and the administration of restrictive medicines; for these prevent nourishment and constrict the callus, so that nourishment does not penetrate it again. Again, one must not allow or permit the binding to be done at an improper time.

### On the quality of splints.
<margin>Chapter 7</margin>

**It is necessary** that the substance of the splints combines hardness with toughness and smoothness, such as oleander wood, pomegranate wood, and similar materials. It is necessary that the thickest part of the splint be at the place that meets the fracture on two sides; for the beginning of the splints should follow the side of the fracture or the more severe part of the fracture. Their sides should be thinner so they have full extremities, lest they oppose the healing; rather, let there be a smooth bandaging. If splints are placed on four sides, then it is more protective, and it is not bad if there is an excess of length, as there is no harm in that nor detriment in this, especially if they catch the joint without covering the joints themselves. The longer of its sides should be toward the side to which the motion of the limb's inclination tends, provided it is not so heavy that it weighs down.

And when you see anything regarding this, you should oppose it by loosening until you find equality. ->### On the quality of the administration of splints with distinction and explanation. Chapter 8.<-

<margin>Chapter 8</margin>
**The hour** that requires splints to be placed is after five days or more, until there is security from harmful effects; for the more the fear of complications increases, the more the positioning of the splints must be delayed. Often haste in this brings harm from swellings <note>original: "apatibus," likely "apostematibus"</note>, itching, and blisters. When the splints are delayed, it is necessary that something else stands in their place through the goodness of the binding with a cloth and the quality of the preparation. But if it is then necessary, the splints are required even in the beginning of the matter. Therefore, the bandages and small pads <note>original: "puluilli"</note> must be applied before the splints, descending in an equal manner, covering and fitting properly; the pads should be thicker at the site of the fracture. One should not bind them tightly, but rather increase the tightness little by little according to the experience and condition of the patient. If the bandages and pads are heavy, they should not be multiplied. Among the harms that occur when they are brought down is a bandage that is too soft. The bandages must not be bound over the ends of the splints in a way that loosens them or removes them from their proper placement. The bandages must be loosened by choice every two days in the beginning, especially when itching occurs; then that which we have prescribed must be done. When the seventh day has passed from the tightening, they should be loosened at longer intervals, every four or five days; for at this time one is secure from itching and swelling. Then the bindings should be softened gradually so as not to prevent the penetration of nourishment. If it is possible for you to retain the splints without loosening them even up to twenty days, it will not be harmful; then loosen them. However, they are sometimes loosened at certain hours, not because of a visible cause but for protection, to see what has happened. Consider the flesh that is uncovered to see if its color or condition has been corrupted. You already know that the final tightening should not be so extreme as to prevent the arrival of nourishment to the fracture; for the bone is not restored except by the blood and strong nourishment that comes to it. Do not be in haste to remove the splints and cast them aside, even if it is believed they are ready; for perhaps it may happen that the callus <note>original: "alrosboth"; the bony healing tissue</note> is not yet confirmed, whereby the limb might twist. It is better for the splints to remain upon the limb when they are no longer necessary than for them to be removed before they have finished their work. Therefore, do not hasten, but delay.

---

->### On a fracture with a wound. Chapter 9.<-

<margin>Chapter 9</margin>
**When** a fracture and a wound <note>a compound fracture</note> occur together, the restorer should greatly lighten the reduction and make the splints pass away from the site of the wound. He should place upon the wound what is required of plasters, especially those made with pitch. Some prescribe beginning the tightening from the two sides of the wound, leaving the wound uncovered. This is indeed better if the wound is directly over the fracture. Then there should be a veil over it to protect it from the air. If the wound is over the fracture, one must be clever in the arrangement of the tightening, so that it is cleaned on every side and repaired slightly away from the wound itself with a suitable preparation. Pads should be soaked in an astringent black wine. The trick is to place the end of the bandage upon the lip of the wound, then twist it back and secure it with another bandage. Place it below the other lip and then arrange the rest of the bandage as required, so that the wound remains open and what is beyond it remains firm. Thus the bandage ascends and descends, and the firm tightening falls upon the fracture while the wound remains open so it can be uncovered. A hole should be placed in the splints opposite the wound so that the excess of the wound medicine can reach it. If a hole is placed over the splints opposite the wound, the goodness of the medicine reaches the wound, and it becomes possible for the pus <note>original: "virus"</note> to exit. It should be such that both can be covered; for to leave a wound uncovered is bad, especially in the cold; rather, it should not be too constricted and should be guarded at night. If the wound is healing, splints should be applied even if it is already joined, and the splint should be firmed in that place if the area has declined from it. When there is a desire to loosen what covers the wound, doing so in the morning and evening is more possible for its proper cure. There should be no conflict between this and the bandage of the fracture restoration. Hippocrates says the wound should be bound from the middle of the bandage if it is fresh; if it is old and has produced pus after ripening, it should be bound from the upper part until the middle is reached. It is good that the bandages following the wound be tightened more at the top so that the pus can flow, provided the tightness is tolerable. The further it is from the wound, the lighter it should be placed. When the wound has great depth, the binding of the bandage should be tightened over the place of depth. 

<column-break/>

If the tightness of the bandage suits the site of the restoration, then the intention is achieved; if not, begin to cover the wound with what we have said, and when you reach the fracture, place the bandage more tightly again. The limb should be positioned so that the flow of pus is easy if it gathers in the wound. In summer, the bandages containing the wound should be cooled, which also helps to prevent swelling. Waxy ointments <note>original: "ceratum"</note> should not be brought near the site, especially in summer, as the limb might perhaps rot. Instead, if a repressive treatment is necessary, it should be with astringent wine as we have previously declared. When the fracture is crushed and death <note>gangrene</note> of the limb is feared, then it should be incised with a scalpel. Know that when a wound is bound as is proper, it expels the descending bandage; but if an error is made in the binding, swelling occurs, especially when it is softened over the site of the wound and tightened behind it. If it is not uncovered, the pus will not flow from it, nor will the medicine reach it; and if it is left uncovered, it rots and grows cold, and death of the limb follows, leading to pains and fevers. Therefore, it is necessary for the physician to act between these two options, considering what happens and aiding it before the condition is confirmed.

->### On a poorly restored fracture. Chapter 10.<-

<margin>Chapter 10</margin>
**Sometimes** a fracture is restored improperly, and it is necessary to repeat the breaking of it. The restorer must know the condition of the callus <note>original: "alrosboth"</note> that restored the bone. If it is large and strong, do not go about breaking it forcefully; for perhaps it will not be possible to break it at the original site of the fracture because of the strength of the callus, and it might break in another part of the area. If there is no other choice, he should proceed gently until he softens the callus. The medicines for softening it are those mentioned in the chapter on hard swellings, such as cures of "alleliani" and dates, and types of oils, and bone marrow, and the marrow of cooked grains and similar things. Then let it be broken. Constant douching <note>original: "embrocatio"</note> with hot water and the application of wine many times a day should be used with this. If this does not help, and movement shows great firmness, then it will be necessary to cut the flesh so that it is possible to scrape the callus from the side and destroy it; then let it be broken, reset, and the wound cured with its own treatment. Often it is possible to cure a poorly restored fracture without a second breaking by softening the callus with what you know, and then applying pressure upon it while it is being saved; the fracture is often excused in lean bodies.

---

->### On the poultices of a fracture that follow their course. Chapter 11.<-

<margin>Chapter 11</margin>
**Among poultices** <note>original: "epithimatū"</note>, some prevent swelling and correct itching. Others are for hardening the callus and creating a joining within it. Others are for smoothing a large callus. Others are for removing the stiffness of joints that occurs after restoration. And others are for removing softness if it should fall into the joints.

---

->### On beneficial poultices that correct itching. Chapter 12.<-

<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
**We have already** spoken in the chapter on bandages about the cloths and what must be known; and we spoke of waxy ointments and douches with astringent wine and similar things. We repeat now and say that whatever is administered of waxy ointment or other things should not be rough in any way, but as smooth and soft as possible. Waxy ointments should not be used where rot is feared, nor where the pieces of the fracture are many. Such a thing is prepared to receive rot when it is used with ulcers. We have already spoken of hot waters and their infusion, and made it known that their utility is in resolving the matters that cause itching and in attracting nutritional matter. They are also sometimes necessary when a limb has been weakened and dried out by the tightness of the binding.

---

->### Poultices to harden the callus. Chapter 13.<-

<margin>Chapter 13</margin>
**Helpful** in this are subtle astringent douches and poultices made from them, such as a decoction of myrtle and its oil—if oil is necessary—and oil of henna <note>original: "alcāne"</note>, and poultices with the water of myrtle leaves and its berries, and a decoction of the "alcort" tree, and a decoction of the "aldir dar" root; a decoction of its leaves promotes flesh growth and hardening. A plaster made from honey, especially when saffron and myrrh are added to it and it is mixed with fragrant wine, is very good. The distillation of palm spathes is also good.

---

->### On the management of smoothing the callus. Chapter 14.<-

<margin>Chapter 14</margin>
**In the beginning**, when it is still fresh, let the aforementioned astringents remain, for they gather and constrict it and lessen its quantity. After that, when it flows out, and especially near a joint, it is necessary to cut from it and rub it until it is made even.

### Medicines that soften joint stiffness. Chapter 15.

You should use lotions <note>original: "ebroces," referring to liquid applications or embrocations</note> and begin with warm water, then apply plasters and ointments over them. These should be applied with a softening friction and made from mucilages, gums, fats, and oils. If strong vinegar is added to them, it allows them to penetrate more deeply. Among those things that are useful are dates, *alleliarum* <note>possibly a specific herbal preparation or "al-haliyal," a type of myrobalan</note>, and sesame oil, as it is a light fat and very softening. Furthermore, a softening agent made from bitter vetch is permitted with as much butter as half its weight, and honey at a quarter of its weight. Perhaps a wax-salve <note>term: "ceratum," a mixture of oil and wax</note> made only of lily oil is sufficient, and sometimes it helps to use all the softening agents previously mentioned in the chapter on hard swellings <note>original: "sephiros," likely referring to scirrhus, a hard tumor or swelling</note>. When you sense a change in the temperament toward coldness, then add castoreum <note>term: "castoreo," a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, sagapenum <note>original: "serapino," a medicinal resin</note>, and opopanax.

**A good medicine:** Take the dregs of linseed oil and sesame oil, and fenugreek boiled in milk, and add to it; then also marshmallow roots, squirting cucumber roots, bdellium, salt ammoniac, and opopanax dissolved with strong vinegar, and let them be smeared on. An ivory ointment is also good.

**A good medicine:** Take mucilage of fenugreek and linseed, mucilage of squirting cucumber, salt ammoniac, laudanum, moist hyssop, lily oil, dill fat, soft and pure bdellium, and calf marrow; let them be dissolved in oil and made into an ointment.

**Another strong one:** Take 2 pounds of old oil, 5 pounds of lily oil, a quarter pound of liquid storax, half a pound of yellow wax, 2 ounces of white glue, 2 ounces of euphorbium, and 3 ounces of deer bone marrow; let an ointment be made.

**A good ointment for the stiffness of joints acquired after bone-setting:** 1 part salt ammoniac, 1 part Jewish bdellium, half a part laudanum, alkanet oil, and duck fat, a quarter part of each; dissolve the gums and combine everything.

**A good ointment of salt ammoniac:** 6 ounces of salt ammoniac and the same of yellow wax; 8 ounces each of white gum, bdellium, and galbanum; 3 ounces of alkanet oil. Let the gums be ground in vinegar, then combined in a mortar joined with lily oil. This also works for their spasms and the knotting that occurs like a gland where it is located. We also discussed this in its own chapter; let the ointments we described there be applied, using castoreum, costus, pigeon dung, and mustard; the plaster is the final step.

**A good softening agent:** Take 1 ounce of the dregs of lily oil, 1 ounce of the dregs of linseed oil, and half an ounce each of liquid storax, galbanum, sagapenum, opopanax, and salt ammoniac; 1 ounce of soft bdellium; and bear, chicken, or pork fat (according to the preference of the wise and wealthy); let an ointment be made from them.

### Things that provide strength to the softening process. Chapter 16.

The support in its treatment is based on subtle styptics <note>substances that contract tissues or stop bleeding</note> like flour and immature dates and similar things, or on thick styptics. Sometimes things like saffron, cinnamon, and myrrh are mixed with these. Elecampane <note>original: "enula"</note> is very good, especially when combined with sweet flag <note>original: "acorus"</note>, vine ash with old fat, palm frond bark, and everything mentioned for hardening the callus <note>original: "atrosbotb," from the Arabic "al-ruthūbah," referring to the restorative moisture or callus that knits a bone</note>.

### On the administration of hot water and oil. Chapter 17.

Others say that hot water and oil are not suitable during the bone-setting <note>original: "restauratione"</note> because they hinder the reduction, but they are suitable *before* it, as both prepare the area for setting. They are also useful *after* setting because they wipe away what remains of the swelling, the stiffness, the callus, and the blisters that the bandages caused on the nerves, which makes movement difficult. Therefore, when hot water, oil, fats, and marrows are administered, they help these injuries. Between those, however, water and oil strongly prevent the healing of the flesh. Perhaps they are administered to infants, but they cause them pain, so they need to be dried off; then the painful spot should be joined with oil, then supported and set. Among some people, this is not permitted. Physicians sometimes use a lotion of hot water when they first loosen the bandage, seeking help from it to draw the matter out. This water must be of such a temperature that it is lukewarm when it touches the patient. Indeed, hot water perhaps dissolves more from a clean body than it draws out, especially when the pouring lasts a long time; it draws from a full body more than it should, especially if the time is short. Rather, the water should be of a quality tending toward balance, and the time of pouring should be according to the amount of swelling and inflation of the limb, and it should not be poured when it begins to subside. We have already discussed the judgments regarding lotions in the chapter on dislocations, which should also be observed here. My preferred method, when there is no pain, is that neither oil nor hot water should come near the limb at all, except what precedes it at the very beginning for protection. For joints that harden after setting following a twist or bruising, dates and *alleliarum* are used as a plaster.

<column-break/>

### On the food and drink of the set patient. Chapter 18.

Their food should be of the kind that generates thick, dry blood, yet not too thick and dry; rather, it should be thick and viscous so that it generates a tenacious, strong callus <note>original: "alrosbotb"</note>, not a weak or soft one. These are things like trotters, wheat boiled with much water until it is like a pulse <note>a thick porridge or pottage</note>, boiled bellies, heads, and the skin of a kid or ram, and similar things, along with thick, styptic wine. For the second course, chestnuts and grains that have no bitterness are given. One should avoid everything that thins the blood, heats it, or prevents it from coagulating, such as thin wine and very strengthening things. Their overall regimen should aim for "thickening" unless there is a wound requiring a thinning of the food, depending on the size or smallness of the wound and the fear of pain. He who is safe from that may be more liberal with food and drink. He who desires protection should begin with a thinning regimen to be safe from the malice of an abscess <note>original: "apostematis"</note>. This is as if he needs to be bled again or have his bowels loosened. Then, after a few days, let him administer the other diet, though it is sometimes necessary to abandon this regimen when the callus becomes excessive in size and must be managed. **A suitable meal for the time of coagulation:** Take bread of fine flour, rice flour, fat cow suet, and milk, and make from them a meal similar to boiled wheat or pulse, well-beaten. The medicine he should take for bone-setting is mummy <note>term: "mumia," a medicinal substance often thought to be mineral pitch or bitumen, highly valued for healing fractures</note>, which is wonderful.

### On things that follow a fracture and setting, and the necessity of helping them. Chapter 19.

Sometimes a tearing of the flesh occurs from the breaks which does not knit together; if it is not cut, it rots and causes the underlying bone to rot, so it is necessary to cut and treat it. Sometimes a flow of blood occurs, which must be stopped. Sometimes a severe bruise and crushing of the flesh occurs; if these are not cured with a lancet or medicines that prevent rotting, it leads to gangrene <note>original: "estionemum," likely a corruption of "esthiomenos"</note>, so this must be watched for. Sometimes a hot abscess occurs, which must be managed by its own regimen. Sometimes wounds occur that need to be cured as previously narrated. Sometimes an excessive callus <note>original: "atrosbotb"</note> occurs in a fracture, the quantity of which is unnecessary; therefore the nourishment must be decreased and its generation prohibited by restricting food, applying friction over it, and the other methods mentioned. Sometimes a softening of the joints occurs from stretching. And sometimes it happens that pus runs to the marrow generated in the bone; then it is necessary to remove the bone and uncover the path for the pus to exit.

### Treatise Three: On the fracture of the skull. Chapter 1.

It often happens that the skull is split, but the skin is not split; rather, it swells <note>original: "apostemef"</note>. When the focus is on curing the swelling and the wound is not reached, it may happen that the bone underneath rots. This causes bad illnesses like fevers and tremors before or after the skin heals.

<column-break/>

**It often happens.** Previously, the text determined the nature of fractures in general; here it treats them specifically. First, it covers the fracture of the skull for three reasons: 1. Because it is the first part we encounter; 2. Because it is highly suspicious/dangerous; 3. Because it is close to the method for curing wounds and ulcers. It is not helped by a mold or binding alone, and therefore it is placed in the middle. First, he shows the necessity of knowing about this fracture because it is often doubted. Then he places the cures there.

He shows how a skull fracture is sometimes hidden from the senses and shows the harms that result from this. <margin>b</margin> When the focus is on the swelling, he shows the harms that happen from ignorance—first from total ignorance, then partial (where one part is seen and another is not). First, consider the harm to the bones: they rot. This is because the moisture from the broken veins and from the bone itself and the bruised skin rots when retained, and this rots the bone. Second, he touches on the common harms: tremors of the heart and body. Third, consider other things: namely, epilepsy and spasms. Fourth, he says "perhaps" as a way of speaking, or because sometimes the bone fracture is so small and the person so well-disposed that he does not suffer these accidents. He says it happens "before or after health," meaning the healing of the skin. If a patient with a fracture, even though the skin is healed, points to the spot with his hand, it signifies a problem in that broken part. It is necessary that the skin be split open so the wound returns to the proper state for treating a fracture.

**Why is it possible for the skull to split but not the skin?** One might think the soft skin would suffer more easily than the hard bone. This happens when the skull is split by a blunt force that causes a "folding" break. A hard thing like dry wood does not bend but breaks; a soft thing like skin bends. Thus, that which yields to the blunt object is not torn (the skin), but is bruised and swells. But the bone, being dry, does not bend that way. This happens more in youths than in infants, for in infants and women, the bone actually bends. To the logic that the soft suffers less, it is because of its yielding nature.

**And so that it may be cured.** It should be considered that a fissure is often larger in several places than the wound in the skin. Therefore, it is seen that an incision should be made so that it does not retain poison <note>original: "virus," here referring to pus or morbid matter</note> or any other matter. This must be granted, unless there is an exception to the incision; for sometimes a physician does not make the skin incision equal to the fracture for two reasons: first, because he is certain there will be no increase in the abscess <note>original: "apostematis"</note> or other bad accidents, and because the person is of good humors and strong virtue. The fracture is not bad even if it is longer than the wound. If an abscess breaks out, or a fissure appears during the breakout, this is an error, because there might be another fissure in the bone. It is doubted whether, when a blow is made on one part of the head, another part can be broken. It seems so, because we see this in vessels of glass and earth. Or it is not; and this is the opinion of Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine surgeon</note>, where he refutes those who say this, saying it is not similar for three reasons. First, because the bone of the head is full <note>meaning it contains the brain</note>, while vessels struck in one part break in another because of the air included within. The second reason is that the bone of the head is very strong. The third is that it is discontinuous; hence one part does not suffer from the other. A continuous glass vessel removes this deception. For it happens that from a blow, a person suffers a fissure of the skull in several parts, but the injury appears more in one part; therefore, it is believed to have been a blow only there, even though it was in different parts. I have heard from a trustworthy source that the opposite of what Paul holds can happen. And because of this, etc.

This is divided into three, as he sets down three signs. An example is a dog bite; so in this case, if it is a great fall or force and the skin is not broken, we suspect a rupture of the skull. Consider that this judgment is estimative, because in small falls we sometimes see a rupture, and in large ones we do not.

<margin>c</margin>
**And similarly it happens.** Consider that those accidents happen simultaneously with the fracture of the bone, as when the bone of the fracture pricks the membrane <note>original: "panniculum," likely the dura mater</note>; others happen afterward, as when an inflammation follows the fracture around the membrane, from which the brain suffers. Similarly, whether that corruption of humors happens quickly or slowly depends on these accidents, and they happen more quickly in summer. Therefore, the uncovering of the bone must be done more quickly. Consider that these accidents sometimes occur without a fracture of the bone, but because the brain is agitated by a strong commotion, or some small veins are opened by the blow and moisture sweats from them onto the membranes of the brain, which then corrupts and causes the said accidents. Therefore, good surgeons sometimes uncover the bone even when no fracture exists.

<margin>d</margin>
**And sometimes.** Furthermore, a fissure of the skin that is manifold and diverse signifies a strong cause impressing it and signifies a disposition toward rupture. In its cause, etc., diverse and not straight, or even if it is straight, as long as it is large, it signifies that the blow was strong. Therefore, it is likely that the bone is fractured. It can be explained that the multitude signifies the disposition of the bone fissure; as the skin fissure is multiplex or straight, so is the bone's. Though an error may occur, it is clear that the condition of the fracture must be known through signs like apoplexy <note>term: "apoplexia," a sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis</note>, scotoma <note>term: "scothomia," dizziness with dimmed vision</note>, or a numbing of the limb, which confirms the judgment of the limb. Such an investigation must be done with great care.

<margin>e</margin>

Consider that the incision of the skin should not be made except after having a suspicion or signs of bone rupture according to Dionysius. Whence Avicenna says that in such a disposition—namely, of opening—it is a sign of bone rupture. For if they do not appear, it should not be done because there is strong pain, and pain draws inflammation because the bone is exposed to the air. These words do not please me, because the physician should not wait for time, but if he suspects it, it is the lesser evil to incise the skin.

He means that if the wound reaches this skin but does not break the bone, it should be treated as in the chapter on ulcers or wounds, according to whether they are recent or old.

# Fen V, Treatise III

<margin>
...on the discovery of the injury. But here he compares it to wounds with a fracture. And he says, according to one interpretation regarding fissures—that is, wounds in which there is nothing but a fissure, which is a break in the continuity <term>solutio continuitatis: a medical term for a wound or break where the flesh or bone is no longer joined</term> of the skin—but if there are many, it appears that the cause is the break in continuity. That fissure of the skin, between which and the bone there is nothing but the "bark"—that is, the little skin called the "gingiva" <note>likely referring to the periosteum, the thin membrane covering the bone</note>—is thus a simple break of the skin. Often, tight bandaging and dressings, as well as cooling agents that prevent the formation of an abscess <note>original: "apostematio"</note>, are sufficient. Truly, the more correct way to treat it is to begin and base the treatment upon the fissure—that is, all around it, and not just inside the fissure. Use warm rose oil, because cold would be harmful. Use a powder to promote scarring <note>original: "cicatrizatione"</note> and the growth of new flesh. Use small compresses <note>original: "puluilli"</note> to hold the reduced parts in place. Use styptic wine <note>a wine that shrinks tissues to stop bleeding</note> because it dries the area, and rose oil to ensure the area remains still so that the flesh may regrow. It is determined that the head should be kept still; if the patient is in pain, matter is drawn to the site. Another interpretation is that this discussion concerns a fracture of the skull in which there is no significant displacement of the "small cloth"—that is, the hard membrane of the brain <note>original: "dure matris"</note>. In that case, bandaging is sufficient. Explain according to your reasoning that between the wound of the bone there is only the "bark"—that is, the hard membrane which adheres to it. But it is doubted whether it can be cured without scraping <note>original: "rasura": the surgical scraping of the bone</note>. The answer is that sometimes it can be, in a person of good humors and strong virtue. Or, if in that break the parts of the bone are tight, then one must scrape; if they are not tight but rather wide apart, then it is not necessary, as the poison <note>original: "virus": here meaning pus or infection</note> is well purged without scraping. Therefore, one must hold the skin with bandages and perhaps stitches so it does not cover the bone, and despite all this, a proper opening should remain for a sufficient space of time...
</margin>

...the two ends of the wound, and it is enough if it is necessary to pulverize the "capital powder" <note>a medicinal powder specifically for head wounds</note> over them. Place over them compresses soaked in styptic wine mixed with oil. Then, apply the remaining bandages so that the "isthmus" <note>the bridge of tissue</note> stays still and is comfortable; let the patient sleep and, if necessary, be monitored.

¶ It is not required in every crack or fracture that the entire bone be removed, as this is not possible in every bone. However, remember what we commanded in the general chapter on fractures and restoration. Yet, many men have had bone removed from their heads by cutting, and according to the way the flesh and skin grew over the wound, they survived. In those who suffer bone fractures and subsequent cracks, the bones of the head differ from other bones when they are broken. When they are broken, nature does not restore a strong bony callus <note>original: "asrosboth": a medieval Latinization of an Arabic term for the hard healing tissue of a bone</note> over them as it does on other bones; rather, it creates something weak. Therefore, so that pus does not pour into the interior, it is necessary that the bone be extracted if the head wound is complete <note>meaning the skull is fully breached</note>, or it should be cut if it is not complete. One should not be preoccupied with its restoration. This must not be delayed beyond seven days in summer, or beyond ten days in winter. The faster it is done, the better it will be, and the further removed from great dangers. Among the things that are harmful and make this necessary is that in bones other than the skull, a bandage can be used to bring the parts back together; but this bandage cannot be placed over the head in the same way. Therefore, it is necessary to remove the bone and the fracture—whatever its size—until the matter can exit as needed. Furthermore, if pus should collect between the restored bone and a bandage that is pressing down and driving the matter inward, that pus would be generated in that very spot and penetrate to the marrow <note>the brain itself</note>. It would then be necessary for us to uncover and clean it. Therefore, in such a member, there is no excuse for failing to gather the tissue, make the incision, detect the site, and prevent the flesh from growing over it until you are certain of recovery and there is no fear of pus running to the interior of the bone we have cut. The incision must be made in the most suitable place, choosing a spot that allows the pus to run out better, facilitates the cutting, and requires the least movement. It should be far from the nerves, such as the *synciput* <note>the front part of the skull</note>. For the middle of it does not interfere with the origin of the nerves. And take care that cold does not reach the membrane <note>the dura mater</note>, for that is evil and fearful; use a subtle regimen and a constant pouring of warm oil. And if blackness appears on the membrane, it is perhaps in the...

<margin>
...so that a good cleansing may take place.
a ¶ **And it is not required.** Here he discusses the quantity of bone that must be elevated. Consider that removing the entire bone could be a great danger, but it suffices to remove some part. It was said above that if the bone is entirely shattered, the whole part must be removed; but if not, and it is only a fissure, take a portion from the site. He wants to show the remarkable growth of flesh in those who have had bone elevated; though it seems incredible, the flesh grew and they were healed.
b ¶ **In those who suffer bone fractures.** Here he explains why we proceed with uncovering and elevating the bone in a skull fracture, rather than rejoining the parts as in other bone fractures. He gives four reasons. First, because of the nature of the bone; the skull is not as hard or "bony" as the hand or foot. Second, so that a hard, protruding callus does not press upon the membranes of the brain. Third, because of the curvature of the bone, a callus cannot surround it on all sides as it does in other bones. Fourth, the moisture of the brain always keeps the callus soft. Since we need a hard callus in other bones, they must be rejoined, but not so in the bone of the head.
</margin>

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

<margin>
c ¶ **Therefore.** Here he gives the second cause. First he does this, and second he sets the time in which it must be done. Consider first that when a bone is broken, there is fear of pus pouring into the interior of the brain—that is, the hard and pious membranes <note>the dura mater and pia mater</note>. This is because the vessels above the hard membrane are ruptured, and even in abscesses of the bone, matter falls inward. This kind of fear does not occur in other bones. Therefore, one should not use rejoining in the skull, but the bone should be extracted...
</margin>

...that which appears of it and is not harmful. Perhaps the cause is the medicines; in that case, treat it with honey mixed with triple the amount of rose oil until the blackness is removed, and sprinkle "capital medicine" over it. If the blackness is confirmed <note>meaning the tissue is dead or necrotic</note>, then flee <note>a common medieval medical way of saying the case is likely terminal</note>. When the necessity of cutting or extracting something is verified, let the physician hurry and not wait for the full formation of pus in the site. This procedure is only tolerated where there is no membrane, or where there is a "pinched" or punctured spot; for a puncture causes spasms and perhaps leads to apoplexy <note>a stroke or loss of consciousness</note>. Therefore, that bone must be extracted immediately, and his senses will return quickly if it was apoplexy. If there is a hole, the matter requires even more haste. When the skull is broken, and the membrane grows cold and an abscess forms, it is called "furrate" <note>likely an encrusted or morbid state</note>; then one must act with the haste we described. Or, if waiting is necessary, let it be for two or three days. At first, the bone should be treated with an incision; sometimes this is done with the delicate care mentioned before. And sometimes it is done by making small holes similar to the holes made by needles, where the matter must fall out of them, though there is fear in this because they might penetrate down to the membrane. In that case, use the method we described, as it is safer. How this cure is performed, we shall say according to what the ancients described. They say the wounded head must first be shaved, and two fissures made in it, crossing each other at right angles in the shape of a cross. One of the cuts should be the original wound from the blow. Then the skin should be peeled back from the four corners to uncover the entire bone that needs to be hollowed out. d ¶ If a flow of blood occurs there, it should be filled with a cloth soaked in water and vinegar; if not, fill it with a dry cloth. Then place over it a compress soaked in wine and oil, and apply the appropriate bandage. In the morning, if no bad accidents have occurred, you must begin to hollow out the broken bone. For this, you should have the patient sit or lie down in a position suited to the fracture. Then, stop up his ears with wool or cotton so he is not harmed by the sound of the striking <note>the sound of the surgical hammer and chisel</note>. Loosen the bandage of the wound, remove the cloth, and wipe the area. Then, command two assistants to hold the four corners of the skin—which has already been cut—with thin cloths and stretch them upwards; that is, the skin that is over the broken bone. If the bone is weak by its nature or from the fracture that occurred...

<margin>
...if the rupture of the bone is complete—that is, down to the membrane—and it is wide enough that I do not need deep scraping or elevation.
d ¶ **And it must not be delayed.** The reason is that in summer, matter putrefies more quickly.
e ¶ **And among those.** Consider that as was taken from Galen <note>the famous Greek physician</note> in *On the Method of Healing*, in other broken bones we use a bandage that holds the parts together and prevents an abscess by pressing on the fracture site with many wraps. However, one cannot do this on the bone of the head because of its shape, and also because pressing on the matter beneath the bone would cause it to flow onto the membranes of the brain. Therefore, it is necessary to remove the skull bone and the fracture—that is, the broken parts. One must make the fracture site large and wide by scraping.
f ¶ **And it should be an incision.** Above, he gave the necessity for breaking and elevating the bone. Here he shows the suitable place for cutting and elevating the bone, and he sets those conditions.
g ¶ **And take care that cold.** He teaches how to prevent or remove accidents, such as the formation of an abscess or the blackening of the hard membrane. Prevention of an abscess is done by warding off cold, and by thinning and rubbing the area.
h ¶ **And if it appears.** See how all things are revealed.
i ¶ **When therefore.** He sets the time in which the elevation must be done. It should be done immediately in three cases: if the hard membrane is punctured and pressed, if it is perforated, or if it grows cold and an abscesses.
</margin>

<margin>
If a widening of the wound is made, let it be within two or three days.
k ¶ **And sometimes it is so.** He shows with which tools the elevation of the bone part is done, namely with a scraper or a trepan <note>a surgical drill for the skull</note>.
l ¶ **How truly it shall be.** Here he shows the method for the incision and the uncovering of the bone. First, he teaches the method of detection and elevation; second, he shows how much should be elevated; third, he teaches how to clean the area.
m ¶ **Further it is necessary.** He shows what must be done after the elevation of the bone. First, what to do for up to three days, and second, what to do after. Consider that the order in these things is: first, place a cloth in rose oil over the hard membrane to prevent the abscess feared because of the commotion. Then, use wool tufts as Paul <note>Paul of Aegina</note> says, so the hard membrane is not pressed. Finally, place a cloth soaked in wine and oil over it for comfort and drying, and to prevent the air from entering.
</margin>

Note that this is a warm abscess because warm humors are seen to flow to the abscess. Note that for "part" he understands the dura and pia mater <note>the tough and delicate membranes surrounding the brain</note> and that they are close; it is rare to find a case where both are similarly affected by an abscess. Starting from those that are wider, change to thin cutters, then reach the capillary <note>fine, hair-like</note> ones, and use ease in striking [the mallet]—even if the blow is wrong or large—so that it does not harm the head or disturb it. If the skull is strong, it will first be necessary to perforate it with trepans <note>original: "tripanis"; surgical drills</note> that are not deep-diving; these are perforators that have a small projection <note>a safety guard</note> on the inside of their sharp points to prevent that projection from going too deep and reaching the membrane <note>original: "sipbac"; likely from the Arabic 'sifaq', referring to the pericranium or dura mater</note> until you hollow out the split bone with them. Eradicate the bone not suddenly, but little by little. If we can use a thumb to pull it out with our fingers, then let it be so; if not, use pincers or forceps or similar tools. It is necessary that the space between those exit holes be the size of a stylus so they are near the surface of the inner bone. It is necessary that some part of the membrane remains untouched by the hole. Because of this, the perforators must be made according to the measure of the bone’s thickness, and many perforators should be used in this task. When the fracture is only at the bone's origin, then the change should only be made to those things; so that when the bone is hollowed out, you must then level the roughness of the skull bone caused by the cutting and crushing, either with a razor or with one of the cutters resembling the edge of a sword, after you have placed an instrument that covers and protects the membrane. If any small bones or fragments remain, they must be removed with ease, and then proceed to the cure with surgery or ointments. For this is the easiest method of treatment and causes the least harm. Galen says that when you uncover a part of the skull bone, place under it a cutter at the end of which is a part resembling a protruding lentil—if it is smooth and the sharpness is along its length—until the width becomes like a lentil supported upon the membrane. It must be struck from above with a small mallet to cut the skull bone. When we have done this, it will fulfill all that we need, because the membrane does not move then, even if the physician were sleeping, because the membrane is opposed to the wide side of the lentil-like instrument. If this instrument reaches the skull bone, it eradicates it without injury. This is because the end of the lentil-like shape surrounding these cutters cuts the skull bone from behind; there is no other way to find a species of tool to eradicate this bone more easily or with faster operation than this kind. As for the cure performed with irons and instruments that the moderns call "vituperable" <note>shameful or poorly made</note> because of their poor quality: this is our discourse on the treatment of the skull bone when a crack occurs. This same treatment is suitable for other types of fractures that happen to the skull, even though we have only spoken of the treatment of a fissure and used it as an example for others. Paulus says in Book I that he again taught us the quality of the bones that must be cut, and this is his discourse: Now, nothing should be cut from the bone except that which is infirm; for that which is greatly shattered must be removed entirely. However, in cases where the cracks extend a great deal, when that happens to the bone, you must follow the cracks to their very end so you know that no harmful thing remains; in other operations, one must do what is required. Furthermore, after the treatment with the iron, you must take a linen cloth the size of the bone wound and soak it in rose oil. Cover the bone wound with it, then take a cloth doubled or tripled and soak it in wine and rose oil, and smear the whole wound with rose oil.
