# Treatise III

...and other methods so that venomous creatures do not approach them. The fumigations <note>The practice of burning substances to create medicinal or protective smoke</note> are like the smoke of pomegranate wood, for it puts venomous things to flight; similarly, lily root and pomegranate branches are wonderful for this. Likewise, galbanum <term>galbanum (a bitter aromatic gum resin used in incense and medicine)</term>, and horns, and hooves that are split like an ox’s, and hooves that are not split like a horse’s, and hair, and asafetida, and bay leaves and its berries, and calamint, and sceba <note>possibly a transliteration of an Arabic plant name</note>, and straw with them; and similarly nasturtium, and similarly the ash of pine wood—and especially with galbanum. If a fumigation is made from opium, black cumin, galbanum, deer horn, sulfur, and goat horns.

### Chapter VI: On the repelling of snakes and venomous animals.
Again: storax <term>storax (a fragrant resin from the Liquidambar tree)</term>, deer horn, black cumin, and asphalt; one part of each. Let the bed be fumigated with this.
Another: one drachm each of cardamom, black lily root, and storax; two drachms each of ostrich eggshell, black cumin, and harmel seeds <term>harmel (Syrian Rue, used as a dye and a sedative)</term>. And again: one gold-weight <note>original: "aureus," a unit of weight equal to a gold coin</note> each of white henbane seeds, cypress leaves, pine, and black cumin; one gold-weight of mandrake root bark; three gold-weights of goat hair; one drachm of calamint; four gold-weights of asphalt. Let it all be mixed and a fumigation made with it over the mouth of the windows; there is safety in its smoke. And among those things from which the species of venomous animals flee when the place is strewn with them are water-parsnip, basil, and chaste tree.

### Chapter VII: A miraculous caution against venomous animals.
When the area around a sleeping chamber is strewn with water-parsnip, and again with sceba, and again with asafetida; and bay is wonderful for this. Similarly, when a circle is made around the place where one sits with a cloth using pine wood ash. And among those things which have an effect in distancing them is to place wax lights and candles in a place far from the bedroom, for they turn aside toward them. And among those things which have an effect in expelling venomous things and "albaguarez" <note>likely an Arabic term for crawling insects</note> is to keep animals such as cranes, peacocks, swans, deer, cats, and weasels, which run after them. For venomous animals are terrified of these because they appear and bite them. And some have said that if one makes a bed for oneself from the hide of leopards, a snake will not approach; and similarly if one makes a coverlet for oneself from them—but this was narrated by one in whose speech there is no confidence.

### Chapter VIII: Things which some have said regarding the destruction of predators.
They say hellebore kills dogs and flies. And "leopard-strangler" <term>leopard-strangler (likely Doronicum or Aconite, plants famously toxic to large cats)</term> kills the leopard. And "wolf-strangler" kills the wolf and the dog. And "ibenaguæ" and bitter almonds kill foxes; and oleander and "alzeridaraet" leaves kill "albeibē" <note>Transliterated Arabic terms for specific local predators or pests</note>. And the juice of the box tree is well known for this.

### Chapter IX: On the repelling of snakes.
Among those things that put them to flight by fumigation are deer horns, lily root, pyrethrum <note>a plant in the daisy family used as an insecticide</note>, and sulfur. And if one anoints one's hands with the "skin" of the dragonwort <note>original: "spolio dragontee," likely the peeled bark or skin of the Dracunculus plant</note>, and its juice and its decoction, a viper will not bite him. And the sprinkling of a place with water in which sal ammoniac has been dissolved is among those things from which they flee; and mustard kills them, and when it is placed upon their paths, they flee from it. And among the things that kill snakes is the spit of a fasting person <note>In medieval lore, fasting saliva was considered toxic to serpents</note> thrown into its mouth, especially when one takes sal ammoniac into their mouth.

### Chapter X: On the repelling of scorpions and their destruction.
The spit of a fasting person of a hot complexion thrown upon them kills scorpions; also chewed radish and its juice when it touches it or them, and its leaves; and similarly "albedaruʒ."
A fumigation to draw out scorpions: take equal parts of storax, arsenic, sheep dung, and the fat from a sheep’s caul; let it be dissolved with wine and the medicines mixed with it. Let a fumigation be made at the hole of the scorpions. And when a sliced radish is placed over the hole of the scorpions, it is not feared that they will emerge from it. And among the fumigations for scorpions themselves is when a fumigation is made from the scorpion itself, and similarly from arsenic.

### Chapter XI: On the repelling of fleas.
When a house is sprinkled with an infusion of colocynth <term>colocynth (a desert vine known as "bitter apple," used as a powerful purgative and insecticide)</term>, the fleas jump and flee; and similarly from a decoction of bramble. And they said that when goat's blood is placed in a pit in the house, the fleas gather at it and then die; similarly they gather upon wood anointed with the fat of a hedgehog. They also flee from the odor of cabbage and oleander leaves. And there is a well-known herb called "cimeu," that is, the flea-herb <note>likely Fleabane</note>, which when placed in a bed intoxicates and stupefies them so that they do not survive.

### Chapter XII: Repelling mosquitoes and bedbugs.
Make a smoke with pine wood shavings, or with "calcadis" <note>possibly a mineral salt</note>, or with black cumin; it is best that a mixture be made between them. And similarly a fumigation with dry myrtle, sulfur, bdellium <term>bdellium (a semi-transparent oleo-gum resin)</term>, the foul thorn called "coru," and cow dung...

<column-break/>

...and crushed harmel placed upon beds and windows, and with cypress leaves and its nut. When a house is sprinkled with a decoction of lupine root it helps, or with a decoction of black cumin, or a decoction of harmel, or a decoction of wormwood, or a decoction of rue.

### Chapter XIII: On the repelling of the weasel.
The odor of rue puts it to flight.

### Chapter XIV: On the repelling of the mouse and its destruction.
Concerning the repelling of the mouse, this is more effective: it is said
Litharge <term>litharge (lead monoxide, used in refining and medicines, though toxic)</term> and hellebore kill mice; and again hellebore and the seed of white henbane; and similarly cabbage root, and similarly "mouse onion" <note>likely Squill, used since antiquity as a rodenticide</note>, and its juice, and iron dross, and its saffron. A male mouse puts them to flight when it is skinned and left in the house, or castrated, or its tail cut off—the skinning is the most effective. And it is said that if one of their mice is tied in the house by its foot with a thread to a peg, the rest flee, though this requires consideration.

### Chapter XV: On the repelling of ants.
When "kitram" <note>likely an Arabic term for tar or pitch</note> is placed over their cavern, they flee from it; similarly from a magnet, bull gall, pitch, and asafetida; and they flee from the smoke of the ants themselves.

### Chapter XVI: On the repelling of flies and their destruction.
Arsenic kills them when a little of it is placed in milk; and its smoke, the smoke of frankincense, and a decoction of black hellebore put flies to flight and kill them.

### Chapter XVII: On the repelling of wasps.
They flee from a fumigation of sulfur and garlic, and they do not approach one who is anointed with marshmallow or the juice of mallow and oil.

### Chapter XVIII: On the repelling of beetles.
The smoke of what is called "aldulb" <note>possibly the plane tree (Platanus)</note> puts them to flight, and especially the smoke of its leaves.

### Chapter XIX: On the repelling of "albaratbati."
The "albaratbati" <note>This term likely refers to cockroaches or a specific crawling household pest</note> do not gather in a house in which there are "budud" <note>bedbugs</note>. And a fumigation with the parts and feathers of the "budud" kills the "albaratbati," according to what is said.

### Chapter XX: On the repelling of moths.
Wormwood prevents moths from getting into clothes, and similarly calamint and citrus peels.

### Chapter XXI: On the species of snakes.
The wise divide the species of snakes and their natures into three parts. First: those of vehement sharpness, not delaying beyond three hours. Neither are their bites cured, for they are "deaf" <note>original: "surdi," meaning they strike silently or the bite goes unnoticed until it is too late</note> and "alafilet." Nothing avails against them except the immediate amputation of the limb or a deep cauterization <note>burning the wound to stop the poison</note> that penetrates, for it burns the venom and constricts the pathways. Sometimes vomiting helps in their cure if done after a full meal of salted fish; then other treatments follow. And if the snake is a little weaker, a strong binding <note>a tourniquet</note> suffices followed by common treatment. A slightly weak part I would kill <note>likely meaning the venom’s effect is easily neutralized</note>, and the middle part which is not delayed from three hours up to seven. They say the bite of the sea dragon and similar large-bodied snakes is treated only as much as it is an ulcer, and not as much as it is venom, regarding which a cure must be made. 
And they said the first order is general. For among them is the snake called the "little king," and in Greek the **basilisk**, which indeed kills by its sight and the hearing of its voice. And among them is the snake called the **swallow**, whose color is like that of a swallow and its length is about one cubit, and it kills before two hours. And among them is the snake called the **aspisicca** <note>the Asp</note> on account of the vehemence of the dryness it causes; it is between three and five cubits in length; its color is ashen, declining toward yellow, and its eyes are of vehement light, and it kills in two to three hours. And among them is the **spitter**, for it can kill by its spit; and some say its teeth are constricted..., and others [say] that whatever its spit falls upon, it kills, and the pain of its spit [is great]. Its length is up to two cubits, its color is ashen declining toward yellow, and it kills the one it bites before he can return home. And there is an order which is not mentioned here in the books because of the many species that may be in its treatment; but no treatment avails it except that operation we described, for it sometimes helps with what we said there. And the "arched deaf ones" are other species that multiply in the lands of Egypt. Sometimes some of them have two horns, their color is diverse: white, off-white, reddish ermine, and ashen; and sometimes they have the form of vipers. Some of them have teeth like hooks, and the dragons that kill instantly are of this kind.
The second order concerns **vipers**, whose species are again diverse. For among them are the "alesilari" vipers, and the Greek vipers, and the "fittie" faces, and the others we shall name. Diversity happens to snakes not only in species but also according to sex within a species: the males are fewer, have [fewer?] teeth but more venom and sharpness, although some say the females are worse because of the multitude of their teeth and again because of age, for the old ones...

# Book IIII

...older snakes are more dangerous than the young because of their bodies; for larger ones are worse than the small and short ones when they are of the same species. Toxicity also depends on location, for those that inhabit watery places and mountains are worse than those living on the shore or in areas with many waters. Toxicity also changes according to the fullness or emptiness of their own ducts <note>original: "sipho," referring to the venom glands or channels</note>; for those who are hungry are more dangerous in their venom. It also depends on their animal passions: for the angry and bold are worse than others. It also depends on the season, for their venom is worse in summer. Certain people have mistakenly thought that the venom of serpents and vipers is cold, but this is an error. The coldness that occurs in one bitten by them happens because of the killing of the innate heat <term>innate heat (the vital warmth believed to sustain life in medieval medicine)</term> due to the opposition of the venom. For innate heat is what warms the body through its dispersion and inflammation. When there is no innate heat, even if the body is inflamed by a mild fire, the extremities do not warm up. Some believed that the venom of the *aselisan* <note>likely a transliteration of an Arabic name for a type of asp</note> is specifically cold and that it aggregates the blood of the heart and congeals it, and for this reason it causes great stupor; but it is not so: rather, perhaps it dissolves the innate heat and kills it. The reasoning for this is that animals of a cold complexion appear dead in winter, but when heat is added, they regain sharpness. Whoever says this should know that his reasoning is not sound; nor is this statement true of small venomous creatures, but only of animals with large bodies. What proves the error of this discourse is the wasp, which is of a very hot complexion, yet is among those that are numbed in winter so that it does not move. It is not far-fetched that a serpent, despite its hot natural complexion, might not move because of the opposition of the natural environment and other things that happen to it.

<margin>Chapter 22.</margin>
### ¶ On the bite of the basilisk, which is the first of the "deaf" snakes, or the *harmene*, of which I do not know if it is the same or another.

It is sometimes called the *regulus* <note>meaning "little king"</note> because it has a crowned head. Its length is two palms, its head is very sharp, its eyes are red, and its color inclines toward black and yellow. It burns everything it falls upon, and nothing grows around its cave. When a bird is exposed to its breath, it falls dead. No animal that is not terrified senses it; if it is near, the animal becomes so stunned that it cannot move. It kills with its hiss if it raises itself up, and anyone upon whom its gaze falls from a distance dies. It is not as they say, that he who looks upon it dies <note>correcting the myth that the victim must see the basilisk first</note>. For him whom it bites, the body melts away and swells, the virus <note>original: "virus," meaning venom or potent liquid</note> runs, and he dies immediately; everyone who approaches the dead body also dies. Rarely does anyone escape who has been in its vicinity. Yet it is possible in some cases to touch it with a rod; but according to many, he who touches it with a rod dies even though the rod is in between. Because of this, a certain soldier once struck it with his lance, and the soldier and his horse died, even though it only touched the horse's lip. This serpent multiplies in the land of the Arabs and Nubia. The signs of its bite are if you see someone die suddenly without any apparent primary cause, especially when it is in a place where that animal is known to be. There is no cure for it at all.

<margin>Chapter 23.</margin>
### ¶ On the harmene.

We have said that the *harmene* shares properties close to the *regulus* in that it is not countered and kills not only by its bite, but by its sight and the sound of its hiss. Any animal it bites dissolves, and any animal that approaches it dies. However, they describe its size differently from the *regulus*: for they believe it is one cubit up to a cubit and a half. They say that nothing helps one bitten by it, but if anything does help, then poppy seed is effective up to the weight of one drachm <term>3. i. (the symbol for one drachm, approx. 3.5 grams)</term> and castoreum <term>castoreum (a medicinal secretion from beaver sacs)</term> up to one drachm. Some have already testified to this.

<margin>Chapter 24.</margin>
### ¶ Sign of the bite of the serpent called the hirudo, which is of the "deaf" kind.

Hiccups occur, along with an alteration of the body, stupor, coldness of the limbs, deep sleep, and closing of the eyelids with a violent pulsing of the heart and great pain. Its cure is the same as the cure for the "deaf" snakes <note>original: "surdarum," a category of highly lethal snakes believed to be "deaf" to charms</note>.

<margin>Chapter 25.</margin>
### ¶ Signs of the bite of the dry asp, which is of the "deaf" kind.

To another whom it bites, the same things happen as to one bitten by the *hirudo*: his heat is altered, he becomes stunned, his hiccups multiply, his limbs grow cold, his eyelids close, and he sleeps deeply. The cure is the cure for the "deaf" ones, which we have already mentioned.

<margin>Chapter 26.</margin>
### ¶ On the bite of the spitter and the asilus.

He who is bitten remains without sense or motion, resting and sleeping deeply after the other things mentioned in the chapter on the asp, followed by continuous jumping, the closing of the eyes, twisting of the neck muscles, spasms, and an irregular pulse. He feels no pain; or if he feels pain in the beginning, it is in the intestines, and you will see him putting his fingers down his throat to vomit. Some have already remembered the *asilus* and reported that it raises its head and spits venom.

<column-break/>

I do not know, therefore, whether it and the one we mentioned are of one species; it is of the genus of spitters. Regarding the accidents <note>symptoms</note> of its bite, it is said that the site of the bite is small, about the size of a needle prick, without a swelling, and a little black blood runs from it. For the one bitten, darkness of the eyes and pain in the viscera and the mouth of the stomach occur first; then comes the closing of the eyes and deep sleep. He does not live beyond the third hour of the day. Its cure is of the kind used for the "deaf" snakes, and we have already stated it.

<margin>Chapter 27.</margin>
### ¶ On the horned viper.

The *cornuta* <note>Horned Viper</note> is a genus of "deaf" snakes whose length is from one to two cubits. There are two protrusions on its head like two horns. The color of its body is the color of ash, and its belly has scales like dry, hard plates that rattle against the ground with a noise. Its teeth are even and not curved, and it is mostly found in sandy places. Some say there is a variety called the "small one," either because its horns are short or they have fallen off, and it is also quite short; it is of many kinds and is similarly named in Greek.

<margin>Chapter 28.</margin>
### ¶ Sign of its bite.

They feel as if needles or nails have been driven into the site of the bite. They say a great heaviness remains in the body, the lips swell, and vertigo, darkness of the eyes, and the destruction of reason follow. Its cure is again the cure for the "deaf" ones. What is specific to it is that radish seed should be given in wine to drink, especially if it causes vomiting. When he has vomited, Indian cumin is beneficial. Similarly, sesame with wine, castoreum with wine, and field calamint with wine are beneficial to the bitten person. Radish seed is of miraculous help for this. Crushed salt mixed with pitch <term>alkitram (Arabic term for pitch or tar)</term> or crushed onion with vinegar should be placed upon the bite.

<margin>Chapter 29.</margin>
### ¶ On the serpent called the andrius and the hard kedusu.

When this serpent is in the water, the Greeks call it the *andrius*; when its habitat is in the field, it is called the *hard kedusu*. It is smaller than the "deaf" *aselisan*, with a wider head, and is worse and more harmful. From its bite, the wound begins with vehement pain and becomes inflamed; then it turns green and corrodes. The bitten person suffers vertigo, vomiting of foul bile, irregular movement, and weakness of strength. He usually dies in the third hour and does not survive past the third. If he does escape because the snake was watery <note>diluted venom</note> or because the victim's constitution is strong, he will be plagued by illnesses from which he may never be healed.

<margin>Chapter 30.</margin>
### ¶ Cure.

Its treatment is the common cure, but what is specific to it is drinking cleaned cypress nuts with myrtle berries—one gold-weight <note>original: "aureum unum"</note> of each—with honey-water or wine. Similarly, two drachms weight of aristolochia <term>aristol' (Birthwort, used as an antidote)</term> with wine or vinegar mixed in. Likewise, the juice of horehound <term>praffii (likely a corruption of prassii/horehound)</term>. It should be plastered with lime and oil, mountain calamint, and the bark of oak roots and similar things, both singly and in combination. Barley flour is among the things mixed with these.

<margin>Chapter 31.</margin>
### ¶ On the Hydra.

I mentioned the *hydra* in the summary, though I am not certain whether it and the *andrius* are one, as they may differ only by derivation and name—as occurs in the writing of Greek discourses—or if it is another serpent. A better place from which this can be considered was stated by one describing the other accidents of its bite. He said that the bite seeps and spreads, its color becomes dark, and a very foul-smelling, black, leaden moisture comes out of it. Its treatment is prolonged and difficult, so it should be considered by someone else after me to recognize its disposition, so it may be properly placed in the order of serpents.

<margin>Chapter 32.</margin>
### ¶ Universal discourse on the bite of vipers and their judgment.

The worst of the vipers and dragons are those that are male. The females are less colorful. The bite of a female is recognized by finding many punctures instead of just two teeth in the part she bit; at the beginning, blood flows from the site of the two teeth or multiple teeth, then a burning virus. Perhaps it begins as watery, then foamy, then like the rust of copper <note>verdigris</note>; then that which remains turns into the substance and color of the venom. The site hurts, and then the pain travels through the body, followed by a hot swelling...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the nature of snake venom, moving from general biological descriptions to the specific clinical symptoms and treatments for various types of serpent bites, particularly the common viper and several specialized species.</meta>

...it becomes red, having pustules and blisters just like those from a fire burn; and sometimes it spreads, after which that swelling near the bite and under the mouth becomes green. Inflammation occurs in the internal organs and redness in the body accompanied by shivering, followed by a cold sweat and a loss of color declining toward greenness, a whirling of dizziness, frequent panting, nausea, and hiccups. Sometimes the patient vomits bilious humor <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that medieval doctors believed controlled health.</note>, and there is difficulty urinating, the head feels heavy, and sometimes a flow of blood from the nostrils occurs. Heaviness appears in the back, followed by a cold sweat, violent trembling, and fainting. Most people die within three days, though sometimes the condition lasts up to seven.

# ¶ The Treatment of Viper Bites According to Standard Rule. Chapter 34.

Consider the common foundations in treatment; then, the most powerful cure is to hasten to apply theriac <term>theriac (a famous ancient and medieval "universal" antidote made from dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh)</term> made from vipers. When the theriac is delayed, it is possible it may still help if given many times, but it is also possible it may not help. The harm of the venom to the senses is not bad because nature is what unites the senses. <note>The author suggests that if the patient is still conscious and their senses are functioning, nature is still fighting the poison.</note> If the poison remains external, one cannot use these cures unless both conditions occur at once. If possible, use a great deal of sleep and wine, which perhaps spares one from all other treatment, and likewise onions and leeks with wine if garlic cannot be found.

Some have already said that the rod of the *alfara* deer <note>original: "virga cervi alfara," likely referring to a specific species of deer mentioned in Arabic medical texts</note>, which is eaten during this condition, is helpful. Syrian rue <note>original: "albarmel," the Arabic name for *Peganum harmala*</note> is among the delivering medicines, as are citron seeds. Among the specific theriacs for these bites, a powerful one is that which contains: 1 drachm <note>The symbol "3" represents a drachm, a unit of weight</note> of anise; 4 gold-weight units of pepper; 1 gold-weight unit each of round birthwort <term>birthwort (a plant of the genus Aristolochia, used since antiquity for snakebites and labor)</term> and castoreum <term>castoreum (a yellowish secretion from the scent glands of beavers, used in medicine for its strong odor and chemical properties)</term>. Let these be prepared with wine. Another recipe: 2 drachms each of myrrh, castoreum, pepper, and red arsenic; 2 drachms of dill seed; let these be prepared with wine.

Another includes: seeds of *andacoche* <note>likely a transliteration of an Arabic plant name</note>, round birthwort, and wild rue. Syrian rue is not what some have thought; rather, it is a species of rue itself. One should give only aged butter and have the patient sit in a vat of milk; one should command him to stay awake and walk in a bathhouse at certain hours, specifically a bath that induces sweating. Rennet <term>rennet (the curdled milk found in the stomach of a young mammal, used here as a biological antidote)</term> and similar substances should be given in succession; the best of these is fresh hare rennet. This is even better when taken as a drink with 4 drachms of wine vinegar mixed in equal parts. Deer rennet is also good. Some have said that if a person takes wild onion and chews it, swallowing what comes from it and making a plaster from the dregs, he will not die at all. Some have experimented with frog broth, and it was a helpful lifesaver when eaten; also weasel meat preserved in vinegar and salt, sea crabs, and the blood of a sea turtle. Some have said that there is healing in a stone called the "serpent stone" <note>An amulet or fossil thought to draw out poison</note> when it is suspended around the neck.

# ¶ Other Praised Drinks for Viper Bites. Chapter 34.

Some have said wild celery is marvelous for this, as are the root of sweet flag, the leaves and roots of birthwort, and the roots of *almaru*, *alsetir*, *alsefireiz*, or agaric—whichever of these is available, one gold-weight of it should be taken in a drink with sweet wine. Likewise, the juice of pimpernel (that is, mouse-ear); and likewise cumin, especially mountain cumin; and cabbage juice with two gold-weights of costus, two *obols* <note>a small unit of weight</note> of pepper, the root of *buchormariene*, the seeds or root of *kesiz*, and Syrian rue seed with leek juice or thistle juice. Again, hare rennet, vetch flour specifically, and ginger in breast milk. Give to drink the root of *baucia* or *barmel*, which is known in cold regions and is of great help, along with birthwort bark and *adancoche* root. Some have believed that when turbith <term>turbith (the root of a plant in the morning glory family, used as a purgative)</term> is taken in a drink with sweet milk, it is very helpful, as is the milk of the *alagiati* plant and samphire <note>original: "cristimo"</note>, which is said to be the theriac of Al-Farabi and Al-Kusaki.

Again, among those things said for the bite of vipers and all poisonous animals: 2 drachms of opopanax <term>opopanax (a medicinal gum resin obtained from certain herbs)</term> with vinegar; and again, take 3 gold-weights of costus and gentian. Also good is goat dung crumbled in wine and given as a drink. All sharp, cutting things are good, specifically garlic, onions, leeks, and radishes, and the water from them; also all salted things, specifically the belly of a weasel, roasted scorpion, the gall of a rooster and of other animals. Among juices of great help are rue juice, juice of apple leaves, marjoram juice, and vinegar itself (of which 4 drachms should be boiled and given in a drink), juice of the tips of Nabataean cabbage, and—as it is said—human urine.

# ¶ External Plasters. Chapter 35.

These plasters are "attractive" <note>Meaning they are intended to "draw out" the poison from the wound</note> and are administered before an opening is made. They are made from savin, laurel berries, chamomile, and especially roasted squill, and vetch flour—all of these either alone or mixed with wine. A plastering with old cheese is extremely good. Plastering with split gall-nut is also

<column-break/>

extremely good. Likewise with viper flesh and with split frogs. Among oils, use laurel oil and oil in which laurel has been decocted.

# ¶ On the Species that Make Blood Flow from All Pores. Chapter 36.

The *Asudi* and the *Sabrin* are evil serpents; when they bite, they break open all the pores and flowing channels, so that blood flows from closed-up wounds with continuous pain, along with the vomiting and spitting of blood. Certain wise men have said these two serpents have sandy bodies, and upon their bodies are black and white spots; their length is that of a horned viper. Some said they are smaller than common vipers, and their heads and tails are thin, and they are sandy-colored. Sometimes they are black, red, and white, and upon their heads are white, incised scales. There is a rustling sound to their movement because of the dryness of the scales on their bellies, as if it were the rustling of leaves on a branch. They have a heavy movement of the teeth, and they are categorized with certain species of the first rank. The bite of these serpents breaks the pores and natural channels, making blood flow from them, as well as from the corners of the eyes, and blood is found in the stool, the spit, the nostrils, and the vomit, with pain in the stomach. Some said the site of the bite swells and turns black, and a small watery substance runs from it; the belly is loosened, breathing is constricted, there is difficulty urinating, the voice is cut off, the limbs become soft, a state of forgetfulness overcomes the body, spasms occur, teeth fall out, and the patient dies.

# ¶ On the Cure. Chapter 37.

Their cure is primarily the cure for the *alafiler* <note>likely another species of snake</note> and vipers, in that they are given pure wine to drink, and they should vomit after eating things like *taraca* eggs and salted fish and other things; then they should vomit again. Afterward, they should eat bread and fish placed over coals, and eat raisins; radish seed is also among the things that help them, especially with wine. Also poppy juice with the root of "heavenly lily" and wine; sometimes the white of an egg with wine helps them. Regarding the expulsion of blood, a plaster with purslane and barley flour, or boiled vine leaves, or ribwort <term>ribwort (a common medicinal weed, Plantago lanceolata, used to stop bleeding)</term>, or gall-nuts is helpful. Among those things that restrain the blood by cautery are leeks, nettle, and rue with barley flour and egg white.

# ¶ On the One that Causes Thirst. Chapter 38.

They said the length of the serpent that causes thirst <note>Likely the Dipsas snake of classical myth</note> is one palm, and upon its body are many black marks; its head is small and its neck is thick, and its body tapers from a thick neck down to a thin tail. Some said it is mostly found in the regions of *Lokiati* and *Afiz*. Its form is that of a viper, and the color of its rear parts down to the tail declines toward blackness; it moves by shaking its tail. Some said it lives on shores and that the bite from it causes the belly to be scorched and inflamed, so that the patient is not satisfied by water; rather, he does not cease drinking without any result through urine or sweat, until his whole belly swells and water runs into his veins.

# ¶ On the Cure. Chapter 39.

Their regimen, after the common regimen, is to unceasingly make them drink a great deal of oil and then vomit; then give them enemas with things that draw out feces and moisture and pull the water downward. Diuretics should be given, such as a decoction of celery, spikenard, cinnamon, ginger, *siselios*, parsley, and *silium*. Let it be plastered externally with salt, lime, and oil. The plastering which we will describe for the bite of a rabid dog is also helpful.

# ¶ On the Casezati and Altararati. Chapter 40.

These serpents are small, short, and tiny, and sometimes they hide in trees, lying in wait to throw themselves upon whoever passes by them, coming out to attack them. I myself say that I saw this kind of serpent in the regions of *Debestem*; they decline toward redness and are very hot. They said that from their bite a violent pain occurs that passes through the whole body (if it is of the kind I saw), and death results from it. They said their cure is the common cure and the cure for vipers.

# ¶ On the One that Jumps to Both Sides. Chapter 41.

Some have spoken of a serpent whose name is *Ankesime* <note>Likely the Amphisbaena, a snake traditionally said to have a head at both ends</note>, and they said it jumps to both sides. However, I have not verified that its extremities are equal in thickness and equal to the middle; I believe this is what I saw in truth.

# ¶ The Illicinus, which is very hard. Chapter 42.

This one lives in holm oaks <note>original: "illicibus," the ilex tree</note>. From its bite occurs the peeling of the skin of the one it bites, and even the peeling of the skin of the one who handles and treats him. It has a malignant odor that kills whoever is present at the death, whether sitting or not sitting. From it also occur the symptoms of a viper bite.

# ¶ On the Cure. Chapter 43.

Its cure is the cure for vipers, and these things help specifically...

**BOOK**

**Left Column**

<margin>
In this section, the author decides on the treatment for bites from four-legged animals and humans. First, he provides the Heading; second, he carries it out. He does this there: "worse." First in general, then in specific. He does this there: "let them be placed." First, he presents a certain [case]; second, the cure. There: "And he who wishes." It should be noted that the face contains malice from saliva; for saliva is a poison. However, the saliva of one who is fasting is stronger, more wicked, and worse—especially that of an evil person or one who has abstained for a long time. The saliva of a black man and a black animal is worse. The Jewish man <note>Likely referring to the physician Isaac Judaeus, a common authority in medieval medicine.</note> says the same thing.

I shall speak on this.

### Miliares. Ch. 44.
The color of snakes of this genus is like the color of millet because of its yellowness <note>original: "citrinitatem," a yellow-green hue</note>. The symptoms that happen to those they bite are the symptoms of wicked vipers; their cure is the same as that cure.

### The snake named Sciferati. Ch. 45.
Its color is similar to the one that leaps in two directions, but this one is worse. Its symptoms and its cure are the same as the previous one.

### The snake Aracis, or the Asp, having diverse colors. Ch. 46.
Some have said that it is a malignant killer on the second day, causing the erosion of the liver and the shattering of the intestines. Its treatment is the same as for small vipers.

### The Trificalis snake. Ch. 47.
It is told of this snake that its symptoms are similar to those of vipers, but they include swelling of the bite location, blisters, apparent hardness, and a flow of black bloody fluid from the site. There also occurs an alteration of reason <note>delirium or confusion</note>, darkness of vision, and a deadly spasm. Its cure is the same as for vipers. I speak of this snake in this place by estimation; I do not know it, nor its order, nor its genus with certainty, nor do I know if it is found in our regions or not.

### The Famusus. Ch. 48.
They say its bite is similar to the bite of vipers, but a corruption and softening happens to the flesh of the one bitten, just as happens to someone who has dropsy <term>dropsy (edema or swelling caused by excess fluid)</term>. Deep sleep, forgetfulness, and diseases in the liver, the small intestine, and the colon also occur. I have brought up the discourse on this snake in this place by estimation, just like the discourse on the one before it; perhaps it is not of this order, but rather belongs to the category of putrefying snakes. Its cure is that of vipers.

### Concerning the Amudutus and the Cauharus. Ch. 49.
Some say that the length of each of these snakes is up to one cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> and their color is the color of sand, and there are tracks upon their bodies. They say that whoever is bitten suffers vehement pain at the site of the bite and a massive swelling. Venom <note>original: "virus"</note> flows from it; they kill on the third day, or at most after the seventh.

### Their Treatment. Ch. 50.
They say the treatment for these is the common treatment, and it is specific to them to give in a drink: castoreum <term>castoreum (a yellowish exudate from beaver sacs, used in medicine)</term>, cinnamon, and the root of centaury—whichever of these is available. Give 2 drams with wine. Birthwort <note>original: "aristol." for aristolochia</note> also helps them, especially the "long" variety, which is of great benefit. Likewise, the "assasir" root, and its juice taken with boiled, dried, and ground honey, pomegranate roots, and similarly centaury, flaxseed, lettuce, harmel seed <note>Peganum harmala</note>, bindweed, and wild rue. Appropriated plasters for putrid ulcers also benefit them.

### The snake named Selsir, which is a putrefying snake. Chapter 51.
Some have reckoned that there are snakes in the regions of Asia and Egypt having broad heads, small necks, short tails, and round bellies. There are no lines or scales upon their heads, but upon their bodies are lines of diverse colors. When they move, they do not go straight but rather contract themselves, and they cause a painful swelling in those they bite...

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

...and a putrefaction of the entire body following its crushing, and the falling out of the hair. Sometimes the putrefaction hastens, destroying that which is healthy; they are like a species of viper.

### Concerning the Cure. Ch. 52.
Their treatment should be the common treatment, halfway between the treatments for vipers, followed by the treatment for what occurs from their bite regarding the dispositions and symptoms.

### Concerning the species of serpents that harm when they bite through a wound, not arriving [by venom alone], which must be treated; and these are snakes of very large bodies.

### Concerning the Dragon. Ch. 53.
They say the smaller species of dragons, according to what some have said, is five cubits long; the large ones, however, are thirty cubits and more. They say dragons have two large eyes, and under the lower jaw is an eminence like a crest, and they have very many teeth. Some say they multiply in the parts of Nubia and India; those are larger. Those of Nubia, which are in the region of Asia, are up to four cubits, but the Indian ones are very large. They say of those which we describe that they have yellow and black faces, and their mouths have a vehement width, and eyebrows cover their eyes, and there are scales upon their necks. In every jaw there are three teeth. And I say that I have already seen one of this genus that had thick hairs on its neck, descending in width. They say that from their bite a small pain occurs, then it inflames; the males are worse than the females. I say it has been verified that in regions other than India there are very large dragons. They say their cure is only the cure for evil ulcers.

### The Persian Albedisimoi. Ch. 54.
It seems this one is of the genera of dragons. They say that for the person bitten by the Albedisimoi, those things do not happen which happen with other dragon bites; but they say of these dragons that their teeth are powerful. It is a property of this creature that it tears the flesh <note>original: "carmiat carinem"</note> and digs into it, so that the fear of the wound is magnified, and it requires the treatment for very evil wounds.

### Concerning the bite of the Sea Dragon. Ch. 55.
They say its bite is smeared with sulfur and vinegar; they say crocodile fat plasters and the fish named "trica" benefit it, and lead, when it is rubbed over it, helps.

### Concerning the medicines which we shall write of in the chapter on rue, and specifically the "First Theriac," and "Albedarigum" drunk and as a plaster helps it. Concerning the "Carman" thing. Ch. 56.
Certain wise Arabs said—and I reckon they are of the genus of sea dragons or others whom the wise Abos named "Sermurion"—saying that from their bite happens that which happens from the bite of vipers. And it is similar that their cure is the cure for vipers.

### Concerning the Albatrak and Baudeu. Ch. 57.
They say when the Albatrak and Baudeu bite, there occurs vehement pain, profound coldness, stupor, and death without a doubt—unless one reaches the point of using the treatment for cold poisons. Some said the bite should be bathed <note>original: "embroicetur"</note> with warm vinegar, or fill the place with laurel leaves, and join it with oil of costus and oil of pyrethrum, and oils similar to those which have the power of heating. That which is given to them in a drink is the juice of laurel leaves with vinegar, and anise with rue; or let them take equal parts of myrrh, pepper, and rue, the dose of which should be one "aureus" <note>a weight roughly equal to a gold coin</note> in wine, and the "First Theriac" mentioned in the chapter on rue.

## Fourth Treatise: Concerning the bites of humans and quadrupeds. Ch. 1.

In this treatise, I shall discuss the injuries from the bite of a man, and the bite of a dog, a hare, and similar things; and the bite of a rabid dog, wolves, a crocodile, the bite of a monkey, the bite of a weasel, and the bite of the "alcale" and "mugali" <note>obscure names for small mammals or lizards</note>.

### General discourse and the treatment of bites. Ch. 2.
I say that no one should treat a bite unless he first places upon the bite a cloth soaked in oil, or wipes it clean with that oil. Then, if the intention is followed, let it be filled with things such as honey, onions, and chewed raw beans—for that is marvelous in healing. Again, boiled wine and litharge <term>litharge (lead monoxide, used in ointments)</term> and a plaster with "borbi" oil is marvelous. If corruption <note>infection or gangrene</note> is seen in it, let it be cleansed first with the application of cupping glasses or sharp medicine, and leave it until it produces pus. Let it be considered: when suppuration and putrefaction are seen, know that the cleansing and drawing out of the injury was not final; therefore, let it be treated with the strong "drawing" medicines which we mentioned in the chapter on snake bites. If there is no corruption in the bite...

Fen 6, Treatise 3

<margin>
Let this be set forth specifically: first concerning the bite of a human; second, the dog; third, the leopard and others. The second section begins there; the third section begins there. I manage these in order: first, the general cure of a human bite on a human; second, specifically. The second part is there: "And sometimes." 

Note that in saliva there is a trace of the natural heat belonging to the one whose saliva it is, which is why it helps in the digestion of food. However, because one person may have a physical temperament <note>original: "complexionem," referring to the balance of the four humors</note> that does not harmonize with another's, the saliva of one person is transformative in respect to another and has the nature of a poison—especially in the case of a person with a bad temperament or a person of dark skin <note>Medieval medicine often associated "black bile" and darker complexions with more potent or "melancholic" humors.</note>. 

Note secondly that in a human bite, because humans do not have sharp fangs, much bruising occurs. From this, it is clear what kind of medicines should be applied: namely, those that are "resolutive" <note>treatments that break up or disperse "bad matter" in the body</note> and those that dry out the fluids and open the pores, such as nitre. And when the author determines the specific treatment for a human bite, note that these core principles apply: a human bite is dangerous because the teeth bruise the flesh and the person may "chew" the wound; if the saliva is "corrupted," it becomes even more poisonous. This corruption occurs at the site of the bite, and therefore one must focus on dilating (widening) the wound and cleansing it, as is appropriate here. 

There is a question of whether we should apply pain-relief to a human bite. To this, it is answered: if there is no suspicion of poison, then yes. If the biter is not suspected of being toxic, we should not worry about this; rather, "attractive" medicines (those that draw out fluids) should be applied. I want you to use them; therefore, oil is applied with the intent of widening the wound, not for the intent of sedating the pain, even though we sometimes use it when the pain is very intense.
</margin>

...the abscess should be drained and the wound should be closed up. Among the better ointments for bites and the scratches from birds' claws, thorns, and similar things is the **black ointment**, administered after the extraction of any "malice" (if required) and after washing the area with salt water.

### Chapter 3: The Bite of a Human on a Human

When a severe bite occurs, onion, salt, and honey should be placed over it for a day and a night. Then, it should be treated with a black ointment made from fat, wax, oil, and **white lead** <note>original: "albe zard," likely a Latinization of the Arabic "al-bayad," meaning white lead or ceruse</note>. For this is the best plaster for a bite. Similarly, ashes mixed with vinegar and honey are helpful. Furthermore, bread crumbs with wine and oil may be used, or the offal of calves burned until it turns white and mixed with honey. Again, three-part salt with honey, autumn herbs, and white gum may be used; once the wound is filled with a burnt soothing agent <note>original: "anetico," possibly anodyne or dill-based</note>, let it be smeared with this and bandaged. It should also be smeared over with cabbage leaves. 

Sometimes a human bite occurs, particularly from those who are fasting, where the saliva carries the corruption of digested grains or lentils. Therefore, the bite must be anointed with cleansing oil and covered with a plaster made of fennel root and honey, or bean flour with water and vinegar. The plaster should be changed every time.

### Chapter 4: The Bite of a Non-Rabid Domestic Dog and Similar Bites

The specific cure for these is found in the things we said in the general chapter and the treatment for human bites. Perhaps it suffices for the area to be immediately sprinkled with vinegar and massaged by hand many times; then, let nitre with vinegar be applied and changed every three days, especially when the malice of rabies is feared. 

Sometimes it suffices to treat it with onion, salt, rue, beans, and bitter almonds with honey, or **plantain** <note>original: "arnaglōffa," a corruption of "arnoglossa," the Greek name for plantain</note> with salt, cucumber leaves, citron leaves, and calamint crushed with wine. Furthermore, a poultice may be placed over it made of litharge (lead oxide), especially when there is intense swelling, using barley flour with honey. Other helpful remedies include wild oregano with salt and honey, and **brine** <note>original: "almuri," a fermented salty condiment</note> dissolved in liquid vinegar and left for a few days; this indeed helps with all puncture wounds.

### Chapter 5: The Bite of a Rabid Dog, Rabid Wolf, Rabid Fox, and Other Such Animals

Rabies occurs in a dog as a conversion of its physical temperament into a wicked, malignant, and poisonous malice. This conversion happens either from the air or from food and drink. From the air, because intense heat burns its humors, which is why it becomes rabid in the autumn; or because intense cold congeals its blood, making it prone to...

<margin>
...blackness, because respiration is blocked and the body is constricted when the cold arrives. It can, however, hasten toward summer but not so much toward winter, as Aristotle notes in the *History of Animals*, Book 8. If it occurs through freezing, then it happens in spring or summer. From this it is clear that autumn rabies is the worst, and mid-day is similarly dangerous, but spring is less bad and winter is the safest. 

Regarding food: Note that a man would not immediately eat and wound another because human flesh is similar to man and provides good nourishment; however, some have sold such meat, which causes putrefaction. Note that all rabid conditions can be treated with honey. 

The question is asked: can a man become so rabid that by biting another he kills him? This is discussed in the following chapter. A man can indeed become rabid. Aristotle says in the *Politics* that man is a social and political animal; yet a man can be sicker with melancholic disease than a rabid one, because rabies is a type of melancholic disease. On the contrary, Aristotle does not list man here among the animals that get rabies. Rabies occurs first in the "marine dog" <note>likely a shark or seal</note> because that animal is very dry and its blood is easily converted into black bile (melancholy). 

One might ask: since foxes, hares, and wolves are also dry, why don't they always become rabid? I say because even if they do, they do not encounter humans as frequently as dogs. Because the dog lives domestically, it eats various and diverse foods that cause indigestion and putrefaction in the blood, leading to rabies; wild animals do not suffer such indigestions. 

I say, however, that a man can become rabid from an external cause, such as a dog bite. For instance, two men bitten by a man who had been bitten by a rabid dog incurred a fear of water (hydrophobia). A rabid dog's bite makes a man rabid just like a dog, as does a bite from a rabid wolf. Fifthly, I say it is not impossible for a man to become rabid from an internal cause; if a man's temperament—even without a bite—is changed into a fraudulent melancholic nature, it can lead to rabies, just as it can lead to cancer, leprosy, or other such conditions. The types of melancholy that can affect a man are infinite, and so it is possible for rabies to occur. Therefore, one must flee from melancholic and wicked people, for their saliva is poisonous. 

In response to the contrary: usually rabies comes from a dog bite. Therefore, the author provides the signs by which we recognize a rabid dog, comparing the rabid dog to the wolf and fox, and listing other animals that become rabid. 

Regarding the signs of a bite from a rabid dog: there are two types. First, certain dispositions that follow the bite; and second, signs that indicate whether the bite was from a rabid dog or not, because sometimes the signs do not appear immediately.
</margin>

...blackness, which is why it becomes rabid in the spring. From food and drink, it happens because the dog licks the blood of the slain, eats from carcasses, and drinks from putrid waters. Thus it is filled with putrid melancholy, causing its nature to change and its temperament to be altered, just as happens to lepers. Sometimes its body breaks out in abscesses and its color turns ashen. It stops eating and drinking. When it encounters water, it fears and loathes it; sometimes its hair stands on end and it trembles. This hair-standing is especially visible on the skin of its face. Sometimes it dies from this fear, especially at the end of the illness. 

Its eyes become cloudy and dark; it is always solitary and does not recognize its own master. You will see it with red eyes and a fierce, horrible gaze. It sticks out its tongue, foamy saliva runs out, and its nose drips. Its head hangs down and its ears go limp. Its back becomes curved and twisted to the side. If its tail is tucked, it walks timidly and drooping, as if it were drunk, sad, and distressed, stumbling at every step. When it sees a shape, it runs at it to attack, whether it be a wall, a tree, or another animal. It rarely barks when it attacks, unlike the habit of normal dogs; instead, it is silent and filthy. When it does bark, other dogs flee from its path. If it suddenly encounters another dog, that dog will fawn and become submissive but then try to flee. A rabid wolf is even worse, as are the other animals we have mentioned.

### Chapter 6: On the Account of Other Animals That Become Rabid

It is known that foxes and weasels become rabid. Some have said that many people have become rabid and bitten their own masters, falling into the same mania that happens with other forms of rabies.

### Chapter 7: The Condition of One Bitten by a Rabid Dog

When a rabid dog bites a person, it initially appears to be nothing but a painful wound like any other. Then, after a few days, corrupted thoughts and strange sounds appear...

<margin>
The condition is evil. The author handles it in two parts: first, the signs; second, he teaches how to distinguish between life-bearing (survivable) and death-bearing (fatal) conditions. 

Note that this poison is very deep-seated, and because melancholy is slow-acting, this poison does not cause much pain at the start of the bite. This is clear because later, the patient has nightmares that infect the brain, and the imaginative and memory powers are altered. Dryness in the body causes spasms and the corruption of the imagination. It makes the victim sometimes crave light and other times flee from it. In the final stages, it leads to fainting, heart damage, and symptoms of a stroke (apoplexy), which is the ultimate damage to the brain. It leads to the loss of sense and motion, which is why the patient cannot tolerate being spoken to or called.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book III, Treatise 6, focusing on the specific pathology of rabies (hydrophobia). The text shifts from general human bites to the terrifying signs and symptoms of a rabid dog's bite, including medieval theories about the transformation of bodily humors and the strange "dog-like" forms reportedly seen in patients' urine.</meta>

# Book III

<margin>The severity is shown by many signs taken from various authorities. First, assess the bite. Then, distinguish the signs. First this. Second, assign the causes of the symptoms sought. There, they said. Note that fear of water and not recognizing oneself in a mirror, or misjudging it, signifies the ultimate malignancy and a transformation in the brain. Therefore, it follows that death follows; for a poison received through another medium <note>likely referring to a bite through clothing</note> is not of such great power, which is perhaps why those two men escaped. Note secondly that the diversity in this power depends on the diversity of the bodies suffering it and the diversity of the dogs; for some are more rabid, others less so.</margin>

And since he [the author] discusses it, he places the signs taken from many experienced men. It is doubted whether the urine of one bitten by a rabid dog can appear as dogs, and it is not the same with poison from a human and from this dog in the disposition of the body; but a bite from a serpent does not produce urine in which a serpent appears, therefore nor does this. Second, where the material, the agent, and the place do not concur, generation cannot happen; but the material of a dog is the menstrual fluid of a bitch <note>medieval medical theory often associated animal generation with menstrual blood</note>, the agent is the seed of the male dog, and the place is the womb. In the opposition, let it be noted: likewise, from a contradiction, Averroes <note>original: "Auenzoar," though often referring to the lineage of Andalusian medical thought including Avenzoar and Averroes</note> posits that if the urine is strained, nothing appears of the form of such dogs in the cloth, but if it is left within, it will appear in the urine. Now he says the matter is fleshy. The *Conciliator* <note>original: "conciliator," referring to Pietro d'Abano, a 13th-century physician-philosopher</note> replies in item 179; at the end he says that these forms are the result of the separation of the substances in the urine. Because every effect is drawn out by the strength of the acting matter and the suitability of the material, which here coincides, since that poison is excessively hot and dry, being sharp like a gadfly. For everything that is reduced from something else retains a mark of that from which it was reduced; for the principles that have arisen attest to what they generate. For the material in which the effect is considered is subtle, moist, and easily changeable according to Galen. Because of this, the strong effect of the dogs can assist and appear in the urinal. How does the *Conciliator* resolve this? It happens that nothing appears to remain [if strained]. That, however, is persuaded by the formative power of the seed. Also, the disposition of the urine in the vial—as they denote large grains at the top of the urine, at the bottom, or in the middle—is due to the rheum <note>bodily discharge</note> which the parts distribute through the skin. These are the *hypostasis* <note>sediment in urine</note> and the *circulus* <note>the ring at the top of a urine sample</note>, along with other contents. Here the *Conciliator*, whom I, Gerard, have added to Gentile <note>likely referring to the commentator Gentile da Foligno</note>, responds that this poison, because it is hot and dry, is very powerful, and therefore it induces the effect from that other thing from which it is said. This reason is doubly false: because some poison from a rabid dog is cold and dry, since he is rabid from melancholy produced by congealing. Secondly, this is the cause: because the poison of serpents is hotter and drier than that of a rabid dog; therefore a serpent ought more so to appear in the urine. For the declaration of this, I premise a probable mode. First, that the superfluity separated from an animal through the act of the final digestion (that is, the third) is that which is in this superfluity; it is the power of the composition of the members from which the action is separated. Second, that the foam of the rabid dog is decided everywhere, even made around parts such as the heart, brain, and liver, as is manifest enough. Third, that what is powerful enough to change the matter to a certain temperament can change it to the figure following that temperament. Fourth, if all poison injected by a bite disposes all the humors of the body according to its own temperament, then the form of that animal follows. Fifth, that this does not happen except from a rabid dog is the cause. If the poisons of other animals arrive by killing first, whence all other humors of the body are governed by the animal or by the temperament of the poison, then other poisons will not be able to make the forms of their animals appear; but so it is. Then, reasoning, I say: that the poison of a rabid dog is slow to kill, and therefore all the humors of the body are first dissolved into a canine disposition, and therefore they are ejected with the urine having a canine temperament, the liver acting there; because the canine heat disposing it, they are reduced to a canine form. I infer from this: that if the poison of a rabid dog kills quickly, it will not have made these marvels appear from which it might appear. And sometimes, if some serpent delayed killing as a dog does, it could make these things appear; and perhaps without this, the humors are now more fit to be transformed into canine ones and are conserved more quickly for us because of our natural figure. See other things regarding the accidents of protection. Note regarding the proposition previously made in the discussion of the person who said to me that in a man bitten by a rabid dog, the signs, figures, and forms of a dog ought not to appear. He argued thus: then in the urine of a menstruating woman, the forms of a woman ought to appear. Secondly, this is false as is the consequence: because a menstruating woman is no less able to be restored than a dog is to a man; for then the menstrual blood and sperm can be made poisonous, as in Book 5, Treatise 1, Chapter 3 on epilepsy. Similarly, on account of the great delay it makes in the body before it kills, the various digestions could form such female forms in the urine. Simply no less—rather more principally and immediately—the menstrual blood alters the members which have to digest, separate, and produce urine, than the rabies of a dog alters when it bites someone in the hand or foot; therefore etc. Third, because those forms in the urinal are either in thick matter or in subtle matter. It happens that with the urine something subtle, dewy, or vaporous escapes from the humors, and then those forms of dogs are fleeting in the collection of urine, just as the figures of clouds in the air quickly disappear; and of these Averroes speaks. Or, because the urine is thick and more compact, then something fleshy and more constant could more likely appear. And thus the contradiction of Avenzoar ceases. But regarding what is commonly said—that dogs are heard barking in his belly—I do not affirm it; but they themselves make voices like dogs. It is doubted: since the blood is of a canine temperament, why does the dog not urinate dogs? I say that the blood is compact and the matter of the members is all transformable into that. It is doubted why the saliva of a dog that is not rabid cannot induce a canine temperament. The solution: because the heat does not overcome it. But it is doubted: if a rabid human bites a human, whether the urine would show the form of a dog or a man. It is replied that either the man will take the malice and the rabid effect, and if any figure appears it will be in the form of a man; or he is made rabid by a dog biting him, and thus the form of a dog will appear. To the first of the three, it appears alone; to the second, it is replied that neither the agent, nor the matter, nor the place is near here; therefore it is not a dog but a likeness. In many cases the urine is subtle on account of dryness; therefore sometimes it thickens on account of the melancholic evacuation. It is retained on account of dryness, the expulsive power failing. Concerning the marvels: because from this it is seen that as the man is made like a dog, it is so marvelous that his superfluities appear in the form of a dog, so that the whole body is tempered like a dog. Therefore, if the form of the man could be fortified, the figure would tend toward the figure of a dog. He speaks here of the behaviors and the canine temperament. And similarly of his superfluity, namely of the dog or the man, where urine, saliva, and sweat are concerned; why if they are taken in, they introduce the sharpness of madness or otherwise from the superfluities—that is, from what remains of the dogs in the eating of a morsel or where he drank. You have seen that it is not so. He teaches how to judge concerning safety or death.

<column-break/>

<margin>The poison of some is sharp and hotter, and thus it is summer-like and autumnal, and of males and youths; of some others, however, it is weaker and thicker, as in winter and spring, and of females, the old, and children. Therefore, it can kill quickly or slowly. However, it is not believable that it could stay for 7 years before taking effect and hide its malice until then. They said: he posits the cause of the appearance, namely the fear of water. First he posits the opinion of others. Second, he disproves it. And still it can be explained in two ways according to the *Conciliator*. Over 7 years, the temperament is twofold: one is acquired over a long time so that it is made natural in the member and makes it incline to the contrary. When, therefore, it is acquired from a rabid dog, it is acquired from a near time and is not natural; therefore it makes one desire the contrary, namely moist things, and does not make one abhor them; and this is what he says: "declination." This is the inclination and appetite toward that which is suitable and not near, i.e., acquired from a near time. There is another thing which will not be: because the acquired [temperament] declines to the contrary because it would desire water which would be contrary to it. This was the mind of the Lord <note>likely referring to a specific teacher or "Dominus"</note>; it is poorly applied to the text. The *Conciliator* in item 179: second, an equal temperament will not induce it from a near time, but naturalness is induced so that it may desire it. Against both: because if a confirmed temperament makes one desire the like and abhor the contrary, then a person with a "hectic" fever <note>a dry, wasting fever</note> would desire dry things. Second, the adversary will say that the temperament of this poison is lively and confirmed, and they fear water, and therefore they would abhor contraries. Otherwise, it is explained according to the reason of the container. If their temperaments love dryness through an alteration toward dryness, it follows that they declare the accidents which properly follow dryness; the falsehood is clear, because from dryness of the brain follows the persistence of wakefulness, which these people do not have. Whence Razes <note>Rhazes/Al-Razi, 9th-century Persian physician</note> says: some say they fear water because their temperament is changed to dryness even in the brain, and always this moisture is contrary to them. If it were so, they ought to have continuous wakefulness. And this is what Avicenna says: "declination," this is the inclination toward that which nearly fits the temperament, namely the dry, whence comes the wakefulness which is nearly joined to dryness just as the effect of a near cause is from those things which were not, i.e., toward which it does not incline, namely vehemently.</margin>

...and he is unable to urinate, and his belly is mostly dry. Among his marvelous dispositions is that he is ready to bite a man. But if he has bitten a man after his own eating, that happens to that man which happens to him, and similarly it happens from the superfluity of his food. And not one of them was terrified of water who escaped through a cure or without it, especially when he saw his face in a mirror and did not recognize himself, or when a dog was imagined in him, except for two men. For they, as the first believe, lived in such a disposition. And the dog itself did not bite both of them; rather, no one bit them both except a man whom a rabid dog had bitten. Before the terror of water, the cure is near. And sometimes it kills within a week and similar periods up to six months, and the temperate span is 40 days. And some have said—though it is not believed—that sometimes one is terrified after seven years. Some have said, and it is like a redhead, he is not terrified of water and they love to roll on the ground, except that their temperaments have already chosen dryness, wherefore they abhor the contrary of the temperament and love the suitable; and toward this discourse there is no "declination." For declination toward that which fits the temperament is near from those things to which it does not run. And of a healthier disposition is the one whom this dog bit, from whose bite mostly...

<margin>and the disposition is like rage and murmuring, and a mixing of reason, and responding without that which is asked of him; and you see his extremities spasming by contracting them toward himself; and he flees light, and the jumping of the veil <note>likely involuntary muscle twitches or starts</note>, and hiccups, and thirst, and dryness of the mouth; and he flees from pressure, and loves the approach of light, and sometimes he abhors light; and his members are disturbed, especially their faces, and their voices become hoarse; and they weep in fear of water and moistures; and as often as water is brought near them, they imagine a dog, wherefore they fear because of it; and sometimes they are not terrified, rather they are nauseated by it; and sometimes they love to roll on the ground. And sometimes a projection of sperm occurs to them without desire, and it leads without doubt to spasm and [unclear]; and sometimes it reaches a cold sweat and syncope and death. And sometimes he dies before these dispositions from thirst; and sometimes he desires water, then cries out because of it when it meets him; and sometimes he swallows it, whereby he is strangled by it and dies; and sometimes he barks like a dog and there is a hoarseness with it; and sometimes his voice is cut off. And he becomes like an apoplectic, not being able to endure being shouted at. And sometimes he urinates fatness in which are marvelous fleshy things, which are as if they were animals and like small dogs. But in most dispositions, his urine is subtle, and sometimes he urinates black, and sometimes his urine is retained, whereby he is entirely unable to urinate.</margin>

...near time it is not natural, therefore it makes him desire the contrary, namely moist things, and does not make him abhor them; and this is what it says. Declination: this is the inclination and appetite for that which is suitable and not near, i.e., acquired from a near time. There is another thing which will not be: because the acquired [temperament] declines toward the contrary, for he would desire water which would be contrary to him. This was the mind of the Lord; it is poorly applied to the text. The *Conciliator*, item 179: second, an equal [temperament] will not induce it from a near time, but naturalness is induced [so that] he may desire it. Against both: because if a confirmed temperament makes one desire the like and abhor the contrary, then a "hectic" person desires dry things. Second, the adversary will say that the temperament of this poison is lively and confirmed, and they fear water, and therefore they would abhor contraries. Otherwise, it is explained according to the reason of the container. If their temperaments love dryness through an alteration toward dryness, it follows that they declare the accidents which properly follow dryness; the falsehood is clear, because from dryness of the brain follows the persistence of wakefulness, which these people do not have. Whence Razes says: some say they fear water because their temperament is changed to dryness even in the brain, and always this moisture is contrary to them. If it were so, they ought to have continuous wakefulness. And this is what Avicenna says: "declination," this is the inclination toward that which nearly fits the temperament, namely the dry, whence comes the wakefulness which is nearly joined to dryness just as the effect of a near cause is from those things which were not, i.e., toward which it does not incline, namely vehemently. 

And "of a healthier [disposition]" he teaches how to signify by signs taken from the disposition of the bite. The cause is because: the poison is evacuated. The author says with them [the signs], security is made as is demonstrated, and yet it [the urine] is passed after three days of treacle <note>original: "tri_vniace," referring to Theriac, a famous universal antidote</note>. It is doubted why these things fear water, whence it is called the bite of the *linifaticus* <note>a term for the 'water-fearer' or 'lymphatic'</note> or *hydroformis* or the disease of tetanus; it is also in Apuleius' *Metamorphoses* Book 6. In this, the cause is given on account of dryness, against which they desire but they fear. Likewise, the "hectic" or "marasmic" <note>wasting</note> person is drier and yet does not fear it. Others say, as Cassius? the *Conciliator* recites, and others whom Gilbertus <note>Gilbertus Anglicus, a medieval medical author</note> narrates, that the cause is the inhibition of some moisture in the pores of the stomach and brain. Therefore it is called *linifaticus*: upon the arrival of the imagination of water and even things, that moisture is moved, and thus it is moved toward the contrary. On the contrary, in many passions it moistens the brain more than in this passion, as in apoplexy, paralysis, and lethargy. And the mode which Dionysius? appropriates to himself, and yet so says the *Conciliator*, is that they fear water and all ground and polished things because they imagine for themselves the viscera of dogs and dogs. The reason is that it happens to some in wakefulness as it does to others in sleep and dreaming. For there is a movement of the "species" <note>mental images</note> from the memory to the imagination, as the *Principator* <note>referring to Avicenna</note> says; Averroes in the 3rd *Colliget*. Their brain, therefore, receives many melancholic vapors as others do. These vapors make that which is not appear to be, because it alters the imagination. And the imagination [acts as the] *Principator*, and then in water and in a mirror, he believes it to be, although it is within their brain. But he believes more that it is the form of a dog because that vapor is infected by the canine temperament, which he has made for this—the memory of a dog from the "species" of a dog through the bite. But why more in water and in a mirror? It is replied: because that is reflective of figures and the air is not. Whatever they see, therefore, they judge; they judge it to be a dog because the imagination is so infected. The second cause is because this vapor coming to a mirror and polished surface is refracted; for a certain vapor is thick. Likewise, whence of itself a certain part is subtle and this is not seen unless it is imagined or reflected; and it is seen in a form in which of itself it is not seen, just as appears from vapors in the eye in those prepared for a cataract; because on account of subtlety, determined forms do not appear unless they are condensed. Thus these vapors existing in the eye, coming to the eye, are refracted and condensed at the water and mirror, appearing in the form of dogs. I believe he wants to say "univocally": that these vapors are judged by the eye looking at something deep like water or something polished, or at something rare like air. Or they want to say that on account of the noted subtlety, they do not...
