# Fen VI. Treatise III.

<margin>It appears that unless it is resisted or aided by something polished. Against these sayings, first, a person should be terrified by any visible thing. Likewise, the cause seems to be the corruption of the spirit. Against the second saying, vapors in the eye are judged or determined by looking; therefore, if vapors are in the eye with fear, they will fear when looking at a person just as they fear water. Likewise, these vapors are melancholic, and thus thick. It is wonderful, then, that it is not resisted. I say, therefore, that this symptom communicates to another poison, such as the core of the spirit. But concerning the second point, it must be said that, as everyone says, this condition is a significant affliction, as noted by Al-Abbas in Book 8 of his Practice, Avicenna in Book 5, and in the *Practice of the Canticles* [of Avicenna]. All conclude, and thus all generally proceed toward the evacuation of the melancholy. In this affliction, many corruptions of the imagination and estimation occur, such that water is feared; whence Galen, in the book *On the Benefits of Theriac*, says they fear water, and yet due to great dryness they have a desire for water, but they abstain from drinking due to alienation <note>original: "alienationem," referring to a state of mental derangement or "being beside oneself"</note>. And if it were asked why there is such a corruption that they fear water and not air or earth or the like, it must be said that the cause is nothing other than such a melancholic humor. Just as if I were to ask you why a certain melancholic person imagines himself to be a glass vessel, and another imagines that the sky is falling—there is no other cause than such corruption from that mode of melancholy. Because of this, note that as was said earlier in the first book of the Practice, the diversity of corruptions is imagined according to the truth of those things about which a person is concerned, just as a tanner is altered by things concerning tanning. When this happens from the diversity of the humors impressing themselves, and according to the different species of melancholy, the imaginations are diverse. Among all humors, that which is apt to create such corruptions of the imagination is the melancholic humor, as Aristotle says in the third Problem. Thus, the cause of such fear of water is such an impression made by that mode of melancholy. And because Avicenna understood this from the chapter on melancholy, he did not include it here. It is argued to the contrary: if such a melancholic humor did this, it would seem the patient would have false imaginations regarding two things: first, because it happens slowly, and second, because they drink and are not strangled. Therefore, the imaginations are not so corrupted toward fleeing water that they would not drink it. To the first, it must be said that the thickening of that poisonous humor is required, and thus it does not impress immediately. Likewise, a specific determined melancholy is required, and not just any melancholy produced by a rabid dog, but such as comes from a dog and not from a man. To the second, it is said that in those who drink water, reason and intellect overcome the corruption of the imagination, as happens to the sick: some eat by their own will, and then in the movement of the water through the media, the corruption of the imagination prevails over reason, and then it strangles them. Such is that corruption of melancholy.</note></margin>
It occurs. And because of this, when one moves toward the drinking of theriacal medicines, the blood is secured from the fear of water, as you should know.

<margin>On the difference between the bite of a rabid and non-rabid dog. Chapter VIII.</margin>
**S**ometimes a dog bites men, and if the confirmation of its form and the visualization of its condition are brought forward, its cure is required. Its cure, insofar as it is a wound, is consolidation <note>closing the wound</note>; but insofar as it is the bite of a rabid dog, it is the discharge of pus and keeping it open. For if it is consolidated, perdition is in it, which is why it needs a sign by which its condition may be known. And among the things they have said in this regard is to take a royal nut <note>original: "nur regal," likely a walnut</note> or another and place it over the wound and leave it there for one hour; then take it and offer it to a hen. Then, if the hen refuses it, the dog is rabid; and if she eats it and does not die, then the dog is again [judged] rabid. And take a piece of bread and smear it with what runs from that wound, whether it be blood or not, and throw it to dogs. If they refuse it, then the bite is the bite of a rabid dog. And they said that among its signs is that when cold water is poured over it, the body becomes hot by its succession, though I say this sign is not specific.

<margin>On the cure. Chapter IX.</margin>
**I**t is necessary in the beginning of the matter that you do not allow the wound to consolidate; rather, let a dilation be made if it was not wide, and do with it the suction and placement of cupping glasses as was told to you in the chapter on the bites of serpents. And the time in which the wound ought not to be consolidated is the space of forty days. And if you have drawn [poison] out in the beginning and then did not consolidate it, you will perform a very helpful operation. And if an error has occurred and it is consolidated, then it must be reopened and pursued to the end. And you must place upon it opening medicines when you have pursued it in the first days, such as opopanax, walnut, and garlic. And a plaster of pitch with opopanax and vinegar; and take one *kist* <note>a unit of measure</note> of vinegar—it ought to be vinegar—and one pound of pitch and three ounces of opopanax. Infuse the opopanax in the vinegar until it is dissolved, then mix all; and perhaps garlic, onions, and rocket <note>arugula</note> again, and beet and other compounds and simples suffice. And with beet again, sometimes elecampane is placed. And perhaps it will be necessary for you to use corrosive medicines such as *alcalcadico* <note>vitriol or copper sulfate</note>, and subsequently butter should be applied. And among the dilating agents is to take three parts of salt, two parts of sal ammoniac, eight parts of vitriol, sixteen parts of burnt gallnuts, four parts of rue, ten parts of coral, three parts of burnt copper, three parts of flower of copper, and two parts of leek seeds; let it be placed over it, sifted with honey-water. And it is necessary in the beginning to make the patient sweat by whatever means possible, from walking and bathing. And you ought not to hurry in the first days toward evacuation <note>purging</note> so as to be occupied in drawing it to the exterior; for evacuation sometimes helps the poison to penetrate to the depths and prohibits the attraction to the exterior. And since it draws

<column-break/>

the humors to the interior, it then draws the poison with them. When, therefore, you have drawn out what is possible for you after two or three days, then occupy yourself in the evacuation of what perhaps has already penetrated. And if the attraction [to the surface] was not done and negligence occurred, then evacuation at that hour will be more necessary and it is better that it be stronger. And if you see the repletion increased, perform phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note>; if not, then do not. And when you bleed them, do not let them look at their own blood, especially at the end of the matter. Let the cathartic be that which leads out the melancholy, such as hellebore and pills of hellebore and similar things that are necessary, and *hiera ruffi* <note>a traditional compound medicine</note> is wonderful for them. And among the things that should loosen them is wild cucumber. A cathartic confection for them: Take two ounces each of chebulic myrobalans, one ounce each of opium, five drachms of golden Indian salt, one ounce each of polypody and Armenian stone, one ounce and five drachms of agaric, and two ounces of black hellebore; let two ounces of the pills made from all these be given. When, therefore, strong cathartics have loosened the bowels, it is then necessary to administer every day or two an enema that does not harm the anus; let it be oil and beet-water or a fatty laxative. And administer diuretics and thinning agents after that, and sweet wine, especially old wine with sweetness, and cooked wine again, and milk; and wine is of vehement help to them, and the most necessary things are the quality of food and its moistening, for that is necessary for the case. These include things like... <note>text becomes specific to diets</note> and bread soaked in cold water. And give them water in which iron has been extinguished many times. Brassica, onions, and garlic are among the foods that resist poisons and cut them and repel them from the body where their use is not excused, although they are medicines themselves. And as for you, prepare and give them the great theriac to drink, and a medicine made of crabs, which is specific. And it is said that the *Theriaca Diatesseron* is vehemently beneficial to them, and similarly the *Theriaca Alanesca* which we shall describe; and feed them river crabs. And it has already been proven that one should take the flesh of river crabs burnt over the wood of white vine in an equal quantity with which it is ground, and gentian charcoal over that same wood in the same quantity. Give it in a drink with pure wine; let its dose be four spoonfuls in that wine, and both must be ground like a fine powder <note>original: "alcohol," used here in the ancient sense of a fine powder, not a liquid</note>. And of this again there is another description: take the charcoal of river crabs caught while the sun is in the sign of Leo, roasted in an oven or in a bronze vessel in equal parts; and let there be five parts of these, five parts of gentian, and one part of pepper; let them be ground and mixed together, and let the dose in the first days be one spoonful in water, and after the passing days let two spoonfuls be given in drink, and similarly add to it up to four spoonfuls. And from medicines...

He places the cure: first the local cure, second the disposition, third the description of plasters, fourth the ingenuity regarding the symptom which is the fear of water. The second part starts at "And it is necessary," the third at "this is the plaster," the fourth at "some have said." Under "it is necessary," he first places the cause of the cure by placing three medicines, the second being simple... he gives the cure when they do not yet fear, and second when they do fear, starting at "And when..." The first part has two sections: first, the cure in the beginning so that they might live in the process; second, the cure in the process. In the beginning, he treats three things: first, the general cure in their evacuation; second, the cause in the food; third, in the medicines. Note that the beginning, according to Avicenna, is taken as up to three days. Therefore, Rhazes in Book 8 of *Ad Almansorem* says the cure in the beginning should be understood as the local cure previously mentioned, as appears there, and not as the Counselor says. For first he proves that in the beginning if evacuation ought to happen, second when it ought to happen, third he shows what kind of substance should be used for evacuation. It is said that evacuation should be done with pharmacy, second when with phlebotomy. And if you see... if it happened that, as was demonstrated above in the general chapter, evacuation is suitable when the poison is spread in the body; it is spread after 2 or 3 days as Avicenna hints and will place below; therefore evacuation is suitable then. Either you have protected what you could from the poison and then it is suitable, or there was negligence, and then it is more necessary to evacuate and more strongly. He shows how evacuation should happen with phlebotomy. It is doubted whether the judgment is the same for phlebotomy and pharmacy, as he says that poison with evacuation in the beginning by phlebotomy empties the body and moves the humors. Whence Rhazes in the second book of *The Continent* [says] laxative medicine is not consumed because it draws the poisonous matter to the interior; if it is necessary in the process, let it be done, etc. It is doubted why he says not to look at the blood; because it is liquid, lest the fear of water and liquids generally begins to be incurred. For men commonly fear at the sight of blood in the process of much blood; that then he must be cured by a cathartic. He places the cause in feeding: first he places suitable foods before medicine, second specific suitable ones. First he names some, second he describes some... it has already been proven. # Book III

<margin>
2. Regarding the properties of the medicine: I say that it contributes primarily through its specific property, and this we must believe. Likewise, it aids in the provocation of urine and the expulsion of poisons to the interior parts. Likewise, the power of the gentian root <note>Gentian was a staple of medieval medicine, used to treat exhaustion and as an antidote to poison.</note> contained within it is effective, as is noted in the second section. To the contrary, some say that authors could not explain all its effects. To another point, I say this case is hotter and drier, and thus it is beneficial.

Regarding medicines, it is doubted whether medicine made from crabs <note>River crabs were often burnt and ground into powder for rabies treatments because they were believed to have a cooling property that countered the "heat" of the poison.</note> is suitable at the beginning of the illness. According to Avicenna, yes. Likewise, in the second part of the *Continens* [of Rhazes], it says they are given before the fear of water appears. Likewise, Galen in his *Book of Secrets* mentions it. Therefore, that old man used to cure patients with medicine from crabs. On the opposite side, Avicenna says yes. The reason is because it has the property among all things that cure. Regarding Avicenna, he says that perhaps he is speaking of a medicine of larger composition; otherwise, it must be said that Avicenna proves—indeed concedes—that you should give it in the beginning when you doubt if the patient might fall into the fear of water, because this is the middle ground where it is most suitable.

a. If however. First, he places the cure in the process through medicines taken locally. Second, he clarifies certain things. Third, he places the cure through those things that resist corruption and through phlebotomy <note>phlebotomy: bloodletting</note>. And note the reason why a larger dose is given: because the poison has made a deeper impression. And the wound does not remain open. On the contrary, whether after three days or five, it must stay open for at least 40 days. I say that the text requires interpretation or correction; that is, it should not be opened just to dilate it, but it is sufficient that it is open. It seems Avicenna understood this when he said: "For the time for dilation has passed." Avicenna's reason is that by then the poison is already dispersed.
</margin>

...having narrated these things, that is, the last resort for them is the medicine from Spanish flies <note>original: "cantharidibz." These beetles were used as a drastic measure to induce urination.</note>; I shall speak of them in their own section. The medicine from crabs does not fail in a drink at the beginning, unless it is for one who already has the fear of water. And sometimes he puts in its description gentian, which is half the amount of the sea-crabs. If, however, you treat him after two or three days, you must double the dose of the medicine of the two deer in the drink, compared to what you would have weighed out if you had treated him at the beginning. The arrangement of the other medicines we shall mention is similar.

And if it is after seven days, then the doses should be tripled, and then use the scalpel with laborious cutting and perform vigorous cupping and suction. And if you have treated him after many days have passed, then do not bother with dilating the wound or laboring excessively over it, for it will harm the patient without much utility; rather, it is better if it just remains open. For the time for dilation has passed after the first three days and those close to them, because the poison is already dispersed. Be content then that the wound remains open and join to it the rest of the regimen by giving theriac <note>theriac: a famous "universal" herbal jam used as an antidote to all poisons</note> in a drink and administering other things, for the poison is dispersed within four days—or even in a shorter time. Indeed, it often kills within one week. And without doubt, it spreads more quickly or slowly as we have said.

There is nothing among the drawing remedies quite like cautery <note>cautery: branding or burning the flesh with a hot iron to "seal" the wound or draw out toxins</note>. Thus, when a long time has passed and one fears an error, hasten to use a large cautery. There is no attraction or corruption of the poison's substance like the attraction of cautery. If something prohibits this, administer medicines that take the place of cautery, such as an emplaister <note>emplaister: a medicated paste spread on cloth and applied to the skin</note> of salt and "reddening" medicines like a mustard emplaister and similar things. 

Do not put him in a bath at this hour at all. For if you bathe him, you will kill him. Yet it is said that sitting in a tub <note>original: "tuna," likely a typo for "tunna" or "tinna," a bathing vat</note> is among the things that help, and I believe that is in the early stages. Cold is among the things to be avoided. A covering is necessary for you at this hour and after it, so that you may protect him; therefore, protect him and do not permit him to see his own image. 

If you see him already tending toward health, gradually have him use balanced exercise and baths, and pour warm water over him and rub him with oil. When he reaches the time of the fear of water, then do not be afraid as long as he is not so far gone that he does not recognize his own face in a mirror. For they said: "Perhaps this man recognizes his own face, and perhaps he imagines that the thing in the mirror is a dog." 

And give him that drink we mentioned of water in which iron has been extinguished <note>Chalybeate water: water "strengthened" by dipping hot iron into it</note> with the skill we shall describe. For it is an excellent cure. Use every skill to give him water to drink. And if it is necessary for you to bind him and use force, then emplaister his stomach with cooling things. And indeed, wine mixed half-and-half has been tested and brought wonderful help. And at this hour, a medicine of this kind helped:

**Recipe:** Rennet of a hare, "Lacie" earth brought from Alexandria, juniper berries, and gentian—four gold coins' weight of each. Mix with honey; the dose should be the size of an Egyptian bean.

**Another:** Sealed earth <note>Terra sigillata: a medicinal clay stamped with a seal of authenticity</note> and juniper berries, both in equal parts; fox rennet, four parts; hare rennet, five parts; roots of round birthwort <note>original: "aristol. rotūde"</note>, laurel berries, amomum, and wild rue—three gold coins' weight of each. Let a mass be cooked with sweet wine and mixed with honey. The dose is one bean.

**Another:** Sealed earth, eight gold coins' weight; "aldemest" grains; hare rennet, six parts; gazelle rennet, thirty-two parts; gentian roots, four parts; myrrh, four parts. Let them be gathered with honey and kept. The dose is the size of a chickpea with warm water.

Among the compound medicines is Galen’s theriac, close to what we described in the past. 
**Recipe:** Burnt river crabs and gentian, five parts of each; frankincense and calamint, three parts of each; sealed earth, two parts. Let him take 3 drams <note>original: "ʒ" (the symbol for a drachma or dram)</note> of this in powder while fasting with warm water, and 2 others in the evening. Let him use this for many days. 

**Another:** Take large fat Spanish flies <note>original: "cātaridarū"</note> with the feet, heads, and wings removed, 1 part; peeled lentils, 1 part; saffron, spikenard, cloves, cinnamon, and pepper—a small amount of each. Let them all be ground perfectly. Prepare the Spanish flies and mix with water, and let troches <note>troches: medicinal lozenges</note> be formed from them, each containing 1 dram. Give one troche in a drink every day with warm water. And if a stinging in the bladder occurs <note>Spanish fly is notorious for irritating the urinary tract.</note>, let him drink a decoction of peeled lentils and almond oil or raw and cooked butter. And let them enter a bath every day after the drink, where he should sit until he urinates in the tub. And let moistening food be administered, like "alessidabegi" <note>An Arabic-derived term for a type of stew or medicinal broth.</note> with a fattened chicken; and let him drink wine and guard himself against the cold.

### Abbreviated description of the medicine of Spanish flies.

Take Spanish flies according to the number and soak them in sour milk for a day and a night; then pour off that sour milk from them and change it for other sour milk, and let it sit for a day and a night. Do this three times. Then let them be dried in the shade and ground with as many peeled lentils as there are flies. Let troches be made from them, the dose being 1 dram with wine or warm water. When he has drunk it, let him be made to sweat by walking or by covering him up. If that which he drank causes him distress, let him drink a sugary mixture of cooked butter or oil, and let him use the tub and urinate in it. When he has mixed blood [in his urine], he will then be safe from the fear of water.

### Emplaisters and similar things to draw out the poison.

Assafetida is a good emplaister, and it is said that its application with the liver of a mad dog is very helpful, as the community testifies. And another is applied as an emplaister and drunk, and salted fish meat is a good help. And among those things that draw the poison from him with strength: place upon the bite the urine of a young man (especially with nitre), ashes of vine alone, vinegar, mint with salt, and opopanax <note>opopanax: a medicinal gum resin</note> is very wonderful. And the leaves of a wild cucumber are of great help for this, as is fennel root. And they said sometimes a wonderful help is conferred if the place is softened with fish glue many times. And again, let it be emplastered with "sad ants" <note>original: "formicis tristis." Likely refers to a specific species or condition of ants used in topical remedies.</note>. And again, take copper flowers and salt, four parts of each; calf fat, two parts. Let an emplaister be made from them. And again: bindweed, 2 drams; borax, 2 drams; sea foam, 1 dram; salt, 4 drams; goose fat, 10 drams; and as much henna oil as is necessary.

Some said, such as the physicians, that when he fears water, then give...

# Book IV

<margin>
He applies his ingenuity against <term>hydrophobia</term> <note>original: "accis qd est timor aq," referring to the fear of water seen in rabies</note>. These predators follow after the bite of the leopard and the dog...

"And they said..." and this is in two parts. First, concerning the poison of certain land-dwelling stingers; second, sea and land; third, certain other sea creatures. ## On the bite of the leopard from the genus of the lion and the wound of their claws. .L.x.

These predators and those that live wild are not like dogs or humans; rather, their teeth and their claws are not empty of a poisonous nature. Therefore, one should first run with a treatment that draws out the poison, and then with one that heals the wound. For drawing it out, even a small thing may suffice.

<margin>
There were certain notes: the female is larger than the male by a push of nature because of a primary excess, as in certain types of fish; because of a honey-like heat coming to dry out, they change into the opposite, as happens in birds, as is demonstrated in the first book on the complexions of animals. If, therefore, it is in the scorpion, it will be because of great dryness. Note: in this our region, this diversity is not found; for all are black in the upper part, though some are lemon-yellow elsewhere. It is doubted whether the poison of the scorpion is hot.
</margin>

## On the bite of the crocodile. .L.xi.

Let him who the crocodile bites be guided by the regimen mentioned before in the chapter on the bite of a non-mad dog, drawing out the poison. From this, the bite may not escape, and the person may be saved. And let this be done with things that are like <term>nitre</term> <note>a mineral salt, often potassium nitrate</note> and honey. And when the crack and the line of the wound are separated, treat it with deer fat, goose fat, and honey; then let it be healed. Its own fat is even more helpful for its bite. They said that for the healing of its wound, when a crocodile gnaws a part of someone's body, the fat of the crocodile is used.

## On the bite of the monkey. .L.xii.

In the case of one whom a monkey bites, let there be a drawing out of the poison that was in its bite. And let that be done with things like a plaster of ash, vinegar, and honey, or bitter almonds, figs, and unripe grapes, and <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide, used in drying ointments</note> with salt and fennel root. The litharge, dissolved in water, soothes its swelling; and let it be covered with <term>nigella</term> <note>black cumin</note> and honey, or the herb and honey.

## On the bite of the cat. .L.xiii.

Sometimes from the bite of a cat, there occurs vehement pain and a greenness <note>likely referring to a sickly, pale, or bruised hue</note> in the whole body. Their treatment is as follows: a plaster of onion helps, as does a plaster of <term>calamint</term> <note>a medicinal herb in the mint family</note> of the field, and a mixture of water, and again with a second plaster made from nigella and sesame with water.

## On the bite of the weasel. .L.xiiii.

They said that its bite brings swift pain; its color is inclined toward a dark shadow. And its first cure is the treatment we described from a plaster of onions and garlic, and a mixture of water with pure wine over both. Unripe figs with barley flour are also beneficial. And indeed, in the book of <term>theriacs</term> <note>antidotes for poison</note>, it is said that if a plaster of it is placed over its bite, and over the bite of a mad dog, it is a good help, healing immediately.

## On the bite of the shrew and the alcale. .L.xv.

They said that this animal is smaller than a weasel in its size. And its color is inclined toward ashiness with a subtle thinness, and the length of its mouth is extreme, and its lip is at the very end. They also said that when it sees an animal, it leaps upon it and hangs from its testicles. And some said its form and color are like a mouse, but its snout is sharp, its eyes are small, and its teeth have three rows, of which some are twisted over others in their upward turn. And some said that from its bite there occur vehement pains and a piercing in the body, and the appearance of redness in the places according to its teeth. It happens in the area around the bite that a blister full of bloody moisture forms on dark bases; and that

<column-break/>

which they contain is dark, and they split away from what is beneath them: white flesh of the color of a nerve emerges, having layers. And sometimes a certain burning appears in them, and sometimes it corrodes and falls away; rather, it first runs with pus, then putrefies and corrodes, and its flesh falls away. And sometimes the matter reaches a piercing in the intestines, difficulty of urine, and a cold, corrupt sweat.

**CLEAR NOTE.** They said that one should place upon the location <term>galbanum</term> <note>a bitter aromatic gum resin</note> on its own or with vinegar, and soak it with water and barley flour and sour syrup. Let the animal itself be split open and placed upon the wound, or <term>pyrethrum</term> <note>pellitory-of-Spain, a root used for its heating effect</note>, or mallows, or <term>centaury</term>, or mustard—all of this if there is no swelling. When swelling appears, give the bark of sweet pomegranate decocted with wine, or rocket, or <term>water-mint</term>, or <term>walnut</term> with wine, or boiled with wine, or rocket, or water-mint, or walnut with wine, or pyrethrum, and rocket seed, and <term>safflower</term>. And among the things that are strong helps are <term>buckthorn</term> with sour syrup, or <term>opopanax</term> <note>a medicinal gum resin</note>, or gentian root, or the rennet of a lamb and the rennet of a kid—both are very good. And milk with sour syrup is a useful ointment for it. And they said that among the most helpful things are the juice of laurel leaves, and fresh laurel leaves with decocted wine, or rocket, or a decoction of <term>southernwood</term>, or a decoction of <term>bindweed</term> with wine. Again, <term>storax</term> <note>a fragrant resin</note> is good for it when given in a drink with wine, and similarly when the aforesaid things are eaten in their proper preparation. Now, therefore, the corrupt flesh falls away when the wound is treated by its own extraction.

### Fifth Treatise: On the sting of small poisonous creatures and their bite. .L.i.

In this treatise, I will address the stinging of scorpions, tarantulas, wasps, and spiders, and those that follow their course; and I will begin with those among them that have stingers.

## On the species of the wild scorpion. .L.ij.

Some have said that the female scorpion is larger than the male: for the male is slender and small, while the female is fat and large. The stinger of the female is finer, and the stinger of the male is thicker. It happens that some scorpions have two stingers; at least, so they think because they leave two holes at their sting. The sting grows red, the rest of the body grows hot, and sweat breaks out again. Now, the scorpion is large compared to others, and the wind prevents its multitude when it flies <note>some ancient/medieval sources believed scorpions could fly or be carried by the wind</note> from falling, because it travels with the wind from region to region. And in the arrangement of the tails of scorpions, there is diversity. For among them are those that have six segments, whose malice becomes strong in the time when the star <term>Aldebaran</term> <note>original: "altiebara"</note> rises, and its bite kills; and among them are those that have fewer. And some have believed that scorpions come in nine colors: white, yellow, red, ashen, iron-grey, and green; and among them are golden ones having black tails and tail-tips; and among them are those of a wine-like color, from whose strike a needle-like puncture is felt and a harmful pain; and among them are smoky ones, and from their bite comes laughter and a confusion of reason.

## What happens from their sting. .L.iij.

It happens to its sting that it appears from its onset as a hard, red, and painful swelling, hanging down; sometimes it inflates and sometimes it subsides, and one imagines the swelling throughout the body. And it is compressed with grains of salt. Pains occur suddenly, and a puncture like the prick of a needle; this is followed by sweat, a trembling of the lip and its coldness, and the expulsion by vomiting of a viscous matter which congeals upon it; and the hair stands on end, a breaking of the hairs, and trembling and coldness of the extremities near the wound follows, and a softening of the whole body, and a swelling of the groin area, and a retention of urine. And a swelling happens in the belly, and perhaps moisture is stirred up over the bite nearby if the bite was in the lower parts. And there occur swellings of the armpits and excessive belching, especially if the strike was in the upper parts, and the color is altered. If, however, the scorpion is of vehement malice, the symptoms will be very bad: the aforesaid conditions flow together, and the sting is like a branding iron in its burning. The whole body suffers stiffness with cold, and a viscous moisture rises over the lip which congeals upon it, and similarly moisture runs from the eye, then congeals as <term>rheum</term> <note>eye discharge</note> in the corners. And there is an alteration of form, and the anus protrudes, and the breasts swell, and the tongue thickens, and the teeth grind, and the posterior limbs spasm, and sometimes the teeth are set one upon another and do not open—and this is a bad sign. Galen says: if by its strike it finds the arteries, fainting will occur; or if it finds the nerves, spasms will occur; or if it finds the veins, putrefaction will occur.

**CLEAR NOTE.** Let it be cured by common rules and by steaming with things like salt, millet, and similar things. The first thing you do is suction with its proper conditions, and the rest which were mentioned regarding extraction. And let sharp, subtle medicines of swift inflammation be administered over it, such as garlic and pyrethrum. <term>Asafoetida</term> <note>original: "Aez tercen?" (likely "asa foetida")</note> is among the better medicines for it. And similarly there is the "Idaean hazelnut" and the "otis hazelnut," and a herb whose leaves are sometimes like those of marjoram, spread over the earth in a circle whose diameter is one palm, and in its flavor there is a viscosity whose taste is like the taste of fresh <term>jujube</term>, and it is drunk with water and soothes the pain immediately. And they mentioned again herbs and trees with their names which I do not know. And again a tree whose trunk rises above the earth the height of one finger, then equal branches are born...

# Book III

...and so: because it inflames and forms an abscess. The opposite is noted in the third [book] of *On the Internal Parts* <note>original: "de interioribus," referring to Galen's *De Locis Affectis*</note>, specifically in the first chapter, where it says that a puncture from a scorpion burns; therefore, it is like being struck by hail and snow. Likewise, in the last [part of] the eighth [book], it should be said that the common scorpions found among us have a cold venom. Avicenna [discusses] this regarding what is eaten and drunk. The sign is that they induce symptoms of cold, and medicines that are vehemently hot are beneficial, such as a bit of <term>monkshood</term> <note>original: "napello," or aconite</note>. There is, however, a certain scorpion called the *iarta* which has hot venom, as Avicenna mentions below and in the second [book] of the *Continens*. ¶ To the contrary, it should be said that it becomes colder because of the accident [of the sting], but the abscess occurs because of a defect in the specific part; from there, the humor is drawn out, or it has the property of attracting [poison] even if it is cold in its temperament.

And it is necessary after taking the garlic and wine that he be prepared in a place of intense heat. And if it can be arranged that his preparation be over the vapor of hot water, it will be helpful. And the intent in this is that he should sweat; the intent in sweating is to move the materials to the exterior. Sweating in a bath is of vehement help to him. **A Good Theriac.** Long <term>aristolochia</term> <note>birthwort</note>, gentian, laurel berries, caper root bark, <term>colocynth</term> <note>bitter apple</note> roots, wormwood, rhubarb, yellow veins, white vine; let it be gathered with honey. **Another good one.** Half [part] of field rue, Ethiopian cumin, half [part] of *andachoca*; of all these, a sufficient amount of vinegar to make a gum that will stick together with the vinegar; gather the medicines, and let the dose be one *aureus* <note>a weight of about 1 dram</note>; do not add more than that, for in it there is fear [of danger]. Indeed, if it is necessary after another hour to add more, give it in a drink... among others. **Another theriac.** Take of garlic and nuts, one part each; of dry rue leaves, <term>barley meal</term> <note>original: "alfit"</note>, and myrrh, half a part of each; let them be prepared with milk, and let the dose be three [drams] with wine. **A good theriac for it.** Of <term>castoreum</term> <note>a secretion from beavers</note>, white pepper, myrrh, and opium; equal parts of all; let <term>troches</term> <note>medicinal lozenges</note> be formed from them, of which the dose is three *obols* with four [drams] of wine; it also benefits the bite of the *rutela* spider. ### On the Algerarat Scorpions. .L.iiij.

These are like scorpions having a hunched body and sharp tails, and their venom is hot. They multiply in Alcoz and in Ascari Bononito and near the mines of *Alaniude*. When they bite, it is not cared for in that hour, but rather in the morning or afterward; then distress occurs and the color [of the skin] changes. And sometimes jaundice occurs, and the tongue swells, and the place of the puncture becomes ulcerated, and the person urinates blood. And sometimes the bowels are constricted, and perhaps his condition turns toward destruction [death], and it begins with a thumping of the heart and <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting</note>. It must not be neglected because of the mildness of its [initial] sting, for it is an evil venom.
**THE CURE.** After the common cure, the best treatments are to cauterize the place and the application of bitter *laciuce* water, dandelion water, barley water, and all things that are cooling, specifically when the swelling becomes strong. And the best of the tested cures for it is <term>citron</term> <note>original: "fawicū malorū"</note> with cold water. And some have said the root of *spolij*, when drunk with water, helps. And <term>elecampane</term> <note>original: "enula"</note> is a good medicine for it according to...

# Fen VI. Treatise V.
### 3

...is described. And the *alhascari* theriac <note>A specific compound medicine named after an Arabic source or region.</note> is good, the description of which is this: take bark of capers, gentian, Roman wormwood, and round birthwort, one part of each. Let them all be ground, and let the dose be two drams in weight.
¶ Another theriac for these: take dried dandelion, leaves of sour apples, coriander—equal parts of all. Let the patient take as much of the powder as fits in the palm of the hand. And when a vehement bloating occurs, let the patient sit in endive water and the juice of cooling herbs. And if heart palpitations occur, a syrup of *alsemiz* apples <note>original: "de malis alsemi," likely a specific variety of apple used in syrups</note> and a barley drink (*savich*) of apples is beneficial, along with very sour milk and camphor lozenges. And if the distress is stronger, then fruit waters with cooled rose oil should be applied. Now, if nature retains [the bowels], let him be given a clyster <note>an enema</note>, and if he urinates blood, let him be bled and the treatment for bloody urine administered. And if the tongue swells, let the vein under it be bled, and let him gargle with endive water and vinegar syrup. And if corrosion occurs at the site of the bite, let it be treated with a sharp medicine, and in those parts, smear it with Armenian bole <note>a medicinal red clay</note> and vinegar. And let it be treated with the cure for malignant ulcers. 

### Chapter VII.

<margin>Species of spiders, *ascehibe*, and *rutelae*.</margin>
**Regarding the *rutelae*** <note>In medieval medicine, *rutela* usually refers to the tarantula or other large, venomous spiders</note> which those who study and have experience in these matters say are of six species; thereafter they have differed in the interpretation of the properties of each species. For some of the ancient physicians said that the first species is called the *albarbasiōn*, round in shape and grape-colored—and by "grape-colored" they mean a color leaning toward blackness. And the second is called the *anchos*, and it is of a broader body than that round shape, and in the parts where its mouth is, there are scales appearing, and there are three protruding bodies sticking out that are thin and smooth. And the third is the *murkiōn*, which is the size of a large bee called an *agerus*, and its color leans toward ash-gray, and small red protrusions cover its body, especially near its back. And the fourth is the *saglauco-slon*, whose whole body and head are hard, and it has wings like those of a large ant. And the fifth is the *suction*, for it has a long, slender body, and there are spots upon its body, specifically near its head and neck. And the sixth is the *furbulēntis*, for it has a long body of a green color, with something like a stinger under its neck. And this physician placed the symptoms of the stings of all species of *rutelae* into one category, but another added specific symptoms. And another man, different from these two, said the *rutela* is an animal like the spider called the *alfebed*, which is a hunter of flies, and that its species are many. And according to what Galen said, there are twelve species, and the worst of them is the Egyptian one. For among them is a red one which is a round spider. And among them is a white one having a round belly and a small mouth, star-patterned, and it has a sharp back with shiny lines. And among them is a yellow, hairy one; and among them is the "grape-like" one (*uvea*) called by this name. And among them is one whose middle of the head and feet are short, leaning toward the rear; and when it wants to sting, it balances on its feet, and when it wants to drink, it vomits a little moisture, and it is more slender than the first grape-like one. And among them is the ant-like one, similar to an ant, having a red neck, a black head, a white back, and a sting of various colors. And among them is the wasp-like one, red and similar to a wasp. Then he lists the symptoms for each of them. And among them is the *alkefenati*, which is named thus because of its smallness; it is as if it were a round chickpea, having a small mouth, a whitish belly, white feet, and many hairs. The Egyptian one, however, which was mentioned before, is malignant, having a large belly and a large head, similar to the insects that fly around a candle <note>i.e., a moth</note>.

<margin>On what happens to one bitten by a spider generally, and on the distinctions between them.</margin>
**Galen says** that the bite of a *rutela* does not result in the same things as the sting of a scorpion, because it does not block the veins by damaging them, although it usually causes difficulty in breathing. And he who described the species of *rutelae* and named them by the first names says that all of them share a common appearance at the site of the bite: in the first hours, the site of the bite is red, and in most cases there is a greenish coagulation of blood in which there is itching and that which follows it. And sometimes it extends as far as the leg, and others added that there is very much protrusion and swelling there. And the first physician said that coldness always happens to the nervous members and the bones, namely those like the knees, the hips, the back, and the spine; and perhaps the whole body becomes chilled, trembles, and feels gooseflesh. He says there is also vehement, crying pain there, along with sleeplessness, a yellowing of the complexion, and it is imagined in the eyes that both are wetter than they usually are, and tears distill in frequent drops; and the patient feels a sensation like emptying and evacuation in the lower part of the belly and near the pubic bone. 

### Chapter VIII.

<column-break/>

Nature begins to expel watery matter both upwards and downwards, and sometimes there appears in that matter something like a spider's web. Swelling occurs in the groin and testicles, and a contraction of the joints like a spasm occurs, the extent of which is perhaps unequal [on both sides]. Pain in the mouth of the stomach and nausea occur, and the body emits a cold sweat; perhaps the head incurs pain like the headache of a patient suffering from *birsen* <note>original: "birsen," a medieval term for phrenitis or inflammation of the brain or its membranes</note>. And others added that a yellowness of the face and a heaviness of the body occur, along with a movement of the urine, which is perhaps associated with a stinging sensation, and sometimes it comes out looking like a spider's web. A vehement tension occurs in the nerves, knees, and pubic region, and similarly in the stomach; there is a shortening and halting of the tongue, and the pains become severe. The first authority says that from the sixth species, according to what has been told, there occurs vehement pain in the intestines and a very severe rigor with very much trembling. 

¶ One distinction which Galen and others stated is that from the bite of the red spider, a small pain of fast duration occurs. In the bite of the black or variegated one, however, there is strong pain with gooseflesh, cold, trembling, heaviness in the heart, itching, putrefaction, and a softening and flow of the bowels. In the bite of the star-patterned one, there is strong pain with itching, gooseflesh, stupor, heaviness of the head, and a softening [weakness] of the body. From the grape-like one (*uvea*), there occurs vehement pain at the site of the strike, coldness of the whole body, gooseflesh, trembling, spasm, a cold sweat, loss of voice, stupor in the whole body, swelling in the belly, tension in the penis and pubic bone, involuntary vomiting, and turbid urine. The "great smoky" one is malignant, and from it occurs stomach pain, frequent vomiting, headache, a persistent cough, and difficulty in breathing, killing quickly. From the bite of the yellow hairy one, there is very strong pain, and trembling and cold sweat occur with bloating of the belly, and it often kills. And some of them add in their account of a certain grape-like spider that it causes an erection of the penis and *priapism* <note>a persistent, painful erection</note>, loss of voice from the expulsion of sperm, and spasm—though that is not certain from the things we have verified. The bite of the ant-like spider is vehement but only slightly painful; however, it causes blistering of the body and heaviness of the tongue. From the *cruespali*, swelling occurs at the site, along with spasm, a deep sounding voice, and weakness of both knees. The *alkefinati* is malignant, whose symptoms are of the same kind as the grape-like spider, but they are more difficult. The Egyptian one is truly malignant and causes a vehement headache and a depth of sleep [coma], and death and life hang in the balance.

---

### Chapter IX.
**The cure** for them is again administered through drawing out [the poison] and suction; the site is smeared with salt water, and the theriacs mentioned before in the chapter on scorpions are given. Baths and tubs are the fastest things for quieting their pains. For when they are moistened in the tub, their pain is quieted, but if they leave it, the pain returns, so they should be bathed every hour. 

A good theriac for the *rutela*, the sea dragon, and kinds of snakes: they said it should be given as a drink for the bite of those like the *surutrugo*. A medicine of this kind: take bdellium, birthwort, root of the celestial lily, Celtic nard, rocket seed, pellitory, carrot seed, black hellebore, cumin, asphodel, leaves of *agebin*, pomegranate heads, hare rennet, cinnamon, river crab, storax, poppy juice, and balsam fruit—one dram of each. Let them be ground and prepared, and formed into lozenges, each of which should be one *aureus* <note>a weight equal to a gold coin</note>. One dose should be given in a drink with wine, and seeds of *andacocbe*, cypress nut, and celery seed. 

¶ Remaining medicines: Pine nuts, Ethiopian cumin, leaves and bark of the *aldulb* tree <note>the plane tree</note>, *andacocbe* seed, black chickpeas (especially the field variety), and "large grains" are very good; also southernwood seed, dill seed, birthwort, tamarisk fruit, and the juice of houseleek and wild lettuce. The dose of any of these should be the weight of two *aurei* with wine. And again, wine in which a cypress nut has been boiled, taken with cinnamon, crab broth, goose broth, and a decoction of asparagus roots with wine and water. And among those things given to them in a drink, equal parts of birthwort and cumin are set down; let the dose be three drams in warm water. 

¶ A theriac proven for this: namely, ten drams of fennel flower (*nigella*); five drams each of carrot and cumin; three drams each of cypress nut and its root; two drams each of nard, laurel berries, round birthwort, balsam fruit, cinnamon, gentian, *andacocbe* seed, and celery seed. Let them be prepared with honey, and let the dose be the size of a nut with old wine. 

¶ External applications (*epithems*) and similar things: Among the good ones for these is the ash of fig wood prepared with wine and salt, water chestnut (*culcasia*), a sponge soaked in vinegar and squeezed out, and birthwort with barley flour prepared with vinegar, and leaves of *alcorfus* <note>likely wild celery</note>, leeks, shepherd's purse, and birthwort with fig wood. A good plaster: take pomegranate bark, birthwort, and barley flour with vinegar; let them be applied after washing the wound with salt water. And among the ointments is the oil of *andacocbe* applied as a warm lotion. And among the lotions is warmed sea water, any salt water, a decoction of *alcorfus*, and a decoction of nuts.

Book III.

...pressed.

### Chapter X: On the *sciebi* and its cure.
<note>original: "sciebi," likely a Latinization of the Arabic *shabth*, referring to a sun spider or solifuge.</note>

This is like a spider having long legs, and they say: from its bite occur stomach pain, vomiting, difficulty urinating, and agony, and it is deadly; the Egyptian variety is the worst. I say, however, that I do not know whether this Egyptian one is that which was mentioned in the chapter on the *rutela* <note>original: "rutele," referring to a venomous spider, likely a tarantula or phalangium</note> or another. Its cure is the same as the cure for the *rutela*.

### Chapter XI: The spider, its signs, and treatments.

From its bite, many gases occur in the belly along with shivering, coldness of the extremities, and the penis becomes erect. Their cure is of the same kind as the cure for the *rutela*. It is beneficial for them to take wine in some quantity, dose after dose throughout the whole day, to place the bitten part in wine, and to sweat in a bath. Among their medicines are black cumin <note>original: "nigella"</note>, wine, and dried rue with wine alone or with cypress-grass.

### Chapter XII: Two animals mentioned by certain wise physicians.

Both are again of a kind for which memory has passed. However, I do not know about them—whether they were included in those mentioned previously or not—but they are recognized by the fact that they have four mandibles. That wise physician says both are of the *rutela* kind; one of them is broad, having white feet, and upon its head are two protrusions, one of which descends into the back part of the head in a straight line, and the other crosses through it in width, which makes one imagine that it has two mouths and four mandibles. In another place on the protrusions, there are two lines that create that illusion. From their bite occurs what occurs from the bite of scorpions: vehement pain, whiteness of the color of the bite, a wasting away of the face and head, and insomnia. Its cure is the cure for the *rutela* bite, and the medicines more specific to those than to the *rutelas* are basil <note>original: "ozimuz"</note>, opopanax root, *alandacocba* <note>likely an Arabic plant name</note>, and southernwood <note>original: "abrotanum"</note>.

### Chapter XIII: Another animal called the *tubarse*.

The wise physician reported on this animal and said: from its bite occur vehement pain, redness, and difficulty urinating. They provide the patient with tamarisk fruit, field cumin, walnut leaves, and sweet wine.

### Chapter XIV: The "vulture-louse" called *debeperice*, *meluce* in Greek, and *ragarius* in Indian; this beast is like a louse or a small *alcandam*.
<note>original: "pediculus vulturis," likely a specific parasitic insect or tick.</note>

Galen says it is small and one does not guard against it, and perhaps the bite is not seen—

### Chapter XV: On the bite of the *gala*.
<note>original: "gale," likely referring to a shrew or a small venomous lizard.</note>

Its bite: it is among those things that cause blood to break out in the urine, through the nostrils, in the anus, from the stomach through vomiting, from the chest and lung, and from the roots of the teeth. Sometimes the fear in this matter is magnified because it does not respond to medicine. Its cure is similar to the cure for the *algerarati* <note>another specific medical term or authority</note>. Among the things specific to it: the bite should be joined with bezoar <note>original: "bezabar"</note>, lettuce juice, and red sandalwood. Lettuce milk, capers, raw butter, sealed earth <note>original: "terra sigillata," a medicinal clay</note>, zedoary <note>original: "algeduar"</note>, purslane and its juice, and its mucilage are all beneficial to the bite, along with other cooling things such as endive water, lettuce water, gourd, and cucumber.

### Chapter XVI: The *altamula* and the "wolf-pig."
<note>original: "porcus lupi," likely referring to woodlice or millipedes.</note>

These are beasts having many feet and sharp poison; they are judged similarly to the vulture-louse and wasps.

### Chapter XVII: On the wasp.

They have a more vehement heating effect than the bee. From its bite occur pain, redness, and swelling. Among the large wasps, there is a kind having black heads and many stingers, which is deadly. The large ones indeed require greater caution and are more harmful, because they perhaps lead to spasms and weakness of the knees; but even from the bite of the small ones, fear is sometimes magnified because they cause blisters to occur and weigh down the tongue.

### Chapter XVIII: On the cure.

Let what you know be applied from above by suction. If the fear is magnified, then what provides relief is a weight of half a *semis* of "holy-salt" <note>original: "sanfuci"</note>, for it calms the pain in that place; or three palmfuls of dry coriander. Let the patient take known cooling juices and cooling drinks. Sometimes ice is applied like a salve, and it helps. Among the things that assist are mallow water, *albedarungi* water <note>likely a type of cucumber or melon</note>, and cucumbers, which are wonderful in their properties; also beets, nightshade <note>original: "solatrum"</note>, crushed sesame and its leaves, and also figs, vinegar, mud, and verjuice <note>original: "aqua acreste," juice of unripened grapes</note>. Also, cow dung prepared with vinegar is helpful, as are watercress leaves and fresh laurel leaves. They also use opium, black henbane seed, and camphor; let it be smeared with cold juices and covered with a linen cloth soaked in cold water, and let mud and vinegar be smeared around it. Likewise, the herb *slumis* with vinegar is wonderful, as is the green growth <note>algae</note> that occurs on running water. Also, according to what some think, let it be steamed with *ralea* water and smeared with the milk of a fig.

<column-break/>

Also, soot from a cooking pot with vinegar; and sometimes compresses <note>original: "embroce"</note> are made from the decoctions of these waters. It has been tested that when a limb is left in hot water for one hour and then suddenly changed to salt water mixed with vinegar, the pain is immediately calmed. And regarding rubs: there are flies <note>original: "muscae"</note>, for they themselves calm the pain.

### Chapter XIX: On bees and their cure.

It has the same primary characteristics as the wasp, except that it leaves its stinger in the puncture. Its primary cure is the cure for wasps.

### Chapter XX: The flying ant and another thing similar to it.

That has the primary characteristics of the bee but is healthier. I say that among those having a point and a stinger, there is a thing similar to a flying ant; however, it is much longer, and it is not in its length [lacuna?]. It has long spider-like legs, yellow or even longer than the legs of wasps. The belt it has is yellow, and it has no skill for building its own dwelling as wasps do; rather, it builds it from mud, having wide openings, and it produces young like a spider, which come out of their hollows and walk with the gait of a spider as if they are being drawn from behind; they fly, and in my judgment, they are like wasps.

### Chapter XXI: The gecko and the lizard.
<note>original: "stellio," the starred lizard or gecko.</note>

When it bites, it leaves small, thin, black teeth in the site of its bite, and the place does not stop hurting and itching until they are removed with a blade or a hood passing over them to take them up and collect them, whereby the pain is calmed. Sometimes oil and ash extract the teeth; then let the place be sucked and placed in hot water. It is said that eating dandelion <note>original: "altararacum"</note> is very helpful for its bite. If the pain is magnified, let the *rutela* theriac be given in a drink.

### Chapter XXII: The animal having forty-four feet.
<note>The centipede.</note>

It is recognized by its entry into the ear; sometimes it is one palm in length, and it has twenty-two feet on each side. Sometimes it walks backwards, and sometimes its disposition changes. According to what is said, it has a certain poison with which a small pain occurs that is calmed immediately. The flower of the asphodel is among its theriacs; sometimes the administration of salt with vinegar is sufficient for it.

### Chapter XXIII: On the bite of the salamander.

It is thought that it is a beast similar to a lizard, having four short, cautious feet. Some think that it does not burn, and if it is thrown into a hearth, it extinguishes the fire. For the one it bites, there occur vehement pain, bloating in the body, heaviness of the tongue, a stinging sensation, tremors, and stupor. Many times a blackening of the limb occurs in a rounded shape, and it may fall off.

### Chapter XXIV: On the cure.

Again, some say its cure is the cure for the Spanish fly <note>original: "cantaridis"</note>. More specifically, they are cured by being given pine resin from whatever pine it may be with honey in a drink; let a decoction of ground-pine <note>original: "camepitheos"</note> and a decoction of lily with nettle leaves and oil be given to them in a drink. Among the remedies are those where they give them boiled frogs and give them the broth of the same in a drink, and plaster them with the flesh of the frogs, and sometimes they eat them. Likewise, the suction of land and sea turtles, boiled, is helpful.

### Chapter XXV: Land and sea scolopendra.

I myself do not know it, and it is not unlikely that we have already completed the account of them. Some have said that from the bite of the land variety, the bite becomes dark and turns a rose color, or it reddens slightly with a clear redness—but only very slightly; and there occur vehement pain and itching in the body. The bite of the sea variety is of a watery color. It is similar, so that its cure is the cure for the *rutela* and similar creatures. Some have said to plaster it with salt or ash with wine, or ash prepared with squill vinegar, or with burnt sesame and wine, and let it be bathed first with the best oil and hot water, and then let the plaster be placed upon it.

### Chapter XXVI: The sea scorpion.

Finally, from the bite of the sea scorpion occur bloating of the belly and a dropsical appearance; sometimes an involuntary exit of gas occurs from it. One must be careful in identifying it. Its cure is the cure for the sea dragon and the *rutela*. A certain person in whose speech one cannot trust said that the water scorpion has a hot poison.

### Chapter XXVII: The sea spider.

It seems its characteristics are close to the characteristics of the sea scorpion.

### Chapter XXVIII: On the bite of the red sea-frog.
<note>Possibly the anglerfish or a similar venomous marine fish.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the final sections on venomous creatures and theriacs into the seventh "Fen" (a major division of Avicenna’s medical encyclopedia), which focuses on "decoration" or the aesthetic health of the body—specifically the hair and skin.</meta>

<margin>Hair. In the preceding <term>Fen</term><note>A "Fen" is a specific section or book within Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*.</note>, etc. Here he determines the nature of decoration: which this Fen receives in the book's beginning, the tenth Fen, etc. Decoration is observed regarding hair, the skin, the habits of the body, and the extremities. Here he does three things: secondly, the second part begins in the second treatise, and in the fourth treatise; from which it appears how the rubric is verified which says that this Fen contains three treatises although it actually makes four. For there are three in the first division. First, he makes known to us the hair. Secondly, he gives his intention in speaking. Thirdly, he proceeds. Hair: whenever speaking of hair, it is taken strictly and broadly for all hair. Here I respond for all hair. Thirdly, it must be considered that Avicenna defines hair through the four causes: the material, the form, and the efficient cause. The material is twofold: that from which a smoky vapor arises, and the pores themselves. The form of the hair is its end, which is length along with thinness and roundness. He indicates this when he speaks of the pores; for a pore is a narrow opening so that according to this form it has its shape. The efficient cause is touched upon when he says "coagulated in the pores," which is either the heat or the coldness that coagulates that vapor. One might doubt why he did not touch upon the "final cause" (the purpose). It must be said that for many hairs there is no purpose; for others, a purpose is implied. He placed the purpose of some elsewhere, such as the hair of the eyelids for protection. There is a common final cause in respect to the body. Secondly, he collects specific ones for certain parts, like the hair of the eyebrows and eyelids: which are ordered lest any dirt enter, as Galen says in the 14th chapter on the utility of parts. Also the hair of the head and the beard: the beard is for the decoration of men, etc. Fourthly, it must be considered that Avicenna first implies the material for the growth and perseverance of hair: for this material is a viscous, oily moisture. For hair arises above the pores where it is extended and increased. That moisture is fit to maintain the continuity of the hair, and this he proves by a comparison to oily trees like the olive, etc. For a muddy or dry terrestrial moisture, or one that is less thick and watery, is not fit for continuity. It is doubted whether hair is generated from smoky vapor: because the material for generation and nutrition is the same; but hair is nourished by the oily-viscous, as Avicenna says, therefore it is generated from the same. Its material is multiplied by a multitude of moistures and diminished by their decrease. But the material of hair is multiplied by a multitude of moisture, as seen in the <note>original: "problemate"</note> problems of Aristotle, specifically problem 58, regarding why eunuchs are not bald. It is clear hair is most multiplied on the head because the brain is moist. According to Avicenna and Galen in the second book on temperaments, chapter 5, it must be said that the material of hair is in a vaporous form, not a humoral one. I respond that in this vaporous form is the material of hair which seeks to go to the places where hair multiplies. It is a dry vapor and thus called smoke. It is a sign that in hot and dry temperaments... I respond that such a vapor must be the material of hair as is most conformable to the temperament. But smoky vapor is dry and hair is dry in the body as Avicenna proves. It must be considered, however, that although it is a dry vapor, it is not entirely dry since it must have a connective moisture, otherwise it would not be a continuous body. Because its continuation is successive and permanent, it has a moisture that is somewhat fatty and viscous.</margin>

# Because many of the wise have erred, thinking that it is a malignant evil invading animals and bodies and that it leaps at them from afar to bite them; and if it cannot bite, it blows a harmful breath upon them, and from its movement a great and swift destruction follows. I say it is similar to those that must be cured by the Great Theriac <note>A famous ancient universal antidote made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh.</note>, which is of its kind.

### Summary of the treatment for poisonous sea reptiles. Chapter 28.

# They said further that they should be cured with theriacs and with those things by which "cold poison" is cured, and with the medicines for <term>rutelae</term><note>A type of venomous spider or small creature.</note> and their specific theriac.

->Fen VII on decoration, which consists of three treatises.<-
->The first treatise is on the condition of the hair; in it is dandruff.<-

### Chapter 1.
# Hair is born from a smoky vapor which coagulates in the pores and grows above them, specifically through that which is assumed from nourishment, and especially when there is a viscous, oily moisture in the body; if it is not entirely watery, just as in an oily tree the leaves do not fall. And it has already been said in the first book concerning the darkening of hair and its greying, and other colors. Truly, that which depends on the discourse on decoration is the management of its substance, its growth, and its blockage. And the management of its number, including its multiplication and its thinning. And the management of its quality, including its thickening and thinning and lengthening. And the management of its shape, including its straightening and curling. And the management of its color, including its blackening, lightening, and whitening. And we shall speak in this treatise according to this intention.

### On the destruction of hair. Chapter 2.
# Hair is destroyed or diminished either because of a cause in the material or because of a cause in the thing in which it grows. And the cause in the material is that it is either diminished or [its quality] is advanced. Smallness of quantity is either a cause which submerges it or alters it, or it is a cause of the smallness of the substance of the form; thus is the smallness of the smoky vapor in children and women because of the multitude of moist vapor, which is why a beard does not grow on them. The smallness of the substance of the root is either due to an accident or because nature consumes the cause. That which is due to accident is like what happens to those recovering from illness, when long diseases like <term>phthisis</term><note>A wasting disease, usually tuberculosis.</note> and <term>hectic fever</term> dry them out; hence there does not remain for them the material from which hair is fed, so it falls and does not grow back, just as happens to plants that are usually irrigated when they are not watered. This also happens to eunuchs because of their similarity to women in moisture and coldness, due to the condition of their testicles. Because of this, that which generates the seed is crushed in them and cooled, and

<column-break/>

this coldness reaches the higher members and cools them; therefore their moisture does not resolve into dryness. Or that which is resolved does not remain in the pores because of its smallness and thinness, but rather escapes. And if it happens that it flows like a heavy substance upon the head. That which is from the way of nature is like baldness. For baldness happens because of the shortening of the material of the hair. And this happens either because of its smallness or because of the brain being "submerged" by that which touches it from the skull; therefore it does not absorb it with that absorption it would have if it were unobstructed. That which happens because of a cause in the thing in which they grow occurs in three ways: either so that the hair material does not penetrate into it; or so that it penetrates but is not retained; or so that it is corrupted within it and resolved into an unsuitable quality so that hair cannot be generated. It does not penetrate except because of a blockage of the pores; and the pores are not blocked except because of an intense solidity due to dryness, as is the case with factors contributing to baldness; it hastens in a hot temperament because of the speed of its drying, and because of this, hair multiplies on the body and chest of those prone to baldness due to the heat of their temperament. For the little hair they have is difficult to pull out. Or it is due to the solidity of the scars of past ulcers, as is the case in <term>glabria</term><note>Smoothness or a hairless patch on the skin.</note>. That which is not retained is due to extreme thinness and the width of the pores, as is the case with some factor that prevents a beard from growing even until the end of life, or because of the dryness of the temperament. Thus the pores are constricted with the moisture of the temperament because of the smallness of the heat. Do you not see that baldness does not occur [in such cases]? And the residue of these hairs is weak and easy to pull out, as it is in women and eunuchs. That which is corrupted in the place is either due to a malignant humor, as in <term>alopecia</term><note>Loss of hair, often compared to the mange of a fox.</note> and <term>tyria</term><note>A skin disease causing scaling, possibly related to tinea or ringworm.</note>, or due to bad corrosive ulcers as in certain types of baldness. The cure for baldness is indeed difficult, although it is possible to repel it before it begins or to delay it. And because of that which Hippocrates said—that when bald men develop varicose veins, their hair grows back—he wanted it to be understood as those depilated by alopecia and similar things. The hair of the eyebrows and eyelids does not fall out quickly because their origin is thick, cartilaginous, and preservative. Because of this, baldness is delayed in Ethiopians and... <unclear>sigis</unclear> because their skin strongly retains their hair; for that which is hard is not easily pulled out, and because of this, the hair is diminished along with it. But...

<margin>First he speaks of the material of generation: afterward of the material of growth in another way. He speaks again about the material of growth being a fatty moisture; yet this is dry, so that the fatness does not exclude the virtual dryness, just as sulfur has a certain fatness yet is dry. To this it must be said that the material of eunuchs, in passing into the hair, passes into a smoky nature. **b** And now indeed it is clear. **c** Hair is created. **d** Now concerning the dispositions of hair: secondly concerning a certain general condition called dandruff. And this the second rubric says there. Every discourse is first in five parts: first on the condition of growth and deprivation, and on multitude and paucity; second on the condition of thickness and flatness; third on their splitting, though he made no mention of it; fourth on thickness and thinness; fifth on the condition of color. Just as fenugreek flour... also there... because of dryness... Borax... We have already spoken. For the first point of evidence, consider that deprivation and paucity are unsightly; presence with multitude is beauty. Therefore Avicenna investigates the cause of paucity and deprivation of hair and their cures. And first in general, secondly specifically. You already know the cause in the generation of alopecia. First he investigates the cause, secondly the cure or management. Medicines for deprivation... the first in two parts: first he provides the division, second he declares the members. And the cause in the material: he says when he speaks of the efficient cause that it is included as will appear. First he declares the cause in the material, second the cause in the thing in which they grow. **d** That which happens because of a cause in the thing: first he puts the division, second he declares it. **e** Just as it is smallness. In the first part, he wishes the cause of the destruction and paucity of hair to be on the part of the material.</margin>

### Chapter 4: On making hair grow strongly on the face.

And for these cases, there is a cure for baldness, the reason for which is the placement and falling out of the eyebrows and similar parts. All the medicines we shall mention in the chapter on <term>alopecia</term> <note>Literally "fox-mange," a general term for patchy hair loss.</note>—and every method of treatment involving the rubbing of the head until it reddens, and the administration of medicines of strong attraction and resolution—are helpful in treating baldness and in making hair grow in depilated areas, the eyebrows, and the beard. And in the bark of the willow root mixed with oil, there is a wonderful strengthening and preservation, along with a darkening effect. The medicines which it is our intention to describe here (although they are also helpful in alopecia), after we have performed what we said at the end of the chapter on hair preservation, are as follows: take fresh <term>cantharides</term> <note>Spanish fly; used here as a counter-irritant to stimulate blood flow to the scalp.</note> with the feet and heads removed, dried in the shade. Let them be ground in violet oil, or boiled in it, or in olive oil until it thickens; then smear it where you wish, for it will cause blistering, and afterward the hair will grow. Similarly, the "honey" of the <term>marking nut (original: "anacardi")</term>, when placed upon the spot where hair has been lost, or if it is ground and mixed with oil of eggs and smeared on well—unless one wants it to be very strong—will cause the hair to grow. Or take the burnt hoof of a donkey and burnt horns, and let them be smeared on with sesame oil, for it is powerful. Also, <term>ants</term> with oil of ben are suitable for making hair grow; and among the common people, these are among the things that prevent hair fall. And among the things that have been tested is the house lizard, which should be killed, dried, ground, and smeared on with oil. And again, a grinding of "Pharaoh’s nitre" with beans. Among the lighter treatments is to make a plate or sheet of lead and place between two of them some hair oil or fat, and let them be rubbed together until it dissolves into a leaden ointment, and let it be smeared on; then fill the place with well-boiled fig leaves, which have a certain power. ### Chapter 5: On Alopecia and Tyria.

You have already learned what it is: alopecia is a bad humor remaining in the skin and in the origins of the hair roots, whereby it corrupts the roots, corroding them and preventing good nourishment to them. It is named **alopecia** because it happens to foxes (original: "vulpibus"). The difference between it and **tyria** is that in tyria, not only does the hair fall out, but the thin skin itself is corroded with it, as happens to a snake (original: "serpenti"). And perhaps it takes on the shape of a serpent’s scales. The matter which causes alopecia and tyria to occur is sometimes choleric, sometimes melancholic, sometimes phlegmatic, and sometimes from corrupt blood. This is signaled above all by what appears when the skin is scraped—by its color and by how it reddens when rubbed. Sometimes it is signaled by the preceding regimen and the symptoms associated with it. From these things, the dominant humor is known. Sometimes the speed or slowness of its cure is signaled by how quickly it reddens upon rubbing: this indicates the speed or slowness of the attraction of good blood to the area, although excessive rubbing may cause ulceration, which prevents the origin of the hairs.

### Chapter 6: On the Cure.

There is no doubt that the rectification of the regimen in this case consists first in the evacuation of that humor which causes it, and the introduction of foods that produce very good <term>chyme</term> <note>The partially digested mass of food; here referring to the quality of nutrients entering the bloodstream.</note>. These should be temperate, leaning toward sweetness, thin and clear, for this is more nourishing. A bath is helpful both before and after any rubbing. Let the practitioner begin first with the evacuation of the body from the causing humor with medicines that draw it out, or with <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>Bloodletting.</note> if the matter requires it. Then, evacuate the head using head-purgers, scents, and gargles mentioned in the chapter on cleansing the head according to each type of superfluity. Next, one must move to the skin to cleanse it of what has remained in it, and to resolve it. One must hasten in this so that the skin does not take on a permanent bad quality. There is no doubt that the medicines for evacuating these regions must be "cutting" and "resolutive," but without causing excessive dryness through intense heating; for if the skin becomes too hot, it may cause future hair loss even if it destroys the alopecia in the present. If the medicine is very hot, like the gum of wild rue, its heat should be broken with temperate oils or with thinning waters. Of these, the fresh is better; that which is over three years old is weak. The sign of a strong medicine is that its quantity should be reduced and its potency broken; it should be removed quickly from where it is smeared. The sign of a weak one is that it should be applied externally. It must be thin, otherwise it will not penetrate deep into the skin. These medicines should also provide strength and protection so the head does not receive more malignant matter. But this power should not be joined by extreme <term>stypticity</term> <note>Astringency that constricts tissues.</note>, which would prevent the medicine from reaching the place and penetrating its pores. Therefore, once the body is cleansed, these medicines should have the power to attract good blood and temperate vapors after the corrupt matter in the skin has been resolved, so that the resolution of the corrupt matter is followed by the attraction of good nourishment. When you administer these medicines, you must consider their impact. Begin with the weaker ones and observe the effect; if the patient is young...
