Secondly, it should be considered that **alopecia** <note>original: "alopecia o[ritur] ab alope. i. vulpe"</note> takes its name from the fox, and **tyria** <note>original: "tiria a tyro. i. serpente"</note> from the serpent. This is because the skin peels away either finely or in large quantities, sometimes continuously and sometimes rarely; and this is the defined form. Or it is because the hairs are shaped [like these animals], etc., though this does not please **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Aliaba"</note> in his 4th book, 14th chapter. It should be considered that he treats them as species of tyria. First, he lists the signs of various causes. Second, he treats the difficult cases, where he says "secondly." Sometimes it is not manageable. First, he commends the cure in general discourse. Second, note that here he declares the cause, and there the judgment on the regimen, which he explains sufficiently. First, therefore, he deals with local medicines. Second, with evacuation [purging]. Third, he lists the medicines for evacuation. Third of the medicines: first, regarding the power of the medicines; second, in the combination of their actions; third, he lists the medicines and local things which are mentioned where he says "secondly." And when you... third, and concerning those things which are needed.
</margin>

...tolerate the impression and remain unharmed, add to the strength of the medicine. But if the body does not tolerate it and the impression is too great, diminish the quantity and the mixture, and strive to produce an ulceration or a pustule—properly so in bodies of a light complexion, or due to age or the season. And if it leads to pustules and ulceration, come to the aid of the skin with fats and smear them over it; let it be **duck fat** or **hen fat**, treating it as a light cure. When the condition is thus calmed, repeat the treatment with a quantity the patient can tolerate. Small efforts will accomplish a great cleansing if you do not cease until the corrupt matter is resolved and good matter is attracted. The sign that the medicine is making an impression is that the skin turns red with fewer rubbings than were required to make it red before the medicine was administered. If the condition does not change, then know that it requires a stronger medicine. If it does not redden, scrub it vigorously with a rough cloth until the skin is abraded; then scrub it with things like **onions**. If it still does not redden, there is no excuse: the place must be scraped with a **scalpel** and smeared with things like **garlic**. 

Among those things needed to cleanse the skin of the "evil matter" of alopecia are **leeches**, **cupping**, and piercing with medical needles. Furthermore, blistering with sharp medicines (which I shall mention), cleansing the blistered area, and healing it so that hairs may emerge from it. Among things that help resolve the matter is covering the head with a cap made of **serpent skins** night and day; this resolves the matter and causes sweating. It is also advised that the head be shaved every two or three days with a razor, as often as the hair grows. Before applying any <term>epithems</term> <note>Topical liquid applications or poultices.</note>, the head should be shaved and scrubbed with a rough cloth, or with onions or **radish peels**, until it reddens and becomes receptive to the power of the medicine through opened pores. Sometimes a bath makes this unnecessary, for if the head is not shaved, the medicine will reach the area regardless.

Regarding **evacuants** <note>Medicines used to purge "humors" like bile from the body.</note>, the choleric humor should be evacuated with a decoction of **myrobalans** combined with the power of **hellebore**, **epithyme**, <term>cochiae pills</term> <note>A common medieval purgative pill containing aloes, scammony, and colocynth.</note>, and with <term>hiera picra</term> <note>Literally "holy bitter," a traditional purgative made of aloes and spices.</note>. Again, <term>hieradya</term> <note>A purgative compound.</note> of **colocynth** is good, especially for persuasive reasons. If there is <term>melancholy</term> <note>The "black bile" humor, thought to cause skin diseases.</note> there, mix in some **black hellebore**. If there is <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile.</note>, mix in **scammony**, and **Hiera of Rufus** and **Logodion** are good by themselves; often the condition is cured by a single evacuation. The types of good evacuants are among those whose science you have gathered in the aforementioned sections. If you wish for a lighter treatment, give a drink of **bitter hiera** composed with the pulp of colocynth and **turbith**, three or four doses in a month. When one evacuation is not enough, repeat it among the people in that place. When you see the skin of the head redden, or the veins of the head, forehead, and temples appear full, the advice is to perform **phlebotomy** <note>Bloodletting.</note> on those veins. But if you do not wish for this, do not draw any blood, as it is not needed there. **Gargles** and **nasal sprays** and similar things are known from the chapter on curing the head.

Of the stronger topical medicines to be applied, the most potent is <term>euphorbium</term> <note>A caustic resin from Euphorbia plants.</note>, prepared for no more than three years according to the rule we gave in the Canon. After that is the gum of **wild rue**, which is truly marvelous. Then **watercress**, **mustard**, and the droppings of <term>cantharides</term> <note>Blister beetles, used to irritate the skin and draw out "bad humors."</note> prepared with liquid pitch; or **stavesacre** prepared with **laurel oil**, or the milk of the **castor bean** with which the skin is blistered, and hasten so that what is beneath it may flow out. When the crust falls off, hairs grow beneath it. <term>Alzeg</term> <note>A mineral or vitriol compound.</note> is placed upon the limb for a short time; it is needed in severe cases of alopecia. After that, **sulfur**, both types of **hellebore**, **arugula seed**, <term>baurach</term> <note>Nitre or borax.</note>, two types of sea-foam, **reed bark** and their burnt roots, **mouse dung**, and burnt **sheep dung** joined with long pitch,

<column-break/>

**mustard**, or burnt **hazelnuts**, **fig leaves**, and **condisi** <note>Possibly a corruption of a botanical name like "coniza" (fleabane).</note>, and veins of **celandine**, and <term>alkitran</term> <note>Liquid pitch or cedar tar.</note>; and sometimes **bull's gall** is beneficial; then that which is like burnt **bitter almonds** with their skins, and **figs** rubbed for several days in good vinegar. And <term>rilocarcte</term> <note>Unclear; likely a transcription of a Persian or Arabic herbal term.</note> of **rhubarb** are among the medicines for this sickness. Of the oils administered in this case, the best are **laurel oil** and **castor oil**. Of the medicines that are waxy, the best is **alkitran**, then **pitch**; of the fats, the best is **bear fat**, especially that which is aged. 

A strong liniment: **euphorbium**, gum of **wild rue**, **laurel oil**, take 2 ounces of each; **live sulfur** and **hellebore** (whichever of the two, black or white), 1 ounce of each; make a <term>cerate</term> <note>A stiff ointment made of wax, oil, and medicinal ingredients.</note> with as much wax as is sufficient. And again, take 2 parts of <term>baurach</term> and 1 part **sal ammoniac**; let both be burnt and ground in strong vinegar and smeared on the places after scrubbing, making a light epithem. Again, apply it for hours when the medicine has dried, three times a day. If it blisters, do what you know [to treat the blister]. And again, **cantharides** and **mustard** are boiled in oil until it becomes like a thick paste; then the place is blistered strongly with it, and its strength is broken with a weak mixture. Among those things which are lighter than this and of marvelous help: take strong vinegar with as much good **rose oil** as a third part of it, along with **galangal**; then scrub the place with a rough cloth and smear this on. And again, anointing with the paste in which there is some gum of wild rue. Know that for infants, abstinence [from treatment] is enough, but youths can tolerate 3 to 5 <term>cochiae pills</term>. And for those of advanced years...

### Chapter 7: On those things which remove hair [Depilatories].

Take 2 parts **lime** and 2 parts **arsenic**; smear them both with a little oil placed in them, and it will remove hair naturally and immediately. If you use equal parts lime and less arsenic, it will be more balanced; and if more lime is added, it will be slower in operation, but it will still work. Sometimes 2 parts lime and 1 part arsenic are taken and boiled in **lye water** until it can strip a feather. If the operation is repeated in that water, it will be better; and the more it is prepared with heat, the better it is. Take that water and boil in it oil, according to the proper way, until it receives the strength of it, and smear with it. Sometimes that water is allowed to coagulate into a salt, and that salt is administered in water. The **lime of shells** performs the work of lime with arsenic even more subtly. If instead of lime you take **lime water** (in which lime is repeatedly placed under the sun or boiled) and ground arsenic is placed in the water, it will be good. Sometimes the properties of **leeches** found under copper vessels are also used. If you wish for the hair that grows back to be fine, first apply **vine ashes** or **baurach** and increase the irritation; then wash with **barley flour**, **bean flour**, and **melon seed**. Sometimes lime and arsenic are compounded with things like **alkitran water** and **castor water**. Sometimes **myrrh** and **mastic** are put in it, and sometimes it is helped by sea-foam.

### Chapter 8: On the cure for that which a depilatory has burned.

It is necessary to reduce movement and hasten the washing with **rose oil** if it was applied before; sometimes it is washed with warm water followed by cold water; for that is a good treatment. Then smear over it peeled **lentils** ground with rose water; it calms and is especially good if it burns. If the burning is severe, then it is necessary to apply something like **white lead ointment** <note>original: "vnguentum ceruse"</note> and like an epithem with <term>litharge</term> <note>Lead monoxide, used in healing ointments.</note> nourished with **egg white**, rose oil, and **camphor**.

### Chapter 9: On those things which block the odor of the depilatory.

After the depilatory, smear with **clay** mixed with aromatics, or clay with vinegar and rose water. **Peach leaves** are marvelous for this, as are **vine leaves**, ground **leaves of citron**, **henna**, the dregs of garden **saffron**, **roses**, **cyperus**, **galia**, **schoinanthos** <note>Camel grass or lemon grass.</note>, and **cloves**, either individually or in compounds.

### Chapter 10: On those things which prevent the growth of hair.

The area should be prepared and depilated; then smear with **white henbane** <note>original: "hyusgamo albo"</note>, **opium**, vinegar, and **black henbane** water; and if the henbane alone is boiled in vinegar, it will be better. The dried heart of a **lizard** is among the preventatives when it is ground and mixed with the mucilage of <term>psyllium</term> <note>Seed husks that create a gel when wet.</note> or henbane juice or vinegar; repeat this. Also, if smeared with oil in which a lizard was dissolved by boiling, it is among those things that prevent growth. And a felt cloth with oil in which **critius** <note>Unclear; possibly a mineral or plant name.</note> is boiled. Perhaps all these belong to what are called "cold" medicines. Take <term>cimolean earth</term> <note>A type of medicinal clay from the island of Kimolos.</note> and **white lead** equally, and half a part of **aloes**, and grind them with the juice of white henbane. Some have believed that the **blood of pond frogs** and the **blood of river turtles** prevent growth; likewise the **blood of bats** and their **brains**; they have composed medicines from these. They said...

<meta>This page continues the medieval dermatological and cosmetic instructions from the previous treatise. <header>Book 7, Treatise 1.</header>

<margin>
a) We have already spoken of this. Above, the author set out the decorative regimen regarding the destruction of hair, such as <term>alopecia</term> <note>patchy hair loss</note> and <term>tyria</term> <note>a skin condition where hair falls out in flakes, named after the shedding of a snake's skin</note>, and the regimen for shaving and preventing hair growth. Here he sets out the decorative regimen concerning color. Because <term>canities</term> <note>graying of the hair</note> is a certain kind of foul defect, he focuses on it: first, he shows the cause of graying; second, he sets out the cure where he says "secondly, regarding things." It is reinforced that **Avicenna** <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> suggests two types of graying: namely, the graying of youth and the graying of old age. He does not specifically address the graying of old age. It should be noted that Avicenna investigates the cause of graying and color absolutely: first indeed regarding coloration, that "if the blood remains..." etc. I respond that there is a colorable moisture and a staining heat; the cause of graying is a tendency toward "aquosity" <note>wateriness</note>. The reason is that graying occurs by way of putrefaction or "moldiness," as they say in the second chapter of Book 2 on signs.
b) Whether, as **Aristotle** says in the 5th book of *On the Generation of Animals*, graying is a weakness of the hair: either because it is too moist, watery, or cold, and putrefies with heat, etc. Perhaps Avicenna’s cause is better; and because of the cause mentioned by **Galen** <note>the Greek physician whose theories dominated medieval medicine</note>. Regarding the remedies: he sets out the regimen for graying: first, the preservative and delaying regimen; second, the removal regimen by way of dyes, where he says "secondly."
</margin>

Take frogs from a reed-filled pond and dry them; take their dried flesh and the dried blood of a river turtle, red roses, <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide</note>, and burnt sea-shells in equal parts. Prepare these with water and apply them over the area where hair has been plucked on the pubes and armpits. Also, the seed of <term>vutice</term> <note>likely a variant of vitex or chasteberry</note> with oil is among those things that depilate hair with great strength.

### Chapter 11. Regarding things that curl the hair.

**O**r thus: take fenugreek meal and its oil, white <term>allidre</term> <note>likely white hellebore or a similar mineral</note>, myrrh, oak galls, lime, and litharge. Let them be mixed, and a sufficient amount of some of these should be moved through the head by touching. Sometimes white henbane seed and its oil are placed in them, and sometimes white henbane is administered like a leaf. Lime is among those things that make the hair flat, and it burns a little when dissolved in this summary; because of this, when using it, two-thirds of it should be <term>sidre</term> <note>likely cedar or a specific alkali</note>, both of which are prepared with cold water. Similarly, the "foam of bitter salt" curls the hair vehemently. A good curling agent: a recipe of galls, <term>al-kermes</term> <note>a red dye made from insects</note>, needle filings, cypress leaves and its berries, quince seeds, litharge, tragacanth, <term>bole</term> <note>medicinal clay</note>, <term>alcauizi</term> <note>possibly a variant of a nut or seed</note>, and <term>emblic myrobalans</term> <note>Indian gooseberry</note>—all in one part each. Add a half-part of unslaked lime. Let it be prepared with water; for it is a good curler and darkener.

### Chapter 12. Concerning those things that make hair smooth.

**T**he care for this is the same as the treatment for split ends mentioned previously, and it consists entirely of the administration of softening oils and moistening mucilages.

### Chapter 13. Concerning the splitting of hair.

**T**he cause of this is dryness and dry food. It is prevented by mild, balanced oils and viscous mucilages, such as the mucilage of marshmallow, the mucilage of psyllium, the mucilage of willow leaves, and everything in which there is moisture.

### Chapter 14. Concerning those things that thin the hair.

**S**affron <note>original: "auranti"</note> placed in hair medicines thins them.

### Chapter 15. Discourse on youth and graying.

**W**e have already spoken in another place about the graying of youths. And the graying of which we speak here is this: while the blood remains healthy, fatty, thick, hot, and viscous, the hairs are black; but when it begins to tend toward wateriness, the hairs decline into grayness.

### Chapter 16. Concerning those things that delay graying.

**R**egarding things that delay graying: there is a regimen of primary things. Among these is the regimen of what reaches the hairs themselves. First is the preservation and curing of the <term>phlegmatic humors</term> <note>cold, wet bodily fluids believed to cause graying</note> at every hour, and especially by vomiting after food, and by clysters <note>enemas</note> repeatedly, to cool and repeat. Then, let there be administered confections and medicines that preserve youth, which we shall describe, along with the administration of foods of "good chyme" <note>healthy digestive juices</note> in balance—specifically those from which laudable, thick blood is generated. Such are fried things prepared in pans, and those things cooked covered without water, and roasted meats without broth, and things placed in broth. One should strive so they are in a quantity suited to digestion, for that is the root; for when digestion is corrupted, the blood is corrupted. And when the <term>complexion</term> <note>the body's constitutional balance</note> is very moist, hot things should be administered, such as mustard, pepper, and seasoning spices, and <term>cauguamich</term> <note>an herbal preparation</note>, and <term>almuri</term> <note>a salty condiment</note>, especially while fasting. Beets with mustard are sufficient, and there should be a sufficiency in drinking a little wine. One should avoid moistening fruits and vegetables, types of milk, fish, and wheat cooked with water like pulse or porridges. Avoid drinking too much water and too much <term>probloma</term> <note>possibly a corruption of 'phlegm' or a specific discharge</note>. Avoid too much hair-combing, excessive drunkenness, and too much sexual intercourse. Avoid touching the hair with things such as camphor, rose water, jasmine oil, or jasmine water. Avoid the frequent use of fresh water. If one does use it, dry it quickly.

<column-break/>

For the washing of the hair preserves its strength. But if one bathes, one should use things such as colocynth pulp, nigella <note>black cumin</note>, <term>borax</term> <note>original: "baurac"</note>, and bull's gall for washing. Confections and spices that cut off the matter of "phlegm" and delay graying are things like chewing <term>chebulic myrobalans</term> <note>a fruit from the Terminalia chebula tree</note>, which should be taken every day in an increasing number, chewed, and swallowed; for this perhaps preserves youth until the end of life. Similarly, <term>tripheras</term> <note>a type of electuary</note> made from lesser and greater myrobalans and a preparation of iron dross. It is even better if it contains gold. Take this: black myrobalans and emblic myrobalans, one part of each; "honey of anacards" <note>marking nut oil</note> extracted from them, half of an eighth part. Let it be mixed with cooked butter and prepared with honey, and administered; this is very good. It must be administered little by little in such a quantity that it does not make a bad impression. <term>Mithridatum</term> <note>a famous ancient panacea</note> is strong, and <term>thyme</term> <note>original: "tyriaca," likely referring to Theriac</note> is strong, and viper's flesh preserves youth and strength when its consumption is frequent.

### The method for a balanced, good preparation.

**B**lack myrobalans, <term>dirungi</term> <note>possibly doronicum or leopard's bane</note>, long pepper, and emblic myrobalans; sometimes iron dross is used in place of long pepper, and sugar. Let a <term>triphera</term> be made from these. Among the well-tested things: take ginger, chebulic myrobalans, and long pepper in equal parts and administer it. Again: take 10 drams of chebulic myrobalans, 3 drams of iron dross, 5 drams of agaric <note>a medicinal mushroom</note>, and 3 drams each of ginger, long pepper, and cloves. Prepare it with honey. He who loves youth should take these youth-preserving things for an entire year from these types of preparations, after which he should wait until midday before eating food.

### Chapter 17. Liniments that prevent graying.

**A**ll warm, strengthening oils and all flowing things similar to them in nature preserve the complexion of the hair based on innate heat, so that the nourishment penetrating them does not "shrivel." These are things like <term>alkitran</term> <note>cedar tar or pitch</note>; when smeared with it, leave it for four hours, then enter the bath. He also mentioned the treatment for one having a head of a warm temperament, and similarly the prevention with thin flowing things, and similarly oil of <term>costus</term> <note>an aromatic root</note>, for it is very strong. Oil of <term>bec</term> <note>possibly a nut or seed oil</note> and oil of nigella are very strong—stronger than anything—and oil made with colocynth pulp and mustard oil. It is very good to take mustard oil and nigella, and cook the nigella in it; then cook the colocynth in it, either because of itself or with the others. Oil expressed from wild olives, when used regularly every day, prevents grayness. A good oil: 1.5 drams of <term>omphacine oil</term> <note>oil from unripe olives</note>, 1 dram of spikenard, 0.5 drams each of <term>blatta byzantia</term> <note>the operculum of a marine snail</note> and <term>flos lignanti</term> <note>likely "flower of wood" or a specific spice</note>. Let the medicines be boiled: either in the oil until a third remains, or in water until it vehemently takes on their virtue; then the oil is boiled again in that water until the water is consumed. It is more correct then to reduce the quantity of oil so that 1 or 1.5 <term>kists</term> <note>a measure of volume</note> suffice; then take 1 dram of acacia, dissolve it with wine, grind it excellently, mix the acacia with it, and administer. Another good oil: equal parts of oil of walnut kernels, myrtle oil, and emblic oil; measure 1 pound of the total. Take <term>cyperus</term> <note>nut-grass</note>, cassia, spikenard, nigella, cloves, colocynth pulp, costus, raw aloes-wood, <term>flos lignanti</term>, and aromatic calamus in equal parts; take 100 drams of their weight and boil in colocynth juice if found, or in the juice of walnut husks, the quantity of which should be 4 pounds. When the water is halved, put the oil on it and boil incessantly until the oil remains and the water is consumed. Strain and administer. A liniment so good that it destroys recent grayness:

**T**ake acacia, galls, fenugreek, melon seed, dry coriander, spikenard, <term>laudanum</term> <note>here referring to labdanum resin, not the opium tincture</note>, dried juice of walnut husks, dried red poppy juice, iron rust, <term>calcucecaumenum</term> <note>burnt copper</note>, <term>remeab</term> <note>an unidentified substance, possibly a mineral</note>, and black alum. From these, let thin lozenges be made and dried; they are administered three times a month by smearing with emblic water or myrtle water.

### A good liniment with which the head is smeared by touching.

**T**ake 10 parts of laudanum, 30 parts each of myrtle leaves and myrtle berries. Place them in 3 pounds of oil and leave them in it for three days; then boil until they thicken, and rub the hair with it. And of those things tested by those who were before us and tested in our time: carry one dram of <term>red tragacanth of Balkh</term>. For it depilates the gray hairs and makes black hairs grow in their place; however, only those with a strong and moistened body can tolerate it. And it should be administered with something that cleanses the lungs and moistens them.

### Chapter 18. Recalling the dyes.

**T**here are found in books oils which are thought to be dyes. Experiment shows that the virtues of the prepared spices are necessary; when the oil rises above them, it dissolves between them and the hair. For they do not penetrate them or work anything unless there is a vehement virtue or a great property there. Vehement virtue is not hoped for except from things of strong dye, such as iron rust, and such as...

<page-num>IV</page-num>
<header>Book IV</header>

<margin>
They repeat in the book: first, he places the preservative regimen against <term>canities</term> <note>graying hair</note> regarding all "non-natural" things <note>in medieval medicine, the 'six non-naturals' were lifestyle factors like diet, sleep, and exercise</note>. Second, he provides medicines for this: there, the second part. Confections. And here first he lists things taken internally. Second, things applied externally: there, the second part: all oils. The first part is in two sections. First he provides the cases, second the rules in them. First he enumerates many things showing the way in which he does this: because it strengthens. Second, he provides the description of some of them. Perhaps they are directed. Here he provides the remote regimen by way of a dye. And first in general and mixed. Second in specific among species. First he introduces it. Second he executes it: there, the bran indeed. It should be noted that "furfures" <note>dandruff or scurf</note> are named from the outer bran (furfure), which these resemble as an exhalation. It should be considered that this is a condition much tainted by the foulness of the hair within. For through the hairs they are scattered and stay at the root. First he provides the species and causes of dandruff; second the cure. The first in two: species and cause. It should be considered that first he provides two species: namely, the light kind and the strong kind leading to ulceration. Immediately he intimates that there are other species that are intermediate between those.
</margin>

...as lead and like nut husks: for then perhaps these and things similar to them, when their virtues are repeated in oils, and the virtues of medicines that make them penetrate, the medicines intervene; thus vinegar and wine work: for if it is possible for anything to be effective, then it is this.

I see and hear some testifying to the truth of what is said concerning one of the veins of a nut when it is cut at the beginning of spring and placed like a morsel in a glass vessel in which there is oil; then they bury it in the earth, and it dries out that which is in the vessel by drying and sucking; then he returns it in autumn and returns its surplus to the vessel, and it is a dye. And most of what happens in this chapter and is imprinted does not occur except with repetition. Furthermore, the species of dyes with which hairs are tinted are blackening, yellow-making, and whitening: and we will now begin to narrate the good blackening agents.

### Blackening Agents. Chapter XIX.
<term>Alcana</term> <note>henna</note> indeed and <term>indicum</term> <note>indigo</note> are the root upon which people agree, though they differ in their preparation according to the diversity and preparation of the hair. People begin with henna, then subsequently apply indigo after washing, and they wait for a certain duration for each of them; the more they wait, the better it is. And there are those who mix them together; and there are those who are content with henna and delight in its yellow-redness; and there are those who are content with indigo and delight in the "peacock color" <note>an iridescent blue-black sheen</note> resulting from it. The indigo which is from India is better for a faster dye, but it produces a more vehement peacock color and yellowness. The indigo of <term>carmenum</term> <note>likely Kerman, Persia</note> dyes less and more slowly, but its tint leans toward a yellowish-black and there is not a great amount of peacock color in it. He who wants the indigo dye to return to the natural color of the hair and wants to block its yellow-redness should mix other things with the henna. And if it is administered before the henna, then it will destroy the peacock color and reduce it to a yellowish color. And it is better not to prolong the duration, but rather to hasten to wash it—namely, the henna which was applied after the first dyeing.

And there are those who join these with <term>sicle</term> <note>beet or chard</note> water and with pomegranate water, or with sour milk water; or they compose them with <term>almasal</term> <note>a scented cosmetic paste</note>, and nut-husk water, and that whole mixture is helpful. And there are those who join them with water in which they throw lime and <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide</note> by boiling, or by leaving it under the sun until it blackens wool. And this again is good: if a weight of one <term>drachm</term> <note>approx. 3.5 grams</note> of cloves (<term>gariofilorum</term>) is placed in the dye, it blackens greatly and prevents its harmfulness from reaching the brain. 

Another dye which is administered many times, though less than the first, is to take <term>galle</term> <note>oak galls</note> and anoint them with oil and burn them with oil. And what is better regarding this is that it be done in a vessel sealed with clay, and the end of the burning is when they are sufficiently blackened. Then take a weight of 20 drachms of these, and 10 drachms of <term>calcucecaumenon</term> <note>burnt copper</note>, and 2 drachms of alum, and 1 drachm of rock salt, and let a dye be made from them. For it blackens the hair with a lasting blackness. And sometimes it is administered according to this description: Take a pound of galls which are joined with oil and fried until they split, and take burnt copper, alum, and <term>dragant</term> <note>tragacanth gum</note>, 20 drachms of each, and 8 drachms of salt. Let all be well ground and prepared with warm water, and let them be dyed with these and left for three hours; and sometimes henna and indigo are mixed with them. And that which is famous after this is that which is made from lime and litharge and "eating chalk" <note>creta quae comedit</note>, or henna, or <term>cimolean earth</term> <note>a type of medicinal clay</note>, or whatever chalk you wish from the species of chalk, taking equal parts, and let it be prepared with water

<column-break/>

in the confection of the dye and administered, and let it be covered with beet leaves; the essential part of the matter is the intensity of the grinding of the litharge. And if the water is also the water of henna and indigo made by repeating the boiling of both, or by placing them under the sun in it, then it is better. But it is necessary that it be left for about six hours so that its moisture is consumed upon it.

And again, take equal parts of henna, indigo, litharge ground like <term>alcohol</term> <note>here meaning a fine powder</note>, lime, fried galls, burnt copper, alum, tragacanth, and cloves, and dye with them. These are the blackening dyes which have already been mentioned in the books from which I brought those that are more suitable for people to like or in which confidence may be placed.

**The Method for a Good Dye:** Take 1 part henna and 2 parts indigo, and equal parts of burnt copper, alum, rock salt, fried galls, and iron dross. Let them be ground with vinegar and left until it ferments, then administered. And regarding those things said about this, one should take iron dross after grinding it in wine vinegar, with four fingers of vinegar standing above it, with intense grinding; and let it be boiled down to half its volume, then let it be left in that for two weeks until it rusts. Then take the syrup of the dross of black <term>myrobalans</term> <note>astringent fruit</note> and pour that vinegar over them after grinding them, and let it be boiled until that vinegar is dried out and it becomes like a fine powder. Then let it be submerged with oil and boiled until it becomes like a thick ointment (<term>algalla</term>). And if you wish, aromatize it. And this, if it dyes with oiliness, then it is because of the power of the iron rust. 

And again, silver dross boiled in vinegar intensely... is counted among the highest of strong blackening agents. And what is more pleasing to me is that in place of vinegar, one uses the acidity of <term>citrangulum</term> <note>bitter orange</note> or citron, and that in place of boiling, the iron is left in them for some space of time. 

They also said: if barley is placed in a row, then a row of red poppy flowers, then another row of alum, and buried in dung, it dissolves into a good dye. They said similarly: if a moist barley plant, before it has ears, is buried with half its weight of alum in dung in the cavity of a vessel like a urinal, it will all become black water and a blackening liniment. They said similarly: if a moist gourd, coming out upon its stem, is opened with a circular cut and what is inside is removed, and salt and a little iron dross are placed in it, and the rind that was removed is replaced and sealed with clay, then all that is in it will dissolve into a black water which will be a dye like <term>encaustum</term> <note>a purple-black ink</note>. 

They said also: if caper leaves are ground and boiled with milk—especially woman’s milk—until it reaches a third of its volume, and left for a whole night, it will be a good dye. And what is best in my opinion is that it be among the highest of preservatives. And <term>Galen</term> <note>the famous Greek physician</note> indeed testifies concerning this dye: therefore take the flower which is like a grape on the stem of a walnut and grind it with oil and smear it with moist cow’s butter. And they said that when goat’s dung is mixed with it, it becomes good. And they said similarly that when the barks of the roots of <term>algazab</term> <note>possibly an Arabic term for a specific shrub</note> are ground with oil and anointed with it, it blackens the hair itself. In my opinion, even if it is a dye, the oil weakens its effect; if water were used in place of oil, perhaps it would be better. 

And similarly it is in my opinion regarding what **Paulus** <note>likely Paul of Aegina</note> gave: that red poppy roses ground in oil until they become like an ointment make a dye. For if the intention is toward this, the sweating of alum is necessary. And similarly it is my opinion to nourish the oil with nut husks and boil it in its own water, and to put a little alum in it; all of this is good. Among those things which weaken the dye: let that be done in the boiling of oil in red poppy water until it is finished. And thus that which they said: namely, take sesame oil and throw upon it the foam of <term>embricorum</term> <note>uncertain, possibly a mineral or plant byproduct</note> and boil for one hour gently and strain; and take for every pound a quarter-pound of lead filings finely ground; then fry it gently so the lead does not melt and the oil does not catch fire, and stir always; then let it be left for three days; then take it. And I say there is some confidence in this because of the alum in it. 

They said similarly: when oil of <term>ben</term> <note>Moringa oil</note> is placed in the cavity of a <term>auerguleti</term> <note>uncertain vessel name</note>, then sealed with clay and placed in an oven with caution, an oil comes out that dyes, and it is better that this be counted among those things that prevent graying. They said also: if raisins are cleaned and ground very well like fine powder and submerged in sesame oil and buried for one month in dung, it will be a good dye. And among those things which are like that upon which there is agreement: a lizard's egg is a strong dye, and similarly the egg of a "slow bird" <note>perhaps an ostrich or a specific owl</note>. And it happened indeed in our time, in the days of the life of King <term>Sedubelaa</term> <note>likely a Latinization of an Arabic or Spanish name</note>, that one of his kin urinated upon one part of the beard of another sleeping kin, and it rubbed it with blackness.

### Galia which they chose.
They said: take 1 drachm of salt... and 1 drachm of moist pressed myrtle water... 4 pounds of water, boil until half remains; then remove from the fire and take 3 pounds of <term>evisci</term> <note>marshmallow or a similar mucilaginous plant</note>, 1 drachm of henna, 30 drachms of indigo, and 20 drachms of fried galls...

Fen VII. Tractate I.

<margin>
And it is done. It should be considered that this <note>the term "bran"</note> can be referred to all species of dandruff—that is, the light and the harsh—or it can be referred only to the harsh kind. And here several medicines of Avicenna <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> are seen. It should be further considered that his intent is that it be caused by a cold, biting, and sharp humor. And here Avicenna strengthens that understanding. Regarding dandruff, he provides a cure according to the different degrees of the dandruff. And he places the medicine there: "Take the juice..." The color is transformed: Above, he placed the decorative regimen with respect to the disposition of the hairs where they were falling out. Second, concerning dandruff. Here he places the decorative regimen with respect to the disposition of the skin, and first he determines the dispositions of the skin according to itself; second, as to certain additions of pustules and other foul dispositions according to the color of the skin. First, indeed, he determines the disposition of bad color—namely black, yellow, etc. Second, concerning the disposition of bad color from the traces of ulcers. Third, concerning the disposition of bad color from freckles. Fourth, some others. Fifth, from excessive redness. Sixth, from <term>albaras</term> <note>a skin condition involving white patches, often equated with leukoderma or vitiligo</note>. The first part is in two: first he provides the causes of foul color, second he provides the regimen. The first is in two: first he provides the causes of the conversion to black; second, to yellow: there, "or it is converted."
</margin>

Take tragacanth, and let gum and pitch be dissolved in it, and let it be thickened with a decoction and scented with musk and <term>galia</term> <note>a complex aromatic compound used in perfumes and medicines</note>. By covering [the hair] with it and touching that which they wish to dye with such a quantity as shines upon it. They said: let him take oil of cotton seeds to the weight of 30 drachms, and let iron filings and lead filings and <term>calcucecaumenon</term> <note>original: "calcucecaumenō"; from the Greek for "burnt copper"</note> all be dissolved in it, each to the weight of 3 drachms. Let the whole be rubbed with it and left until it turns black; then let it be rubbed and scented with musk. And you should know that burnt barley or bean husks or pomegranate husks are among the chief things that enter into dyes by the introduction of henna, and similarly walnut shells. And we have already distinguished the medicines for dyeing in the section on simple medicines, such as <term>capha</term> <note>likely camphor or a similar aromatic</note>, myrrh, <term>litinum</term>, mustard, salt, hellebore, orach, myrobalans, maidenhair fern, red poppy roses, henna, indigo, burnt copper, iron dross, bean husk water, the moisture of walnut shells and their juice, acacia, fenugreek, <term>ficle</term> <note>possibly a corruption of "fig"</note> seed, myrtle, and grains, and labdanum, litharge, lime, and all <term>icoze</term> and filings.

### On those making it yellow which follow the course of specific regions. Chapter 20.

They said that it runs from the Nabatean reed, the bark having been recently removed from it, which burns upon it from the high side and stiffens like gold. And similarly, iron rust with tragacanth water, upon which you should wait as you wait for henna. Or let equal parts of henna, wine dregs, and gum be taken, and something of <term>sgnato</term> <note>unclear, perhaps a mineral or plant extract</note>, and let it be dyed with it. Or let henna be taken and moistened with it after it is prepared with a decoction of <term>condisi</term>; let it be digested and dyed with alum, <term>alissireo</term> <note>possibly a reference to a yellow dye plant</note>, and saffron; or with myrrh and stavesacre. And let it be left for a day and a night with water and ground for several days. And when "perfect wolves" <note>likely a colorful name for a specific herb or strong chemical agent</note> are added upon it with vinegar, it is good. And let them take 10 drachms of ground "black wolves," 5 drachms of myrrh, 50 drachms of <term>rigenū</term> salt, 3 drachms of <term>asauregi</term>, 3 drachms of dried and burnt wine dregs, and as much water of the ash of vine wood as suffices.

### On strong reddening agents. Chapter 21.

Take 2 drachms of sumac, 3 drachms of gallnuts, 2 drachms of citron <term>alidriū</term>, two handfuls of maidenhair fern, 50 berries of wormwood, and two handfuls of dried, peeled lupines; let them be ground and soaked in 10 pounds of water for several days. Then let the head be filled with it while it is warm. They said that a decoction of lentils and <term>pdiī</term> in water is a good thing for making it all yellow. They said: take burnt wine dregs and mix them with "oil of <term>bec</term>" <note>likely oil of ben or Moringa</note> or oil of camel grass.

### On whitening agents. Chapter 22.

Among these are swallow droppings, and among these are <term>vesty</term>, and among these are <term>almes</term>, and among these are white flowers, and among these are radish skins, bull's gall, sulfur vapor, caper tips, and olive tips—singly or combined. Especially with vinegar, and especially after its vaporization with sulfur. Let elecampane seed and dried radish skins and alum be taken and gathered by grinding with half a part of gum arabic. And again, let leaves of <term>aluefri</term> and poppy husks be taken, and mandrake; and if in place of both there be white henbane, it will be strong. Let the dye be mixed, and if there be camphor and rose water in it, it will be better. And when the hairs are moistened, then let them be wrapped in bran, then let it be smoked with it; let it be done once in the night, or twice.

### Assistance for conditions following dyes. Chapter 23.

Many species of dye chill the brain and corrupt it, and cause it to fall into preparation for catarrhs <note>downward flows of mucus or humors</note> and for apoplexy and the like. Therefore, let it be cured with those things

<column-break/>

which are near to dyes: or let warm aromatics be administered in succession to them, such as musk, cloves, and the like. And when it happens from the dye that the hairs become stretched like cords and their curliness is removed and they become foul, it is remedied if that which thins and curls is placed with the dye, especially in the kind of hairs that do this. And when it happens from the dye that the hairs are weakened and the beard is dried out and the face is blackened and the hairs are broken, it is remedied if violet oil and <term>alkeiri</term> oil are applied. And when it happens from the dye that the face is blackened, some people wash it with bean and chickpea flour and similar things, and the best washing for that is with warm oil. And when "alnusul" <note>an Arabic term for the shedding of hair or dye residue</note> happens after dyeing. The best thing to be mixed in them is to take as much of the dye as is necessary and dry it, specifically of the dye in which there is a deep-reaching virtue. And as often as the <term>alnusul</term> or the shedding appears, take a piece of wood—like that with which the gums are rubbed—and wrap a cloth over its end with a solution of that congealed dye and follow the <term>alnusul</term> with it. And some take the smoke of aromatic oil, like oil of ben and labdanum, or wax, and they anoint the <term>alnusul</term> with it when it is dried and smeared.

### On dandruff. Chapter 24.

Since the discourse on dandruff <note>original: "furfuribus"</note> is proportional to the discourse on hair in some ways, then let us speak of them. Dandruff is <term>alabirati</term>, that is, <term>cantabrum</term> <note>bran-like scurf</note>, which is a mode of light skin-peeling in the head; it happens to the head because of a corruption occurring in the complexion, especially with a thickening in the upper surface of the skin, and more severely it leads to ulcers and to corrupting the roots of the hairs. And it is made from an acute, borax-like <note>original: "bauracbiat"</note> matter or melancholic blood. And sometimes it is because of the malice of the complexion in the head, because that which reaches it is corrupted. And perhaps it is that which simple dryness creates; and there is no remaining composition in the body except the good kind, and sometimes it happens through contrast.

### On the cure. Chapter 25.

For dandruff which is light, a light cure suffices, and to apply a poultice to the head with rose and violet oil and with mucilages destroys it. And there is a type of dandruff that is more vehement than that and requires things that have a strong cleansing and resolving power; then afterwards let those things which moisten and equalize be applied. And of this type, there is a very bad kind leading to ulceration; and it is necessary in its treatment that the body be cleansed with bloodletting and purging of the belly if that be necessary, and if the cause is seen in the head to be from a fullness of the body. Then let it be cured, and as often as it is cured with that which scrapes, let oils be applied at the same time.

->Light medicines for dandruff without biting sharpness.<-

A weak washing with <term>ficle</term> water affects the nearby dandruff; and with fenugreek water, and with melon seeds, and with chickpea and lupine and bean flour, and a decoction of <term>alice</term> silk in oil, and with mucilage of quinces and marshmallow and tragacanth, and with <term>alcanzi</term> chalk and <term>chimolea</term> <note>Cimolean earth, a type of medicinal clay</note>, and especially with the juice of <term>ficle</term> after it is left on the head for one hour. And let it be satisfied with moist willow leaves, as they are the ultimate [remedy]. And with tamarinds and celery and its juice, and a decoction of <term>alzedaract</term> <note>the Chinaberry tree</note> and hemp leaves and sesame leaves, and perhaps with the rubbing of both it destroys the strong kind, and similarly the juice of both and peeled almonds with vinegar and fenugreek flour with vinegar. Or let chickpea flour be taken with crushed sesame leaves and let them be mixed with <term>ficle</term> water and a little wine vinegar. Or let crushed chickpeas and marshmallow be taken and prepared with vinegar and smeared. Or let the head be washed with the tips of mulberry ground like powder, administered like marshmallow; or marshmallow with oil; or frankincense dissolved in violet [oil] which is mixed with oil; let that be used for two weeks. And among the subtle and easy things is the washing of the head with water of moist willow leaves; for it is an excellent, tested, and safe remedy; and the point is that it should be washed with whatever is used, then let it be anointed with an oil like violet or rose oil.

->Medicines for dandruff which are stronger.<-

Let there be mixed with the washing some borax <note>original: "bauracb"</note>, or sulfur, or bull's gall, or the pulp of colocynth <note>bitter apple</note>, or wine dregs and mustard, or stavesacre, or burnt nitre, or the gum of wild rue and similar things. And again, let <term>chimolea</term> be taken and prepared with ox gall and administered and left for two hours. Or white grains and bean flour taken in equal parts with one pound of rue oil and one ounce of soap and three drachms of borax; let the whole be gathered and the head smeared with it; then let it be washed with <term>ficle</term> water and chickpea flour. Then let myrtle oil be administered; and the head is also smeared with cow dung, and it profits much; let it rest for one night and be smeared another night. And the washing of it with a <term>caeli</term> <note>unclear measurement</note>, especially Arabic, is of vehement help. And nitre is very strong in the chapter on bad dandruff. And among those things which are useful in it are <term>calcatum</term> <note>copperas/vitriol</note> and stavesacre. Or let the foam of borax and <term>calcatum</term> be taken in equal measure and smeared upon the head by reason; and perhaps they are gathered with oil, or stavesacre is ground in oil and joined with it. Or let sulfur and <term>calcatum</term> and borax be taken in equal measure and gathered with labdanum dissolved in mastic oil and let them be placed upon the head; and perhaps hellebore is put in it.

A medicine which some moderns attribute to the <term>iubi</term> <note>possibly a group of practitioners or a specific location</note> and which is tested and found to be good and strong: take half a grain of moist hyssop and colocynth pulp...

Book III

<margin>
It is debated why he did not list other "bad" colors, such as a livid or leaden hue, or greenness. It should be said that in Book I, yellow and black are more relevant; or it may be said that by these he intends the reader to understand the others. For the causes of blackening are not only those that make the skin green or livid; he spoke more diffusely on this in Book I, Section 2, Chapter 4, regarding the signs of complexions. Here he presents a regimen: not for each color individually, because the cause is known; fourth is the removal of these causes. And to the extent that a bad color proceeds from an internal illness, it is understood. And in the third canon, he gives only the regimen for a good color: first, he presents those things by which the skin acquires a good color. It should be considered that he suggests three things that make a good color: first, moving the blood to the skin, which is done by the natural heat (from which redness and heat arise); second, that which cleanses and draws out clarity, so that the skin can be cooled; third, caution against the cold. And he first declares the things that make a good color by moving the blood to the skin. Second, by cleansing. Third, caution against heat and cold. The first part is divided into two: the modes by which things move the blood, and then he declares what those things are.
</margin>

### Second Treatise on the dispositions of the skin regarding the skin itself. Chapter 1.

**Color** tends toward blackness from the cause of the sun, cold, wind, dirt, poor bathing habits, the eating of "false" <note>unhealthy or corrupted</note> foods, or the withdrawal of blood into the internal organs. And it turns to yellow <note>original: citrinitatem</note> from causes of yellowing, which are illnesses, sorrows, lack of nutrition, excessive sexual intercourse, hunger, vehement heat of the air, and the drinking of stagnant water. Also from the eating of figs, <term>ameos</term> <note>bishop's weed</note>, and the smell and sight of it, for it is said that the constant presence and use of it yellows the face; also cumin drunk or dissolved with vinegar. And a long stay in a house in which there is much cumin and vinegar. Also the eating of clay <note>original: crete</note>, which causes blockages in the openings of the veins so that the red blood does not reach the skin, but rather a vapor of bile <note>original: cholere</note>.

### On things making for a good color with brightness, redness, and subtle cleansing. Chapter 2.

**Know** <note>original: Dias, likely a transcription error for Scias</note> also that whatever moves the blood and the spirit to the skin induces in it a youthful beauty, purity, and redness. It is aided by that which cleanses with a light scouring, making the skin thinner and uncovering that which is dead upon its surface—uncovering it subtly, especially if there is a stain—and with all this, it requires caution against heat, cold, and wind. Indeed, the things moving blood to the skin do so in three ways. Among them are those that generate blood, especially "subtle" <note>thin or refined</note> blood; for when good blood is generated and multiplied and spread, it fills every place. And among them are those that purify the blood. And among them are those that scatter the blood and dilate it, which is why it moves to the exterior; they open the passages, drawing the blood violently from the internal parts to the external.

The things that make a good color by the first way are: taking figs, chickpeas, soft-boiled eggs, meat-broth, fragrant wine, and the consumption of "royal" figs <note>original: ficuum imperi.</note>, for they generate subtle blood that is expelled toward the skin, though for that reason they may cause lice. And if someone’s color becomes ugly, then if they wish to return to their natural color, they are especially helped by dry figs and the water of immature dates; both of these add to the subtle blood and internal heat. And among the external things for this: one should drink wine and milk for consecutive days while fasting.

The things that work by purifying the blood are: small <term>trifera</term> <note>a compound herbal medicine</note> and yellow myrobalan <note>original: myrabolani pdiu</note> when administered regularly; and Chebulic myrobalans are stronger than the *trifera*.

The things that do this by dilating and spreading the blood are: <term>alrit</term> <note>possibly a transcription of an Arabic herb</note>, pepper, cypress, and cloves when put in food; and likewise saffron <note>original: crocus</note>, for saffron waters the blood again, especially when cooked in wine in a dose of up to one drachm; and likewise hyssop. Take two drachms of hyssop and half a drachm of saffron and drink them with sugar. Sweet flag <note>original: acorus</note> also makes a good color. And using "Barbary turnips" from one to two drachms, when drunk with <term>sauic</term> and <term>kilch</term> <note>likely Arabic preparations of barley or cereals</note>, is a powerful aid for this, provided it does not cause ugly bloating. And among pot-herbs: radish, leeks, onions, and especially cabbage, if eaten regularly; and also garlic.

And from actions and movements: anger and wrath, and scents, and moderate exercise, and "incuration" <note>likely care of the body</note>, and again joy, gladness, and looking at things that delight; and from actions like singing with instruments, joy, and sitting with beautiful people who are decently

<column-break/>

clothed, and looking at the hopes of litigants for victory in their pledges and rights, and other such things.

The things that work from the outside with attraction and cleansing are: liniments and washes made from de-husked bean flour, barley flour, vetch flour <note>original: orobi</note>, wheat flour, starch <note>original: amilo</note>, chickpea flour, and especially lentil flour, rice flour, fish glue, iris, <term>laudanum</term> <note>a resin from rockrose, not the opiate</note>, figs, frankincense, mastic and its oil, eggshells, the flesh of shellfish <note>original: ostracoz</note>, bdellium, litharge <note>original: lithargyrio</note>, white lead <note>original: cerusa</term>, ivory shavings, aged bones, <term>almabaleb</term> <note>perfumed cherry pits</note>, and aromatic madder is also strong; also sweet and bitter almonds, the seeds of citron, melon, orach, and pumpkin, radish seed flour, and rocket seed.

And many times an <term>epithema</term> <note>a liquid poultice or wash</note> of starch and tragacanth with milk applied all day clarifies and cleanses the face; also the juice of wild cucumber, the "bachar" <note>likely a preparation</note> of garden saffron, milk freshly milked, and a decoction of calves' hooves. I have also experienced success with a decoction of shellfish meat, egg white, and a decoction of fenugreek or melilot.

**A Good Wash.** Take de-husked bean flour, wolf-herb <note>lupine</note>, radish seed, de-husked melon seed, chickpeas, and starch; make a wash from these.

**A Good Ointment.** ℞. Bean flour and barley flour, one part each; chickpea flour, one part; de-husked lentils, tragacanth, and starch, half a part each; melon seeds, two parts; a quantity of saffron to color it. Apply it at night and wash it off in the day with a decoction of melon rind, violet decoction, and lily.

Another. ℞. Sweet almonds, tragacanth, gum, bean flour, iris, and fish glue in equal parts. Melt the glue in enough water for all the ingredients, then add the medicines and make an epithem.

Another. Take bean, barley, and chickpea flour and lilies, and apply them with egg white.

Among those things that cleanse with a strong scouring are: bulbs, onions, borax <note>original: baurach</note>, bishop's weed with honey, salt ammoniac, chamomile oil, and liquid storax—these are of great help—as are sulfur, arsenic, lizard dung, and narcissus root.

**A Strong Ointment.** Take garden saffron and boil it until it thickens; take one drachm of it and mix it with the previously mentioned epithem medicines: sparrow dung, lupine flour, chickpea flour, and de-husked melon seeds. Grind them and combine them with the saffron and apply.

Another strong ointment. ℞. Tragacanth, nitre, ground radish seed, saffron, lupines, and the pith of grain husks, one ounce each. Apply with almond oil.

And when the face is smeared every night with white mustard and red and yellow arsenic with milk, and washed in the morning, the face becomes very red. These strong cleansing medicines are useful for the beginning of leprosy, which is called *afork* and *bothor* <note>terms for skin eruptions or pustules</note>; and boiled butter administered over them destroys them.

**Among those things specifically for this** that cleanse with strength are: white gum, burnt borax, and yellow sulfur in equal measure. Make lozenges with vinegar; let them be dried and administered when necessary with vinegar and honey. The "foam" of borax is better for this than the borax itself. Again, take a measure of soap and salt ammoniac, pound them and dissolve them in three pounds of water; then throw in equal parts of frankincense, mastic, and nitre (seven drachms). Grind all in a glazed vessel vigorously and apply at night. Again, lupine flour, chickpea flour, bean flour, barley flour, iris, and narcissus root in equal parts, with half a part each of gum and lily root; make lozenges. **And know** that everything that helps against skin discolorations <note>original: panno</note>, freckles, marks, and the darkness of blood helps in this with greater benefit; and a portion of those is sufficient.

### On the preservation of the skin from the sun, wind, and cold. Chapter 3.

**It is necessary** to apply egg white, or gum water, or wax; or take thick thread <note>or fiber</note> soaked in strained water and mix it with an equal measure of egg white and anoint the face with it.

### On the marks of bruising and black marks. Chapter 4.

**Litharge** <note>lead monoxide</note> made white eradicates them when applied with some fat or with breadcrumbs; and similarly, common pepper is used for this and helps visibly. Also "water pepper" and similar things, pounded, with cabbage leaves, coriander, radish, wild mint, and arsenic—all of this with coriander and celery water. When the place is smeared with lime <note>original: calce</note> or red nitre with strong vinegar, it removes green marks; similarly with frankincense and nitre. Aloe eradicates marks of a "melon-colored" <note>dark yellow/bruised</note> hue, as does wormwood with honey, and similarly white fish glue and <term>laudanum</term>. This should be left on the place for several days. A "diachylon" plaster is also good. **A good epithem for this: de-husked almonds (one ounce), burnt shellfish, and white mustard.**

### On the traces of ulcers and smallpox. Chapter 16.

Everything that is strong among those remedies we have mentioned is also effective for faint traces of ulcers. Among the medicines described for this, and those that are tried and tested, are donkey fat, the juice of reed roots mixed with some honey, and salted cheese massed together with bee's honey. ### On Bruised Blood, Large Freckles, and Skin Patches. Chapter 17.

Freckles <note>original: "Lentigines"</note> and bruised blood <note>original: "sanguis mortuus," literally 'dead blood'</note> occur because of blood for which the opening of a vein was suited to vomit out its fullness, or because its opening was ruptured by a blow, or by some other provocation beneath the upper layer of the skin, appearing there in its color and shape. That which inclines toward redness is called a freckle <note>lentigo</note>. That which is smeared or spread out is called a skin patch <note>pannus</note>, which some call a "pointed patch." That which inclines toward blackness is called *baraffen*. 

Frequently, those who have freckles also suffer from cracked lips due to the dryness of their constitution. It should be apparent that for the cure of all these, one must act before the redness of the blood becomes too intense and turns black; for after that, their cure is difficult. Indeed, bruised blood and *baras* <note>white leprosy or vitiligo</note> are sometimes removed by taking away the thin layer of skin without causing an ulcer. If there is anything congealed there, it will be removed easily; if it is not yet congealed, it should be made to flow easily, then cured through a process of cleansing with medicines. 

Indeed, we have already cured *albaras* and freckles and the like, and they were removed; but it is necessary to follow this with a poultice that has astringency, so that the blood does not flow from the vein openings another time. It is necessary to mix astringent medicines with those that are resolutive <note>substances that disperse humors</note>, so that the resolutives do not draw more material through the path of the veins which has been dilated, especially at the onset of a skin patch. Similarly, avoid anything that causes intense stinging. However, for old, stagnant cases, this is not a concern; rather, one must apply stinging resolutives, removing and reapplying them continuously—and for old black marks, nothing else will do. 

Sometimes it is useful to resolve bruised blood at the beginning of the condition by bathing it with much hot water for a long time, especially if that water has a resolutive quality. Sometimes we first use a scalpel; sometimes a collyrium <note>medicated wash</note> of myrrh or a collyrium of roses is smeared on and repeated twice a day after the place is washed with a decoction of melilot. The best way to administer these two medicines and others is with fenugreek water. A collyrium made of myrrh eradicates whatever remains after cleansing with weaker medicines. 

Figs infused in vinegar sometimes resolve bruised blood; also nitre, pigeon dung, and borax taken in equal parts and smeared on with honey. Again, wash the place with nitre, then cover it with tree gum and bind it tightly for six days. Afterward, wash it and prick it with needles until it bleeds; then let the blood dry and leave it for six days. Then rub it with salt and leave it for half an hour. Finally, place upon it this medicament which we shall describe for five days, so that all the residual blood is drawn out. The medicament is this: frankincense, nitre,

<margin>
Here he determines the nature of freckles <note>lentigines</note>. First, he sets forth the causes and definitions; second, the cure. In the first part, he provides the cause, and second, the difference between them. Third, he assigns the cause of a certain appearance. 

It should be considered that Avicenna suggests three things: First, regarding the blood, he takes it to be either actual blood or a melancholic humor, especially in a vaporous or misty form. Second, regarding the location in the upper part of the skin where color and shape appear—whether round, as in a freckle, etc. Third, the manner of arrival at the spot: through an open orifice, or by what means it came there, and why the blood was the cause of the opening. 

Consider that blood can arrive at a spot in three ways: either due to fullness in the veins, which forces it to "vomit" out; or due to a rupture from a blow; or due to dilation or seeping. Thus he says, "or another." 

Regarding "And he": Consider that Avicenna places the differences and definitions between a freckle, a skin patch <note>pannus</note>, and *baraffen* (that is, a large freckle). All these come from a bloody material that has been vomited out or otherwise reached the upper part of the skin. A freckle is red in color and round. A *pannus* is "smeared," meaning expanded without a round shape. *Baraffen* is a black freckle. 

But you may ask why he does not speak of "dead blood" <note>bruising</note>; it should be said that it was very well known and included under the category of freckles. In the first type, the shape of a lentil <note>the root of 'lentigo'</note> correctly appears; in the second, the blood is more corporeal and united. And just as dead blood exists there, so there may be a thin, cold vaporous form, which is called a "pointed freckle"—that is, blood in the form of a point or round shape. This is said to distinguish it from what he said about blood in a *pannus* being smeared.

### On Alguassem. Chapter 7.

### On the treatment of whiteness and redness of the surface. Chapter 8.

The whiteness and redness that is common, similar to the redness of that in which leprosy begins, which appears on the face and on the extremities, especially in winter and cold, and perhaps there are ulcers with it. He explains how the nutrient is changed, saying that we do not consider morphea and albaras in respect to health and thus to nutrition; and bad matter acts, and we consider the preservation of morphea and albaras. And as such, the limb acts and transforms. Consider that all these three things prove one point: that the limb changes and the nutrient is changed. In the first nutrition of the flesh, if it were healthy and albaras begins, or morphea, one can say of the nutrient that it was the cause of the change in the flesh, and the result was ultimately bad flesh. Afterward, the nutrient changed itself. In the second example, we consider the change made from a place into the substance of albaras, because it gave it such a quality that it thus changes the nutrient, etc. It is clear how the limb itself causes the change in nutrition. Afterward, we consider that something is an equivalent nutrient, and another profits it; and in this is shown how the nutrient changes because it acts, as Galen says in the multiplication of cancers and the knife. Thirdly, on complexions, that cancer and the knife. Sixthly, on accidents and disease: and just as it is, etc. But the consideration clarifies that the nutrient changes the flesh when he says: when a limb becomes phlegmatic; and likewise when the changed flesh is changed, the nutrient changes by itself even if it is a good nutrient. And all these: here he places the distinction between the two types of morphea, namely between themselves. Secondly, between the two types of albaras, namely between themselves. There, the second: "but the matter." Therefore, let the blister <note>the result of applying a vesicant or blistering agent</note> rest for some days until the skin falls off; then repeat it if there is a necessity. And sometimes it does not let it fall; rather, as often as it begins to bite <note>meaning to sting or irritate</note>, let it be removed until it rests; then repeat. And these medicines are such as: gum of wild rue, pepper, mustard, watercress, spurge, cassia, harmel <note>Syrian rue</note>, radish seed, bark of caper roots, and kebikek <note>likely *Ranunculus sceleratus*, used as a blistering agent</note>. And *alkebikengi* <note>Winter cherry</note> again is helpful in morphea and albaras, because it vehemently attracts blood. Also old, putrid olive pits collected from walls, and all the aforementioned strong attractants for the purpose of eradicating marks. And the waters with which they are smeared are cucumber water, its dregs, and a decoction of colocynth <note>bitter apple</note>.

### Method for a Good Epithema <note>A topical application or poultice</note>

Take radish seed and grind it with the aforementioned water, and let the black morphea be smeared with it in the bath. And again, take radish seed and mustard seed prepared with some things decocted in vinegar.

### Method of Epithema

Take: toasted nigella <note>black cumin</note>, cassia, ten drams each; alumen iamen <note>Yemen alum</note>, two drams; tragacanth and galls, two drams of each; toasted harmel seeds, five drams. Let it be smeared with strong vinegar; then help the stinging marks with woman’s milk. And all the strong epithems mentioned in the chapter on albaras, freckles, and others are helpful for black morphea.

### On the Cure of Alguada and Albaras. Chapter XVII.

One ought to say phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note>, but do not make it necessary unless for a strong cause, and avoid intercourse, except rarely; but observe fasting and use only pure wine. And sweating in the bath is preferred if the body has been cleansed. First, administer a vomit; then evacuating medicines for the phlegm if the body is not clean; then diuretics and things that loosen the belly, such as the "Great Hieras" <note>a class of bitter purgative powders</note>. Especially the *hiera* made from the pulp of colocynth and pills that are similar to it. The *hieras* should be given in a drink with a decoction of myrobalans <note>dried medicinal fruits</note>, epithyme <note>dodder of thyme</note>, polypody, raisins, and salt. And in the grains of *alnil* <note>indigo</note> there is a miraculous property in evacuating the residual humor of white morphea and albaras. Among the laxatives suitable for them is *hiera picra* <note>the 'holy bitter' purgative</note> compounded with the pulp of colocynth. Or according to this description: Take cinnamon, spices, wood of the balsam tree, mastic, storax, saffron, leaf, river calamint, and pulp of colocynth, one dram of each; aloes, eighteen drams. The dose of which is one dram or one *aureus* <note>a gold coin weight, about 4-5 grams</note> with acetous syrup of honey and calamint water. And among the laxatives suitable for them is to take chebulic and emblic myrobalans, one part of each, and turbith <note>a purgative root</note>, three parts; let each part be one dram. Dissolve it in half a pound of *penidion* <note>a type of pulled sugar candy used as a vehicle</note> with water, and let it thicken; let the dose be from three to five drams. And I prefer that one dram of ginger be placed in it. And let there be administered the "triferal" <note>from *tryphera*, a delicate electuary</note> confections and our electuary of this kind: Take black myrobalans, white frankincense, one part of each; a quarter part of one part of ginger. Let it be compounded with honey of raisins and take a quantity the size of an egg every day. And again: black myrobalans, black emblics, nigella, equal parts; half a part of ginger. Drink three drams of it every day, and stop when it takes effect. And take equal parts of calamus, long pepper, chebulic myrobalans, mastic, frankincense, nigella, and laurel berries; let the dose be three drams. And among those things said in the book of abbreviations is to take a measure of *savich* <note>a roasted grain flour/gruel</note> made from wheat very strongly toasted; and if necessary, let the toasting be repeated. Let it be drunk and a medicine of three drams of Nabatean brine be made upon it, which allows one to endure thirst until midday. And in *zukera* <note>possibly a variant of sugar or a specific plant</note> and its seed in wine, there is a miraculous property in this chapter. And of the juice from the bitter extremities of the vine, let one *cadus* <note>a jar or measure</note> be drunk every day, for it dries up albaras and prohibits its increase. Let there be sufficiency in the treatment of the limb with what is applied to it of epithems and things similar to them. To distinguish between *alguada* and the grades of *albaras*: the first rule is that they should be of vehement cleansing, strongly attracting blood, and vehemently heating the complexions of the limb; after that, they should be ulcerating and excoriating. And among the aids to the help of medicines is to apply the liniment in the sun. And the best of medicines for *albaras* is that which ulcerates or blisters, because it makes the matter flow and they are healed; and let it be repeated, and perhaps it will not allow it to blister, but rather bite it and be repeated after resting. ...and added a third, it should be said that it can be reduced to black. "But the matter" distinguishes everything between black and white albaras, etc. It should be considered that the two morpheas were one in genus, because they are superficial defects. But white morphea is made from white matter, and black is made from black. But the two albaras, although they agree in genus because both are deep in their section, nevertheless differ; because although the white is made from white phlegmatic matter, and the black is made from black or melancholic matter, then black albaras is a distinct genus from white albaras and morphea. From this, it is clear that it is *impetigo* <note>a skin infection</note>, etc. And it can be in a bad or good way; it is accepted as that through which the parts of the skin are corrupted and it produces scales. But white albaras is that which does not have scales and this malice; it is made from white matter having the nature of phlegm. Therefore it appears that it is like a genus outside the distinction, and it appears that black albaras is the worst and difficult to cure, or even impossible; and morphea is of far easier cure than it. And why is this? He proves it thus: ancient morphea is "healthier" than white albaras, therefore it is much more easy than black albaras, and the cause of all this is known. Namely, the cause of these passions: black albaras which is excoriating impetigo, and white albaras which is a corruption of the color toward white in the surface and depth without excoriation or the cause of it, etc. That is, why ancient morphea is "healthier" than white albaras and much more "healthy" than black albaras, because the infections of these are from a stronger cause and with a greater effect of the virtue, as was found. And know: it should be considered that *albaras* here is taken broadly to include morphea; in which he places the causes. First: because it attracts blood that is not avoided, etc. Second: because on account of the ulceration it weakens, etc., namely the expulsive and digestive [faculties]. He states the signs of morphea: and first the distinction between white morphea which is called *alfuada* and bad *albaras*. Second, between black morphea and that which is called *alguada* according to a certain division. There the second: "but they differ." Third there: "furthermore albaras." Because *alguada* is not called black morphea just as the white is called; it should be said that it could be called so: as it appeared before concerning white and black morphea. ## On the cure of black albaras. Chapter xii.

**I**f the cure of black morphea <note>discolored skin patches</note> also requires a
more vehement moistening of the body and a
stronger cleansing: then let more

The third treatise is concerning those things which happen in the skin, not in the
color of it: concerning sabafati, and refrengi, and balkiati, and
aluathim.

## On sabafati. Chapter i.

**S**abafati is from the sum of
ulcerous pustules <note>original: "bothor"; from the Arabic for papules or pustules</note> and it is the
custom in many books that it
be discussed in the chapter on decoration <note>cosmetic medicine</note>. And
sabafati indeed begins as pustules,
small, almost light, divided in
innumerable places: then they are
ulcerated with crusty ulcers and are
inclined toward redness; sometimes it even emits poison <note>original: "virus"; here meaning pus or discharge</note> and is named
refrengi and moist sabafati: and sometimes dry scales begin there,
and many times it appears in winter and is removed
quickly: and the cause indeed of sabafati is the divided, sharp,
corrosive bad humors which are mixed with the blood and the gross
bad ones again: sometimes the gross is fixed and the subtle is dried out.
And the cause of that which is dry is mostly a melancholic humor
to which is mixed a sharp moisture which
is expelled to the skin and is corrupted and corrodes.
Balkiati indeed is of the genus of bad sabafati: but
aluathim are melancholic ulcers which appear on the legs from
the same matter from which varices <note>varicose veins</note> are made, and its
cure approaches the treatment of them.
